## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age up to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully corrected by comparison with one another and with several manuscript codices; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the ample editions to which the last three centuries are indebted; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which everything each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture, and in what passages of their works they have done so. The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes—consistently similar throughout the entire work—the low price, and above all this collection, unique, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but for the first time assembled in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form, are taken into account.*

**FIRST SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# Preface to the Third Volume

Since Augustine cultivated the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures as the chaste delights of his soul (*Confessions*, book 11, chapter 2), and cultivated it above all from the beginning of his priesthood, it was worthwhile that his sacred commentaries should immediately follow his earliest writings and letters, and that they should be arranged in a proper and natural order. For if the editors, for the benefit of students, have arranged in a single class the polemical books that he composed against the Manichaeans, Donatists, Pelagians, and other heretics, the same treatment certainly ought to have been given to his exegetical works, as was recently done in the case of the Fathers Ambrose, Gregory, and others. This seemed to be demanded not only by the dignity of the subject but also for the sake of devout readers who love to listen to Augustine discoursing on the sacred Scriptures, so that, once the Scriptures had been arranged in order, they might have the saintly Doctor’s continuous expositions readily available. Hence, whereas these works had previously existed, inelegantly divided and scattered here and there through various volumes, into something like scraps, we have thought it best at last to bring them together in one place. Otherwise that part which deservedly claimed our more important attention and greater reverence might have seemed less carefully treated by us if we had retained the disorderly and confused arrangement of earlier editions.

Accordingly, the works in which Augustine labored over the sacred Scriptures, which had been dispersed through the third, fourth, and ninth volumes, we have arranged in this volume in the sequence of the Old and New Testaments. At the beginning we have placed the books *On Christian Doctrine*, which are, as it were, the key and the art of the method of correct interpretation employed by Augustine and, after him, by Catholic commentators. We have established this order with no desire for novelty, but on the advice of learned men and with the intention of helping Christian readers who prefer to draw out and learn the hidden meanings of Scripture from the tradition of the Fathers rather than from the books of more recent authors, judging that greater latent power and heavenly virtue are present in those who approach the very sources more closely—not only in time but also in holiness.

Since the exposition of Holy Scripture consists chiefly of two parts—namely, bringing out its true and genuine meaning, and stirring the minds of readers toward piety—most devout and learned men are so disposed that not only does the authority of the ancients weigh more with them than that of the moderns, but they are also inflamed far more intensely to the worship and love of God by reading the former. Whether this arises from an inborn reverence for their ancestors, or from some heavenly virtue infused into their books, or from a kind of natural sap and flavor of holiness perceived in their writings, the result is the same. Even if certain modern writers have sometimes grasped the literal or grammatical meaning more successfully than the ancients, the latter nevertheless contribute more to strengthening faith than the former. But if one compares the sense of inward piety in both, among the moderns the understanding of Scripture lies almost withered and languishing, whereas among the ancients it is kindled by the sacred fire of charity and warms and refreshes the minds of readers.

This may be experienced especially in Augustine; indeed, all who have devoted diligent labor to his commentaries and writings have experienced it. If readers are to be taught, then, just as the sun surpasses all the planets in light, so Augustine surpassed everyone in expounding the sacred Scriptures, says Remigius of Auxerre (*Commentary on 2 Corinthians*). If the affections of readers are to be moved and stirred, no one accomplishes this more sweetly or effectively than Augustine. Fulgentius, once a disciple of so great a teacher, demonstrated this long ago. After he had experienced everything that seemed difficult to him and had felt that, through the assistance of spiritual grace, the power to fulfill his will was supplied, he was admonished and moved to compunction by blessed Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 36 and decided to make public the vow he had conceived concerning the monastic life (*Life of Saint Fulgentius*, chapter 3).

The gifts of this holy Doctor in expounding Scripture were so highly esteemed not only by later generations but also by his contemporaries that, when faced with obscure and doubtful passages, Simplicianus of Milan, Paulinus of Nola, and Evodius of Uzalis, all bishops, fled to him by letter as to a heavenly oracle. Indeed, the priest Orosius came to him from the farthest part of Spain, inflamed solely by his ardor for the Holy Scriptures (*Augustine, Letter* 169, no. 13). Hence Audax calls Augustine “the bold Oracle of the Law” (*Letters among Augustine’s works*, 260), while Volusianus asserts that whatever might happen to be unknown to Augustine is lacking from the Law itself (*ibid.*, 135, no. 2). But this above all deserves commendation: not merely individual men of outstanding learning, but the Councils themselves—namely those of Numidia and Carthage—entrusted the most holy Doctor, as a canonical interpreter, with the care and responsibility of expounding the sacred Scriptures (*Letter* 213, no. 4), so that what divine providence had already entrusted to him might also be carried out with the support and request of the Church.

The most holy man had attained this understanding of the sacred books above all through the integrity and purity of his life. Hence Paulinus wrote to him: “I do not doubt that the light of your holy soul shines forth, since through the purity of its inward eye it has deserved the illumination of the Holy Spirit, by whom it can search out and behold the depths of God” (*Letters among Augustine’s works*, 121, no. 18). Further, his reverence and religious devotion toward Holy Scripture had impressed such veneration upon his mind [Col. 0011] that he continually marveled at the depth of the divine utterances, and it was itself a source of awe for him to gaze intently upon it (*Confessions*, book 12, chapter 14). Thus, just as the rash investigator of Scripture is overwhelmed by glory (*Proverbs* 25:27), so, conversely, the devout admirer was wholly illuminated by its splendor.

To this was added Augustine’s ardent and tireless study of those same Scriptures, to such a degree that he burned wholly with the desire to meditate on God’s law and was unwilling to let the hours he found free from life’s necessities flow away into anything else (*Confessions*, book 2, chapter 2). Therefore, when he had reached the final period of his life, he arranged for a successor to be appointed in his place, so that, freed from pastoral concerns, he might devote his entire mind to this meditation (*Letter* 213, no. 4), as though he could undertake no other service more useful and necessary to the universal Church.

His charity and modesty seem to have brought this understanding to perfection. His modesty sometimes openly professes his lack of skill and knowledge; at other times it cautiously offers his interpretations as conjectures. Then he urges others to find better interpretations; and if he himself has made progress, he attributes it not to his own industry but to the merits and prayers of others. Finally, charity causes him to adapt himself in various ways and to descend to the smallest matters, such as the interpretation of numbers, so that he may accommodate himself to the character and studies of his age. This is so far from diminishing the esteem of his commentaries that, on the contrary, it ought to win them greater favor, since he comes closer to that form of divine wisdom which, for the sake of the uneducated and inexperienced, was not ashamed in a certain manner to become childlike.

Therefore certain insufficiently reverent critics should not be heeded—men who, weighing in the sacred books scarcely anything beyond grammatical rudiments, have dared to find fault in the most holy Doctor with a humble manner of interpretation that is wholly adapted to the rules of the divine art, not to that display of human eloquence which they pursue with such zeal.

Nor should anyone be offended by the allegories that the holy man occasionally used, especially in explaining the Old Testament. In such matters he acted with such reverence that he preferred above other interpreters the one who accepted everything that had been said according to the letter, provided that blasphemies could be avoided (*On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book 2, chapter 2)—that is, a meaning unworthy of God. If this could not be done, he taught that one should have recourse to the allegorical meaning, following the example of the Apostles, who used that meaning more than once.

Certainly, since the Old Scripture possesses the character of history, prophecy, and law, a threefold meaning has rightly been employed by sacred interpreters in accordance with this threefold character: the literal meaning, corresponding to history; the allegorical meaning, corresponding to prophecy; and the moral meaning, corresponding to the law. Therefore, although that mystical meaning alone is insufficient for establishing and confirming the Church’s doctrines unless it is contained in the sacred Scriptures, it is nevertheless extremely useful when it serves to advance the perfection of the law—namely, charity—and when it leads to Christ, who is the end of the law and of charity.

Augustine proposes this twofold goal, as though it were a twofold rule, in his commentaries. Hence they seem to breathe nothing but Christ and inspire nothing but charity. Moreover, he introduces this meaning with very great prudence and draws it chiefly from the literal meaning. He does not have recourse to it too readily, even in those books that he published against the Manichaeans—except in his first work on Genesis—although this method might have seemed suitable to his purpose in explaining certain actions of the ancient Fathers that those heretics abused.

Whenever the most learned Doctor presents a single allegorical meaning, he does so either because he confesses that the literal meaning is obscure or unknown to him; or because the literal meaning is itself so clear that it requires no explanation; or, finally, because he has explained it elsewhere. For this belongs to the prudence of a Catholic Doctor: not to insist on the literal meaning at every opportunity, lest it become cheapened, but sometimes to prefer the mystical and spiritual meaning when the interests and affections of his hearers seem to require it; indeed, even when the subject itself calls for it, with the allegorical meaning taking the place of the literal.

Here it might perhaps be necessary to address the criticism of certain men of little authority who, in shameless words, dared to reproach Augustine for ignorance of the languages, on account of which he occasionally fell into error—to put more gently the statement of a certain modern writer who expressed it in an atrocious and impudent term. But such insults recoil upon their author. Fair-minded judges of these matters recognize that Augustine was sufficiently equipped for understanding the New Testament by means of the Greek language, on which all the Latin editions were based. This is proved by the various readings derived from Greek sources that the holy man employed in doubtful or corrupt passages.

The most modest man does indeed confess in his *Confessions* that, when as a little boy he loved Latin literature, he hated Greek (*Confessions*, book 1, chapter 13). But, says Erasmus, once he had become a bishop and an old man, Augustine returned to the Greek literature that he had loathed as a boy. In this matter he gave an outstanding example of his diligence and reverence toward the sacred Scriptures: although already old and distracted by so many affairs, he did not disdain to descend to the elements of Greek so that he might be better equipped to understand the text of the sacred Scriptures.

As for the Old Testament, in expounding it the holy man kept before his eyes the version of the Septuagint translators, which alone then possessed authority, ever since the time of the Apostles. Yet he followed it in such a way that he was led into no serious error, although his commentaries might perhaps have been fuller and richer if he had penetrated the Hebrew language.

The Greek text of the Septuagint accepted by him is the very one that Nobilius revised. Most of the variant readings from Augustine arise from defects in the editions; with the help of ancient books we have removed those defects in this edition. We believe that this translation is the one that Jerome calls the “common” version (*On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book 2, chapter 66), and which Jerome calls the “Old” and “Vulgate” version (*Book on the Best Kind of Interpretation* and commentary on *Ecclesiastes* 1:7 and following). It may perhaps be the same version that Augustine prefers to the others, namely the Italic, which he praises in book 2, chapter 15 of *On Christian Doctrine* as more faithful to the words while preserving clarity of meaning—if, that is, this Italic version embraced anything beyond the New Testament; for this has not been established with complete certainty from Augustine’s words.

In the books *On Expressions* and *Questions on the Heptateuch*, which he composed in old age, he generally consults a version derived more directly from Hebrew sources and corresponding to our common version—perhaps the version issued under Jerome’s authority. In book 4 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 7, no. 13, written around the time when he was revising his minor works, he finally acknowledges this version as more accurate than the Septuagint.

Shortly afterward, that is, toward the end of his life, he used this version in composing the *Mirror*, which he was then preparing from passages collected from Scripture for the use of ordinary people. Thus it came about that, once handed down by Augustine into the hands of the people, this version became the commonest and most widely received, while the Septuagint continued to retain a certain authority even in the Roman Church, as the letter of Saint Gregory to Leander of Seville concerning his exposition of Job testifies.

Finally, if it is useful to mention our labor in revising these books of Augustine, we have judged that the utmost care and fidelity were required everywhere, and especially wherever anything, however small, had to be altered in the sacred text. Accordingly, when the reader finds a variation among Augustine’s biblical citations, and finds that we have not everywhere restored the same passage in its entirety with complete consistency, but only in certain places, he should attribute this not to negligence or rashness but to our reverence and sincere fidelity.

For in this matter we followed the authority of the ancient codices, retaining or correcting a reading wherever necessary. If, on our own authority, we had corrected the same passage in one place—where manuscripts of better quality showed that it ought to be corrected—and then similarly altered it elsewhere without the support of manuscripts, the important benefit that can be derived from Augustine’s various writings would have been lost. That benefit is this: from his variant readings, arguments may be drawn both for restoring the integrity of the Bibles now read in the Church and for establishing their authority.

# [On Christian Doctrine]

[Col. 0013]

## Notice concerning the books *On Christian Doctrine*

We have arranged that the books *On Christian Doctrine* should precede the exegetical works contained in this third volume. Their subject is precisely that we should be instructed in certain necessary principles and precepts for understanding and treating the sacred Scriptures. The work was carefully composed in keeping with the importance of its subject and is certainly not unworthy of a place at the threshold of the Bible, alongside Jerome’s prefaces.

As we learn from the sequence of the *Retractations*, Augustine began it not long after he had undertaken the episcopate, that is, around the year of Christ 397. When he had reached only that part of the third book which now bears the numeral 36, he could not prevent it from immediately being published. For in the books against Faustus, written around the year 400, he recalls a passage from it concerning the Egyptians despoiled by the Hebrews at God’s command, in these words: “I remember that I placed an interpretation of what this prefigured, insofar as it occurred to me at the time, in certain books that I entitled *On Christian Doctrine*” (*Against Faustus*, book 22, chapter 91).

Later, when reviewing his works and discovering that this one was incomplete, he wished to finish it before proceeding to revise anything else. At that time he not only completed the third book but also added a fourth, around the eighth year after his departure for Caesarea in Mauretania—that is, in the year of Christ 426 or 427—as we observe here at chapter 24 of the fourth book.

The subjects of the books are as follows.

In the first book, after dividing the work into parts, he undertakes a discussion of things. Once these have been explained, he teaches that the fullness and end of the Law and of all the divine Scriptures is love: love of the thing that is to be enjoyed and of the thing that can enjoy that thing together with us—that is, love of God and of our neighbor.

In the second book he discusses the signs and words of Holy Scripture. Since its meaning is generally not perceived either because of ignorance of the signs or because of their ambiguity, Augustine first sets forth the canon of the divine books and then proceeds to explain knowledge of which languages, and which disciplines and branches of learning, contribute to removing that ignorance of signs. Taking the opportunity, he also discusses the rejection of superstitious arts. At the beginning and end of the book he likewise explains how the mind of one who intends to devote himself to the study of Scripture ought to be disposed.

In the third book the holy Doctor moves on to consider the ambiguity that may occur both in proper and in transferred signs. He carefully examines the sources from which this ambiguity arises and the means by which it can be removed. From this he gives rules for recognizing whether an expression is figurative and, if it is figurative, how it ought to be explained. Then he considers, one by one, the seven Rules of Tichonius.

Thus far the subject has been the investigation of the meaning of Scripture. In the fourth book he now treats of exposition and pursues the parts and duties of the Christian orator. He proposes the authors of the sacred writings and the ecclesiastical Doctors for imitation, presenting from their works examples of sound eloquence in various styles of speaking. Finally, he exhorts the preacher himself [Col. 0015] above all to devote himself to prayer and to exhibit fully in his life and conduct what he teaches others in words.

Long ago Angilbert, abbot of Corbie, had this work copied for the use of Louis, king of the Franks and brother of Carloman, as the verses placed at the front of the Corbie codex testify. Among others, they read:

> This little book the humble Abbot ordered made,  
> Angilbert, lowly and insignificant,  
> To give it to Louis, supported by heavenly power,  
> A pious and humble king.

[Col. 0015]

# Prologue  
## Instruction on how Scripture is to be treated is not superfluous

### 1

There are certain principles for treating the Scriptures which, as I see, can appropriately be taught to those devoted to them, so that they may progress not only by reading others who have opened what was hidden in the divine Scriptures, but also by opening it themselves for others. I have undertaken to teach these principles to those who wish and are able to learn, if God and our Lord does not deny me, as I write, those things which he is accustomed to suggest to me when I reflect upon this subject.

Before I begin, it seems to me that I must answer those who are going to criticize this work—or would criticize it if we did not first disarm them. If some should criticize it even afterward, at least they will not move others or call them back from useful study to the laziness of ignorance—people whom they might move if they did not find them forewarned and prepared.

### 2

Some will criticize this work of ours because they will not have understood the things we are about to teach. Others, having understood them and wishing to use them, will attempt to treat the divine Scriptures according to these principles but will not be able to open and explain what they desire. They will then think that I have labored in vain; and because they themselves are not helped by this work, they will conclude that no one can be helped by it.

There is a third kind of critic: those who either truly treat the divine Scriptures well or think that they treat them well. Since they either see or suppose that they have acquired the ability to explain the sacred books without having read any observations of the kind I am now undertaking to transmit, they will loudly declare that these principles are necessary for no one, but rather that everything which is laudably opened up concerning the obscurities of those writings can take place through a divine gift.

### 3

Briefly answering all of them, I say to those who do not understand what we are writing that I should not be criticized because they do not understand it. It would be as if they wished to see the old or new moon, or some star that was not very bright, which I was pointing out with an extended finger, while their eyesight was not strong enough even to see my finger. They ought not therefore to be angry with me.

Those, however, who, even after learning and grasping these principles, have been unable to see what is obscure in the divine Scriptures should suppose that they can indeed see my finger, but cannot see the stars toward which I am pointing. Let both groups cease criticizing me and pray that the light of their eyes may be divinely supplied. For if I am able to move one of my limbs in order to point something out, I am not thereby able to kindle the eyes by which either my pointing or the thing I wish to point out may be seen.

### 4

As for those who rejoice in a divine gift and boast that, without principles such as those I am now undertaking to teach, they understand and treat the sacred books, and who therefore think that I have wished to write something superfluous, their agitation should be calmed in this way: although they are rightly pleased with so great a gift of God, they should nevertheless remember that they learned at least their letters from human beings.

They should not therefore think that Saint Antony, an Egyptian monk and a perfect man, insults them. He is said, without any knowledge of letters, to have committed the divine Scriptures to memory by hearing them and to have understood them through wise reflection. Nor should they think themselves insulted by that Christian barbarian slave **[Note: [Col. 0017] Two Vatican manuscripts read *Barbarico Macario*. We have searched in vain for the slave’s name in the other codices and in Cassiodorus Senator, who relates this miracle in the preface to his books of the *Institutions*.]**, about whom we have recently learned from men of the greatest gravity and trustworthiness. Without being taught by anyone, he received knowledge even of the letters themselves by praying that they be revealed to him, and after obtaining this through three days of prayer, he proceeded to read through a codex that was placed before him, to the astonishment of those who were present.

### 5

**[Note: [Col. 0017] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions instead have: “But if anyone thinks these things false …”]**

Or if anyone thinks these things false, I will not argue aggressively. Certainly, since we are dealing with Christians who rejoice in knowing the Holy Scriptures without a human guide—and if this is so, they rejoice in a true and no small blessing—they must nevertheless concede that each of us learned our own language from infancy through the habit of hearing it, and that we acquired some other language, whether Greek, Hebrew, or any of the others, either in the same way, by hearing it, or through a human teacher.

So, if it pleases us, let us warn all the brethren not to teach these things to their little children, since, when the Holy Spirit came in a single moment, the Apostles were filled and spoke in the languages of all nations. Or let anyone to whom such things have not happened conclude that he is not a Christian, or doubt that he has received the Holy Spirit.

Rather, let him learn without pride what must be learned through a human being; and let the person through whom another is taught transmit without pride and without envy what he has received. Let us not put the one in whom we have believed to the test, lest, deceived by such crafty devices and perversity of the enemy, we should refuse to go to churches even to hear and learn the Gospel, or to read a codex, or to hear a person reading and preaching. Instead, let us wait to be snatched up into the third heaven, whether in the body or outside the body, as the Apostle says, and there hear “ineffable words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak” (2 Corinthians 12:2–4), or there see the Lord Jesus Christ and hear the Gospel from him rather than from human beings.

### 6

Let us beware of such exceedingly proud and dangerous temptations. Let us rather remember that the Apostle Paul himself, although struck down and instructed by a divine and heavenly voice, was nevertheless sent to a human being [Col. 0018] so that he might receive the sacraments and be joined to the Church (Acts 9:3–7).

Likewise, although an angel announced to the centurion Cornelius that his prayers had been heard and his almsgiving regarded, Cornelius was nevertheless handed over to Peter to be instructed. Through Peter he was to receive not only the sacraments but also to hear what he ought to believe, hope for, and love (Acts 10:1–6).

Certainly everything could have been done through an angel; but the human condition would have been degraded if God had seemed unwilling to administer his word to human beings through human beings. For how would the statement “You are God’s holy temple” be true (1 Corinthians 3:17) if God gave no responses from a human temple, and if everything that he wished to be taught to human beings resounded from heaven and through angels?

Moreover, charity itself, which binds human beings to one another by the bond of unity, would have no opportunity to pour out and, as it were, mingle souls with one another if human beings learned nothing through human beings.

### 7

Certainly, when the eunuch was reading the prophet Isaiah without understanding him, the Apostle did not send him to an angel. Nor was what he did not understand explained to him through an angel, nor was it revealed to his mind divinely without human ministry. Rather, by divine prompting Philip was sent to him. Philip sat with him, knew the prophet Isaiah, and opened with human words and language what was hidden in that Scripture (Acts 8:27–35).

Was it not God who spoke with Moses? Yet Moses nevertheless received counsel about governing and administering so great a people from his father-in-law, a foreigner—one who was exceptionally prudent and entirely free from pride (Exodus 18:14–26). For that man knew that, regardless of the soul from which true counsel proceeded, it ought to be attributed not to that soul but to him who is the truth, the unchangeable God.

### 8

Finally, whoever boasts that, without being instructed by any principles, he understands by a divine gift whatever is obscure in the Scriptures certainly believes rightly—and it is true that this ability of his does not exist as though it came from himself, but was divinely bestowed. In this way he seeks God’s glory, not his own.

But when he reads and understands without anyone explaining it to him, why does he desire to explain it to others? Why does he not rather send them back to God, so that they too may understand not through a human being but with God teaching them inwardly?

Perhaps he fears hearing from the Lord: “Wicked servant, you should have put my money with the money-changers” (Matthew 25:26–27). Therefore, just as those who reveal to others the things they understand, whether by speaking or writing, so too, if I reveal not only the things they understand **[Note: [Col. 0018] Twenty-three manuscripts read: “the things I understand.”]**, but also the things they should observe in understanding, I certainly ought not to be blamed by them.

Nevertheless, no one ought to possess anything as though it were his own property, except perhaps a lie. For every truth comes from him who says, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). For what do we have that we have not received? And if we have received it, why do we boast as though we had not received it? (1 Corinthians 4:7).

9. He who reads a letter aloud to listeners naturally pronounces the letters he recognizes; but he who teaches the letters does so so that others too may learn how to read. Yet each conveys what he has received. So also the person who explains to listeners what he understands in the Scriptures pronounces, in the role of a reader, letters that he recognizes; but the person who teaches how it should be understood resembles one who teaches letters—that is, one who teaches how it should be read. Thus, just as one who knows how to read does not need another reader when he has found a manuscript from which he can learn what is written there, so the person who has received the rules we are attempting to teach, when he encounters something obscure in books, will possess certain rules like letters and will not require another interpreter through whom what is hidden from him may be disclosed. Rather, by tracing certain clues, he will himself reach the hidden meaning without error, or at least will not fall into the absurdity of a perverse interpretation. Therefore, although the work itself may sufficiently show that no one can rightly oppose this serviceable labor of ours, nevertheless, if this kind of prologue seems a suitable answer to any objectors, the following beginning presented itself to us for the path we wish to enter in this book.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0019]

At the outset, the whole work is divided, so that the student of Scripture may be equipped both to investigate its meaning and to explain it. Then, after observing the distinction between the things about which instruction is to be given—namely, things and signs—this first book undertakes the treatment of things. Some things, moreover, are those which we are to enjoy, others those which we are permitted only to use; and indeed we must cleave in enjoyment to God alone, while we are advanced toward him by the incarnation of his Word, by the deeds he accomplished in time, and by the keys entrusted to the Church. Among the things that serve for use, some are rightly objects of love, but only as referred to God. Once these matters have been explained, it is taught that the fullness and end of all sacred Scripture is the twofold charity: love of God for his own sake, and love of one’s neighbor for God’s sake.

# CHAPTER ONE  
## The treatment of Scripture rests on discovery and expression; both must be undertaken with God’s help

1. There are two things on which every treatment of the Scriptures rests: the method of discovering what is to be understood, and the method of presenting what has been understood. We shall discuss discovery first and presentation afterward. It is a great and arduous work [Note: [Col. 0019] Am., Er., and five manuscripts read onus (“burden”).], and, if difficult to sustain, I fear it may be rash even to undertake it. That would indeed be so if we relied on ourselves; but now, since our hope of completing this work rests in the one from whom we already hold, in our thinking, many things concerning it that have been handed down to us, we need not fear that he will cease to give the rest once we have begun to distribute what has been given. For every possession that is not diminished by being given, while it is held and not given, is not yet possessed in the manner in which it ought to be possessed. But he says: “To the one who has, it will be given” (Matt. XIII, 12). Therefore he will give to those who have—that is, to those who use with kindness what they have received—and will complete and increase what he has given. The five loaves and the seven loaves existed before they began to be given to the hungry; but once this began, they filled baskets and hampers when so many thousands had been satisfied (ibid. XIV, 17–21; and XV, 34–38). Therefore, just as that bread increased while it was being broken, so what the Lord has already supplied for undertaking this work will multiply when it begins to be distributed, since he himself will furnish it. Thus, in this ministry of ours, we shall not only suffer no want, but shall also rejoice in wondrous abundance.

# CHAPTER TWO  
## What things are, and what signs are

2. Every doctrine concerns either things or signs, but things are learned through signs. Properly speaking, I now call “things” those entities that are not employed to signify something, such as wood, stone, cattle, and other things of this kind. I do not mean that wood which we read Moses placed in the bitter waters so that they might lose their bitterness (Exod. XV, 25); nor that stone which Jacob placed under his head (Gen. XXVIII, 11); nor that animal which Abraham sacrificed in place of his son (ibid. XXII, 13). For these are indeed things, but they are also signs of other things. There are other signs whose entire use consists in signifying, such as words. No one uses words except for the purpose of signifying something. From this it is understood what I call “signs”: namely, those things that are employed to signify something. Consequently, every sign is also some thing; for what is no thing is altogether nothing. But not every thing is also a sign. And so, in this division between things and signs, when we speak of things, we shall speak in such a way that, even if some of them can be employed to signify something, they do not obstruct the division by which we shall discuss things first and signs afterward. Let us carefully remember that what is now to be considered in things is what they are, not what else they may signify besides themselves.

# CHAPTER THREE  
## The division of things

3. Some things, then, are to be enjoyed, others are to be used, and others both enjoy and use. Those which are to be enjoyed make us blessed. By those which are to be used, we are helped and, as it were, supported as we move toward blessedness, so that we may reach and cling to those things which make us blessed. But we who enjoy and use things, placed between the two, are hindered in our course if we wish to enjoy the things that are to be used; and sometimes our course is even diverted, so that, impeded by love of inferior things, we are delayed or even recalled from obtaining those things which are to be enjoyed.

# CHAPTER FOUR  
## What it is to enjoy and to use

4. To enjoy is to cling to something in love for its own sake. To use, however, is to refer what has come into use to the attainment of what you love, provided that it is something that ought to be loved. For illicit use should rather be called misuse or abuse. Therefore, if we were travelers who could live happily only in our homeland, and if in that journey we were naturally miserable and desired to end our misery, we would wish to return to our homeland. We would need either land or sea vehicles, which we would use in order to reach the homeland that was to be enjoyed. But if the pleasantness of the journey and the very transport of the vehicles delighted us, and if, turning toward the enjoyment of the things we ought to have used, we did not wish to bring the journey quickly to an end, and if, entangled in a perverse pleasure, we were alienated from our homeland, whose pleasantness would make us blessed—so, in this life of mortality, while we are travelers away from the Lord (II Cor. V, 6), if we wish to return to our homeland where we can be blessed, we must use this world, not enjoy it, so that “the invisible things of God may be perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. I, 26)—that is, so that from bodily and temporal things we may grasp eternal and spiritual things.

# CHAPTER FIVE  
## The Triune God is the thing to be enjoyed

5. The things, therefore, that are to be enjoyed are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the Trinity itself—which is one supreme thing and common to all who enjoy it, provided that it is a thing and not the cause of all things, and provided also that it is a cause. For it is not easy to find a name suitable to such excellence, except that this is better said as follows: the Trinity is one God, “from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things” (Rom. XI, 36). Thus the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each individually God, and all together one God; each individually is complete substance, and all together one substance. The Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit; the Son is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. The Father is Father alone, the Son Son alone, and the Holy Spirit Holy Spirit alone. The three have the same eternity, the same immutability, the same majesty, and the same power. In the Father there is unity, in the Son equality, and in the Holy Spirit the harmony of unity and equality: and these three are one in all things because of the Father, equal in all things because of the Son, and joined together in all things because of the Holy Spirit.

# CHAPTER SIX  
## God is ineffable: in what sense

6. Have we said anything, or uttered anything, worthy of God? Indeed, I realize that I intended to say nothing other than this. But if I have said something, it is not what I intended to say. How do I know this, except because God is ineffable? Yet if what I have said were ineffable, it would not have been said. Accordingly, God cannot even properly be called ineffable, because when this is said, something is said. And there arises some strange conflict of words: if that is ineffable which cannot be said, then what can be called ineffable is not ineffable. This conflict of words is better avoided by silence than settled by speech. Nevertheless, although nothing worthy can be said about God, he has accepted the service of human speech and has wished us to rejoice in our words of praise to him. For this is also the reason he is called “God.” He is not truly known in the sound of these two syllables; yet, when this sound reaches the ears of all who know the Latin language, it moves them to conceive of some supremely excellent and immortal nature.

[Note: [Col. 0021] In Ambrose, Erasmus, and seventeen manuscripts: socios (“associates”), rather than scios (“those who know”).]

# CHAPTER SEVEN  
## Everyone understands “God” as that than which nothing is better

[Col. 0022]

7. For when the one God of gods is conceived, even by those who suspect, call upon, and worship other gods, whether in heaven or on earth, he is conceived in such a way that their thought attempts to attain something than which nothing is better or higher. Since people are moved by different goods—some by those pertaining to bodily sensation, others by those pertaining to the understanding of the mind—those devoted to bodily senses regard either heaven itself, or whatever they see shining most brightly in heaven, or the universe itself, as the God of gods. Or, if they attempt to go beyond the universe, they imagine something luminous and posit it, on the basis of empty conjecture, either as infinite or in whatever form seems best; or they conceive a human bodily form, if they place it above all others.

[Note: [Col. 0022] The printed editions read sic eam (“if they place it thus”); almost all manuscripts read si eam (“if they place it”).]

If they do not think there is one God of gods, but rather many or innumerable gods of equal rank, they still hold them in their minds as formed according to whatever each person regards as bodily excellence. Those, however, who proceed by understanding to see what God is place him above all visible and bodily natures, and also above all intelligible and spiritual natures, and above everything mutable. Nevertheless, all contend eagerly for God’s excellence; and no one can be found who believes that God is something than which there is anything better. Thus everyone agrees that God is that which they place above all other things.

# CHAPTER EIGHT  
## Since God is immutable wisdom, he must be placed above all things

8. Since all who think about God think of something alive, only those can hold views about God that are neither absurd nor unworthy who think of life itself. Whatever bodily form presents itself to them, they determine whether it lives by life or does not live, and they place what lives above what does not. They understand that the living bodily form itself—however great its light, however immense its size, however adorned its beauty—is one thing, while the life by which it is animated is another; and they place that life, by which the mass is animated and given vitality, above the mass with incomparable dignity.

Next they continue to examine life itself. If they find it nourishing without sensation, as in trees, they place above it life that possesses sensation, as in animals; and above this again, life that possesses understanding, as in human beings. When they see that this too is mutable, they are compelled to place above it some immutable life—namely, that life which is not at one time foolish and at another wise, but which is Wisdom itself. For a wise mind, that is, a mind which has acquired wisdom, was not wise before it acquired wisdom; but Wisdom itself was never foolish and can never be so. If they did not see this, they would in no way confidently place an immutably wise life above a mutable life. They see the very rule of truth by which they proclaim it better to be immutable; and they see it nowhere except above their own nature, since they see themselves to be mutable.

[Note: [Col. 0022] Most manuscripts read Ipsam (“it itself”); the printed editions have Ipsam quoque (“it also”).]

# CHAPTER NINE  
## Everyone knows that immutable wisdom must be preferred to mutable wisdom

9. No one is so shamelessly foolish [Note: [Col. 0023] The printed editions read tam imprudenter (“so foolishly”); thirteen manuscripts read tam impudenter (“so shamelessly”).] as to say: “How do you know that an immutably wise life ought to be preferred to a mutable one?” For the very thing he asks—how I know this—is present to everyone for contemplation, equally and immutably. Whoever does not see it is like a blind man in the sun, for whom the radiance of such clear and present light, poured into the very places of his eyes, is of no benefit. But whoever sees it and turns away has a feeble sight of mind because of the habit of carnal shadows. Thus, as if by opposing winds, people of wicked character are driven back from their homeland itself, pursuing what is behind and below rather than what they acknowledge to be better and more excellent.

# CHAPTER TEN  
## The mind must be purified in order to see God

10. Therefore, since we are to enjoy that truth which lives immutably, and since in it the Triune God, author and creator of the universe, cares for the things he created, the mind must be purified, so that it may both perceive that light and cling to it once perceived.

[Note: [Col. 0023] The printed editions read inhaerere perfecte (“to cling perfectly”); the manuscripts more elegantly read inhaerere perspectae (“to cling to what has been perceived”).]

Let us consider this purification as a kind of journey, and as a kind of voyage to our homeland. We are not moved toward him, who is present everywhere, by changes of place, but by good desire and good conduct.

# CHAPTER ELEVEN  
## The incarnate Wisdom is the example of the mind’s purification

11. We could not do this unless Wisdom itself deigned to accommodate itself even to our great weakness and provided us with an example of how to live, in no other way than in a human being, since we too are human beings. But because, when we come to Wisdom, we act wisely, while when Wisdom comes to us it was thought by proud human beings to have acted foolishly. And because, when we come to Wisdom, we grow strong, while when Wisdom comes to us it was regarded as weak. Yet “the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men” (I Cor. I, 25). Since Wisdom itself is the homeland, it also made itself the way to the homeland for us.

# CHAPTER TWELVE  
## How the Wisdom of God came to us

Although it is everywhere present to the sound and pure inner eye, Wisdom also deigned to appear to the bodily eyes of those who possess an impaired and unclean eye. For “because, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (I Cor. I, 21).

12. It is therefore said to have come to us, not by traveling through regions of space, but by appearing in mortal flesh to mortals. It came there where it was, because it was in this world, and the world was made through it. But because human beings, shaped according to this world by their desire to enjoy the creature in place of the Creator—and most appropriately called by the name “world”—did not recognize it, the Evangelist said: “And the world did not know him” [Col. 0024] (John I, 10). Thus the world could not know God through Wisdom in the wisdom of God. Why, then, did Wisdom come, since it was already here, except because it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe?

# CHAPTER THIRTEEN  
## The Word became flesh

How did Wisdom come, except that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14)? When we speak, so that what we hold in our mind may enter the mind of the listener through bodily ears, the word we carry in our heart becomes a sound and is called speech. Yet our thought is not changed into that same sound; remaining whole within itself, it assumes the form of a voice by which it may insinuate itself into the ears without any blemish from its own change.

[Note: [Col. 0024] Ambrose and Erasmus read: “without any injury, without change.”]

So the Word of God, without being changed, nevertheless became flesh in order to dwell among us.

# CHAPTER FOURTEEN  
## How the Wisdom of God healed humanity

13. Just as treatment is a way to health, so this treatment undertook to heal and restore sinners. And just as physicians, when they bind wounds, do so not without order but suitably, so that a certain beauty also arises from the usefulness of the bandage, so the medicine of Wisdom was adapted to our wounds through the assumption of humanity, healing some by opposites and others by likenesses.

For the person who treats a bodily wound applies certain opposites, such as cold to hot or moisture to dryness, or anything else of this kind. He also applies certain likenesses, such as a round piece of linen to a round wound or an elongated one to an elongated wound, and he fits the bandage itself not identically to every limb but similarly to similar limbs. So the Wisdom of God, healing humanity, presented itself for healing: itself the physician, itself the medicine.

Because humanity fell through pride, Wisdom applied humility for healing. Deceived by the serpent’s wisdom, we are freed by the foolishness of God. Just as that Wisdom was called wisdom but was foolishness to those who despised God, so this which is called foolishness is Wisdom to those who conquer the devil. We made bad use of immortality, so that we might die; Christ made good use of mortality, so that we might live. Disease entered through the corrupted soul of a woman; salvation proceeded through the intact body of a woman. To the same category of opposites belongs the fact that our vices are also healed by the example of Christ’s virtues.

The likenesses applied as bands to our limbs and wounds include this: he who was born through a woman freed those deceived through a woman; a human being freed human beings, a mortal freed mortals, and through death he freed the dead. Many other aspects of Christian medicine will also become apparent to those who examine them carefully, provided that the necessity of completing the work undertaken does not hurry them away, whether by way of opposites or by way of likenesses.

# CHAPTER FIFTEEN  
## Faith is strengthened by Christ’s resurrection and ascension, and the judgment awakens us

14. The resurrection of the Lord from the dead, which we have believed, and his ascension into heaven, strongly support our faith with great hope. For he showed how willingly he laid down his life for us by possessing such power to take it up again. How confidently, then, does the hope of believers console itself when it considers how great he is and how great things he suffered for those who did not yet believe?

When he is awaited from heaven as judge of the living and the dead, he instills great fear in the negligent, so that they may turn to diligence and desire him more by doing good than fear him by doing evil.

What words can express, or what thought can grasp, the reward he will give at the end, when, for the consolation of this journey, he has given so much of his Spirit that in the adversities of this life we may possess such confidence and love for him whom we do not yet see, and when he has given gifts proper to each person for the instruction of his Church, so that we may do what he shows ought to be done not only without complaint but also with delight?

[Note: [Col. 0025] Bad., Am., and Er. read indulgentiam (“indulgence”); the other copies more correctly read diligentiam (“diligence”).]

[Note: [Col. 0025] Lovaniensis reads donat (“he gives”); we have substituted dona (“gifts”), following Ambrose, Erasmus, and most of the better manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0025] Five manuscripts read cum dilectione (“with love”) rather than cum delectatione (“with delight”).]

# CHAPTER SIXTEEN  
## The Church, Christ’s body and spouse, is cleansed by him through medicinal afflictions

15. The Church is his body, as apostolic teaching commends (Eph. I, 23), and she is also called his spouse. He therefore binds his body, whose many members perform diverse functions (Rom. XII, 4), with the bond of unity and love as with a bond of health. At the present time he exercises and purifies it through certain medicinal afflictions, so that, once rescued from this world, the Church may be joined to him eternally as a spouse “without spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind” (Eph. V, 23–32).

# CHAPTER SEVENTEEN  
## By forgiving sins, Christ opened the way to the homeland

16. Since we are on a way—and this way is not one of places but of affections—which the wickedness of past sins had blocked as if with thorny barriers, what could he do more generously and mercifully? He wished to place himself beneath us as the way by which we might return. He therefore forgave all sins to those who turned back and, by being crucified for us, pulled out the firmly fixed prohibitions that barred our return.

[Note: [Col. 0025] The printed editions read intercludebant … malitiae (“the wickednesses … were blocking”); the manuscripts, with great agreement, read intercludebat … malitia (“the wickedness … was blocking”).]

[Note: [Col. 0025] The printed editions read quo rediremus (“by which we might return”); seventeen manuscripts read qua (“by which”), apart from five others that have viam qua (“the way by which”).]

# CHAPTER EIGHTEEN  
## The keys entrusted to the Church

17. Therefore he gave these keys to his Church, so that whatever she loosed on earth would be loosed in heaven, and whatever she bound on earth would also be bound in heaven (Matt. XVI, 19). This means that whoever in his Church did not believe that his sins could be forgiven would not have them forgiven; but whoever believed, and, corrected, turned away from them, would be healed within the bosom of that same Church by the same faith and correction. For whoever does not believe that sins can be forgiven becomes worse through despair, as though nothing remained for him but evil, since he is distrustful of the fruit of his conversion.

# CHAPTER NINETEEN  
## The death and resurrection of body and soul

18. Just as there is a kind of death of the soul—the abandonment of one’s former life and conduct, which occurs through repentance [Note: [Col. 0025] Ambrose and Erasmus read rejectio (“rejection”) rather than relictio (“abandonment”).]—so there is also a death of the body, the dissolution of its former animation. And just as the soul, after repentance, by which it puts to death its former ruined conduct, is reformed for the better, so also the body, after this death which we all owe to the bond of sin, must be believed and hoped to be changed for the better at the time of resurrection. Thus “flesh and blood” will not possess the kingdom of God, which cannot happen; rather, “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (I Cor. XV, 50, 53). It will cause no trouble, because it will suffer no want, and it will be given life in complete peace by a blessed and perfect soul.

# CHAPTER TWENTY  
## Those who are reborn not to life but to punishments

19. But the soul that does not die to this world and does not begin to be conformed to the truth is dragged, through the death of the body, into a more grievous death. It will rise again not for a transformation into heavenly condition [Note: [Col. 0026] Three Vatican manuscripts read ad communicationem (“for participation”), and another Vatican manuscript ad communionem (“for communion”). Erasmus agrees with this; but the other books read ad commutationem (“for transformation”). Shortly afterward, nearly all the manuscripts read coelestis habitudinis (“of heavenly condition”); Ambrose has habitationis (“of habitation”), while Erasmus and Lovaniensis have beatitudinis (“of blessedness”).], but to undergo punishments.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE  
## Again, concerning the resurrection of the body

This, then, is what faith holds, and what must be believed to be the case: neither the human soul nor the human body suffers complete destruction. Rather, the impious rise again for immeasurable punishments, while the devout rise again for eternal life.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO  
## God alone is to be enjoyed

20. Among all these things, therefore, only those are to be enjoyed which we have identified as eternal and immutable. The rest are to be used, so that we may reach the enjoyment of those things. We, then, who enjoy and use other things are ourselves certain things. For the human being is a great thing, made in the image and likeness of God—not insofar as he is enclosed in a mortal body, but insofar as he surpasses beasts through the dignity of a rational soul.

[Note: [Col. 0026] Eleven manuscripts read praecellit (“surpasses”) rather than praecedit (“precedes”).]

Thus it is a great question whether human beings ought to enjoy themselves, or use themselves, or do both. We have been commanded to love one another, but the question is whether one person ought to be loved by another for his own sake or for the sake of something else. If for his own sake, we enjoy him; if for the sake of something else, we use him. It seems to me that he is to be loved for the sake of something else. For in that which is to be loved for its own sake blessed life is established; and although we do not yet possess it, its hope consoles us in this present time. But “cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. XVII, 5).

21. Nor should anyone enjoy himself, if you observe the matter clearly, because he ought not to love himself for his own sake but for the sake of him whom we are to enjoy. A person is best when his whole life proceeds toward immutable life and he clings to it with his entire affection. But if he loves himself for his own sake, he does not refer himself to God; turning toward himself, he does not turn toward anything immutable. Consequently, he already enjoys himself with some defect, because he is better when he wholly clings and is bound to the immutable good than when he relaxes his attachment from it even toward himself.

If, therefore, you ought not to love yourself for your own sake but for the sake of him in whom the most rightful end of your love lies, another person should not be angry if you love him also for God’s sake. For this is the rule of love established by God: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”; but you shall love God “with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Lev. XIX, 18; Deut. VI, 5; and Matt. XXII, 37, 39). Thus you are to direct all your thoughts, your whole life, and your entire understanding toward him, from whom you have the very things you direct toward him.

When he says “with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind,” he leaves no part of our life that ought to be vacant and, as it were, make room for us to wish to enjoy some other thing. Rather, whatever else comes into the mind as something to be loved must be carried there where the whole impulse of love runs.

Therefore, whoever rightly loves his neighbor ought to act with him in such a way that he too may love God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind. For by loving him as himself, he refers his entire love of himself and of the other person to that love of God which permits no stream to be diverted away from itself and diminished by such a diversion.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE  
## No command is needed that a person love himself and his body; the perverse love of self

22. Not everything that is to be used, however, is to be loved, but only those things which either, through a certain fellowship with us, are referred together with us to God—such as a human being or an angel—or which, when referred to us, depend on us for God’s benefaction, such as the body. Certainly the martyrs did not love the crime of those who persecuted them, although they used it to gain God’s favor.

Since there are four things to be loved—one above us, another which we are, a third beside us, and a fourth below us—no commands needed to be given concerning the second and the fourth. However far a human being may fall from the truth, love of himself and love of his body remain with him. For the soul that flees from the immutable light ruling over all things acts so that it itself may rule itself and its body; and therefore it cannot help loving both itself and its body.

23. He considers himself to have attained something great if he can also dominate his companions, that is, other human beings. For a vicious soul is inclined to desire and claim for itself as if it were owed to it what is owed properly to God alone. Such love of self is better called hatred. It is unjust, because it wants what is below it to serve it, while it refuses to serve what is above it. Hence it is most rightly said: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 6). Therefore the soul becomes weak and is tormented by the mortal body. It must love that body and is weighed down by its corruption.

The immortality and incorruption of the body arise from the health of the soul; and the health of the soul consists in clinging most firmly to what is superior, namely, the immutable God. But when it also desires to dominate those who are naturally its equals—that is, human beings—this is utterly intolerable pride.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR  
## No one hates his own flesh, not even those who rise up against it

24. No one, then, hates himself. On this point there was indeed no dispute with any sect.

[Note: [Col. 0028] Bad., Am., and Er. read: “On this point there was some dispute with a certain sect.”]

Nor does anyone hate his own body. What the Apostle says is true: “No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V, 29). Some say that they would prefer altogether to be without a body, but they are entirely mistaken. They do not hate their body, but its corruptions and its burden. They therefore do not want no body at all, but an incorruptible and extremely swift body.

[Note: [Col. 0028] Bad., Am., and Er., supported by only one manuscript, read integerrimum (“most perfect”) rather than celerrimum (“extremely swift”).]

But they think that there would be no body if it were such, because they think that the soul is something of this kind. When they appear to persecute their bodies through a certain continence and through labors, those who do this rightly are not acting so as to be without a body, but so as to have it subjected and ready for necessary works. They desire to extinguish, through a kind of laborious military service of the body, the lusts that make bad use of the body—that is, the habits and inclinations of the soul toward enjoying inferior things. For they do not kill themselves; rather, they take care of their health.

25. Those who act perversely, however, as though their body were naturally their enemy, wage war against it. They are misled by what they read: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another” (Gal. V, 17). This was said of the uncontrolled carnal habit, against which the spirit desires—not in order to destroy the body, but so that, once its desire, that is, its evil habit, has been subdued, it may make the body subject to the spirit, as the natural order requires.

For after the resurrection the body will be completely subject to the spirit, flourish immortally in supreme peace, and this must also be practiced in the present life: the carnal habit must be changed for the better and must no longer resist the spirit with disordered movements.

Until this happens, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” The spirit does not resist through hatred but through mastery, because it wants what it loves to be subject to what is better. Nor does the flesh resist through hatred, but through the bond of habit, which, having grown old from the lineage of our parents, has developed according to the law of nature.

The spirit therefore acts in subduing the flesh so as to dissolve the perverse agreements of evil habit, as it were, and to establish the peace of good habit. Yet even those who, corrupted by a false opinion, detest their bodies would not be willing to lose one eye without feeling pain, even if the power of sight remaining in the other were as great as that which had been present in both, unless some consideration requiring preference compelled them.

This and similar evidence sufficiently shows, to those who seek the truth without obstinacy, how certain the Apostle’s statement is when he says: “No one has ever hated his own flesh.” He added: “But he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.”

# CHAPTER TWENTY-FIVE  
## Even if something is loved more than the body, the body is not therefore hated

26. A rule of loving must therefore be taught to a human being: namely, how he should love himself so as to benefit himself. That he loves himself and wishes to benefit himself is something only a madman would doubt. It must also be taught how he should love his body, so that he may care for it in an orderly and prudent manner. For it is equally clear that he loves his body and wishes to keep it safe and sound.

A person may therefore love something more than the health and soundness of his body. Many are found to have voluntarily accepted both pain and the loss of certain limbs in order to obtain other things that they loved more. No one should therefore be said not to love the health and safety of his body simply because he loves something more. Even a miser, although he loves money, buys bread for himself. In doing so, he gives money that he loves greatly and desires to increase, because he values more highly the health of his body, which is supported by that bread.

It is unnecessary to argue at greater length about something so evident, though the error of the impious often compels us to do so.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX  
## The command to love God and one’s neighbor also includes oneself

27. Since no command is needed for each person to love himself and his body—that is, since we love, by an unshaken law of nature, both what we are and what is below us but nevertheless belongs to us, and this law has even been promulgated among beasts, for beasts also love themselves and their bodies—it remained that we should receive commands concerning what is above us and what is beside us.

“You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII, 37–40). The end, therefore, of the commandment is love (I Tim. I, 5), and it is twofold: love of God and love of neighbor.

If you understand yourself as a whole—that is, your soul and your body—and your neighbor as a whole—that is, his soul and his body, for a human being consists of soul and body—then no kind of thing that ought to be loved has been omitted from these two commandments.

Since the love of God comes first and the measure of that love is prescribed, so that everything else flows into it, nothing may seem to have been said about your love of yourself. But when it is said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” your love of yourself by yourself has not been omitted either.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-SEVEN  
## The order of love
## 28.

But he lives justly and holily who is an unimpaired evaluator of things. He is the one who possesses an ordered love, so that he does not love what ought not to be loved, fail to love what ought to be loved, love more what ought to be loved less, love equally what ought to be loved either less or more, or love less or more what ought to be loved equally. Every sinner, insofar as he is a sinner, is not to be loved; and every human being, insofar as he is a human being, is to be loved for God’s sake, while God is to be loved for his own sake. And if God is to be loved more than any human being, each person ought to love God more than himself. Likewise, another human being is to be loved more than our own body, because all these things are to be loved [Col. 0030] for God’s sake; and another human being can enjoy God together with us, which the body cannot do, since the body lives through the soul, by which we enjoy God.

## Chapter XXVIII. Whom One Should Help When One Cannot Help Everyone, or Even Two People

All are to be loved equally; but since you cannot benefit everyone, you must take particular thought for those who, by the circumstances of place, time, or any other matter, are bound to you more closely, as though by a certain lot. For just as, if you had an abundance of something that ought to be given to someone who lacked it, and it could not be given to two people, and two people met you, neither of whom surpassed the other either in need or in any claim upon you, you could do nothing more just than choose by lot to whom the thing should be given which could not be given to both; so, among people for whom you cannot provide for all, it should be regarded as a matter of lot according to how much more closely each person may be temporarily attached to you.

## 29. We Should Desire and Endeavor That Everyone Love God

Among all those who can enjoy God together with us, we love [Note: [Col. 0030] Printed editions have “we should love”; the manuscripts, except one, have “we love.”] some whom we assist, some by whom we are assisted, some whose assistance we need and whose need we relieve, and some to whom we ourselves contribute no advantage and from whom we do not expect any advantage to be contributed to us. Nevertheless, we ought to desire that all should love God together with us, and everything by which we assist them or are assisted by them must be referred to that one end.

For if, in the theaters of wickedness, someone loves a particular actor and enjoys his art as a great or even supreme good, he loves all those who love that actor along with him—not for their sake, but for the sake of the one whom they love together. And the more fervent he is in his love for the actor, the more he strives by whatever means he can to make him loved by more people, and the more people he wants to display him to. When he sees someone less enthusiastic, he arouses him as much as he can by praising the actor; but if he finds someone opposing him, he vehemently hates in that person the hatred of his beloved, and presses by whatever means he can to remove it. What, then, ought we to do in the fellowship of the love of God—God whose enjoyment is blessed life; from whom all who love him receive both what they are and the fact that they love him; concerning whom we have no fear that he could displease anyone once known; and who wishes to be loved not so that anything may be bestowed on him, but so that an eternal reward may be bestowed on those who love him—God himself, that is, whom they love?

From this it follows that we should love even our enemies. We do not fear them, because they cannot take away from us what we love; rather, we pity them, because they hate us all the more the farther they are separated from the one whom we love. If they turn to him, they must love both him as the source of blessedness and us as companions in so great a good.

## 30. Our Neighbors Are All Human Beings, and the Angels Themselves

A certain question concerning the angels arises at this point. They too are blessed by enjoying the one whom we desire to enjoy; and insofar as we enjoy him in this life either through a mirror or in a riddle (1 Cor. 13:12), we endure our pilgrimage more tolerably and desire its end more ardently.

But whether the love of angels also belongs to those two commandments may reasonably be asked. That the one who commanded us to love our neighbor excluded no human being is shown by the Lord himself in the Gospel, as well as by the apostle Paul. When the man to whom the Lord had given those two commandments and had said that the whole Law and the Prophets depended on them asked him, “And who is my neighbor?” [Note: [Col. 0031] Nearly all manuscripts have, “And who is a neighbor to me?”], he set before him a certain man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, who fell among robbers, was severely wounded, and was left injured and half-dead. He taught that the man’s neighbor was the one who showed mercy in restoring and caring for him; and the questioner himself, when questioned, acknowledged this. The Lord said to him, “Go, and do likewise” (Luke 10:27, 37), so that we may understand that the neighbor is the person to whom we ought to show the service of mercy if he is in need, or would have to show it if he were in need.

It follows from this that the one from whom such service must likewise be shown to us is also our neighbor. “Neighbor” is a relational term, and no one can be a neighbor except in relation to another. Who does not see that no one has been excluded from the service of mercy, since it is extended even to enemies, as the same Lord says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44)?

Paul the apostle teaches the same thing when he says: “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not murder, you shall not steal, you shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love does no evil to the neighbor” (Rom. 13:9–10). Whoever therefore thinks that the apostle was not speaking of every human being is forced to admit something utterly absurd and criminal: that the apostle considered it no sin if someone committed adultery with the wife of a non-Christian or an enemy, murdered him, or coveted his property. Since it is madness to say this, it is clear that every human being must be regarded as a neighbor, because evil must be done to no one.

Moreover, if the person to whom we are to show the service of mercy, or from whom that service is to be shown to us, is rightly called a neighbor, it is clear that the holy angels too are included in this commandment by which we are ordered to love our neighbor. They render us services of mercy so great that this can easily be observed in many passages of the divine Scriptures.

From this it also follows that God himself and our Lord wished to be called our neighbor. For the Lord Jesus Christ also indicates that he came to the aid of the half-dead man who was lying afflicted on the road and had been abandoned by the robbers. And the prophet says in prayer: “Like a neighbor, like our brother, so I pleased” (Ps. 34:14).

But because the divine substance is more excellent and above our nature, the commandment by which we are to love God is distinguished from the love of our neighbor [Note: [Col. 0032] Two Vatican manuscripts add here: “But because we are equal by nature, and, leaving aside boasting, are all nothing other than human beings, the commandment by which we are to love our neighbor is not distinguished from love of ourselves.”]. He shows us mercy because of his goodness, whereas we show mercy to one another because of him; that is, he has mercy on us so that we may enjoy him, while we have mercy on one another so that we may enjoy him.

## 31. God Does Not Enjoy Us but Uses Us

Therefore, when we say that we enjoy the thing that we love for its own sake, and that we ought to enjoy only that by which we are made blessed, while we ought to use the other things, an ambiguity still seems to remain. God loves us, and divine Scripture strongly commends his love toward us: how, then, does he love us? Does he use us, or does he enjoy us?

But if he enjoys us, he needs our goodness—which no sane person would say. For all our good is either God himself or comes from him. Who, then, does not understand or doubt that light has no need of the splendor of those things which it itself illuminates? The prophet also says most plainly: “I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods’” (Ps. 15:2). Therefore he does not enjoy us, but uses us. For if he neither enjoys nor uses us, I do not see how he could love us.

## 32. How God Uses the Human Being

But neither does he use us in the way we do. We refer the things we use to the end that we may enjoy God’s goodness; God, however, refers our use to his own goodness. Because he is good, we exist; and insofar as we exist, we are good. But because he is also just, we are not evil with impunity; and insofar as we are evil, to that extent we exist less fully.

For he is supremely and primarily the one who is wholly unchangeable, and who could say most completely: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to them, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14). The other things that exist cannot exist except from him, and are good insofar as they have received existence [Note: [Col. 0032] Printed editions have: “But the other things that exist cannot exist except from him, and are good to the extent that they exist.” This is not incorrect, but the manuscript reading seemed preferable.].

Therefore, that use of us which is called God’s use of us is directed not to his utility but to ours, and only to his goodness. When we pity someone and take thought for his welfare, we do this for his benefit and have his benefit in view; but somehow it also becomes our benefit, since God does not leave the mercy we show to the needy without reward [Note: [Col. 0032] Printed editions have, “becomes”; manuscripts have, “is”]. The highest reward is that we may enjoy God himself, and that all who enjoy him may also enjoy one another in him.

## 33. How It Is Appropriate to Enjoy the Human Being

For if we do this in ourselves, we remain on the way and place the hope of our blessedness in a human being or an angel. The proud human being and the proud angel arrogate this to themselves and rejoice that the hope of others is placed in them. But the holy human being and the holy angel, when we are weary and wish to rest in them and remain with them, instead refresh us—by the provision they have received for our sake, or even by that which they have received for their own sake, though they have received it nonetheless—and thus, once refreshed, compel us to go to the one whose enjoyment makes us blessed together.

The apostle also cries out: “Was Paul crucified for you?
