Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:13); and, “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (ibid. 3:7). And the angel warns the human being who worships him that he should rather worship the one under whose Lordship the angel himself is also a fellow servant (Rev. 19:10).

When you enjoy a human being in God, therefore, you enjoy God rather than the human being. You enjoy the one by whom you are made blessed, and you rejoice that you have reached the one in whom you place your hope of arriving. Hence Paul says to Philemon: “Yes, brother, let me enjoy you in the Lord” (Philem. 20). If he had not added “in the Lord” and had said only “let me enjoy you,” he would have placed the hope of his blessedness in him.

Although one may also say “enjoy” in a very near sense when one uses with delight [Note: [Col. 0033] Older manuscripts have, “when one uses with love.”]. For when the thing that is loved is present, it necessarily brings delight with it. If you pass through that delight and refer it to the place where one ought to remain, you use it, and are said to enjoy it improperly and figuratively. But if you cling to it and remain in it, placing the end of your joy in it, then you are said to enjoy it truly and properly. This is to be done only in that Trinity, the supreme and unchangeable good.

## 34. The First Way to God Is Christ

Consider how, although Truth itself and the Word through whom all things were made became flesh in order to dwell among us (John 3:3, 14), the apostle nevertheless says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16).

He who wished to provide not only possession for those arriving, but also the way for those coming to the beginning of the ways [Note: [Col. 0033] Am., Er., and the Theoderician manuscript have: “to himself, the beginning of the ways.”], wished to assume flesh. Hence there is also the statement: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. 8:22), so that those who wished to come might begin from there.

The apostle, then, although he was still walking on the way and following the God who called him toward the prize of the heavenly calling, nevertheless, “forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. 3:12–14), had already passed beyond the beginning of the ways. That is, he no longer needed the one from whom, nevertheless, the journey must be undertaken and begun by all who desire to arrive at the truth and remain in eternal life.

For he says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6): that is, through me one comes, to me one arrives, in me one remains. When one arrives at him, one also arrives at the Father, because through the one who is equal to him, the one to whom he is equal is recognized, with the Holy Spirit binding and, as it were, gluing us together, so that we may remain in the supreme and unchangeable good.

From this we understand how no thing [Note: [Col. 0033] Printed editions have “because”; manuscripts of better quality have “how no thing.”] ought to hold us on the way, since even the Lord himself, insofar as he deigned to be our way, did not wish to hold us but to be passed beyond. He does not want us to cling weakly to temporal things, even though he assumed and accomplished them for our salvation; rather, through them we should run eagerly, so that we may deserve to be carried and conveyed to him himself, who liberated our nature from temporal things and placed it at the right hand of the Father [Note: [Col. 0034] The Vulgate has “to arrive”; manuscripts have “to be conveyed,” in place of it.].

## 35. The Fullness of Scripture and Its End Is the Love of God and Neighbor

The sum of all that has been said, then, insofar as we have been treating things, is that the fullness and end of the Law and of all the divine Scriptures is love (Rom. 13:10; 1 Tim. 1:5) of the thing that is to be enjoyed and of the thing that can enjoy it together with us, because no commandment is needed for each person to love himself.

The whole temporal dispensation, therefore, which was arranged by divine providence for our salvation, was made so that we might know and be able to do this. We ought to use that dispensation, not with a stationary kind of love and delight, but with a passing one, as a road, as vehicles, or as any other instruments—or whatever more suitable expression may be used—so that we may love the things by which we are carried for the sake of that to which we are being carried.

## 36. A Faulty Interpretation of Scripture Is Not Lying or Harmfully Deceptive If It Is Useful for Building Love; Nevertheless, the Interpreter Who Is Thus Mistaken Must Be Corrected

Whoever, therefore, thinks that he has understood the divine Scriptures, or any part of them, in such a way that his interpretation does not build up that twofold love of God and neighbor has not yet understood them.

But whoever derives from them a meaning useful for building this love, although he has not said what the author whom he is reading can be shown to have meant at that place, is not harmfully deceived and is not lying altogether [Note: [Col. 0034] Am. and eleven manuscripts have “has said.”]. For a false will to speak falsely is present in the liar; and therefore we find many who wish to lie, but no one who wishes to be deceived.

Since a person knowingly does the one and unknowingly suffers the other, it is sufficiently clear in one and the same matter that the person who is deceived is better than the person who lies, since it is better to suffer injustice than to commit it. Everyone who lies commits injustice [Note: [Col. 0034] Eighteen manuscripts have, “who lies acts unjustly.” One has, “an unjust person.”]. And if it seems to anyone that a lie is sometimes useful, it may also seem that injustice is sometimes useful. For no liar keeps faith in the matter about which he lies. He certainly wants the person to whom he lies to have faith in him, yet by lying he does not keep faith with that person. Everyone who violates faith is unjust. Either, then, injustice is sometimes useful—which cannot be—or a lie is always useless.

But whoever in the Scriptures understands something other than what the author wrote is deceived, though the Scriptures themselves do not lie. Nevertheless, as I began to say, if he is deceived in a meaning by which he builds love, which is the end of the commandment, he is deceived as someone might be who, by mistake, leaves the road but nevertheless proceeds across the field to the place to which the road also leads. Yet he must be corrected, and it must be shown how much more useful it is not to leave the road, lest, through the habit of straying, he be forced to go crosswise or astray.

## 37. Great Danger Lies in This Faulty Interpretation

[Col. 0035]

For by rashly asserting what the author he is reading did not mean, he generally encounters other matters that he cannot connect with that interpretation. If he agrees that those matters are true and certain, then what he had understood cannot be true; and somehow it happens that, by loving his own interpretation, he begins to be more offended by Scripture than by himself.

If he allows this evil to spread, he will be overthrown by it. “We walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:7); but faith will stumble if the authority of the divine Scriptures wavers. When faith stumbles, love itself also grows weak. For if someone falls away from faith, he must also fall away from love, since he cannot love what he does not believe to exist. But if he both believes and loves, then by acting well and obeying the commandments of good conduct he brings it about that he also hopes to reach what he loves.

Thus there are three things by which all knowledge and prophecy serve: faith, hope, and love.

## 38. Love Remains Forever

Faith will be succeeded by sight [Note: [Col. 0035] Thirteen manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead have “hope succeeds faith,” incorrectly, as is clear from the following words, “which we shall see.”], which we shall see; and hope will be succeeded by blessedness itself, to which we shall come. But love will rather increase when those things pass away.

For if we love by believing what we do not yet see, how much more will we love when we begin to see it? And if we love by hoping for what we have not yet reached, how much more when we have reached it?

The difference between temporal and eternal things is that a temporal thing is loved more before it is possessed, but becomes worthless when it arrives. It does not satisfy the soul, whose true and certain dwelling-place is eternity. An eternal thing, however, is loved more ardently once attained than when desired. No one who desires it is permitted to form a higher estimate of it than it possesses, so that it may seem worthless when he finds less than he expected. Rather, however much anyone who is approaching may have been able to imagine, he will find more upon arriving.

## 39. A Person Equipped with Faith, Hope, and Love Does Not Need the Scriptures

A human being supported by faith, hope, and love, and holding them firmly, does not need the Scriptures except for instructing others. Thus many people, through these three things, live even in solitude without books.

In them, I think, what was said has already been fulfilled: “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be abolished.” Through these instruments, as it were, such an instruction in faith, hope, and love has arisen in them that, possessing something perfect, they do not seek what exists only in part. It is perfect, certainly, insofar as this life permits; for compared with the life to come, the life of no just and holy person is perfect.

“Faith, hope, and love remain,” he says, “these three; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Cor. 13:8, 13), because when anyone reaches eternal things, and those two pass away, love will remain more abundant and more certain.

## 40. What Kind of Reader Scripture Requires

Therefore, when someone recognizes that the end of the commandment is love “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5), he should approach the interpretation of those books confidently, referring every understanding of the divine Scriptures to these three things.

When he said “love,” he added “from a pure heart,” so that nothing other than what ought to be loved may be loved. He joined a good conscience to it because of hope. A person who has a scruple of bad conscience despairs of reaching what he believes and loves.

Third, he says, “and from an unfeigned faith.” For if our faith is free from falsehood, then we neither love what should not be loved nor, by living rightly, hope in such a way that our hope can be deceived.

For this reason I wished to speak about matters concerning faith as much as I judged sufficient for the present, since much has already been said about them in other volumes, either by others or by us. Let this, then, be the end of this book. Concerning signs we shall discuss as much as the Lord grants.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0035]

Augustine now begins his discussion of the signs and words of sacred Scripture, and shows that its genuine meaning is often not perceived because those signs are either unknown or ambiguous. Accordingly, after first setting forth the canon of the divine books, he proceeds to explain knowledge of which languages, and which disciplines and sciences, contribute most to removing ignorance of those signs. Taking the opportunity, he also discusses briefly but profoundly the rejection of superstitious arts and teachings. At the beginning and end of the book he explains what disposition of mind is required of one who is about to devote himself to the study of Scripture.

## Chapter 1. What a Sign Is and How Many Kinds There Are

Since, when writing about things, I prefaced my discussion by warning that no one should attend to anything in them except what they are, and not also to whether they signify something beyond themselves, so, conversely, when discussing signs I say that no one should attend in them to what they are, but rather to the fact that they are signs—that is, to what they signify.

A sign is a thing which, besides the appearance that it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into thought from itself. Thus, when we see a footprint, we think that the animal whose footprint it is has passed; when we see smoke, we recognize that fire is present beneath it; when we hear the voice of a living creature, we perceive the affection of its mind; and when a trumpet sounds, soldiers know that they must advance or retreat, or do whatever else the battle requires [Note: [Col. 0036] Am., Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., and Helm. read “either advance or retreat” and omit “themselves.” M.].

Signs, then, are of two kinds: natural and given.

Natural signs are those which, without any will or desire to signify, cause something other than themselves to be known from them, as smoke signifies fire. Smoke does not do this because it wishes to signify, but through observation and recognition of experienced things it is understood that fire is present, even if only smoke appears.

The footprint of a passing animal also belongs to this class. An angry or sad expression signifies an affection of the mind even without the will of the person who is angry or sad. The same is true if some other movement of the mind is revealed by the face as its indicator, even though we are not trying to reveal it.

But it is not our purpose to discuss this entire class now. Since it has nevertheless entered into our division, it could not be passed over altogether; and it is enough that we have noted it thus far.

## Chapter 2. The Kind of Signs to Be Discussed Here

Given signs, on the other hand, are those which living beings give to one another in order, as far as they can, to display the movements of their minds, or whatever sensations or thoughts they may have. We have no reason for signifying—that is, for giving a sign—except to bring forth and transfer into another’s mind what the person giving the sign has in his own mind.

We have therefore decided to consider and discuss this kind of sign as it concerns human beings, because even the signs given by God and contained in the sacred Scriptures were made known to us through human beings who wrote them down.

Some animals also have signs among themselves by which they reveal the desire of their minds. A rooster, for example, when it finds food, gives a vocal sign to a hen so that she may run to it; and a dove calls another dove by its cooing, or is called by it in turn. Many such things are commonly observed.

Whether these signs follow the movement of the mind without a will to signify, as does the expression or cry of one who is suffering, or whether they are actually given for the purpose of signifying, is another question and does not concern the matter at hand. We therefore remove that part from this work as unnecessary.

## Chapter 3. Words Hold Primacy Among Signs

Of the signs by which human beings communicate their thoughts to one another, some belong to the sense of sight, most to the sense of hearing, and very few to the remaining senses.

When we gesture, we give a sign only to the eyes of the person whom we wish, through that sign, to make a participant in our intention. Some things are signified by the movement of the hands [Note: [Col. 0037] Several printed editions and many manuscripts have, “and some movements.” Other manuscripts read more appropriately, “through movements,” or “by movement.”]. Actors give signs to those who understand them through the movements of all their limbs, and converse, as it were, with their eyes. Military standards and dragon-emblems convey the commanders’ wishes through the eyes. All these are, as it were, visible words.

The signs that pertain to the ears, as I said, are more numerous, especially words. A trumpet, flute, and lyre often produce not merely a pleasant sound but also a significant one. Yet all these signs are very few compared with words.

Words have acquired complete primacy among human beings for signifying whatever is conceived in the mind, if one wishes to disclose it. The Lord also gave a sign through the fragrance of the ointment with which his feet were anointed (John 12:3, 7); and through the sacramental tasting of his body and blood he signified what he wished (Luke 22:19–20) [Note: [Col. 0037] The printed editions read this way, supported by very few manuscripts; most have “having tasted,” while five manuscripts of excellent quality have “through tasting.” Another reading found in three manuscripts is “through taste”; for in ancient books one frequently finds “tasting” in place of “taste.”]. When the woman touched the fringe of his garment and was healed, she also signified something (Matt. 9:21).

But the innumerable multitude of signs by which human beings express their thoughts is constituted in words. I have been able to state in words all the signs whose kinds I have briefly touched upon; but I could in no way state words through those signs.

## Chapter 4. The Origin of Letters

But because sounds, once the air has been struck, immediately pass away and remain no longer than they resound, signs of words were established through letters. Thus voices are displayed to the eyes, not in themselves, but through certain signs belonging to them.

These signs could not be common to all peoples, because of a certain sin of human dissension, when each person seizes primacy for himself. The sign of this pride is that tower raised toward heaven, where the impious human beings deserved to have not only their minds but also their voices made discordant (Gen. 11:1–9).

## Chapter 5. The Diversity of Languages

From this it came about that the divine Scripture also—by which such great remedies are provided for the diseases of human wills—having originated in one language through which it could suitably be disseminated throughout the world, became known to the nations after being spread far and wide through the various languages of translators, for their salvation.

Those who read it desire nothing other than to discover the thoughts and will of those by whom it was written, and through them the will of God, according to which we believe such people spoke [Note: [Col. 0038] Bad., Am., Er., and several manuscripts have “which.”].

## Chapter 6. The Usefulness of Scripture’s Obscurity in Tropes and Figures

Those who read rashly are deceived by many and manifold obscurities and ambiguities, understanding one thing in place of another. In some passages they cannot even discover what they might falsely suppose, because certain statements cast over themselves an extremely dense darkness.

I do not doubt that all this has been divinely arranged to subdue pride through labor and to recall the mind from boredom, since what is easily discovered generally becomes worthless through familiarity [Note: [Col. 0038] Lovaniensis and some manuscripts have “to renew.” Others, with Augustine and Erasmus, have “to recall.”].

For what, I ask, would happen if someone said that there are holy and perfect human beings whose life and conduct cause Christ’s Church to cut away from every superstition those who come to her and, by the imitation of good people, incorporate them into herself, as it were; that these good believers and true servants of God [Note: [Col. 0038] Two manuscripts have “true.” Three others have “truly.”], laying down the burdens of the world, came to the holy baptismal washing, and, ascending from it, bear the fruit of twofold love, that is, love of God and neighbor?

Would this be less pleasing to the hearer than if, with the same meaning, he explained that passage from the Song of Songs where the Church is addressed as a beautiful woman and praised in these words: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep, coming up from the washing, all of which bear twins, and none among them is barren” (Song 4:2)?

What does a person learn that is different from what he would learn by hearing the same thing in the plainest words, without the aid of this comparison? And yet, somehow, I contemplate the saints more sweetly when I see them as the teeth of the Church, cutting people away from errors and transferring them into her body, their hardness softened, as though they had been bitten and chewed.

I also recognize with great delight the sheep shorn of their fleeces—that is, having laid aside their worldly burdens—ascending from the washing, that is, from baptism, and all bearing twins, that is, the two commandments of love. I see that none is barren of this holy fruit.

But why I see this more sweetly than if no such comparison were drawn from the divine books, although the thing and the knowledge are the same, is difficult to say and is another question.

For now, however, no one doubts that things are more readily learned through comparisons, and that what is sought with some difficulty is found with much greater pleasure. Those who do not find at all what they seek suffer hunger; those who do not seek because they have everything readily available often languish from boredom. Both kinds of weakness must be avoided.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, has magnificently and beneficially arranged the sacred Scriptures so that their more open passages might meet hunger, while their more obscure passages might wipe away boredom. For scarcely anything is drawn from those obscurities that is not found stated with complete clarity elsewhere.

## Chapter 7. The Steps Toward Wisdom: First, Fear; Second, Piety; Third, Knowledge; Fourth, Fortitude; Fifth, Counsel; Sixth, Purification of the Heart; Seventh, Wisdom, or the End

Above all, it is necessary to be converted by the fear of God toward learning his will—what he commands us to desire and to avoid. This fear must necessarily bring to mind our mortality and future death, and, as though our flesh had been nailed down, fasten every movement of pride to the wood of the cross.

Next, it is necessary to become gentle through piety and not contradict divine Scripture, whether it is understood and strikes at some of our faults, or is not understood, as though we could know better and give better commands [Note: [Col. 0039] Augustine and four manuscripts have “perceive.”]. Rather, we should think and believe that what is written there, even if hidden, is better and truer than anything we can know by ourselves.

After these two steps, fear and piety, one comes to the third step, knowledge, which I have now undertaken to discuss. In it every student of the divine Scriptures exercises himself, finding nothing in them other than that God must be loved for God’s sake and one’s neighbor for God’s sake: God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind; one’s neighbor as oneself (Matt. 22:37, 39), that is, so that the whole love of one’s neighbor, just as the love of oneself, may be referred to God.

We discussed these two commandments in the preceding book when treating of things. It is therefore necessary that, in the Scriptures, each person first discover himself entangled in love of this world—that is, of temporal things—and separated from such love of God and such love of neighbor as Scripture itself prescribes.

Then the fear by which he thinks about God’s judgment, and the piety by which he cannot help but believe and submit to the authority of the holy books, compels him to mourn for himself. For this knowledge makes a person of good hope not boastful but mournful. Through this disposition he obtains, by persistent prayers, the consolation of divine assistance, lest he be broken by despair; and he begins to be at the fourth step, that of fortitude, by which he hungers and thirsts for righteousness.

Through this disposition he withdraws from every deadly delight in passing things and, turning away from them, turns toward love of eternal things—namely, the unchangeable unity and the same Trinity.

When he has seen it radiating as far as possible into the distance, and has recognized that, because of the weakness of his sight, he cannot endure that light, he reaches the fifth degree—that is, the counsel of mercy—in which he purifies the soul that is, as it were, agitated and clamoring against itself because of the filth conceived from its desire for inferior things. Here he exercises himself gently in love of neighbor and is perfected in it; and, already full of hope and possessing his full strength, when he has advanced as far as love of the enemy, he ascends to the sixth degree, where he now purifies the very eye by which God can be seen, insofar as he can be seen by those who die to this world as much as they are able. For they see in proportion as they die to this world; but insofar as they live for this world, they do not see. And therefore, although a more certain form of that light has now begun to appear—not merely more bearable but also more delightful—it is nevertheless still said to be seen “in an enigma and through a mirror” (I Cor. XIII, 12), because, while we are pilgrims in this life, “we walk more by faith than by sight” (II Cor. V, 6–7), although “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philipp. III, 20). At this degree he so purifies the eye of the heart that he does not place or compare even his neighbor before the truth; therefore neither does he place himself before it, since he does not place before it the one whom he loves as himself. This holy man will therefore be of so simple and pure a heart that he will be turned aside from the truth neither by the desire to please human beings nor by regard for avoiding any of his own troubles that are hostile to this life. Such a son ascends to wisdom, which is the final and seventh degree, and enjoys it in peace and tranquility. For “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Psal. CX, 10; Eccli. I, 16). From that beginning one stretches toward wisdom itself and arrives at it through these degrees.

## CHAPTER VIII—The Canonical Books

12. But let us return our consideration to that third degree, about which we have undertaken to discuss and treat what the Lord may suggest. The most diligent investigator of the divine Scriptures will therefore be one who has first read them all and committed them to memory—not yet necessarily in understanding, but at least through reading—namely, those called canonical. For he will read the others more safely when instructed by the faith of truth, lest they seize upon a weak mind and, deceiving it with dangerous lies and fantasies, prejudice it against sound understanding.

In the canonical Scriptures, let him follow the authority of the many Catholic Churches; among these, certainly, those should be included that have deserved to possess apostolic sees and to receive apostolic letters. He will therefore observe this rule in the canonical Scriptures: he will place before those books accepted by some Catholic Churches those accepted by all; among those not accepted by all, he will place before those held by fewer and less authoritative Churches the books accepted by the greater number and by the more authoritative Churches. But if he should find that some books are held by a greater number and others by more authoritative Churches—although he could scarcely find such a situation—I think that they should nevertheless be regarded as of equal authority.

13. The entire canon of Scripture, in which we say that this consideration is to be pursued, is contained in these books [Note: [Col. 0041] Compare the Council of Hippo, in the year 393, canon 38; and the Third Council of Carthage, in the year 397, canon 47.]: the five books of Moses—that is, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy; one book of Jesus Nave, one of Judges, and one little book called Ruth, which seems rather to belong to the beginning of the Books of Kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0041] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *principia*, “beginnings.”]; then four Books of Kingdoms and two of Chronicles, not following one another but, as it were, attached alongside them and proceeding together.

This is the history that contains connected periods of time and the order of events. There are other books, as though arranged according to a different order, which are connected neither with this sequence nor with one another, such as Job, Tobit, Esther, Judith, the two Books of Maccabees, and the two of Ezra, which seem rather to follow that ordered history after it has reached its conclusion in the Books of Kingdoms or Chronicles.

Then come the Prophets, among whom David is represented by one book, the Psalms, and Solomon by three: Proverbs, the Song of Songs, and Ecclesiastes. For the two books, one entitled Wisdom and the other Ecclesiasticus, are said to belong to Solomon by a certain resemblance; for it is most consistently reported that Jesus Sirach composed them [Note: [Col. 0041] As regards the Book of Wisdom, Augustine later learned that Jesus son of Sirach was not its author, as he warns in *Retractations* II, 4, §2. Whoever the author of the work *On the Creed for Catechumens* may be, he praises it under Solomon’s name, II, 2; so too Cyprian in *On Mortality*, Basil in Book V *Against Eunomius*, and Ambrose in many places. Augustine, however, both here and in his preface to the *Speculum*, considers the Book of Wisdom to have been attributed to Solomon “because of a certain similarity of style. For the more learned,” he says, “have no doubt that it is not Solomon’s”; and he adds that it is not apparent who its author was. Jerome calls the same book, which had long borne the title *The Wisdom of Solomon*, pseudepigraphal, and says that ancient writers attributed it to Philo the Jew and that its style bears the fragrance of Greek eloquence. Some now wish to maintain that its sayings came from Solomon, while its collection and Greek phrasing came from Philo.], but because they have deserved to be received as authoritative, they must be counted among the prophetic books.

The remaining books are those properly called Prophets: the twelve individual books of the Twelve Prophets, which, because they have never been separated from one another, are regarded as one book. Their names are these: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. Then there are four Prophets of greater volumes: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and Ezekiel.

With these forty-four books the authority of the Old Testament ends [Note: [Col. 0041] *Retractations* II, 4, §2.]. The New Testament is contained in the four books of the Gospel: according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, and according to John; in the fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul: to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, to the Colossians, two to Timothy, to Titus, to Philemon, and to the Hebrews; in two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude, and one of James; in one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and in one book of the Apocalypse of John.

## CHAPTER IX—How One Should Devote Oneself to the Study of Scripture

[Col. 0042]

14. In all these books, those who fear God and are gentle through piety seek the will of God. The first observance in this work and labor is, as we said, to know these books: even if not yet in understanding, nevertheless by reading either to commit them to memory or at least not to leave them wholly unknown. Next, the things plainly set forth in them—whether precepts for living or rules for believing—must be investigated with greater diligence and care. Each person discovers more of them according to the capacity of his understanding [Note: [Col. 0042] The printed editions have *intelligentia*, “understanding.” Several manuscripts have *intelligentiae*, “of understanding.”].

For in the things plainly set forth in Scripture are found all that contains faith and the manner of life—namely, hope and charity, which we discussed in the preceding book. Then, after becoming familiar with the language of the divine Scriptures themselves, one must proceed to open up and examine what is obscure, so that examples may be taken from the clearer passages to illuminate the more obscure expressions, and so that certain testimonies of definite meanings may remove uncertainty from uncertain ones. In this matter memory is of the greatest importance; if it is lacking, these precepts cannot be applied.

## CHAPTER X—Scripture May Be Unintelligible Because of Unknown or Ambiguous Signs

15. What is written is not understood for two reasons: either it is concealed by unknown signs or by ambiguous signs. Signs are either proper or transferred. They are called proper when they are used to signify the things for which they were instituted, as when we say “ox” while understanding the animal that all speakers of the Latin language, together with us, call by this name [Note: [Col. 0042] The printed editions read: “As when we say ‘ox,’ we understand the animal.” Several manuscripts read: “As when we say ‘ox,’ and understand the animal.” Others read: “As when we say ‘ox,’ while understanding the animal.”].

They are transferred when the things themselves that we signify by their proper words are employed to signify something else. Thus we say “ox,” and by these two syllables we understand the animal customarily called by this name; but then, by that animal, we understand the evangelist whom Scripture signified when the Apostle interpreted it, saying: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (I Cor. IX, 9).

## CHAPTER XI—Knowledge of Languages Is Necessary for Removing Ignorance of Signs, Especially of Greek and Hebrew

16. Against unknown proper signs, knowledge of languages is a great remedy. Speakers of Latin—the people whom we have now undertaken to instruct—need two other languages for knowledge of the divine Scriptures, namely Hebrew and Greek, so that one may return to the earlier exemplars if the endless variety of Latin translators has introduced any doubt.

Although we often find Hebrew words untranslated in the books—such as *Amen*, *Alleluia*, *Racha*, and *Hosanna*, together with any others of this kind—some have been preserved in their antiquity because of their more sacred authority, even though they could have been translated, as with *Amen* and *Alleluia*. Others, however, are said not to have been transferable into another language, as with the other two just mentioned. For there are words belonging to particular languages that cannot pass by translation into the usage of another language [Col. 0043]. This happens especially with interjections, which signify an emotional movement more than any part of a formulated statement [Note: [Col. 0043] Three manuscripts read *contextae*, “of a connected statement.”]. These two words are said to be of this kind: they say that *Racha* is the cry of an angry person, and *Hosanna* that of one rejoicing.

Knowledge of those languages is necessary, however, not because of these few words—which are very easy to note and investigate—but because of the differences among translators, as has been said. Those who translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek can be counted; Latin translators, however, cannot possibly be counted. For whenever, in the earliest times of the faith, a Greek codex came into someone’s hands and he seemed to possess even a little ability in both languages, he ventured to translate it.

## CHAPTER XII—The Diversity of Translations Is Useful; How Error Arises from Ambiguous Words

17. This circumstance has helped understanding more than it has hindered it, provided that readers are not negligent. For examination of several codices has often clarified some more obscure passages. Thus, in the following passage of the prophet Isaiah, one translator says, “And do not despise the members of your seed,” while another says, “And do not despise your flesh” (Isa. LVIII, 7); each bears witness to the other.

For one is explained by the other. “Flesh” could be understood literally, so that someone might think he had been warned not to despise his own body; while “the members of your seed,” taken figuratively, could mean Christians, born spiritually with us from the same seed of the word. But when the translators’ meanings are compared, the more probable interpretation appears to be that one is commanded literally not to despise one’s relatives. For when “the members of your seed” is referred to the flesh, relatives are the most natural meaning. Hence, I think, comes what the Apostle says: “If by any means I may provoke my flesh to emulation, and may save some of them” (Rom. XI, 14)—that is, so that, by imitating those who had believed, they too might believe. He called the Jews his flesh because of their blood relationship.

Likewise, in that passage of the same prophet Isaiah, “Unless you believe, you will not understand,” another translator rendered it, “Unless you believe, you will not remain” (Isa. VII, 9). Unless the exemplars in the earlier language are read, it is uncertain which of the two translators followed the words of the original [Note: [Col. 0043] Thus three manuscripts. Others, with the printed editions, have *vera*, “true.”]. Nevertheless, something great is suggested to readers who understand from both versions. It is difficult for translators to differ so much that they do not touch one another in some proximity.

Therefore, since understanding concerns the eternal form, while faith nourishes the little ones, as it were with milk, in the beginnings of temporal things—and “we walk by faith, not by sight” (II Cor. V, 7)—unless we walk by faith, we cannot arrive at the form that does not pass away but remains, by which, through purified understanding, we cleave to the truth. For this reason one translator says, “Unless you believe, you will not remain,” while the other says, “Unless you believe, you will not understand.”

18. An interpreter is also frequently misled by an ambiguity in the earlier language when the meaning is not well known to him, and he transfers a meaning utterly alien to the author’s sense. Thus some codices read, “Sharp are their feet for shedding blood.” For among the Greeks, *oxys* (ὀξύς), “sharp,” also means “swift.” The translator who rendered it, “Their feet are swift for shedding blood” (Psal. XIII, 3), therefore saw the meaning; the other, carried in another direction by an ambiguous sign, went astray.

Such readings are not obscure but false, and their treatment is different: one must not be instructed to understand such codices but rather to correct them. This is also what happened because *moschos* (μόσχος) in Greek means “calf”: some did not understand *moscheumata* (μοσχεύματα) to mean “plantations,” and translated it as “calf-shoots.” This error so occupied many codices that it is scarcely possible to find the passage written otherwise. Yet the meaning is perfectly clear from the words that follow, for “Adulterous plantations will not take deep root” (Wis. IV, 3) is more suitable than “calf-shoots,” which walk upon the ground with their feet and do not cling by roots. The surrounding context in that passage also preserves this translation.

## CHAPTER XIII—From Where Errors of Translation May Be Corrected

19. Yet the actual meaning, which several translators attempt to express, each according to his ability and judgment, is not apparent unless one examines the language from which they translate. An interpreter frequently strays from the author’s meaning if he is not highly learned. Knowledge must therefore be sought of the languages from which Scripture came into Latin; or translations should be consulted that adhere too closely to the words—not because they are sufficient, but so that the truth or error of the others may be detected [Note: [Col. 0044] The printed editions have: “Freedom or error may be directed by the others.” On the authority of eleven manuscripts we have restored *veritas*, “truth”; then, conjecturally, *detegatur*, “may be detected.” This conjecture is supported by a single Floriacensis manuscript, in which one reads *deligatur*, “may be chosen.”]—those who, in translating, preferred to follow meanings rather than words.

For not only individual words but also expressions are often transferred, and these cannot at all pass into the usage of the Latin language if someone wishes to preserve the custom of the ancients who spoke Latin. Such things sometimes deprive understanding of nothing, but nevertheless offend those who take greater delight in the subject matter, since they wish a certain integrity to be preserved even in its signs.

What is called a solecism is nothing other than the joining of words according to a rule different from that followed by those who spoke before us, not without some authority. For whether one says *inter homines*, “among human beings,” or *inter hominibus*, “among human beings” with the wrong case, makes no difference to the person who understands the subject matter.

Likewise, what is a barbarism other than a word pronounced with letters or a sound different from that in which those who spoke Latin before us usually pronounced it? Whether *ignoscere*, “to forgive,” is pronounced with the third syllable long or short matters little to one who asks God to forgive his sins, whatever sound that word may have.

What, then, is integrity of expression except the preservation of a foreign usage [Note: [Col. 0044] Thus most manuscripts. The printed editions have: “except the preservation of Latin usage.”] confirmed by the authority of earlier speakers?

20. Nevertheless, people are offended by this all the more as they are weaker; and they are weaker in proportion as they wish to appear learned—not in the knowledge of things by which we are built up, but in the knowledge of signs, by which it is exceedingly difficult not to become inflated, since even knowledge of things often makes the neck stiffen unless it is restrained by the Lord’s yoke.

What harm does it do to one who understands that it is written: “What is the land in which these men sit upon it, whether it is good or bad; and what are the cities in which they themselves dwell in them?” (Num. XIII, 20). I think this expression belongs more to a foreign language than to any deeper meaning.

The passage that we can no longer remove from the mouths of singing peoples—“Upon him, however, my sanctification will flower” (Psal. CXXXI, 18)—takes nothing away from the meaning. A more learned listener, however, would prefer that it be corrected so that it says not *floriet* but *florebit*, “will flower”; and nothing prevents the correction except the singers’ custom.

Such things can therefore easily be disregarded if one does not wish to avoid what takes nothing away from sound understanding. But when the Apostle says, “What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (I Cor. I, 25), if someone wished to preserve the Greek expression by saying, “What is foolish in God is wiser than that of human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than that of human beings,” the attentive reader’s mind would indeed proceed to the truth of the meaning; but someone slower might either fail to understand or understand perversely.

For such an expression is not merely faulty in Latin; it also falls into ambiguity, so that what is foolish or weak among human beings might seem wiser or stronger than what is foolish or weak in God. Even the expression “wiser than human beings” is not free from ambiguity, although it avoids solecism. For it is not apparent without the illumination of the meaning whether it means “wiser for human beings,” from the expression “to this human being,” or “wiser than human beings,” from the expression “from this human being.” It is therefore better to say, “It is wiser than human beings” and “It is stronger than human beings.”

## CHAPTER XIV—From Where Knowledge of an Unknown Word or Expression Is to Be Obtained

21. We shall speak about ambiguous signs later; for now we are dealing with unknown signs, of which there are two forms as far as words are concerned. Either an unknown word causes the reader to hesitate, or an unknown expression does so. If they come from foreign languages, they must either be sought from speakers of those languages, or, if there is leisure and ability, those languages themselves must be learned, or the comparison of several translators must be consulted.

If, however, we do not know certain words or expressions belonging to our own language, they become familiar through the practice of reading and listening. Nothing should be committed to memory more carefully than those classes of words and expressions that we do not know. Thus, when either a more learned person appears from whom they may be investigated, or a passage occurs that shows from what precedes, what follows, or both, what force the unknown expression has and what it signifies, we may easily notice and learn it with the help of memory.

Indeed, the power of habit is so great even in learning that those who have been, so to speak, nourished and brought up in the sacred Scriptures are more surprised by other expressions and regard them as less Latin than those they learned in Scripture and do not find in authors of the Latin language.

Here too the abundance of translators, examined and discussed through comparison of codices, is of great assistance—provided that falsehood is absent. For the diligence of those who desire to know the divine Scriptures must first devote itself to correcting the codices, so that the uncorrected may yield to the corrected, even when they derive from merely one kind of translation.

## CHAPTER XV—The Latin Itala Version and the Greek Septuagint Are Commended

22. Among the translations themselves, the Itala should be preferred to the others, for it is more faithful to the words while preserving clarity of meaning. In correcting any Latin texts, Greek texts should be consulted; among these, as far as the Old Testament is concerned, the authority of the translators known as the Seventy excels [Note: [Col. 0046] *City of God* XVIII, 43.]. They are said to have translated throughout the more learned Churches with such a manifestation of the Holy Spirit that the mouths of so many men were one mouth.

If, as is reported and proclaimed by many trustworthy witnesses [Note: [Col. 0046] Among them are Irenaeus, III, 25; Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Stromata*; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 4; Hilary, on Psalm 2, and others. Before these came Justin Martyr, who says in his *Address to the Greeks* that he saw at Alexandria certain remains of the chambers in which the seventy translators, by order of Ptolemy, devoted themselves separately to translating the Scriptures. Jerome, however, says in his preface to the Pentateuch that he does not know “who first constructed by his lie the seventy chambers at Alexandria, in which they wrote the same things while separated; for Arist[e]as, Ptolemy’s *hyperaspistes*—“champion” or “defender”—and, much later, Josephus report nothing of the kind, but write that they gathered in one basilica and compared their work, not that they prophesied.”], each of them having been separated in an individual chamber while translating, nothing was found in any one of their codices that was not found in the others in the same words and the same order of words, who would dare to compare anything with this authority, much less prefer anything to it?

But if they compared their work so that, through the common deliberation and judgment of all, one voice might result, even then no one person, however skilled, ought or should aspire to correct the agreement of so many senior and learned men.

Therefore, even if something is found in the Hebrew exemplars differently from the way these translators rendered it, I think that one should yield to the divine dispensation accomplished through them: books that the Jewish nation, whether from religion or envy, did not wish to reveal to other peoples were, long beforehand, revealed by the authority of King Ptolemy to the nations who were to believe in the Lord.

It may therefore be that they translated in the manner judged suitable for the nations by the one who directed them—the Holy Spirit, who made one mouth for them all. Nevertheless, as I said above, comparison with these translators also—those who adhered more closely to the words—is often useful for explaining the meaning.

As I had begun to say, Latin codices of the Old Testament, when necessary, should therefore be corrected by the authority of the Greek codices, especially those of the translators who, being the Seventy, are said to have translated with one mouth. As for the books of the New Testament, if anything wavers amid the Latin variations, there is no doubt that it ought to yield to the Greek texts, especially those found among the more learned and more diligent Churches.

## CHAPTER XVI—Knowledge Both of Languages and of Things Helps One Understand Transferred Signs

23. If any unknown transferred signs happen to force the reader to hesitate [Col. 0047], they must be investigated partly through knowledge of languages and partly through knowledge of things. Something contributes to a resemblance and undoubtedly suggests a hidden meaning in the pool of Siloam, where the Lord ordered the man whose eyes he had anointed with mud made from spittle to wash his face (John IX, 7). Yet, unless the Evangelist had interpreted that name, so great a meaning would have remained concealed in an unknown language.

Likewise, many Hebrew names that have not been interpreted by the authors of those same books undoubtedly possess considerable force and assistance for solving the riddles of Scripture, if someone can interpret them. Certain skilled men of that language have conferred no small benefit on posterity by separately interpreting all those words from Scripture, explaining what Adam means, what Eve means, what Abraham means, and what Moses means; and likewise the names of places—what Jerusalem means, or Zion, or Jericho, or Sinai, or Lebanon, or Jordan—or whatever other names in that language are unknown to us. Once these have been disclosed and interpreted, many figurative expressions in Scripture are made clear.

24. Ignorance of things, however, makes figurative expressions obscure when we do not know the natures of animals, stones, herbs, or other things that are often introduced in Scripture for the sake of some comparison.

For even what is known about the serpent—that it exposes its whole body to those striking it in place of its head—how much does this illuminate the meaning in which the Lord commands us to be “wise as serpents” (Matt. X, 16)! We should offer our body to persecutors in place of our head, which is Christ, lest the Christian faith be killed in us if, while sparing our body, we deny God.

Likewise, the claim that the serpent, constricted by the narrowness of a cave, is said to receive new strength after casting off its old skin, how well does this accord with imitating the serpent’s cunning and casting off the old person, as the Apostle says, so that we may put on the new (Eph. IV, 22, 24; Col. III, 9–10)—casting it off through narrow places, as the Lord says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. VII, 13)!

Thus, just as knowledge of the serpent’s nature illuminates many comparisons that Scripture commonly draws from this animal, ignorance of certain other animals, which Scripture likewise frequently mentions by way of comparison, greatly obstructs the interpreter [Note: [Col. 0047] The Vulgate editions have *lectorem*, “reader.” The manuscripts have *intellectorem*, “interpreter.”].

The same is true of stones, herbs, and whatever is held by roots. Knowledge of the carbuncle, which shines in darkness, illuminates many obscure passages of the books wherever it is used by way of comparison; ignorance of the beryl or diamond often closes the doors of understanding.

Nor is there any other reason why it is easy to understand that perpetual peace is signified by the olive branch that the returning dove carried to the ark (Gen. VIII, 11), except that we know both that the gentle touch of oil is not easily corrupted by another liquid and that the tree itself remains perpetually green.

Because of ignorance of hyssop, however, many people, while not knowing what power it has either for cleansing the lungs or, as is said, for penetrating rocks with its roots, since it is a short and low-growing plant, cannot discover at all why it is said: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Psal. L, 9).

25. Ignorance of numbers also causes many things placed figuratively and mystically in Scripture not to be understood. An ingenuous mind, so to speak, cannot fail to be moved by the question of what is meant by the fact that Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for forty days (Exod. XXIV, 18; III Kings XIX, 8; Matt. IV, 2).

The figurative knot of this action cannot be untied without knowledge and consideration of this number. It contains four times ten, as though the knowledge of all things were woven into the periods of time. For the cycles both of day and of year are completed by the number four: the day by the spaces of morning, midday, evening, and night; the year by the months of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

Because we live in time and desire to live for eternity, we must abstain and fast from delight in temporal things, although the very cycles of time suggest to us the doctrine of despising temporal things and desiring eternal things.

Moreover, the number ten signifies the knowledge of the Creator and of creation. For the Trinity is the Creator, while the number seven indicates creation, because of life and body. In life there are three, which is why God is to be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind (Matt. XXII, 37); in the body four elements are most clearly apparent, of which it consists.

Thus, when this ten is presented to us temporally—that is, when it is multiplied by four—we are warned to live chastely and continently, separated from delight in temporal things: this is what it means to fast for forty days.

The Law, represented by Moses, gives this warning; Prophecy, represented by Elijah, gives it; and the Lord himself gives it. He appeared as though bearing testimony from the Law and the Prophets, shining between them on the mountain in the sight of the three disciples, who saw and were amazed (Matt. XVII, 2–3).

Next, one may ask how the number fifty arises from the number forty—a number that has been especially consecrated in our religion because of Pentecost (Acts II)—and how, when multiplied by three because of the three periods, before the Law, under the Law, and under Grace, or because of the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, with the Trinity itself added in a more eminent way, it is referred to the mystery of the most purified Church and reaches the one hundred and fifty-three fish that the nets cast to the right side caught after the Lord’s resurrection (John XXI, 11).

In this way, many other forms of numbers contain certain hidden comparisons in the sacred books, which remain closed to readers because of their ignorance of numbers.

26. Ignorance of certain musical matters also closes and conceals no small number of things. Through the difference between the psaltery and the lyre, someone has not inelegantly disclosed certain figurative meanings. Among the learned, the ten-stringed psaltery (Psal. XXXII, 2; XCI, 4) is appropriately questioned: does it possess some musical law that requires such a number of strings, or, if it does not, should the number itself be understood as all the more sacred, either because of the Decalogue of the Law—for if anything is asked concerning that number, it must be referred only to the Creator and creation—or because of the ten explained above?

The number of years mentioned in the Gospel for the construction of the temple—forty-six years (John II, 20)—also seems to sound some musical note. Referred to the structure of the Lord’s body, for which the temple was mentioned, it compels some heretics to confess that the Son of God was clothed not falsely but truly in a human body. We find both number and music honorably placed in many passages of the sacred Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XVII—The Origin of the Fable of the Nine Muses

27. We must not listen to the errors of pagan superstitions, which invented the story that the nine Muses were daughters of Jupiter and Memory [Note: [Col. 0049] Two Vatican manuscripts have “of Minerva.” All the others have “of Memory.” The same is found in Book II of *On Order*, chapter 14, §41.].

Varro refutes them; I do not know whether among them anyone could be more learned or more curious about such matters. He says that a certain city—I do not recall its name—commissioned three artists to make three statues of the Muses each, intending to place a gift in the temple of Apollo. It proposed to buy whichever statues each artist had made most beautifully.

It happened that the works of all three artists were equally beautiful, and the city liked all nine and bought all of them, intending to dedicate them in the temple of Apollo. Varro says that the poet Hesiod later supplied them with names.

Jupiter, therefore, did not beget nine Muses; three craftsmen created three each. The city did not commission three sets because it had seen them in a dream, or because so many had appeared before the eyes of any one of the artists. Rather, it was easy to observe that every sound—the material of songs—is naturally threefold. For sound is produced either by the voice, as among those who sing with their throats without an instrument; or by breath, as with trumpets and flutes; or by striking, as with lyres and drums and any other things that become musical when struck.

## CHAPTER XVIII—If Pagans Have Said Anything Good, It Should Not Be Rejected

28. But whether what Varro reported is so or not, we nevertheless ought not to flee music because of the superstition of pagans, if we can seize from it anything useful for understanding the sacred Scriptures. Nor should we turn to their theatrical frivolities if we discuss lyres and instruments in whatever way may be useful for grasping spiritual matters.

We should not refuse to learn letters merely because they say that Mercury was their inventor [Note: [Col. 0049] Almost all manuscripts say, “they say that he was their god.”]. Nor, because they dedicated temples to justice and virtue and preferred to worship in stones what ought to be carried in the heart, should justice and virtue therefore be avoided by us.

Indeed, whoever is a good and true Christian should understand that his Lord’s property belongs wherever he finds truth. By acknowledging and recognizing it, he should also reject superstitious fictions in the sacred Scriptures, and grieve over and guard against those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents (Rom. I, 21 ff.) [Col. 0050].

## CHAPTER XIX—Two Kinds of Learning Found among the Pagans

29. But so that we may explain this entire passage, which is especially necessary, with greater care, there are two kinds of learning practiced even in pagan customs. One concerns things instituted by human beings; the other concerns things they have observed as already accomplished or divinely instituted. That which belongs to human institutions is partly superstitious and partly not.

## CHAPTER XX—Some Learning Instituted by Human Beings Is Full of Superstition; Cato’s Witty Saying
30. Whatever human beings have instituted that pertains to making and worshiping idols, or to worshiping a creature, or any part of a creature, as though it were God, is superstitious; so too are consultations and certain agreements concerning signs, settled and covenanted with demons, such as the devices of magical arts, which poets are accustomed to mention rather than teach. Of this kind are also the books of haruspices and augurs, though they proceed with something like a freer frivolity. To this category belong all amulets and remedies as well, which even medical learning condemns—whether they involve incantations, certain marks called “characters,” or the hanging and tying, or even in some fashion attaching, of various objects—not for regulating the body, but for certain meanings, hidden or even manifest. These they call “natural remedies” (*physica*), by a milder name, so that they may seem not to entangle people in superstition but to benefit them through nature. Such are earrings at the upper part of each ear, little loops made from ostrich bones on the fingers, or the instruction given to someone suffering from hiccups to hold the left thumb with the right hand.

[Note: Codices, both printed and manuscript, read *saltandis quodammodo* (“as if for dancing”), except one Remigian manuscript, on whose authority we restore *aptandis* (“attaching”).]

31. To these are added thousands of utterly empty observations: whether some limb has twitched; whether, while friends are walking together, a stone, dog, or child has come between them; and the belief that stepping on a stone, as though it were a divider of friendship, is less troublesome than striking an innocent child with a slap if he crosses between people walking together. Yet it is amusing when children are sometimes avenged by dogs. For some people are so superstitious that they even dare to strike a dog that has come between them—and not without penalty: for, in consequence of a futile remedy, the animal sometimes quickly sends its striker to a real physician.

Hence also come such practices as stepping over the threshold when passing in front of one’s house; returning to bed if someone sneezes while one is putting on one’s shoes; returning home if one stumbles while setting out; and trembling more at the suspicion of future misfortune when mice have gnawed one’s clothing than grieving over the present damage. Hence that elegant saying of Cato. When someone consulted him, saying that mice had gnawed his boots, he replied that this was not an omen; rather, it would truly have been an omen if mice had been gnawed by boots.

## CHAPTER XXI — The Superstition of Astrologers

32. Nor should those who are called *genethliaci*—because of their consideration of birth-days, but now commonly called “mathematicians”—be separated from this kind of pernicious superstition. For although they pursue, and sometimes even investigate, the true position of the stars at the time each person is born, they nevertheless err greatly when they attempt from this to predict either our actions or the outcomes of our actions, and they sell ignorant people a pitiable slavery. For every free person who enters such an astrologer’s establishment gives money in order to leave as the slave either of Mars, Venus, or rather of all the stars—those stars to which the first people who went astray, and handed their error down to later generations, assigned names either from their resemblance to animals or in order to honor human beings themselves.

It is not surprising that, even in more recent and nearer times, they attempted to dedicate to the honor and name of the Roman Caesar the star that we call Lucifer.

[Note: Thus Virgil, *Eclogue* 9:

> Behold, Caesar’s star, offspring of Dione, has risen.]

And perhaps this would have happened and the name would have passed into antiquity, if his grandmother Venus had not already preempted this estate of a name; nor could he lawfully transfer to his heirs what she had never possessed while alive or sought to possess. For when the place was vacant and was not held by the honor of any earlier dead person, what usually happens in such matters took place. In place of the months Quintilis and Sextilis, we call them July and August, named from the honors of Julius Caesar and Augustus Caesar. Thus anyone who wishes can easily understand that those stars too had previously wandered through heaven without these names. When the people whose memory they were compelled by royal power, or pleased by human vanity, to honor had died, human beings seemed, by assigning their names to the stars, to lift those very dead persons into heaven for themselves.

But whatever names human beings give them, the stars remain things that God established and ordered as he willed; and their movement is fixed, by which times are distinguished and varied. To note what that movement is when someone is born is easy, by means of the rules they have devised and written down—rules that Holy Scripture condemns when it says: “If they were able to know enough to estimate the age of the world, how did they not more easily find its Lord?” (Wisdom 13:9).

## CHAPTER XXII — The Observation of the Stars for Discovering the Course of Life Is Futile

33. But to wish to predict from that observation the character, actions, and fortunes of those being born is a great error and great madness. Indeed, among those who have learned such matters only in order to unlearn them, this superstition is refuted beyond doubt. The “constellations” they call them are a record of the stars—how they stood when the person was born—for whom these wretched people are consulted by people even more wretched.

Now it can happen that some twins are delivered from the womb so closely together that no interval of time can be detected between them or recorded in the numerical calculations of the constellations. Hence some twins must have the same constellations, although the outcomes of the things they do or suffer are not alike, and are often so different that one lives most fortunately while the other lives most unhappily. Thus we are told that Esau and Jacob were born as twins, so that Jacob, who was born later, was found holding with his hand the heel of his brother who preceded him (Genesis 25:25). Their day and hour of birth could certainly not have been recorded differently, except so that the constellation of both would be one. Yet Scripture bears witness to how greatly their characters, deeds, labors, and successes differed—a Scripture already spread throughout the mouths of all nations.

[Note: Three manuscripts read *pervulgata* (“spread abroad”); the printed editions read *pervagata* (“spread throughout”).]

34. It is irrelevant that they say that the smallest and narrowest moment of time separating the birth of twins has great force in nature and in the exceedingly swift motion of the heavenly bodies. For even if I grant that it has very great force, it still cannot be found by the astrologer in the constellations from which, once he has inspected them, he claims to pronounce the fates. Since, therefore, he does not find it in the constellations—which he must inspect as one and the same, whether he is consulted about Jacob or about his brother—what benefit is it to him if something differs in the heavens, which he rashly and confidently slanders, but does not differ in the chart at which he gazes with useless anxiety?

[Note: In all editions printed until now, the reading is: *si discat in coelo . . . . . et non discat in tabula* (“if he learns in heaven . . . and does not learn in the chart”). But the reading *distat* (“differs”) should unquestionably be restored from the manuscripts in both places, since what is being refuted is the astrologers’ chatter that the smallest moment separating the birth of twins has great force amid the rapidity of the heavenly bodies.]

Therefore these opinions too, which are based on certain signs established by human presumption, must be referred to those same supposed agreements and covenants with demons.

## CHAPTER XXIII — Why the Science of Astrologers Must Be Rejected

35. For this is how it comes about that, by a certain hidden divine judgment, people greedy for evil things are handed over, in accordance with the deserts of their desires, to be mocked and deceived by transgressing angels. According to the most beautiful order of things, this lowest region of the world has been subjected to those angels by the law of divine providence.

Through these illusions and deceptions it happens that these superstitious and pernicious kinds of divination tell many things, past and future, and that they occur exactly as foretold. Many things also happen to those who observe them according to their observations; and those entangled in them become more curious and insert themselves ever more deeply into the manifold snares of the most destructive error.

Holy Scripture did not leave this kind of fornication of the soul unmentioned. Nor did it deter the soul from it merely by denying that such things should be pursued because their practitioners speak falsely. Rather, it also says: “Even if they tell you, and it happens in this way, do not believe them” (Deuteronomy 13:1–3).

For it does not follow, because the apparition of the dead Samuel foretold the truth to King Saul (1 Samuel 28:14–20; Sirach 46:23), that the sacrileges by which that apparition was produced are therefore less detestable. Nor, because in the Acts of the Apostles a ventriloquist woman gave true testimony to the Lord’s apostles, did the Apostle Paul spare that spirit rather than cleanse the woman by driving out the demon that possessed her (Acts 16:16–18).

[Note: Three manuscripts read *ventiloqua*; other manuscripts, more correctly, read *ventriloqua*. The Greek is *engastrimythos*, “belly-speaker,” the term by which the woman at Philippi is called, as the woman of Python is called in 1 Samuel 27:7 in the Septuagint. The Septuagint writers use this word frequently. Basil, in his commentary on Isaiah 8:19, interprets the words “consult the ventriloquists” (*zētēsate engastrimythous*) as follows: “That is, those who prophesy future things in Python, possessed through the belly, with the spirit itself speaking, and who also speak from the earth, babbling certain empty things.” Erasmus noted in the margin of his book that even in his own time there was among the Italians a class of diviners so called because, without producing a sound through the mouth, they seemed to speak through the belly.]

36. All arts of this kind, whether belonging to frivolous or harmful superstition, established through a kind of pestilential partnership of human beings and demons—as agreements of an unfaithful and deceitful friendship—must be utterly rejected and shunned by a Christian. “Not that an idol is anything,” says the Apostle, “but because what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God; and I do not want you to become partners with demons” (1 Corinthians 10:19–20).

What the Apostle said about idols and about sacrifices offered in their honor must be understood also of all imaginary signs that draw people either to the worship of idols, or to the worship of a creature and its parts as God, or to the care of remedies and other observances. These practices have not been publicly established by God for the love of God and neighbor; rather, through private desires for temporal things, they scatter the hearts of the wretched.

In all these teachings, therefore, the partnership of demons must be feared and avoided. They attempt nothing with their prince, the devil, except to close and bar our return.

Just as human and deceptive conjectures concerning the stars—which God created and ordered—have been established by human beings, so also many people have committed to writing many conjectures, based on human suspicions as though they were regular predictions, concerning whatever is born or exists in any way under the administration of divine providence, in case unusual events should occur—for example, if a mule should give birth or something should be struck by lightning.

[Note: The printed editions read *conjecta litteris* (“cast into writing”); the manuscripts read *conjectata*, which is the better reading.]

## CHAPTER XXIV — Partnership and Covenant with Demons in the Superstitious Use of Things

37. All these practices have whatever power they possess because, through the presumption of minds, they have been allied with demons by a kind of common language. Yet they are all full of pestilential curiosity, tormenting anxiety, and deadly slavery.

They were not first noticed because they had power; rather, by being noticed and marked, it was brought about that they should have power.

[Note: Five manuscripts read *servando* (“by preserving”) rather than *signando* (“by marking”).]

And therefore they produce different results for different people, according to their thoughts and presumptions. For those spirits who wish to deceive arrange such things for each person in accordance with the suspicions and agreements by which they see that person entangled.

For example, the single figure of the letter X, marked crosswise, means one thing among the Greeks and another among the Latins—not by nature, but by the convention and agreement of signification. Therefore someone who knows both languages, if he wishes to signify something in writing to a Greek, does not use this letter with the meaning it has when he writes to a Latin. Likewise, beta, with one and the same sound, is the name of a letter among the Greeks but the name of a vegetable among the Latins. And when I say *lege* (“read” in Latin), in these two syllables a Greek understands one thing and a Latin another.

Just as all these meanings move people’s minds according to the agreement of each society—and because the agreements differ, they move them differently—so human beings did not agree upon them because they already possessed power as signs; rather, they possess power because human beings agreed upon them. In the same way, those signs through which the destructive partnership of demons is acquired have power according to each person’s observances.

This is demonstrated most clearly by the ritual of augurs. Before they observe, and after they have retained the signs observed, they act so as not to see the birds’ flights or hear their cries, because none of these are signs unless the observer’s agreement is added.

## CHAPTER XXV — Among Human Institutions That Are Not Superstitious, Some Are Superfluous and Others Useful and Necessary

38. Once these things have been cut away and uprooted from the Christian mind, we must next examine human institutions that are not superstitious—that is, institutions established not with demons but with human beings themselves. Everything that has power among human beings because they have agreed among themselves that it should have power is a human institution. Some of these institutions are superfluous and luxurious; others are useful and necessary.

If the signs made by actors through dancing had power by nature rather than by human institution and agreement, an announcer would not, in the earliest times, have declared to the people of Carthage, while a pantomime was dancing, what the dancer intended to signify.

[Note: Pantomimes expressed any gestures and behaviors required of them.]

Many old people still remember this, and we commonly hear it from their reports. It must be believed because even now, if someone inexperienced in such theatrical amusements enters a theater, he is concentrating in vain unless someone else tells him what those movements signify.

Nevertheless, everyone seeks some likeness in signification, so that the signs themselves, insofar as they can, may resemble the things signified. But because something may resemble something else in many ways, such signs do not remain established among human beings unless agreement is added.

39. In paintings, statues, and other artificial works of this kind, especially those produced by skilled craftsmen, no one errs when he sees likenesses and recognizes the things to which they are like. This entire category must be counted among superfluous human institutions, except when it matters what is done, for what reason, where, when, and by whose authority.

Finally, the thousands of invented stories and falsehoods whose lies delight human beings are human institutions. Nothing should be regarded as more distinctively human—things that human beings possess from themselves—than falsehoods and lies of every kind.

Useful and necessary human institutions established among human beings include whatever differences in dress and bodily adornment have been agreed upon for distinguishing the sexes or honors; the countless kinds of signs without which human society either cannot function at all or functions less conveniently; and the conventions proper to each state and people concerning weights and measures and the stamping or valuation of coins. The same applies to other things of this kind. If they were not human institutions, they would not vary among different peoples, nor would they be changed within individual peoples at the discretion of their rulers.

40. But this entire class of human institutions, which contributes to the necessary uses of life, is by no means to be avoided by a Christian. Rather, it should be examined and retained in memory to the extent that is sufficient.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Which Human Institutions Are to Be Avoided and Which Embraced

There are certain human institutions that are shadowy and in some fashion resemble natural things. Those belonging, as has been said, to partnership with demons must be utterly rejected and detested. But those that human beings possess with other human beings should be adopted insofar as they are not luxurious or superfluous—especially the forms of letters, without which we cannot read, and the diversity of languages to the extent that is sufficient, concerning which we discussed above.

Also belonging to this category are shorthand signs (*notae*), and those who have learned them are now properly called notaries. These things are useful; they are not learned illicitly, do not involve superstition, and do not enervate through luxury, provided that they occupy only so much time that they do not obstruct greater matters, for the attainment of which they ought to serve.

## CHAPTER XXVII — Some of the Sciences Not Instituted by Human Beings Assist the Understanding of Scripture

41. Those things which human beings have handed down not by instituting them but by investigating events that have occurred over time or things established by God are not to be considered human institutions, wherever they are learned. Some of these pertain to the bodily senses, others to the reasoning of the mind.

But those things apprehended by the bodily senses we either believe because they have been reported, perceive because they have been demonstrated, or infer because we have experienced them.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — The Extent to Which History Is Helpful

42. Whatever the discipline called history indicates concerning the sequence of past times greatly helps us to understand the holy Books, even if it is learned outside the Church through childish education. We are often asked about many things by reference to Olympiads and the names of consuls.
