Ignorance of the consulship in which the Lord was born and that in which he suffered led some people into error, so that they thought the Lord suffered at the age of forty-six, because the Jews were said to have built the Temple over that many years—a Temple that bore the image of the Lord’s body.

We retain, on evangelical authority, that he was baptized at about thirty years of age (Luke 3:23). But although the number of years he spent in this life afterward can be perceived from the text itself describing his actions, it is nevertheless gathered more clearly and certainly from the history of the nations compared with the Gospel, lest the darkness of doubt arise from another source.

Then it will be seen that it was not said without reason that the Temple was built over forty-six years. Since that number cannot be referred to the Lord’s age, it may be referred to the more secret instruction concerning the human body with which, for our sake, the only Son of God did not disdain to clothe himself—the one through whom all things were made.

43. To say nothing of the Greeks, how great a question our Ambrose resolved concerning the usefulness of history when readers and admirers of Plato slandered him! They dared to say that all the sayings of our Lord Jesus Christ—sayings they are compelled to admire and praise—he had learned from Plato’s books, since it cannot be denied that Plato lived long before the Lord’s human coming.

Did not the aforementioned bishop, when he considered the history of the nations and discovered that Plato had gone to Egypt in the time of Jeremiah, when that prophet was there, show that it was more probable that Plato had instead been imbued through Jeremiah with our Scriptures, so that he could teach or write the things that are rightly praised?

[Note: *Retractations* II, chapter 4, section 2.]

Before the writings of the Hebrew nation—in which the worship of the one God shone forth and from which, according to the flesh, our Lord came—not even Pythagoras existed, from whose followers these men claim that Plato learned his theology. Thus, when the times are considered, it becomes much more believable that these men derived from our Scriptures whatever good and true things they said, rather than that the Lord Jesus Christ derived them from Plato—which it would be utterly insane to believe.

44. When historical narration also recounts past human institutions, history itself should not be counted among human institutions, because things that have already passed away and cannot be made not to have happened must be placed within the order of times, whose creator and administrator is God.

For it is one thing to narrate what has been done and another to teach what ought to be done. History faithfully and usefully narrates deeds; the books of haruspices and writings of similar kinds, however, aim to teach what should be done or observed, with the audacity of an adviser rather than the fidelity of a reporter.

[Note: The printed editions read *judicis* (“of a judge”); the better manuscripts clearly require *indicis* (“of a reporter” or “indicator”).]

## CHAPTER XXIX — The Extent to Which Knowledge of Animals, Plants, and Other Things, Especially the Stars, Contributes to Understanding Scripture

45. There is also a kind of account resembling demonstration, by which present things are indicated to those ignorant of them rather than past things being narrated. This category includes whatever has been written about the location of places and the natures of animals, trees, plants, stones, and other bodies.

We discussed this category above and showed that such knowledge is useful for solving the riddles of Scripture—not so that these things may be employed as certain signs, as remedies or devices of some superstition. For we have already distinguished that category from this lawful and free one.

It is one thing to say, “If you drink this crushed herb, your stomach will not hurt,” and another to say, “If you hang this herb around your neck, your stomach will not hurt.” In the first case, a wholesome physical effect is demonstrated; in the second, a superstitious signification is condemned.

Nevertheless, where there are no incantations, invocations, or characters, it is often uncertain whether the thing that is tied on or in some way attached to the body for healing has power by the force of nature—which may be freely employed—or whether the result arises from some symbolic obligation. A Christian must be the more careful to avoid the latter the more effective it may appear to be.

But where the reason why something has power is hidden, what matters is the intention with which each person uses it, provided that the matter concerns only the healing or regulation of bodies, whether in medicine or agriculture.

46. Knowledge of the stars is not a narrative but a demonstration. Scripture mentions very few of them. Just as the course of the moon is known to very many people and is also solemnly used for the annual celebration of the Lord’s Passion, so the risings, settings, and other occurrences of the remaining stars are known without error to very few people.

Knowledge of these things in itself, although it does not bind one with superstition, nevertheless contributes little or almost nothing to the interpretation of divine Scripture; and, because it occupies the mind with an unproductive purpose, it impedes it more than it helps. Since it is also closely associated with the most pernicious error of those who foolishly chant fates, it is more usefully and honorably disregarded.

Yet besides the demonstration of present things, it also contains something resembling a narration of past things, since from the present position and movement of the stars one may regularly trace back their earlier positions. It also contains regular predictions of future things—not suspicious and ominous predictions, but fixed and certain ones; not so that we may attempt to derive from them anything concerning our own deeds and fortunes, as in the ravings of astrologers, but only insofar as the stars themselves are concerned.

For just as someone who calculates the moon can say, after observing what day it is today, what day it was any number of years ago and what day it will be any number of years from now, so those who skillfully calculate each of the stars customarily give corresponding answers. I have explained what I think about this entire field of knowledge insofar as its use is concerned.

[Note: Bad., Am., Er., and six manuscripts read *in nostra fata* (“into our fortunes”); the principal text has *in nostra facta* (“into our deeds”).]

## CHAPTER XXX — What the Mechanical Arts Contribute to the Same Purpose

47. The other arts, by which something is made—either something that remains after the craftsman’s activity has produced it, such as a house, bench, vessel, or anything of that kind; or arts that provide a kind of service to God at work, such as medicine, agriculture, and navigation; or arts whose entire product is an action, such as dancing, running, and wrestling—all these arts also make it possible to infer future things from past experience. For no practitioner of any of them moves his limbs while working without weaving together the memory of past things with expectation of future things.

Knowledge of these arts should be used lightly and briefly in human life, not for practicing them—unless some duty compels this, which is not our present subject—but for judging, so that we may not be entirely ignorant of what Scripture intends to suggest when it inserts figurative expressions drawn from some of these arts.

## CHAPTER XXXI — The Usefulness of Dialectic: Sophisms

48. There remain those matters that concern not the bodily senses but the reasoning of the mind, where the disciplines of argument and number prevail.

The discipline of argument is of the greatest value for penetrating and resolving every kind of question found in the holy Scriptures. Only the desire to quarrel and a certain childish display of deceiving one’s opponent must be avoided there.

There are many things called sophisms: false conclusions in reasoning, usually imitating the truth so closely that they deceive not only the slow-witted but also the clever when they are insufficiently attentive.

Someone proposed the following to a person with whom he was speaking: “What I am, you are not.” The other agreed, and in part it was true, since one was devious and the other simple. Then the first added: “But I am a human being.” When the other had granted this too, he concluded: “Therefore you are not a human being.”

[Note: Someone used this syllogism against Diogenes, but was caught when Diogenes reversed it and was mocked.]

Scripture, I think, detests this kind of deceitful conclusion where it says: “One who speaks sophistically is hateful” (Sirach 37:23). Yet even speech that is not deceptive may be called sophistic if it pursues verbal ornament more abundantly than dignity permits.

49. There are also true connections of reasoning that contain false propositions, which follow from the error of the person with whom one is dealing. A good and learned person introduces such propositions so that the person whose error they follow will be ashamed and abandon that same error. For if he wishes to remain in it, he will necessarily be compelled to hold even the consequences that he condemns.

The Apostle was not asserting true things when he said, “Neither has Christ been raised,” and then, “Our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty” (1 Corinthians 15:14), followed by other statements that are altogether false. Christ has in fact been raised, and the preaching of those who proclaimed this was not empty, nor was the faith of those who believed it. But these false statements were connected most truly to the proposition that there is no resurrection of the dead.

Once these false statements are rejected, since they would be true if the dead are not raised, the resurrection of the dead follows. Since, therefore, there are true connections not only of true propositions but also of false ones, it is easy to learn the truth of connections even in those schools that exist outside the Church. But the truth of propositions must be sought in the holy ecclesiastical Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XXXII — The Truth of Connections Was Not Instituted by Human Beings but Merely Observed

50. The truth of connections itself was not instituted by human beings; it was noticed and recorded by them so that they might learn or teach it. For it is perpetual in the rational structure of things and was instituted by God.

Just as someone who narrates the sequence of times does not himself compose it; and someone who displays the location of places or the natures of animals, plants, or stones does not display things instituted by human beings; and someone who demonstrates the stars and their movements does not demonstrate something instituted by himself or by any human being—so also the person who says, “When the consequence is false, the antecedent must be false,” speaks most truly. He does not make it so; he merely demonstrates that it is so.

From this rule comes what we mentioned concerning the Apostle Paul. The claim that there is no resurrection of the dead comes first; this was asserted by those whose error the Apostle wished to destroy. The proposition “Christ has not been raised” necessarily follows from that preceding proposition, “There is no resurrection of the dead.” But the consequent is false, for Christ has been raised. Therefore the antecedent is also false. The antecedent is “There is no resurrection of the dead”; therefore there is a resurrection of the dead.

The whole argument is stated briefly as follows: “If there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised. But Christ has been raised; therefore there is a resurrection of the dead.”

Human beings did not institute this rule—that when the consequent is removed, the antecedent must also necessarily be removed. They demonstrated it. This rule concerns the truth of connections, not the truth of propositions.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — True Conclusions Can Be Drawn from False Propositions, and False Conclusions from True Ones

51. In the case of the resurrection, both the rule of connection is true and the proposition in the conclusion is itself true. But the truth of a connection involving false propositions is as follows.

Let us suppose that someone has granted: “If an animal is a snail, it has a voice.” Once this has been granted, and once it has been established that a snail has no voice, then, because removal of the consequent removes the antecedent, the conclusion follows that there is no animal that is a snail. That proposition is false, but the connection of the conclusion is true because it follows from a false proposition that was granted.

The truth of a proposition therefore has validity in itself; the truth of a connection depends upon the opinion or concession of the person with whom one is dealing. As we said above, a false conclusion is introduced through a true connection so that the person whose error we wish to correct will regret having granted the antecedent, whose consequence he sees must be rejected.

It is now easy to understand that, just as true conclusions can be drawn from false propositions, so false conclusions can be drawn from true propositions. Suppose someone proposes: “If that man is just, he is good,” and this is granted. Then he assumes: “But he is not just,” and this too is granted; finally he draws the conclusion: “Therefore he is not good.”

Although all these propositions may be true, the rule of the conclusion is nevertheless not true. For just as removing the consequent necessarily removes the antecedent, removing the antecedent does not likewise necessarily remove the consequent. It is true to say, “If he is an orator, he is a human being.” But if we assume, “He is not an orator,” it does not follow that we may conclude, “Therefore he is not a human being.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV — Knowing the Laws of Conclusions Is One Thing; Knowing the Truth of Propositions Is Another

52. Accordingly, knowing the rules of connections is one thing, and knowing the truth of propositions is another. In the former one learns what follows, what does not follow, and what is incompatible.

An example of a consequence is: “If he is an orator, he is a human being.”

An example of a non-consequence is: “If he is a human being, he is an orator.”

An example of an incompatibility is: “If he is a human being, he is a quadruped.”

Here, therefore, the connection itself is being judged. In the truth of propositions, however, the propositions themselves must be considered in their own right, not their connection. But when true and certain propositions are joined by a true connection to uncertain propositions, the latter too must necessarily become certain.

Some people boast when they have learned the truth of connections, as though that were the truth of propositions itself. Others, meanwhile, often retain a true proposition but despise themselves because they do not know the laws of conclusions. Yet the person who knows that there is a resurrection of the dead is better than the one who knows that it follows that, if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised.

## CHAPTER XXXV — The Science of Defining and Dividing Is Not False Even When Applied to False Things: What Is False

53. Likewise, although the science of defining, dividing, and partitioning is often applied to false things, it is not itself false. Nor was it instituted by human beings; it was discovered in the rational structure of things.

The fact that poets have been accustomed to apply it to their fables, false philosophers or heretics—that is, false Christians—to the opinions of their error, does not make it false. It remains true that, in defining, dividing, or partitioning, one must not include anything that does not pertain to the matter itself, nor omit anything that does pertain to it. This is true even when the things being defined or distributed are not themselves true.

For falsehood itself can be defined when we say that falsehood is the signification of a thing that is not as it is signified, or is otherwise than it is represented. This definition is true, although falsehood itself cannot be true.

We can also divide falsehood, saying that there are two kinds of false things: those that cannot exist at all, and those that do not exist although they could exist. Someone who says that seven and three are eleven says something that cannot exist at all. Someone who says that it rained on the Kalends of January, although this did not happen, nevertheless says something that could have happened.

The definition and division of false things can therefore be entirely true, although false things themselves are certainly not true.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — The Rules of Eloquence Are True Even Though Falsehoods Are Sometimes Persuaded by Means of Them

54. There are also certain rules of more extensive argument, which is now called eloquence. These too are true, although falsehoods can sometimes be made persuasive through them. But because truths can also be made persuasive, the faculty itself is not blameworthy; the fault lies in the perversity of those who use it badly.

Nor was it instituted by human beings that an expression of charity should win over an audience, or that a brief and clear account should easily convey what one intends, or that variety should hold the attention without producing weariness, or that other observations of this kind should have their effects. Whether used in false or true cases, these rules are nevertheless true insofar as they cause something to be known or believed, or move the mind to seek or avoid something. They were discovered because things are so, rather than instituted so that they would be so.

[Note: The printed editions read *veritatis expressio* (“an expression of truth”). Eighteen manuscripts read *charitatis* (“an expression of charity”).]

## CHAPTER XXXVII — The Usefulness of Rhetoric and Dialectic
55. But this branch, when learned, should be employed more for expressing what has been understood than for understanding. [Note: One manuscript reads “this art.” Shortly afterward Bad., Am., Er., and nine manuscripts read “when it is learned”; ten other codices, “when it is said”; Lov., “when it is discussed.”] The branch of conclusions, definitions, and divisions, however, greatly assists understanding—provided only that the error is absent by which people seem to themselves to have learned the truth of the blessed life once they have learned these things. Although it generally happens that people more easily attain the things for whose attainment these disciplines are learned than they master the extremely intricate and thorny principles of such instruction.

It is as if someone wishing to give instructions for walking should warn that one must not lift the rear foot until one has put down the front foot, and then describe in minute detail how the joints of the ankles and knees ought to be moved. For he speaks truly, and one cannot walk otherwise; but people walk more easily by doing these things than they notice them while doing them, or understand them when they hear them. Those who cannot walk are much less concerned with matters they cannot attend to even through experience.

So, generally, an intelligent person sees more quickly that a conclusion is invalid than he grasps its rules; a slow person does not see that, and understands still less what is prescribed concerning it. In all these matters, the spectacles of truth themselves often give more pleasure than they help us in arguing or judging—unless, perhaps, they render minds more practiced without making them more malicious or conceited: that is, unless those who have learned these things become enamored of deceiving others by plausible speech and questions, or think they have attained something great by which they may place themselves above the good and innocent.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — The science of numbers was discovered by human beings, not instituted by them, but arises from the nature of things.

56. Now it is clear even to the slowest person that the discipline of numbers was not instituted by human beings but rather investigated and discovered. For it is not as Virgil wished the first syllable of *Italia* to be, when the ancients pronounced it short and it became long, so that anyone can make it happen, whenever he wishes, that three times three should not be nine, or that they should not be capable of producing a square figure, or that they should not be three times the number three, one and a half times the number six, and twice no number, because intelligible numbers do not have a half.

Whether numbers are considered in themselves, therefore, or are applied to the laws of figures, sounds, or other movements, they possess immutable rules. These rules were not instituted in any way by human beings, but discovered through the acumen of the intelligent.

57. Yet whoever loves all these things so much that he wishes to boast of them among the unlearned, rather than seek the source of truths that he has merely perceived to be true, and the source of certain things that are not only true but also immutable, whose immutability he has comprehended; and whoever, proceeding in this way from the appearance of bodies to the human mind, finds that the mind itself is mutable—now learned, now unlearned—yet is situated between the immutable truth above it and all other mutable things below it, and turns everything toward the praise and love of the one God, from whom he knows that everything exists: such a person may appear learned, but in no way is he wise.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — To which of the disciplines noted above, and with what disposition, one should devote oneself. Human laws.

58. For this reason, it seems to me salutarily prescribed for diligent and talented young people who fear God and seek the blessed life that they should not dare confidently to follow, as a means of attaining the blessed life, any doctrines practiced outside the Church of Christ, but should judge them soberly and carefully. If they find any doctrines instituted by human beings, varying because of the differing wishes of their institutors, and unknown because of the suspicions of those who err—especially if they also involve a pact with demons through certain agreements and covenants resembling signs—they should wholly reject and detest them. They should also withdraw their diligence from the superfluous and luxurious institutions of human beings.

They should not, however, neglect those human institutions that contribute to the society of people living together [Note: Er. and Lov. read “people coming together”; Bad., Am., and the manuscripts read “people living together.”], since these are necessary for the present life. In the other doctrines found among the nations, apart from history—whether of past or present events pertaining to the bodily senses, to which the experiments and conjectures of useful bodily arts are also to be reckoned—and apart from the principles of argument and number, I believe that nothing useful is found. In all these matters one must observe:

> Nothing in excess (*Ne quid nimis*; Terence, *Andria*, act 1, scene 1),

especially in those matters that concern the bodily senses, unfold in time, and are contained in places.

59. Just as certain people have separately interpreted all the Hebrew, Syriac, Egyptian, and other words that may be found in the holy Scriptures and that have been placed there without interpretation; and just as Eusebius did this with the history of time because of the questions concerning the divine Books that require its use—so, what these people did concerning such matters, so that a Christian need not labor over many things for the sake of a few, could, as I see it, also be done if one of those capable of doing so took pleasure in devoting a kindly service to the benefit of his brothers: namely, by arranging by category whatever places on earth, animals, herbs, trees, stones, metals, and whatever kinds of things the Scripture mentions, and committing to writing only an exposition of them.

This could also be done with numbers, so that an account would be written only of those numbers mentioned by divine Scripture. Perhaps some or all of these works have already been produced, just as we have found many things worked out and written by good and learned Christians that we had not supposed existed [Note: Nineteen manuscripts read thus. The printed editions have: “And written, we suppose, not discovered.”]; but whether because of the negligence of the multitude or because of the concealment practiced by the envious, they remain hidden.

Whether this can be done with the principles of argument, I do not know. It seems to me that it cannot, because these principles are linked throughout the entire text of Scripture like sinews; and therefore they help readers more in resolving and explaining ambiguities, about which we shall speak later, than in learning unknown signs, which is the subject now under discussion.

## CHAPTER XL — Whatever has been said correctly by the pagans is to be converted to our use.

60. As for the philosophers, if they have perhaps said anything true and suited to our faith—especially the Platonists—not only need we have no fear of them, but we must also claim such things for our use from them as from unjust possessors.

For just as the Egyptians possessed not only idols and heavy burdens that the people of Israel were to detest and flee, but also vessels and ornaments of gold and silver, and clothing, which that people, when leaving Egypt, secretly claimed for themselves as suited to a better use—not by their own authority, but at God’s command, while the Egyptians unknowingly lent them the things they were not using well (Exod. 3:22; 12:35)—so the teachings of all the nations contain not only fabricated and superstitious notions and burdens of unnecessary labor, which each of us, leaving the society of the nations under Christ’s guidance, must abominate and avoid, but also liberal disciplines more suited to the use of truth, and certain extremely useful moral precepts. They contain, moreover, some truths concerning the worship of the one God.

These things, like their gold and silver—which they did not themselves create, but extracted, as it were, from certain veins of divine providence spread everywhere—and which they perversely and wrongfully abuse in the service of demons, the Christian, when separating himself in spirit from their wretched society, ought to take from them for the just use of preaching the Gospel. Their clothing also—that is, human institutions, indeed, but nevertheless adapted to human society, without which we cannot live in this life—may be received, retained, and converted to Christian use.

61. For what else have many of our good and faithful people done? Do we not see how laden with gold, silver, and clothing Cyprian, that most gracious teacher and most blessed martyr, came out of Egypt? How much Lactantius? How much Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary—to say nothing of the living? How much the innumerable Greeks?

The most faithful servant of God, Moses himself, had done this earlier; it is written of him that he had been educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22). The superstitious practice of the nations—and especially in those times when, shaking off Christ’s yoke, it persecuted Christians—would never have lent the disciplines it possessed that were useful, if it had suspected that they would be converted to the worship of the one God, by which the empty cult of idols would be destroyed.

But they gave their gold, silver, and clothing to the people of God as they left Egypt, not knowing how the things they gave would contribute to Christ’s service. What happened in Exodus is undoubtedly a figure, prefiguring this; I say this without prejudice to another, equal, or better interpretation.

## CHAPTER XLI — What sort of soul the study of Holy Scripture requires. The properties of hyssop.

[Col. 0064]

62. But the student of the divine Scriptures, instructed in this way, when he begins to approach them for careful examination, should never cease to ponder the apostolic saying: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1).

For he will understand that, although he may come out rich from Egypt, nevertheless, unless he has celebrated Passover, he cannot be safe. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (ibid., 5:7), and nothing does Christ’s sacrifice teach us more than what he himself cries out, as though addressing those whom he sees laboring in Egypt under Pharaoh:

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:28–30).

To whom does this apply, if not to the gentle and humble in heart—those whom knowledge does not puff up, but love builds up?

Let them therefore remember those who at that time celebrated Passover symbolically under the shadow of images [Note: Bad., Am., and Er. read “under an imaginary shadow.”], when they were commanded to mark the doorposts with the blood of a lamb: the doorposts were marked with hyssop (Exod. 12:22).

This herb is gentle and humble, yet nothing is stronger or more penetrating than its roots. Thus, being rooted and grounded in love, we may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth—that is, the cross of the Lord.

Its breadth is represented by the transverse wood on which the hands are extended; its length, from the ground up to that breadth, where the entire body is fastened from the hands downward; its height, from the breadth upward to the top, to which the head is attached [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and most manuscripts read: “to the top, to which the head is attached.”]; and its depth is what is hidden, fixed in the earth.

By the sign of the cross every Christian action is represented: to do good in Christ and remain steadfastly attached to him; to hope for heavenly things; and not to profane the sacraments [Note: It seems that *propalare*, “to disclose,” should be read, so that the analogy with the preceding words may stand: “But the depth is what is fixed in the earth and represents the hidden mystery.” Thus also in Letter 55 to Januarius, chapter 14, section 25, where Augustine likewise transfers the parts of the Lord’s cross—and the same passage from the Apostle in Ephesians 3—to Christian conduct: “The depth,” he says, “prefigures the secret of the sacrament, which is fixed in the earth.”].

Through this action, once purified, we shall also be able to know “the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” [Note: The editions read: “the knowledge of the love of Christ that surpasses [knowledge].” But many manuscripts, and those of better quality, read: “the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.”], who is equal to the Father, through whom all things were made, so that we may be filled unto all the fullness of God (Eph. 3:17–19).

There is also a purifying power in hyssop, so that, when knowledge puffs us up because of the riches taken from Egypt, our swollen lungs may not proudly breathe out some arrogance:

> “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; you shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. You shall make me hear joy and gladness.”

Then, continuing, he connects this with the demonstration that hyssop signifies purification from pride:

> “And the humbled bones shall rejoice” (Ps. 50:9–10).

## CHAPTER XLII — Comparison of Holy Scripture with profane learning.

63. As much less is the abundance of gold, silver, and clothing that the people carried away with them from Egypt [Col. 0065] in comparison with the riches they later acquired at Jerusalem—riches displayed especially in King Solomon (3 Kings 10:14–23)—so all learning gathered from the books of the nations becomes of little account when compared with the knowledge of the divine Scriptures.

For whatever a person has learned outside them, if it is harmful, is condemned there; if it is useful, it is found there. And when someone has found there everything useful that he has learned elsewhere, he will find there, much more abundantly, those things that are learned nowhere else at all, but only in the wondrous depth and wondrous humility of those Scriptures.

[Col. 0066] Equipped, therefore, with this instruction, when unknown signs no longer impede him, let the reader approach the ambiguous signs in Scripture for consideration and investigation—gentle and humble in heart, gently subjected to Christ, burdened with a light load, grounded, rooted, and built up in love, whom [Note: The editions read: “in love, which knowledge may puff up.” Most manuscripts read: “whom knowledge cannot puff up.”] knowledge cannot puff up. Of these matters I shall now undertake to speak in the third volume, if the Lord grants it.

# BOOK THREE.

[Col. 0065]

Having dealt in the preceding book with the removal of ignorance concerning signs, the holy Doctor now proceeds to consider ambiguity, which occurs both in proper and in figurative signs. In proper signs, ambiguity arises from the punctuation of words, their pronunciation, and their uncertain meaning. He shows that this kind of ambiguity can be resolved from the context of the speech, by comparison of translators, or by examining the language from which the Scripture was translated. In figurative signs, ambiguity occurs when the expression itself is not used in Scripture according to the literal sense of the words. On this subject he argues at greater length and gives rules by which one may discern whether an expression is figurative and, if it is figurative, how it ought to be explained. Finally, he examines individually the seven rules of Tichonius.

## CHAPTER I — Summary of the preceding books and the aim of what follows.

1. A person who fears God diligently seeks his will in the holy Scriptures. To avoid loving quarrels, he should be gentle through piety; he should also be fortified by knowledge of languages, so that he does not become stuck on unfamiliar words and expressions; and he should be fortified by knowledge of certain necessary things, so that he does not remain ignorant of the force or nature of things employed by way of likeness. With the assistance also of the textual accuracy of the manuscripts, secured by painstaking care in correction, he should come thus equipped to examine and resolve the ambiguities of Scripture.

To prevent him from being deceived by ambiguous signs, insofar as we are able to instruct him [Note: The Remigius, Theoderic, and Cistercian manuscripts add here: “With the Lord’s help, all our effort has been to demonstrate these things.” The Floriacensis inserts the single word *explicabo*, “I shall explain”; both are inept glosses.], it may happen that he laughs at the methods we wish to show him as childish, either because of the greatness of his intellect or because of the brightness of a greater illumination.

Nevertheless, to repeat what I had begun to say: insofar as he can be instructed by us—and he should know that he can be instructed by us if he is in the kind of spiritual condition that makes this possible—Scriptural ambiguity is either in proper words or in figurative ones. We demonstrated these kinds in the second book.

## CHAPTER II — How ambiguity arising from the division of words is to be removed.

2. When proper words make Scripture ambiguous, one must first see whether we have divided or pronounced them incorrectly. When attentive consideration has made it clear that there is uncertainty about how the words should be divided or pronounced, one should consult the rule of faith, which has been received from the clearer passages of Scripture and from the authority of the Church. We dealt sufficiently with this when speaking about things in the first book.

But if both divisions—or all of them, if there are several—produce a meaning consistent with the faith, the text of the speech itself must then be consulted, examining the preceding and following passages that have placed the ambiguity in the middle, so that we may see which of the several apparent meanings it supports and allows to be woven into itself.

3. Consider examples now. The heretical division, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was,” so that the meaning becomes, “This Word was in the beginning with God,” refuses to confess that the Word is God.

But this must be refuted by the rule of faith, which prescribes for us, concerning the equality of the Trinity, that we say, “And the Word was God,” and then add, “This was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2).

4. Another ambiguity of division does not resist the faith on either side and must therefore be judged by the text itself, where the Apostle says:

> “And what I shall choose I do not know; I am compelled by the two: having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23–24).

For it is uncertain whether “having the desire” is to be joined with “to depart and to be with Christ,” or whether “I am compelled by the two” is to be followed by “having the desire to depart and to be with Christ.”

But since the sentence continues, “for that is much better,” it is clear that he says he has a desire for the better of these options: although compelled by two alternatives, he has a desire for one and a necessity for the other—the desire to be with Christ, and the necessity of remaining in the flesh.

This ambiguity is settled by the one following word *enim*, “for.” Translators who removed this particle were led instead to the interpretation that he appeared not only to be compelled by two alternatives, but also to have a desire for both.

The passage should therefore be divided as follows: “And what I shall choose I do not know; but I am compelled by the two.” This division is followed by: “having the desire to depart and to be with Christ.” And as though someone asked why he has a desire for this particular alternative, he says: “for that is much better.”

Why, then, is he compelled by the two? Because there is a necessity of remaining, which he adds in these words: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.”

5. When ambiguity can be explained neither by the rule of faith nor by the text of the speech itself, there is no harm in dividing the words according to any of the meanings that present themselves.

For example, there is the passage addressed to the Corinthians:

> “Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. Receive us. We have wronged no one” (2 Cor. 7:1–2).

It is uncertain whether the meaning is, “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit,” in accordance with the passage, “that she may be holy both in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7:34); or whether it is, “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of the flesh,” with another meaning following: “and, perfecting holiness in the fear of God, receive us.”

Such ambiguities of division, therefore, lie within the reader’s discretion.

## CHAPTER III — How ambiguity arising from pronunciation is resolved. The difference between inquiry and interrogation.

6. Whatever we have said about ambiguous divisions must also be observed with ambiguous pronunciations. Unless these too are corrupted by the reader’s excessive negligence, they are corrected either by the rules of faith, or by the connection of the preceding and following speech. If neither of these is applied for correction, they nevertheless remain uncertain, so that whichever way the reader pronounces them, he is not at fault.

Unless faith recalls us—for we believe that God will not bring an accusation against his elect, and that Christ will not condemn his elect—the passage may be pronounced in this way:

> “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?”

Then the following words would be taken as the answer:

> “God, who justifies.”

Again, the question would be asked:

> “Who is the one who condemns?”

And the answer would be:

> “Christ Jesus, who died.”

Since it would be utterly foolish to believe this, the passage should be pronounced so that an inquiry precedes and an interrogation follows.

The ancients said that an inquiry and an interrogation differ in this respect: many answers may be given to an inquiry, but to an interrogation the answer is either “No” or “Yes.”

It should therefore be pronounced so that, after the inquiry, “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” the following words, “God, who justifies,” are spoken in the tone of an interrogator, so that the unspoken answer is “No.” Likewise, we should ask, “Who is the one who condemns?” and then again question the words, “Christ Jesus, who died—rather, who also rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:33–34), so that everywhere the unspoken answer is “No.”

But in the passage where he says:

> “What then shall we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness” (Rom. 9:30),

unless the words “That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness” are supplied as the answer after the inquiry “What then shall we say?”, the following text will not cohere.

However one pronounces what Nathanael said, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” (John 1:46)—whether as an affirmation, so that only the words “From Nazareth?” belong to the question, or with the whole sentence as a doubtful question—I do not see how the distinction can be made. Neither meaning, however, impedes the faith.

7. There is also ambiguity in the uncertain sound of syllables, and this certainly pertains to pronunciation. For in the words written, “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret” (Ps. 138:15), it is not clear to the reader whether *os* should be pronounced with a shortened vowel or a lengthened one.

If the vowel is shortened, the word is understood from the term for “bone”; if lengthened, it is understood from the term for “mouth,” and represents the singular number. Such matters, however, are settled by examining the earlier language: for in Greek the word is not *stóma* (στόμα), “mouth,” but *ostéon* (ὀστέον), “bone.”

Hence ordinary speech is often more useful for making things understood than literary correctness. I would rather have someone say, with a barbarism, “My bone was not hidden from you,” than have the meaning be less clear because the expression is more Latin.

Sometimes, however, the uncertain sound of a syllable is settled by a neighboring word belonging to the same meaning, as in the Apostle’s words:

> “The things I proclaim to you, as I have already proclaimed, are these: those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21).

If he had said only, “The things I proclaim to you,” and had not added “as I have already proclaimed,” we would have had to return to the manuscript of the earlier language to discover whether the middle syllable in *praedico*, “I proclaim,” should be lengthened or shortened. But now it is clear that it should be lengthened: he does not say, “as I have proclaimed” (*praedicavi*), but “as I have already declared” (*praedixi*).

## CHAPTER IV — How ambiguity of expression is resolved.

8. Not only these ambiguities, but also those that do not pertain to division or pronunciation, must be considered in a similar way. Such is the passage addressed to the Thessalonians:

> “Therefore we were comforted, brothers, in you” (1 Thess. 3:7).

It is uncertain whether the meaning is “Therefore, O brothers,” or “Therefore, these brothers.” Neither meaning is contrary to the faith. But the Greek language does not have these cases in the same form, and therefore, by examining it, the expression is recognized as a vocative: “O brothers.”

If the translator had wished to say, “Therefore we received consolation, brothers, in you,” he would have adhered less closely to the words, but there would have been less uncertainty about the meaning. Or certainly, if he had added *nostri*, “our,” scarcely anyone would doubt that the case was vocative upon hearing, “Therefore we were comforted, our brothers, in you.”

But this is permitted with greater danger. Thus it happened in the passage addressed to the Corinthians, when the Apostle says:

> “I die daily, by your glory, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 15:31).

One translator rendered it, “I die daily; by your glory I swear,” because in Greek the oath-word *nē* (νή) is clear and has no ambiguous sound.

Thus, as far as the books of the divine Scriptures are concerned, ambiguity in proper words is found only very rarely and with great difficulty when it cannot be resolved either by the surrounding speech itself, through which the writer’s intention is recognized, by comparison of translators, or by examination of the earlier language.

## CHAPTER V — To take the figurative expressions of Scripture literally is a wretched slavery.

9. But the ambiguities of figurative words, which must be discussed next, require no small care and diligence. For at the outset one must beware of accepting a figurative expression literally. This is also the point of the Apostle’s statement:

> “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

When something said figuratively is accepted as though it had been said literally, one reasons carnally. No death of the soul can more appropriately be called death than when what distinguishes the soul from beasts—namely, understanding—is subjected to the flesh by following the letter.

For someone who follows the letter treats figurative words as though they were proper words, and does not refer what is signified by the proper word to another meaning. If, for example, he hears “Sabbath,” he understands nothing except one of the seven days that recur in continuous succession. When he hears “sacrifice,” he does not go beyond the thought of what is usually performed with animal victims and earthly fruits.

This, then, is the wretched slavery of the soul: to take signs for things, and to be unable to raise the eye of the mind above bodily creation in order to drink in eternal light.

## CHAPTER VI — The servitude of the Jews under useful signs.

10. Yet this slavery differed greatly among the Jewish people from the custom of the other nations [Note: An old Corbie manuscript reads “death” instead of “custom.”]. They were so subjected to temporal things that one God alone was commended to them in everything.

Although they observed the signs of spiritual things in place of the things themselves, not knowing what they referred to, they nevertheless had this implanted in them: that through such slavery they pleased the one God of all, whom they did not see. The Apostle writes that this guardianship existed “under a tutor,” like that of children (Gal. 3:24).

Therefore, when the time of their revelation had come, those who obstinately clung to such signs could not endure the Lord’s contempt for them (Matt. 12:2). Their leaders consequently contrived accusations because he healed on the Sabbath (Luke 6:7). The people, bound to those signs as though they were the things themselves, did not believe that the one who was unwilling to observe them as the Jews observed them was God or had come from God.

But those who believed—and from them the first Church at Jerusalem was formed—clearly demonstrated how beneficial it had been to be kept under a tutor in that manner: the signs imposed temporarily upon servants bound the minds of those who observed them to the worship of the one God who made heaven and earth.

For they were near to spiritual things—for in their temporal and carnal vows [Note: Am. reads *vocis*, “of the voice,” for which Erasmus unhappily substituted *vocibus*, “voices.” Bad. and the manuscripts, with broad agreement, read *votis*, that is, “offerings”—and signs, although they did not know how these were to be understood spiritually, they had nevertheless learned to venerate the eternal God. They therefore became so receptive to the Holy Spirit that they sold all their possessions and laid the proceeds at the feet of the Apostles to be distributed to those in need (Acts 4:34). They dedicated themselves wholly to God as a new temple, whose earthly image—that is, the old temple—they had served.

11. It is not written that any Gentile churches did this, because among them those who possessed handmade images as gods were not found so near to spiritual things.

## CHAPTER VII — The servitude of the nations under useless signs.

[Col. 0070]

And if some of them occasionally attempted to interpret those things as signs, they referred them to the worship and veneration of a creature.

For what benefit is it to me, for example, that the image of Neptune should be understood not as Neptune himself, but as signifying the whole sea, or even all the other waters that gush forth from springs? One of their poets describes him, if I remember correctly, saying:

> “You, Father Neptune, whose gray temples, encircled  
> by the resounding sea, roar; from whose perpetual chin  
> the great ocean flows, and rivers wander through your hair.”

This pod shaken with rattling pebbles within a sweet covering is not human food but food for pigs. Whoever knows the Gospel knows what I mean (Luke 15:16).

What benefit, then, is it to me that the image of Neptune is referred to that meaning, unless perhaps it is so that I worship neither one? Any statue is no more God to me than the whole sea is God.

I admit, nevertheless, that those who think human works are gods are more deeply sunk than those who think God’s works are gods. But we are commanded to love and worship the one God (Deut. 6:5), who made all these things whose images they venerate, whether as gods or as signs and images of gods.

If, therefore, to follow a usefully instituted sign as though it were the thing itself, for signifying which it was instituted, is carnal slavery, how much more is it slavery to take signs instituted for useless things as though they were the things themselves? Even if you refer them to the things signified by them and bind your mind to their worship, you will still not escape the servile and carnal burden and veil.

## CHAPTER VIII — The Jews and the Gentiles were liberated from the slavery of signs in different ways.

12. Therefore Christian freedom, finding those who were under useful signs as though they were near at hand, liberated them by interpreting the signs to which they had been subjected and raising them to the things of which those signs were signs. From these people the churches of the holy Israelites were formed.

But those whom it found under useless signs it freed not only from servile activity under such signs, but also from the signs themselves: it removed them all. Thus the Gentiles could be converted from the corruption of the multitude of false gods—which Scripture often and properly calls fornication—to the worship of the one God. They would no longer be enslaved even under useful signs, but would rather exercise their minds in understanding them spiritually.

## CHAPTER IX — Who is oppressed by the slavery of signs and who is not. Baptism. The Eucharist.

13. A person is enslaved under a sign when he performs or venerates some signifying thing without knowing what it signifies. But someone who performs or venerates a useful sign instituted by God, and understands its power and meaning, does not venerate what is seen and passes away, but rather that to which all such things are to be referred.

Such a person is spiritual and free even during the time of slavery, when those signs ought not yet to be revealed to carnal minds, which must be subdued beneath their yoke. Such were the Patriarchs and Prophets, and all in the people of Israel through whom the Holy Spirit supplied us with both the aids and the consolations of the Scriptures.

But now, after the resurrection of our Lord has made the clear sign of our freedom shine forth, we are not burdened by the performance even of those signs that we already understand. Instead, the Lord and the apostolic discipline have handed down a few signs in place of many—signs extremely easy to perform, sublime in their meaning, and most pure in their observance—such as the sacrament of Baptism and the celebration of the Lord’s body and blood.

When each person receives these, instructed in what they signify, he recognizes their meaning, so that he venerates them not with carnal slavery but rather with spiritual freedom.

Just as it is the weakness of a slave to follow the letter and take signs for the things they signify, so it is the error of someone wandering badly to interpret signs uselessly. Whoever does not understand what a sign signifies, yet understands that it is a sign, is not himself oppressed by slavery.

It is better to be oppressed by unknown but useful signs than, by interpreting them uselessly, to insert a neck brought out from under the yoke of slavery into the snares of error.

## CHAPTER X — How one may discern whether an expression is figurative. The general rule. Love. Desire. Sin. Crime. Usefulness. Beneficence.

14. To this practice—by which we take care not to follow a figurative, that is, a transferred, expression as though it were proper—another must also be added: we must not wish to take a proper expression as though it were figurative.

First, therefore, the method by which one discovers whether an expression is proper or figurative must be demonstrated. The method is altogether this: whatever in divine speech cannot be properly referred either to moral uprightness or to the truth of faith, you should recognize as figurative.

Moral uprightness pertains to loving God and one’s neighbor; the truth of faith pertains to knowing God and one’s neighbor. Each person’s hope lies in his own conscience, according to how he perceives himself to be progressing in love of God and neighbor and in knowledge of them. These matters were discussed in the first book.

15. But since it is easy for the human race to judge sins not by the impulses of lust themselves, but rather by its own customs, it generally happens that people consider only those things blameworthy which the people of their own region and time are accustomed to censure and condemn; and approve and praise only those things which the custom of those with whom they live permits. Consequently, if Scripture either commands something that conflicts with the custom of its hearers, or condemns something that does not conflict with it, they suppose it to be figurative speech—provided that the authority of the word has already bound their minds. Scripture, however, commands nothing except charity, and condemns nothing except lust; and in this way it forms human conduct. Likewise, if an opinion based on some error has already taken possession of the mind, people consider figurative whatever Scripture asserts differently. Scripture, however, asserts only the catholic faith, concerning past, future, and present things. It narrates past events, foretells future ones, and demonstrates present ones; but all these serve to nourish and strengthen the same [Col. 0072] charity and to conquer and extinguish lust.

16. By “charity” I mean the movement of the soul toward enjoying God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake; by “lust,” the movement of the soul toward enjoying oneself, one’s neighbor, or any bodily thing not for God’s sake. What untamed lust does to corrupt its own soul and body is called an outrage; what it does in order to harm another is called a crime. These are the two classes of all sins, but outrages come first. When they have emptied the soul and brought it to a kind of poverty, one rushes into crimes, either to remove obstacles to outrages or to seek aids for them. Likewise, what charity does for its own benefit is usefulness; what it does in order to benefit one’s neighbor is called benevolence. Usefulness comes first here too, since no one can benefit another from what he does not possess. The more the kingdom of lust is destroyed, the more charity grows.

### CHAPTER XI — Rule concerning passages that have the flavor of cruelty but are nevertheless related as spoken by God or by the saints

17. Whatever harsh or seemingly cruel thing is read in the holy Scriptures as spoken by God or by his saints serves to destroy the kingdom of lust. If it sounds plainly as such, it should not be referred to something else on the assumption that it was spoken figuratively. Such is the Apostle’s statement:

“You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each according to his works: eternal life to those who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory and honor and incorruption; but wrath and indignation to those who are contentious and disbelieve the truth but believe in iniquity. Tribulation and distress upon every human soul that works evil, upon the Jew first and also the Greek” (Romans 2:5–9).

But this applies to those in whom lust itself is overthrown—those who were unwilling to conquer it. When the kingdoms of lust are subverted in a person whom it had dominated, the language is plain:

“But those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified their flesh with its passions” (Galatians 5:24).

[Note: [Col. 0072] The printed editions have *vitiis* (“vices”), whereas the manuscripts have *passionibus* (“passions”). Augustine regularly renders the Greek *tois pathêmasi* by this word.]

Unless, indeed, certain words here too are used metaphorically, such as “the wrath of God” and “they crucified”; but there are not so many of them, nor are they arranged in such a way as to conceal the meaning and create an allegory or enigma of the sort that I properly call figurative speech. When Jeremiah is told, “Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, to destroy, to ruin, and to overthrow” (Jeremiah 1:10), there is no doubt that the whole passage is figurative speech, to be referred to the end we have mentioned.

### CHAPTER XII — Rule concerning statements and actions that seem outrageous to the judgment of the unlearned and are attributed to God or to holy men; actions are judged by their circumstances

18. Whatever seems outrageous to the unlearned, whether it consists only of words or also of actions, when it is spoken or done by God [Col. 0073] or by people whose holiness is commended to us, is wholly figurative; its hidden meaning must be brought out for the nourishment of charity. Whoever uses transient things with greater restraint than is customary among those with whom he lives is either temperate or superstitious; whoever uses them in such a way as to exceed the bounds of the customary conduct of the good among whom he lives either signifies something or is outrageous. In all such matters, it is not the use of things but the lust of the user that is blameworthy.

Nor would any sober person believe that the Lord’s feet were anointed by a woman with precious ointment (John 12:3) in the manner customary among luxurious and wicked people, whose banquets we detest. A good fragrance is a good reputation: whoever possesses one through the works of a good life, while following Christ’s footsteps, pours precious fragrance upon his feet, so to speak. Thus, what is generally an outrage in other persons is a sign of some great reality in a divine or prophetic person. The union with a prostitute in the prophet Hosea’s case is one thing (Hosea 1:2), and the union of people with depraved morals is another; nor, if bodies are indecently exposed at the banquets of drunkards and lechers, is it therefore outrageous to be naked in the baths.

19. We must therefore carefully consider what is appropriate to places, times, and persons, lest we rashly condemn outrages. It can happen that a wise person uses extremely costly food without any fault of daintiness [Note: [Col. 0073] The printed editions have “without any fault of lust” (*vitio cupiditatis*), or “of desire” (*cupidinis*). The manuscripts have “without any fault of daintiness” (*vitio cupediae*), that is, a faulty appetite for more elaborate and agreeable foods.] or gluttony, while a foolish person burns with the foulest flame of appetite for the cheapest fare. And any sane person would prefer to eat fish, as the Lord did (Luke 24:43), rather than lentils, as Esau, Abraham’s grandson, did (Genesis 25:34), or barley, as beasts of burden do. For most animals are not more temperate than we are simply because they are fed cheaper foods. In all such matters, what we do must be approved or condemned not on the basis of the nature of the things we use, but on the basis of the reason for using them and the manner of desiring them.

20. By the earthly kingdom, the righteous of old imagined and foretold the heavenly kingdom. The customary practice of one man having several wives simultaneously was blameless for the purpose of producing offspring [Note: [Col. 0073] Some manuscripts have *suscipiendae* (“to be undertaken”) instead of *sufficiendae* (“for supplying” or “begetting”). Others agree with the printed editions, *sufficiendae*, a Virgilian word, *Georgics* 3.65: “Begetting one offspring after another, supply a new generation.”] (Genesis 16:3; 25:1; and 2 Samuel 5:13); and therefore it was not honorable for one woman to have several husbands. A woman is not more fertile on that account; rather, it is the shame of prostitution to seek either profit or children indiscriminately. In such customs, whatever the holy men of those times did without lust, although they did things that in our time cannot be done except through lust, Scripture does not condemn. And whatever of this kind is narrated there must be interpreted not only historically and literally but also figuratively and prophetically, toward that end of charity—whether charity toward God, toward one’s neighbor, or toward both.

[Col. 0074] Just as among the ancient Romans it was outrageous to wear ankle-length and sleeved tunics, whereas now, among those born to respectable families, when they wear tunics it is outrageous not to have them, so we must recognize that in the rest of the use of things too, lust ought to be absent. Lust not only wickedly abuses the custom of those among whom it lives, but often also oversteps its limits and, in a most outrageous eruption, reveals its foulness, which had been concealed within the restraints of established morals.

### CHAPTER XIII — Continuation of the same argument

21. Whatever accords with the custom of those among whom this life is either imposed by necessity or undertaken as a duty must, in good and great people, be referred to usefulness and benevolence—either literally, as we too ought to do, or figuratively, as is permitted to the prophets.

### CHAPTER XIV — The error of those who think that justice does not exist in itself

22. When the unlearned encounter these actions while reading, coming from a different custom, they consider them outrageous unless restrained by authority. They cannot observe that their entire way of life—whether in marriages, banquets, clothing, or the rest of human food and adornment—may appear outrageous to other peoples and other times.

Moved by this diversity of innumerable customs, certain people—drowsy, so to speak, who were neither lulled into the deep sleep of folly nor able to awaken into the light of wisdom—supposed that justice did not exist in itself, but that each nation considered its own custom just. Since custom is different among all nations, while justice ought to remain unchangeable, they concluded that it must be evident that justice exists nowhere.

They did not understand, to mention only one example, that “Whatever you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16; Matthew 7:12) cannot in any way be altered by the diversity of any people. When this saying is referred to love of God, all outrages die; when it is referred to love of one’s neighbor, all crimes die. No one wishes his own dwelling to be corrupted; therefore he must not corrupt God’s dwelling, namely, himself. And no one wishes to be harmed by anyone; therefore he too must harm no one.

### CHAPTER XV — Rule to be observed in figurative speech

23. Thus, once the tyranny of lust has been overthrown, charity reigns by the most just laws of love: love of God for God’s sake, and love of oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. In figurative speech, therefore, the following rule must be observed: what is read must be examined with careful attention for as long as necessary, until interpretation leads to the kingdom of charity. But if the passage already sounds literal, it should not be considered figurative speech.

### CHAPTER XVI — Rule concerning imperative speech

24. If an imperative statement forbids an outrage or a crime, or commands usefulness or benevolence, it is not figurative. But if it seems to command an outrage or a crime, or to forbid usefulness or benevolence, it is figurative.

“Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,” he says, “you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). This appears to command a crime or an outrage; [Col. 0075] it is therefore a figure, commanding participation in the Lord’s passion and the pleasant and useful preservation in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.

Scripture says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink.” Here it unquestionably commands benevolence. But what follows—“For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Proverbs 25:21–22; Romans 12:20)—might seem to command an act of malevolence. Therefore do not doubt that it was spoken figuratively; and since it can be interpreted in two ways, one toward harming and the other toward helping, let charity draw you rather toward benevolence, so that you understand the burning coals to be the burning groans of repentance by which the pride of the one who grieves that he was an enemy of the person who comes to his misery’s aid is healed.

Likewise, when the Lord says, “Whoever loves his life will lose it” (John 12:25), we should not suppose that he forbids the usefulness by which each person ought to preserve his life. Rather, the saying is figurative: “let him lose his life,” that is, let him destroy and abandon the use he now makes of it—the perverse and disorderly use by which he is inclined toward temporal things, so that he does not seek eternal things.

It is written: “Give to the merciful, and do not receive the sinner” (Sirach 12:4). The latter part of this statement appears to forbid benevolence, for it says, “Do not receive the sinner.” Understand, therefore, that “sinner” is figuratively used for “sin,” so that you do not receive his sin.

### CHAPTER XVII — Some commands are given to all in common, others separately to individuals

25. It often happens that someone who is—or thinks himself to be—in a higher degree of spiritual life considers figurative what is commanded to those in lower degrees. For example, if he has embraced a celibate life and has castrated himself for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 19:12), he may insist that whatever the holy books command concerning loving and governing a wife should be understood not literally but figuratively. Or, if someone has decided to preserve his unmarried virgin daughter, he may try to interpret figuratively the statement, “Give your daughter in marriage, and you will have accomplished a great work” (Sirach 7:27).

This too must therefore be included among the principles for understanding Scripture: we must know that some things are commanded to everyone in common, and others to each individual class of persons. Medicine applies not only to the general condition of health but also to the particular infirmity of each member [Note: Twelve manuscripts have *perveniat* (“may reach”) instead of *pertineat* (“may pertain”).]. What cannot be raised to a higher condition must be cared for within its own condition.

### CHAPTER XVIII — The time at which something was commanded or permitted must be considered

26. We must also take care lest someone suppose that what was understood in the ancient Scriptures as appropriate to the conditions of those times—even if it is understood literally and is neither an outrage nor a crime—can be transferred for use in the conduct of life today. No one will do this unless lust is dominant and seeks the support even of the Scriptures themselves, by which it ought to be overthrown. In his misery he does not understand that these matters were placed there for this purpose: [Col. 0076] so that people of good hope might see salutarily that a custom they reject can have a good use, and that the custom they embrace can be condemnable, if in the former case the charity of those who use it is considered, and in the latter their lust.

27. For if someone could once use many wives chastely, another person can use one wife lustfully. I approve more highly of the person who makes use of the fertility of many for some other purpose than of the person who enjoys the flesh of one for its own sake. In the former case, a usefulness suited to the opportunities of the times is sought; in the latter, lust entangled in temporal pleasures is satisfied.

Those who, because of their lack of self-control, are granted by the Apostle, as a concession, sexual relations with individual spouses (1 Corinthians 7:2) are of a lower degree before God than those who, although each had several wives, regarded sexual intercourse only for the procreation of children, just as a wise person looks to nothing but bodily health in food and drink.

Thus, if the Lord’s coming had found them in this life, when it was already time not to send out stones but to gather them (Ecclesiastes 3:5), they would immediately have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. For abstaining is difficult only when there is lust in possessing.

Those men knew that even within marriage there can be the intemperance of misuse through lust. Tobit’s prayer bears witness to this when he was joined to his wife. For he says:

“Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers, and blessed is your name throughout all ages. Let the heavens and all your creation bless you. You made Adam and gave him Eve as his helper. And now, Lord, you know that I am taking my sister not because of lust, but in truth, so that you may have mercy on us, Lord” (Tobit 8:7–9).

### CHAPTER XIX — The wicked judge others by their own disposition

28. But those who, driven by unrestrained lust, either wander about indulging in numerous acts of fornication, or, even with one wife, not only exceed the measure appropriate to the procreation of children but also accumulate the filth of a more inhuman [Note: [Col. 0076] Eight manuscripts have *immanioris* (“more savage”) instead of *inhumanioris* (“more inhuman”).] lack of restraint with the utterly shameless license of a kind of servile freedom, do not believe that the men of old could have used several women temperately, preserving in that practice nothing except the duty appropriate to the time of propagating offspring. Bound themselves in the snares of lust, and not doing even with one woman what they should, they think that it could in no way have been done with many.

29. But such people could also say that good and holy men ought not to be honored and praised, because when they are honored and praised they swell with pride; the more often and more widely an ingratiating tongue fans them, the more avid they become for the emptiest glory. They become so light that the breeze of rumor—whether what is considered favorable or unfavorable—carries them into whatever abysses of outrage, or dashes them even against the rocks of crime.

Let them therefore see how arduous and difficult it is neither to be enticed by the food of praise nor pierced by the barbs of insult, and let them not measure others by themselves.

### CHAPTER XX — In every manner of life, the good are like one another

Let them rather believe that our Apostles were neither puffed up when they were admired [Col. 0077] by people nor crushed when they were despised. Neither temptation was absent from those men: they were celebrated by the praise of believers and branded by the curses of their persecutors. Just as these men used all such things according to the time and were not corrupted by them, so those men of old, referring their use of women to what was appropriate to their time, did not suffer the domination of lust to which those who do not believe this are enslaved.

30. And therefore these people would in no way restrain themselves from an unforgiving hatred of sons whom they discovered to have assaulted or touched their wives or concubines, if something of that kind had happened to them.

### CHAPTER XXI — Although David fell into adultery, he was far removed from the intemperance of the lustful

But when King David had suffered this at the hands of his wicked and savage son, he not only endured the son’s ferocity but also mourned him when he was dead (2 Samuel 18:33). He was not held fast by carnal jealousy; he was moved not by the injury done to himself but by his son’s sins. For this reason, he had forbidden him to be killed if he were defeated, so that, once subdued, he might retain an opportunity for repentance. And because this did not happen, David did not grieve the loss of a son at his death; he knew into what punishments that impious, adulterous, and parricidal soul was being swept [Note: Am. and Er., and seven manuscripts, have *tam impia et adultera* (“so impious and adulterous”); Bad. has *tam impii adultera* (“the adulteress of so impious a man”).]. For earlier, when another son who was innocent died—the son whose illness had afflicted him—he had rejoiced.

31. The moderation and temperance with which those men used women is especially evident from the fact that when this same king unlawfully attacked one woman, carried away by the heat of youth and the prosperity of temporal affairs, and even ordered her husband to be killed, he was accused by the prophet.

When the prophet came to convict him of his sin, he presented him with the story of a poor man who had one sheep, while his neighbor had many. When a guest arrived, the neighbor took the poor man’s single little ewe rather than one of his own and prepared it for the guest to eat. David, angered against him, ordered that he be killed and that the poor man’s sheep be restored fourfold, thereby unknowingly condemning himself, who had sinned knowingly.

When this was disclosed to him and divine vengeance was announced, he washed away his sin through repentance (2 Samuel 12:1–14). Yet in this likeness only the violation was represented by the poor neighbor’s sheep. David was not questioned by way of the comparison about the murdered husband—that is, about the poor man who had one sheep and was killed—so that he might pronounce judgment on himself only for the adultery [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “so that in the case of adultery alone he might learn the sentence of his condemnation.”].

From this it is understood with what temperance he had possessed many women, since, for exceeding the measure with one, he was compelled to punish himself. But in this man there was not a continuance of such immoderate lust, but a passing episode. For this reason the unlawful desire was called a guest by the accusing prophet. He did not say that the king had presented his poor neighbor’s sheep to his own guest for eating, but to his neighbor’s guest.

In his son Solomon, however, this lust did not pass through like a guest; [Col. 0078] it took possession of his kingdom. Scripture did not conceal this, but blamed him for being a lover of women (1 Kings 11:1). Yet at the beginning his desire had burned for wisdom (2 Chronicles 1:7–12); when he had attained it through spiritual love, he lost it through carnal love.

### CHAPTER XXII — Rule concerning passages of Scripture in which certain actions contrary to the customs of good people today are praised

32. Therefore, although everything—or nearly everything—contained in the books of the Old Testament must be understood not only literally but also figuratively, nevertheless, when a reader understands literally those things in which the people who did them are praised, but which are contrary to the custom of good people who keep the divine commands after the Lord’s coming, let him refer the figure to understanding but not transfer the action itself to conduct. Many things were done dutifully in that time which now cannot be done except lustfully.

### CHAPTER XXIII — Rule concerning passages in which the sins of great men are recounted

If someone reads of sins committed by great men, even if he can discern and investigate in them some figure of future things, he should nevertheless take the literal fact of what happened for this purpose: that he dare not boast of his own righteous deeds or despise others as sinners on the strength of his own righteousness, when he sees the storms that such great men had to avoid and their shipwrecks to mourn.

Their sins were written down for this purpose also, so that the apostolic saying, which ought everywhere to inspire fear, may be remembered: “Therefore, whoever thinks that he stands, let him take care lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). For there is scarcely a page of the holy books in which the truth does not sound forth that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

### CHAPTER XXIV — Above all, the kind of speech must be considered

34. We must therefore investigate above all whether the speech we are trying to understand is literal or figurative. Once it has been established that it is figurative, it is easy, by applying the rules concerning matters that we set out in the first book, to turn it over in every way until we arrive at the meaning of truth, especially when practice has been strengthened by the exercise of devotion. We determine whether speech is literal or figurative by considering the matters discussed above.

### CHAPTER XXV — The same word does not signify the same thing everywhere

When this has become clear, the words in which the speech is contained will be found to have been drawn either from similar things or from things that touch it through some form of proximity.

35. But since things appear similar to other things in many ways, we must not suppose that, when something signifies a particular thing by likeness in one passage, it always signifies that same thing. The Lord used leaven as a reproach when he said, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matthew 16:11), and as praise when he said, “The kingdom of heaven is like a woman who hid leaven in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened” (Luke 13:21).

[Col. 0079]

36. [Note: [Col. 0079] Augustine added the remainder of this book and the whole of Book IV when he revised this work in its order; see *Retractations*, Book II, chapter 4.] This observation of such variation has two forms.
