Things signify different things either by signifying opposites or by signifying merely different things.

They signify opposites when the same thing is used by likeness sometimes for good and sometimes for evil, as in the example of leaven just mentioned. The lion likewise signifies Christ where it is said, “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5); but it signifies the devil where it is written, “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8).

So the serpent is used for good in “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16), but for evil in “The serpent deceived Eve by its craftiness” (2 Corinthians 11:3). Bread is used for good in “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51), and for evil in “Eat gladly the bread of secrecy” (Proverbs 9:17), and so with many other things.

These examples have an unmistakable meaning, since examples should be cited only when they are clear. But there are things concerning which it is uncertain in which direction they should be understood, such as: “The cup in the Lord’s hand is full of pure wine, yet mixed.” It is uncertain whether this signifies God’s wrath, not extending to the final punishment—that is, to the dregs—or rather the grace of Scripture passing from the Jews to the Gentiles, because he “inclined it from this to that,” while the observances that the Jews understand carnally remain with them, since “its dregs have not been emptied” (Psalm 74:9).

When, however, the same thing is used not for opposite but merely for different meanings, water provides an example. Water signifies a people, as we read in Revelation (17:15; 19:6), and the Holy Spirit, as in “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38); and it is understood to signify one thing and another according to the passages in which it occurs.

37. Other things likewise, each one of them—not merely two different things but sometimes many—signify different things according to the context of the meaning in which they are found.

### CHAPTER XXVI — Obscure passages are to be explained by clearer passages

Where things are stated more clearly, we must learn how they are to be understood in obscure passages. For what was said to God, “Take hold of weapons and shield, and rise up to help me” (Psalm 35:2), cannot be understood better than from the passage where we read, “Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Psalm 5:13).

Yet this does not mean that whenever we find “shield” used for some protection, we must understand it only as God’s good will. For Scripture also speaks of “the shield of faith,” “with which,” he says, “you will be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one” (Ephesians 6:16). Nor, again, should we therefore attribute only faith to the shield among such spiritual weapons, since in another passage faith is also called a breastplate: “Put on the breastplate of faith and charity” (1 Thessalonians 5:8).

### CHAPTER XXVII — Nothing prevents the same passage from being understood in different ways

[Col. 0080]

38. When the same words of Scripture yield not one meaning but two or more, even if what the writer meant remains hidden, there is no danger provided that any one of those meanings can be shown from other passages of the holy Scriptures to accord with the truth. The person who searches the divine utterances should nevertheless strive to arrive at the author’s intention, through whom the Holy Spirit produced that Scripture—whether he succeeds in doing so, or extracts from those words another meaning that does not conflict with sound faith and has testimony from some other passage of the divine utterances.

For perhaps that author himself saw the very meaning we are trying to understand in those same words; and certainly the Spirit of God, who worked these things through him, foresaw without doubt that this meaning too would occur to the reader or hearer. Indeed, he provided for it to occur, because it too is supported by the truth. For what could God have provided more generously and abundantly in the divine utterances than that the same words should be understood in several ways, with other equally divine testimonies confirming those interpretations?

### CHAPTER XXVIII — An uncertain passage is more safely made clear through other passages of Scripture than through reasoning

39. When a meaning is drawn out whose uncertainty cannot be clarified by certain testimonies of the holy Scriptures, it remains for it to become clear through a reasoned explanation, even if the person whose words we are trying to understand perhaps did not perceive that meaning. But this practice is dangerous. It is much safer to walk through the divine Scriptures: when we wish to investigate them, veiled as they are by figurative words, either the result should be something that admits of no dispute, or, if it does admit of dispute, the matter should be settled by witnesses found and applied from that same Scripture wherever possible.

### CHAPTER XXIX — Knowledge of tropes is necessary

40. Let the educated know that our authors used every kind of expression that grammarians call, in the Greek term, *tropes*—and used them more abundantly and extensively than those who do not know them, and learned them only in other authors, can imagine or believe. Those who know these tropes recognize them in the sacred writings, and their knowledge helps them to understand those writings to some extent.

But it is not appropriate to teach them here to the ignorant, lest we appear to be teaching grammar. I do advise that they be learned elsewhere, although I already gave this advice above, in the second book, where I discussed the necessity of knowing languages. For the letters from which grammar itself takes its name—the Greeks call letters *grammata* (Γράμματα)—are signs of the sounds belonging to the articulated voice by which we speak.

Examples of these tropes, as of all tropes, and even the names of some of them, are found in the divine books: allegory, enigma, and parable. Nearly all the tropes said to be learned through the liberal art are also found in the speech of people who have never listened to grammarians and are content with the language used by the common people.

Who does not say, “May you flourish”? This is the trope called metaphor. Who does not call something a *pool* even [Col. 0081] when it has no fish and was not made for fish, although it took its name from fish? This trope is called *catachresis*.

41. It would take too long to pursue the other tropes in this way. Popular speech reaches even those that are more remarkable because they signify contrary to what is said, such as the trope called irony or antiphrasis.

Irony indicates by pronunciation what it wishes to be understood, as when we say to someone doing bad things, “You are doing good things.” Antiphrasis, however, signifies the contrary not through the speaker’s tone of voice but either by using words whose origin is contrary, as when a grove is called a *lucus* because it has very little light; or because something has become customarily expressed in that way, even though it is not said in the contrary sense—for example, when we ask to receive something that is not there and are answered, “There is plenty”; or by adding words that make what we say understood in the contrary sense, as when we say, “Be careful of that man, because he is a good man.”

What unlearned person does not say such things, even without knowing altogether what these tropes are or what they are called? Knowledge of them is necessary for resolving the ambiguities of Scripture because, when a meaning is absurd if taken according to the literal meaning of the words, we must investigate whether what we do not understand may have been spoken by one trope or another. In this way many things that lay hidden have been discovered.

### CHAPTER XXX — The rules of Tichonius the Donatist are examined

42. A certain Tichonius, who wrote most vigorously against the Donatists, though he himself was a Donatist—and whose mind is found to be most absurd precisely where he did not wish to abandon them entirely—wrote a book called *The Rules* [Note: [Col. 0081] It is extant in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume 15, Cologne edition of 1622, and in the Lyons edition of 1677, volume 6.]. In it he expounded seven rules by which, as though by keys, the hidden things of the divine Scriptures might be opened.

He makes the first rule “Concerning the Lord and his body”; the second, “Concerning the Lord’s bipartite body”; the third, “Concerning the promises and the Law”; the fourth, “Concerning species and genus”; the fifth, “Concerning times”; the sixth, “Concerning recapitulation”; and the seventh, “Concerning the devil and his body.”

These rules, considered as he unfolds them, provide no small help for penetrating what is concealed in the divine utterances. Nevertheless, not everything written in such a way that it cannot easily be understood can be discovered through these rules. There are many other methods, which he has by no means comprehended within this number seven. Indeed, he himself explains many obscure passages without applying any of these rules, because there is no need to do so.

For example, in the Apocalypse of John he asks how the seven angels of the churches to whom he is commanded to write should be understood, reasons about it in various ways, and arrives at the conclusion that we should understand the angels themselves to be the churches (Revelation 1:20). In this very extensive discussion none of these rules appears, although an extremely obscure matter is being investigated. This example should suffice; for it would be excessively long and laborious to gather all the passages in the canonical Scriptures that are so obscure that none of these seven rules needs to be sought in them.

[Col. 0082]

43. When recommending these rules as though they were such, he attributed so much to them that he seemed to claim that, once they were properly known and applied, we could understand everything obscurely set forth in the Law—that is, in the divine books.

He began that same book by saying:

“I considered it necessary above all to write a little book of Rules, as I see fit, and to construct something like keys and lamps for the secrets of the Law. For there are certain mystical rules that possess the recesses of the entire Law and make the treasures of truth, invisible to some, visible. If the method of these rules is received without envy, as we share it, everything closed will be opened and everything obscure will be made clear, so that whoever travels through the immense forest of prophecy, led by these rules along paths of light, may be protected from error.”

If he had said, “There are certain mystical rules that possess some recesses of the Law,” or at least, “that possess the great recesses of the Law,” rather than saying “the recesses of the entire Law”; and if he had not said, “Everything closed will be opened,” but rather, “Many closed things will be opened,” he would have spoken truly. He would not then have led his reader and student into a false hope by attributing more to his elaborate and useful work than the matter itself warrants.

I have thought this worth saying so that the book itself may be read by serious students, since it contributes a great deal to the understanding of Scripture, but that no one may expect from it more than it contains. It must be read cautiously, not only because of certain matters in which he erred as a human being, but especially because of those matters in which he speaks as a Donatist heretic. I shall briefly show what these seven rules teach or recommend.

### CHAPTER XXXI — The first rule of Tichonius
44. The first concerns the Lord and his body. In this rule, knowing that the head and the body—that is, Christ and the Church—are sometimes presented to us as one person (for it was not said to the faithful without reason, “Therefore you are Abraham’s offspring” [Gal. 3:29], although there is one offspring of Abraham, namely Christ), we need not hesitate when the transition is made from the head to the body, or from the body to the head, while nevertheless remaining within one and the same person. For one person speaks, saying, “As a bridegroom he placed a mitre upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament” (Isa. 61:10); yet it must certainly be understood which of these two statements applies to the head, and which to the body—that is, which to Christ and which to the Church.

## CHAPTER XXXII — Tichonius’s Second Rule

The second concerns the Lord’s divided body, though this should not really have been called so. For what will not be with the Lord forever is not truly the Lord’s body. It should rather have been called “concerning the Lord’s true and mixed body,” or “true and counterfeit,” or something similar; for hypocrites must be said not to be with him not only eternally but even now, although they appear to be in his Church. Accordingly, this rule could also have been called “concerning the mixed Church.”

This rule requires an attentive reader whenever Scripture, although it has already begun speaking to others, appears to speak as though to the very people to whom it had been speaking; or when it appears to speak about the same people, although it has already begun speaking about others—as though both groups constituted one body, because of their temporal mixture and their fellowship in the sacraments [Col. 0083].

This applies to the Song of Songs: “I am dark and beautiful, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon” (Song 1:5). It does not say, “I was dark like the tents of Kedar, and I am beautiful like the curtains of Solomon,” but says that it is both, because of the temporal unity within one net of good and bad fish (Matt. 13:48). The tents of Kedar belong to Ishmael, who will not be heir with the son of the free woman (Gen. 21:10; Gal. 4:30).

Thus, when God says of the good part, “I will lead the blind by a way they do not know, and they will walk by paths they do not know; I will turn darkness before them into light and crooked things into straight. These things I will do for them, and I will not abandon them,” he immediately says of the other part, which is wrongly mixed in with it, “But they turned backward” (Isa. 42:16–17), although by these words others are now signified. But because they are presently together in one, he speaks as though he were speaking about the very people about whom he had been speaking; nevertheless, they will not always remain together in one. For this is that servant mentioned in the Gospel whose master, when he comes, “will cut him in two and appoint his portion with the hypocrites” (Matt. 24:51).

## CHAPTER XXXIII — Tichonius’s Third Rule. *The Book Concerning the Spirit and the Letter*

46. The third rule concerns the Promises and the Law. It may also be called “concerning the spirit and the letter,” as we called it when we wrote a book on this subject [Note: [Col. 0083] *The Book Concerning the Spirit and the Letter*]. It may likewise be called “concerning grace and commandment.”

This seems to me more a major question than a rule to be employed in solving questions. The Pelagians, because they did not understand it, either founded their heresy or increased it. Tichonius labored well at resolving it [Note: [Col. 0083] Nine manuscripts: “at discussing it”], but not completely. For, discussing faith and works, he told us that works are given by God on account of the merit of faith, but that faith itself comes from us in such a way that it does not come to us from God. He did not heed the Apostle, who says, “Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. 6:23).

But he had not encountered this heresy, which arose in our own time and exercised us greatly, so that we might defend against it the grace of God that comes through our Lord Jesus Christ. In accordance with the Apostle’s statement, “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19), it made us much more watchful and diligent, so that we might observe in the holy Scriptures what escaped Tichonius because he was insufficiently attentive and insufficiently troubled by an adversary: namely, that faith itself is also the gift of the one who distributes its measure to each person (Rom. 12:3).

On the basis of this statement some have been told, “It has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29). Who, then, could doubt that both are God’s gifts, when he faithfully and intelligently hears that both have been granted? There are also many other testimonies by which this is demonstrated; but that is not our concern now. We have treated it elsewhere, and very often elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — Tichonius’s Fourth Rule

47. Tichonius’s fourth rule concerns species and genus. He calls a species a part, and a genus the whole of which that part is a part. Thus, each individual city is certainly a part of the totality of the nations: he calls this a species, while he calls all the nations the genus. Here we should not apply the subtle distinction taught by dialecticians, who argue with great precision about the difference between a part and a species.

The same principle applies if something of this kind is found in the divine utterances not about each individual city but about a province, nation, or kingdom. For Scripture says not only of Jerusalem or of some city of the nations—whether Tyre, Babylon, or any other city—something that exceeds its own limits and applies rather to all the nations; it also says of Judaea, Egypt, Assyria, or any other nation containing many cities—though it is not the whole world but a part of it—something that goes beyond its limits and applies rather to the whole of which it is a part, or, as he calls it, to the genus of which it is the species.

Hence these expressions have entered common knowledge, so that even uneducated people understand what has been established specifically and what generally in any imperial decree. The same thing occurs with individuals. For example, what is said about Solomon exceeds his limits and becomes clear when referred rather to Christ or to the Church, of which he is a part.

48. The species is not always exceeded. Often statements are made that clearly apply either to it as well or perhaps to it alone. But when Scripture passes from the species to the genus, while appearing still to speak about the species, the reader’s attention must remain vigilant, lest he seek in the species what he can find more properly and certainly in the genus.

It is easy, for example, to understand the following words of the prophet Ezekiel as referring to that house of Israel of which the Apostle says, “Consider Israel according to the flesh” (1 Cor. 10:18): “The house of Israel dwelt in the land, and they defiled it by their way and by their idols and by their sins. Their way became before my face like the uncleanness of a menstruating woman. And I poured out my anger upon them, and I scattered them among the nations, and I dispersed them throughout the regions; I judged them according to their ways and according to their sins” (Ezek. 36:17–19). For the carnal people of Israel both did and suffered all these things.

Other statements that follow can likewise be understood as applying to that same people. But when he begins to say, “And I will sanctify my holy name, that great name which has been profaned among the nations, which you profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am the Lord,” the reader must now be attentive to how the species is exceeded and the genus joined to it.

For he continues:

“And when I am sanctified in you before their eyes, I will take you from the nations, and gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your land. I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your idols, and I will cleanse you. I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh, and I will put my spirit within you. I will make you walk in my ordinances, keep my judgments, and perform them. You shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers; you shall be my people, and I shall be your God. And I will cleanse you from all your impurities” (Ezek. 36:23–29).

Anyone who observes that the washing of regeneration is here promised—something that we now see granted to all nations—does not doubt that this was prophesied of the New Testament. It does not concern only that one nation in its remnant, concerning which it is written elsewhere, “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be saved” (Isa. 10:22), but also the other nations that were promised to their fathers, who are also our fathers.

When the Apostle was commending the grace of the New Testament so that it might stand out in comparison with the Old, he said, “You are our letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on stone tablets but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (2 Cor. 3:2–3). Anyone who observes this understands that the Apostle’s words are drawn from the passage in which the prophet says, “I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; I will take the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.”

The heart of flesh, of which the Apostle says, “on tablets of fleshly hearts,” was intended to be distinguished from the heart of stone by a life capable of feeling; and by that life capable of feeling he signified understanding. Thus the spiritual Israel comes into being—not of one nation, but of all the nations promised to the fathers in their offspring, which is Christ.

49. This spiritual Israel is therefore distinguished from that carnal Israel, which consists of one nation, by the newness of grace, not by nobility of ancestry, and by mind, not by nation. Yet prophetic elevation, while speaking about or to the former, secretly passes over to the latter; and when it is already speaking about or to the latter, it still appears to speak about or to the former. Scripture does not maliciously begrudge us its meaning; rather, it exercises us for our healing.

Accordingly, what it says, “I will bring you into your land,” and shortly afterward, as though repeating the same statement, “You shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers,” must be understood not carnally, as it applies to carnal Israel, but spiritually, as it applies to spiritual Israel.

The Church, gathered from all nations, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27), and destined to reign with Christ forever, is itself the land of the blessed, the land of the living (Ps. 26:13). It is to be understood as having been given to the fathers when, by God’s certain and unchangeable will, it was promised to them. For by the firmness of the promise or predestination it has already been given, although the fathers believed that it would be given in its own time.

Thus, concerning the same grace given to the saints, the Apostle wrote to Timothy: “Not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages, but has now been manifested through the appearing of our Savior” (2 Tim. 1:9–10). He said that grace was given when those to whom it would be given did not yet exist, because in God’s ordering and predestination what would occur in its own time had already been accomplished—what he says has now been manifested.

These words can also be understood of the land of the age to come, when there will be a new heaven and a new earth (Rev. 21:1), in which the unrighteous will not be able to dwell. Therefore it is rightly said to the righteous that this land is theirs, since it will in no respect belong to the ungodly. It too was given when its future giving was made certain.

## CHAPTER XXXV — Tichonius’s Fifth Rule

50. Tichonius sets down a fifth rule, which he calls “concerning times.” By this rule the quantity of time hidden in the holy Scriptures can often be discovered or inferred.

He says that this rule operates in two ways: either through the figure of synecdoche or through canonical numbers. Synecdoche makes the whole understood from a part, or the part from the whole. Thus one evangelist says that something occurred after eight days, while another says after six days, when, with only three disciples present on the mountain, the face of the Lord shone like the sun and his garments became white as snow (Luke 9:28; Matt. 17:1–2; Mark 9:1–2).

Both statements could not be true concerning the number of days unless the one who said “after eight days” is understood to have counted as whole days the final part of the day on which Christ foretold that this would happen and the first part of the day on which he showed it fulfilled—thus counting two days along with the intervening days as complete days—while the one who said “after six days” counted all the days as complete but counted only the days in between.

This manner of speaking, in which the whole is signified by a part, also resolves the question concerning Christ’s resurrection. The final part of the day on which he suffered cannot constitute one of the three days and three nights during which he foretold that he would be in the heart of the earth (Matt. 12:40), unless it is taken for the whole day, with the preceding night included. Likewise, the night during whose final part he rose cannot constitute another day unless the day that dawned on Sunday is included.

51. By “canonical numbers” he means those that divine Scripture commends especially, such as seven, ten, and twelve, and whatever other numbers attentive readers readily recognize as they read. Such numbers often stand for the whole of time. Thus, “Seven times a day I praise you” (Ps. 118:164) means nothing other than, “His praise is always in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2).

The same numbers retain this force when multiplied, whether by ten, as in seventy and seven hundred—hence Jeremiah’s seventy years (Jer. 25:11) can also be understood spiritually as the whole period during which the Church is among strangers—or by themselves, as ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred, and twelve multiplied by twelve makes one hundred forty-four, the number that signifies the totality of the saints in Revelation (Rev. 7:4).

It is therefore clear that these numbers do not solve only questions concerning time. Their meanings extend more broadly and spread into many things. For the number in Revelation does not refer to times but to people.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — Tichonius’s Sixth Rule

52. Tichonius calls his sixth rule “Recapitulation,” a rule discovered with considerable vigilance amid the obscurity of Scripture. Some things are narrated as though they follow in temporal order or continue the sequence of events, when in fact the narrative secretly returns to earlier matters that had been passed over. Unless this is understood by means of the rule, one goes astray.

Thus in Genesis it says, “And the Lord God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the east, and there he placed the man whom he had formed. And God brought forth from the earth every tree that is beautiful and good for food.” This appears to say that the event occurred after God had placed the man in the paradise. Yet, after briefly mentioning both events—namely, that God planted the paradise and placed there the man whom he had formed—the narrative returns by recapitulation to what it had omitted: namely, how the paradise was planted, since God brought forth from the earth every tree that was beautiful and good for food.

Finally it adds: “And the tree of life in the midst of the paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” Then the river by which the paradise was watered is described as divided into four sources, four rivers. All this belongs to the establishment of the paradise.

When this has been completed, the narrative repeats what it had already said, and what in fact followed these events, saying: “And the Lord God took the man whom he had formed and placed him in the paradise” (Gen. 2:8–9), and so forth. The man was placed there after these things had been done, as the order itself now demonstrates—not after the man had been placed there were these things done, as it might earlier be thought to say, unless recapitulation is attentively understood, by which the narrative returns to what had been omitted.

53. Likewise, in the same book, when the generations of Noah’s sons were being enumerated, it says: “These are the sons of Ham in their tribes, according to their languages, in their regions [Note: [Col. 0087] Four manuscripts: ‘in their generations.’ Other copies: ‘in their regions,’ in accordance with the Septuagint version, *en tais chorais* (‘in the regions’)], and in their nations.”

After the sons of Shem have also been listed, it says: “These are the sons of Shem in their tribes, according to their languages, in their regions and in their nations.” It then adds concerning them all: “These are the tribes of the sons of Noah according to their generations and according to their nations. From these the islands of the nations were dispersed over the earth after the flood. And the whole earth had one language and one speech for all” (Gen. 10:20, 31–32; 11:1).

The addition, “And the whole earth had one language and one speech for all”—that is, one language belonging to all—appears to say that, at the time when they had already been dispersed throughout the earth, even among the islands of the nations, there was still one language common to all. This clearly conflicts with the preceding words, where it said, “in their tribes according to their languages.” For individual tribes that had already become individual nations would not be said to have had their own languages if one common language existed for all.

Accordingly, the words, “And the whole earth had one language and one speech for all,” have been added by recapitulation. The narrative secretly returns in order to explain how they came to be divided from one common language into many. It immediately proceeds to narrate the building of the tower, where this punishment for their pride was inflicted upon them by divine judgment. After that event they were dispersed over the earth according to their languages.

54. This recapitulation also occurs more obscurely. In the Gospel the Lord says: “On the day when Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire from heaven and destroyed them all. So shall it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. In that hour, whoever is on the housetop, with his vessels in the house, must not come down to take them; and whoever is in the field likewise must not turn back. Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:29–32; Gen. 19:26).

Are these instructions to be observed when the Lord has been revealed, so that no one looks back—that is, seeks again the former life to which he has renounced—or rather during the present time, so that, when the Lord is revealed, each person may receive recompense for what he preserved or despised? Yet because it says, “In that hour,” people think that these things must be observed when the Lord has been revealed, unless the reader’s understanding remains alert to recognize recapitulation, aided by another Scripture that cried out even in the time of the Apostles, “Children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).

The period itself, therefore, during which the Gospel is preached until the Lord is revealed, is the hour in which these things must be observed. For the Lord’s revelation itself belongs to this same hour, which will end on the day of judgment (Rom. 2:5; 13:11).

## CHAPTER XXXVII — Tichonius’s Seventh Rule

55. Tichonius’s seventh and final rule concerns the devil and his body. He too is the head of the ungodly, who are in some manner his body and will go with him into the punishment of eternal fire (Matt. 25:41), just as Christ is the head of the Church, which is his body and will be with him in eternal kingdom and glory (Eph. 1:22).

Therefore, just as in the first rule, which he calls “concerning the Lord and his body,” one must remain attentive in order to understand, when Scripture speaks of one and the same person, what applies to the head and what to the body, so also in this final rule something is sometimes said of the devil that can be recognized not in him personally but rather in his body. His body consists not only of those who are manifestly outside, but also of those who, although they belong to him, are for a time mixed with the Church, until each person departs from this life or the chaff is separated from the wheat by the final winnowing (Luke 3:17).

What is written in Isaiah—“How Lucifer fell from heaven, rising in the morning” (Isa. 14:12)—and the other statements that, within the same sequence of speech, are spoken under the figure of the king of Babylon about the same person or to the same person, are certainly understood of the devil. Yet what is said there, “He who sends to all the nations has been crushed upon the earth,” does not entirely apply to the head himself.

For although the devil sends his angels to all the nations, it is his body, not he himself, that is crushed upon the earth—unless it is because he himself is in his body, which, once crushed, becomes like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth (Ps. 1:4).

56. All these rules, except one—the one called “concerning the Promises and the Law”—make one thing understood from another. This is characteristic of figurative speech, whose range, as it seems to me, is too extensive for anyone to encompass in its entirety.

Wherever one thing is said as though another were meant, even if the name of the particular figure is not found in the art of speech, the expression is figurative. When this occurs where it commonly occurs, understanding follows without difficulty. But when it occurs where it is not customary, effort is required for it to be understood—more by some, less by others, according as the gifts of God in human minds are greater or less, or as assistance is granted.

Therefore, just as with literal expressions, which we discussed above, things are to be understood as they are said, so with transferred expressions that produce figurative speech—where one thing is to be understood from another—we have dealt with these matters as far as seemed sufficient. Students of the venerable Scriptures must not only be instructed to recognize the kinds of expression found in the holy Scriptures and to observe attentively how something is customarily said in them and retain this in memory; they must also, and above all—for this is most important and necessary—pray that they may understand.

For in the Scriptures whose students they are, they read that “the Lord gives wisdom, and from his face come knowledge and understanding” (Prov. 2:6). From him they received even their study, if it is accompanied by piety.

Let this suffice concerning signs, insofar as words are concerned. It remains for us, in the following book, to discuss the setting forth of what we perceive, insofar as the Lord grants it.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0089]

Up to this point the subject has been the investigation of the meaning of Scripture; now at last it concerns its exposition. Augustine does not intend the precepts of rhetorical art to belong to the purpose of this book. Nevertheless, he pursues with the greatest diligence the duties of the Christian orator. He presents the authors of the sacred Scriptures and the ecclesiastical teachers as models to be imitated, since they are far superior in the wisdom of speech, indeed in eloquence as well, and he supplies from their writings examples of expression in various kinds of discourse. Finally, he urges the ecclesiastical speaker above all to devote himself to prayer, and to make his life and conduct entirely accord with what he teaches others by his words.

## CHAPTER I — Giving the Precepts of Rhetoric Is Not the Purpose of This Work

1. In my first division I had divided this work of ours, entitled *On Christian Doctrine*, into two parts. For, after the preface in which I replied to those who were going to criticize it, I said: “There are two things on which every treatment of the Scriptures depends: the method of discovering what is to be understood, and the method of presenting what has been understood. We shall discuss discovery first and presentation afterward.”

Since we have already said much about discovery, and, with the Lord’s help, completed three books on this one part, we shall say a little about presentation, so that, if possible, we may enclose everything in a single book and bring this entire work to an end in four books.

2. I therefore begin by restraining the expectation of readers who may perhaps think that I am going to give the rhetorical precepts that I both learned and taught in secular schools. I warn them not to expect these from me—not because they have no usefulness, but because, if they possess any, they must be learned separately, if perhaps some good man has time to learn them as well. They should not be sought from me either in this work or in any other.

## CHAPTER II — It Is Appropriate for a Christian Teacher to Use Rhetorical Skill

3. Since rhetorical art is used to persuade both truth and falsehood, who would dare say that truth should stand unarmed against falsehood in its defenders, so that those who attempt to persuade others of false things know how to make their hearer favorable, attentive, or teachable in the introduction, while the defenders of truth do not?

Should those others narrate falsehoods briefly, clearly, and plausibly, while these narrate truths in such a way that hearing them is tedious, understanding them impossible, and believing them finally undesirable? Should those others attack the truth with deceptive arguments and assert falsehood, while these are unable either to defend the truth or refute falsehood? Should those others, by moving and driving the minds of their hearers into error, terrify, sadden, cheer, and ardently exhort them in speech, while these, on behalf of the truth, remain sluggish and cold and fall asleep?

Who would be so foolish as to think that this is wisdom? Since the power of eloquence is placed in the midst of things and is extremely effective for persuading people either to what is wrong or to what is right, why should it not be acquired through the zeal of the good, so that it may serve the truth, if the wicked seize it for the purposes of injustice and error in order to obtain their perverse and empty causes?

## CHAPTER III — At What Age and by What Method the Precepts of Rhetoric Can Be Learned

4. Whatever observations and precepts there are concerning this matter—which, when joined to extensive practice and the highly skillful habit of a practiced tongue in many words and verbal ornaments, produce what is called facility or eloquence—should be learned outside these writings of ours, with a suitable amount of time set aside for that purpose, and at an appropriate age, by those who can learn them quickly.

For even the leading Roman authorities in eloquence were not reluctant to say that, unless someone can learn this art quickly, he can never learn it completely (Cicero, *On the Orator*). Whether this is true is not worth investigating. For even if slower learners could eventually learn these things, we do not value them so highly that we would wish the already mature, or even advanced, years of human beings to be spent learning them.

It is enough that this should be the concern of the young—not of all those whom we wish to educate for the usefulness of the Church, but of those who have not yet been occupied by a more urgent necessity, which must unquestionably take precedence over this matter.

For if a sharp and fervent intellect is present, eloquence adheres more easily to those who read and hear eloquent speakers than to those who pursue the precepts of eloquence. Nor are ecclesiastical writings lacking—not only the canon placed salutarily in the citadel of authority, but also other writings—from which a capable person, by reading, may become imbued with the very manner of expression in which their contents are expressed, even if he does not intend this but merely concentrates on the matters discussed there.

This is especially the case when practice is added, whether in writing, dictating, or finally speaking, what one thinks in accordance with the rule of piety and faith.

But if such an intellect is lacking, neither are those rhetorical precepts grasped, nor, if they are absorbed with great labor in however small a part, do they provide any benefit. Indeed, even those who have learned them and speak copiously and ornamentedly cannot all think about them while speaking, so as to speak according to them, unless they are discussing the precepts themselves. In fact, I scarcely think that any of them can do both: speak well and, while speaking, think about those precepts of speaking by which this is done.

One must take care that the things to be said do not escape from the mind while attention is directed toward saying them according to the art. Yet in the speeches and discourses of eloquent speakers the precepts of eloquence are found fulfilled, although they did not think about them either in order to speak or while speaking, whether they had learned them or had never even encountered them. They fulfill them because they are eloquent; they do not employ them in order to become eloquent.

5. Therefore, since speaking infants become speakers only by learning the expressions of speakers, why should people not become eloquent without being taught any art of speaking, simply by reading and hearing the expressions of eloquent speakers and imitating them as far as they are permitted to attain?

Why, indeed, do we not observe that this happens even by the examples of the speakers themselves? For we know many people who are more eloquent than many who have learned the rhetorical precepts, although they have learned no precepts of rhetoric; but without reading and hearing the discussions or speeches of eloquent people, we know of no one who has become eloquent.

Indeed, boys would not need even the grammatical art by which correctness of speech is learned if they were allowed to grow up and live among people who spoke correctly. Without knowing any of the names of faults, they would criticize and avoid by their sound habitual usage whatever faulty expression they heard from someone speaking, just as city dwellers criticize country people, even those who do not know letters.

## CHAPTER IV — The Duty of the Christian Teacher

6. The interpreter and teacher of the divine Scriptures, therefore, the defender of the right faith and vanquisher of error, must teach what is good and unteach what is evil. In this work of speech he must make opponents favorable [Note: [Col. 0091] Bad., Am., Er., and seven manuscripts: “those who are averse”], raise up the indifferent, and disclose to those who do not know what is happening what they ought to expect.

When he has found—or himself made—people favorable, attentive, and teachable, the remaining tasks must be carried out as the case requires. If those who hear are to be taught, this must be done through narration, provided that the matter under discussion requires explanation so that it may become known. But if doubtful things are to be made certain, reasoning must be employed with supporting evidence.

If, however, those who hear must be moved rather than taught, so that they do not grow sluggish in acting upon what they already know and may give their assent to matters they acknowledge to be true, greater powers of speech are required. There, entreaties and rebukes, incitements and restraints, and whatever else is effective in stirring the emotions are necessary.

7. Nearly all people, in the things they undertake by speaking [Note: [Col. 0091] Two manuscripts: “in the things they argue by speaking”], do not cease doing all the things I have mentioned.

## CHAPTER V — It Matters More That the Christian Orator Speak Wisely Than That He Speak Eloquently; How This Can Be Achieved

But while some do these things bluntly, awkwardly, and coldly, and others sharply, ornamentedly, and forcefully, the person who can argue or speak wisely, even if he cannot speak eloquently, should now approach the work we are discussing. He will benefit his hearers, even if less than he would benefit them if he could also speak eloquently.

But someone who overflows with foolish eloquence is all the more to be avoided because the hearer takes greater pleasure in him precisely where it is useless to listen to him, and, because he hears him speak fluently, also thinks that he speaks truthfully.

This judgment did not escape even those who thought that the art of rhetoric should be taught. They confessed that wisdom without eloquence does little good for communities [Note: [Col. 0092] Lov.: “for citizens.” Other printed editions and manuscripts: “for communities”], while eloquence without wisdom usually does great harm and never does good (Cicero, *On Invention*, book 1).

If those who transmitted the precepts of eloquence were compelled by the prompting of truth to confess this in the very books in which they treated the subject, although they did not know the true—that is, the heavenly—wisdom that descends from the Father of lights, how much more ought we, who are children and ministers of this wisdom, to hold the same view?

A person speaks wisely to the greater or lesser extent that he has made greater or lesser progress in the holy Scriptures. I do not mean merely reading many of them and committing them to memory, but understanding them well and diligently investigating their meanings.

There are some who read them and neglect them: they read in order to retain the words, but neglect them in order not to understand. Those who retain fewer of their words but see their meaning with the eyes of their heart are unquestionably to be preferred to these by far. But better than both is the person who, whenever he wishes, can recite them and understands them as he ought.

8. For the person who must speak wisely, even if he cannot speak eloquently, it is especially necessary to retain the words of Scripture. The poorer he sees himself in his own words, the richer he ought to be in these, so that he may prove what he says in his own words from them; and he who was lesser in his own words may, through the testimony of great ones [Note: [Col. 0092] Two Vatican manuscripts: “greater ones”], in some way become greater.

By proving his statements he gives pleasure, although he is less able to give pleasure by his manner of speaking.

But whoever wishes to speak not only wisely but also eloquently—for he will certainly be more useful if he can do both—I would more willingly send to read or hear eloquent speakers and to imitate them through practice than instruct him to devote himself to teachers of rhetorical art, provided that those who are read and heard are praised with a truthful commendation as having spoken or as speaking not only eloquently but also wisely.

Those who speak eloquently are heard pleasantly; those who speak wisely are heard profitably. For this reason Scripture does not say, “A multitude of the eloquent,” but, “A multitude of the wise is the health of the world” (Wis. 6:26).

Just as bitter medicines must often be taken for the sake of health, so pernicious sweetness must always be avoided. But what is better than a healthful pleasantness, or a pleasant healthfulness? The more pleasantness is sought there, the more easily healthfulness benefits.

There are therefore ecclesiastical men who have treated the divine utterances not only wisely but also eloquently. Those who wish to read them more often lack time than these writings can lack for students and those who have leisure.

## CHAPTER VI — Wisdom Joined with Eloquence in the Sacred Authors
### 9

Someone may perhaps ask whether our authors—whose writings, divinely inspired, established the canon for us by their most salutary authority—should be called merely wise, or also eloquent. This question is very easily resolved, both for me and for those who share my view. For when I understand them, I can imagine nothing wiser than they are, and nothing more eloquent either. And I dare say that all who rightly understand what they say at the same time understand that they could not have spoken otherwise.

For just as there is one kind of eloquence that suits youth better, and another that suits old age—and eloquence should no longer be called eloquence if it does not suit the speaker’s person—so there is an eloquence that plainly suits men worthy of the highest authority and wholly divine. They spoke in this manner; no other manner suits them, nor does this manner suit others: it suits them. Yet the more humble it seems to others, the more profoundly it surpasses them—not through ostentation, but through solidity.

When I do not understand them, their eloquence indeed appears less to me; yet I do not doubt that it is of the same quality as where I do understand it. The very obscurity of their divine and salutary sayings had to be mingled with such eloquence, so that our understanding might make progress not only through discovery but also through exercise.

### 10

I could, if I had the leisure, point out in these sacred writings all the virtues and ornaments of eloquence about which those men puff themselves up who place their own language above the language of our authors—not because of its greatness, but because of its swelling. These are the authors whom divine providence supplied for educating us and transferring us from this wicked age to the blessed age.

But it is not the features these men share with the orators and poets of the Gentiles that delight me in that eloquence more than words can express. Rather, I admire and marvel at this: they used our eloquence through another eloquence of their own in such a way that it was neither absent from them nor conspicuous in them. For it ought neither to be condemned nor displayed by them: the former would happen if they avoided it; the latter might be supposed if it were easily recognized.

And in those passages where it is perhaps recognized by the learned, such things are said that the words in which they are said seem not to have been employed by the speaker but to have been added, as it were, spontaneously by the things themselves. You seem to understand wisdom as proceeding from its own house—that is, from the breast of the wise man—and eloquence following it like an inseparable servant, even when not summoned.

## CHAPTER VII

He aptly teaches, by adducing examples, that genuine eloquence is present in the sacred writings, adhering to wisdom like an inseparable companion. Examples are given from Paul’s Epistles and from the prophet Amos. Another example of sound eloquence from Amos 6:1.

### 11

Who does not see what the Apostle wished to say, and how wisely he said it: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:3–5)?

If someone who is, so to speak, unskilled yet considers himself skilled were to insist that the Apostle followed the rules of the art of eloquence, would he not be laughed at by learned and unlearned Christians alike? And yet a figure is recognized here, called in Greek κλίμαξ (*klimax*), and in Latin by some *gradatio* (“gradation”), because they did not wish to call it a “ladder”: words or thoughts are connected, each arising from the preceding one. Here we see endurance connected with tribulation, testing with endurance, and hope with testing.

Another ornament is also recognized. After several units have been completed individually by the voice of delivery—units which our writers call *membra* and *caesa*, while the Greeks call them κῶλα (*kōla*) and κόμματα (*kommata*)—there follows an entire period or circuit, which they call περίοδος (*periodos*), whose members are held in suspense by the speaker’s voice until the final ending.

Of the elements preceding the period, the first member is “tribulation produces endurance”; the second, “but endurance, testing”; the third, “and testing, hope.” Then the period itself follows, formed of three members. The first is “but hope does not disappoint”; the second, “because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts”; the third, “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

These and similar features are taught in the art of expression. Therefore, just as we do not say that the Apostle followed the rules of eloquence, so we do not deny that eloquence followed his wisdom.

### 12

In the Second Epistle, writing to the Corinthians, he rebukes certain people who were pseudo-apostles from the Jews and who disparaged him. Since he is compelled to praise himself, attributing this to himself as a kind of folly, how wisely he speaks—and how eloquently! Eloquence is wisdom’s companion, and wisdom eloquence’s guide: wisdom goes before, eloquence follows, and he does not reject her as she follows.

“Again I say,” he says, “let no one think me foolish; otherwise receive me as foolish, so that I too may boast a little. What I speak, I do not speak according to the Lord, but as if in folly, in this matter of boasting. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. For you gladly tolerate fools, since you yourselves are wise. For you tolerate it if someone brings you into slavery, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face. I say this according to dishonor, as though we had been weak. In whatever anyone dares—in folly I speak—I too dare. Are they Hebrews? I too. Are they Israelites? I too. Are they the seed of Abraham? I too. Are they ministers of Christ?—I speak as one insane—I am more” [Note: Two manuscripts read *plus ego* (“I am more”). All the others, with the printed editions, read *super ego* (“I am above”). The Greek has *hyper egō*, where the translator rendered the words more than the sense.]. “In labors more abundantly, in prisons more extensively, in blows beyond measure, in deaths often. Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck; I was in the depths of the sea night and day; often on journeys, in dangers from rivers, in dangers from robbers, in dangers from my own people, in dangers from the Gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers at sea, in dangers among false brothers; in labor and hardship, in frequent vigils, in hunger and thirst, in frequent fastings, in cold and nakedness; besides those external things, there is my daily pressure, the care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning? If it is necessary to boast, I will boast in the things that belong to my weakness” (2 Cor. 11:16–30).

Those who are watchful see how much wisdom these words contain. But even one who snores notices how abundantly the stream of eloquence flows through them.

### 13

Moreover, anyone who understands recognizes that the *caesa*—which the Greeks call κόμματα (*kommata*)—the members, and the periods about which I discussed a little earlier, were interposed with most fitting variety and thereby formed the entire appearance of this discourse, so to speak, its face, by which even the unlearned are delighted and moved.

For the passage with which we began consists of periods. The first is the smallest, that is, two-membered; a period cannot have fewer than two members, though it may have more: “Again I say, let no one think me foolish.” Another follows, of three members: “Otherwise receive me as foolish, so that I too may boast a little.” The third has four members: “What I speak, I do not speak according to the Lord, but as if in folly, in this matter of boasting.” The fourth has two: “Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.” The fifth also has two: “For you gladly tolerate fools, since you yourselves are wise.” The sixth is likewise two-membered: “For you tolerate it if someone brings you into slavery.”

Three *caesa* follow: “If someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself.” Then come three members: “If someone strikes you in the face; I say this according to dishonor, as though we had been weak.” A three-member period is added: “In whatever anyone dares—in folly I speak—I too dare.”

From this point, each individual *caesum* is presented as a question, and each receives a corresponding *caesum* in reply: “Are they Hebrews? I too. Are they Israelites? I too. Are they the seed of Abraham? I too.” But when a fourth *caesum* is presented in the form of a similar question, it is answered not by another *caesum* but by the contrast of a member: “Are they ministers of Christ?—I speak as one insane—I am more.”

The next four *caesa* are poured forth, with the questions most appropriately removed: “In labors more abundantly, in prisons more extensively, in blows beyond measure, in deaths often.” Then a brief period is inserted, since it should be divided by a suspended delivery: “Five times from the Jews”—this is one member—to which the second is joined: “I received the forty lashes minus one.”

Then the discourse returns to *caesa*, and three are placed: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck.” A member follows: “Night and day I was in the depths of the sea.” Then fourteen *caesa* flow forth in a most fitting rush: “Often on journeys, in dangers from rivers, in dangers from robbers, in dangers from my own people, in dangers from the Gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers at sea, in dangers among false brothers; in labor and hardship, in frequent vigils, in hunger and thirst, in frequent fastings, in cold and nakedness.”

After this he inserts a three-member period: “Besides those external things, there is my daily pressure, the care of all the churches.” To this he adds two members in the form of questions: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?”

Finally, this entire passage, as though panting, is brought to an end by a two-member period: “If it is necessary to boast, I will boast in the things that belong to my weakness.”

After this rush, a short narrative is interposed, so that the discourse somehow rests and causes the listener to rest. Its beauty and delight cannot adequately be expressed. He continues: “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying” (2 Cor. 11:31). Then he briefly relates how he was endangered and how he escaped.

### 14

It would take too long to pursue the rest, or to point out these features in other passages of the sacred Scriptures. What if I had also wished to demonstrate, in at least those passages from the Apostle’s eloquence that I have recalled, the figures of speech taught in that art? Would not serious men more readily think me excessive than any student think himself adequately instructed?

Whenever these things are taught by teachers, they are considered highly valuable, purchased at a high price, and sold with great self-display. I fear that I too may give off the scent of such display while discussing them in this way. But an answer had to be given to poorly educated people who think our authors should be despised—not because they lack eloquence, but because they do not display the kind of eloquence these people love excessively.

### 15

But perhaps someone thinks that I deliberately chose the Apostle Paul as our eloquent author. For when he says, “Even if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Cor. 11:6), he seems to have spoken as though conceding something to his detractors, not as though he acknowledged its truth by confessing it. If he had said, “I am indeed unskilled in speech, but not in knowledge” [Note: Thus the manuscripts and the editions of Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus. The edition of Lovaniensis omits *et* (“indeed”) and reads, “but not in knowledge.”], it could in no way be understood otherwise.

He plainly did not hesitate to profess knowledge, without which he could not have been a teacher of the Gentiles. Certainly, if we produce any of his words as an example of eloquence, we produce them from those Epistles which even his detractors—who wanted his speech in person to be considered contemptible—admitted to be weighty and powerful (2 Cor. 10:10).

I see, therefore, that I must say something about the eloquence of the prophets as well, in which many things are concealed through tropology. The more they appear to be covered by figurative words, the sweeter they become when they are disclosed. But here I ought to recall an example in which I am not compelled to explain what was said, but only to commend how it was said.

I shall take it especially from the book of that prophet who says that he was a shepherd, or a herdsman, and that from there he was taken away and sent by divine command to prophesy to the people of God (Amos 7:14–15). I shall not use the version of the Septuagint translators. Although they too translated under the influence of the divine Spirit, they sometimes seem to have said things differently so that the reader’s attention might be more strongly urged to search out the spiritual meaning. Hence some of their passages are also more obscure, because they are more figurative. I shall use instead the version translated from Hebrew into Latin by the presbyter Jerome, who was skilled in both languages.

### 16

When this prophet—rustic, or sprung from rustic stock—was rebuking the impious, the proud, the luxurious, and those who were therefore utterly negligent of brotherly love, he exclaimed:

“Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and put your trust in Mount Samaria, nobles, heads of the peoples, entering the house of Israel with pomp! Cross over to Calneh and see; go from there to great Hamath, and descend to Gath of the Philistines, and to the best of these kingdoms, if their territory is wider than your territory. You who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the throne of iniquity. You who sleep on ivory beds and lounge upon your couches; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; who sing to the sound of the psaltery. Like David, they thought they had vessels for song, drinking wine from bowls and anointing themselves with the finest ointment, and they suffered nothing over the ruin of Joseph” (Amos 6:1–6).

Would those people who, as though learned and eloquent, despise our prophets as uneducated and ignorant of expression, if they had had to say something like this or against people like these, have wished to say it differently—provided they did not wish to rave like them?

### 17

What is there in this eloquence that sober ears could desire more? First, how forcefully the very denunciation strikes, as though to awaken sleeping senses:

“Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and put your trust in Mount Samaria, nobles, heads of the peoples, entering the house of Israel with pomp!”

Then, wishing to show them ungrateful for the benefits of God, who had given them broad expanses of kingdom because they trusted in Mount Samaria, where idols were certainly worshiped, he says:

“Cross over to Calneh and see; go from there to great Hamath, and descend to Gath of the Philistines, and to the best of these kingdoms, if their territory is wider than your territory.”

At the same time, while these things are being said, the eloquence is adorned as though by lights through the names of places: Zion, Samaria, Calneh, great Hamath, and Gath of the Philistines.

Then the words attached to these places are varied most fittingly: “you are wealthy,” “you trust,” “cross over,” “go,” “descend.”

### 18

In due sequence, captivity under an unjust king is announced as approaching when he adds:

“You who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the throne of iniquity.”

Then the practices of luxury are set forth:

“You who sleep on ivory beds and lounge upon your couches; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd.”

These six members produced three two-member periods. For he does not say:

“You who are set apart for the evil day; you who draw near to the throne of iniquity; you who sleep on ivory beds; you who lounge upon your couches; you who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd.”

If it were said in that way, it would indeed also be beautiful, since six individual members would flow from the repeated pronoun and each would be completed by the speaker’s voice. But it was made more beautiful by attaching two members to the same pronoun, so that they expressed three sentences:

One concerning the prediction of captivity: “You who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the throne of iniquity”;

another concerning lust: “You who sleep on ivory beds and lounge upon your couches”;

and a third concerning gluttony: “You who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd.”

The speaker is thus free either to end each phrase individually, making six members, or to suspend his voice after the first, third, and fifth, joining the second to the first, the fourth to the third, and the sixth to the fifth, and thereby forming three most elegant two-member periods: one displaying the impending calamity, one the impure couch, and one the lavish table.

### 19

Then he attacks the luxurious pleasure of their ears. After saying, “You who sing to the sound of the psaltery”—since music can be practiced wisely by wise people—he relaxes the force of his denunciation with a marvelous beauty of expression and, no longer speaking to them but about them, reminds us to distinguish the music of the wise from the music of the luxurious.

He does not say, “You who sing to the sound of the psaltery and think that you have vessels for song, like David.” Rather, having said to them what the luxurious ought to hear, “You who sing to the sound of the psaltery,” he also indicated their ignorance to others, adding:

“Like David, they thought they had vessels for song, drinking wine from bowls and anointing themselves with the finest ointment.”

These three phrases are better delivered if the first two members are suspended in a period and the third brings it to completion.

### 20

What is added to all this—“and they suffered nothing over the ruin of Joseph”—may either be spoken continuously as one member, or, more elegantly, be suspended after “and they suffered nothing,” with “over the ruin of Joseph” introduced after the pause, so that it becomes a two-member period.

With marvelous beauty he did not say, “They suffered nothing over the ruin of their brother,” but instead put “Joseph” in place of “brother,” so that every brother might be signified by the name of one whose reputation among his brothers is illustrious, whether because of the evils he endured or because of the good things he returned.

This trope, in which Joseph is understood to mean any brother, I do not know whether it is taught in the art that we have learned and taught. How beautiful it is, however, and how it affects readers and those who understand, need not be explained to anyone who does not himself feel it.

### 21

Many more features belonging to the rules of eloquence can indeed be found in this very passage, which we have set forth as an example. But it instructs a good listener less when it is carefully dissected than when it is ardently delivered.

For these things were not composed by human industry, but poured forth by a divine mind, both wisely and eloquently—not with wisdom intent upon eloquence, but with eloquence that does not depart from wisdom. If, as certain highly eloquent and acute men have been able to see and say, the things learned as though through the art of oratory would not have been observed and noted, nor reduced to this discipline, unless they had first been discovered in the minds of orators, what wonder is it if they are also found in these authors whom the one who creates minds sent?

Therefore let us acknowledge that our canonical authors and teachers were eloquent as well as wise, with an eloquence of the kind suited to persons of this sort [Note: Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and seven manuscripts read *tali eloquentia usos* (“that they used such eloquence”).].

## CHAPTER VIII

The obscurity of the sacred authors, although eloquent, is not to be imitated by Christian teachers.

### 22

Although we take some examples of expression from their writings—those passages that are understood without difficulty—we must by no means think that we should imitate them in those passages where, in order to exercise and refine the minds of readers, to break their weariness, and to sharpen the eagerness of those wishing to learn, they spoke with a useful and salutary obscurity, concealing the minds of the impious, whether so that they might be converted to piety or so that they might be excluded from the mysteries.

They spoke in such a way that later generations, who rightly understood and expounded them, would find in the Church of God another grace—different, certainly, but nevertheless subsequent. Their interpreters, therefore, ought not to speak as though they themselves were presenting themselves for interpretation with similar authority. Rather, in all their discourses they should strive first and foremost to be understood, with as much clarity of expression as possible, so that either the person who does not understand is exceptionally slow, or the obstacle lies in the difficulty and subtlety of the matters we wish to explain and display, not in our manner of speaking, which prevents or delays understanding.

## CHAPTER IX

Where and how difficult matters are to be treated.

### 23

There are certain things that cannot be understood, or can scarcely be understood, by their own force, no matter how much or how often they are treated in the speaker’s eloquence, even if he speaks with complete clarity. Such matters should be brought before the hearing of the people either rarely, when some urgent need requires it, or never at all.

But in books written so that, when understood, they hold the reader by themselves, as it were, and, when not understood, are not burdensome to those who wish to read; and in conversations with certain people [Note: Earlier editions read: “when they are understood, they are not burdensome to those wishing to read; when they are not understood, they are not burdensome to those unwilling to read. And in conversations with certain people …” With the help of the manuscripts, we have freed this passage from an inept gloss and faulty punctuation, which separated from one another the parts of this proposition: “But in books … this duty must not be abandoned.”], this duty must not be abandoned: if the hearer or interlocutor is held by a desire to learn and possesses sufficient mental capacity to receive what is conveyed in some manner, we should bring to the understanding of others truths that we ourselves have already grasped, however difficult they may be to understand, with whatever labor of discussion is required.

The teacher should not be concerned with how eloquently he teaches, but with how clearly.

## CHAPTER X

The pursuit of clarity in speaking.

### 24

A diligent desire for this clarity sometimes neglects more polished words and does not care what sounds good, but what clearly indicates and conveys what one intends to show. Hence someone, speaking about this kind of expression, said that it contains a certain “careful negligence” (Cicero, *Orator*).

Yet this removes ornament in such a way that it does not become shabby. Indeed, good teachers have, or ought to have, such concern for teaching that a word which cannot be Latin without being obscure or ambiguous, but which in popular usage is spoken so as to avoid ambiguity and obscurity, should be spoken not as the learned customarily speak, but rather as the unlearned do.

For if our translators were not ashamed to say, “I will not gather their assemblies from bloods” (Ps. 15:4), because they judged it relevant that the word be expressed in the plural at that point, although in Latin it is used only in the singular, why should a teacher of piety be ashamed, when speaking to the unlearned, to say *ossum* rather than *os* (“bone” rather than “mouth”), lest this syllable be understood as referring not to bones but to mouths, when African ears do not distinguish between shortened and lengthened vowels?

What benefit is there in correctness of expression if it is not followed by the listener’s understanding? There is no reason to speak at all if those for whose understanding we speak do not understand what we say.

Therefore, the teacher will avoid every word that does not teach; and if he can use in its place another correct word that is understood, he will choose that one. But if he cannot—whether because such a word does not exist or because it does not occur to him at the moment—he will use even less correct words, provided that the matter itself is taught and learned correctly.

### 25

This principle applies not only in conversations, whether with one person or with several, but much more when a sermon is delivered before a crowd: one must strive to be understood.

In conversation, each person has the opportunity to ask questions. But when everyone is silent so that one person may be heard, and all turn their attentive faces toward him, it is neither customary nor seemly for each person to ask about what he has not understood. Therefore the speaker’s care must especially come to the aid of the silent listener.

A crowd eager to understand usually indicates by its movements whether it has understood. Until it gives that indication, the subject must be handled through many kinds of variation in expression—something those who deliver prepared and memorized words cannot control.

As soon as it is clear that the matter has been understood, the discourse must either end or move on to something else. For just as the person who dispels obscurity from what is to be learned is welcome, so the person who repeats what is already known is burdensome—except to those whose entire expectation depended upon resolving the difficulty of what was being explained.

Known things are also spoken for the sake of delight, when attention is directed not to the things themselves but to the manner in which they are said. If that manner too is already familiar and pleases the hearers, it makes almost no difference whether the speaker is a reciter or a reader.

Things that have been well written are often read pleasantly not only by those to whom they first become known, but also reread with pleasure by those to whom they are already familiar and from whose memory oblivion has not yet erased them; or they are gladly heard by both groups.

When something has been forgotten, a person is taught when reminded of it. But I am not now discussing the manner of pleasing; I am speaking about the manner in which those who wish to learn should be taught. The best manner is that by which the listener hears the truth and understands what he hears.

Once this goal has been reached, one should no longer labor over the matter itself as though it still required teaching, though perhaps one may commend it so that it may be fixed in the heart. If that seems necessary, it should be done modestly, lest weariness result.

## CHAPTER XI

Why one who strives to teach should speak clearly, but not without pleasantness.

### 26

This is precisely the eloquence proper to teaching: through speech it brings about not that what was dreaded becomes pleasing, or that what was disliked gets done, but that what was hidden becomes apparent.

If this is done without pleasantness, its proper benefit reaches only a few exceptionally devoted students, who desire to know what must be learned even when it is expressed meanly and without refinement. Once they have attained it, they are nourished delightfully by the truth itself. It is a mark of good minds to love the truth in words, not the words themselves.

What use is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish to open? Or what harm is there in a wooden one if it can? We seek nothing except that what is closed may be opened.

But because those who eat and those who learn have some similarity to one another, and because of the distastefulness felt by many, even the food without which one cannot live must be seasoned.

## CHAPTER XII

It is the orator’s task to teach, delight, and move, according to Cicero, *On the Orator*. How he should accomplish these three things.

### 27

A certain eloquent man spoke—and spoke truly—when he said that the eloquent speaker ought to speak so as to teach, delight, and move. He then added: “Teaching is a matter of necessity, delight of pleasantness, and moving of victory” (Cicero, *On the Orator*).

Of these three, the first—namely, the necessity of teaching—is established in the matters we discuss; the other two lie in the manner in which we speak.

Therefore, when someone speaks in order to teach, he should not think that he has said what he wishes to say to the person whom he wishes to teach for as long as he is not understood. For even if he has said what he himself understands, he should not yet be considered to have said it to the person by whom it has not been understood. But if it has been understood, then, however he said it, he has said it.

If he also wishes to delight or move the person to whom he speaks, he will not accomplish this by speaking in just any manner; the manner of speaking matters. Just as the listener must be delighted in order to keep him listening, so he must be moved in order to impel him to action.

He is delighted if you speak pleasantly; he is moved if he loves what you promise, fears what you threaten, hates what you condemn, embraces what you commend, grieves over what you emphasize as grievous, rejoices when you proclaim what should bring joy, pities those whom you set before his eyes in speech as deserving pity, flees those whom you present in a terrifying manner as people to be avoided, and responds in whatever other way great eloquence can move the minds of listeners—not so that they may know what ought to be done, but so that they may do what they already know ought to be done.

### 28

If they do not yet know, they must of course first be taught before they are moved. Perhaps, once they have learned the facts themselves, they will be moved in such a way that there will be no need to move them further with greater force of eloquence.

Nevertheless, when this is necessary, it must be done. It is necessary when people know what ought to be done but do not do it. Thus teaching is a matter of necessity. People can do, or fail to do, what they know. But who would say that they ought to do what they do not know?

Moving, therefore, is not a matter of necessity, because it is not always needed if the listener merely agrees with the teacher or even takes delight in him.
