It is a matter of victory because someone may be taught and delighted yet not assent. What benefit would the other two provide if this third were lacking?

Nor is delight a matter of necessity. When truths are displayed through speech—which belongs to the duty of teaching—the speech itself need not be made an object of attention or enjoyment. The truths, once manifested because they are true, delight by themselves.

Thus even falsehoods, once exposed and refuted, often delight. They do not delight because they are false, but because it is true that they are false; and the expression by which this truth has been demonstrated is also pleasing.

## CHAPTER XIII

The mind is finally moved by speaking.

### 29

For those who are disgusted by the truth and do not like it unless it is expressed in some manner that makes the speaker’s discourse itself pleasing, eloquence has also been given a considerable place for delight.

Yet this addition is not enough for the hard-hearted, for whom neither understanding nor delight in the teacher’s expression has been of benefit. What do these two things contribute to a person who acknowledges the truth and praises the eloquence, yet does not incline his assent—the very thing toward which the speaker’s attention is directed when something is being urged?

If matters are taught that require only belief or knowledge, consenting to them means nothing other than confessing that they are true. But when something is taught that ought to be done, and it is taught so that it may be done, it is useless to persuade someone that what is said is true, and useless for the manner of speaking itself to please, if the lesson is not learned in such a way that it is acted upon.

Therefore, when an ecclesiastical speaker urges something that ought to be done, he must not only teach in order to instruct and delight in order to hold the listener, but also move in order to conquer. The person in whom demonstrated truth, joined with pleasant expression, has not accomplished this task up to the point of acknowledgment still remains to be moved toward assent by the grandeur of eloquence.

## CHAPTER XIV

The pleasantness of expression should be proportioned to the subject of the argument.

### 30

Human beings have devoted so much effort to this pleasantness that they repeatedly read, solely for the sake of delight, so many great evils and shameful things—evils and shameful things persuasively presented with the utmost eloquence—which ought not merely not to be done but avoided and detested.

May God avert from his Church what the prophet Jeremiah records concerning the synagogue of the Jews:

“Dread and horrible things have occurred upon the earth: the prophets prophesied wickedness, and the priests applauded with their hands, and my people loved it so. And what will you do in the future?” (Jer. 5:30–31).

O eloquence, all the more terrible the purer it is, and all the more vehement the more solid! O true axe cutting through rocks! God himself said through this same prophet that his word, which he spoke through the holy prophets, would be like this (Jer. 46:22).

Therefore, far be it from us—far be it—that priests should applaud those who speak wickedness and that God’s people should love it so. Far be it from us, I say, that such madness should prevail. For what shall we do in the future?

Let what is said be understood less, please less, and move less; nevertheless, let it be said. And let what is just—not what is wicked—be willingly heard [Note: The manuscripts of better quality read this way. The printed editions have: “but let true and just things nevertheless be spoken.”]. This would certainly not happen unless it were spoken pleasantly.

### 31

But among the serious people of whom it is said to God, “Among a serious people I will praise you” (Ps. 34:18), even that pleasantness is not delightful by which small and fragile goods are adorned with a frothy abundance of words—not wicked things, certainly, but goods that would not be appropriately or gravely adorned in such a manner if they were great and enduring.

There is something of this sort in a letter of the blessed Cyprian. I think it either happened accidentally or was done deliberately so that posterity might know how the soundness of Christian teaching recalled its language from this excess and restrained it toward a more serious and moderate eloquence—an eloquence that can safely be loved and religiously desired in his later writings, but is fulfilled only with the greatest difficulty.

In one passage he says:

“Let us seek this seat: the neighboring retreats grant seclusion; where, while the wandering slips of vines creep through the supporting reeds in hanging interlacements, they have made a vine-covered portico under a leafy roof” (Cyprian, *Letter 1 to Donatus*).

Such words are spoken only through an astonishingly overflowing abundance of eloquence, but their excessive profusion displeases seriousness. Those who love this style naturally think that people who do not speak in this way but express themselves more chastely are unable to speak so, and avoid such language not by judgment.

Therefore this holy man demonstrated that he could speak in this manner, since he did so somewhere, and that he did not wish to, since afterward he did so nowhere.

## CHAPTER XV

The ecclesiastical teacher should pray to God before preaching.

32. Our eloquent speaker, then, when he says what is just, holy, and good—for he ought to say nothing else—does everything in his power, when saying these things, to be heard intelligently, willingly, and obediently. Let him not doubt that, if he can and insofar as he can, he is able to do this more through the devotion of his prayers than through the ability of an orator; by praying for himself and for those whom he is about to address, let him be an orator before he becomes a speaker. When he approaches the very moment of speaking, before he brings forth his uttering tongue, let him lift his thirsting soul to God, so that he may pour out what he has drunk or what has filled him.

Since, concerning every matter that must be treated according to faith and love [Note: [Col. 0103] Printed editions have *delectationemque*, “and delight”; the better manuscripts have *dilectionemque*, “and love.”], there are many things that can be said, and many ways in which they can be said by those who understand these matters, who knows what it is appropriate for us to say at the present moment, or what it is appropriate for the hearers to hear through us, except the one who sees the hearts of all? And who causes us to say what ought to be said, and in the way it ought to be said, except the one in whose hand are both we and our words (Wis. 7:16)?

Accordingly, let the person who wishes both to know and to teach learn everything that must be taught, and acquire the ability to speak as befits an ecclesiastical man. At the actual moment of speaking, however, let him think rather that what accords with a good mind is what the Lord says: “Do not consider how or what you are to speak; for what you are to speak will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19–20). If, then, the Holy Spirit speaks in those who are handed over to persecutors for Christ’s sake, why should he not also speak in those who hand Christ over to learners?

## CHAPTER XVI — The precepts of teaching are not given needlessly by a human being, even though God makes teachers.

33. Whoever says that human beings should not be instructed concerning what or how they are to teach, if the Holy Spirit makes them teachers, may also say that we ought not to pray, because the Lord says, “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (ibid. 6:8); or that the apostle Paul ought not to have instructed Timothy and Titus concerning what or how they should instruct others.

Anyone who has been assigned the role of teacher in the Church ought to keep these three Apostolic Epistles before his eyes. Is it not written in the First Epistle to Timothy: “Announce and teach these things” (1 Tim. 4:11)? What these things are has been stated above. Is it not written there: “Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father” (ibid. 5:1)? Is he not told in the Second Epistle: “Hold the pattern of sound words which you have heard from me” (2 Tim. 1:13)? Is he not told there: “Be diligent to present yourself approved to God, a worker who does not need to be ashamed, handling the word of truth rightly” (ibid. 2:15)? There too is the instruction: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and teaching” (ibid. 4:2).

And in the Epistle to Titus, does he not say that a bishop must adhere to the faithful word according to the teaching, so that he may be powerful in sound doctrine and able to refute those who contradict it (Tit. 1:9)? There also he says: “But speak what accords with sound doctrine: that older men are to be sober” (ibid. 2:1–2), and what follows. There too is the instruction: “Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you” (ibid. 15). “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities” (ibid. 3:1), and so forth.

What, then, are we to think? Does the Apostle contradict himself when, although he says that teachers are made through the activity of the Holy Spirit, he himself instructs them concerning what and how they should teach? Or should we understand that, with the same Holy Spirit bestowing human responsibilities, human instruction must not cease even in the teaching of teachers themselves—and yet that neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth (1 Cor. 3:7)?

Therefore, even when holy human ministers, or even holy angels, are at work, no one rightly learns what pertains to living with God unless he is made teachable by God for God [Note: [Col. 0104] The common editions omit *Deo*, “for God”; the manuscripts contain it, as they also contain *nec superfluo*, “nor needlessly.”], to whom it is said in the Psalm: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God” (Ps. 142:10). Hence the Apostle says the same thing to Timothy, speaking, of course, to a disciple who is a teacher: “But continue in the things which you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them” (2 Tim. 3:14).

For just as medicines for the body, administered to human beings by human beings, benefit only those for whom God works salvation—he who can heal without them, although they can do nothing without him—and yet they are administered, and, when this is done dutifully, it is counted among works of mercy or benevolence, so also the aids of teaching, when administered through a human being, benefit the soul only when God works so that they may benefit it. Yet God could have given the Gospel to a human being even without human beings and without a human intermediary.

## CHAPTER XVII — The threefold manner of speaking belongs to teaching, delighting, and moving.

34. Whoever endeavors by speaking to persuade people of what is good, despising none of these three aims—namely, teaching, delighting, and moving—should pray and act so that, as we said above, he may be heard intelligently, willingly, and obediently. When he does this suitably and appropriately, he may rightly be called eloquent, even if the assent of the hearer does not follow.

These three aims—teaching, delighting, and moving—are apparently also what that same author of Roman eloquence intended by the following three styles when he said: “He, then, will be eloquent who can speak of small matters in a subdued manner, of moderate matters in a temperate manner, and of great matters in a grand manner” (Cicero, *On the Orator* [*De Oratore*]). It is as though he had added those other three and explained one and the same idea in this way: He will be eloquent who, in order to teach, can speak of small matters in a subdued manner; in order to delight, of moderate matters in a temperate manner; and in order to move, of great matters in a grand manner.

## CHAPTER XVIII — The ecclesiastical orator is always engaged with a grand subject.

35. Cicero could have illustrated these three styles, as he described them, in forensic cases; but not here—that is, in ecclesiastical questions, which are the subject of the speech of the person we wish to form.

In forensic cases, those matters are called small in which judgments concern money; great, where the safety or life of human beings is at issue; while those cases in which neither of these is to be judged, and nothing is being done in order that the judge may act or decide, but only in order that the hearer may be entertained, were called intermediate and therefore moderate—that is, temperate. For *moderate* derives its name from *measure*; we use *moderate* for *small* improperly, not strictly.

In our matters, however, since everything—and especially what we say to the people from an elevated place—must be referred to the salvation of human beings, not temporal but eternal, and since eternal destruction must also be avoided, everything we say is great. So much so that even concerning monetary matters, whether acquiring or losing them, what the ecclesiastical teacher says should not be regarded as small, whether the sum of money is great or small.

For justice is not small; indeed, we ought to preserve it even in a small amount of money, since the Lord says: “The one who is faithful in the least is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). What is least is therefore least; but to be faithful in what is least is great. For just as the principle of roundness—that all lines drawn from the center to the circumference should be equal—is the same in a large disk as in a tiny coin, so when small matters are handled justly, the greatness of justice is not diminished.

36. Finally, when the Apostle was speaking about secular lawsuits—which surely concerned monetary matters—he said:

“Does any one of you, having a dispute with another, dare to be judged by the unrighteous, and not by the saints? Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we shall judge angels, to say nothing of secular affairs? If, then, you have secular lawsuits, appoint those who are despised in the Church to judge” [Note: [Col. 0105] The manuscripts have *collocate*, “appoint”; and almost all omit *ad judicandum*, “to judge,” which is also absent from the Greek text of the Apostle.]. “I say this to your shame. Is there no wise person among you who can judge between his brothers? But brother goes to law against brother—and this before unbelievers. In any case, it is already a complete failure in you that you have lawsuits among yourselves. Why not rather suffer injustice? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves do injustice and defraud—and this to your brothers” [Note: [Col. 0105] Five manuscripts have *et hoc apud fratres*, “and this before brothers.” Three others have *et hoc fratribus*, “and this to brothers.”]. “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?” (1 Cor. 6:1–9).

What is the reason that the Apostle is so indignant, so sharply reproves, so reproaches, so rebukes, and so threatens? What is the reason that he testifies to the emotion of his mind through such frequent and harsh changes of tone? Finally, what is the reason that he speaks so grandly about such small matters? Have secular lawsuits deserved so much from him? Certainly not. Rather, he does this on account of justice, love, and devotion, which, as no sober mind can doubt, are great even in matters of whatever smallness.

37. Certainly, if we were advising people how they should conduct secular lawsuits on their own behalf or on behalf of their relatives before ecclesiastical judges, we would properly advise them to conduct them as small matters, in a subdued manner. But when we are discussing the eloquence of the man whom we wish to make a teacher of those matters by which we are delivered from eternal evils and attain eternal goods, wherever these matters are discussed—whether before the people or privately, whether to one person or to many, whether to friends or enemies, whether in a continuous speech or in conversation, whether in treatises or books, whether in very long or very short letters—they are great.

Unless, perhaps, because a cup of cold water is a very small and worthless thing, the Lord therefore said that it was something small and worthless, so that the one who gave it to his disciple would not lose his reward (Matt. 10:42); or unless, when this teacher in the Church makes a speech about it, he ought to think that he is saying something small, and therefore that he should speak not in a temperate or grand manner, but in a subdued manner.

When it happened that we were speaking to the people about this matter, and God was present so that we spoke appropriately, did not a kind of flame rise from that cold water (2 Macc. 1:32), one that would kindle even the cold breasts of human beings to perform works of mercy through hope of heavenly reward?

## CHAPTER XIX — A different style of speaking must be used for different purposes.

38. Although this teacher ought to be a speaker about great matters, he should not always speak of them in a grand manner. He should speak in a subdued manner when something is being taught, and in a temperate manner when something is being blamed or praised. But when something must be done and we are speaking to those who ought to do it but are unwilling, then great matters must be spoken of grandly, in a manner suited to moving their minds.

Sometimes one and the same great matter is spoken of in a subdued manner when it is being taught, in a temperate manner when it is being praised, and in a grand manner when a mind turned away from it is driven to turn back.

For what is greater than God himself? Is he therefore not to be taught? Or when someone teaches the unity of the Trinity, ought he to proceed in any way except by subdued argument, so that a matter difficult to discern may, insofar as possible, be understood? Are ornaments being sought here rather than instruction? Is the hearer to be moved in order to make him do something, rather than instructed so that he may learn?

Moreover, when God is praised, whether for himself or for his works, what a display of beautiful and splendid speech arises in one who can praise him as much as he can—him whom no one praises adequately, yet no one fails to praise in some manner! But if he is not worshiped, or if idols, demons, or any created thing are worshiped alongside him or even before him, how great an evil this is, and how grandly it must be said so that people may be turned away from this evil.

## CHAPTER XX — Examples from Sacred Scripture, first of subdued speech, then of temperate speech, and finally of grand speech: all three from Paul’s Epistles.

39. An example of subdued speech is found in the Apostle Paul, to mention something especially clear, where he says:

“Tell me, you who desire to be under the Law, do you not hear the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through the promise. These things are an allegory. For these women are two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem that now exists, and she is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:21–26), and so forth.

Likewise, when he reasons and says:

“Brothers, I speak in human terms: even a humanly ratified covenant no one annuls or adds conditions to. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say, ‘And to offsprings,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘And to your offspring,’ who is Christ. This is what I mean: the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to cancel the promise. For if the inheritance comes from the Law, it no longer comes from the promise. But God granted it to Abraham through the promise.”

And because the question might occur to the hearer’s mind, “Why, then, was the Law given, if the inheritance does not come from it?” he raised the objection himself and said, as though asking: “Why, then, the Law?” Then he answered: “It was established because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, arranged through angels by the hand of a mediator” [Note: [Col. 0107] Most manuscripts have *dispositum*, “arranged,” rather than *disposita*.]. “Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one.”

Here too the question arose which he himself proposed: “Is the Law, then, against the promises of God?” And he answered: “Certainly not.” Then he gave the reason, saying: “For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly come from the Law. But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ,” and so forth (Gal. 3:15–22), or something of that kind.

The responsibility of teaching therefore includes not only opening what is closed and solving the knots of questions, but also, while this is being done, anticipating other questions that may perhaps arise, lest through them what we are saying be rejected or refuted—provided that the solution to those questions also presents itself at the same time, lest we raise a question that we cannot remove.

It happens, however, that when other questions arise within a question, and still others arise within those questions, and all are treated and solved, the attention is extended into such a lengthy chain of reasoning that, unless the memory is exceptionally strong and active, the disputant cannot return to the point from which the discussion began.

It is nevertheless very good that whatever can be objected, if it occurs to us, should be refuted, lest it occur where no one will be present to answer it; or lest it occur to someone who is present but silent, and he depart less completely healed.

40. The following apostolic words, however, are temperate in style:

“Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters” (1 Tim. 5:1–2).

And also:

“I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.”

Almost the whole passage of this exhortation has a temperate style of expression. Its most beautiful features are those in which corresponding things proceed gracefully, each being appropriately assigned to its counterpart, as in the following:

“Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, according to the measure of faith; whether ministry, in serving; whether one who teaches, in teaching; whether one who exhorts, in exhortation; one who gives, in simplicity; one who presides, with diligence; one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

“Love without hypocrisy; hating evil, clinging to what is good; loving one another with brotherly affection; anticipating one another in honor; not sluggish in diligence; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord; rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; persistent in prayer; sharing in the needs of the saints; pursuing hospitality.

“Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep; having the same mind toward one another” (Rom. 12:1, 6–16).

And how beautifully all these flowing statements are brought to an end by a two-member period: “Not being wise in high things, but consenting to the humble.”

A little later he says:

“Persevering in this, render to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is due; tax to whom tax is due; fear to whom fear is due; honor to whom honor is due.”

These statements, spread out in separate members, are likewise closed by a period formed of two members: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another.”

A little afterward:

“The night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in reveling and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and sexual impurity, not in quarrels and jealousy; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:6–8, 12–14).

If someone were to say, “And do not make provision for the flesh in its desires,” he would undoubtedly delight the ears with a more rhythmical closing. But the more serious translator preferred to preserve the order of the words. How this sounds in the Greek eloquence in which the Apostle spoke, let those more learned in that eloquence determine. To me, however, what has been translated for us in the same order of words does not seem to flow rhythmically even there.

41. Certainly, it must be acknowledged that this ornament of expression, which is produced by rhythmical endings, is lacking in our authors. Whether this happened through the translators, or whether—as I am more inclined to think—they deliberately avoided such applause-winning effects, I do not dare to affirm, since I confess that I do not know.

I do know this: if someone skilled in such rhythm were to arrange their clauses according to the same rules of rhythm—which is very easily done by changing certain words that have the same meaning, or by changing the order of the words he finds—he would recognize that those divine men lacked none of the things which he himself had learned in the schools of grammarians or rhetoricians as if they were great [Col. 0109]. He would also find many forms of expression of such great beauty, which are elegant in our language but especially beautiful in their own language; none of these is found in the writings by which those people are puffed up.

But care must be taken lest, when rhythm is added to divine and weighty statements, their weight be taken away. For the discipline of music, in which this rhythm is learned most fully, was not lacking in our prophets. Indeed, the very learned Jerome records the meters of some of them, at least in the Hebrew language (Jerome, Preface to the Book of Job). To preserve the truth of the words, he did not translate these meters from it.

As for myself, to speak of my own judgment—which is necessarily better known to me than to others, and than that of others—I do not omit these rhythms of clauses in my own eloquence, insofar as I modestly judge that this can be done. Yet in our authors I prefer the fact that I find them there exceedingly rarely.

42. The grand style of speaking differs most of all from the temperate style in this respect: it is not so much adorned with verbal ornaments as driven by emotional force. It embraces almost all those ornaments, but if it lacks them, it does not seek them. It is carried forward by its own impulse, and if the beauty of expression happens to appear, it seizes it through the force of the subject matter rather than adopting it out of concern for elegance.

For it is enough for it, because of the matter at hand, that suitable words be chosen—not by the craft of the mouth, but that they follow the ardor of the heart. If a brave man is armed with a sword covered in gold and jewels, intent upon battle, he performs with those weapons what he performs not because they are costly but because they are weapons. Yet he remains the same man and is fully effective even when anger makes a weapon for him from whatever he finds while searching [Note: [Col. 0109] Lovaniensis has *rimanti telo mira facit*, “makes wonderful things for the searching weapon.” But the other editions and the manuscripts more correctly have *rimanti telum ira facit*, “anger makes a weapon for the one searching for it.” This is taken from Virgil, *Aeneid* 7:

“Here one armed with a fire-hardened trunk,

another with a heavy club knotted with branches:

whatever each found while searching,

anger made into a weapon.”]

The Apostle is acting so that, for the sake of evangelical ministry, all the evils of this present age may be endured patiently, with the consolation of God’s gifts. The subject is great, and it is treated grandly, nor are ornaments of speech lacking:

“Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. We give no offense in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed; but in everything we commend ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in imprisonments, in riots, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in purity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unhypocritical love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left [Note: [Col. 0109] Several manuscripts of excellent authority have *arma justitiae dextra et sinistra*, “weapons of righteousness, right and left.”]; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful; as unknown and yet recognized; as dying, and behold, we live; as disciplined and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.”

Observe him still burning:

“Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:2–11), and so forth, which it would be lengthy to pursue.

43. Likewise, in the Epistle to the Romans he acts so that the persecutions of this world may be conquered by love, through certain hope in God’s help. He acts both grandly and ornamentally:

“We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose” [Note: [Col. 0110] The printed editions have *vocati sunt sancti*, “who are called saints,” and a little later *conformes fieri*, “to be made conformed.” The manuscripts lack the words *sancti* and *fieri*, which Augustine commonly omits and which are absent from the Greek text.]. “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.

“What, then, shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how will he not also give us everything with him? Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies? Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—more than that, who was raised—who is at the right hand of God and also intercedes for us?

“Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter’ (Ps. 43:22). But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us.

“For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, neither powers, neither height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:28–39).

44. Although the whole Epistle to the Galatians is written in a subdued style, except in its final sections, where the expression is temperate, it nevertheless inserts a passage in which the emotion of the mind is so moved that it could not be spoken except grandly, even without any of the ornaments found in the passages we have just presented:

“You observe days, months, seasons, and years. I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you for no purpose” [Note: [Col. 0110] The printed editions have *in vobis*, “among you.” The manuscripts have *in vos*, “toward you,” in accordance with the Greek *eis hymas*.].

“Become as I am, because I also am as you are. Brothers, I entreat you; you have done me no wrong. You know that it was because of an infirmity of the flesh that I first preached the Gospel to you, and you did not despise or reject your trial [Note: [Col. 0110] Most manuscripts have *et tentationem vestram*, “and your trial.”] in my flesh; but you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus. What, then, has become of your blessedness? For I bear you witness that, if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth? They are zealous for you, but not rightly; rather, they wish to exclude you so that you may be zealous for them. It is always good to be zealous for what is good, and not only when I am present with you. My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you, I wish that I could now be present with you and change my voice, because I am perplexed about you” (Gal. 4:10–20).

Are contrary words here set against contrary words? Are any linked to one another by a progression? Do any clauses or members or periods resound? And yet the grand emotion through which we feel the speech burning is not therefore lukewarm.

## CHAPTER XXI — Examples of these three kinds of speech are taken from ecclesiastical teachers, namely Cyprian and Ambrose.

[Col. 0111]

45. These apostolic passages are so clear and yet so profound; they have been composed and committed to memory in such a way that they require not only a reader or hearer but also an interpreter, if someone seeks depth in them and is not content with their surface. Let us therefore examine these styles of speaking in those who, through reading these authors, advanced in knowledge of divine and saving matters and ministered that knowledge to the Church.

The blessed Cyprian uses the subdued style in the book in which he discusses the sacrament of the cup. A question is settled there: whether the Lord’s cup ought to contain water alone or water mixed with wine.

For the sake of an example, something from that work should be presented. After the beginning of the letter, when he begins to resolve the proposed question, he says:

“Know that we have been admonished that, in offering the cup, the Lord’s tradition must be observed, and that we must do nothing other than what the Lord first did for us, so that the cup offered in his remembrance may be offered mixed with wine.

“For when Christ says, ‘I am the true vine’ (John 15:5), the blood of Christ is certainly not water but wine. Nor can his blood, by which we have been redeemed and given life, be regarded as present in the cup when the wine is absent from the cup by which Christ’s blood is manifested—the blood proclaimed by the sacramental meaning and testimony of all the Scriptures.

“For we find in Genesis that this same thing was foreshadowed in connection with the sacrament of Noah, and that a figure of the Lord’s passion was set forth there: he drank wine, he became drunk, he was uncovered in his house, and he lay there with his thighs naked and exposed; that the nakedness of that father was indicated by the middle son, while it was covered by the elder and the younger” (Gen. 9:20–23), and the rest, which there is no need to pursue, since it is enough to grasp this one point: Noah, displaying a type of the future reality, drank not water but wine, and thus expressed an image of the Lord’s passion.

“Likewise, in the priest Melchizedek we see the Lord’s sacrament prefigured [Note: [Col. 0111] Thus in the manuscripts. Earlier editions have: “we see the mystery of the Lord’s sacrament prefigured.” In Cyprian, however, the reading is: “the sacrament of the Lord’s sacrifice.”], as divine Scripture testifies and says: ‘And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High, and he blessed Abraham’ (Gen. 14:18).

“That Melchizedek bore a type of Christ, the Holy Spirit declares in the Psalms, speaking from the person of the Father to the Son: ‘Before the morning star I begot you. You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’ (Ps. 109:4).”

These and the other passages that follow in this letter (Cyprian, *Letter 63 to Caecilius, On the Sacrament of the Cup*) preserve the manner of subdued speech, as readers can easily determine.

46. Saint Ambrose also uses the subdued style when treating a great subject, the Holy Spirit, in order to demonstrate that he is equal to the Father and the Son. The matter undertaken requires not verbal ornaments or emotional agitation for moving minds, but instruction concerning the facts.

Thus, among other things, at the beginning of his work he says:

“Moved by Gideon’s oracle, when he heard that, although the thousands of the peoples were failing, the Lord would deliver his people from their enemies through one man, he offered a kid of the goats. According to the angel’s command, he placed its flesh and unleavened bread upon the rock and poured broth over them. As soon as the angel of God touched them with the tip of the staff he was carrying, fire burst from the rock, and thus the sacrifice that was being offered was consumed” (Judg. 6:11–21).

“By this sign it appears to have been declared that that rock represented a type of Christ’s body, because it is written: ‘They drank from the rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ’ (1 Cor. 10:4). This, of course, refers not to his divinity but to his flesh, which flooded the thirsty hearts of the peoples with the perpetual stream of its blood.

“Thus it was already declared in mystery that the Lord Jesus, crucified in his flesh, would abolish the sins of the whole world—not only sins committed in deeds but also the desires of souls.

“For the flesh of the kid refers to guilt, while the broth refers to the allurements of desires, as it is written: ‘The people desired an evil desire, and they said, “Who will feed us meat?”’ (Num. 11:4).

“When, therefore, the angel extended the staff and touched the rock from which fire came forth, he showed that the Lord’s flesh, filled with the divine Spirit, would burn away all the sins of the human condition. Hence the Lord also says: ‘I have come to cast fire upon the earth’ (Luke 12:49),” and so forth, in the passages in which he is chiefly concerned with teaching and proving the matter (Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, Book 1, Preface).

47. Cyprian’s praise of virginity is an example of the temperate style:

“Now our speech is addressed to virgins, whose care is all the greater because their glory is higher. They are the flower of ecclesiastical growth, the beauty and adornment of spiritual grace, a joyful product of praise and honor, a work whole and undefiled, the image of God corresponding to the holiness of the Lord, the more illustrious portion of Christ’s flock.

“Through them the Church rejoices, and in them the glorious fecundity of the mother Church flourishes abundantly. The more glorious [Note: [Col. 0112] Cyprian has *copiosa*, “abundant”; the manuscript of Fleury has *generosa*, “noble” or “generous.”] virginity becomes through its increase in number, the more the mother’s joy grows.

“And elsewhere, at the end of the letter, he says:

“‘Just as we have borne the image of the one who is from the dust, so let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven’ (1 Cor. 15:49). Virginity bears this image; integrity bears it; holiness and truth bear it. Those who remember God’s commands bear it, retaining justice with devotion; steadfast in faith, humble in fear, strong in every endurance, gentle in bearing injuries, ready to show mercy, united and harmonious in fraternal peace.

“You, good virgins, must observe, love, and fulfill each of these things. Since you are devoted to God and Christ, you precede the Lord, to whom you have consecrated yourselves, with the greater and better portion.

“Those advanced in years, provide instruction to the younger; those younger in age, offer service to the older and encouragement to your peers. Stir one another up through mutual exhortations; challenge your rivals to glory by examples of virtue. Endure bravely; advance spiritually; arrive happily. Only remember us when virginity begins to be honored in you” (Cyprian, *Treatise on the Conduct and Dress of Virgins*).

48. Ambrose likewise presents to professed virgins, in a temperate and ornate style, an example to imitate in their conduct. He says:

“She was a virgin, not only in body but also in mind, whose sincere affection no deceitful artifice corrupted; humble in heart, grave in speech, prudent in mind, sparing in speaking, more devoted to reading; placing her hope not in the uncertainty of riches but in the prayer of the poor; intent upon work, modest in conversation; accustomed to seek as the arbiter of her mind not a human being but God; harming no one, wishing well to all; rising before her elders, not envying those of her own age; fleeing ostentation, following reason, loving virtue.

“When did she ever offend her parents even by her expression? When did she disagree with her relatives? When did she despise the humble? When did she laugh at the weak? When did she avoid the needy? She was accustomed to visit gatherings of men only when mercy would not be ashamed of them and modesty would not pass them by.

“There was nothing harsh in her eyes, nothing bold in her words, nothing immodest in her conduct; no excessively languid gesture, no overly relaxed walk, no more wanton voice, so that the appearance of her body itself was an image of her mind and a representation of her integrity.

“For a good house ought to be recognized in its very vestibule, and at the first entrance it should show that no darkness is hidden within, just as the light of a lamp placed inside shines outward.

“Why should I describe the frugality of her food and the abundance of her duties, when the one exceeded nature and the other was almost lacking even to nature? There, no times were allowed to pass unused; here, days were doubled by fasting. And if at some point the desire for refreshment arose, the food usually at hand was enough to ward off death, not to provide indulgence” (Ambrose, *On Virgins*, Book 2, beginning), and so forth.

I have placed these passages here as an example of the temperate style for this reason: the purpose here is not to persuade those who have not yet vowed virginity to make such a vow, but to show what those who have already vowed it ought to be like.

But when the mind is to undertake so great and demanding a commitment, it must certainly be aroused and kindled by the grand style of speaking. The martyr Cyprian, however, wrote about the conduct of virgins, not about undertaking the purpose of virginity. This bishop, on the other hand, also kindles them to that purpose with grand eloquence.

49. But from what both of them did, I shall recall examples of elevated diction. For both inveighed against women who color—or rather discolor—their natural appearance with cosmetics. The earlier of the two, when dealing with this matter, said among other things:

“If some painter wished to mark out the face and appearance, and the bodily form, of a person with a lifelike color, and, once the likeness had been marked out, completed, and finished, another were to lay hands upon it in order to refashion what had already been formed and painted, as though he were a more skilled artist, the first artist’s grave injury and justified indignation would be apparent. Do you imagine that you will escape with impunity from the audacity of so improper an act, from offending God the creator? For, lest you be unchaste toward men and incestuous toward the lights through seductive adornments, by corrupting and violating what belongs to God you are accounted worse than an adulteress. What you think adorns you, what you think beautifies you, is an attack upon the divine work; it is a transgression against truth.

“The Apostle’s admonishing voice says: ‘Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth’ (1 Corinthians 5:7–8). Does sincerity endure, and truth, when what is sincere is polluted, and true things are changed into falsehood by adulterations of colors and by the disguises of cosmetics?”

[Col. 0114]

Your Lord says, “You cannot make one hair white or black” (Matthew 5:36); and you wish to prove yourself more powerful than the word of your Lord. With audacious effort and sacrilegious contempt you dye your hair; with an evil foreboding of things to come, you already prophesy flaming hair for yourself (Cyprian, *Treatise on the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*).

[Note: [Col. 0114] Printed editions and manuscripts in Augustine read *et colorum adulterinis medicaminum* (“and by the adulterous cosmetics of colors”). We correct this from Cyprian’s book to *et colorum adulteriis, et medicaminum* (“both by adulterations of colors and by cosmetic disguises”).]

It would be too long to insert everything that follows.

50. The latter, in speaking against such women, says:

“Hence,” he says, “arise those incentives to vice, that they paint their faces with artificial colors, while they fear displeasing men and contemplate the adultery of chastity through the adultery of the face. What madness this is—to alter nature’s image, to seek a painting; and, while they fear a husband’s judgment, to betray their own! For the woman who desires to change what she was born as first pronounces judgment against herself: while she strives to please another, she first displeases herself.

“What judge of your ugliness, woman, shall we seek who is more truthful than yourself, since you fear being seen? If you are beautiful, why do you hide yourself? If you are ugly, why do you pretend to be beautiful, when you will possess neither the favor of your own conscience nor that of another’s mistaken judgment? For he loves one woman, while you wish to please another; and you become angry if the man who is being taught to commit adultery with you loves another.

“You are a bad teacher of your own injury. Even the woman who has endured a procurer refuses to play the procurer; and although she is a base woman, she sins not against another but against herself. Crimes in adultery are, in a way, more tolerable: there chastity is adulterated, here nature.”

[Note: [Col. 0114] So it stands in Ambrose. But in several Augustinian manuscripts: *perdere* (“to destroy”). In others: *perdidere* or *perdiderunt* (“they destroyed” / “they have destroyed”).]

As I think is sufficiently apparent, women are vehemently driven by this eloquence both toward shame and toward fear, so that they do not adulterate their natural appearance with cosmetics. Accordingly, we recognize in this discourse not a subdued or moderate style, but an altogether elevated one. In these two men whom I have wished to present from among all the others, as well as in other ecclesiastical writers who speak well and appropriately—that is, sharply, elegantly, and ardently, as the matter requires—these three styles may be found throughout many of their writings or speeches. Through constant reading or hearing, combined also with practice, they can grow familiar to those who devote themselves to them.

## CHAPTER XXII — Diction Must Be Varied among All the Styles

51. No one should suppose that mixing these styles is contrary to discipline. Rather, insofar as it can appropriately be done, diction should be varied among all the styles. For when a speech is prolonged in a single style, it holds the listener less effectively. But when there is a transition from one style to another, the speech proceeds more gracefully, even if it becomes longer. Each individual style, moreover, has its own variations in the speech of eloquent persons, by which the sensations of those who listen are prevented from growing cold or lukewarm.

Nevertheless, the subdued style alone can be endured for a longer time than the elevated style alone. For the more intensely the mind must be stirred so that the listener may agree with us, the less long can it be held in that state once it has been stirred as far as necessary. Therefore we must take care that, while we wish to raise still higher what has already been raised, it does not fall from the height to which it had been brought by the arousal.

When matters that should be stated more quietly have been inserted, one returns effectively to what needs to be said in an elevated manner, so that the force of the diction alternates like the swell of the sea. Hence, if the elevated style must be sustained for a longer time, it should not stand alone, but should be varied by the interposition of the other styles. Nevertheless, the whole speech is assigned to that style whose abundance predominates.

## CHAPTER XXIII — How the Styles of Diction Are to Be Intermingled

52. It matters which style is inserted into, or employed alongside, which other style, and in what definite and necessary places. For even in an elevated style, the beginnings should always, or almost always, be moderate. It is also within the power of an eloquent speaker to state somewhat quietly even things that could be said in an elevated manner, so that what is said with elevation may become more elevated by comparison with those quieter passages, and may be rendered brighter, as it were, by their shadows.

In whatever style certain knots of questions have to be untied, sharpness is required, and this belongs properly to the subdued style. Consequently, that style must also be used in the other two styles whenever such matters arise. Likewise, whenever something is to be praised or blamed, where neither anyone’s condemnation or acquittal nor assent to any action is required, but the matter occurs within some other style, the moderate style should be employed and inserted.

Thus, in the elevated style the other two styles find their proper places, and likewise in the subdued style. The moderate style, however, does not always—but does sometimes—need the subdued style, if, as I have said, a question whose knot must be untied should arise; or when certain matters that could be adorned are deliberately not adorned, but are stated in subdued speech, so that they may provide, as it were, certain cushions against which the ornaments can occupy a more prominent place.

The moderate style does not require elevated diction. For it is itself undertaken to delight minds, not to move them.

## CHAPTER XXIV — What the Sublime Style of Speaking Accomplishes

53. A speaker should not be thought to speak in an elevated manner merely because he is applauded frequently and vehemently. The sharpness of the subdued style and the ornaments of the moderate style can produce this as well. The elevated style, however, generally weighs down the voice by its own force, but draws out tears.

Thus, when I was dissuading the people of Caesarea in Mauretania from civil—or rather, more than civil—war, which they called the *Caterva* (for not only citizens, but also relatives, brothers, and finally parents and children, divided into two parties, used to fight one another with stones for several successive days at a fixed season of the year, and each killed anyone he could), I certainly spoke with elevation, as far as I was able, in order by speaking to tear out and drive away from their hearts and habits so cruel and long-established an evil.

Yet I did not think that I had accomplished anything when I heard them applauding, but when I saw them weeping. By their applause they indicated that they were instructed and delighted; by their tears, that they were moved. When I saw those tears, I believed that the monstrous custom handed down from their fathers and grandfathers, and from ancestors still more remote, which occupied—or rather possessed—their hearts like an enemy, had been defeated, even before they showed this in action.

As soon as my speech was finished, I turned their hearts and mouths toward giving thanks to God. And behold, it is now nearly eight years or more, by the favor of Christ, since anything of that kind has been attempted there.

[Col. 0116]

[Note: [Col. 0116] Thus this book was completed around the year 426. For Augustine’s intervention in Caesarea of Mauretania belongs to the year 418, according to Letters 190 and 193.1. At Caesarea, where he says that he had delivered that sermon eight or more years earlier, Saint Augustine was active in September of that same year 418, according to the book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*.]

There are also many other experiences by which we have learned that people have shown what the greatness of a wise speaker’s diction has accomplished in them not by shouting rather than groaning, sometimes even by tears, and finally by a change of life.

54. Many have also been changed by the subdued style of speaking; but it was so that they might know what they did not know, or believe what had seemed incredible to them—not so that they might do what they already knew ought to be done but did not wish to do.

To bend such hardness, therefore, one must speak with elevation. For when praise and blame are spoken eloquently, although they belong to the moderate style, they affect certain people in such a way that they are delighted not only by eloquence in praise and blame, but also desire to live laudably themselves and avoid living blameworthily.

But surely not all who are delighted are changed, just as all who are moved in the elevated style act; and in the subdued style, not all who are instructed know, or believe to be true, what they did not know?

[Note: [Col. 0116] Four manuscripts read *imitantur* (“imitate”).]

## CHAPTER XXV — To What End the Moderate Style of Speaking Should Be Directed

55. From this it follows that the two styles whose intended effect is described are especially necessary to those who wish to speak wisely and eloquently. But what is done in the moderate style—that eloquence itself should give pleasure—is not to be employed for its own sake. Rather, when matters are spoken that are useful and honorable, and the listeners need neither instruction nor emotional movement because they already know and approve, the assent of the audience may through the pleasure of the diction itself approach somewhat more readily or adhere more firmly.

For since the universal task of eloquence, in whichever of these three styles, is to speak appropriately for persuasion, and its goal is to persuade by speaking what one has intended, the eloquent speaker does indeed speak appropriately for persuasion in whichever of the three styles he uses. But unless he persuades, he does not reach the goal of eloquence.

In the subdued style he persuades that what he says is true; in the elevated style he persuades people to do what they already know ought to be done but are not doing; in the moderate style he persuades them that he speaks beautifully and elegantly. What need have we of this goal? Let those who glory in their eloquence and boast in panegyrics and similar speeches pursue it, where the listener needs neither instruction nor motivation toward any action, but only to be delighted.

Let us, however, refer this goal to another goal: namely, when we speak with elevation, let us wish to accomplish through the moderate style also what we seek to accomplish through the elevated style—that good moral conduct should be loved and evils avoided—if people are not so alienated from this action that they seem to need to be urged toward it in an elevated style; or, if they already do it, that they may do it more zealously and persevere firmly in it.

[Col. 0117]

Thus we use the ornament of the moderate style not ostentatiously but wisely: not content with its goal, by which the listener is merely delighted, but acting rather so that through this very delight the listener may also be helped toward the good we wish to persuade him to embrace.

## CHAPTER XXVI — In Every Style the Orator Should Aim to Be Heard Intelligently, Willingly, and Obediently

56. The three things mentioned above—that one who speaks wisely, if he also wishes to speak eloquently, should strive to be heard intelligently, willingly, and obediently—should not be understood as though each were assigned so exclusively to one of the three styles that intelligent hearing belonged to the subdued style, willing hearing to the moderate style, and obedient hearing to the elevated style.

Rather, he should always aim at all three and, as far as he can, pursue all three even while employing any one of them. For we do not wish even what we say in a subdued manner to become wearisome; therefore we wish it to be heard not only intelligently but also willingly.

When we teach what we say by divine testimonies, what are we doing except striving to be heard obediently—that is, so that people may believe them—with the help of the one to whom it was said: “Your testimonies have been made exceedingly trustworthy” (Psalm 92:5)?

What else does someone wish who tells learners something, even in subdued language, except to be believed? And who would wish to hear him unless he also held the listener through some pleasantness? For if he is not understood, who does not know that he cannot be heard either willingly or obediently?

Often, however, the subdued diction itself, while it disentangles the most difficult questions and displays them through an unexpected revelation; while it draws forth and exhibits from certain caves, as it were, the sharpest judgments, from places where they were not expected; while it refutes an opponent’s error and teaches that what seemed to be said by him with invincible force is false—especially when it possesses a certain beauty that is not sought after but in some way natural, and a certain rhythmic structure in its clauses that is not boastful but almost necessary and, so to speak, forced out by the matters themselves—often arouses such applause that it can scarcely be understood to be subdued.

For although it does not advance adorned or armed, but engages as though naked, it nevertheless smashes its opponent with sinews and muscles and overthrows and destroys the falsehood that resists it with its strongest limbs.

Why, then, do such speakers receive frequent and prolonged applause, except because truth displayed, defended, and shown to be unconquered gives pleasure? Therefore, in this subdued style also, our teacher and speaker should strive to be heard not only intelligently, but also willingly and obediently.

[Note: [Col. 0117] Printed editions read *dissolvit* (“dissolves”); shortly below, they also read *et quando nonnulla non jactanticula* (“and when certain things are not boastful”). In this passage the word *quando* (“when”) is absent from the manuscripts and is plainly superfluous if the reading above is *dum solvit* (“while it unties”), as all the manuscripts in fact give.]

[Note: [Col. 0117] Several manuscripts read *exorta* (“arising”).]

57. The eloquence of the moderate style in an eloquent ecclesiastical speaker is neither left unadorned nor adorned inappropriately. Nor does it seek merely to delight, which is the only aim it professes among others; rather, even in the things it praises or blames, it wishes to be heard obediently, so that the former may be pursued or held more firmly, and the latter avoided or rejected.

But if it is not heard intelligently, it cannot be heard willingly. Therefore, in this style as well, where delight holds the leading place, one must strive for all three: that those who listen may understand, be delighted, and obey.

58. But where it is necessary to move and bend the listener through the elevated style—which is necessary when he acknowledges that what is said is both true and pleasantly expressed, and yet does not wish to do what is said—one must unquestionably speak with elevation.

But who is moved if he does not know what is being said? Or who is held so as to listen if he is not delighted? Therefore, even in this style, where the hardness of the heart must be bent toward obedience by the grandeur of the diction, the speaker cannot be heard obediently unless he is also heard intelligently and willingly.

## CHAPTER XXVII — One Is Heard More Obediently When One’s Life Corresponds to One’s Speech

59. However great the grandeur of his diction may be, the speaker’s life gives greater weight to his being heard obediently. For one who speaks wisely and eloquently but lives wickedly does indeed instruct many who are eager to learn, although he is useless to his own soul (Ecclesiasticus 37:22), as it is written:

[Note: [Col. 0118] Printed editions add: “As it is written: ‘The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat. Whatever they say, do; but whatever they do, do not do, for they say and do not do.’” This sentence of Scripture is absent from all the manuscripts. We think it was inserted here because of the closing phrase “as it is written,” which should instead refer to the preceding words from Ecclesiasticus 37:22, where we read: “There is a shrewd man who instructs many, but is useless to his own soul.” In the ancient Greek text now extant, the word is *achrēstos* (“useless”), whereas the reader of the Latin version [lacuna] read *chrēstos* (“useful” or “good”), since he rendered [lacuna], the reading found in one of the manuscripts of our Bibles; [lacuna] both are found together.]

Hence the Apostle also says: “Whether by pretext or in truth, Christ is proclaimed” (Philippians 1:18). Christ, however, is truth, and yet truth can be proclaimed not in truth—that is, so that what is right and true may be preached with a wicked and deceitful heart.

Thus Jesus Christ is proclaimed by those who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But because good believers hear obediently not just any human being but the Lord himself, who says, “Whatever they say, do; but whatever they do, do not do, for they say and do not do,” those who do not themselves act rightly may nevertheless be heard profitably.

They strive to seek their own interests, but they do not dare to teach their own interests, because of the higher seat of ecclesiastical authority, which sound doctrine has established. For this reason the Lord himself, before saying what I have recalled about such people, prefaced it with: “They have taken their seat on Moses’ chair” (Matthew 23:2–3).

That chair, therefore—not theirs but Moses’—compelled them to say good things even though they did not do good things. Thus they pursued their own interests in their lives, but the chair belonging to another did not permit them to teach their own interests.

60. Thus they benefit many by saying what they do not do; but they would benefit far more by doing what they say. For there are many who seek a defense of their wicked life from their own superiors and teachers, replying in their hearts—or even bursting forth and saying it with their mouths: “Why do you yourself not do what you command me?”

Thus they do not hear obediently the one who does not himself hear himself, and they despise together with the preacher the word of God that is preached to them. Finally, when the Apostle wrote to Timothy and had said, “Let no one despise your youth,” he added what would prevent him from being despised, saying: “But be an example to the faithful in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity” (1 Timothy 4:12).

## CHAPTER XXVIII — One Should Devote Oneself to Truth Rather Than to Words; What It Means to Quarrel over Words

61. Such a teacher, in order to be heard obediently, speaks not shamefully—not only in a subdued and moderate manner, but also with elevation—because he does not live contemptibly. He chooses a good life in such a way that he does not neglect a good reputation either, but “takes thought for what is honorable before God and men” (2 Corinthians 8:21), fearing him and taking thought for them, as far as he can.

In his speech also, he should prefer to please by the matter itself rather than by words. He should not consider anything better said than what is said more truthfully; the teacher should not serve words, but words the teacher.

This is what the Apostle says: “Not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power” (1 Corinthians 1:17). The same applies to what he says to Timothy: “Do not quarrel over words; for it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear” (2 Timothy 2:14).

This was not said, however, so that we should say nothing in defense of truth when opponents attack it. Otherwise, what becomes of the statement he made when showing what a bishop ought to be, among other things: “So that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it” (Titus 1:9)?

To quarrel over words is not to care how error may be conquered by truth, but how one’s diction may be preferred to another’s diction. But one who does not quarrel over words—whether he speaks in a subdued, moderate, or elevated manner—uses words in order that truth may be revealed, truth may please, and truth may move. For love itself, which is “the end of the commandment and the fullness of the Law” (1 Timothy 1:5; Romans 13:10), cannot in any way be right if the things loved are not true but false.

Just as a person whose body is beautiful but whose soul is deformed deserves more pity than one whose body too is deformed, so those who eloquently say what is false deserve more pity than if they expressed such things clumsily.

What, then, is it to speak not only eloquently but also wisely, except to apply words that are sufficient in the subdued style, shining in the moderate style, and forceful in the elevated style, to true matters that ought to be heard?

But one who cannot do both should speak wisely without speaking eloquently, rather than speak eloquently while speaking foolishly.

## CHAPTER XXIX — An Ecclesiastical Preacher Is Not to Be Blamed When He Takes from a More Skilled Person a Written Speech to Deliver to the People

If he cannot even do this, let him conduct himself in such a way that he not only secures a reward for himself but also provides an example to others, and let the form of his life be, as it were, his abundance of speech.

62. There are certainly some who can deliver a speech well but cannot devise what they should deliver. If they take from others something written eloquently and wisely, commit it to memory, and deliver it to the people, they do not act improperly if they are fulfilling that role.

For in this way—which is certainly useful—many become preachers of the truth, though there are not many teachers, if all say the same thing belonging to the one true teacher and there are no divisions among them (1 Corinthians 1:10).

Nor should they be deterred by the words of the prophet Jeremiah, through whom God rebukes those who steal his words, “each one from his neighbor” (Jeremiah 23:30). Those who steal take away what belongs to another; but the word of God is not foreign to those who obey it. Rather, the one who says what belongs to another is the person who speaks well while living badly. Whatever good things he says seem to have been devised by his own intellect, but they are foreign to his conduct.

God therefore said that those steal his words who wish to appear good by speaking the things of God while being evil by doing the things that are their own. Indeed, if you pay close attention, they themselves do not say the good things they say. For how do they say in words what they deny by their deeds? The Apostle does not say of such people without reason: “They profess that they know God, but they deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16).

In one sense they themselves say these things, and again in another sense they do not say them themselves, because both statements are true, as Truth says. Speaking of such people, he says: “Whatever they say, do; but whatever they do, do not do.” That is: “Do what you hear from their mouths; do not do what you see in their actions. For they say,” he says, “and do not do” (Matthew 23:3).

Thus, although they do not do these things, they nevertheless say them. But elsewhere, rebuking such people, he says: “Hypocrites, how can you speak good things, when you are evil?” (Matthew 12:34). Consequently, when they say good things, they do not themselves say what they say, since by their will and conduct they deny what they say.

It therefore happens that an eloquent but wicked person composes a speech in which truth is proclaimed, for it to be delivered by someone who is not eloquent but good. When this happens, the former hands over something foreign to himself from himself, while the latter receives from another what is his own.

When good believers, however, lend this service to good believers, both say what is their own: God belongs to both of them, and the things they say belong to God; and they make their own what they were unable to compose themselves, since they live in accordance with it.

## CHAPTER XXX — A Preacher Should Begin with Prayer to God

63. Whether he is about to speak before the people or before any others, or whether he is about to compose what is to be said before the people or read by those who wish or are able to read it, he should pray that God may place a good word in his mouth.

For if Queen Esther prayed, when she was about to speak before the king for the temporal safety of her people, that God might place an appropriate speech in her mouth (Esther 14:13), how much more should one pray to receive such a gift when laboring in word and doctrine for the eternal salvation of human beings?

Those who are going to say what they have received from others should, before receiving it, pray for those from whom they receive it, that what they wish to receive through them may be granted to them. Once they have received it, they should pray that they themselves may deliver it well and that those to whom they deliver it may receive it. They should give thanks for the successful outcome of their speech to the one from whom they do not doubt that they received it, so that “whoever glories may glory in him,” in whose hand are both we and our words (Wisdom 7:16).

## CHAPTER XXXI — The Length of the Book Is Excused

[Col. 0121]

64. This book has turned out longer than I wished and longer than I had expected. But to one who finds it agreeable, whether reading or hearing it, it is not long; and whoever finds it long should read it in sections, if he wishes to understand it. Let him who is wearied by understanding it not complain about its length.

[Col. 0122]

Nevertheless, I give thanks to our God that in these four books I have explained, with whatever small ability I possessed, not what I myself am—for I lack much—but what the person ought to be who strives to labor in sound doctrine, that is, Christian doctrine, not only for himself but also for others.

## [ON TRUE RELIGION]

[Col. 0121]

### EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK, *ON TRUE RELIGION*

[Note: [Col. 0121] In B., the book *On True Religion* follows the book *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*. It seems better placed here, as being a natural complement to the book *On Christian Doctrine*. M.]

Among the minor works that Saint Augustine, while not yet a presbyter—the dignity which he attained in the year 391—published, he assigns the last place in the *Retractions* to the book *On True Religion*. For this reason we think it should be assigned to the year 390.

Several years earlier he had promised his fellow citizen and patron Romanianus that he would treat this subject, as he recalls in chapter 7, section 12. He had undertaken the work when writing against the Academics in the year 386, book 2, chapter 3, section 8. Furthermore, in his fifteenth letter to Romanianus, section 1, he mentions that the work had been completed by him and would shortly be sent to him.

Later, when Evodius proposed certain doubts concerning the existence of God, Augustine referred him to this book in Letter 162, section 2. It is clear from Letter 27, section 4, to Paulinus that this same book is one of the five that Paulinus calls the *Pentateuch against the Manichaeans*. Paulinus had received these books as a gift from Alypius, and on that occasion he exclaims in praise of Augustine in Letter 25, section 1:

“O truly the salt of the earth, by which our inmost hearts are preserved, so that they cannot waste away through the world’s error! O lamp worthy to be placed upon the Church’s lampstand, which, pouring forth light nourished by the oil of joy from its sevenfold wick throughout the Catholic cities, dispels the dense darknesses of the heretics and, by the splendor of its brilliant speech, clears the light of truth from the confusion of darkness!” and so forth.

Certainly, if any book deserved this praise of Augustine, it was the book *On True Religion*. For although, when he wrote it, he had only recently been led over to the side of true religion and bore no other name than that of a Catholic Christian, he nevertheless expounds the mysteries of the Christian religion in so sublime a manner and above all tears out the foundations of the opposing doctrines, especially those of the Manichaeans, that even then he fulfilled the role of a most accomplished teacher and most vigorous bishop.

[Col. 0121]

[Note: [Col. 0121] See Book 1, chapter 13 of the *Retractions*, column 602, from the words “At that time also, concerning *On True Religion*,” section 1, through column 605, section 9, ending with the words “the way of the good and blessed life.” M.]

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo: One Book *On True Religion***

[Note: [Col. 0121] Written around the year of Christ 390.]

[Note: [Col. 0121] In preparing this recension of the book, we consulted the Thuane, Royal, Navarre, Sorbonne, Victorine, Casal, Corbie, Gembloux, Audoen, Bec, and German manuscripts; one manuscript from the library of the church of Rheims; readings sent to us from the Cistercian, Arnulfian, and Vatican manuscripts; and the readings of five Belgian manuscripts apud Lov. Finally, we consulted the editions of Bad., Er., Lov., and Arnold.]

[Note: [Col. 0121] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

After first establishing that true religion is not found among the pagans or in any sect other than the Catholic Church, Augustine immediately explains the history of the divine providence directed toward human salvation—which is indeed the chief point and foundation of the Christian religion—in such a way that the Manichaean errors, especially concerning the two natures and concerning the origin and nature of evil, are refuted.

Accordingly, he discusses the twofold way in which God provides for human beings: by authority calling those who believe to salvation, and by reason those who understand. For the human being, supported by reason, rises from lower things to God; indeed, he is urged to pursue God even by the vices themselves, concerning whose threefold kind Augustine here offers an extended discussion. Finally, he concludes that the one true God—that is, the Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is to be worshiped by true religion.

## CHAPTER I — Philosophers Taught One Thing in Their Schools and Professed Another in Their Temples

1. Since the whole way of a good and blessed life is established in true religion, through which the one God is worshiped and, with the purest devotion, recognized as the source of all natures—from whom the whole universe both begins and reaches completion and is sustained—

[Col. 0122]

[Col. 0123]

the error of those peoples is thereby detected more clearly who preferred to worship many gods rather than the one true God and Lord of all. Their wise men, whom they call philosophers, had schools in which they disagreed, but temples they shared.

For neither the people nor the priests were unaware how differently the philosophers thought about the nature of their gods, since each one did not fear to profess his own opinion publicly and to strive to persuade everyone of it, if he could. Yet all of them, together with their followers, who held different and opposing opinions, came without hindrance to the common rites.

The question now is not which of them held the truer opinion. But this much, at least, seems sufficiently clear to me: in matters of religion they undertook one thing together with the people, while privately, in the hearing of those same people, they defended something else.

## CHAPTER II — What Socrates Thought about the Gods; This World Regarded as God

2. Socrates, however, is said to have been bolder than the others, swearing by any dog, any stone, and whatever happened to be at hand or came, as it were, readily to the hand of one taking an oath.

I believe that he understood that all the works of nature, which are brought forth under the administration of divine providence, are far better than the works of human beings and of any craftsmen, and therefore more worthy of divine honors than the things worshiped in temples.

He did not mean that stones and dogs truly ought to be worshiped by wise people, but that in this way those who were capable of understanding might recognize that human beings were so deeply submerged in superstition that, for them to emerge from it, such a shameful step had to be pointed out. If they were ashamed to approach that level, they would see how much more shameful it would be to remain fixed in something worse.

At the same time, he was warning those who thought that this visible world was the supreme God of the disgracefulness of their position, teaching that it necessarily followed that every stone ought rightly to be worshiped as a particle of the supreme God.

If they recoiled from this, they should change their opinion and seek the one God, who alone is above our minds and from whom it is evident that every soul and this entire world were fashioned.

[Note: [Col. 0123] Sixteen manuscripts read: “so that they might seek the one God.”]

Later Plato wrote more agreeably for reading, though less powerfully for persuasion. For these people were not born in such a condition that they could turn the opinion of their peoples toward the true worship of the true God, away from the superstition of images and the vanity of this world.

Thus Socrates himself worshiped images together with the people; and after his condemnation and death no one dared to swear by a dog or call any stone Jupiter, but only to commit these things to memory and writing.

Whether they did this out of fear of severity—

[Note: [Col. 0123] Nine manuscripts omit *severitatis* (“of severity”); one of them, the Gembloux manuscript, continues: “or from some other understanding of the times,” and so forth.]

—or because of some understanding of the times, it is not for me to judge.

## CHAPTER III — The True Christian Religion, Which Persuaded Human Beings of What Plato Did Not Believe Could Be Persuaded to Them
3.
