Nevertheless, with the leave of all those who obstinately cherish their books, let them say with complete confidence that there can be no doubt, in Christian times, which religion ought above all to be held, and which is the way to truth and blessedness. For if Plato himself were alive and did not disdain to answer my questions [Col. 0124]—or rather, if one of his disciples had questioned him at the very time when he was alive—when Plato had persuaded him that truth is seen not with bodily eyes but with a purified mind; that whatever soul had clung to it would become blessed and perfect; that nothing impeded its apprehension more than a life devoted to lust and the false images of sensible things which, impressed upon us through the body by this sensible world, generate various opinions and errors; and that therefore the soul must be healed so that it might behold the unchangeable form of things and the beauty that always remains in the same condition and is everywhere like itself, neither extended through space nor altered by time, but preserving itself wholly one and the same—which men would not believe to exist, although it truly and supremely exists; while all other things are born, perish, flow, and pass away, yet, insofar as they exist, are established as fashioned by that eternal God through his truth; and that only the rational and intellectual soul has been granted to enjoy and be affected and adorned by contemplation of his eternity, and to merit eternal life; but that, while it is wounded by love and grief for things that are born and pass away, and, devoted to the habits of this life and to bodily sensations, dissipates itself in empty images, it mocks those who say that something exists which is perceived neither by these eyes nor conceived by any phantasm, but which can be discerned by mind and understanding alone—if, then, that disciple, having been persuaded of these things by his teacher, had asked him whether, supposing there existed some great and divine man who could persuade peoples to believe such things at least, if they were unable to comprehend them—or, if some were able to comprehend them, could prevent them from being entangled in the multitude’s depraved opinions and overwhelmed by popular errors—he would judge that man worthy of divine honors, I believe Plato would have replied that this could not be accomplished by a human being unless that person had perhaps been set apart from the very nature of things by the Power and Wisdom of God himself, enlightened from the cradle not by human instruction but by an inward illumination, ennobled by such grace, strengthened by such firmness, and finally raised up by such majesty that, by despising everything wicked people desire, enduring everything they dread, and doing everything they admire, he would turn the human race toward so salutary a faith with supreme love and authority. As for his honors, it would be futile to consult him, since it can readily be judged how great are the honors due to the Wisdom of God, which, bearing and governing that man for the true salvation of the human race, would enable him to deserve something great and distinctive, something above humanity.

4. If these things have happened; if they are celebrated in writings and memorials; if, from one region of the earth where alone one God was worshiped and where such a man ought to have been born, chosen men have been sent throughout the whole world, kindling fires of divine love by their virtues and words; if, having established a most salutary discipline, they have left the lands enlightened to later generations; and—to say nothing of the past—if anyone can fail to believe what is now proclaimed among nations and peoples:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. [Col. 0125] He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1–3).

If, for the purpose of perceiving, loving, and enjoying this, so that the soul may be healed and the mind’s vision strengthened to drink in so great a light, the greedy are told:

> Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal; but store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroy, and where thieves neither break in nor steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart also is (Matthew 6:19–21);

if the lustful are told:

> Whoever sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; whoever sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit (Galatians 6:8);

if the proud are told:

> Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11);

if the angry are told:

> You have received a blow; prepare the other cheek (Matthew 5:39);

if the quarrelsome are told:

> Love your enemies (ibid. 44);

if the superstitious are told:

> The kingdom of God is within you (Luke 17:21);

if the curious are told:

> Do not seek the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Corinthians 4:18);

and finally if everyone is told:

> Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; for everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age (1 John 2:15–16);

5. If these things are now read to peoples throughout the whole world and heard with the greatest willingness and reverence; if, after so much blood, so many fires, and so many crosses of martyrs, the Churches have sprung up with such greater fertility and abundance even among barbarian nations; if no one is now astonished at the many thousands of young men and virgins who disdain marriage and live chastely—which, when Plato had done it, he feared the perverse opinion of his times so greatly that he is said to have sacrificed to nature [Note: [Col. 0125] In seven manuscripts: “having execrated nature, he sacrificed to nature, so that, as it were, …”] so that the supposed sin might be abolished; if these things are received in such a way that, just as it was formerly monstrous to argue for them, so now it is monstrous to argue against them; if Christian rites are handed down throughout all the regions of the earth inhabited by human beings with such a promise and pledge; if these things are read daily in churches and expounded by priests; if those who strive to fulfill them beat their breasts; if so countless a multitude undertakes this way that the deserted islands and the solitude of many lands are filled with people from every class who, abandoning the wealth and honors of this world, wish to dedicate their whole lives to the one supreme God; and finally, if throughout cities and towns, fortified places, villages, and fields, even in private estates, withdrawal from earthly things and conversion to the one true God are openly urged and desired to such an extent that every day throughout the whole human world nearly one voice responds that they have their hearts lifted up to the Lord [“Lift up your hearts,” from the canon of the Mass]—why do we still yawn off yesterday’s drunkenness and search through the divine utterances among dead animals? Whenever discussion arises, why do we desire to have mouths resounding with Plato’s name rather than hearts filled with truth?

## CHAPTER IV — Philosophers who cling wholly to sensible things are to be despised

[Col. 0126]

6. Those, then, who think it vain or evil to despise this sensible world and to purify the soul by virtue, subjecting and subjugating it to the supreme God, must be refuted by another method—if, indeed, it is worthwhile to dispute with them. But those who acknowledge that this is good and desirable should acknowledge God and yield to God, through whom all peoples have now been persuaded that these things ought to be believed. They would certainly have done this themselves if they had possessed such power; or, if it had not happened, they could not have avoided the guilt of envy. Let them therefore yield to him by whom this has been accomplished, and not allow curiosity or empty boasting to prevent them from recognizing the difference between the timid conjectures of a few [Note: [Col. 0126] Thus in the manuscripts of better quality. In the common text: “swelling conjectures.”] and the manifest salvation and correction of peoples. For if those men whose names these people boast of were to come back to life, and were to find the churches filled, the temples deserted, and the human race summoned and hastening away from desire for temporal and transitory goods toward hope of eternal life and spiritual and intelligible goods, they might say—if they were such as they are reported to have been:

> These are the things we did not dare to persuade peoples to believe; instead, we yielded to their customs rather than bringing them over to our faith and will.

7. Therefore, if those men could live this life again with us, they would surely see under whose authority it would be easier to provide for human beings, and, with a few words and opinions altered, they would become Christians, as many Platonists of more recent times, including our own, have done. But if they neither confessed nor did this, remaining in pride and envy, I do not know whether they could fly back with these stains and this sticky residue to those very things which they had said ought to be desired and sought. As for the third vice, curiosity in questioning demons, by which these Pagans with whom we are now dealing are especially drawn away from Christian salvation—because it is excessively childish—I do not know whether such men would have been hindered by it.

## CHAPTER V — In which sects true religion is found. The divine Gift. The Holy Spirit

8. Whatever may be the case with the philosophers’ boasting, anyone can easily understand that religion is not to be sought from those who accepted the same rites as the peoples, while in their schools, with the same multitude bearing witness, they proclaimed differing and contradictory opinions about the nature of their gods and the supreme good. If we saw that Christian discipline had healed only this one vice, no one ought to deny that it deserved to be proclaimed with inexpressible praise. For the countless heresies that have turned away from the rule of Christianity testify that those who think differently about God the Father, his Wisdom, and the divine Gift, and who try to persuade others of their views contrary to what truth requires, are not admitted to share the Sacraments. For this is believed and taught—and it is the foundation of human salvation—that philosophy, that is, the pursuit of wisdom, is not one thing and religion another, since those whose teaching we do not approve do not share the Sacraments with us.

9. This is less surprising in those who also chose to observe differing rites of those Sacraments, such as certain people called Serpentines [Note: [Col. 0127] Ophites.], such as the Manichaeans, and certain others. But it is more important, and more worthy of emphasis, in those who celebrate the same Sacraments yet, because they differ in doctrine, have preferred to defend their errors more boldly than to correct them cautiously. Excluded from Catholic communion and from participation in the Sacraments, although those Sacraments were the same, they thereby earned their own names and their own assemblies—not merely in speech but also in superstition—as the Photinians, Arians, and many others did. The case of those who created schisms is different. The Lord’s threshing floor could have endured them as chaff until the time of the final winnowing (Matthew 3:12), unless they had yielded with excessive lightness to the wind of pride and voluntarily separated themselves from us.

The Jews, although they pray to the one omnipotent God, nevertheless expect from him only temporal and visible goods. Thus, with excessive confidence, they failed to recognize in their own Scriptures the beginnings of the new people rising from humility, and so they remained in the old man.

Since this is so, religion is to be sought neither in the confusion of the Pagans, nor in the refuse of the heretics, nor in the weakness of schismatics, nor in the blindness of the Jews, but only among those who are called Christian Catholics, or orthodox—that is, guardians of integrity and followers of what is right.

## CHAPTER VI — True religion exists in the Catholic Church alone, which uses all who err for its own advancement. Good people sometimes expelled from the Church by seditious persons

10. For this Catholic Church, powerfully and extensively spread throughout the whole world, makes use of all who err for its own advancement and for their correction when they wish to awaken. It uses the Gentiles as material for its work, heretics as a test of its doctrine, schismatics as evidence of its stability, and Jews as a comparison by which its beauty is shown. Thus it invites some, excludes others, leaves others behind, and goes before others; yet it grants all the power to share in the grace of God, whether they still need to be formed [Note: [Col. 0127] The printed editions read: “whether they still need to be shaped.” The manuscripts more accurately read “formed.”], reformed, gathered again, or admitted.

As for its carnal members—that is, those who live or think carnally—it tolerates them as chaff, by which the grain on the threshing floor is kept safer until they are stripped of such coverings. But because on this threshing floor each person is, according to his will, either chaff or grain, the sin or error of each is tolerated until it either finds an accuser or defends its false opinion with obstinate hostility.

Those who are excluded either return through repentance; or, in a bad freedom, drift into wickedness, as a warning to our diligence; or create a schism, as an exercise of our patience; or produce some heresy, as a test or opportunity for our understanding. These are the outcomes of carnal Christians who could neither be corrected nor tolerated.

[Col. 0128] 11. Divine providence also often permits good men to be expelled from the Christian congregation through the seditions of certain excessively turbulent carnal people. When they bear this insult or injury to themselves with the greatest patience for the sake of the Church’s peace, and attempt no innovations, whether of schism or heresy, they teach people with what true devotion and how great a sincerity of charity God ought to be served.

The purpose of such men, therefore, is either to return when the storms have been calmed, or, if they are not permitted to do so—whether the same disturbance continues or lest their return give rise to an even more savage disturbance—to maintain until death their resolve to benefit even those whose agitation and disturbances they have yielded to, without forming any separate assemblies, defending and supporting by their testimony the faith which they know is proclaimed in the Catholic Church. The Father, who sees in secret, crowns them in secret.

This kind of person seems rare, but examples are not lacking—indeed, there are more than one might believe. Thus divine providence makes use of every kind of person and example for the healing of souls and the instruction of the spiritual people.

## CHAPTER VII — The religion of the Catholic Church must be embraced. What it professes

12. Therefore, since a few years ago I promised you, my dearest Romanianus, that I would write what I thought about true religion (Against the Academics, Book 2, chapter 3, §8), I have judged that the time has now come, since I could no longer endure your most searching questions, which wandered without any definite conclusion, with the charity by which I am bound to you. Accordingly, I have rejected all those who neither philosophize within sacred things nor are consecrated in philosophy; those who, whether through a depraved opinion or some hostility, have proudly departed from the rule and communion of the Catholic Church; and those who have refused to possess the light of the Holy Scriptures and the grace of the spiritual people, which is called the New Testament—all of whom I have touched upon as briefly as I could.

We must therefore hold the Christian religion and communion with that Church which is Catholic and is called Catholic, not only by its own members but also by all its enemies. For whether they wish it or not, heretics and the offspring of schisms themselves, when they speak not with their own people but with outsiders, call it nothing other than Catholic. They cannot be understood unless they distinguish it by this name, by which it is designated throughout the whole world.

13. The foundation of this religion is the history and prophecy of the temporal dispensation of divine providence, by which the human race is to be reformed and restored to eternal life. Once this has been believed, a manner of life reconciled to the divine commandments will purify the mind and make it fit to perceive spiritual realities—realities that are neither past nor future, but always remain in the same condition, subject to no change: namely, the one God himself, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

When, insofar as this is granted in the present life, this Trinity has been known, it is perceived without doubt that every intellectual, animate, and bodily creature is from that same creative Trinity insofar as it exists, has its own form [Note: [Col. 0129] Eleven manuscripts omit the words “and has its own form,” but they are especially appropriate here because of the second person of the Trinity.], and is administered in the most orderly fashion. This does not mean that the Father made one part of the whole creation, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; rather, the Father made all things together, and each nature, through the Son in the gift of the Holy Spirit.

For every thing—whether it is called substance, essence, nature, or by some other, better term—possesses these three things together: it is one thing, it is distinguished from other things by its particular form, and it does not exceed the order of things.

## CHAPTER VIII — What we first believed under the authority of faith we later understand through reason. Heretics benefit the Church

14. Once this has been understood, it will sufficiently appear, insofar as a human being can grasp it, by what necessary, invincible, and just laws all things are subject to God and their Lord. From this it follows that all those things which we first believed, following authority alone, are partly understood in such a way that we see them to be absolutely certain, and partly understood in such a way that we see how they could and ought to have happened; and we grieve that those who did not believe these things preferred to mock us when we believed them rather than believe together with us.

For once the eternal nature of the Trinity and the mutability of creation are known, we no longer merely believe but also judge that the sacred taking-on of humanity, the birth from a Virgin, the death of the Son of God for us, the resurrection from the dead, the ascension into heaven, the sitting at the right hand of the Father, the abolition of sins, the day of judgment, and the resurrection of bodies belong to the mercy of the supreme God, which he displays toward the human race.

15. But since it has been said most truly, “There must be many heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19), let us also make use of this benefit of divine providence. For those people become heretics who, even if they were in the Church, would nevertheless err. When they are outside, they are of great benefit—not by teaching the truth, which they do not know, but by rousing the carnal to seek the truth and the spiritual Catholics to disclose the truth.

There are countless men approved by God in the holy Church, but they do not become manifest among us so long as we prefer to sleep, delighting in the darkness of our ignorance, rather than gaze upon the light of truth. Therefore many are awakened from sleep by heretics, so that they may see and rejoice in the day of God.

Let us therefore make use of heretics—not to approve their errors, but, by asserting Catholic discipline against their snares, to become more vigilant and cautious, even if we cannot call them back to salvation.

## CHAPTER IX — The Manichaean error concerning two principles and two souls

16. I believe that God will grant that this writing, when read by good people with piety preceding it, may be effective not merely against one particular opinion but against all depraved and false opinions. It is directed especially, however, against those who think that two natures or substances, each with its own principle, are mutually opposed.

Offended by certain things and delighted by others, they wish God to be the author not of the things that offend them but of those that delight them. And because they cannot overcome their habits, already ensnared in carnal bonds, they think that there are two souls in one body: one from God, naturally what God himself is; the other from the race of darkness, which God neither begot, made, brought forth, nor cast away, but which possessed its own life, its own earth, its own offspring and animals, and finally its own kingdom, with an unbegotten principle. They imagine that at a certain time it rebelled against God; that God, having nothing else to do and finding no other way to resist the enemy, compelled by necessity sent here the good soul and a certain particle of his substance; and that, by the commixture and mingling of this particle with the enemy, the enemy was tempered [Note: [Col. 0130] Nineteen manuscripts read “by whose commixture and misery.” Bad. and Er. likewise have “misery.”], and the world was fashioned.

17. We are not now refuting their opinions—for some of this we have already done, and as much as God permits we shall do in part later—but in this work we demonstrate, as far as we can, by arguments which the Lord deigns to grant, how the Catholic faith is secure against them and how those things that move people to adopt their opinion need not disturb the mind.

I want you above all to keep this in mind—you who know my character well—not because I am trying to avoid arrogance, as though making a solemn declaration, but because whatever error may be found in these writings is to be attributed solely to me, whereas whatever is true and properly explained belongs to God, the one giver of all good gifts.

## CHAPTER X — As he is about to narrate the history of the divine dispensation for our salvation, he first shows where error in religion arises and how perfect religion is restored with God’s help

18. Let it therefore be clear and understood by you that no error could have arisen in religion if the soul had not worshiped, in place of its God, either another soul, or the body, or its own phantasms [Note: [Col. 0130] Retractations, chapter 13, §2], or any two of these joined together, or certainly all of them together. Instead, while temporally and without deceit conforming to the fellowship of the human race in this life, it would have contemplated the eternal, worshiping the one God, who, unless he remained unchangeable, would leave no changeable nature in existence.

Everyone recognizes that the soul can change—not indeed locally, but temporally, through its own affections. It is easy for anyone to observe that the body is changeable both in time and in place. Phantasms, moreover, are nothing other than images drawn from the appearance of bodies through bodily sense. It is very easy to commit them to memory as they are received, or to divide, multiply, contract, expand, arrange, disturb, or shape them in thought in any way; but when truth is being sought, it is difficult to guard against and avoid them.

[Col. 0131] 19. Let us therefore serve the Creator rather than the creature, and let us not dissipate ourselves in our thoughts; this is perfect religion [Note: [Col. 0131] Retractations, chapter 13, §2]. For by clinging to the eternal Creator, we too must be affected by eternity. But because the soul, weighed down and entangled by its sins, could not see or hold this by itself, and because no intermediate step had been placed in human affairs by which a human being might strive from earthly life toward likeness to God, the ineffable mercy of God comes to our aid through a temporal dispensation carried out by mutable creation, though creation remains subject to eternal laws, recalling our first and perfect nature—partly to individual human beings and partly to the human race itself.

This is the Christian religion of our times, to know and follow which is the surest and most certain salvation [Note: [Col. 0131] Ibid., §3].

20. It can be defended against talkative opponents and opened up to those who seek it in many ways, with God himself, the Almighty, demonstrating through himself what is true and assisting good wills in beholding and grasping these things through good angels and through all kinds of human beings. Each person, however, uses the method he sees as fitting for those with whom he is dealing.

I therefore considered at length the kinds of barking opponents and seekers whom I have experienced, and what sort of person I myself was when I barked or sought. I decided that I ought to use the following method:

What you perceive to be true, hold fast and attribute to the Catholic Church. What is false, reject, and forgive me, who am a human being. What is doubtful, believe until either reason teaches you that it must be rejected, that it is true, or that it must always be believed, or until authority commands it.

Attend, therefore, carefully and devoutly, as far as you can, to what follows; for God helps people of this kind [Note: [Col. 0131] Ibid., §4].

## CHAPTER XI — All life is from God. The death of the soul is wickedness

21. There is no life that is not from God, because God is certainly the supreme life and himself the source of life. No life, insofar as it is life, is evil; it is evil insofar as it tends toward death. But the death of life is nothing other than wickedness (nequitia), so called from “not being anything” (ne quidquam sit); hence the most wicked are called worthless people.

Life, therefore, declining voluntarily from the one who made it and whose essence it enjoyed, and wishing to enjoy bodies over which God appointed it, tends toward nothingness; and this is wickedness—not because the body is already nothing. For the body itself possesses some harmony among its parts, without which it could not exist at all. Therefore the body too was made by the one who is the source of all harmony.

The body possesses a certain peace of its form, without which it would altogether be nothing. Therefore he is also the creator of the body from whom all peace comes, who is the unmade form and the most beautiful of all. The body possesses some form, without which it is not a body. If, then, one asks who established the body, one should seek the one who is most beautiful of all. For every form is from him.

Who is this, then, except the one God, the one truth, the one salvation of all, and the first and supreme essence, from which everything that exists derives its existence insofar as it exists? For insofar as anything exists, it is good.

22. Therefore death is not from God. For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living (Wisdom 1:13), since the supreme essence gives existence to everything that exists—hence it is called “essence.” Death, however, compels whatever dies not to exist, insofar as it dies. For if things that die were to die completely, they would undoubtedly arrive at nothingness; but they die only insofar as they participate less in essence. This can be stated more briefly: they die more, the less they are.

The body, however, is less than any life, since whatever small amount of form remains in it remains through life, whether through the life by which each animal is governed or through the life by which the whole nature of the world is administered. The body, therefore, is more subject to death and consequently nearer to nothingness. Hence life, which delights in the fruit of the body and neglects God, inclines toward nothingness—and this is wickedness.

## CHAPTER XII — The fall and restoration of the whole human being

23. In this way life becomes carnal and earthly, and for this reason it is also called flesh and earth. As long as it remains so, it will not possess the kingdom of God, and what it loves is taken away from it. For it loves what is less than life, since it is the body; and because of the very sin, what is loved becomes corruptible, so that by passing away it abandons its lover, just as the lover, by loving it, abandoned God.

For the soul neglected God’s command when he said: “Eat this, and do not eat that” (Genesis 2:16–17). It is therefore dragged toward punishments, because by loving inferior things it is ordered in the poverty of its pleasures and in pains among the underworld.

For what is the pain called bodily pain except the sudden corruption of the health of that thing which the soul, by using it wrongly, made subject to corruption [Note: [Col. 0132] Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “which it made subject to corruption.”]? And what is the pain called pain of the soul except being deprived of changeable things in which it had enjoyed itself or had hoped that it could enjoy itself? This is the whole of what is called evil—that is, sin and the punishment of sin.

24. But if, while the soul dwells in this stage of human life, it conquers the desires which it nourished against itself by enjoying mortal things, and believes that the grace of God assists it in conquering them, serving him with mind and good will, it will undoubtedly be restored. It will return from many changeable things to the one unchangeable thing, reformed by Wisdom—not by a wisdom that was formed, but by the Wisdom through which all things are formed—and will enjoy God through the Holy Spirit, who is the Gift of God.

Thus the human being becomes spiritual, judging all things while being judged by no one (1 Corinthians 2:15), loving the Lord his God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind, and loving his neighbor not carnally but as himself. He loves himself spiritually when he loves God with everything in him that lives. For on these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets (Matthew 22:37–40).

25. It will then follow that after bodily death—which we owe to the first sin—this body, in its proper time and order, will be restored to its original stability [Note: [Col. 0133] Retractations, chapter 13, §4]. It will not possess this stability by itself, but through the soul established in God. Nor will the soul itself be established by itself, but by the God whom it enjoys; and therefore it will be stronger than the body. For the body will be strong through the soul, and the soul through the unchangeable truth, who is the only Son of God. Thus the body too will be strong through the Son of God, because all things were made through him.

Through his Gift, which is given to the soul—that is, through the Holy Spirit—not only is the soul to which it is given made safe, peaceful, and holy, but the body itself will also be brought to life and will be utterly pure in its nature. For he said: “Cleanse what is within, and what is outside will be clean” (Matthew 23:26). The Apostle also says: “He will give life even to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:11).

When sin is removed, therefore, the punishment of sin will also be removed. And where is evil? Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death? For essence conquers nothingness, and thus death is swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54–55).

## CHAPTER XIII — The distinction among angels

26. Nor will the evil angel, who is called the devil, do any harm to those who have been sanctified. For he too, insofar as he is an angel, is not evil, but is evil insofar as he is perverse by his own will.

We must acknowledge that angels are mutable by nature, if God alone is unchangeable. Yet by that will through which they love God more than themselves, they remain firm and stable in him and enjoy his majesty, willingly subject to him alone.

But that angel, loving himself more than God, refused to be subject to him; he swelled with pride, fell away from the supreme essence, and fell. For this reason he is less than he was, because he wished to enjoy what was less, preferring to enjoy his own power rather than God.

Although he was not supreme, he was nevertheless greater when he enjoyed that which is supreme, since God alone is supreme. Whatever is less than it was is evil not insofar as it exists, but insofar as it is less. For insofar as it is less than it was, it tends toward death.

What wonder, then, if from decline comes want, and from want envy—the envy by which the devil is truly the devil?

## CHAPTER XIV — Sin proceeds from free choice

27. If this decline, which is called sin, seized an unwilling person like a fever, the punishment that follows the sinner and is called condemnation would rightly seem unjust. But sin is so entirely a voluntary evil that there is no sin at all if it is not voluntary [Note: [Col. 0133] Ibid., §5]. This is so evident that neither the small number of the learned nor the multitude of the unlearned disagrees about it.

Therefore either we must deny that sin is committed, or we must admit that it is committed by the will. But someone does not rightly deny that the soul has sinned if he admits that it is corrected through repentance, that forgiveness is granted to the repentant, and that the one who persists in sins is condemned by God’s just law.

Finally, if we do not do evil by our will, then no one ought to be reproved or admonished at all; and once these have been removed, the whole Christian law and the discipline of every religion must necessarily be abolished.

Sin is therefore committed by the will. And since there is no doubt that sin is committed, I see no reason to doubt that souls possess free choice of the will. God judged that his servants would be better if they served him freely; and this could in no way happen if they served not by will but by necessity.

28. Angels therefore serve God freely, and this benefits not God but themselves. God does not need another’s good, since he is from himself. Whatever has been begotten by him is the same as he is, because it was not made but begotten.

Those things, however, which have been made need his goodness—namely, the supreme good, the supreme essence. They are less than they were when, through the soul’s sin, they are moved less toward him; yet they are not separated from him completely, for then they would not exist at all.

What happens to the soul through its affections happens to the body through places: the soul is moved by the will, whereas the body is moved through space. Whatever is said to have been persuaded to human beings by the perverse angel, the human being consented to this by will as well. For if he had done it by necessity, he would not be held by any charge of sin.

## CHAPTER XV — Through punishment itself we are instructed to return to our senses
29. But although the human body, which before sin was supremely excellent within its kind, became after sin weakened (*imbecillosum*) and destined for death [Note: [Col. 0134] Erasmus, Lovaniensis, and Arnoldus read *imbecillum*, “weak”; instead, Badius and the manuscripts read *imbecillosum*.], this, though a just punishment for sin, nevertheless displays more of the Lord’s mercy than of his severity. For in this way we are taught by bodily pleasures that our love ought to be turned toward the eternal essence of truth. It is also the beauty of justice, harmonizing with the grace of goodness, that since we were deceived by the sweetness of inferior goods, we should be instructed by the bitterness of punishments. For divine providence has so ordered our penalties that even in this body, so corruptible, we may strive toward justice; laying aside all pride, we may submit our neck to the one true God, place no confidence in ourselves, and entrust ourselves to him alone to be governed and protected. Thus, with God himself as guide, a person of good will turns the troubles of this life to the use of fortitude; amid abundance of pleasures and successful temporal circumstances, he tests and strengthens his self-control; in temptations he sharpens his prudence, so that he is not merely kept from falling into them but becomes more watchful, and grows more ardent in love for the truth, which alone does not deceive.

### CHAPTER XVI  
### Through the Incarnate Word, provision was made for humanity with greater benevolence

30. But although God provides remedies for souls in every way according to the opportunities of the times, which are ordered by his wondrous wisdom—matters that should either not be discussed or should be discussed among the devout and spiritually mature—he provided for the human race in no way more benevolently than when Wisdom itself, the only-begotten Son consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, deigned to assume the whole human being: “and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). In this way he demonstrated to those who were carnal and unable to contemplate the truth with the mind, being devoted to bodily senses, how exalted a place human nature occupies among creatures. He appeared not merely visibly—for he could have done that in some ethereal body adapted to the endurance of our sight—but to human beings in a true human being. For it was precisely the nature that was to be liberated that had to be assumed. And lest anyone perhaps think that either sex had been scorned by its Creator, he assumed a man, born of a woman.

31. He did nothing by force, but everything by persuasion and admonition [Note: *Retractations* I.13.6.]. For the old servitude had passed away, and the time of freedom had dawned; and now it was appropriately and salutarily impressed upon humanity how freely it had been created. By miracles he won faith for the God that he was [Note: Badius and Erasmus read *qui in eo erat*, “who was in him.” Shortly afterward, three manuscripts of the highest authority read *homini quem regebat*, “the man whom he governed.” Others, with the printed editions, read *gerebat*, “whom he carried/bore.” Both readings were accepted by Augustine, who above, chapter 3, section 3, says that the man assumed had merited this because the Wisdom of God carried and governed him.], and by suffering for the man whom he bore. Speaking to the crowds as God, he denied that the mother announced to him was his mother (Matthew 12:48); and yet, as the Gospel relates, as a child he was subject to his parents (Luke 2:51). In his teaching he appeared as God, but in his ages as a human being.

Likewise, when he was about to turn water into wine as God, he said: “Withdraw from me, woman: what is it to me and to you? My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4). But when the hour had come in which he was to die as a human being, from the cross he entrusted his known mother to the disciple whom he loved more than the others (John 19:26–27). The servants of pleasure were wickedly coveting riches: he chose to be poor. They were eager for honors and commands: he refused to become a king. They considered carnal children a great good: he rejected such marriage and offspring. They regarded insults with the utmost horror: he endured every kind of insult. They thought injuries intolerable: what greater injury is there than for a just and innocent person to be condemned? They cursed bodily pains: he was scourged and tortured. They feared death: he was condemned to death. They considered the cross the most shameful kind of death: he was crucified.

Everything that we desired to possess and therefore lived wrongly, he made worthless by going without it [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read *vilia fecit*, “he made them worthless.”]. Everything that, in our desire to avoid it, caused us to stray from the pursuit of truth [Note: The manuscripts do not contain the word *veritatis*, “of truth.” Some critics think that the word was added by scribes, and that through the same scribal error *studio* was substituted for *stadio*. M.], he overthrew by enduring it. For no sin can be committed except either while things that he despised are being pursued, or while things that he endured are being avoided.

32. Thus his entire life on earth, through the man whom he deigned to assume, was a discipline of conduct. His resurrection from the dead sufficiently indicated that nothing belonging to human nature perishes, since everything is safe with God. It also showed how all things serve their Creator, whether for the punishment of sins or for human liberation, and how readily the body serves the soul when the soul itself is subject to God. When these things have been perfected, not only is no substance evil—which can never happen—but neither is anything afflicted by the evil that could arise through sin and punishment.

This is the natural discipline [Note: He alludes to the ancient division of philosophy into natural, moral, and rational philosophy. He mentioned the moral discipline above, when he said that Christ’s life was a discipline of conduct; here he refers to the natural, and in the following chapter to the rational.], worthy of complete credence among Christians who understand less, and purified of every error for those who understand.

### CHAPTER XVII  
### The method of teaching in the true religion is supremely good, whether the Old or the New Testament is considered

33. Moreover, the very method of the entire teaching—partly most explicit [Note: So thirteen manuscripts and Arnoldus. Badius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read: “partly by the most explicit arguments, partly by comparisons,” etc.], partly conveyed through comparisons—in words, actions, and sacraments, adapted to every instruction and exercise of the soul: what else did it fulfill than the rule of rational discipline? For the exposition of the mysteries is directed toward those things that have been stated most explicitly. And if Scripture contained only what is easily understood, truth would neither be sought with care nor found with delight. Nor, if there were sacraments in Scripture [Note: The word *sacramenta*, “sacraments,” is absent from the manuscripts of Germanensis and Gemmeticensis, and from several others of no inferior authority.], and if the sacraments did not contain seals of truth, would action correspond sufficiently with knowledge.

But now, since piety begins with fear and is perfected by love, the people, bound by fear during the time of servitude, were burdened under the Old Law with many sacraments. This was useful for such people, so that they might desire the grace of God, which was sung as destined to come through the prophets. When that grace came through Wisdom itself, God having assumed humanity, through whom we were called into freedom [Note: Most manuscripts read: “God’s Wisdom having assumed humanity, and we were called into freedom.”], a few most salutary sacraments were established, which would preserve the fellowship of the Christian people—that is, of a free multitude under one God. Many practices that had been imposed upon the Hebrew people—that is, upon a multitude bound in fetters under the same one God—were removed from performance but remained in faith and interpretation. Thus they now neither bind us in a servile manner nor cease to exercise the soul freely.

34. Whoever therefore denies that both Testaments can come from one God because our people are not bound by the same sacraments by which the Jews were or still are bound may say that it is impossible for one supremely just head of a household to command one thing to those for whom he judges a harsher servitude useful, and another to those whom he deigns to adopt into the rank of sons.

But if the commandments concerning life cause concern—because they are less demanding in the Old Law and more demanding in the Gospel, and therefore both are thought not to belong to one God—whoever thinks this may be disturbed by the example of one physician prescribing one treatment through his assistants for the weaker and another treatment directly for the stronger, in order to restore or preserve health. For just as the art of medicine remains the same and is not itself changed in any way, yet changes its prescriptions for the sick because our health is changeable, so divine providence, although itself wholly unchangeable, nevertheless assists changeable creatures in various ways. According to the diversity of their illnesses, it commands or forbids different things, so that it may lead back and restore to their own nature and essence those things that are failing—things that are tending toward nothingness—from the vice from which death begins and from death itself.

### CHAPTER XVIII  
### Why creatures are changeable

[Col. 0137]

35. But you say to me: “Why do they fail?” Because they are changeable. “Why are they changeable?” Because they are not supreme. “Why are they not supreme?” Because they are inferior to the one by whom they were made. “Who made them?” The one who is supreme. “Who is this?” The unchangeable Trinity, God, since he made them through supreme Wisdom and preserves them by supreme goodness.

“Why did he make them?” So that they might exist. For existence itself, however limited, is good, because supreme goodness is supreme being. “From what did he make them?” From nothing. Since whatever exists must possess some degree of form, however slight [Note: Seven manuscripts read: “whatever its form, however slight, it must exist,” etc. This is no less satisfactory.], even if it is the least good, it will nevertheless be good, and it will be from God. For since supreme form is supreme good, the least form is the least good. Every good is either God or from God. Therefore even the least form is from God.

Certainly, what can be said of form (*species*) can also be said of shape (*forma*). For it is not without reason that something is praised as both most splendid and most beautiful. Therefore, that from which God made all things is what possesses no form and no shape—nothing other than nothingness. But that which is called formless in comparison with perfect things, if it possesses some form, however slight or rudimentary, is not yet nothing; and therefore, insofar as it exists, it too is from God.

36. Consequently, even if the world was made from some formless matter, that matter itself was wholly made from nothing. For even what has not yet been formed is nevertheless, in some way, already begun so that it can be formed; by God’s gift it is capable of form. For being formed is good. Thus the capacity for form is also some good; and therefore the author of all good, who bestowed form, himself also made the capacity to be formed.

Thus everything that exists, insofar as it exists, and everything that does not yet exist, insofar as it can exist, possesses this from God. The same may be stated in another way: everything formed, insofar as it is formed, and everything not yet formed, insofar as it can be formed, possesses this from God. No thing, however, possesses the integrity of its nature unless it is preserved within its own kind. All preservation comes from the one from whom all good comes; and all good is from God. Therefore all preservation comes from God.

### CHAPTER XIX  
### Things that can be corrupted are good, but not supreme goods

37. From this, anyone whose eyes of the mind are open and are not clouded or disturbed by the destructive zeal for empty victory easily understands that everything that is corrupted and dies is good, although corruption itself and death itself are evil. For unless such things were deprived of some preservation, corruption or death would not harm them; but if corruption did not harm them, it would in no way be corruption.

If corruption therefore opposes preservation, and preservation is undeniably good, then everything opposed by corruption is good. But what corruption opposes is itself corrupted. Therefore the things that are corrupted are good; but they are corrupted because they are not supreme goods. Since they are good, they are from God; since they are not supreme goods, they are not God.

The good that cannot be corrupted is therefore God. All other goods are from him; they can be corrupted in themselves because in themselves they are nothing, but through him some are not corrupted and others, once corrupted, are healed [Note: In the Cistercian manuscript it reads: “Some are not corrupted, such as angels; others, once corrupted, are healed, such as human beings.”].

### CHAPTER XX  
### The source of the soul’s corruption

38. The first corruption of the rational soul is the will to do what supreme and inward truth forbids. Thus the human being was expelled from paradise into this present age—that is, from eternal things to temporal things, from abundance to poverty, from stability to weakness. Not from substantial good to substantial evil, because no substance is evil, but from eternal good to temporal good, from spiritual good to bodily good, from intelligible good to sensible good, from supreme good to the lowest good.

There is therefore a certain good which, if the rational soul loves it, sins, because it has been ordered below the soul. Consequently, sin itself is evil, not the substance that is loved in sinning. That tree, then, which Scripture says was planted in the middle of paradise, is not evil, but the transgression of the divine command. Since a just condemnation follows that transgression, knowledge of good and evil results from the tree that was touched contrary to the prohibition. For once the soul has become entangled in its sin, it learns by paying the penalty what difference there is between the command that it refused to keep and the sin that it committed. In this way it learns through suffering the evil that it did not learn by avoiding it; and by comparison it loves more ardently the good that, through disobedience, it had loved less [Note: Some manuscripts read: “the good that, in obeying, it loved less.” Others read: *obtem[lacuna]*.].

39. The soul’s corruption, then, is what it has done, and the difficulty arising from corruption is the punishment it suffers; and this is the whole of evil. But doing and suffering are not substances; therefore substance is not evil.

Thus neither is water evil, nor an animal that lives in the air; for these are substances. Evil consists in the voluntary plunge into the water and in the suffocation suffered by one who is submerged. An iron stylus, made skillfully with one end for writing and another for erasing, is beautiful in its kind and suited to our use. But if someone wished to write with the end used for erasing and erase with the end used for writing, he would not thereby make the stylus evil, although the action itself would rightly be condemned. If he corrected it, where would the evil be?

If someone suddenly looks at the midday sun, his eyes, struck by its brightness, will be disturbed. Is the sun therefore evil, or are the eyes evil? In no way; they are substances. The evil consists in the disordered gaze and the disturbance that follows it. That evil will no longer exist when the eyes have recovered and look upon their proper light in the proper manner.

Nor, when the same light belonging to the eyes is worshiped in place of the light of wisdom belonging to the mind, does the light itself become evil. Superstition is evil—the practice by which the creature is served rather than the Creator. That evil will wholly disappear when the soul, having recognized its Creator, has submitted itself to him alone and has perceived that all other things are subject to it through him.

40. Thus every bodily creature, if it is merely possessed by a soul that loves God, is a lowest good and beautiful within its kind, since it is held together by form [Col. 0139] and appearance. But if it is loved by a soul that neglects God, it does not thereby itself become evil. Rather, because the sin by which it is loved is evil, it becomes punitive for the one who loves it, entangles him in hardships, and feeds him with deceptive pleasures. For these pleasures neither endure nor satisfy; they torment with pain.

When the beautiful mutability of temporal things completes its proper order, the desired appearance abandons its lover; through the torment of the one who perceives it, it withdraws from the senses and drives him into error, so that he thinks this to be the first form—the lowest of all, namely, bodily nature [Note: The printed editions read: “namely, bodily nature.” Ten manuscripts read: “namely, of bodily nature.”]—which the flesh, wrongly delighted through slippery senses, has reported [Note: The printed editions read: “which the flesh, wrongly loved, had reported.” Eight manuscripts read: “which the accursed flesh had reported.” Two others read “the badly instructed flesh”; one reads “the badly led flesh”; several others read: “which the flesh, wrongly delighted, has reported.”].

Thus, when he thinks about something, he believes that he understands, deceived by the shadows of images. But if, without possessing the discipline of divine providence in its entirety, he merely thinks that he possesses it and tries to resist the flesh, he reaches the images of visible things. He then vainly constructs in thought immense spaces for the light of this world, which he sees enclosed within definite boundaries, and promises himself this form [Note: Lovaniensis and Arnoldus read *spem*, “hope.” The older editions and the manuscripts more suitably read *speciem*, “form.”] as the dwelling-place of the future. He does not know that he is dragging along the desire of the eyes and wants to go outside the world together with the world. He therefore thinks that the world itself does not exist because, through false thought, he stretches its brighter part into infinity.

The same thing can very easily happen not only with this light but also with water, and finally with wine, honey, gold, silver, even the flesh, blood, or bones of any animals, and other things of this kind. For there is nothing bodily whose appearance cannot be imagined innumerably, or whose appearance, seen within a small space, cannot by the same imaginative faculty be spread out through infinite expanses. Nothing is easier than to condemn the flesh; nothing more difficult than to think without carnality.

### CHAPTER XXI  
### The soul is led astray while it pursues the fleeting beauties of bodies

41. Through this perversity of the soul, which results from sin and punishment, all bodily nature becomes what is said through Solomon: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What abundance has a human being in all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” (Ecclesiastes 1:2–3). The addition “of those who are vain” is not without reason. For if you remove those who are vain—those who pursue extremes as though they were first things—the body will not be vanity; rather, within its own kind, although it is an extreme, it will display beauty without any error.

The manifold diversity of temporal forms, striking the human being who has fallen from God’s unity through bodily senses, has multiplied his affection through changeable variety. Thus there has arisen a laborious abundance and, if it may be said so, an abundant poverty, as he pursues one thing after another and nothing remains with him. Thus he has been multiplied “from the time of his grain, wine, and oil,” so that he does not find that same thing (Psalm 4:8–9)—that is, the unchangeable and singular nature which, when pursued, does not lead him astray and, when attained, does not cause him grief.

He will also receive the redemption of his body (Romans 8:23), which will no longer be corrupted. But now “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15), because the lowest beauty of bodies is swept into the order of succession. It is lowest for this reason: it cannot possess everything simultaneously. But while some things yield and others succeed them, the number of temporal forms completes a single beauty [Note: So most manuscripts. Erasmus, Lovaniensis, and Arnoldus read: “they complete numbers in beauty.”].

### CHAPTER XXII  
### Only the ungodly dislike the administration of passing things

42. None of this is evil merely because it passes away. A verse, too, is beautiful within its kind, although its two syllables can in no way be spoken simultaneously. The second is not pronounced unless the first has passed; and one reaches the end in an ordered sequence, so that when only the final syllable sounds, without the preceding syllables sounding with it, it nevertheless completes, together with those that have passed, the verse’s form and metrical beauty.

Yet the art by which the verse is constructed is not thereby so subject to time that its beauty is distributed according to measured durations. Rather, it possesses simultaneously everything by which it produces a verse that does not possess everything simultaneously, but removes the earlier elements through the later ones. It is beautiful for this reason: it displays the final traces of the beauty that the art itself preserves consistently and unchangeably.

43. Accordingly, just as some perverse people love a verse more than the art itself by which the verse is composed, because they have surrendered themselves more to the ears than to the understanding, so many love temporal things but do not seek the divine providence that creates and governs time. In their very love of temporal things they do not want what they love to pass away, and they are as absurd as someone who, while a splendid poem was being recited, wanted to hear one particular syllable alone forever.

Such listeners to poems are not found; but the world is full of such judges of things, because anyone can easily hear not only an entire verse but even an entire poem, whereas no human being can perceive the entire order of the ages. Moreover, we are not parts of a poem, but through condemnation we have become parts of the ages. The poem is sung under our judgment; these things are brought to completion through our labor.

No defeated contestant in the athletic games takes pleasure in the games, yet the games remain beautiful despite his disgrace; for this too is a kind of imitation of truth. We are prohibited from such spectacles for no other reason than that, deceived by shadows of things, we might stray from the things themselves whose shadows they are.

Thus the constitution and administration of this universe do not please only ungodly and condemned souls; they also please many who, amid their misery, are either victorious on earth or view them without danger in heaven [Note: Erasmus and the Casalensis manuscript read: “But they also please holy souls amid their misery.” Lovaniensis reads: “but also holy animals amid their misery,” etc. This is an interpolated passage, which most manuscripts and the editions of Badius and Arnoldus present as follows: “but they also please amid their misery,” etc.]. For nothing just displeases the just.

### CHAPTER XXIII  
### Every substance is good

44. Consequently, since every rational soul is either miserable through its sins or blessed through right actions; since every irrational creature either yields to what is more powerful, obeys what is better, is compared with what is equal, exercises one who contends [Note: Lovaniensis and Arnoldus read *certamen*, “a contest.” Badius, Erasmus, and eight manuscripts more smoothly read *certantem*, “what contends with it.”], or harms what has been condemned; and since every body serves its soul insofar as this is permitted by the soul’s merits and by the order of things, no evil belongs to the universe of nature. Rather, each person’s own fault becomes his evil.

Moreover, when the soul has been regenerated by God’s grace, restored to wholeness, and subjected to the one from whom it was created; when the body too has been restored to its former firmness; and when the soul has begun not to be possessed along with the world but to possess the world, it will have no evil. For the lowest beauty of temporal changes, which was then being accomplished along with it, will then be accomplished beneath it. There will be, as Scripture says, “a new heaven and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17; Revelation 21:1), not in souls laboring in part, but in the whole universe reigning.

“For all things are yours,” says the Apostle, “and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Corinthians 3:22); and: “The head of a woman is man, the head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (ibid. 11:3).

Since the soul’s corruption is therefore not its nature but contrary to its nature, and is nothing other than sin and the punishment of sin, it follows that no nature—or, to put it more suitably, no substance or essence—is evil. Nor do the sins and punishments of the soul cause the universe to be disfigured by any deformity. The rational substance that is free from every sin, subject to God, rules over the other things subject to it. The soul that has sinned, however, has been placed where such souls ought to be, so that all things may be beautiful under God, the Creator and governor of the universe.

The beauty of the entire creation is blameless through these three things: the condemnation of sinners, the testing of the just, and the perfection of the blessed.

### CHAPTER XXIV  
### Human salvation is provided for by a twofold path, authority and reason; first, the aid of authority is discussed through chapter 29

45. Therefore even the soul’s medicine, administered by divine providence and ineffable benevolence, is supremely beautiful in its gradual and ordered arrangement. It is divided into authority and reason. Authority demands faith and prepares a person for reason. Reason leads to understanding and knowledge.

Yet reason does not entirely abandon authority when it considers whom one ought to believe; and certainly the highest authority is that of truth itself, once known and made evident. But because we have descended into temporal things and are hindered from eternal things by our love of them, a certain temporal medicine—which calls us to salvation not by knowing but by believing—is prior, not in nature or excellence [Note: Many manuscripts read: “not by the excellence of nature.”], but in the order of time. For wherever someone has fallen, there he must apply himself in order to rise.

Therefore we must use the very bodily forms by which we are held captive in order to come to know those things that the flesh does not announce. By “bodily” forms I mean those that can be perceived through the flesh—that is, through the eyes, ears, and the other bodily senses. It is therefore necessary for children to cling in love to these bodily or corporeal forms; for adolescents it is almost necessary; but as age advances beyond this point, it is no longer necessary.

### CHAPTER XXV  
### Whose authority, whether of persons or books, is to be believed concerning the worship of God

46. Since divine providence provides not only for individual human beings privately, as it were, but also for the entire human race publicly, God, who acts, and the individuals with whom he acts, know what takes place with each person. But what takes place with the human race he wished to be preserved through history and prophecy.

Faith concerning temporal things, whether past or future, has greater force through believing than through understanding. But it is our task to consider which people or books we ought to believe in order rightly to worship God, which is the one salvation.

The first question in this matter is whether we should rather believe those who call us to worship many gods, or those who call us to worship one God. Who would doubt that we should chiefly follow those who call us to one, especially since the worshipers of many gods agree concerning this one Lord and governor of all? And certainly number begins from one.

Those, then, must first be followed who say that there is one supreme God, the only true God, and that he alone ought to be worshiped. If the truth does not shine forth among them, only then should one move elsewhere [Note: *Retractations* I.13.6.]. For just as, in the nature of things itself, greater authority belongs to the one who reduces everything to unity, and in the human race no power belongs to a multitude unless it is consenting—that is, unless it thinks as one—so in religion the authority of those who call us to one God ought to be greater and more worthy of faith.

47. The second consideration concerns the disagreement that has arisen among human beings concerning the worship of the one God. We have received the tradition that our ancestors, at that level of faith [Note: The word *fidei*, “of faith,” is absent from fifteen manuscripts and also from Badius and Erasmus.], by which one ascends from temporal to eternal things, followed visible miracles—for they could not have proceeded otherwise. Through them it was brought about that such miracles would no longer be necessary for later generations.

For since the Catholic Church has been spread and established throughout the whole world, those miracles were not permitted to continue into our times, lest the human mind should always seek visible signs and the human race grow cold through familiarity with what had once inflamed it by its novelty [Note: Ibid. section 7.]. Nor should we now doubt that we ought to believe those who, while proclaiming things that few attain, were nevertheless able to persuade the masses to follow them.

The question now is whom one ought to believe before each person is capable of undertaking rational inquiry into divine and invisible matters. For no human authority is in any way placed above the purified reason of the soul that reaches clear truth. But no pride leads to this reason [Note: The printed editions read: “no human pride leads to this.” The word “human” is absent from the manuscripts.]. If pride did not exist, there would be no heretics, schismatics, people circumcised in the flesh, or worshipers of creatures and images. If these groups did not exist before the perfection of the people that is promised, truth would be sought much more sluggishly.

### CHAPTER XXVI  
### Divine providence for our salvation through the six ages of the old and the new human being

[Col. 0143]

48. The temporal dispensation and the divine medicine of providence are therefore communicated in this way to those who, through sin, have merited mortality.

First, the nature and education of every individual human being who is born are considered. The first age of this life, infancy, is spent in bodily nourishment and must be completely forgotten by the growing person. Childhood follows, from which we begin to remember something. Adolescence succeeds childhood; nature now permits the propagation of offspring and makes the person a father. Then youth follows adolescence, an age already requiring the performance of public duties and subjection to laws.

At this stage, the more forceful prohibition of sins and the servile punishment that restrains sinners produce more savage eruptions of lust in carnal souls, and multiply every offense. For it is not a simple sin to commit not merely something evil but something forbidden.

After the labors of youth, some peace is granted to old age. From there until death comes a worse and more discolored age, more subject to disease and weakness. This is the life of the human being who lives from the body and is bound to desires for temporal things.

This is called the old, exterior, and earthly human being, even if he possesses what the common people call happiness in a well-ordered earthly state—whether under kings, rulers, laws, or all of these together. For a people that pursues earthly things cannot otherwise be well ordered; it too possesses a certain measure of beauty.

49. Some people carry out this human being whom we have described as old, exterior, and earthly—whether moderate within his own kind or even exceeding the measure of servile justice—from the beginning of this life until its end. Others necessarily begin this life from him but are reborn inwardly; through their spiritual strength and growth in wisdom they corrupt and kill the remaining parts of the old human being and bind them to heavenly laws, until the whole person is restored after visible death.

This is called the new, interior, and heavenly human being. He too possesses, in proportion not to years but to progress, certain distinct spiritual ages of his own.

The first age is spent at the breasts of useful history, which nourishes by examples. The second has already begun to forget human things and to strive toward divine things. In this age the person is not held within the embrace of human authority but relies, through the steps of reason, upon the supreme and unchangeable law.

The third is already more confident; it tames carnal desire by the strength of reason and rejoices inwardly in a certain conjugal sweetness, when the soul is joined to the mind and veiled by modesty, so that it is no longer compelled to live rightly, but even if everyone gave permission, it would have no desire to sin.

The fourth does the same thing much more firmly and orderly, shining forth as a perfect human being, prepared and capable of enduring and breaking every persecution and all the storms and waves of this world.

The fifth is peaceful and tranquil in every respect, living amid the riches and abundance of the unchangeable kingdom of supreme and ineffable wisdom.

The sixth consists in complete transformation into eternal life, passing over into the perfect form that was made in the image and likeness of God, until the life of temporal things is wholly forgotten [Col. 0144].

The seventh is already eternal rest, perpetual blessedness not to be divided into ages. For just as death is the end of the old human being, so eternal life is the end of the new human being. The one is the human being of sin; the other, of justice.

### CHAPTER XXVII  
### The course of the two human beings in the whole human race

50. Just as these two human beings unquestionably exist in such a way that one person can live out the old and earthly one through the entirety of this life, while no one in this life can live out the new and heavenly one except together with the old—for he must necessarily begin from the old and continue with it until visible death, although the old declines as the new progresses—so, by analogy, the entire human race, whose life is like that of a single human being from Adam to the end of this age, is governed under the laws of divine providence in such a way that it appears divided into two groups.

In one is the multitude of the ungodly, bearing the image of the earthly human being from the beginning of the age to its end. In the other is the succession of the people devoted to the one God. From Adam to John the Baptist this people lived the life of the earthly human being according to a certain servile justice. Its history is called the Old Testament, as though promising an earthly kingdom. In its entirety it is nothing other than an image of the new people and of the New Testament, which promises the kingdom of heaven.

The temporal life of this people begins meanwhile with the Lord’s coming in humility and continues until the day of judgment, when he will come in glory. After that judgment, when the old human being has been extinguished, there will be the transformation that promises angelic life: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51).

The devout people will therefore rise so that the remnants of their old human being may be transformed into the new. The ungodly people, who carried the old human being from beginning to end, will also rise, so that they may be hurled into the second death.

Those who read carefully discover the divisions of the ages; they do not shrink back in horror from the weeds or the chaff. For the ungodly live for the devout, and the sinner for the just, so that by comparison the latter may rise more vigorously until perfection is achieved.

### CHAPTER XXVIII  
### What is to be handed down, to whom, and in what manner
51. Whoever, however, among the people of the earthly age has deserved to advance as far as the illumination of the inner person has, in his own time aided the human race, presenting to it what that age required and announcing prophetically what it was not opportune to present. Such are the Patriarchs and Prophets, as they are found by those who do not rush in childishly [Note: [Col. 0144] As the Manichaeans do], but piously and carefully examine the good and very great mystery of divine and human affairs.

I also see this most cautiously provided for in the times of the new people by great and spiritual men, foster-children of the Catholic Church: they take care not to do anything publicly which they understand is not yet timely to be done with the people; they abundantly and persistently pour milk-food into the eager, weaker multitude, but partake of stronger foods with the few who are wise. [Col. 0145] For “among the perfect” they speak wisdom, while to the carnal and natural, even though they are new persons, yet still little ones, they conceal certain things—but they assert nothing false. They do not look to their own empty honors and hollow praises, but to the usefulness of those with whom they have deserved to enter into the fellowship of this life.

For this is the law of divine providence: no one is aided by those above him in knowing and receiving the grace of God unless he, with pure affection, has aided those below him in receiving that same grace. Thus, from our sin—which our very nature committed in the sinful human being—the human race has become a great glory and adornment of the earth; and it is so fittingly administered by the governance of divine providence that the ineffable art of healing turns the very ugliness of its vices into some beauty of its own kind.

## CHAPTER XXIX — On the second aid to salvation, namely reason; how, under its guidance, a human being is raised up to God; it is first discovered to exercise its function through the senses

52. And since we have spoken, as much as seemed sufficient for the present, about the beneficence of authority, let us see how far reason can advance from visible things to invisible things, ascending from temporal things to eternal ones.

For it is not without purpose or profit that one should contemplate the beauty of heaven, the order of the stars, the brightness of light, the alternation of days and nights, the moon’s monthly courses, the fourfold ordering of the year corresponding to the four elements, the great power of seeds producing forms and numbers, and all things preserving in their own kind their proper measure and nature. In considering these things, one should not exercise a vain and perishable curiosity, but make them a step toward things immortal and everlasting.

The next step is to attend to the nature of this living being that perceives all these things. Since it gives life to the body, it must necessarily be superior to the body. For no mass, however great, even if it shines with visible light, is to be highly valued if it lacks life. Every living substance, by the law of nature, is preferred to any nonliving substance. [Note: [Col. 0145] Consult *On Free Choice of the Will*, Book 2, chapters 3 and following.]

53. But since no one doubts that irrational animals also live and perceive, what is most excellent in the human mind is not that by which it perceives sensible things, but that by which it judges concerning sensible things. Most beasts see more sharply and encounter bodies through the other bodily senses more keenly than human beings do; but judging concerning bodies belongs not merely to a perceiving life, but also to a reasoning one. They lack this, whereas we excel in it.

Now it is very easy to see that the one who judges is superior to the thing about which judgment is made. Rational life judges not only concerning sensible things, but also concerning the senses themselves: why an oar in water ought to appear broken although it is straight, and why it must necessarily be perceived in this way through the eyes. The eyes’ own visual perception can report this, but it cannot judge it in any way. Therefore it is clear that, just as the sentient life is superior to the body, so the rational life is superior to both.

## CHAPTER XXX — The immutable law is superior to reason, namely the truth according to which reason judges

54. Therefore, if rational life judges according to itself, there is now no nature superior to it. But since it is clearly changeable, being found at one time knowledgeable and at another ignorant—and since it judges better the more knowledgeable it is, and is more knowledgeable insofar as it participates in some art, discipline, or wisdom—the nature of the art itself must be sought.

I do not now mean by “art” what is recognized through experience, but what is investigated by reasoning. What remarkable knowledge does someone possess who knows that stones adhere more firmly in mortar made with lime and sand than in mud? Or what remarkable knowledge belongs to one who builds so elegantly that the greater number correspond to one another as equals, while individual elements occupy the middle position? Yet this sense is already nearer to reason and truth.

But certainly we must ask why it offends us if, when two windows are placed not one above the other but beside one another, one is larger or smaller than the other, although they could have been equal; whereas, if they are placed one above the other, and both are unequal by half [Note: [Col. 0146] Thus the better manuscripts. The printed editions, however, have “from the middle”], such inequality does not offend us so much. We must also ask why we care little how much one of the two is larger or smaller, simply because there are two.

With three, however, the sense itself seems to demand either that they not be unequal, or that the middle one stand between the largest and the smallest in such a way that it exceeds the smaller by as much as it is exceeded by the larger. Thus, in the first instance, nature herself, as it were, is consulted concerning what she approves.

Here we must especially note how something that, considered by itself, was less displeasing is rejected when compared with something better. Thus it is found that ordinary art is nothing other than a memory of things tested and approved, joined to a certain bodily practice and activity. If one lacks this, one can still judge works—which is much more excellent—although one cannot perform artistic operations.

55.
