But since proportion pleases in all the arts, and through it alone all things are beautiful, while proportion itself seeks equality and unity, either through the similarity of equal parts or through the gradation of unequal ones, who could find perfect equality or similarity in bodies and dare to say, after carefully considering any body whatsoever, that it is truly and simply one, when all bodies change either by passing from one form to another or from one place to another, and consist of parts occupying their own places, through which they are divided into different spaces?

Moreover, true equality and similarity, and true and first unity itself, are perceived not by bodily eyes or by any such sense, but by the mind. For how could any equality in bodies be sought, or how could it be shown to differ so greatly from the perfect, unless that which is perfect were seen by the mind?—provided, that is, that something not made can properly be called perfect.

56. And since everything that is beautiful in a sensible way—whether produced by nature or wrought by art—is beautiful in places and times, as are a body and the movement of a body, that equality and unity known only to the mind, according to which judgment is made concerning bodily beauty through the mediation of the senses, is neither swollen by place nor unstable through time.

For one cannot rightly say that according to it a round rim is judged round, but not a round little vessel; or that according to it a round little vessel is judged round, but not a round coin. Similarly, in times and bodily movements, it is absurd to say that according to it equal years are judged equal, but not equal months; or that according to it equal months are judged equal, but not equal days.

Whether something moves proportionately through these spans, through hours, or through briefer moments, it is judged by the same one and unchangeable equality. If smaller and larger spatial intervals of figures and movements are judged according to the same law of equality, similarity, or proportion, then that law is greater than all these things in power. In spatial or temporal extent, however, it is neither greater nor smaller. If it were greater, we would not judge smaller things according to it in its entirety; if it were smaller, we would not judge larger things according to it. [Note: [Col. 0147] The printed editions read: “We would not judge larger things according to it.” The manuscripts more correctly read: “According to it in its entirety.”]

Now, since according to the entire law of squareness we judge a square forum, a square stone, a square tablet, and a square gem; and since, again, according to the entire law of equality we judge that the movements of the feet of a running ant and of a walking elephant correspond to one another, who could doubt that this law is neither greater nor smaller than intervals of place and time, since in power it surpasses all things?

Since this law of all the arts is altogether unchangeable, while the human mind, which has been granted the vision of such a law, can suffer the mutability of error, it is sufficiently clear that there is above our mind a law called truth.

## CHAPTER XXXI — God is that supreme law according to which reason judges, but which it is not permitted to judge

57. Nor should there now be any doubt that the unchangeable nature which is above the rational soul is God, and that the first life and first essence are where the first wisdom is. For this is that unchangeable truth which is rightly called the law of all the arts and the art of the omnipotent Craftsman.

Therefore, when the soul perceives that it does not judge the form and movement of bodies according to itself, it must at the same time acknowledge that its own nature is superior to the nature about which it judges; yet that nature according to which it judges is superior to it, and it cannot judge that nature in any way.

I can say why the corresponding limbs of every body ought to answer one another equally on both sides: because I delight in supreme equality, which I contemplate not with bodily eyes but with the mind. Accordingly, I judge the things I see with my eyes to be better insofar as, according to their own nature, they are nearer to the things I understand in my mind.

But why those things are as they are, no one can say; nor would anyone soberly say that they ought to be so, as though they could be otherwise.

58. Nor will anyone who understands these things properly dare to say why they please us, or why, when we have better judgment, we love them most intensely. For just as we and all rational souls judge inferior things rightly according to truth, so, when we cleave to that same truth, truth alone judges us.

As for truth itself, not even the Father judges it—for it is not less than he himself [Note: [Col. 0148] Twelve manuscripts read: “For it is not less than he himself”]—and therefore whatever the Father judges, he judges through it. For everything that seeks unity has this as its rule, form, or model, or whatever other word it permits itself to be called, since it alone has fulfilled the likeness of the one from whom it received being.

Yet if it is said to have received being, this is not inappropriate according to the meaning in which the Son is called the Son: he is not from himself, but from the first and highest Principle, who is called the Father, “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Ephesians 3:15).

Therefore the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). And “the spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2:15)—that is, by no human being, but by the very law according to which he judges all things. For this too was said most truly: “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

He judges all things, then, because he is above all things when he is with God. He is with God when he understands with the greatest purity and loves with complete charity what he understands. Thus, insofar as he can, he himself also becomes the law according to which he judges all things and concerning which no one can judge.

So it is with temporal laws: although human beings judge concerning them when they establish them, once they have been established and confirmed, a judge may not judge the laws themselves, but must judge according to them. Yet the maker of temporal laws, if he is a good and wise man, consults that eternal law concerning which no soul has been granted the right to judge, so that according to its unchangeable rules he may discern what ought to be commanded or forbidden at a particular time.

It is therefore lawful for pure souls to know the eternal law, but not lawful to judge it. The distinction is this: for knowing, it is sufficient that we see that something is so or is not so; but for judging, we add something by which we signify that it could also be otherwise—for example, when we say, “It ought to be so,” or “It ought to have been so,” or “It will have to be so,” as craftsmen do in their works.

## CHAPTER XXXII — There is a trace of unity in bodies, but unity itself is perceived only by the mind

59. But for many, human pleasure is the end, and they do not wish to ascend to higher things in order to judge why visible things please. Thus, if I ask a craftsman, after he has built one arch, why he constructs another of equal size opposite it on the other side, he will answer, I suppose, “So that equal members of the building may correspond to equal members.”

If I continue asking why he chooses this very arrangement, he will say, “Because it is fitting, beautiful, and pleasing to those who see it.” He will dare say no more. Inclining and reclining toward his eyes, he does not understand upon what they depend.

But I shall not cease to admonish the inwardly sighted man, who sees invisibly, asking why these things please, so that he may dare to be the judge of human pleasure itself. In this way he rises above it and is not held by it, because he judges it rather than judging according to it.

First, then, I shall ask whether things are beautiful because they please, or please because they are beautiful. Here he will answer me without hesitation: they please because they are beautiful. I shall next ask why they are beautiful; and if he falters, I shall add: Is it because their parts are similar to one another and are brought together into one harmony by some joining?

60. When he has discovered that this is so, I shall ask whether they fully realize the unity they are shown to seek, or whether they lie far below it and in some way falsely represent it. For if this is so—and who, once warned, would not see that no form and no body whatsoever lacks some trace of unity, yet that no matter how beautiful a body may be, since it necessarily has one thing in one place and another elsewhere, separated by intervals of space, it cannot attain the unity it pursues?—then, if this is so, I shall demand that he answer where he himself sees this unity, or from where he sees it.

If he did not see it, how would he know what bodily forms imitate and what they could not fulfill? But when he says to bodies, “Unless some unity held you together, you would be nothing; yet if you were unity itself, you would not be bodies,” he is rightly asked: “From where do you know that unity according to which you judge bodies, which you could not judge to be deficient in it unless you saw it? If you saw it with these bodily eyes, you would not rightly say that, although bodies are held by its trace, they are nevertheless far removed from it.”

For with these bodily eyes you see only bodily things. Therefore we see unity with the mind. But where do we see it? If it were situated in the place where our body is, the person who judges bodies in the East in this way would not see it. It is not therefore contained in a place; and although it is present wherever one judges, it is nowhere extended through intervals of place, and through its power it is nowhere absent.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — It is not bodies or the bodily senses that deceive, but judgment. The difference between lying and deceiving

61. If bodies imitate unity falsely, we must not believe those that lie, lest we fall into the vanities of those who make themselves vain; rather, we must ask this: since they seem to lie because they appear to display unity to bodily eyes, although unity is seen by a pure mind, do they lie insofar as they are similar to it, or insofar as they fail to attain it?

If they attained it, they would fulfill what they imitate. If they fulfilled it, they would be completely similar. If they were completely similar, there would be no difference between that nature and this one. If that were so, they would not lie about it, for they would be what it is.

Yet they do not lie to those who consider the matter carefully. For one lies who wishes to appear to be what he is not. But when something unwillingly is thought to be other than it is, it does not lie; it merely deceives. The distinction between lying and deceiving is therefore this: every liar has the will to deceive, even if no one believes him; but there can be no deceiver who does not deceive.

Thus bodily form, since it has no will, does not lie. And if it is not thought to be what it is not, it does not deceive either.

62. But not even the eyes themselves deceive. They can report to the mind only the condition in which they are affected. If not only the eyes, but all the bodily senses report things in accordance with the way they are affected, I do not know what more we ought to demand from them.

Remove, then, those who make themselves vain, and there will be no vanity. If someone thinks that an oar is broken in water and becomes whole when removed from it, the messenger is not defective; the judge is. For according to its nature the eye could not perceive otherwise in water, nor ought it to have done so. If air is one thing and water another, it is right that something should be perceived one way in air and another way in water.

The eye is therefore right, for it was made to see only as much as it sees. But the mind is wrong, for the mind, not the eye, was made to contemplate supreme beauty. The mind, however, wishes to turn itself toward bodies and its eyes toward God. It seeks to understand carnal things and to see spiritual things; this cannot happen.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — How fabricated images are to be judged

63. This perversity must therefore be corrected, because unless it makes what is above into what is below and what is below into what is above, it will not be fit for the kingdom of heaven.

Let us not seek the supreme in the lowest things, nor cling to the lowest things themselves [Note: [Col. 0150] Twelve manuscripts read, “let us not envy them”]. Let us judge them, lest we be judged along with them; that is, let us assign them only as much value as the lowest form deserves, lest, when we seek the first things among the last, we ourselves be numbered among the last by the First.

This harms nothing in the lowest things themselves, but harms us greatly. Nor does the administration of divine providence thereby become less beautiful, because both the unjust are ordered justly and the ugly beautifully.

And if the beauty of visible things deceives us because it is held together by unity but does not fulfill unity, let us understand, if we can, that we are not deceived by what is, but by what is not. Every body is indeed a true body, but a false unity. It is not supremely one, nor does it imitate the One sufficiently to fulfill it. Yet the body itself would not exist unless it were in some way one. Moreover, it could not be in any way one unless it possessed this from the One who is supremely one.

64. O stubborn souls [Note: [Col. 0150] The Manichaeans, devoted to phantasms; *Confessions* 3.6 and 9.4], give me one who sees without any imagination of things viewed by the flesh. Give me one who sees that the beginning of every unity is nothing other than the one alone from whom every one thing derives its unity, whether it fulfills that unity or not.

Give me one who sees—not one who quarrels, nor one who wants it to appear that he sees what he does not see. Give me one who resists the bodily senses and the blows by which, through them, the soul has been beaten; who resists human custom and human praise; who is pierced in his chamber; who renews his spirit; who does not love vanities outside and seek lies (Psalm 4:3–4).

Let him already know how to say to himself: If there is only one Rome, which some Romulus is said to have founded beside the Tiber, then this Rome that I imagine while thinking is false. For it is not the same Rome, nor am I there in mind [Note: [Col. 0150] Bad., Lov., and Arn. read, “nor am I there now.” But the reading of Er. and ten manuscripts, “nor am I there in mind,” appears preferable]. For surely I would know what is happening there now.

If there is only one sun, this sun that I imagine while thinking is false. The real sun completes its courses in fixed places and times; I establish this imagined one wherever and whenever I wish.

If there is only one friend of mine, this friend that I imagine is false. For I do not know where the real one is; the imagined one is placed wherever I wish.

I myself, certainly, am one, and I perceive my body to be in this place; yet by the fiction of thought I go wherever I please and speak with whomever I please. These things are false, and no one understands what is false. Therefore, when I contemplate these things and believe them, I do not understand them, because what I contemplate through understanding must be true.

Could these perhaps be what are usually called phantasms? How, then, has my soul been filled with illusions? Where is the truth that is contemplated by the mind?

To one who thinks in this way it can now be said: That is the true light by which you recognize that these things are not true. Through it you see that One by which you judge everything else you see to be one, yet you do not judge that anything mutable is the same as that One.

## CHAPTER XXXV — One must have leisure in order to know God

65. If the gaze of the mind struggles to contemplate these things, be still. Do not fight except against the habit of bodily things. Conquer that habit, and all things will be conquered.

Certainly we seek the One, than whom nothing is simpler. Let us therefore seek him in simplicity of heart. “Be still,” he says, “and know that I am God” (Psalm 45:11)—not the leisure of idleness, but the leisure of thought, so that the mind may be free from places and times.

For the phantasms of swelling and changeability do not allow us to see abiding unity. Places offer what we love; times snatch away what we love; and they leave in the soul crowds of phantasms by which desire is driven toward one thing and then another. Thus the mind becomes restless and wretched, vainly desiring to hold what holds it.

It is therefore called to leisure—that is, not to love the things that cannot be loved without labor. In this way it will rule them; it will not be held by them, but will hold them.

“My yoke,” he says, “is easy” (Matthew 11:30). Whoever is subject to this yoke has the rest subject to him. He will not labor, for what is subject does not resist.

But the wretched friends of this world—whose masters they will be if they wish to be children of God, since he gave them power to become children of God (John 1:12)—are so afraid to be separated from its embrace that nothing seems more burdensome to them than not to labor.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — The Word of God is truth itself, because it completely fulfills that from which, as the Principle, everything that is one is one. Falsity arises not from things but from sins

66. Whoever at least understands that falsity consists in thinking that something is what it is not also understands that truth is what reveals what is.

But if bodies deceive insofar as they do not fulfill that One which they are shown to imitate—the Principle from which whatever is, is one, and toward whose likeness whatever strives we naturally approve, because we naturally disapprove whatever departs from unity and tends toward its unlikeness—it is given us to understand that there is something so like that sole One, from the Principle from which everything that is in any way one is one, that it completely fulfills this and is the selfsame thing.

This is Truth, and the Word in the Beginning, and the Word, God with God. For if falsity belongs to things that imitate unity not insofar as they imitate it but insofar as they cannot fulfill it, then the Truth is what was able to fulfill it and to be what that One is. It is the Truth that reveals the One as it is; hence it is rightly called his Word and his Light (John 1:9).

The other things may be called like that One insofar as they exist; for insofar as they exist, they are also true. But this is its very likeness, and therefore it is Truth. Just as truth is the form of true things, so likeness is the form of things that are alike. Therefore, since true things are true insofar as they are, and are insofar as they are like the principal One, the form of all things that exist is that supreme likeness of the Principle. It is Truth because it has no unlikeness at all.

67. Falsity arises neither from the things themselves, which deceive no one but display to the perceiver only their own appearance, received according to the degree of their beauty, nor from the senses themselves, which, being affected according to the nature of their bodies, report to the presiding mind nothing other than their own affections.

Rather, sins deceive souls when they seek the truth but have abandoned and neglected it. For because they have loved works more than the Craftsman and the art itself, they are punished by this error: they seek the Craftsman and the art in the works; and when they cannot find them—for God is not subject to bodily senses but surpasses the mind itself—they suppose that the works themselves are both the art and the Craftsman.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — The impiety of manifold idolatry arising from love of the creature

68. From this arises all impiety—not only that of sinners, but also that of those condemned for their sins. For they do not merely scrutinize the creature contrary to God’s command and wish to enjoy it rather than the law and truth themselves, which is recognized as the sin of the first human being, who misused free will. In their very condemnation they add this: they not only love the creature but also serve it rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25), and they worship it through its parts, descending from the highest to the lowest.

Some, however, hold to this position: instead of the supreme God, they worship the soul and the first intellectual creature, which the Father fashioned through the Truth so that it might always contemplate the Truth itself, and itself through that Truth [Note: [Col. 0152] Lov. reads, “and through itself.” But the reading found in the other editions and in all the manuscripts, “and itself through that Truth,” should be retained], because it is in every way like it.

Next they come to generative life, through which the eternal and unchangeable God produces visible and temporal things. From there they slip down to the worship of animals, and then of bodies themselves. Among these they first choose the more beautiful, in which the heavenly bodies excel most greatly.

Thus the body of the sun is encountered first, and some remain there. Others consider the brightness of the moon also worthy of religious veneration; it is said to be nearer to us, and therefore is perceived to possess a more familiar appearance.

Others add the bodies of the remaining stars, and the whole heaven with its stars. Others join the air to the ethereal heaven and subject their souls to these two higher corporeal elements.

But among them, those seem to themselves most religious who regard the whole of creation at once—that is, the entire world with everything in it, and the life by which it breathes and is animated, which some have believed to be corporeal and others incorporeal—as one great God, whose parts the other things are. For they do not know the author and creator of the whole of creation.

From there they plunge into images and sink from the works of God into their own works, which nevertheless are still visible.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — Another kind of idolatry, by which the sinner serves a threefold desire

[Col. 0153]

69. There is another, worse and lower, worship of images, by which people worship their own phantasms and, under the name of religion, observe whatever they have imagined in thought with a wandering mind, in pride or swelling conceit. Eventually the soul comes to believe that nothing at all ought to be worshiped, that those who entangle themselves in superstition are mistaken, and that they involve themselves in miserable servitude.

But they think this in vain. They do not thereby cease to serve; the very vices remain by which they were drawn into thinking that such things should be worshiped. For they serve a threefold desire: pleasure, superiority, or spectacle.

I deny that any of those who think that nothing ought to be worshiped exists who is not either subject to carnal pleasures, cherishing empty power, or driven mad by delight in some spectacle. Without knowing it, they love temporal things in such a way that they expect blessedness from them.

But one must necessarily serve the things by which each person wishes to become blessed, whether he wishes to or not. Wherever they lead, he follows; and whoever appears able to take them away is feared. Yet fire and even some small animal can take these things away. Finally, to omit innumerable adversities, time itself must take away everything that passes.

Since this world therefore encloses all temporal things, those who think that nothing should be worshiped lest they serve anything are serving all the parts of the world.

70. Nevertheless, although in this lowest condition of things the miserable lie prostrate, allowing their vices to dominate them—condemned by lust, pride, or curiosity, or by two of these, or by all of them—as long as they are in this arena of human life, they may fight and conquer, provided that they first believe what they are not yet able to understand and do not love the world.

For, as it is divinely said, everything that is in the world is “the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (1 John 2:16). In this way those three things are identified: “the desire of the flesh” signifies lovers of the lowest pleasures; “the desire of the eyes,” the curious; and “the ambition of the age,” the proud.

71. A threefold temptation was also shown to be something to be guarded against in the human being whom Truth itself assumed.

“Tell these stones,” says the tempter, “to become loaves of bread.” But that one and only Teacher replied: “Human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” Thus he taught that the desire for pleasure must be subdued, so that one must not yield even to hunger.

But perhaps he could be deceived by the arrogance of temporal domination, although he could not be overcome by bodily pleasure. Therefore all the kingdoms of the world were shown to him, and it was said: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.” He replied: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” Thus pride was trampled down.

The final enticement of curiosity was also subjected. For nothing compelled him to throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple except the desire to test something. Yet he was not overcome here either, and he replied in such a way that we might understand that there is no need to explore divine things visibly through temptations in order to know God: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matthew 4:1–10; Luke 4:2–12).

Therefore whoever is nourished inwardly by the word of God does not seek pleasure in this wilderness. Whoever is subject to God alone does not seek boastfulness on the mountain—that is, in earthly exaltation. Whoever clings to the eternal spectacle of unchangeable truth is not thrown down through the height of this body—that is, through these eyes—in order to know temporal and inferior things.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — From its own vices the soul is admonished to seek the first beauty; this is first shown from the vice of pleasure, through chapter 43

72. What, then, remains from which the soul could not recall the first beauty that it abandoned, since it can recall it even from its own vices? For “the Wisdom of God reaches mightily from end to end” (Wisdom 8:1). Through it the supreme Craftsman has woven together his works, ordered toward one end of beauty.

That goodness, from the highest to the lowest, did not begrudge any beauty that could exist from it alone, so that no one is cast down from the truth itself without being received by some image of truth.

Seek in bodily pleasure what holds it, and you will find nothing other than proportion. For just as resistance produces pain, so proportion produces pleasure. Recognize, then, what supreme proportion is.

Do not go outside yourself; return into yourself. Truth dwells in the inner person. And if you find your nature changeable, transcend yourself. But remember, when you transcend yourself, that you transcend a reasoning soul.

Strive, then, toward the place from which the very light of reason is kindled. For where does every good reasoner arrive except at truth? Truth itself does not arrive at itself by reasoning; rather, it is what those who reason seek.

There behold the proportion beyond which no higher proportion can exist, and bring yourself into harmony with it. Confess that you are not what it is, since it does not seek itself, whereas you came to it by seeking—not through a distance of place, but through the mind’s affection—so that the inner person himself might come into harmony with his inhabitant, not through the lowest and carnal pleasure but through the highest and spiritual pleasure [Note: [Col. 0154] Lov. and Arn. read “will” instead of “pleasure”; Bad., Er., and seven manuscripts have “pleasure”].

73. Or, if you do not see what I am saying and doubt whether it is true, at least see whether you doubt that you doubt these things. And if it is certain that you are doubting, seek the source of that certainty.

There the light of this sun will not meet you—not at all [Note: [Col. 0154] Ven. and Lov. read this passage as: “There the light of this sun will not meet you at all.” M.], but the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9).

This light cannot be seen with these eyes, nor with those by which phantasms are imagined, having been driven into the soul through those same eyes. It is seen with those by which the soul says to the phantasms themselves: “You are not what I seek, nor are you that from which I arrange you. Whatever appears ugly among you I reject; whatever beautiful, I approve—although that from which I reject and approve is more beautiful. Therefore I approve it more than I approve not only you, but all those bodies from which I drew you.”

Next, conceive the rule itself that you see in this way: Everyone who understands that he is doubting understands something true, and is certain of the matter that he understands; therefore he is certain of truth.

Everyone, then, who doubts whether truth exists has within himself something true of which he cannot doubt. And nothing is true except through truth. Therefore someone who has been able to doubt in any way ought not to doubt truth.

Where these things are seen, there is a light without spatial or temporal extension and without any phantasm of such extensions. Can these things be corrupted in any respect, even if every reasoner should perish or grow old among carnal punishments below?

Reasoning does not make such things; it discovers them. Therefore, before they are discovered, they remain in themselves, and when they are discovered, they renew us.

## CHAPTER XL — On the beauty of bodies and the pleasure of the flesh, and on the punishment of sinners
74. Thus the inner man is reborn, while the outer man decays from day to day (II Cor. 4:16). But the inner man looks upon the outer and sees it as ugly in comparison with himself; yet, within its own kind, he sees it as beautiful and rejoicing in the fitting arrangement of bodies, and as corrupting what it converts to its own good—namely, the nourishment of the flesh. These things, once corrupted—that is, losing their form—pass into the construction of these limbs; and, when corrupted, they restore them, passing over into another form through their fittingness. Through the vital movement they are, in a sense, sorted, so that what is suitable is taken up into the structure of this visible beauty, while what is unsuitable is expelled through appropriate passages [Note: [Col. 0155] Lovaniensis and certain manuscripts read “inappropriate.” But Badius, Erasmus, Arnobius, and twelve other manuscripts, more correctly, read “appropriate.” For the beauty of the outer man is here described, and in its structure there is nothing inappropriate.].

Of these substances, one, rendered most foul, is returned to the earth to be taken up into other forms; another is exhaled throughout the body; another receives the hidden rhythms of the whole animal and begins to develop into offspring; and, whether stirred by the fittingness of two bodies or by some such image, it flows down through the genital passages from the very summit into the lowest pleasure [Note: Eight manuscripts read, “it flows down into lowest pleasure.”].

Then, in the mother, through the appointed rhythms of time, it is fitted into the rhythm of place, so that each limb occupies its own region. And if they preserve the measure of equality, with the light of color added, a body is born that is called beautiful and is loved most passionately by those who cherish it. Yet what pleases in it is not the moving form more than the life that moves it. For if that animal loves us, it attracts us more powerfully; but if it hates us, we become angry and cannot endure it, even if it presents the very form that delights the beholder. This is the whole realm of pleasure, and beauty at the lowest level; for it is subject to corruption. If it were not, it would be thought supreme.

75. Yet divine providence is present, showing that this is not evil, on account of the plainly evident traces of the primordial numbers, of which there is no number in God’s wisdom; and nevertheless showing that it is the lowest level, by mixing with it pains, diseases, distortions of the limbs, darkness of color, and conflicts and dissensions of minds, so that from these we may be warned to seek something unchangeable.

And it does this through the lowest ministries [Note: Printed editions have, “through the lowest ministries of those by whom,” etc. But the word “of those” is absent from the manuscripts. Hence we understand that these words do not designate certain offices, but the evil angels themselves, who are immediately called “the lowest servants.” By contrast, the good angels are called below, in chapter 55, “the most excellent and holy ministries of God.”], [Col. 0156] to whom doing this is a pleasure—those whom divine Scripture calls destroyers and angels of wrath, although they themselves do not know what good is being brought about concerning them.

Like them are people who rejoice in the miseries of others and provide, or wish to have provided, laughter and entertaining spectacles for themselves through the ruin and errors of others [Note: *Confessions*, book 3, chapter 3, no. 6]. And so, in all these things, the good are warned, exercised, conquer, triumph, and reign. But the wicked are deceived, tormented, conquered, condemned, and serve—not the one supreme Lord of all, but the lowest servants, namely those angels who feed upon the pains and misery of the condemned and, because of this malevolence, are themselves tormented by the liberation of the good.

76. Thus all things are ordered, according to their offices and ends, into the beauty of the universe, so that what horrifies us in a part, if considered together with the whole, pleases us greatly. For in judging a building we must not consider only one corner; nor, in a beautiful person, only the hair; nor, in someone speaking well, only the movement of the fingers; nor, in the course of the moon, merely certain figures belonging to three days.

These things, which are therefore lowest because they are imperfect as parts but perfect as wholes, whether perceived as beautiful in their state or in their movement, must all be considered if we wish to judge correctly. Our judgment itself, whether it judges the whole or a part, is beautiful when it is true; for it is set above the entire universe, and, insofar as we judge truly, we cling to none of its parts. But our error, clinging to a part of it, is ugly in itself.

Yet just as the color black becomes beautiful in a painting when considered with the whole, so unchangeable divine providence fittingly stages this entire contest, assigning one thing to the defeated, another to those who are fighting, another to the victors, another to the spectators, and another to those who are at rest and contemplate God alone. In all these things there is no evil except sin and the punishment of sin: that is, the voluntary falling away from the supreme essence, and involuntary suffering in the lowest condition. This may also be expressed in another way: freedom from righteousness and enslavement under sin.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### Beauty in the punishment of the sinful soul

77. The outer man is corrupted either through the progress of the inner man or through his own failure. Through the progress of the inner man he is corrupted in such a way that he is wholly reformed for the better and restored to integrity at the last trumpet, so that he may no longer be corrupted or corrupt. Through his own failure, however, he is plunged into more corruptible beauties—that is, into the order of punishments.

Nor should we be surprised that I still call them beauties. Nothing is ordered that is not beautiful; and, as the Apostle says [Note: *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 13, no. 7], every order is from God (Rom. 13:1).

We must nevertheless admit that a weeping human being is better than a cheerful little worm. Yet I can speak at length and without any falsehood in praise of the worm, considering the brilliance of its color, the smooth shape of its body, the fitting relation of its front parts to its middle parts and of its middle parts to its hind parts, and the preservation, according to the lowliness of its nature, of its desire for unity—nothing formed on one side failing to correspond on the other side by an equal dimension.

What shall I now say of the soul itself, which animates the small body, how it moves it rhythmically, how it seeks what is fitting, how it overcomes or avoids obstacles as far as it can, and, referring everything to one sense of preservation, reveals that unity which creates all natures much more clearly than the body does? I am speaking of a soul animating any sort of little worm.

Many have spoken most truthfully and abundantly in praise of ash and dung (Cato in Cicero, *Cato the Elder*). What wonder, then, if I say that the human soul—wherever and whatever it may be—is better than every body, and that it is beautifully ordered, and that other beauties are made from its punishments, since, when it is miserable, it is not where it ought to be blessed, but where it ought to be miserable?

78. Let no one deceive us at all. Whatever is rightly censured is rejected in comparison with something better [Note: *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 13, no. 8]. Every nature, however extreme or lowly, is rightly praised in comparison with nothingness. And each thing is not well situated when it can be better.

Therefore, if we can be well situated with truth itself, we are badly situated with any trace of truth; much worse, then, with the extremity of a trace, when we cling to the pleasures of the flesh. Let us therefore conquer either the allurements or the troubles of this desire; let us subject this woman to ourselves, if we are men. Under our leadership she too will become better, and will no longer be called desire, but self-control.

For when she leads and we follow, she is called desire and lust, while we are called recklessness and folly. Let us follow Christ, our head, so that the one of whom we are the head may also follow us. This may also be commanded to women—not under marital right, but under fraternal right, by which in Christ there is neither male nor female.

They too possess something manly by which they may subject feminine pleasures, serve Christ, and rule desire. This is manifest in many widows and virgins of God, and also in many married women who already preserve the rights of marriage in a fraternal manner, according to the administration of the Christian people.

But if the man is subjected through negligence and impiety to that part over which God commands us to rule, and by which he both urges and helps us to be restored to our possession—that is, if the mind and reason are subjected—then the man will indeed be ugly and miserable. Yet he is destined in this life and ordered after this life to the place to which that supreme ruler and Lord judges that he should be destined and where he should be ordered. Therefore the whole creation is not permitted to be stained by any ugliness.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### The pleasure of the flesh urges us to seek indivisible numbers; whether such numbers exist in any vital movement

79. Let us walk while we have the day—that is, while we are able to use reason—so that, turned toward God, we may deserve to be illumined by his Word, which is the true light, lest darkness overtake us (John 12:35).

For day is the presence of that light which illumines every human being coming into this world (John 1:9). [Col. 0158] He said “human being” because one can use reason [Note: The printed editions read, “who can use reason”; and a little later Lovaniensis and Arnobius read, “must strive to rise.” But the manuscripts have, “because he can use reason,” and in the other passage they lack the word “must,” which is also absent from the editions of Badius and Erasmus]. And where he has fallen, he should lean there in order to rise.

If, then, the pleasure of the flesh is loved, let it itself be considered more carefully. And when traces of certain numbers have been recognized in it, we must seek where they exist without swelling. For there that which is one is more truly one.

And if such numbers exist in the very vital movement that operates in seeds, they are more wondrous there than in the body. For if the numbers of seeds swelled like the seeds themselves, half a fig-seed would produce half a tree; nor would whole and complete animals be generated from the seeds of animals, even when those seeds are not whole; nor would one tiny seed possess the immeasurable power proper to its kind.

From one seed, according to its nature, crops of crops, forests of forests, herds of herds, or peoples of peoples can be propagated through the ages, so that there is no leaf or hair, through such a vast succession, whose pattern was not present in that first and single seed.

Then we must consider how many and how pleasing are the beauties of sound that the struck air conveys when the nightingale sings—beauties that the soul of that little bird could not fashion so freely when it gives expression to them unless it possessed them impressed within itself incorporeally through vital movement [Note: The manuscripts do not contain “so freely.”].

This may also be observed in the other living creatures that lack reason but do not lack sensation. For there is none of them that does not exhibit, either in the sound of its voice or in the rest of the movement and operation of its limbs, something rhythmic and ordered according to its kind—not through any knowledge, but nevertheless through the innermost limits of nature, modulated by that unchangeable law of numbers.

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### In human beings, the power to judge the proportion of bodies and times; the order that exists in perpetual truth

80. Let us return to ourselves and set aside what we have in common with trees and beasts. A swallow builds its nest in one particular way, and each kind of bird in some one way of its own. What, then, is it in us by which we judge all those things—what shapes they desire and to what extent they fulfill them—and by which we, as though masters of all such forms, devise innumerable structures in buildings and other bodily works?

What is it in us that inwardly understands these visible masses of bodies to be large or small in proportion; that every body, however small, has a half; and that, if it has a half, it has innumerable parts? Thus every grain of millet is as large in relation to a part of itself equal in size to that occupied by our body in this world as the world is large in relation to us; and this entire world of forms is beautiful by the principle of its forms, not by its mass.

It appears large not according to its quantity, but because of our smallness—that is, the smallness of the animals with which it is filled. These animals, in turn, although they possess infinite divisibility, are small not in themselves but in comparison with other things, and especially with the universe itself.

Nor is there another principle in the extent of times. For just as every length of place has a half, so does every length of time. However short it may be, [Col. 0159] it begins, advances, and ends. Therefore it cannot fail to have a half while it is divided at the point where it passes toward its end.

Thus the time of a short syllable is short in comparison with that of a long syllable, and a winter hour is shorter in comparison with a summer hour [Note: This reflects the practice of those who consistently counted twelve hours from sunrise to sunset: the hours were shorter in winter and longer in summer].

The duration of one hour is therefore short in relation to a day, a day in relation to a month, a month in relation to a year, a year in relation to a lustrum, a lustrum in relation to longer cycles, and those cycles themselves in relation to the whole of time. Yet that very rhythmic succession and a kind of gradation, whether of spatial or temporal intervals, is judged beautiful not because of swelling or duration, but because of ordered fittingness.

81. The very principle of order lives in perpetual truth. It is neither vast in mass nor changeable through extension, but great in power above all places and immovable in eternity beyond all times. Without it, however, neither can the vastness of any mass be brought into unity nor the extension of any time be restrained from error; nor can anything exist—whether a body, so that it is a body, or movement, so that it is movement.

It is itself the one First Principle, neither thickened by the finite nor by the infinite, neither changed by the finite nor by the infinite. It does not have one thing here and another elsewhere, or one thing now and another later, because the Father of Truth is supremely one: the Father of his Wisdom, which, being in no respect unlike him, is called his likeness and image, because it is from him.

Therefore the Son is rightly said to be from him, while other things are through him. For the form of all things preceded them, supremely filling the One from whom it is, so that all other things that exist, insofar as they are like the One, were made through that form.

## CHAPTER XLIV  
### The Son, the image of God, to whose image certain things were made

82. Some things exist through the form itself and also toward it, such as every rational and intellectual creature, in which the human being is most rightly said to have been made according to the image and likeness of God. For otherwise the mind could not behold unchangeable truth.

Other things, however, were made through it but do not exist toward it. Therefore, if the rational soul serves its Creator—from whom it was made, through whom it was made, and toward whom it was made—then all other things will serve it.

The ultimate life, which is so near to it and is its assistance, by which it rules the body, will serve it; and the body itself, the lowest nature and essence, over which it will rule entirely at will, yielding in every way to its command and causing it no annoyance, will serve it. For the soul will no longer seek blessedness from the body or through the body, but will receive it from God through itself.

It will therefore administer a body restored and sanctified, without the harm of corruption and without the burden of difficulty. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven (Matt. 22:30). Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both the one and the other (I Cor. 6:13), because the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy (Rom. 14:17).

## CHAPTER XLV  
### The weakness of pleasure drives us toward higher things; concerning the vice of pride, through chapter 49: how by this we are urged to embrace virtue

83. Therefore, even in this pleasure of the body we find something that warns us to despise it—not because the nature of the body is evil, but because it wallows shamefully in the love of the lowest good, whereas it was granted to cling to and enjoy the highest goods.

When the charioteer is dragged along and pays the penalty for his recklessness, he accuses whatever it was that he used. But let him implore help; let the Lord of all command; let the horses be restrained, though they are now making another spectacle out of his fall and, unless help is provided, will make one out of his death; let him be restored to his place, set upon the wheels, have the reins returned to his authority, and rule more cautiously over the obedient and tamed beasts.

Then he will understand how well the chariot and that entire combination were constructed, although their collapse had afflicted him and caused him to lose his most decorous course. For the soul’s greed, using it badly in paradise and usurping the forbidden food against the physician’s discipline by which everlasting health is preserved, brought weakness upon this body [Note: In Badius, *malae* (“of the evil [soul]”) is found. We restore *male* (“badly”), following Erasmus, the Venice edition, Lovaniensis, the Paris edition, and others].

84. If, then, in this very visible weakness of the flesh, where blessed life cannot exist, a warning of blessed life is found because of the form descending from the highest to the lowest [Note: The printed editions read, “from the highest good to the lowest,” but “good” is absent from the manuscripts], how much more in the desire for distinction and excellence, and in all the pride and empty pomp of this world?

For what else does a human being desire in these things except to be alone, if possible, with everything subjected to him—a perverse imitation, obviously, of almighty God? If he imitated God as a subject, by living according to God’s commands, he would have all other things subjected through God, and would not reach such deformity that he who wishes to rule human beings fears a little creature.

Pride therefore also possesses a certain desire for unity and omnipotence, but in the rule of temporal things, all of which pass away like a shadow.

85. We wish to be unconquered, and rightly so. For this belongs to the nature of our soul, after God, by whom it was made according to his image. But his commands ought to have been observed; had they been observed, no one would have conquered us.

Now, however, while the very one whose words we shamefully followed is subdued by the pain of childbirth, we labor on the earth and are overcome, with great disgrace, by everything capable of moving and disturbing us. Thus we do not wish to be conquered by human beings, yet we cannot conquer anger. What could be said to be more execrable than such disgrace?

We admit that the human being who conquers us is what we are, and that although he has vices, he is not himself a vice. How much more honorable, then, is it for a human being to conquer us than for a vice to do so? Who could doubt that envy is a monstrous vice, by which the person who does not wish to be conquered in temporal matters must necessarily be tormented and subjected? It is therefore better for a human being to conquer us than for envy or any other vice.

## CHAPTER XLVI  
### The unconquered person is one who loves only what cannot be taken from the one who loves it—that is, God with all his heart and his neighbor as himself

86. Yet the person who has conquered his vices cannot be conquered even by another human being. For no one is conquered unless the adversary takes from him what he loves.

Whoever therefore loves only what cannot be taken from the one who loves it is unquestionably unconquered and [Col. 0161] is tormented by no envy. He loves that which, the more people come to love and attain it, the more abundantly he rejoices with them.

For he loves God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his mind; and he loves his neighbor as himself. Therefore he does not envy his neighbor, wishing him to be what he himself is; indeed, he helps him as much as he can. Nor can he lose the neighbor whom he loves as himself, because he does not love in himself the things that are subject to the eyes or to any other bodily senses. Therefore he possesses within himself the one whom he loves as himself.

87. The rule of love is that one should wish the good to come to another that one wishes to come to oneself, and should not wish for another the evils one does not wish to happen to oneself (Tob. 4:16). He preserves this will toward all human beings. For no evil should be done to anyone, and love of neighbor does no evil (Rom. 13:10).

Let us therefore love, as commanded, even our enemies (Matt. 5:44), if we truly wish to be unconquered. No human being is unconquered through himself, but through that unchangeable law. Whoever serves that law alone is free.

For what they love cannot be taken from them. This alone makes people unconquered and perfect. If a human being loves another human being—not as himself, but as one loves a beast of burden, or baths, or a painted or chattering little bird—that is, in order to obtain from him some temporary pleasure or advantage, then he must serve not the human being but, what is more shameful, that foul and detestable vice by which he does not love a human being as a human being ought to be loved. Under the domination of this vice he is led to the end of life, or rather to death.

88. Nor should one human being love another in the same way that people love blood brothers, children, spouses, relatives, in-laws, or fellow citizens. For this love too is temporal. We would not have any such relationships, which arise through birth and death, if our nature, remaining in God’s commands and image, had not been banished into this corruption [Note: *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 13, no. 8].

Therefore Truth itself calls us back to our original and perfect nature and commands us to resist carnal custom, teaching that no one is fit for the kingdom of God who does not hate these carnal relationships (Luke 9:60, 62; 14:26).

This should not seem inhuman to anyone. It is more inhuman not to love in a human being what is human, but to love what is a son [Note: Lovaniensis and Arnobius read, “what is inferior.” But Badius, Erasmus, and the manuscripts, with strong agreement, have, “what is a son.” This reading is more persuasive because Augustine immediately adds that to love this is to love what belongs to oneself. He uses a similar expression in book 1 of *The Sermon on the Mount*, where, again discussing hatred of such temporal relationships, after explaining what kind of love and hatred a husband should show toward his wife, he says: “That is, to love in her what is human, to hate what is a wife.” He then adds that the same should be understood of father, mother, and the other bonds of the flesh: in them we should hate what the human race has acquired through birth and death, but love what can be carried with us into those kingdoms where no one says, “My father,” but all say to the one God, “Our Father.”].

For this is not to love in that person what belongs to God, but to love what belongs to oneself. What wonder, then, if one does not reach the kingdom who loves not what is common but what is private?

“Indeed, both,” someone may say. [Col. 0162] “Indeed, the one thing,” God says. For Truth speaks most truly: No one can serve two masters (Matt. 6:24). No one can perfectly love that to which we are called unless he hates that from which we are called back.

We are called to the perfect human nature that God made before our sin; we are called back from the love of the condition that we deserved through sinning. Therefore we must hate that from which we desire to be liberated.

89. Let us therefore hate temporal relationships if we burn with love of eternity. Let a human being love his neighbor as himself. Certainly no one is his own father, son, in-law, or anything of that sort, but only a human being. Whoever loves someone as himself ought therefore to love in that person what that person is to himself.

Bodies, however, are not what we are; therefore the body should not be sought or desired in a human being. The command, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20:17), also serves this purpose.

Therefore whoever loves in his neighbor anything other than what that neighbor is to himself does not love him as himself. Human nature itself must be loved without its carnal condition, whether it is to be perfected or is already perfect.

All who love God the Father and do his will are related under one Father. They are also one another’s fathers when they care for one another, sons when they obey one another, and especially brothers, because one Father calls them by his testament to one inheritance.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### True love of neighbor: the person who gives it is unconquered

90. Why, then, is this person not unconquered in loving a human being, since he loves in that person nothing except the human being—that is, God’s creature made according to God’s image—and since the perfect nature he loves cannot be absent from him when he himself is perfect?

For example, if someone loves a person who sings well—not this or that person, but anyone who sings well—and the lover himself is a perfect singer, then he wishes everyone to be such, yet he does not lack what he loves, because he himself sings well.

If he envies someone who sings well, he no longer loves good singing, but either praise or something else that he wishes to attain by singing well; and that could be diminished or taken away from him if someone else also sang well.

Therefore whoever envies someone who sings well does not love good singing. But, conversely, whoever needs another person does not sing well.

This can be said much more appropriately of someone who lives well, because such a person cannot envy anyone. What those who live well attain is the same for all, and it does not become less when more people possess it.

There can be a time when a good singer is unable to sing suitably and needs another’s voice to present to him what he loves—just as if he were dining somewhere where it would be improper for him to sing but appropriate to listen to someone singing. But living well is always appropriate.

Therefore whoever both loves and practices this not only does not envy those who imitate him, but also offers himself to them as willingly and humanely as he can; nevertheless, he does not need them. For what he loves in them he possesses wholly and perfectly in himself.

Thus, when he loves his neighbor as himself, he does not envy him, because he does not envy himself; he grants him what he can, because he grants it to himself; he does not need him, because he does not need himself. He needs only [Col. 0163] God, and by clinging to God he is blessed. No one takes God away from him.

Therefore the truly and certainly unconquered person is the one who clings to God—not so that he may earn some good outside God, but because nothing other than clinging to God himself is good for him.

91. While this man lives in this life, he uses a friend to return kindness, an enemy to exercise patience, those whom he can to practice beneficence, and everyone to practice goodwill.

Although he does not love temporal things, he uses temporal things rightly and, according to their condition, cares for people when he cannot care equally for everyone. Therefore, if he addresses one of his close associates more readily than someone else, he does not love him more, but has greater confidence in him and a more open door of opportunity in time.

He treats those devoted to temporal things better in proportion as he himself is less bound to time. Since he cannot benefit everyone whom he loves equally unless he prefers to benefit those who are closer, he would be unjust if he did not do so.

Closeness of soul is greater than that of the places or times in which we are born in this body [Note: Lovaniensis and Arnobius read, “in which they are joined.” Badius and Erasmus read, “in which we are joined.” But eleven manuscripts read, “in which we are born.”]. But the greatest closeness is that which surpasses all others.

Therefore this man is not distressed by anyone’s death, because the person who loves God with his whole soul knows that nothing perishes for him that does not perish for God. God is Lord of both the living and the dead.

He is not made miserable by anyone’s misery, because he is not made righteous by anyone’s righteousness [Note: Seven manuscripts read, “nor is he made unrighteous by anyone’s unrighteousness.”]. And just as no one takes righteousness and God away from him, so no one takes blessedness away from him.

If he is ever moved by someone’s danger, error, or grief, he does not allow this movement to extend beyond that person’s assistance, correction, or consolation into his own overthrow.

92. In all his labors of service he is not broken, because he confidently awaits future rest. What can harm the person who can use even an enemy well? He does not fear enmity because he is protected and fortified by the one whose command and gift enable him to love his enemies.

For this man, in tribulations it is not enough merely not to grieve; he must also rejoice, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:3–5).

Who will harm him? Who will subject him? The person who advances through prosperity learns through adversity what progress he has made.

When an abundance of mutable goods is present, he does not trust in them. When they are taken away, he learns whether they had captured him. For often, while such things are present, we think that we do not love them; but when they begin to be absent, we discover what we are.

That which was present without our love departs without our grief. Thus the person who reaches, by overcoming, what he will lose with grief appears to conquer when he is conquered; and the person who, by yielding, reaches what he does not unwillingly lose conquers when he appears to be conquered.

## CHAPTER XLVIII  
### What perfect righteousness is

93. Whoever delights in freedom should desire to be free from love of mutable things; and whoever delights in reigning should [Col. 0164] cling in submission to God, the one ruler of all, loving him more than himself.

This is perfect righteousness: that we love better things more and lesser things less. Let him love a wise and perfect soul as he sees it; let him love a foolish soul not as it is, but because it can become perfect and wise. For he ought not to love himself as foolish.

Whoever loves himself as foolish will not progress toward wisdom; nor will anyone become what he desires to be unless he hates himself as he is. But until wisdom and perfection are reached, let him endure the foolishness of his neighbor in the same spirit in which he would endure his own foolishness if he were foolish and loved wisdom.

Therefore, if pride itself is also a shadow of true freedom and true kingship, divine providence uses even it to remind us what our vice signifies and where we ought to return once corrected.

## CHAPTER XLIX  
### Concerning curiosity hereafter: how through this vice we are warned to contemplate truth

94. What else do all spectacles and all that is called curiosity seek except joy in knowledge of things? What, then, is more wondrous, what more beautiful, than truth itself? Every spectator confesses that he desires to reach it, since he watches intently lest he be deceived and boasts when he recognizes and judges something more sharply and vividly than others in watching.

Even the magician, who professes nothing but deception, is watched carefully and observed most cautiously. If the spectators are tricked because they cannot themselves do such things, they delight in the knowledge of the person who deceives them.

For if he himself did not know by what means those watching him were deceived, or were thought not to know, no one would applaud a person who was equally mistaken. But if one person from the crowd detects him, he thinks that he deserves greater praise than the magician—not for any other reason than that he could not be deceived and fooled.

If the trick is exposed to many, the magician is not praised; rather, the others who cannot detect such things are ridiculed. Thus every prize is awarded to knowledge, skill, and apprehension of truth. Yet those who seek truth outside themselves never reach it.

95. We are therefore so deeply immersed in trifles and shameful things that, when asked what is better, truth or falsehood, we answer with one voice that truth is better; yet in jokes and games—where what delights us is certainly not truth but fiction—we cling much more eagerly to them than to the precepts of truth itself.

Thus we are punished by our own judgment and speech: we approve one thing with reason but pursue another through vanity. Something remains playful and humorous only so long as we know in comparison with what truth it is being laughed at.

But by loving such things we fall away from truth and no longer discover the things of which they are imitations—those primary beauties for which we yearn—and, withdrawing from them, embrace our own images.

When we return to investigate the truth, these images meet us on the road and do not allow us to pass. They plunder us not by force but through great ambushes, while we do not understand how widely the saying applies: “Guard yourselves from idols” (I John 5:21).

96. Thus some have wandered through innumerable worlds, being tossed about by a roving imagination. Others thought that God could be nothing except a body of fire. Others imagined a brightness of immense light extending in every direction through infinite spaces, [Col. 0165] yet split on one side by something like a black wedge, and, supposing two opposing kingdoms, composed stories with their fantasies by assigning such principles to reality.

If I compelled them to swear whether they knew these things to be true, perhaps they would not dare, but would answer in turn: “Then you show what is true.” If I gave them no answer except that they should seek that light by which it appears to them and is certain that believing is one thing and understanding another, they too would swear that this light cannot be seen by the eyes, cannot be conceived together with any vastness of place, is everywhere present to those who seek it, and that nothing more certain or more serene can be found than it.

97. All these things that I have now said about this light of the mind are themselves made manifest by no other light than the same light. Through it I understand that what has been said is true, and through it I again understand that I understand these things.

And again and again, whenever someone understands that he understands something and again understands that very understanding, I understand that this proceeds to infinity. I also understand that there are here no intervals of any swelling or movement.

I understand more certainly that I cannot understand unless I live, and that I become more alive through understanding. For eternal life surpasses temporal life by this very vitality. I do not perceive what eternity is except by understanding.

Through the mind’s vision I separate all mutability from eternity, and in eternity itself I discern no intervals of time, because intervals of time consist in the past and future movements of things. But nothing passes away in eternity, and nothing is future, because what passes away ceases to be, and what is future has not yet begun to be.

Eternity, however, merely is. It was not, as though it no longer were; nor will it be, as though it did not yet exist. Therefore eternity alone could most truly say to the human mind, “I am who am”; and of it it could most truly be said, “He who is has sent me” (Exod. 3:14).

## CHAPTER L  
### The method of the Scriptures and of interpretation; the fourfold allegory
98. If we cannot yet cling to it, let us at least rebuke our fantasies and drive from the spectacle of the mind such frivolous and deceptive games. Let us make use of the steps which divine providence has deigned to construct for us. For when, excessively delighted by playful imaginings, we were vanishing into our thoughts and turning our whole life into certain vain dreams, the ineffable mercy of God did not disdain, with the rational creature [Note: [Col. 0165] A learned man thought that *irrationali* should be read. But all the manuscripts and editions have *rationali creatura*: by these words, unless we are mistaken, the angels are to be understood, as below, no. 99, at the end, and in book 3 of *On Free Will*, chapter 10, no. 30. For God spoke through the angels to the ancient Fathers, and through their ministry displayed sounds, letters, fire, smoke, cloud, a column, and similar signs narrated in the sacred books. Most manuscripts continue thus: “serving under its laws,” etc.] serving under its laws, to play in some measure with our childhood through sounds and letters, fire, smoke, cloud, and a column—as it were, certain visible words—and to heal our inner eyes with mud of this kind through parables and likenesses.

99. Let us therefore distinguish what faith we ought to give to history, what faith to understanding, and what we should entrust to memory without knowing it to be true, but nevertheless believing it. And let us determine where the truth is that does not come and pass away but always remains in the same manner. Let us determine how the allegory that is believed to have been spoken through the wisdom of the Holy Spirit should be interpreted: whether it is enough to lead it from older visible things to more recent visible things; or whether it should be carried as far as the soul’s affections and nature; or as far as unchangeable eternity; whether some things signify visible events, others movements of the soul, and others the law of eternity; or whether some are found in which all these things must be sought. Let us determine what stable faith is—whether historical and temporal, or spiritual and eternal—toward which every interpretation of authority ought to be directed. Let us determine what benefit, for understanding and obtaining eternal things, where the end of all good actions lies, is provided by faith in temporal things. Let us determine the difference between the allegory of history, the allegory of an event, the allegory of speech, and the allegory of a sacrament. Let us determine how the very language of the divine Scriptures is to be understood according to the character of each language. Every language has certain proper modes of expression which, when transferred into another language, appear absurd.

Let us determine what benefit comes from such great lowliness of speech that in the sacred books there are found not only the names of God’s anger and sorrow, of awakening from sleep, of remembering and forgetting, and of other things that can occur even in good people, but also the names of repentance, jealousy, drunkenness, and other things of this kind. Let us determine whether God’s eyes, hands, feet, and other bodily members of this kind, which are named in Scripture, should be referred to the visible form of the human body, or to the meanings of intelligible and spiritual powers, such as a helmet, shield, sword, belt, and other similar things. Above all, we must ask what benefit it is to the human race that divine providence has spoken with us in this way through the rational, generative, and bodily creature serving it. Once this is known, every childish arrogance is excluded from human minds [Note: [Col. 0166] Namely, the arrogance of the Manichaeans toward the Old Testament.], and the sacred religion is introduced.

CHAPTER LI.—The examination of Scripture as a remedy for curiosity.

100. Therefore, setting aside and rejecting theatrical and poetic frivolities, let us nourish and refresh the soul, weary and burning with the hunger and thirst of empty curiosity, which vainly longs to be restored and satisfied by empty fantasies, as though by painted banquets, through consideration and treatment of the divine Scriptures. Let us be healthfully instructed by this truly liberal and noble game. If the marvels of spectacles and beauty delight us, let us desire to see that Wisdom which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1). For what is more marvelous than an incorporeal power making and governing a corporeal world? Or what is more beautiful than its ordering and adorning it?

CHAPTER LII.—Curiosity and other vices provide an occasion for virtue.

101. Yet if everyone admits that these things are perceived through the body, and that the soul is better than the body, will the soul itself perceive nothing by its own power? Or can what it perceives be anything other than something far more excellent and superior? Indeed, recalled from those things which we judge, let us look upon what it is according to which we judge; and, turning from works of art to the law of the arts, we shall contemplate with the mind that form in comparison with which those things are ugly which are beautiful through its benevolence. “For the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made, as are his everlasting power and divinity” (Romans 1:20).

This is the return from temporal things to eternal things, and the reformation from the life of the old man into the new man. What is there from which a person cannot be recalled to the pursuit of virtues, when he can be recalled even from vices? For what does curiosity desire except knowledge—knowledge that cannot be certain except of eternal things and of things that always remain the same? What does pride desire except power, which pertains to ease of action—an ease that the perfected soul finds only when subject to God [Note: [Col. 0167] The editions read: “unless the soul is perfect and subject to God.” But manuscripts of good quality read: “a perfected soul only when subject to God.”] and turned toward his kingdom with supreme love? What does bodily pleasure desire except rest, which exists only where there is neither want nor corruption?

Therefore the lower hells must be avoided—that is, the more severe punishments after this life—where there can be no remembrance of truth, because there is no reasoning; and there is no reasoning because the true light does not suffuse it, the light “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). Therefore let us hasten and walk while the day is present, lest darkness overtake us (ibid. 12:35). Let us hasten to be delivered from the second death (Revelation 20:6, 14; 21:8), where no one remembers God, and from hell, where no one will confess to God (Psalm 6:6).

CHAPTER LIII.—The differing aims of fools and wise people.

102. But miserable are those people for whom known things become worthless and who delight in novelty. They prefer learning to knowing, although knowledge is the end of learning. Those for whom ease of action is worthless prefer striving to conquering, although victory is the end of striving. Those for whom bodily health is worthless prefer eating to being satisfied, and prefer to enjoy their generative organs rather than suffer no such agitation. There are even people who prefer sleeping to not being sleepy, although the end of all that pleasure is not to hunger or thirst, not to desire intercourse, and not to have a wearied body.

103. Therefore those who desire the ends themselves first free themselves from curiosity, recognizing that the certain knowledge is the knowledge within, and enjoying it as much as they can in this life. Then, having laid aside stubbornness, they receive ease of action, knowing that the greater and easier victory is not to resist anyone’s hostility; and this they perceive as much as they can in this life. Finally, by abstaining from those things without which this life can be lived, they attain rest of body, and thus taste how sweet the Lord is.

There will be no doubt what is to come after this life [Col. 0167–0168], and they are nourished by faith, hope, and love in their perfection. After this life, knowledge too will be perfected: “For we know in part now, but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will pass away” (1 Corinthians 13:9–10). And complete peace will be present. For now “another law in my members wars against the law of my mind”; but “the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord will deliver us from this body of death” (Romans 7:23–25), because we agree to a great extent with our adversary while we are with him on the way. Complete health, no want, and no weariness will also be present in the body, because “this corruptible body,” at the time and in the order appointed for the resurrection of the flesh, “will put on incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:53).

It is not surprising if this will be given to those who in knowledge love truth alone, in action peace alone, and in the body health alone. For what will be perfected in them after this life is what they love more greatly in this life.

CHAPTER LIV.—The relation of the punishments of the condemned to their vices.

104. Those, therefore, who misuse so great a good of the mind that they desire visible things more than the mind itself—although visible things ought to have recalled them to perceive and love intelligible things—will be given outer darkness. Its beginning is the prudence of the flesh and the weakness of bodily senses. Those who delight in contests will be separated from peace and entangled in the greatest difficulties. For the beginning of the greatest difficulty is war and strife. I think this is signified by their hands and feet being bound—that is, every ease of action is taken away.

Those who wish to thirst and hunger, to burn with lust and to be exhausted so that they may eat, drink, have intercourse, and sleep with pleasure, love want, which is the beginning of the greatest sorrows. Therefore what they love will be perfected in them, so that they will be where there is weeping [Note: [Col. 0168] Most manuscripts read: “so that weeping may be there for them,” etc.] and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 22:13).

105. There are many who love all these vices together. Their life is to watch, compete, eat, drink, have intercourse, sleep, and in their thoughts embrace nothing but the fantasies they gather from such a life. From the deception of these fantasies they establish rules of superstition or impiety by which they are deceived and to which they cling, even if they try to abstain from the allurements of the flesh.

For they do not use well the talent entrusted to them—that is, the sharpness of mind by which all those who are called learned, cultivated, or witty seem to excel. Instead, they keep it bound in a cloth or buried in the earth: that is, entangled and overwhelmed by delicate and superfluous things or by earthly desires. Therefore their hands and feet will be bound, and they will be cast into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

This is not because they loved these things—for who would love them?—but because the things they loved are the beginnings of these punishments and necessarily lead those who love them to them. For those who love going more than returning or arriving must be sent farther away, since they are flesh, “a spirit that walks and does not return.”

106. But whoever makes good use even of the five bodily senses, whether for believing and proclaiming the works of God and nurturing love of him, or uses action and knowledge to pacify his nature and know God, enters into the joy of his Lord.
