Therefore the talent taken away from the one who used it badly is given to the one who used five talents well (Matthew 25:14–30; Luke 19:15–26). This does not mean that the acuteness of understanding can be transferred, but signifies that negligent and impious people who are gifted can lose it, while those who are diligent and pious can attain it, even if they are slower in intellect.

For the talent was not given to the one who had received two; the latter already has it, since he lives well both in action and in knowledge. Rather, it was given to the one who had received five. The person who believes only in visible things—that is, temporal things—does not yet possess a mind sufficiently suited to contemplating eternal things. But such a mind can be possessed by the person who praises God as the maker of all these sensible things, is persuaded of him by faith, awaits him in hope, and seeks him in love.

CHAPTER LV.—Epilogue exhorting to true religion and deterring from false religion. The character of the Manichaean religion. False opinions about the gods. True religion.

107. Since these things are so, I exhort you, my dearest and closest companions—and I exhort myself together with you—to run with all the speed we can toward that to which God exhorts us through his wisdom.

Let us not love the world, because everything in the world is “the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (1 John 2:15–16). Let us not love to corrupt and be corrupted through bodily pleasure, lest we come to a more miserable corruption of pains and torments. Let us not love contests, lest we be handed over to angels who delight in such things, to be humbled, bound, and beaten. Let us not love visible spectacles, lest, wandering away from the truth itself and loving shadows, we be cast into darkness.

108. Let religion for us not consist in our fantasies. For any kind of truth is better than everything that can be invented according to one’s will. Yet we ought not to worship the soul itself, even though the soul is real when it imagines false things. A real straw is better than a light formed in an empty thought according to the will of one who merely suspects; yet it would be madness to believe that the straw which we perceive and touch should be worshiped.

Let religion for us not consist in worshiping human works. The craftsmen themselves who make such things are better than their works, yet we ought not to worship them. Let religion for us not consist in worshiping beasts. Even the lowest human beings are better than beasts, yet we ought not to worship them. Let religion for us not consist in worshiping dead human beings. For if they lived piously, they do not wish to be honored in such a way; rather, they wish us to worship the one by whose illumination they rejoice, and whose fellow servants they want us to be [Note: [Col. 0169] Several manuscripts and Erasmus read: “fellow servants.”]. They should therefore be honored for imitation, not adored as a matter of religion. If, however, they lived wickedly, they should not be worshiped wherever they may be.

Let religion for us not consist in worshiping demons. Since every superstition is a great punishment for human beings and a most dangerous disgrace, it is an honor and triumph for those demons.

109. Let religion for us not consist in worshiping earth and water [Col. 0170], because even the air, though murky, is purer and clearer than these; yet we ought not to worship it. Let religion for us not consist even in worshiping purer and clearer air, because when the light is absent it becomes shadowy; and purer than it is the radiance of even this fire, which nevertheless we certainly ought not to worship, since we kindle and extinguish it according to our will.

Let religion for us not consist in worshiping ethereal and heavenly bodies. Although they are rightly placed above all other bodies, any kind of life is better than they are. Therefore, if they are animate, any soul in itself is better than any animate body; and yet no one would judge that a vicious soul should be worshiped.

Let religion for us not consist in worshiping that life by which trees are said to live, since there is no sense in it. It belongs to the same category as the life by which the structure of our own body is governed, through which even hair and bones live, although they are cut without sensation. But a sentient life is better than this; and yet we ought not to worship the life of beasts.

110. Let religion for us not consist even in worshiping the perfect and wise rational soul itself—whether it has been established in the service of the whole universe, in the service of its parts, or whether, among the highest human beings, it awaits the transformation and reformation of its portion. For every rational life, if it is perfect, obeys the unchangeable truth speaking inwardly to it without noise; but by refusing to obey, it becomes vicious.

It does not therefore excel by itself, but through the one whom it willingly obeys. What the highest angel worships must also be worshiped by the lowest human being, because human nature itself has become lowest by failing to worship it. For the angel is not wise from one source and the human being from another, nor is the angel truthful from one source and the human being from another; rather, both are so from one unchangeable wisdom and truth.

For this very thing was accomplished in the temporal dispensation of our salvation: the very Power and Wisdom of God, unchangeable, consubstantial with the Father, and coeternal with him, deigned to assume human nature, so that through it he might teach us that human beings must worship what every intellectual and rational creature must worship.

Let us believe that the very best angels and the most excellent ministries of God also desire this: that together with them we should worship the one God whose contemplation makes them blessed. For we are not made blessed by seeing an angel, but by seeing the truth, through which we also love the angels themselves and rejoice with them. We do not envy them because they enjoy this more readily or without the hindrance of troubles. Rather, we love them more, because we too have been commanded to hope for such a condition from our common Lord.

Therefore we honor them with love, not with servitude. We do not build temples for them, for they do not wish to be honored by us in this way; when we are good, they know that we ourselves are temples of the highest God. Thus Scripture rightly says that an angel prevented a human being from worshiping him, but directed him to worship the one Lord under whom the angel too was a fellow servant (Revelation 22:9).

111. Those who invite us to serve them and worship them as gods are like proud human beings who, if permitted, would likewise wish to be worshiped. Yet it is less dangerous to endure such human beings, while it is more dangerous to worship those others. Every human domination over human beings—whether of rulers or of subjects—ends in death. But servitude under the pride of evil angels is more to be feared because of the very time that follows death.

It is also easy for anyone to recognize that under a human ruler we are permitted to have free thoughts. But we fear those rulers in our very minds who occupy the one eye by which truth is seen and perceived. Therefore, if we are subject, for the sake of our bond, to all the powers given to human beings for governing the republic, rendering to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s (Matthew 22:21), there is no need to fear that anyone will demand this after our death.

The servitude of the soul is one thing; the servitude of the body is another. Righteous people, who have all their joys in the one God, rejoice with those who praise God when he is blessed through their deeds. But when they themselves are praised as though they were God, they correct those who err, insofar as they can. Those whom they cannot correct, they do not congratulate, and they wish them to be corrected of that fault.

If good angels and all the holy ministries of God are like these people—or even purer and holier—why should we fear offending any of them if we are not superstitious? With their help we strive toward the one God and bind our souls to him alone, from which attachment religion is believed to have received its name, and thus remain free from every superstition [Note: [Col. 0171] See also *Retractions*, chapter 13, no. 9.].

112. Behold, I worship one God, the one Principle of all things, the Wisdom through which every wise soul is wise, and the very Gift through which every blessed thing is blessed. Any angel who loves this God—I am certain—also loves me. Whoever remains in him, and can perceive human prayers, hears me in him. Whoever possesses his own good in him helps me in him and cannot begrudge me participation in him.

Let the worshipers—or flatterers—of the parts of the world tell me whom the person who worships this one reality does not make most favorably disposed to himself: that which every excellent being loves, in the knowledge of which he rejoices, and by returning to which as his principle he becomes excellent.

But any angel who loves his own excesses, refuses to be subject to the truth, and, desiring to rejoice in his private good, has fallen away from the common good of all and from true blessedness [Note: [Col. 0172] Fourteen manuscripts read: “has fallen away from the common good of all good things and from true blessedness,” etc.]—to whom all the wicked must be subjected and oppressed, while no good person is handed over except for exercise—such an angel, no one can doubt, is not to be worshiped. His joy is our misery, and his loss is our return.

113. Therefore let religion bind us to the one almighty God, because between our mind, by which we understand him as Father, and the truth—that is, the inner light through which we understand him—there is no creature interposed. Let us therefore also venerate and hold fast the Truth itself, in no respect unlike him, and with him, the form of all things that were made by the One and strive toward the One.

From this it appears to spiritual minds that all things were made through this form, which alone fulfills what all things desire. Yet none of these things would be made by the Father through the Son, nor would they be preserved within their proper bounds, unless God were supremely good: he neither begrudged any nature that could be good from him, nor, in that good itself, failed to give some things as much as they wished and others as much as they could, so that they might remain.

Therefore it is fitting for us to worship and hold fast the very Gift of God, equally unchangeable with the Father and the Son: the Trinity of one substance, one God from whom we are, through whom we are, and in whom we are; from whom we departed, to whom we became unlike, and by whom we were not permitted to perish; the Principle to which we return, the Form which we follow, and the Grace through which we are reconciled; one God by whose authority we were created, whose likeness forms us toward unity [Note: [Col. 0172] Thus in the manuscripts. But the editions read: “through whom we are reformed toward unity.”], and whose peace keeps us attached to unity; the God who said, “Let it be” (Genesis 1); and the Word through whom everything that was substantially and naturally made came to be; and the Gift of his goodness, through which it pleased and was reconciled to its author that whatever was made by him through the Word should not perish: one God by whose creative power we live, through whom we live wisely after being reformed, whom we love and in whose enjoyment we live blessedly; one God from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things—to him be glory forever and ever. Amen (Romans 11:36).

[ON GENESIS AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS.]

[Col. 0171]

ON THE FOLLOWING TWO BOOKS OF GENESIS AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS [Note: [Col. 0171] In the Benedictine edition these two books of *Genesis against the Manichaeans* follow the three books of *On Free Will*. They have been moved here because of the similarity of their subject. M.].

ST. AUGUSTINE IN BOOK VIII OF *ON THE LITERAL MEANING OF GENESIS*, CHAPTER 2.

Against the Manichaeans, who err by accepting these writings of the Old Testament in a manner other than they ought, but who blaspheme by not accepting and detesting them altogether, I wrote two books shortly after my conversion. I wished either to refute their ravings or to raise their attention toward seeking in the writings they hate the Christian and evangelical faith. Since at that time not everything occurred to me as to how the passages could properly be understood, and many of them seemed incapable of being understood, or barely or only with difficulty, I explained with as much brevity and clarity as I could what they signified figuratively when I could not discover their literal meaning. I did this so that, deterred neither by extensive reading nor by obscurity of argument, they would not cease to take these books into their hands.

[Col. 0173]

[Note: [Col. 0171] See also book 1, chapter 10, of the *Retractions*, volume 1, column 599, no. 1, beginning with the words “Now, in Africa,” through column 600, no. 3, ending with the words “the Manichaeans whom they might deceive.” M.]

TWO BOOKS OF ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON GENESIS AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS [Note: [Col. 0173] Written around the year of Christ 389.] [Note: [Col. 0173] These two books were corrected against the Regius manuscript, approximately one thousand years old, and against manuscripts of the highest quality: the Theoderican, Gemmetican, Martinian, Audoenian, Pratellian, Casalian, Arnulfian, Cistercian, Regiomontan, two Victorine, Sorbonian, Christinaean, Vedastine, and Vatican manuscripts; against readings collected from two Belgian manuscripts through the care of the scholars of Louvain; and against the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.] [Note: [Col. 0173] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.] (C)

BOOK ONE. In this book the beginning of Genesis is defended against the Manichaeans’ calumnies—from the following verse, chapter 1: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” through verse 2 of chapter 2, where God is said to have rested on the seventh day.

CHAPTER ONE.—He is about to write in defense of the Old Law against the Manichaeans in a style lowered to the understanding of the uneducated.

[Col. 0173]

1. If the Manichaeans chose whom they would deceive, we too would choose the words with which to answer them. But since they attack both the educated in letters and the uneducated with their error, and, while promising truth, strive to turn people away from the truth, their vanity must be refuted not with ornate and polished speech but with evident facts.

I approved the judgment of certain truly Christian people who, although educated in the liberal arts, had read other books of ours published against the Manichaeans and perceived that the uneducated either could not understand them or understood them only with difficulty. They very kindly advised me not to abandon ordinary ways of speaking if I intended to drive those pernicious errors from the minds of the uneducated as well. For the educated understand this familiar and simple style, whereas the uneducated do not understand the other.

2. The Manichaeans therefore customarily disparage the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which they do not know. Through this disparagement they mock and deceive our weak and inexperienced people, who cannot find how to answer them. For there is no Scripture that cannot easily be criticized by those who do not understand it.

But divine providence permits many heretics of different errors to exist so that, when they insult us and ask us questions we do not know how to answer, we may at least in this way shake off our laziness and desire to know the divine Scriptures. For this reason the Apostle also says: “There must be heresies” [Note: [Col. 0173] Thirteen manuscripts read: “There must be many heresies.”] “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19).

Those are approved by God who can teach well; but they cannot become manifest to human beings unless they teach. They do not wish to teach, however, except those who seek to be taught [Note: [Col. 0173] Most manuscripts read: “except those who seek,” omitting “to be taught.”]. But many are too lazy to seek unless the troubles and insults of heretics rouse them as if from sleep, make them ashamed of their ignorance, and cause them to realize that, because of this ignorance, they are in danger.

If these people are of good faith, they do not yield to the heretics [Note: [Col. 0174] Erasmus reads: “they believe the heretics.” Louvain reads: “they yield to the heretics.” M.], but diligently seek what they should answer them. Nor does God abandon them, so that those who ask may receive, those who seek may find, and to those who knock it may be opened (Matthew 7:7).

But those who despair that they can find within the Catholic discipline what they seek are worn down by errors. If they persist in seeking, after great labors, exhausted, thirsty, and almost dead, they return to the very fountains from which they had wandered.

CHAPTER TWO.—Verse 1 of chapter 1 of Genesis is defended against the detractors: what God was doing before the creation of the world, and why he suddenly wished to create the world.

3. The Manichaeans usually criticize the first book of the Old Testament, entitled Genesis, in the following way. Concerning what is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” they ask, “In what beginning?” And they say: “If God made heaven and earth at some beginning of time, what was he doing before he made heaven and earth? And why did he suddenly decide to make what he had never before made throughout eternal ages?”

We answer them that God made heaven and earth “in the beginning,” not in the beginning of time but in Christ, when the Word was with the Father, through whom and in whom all things were made (John 1:1, 3). For when the Jews asked our Lord Jesus Christ who he was, he replied, “The Beginning, because I am also speaking to you” (ibid. 8:25).

But even if we believe that God made heaven and earth at the beginning of time, we must certainly understand that before the beginning of time there was no time. For God made time as well; therefore, before he made time, there was no time. We cannot say, then, that there was some time when God had not yet made anything. For how could there have been time that God had not made, when he himself is the maker of all time?

And if time began together with heaven and earth, no time can be found in which God had not yet made heaven and earth. When it is said, “Why did he suddenly decide?” it is said as though some periods had passed during which God did nothing. But time could not pass before God had made it, because no one can be the maker of time except one who exists before time.

Certainly the Manichaeans themselves read the Apostle Paul, praise and honor him, and deceive many by wrongly interpreting his letters. Let them therefore tell us what the Apostle Paul said: “The acknowledgment of the truth that accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal times” (Titus 1:1–2). For what could eternal times have had before them? They must explain this, so that they may understand that they do not understand when they rashly wish to criticize what they ought carefully to have investigated.

4. If they do not say, “Why did God suddenly decide to make heaven and earth?” but remove the word “suddenly” and say only, “Why did God decide to make heaven and earth?” we answer as follows.

We do not say that this world is coeternal with God, because this world does not possess the eternity that God possesses. God made the world, and together with the creature that God made, time began to exist; for this reason time is called eternal. Yet time is not eternal in the same way that God is eternal. God exists before time, since he is the maker of time.

Just as everything God made is very good, but is not good in the same way that God is good—for he made these things, whereas they were made—so he did not beget them from himself so that they would be what he is. Rather, he made them from nothing so that they would not be equal either to him from whom they were made or to his Son through whom they were made. “For it is just” [Note: [Col. 0175] The editions read: “For he is just.” Four manuscripts read: “For it is just.”].

If, then, they say, “Why did God decide to make heaven and earth?” we must answer them by telling them first to learn the force of the human will, since they wish to know the will of God. They seek to know the causes of God’s will, although God’s will itself is the cause of everything that exists. For if God’s will has a cause, then something precedes God’s will—which it is impious to believe.

Therefore, when someone says, “Why did God make heaven and earth?” the answer is: “Because he willed it.” God’s will is the cause of heaven and earth, and therefore God’s will is greater than heaven and earth. But when someone asks, “Why did he will to make heaven and earth?” he seeks something greater than God’s will. Nothing greater can be found.

Let human presumption therefore restrain itself and not seek what does not exist, lest it fail to find what does exist. If anyone desires to know God’s will, let him become God’s friend. For if someone wished to know the will of a human being whose friend he was not, everyone would laugh at his impudence and folly.

No one becomes God’s friend except through the purest conduct and through that end of the commandment of which the Apostle says: “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5). If the Manichaeans had this, they would not be heretics.

CHAPTER THREE.—Verse 2 is defended.

5. What follows in the book of Genesis—“But the earth was invisible and unformed”—the Manichaeans criticize as follows: “How did God make heaven and earth in the beginning, if the earth already existed, invisible and unformed?”

Thus, because they wish to criticize the divine Scriptures before knowing them, they fail to understand even the clearest things. For what could have been said more plainly than this: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed”? That is: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the very earth that God made was invisible and unformed before God arranged the forms of all things in their proper places and settings through an ordered distinction; before he said, ‘Let there be light,’ and ‘Let there be a firmament,’ and ‘Let the waters be gathered together,’ and ‘Let the dry land appear,’ and the other things that are explained in order in the same book, in a manner capable of being grasped by the inexperienced.”

All these things contain such great mysteries that whoever has learned them will either grieve over the vanity of all heretics because they are human beings, or laugh at it because they are proud.

6. It follows in the same book: “And darkness was over the abyss.” The Manichaeans criticize this by saying: “Then was God in darkness before he made the light?” In truth, they themselves are in the darkness of ignorance, and therefore do not understand the light in which God was before he made this light. They know no light except what they see with bodily eyes. Thus they worship this sun—which we see together not only with the larger beasts but even with flies and worms—in such a way as to say that it is a particle of that light in which God dwells.

But let us understand that there is another light in which God dwells, of which it is written in the Gospel: “That was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). For the light of this sun does not enlighten every human being, but the human body and mortal eyes; and in these the eyes of eagles surpass us, since they are said to look upon this sun much better than we do.

That other light, however, does not feed the eyes of irrational birds [Note: Col. 0176. The printed editions read “animals.” But the manuscripts read “birds,” namely eagles], but the pure hearts of those who believe in God and turn themselves away from the love of visible and temporal things toward fulfilling his commandments. All human beings can do this if they wish [Note: *Retractationes* I, chapter 10, no. 2], because that light enlightens every human being coming into this world.

Therefore darkness was over the abyss before this light came into being; and of this the text subsequently speaks here.

## CHAPTER IV — In defense of verse 3, it is shown that darkness is nothing

7. “And God said, Let there be light.” Where there is no light, there is darkness—not because darkness is something, but because the absence of light is called darkness. Just as silence is not some thing, but where there is no sound, that is called silence. Nakedness is not some thing, but where there is no covering on a body, that is called nakedness. Emptiness is not something, but a place where there is no body is called empty. So darkness is not something, but where there is no light, that is called darkness.

We say this because they are accustomed to ask: “Where, then, did that darkness over the abyss come from before God made the light? Who made or generated it? Or, if no one made or generated it, was darkness eternal?” This is as though darkness were something. But, as has been said, the absence of light received this name.

Since, however, they have been deceived by their fables into believing that there was a nation of darkness, in which they imagine that bodies, forms, and souls in those bodies existed, they therefore think that darkness is something. They do not understand that darkness is perceived only when we do not see, just as silence is perceived only when we do not hear. And just as silence is nothing, so darkness is nothing.

Yet just as they say that the nation of darkness fought against God’s light, so another equally foolish person could say that a nation of silences fought against God’s voice. But we have not now undertaken to refute and disprove those follies. For at present we have resolved to defend, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant us strength, the things they criticize in the Old Testament, and to show in them that human blindness has no power against the truth of God.

## CHAPTER V — How it is to be understood that the Spirit of God was borne over the waters, according to verse 2

8. What is written—“And the Spirit of God was borne over the water”—the Manichaeans are accustomed to criticize in this way: “Then was the water the dwelling place of the Spirit of God, and did it contain the Spirit of God?” With their perverse minds they try to pervert everything, and they are blinded by their own wickedness.

When we say, “The sun is borne over the earth,” do we intend this to mean that the sun dwells in the earth and that the earth contains the sun? Yet the Spirit of God was not borne over the water in the same way that the sun is borne over the earth, but in another way that few understand. That Spirit was not borne over the water through intervals of space, as the sun is borne over the earth, but through the power of his invisible majesty.

Let them tell us, then, how a craftsman’s will is borne over the things that are to be fashioned. If they cannot comprehend these ordinary and human matters, let them fear God and seek with simple hearts what they do not understand, lest, when they try with sacrilegious words to cut down the truth they cannot see, the axe return upon their own legs. For that truth, which remains unchangeable, cannot be cut down; rather, whatever blows are directed against it rebound and return with greater force upon those who dare to strike what they ought to believe, so that they might deserve to understand.

9. Next they ask, and mockingly inquire: “Where was that water over which the Spirit of God was borne? For is it written earlier that God made water?” If they asked this reverently, they would discover how it ought to be understood.

For in this passage “water” was not named so that we should understand the water that we can already see and touch. Nor was the “earth” called formless and invisible such as this earth that can now be seen and handled. Rather, when it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” the whole of creation that God made and established was signified by the names “heaven” and “earth.” These names of visible things were used because of the weakness of little ones, who are less able to comprehend invisible things.

First, therefore, matter was made confused and formless, from which all the distinct and formed things were to be made. I believe that the Greeks call this *chaos*. For in another passage we likewise read, in praise of God: “You who made the world from formless matter” (Wisdom 11:18); some books have, “from unseen matter.”

## CHAPTER VI — Formless matter made from nothing, and all things made from it

10. And therefore God is most rightly believed to have made all things from nothing. For even if all formed things were made from this matter, this matter itself was nevertheless made from absolutely nothing.

We must not resemble those who do not believe that almighty God could make something from nothing, because they observe that craftsmen and all sorts of artisans cannot fashion anything unless they have material from which to fashion it. Wood assists the carpenter, silver the silversmith, gold the goldsmith, and earth the potter, enabling each to complete his work. If they are not assisted by the material from which they make something, they can make nothing, since they themselves do not make the material. The carpenter does not make wood, but makes something from wood; and so it is with all other artisans of this kind.

Almighty God, however, needed no assistance from anything that he himself had not made in order to produce what he willed. For if, in making the things he wished to make, he were assisted by something he had not made, he would not be omnipotent. It is sacrilegious to believe this.

## CHAPTER VII — Formless matter designated by various names

11. That formless matter, then, which God made from nothing, was first called “heaven and earth,” and it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”—not because this was already heaven and earth, but because it could become so. For heaven too is written to have been made afterward.

It is like this: if, looking at the seed of a tree, we were to say that roots, trunk, branches, fruit, and leaves are present in it—not because they already exist, but because they are going to come from it—so it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” as though it were the seed of heaven and earth, while the matter of heaven and earth was still in a confused state. But because it was certain that heaven and earth would come from it, the matter itself was already called heaven and earth.

The Lord also speaks in this manner when he says: “I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15)—not because it had already been done, but because it was most certainly going to be done. For shortly afterward he says to them: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). Why, then, had he said, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you,” unless he knew that he would do this?

In the same way, the matter from which heaven and earth had not yet been made could be called “heaven and earth,” although heaven and earth were not to be made from anything else. Innumerable expressions of this kind are found in the divine Scriptures. As in our customary speech, when we say of something that we most certainly hope will happen, “Consider it already done.”

12. He also wished to call this still-formless matter “invisible and formless earth,” because among all the elements of the world the earth appears less beautiful than the others. He called it invisible because of its obscurity, and formless because of its lack of form.

He called this same matter “water,” over which the Spirit of God was borne, just as an artisan’s will is borne over the things being fashioned. Although only a few can attain to this understanding, I do not know whether it can even be explained in human words to more than a few people.

It was not unreasonable, moreover, for this matter to be called “water,” because everything that is born on earth—whether animals, trees, plants, or anything similar—begins to be formed and nourished from moisture.

All these names, therefore—whether “heaven and earth,” or “invisible and formless earth,” or “the abyss with darkness,” or “the water over which the Spirit was borne”—are names for formless matter. Thus an unknown thing was introduced to the less experienced through familiar terms. It was not given a single name, lest, if there were only one, people should suppose it to be what they were accustomed to understand by that name.

It was called “heaven and earth” because heaven and earth were going to come from it. It was called “invisible and formless earth,” and “darkness over the abyss,” because it was formless and could not be seen or handled in any shape, even if there were someone able to see and handle it. It was called “water” because it was pliable and tractable under the work of the one fashioning it, so that all things might be formed from it.

Under all these names, therefore, the matter was unseen and formless, and from it God established the world.

## CHAPTER VIII — The Manichaean slander concerning verse 4 is refuted

13. “And God said, Let there be light. And light was made.” The Manichaeans are not usually accustomed to criticize this, but rather what follows: “And God saw the light, that it was good.” For they say: “Then did God not know the light, or did he not know what was good?”

Wretched people, who are displeased that God was pleased with his works, although they see that even a human craftsman—for example, a carpenter—though almost nothing in comparison with the wisdom and power of God, nevertheless cuts and works wood for a long time, shaping it with an adze, a plane, a lathe, or by polishing it, until it is brought as far as possible to the standards of his art and pleases its craftsman.

Because what he has made pleases him, does this mean that he did not know what was good? He certainly knew it inwardly, in the mind, where the art itself is more beautiful than the things produced by the art. But what the craftsman sees inwardly in his art, he tests outwardly in his work; and that is perfect which pleases its craftsman.

Thus “God saw the light, that it was good” does not show that an unfamiliar good had become evident to God, but that the finished work pleased him.

14. What if it had been said, “God was astonished at the light, because it was good”? How loudly they would have shouted! How much they would have argued! Astonishment in fact ordinarily arises from unexpected things; yet these people read, and praise, our Lord Jesus Christ in the Gospel for having been astonished at the faith of believers (Matthew 8:10).

But who had produced that faith in them except the one who was astonished at it? And if someone else had produced it, why would he who knew it beforehand be astonished? If the Manichaeans resolve this question, let them see that the other question can also be resolved. If they do not resolve it, why do they criticize matters that they do not want to concern them, when they do not understand the things they claim do concern them?

When our Lord is astonished, he indicates that we ought to be astonished—those of us who still need to be moved in this way. All such movements in him, therefore, are not signs of a disturbed mind, but of a teacher instructing.

So too are the words of the Old Testament: they do not teach that God is weak, but accommodate themselves tenderly to our weakness. Nothing can be said about God in a manner worthy of him. Nevertheless, so that we may be nourished [Note: The printed editions have “so that faith may be nourished.” But the very old and excellent Regius manuscript, together with ten other manuscripts, reads “so that we may be nourished.”] and reach those things that cannot be expressed in any human language, things are said that we can comprehend.

## CHAPTER IX — The second part of the same verse and the first part of the following verse are defended

15. “And God divided between the light and the darkness, and God called the light day, and the darkness he called night.”

Here it was not said, “God made the darkness,” because, as was stated above, darkness is the absence of light. Nevertheless, a distinction was made between light and darkness.

We make a voice by shouting; but we make silence by not making sound, because silence is the cessation of voice. Yet by some act of perception we distinguish between voice and silence, and we call one “voice” and the other “silence.” Therefore, just as we are rightly said to make silence, so in many passages of the divine Scriptures God is rightly said to make darkness, because at times and in places he either does not give light to those whom he wishes, or takes it away.

All this, however, has been said for the sake of our understanding. In what language did God call the light “day” and the darkness “night”? Hebrew, Greek, Latin, or some other? The same question could be asked about everything he called by a name. But in God there is pure understanding, without the noise and variety of languages.

“Called” means “caused to be called,” because he distinguished and ordered everything in such a way that it could be discerned and receive names. We shall inquire in its proper place whether “God called” is truly to be understood in this way, since the more we advance in the Scriptures and become accustomed to them, the more their expressions become familiar to us.

For we say, “That head of a household built this house,” meaning “caused it to be built,” and many similar expressions are found throughout all the books of the divine Scriptures.

## CHAPTER X — How it is rightly understood that one day began and passed, according to verse 5

16. “And evening was made, and morning was made, one day.” Here too the Manichaeans bring a charge against the text, thinking that it was said as though the day began at evening.

They do not understand that the whole operation by which light was made, divided from darkness, and called “day,” while darkness was called “night,” belongs to the day. After this operation, as though the day had been completed, evening was made.

But because night also belongs to its day, “one day passed” is not said until the night too had passed and morning had been made. In this way the remaining days are counted from morning to morning.

For now, when morning has been made and one day has passed, the succeeding operation begins from that very morning which has already come to be. After that operation, evening occurs, then morning, and another day passes; and so the remaining days pass in succession.

## CHAPTER XI — The waters divided by the firmament: verses 6–8

17. “And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let there be a division between water and water; and so it was made. And God made the firmament, and God divided between the water that is above the firmament and the water that is beneath the firmament, and God called the firmament heaven; and God saw that it was good.”

I do not remember that the Manichaeans usually criticize this. Nevertheless, since the waters were divided so that some were above the firmament and others beneath the firmament, and since we said that the matter over which the Spirit of God was borne had been called “water,” I believe that by the firmament of heaven [Note: The printed editions have “beneath the firmament of heaven.” The manuscripts lack the word “beneath.”] the bodily matter of visible things was separated from the incorporeal matter of invisible things.

Since heaven is a most beautiful body, all invisible creation surpasses even the beauty of heaven. Therefore, perhaps the invisible waters are said to be above heaven—waters understood by few to surpass heaven not by spatial position but by the dignity of their nature.

Nevertheless, nothing should be rashly asserted about this matter. It is obscure and remote from human senses. But whatever its nature may be, it must be believed before it is understood.

“And evening was made, and morning was made, the second day.” All these repeated expressions are now to be understood and treated as explained above.

## CHAPTER XII — The gathering of the waters mentioned in verses 9 and 10 is their very formation

18. “And God said, Let the water that is beneath heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear; and so it was made. And the water that was beneath heaven was gathered into one gathering, and the dry land appeared. And God called the dry land earth, and the gathering of the water he called sea. And God saw that it was good.”

Here the Manichaeans say: “If everything was full of waters, how could the waters be gathered into one place?” But it was already said above that the matter over which the Spirit of God was borne had been called “waters,” from which God was going to form everything.

Now, however, when it is said, “Let the water that is beneath heaven be gathered into one gathering,” this is said so that that bodily matter might be formed into the appearance possessed by these visible waters. The gathering itself into one, therefore, is the formation of these waters that we see and touch. For every form is brought into conformity with the rule of unity.

And when it is said, “Let the dry land appear,” what else is this to be understood as saying except [Col. 0182] that the matter should receive the visible form possessed by this earth that we now see and touch?

Earlier, therefore, what was called “invisible and formless earth” designated the confusion and obscurity of matter; and what was called “water over which the Spirit of God was borne” again designated that same matter. Now this water and earth are formed from the matter that had previously been called by those names, before it received the forms that we now see.

It is rightly said that in Hebrew usage the whole gathering of waters, whether salt or fresh, is called “sea.”

## CHAPTER XIII — The objection concerning verses 11–13 is exploded: namely, why the earth produces things without fruit and things harmful

19. “And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass producing seed according to its kind and likeness, and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit, whose seed is in itself according to its likeness. And so it was made. And the earth brought forth grass producing seed according to its kind, and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit, whose seed was in itself according to its likeness, according to its kind, upon the earth. And God saw that it was good. And evening was made, and morning was made, the third day” (Genesis 3:17–19).

Here they are accustomed to say: “If God commanded grass for food and a fruit-bearing tree to arise from the earth, who commanded so many grasses—whether thorny or poisonous—that are of no use for food, and so many trees that bear no fruit?”

We must answer them in such a way that the mysteries are not opened to the unworthy, nor revealed in what figure of future things these matters were spoken.

We must therefore say that, on account of human sin, the earth was cursed so that it would produce thorns—not so that it itself, being without sensation, should feel punishment, but so that the guilt of human sin might always be placed before human eyes. Thus people would be warned at some time to turn away from sins and turn toward the commandments of God.

Poisonous plants were created either for the punishment or for the exercise of mortals; and all this was because of sin, since we became mortal after sin.

By fruitless trees, moreover, human beings are reproached, so that they may understand how shameful it is to be without the fruit of good works in God’s field—that is, in the Church—and fear lest God abandon them, since they too abandon fruitless trees in their own fields and give them no cultivation.

Before human sin, therefore, it is not written that the earth produced anything except grass for food and fruitful trees. After sin, however, we see many dreadful and fruitless things arising from the earth, I believe for the reason we have given.

For it is said to the first human being after he had sinned: “Cursed shall the earth be for you in all your works; in sadness and groaning you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the food of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and into earth you shall go.”

## CHAPTER XIV — Difficulties concerning verses 14–19 are resolved

20. “And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth, and divide between day and night, and be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years; and let them be for illumination in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth. And so it was made. And God made two lights, the greater and the lesser: the greater light for the beginning of day, and the lesser light for the beginning of night, and the stars. And God placed them in the firmament of heaven, so that they might shine upon the earth, and rule the day and the night, and divide between day and night. And God saw that it was good. And evening was made, and morning was made, the fourth day.”

Here they first ask how the heavenly bodies—that is, the sun, moon, and stars—were made on the fourth day. How could the preceding three days have existed without the sun, since we now see the day pass with the rising and setting of the sun, while night is made for us by the sun’s absence, when it returns from the other side of the world toward the east?

We answer them that it could have happened that each of the preceding three days was reckoned over as long a period as that in which the sun makes its circuit—from the time it proceeds from the east until it returns again to the east. Human beings could have perceived this duration and length of time even if they lived in caves, where they could not see the sun’s rising and setting.

In this way, it can be understood that such a duration could also have occurred without the sun, before the sun had been made, and that this duration was reckoned as individual days during those three days.

We would give this answer if we were not recalled by the statement, “And evening was made, and morning was made,” which we now see cannot occur without the sun’s course.

It remains, therefore, for us to understand that, within the duration of time itself, the distinctions between the works were called “evening” because a completed work had passed, and “morning” because a future work was beginning. This was based on the resemblance of human works, since they generally begin in the morning and end toward evening. The divine Scriptures have the custom of transferring words from human matters to divine matters.

21. Next they ask why it was said of the heavenly bodies, “And let them be for signs and for seasons.” “Could those three days,” they say, “have existed without seasons, or not belong to the divisions of time?”

But “for signs and for seasons” was said so that by means of these heavenly bodies the seasons might be distinguished and recognized by human beings. For if time runs on without being distinguished by any divisions—and those divisions are marked by the courses of the heavenly bodies—time can indeed run and pass, but it cannot be understood or distinguished by human beings.

Thus hours pass and complete their intervals when the day is cloudy, but they cannot be distinguished or marked by us.

22. What was said—“And God made two lights, the greater light for the beginning of day, and the lesser light for the beginning of night”—was said as if it meant “for the rule of day and for the rule of night.”

For the sun does not merely begin the day; it also carries it through and brings it to an end. The moon, moreover, sometimes appears for us in the middle of the night or at the end of the night. If, then, the nights during which this happens do not begin with it, how was it made for the beginning of night?

But if by “beginning” you understand an origin, and by “origin” a rule, the meaning is clear: the sun holds rule over the day, while the moon holds rule over the night. Even though the other stars then appear, the moon surpasses them all in brilliance and is therefore rightly called their chief.

23. What was said—“And let them divide between day and night”—could give rise here to a charge: “How had God already divided between day and night above, if the heavenly bodies bring about this division on the fourth day?”

The statement here, therefore, “Let them divide between day and night,” is as though it said: “Let them divide day and night among themselves in such a way that day is assigned to the sun, while night is assigned to the moon and the other stars.”

The two had already been divided, but not yet among the heavenly bodies, so that it might now be certain, with regard to the number of the heavenly bodies, what would appear to human beings by day and what by night.

## CHAPTER XV — The misty air is designated by the name “water,” according to verse 20 and following

24. “And God said, Let the waters bring forth reptiles having living souls, and flying creatures flying over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven. And so it was made. And God made the great sea creatures, and every living soul of animals and reptiles which the waters brought forth according to each kind, and every kind of winged flying creature according to its kind. And God saw that they were good; and God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea, and let flying creatures multiply upon the earth. And evening was made, and morning was made, the fifth day.”

Here they are accustomed to criticize the text, asking—or rather bringing a charge—why it is written that not only animals living in the waters, but also those that fly through the air, and all winged creatures, were born from the waters.

Let all those who are troubled by this know that this misty and humid air in which birds fly is commonly reckoned among the waters by highly learned people who investigate such matters carefully. For it thickens and becomes dense from exhalations and, as it were, vapors of the sea and earth; and from that moisture it is somehow enriched so that it can support the flight of birds.

Therefore, even on clear nights it produces dew, whose drops are found in the grasses in the morning.

For that mountain in Macedonia called Olympus is said to be of such great height that at its summit neither wind is felt nor clouds gather, because by its height it rises above all this humid air in which birds fly. For this reason, birds are said not to be able to fly there.

This is said to have been reported by those who used to ascend the summit of that mountain every year for the sake of certain sacrifices—I do not know whose. They would write certain marks in the dust and find them intact the following year. This could not happen if the place were exposed to wind or rain.

Moreover, because the thinness of the air there did not sustain their breathing, they could not remain there unless they applied wet sponges to their nostrils, from which they could draw thicker, ordinary air. These people therefore reported that they had never seen a bird in that place.

Thus Scripture, with complete fidelity, not without reason records that not only fish and the other animals that are in the waters, but also birds, were born from the waters, because they can fly through this air, which rises from the moisture of the sea and the earth.

## CHAPTER XVI — Why harmful animals were created

25. “And God said, Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to each kind: quadrupeds, reptiles, and beasts of the earth. And so it was made. And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kind, and cattle according to their kind, and all the reptiles of the earth according to their kind. And God saw that they were good.”

The Manichaeans also usually raise this question, saying: “What need was there for God to make so many animals, whether in the waters or on the earth, that are not necessary for human beings? Many are even harmful and frightening.”

When they say this, they do not understand how all things are beautiful to their creator and craftsman, who uses everything in governing the universe over which he rules by the supreme law.

If an inexperienced person enters a craftsman’s workshop, he sees many tools whose purposes he does not know; and if he is very foolish, he thinks them superfluous. If, moreover, through carelessness he falls into a furnace, or injures himself with some sharp instrument because he handles it badly, he also thinks that many harmful and dangerous things are present there.

Yet because the craftsman knows how these things are used, he laughs at the ignorant person’s foolishness and, disregarding his inept words, diligently carries on his work.

Human beings are nevertheless so foolish that, in the workshop of a human craftsman, they do not dare criticize what they do not understand. When they see such things, they believe that they are necessary and designed for some use. But in this world, whose creator and administrator is proclaimed to be God, they dare to criticize many things whose purposes they do not see, and in the works and instruments of the omnipotent craftsman they wish to appear to know what they do not know.

26. I confess that I do not know why mice and frogs were created, or flies and worms. Yet I see that all things are beautiful in their own kind, although on account of our sins many things appear hostile to us.

For I consider the body and limbs of any animal, and there I find measures, numbers, and order, all belonging to the unity of harmony. I do not understand where all these come from except from the supreme measure, number, and order, which exist in God’s own unchangeable and eternal sublimity.

If these most talkative and foolish people would consider this, they would not weary us. Rather, by contemplating all beauties, both the highest and the lowest, they would praise God the craftsman everywhere. Since reason is nowhere offended, if bodily sensation is offended somewhere, they would attribute this not to any defect in the things themselves but to the deserts of our mortality.

Certainly all animals are either useful to us, harmful to us, or superfluous. They have nothing to say against useful animals. As for harmful ones, we are either punished by them, exercised by them, or frightened by them, so that we may love and desire not this life, subjected to many dangers and labors, but another and better life where there is complete security, and so that we may obtain it through the merits of piety.

But what concern of ours are the superfluous things? If you dislike them because they are not useful, let it please you that they are not harmful. Even if they are not necessary for our household, they nevertheless complete the integrity of this universe, which is far greater and far better than our household. God governs it much better than each of us governs his own house.

Make use, therefore, of what is useful; beware of what is harmful; leave what is superfluous. Yet whenever you see measures, numbers, and order, seek the craftsman. You will find no other than the one in whom are supreme measure, supreme number, and supreme order—that is, God, of whom it is most truly said that he has arranged all things by measure, number, and weight (Wisdom 11:21).

Perhaps you will receive richer benefit when you praise God in the lowliness of an ant than when you cross a river upon the height of some beast of burden.

## CHAPTER XVII — How it is understood that human beings were made in the image of God, according to verse 26

27. “And God said: Let us make the human being in our image and likeness; and let him have authority over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, all cattle and wild beasts, all the earth, and all reptiles that crawl upon the earth,” and so forth, up to the evening and morning by which the sixth day is completed.

The Manichaeans are especially accustomed to argue about this question at length and to mock us because we believe that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God.

They attend to the shape of our body and unhappily ask whether God has nostrils, teeth, a beard, and even internal limbs and the other things that are necessary in us. In God, however, it is ridiculous—indeed impious—to believe such things. Therefore they deny that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God.

We answer them that these bodily members are often named in Scripture when God is being introduced to the understanding of little ones, and this not only in the books of the Old Testament but also in those of the New.

For God’s eyes and ears and lips are mentioned [Note: The printed editions have “and lips and teeth and feet, etc.”; but “and teeth” is absent from the manuscripts], and the Son is proclaimed to sit at the right hand of God the Father. The Lord himself also says: “Do not swear by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet” (Matthew 5:34–35). Likewise, he himself says that he cast out demons by the finger of God (Luke 11:20).

But all who understand the Scriptures spiritually have learned that these names signify not bodily limbs but spiritual powers, just as do “helmets,” “shield,” and “sword” (Ephesians 6:16–17), along with many other expressions.

First, then, we must ask these heretics with what impudence they bring charges against such words in the Old Testament, when they see them also placed in the New—or perhaps they do not see them, but are blinded by their quarrelling.

28. Nevertheless, let the spiritually faithful in the Catholic discipline know that they do not believe God to be defined by bodily form; and when man is said to have been made in the image of God, this is said according to the inner man, where reason and understanding are found. Hence he also has dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, all cattle and wild animals, all the earth, and all creeping things that creep upon the earth. For when he had said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” he immediately added, “And let him have dominion over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky,” and so forth, so that we might understand that man is said to have been made in the image of God not on account of his body, but on account of that dominion by which he surpasses all cattle. For all the other animals are subject to man, not on account of the body, but on account of the understanding which we possess and they do not—although our body also has been so fashioned as to indicate that we are better than the beasts and therefore like God. For the bodies of all animals, whether they live in water, on land, or fly through the air, are inclined toward the earth and are not upright like the human body. By this it is signified that our soul, too, ought to be upright toward its higher things, that is, toward eternal spiritual realities. Thus man is understood to have been made in the image and likeness of God chiefly in respect of the soul, as is also attested by the upright form of his body.

[Note: We have restored “its higher things” (*sua*) from twelve manuscripts; the word is omitted in the printed editions.]

## CHAPTER XVIII—Man’s Dominion over the Beasts

29. Sometimes they also say: “How did man receive dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and all cattle and wild animals, when we see human beings killed by many wild beasts and harmed by many birds—creatures which we wish either to avoid or capture and often cannot? How, then, did we receive dominion over them?” First, it must be said to them that those who consider man after the Fall are greatly mistaken, when he was condemned to the mortality of this life and lost that perfection in which he was made in the image of God. But if his condemnation is nevertheless so powerful that he rules over so many cattle—for although, because of the frailty of his body, he may be killed by many wild beasts, he can be tamed by none, while he himself tames so many, indeed almost all of them—if, then, this condemnation of man is so powerful, what must we think of his kingdom, which is divinely promised to him when he has been renewed and liberated?

[Note: Published editions here and shortly afterward read “dominion” (*dominatio*); moreover, Lovaniensis has “to rule” (*dominari*). But the manuscripts require the correction “condemnation” (*damnatio*) and “to be tamed” (*domari*).]

## CHAPTER XIX—How Verse 28 Is to Be Understood Spiritually

30. Concerning what is written, “Male and female he made them; and God blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply, and be fruitful, and fill the earth,’” it is entirely proper to ask how the union of male and female before the Fall is to be understood, as well as the blessing expressed in the words, “Increase and multiply, and be fruitful, and fill the earth”: whether it is to be understood carnally or spiritually. For we may also understand it spiritually, so that it may be believed to have been converted into carnal fertility after the Fall.[^c0018-1] Previously, the union of male and female was chaste: the one was suited to rule, the other to obey; and a spiritual offspring of intelligible and immortal joys filled the earth—that is, gave life to the body—and ruled over it, possessing it in such subjection that it suffered from it no opposition and no distress. This should be believed for the reason that, before they sinned, they were not yet children of this age. For the children of this age beget and are begotten, as the Lord says when, in comparison with the future life promised to us, he shows that this carnal generation is to be held in contempt (Luke 20:34–36).

[^c0018-1]: *Retractationes* I.10.2.

## CHAPTER XX—Dominion over the Beasts Allegorically

31. As for what was said to them, “Have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth”: while the literal understanding is certainly valid, namely, that it is evident to everyone that man rules over all these animals by reason, it is nevertheless rightly understood spiritually as well. We should have all the affections and movements of the soul that resemble these animals under our control, and should rule over them through self-restraint and moderation.

For when these movements are not governed, they burst forth and proceed into the most shameful habits; through various and destructive pleasures they carry us away and make us resemble every kind of beast. But when they are governed and subjected, they become altogether tame and live harmoniously with us. For the movements of our soul are not alien to us. They, too, are nourished with us by knowledge of reason, excellent conduct, and eternal life, as though by seed-bearing plants, fruit-bearing trees, and green plants.

This is the human life that is blessed and tranquil, when all its movements agree with reason and truth; and they are called joys, and holy, chaste, and good loves. But if they do not agree, then, while they are heedlessly managed, they nevertheless tear apart and scatter the soul, making life utterly wretched; and they are called disturbances, lusts, and evil desires. Concerning these we are now commanded to crucify them within ourselves with as much effort as we can, until death is swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54). For the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified their flesh with its disturbances and desires” (Galatians 5:24).

From this point, anyone should also be warned that these things are not to be understood carnally: in Genesis, green plants and fruit-bearing trees are given as food to every kind of beast, to all birds, and to all serpents, while we see that lions, hawks, kites, and eagles feed only on flesh and on the slaughter of other animals. I believe the same is true of certain serpents that live in sandy and desert places where neither tree nor plant grows.[^c0018-2]

[Note: Seven manuscripts omit “nevertheless” (*nihilominus*). Three others, shortly afterward, read “are governed” (*reguntur*) instead of “are conducted” (*geruntur*).]

[^c0018-2]: *Retractationes* I.10.2.

## CHAPTER XXI—Why It Is Said in Verse 31, “Very Good”

32. It must certainly not be passed over carelessly that it is said, “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” For when he dealt with each individual thing, he said only, “God saw that it was good”; but when all things together were spoken of, it was not enough to say “good” unless “very” was added. If, when considered by the wise, the individual works of God are found to possess praiseworthy measures, numbers, and arrangements, each established in its own kind, how much more is this true of all things together—that is, of the universe itself, which is made complete by the gathering of these individual things into one?

For every beauty that consists of parts is much more praiseworthy in the whole than in a part. Thus, if we praise only the eyes in the human body, or only the nose, or only the cheeks, or only the head, or only the hands, or only the feet, and praise the other individual features as beautiful when considered alone, how much more should we praise the whole body, to which all the limbs—each beautiful in itself—contribute their beauty? Indeed, a beautiful hand, which was praised even when considered alone as part of the body, if separated from the body would itself lose its grace, and the other parts would be unbecoming without it.

So great is the force and power of wholeness and unity that even things which are many and good please us only when they come together and converge into a whole.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “So that things which are good then also please very much.”] The word “universe” (*universum*) itself derives its name from unity. If the Manichaeans considered this, they would praise God as the author and creator of the universe; and whatever in the condition of our mortality offends them in a part, they would refer back to the beauty of the whole and see how God made all things not only good but also very good.

For even if, in an ornate and carefully composed speech, we consider the individual syllables—or even the individual letters, which pass away immediately after sounding—we find in them nothing that is pleasing or worthy of praise. The speech as a whole is beautiful not because of its individual syllables or letters considered separately, but because of all of them together.

## CHAPTER XXII—The Rest of the Seventh Day Allegorically: Chapter 2, Verses 1–3

33. Let us now consider also that which they are accustomed to ridicule with greater shamelessness than ignorance: that it is written that, after completing heaven and earth and all that he had made, God rested on the seventh day from all his works, and blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because he rested from his works.

They say: “What need was there for God to rest? Was he perhaps wearied and exhausted by the works of the six days?” They also add the testimony of the Lord, where he says, “My Father is working until now” (John 5:17), and by this they deceive many ignorant people, whom they try to persuade that the New Testament is opposed to the Old Testament.

But just as those to whom the Lord says, “My Father is working until now,” held a carnal opinion about God’s rest and, observing the Sabbath carnally, did not see what the significance of that day prefigured, so these people, although their intention is different, likewise fail to understand the sacrament of the Sabbath. Both by observing it carnally and by cursing it carnally, they do not know the Sabbath.

Let each person therefore pass over to Christ, so that the veil may be removed, as the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 3:16). For the veil is removed when, once the covering of likeness and allegory has been taken away, the truth is laid bare so that it can be seen.

34. First, then, the rule governing this manner of expression must be noticed and learned in many passages of the divine Scriptures.[^c0018-3] What else does it signify when God is said to have rested from all his works, which he made very good, except our rest, which he will give us from all our works if we too have done good works?

In accordance with this very figure of speech, the Apostle also says: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Romans 8:26). The Holy Spirit does not groan as though he were in need or suffering distress—he intercedes for the saints according to God—but because he himself moves us to pray when we groan, what we do through his moving us is said to be done by him.

The same manner of speech is found in the words: “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13:3). He does not test us so that he himself may know, since nothing is hidden from him, but so that he may make us know how much we have progressed in his love; he permits us to be tested for this purpose.

In accordance with the same figure of speech, our Lord says that he does not know the day and hour of the end of the age (Matthew 24:36). For what could there be that he does not know? But because he was usefully concealing this from the disciples, he said that he did not know it, since by concealing it from them he made them not know it. According to this figure, he also said that the Father alone knew that day, because he would make the Son know it.

Through this figure, many questions in the divine Scriptures are resolved without difficulty by those who already understand this kind of expression. Our ordinary speech is also full of such expressions when we call a day “joyful” because it makes us joyful; cold “sluggish” because it makes us sluggish; a ditch “blind” because we do not see it; and a tongue “polished” because it produces polished words. Finally, we also call a time “free from all troubles” when it is we who are at rest from all troubles.

God, then, is said to have rested from all his works, which he made very good, because in him we shall rest from all our works if we have done good works. For even our good works must be attributed to him who calls, who commands, who shows the way of truth, who invites us so that we may will, and who supplies the strength to fulfill what he commands.

[^c0018-3]: Five manuscripts read “must be discerned” (*discernenda est*) instead of “must be learned” (*discenda est*).

## CHAPTER XXIII—The Seven Days and the Seven Ages of the World

33. **The First Age.** But why this rest is assigned to the seventh day must, I think, be considered more carefully.[^c0018-4a] For throughout the entire text of the divine Scriptures I see six laborious ages, distinguished by their own fixed boundaries, as it were, so that rest may be hoped for in the seventh. These same six ages resemble the six days in which the things that Scripture records God made were made.

The beginnings of the human race, in which it began to enjoy this light, are appropriately compared with the first day, on which God made light. This age should be regarded as the infancy of the whole age of the world itself, which we must conceive as one human being in proportion to its magnitude. For every human being, when first born and brought forth into the light, passes through the first age, infancy.

This age extends from Adam to Noah through ten generations. The evening of this day is the Flood,[^c0018-4] because our infancy, too, is wiped away as though by a flood of forgetfulness.

[^c0018-4]: Seven manuscripts read “in the Flood” (*in diluvio*).

[^c0018-4a]: Seven manuscripts read “of the seventh day” (*septimo diei*).

36. **The Second Age.** Morning begins from the time of Noah, the second age being like childhood, and this age extends to Abraham through another ten generations. It is appropriately compared with the second day, on which the firmament was made between water and water. For the ark in which Noah and his companions were was a firmament between the lower waters on which it floated and the upper waters by which it was deluged.

This age is not erased by a flood, because our childhood too is not wiped from memory by forgetfulness. We remember having been children, but we do not remember having been infants. The evening of this age is the confusion of languages among those who were building the tower, and its morning begins with Abraham. Yet this second age did not generate the people of God, because childhood is not yet suited for begetting.

37. **The Third Age.** Morning therefore begins with Abraham, and the third age follows, resembling adolescence. It is appropriately compared with the third day, on which the earth was separated from the waters.

For by the name “sea” all the nations are suitably signified, whose unstable error, moved by the vain teachings of idols as by every wind, is unsettled. From this vanity of the nations and the waves of this age, the people of God were separated through Abraham, like earth when it appeared dry—that is, thirsting for the heavenly rain of the divine commandments. By worshiping the one God, this people, like irrigated earth able to produce useful fruits, received the Holy Scriptures and the Prophecies.[^c0018-5]

This age could already beget a people for God, because the third age—that is, adolescence—can already have children.[^c0018-5a] Therefore it was said to Abraham: “I have made you the father of many nations, and I will increase you exceedingly, and I will make nations of you, and kings shall come from you. And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations, for an everlasting covenant, to be your God and the God of your seed after you. And I will give to you and to your seed after you the land in which you dwell, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God” (Genesis 17:5–8).

This age extends from Abraham to David through fourteen generations. Its evening lies in the sins of the people, by which they transgressed the divine commandments, up to the wickedness of the worst king, Saul.

[^c0018-5]: A Regius manuscript and five others read: “so that it could produce the useful fruits of the Holy Scriptures and the Prophets.”

[^c0018-5a]: In the earlier Amedean, Erasmian, and Lovaniensian editions, the following is inserted after “I have made you”: “before God whom you believed, who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were; who, against hope, believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said: ‘So shall your seed be.’” All these words are absent from the manuscripts.

38. **The Fourth Age.** From that point morning begins with the kingdom of David. This age resembles youth. Indeed, youth reigns among all the ages and is itself the firm adornment of every age.[^c0018-5b] It is therefore appropriately compared with the fourth day, on which the stars were made in the firmament of heaven.

For what signifies the splendor of a kingdom more clearly than the excellence of the sun? And the people obedient to the kingdom are shown by the splendor of the moon, as the synagogue itself, while its princes are the stars; everything is founded, as it were, in the firmament of the stability of the kingdom.

The evening of this age, as it were, lies in the sins of the kings, by which that nation deserved to be taken captive and reduced to servitude.

39. **The Fifth Age.** Morning begins with the migration to Babylon, when, in that captivity, the people were placed gently in a foreign leisure. This age extends to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is the fifth age, namely, the decline from youth into old age—not yet old age, but no longer youth—the age of one who is older, whom the Greeks call *presbytēs* (πρεσβύτης). For among them an old man is called not *presbytēs* (πρεσβύτης), but *gerōn* (γέρων).

And truly this age in the Jewish people was bent and broken from the strength of the kingdom, just as a human being becomes older after youth. It is appropriately compared with the fifth day, on which the animals in the waters and the birds of the sky were made, after those people began to live among the nations, as in the sea, and to possess an uncertain and unstable dwelling, like flying birds.

But there were certainly also great sea creatures there—that is, those great men who were more able to rule the waves of the age than to serve in that captivity. They were not corrupted by any terror into the worship of idols.

Here it should be noted that God blessed those animals, saying, “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea, and let the birds multiply upon the earth,” because in truth the Jewish people, since it was scattered among the nations, has multiplied greatly.

The evening of this day—that is, of this age—is the multiplication of sins among the Jewish people, because they were so blinded that they could not even recognize the Lord Jesus Christ.

40. **The Sixth Age.** Morning begins with the preaching of the Gospel through our Lord Jesus Christ, and the fifth day ends. The sixth begins, in which the old man’s old age becomes visible. In this age that carnal kingdom was violently worn down: the temple was thrown down and the sacrifices themselves ceased; and now, so far as the strength of its kingdom is concerned, that nation is living out its final life.

Yet in this age, as in the old age of the old man, the new man is born, who now lives spiritually. For on the sixth day it was said, “Let the earth produce a living soul.” On the fifth day it had been said, “Let the waters produce,” not a living soul, but “creeping things of living souls,” because creeping things are bodies, and that people was still serving the Law through bodily circumcision and sacrifices, as in the sea of the nations.[^c0018-6]

But here he speaks of a living soul, by which eternal things now begin to be desired.[^c0018-7] The serpents and cattle that the earth produces therefore signify the nations that will now believe steadfastly in the Gospel.
