Concerning these it is said in the vessel shown to Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: “Kill and eat.” When he said that they were unclean, the response was made to him: “What God has cleansed, do not call unclean” (Acts 10:13–15).

Then man is made in the image and likeness of God, just as in this sixth age our Lord is born in the flesh, of whom it was said through the prophet, “And he is a man, and who will recognize him?” And just as on that day there were male and female, so in this age there are Christ and the Church.

On that day man is placed above cattle, serpents, and birds of the sky; likewise in this age Christ rules the souls that obey him, who have come to his Church partly from the nations and partly from the Jewish people, so that they might be tamed and made gentle by him: human beings devoted either to carnal desire, like cattle; or darkened by obscure curiosity, like serpents; or lifted up by pride, like birds.

And just as on that day man and the animals that are with him are fed with seed-bearing plants, fruit-bearing trees, and green plants, so in this age every spiritual person who is a good minister of Christ and imitates him well, insofar as he can, is spiritually nourished together with the people by the sustenance of the Holy Scriptures and the divine Law: partly for conceiving the fertility of reasonings and words, like seed-bearing plants; partly for the usefulness of moral conduct in human life, like fruit-bearing trees; and partly for the vigor of faith, hope, and charity unto eternal life, like green plants—that is, flourishing plants—which no heat of tribulations can cause to wither.

But the spiritual person is nourished by these foods in such a way as to understand many things; the carnal person, however—that is, the little one in Christ—is nourished like God’s animal, so as to believe many things that he is not yet able to understand. Nevertheless, they all have the same foods.

[^c0018-5b]: The printed editions read “firmament and adornment”; the manuscripts read “firm adornment,” and some of them shortly afterward read “and the people obedient to the king.”

[^c0018-6]: *Retractationes* I.10.3.  
[^c0018-7]: The manuscripts read this way. Earlier editions read: “by which they begin to desire eternal life.”

41. **The Seventh Age.** The evening of this age—if it has not yet begun, may it not find us—is that of which the Lord says: “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

After this evening, morning will come, when the Lord himself will come in glory. Then those to whom it was said, “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48), will rest with Christ from all their works. For such people perform works that are very good. After such works, rest is to be hoped for on the seventh day, which has no evening.

It is therefore altogether impossible to say in words how God made and established heaven and earth and every creature that he established. Yet this exposition, by arranging things according to the days, indicates them as though it were a history of events, while observing above all the proclamation of future things.

## CHAPTER XXIV—Why the Ages of the World Are Unequal

42. If anyone is troubled by the fact that in these ages of the world we observe the first two ages unfolded through ten generations, while the three that follow are each composed of fourteen generations, and this sixth age is not defined by any number of generations (Matthew 1:1), it is easy to see that in each individual human being the first two ages—infancy and childhood—are attached to the senses of the body.

There are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. The number five is doubled because the human sex is twofold, and thus such generations arise, male and female. Five, then, as I have said, doubled makes the number ten.

But from adolescence onward, when reason begins to prevail in a human being, knowledge and action are added to the five senses; these govern and administer life, so that the number seven begins to appear. Doubled in the same way on account of the twofold sex, it stands out and appears in fourteen generations, which are found in the three succeeding ages, resembling adolescence, youth, and the age of the older man.

The age of old age, however, just as in us is not defined by any fixed period of years, but after those five ages however long a person has lived is assigned to old age, so in this age of the world the generations do not appear. Thus the final day also remains hidden, which the Lord showed it was useful for us not to know (Matthew 24:36).

## CHAPTER XXV—A Higher Allegory of the Seven Days

43. Each one of us also has, in good works and a righteous life, these six days, distinguished, as it were, in sequence, after which he ought to hope for rest.

On the first day there is the light of faith, when he first believes in visible things,[^c0018-8] on account of which faith the Lord deigned to appear visibly.

On the second day there is the firmament of discipline, by which he distinguishes between carnal and spiritual things, as between the lower and upper waters.

On the third day he separates his mind from the stain and waves of carnal temptations, as dry land is separated from the disturbances of the sea, so that he can now say, “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7:25), directing his mind toward bearing the fruits of good works.

On the fourth day, having already become spiritually discerning within that firmament of discipline, he perceives what immutable truth is, shining in the soul like the sun. He perceives how his soul becomes a participant in truth itself and gives order and beauty to the body, like the moon illuminating the night; and how all the stars—that is, all spiritual understandings—sparkle and shine in the obscurity of this life as in night.

On the fifth day, having become stronger through knowledge of these things, he begins to work in the actions of this most turbulent age, as in the waters of the sea, for the benefit of fraternal fellowship. From bodily actions,[^c0018-9] which pertain to the sea itself—that is, to this life—he brings forth creeping things of living souls, that is, works beneficial to living souls; and great sea creatures, that is, very powerful actions by which the waves of the age are broken and despised; and the birds of the sky, that is, voices proclaiming heavenly things.

[^c0018-9]: Three manuscripts read “cognitions” (*agnitionibus*) instead of “actions” (*actionibus*); shortly afterward they read “most powerful cognitions” (*fortissimas agnitiones*).

On the sixth day let him produce from the earth a living soul—that is, from the very stability of his mind, where he has spiritual fruits, namely, good thoughts. Let him govern all the movements of his soul, so that there may be in him a living soul, serving reason and justice rather than rashness and sin.

Thus let man also be made in the image and likeness of God, male and female—that is, understanding and action—whose union may fill the earth with spiritual offspring, that is, subject the flesh, together with the other things already mentioned above concerning human perfection.

In these days, as it were, the evening lies in the completion of each individual work, and the morning in the beginning of the works that follow. After these works, as it were, of the six days—works that are very good—let man hope for perpetual rest and understand what is meant by, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” For he himself works these good things in us, he who commands us to work; and he is rightly said to rest, because after all these works he himself will grant us rest.

For just as a master of a household is rightly said to build a house, although he does not do this by his own labor but by that of those whom he commands while they serve, so he is rightly said to rest from his works when, after the completion of the construction, he permits those whom he commanded to be free and enjoy a pleasant leisure.

## BOOK TWO

This book continues the exposition of Genesis from chapter 2, verse 4—“This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth,” and so forth—up to the passage in which Adam and Eve are expelled from Paradise. At the end, it compares the doctrines of the Church with the errors of the Manichaeans.

## CHAPTER ONE—Recitation of the Second and Third Chapters of Genesis

1. After the enumeration and exposition of the seven days, a kind of conclusion was inserted, and everything said above was called “the book of the creation of heaven and earth,” although it is only a small part of the book. It deserved to be called this because a brief likeness, as it were, of the entire age of the world from beginning to end is represented in these seven days.

Then the account begins to speak more carefully about man. The whole account is explained not openly but figuratively, so that it may exercise the minds of those seeking truth and draw them away from carnal occupations toward a spiritual task. It proceeds as follows:

“This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when the day was made on which God made heaven and earth and all the green plants of the field, before they existed upon the earth, and all the food of the field, before it sprouted. For God had not yet rained upon the earth, nor was there a man to work it. But a spring rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth.

“And then God formed man from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.

“And then God planted Paradise in Eden, toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had formed. And God caused to grow from the earth every tree beautiful to look upon and good for food, and he planted the tree of life in the middle of Paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

“And a river went out from Eden and watered Paradise; from there it is divided into four branches. The name of the first is Pishon; it is the one that surrounds the whole land of Havilah. There is gold there, and the gold of that land is excellent;[^c0018-10] there is also bdellium and the green stone. The name of the second river is Gihon; it is the one that surrounds the whole land of Ethiopia. The third river is the Tigris; it is the one that flows toward Assyria. The fourth river is called the Euphrates.

“And the Lord God took the man whom he had made and placed him in Paradise, to work it and guard it. And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: ‘You may eat for food from every tree that is in Paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat from it, for on the day on which you eat from it, you shall die by death.’

“And the Lord God said: ‘It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.’

“And whatever God had formed from every kind of cattle, every kind of beast of the field, and every kind of flying bird beneath the sky, he brought to Adam, to see what he would call them. Whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name. And after this Adam called the names of all cattle, all birds of the sky, and all beasts of the field; and according to what Adam called them, that is their name to this day.

“But for Adam no helper like himself had yet been found. And God cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he fell asleep. And God took one of his ribs and filled its place with flesh, and God formed the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman. And he brought her to Adam, to see what he would call her.

“And Adam said: ‘This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. She shall be called Woman, because she was taken from her man’;[^c0018-11] and she shall be a helper for me.

“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. And both were naked, Adam and his woman, and they were not ashamed.”

[^c0018-10]: The manuscripts read this way. Amedean, Erasmian, and Lovaniensian editions instead have: “where gold is born, and the gold of that land,” and so forth.

[^c0018-11]: The word “her own” (*suo*) is omitted in the Lovaniensian edition, although it is found in the manuscripts, in the Amedean and Erasmian editions, and in the Greek text of the Septuagint: ἐκ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτῆς, “from her man.”

[Note: The published editions read “she shall adhere” (*adhaerebit*); the manuscripts instead read “she shall be joined” (*adjungetur*).]

2. Now the serpent was more cunning than all the beasts that were upon the earth, which the Lord God had made. And the serpent said to the woman, “Why did God say, ‘You shall not eat from every tree that is in the garden’?” And the woman said to the serpent, “We may eat from the fruit of every tree that is in the garden; but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the garden, God said, ‘You shall not eat from it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die.’” And the serpent said to the woman, “You shall certainly not die. For God knew that on the day when you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasing to the eyes and desirable for acquiring knowledge; and she took its fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband; and Adam took it and ate. Then the eyes of both of them were opened, and they realized that they were naked; and they took fig leaves for themselves and made themselves coverings.

And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden toward evening, Adam and his wife hid themselves from before the face of the Lord God [Note: [Col. 0196] Am., Er., and Louvain read, “of the Lord their God.” But the manuscripts lack the word *their*.—For “from before the face,” Erasmus and Venice have “from the face”; Louvain, “before the face.” M.], by the tree that was in the middle of the garden.

And the Lord God called Adam and said to him, “Adam, where are you?” And he said, “I heard your voice, Lord, in the garden, and I was afraid, and I hid myself, because I am naked.” And the Lord God said, “Who told you that you were naked, unless it is because you ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you that you alone should not eat from it?” And Adam said, “The woman whom you gave me [Note: [Col. 0196] In the printed editions *sociam* (“companion”) is added here; this word is absent from the manuscripts.] gave me some, and I ate.” And God said to the woman, “What have you done?” And the woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

And the Lord God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, cursed are you above every domestic animal and every beast of the field. Upon your breast and belly you shall crawl, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. And I shall put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. She shall watch for your head, and you shall watch for her heel.”

And he said to the woman, “Multiplying, I shall multiply your pains and your sighs; in pains you shall bear your children. Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.”

And then God said to Adam: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat from it alone,’ cursed is the earth for you in all your works. In sorrow and groaning you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall produce for you, and you shall eat the plants of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and into earth you shall go.”

And then Adam gave his wife the name Life, because she is the mother of all the living.

And then the Lord God made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them. And he said, “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest Adam stretch out his hand to the tree of life and take from it for himself, and eat and live forever,” the Lord God sent him away from the garden of delight, to work the earth from which he had also been taken. And when he had been cast out of the garden, he dwelt opposite the garden of pleasure. And God placed the Cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way to the tree of life.

## CHAPTER II — Genesis cannot everywhere be expounded literally

3. If the Manichaeans preferred to examine these mysteries of the words not by censuring and accusing them, but by seeking and reverently investigating them, they would certainly not be Manichaeans. What is sought would be given to those who ask; those who seek would find; and to those who knock, it would be opened. For those who seek with devout diligence raise more questions in this discourse than these wretched and impious men do. But the difference is that the former seek in order to find, whereas the latter take no trouble except to ensure that they do not find what they seek.

This entire discourse, then, must first be examined according to history, and afterward according to prophecy. According to history, events are narrated; according to prophecy, future things are foretold.

Certainly, whoever wishes to accept everything that has been said according to the letter—that is, to understand it in no other way than the letter sounds—and is able to avoid blasphemies and proclaim everything consistent with the Catholic faith, is not merely someone who should not be begrudged this interpretation; he must be regarded as an exceptionally worthy and highly praiseworthy interpreter.

But if no way is available by which what has been written can be understood piously and worthily of God, unless we believe that these things were set forth figuratively and in riddles, then, possessing apostolic authority—since the Apostles resolve so many riddles from the books of the Old Testament—let us maintain the method we have undertaken, with the help of him who exhorts us to ask, seek, and knock (Matt. VII, 7). Thus we may explain all these figures of things according to the Catholic faith, whether they pertain to history or to prophecy, without prejudging a better and more diligent treatment, whether by ourselves or by others to whom the Lord may deign to reveal it.

## CHAPTER III — What “the green plant of the field” signifies, verse 5, chapter 2

4. Thus there came to be a day on which God made heaven and earth, and every green plant of the field, before it existed upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0197] Venice has: “before it existed upon the earth.” M.], and every nourishment of the field. Earlier seven days are counted; now one day is mentioned, the day on which God made heaven and earth, and every green plant of the field, and every nourishment. The name of this day is rightly understood to signify all time. For God made all time together with all temporal creatures, which visible creatures are signified by the name of heaven and earth.

What should move us to inquire is that, after naming the day that was made, heaven, and earth [Note: [Col. 0198] The printed editions read: “When he had named the day on which heaven and earth were made.” But the manuscripts, with substantial agreement, read: “When he had named the day that was made, and heaven and earth.”], he also added “the green plant of the field” and “every plant.” For when it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” it was not then said that every green plant and plant of the field had been made. It is plainly read that every green plant and nourishment of the field was made on the third day.

But what was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” does not refer to one of those seven days. For at that point he was either naming the very matter from which all things were made by the name of heaven and earth, or certainly he had first presented the whole creation by the name of heaven and earth, saying, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”; and afterward, in due order, he set forth and explained God’s works individually through the days, on account of the prophecy mentioned in the first book.

What, then, does it mean that, after naming heaven and earth, he now added “the green plant of the field” and remained silent about so many other things that are in heaven and earth, or even in the sea? It means that he wishes the green plant of the field to be understood as the invisible creation, such as the soul. For in Scripture the field is customarily called figuratively “the world.” Indeed, the Lord himself says, “The field is the world” (Matt. XIII, 38), when he was explaining the parable in which weeds were mixed with the good seed.

Thus by “the green plant of the field” he means the spiritual and invisible creation, on account of the vigor of life; and by the name “nourishment,” plainly on account of life, we rightly interpret this same thing [Note: [Col. 0198] I *Retractations*, chapter 10, no. 3.].

5. Next, what he added, “before they existed upon the earth,” is understood to mean before the soul sinned. For, stained by earthly desires, as though born upon the earth or existing upon the earth, it is rightly so described. Therefore he added, “For God had not yet rained upon the earth.”

## CHAPTER IV — What “he had not yet rained upon the earth” means, verse 5

Even now God makes the green plant of the field, but by raining upon the earth—that is, he makes souls become green again through his word. Yet he waters them from the clouds, that is, from the Scriptures of the Prophets and Apostles.

They are rightly called clouds, because these words, which sound and pass away after striking the air, are also wrapped in the obscurity of allegories, as though covered by a kind of darkness; thus they become like clouds. When they are drawn out and expressed through interpretation, the rain of truth is poured into those who understand well.

But this had not yet occurred before the soul sinned—that is, before the green plant of the field existed upon the earth. For God had not yet rained upon the earth, nor was there a human being to work it. A person laboring upon the earth needs rain from the clouds, concerning which clouds we have already spoken.

After the sin, however, the human being began to labor upon the earth and to need those clouds. Before the sin, when God had made the green plant of the field and the nourishment, by which we have said that the invisible creation is signified, he watered it [Col. 0199] from an inner spring, speaking into its understanding. Thus it did not receive words from outside, as rain from the clouds mentioned above, but was satisfied by its own spring—that is, by truth flowing from its innermost being.

## CHAPTER V — The spring watering the earth allegorically; what pride is

6. “For a spring,” he says, “rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth.” From that earth, certainly, of which it is said: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. CXLI, 6).

When the soul was watered by such a spring, it had not yet cast away its innermost being through pride. For the beginning of human pride is apostasy from God. And because, swelling outward through pride, it began no longer to be watered by the inner spring, the prophetic words rightly taunt it [Note: [Col. 0199] I *Retractations*, chapter 10, no. 3.] and say: “Why does earth and ashes grow proud? Because in its life it cast away its innermost being” (Ecclus. X, 14, 9, 10).

For what else is pride than, after abandoning the secret chamber of conscience [Note: [Col. 0199] The printed editions read *secreto* (“secret place”). Twelve manuscripts read *secretario* (“secret chamber”).], wishing to appear outwardly to be what one is not?

And therefore, now laboring upon the earth, a person needs rain from the clouds—that is, teaching conveyed through human words—in order that he may also by this means become green again after that dryness and once more become the green plant of the field.

Would that he might at least willingly receive the rain of truth from those very clouds! For on account of this our Lord deigned to assume the cloud of our flesh and poured out the most abundant rain of the holy Gospel, also promising that if anyone drinks of his water, he will return to that inner spring and will not seek rain from outside. For he says: “It will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life” (John IV, 14).

I believe that this spring rose from the earth before the sin and watered the whole face of the earth, because it was inward and did not desire the help of clouds: “For God had not yet rained upon the earth, nor was there a human being to work it.”

For after saying, “God had not yet rained upon the earth,” he added the reason why he had not yet rained: because there was no human being to work it. The human being began to work the earth when, after the sin, he was sent away from the blessed life that he enjoyed in paradise.

For it is written: “And the Lord God sent him away from the garden of delight, to work the earth from which he had also been taken.” We shall investigate this in its proper place (below, chapter 22).

I have mentioned it here so that we might understand that a human being laboring upon the earth—that is, established in the dryness of sins—needs divine teaching conveyed through human words, like rain from the clouds. But such knowledge will be destroyed. For now we see in a riddle, as though in cloudy weather, seeking nourishment; but then we shall see “face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 8, 12), when the whole face of our earth shall be watered by the inner spring of leaping water.

For if we wish to understand as some spring of visible water the one of which it was said, “A spring rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth,” it is not credible that, when so many perennial springs—whether streams or rivers—are found throughout the whole earth, only that one should have dried up [Note: [Col. 0199] According to Erasmus and the Louvain edition, *siccuerit* (“should have dried up”); M.].

## CHAPTER VI — By what names invisible things are signified

[Col. 0200]

7. In these few words, then, the whole creation before the soul’s sin has been intimated to us. By the name “heaven and earth,” the whole visible creation is signified; by the name “day,” all time; by the name “the green plants and nourishment of the field,” the invisible creation; and by the name “the spring rising and watering the whole face of the earth,” the flood of truth satisfying the soul before the sin.

This day, whose name we have said signifies all time, teaches us that not only the visible but also the invisible creation can experience time. This is made clear to us by the soul, which is shown to be capable of being changed by the great variety of its affections, by the very fall through which it became wretched, and by the restoration through which it returns again to blessedness.

Therefore it was not said merely, “When the day was made, on which day God made heaven and earth”—names by which the visible creation is intimated—but “the green plant and the nourishment of the field” were also added. By this name we have said that the invisible creation is signified, on account of its vigor and life, as is the soul.

Thus it was said, “When the day was made, on which day God made heaven and earth, and every green plant and plant of the field,” so that we might understand that not only the visible but also the invisible creation belongs to time, on account of mutability. For only God is immutable; he exists before time.

## CHAPTER VII — What mystery the clay contains

8. Now, after the whole creation, both visible and invisible, has been intimated, and after the universal benefit of the divine spring toward the invisible creation, let us see what is specially intimated concerning the human being, which concerns us most closely.

First, the statement that God formed the human being from the clay of the earth commonly raises the question of what kind of clay it was, or what matter is signified by the name “clay.” The enemies of the ancient Books, who regard everything carnally and therefore are always in error, also customarily criticize this sharply: that God formed the human being from clay.

For they say: “Why did God make the human being from clay? Was better and heavenly matter lacking to him, from which he could make the human being, so that he would form such a fragile and mortal creature from earthly filth?”

They do not understand, first, how many meanings the terms “earth” and “water” have in Scripture. For clay is a mixture of water and earth.

We say that the human body became weak, fragile, and destined for death after the sin. For in our body these people are horrified by nothing except mortality, which we deserved by condemnation.

But what is difficult or surprising for God, even if he made the human being from the clay of this earth, in making his body such that it would not be subject to corruption if the human being, keeping God’s commandment, had not wished to sin?

If we say that the very form of heaven was made from nothing or from unformed matter because we believe in an almighty Craftsman, what is surprising if a body made from whatever kind of clay could be made by an almighty Craftsman such that, before the sin, no trouble or want would torment the human being and no corruption would cause him to decay?

9. It is therefore useless to ask from what God made the human body—if, that is, the passage now speaks of the formation of the body. For I have learned that some of our people understand it in this way: after it was said, “God formed the human being from the clay of the earth,” the words “according to his image and likeness” were not added because the passage now speaks of the formation of the body. The interior human being, however, was signified when it was said, “God made the human being according to the image and likeness of God” [Note: [Col. 0201] Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 5, and Hilary on Psalm CXVIII understand the passage in this way.].

But even if we understand the human being here also as made of body and soul, so that this discourse is not the beginning of some new work but a more careful reconsideration of what was briefly intimated above, then, as I have said, if we understand the human being in this passage as made of body and soul, the name “clay” was not inappropriately given to the very mixture.

For just as water gathers, glues, and holds earth together when clay is produced from their mixture, so the soul, by giving life to the matter of the body, forms it into harmonious unity and does not permit it to fall apart and dissolve.

## CHAPTER VIII — What the breathing-in of the spirit means; what Scripture calls the human spirit

10. But what is written—“And he breathed into him the spirit of life, and the human being became a living soul”—if the body alone still existed, we must understand here as the soul being joined to the body.

Either it was already made but was, as it were, in the mouth of God—that is, in his truth or wisdom—from which it nevertheless did not depart as though separated by place when it was breathed in; for God is not contained in a place but is present everywhere.

Or the soul was made at that time, when God breathed the spirit of life into that formation, so that this breathing-in signifies the very action of God by which, through the Spirit of his power, he made the soul in the human being.

But if the human being who had been made already consisted of body and soul, then through this breathing-in a faculty of perception was added to the soul, when the human being became a living soul. This does not mean that the breathing-in was changed into a living soul, but that it acted upon a living soul.

Yet we must not understand that the human being who became a living soul was already spiritual; he was still animal. He became spiritual when, established in paradise—that is, in the blessed life—he also received the commandment of perfection, so that he might be perfected by the word of God.

Therefore, after he sinned, departing from God’s commandment and being sent away from paradise, he remained animal. And so all of us who were born from him after the sin first conduct our lives as animal human beings [Note: [Col. 0201] I *Retractations*, chapter 10, no. 3.], until we attain the spiritual Adam, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, who committed no sin (I Pet. II, 22). Having been recreated and given life by him, we shall be restored to paradise, where that thief deserved to be with him on the very day on which he ended this life (Luke XXIII, 43).

For the Apostle says: “But not first the spiritual, but the animal; as it is written: ‘The first Adam was made a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit’” (I Cor. XV, 44–46).

11. We must therefore understand this passage in such a way that, because it was said, “He breathed into him the spirit of life, and the human being became a living soul,” we do not believe that a kind of part of the divine nature was changed into the human soul and are thereby forced to say that the nature of God is mutable. Truth presses the Manichaeans most forcefully on precisely this error.

For, since pride is the mother of all heretics, they dared to say that the soul is the nature of God. And we press them on this point when we say: “Then the nature of God errs and is wretched, is corrupted by the stain of vices, and sins; or even, as you say, it is defiled by the filth of an opposing nature”—and other such things which it is impious to believe about the nature of God.

But that the soul was made by almighty God, and therefore is not a part or the nature of God, is plainly written elsewhere. The prophet says: “He who formed the spirit of all, he himself made all things” (Ps. XXXII, 15); and elsewhere: “He who formed the spirit of the human being within him” (Zech. XII, 1).

Thus these testimonies plainly establish that the human spirit was made.

In Scripture, the human spirit means the rational power of the soul itself, by which it differs from animals and rules them according to the law of nature. Concerning this the Apostle says: “No one knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him” (I Cor. II, 11).

Lest, if it were proved by these testimonies that the soul was made, there should be people who would say that the human spirit was not made and would suppose that it itself was the nature of God, claiming that a part of God had been changed into it when God’s breathing-in took place. Sound doctrine likewise rejects this, because the human spirit itself, when it sometimes errs and at other times wisely understands, proclaims that it is mutable. It is in no way permissible to believe this of the nature of God.

There can be no greater sign of pride than for the human soul to say that it is what God is, while it still groans under such great burdens of vices and miseries.

## CHAPTER IX — What the delights of paradise signify allegorically

12. Let us now consider the blessedness of the human being itself, which is signified by the name “paradise.” Since human beings commonly find delightful rest in groves, and since light rises for our bodily senses from the east, while the sky rises above us—the upper body, superior to our body—spiritual delights, which belong to the blessed life, are therefore also figuratively explained through these words, and paradise is planted toward the east.

Let us understand every beautiful tree as signifying our spiritual joys, beautiful to the sight of understanding, and good for food that does not decay, by which blessed souls are nourished. For the Lord also says, “Work for the food that does not perish” (John VI, 27), such as every form of reason, which is food for the soul.

Toward the east: the light of wisdom in Eden, that is, in immortal and intelligible delights. For if this word is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin, Eden is said to signify delight, pleasure, or a banquet. It has been left untranslated here so that it may appear to signify a place, thereby making the expression more figurative.

We understand “every tree brought forth from the earth” as every spiritual joy, that is, as surpassing the earth and not being entangled in or overwhelmed by the snares of earthly desires.

The tree of life planted in the middle of paradise signifies that wisdom by which the soul ought to understand that it has been ordered in a kind of center of things: although it has all bodily nature subject to it, it must nevertheless understand that the nature of God is above it. It must neither decline to the right, arrogating to itself what it is not, nor to the left, through negligence scorning what is. This is the tree of life planted in the middle of paradise.

By the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, that same middle and ordered integrity of the soul is signified. For this tree too was planted in the middle of paradise. It is called the tree of discernment of good and evil because, if the soul—which ought to extend itself toward the things that are before it, that is, toward God, and to forget the things that are behind it (Phil. III, 13), that is, bodily pleasures—turns toward itself after abandoning God and wishes to enjoy its own power as though without God, it swells with pride, which is the beginning of every sin.

When punishment follows upon this sin, the soul learns by experience the difference between the good that it abandoned and the evil into which it fell. This is what it means for the soul to have tasted from the fruit of the tree of the discernment of good and evil.

It is therefore commanded to eat from every tree that is in paradise, but not to eat from the tree in which there is the discernment of good and evil—that is, not to enjoy it in such a way as to violate and corrupt, as though by eating, the ordered integrity of its own nature.

## CHAPTER X — What the four rivers signify

13. The river that proceeded from Eden—that is, from delight, pleasure, and banquets—is the river signified by the prophet in the Psalms when he says, “You will give them drink from the torrent of your pleasure” (Ps. XXXV, 9). For this is Eden, which in Latin means “pleasure.” It is divided into four parts and signifies the four virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

Phison is said to be the Ganges, while Geon is the Nile; this too can be observed in the prophet Jeremiah. They are now called by other names, just as the river is now called the Tiber, though previously it was called the Albula. The Tigris and the Euphrates, however, still retain the same names.

Nevertheless, these names signify spiritual virtues, as I have said; the interpretation of the names themselves also teaches this, if one considers the Hebrew or Syriac language.

Thus Jerusalem, although it is a visible and earthly place, nevertheless signifies spiritually the city of peace. And Zion, although it is a mountain on earth, signifies contemplation; this name is also frequently transferred in the allegories of Scripture to the understanding of spiritual things.

Likewise, the man who descended from Jerusalem to Jericho, as the Lord says, and was wounded on the road and left by robbers injured and half-dead (Luke X, 30), compels us to understand these places spiritually, although according to history they are found upon the earth.

14. Prudence, therefore, which signifies the contemplation of truth itself, beyond every human mouth because it is ineffable—if you wish to express it, you make it small rather than bring it forth [Col. 0204]—is the truth that the Apostle also heard: “Ineffable words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (II Cor. XII, 4).

This prudence circles the land that contains gold, carbuncle, and green stone—that is, the discipline of living, which, cleansed of all earthly filth as though refined by fire, shines like the finest gold; truth, which no falsehood conquers, like the radiance of the carbuncle, which is not overcome by night; and eternal life, signified by the greenness of the green stone, on account of the vigor that does not wither.

That river which circles the land of Ethiopia, exceedingly hot and burning, signifies fortitude, made energetic and tireless by the heat of action.

The third river, the Tigris, flows toward the Assyrians and signifies temperance, which resists desire—a force strongly opposed to the counsels of prudence. Hence the Assyrians are often placed in Scripture as a symbol of adversaries.

Of the fourth river it is not said toward what it flows or what land it circles. For justice pertains to every part of the soul, since it is the soul’s order and equity, by which these three are joined together harmoniously: first, prudence; second, fortitude; third, temperance. In this entire joining and ordering, justice consists [Note: [Col. 0204] The printed editions read: “And through this joining and ordering they bring justice to completion.” The manuscripts, however, read: “And in this entire joining and ordering, justice”—with “consists” understood.].

## CHAPTER XI — Human work in paradise; the woman made as a helper

15. The human being was established in paradise to work and to guard it, but that work, though worthy of praise, was not laborious. Work in paradise is one thing; work on the earth, to which the human being was condemned after the sin, is another.

The addition “and to guard it” indicates what kind of work it was. For in the tranquility of the blessed life, where there is no death, all work consists in guarding what one possesses.

The human being also receives the commandment about which we have already treated above (above, chapter 9). Since that commandment is concluded in such a way that it is not addressed to one person alone—for it says, “On the day when you eat from it, you shall die”—the explanation begins of how the female was made.

She is said to have been made as a helper for the man, so that through spiritual union she might produce spiritual offspring, that is, good works of divine praise: while he governs, she obeys; he is governed by wisdom, and she by the man. “The head of the man is Christ, and the head of the woman is the man” (I Cor. XI, 3).

Therefore it is said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” For something still remained to be made, so that not only should the soul rule the body—for the body occupies the place of a servant—but also the masculine reason should subject to itself its animal part, through which assistance it might command the body.

The woman was made as an example of this matter. The order of things subjects her to the man, so that what appears more clearly in two human beings, namely male and female, may also be considered in one human being.

Thus the mind within, as the masculine reason, should have subject to itself the soul’s appetite, through which we act with the members of the body, and by a just law should impose a limit upon its helper, just as a man ought to rule a woman and not permit her to dominate the man. When this occurs, the household is perverted and wretched.

16. First, therefore, God showed the human being how much better he was than cattle and all irrational animals. This is signified by the statement that all the animals were brought to him so that he might see what he should call them and give them names.

For it is evident from this that the human being is better than cattle by reason itself: only reason can distinguish them and separate them by name, since it judges concerning them.

But this is an easy kind of reasoning, for a human being quickly understands that he is better than cattle. The difficult reasoning is that by which he understands that within himself there is one thing that is rational and rules, and another that is animal and is ruled.

## CHAPTER XII — Eve joined to Adam while he slept; what this signifies

Because this is seen by a more secret wisdom, I think that the secret vision itself is signified by the name “sleep,” which God cast upon Adam when the woman was made for him.

For seeing this does not require these bodily eyes. The more anyone withdraws from visible things into the interior of understanding—which is, as it were, falling asleep—the better and more sincerely he sees it.

The very knowledge by which one understands that within us there is one thing that rules by reason and another that obeys reason is itself, as it were, the making of the woman from the man’s rib, signifying union.

Moreover, in order that each person may rightly rule this part of himself and become, as it were, married within himself—so that the flesh does not desire against the spirit but is subjected to the spirit, that is, so that carnal desire does not oppose reason but, by obeying it, ceases to be carnal—perfect wisdom is necessary.

Because contemplation of this wisdom is inward and more secret, and far removed from every bodily sense, it can appropriately also be understood under the name “sleep.”

For the man is most properly the head of the woman when Christ, who is the Wisdom of God, is the head of the man [Note: [Col. 0205] We follow Erasmus, the Venice edition, and the second Louvain edition, which read *quae* (“who” or “which”).].

17. Certainly, he filled the place of the rib with flesh, so that by this name the affection of love might be intimated, by which each person loves his own soul and is not harsh toward it by despising it—what one rules is what one loves.

The flesh is not named in this passage to signify carnal desire, but rather in the sense in which the prophet says that the stony heart is taken away from the people and a fleshly heart is given to them (Ezek. XI, 19).

In this sense the Apostle also says: “Not on tablets of stone, but on fleshly tablets of the heart” (II Cor. III, 3).

One thing is proper expression and another is figurative expression, such as the one we are now considering.

Therefore, even if the visible woman was historically made by the Lord God from the body of the man, this was certainly not done without reason, but so that some secret might be intimated.

Was there a lack of clay from which the woman could be formed? Or, if the Lord had wished, could he not have taken a rib from a waking man without pain?

Whether, therefore, these things were spoken figuratively or were also done figuratively, they were not spoken or done in this manner without reason. They are plainly mysteries and sacraments, and must be interpreted and understood according to sound faith, whether in the manner our limited understanding attempts here or in some other, better manner.

## CHAPTER XIII — Spiritual marriage in the human being

18. The man therefore called his woman, as the superior calls the inferior, and said: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.”

“Bone from bones,” perhaps on account of fortitude; and “flesh from flesh,” on account of temperance. For these two virtues are taught to belong to the lower part of the soul, which rational prudence governs.

But the statement, “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man,” does not display this origin and interpretation of the name in the Latin language. For no resemblance is found between the name *mulier* (“woman”) and the name *vir* (“man”).

In Hebrew expression, however, it is said to sound as though it meant: “She shall be called *virago* [a woman derived from man], because she was taken from her man.” For *virago*, or rather *virgo* (“maiden”), has some resemblance to the name *vir*; *mulier* does not. As I have said, this is caused by the difference between languages.

19. As for the addition, “A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,” I do not find how it relates to history, except insofar as such things often occur among the human race.

But the whole passage is prophecy, of which the Apostle speaks, saying: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. This mystery is great; but I am speaking with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 31–32).

If the Manichaeans were not blind when they read these words—for through the apostolic Epistles they deceive many—they would understand how the Scriptures of the Old Testament should be received, and would not dare, with such sacrilegious speech, to accuse what they do not understand.

As for the fact that Adam and his wife were naked and were not ashamed, this signifies the soul’s simplicity and chastity. For the Apostle also says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and chastity that is in Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2–3).

## CHAPTER XIV — The serpent as the devil; Eve as the affection
20. The serpent signifies the devil, who certainly was not simple. For when he is called wiser than all the beasts, his cunning is figuratively indicated. It is not said that the serpent was in paradise, but that there was a serpent among the beasts that God had made. For paradise signifies the blessed life, as I said above (above, chap. 9), in which the serpent was no longer present, because the devil already existed and had fallen from his blessedness, since he did not stand in the truth.

Nor is it surprising that he could speak to the woman, although she was in paradise and he was not. For either she was not in paradise according to place, but rather according to the disposition of blessedness; or, even if there was a place of the sort called paradise, are we to understand that the devil approached them bodily? Certainly not, but spiritually, as the Apostle says: “According to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience” (Eph. 2:2). Does he therefore appear to them visibly, or approach them as though in bodily places, where he works upon them? Certainly not; but in marvelous ways he suggests through thoughts whatever he can.

Those who truly say what the Apostle also says resist these suggestions: “For we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Cor. 2:11). How did he approach Judas when he persuaded him to betray the Lord? Did he do so in some place, or was he seen by Judas through those eyes? Rather, as it is written, “he entered into his heart” (Luke 22:3).

A man repels him if he guards paradise. For God placed the man in paradise “to work it and guard it”; thus it is said of the Church [Note: [Col. 0207] In Er., Ven., and Lov. the reading is likewise “of the Church.” M.] in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12). The persuader of perversity is certainly not admitted there. Yet he deceives through the woman. For our reason cannot be led into consent to sin unless pleasure has first been stirred in that part of the soul which ought to obey reason as its governing man.

21. Even now, whenever any one of us falls into sin, nothing other than what then occurred among those three—the serpent, the woman, and the man—is taking place. First there is a suggestion, whether through thought or through the bodily senses: seeing, touching, hearing, tasting, or smelling. Once this suggestion has occurred, if our desire is not stirred toward sin, the serpent’s cunning is excluded; but if desire is stirred, it is as though the woman has already been persuaded.

Sometimes, however, reason manfully restrains and checks even desire once it has been stirred. When this happens, we do not fall into sin; rather, after some struggle, we are crowned. But if reason consents and decides that what lust has stirred up ought to be done, the man is expelled from the whole blessed life as though from paradise. For sin is already imputed, even if the deed does not follow, because in the consent the conscience is held guilty.

### CHAPTER XV — How Temptation Casts Down

22. We must carefully consider in what manner that serpent persuaded the woman to sin, for this bears most directly upon our salvation. These things were written so that we might now beware of such things. When the woman, having been questioned, answered what command had been given to them, the serpent said:

“You shall not surely die; for God knew that on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

[Note: [Col. 0207] Lov. here and below reads *scit* (“knows”).]

We see from these words that sin was persuaded through pride. This is the force of the statement, “You will be like gods.” Likewise, when it says, “For God knew that on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened,” what else is meant than that they were persuaded not to remain under God, but rather to exist under their own authority, without the Lord, and thus not to observe his law—as though he begrudged them the ability to govern themselves? They would not need his inward light, but would use their own providence, as though their own eyes, to distinguish good and evil, which he had forbidden.

This, then, was what they were persuaded to do: to love their own power excessively and to wish to be equal with God. They misused, against God’s law, that intermediate position by which they were subject to God and had their bodies subject to them, as though it were the fruit of the tree planted in the middle of paradise. Thus they lost what they had received while attempting to seize what they had not received.

Human nature was not given the capacity to be blessed through its own power, with God not governing it. For without a governor, God alone can be blessed through his own power.

23. “And the woman saw,” it says, “that the tree was good for food, and that it was good to the eyes for seeing and for knowing.” How did she see, if their eyes were closed? This was said so that we might understand that those eyes were opened after they took from that fruit—eyes by which they saw themselves naked and were displeased with themselves: that is, eyes of cunning, by which simplicity is displeasing.

When anyone has fallen away from that innermost and most secret light of truth, there is nothing by which he wishes to please except fraudulent pretenses. From this hypocrisy also arises, in which those who are able to deceive and mislead whomever they wish seem very clever to themselves.

The woman gave to her husband, and they ate, and their eyes were opened—the eyes already mentioned. Then they saw that they were naked, but with perverse eyes, by which that simplicity signified under the name of nakedness appeared shameful to them. Thus, so that they would no longer be simple, they made themselves loincloths from fig leaves, as though covering their private parts—that is, concealing the simplicity of which cunning pride had now become ashamed.

The fig leaves signify a certain itching, if such a term may properly be used of incorporeal things, which the mind experiences in marvelous ways through desire and the pleasure of lying. Hence those who love to jest are also called *salsi* in Latin, “witty” or “saucy.” In jokes, however, pretense certainly holds the leading place.

### CHAPTER XVI — What Concealment, Walking, and Questioning Signify

24. Therefore, when God was walking in paradise toward evening—that is, when he was coming to judge them—before their punishment he was walking in paradise. This means that God’s presence was, as it were, moving within them, when they themselves were no longer steadfast in his command. It was appropriately toward evening, when the sun had already set for them—that is, when that inward light of truth had been taken away from them.

They heard his voice and hid themselves from his presence. Who hides from God’s presence except one who, having abandoned God himself, begins to love what belongs to him? They already had coverings of falsehood; but “the one who speaks falsehood speaks from his own” (John 8:44).

Therefore they are said to hide by the tree that was in the middle of paradise—that is, by themselves, who had been ordered in the midst of things, below God and above bodies. They hid themselves, then, in themselves, so that they might be disturbed by wretched errors after abandoning the light of truth, which they themselves were not. The human soul can participate in truth, but truth itself is the immutable God above it.

Whoever turns away from that truth and turns toward himself, exulting not in God as ruler and enlightener but in his own supposedly free movements, is darkened by falsehood. For “the one who speaks falsehood speaks from his own.” Thus he is troubled and gives expression to the prophet’s words: “My soul is troubled within me” (Ps. 42:6).

Adam is therefore questioned—not because God did not know where he was, but because he was compelling him to confess his sin. For the Lord Jesus Christ did not fail to know the many things about which he questioned others. When Adam heard his voice, he answered that he had hidden himself because he was naked. In his most wretched error he answered as though he could displease God by being naked, although God himself had made him so.

It is characteristic of error that whatever displeases someone, he supposes also displeases God. But the Lord’s words must be understood in a sublime sense: “Who told you that you were naked, except that you ate from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat—from that one you ate?”

He was naked of pretense, but clothed with divine light. Turning away from that light and toward himself—which is signified by eating from the tree—he saw his nakedness and became displeased with himself because he did not possess something as his own.

### CHAPTER XVII — The Rejection of Blame and the Serpent’s Punishment

25. Then, in the customary manner of pride, he does not accuse himself of having consented to the woman, but casts his guilt back upon the woman. Thus, subtly, as though from the cunning he had miserably conceived, he wished to make God himself responsible for his sin. For he did not say, “The woman gave to me,” but added, “The woman whom you gave me.”

Nothing is more familiar to sinners than the desire to attribute to God whatever they are accused of. This also arises from that vein of pride: since man sinned by wishing to be equal to God—that is, free from God’s dominion, as God is free from every dominion because he is Lord of all—and since he could not be God’s equal in majesty, now, fallen and lying in his sin, he attempts to make God his equal. Or rather, he wishes to show that God sinned while he himself was innocent.

When questioned, the woman in turn casts the blame upon the serpent, as though either Adam had received a wife so that he would obey her rather than so that he would make her obey him, or as though she could not have guarded God’s command rather than admitted the serpent’s words.

26. The serpent is not questioned, but receives the punishment first, because he can neither confess his sin nor find any excuse for himself. The condemnation of the devil spoken of here is not that reserved for the final judgment, concerning which the Lord says, “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). Rather, it is the punishment by which he is to be avoided by us.

His punishment is that he has power over those who despise God’s commands. This is explained by the words in which judgment is pronounced against him. His punishment is the greater because he rejoices in this wretched power, although before his fall he used to rejoice in the sublime truth in which he did not remain.

For this reason even the animals are placed above him—not in power, but in the preservation of their nature. [Note: [Col. 0209] Am., Er., and two manuscripts read *conversione*; Lov., supported by several manuscripts, *conversatione*. But the Regius codex and two others more rightly read *conservatione*.] The animals did not lose some heavenly blessedness that they had never possessed; rather, they carry on their lives within the nature they received.

Thus it is said to him: “You shall crawl on your breast and belly.” This is indeed observed in the snake, and from that visible creature the speech is figuratively directed toward this invisible enemy of ours. By the name “breast” pride is signified, because the impulse of the soul dominates there; by the name “belly” carnal desire is signified, because this part is felt to be softer in the body. Since the devil crawls through these things toward those whom he wishes to deceive, it is said: “You shall crawl on your breast and belly.”

### CHAPTER XVIII — The Enmity of the Serpent with Eve

27. “And you shall eat the earth,” it says, “all the days of your life”—that is, throughout all the days in which you exercise this power, before the final punishment of judgment. For this appears to be his life, in which he rejoices and glories.

“You shall eat the earth” may be understood in two ways. Either those whom you deceive through earthly desire will belong to you—that is, sinners, who are signified by the name “earth”—or else these words figuratively indicate a third kind of temptation, namely curiosity. One who eats the earth penetrates into deep and dark things, and yet into things temporal and earthly.

28. Enmity, however, is not placed between the serpent and the man, but between the serpent and the woman. Is this because he does not deceive and tempt men? It is obvious that he does deceive them. Or is it because he did not deceive Adam himself, but Adam’s woman? But does that mean that he is not Adam’s enemy, since the deception reached Adam through his woman—especially because it is said concerning the future, “I will place enmity between you and the woman”?

If the serpent did not afterward deceive Adam, neither did he afterward deceive Eve. Why, then, is it said in this way, unless it is because it is here clearly shown that we cannot be tempted by the devil except through that animal part which, in the one human being, displays something like the image or example of the woman? We have already said much about this above.

That enmity is also placed between the seed of the devil and the seed of the woman signifies, by the seed of the devil, a perverse suggestion, and by the seed of the woman, the fruit of a good work by which the perverse suggestion is resisted.

Therefore the devil watches the sole of her foot, so that, whenever pleasure lapses into what is unlawful, he may seize her. But she watches his head, so that she may repel him at the very beginning of his evil persuasion.

[Note: [Col. 0210] A considerable number of manuscripts read: “If unlawful pleasure slips away.”]

### CHAPTER XIX — The Punishments Inflicted upon the Woman

29. There is now no question concerning the woman’s punishment. She plainly experiences multiplied pains and sighs amid the calamities of this life; and although the statement that she bears children in pain is fulfilled also in the visible woman, consideration must nevertheless be directed toward that more hidden reality.

Female animals also give birth to their young in pain, and in them this is a condition of mortality rather than a punishment for sin. It may therefore be that this condition also belongs to human females as beings with mortal bodies. But the great punishment is that they came to this mortality of bodies from immortality.

Nevertheless, this sentence contains a great sacrament: no abstinence from carnal desire occurs without pain at the beginning, until habit is bent toward the better part. When this has happened, a son has been born, as it were—that is, desire has been prepared by good habit for a good work.

For this habit to be born, the bad habit was resisted with pain. Likewise, what was said after childbirth [Note: [Col. 0211] Thus Am., Er., and the better manuscripts. Lov. reads: “What was said after from childbirth.” Six manuscripts read: “What was said concerning childbirth,” etc.]—“Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you”—cannot mean literally that many, indeed almost all, women give birth when their husbands are absent and afterward do not turn toward them. Nor do proud women who rule their husbands cease, after giving birth, from this vice, so that their husbands rule them. On the contrary, they regard becoming mothers as though it added dignity to them, and they are often even prouder.

What, then, is meant by the statement that after the words “In pain you shall bear children” there was added, “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you”? It means that the part of the soul held by carnal pleasures, when it wishes to overcome some bad habit and has endured difficulty and pain, thereby gives birth to a good habit. It then obeys reason more cautiously and diligently, as a woman obeys her husband. Educated by those very pains, it turns toward reason and gladly serves its command, lest it again fall into some destructive habit.

These things, then, which appear to be curses, are commands, if we read spiritual meanings rather than carnal ones. “The law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14).

### CHAPTER XX — The Punishment of the Man

30. What shall we say, likewise, about the sentence pronounced against the man himself? Are the rich, whose sustenance comes easily and who do not work the land, to be thought to have escaped this punishment, which says:

“Cursed shall the earth be for you in all your works; in sorrow and groaning you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the plants of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go”?

[Note: [Col. 0211] Lov. reads: “For this very thing will have to be feared by him, that in this life, etc.” We have removed the words “will have to be feared by him,” which are absent from the earlier editions and eleven manuscripts.]

Certainly it is clear that no one escapes this sentence. For the difficulty each person born into this life encounters in finding the truth because of his corruptible body—“The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things,” as Solomon says (Wis. 9:15)—these are the labors and sorrows that man has from the earth.

The thorns and thistles are the stings of tortuous questions, or thoughts concerning the provision of this life. Unless they are often uprooted and cast out from God’s field, they choke the word so that it does not bear fruit in a person, as the Lord says in the Gospel (Mark 4:18–19).

Since we are now necessarily reminded of the truth through these eyes and these ears, and since it is difficult to resist the phantasms that enter the soul through these senses—although through them the reminder of truth also enters—in this perplexity, whose face does not sweat in order to eat his bread? We shall suffer this throughout all the days of our life, that is, of this life which will pass away.

This was said to the one who cultivates his field, because he suffers these things until he returns to the earth from which he was taken—that is, until he ends this life. Whoever cultivates this field inwardly and reaches his bread, even with labor, may endure this labor until the end of this life; after this life, however, he need not suffer it.

But whoever has perhaps failed to cultivate the field and has allowed it to be overrun by thorns has the curse of his earth upon all his works in this life, and after this life he will have either the fire of purification or eternal punishment.

Thus no one escapes this sentence. We must act so that, at least, it may be experienced only in this life.

### CHAPTER XXI — Why Adam Called the Woman Eve after the Transgression, and the Meaning of the Garments of Skin

31. Who would not be moved by the fact that after the sin and the sentence of God the Judge, Adam called his woman “Life,” because she was the mother of the living, after she had deserved death and had been destined to bear mortal offspring? The reason is that Scripture has in view those offspring whom, when she has borne them in pain, her turning will be toward her husband and he will rule over her. We have already spoken above of these offspring.

In this sense she is “life” and “mother of the living.” For the life that exists in sins is customarily called death in Scripture, as the Apostle says that a widow who lives in pleasures is dead (1 Tim. 5:6). We also read that sin itself is signified by the name “dead,” where it is said:

“He who is baptized by a dead person and again touches him, what does he gain from his washing?”

[Note: [Col. 0212] The printed editions read *inundationem* (“flooding”); we have preferred the reading of ten manuscripts, *mundationem* (“cleansing”).]

“So also the one who fasts for his sins and again goes and does the same things” So also the one who fasts for his sins and again goes and does the same things” (Sir. 34:30–31).

In place of sin he put “the dead”; abstinence and fasting from sin he placed like baptism—that is, cleansing—from the dead; and returning again to sin is like touching the dead again.

Why, then, should that animal part of us—which ought to obey reason as a woman obeys a man—be called “life” when, through reason, it has rightly conceived from the word of life the burden of living rightly? And when, through the labor of abstinence, resisting a bad habit with pain and groaning, it has given birth to a good habit directed toward right actions, why should it not be called the mother of the living—that is, of those who act rightly? Their opposites are sins, which, as we have shown, can be signified by the name “the dead.”

[Note: [Col. 0212] Er. reads: “Why, when the animal part … conceived, is it called life … when it gave birth, is it called the mother of the living … as we have shown.”]

32. That death, which all of us who are born from Adam began to owe to nature, and which God threatened when he commanded that the fruit of that tree should not be eaten—that death, then, is figured by the garments of skin.

They themselves made loincloths from fig leaves, while God made garments of skin for them. This means that they desired the lust of lying after abandoning the face of truth, whereas God changed their bodies into this mortality of flesh, in which lying hearts are concealed.

Nor should we believe that in those heavenly bodies thoughts can be hidden in the same way that they are hidden in these bodies. Just as certain movements of the soul appear in the face, especially in the eyes, so, in the transparency and simplicity of heavenly bodies, I do not think that any movements of the soul can be hidden at all.

Those, therefore, will deserve that dwelling and transformation into angelic form who, even in this life, although they can conceal lies beneath garments of skin, nevertheless hate and avoid them through the most fervent love of truth. They conceal only what those who hear them cannot bear; they utter no lies. For the time will come when nothing will even be concealed: “There is nothing hidden that will not be revealed” (Matt. 10:26).

They remained in paradise, although already under the sentence of God who condemned them, until they came to the garments of skin—that is, to the mortality of this life. What clearer sign could there be of the death we experience in the body than skins, which are customarily stripped from dead animals?

Thus, because man desired to be God against God’s command—not through legitimate imitation, but through unlawful pride—he was cast down to the mortality of beasts.

33. For this reason the divine law, through God’s mouth, thus mocks him; and through this mockery we are warned, as far as we can be, to beware of pride.

### CHAPTER XXII — The Allegorical Meaning of Adam’s Expulsion

“Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.”

This ambiguous expression creates a figure. For “he has become like one of us” may be understood in two ways: either “like one of us,” as though he himself were also God, which pertains to the mockery—as when one says “one of the senators,” meaning certainly a senator—or because he too would have been a god, though by the beneficence of his Creator and not by nature, if he had wished to remain under his power. In this latter sense “one of us” is like the expression “one of the consuls,” or “among the consuls,” even though he is no longer one.

But for what purpose did he become like one of us? Clearly, for the knowledge of discerning good and evil: so that through experience, by suffering evil, he might learn what God knows through wisdom, and so that through his punishment he might learn that the power of the Almighty—which he had refused to endure while blessed and obedient—is unavoidable.

34. “And then, lest Adam should stretch out his hand to the tree of life and live forever, God sent him away from paradise.”

It is well said that God “sent him away,” not that he “expelled” him, so that he might appear to be driven by the weight of his sins into a place suited to him. This often happens to an evil person when he begins to live among good people and refuses to change for the better. He is driven from the company of the good by the weight of his bad habit; they do not exclude him when he resists, but send him away when he desires to depart.

The statement “lest Adam should stretch out his hand to the tree of life” is also ambiguous. We speak in this way when we say, “I warn you so that you do not do again what you did,” clearly meaning that he should not do it. But we also say, “I warn you so that you may perhaps be good,” clearly meaning that he should be good—that is, “I warn you, not despairing that you may be good.” The Apostle speaks in this way when he says: “Perhaps God may grant them repentance for knowing the truth” (2 Tim. 2:25).

It can therefore be understood that for this reason man was sent into the labors of this life: so that at some time he might stretch out his hand to the tree of life and live forever. The stretching out of the hand aptly signifies the cross, through which eternal life is recovered.

Even if we understand the statement in the other way—“lest he stretch out his hand and live forever”—it is not an unjust punishment, after sin, that access to wisdom should be closed until, through God’s mercy and the ordered measure of time, the mind that died should revive and what had perished should be found.

He was therefore sent away from the paradise of delight so that he might work the earth from which he had been taken—that is, so that he might labor in this body and, if possible, lay up for himself there a merit by which he might return.

He remained opposite paradise in misery, which is certainly contrary to the blessed life. For I believe that the blessed life is signified by the name “paradise.”

### CHAPTER XXIII — What the Cherubim and the Turning Flaming Sword Signify

35. “And God placed the Cherubim and the flaming sword that turns”—which may be called “turning” by a single term—to guard the way to the tree of life.

As those who have interpreted the Hebrew words in Scripture maintain, *Cherubim* is said in Latin to mean “fullness of knowledge.” The turning flaming sword signifies temporal punishments, because times revolve in their succession. It is called “flaming” because every tribulation burns, in a certain sense.

But it is one thing to be burned for destruction and another to be burned for purification. The Apostle says: “Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Yet this feeling purified him all the more, because it proceeded from love.

The tribulations suffered by the righteous also belong to this flaming sword: “Gold and silver are tested in fire, and acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation” (Sir. 2:5). Again: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Sir. 27:6).

Since God chastises the one whom he loves and scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6), as the Apostle says, “knowing that tribulation produces endurance, and endurance produces character” (Rom. 5:3–4), we read, hear, and must believe that the fullness of knowledge and the flaming sword guard the tree of life. [Note: [Col. 0214] Lov. reads: “the fullness is of knowledge, and the flaming sword is guarded.” The earlier editions read likewise, except that they omit “is.” But the sequence of the sentence supports the manuscript reading: “the fullness of knowledge and the flaming sword guard.”]

No one, therefore, can reach the tree of life except through these two things: endurance of hardships and fullness of knowledge.

36. Almost everyone who strives toward the tree of life must endure hardships in this life. The fullness of knowledge, however, seems to come to fewer people, so that it might appear that not all who reach the tree of life come through the fullness of knowledge, although all experience endurance of hardships—that is, the turning flaming sword.

But if we consider what the Apostle says, “The fullness of the Law is love” (Rom. 13:10), and observe that the same love is contained in the twofold commandment, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind,” and “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”—on these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22:37–40)—then we understand without doubt that one comes to the tree of life not only through the turning flaming sword, that is, through endurance of temporal hardships, but also through the fullness of knowledge, that is, through love. For “if I do not have love,” he says, “I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2).

### CHAPTER XXIV — Adam as Christ, Eve as the Church

37. In this discussion I promised to consider the created things, and I believe that this has now been explained. There remains the consideration of the prophecy, which must now be explained briefly. Once a clear sign has been set forth by which the other matters may be directed, this consideration will not, I think, detain us long.

The Apostle says that this is a great sacrament: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” He interprets it by adding: “But I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31–32).

Therefore, what was fulfilled historically in Adam signifies Christ prophetically. Christ left his Father when he said: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16:28). He did not leave him spatially, since God is not contained by place, nor by the turning away of sin, as apostates leave God. Rather, he left him by appearing to human beings as a human being, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

This does not signify a change in God’s nature, but the assumption of the nature of a lower person, that is, a human one.

[Note: [Col. 0215] This is the reading of the printed editions, supported by scarcely any manuscripts.
