The Arnulfensis and two Victorine manuscripts omit *personae* (“of a person”); nine others of better quality—including the Theodericensis, Gemmeticensis, Pratellensis, Regiomontensis, Saint-Ouen of Rouen, Sorbonicus, one manuscript of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, and the royal codex formerly belonging to the church of Verona, which is about a thousand years old—omit *naturae* (“nature”) and read: “But the assumption of a lower person, that is, of a human one.” The collection attributed to Bede, in the fifth chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians, has the same reading, both in printed editions and in the Corbie manuscript copied by Florus. This mode of expression must be understood according to the usage by which the ancients say that the Word assumed a human being—namely, an assumption ordered so that the Word himself, by assuming, exists as a human being and Son of Man, which is the human person. Otherwise Augustine consistently teaches that human nature was assumed by the Word into the unity of the person. His more famous statement is found in Epistle 3 to Volusian: “Thus the Mediator between God and human beings appeared, joining both natures in the unity of one person, elevating the customary by the uncustomary and tempering the uncustomary with the customary.”]

The statement “he emptied himself” (Phil. 2:7) also serves this purpose, because he did not appear to human beings in the dignity in which he exists with the Father. He accommodated himself to the weakness of those who did not yet have a pure heart, by which they might see that the Word was “in the beginning God with God” (John 1:1).

What, then, do we mean by saying that he left the Father? We mean that he ceased to appear to human beings as he is with the Father.

Likewise, he left his mother—that is, the old and carnal observance of the Synagogue, which was his mother according to the seed of David in the flesh—and clung to his wife, that is, to the Church, so that “the two might be one flesh.”

For the Apostle says that he is the head of the Church and that the Church is his body (Col. 1:18). Therefore he too was put into a sleep, the sleep of his Passion, so that the Church, his wife, might be formed for him. The prophet sings of this sleep:

“I slept and took sleep; and I rose again, because the Lord received me” (Ps. 3:6).

His wife, the Church, was therefore formed for him from his side—that is, from faith in his Passion and from Baptism. For when his side was pierced by a lance, he poured forth blood and water (John 19:34).

As I said above, he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, as the Apostle says (Rom. 1:3)—that is, as though from the mud of the earth, since there was no man working the earth, because no man worked in the Virgin from whom Christ was born.

“A fountain rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth.” The “face of the earth,” that is, the dignity of the earth, is rightly understood as the Virgin Mary, the Lord’s mother. The Holy Spirit watered her; in the Gospel the Spirit is signified by the name of the fountain and of water (John 7:38–39). Thus that man was made, as it were, from such mud, and was placed in paradise “to work it and guard it”—that is, in the will of the Father, so that he might fulfill and preserve it.

[Note: [Col. 0216] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “so that, as the mud of the earth was, so that man might be.”]

### CHAPTER XXV — Heretics, and Especially the Manichaeans, Signified by the Serpent

38. We received the command that he received, because every Christian not inappropriately bears the person of Christ, since the Lord himself says: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40).

Would that we might enjoy, as commanded, every tree of paradise, which signifies spiritual delights. “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control,” as the Apostle says (Gal. 5:22–23). And would that we did not touch the tree planted in the middle of paradise, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—that is, would that we did not wish to grow proud of our nature, which, as we have already said, occupies an intermediate place. Then, deceived, we would experience the difference between simple Catholic faith and the deceits of heretics.

For in this way we arrive at the discernment of good and evil. “There must also be heresies,” he says, “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19).

That serpent, then, according to the prophecy, signifies the poisons of heretics, and especially of these Manichaeans and of all who oppose the Old Testament. I do not think that anything was more clearly foretold than that these people are to be avoided in that serpent—or rather, that serpent in these people.

No one promises the knowledge of good and evil more loudly and boastfully than they do. In the human being himself, as in the tree planted in the middle of paradise, they presume to demonstrate that discernment.

And who else speaks more than these people of the statement, “You will be like gods”? Through their proud vanity, while attempting to persuade others of that same pride, they assert that the soul is by nature what God is.

And to whom does the opening of carnal eyes belong more than to those who, having abandoned the inward light of wisdom, compel people to worship this sun, which pertains to the bodily eyes?

All heretics generally deceive through their promise of knowledge and criticize those whom they find believing simply. And because they persuade people of entirely carnal things, they attempt to lead them, as it were, toward the opening of carnal eyes, so that the inward eye may be blinded.

## CHAPTER XXVI — The Heretical Serpent, Manichaean

But these people also dislike their own bodies—not because of the penal mortality that we deserved by sinning, but in such a way that they deny God to be the creator of bodies, as though, with their carnal eyes opened, this nakedness displeased them.

39. Yet nothing marks and exposes them more clearly than what the serpent says: “You shall not surely die; for God knew that on the day you eat, your eyes will be opened.” For these people believe that that serpent was Christ, and they fabricate the claim that some god or other belonging to the nation of darkness—as they assert—gave that commandment, as though he envied human beings the knowledge of good and evil. From this opinion, too, I suppose that certain Serpentines arose, who are said to worship the serpent in place of Christ [Note: [Col. 0217] The Ophites.]; nor do they heed the Apostle, who says: “I fear lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted” (II Cor. 11:3).

I therefore think that these people were prefigured by this prophecy. Our carnal desire, however, is deceived by the words of this carnal serpent, and through it Adam is deceived—not Christ, but the Christian. If he had wished to keep God’s commandment and to live perseveringly by faith until he became capable of understanding the truth—that is, if he had worked in paradise and guarded what he had received—he would not have fallen into that deformity in which, when his flesh displeased him as though it were his nakedness, he gathered more carnal coverings of lies, like fig leaves, with which to make himself a loincloth. This is what these people do when they lie about Christ and proclaim that Christ himself lied; and, as though hiding themselves from the face of God, they turn from his truth to their own lies, as the Apostle says: “They will turn their hearing away from the truth, but they will turn to fables” (II Tim. 4:4).

40. That serpent, then—that error of the heretics which tests the Church, against which the Apostle chants an incantation [Note: [Col. 0217] The printed editions read *clamat*, “cries out”; we have restored *incantat*, “chants an incantation,” from the manuscripts.] when he says, “I fear lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted”—that error creeps on its breast and belly and eats the earth. For it deceives no one except either the proud, who arrogantly claim for themselves what they are not and readily believe that the nature of the supreme God and of the human soul is one and the same; or those entangled in carnal desires, who gladly hear that whatever they do wantonly is not done by them but by the nation of darkness; or the curious, who have earthly concerns and investigate spiritual things with an earthly eye.

“There will be enmity,” however, “between this one and the woman, and between his seed and her seed,” if she gives birth to children, even though with pains, and turns toward her husband, so that he himself may rule over her. For then it can be recognized that one part of us does not belong to God the creator and another part to the nation of darkness, as these people say; rather, both that which has the power to rule in a human being and that lower part which must be ruled are from God, as the Apostle says:

“A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man. For man is not from woman, but woman from man; nor was man created for woman, but woman for man. Therefore a woman ought to have a veil over her head, because of the angels. Nevertheless, neither is woman without man, nor man without woman, in the Lord. For just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman; but all things are from God” (I Cor. 11:7–12).

## CHAPTER XXVII — Adam’s Fall and Punishment Allegorically

41. Let Adam now labor in his field, and let him understand that the fact that the earth produces thorns and thistles for him belongs not to nature but to punishment; and let him attribute this not to some nation of darkness, but to divine judgment, because justice consists in assigning to each what belongs to it.

Let him give the woman the heavenly food that he received from his head, who is Christ; let him not receive from her the forbidden food—that is, the deception of the heretics, offered with a great promise of knowledge and as though it were an opening of secrets, by which the error itself becomes more attractive for deception. For the proud and curious desire of the heretics cries out in the Book of Proverbs under the figure of a woman and says, “Let the foolish turn in to me”; and it urges those who are lacking in understanding, saying, “Eat hidden bread willingly, and drink stolen sweet water” (Prov. 9:16–17).

Yet when someone has believed that woman, having first been driven by a desire to lie through which he believes that Christ lied, he must also receive the tunic of skin by divine judgment. By this name, it seems to me, prophecy signifies not the mortality of the body, which is signified in the historical account and has already been discussed, but the phantasms drawn from carnal perceptions. By divine law, these phantasms follow and cover the person who lies in a carnal manner. Thus he is dismissed from paradise—that is, from the Catholic faith and truth—and made to dwell opposite paradise, that is, to contradict that same faith.

If at some point he turns back to God through the flaming sword—that is, through temporal tribulations—by recognizing and lamenting his sins, and by accusing not some alien nature, which does not exist, but himself, so that he himself may merit pardon [Note: [Col. 0218] The printed editions read, “through conversion he obtains pardon,” and so forth. The manuscripts do not contain the words “through conversion.”]; and if, through the fullness of knowledge, which is charity, he loves God, who is immutable above all things, loving him with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind, and loving his neighbor as himself, he will reach the tree of life and live forever.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — By Way of Epilogue He Refutes the Several Slanders of the Manichaeans

42. What, then, do these people have to criticize in these books of the Old Testament? Let them ask according to their custom, and let us answer as the Lord deigns to grant.

“Why,” they say, “did God make human beings when he knew that they would sin?”

Because he could also bring many good things out of the sinner, ordering him according to the measure of his justice; and because the sinner’s sin did God no harm. If he had not sinned, there would have been no death; but since he did sin, other mortals are corrected by his sin. For nothing recalls human beings from sin as much as the thought of impending death [Note: [Col. 0219] In the Regius manuscript and six other manuscripts of better quality, this sentence is absent: “For nothing recalls human beings from sin as much as the thought of impending death.”].

“They should have been made,” they say, “so that they would not sin.”

Rather, he did make them in that way; for they were made so that, if they had wished, they would not sin.

“The devil,” they say, “should not have been admitted to the woman.”

Rather, she herself should not have admitted the devil to herself; for she was made so that, if she had wished, she would not admit him.

“The woman,” they say, “should not have been made.”

That is to say, “Good should not have been made,” since she too is certainly some good—and such a great good that the Apostle says she is the glory of man; and all things are from God.

Again they say: “Who made the devil?”

He made himself; for he became the devil not by nature but by sinning.

“God should not have made him,” they say, “if he knew that he would sin.”

Rather, why should he not have made him, since through his justice and providence he corrects many from the devil’s wickedness? Or have you perhaps not heard the Apostle Paul say, “Whom I delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (I Tim. 1:20)? And of himself he says, “And lest I should be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (II Cor. 12:7).

“Then,” they say, “the devil is good, because he is useful?”

Rather, he is evil insofar as he is the devil. But God is good and omnipotent, and even from the devil’s wickedness he brings about many just and good things. For only his will is attributed to the devil—the will by which he attempts to do evil—not God’s providence, which brings good out of him.

## CHAPTER XXIX — He Compares the Doctrines of the Church with the Errors of the Manichaeans

43. Finally, since our dispute with the Manichaeans concerns religion—and the question of religion is what is piously to be thought about God—since they cannot deny that the human race is in misery because of sins, they say that God’s nature is in misery. We deny this, but say that the nature in misery is the nature that God made from nothing, and that it came into this condition not under compulsion but by the will to sin.

They say that God’s nature is compelled by God himself to repent of sins. We deny this, but say that the nature which God made from nothing, after it sinned, is compelled to repent of sins.

They say that God’s nature receives forgiveness from God himself. We deny this, but say that the nature which God made from nothing receives forgiveness of sins if it turns from its sins to its God.

They say that God’s nature is necessarily changeable. We deny this, but say that the nature which God made from nothing was changed by its will.

They say that the sins of another nature harm God’s nature. We deny this, but say that sins harm no nature except its own [Note: [Col. 0220] *Retractationes*, I, chapter 10, no. 3.]. And we say that God is of such goodness, such justice, and such incorruptibility that he neither sins nor himself harms anyone who does not wish to sin, nor can anyone harm him who wishes to sin.

They say that there is a nature of evil to which God was compelled to give a part of his own nature to be tormented. We say that no evil is natural [Note: [Col. 0220] The printed editions read, “evil is of nature.” The manuscripts, here and in Book I of the *Retractationes*, chapter 10, no. 3, read, “is natural.”] [Note: [Col. 0220] *Ibid.*]; rather, all natures are good, and God himself is the supreme nature, while the other natures are from him. All are good insofar as they exist, since God made all things very good, but they are ordered in degrees of distinction, so that one thing is better than another. Thus this whole universe is completed by every kind of good: although some things are perfect and others imperfect, the whole is perfect. God, its maker and creator, does not cease to govern it by a just ordering; he makes all things good by his will and suffers no evil by necessity. For one whose will surpasses all things does not in any respect experience anything against his will.

Since they say those things and we say these, let each person choose what he will follow. For I have set forth, in good faith before God, without any desire for contention, without any uncertainty about the truth, and without prejudging a more careful treatment, what seemed to me appropriate.

[Col. 0219]

[Note: [Col. 0219] Concerning the following book, see Book I, chapter 18, of the *Retractationes*, column 613, from the words “When concerning Genesis” through column 614, ending with the words “it must be treated by inquiry.” M.]

SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO,  
THE IMPERFECT BOOK ON THE LITERAL MEANING OF GENESIS

[Note: [Col. 0219] We think this book should be assigned approximately to the year 393, because Augustine places it in the *Retractationes* immediately after the little work, or sermon, on faith and the creed that he delivered at the Council of Hippo in that year, 393.]

[Note: [Col. 0219] You now have this book cleansed of the errors with which it previously abounded, through the aid of the Vatican manuscript. Besides it, the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain were also used for this purpose.]

[Note: [Col. 0219] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractationes* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

The beginning of Genesis is treated up to this verse, 26: “Let us make man in the image,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0219]

1. Concerning obscure matters of nature, which we perceive to have been made by God, the omnipotent craftsman, we must proceed not by making assertions but by inquiry—especially in the books that divine authority commends to us. In these books, the rash assertion of an uncertain and doubtful opinion scarcely avoids the crime of sacrilege. Nevertheless, this doubt in inquiry must not exceed the boundaries of the Catholic faith.

And since many heretics are accustomed to draw the divine Scriptures toward their own opinion, which lies outside the faith of Catholic doctrine, the Catholic faith must first be briefly explained before treating this book.

2. It is as follows: Catholic doctrine commands us to believe that God the Father almighty made and established the whole creation through his only-begotten Son—that is, through his Wisdom and Power, consubstantial and coeternal with him—in the unity of the Holy Spirit, who is likewise consubstantial and coeternal.

This Trinity, therefore, is called one God; and it is to be believed that he made and created all things that exist, insofar as they exist. Thus every creature, whether intellectual or bodily—or, more briefly, in the words of the divine Scriptures, whether invisible or visible—is made by God from nothing, not from God’s nature [Note: [Col. 0221] The Vatican manuscript reads, “not born from God.”]. Nothing in creation belongs to the Trinity except that the Trinity created it. Therefore it is not lawful to say or believe that any creature is consubstantial with God or coeternal with him.

3. Behold, everything that God made is very good. Evils, however, are not natural; rather, everything called evil is either sin or the punishment of sin. Nor is there any sin except the perverse consent of a free will, when we incline toward things that justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain—that is, the fault lies not in these things themselves but in their illegitimate use.

The legitimate use of things is that the soul should remain in God’s law, be wholly subject to the one God in love, and minister to all other things subject to it without covetousness or lust—in accordance with God’s commandment. In this way it will govern without difficulty or misery, with the greatest ease and blessedness.

The punishment of sin, however, occurs when the soul is tormented by creatures that do not serve it, while it itself does not serve God—creatures that obeyed it when it itself obeyed God. Thus fire is not evil, because it is a creature of God; yet our weakness is burned by it as a deserved consequence of sin.

Sins are called natural when, after we have fallen into this life through the sin of free choice, they must be committed before God’s mercy.

4. Human beings are renewed through Jesus Christ our Lord, when the ineffable and immutable Wisdom of God deigned to assume the whole and complete human being, to be born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, to be crucified, buried, raised again, and to ascend into heaven—which has already happened—and to come at the end of the age to judge the living and the dead, and to bring about the resurrection of the dead in the flesh, which is still proclaimed as future.

The Holy Spirit has been given to those who believe in him. The Church, which is called Catholic, has been established by him because it is perfect universally, does not limp in any respect, and is spread throughout the whole world. Earlier sins have been forgiven to those who repent, and eternal life and the kingdom of heaven have been promised.

## CHAPTER II

5. In accordance with this faith, we must consider what can be asked and discussed in this book.

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Some interpreters of Scripture have handed down four modes by which the Law is to be expounded. Their names can be stated in Greek, but in Latin they can be defined and explained [Note: [Col. 0222] Several words are restored here, and other passages are similarly completed, with the aid of the Vatican manuscript—the only handwritten exemplar of this work that we have been able to obtain.]: according to history, according to allegory, according to analogy, and according to etiology.

History is when an event, whether accomplished by divine or human action, is recorded. Allegory is when words spoken figuratively are understood. Analogy is when the agreement of the Old and New Testaments is demonstrated. Etiology is when the causes of words and deeds are supplied.

## CHAPTER III

6. Concerning what is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” it may be asked whether it should be understood only historically, or whether it also signifies something figuratively, and how it agrees with the Gospel, and for what reason this book begins in this way.

According to the historical interpretation, it is asked what “in the beginning” means: whether “in the beginning of time,” or “in the beginning,” that is, in God’s Wisdom itself—for the Son of God also called himself the beginning when he was asked, “Who are you?” and said, “The Beginning, which I also speak to you” (John 8:25).

There is a Beginning without a beginning, and there is a Beginning with another beginning. The Father alone is Beginning without a beginning; therefore we believe that all things are from one beginning. The Son, however, is Beginning in such a way that he is from the Father.

The first intellectual creature itself can also be called a beginning for the things God made, of which it is the head. For although “head” can rightly be called “beginning,” in that hierarchy the Apostle nevertheless did not call woman the head of anyone. He said that man is the head of woman, Christ the head of man, and God the head of Christ (I Cor. 11:3). Thus the creature is joined beneath the Creator.

7. Or was “in the beginning” said because it was made first? Could heaven and earth not have been made first among creatures if the angels and all intellectual powers were made first? For we must believe that the angels too are creatures of God and were made by him. The prophet also enumerated the angels in Psalm 148 when he said: “He commanded, and they were made; he ordered, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5).

But if the angels were made first, it may be asked whether they were made in time, or before all time, or at the beginning of time.

If they were made in time, time already existed before the angels were made. And since time itself is also a creature, we must necessarily suppose that something was made before the angels.

But if we say that they were made at the beginning of time, so that time began together with them, then it must be said that the view held by some is false—namely, that time began with heaven and earth [Note: [Col. 0222] So reads the Vatican manuscript. The printed editions read, “before heaven and earth.”].

8. But if the angels were made before time, it must be asked how the following was said: “And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth, and to divide between night and day; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years.”

Here it may seem that time began when heaven and its lights began to move along ordered courses. But if this is true, how could there have been days before there was time, if time began from the course of the heavenly lights, which are said to have been made on the fourth day?

Or was this arrangement of the days ordered according to the custom of human frailty, by the law of narration, so that sublime matters might be conveyed humbly to the humble? For the speech of the narrator itself cannot avoid having beginnings, middles, and endings.

Or was it said that the lights should exist for these times by which human beings measure intervals of duration through bodily movement? For if there were no movement of bodies, these times would not exist; and such times are more evident to human beings.

If we admit this, it must be asked whether, apart from the movement of bodies, time can exist in the movement of an incorporeal creature, such as the soul or the mind itself. The mind certainly moves through its thoughts, and in that movement one thing is earlier and another later—something that cannot be understood without an interval of time.

If we accept this, time can also be understood to have existed before heaven and earth, if the angels were made before heaven and earth. For there was already a creature whose incorporeal movements brought about time. It is rightly understood that time existed together with it, just as it exists in the soul, which has become accustomed to bodily movements through bodily senses.

But perhaps this is not the case with the first and superior creatures. However this may be—for the matter is exceedingly secret and impenetrable to human conjecture—we must certainly accept in faith, even if it exceeds the mode of our thought, that every creature has a beginning; that time itself is a creature and therefore has a beginning; and that it is not coeternal with the Creator.

9. Heaven and earth may also be understood as standing for the whole creation: the visible ethereal firmament may be called heaven, and the invisible creation of the exalted powers likewise; while earth may mean the whole lower part of the world together with the animals that inhabit it.

Or is all lofty and invisible creation called heaven, and everything visible called earth, so that the words “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” may in this way also be understood of the whole creation?

Perhaps, not incongruously, in comparison with invisible creation everything visible is called earth, so that the invisible is named heaven. For the soul, which is invisible, when it swelled with love of visible things and was exalted by attaining them, was called earth, as it is written: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Ecclus. 10:9).

10. But it may be asked whether he said that all things were already distinct and composed when he spoke of heaven and earth, or whether he called by the name heaven and earth the originally formless matter of the universe, which, at God’s ineffable command, was arranged into these formed and beautiful natures.

Although we read, “You who made the world from formless matter” (Wis. 11:18), nevertheless we cannot say that this matter, whatever its kind, was not made by him, since we confess and believe that all things are from him. Thus the very arrangement and ordering of each formed and distinct thing may be called the world; while the matter itself may be called heaven and earth, as it were the seed of heaven and earth; and heaven and earth may be understood as something confused and mixed, suitable for receiving forms from God the craftsman.

Let this suffice as an inquiry into the statement, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” For none of these matters ought to have been asserted rashly.

## CHAPTER IV

11. “Now the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss; and the Spirit of God was borne over the water.”

The heretics who oppose the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0224] The Manichaeans.] are accustomed to raise a slander against this passage, saying: “How did God make heaven and earth in the beginning, if the earth already existed?” They do not understand that this was added in order to explain what kind of earth it was, the earth of which it had already been said that God made heaven and earth.

It should therefore be understood as follows: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” This earth, which God made, was invisible and unformed until it was distinguished by that same God and established from confusion into a definite order of things.

Or is it better understood in this way: in this further exposition the same matter of things is again commended, the matter previously named heaven and earth, so that the meaning is: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but what was called heaven and earth was earth invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss”?

That is, what was called heaven and earth was a certain confused matter, from which the world—consisting of two chief parts, namely heaven and earth—was to be fashioned when the elements had been arranged and received their form.

This confusion of matter could have been conveyed to popular understanding by saying “earth invisible and unformed,” or “disordered,” or “unprepared,” and “darkness over the abyss,” that is, over an immeasurable depth. This depth perhaps received its name because, on account of its formlessness, no understanding can penetrate it.

12. “And darkness was over the abyss.” Was the abyss below and darkness above, as though places were already distinct? Or, because the confusion of matter is still being explained—what is also called *chaos* (χάος) in Greek—was it said that darkness was over the abyss because there was no light? If light had existed, it would certainly have been above, because it would have been higher and would have illuminated what was subject to it.

Indeed, anyone who carefully considers what darkness is finds nothing other than the absence of light. Thus the statement “Darkness was over the abyss” is equivalent to saying, “There was no light over the abyss.”

Therefore this matter, which by God’s subsequent work is arranged and distinguished into the forms of things, was called invisible and unformed earth, and a depth without light. Earlier it had been called by the name heaven and earth, as it were their seed, as has been said.

This is so, unless by saying “heaven and earth” he first wished to present the universe, and afterward to unfold the parts of the world once the matter had been introduced.

[Col. 0225]

13. “And the Spirit of God was borne over the water.” He had nowhere said that God made the water; yet it must in no way be believed that God did not make the water, or that it already existed before he established anything.

For he is the one from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are, as the Apostle says (Rom. 11:36). Therefore God also made the water, and it is a great error to believe otherwise.

Why, then, was it not said that God made the water? Or did he again wish to call the same matter that he had named by the terms heaven and earth, or invisible and unformed earth and abyss, by the name water?

For why should it not also be called water, if it could be called earth, when there was not yet either distinct and formed water or earth, or anything else?

Perhaps it was first called heaven and earth; second, unformed earth and an abyss without light; third, not incongruously, water. Thus, first, the matter of the whole universe—for whose sake it was made from absolutely nothing—was called by the name heaven and earth. Second, its formlessness was conveyed under the name of unformed earth and abyss, because among all the elements earth is more formless and less luminous than the others. Third, under the name water the matter subject to the work of the craftsman was signified, for water is more mobile than earth. Therefore, because of its suitability for work and its easier movement, the matter subject to the craftsman was more appropriately called water than earth.

14. Air, indeed, is more mobile than water; and ether is believed or perceived, not absurdly, to be more mobile than air itself. But matter would less suitably be called by the name of air or ether.

For these elements are believed to possess more power of making, while earth and water possess more of the capacity to undergo making. If this is obscure, the following seems entirely clear: wind moves water and certain earthly things; but wind is moving air, as it were surging.

Therefore, since air plainly moves water, while the source of its own movement, by which it becomes wind, is hidden, who would doubt that matter is more appropriately called by the name of water, because it is moved, than by the name of air, which moves? To be moved is to undergo action; to move is to act.

It also matters that the things which earth produces are watered so that they may be born and perfected, so that water itself seems almost to be transformed into these growing things.

For this reason matter would more suitably be called by the name water when it is presented as subject to the craftsman’s work, because of its mobility and its transformation into various growing bodies, than by the name air, in which only mobility could be observed, while the other features by which matter is more clearly signified would be lacking.

Thus the whole meaning is: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, matter capable of receiving the form of heaven and earth. This matter was invisible and unformed earth—that is, a formless depth without light—which, nevertheless, because it was subject to the craftsman who moved and worked upon it, was for that very reason also called water, since it yields to the one working upon it.

15. In this signification of matter, its purpose was first intimated—that is, the reason for which it was made; second, its formlessness; third, its service and subjection to the craftsman.

Thus, first, heaven and earth, because the matter was made for this purpose; second, invisible and unformed earth, and darkness over the abyss—that is, formlessness itself without light, which is why it was also called invisible earth; third, water subject to the Spirit for receiving condition and forms.

Therefore the Spirit of God was borne over the water, so that we may understand the Spirit as working and the water as the material upon which he worked—that is, the matter capable of being fashioned.

When we call these three names of one thing—matter of the world, formless matter, and fabricable matter—the first name is appropriately joined to heaven and earth; the second to obscurity, confusion, depth, and darkness; and the third to the ease of yielding, over which the Spirit of the craftsman is already borne for the purpose of working.

16. “And the Spirit of God was borne over the water.” He was not borne over it as oil is borne over water, or water over earth—that is, as though he were contained by it. But, if examples are to be taken from visible things, he was borne over it as this light of the sun or moon is borne over the bodies it illuminates on earth. It is not contained by those bodies; rather, while it is contained with the heavens, it is borne over them.

We must also take care not to suppose that God’s Spirit was borne over matter through intervals of space. Rather, he was borne over it by an effective and creative force, so that what he was borne over might be brought into being and fashioned.

The will of a craftsman is similarly borne over wood or over anything else subject to his work, and even over the limbs of his own body, which he moves in order to work.

Although this comparison is already superior to every body, it is nevertheless small and almost nothing in comparison with understanding how the Spirit of God is borne over the matter of the world, subject to him for his work. But among those things that human beings can grasp in any way, we do not find a clearer or more fitting likeness of the matter under discussion.

Therefore, in such reflection, the command written in Scripture will be held most appropriately: “Blessing God, exalt him as much as you can; for he will surpass even that” (Ecclus. 43:33).

This is said if, in this passage, the Spirit of God is understood to be the Holy Spirit, whom we venerate within the ineffable and immutable Trinity.

17. It can also be understood differently: by “the Spirit of God” we may understand a living creature through which this entire visible world and all bodily things are contained and moved. God almighty granted this creature a certain power of serving him in working upon the things that are generated.

Since this spirit is better than every ethereal body—for every invisible creature precedes every visible creature—it is not absurdly called the Spirit of God.

For what among the things he made is not God’s, since even of the earth it is said, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1), and Scripture says in universal terms, “For all things are yours, Lord, who love souls” (Wis. 11:27)?

But this spirit can be understood in this way only if we take “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” to have been said solely of visible creation. In that case, at the beginning of the world’s fabrication, an invisible spirit was borne over the matter of visible things—though it too would itself be a creature, that is, a nature made and established by God, not God.

But if the matter of the whole creation—that is, of intellectual, animal, and bodily creation—is believed to have been expressed under the name water, then in this passage the Spirit of God can in no way be understood as anything other than the immutable and holy Spirit, who was borne over the matter of all things that God made and established.

[Col. 0227]

18. A third opinion concerning this spirit may arise: the element of air may be indicated by the name spirit, so that the four elements from which this visible world arises are intimated—namely heaven, earth, water, and air.

This would not mean that they already existed as distinct and ordered, but that, within the confused formlessness of that matter, their future emergence was nevertheless foreshadowed. That formless confusion was commended under the names darkness and abyss.

But whichever of these opinions is true, we must believe that God is the author and creator of all things that have arisen, of things visible and invisible—not insofar as they possess defects contrary to nature, but insofar as they are natures themselves. There is absolutely no creature that does not receive from him the beginning and perfection of its kind and substance.

## CHAPTER V

19. “And God said, Let there be light; and there was light.”

We must not understand God’s saying, “Let there be light,” as a sound produced from the lungs, or by tongue and teeth. Such thoughts belong to the carnal. To set one’s mind according to the flesh is death (Rom. 8:6).

Rather, “Let there be light” was spoken ineffably. But it may be asked whether this statement was spoken to the only-begotten Son, or whether the only-begotten Son himself is what was spoken—that is, the Word of God, through whom all things were made (John 1:1, 3).

At any rate, that impiety must be excluded which would lead us to believe that the only-begotten Word of God the Son is like a spoken voice, as occurs with us [Note: [Col. 0227] The Vatican manuscript reads, “lest.”].

The Word of God, through whom all things were made, neither began to exist nor will cease to exist. Born without beginning, he is coeternal with the Father.

Therefore, if “Let there be light” both began to be said and ceased to be said, this word was spoken to the Son rather than being the Son himself.

Yet even this must be understood ineffably. No carnal image should creep into the mind and disturb a devout spiritual understanding. For to suppose that anything begins or ceases in the nature of God, if understood properly, is a rash and precipitate opinion.

Nevertheless, such language may most humanely be granted to the carnal and immature—not so that they remain in it, but so that they may rise from it. Whatever is said to begin or cease in God must in no way be understood of his own nature, but of his creature, which obeys him in wondrous ways.

20. And God said, “Let there be light.” Is this the light apparent to these bodily eyes, or some hidden light, which we have not been given to see through this body? And if hidden, is it corporeal, extending perhaps through the regions of space in the higher parts of the universe; or incorporeal, such as exists in the soul, to which the judgment of what is to be avoided or sought is referred from the bodily senses—a light not lacking even in the souls of animals; or is it that which appears through higher reasoning, from which everything created begins? Whatever light it signifies, we must nevertheless understand it to have been made and created: not that light by which God’s Wisdom itself shines, which was not created but born, lest God be thought to have existed without light before he established this light of which we are now speaking. For concerning this light, as the very words sufficiently show, what is commended is that it was made: “And he said,” it says, “‘Let there be light’; and there was light.” One light was born from God, and another light God made: the light born from God is God’s own Wisdom; the light made by God is any mutable light, whether corporeal or incorporeal.

21. It is usually asked how corporeal light could have existed before the sky and the heavenly luminaries, which are described after this—as though a human being could easily perceive this, or could perceive at all, whether there is some light apart from the sky which is nevertheless divided and diffused through spatial regions and embraces the universe. But since here we may also understand an incorporeal light, if in this book we say that not merely visible creation but every creature is being expounded, why should we linger over this controversy? And perhaps the question people ask—when the angels were made—is answered by this light itself: very briefly, certainly, but nevertheless most appropriately and suitably.

22. “And God saw the light, that it was good.” This statement should be understood as signifying not joy at an unusual good [Note: [Col. 0228] So the Vatican Manuscript. But Am., Er., and Lov. read *insoliti benevolentiam*, “benevolence toward an unusual good.”], but approval of the work. For what more fitting thing can be said about God, so far as anything can be said among human beings, than when it is stated in this way: “He spoke, it came to be, it pleased”—so that in what he said his command is understood, in what came to be his power, and in what pleased his goodness? These ineffable realities had to be expressed by a human being to human beings in such a way that they could benefit everyone.

23. “And God divided between the light and the darkness.” From this it may be understood how readily these things are said to have been accomplished by the divine work. No one would suppose that light was made in such a way that it was confused with darkness and therefore subsequently required separation; rather, by the very fact that light was made, the division between light and darkness also followed. “For what fellowship is there between light and darkness?” (II Cor. 6:14). God therefore divided between light and darkness because he made the light whose absence is called darkness. There is a distinction between light and darkness, just as there is between clothing and nakedness, or fullness and emptiness, and similar things.

24. Above it has already been said in how many ways light can be understood; the corresponding privations can be called darkness. There is one kind of light that is seen by these bodily eyes and is itself corporeal, such as the light of the sun, moon, and stars, and anything of this kind; its opposite is darkness whenever a place lacks that light. There is another kind of light, namely sentient life, able to distinguish what is conveyed through the body to the soul’s judgment: white and black, musical and hoarse, sweet-smelling and foul-smelling, sweet and bitter, hot and cold, and other things of this sort. The light perceived by the eyes is one thing; the light by which perception is effected through the eyes is another. The former is in the body, whereas the latter, although it perceives through the body what it senses, is nevertheless in the soul.

Its opposite is a certain insensibility—or, if one prefers, *insensualitas*, “absence of sensation”—that is, not sensing, even though things that could be sensed are introduced, if this light by which they are sensed were present in that life. This is not the condition that occurs when the bodily instruments are lacking, as in the blind or deaf. In the souls of such people the light of which we are now speaking is present; only the bodily instruments are lacking. Nor is it the condition in which a voice is not heard during silence, although this light is present in the soul and the bodily instruments are present, but nothing that can be sensed is introduced.

Therefore one who does not sense for these reasons is not deprived of this light. Rather, this light is absent when the soul no longer possesses such a power—a being that is not usually called a soul at all, but merely “life,” as is said to exist in a vine, a tree, and every kind of plant, if it can in any way be persuaded that they possess either this or something of this sort. Some heretics, erring excessively [Note: [Col. 0229] The Manichaeans.], suppose that such beings not only sense through the body—that is, see, hear, and distinguish heat and fire—but also understand reason and know our thoughts. But that is another question.

Insensibility, therefore, is the darkness opposed to this light: whenever any form of life lacks the very power of sensation by which whatever is sensed is sensed. Anyone who admits that light is rightly so called by which anything is made manifest will appropriately allow this light to be so called. For when we say, “It is manifest that this is musical; it is manifest that this is sweet; it is manifest that this is cold,” and so on for whatever we apprehend through the bodily senses, this light by which these things are manifest is certainly within the soul, although what is sensed in this way is conveyed through the body.

A third kind of light can be understood among creatures: the light by which we reason. Its opposite is irrationality, as found in the souls of animals.

25. Whether, therefore, this statement is to be understood as referring to an ethereal light, or to the sentient light shared by animals, or to the rational light possessed by angels and human beings, it intends us to understand that God first made this light in the nature of things. We must understand that God divided between light and darkness by the very fact that light was made: light is one thing, and those privations of light that God arranged as their opposites are another. For Scripture does not say that God made darkness, since God made the actual forms and not the privations belonging to nothingness, from which all things were made by the divine craftsman. Yet we understand that he arranged these privations when it says, “And God divided between the light and the darkness,” so that even the privations themselves would not lack their order, with God ruling and governing all things.

Thus, in singing, intervals of silence inserted at definite and measured points, although they are privations of sound, are nevertheless well ordered by those who know how to sing and contribute something to the beauty of the entire song. Shadows in paintings distinguish whatever stands out, and please not by their form but by their arrangement. God is not the author of our vices either; nevertheless, he is their arranger when he assigns sinners their place and compels them to suffer what they deserve. This is the significance of the sheep being placed on the right and the goats on the left (Matt. 25:33).

Some things, therefore, God both makes and arranges; other things he merely arranges. He both makes and arranges the righteous; sinners, insofar as they are sinners, he does not make, but merely arranges. For when he places some on the right and others on the left, and commands that one group go into eternal fire, this serves the order of their merits. Thus he both makes and arranges the forms and natures themselves; but the privations of forms and the defects of natures he does not make—he merely arranges them.

He therefore said, “Let there be light”; and there was light. He did not say, “Let there be darkness”; and there was darkness. He made one of these, but did not make the other; nevertheless, he arranged both when God divided between light and darkness. Thus individual things are beautiful through his making, and all things are beautiful through his ordering.

## CHAPTER VI

26. “And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night.” Since *light* is the name of one thing, and *day* likewise, while *darkness* and *night* are each names, it was necessary for both to be said in such a way that names were imposed on things, so that the thing on which the name was imposed would necessarily be expressed by another name as well—for it could not be expressed otherwise [Note: [Col. 0230] The Vatican Manuscript omits *quoque*, “also”; shortly afterward it reads *poterat enuntiare*, “he could express,” where the printed editions have *poterat enumerare*, “he could enumerate.” The passage has evidently been corrupted by scribes. After the words *nomina rebus imposita esse*, which clearly entered from the margin and should be deleted, it ought to be emended as follows: “both had to be said in such a way that the thing on which the name was imposed would necessarily be expressed by another name (for it could not otherwise be expressed).”].

Thus it was said, “God called the light day,” so that the statement could also, without difference, be reversed and expressed as, “God called the day light, and he called the night darkness.” What shall we answer if someone asks us: Was the name *day* imposed on the light, or was the name *light* imposed on the day? For both of these, insofar as they are uttered with articulated speech to signify things, are names.

The same question can be asked about the other two: Was the name *night* imposed on darkness, or was the name *darkness* imposed on night? And indeed, as Scripture presents it, it is clear that *day* was given as the name of light and *night* as the name of darkness. When it said, “God made the light, and divided between the light and the darkness,” it was not yet dealing with names. Later the names *day* and *night* were introduced, although *light* and *darkness* are unquestionably also names signifying certain things, just as *day* and *night* do.

This should therefore be understood as meaning that the thing which received a name could not be expressed otherwise than by some name. Or should this naming rather be understood as the distinction itself? For not every light is day, nor is every darkness night; rather, light and darkness, arranged and distinguished from one another in definite alternation, are called by the names *day* and *night*. Every name serves to distinguish. Hence a name that marks a thing was called a *name* (*nomen*), as though it were a *marker* (*notamen*). It marks—that is, it distinguishes and instructively assists discernment.

Perhaps, therefore, “he divided between the light and the darkness” is the same as “he called the light day, and the darkness night,” so that calling them is the same as arranging them. Or do these names intend to signify for us what kind of light he called light and what kind of darkness he called darkness—as though he were saying: “God made light and divided between light and darkness; but I call the light day and the darkness night, so that you may not understand any other light that is not day, or any other darkness that is not night”? For if every light could be understood as day, and every darkness counted under the name night, perhaps it would not have been necessary to say, “And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night.”

27. One may also ask which day and which night he means. If we are to understand the day begun by the rising of the sun and closed by its setting, and the night extending from sunset to sunrise, I do not see how these could have existed before the heavenly luminaries were made. Or could the spans of hours and times already have been called by these names even without a distinction of brightness and shadow? And how does this alternation, signified by the names day and night, apply to that rational or sentient light, if that is what is meant? Or were these things indicated not according to what actually occurs but according to what can occur, since error can follow reason and a certain dullness can follow sensation?

## CHAPTER VII

28. “And evening came, and morning came, one day.” The word *day* is not used here in the same way as when it was said, “And God called the light day,” but in the way we say, for example, that a month has thirty days. By this meaning of *day* we include nights as well; above, however, day was spoken of in such a way that it was separated from night.

Since that work of the day was indicated as having been accomplished through the light, it was consequently said that evening came and morning came, one day—that is, one day from the beginning of a day until the beginning of a day, from morning until morning, the kind of days that, as I said, we count together with their nights.

But how did evening come and morning come? Did God take as long to make the light and divide between light and darkness as the duration of the luminous day—that is, without counting the night? And where is the truth of what is written, “You have power whenever you will” (Wis. 12:18), if God requires a process of time in order to complete something? Or are all things perfect for God as though in art and reason, not through a process of time, but through that very power by which he stably brings about even those things that we see not remaining still but passing away?

For when words pass away one after another and others succeed them in our speech, it is not credible that this occurs in the art itself by which, while it operates stably, an artistic utterance arises. Although God, who has power whenever he wills, creates without a process of time, temporal natures nevertheless carry out their movements temporally.

Perhaps, then, “evening came and morning came, one day” was said in the sense that reason perceives that it should or could happen in this way, not in the manner in which it occurs through temporal processes. For in the Holy Spirit he contemplated the operation in its rational structure—the Spirit who said, “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1). Yet in that book the account of the things made by God is most suitably arranged as though they had been made at intervals of duration, so that the very ordering—which weaker minds could not behold through stable contemplation—might be displayed to them as though visible to their eyes through such an arrangement of speech.

## CHAPTER VIII

29. “And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water.’ And so it was made. And God made the firmament, and divided between the water that was beneath the firmament and the water that was above the firmament.”

Are the waters above the firmament of the same kind as the visible waters beneath the firmament? Or, since that water seems to signify the water over which the Spirit was borne, and we understood it to be the very matter of the world, should this water too be understood here as separated by the intervening firmament, so that the lower is corporeal matter and the upper animate matter?

This firmament, Scripture says, is what it later calls heaven. Among bodies, nothing is better than a heavenly body. For there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, and the heavenly are certainly better. Whatever transcends their nature, I do not know how it can be called a body; but perhaps it is a certain power subject to reason, through which God and truth are known. Since this nature can be formed by virtue and prudence, whose strength restrains and compresses its fluctuation, and since for this reason it appears, as it were, material, it was rightly called “water” by divine usage—not because of spatial extent, but because by the merit of its incorporeal nature it exceeds the bounds of corporeal heaven [Note: [Col. 0232] We emend this according to the Vatican Manuscript. The printed editions read: “the nature within the body of incorporeal heaven.”].

And since he called heaven the firmament, it is not unreasonable to understand that whatever lies beneath the ethereal heaven, in which all things are calmed and made firm, is more mutable and more dissoluble. There were some who believed that this kind of corporeal matter, formed before it received its appearance and distinction—from which it was called the firmament—consisted of these visible waters, which surrounded the surface of heaven above and beyond it. They tried to support this view by citing the slowness of one of the seven wandering stars, which is higher than the others and is called by the Greeks *Phaínōn* (Φαίνων); it completes the zodiacal circle in thirty years. They claimed that it is slow because it is nearer the cold waters above heaven.

I do not know how this opinion can be defended by those who have investigated these matters with the greatest subtlety. None of these questions should be affirmed rashly; everything must be handled cautiously and moderately.

30. “And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water.’ And so it was made.” After saying “so it was made,” what need was there to add again, “And God made the firmament, and divided between the water that was beneath the firmament and the water that was above the firmament”? For when he had earlier said, “And God said, ‘Let there be light’; and there was light,” he did not add again, “And God made the light.” Here, however, after saying, “And God said, ‘Let there be …’; and so it was made,” he added, “And God made.”

Does this show that we ought not to understand that earlier light as corporeal, lest God appear to have made it through an intervening creature—by “God” I mean the Trinity? But this firmament of heaven, because it is corporeal, is believed to have received its appearance and form through an incorporeal creature, so that what was to be impressed corporeally was first impressed rationally upon an incorporeal nature by the truth, in order that the firmament of heaven might be made. Therefore it was said, “Let there be”; and so it was made: in the rational nature itself there was perhaps first made that from which the form would be impressed upon the body [Note: [Col. 0233] So the Vatican Manuscript. The printed editions read *facta est*, “was made.”].

## CHAPTER IX

When it was added, “And God made the firmament, and divided between the water that was beneath the firmament and the water that was above the firmament,” is the cooperation itself in that matter signified, so that the body of heaven might be made? Or perhaps, for the sake of variation, so that the flow of the discourse would not become tedious, what was stated below was not stated above, and we should not scrutinize every detail too meticulously [Note: [Col. 0233] The Vatican Manuscript reads *numerare*, “count,” which is no less suitable.]. Let each person choose what he can; only let no one rashly assert as known something that is unknown, and let him remember that he is a human being investigating the works of God insofar as permission is granted.

31. “And God called the firmament heaven.” What was discussed above concerning naming can also be considered here: not every firmament is heaven. “And God saw that it was good.” What was discussed above concerning this too would have to be revisited, except that I do not see the same order here. Above, it says, “And God saw the light, that it was good,” and afterward adds, “God divided between the light and the darkness; and God called the light day, and the darkness he called night.” Here, however, after the work has been narrated—the work that was said to have been made—and after the firmament has been called heaven, it then says, “And God saw that it was good.”

If this variation was not introduced merely to avoid monotony, we are certainly compelled to understand what was said: “And God made all things together.” For why did he first see there that it was good and afterward impose a name, whereas here he first imposed a name and afterward saw that it was good? Unless that difference signifies that there are no intervals of duration in God’s work, although such intervals are found in the works themselves.

According to an interval of duration, something is made first and something afterward—without which an account of things made cannot exist—even though God could have made these things without such intervals. “And evening came, and morning came, the second day.” This has already been discussed above, and I think the same explanations apply here as well.

## CHAPTER X

32. “And God said, ‘Let the waters beneath heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear.’ And so it was made.”

From this it may more probably be believed that what was called “water” above was, as we supposed, the very matter of the world. For if the whole universe was filled with water, from where or to where could it have been gathered? If he had called a certain material confusion “water,” this gathering must be understood as the very act of formation, so that the appearance of the water would be such as we now see.

The statement “Let the dry land appear” can likewise be understood as the formation of the earth, so that the earth would have the appearance we see. For it had been called invisible and unformed when it still lacked the appearance of matter.

God therefore said, “Let the water beneath heaven be gathered”—that is, let corporeal matter be reduced to form, so that this water may be what we perceive. “Into one gathering”: the very power of form is commended by the name of unity. For this is truly to be formed: to be reduced to something one, since the principle of every form is supremely one. “And let the dry land appear”: that is, let it receive a visible appearance and be distinguished from confusion.

And fittingly the water is gathered so that the dry land may appear—that is, what flows is restrained, so that what is obscure may be illuminated. “And so it was made”: perhaps this too was first made in the rational structures of incorporeal nature, so that afterward the statement, “And the water was gathered into one gathering, and the dry land appeared,” would not seem to have been added unnecessarily after “And so it was made” had already been said, but so that we might understand that after the rational and incorporeal operation, a corporeal one followed as well.

33. “And God called the dry land earth, and the gathering of the waters he called sea.” The same issue concerning names remains with us. Not every water is sea, nor is every dry place earth. Therefore it was necessary to distinguish by names what was water and what was dry land. It may still reasonably be understood that the distinction and formation itself was God’s naming.

“And God saw that it was good.” Here too the same order has been preserved. Let this therefore also be compared with what has already been discussed.

## CHAPTER XI

34. “And God said, ‘Let the earth sprout vegetation, plants yielding seed according to their kind and likeness, and fruit-bearing trees making fruit whose seed is in itself according to its likeness.’”

After the earth and sea had been made, named, and approved—something we have often said should not be understood as occurring through intervals of duration, lest some slowness be attributed to the ineffable power of God at work—the statement “And evening came, and morning came, the third day” is not immediately added, as it was on the preceding two days. Instead, another work is joined to it: “Let the earth sprout vegetation, plants yielding seed according to their kind and likeness, and fruit-bearing trees making fruit whose seed is in itself according to its likeness.”

This was not said of the light, the firmament, the waters, and the dry land. Light does not have a succession of propagation; heaven is not born from another heaven; nor do earth or sea produce other seas and other earths to succeed them. Here, therefore, it was necessary to say, “yielding seed according to its kind and likeness,” and “whose seed is in itself according to its likeness,” wherever the likeness of things born preserves the likeness of what passes away.

35. All these things are above the earth in such a way that they adhere to the earth at their roots, remain continuous with it, and are again separated from it in a certain manner. For this reason, I think, the meaning of this nature has been preserved in the narrative: they were made on the same day on which the earth appeared, yet God again said that the earth should sprout. Again it is said, “And so it was made.” Then, according to the earlier pattern, after “And so it was made” has been said, the execution itself is added: “And the earth brought forth vegetation, plants yielding seed according to their kind; and fruit-bearing trees making fruit whose seed is in itself according to its likeness.” And again it says, “God saw that it was good.”

Thus these things are joined together on one day, yet are distinguished from one another by the repeated words of God. I think this distinction was not made with respect to earth and sea because the nature of these things—that is, the plants—needs more to be distinguished: they arise and perish, and are propagated through the succession of seed.

Or was it because earth and sea could have been made together, not only in the rational structures of spiritual creation, where everything was made together, but also in corporeal movement itself, whereas trees and all plants could not be born unless the earth in which they would sprout had preceded them? For this reason God’s command had to be repeated, so that things made at different stages might be signified, although they were not to be made on another day, since they are attached to and continuous with the earth through their roots.

But one may ask why God did not give these things names. Was this omitted because their multitude did not permit it? This question will be considered more suitably later, when we observe other things that God did not name, as he named the light, heaven, earth, and sea.

“And evening came, and morning came, the third day.”

## CHAPTER XII

36. “And God said, ‘Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven, to give light upon the earth and to divide between day and night; and let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years; and let them be for brightness in the firmament of heaven, to give light upon the earth.’”

The luminaries were made on the fourth day, and of them it is said, “Let them be for days.” What, then, do the three days already elapsed without luminaries mean? Or why should these luminaries be for days, if days could exist even without them?

Or is it because the process of time and the interval of duration can be distinguished more clearly by human beings through the movement of these luminaries? Or does the counting of days and nights serve to distinguish between that nature which was not made and those things that were made? Thus morning was named on account of the appearance of things made, and evening on account of privation. For insofar as they derive from the one who made them, they are beautiful and well formed; but insofar as they are considered in themselves, they can fail, because they were made from nothing. And insofar as they do not fail, this is not due to their matter, which is from nothing, but to him who supremely is and causes them to exist in their proper kind and order.

37. “And God said, ‘Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven, to give light.’” Is this said only of the fixed stars, or also of the wandering stars? But the two luminaries, the greater and the lesser, are counted among the wandering stars. How, then, were all of them made in the firmament, when each of the wandering stars possesses its own sphere or circle?

Or, since in Scripture we read both of many heavens and of heaven—as in this passage, where it says “the firmament of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0235] The Vatican Manuscript reads “heaven and firmament.”—]—should we understand the entire ethereal structure to be called by this name, the structure containing all the stars [Note: [Col. 0235] So the Vatican Manuscript. The printed editions read “the substance containing all the stars.”—]? Beneath it lies the serenity of the pure and tranquil air; beneath that again this turbulent and stormy air is set in motion.

“To give light upon the earth and to divide between day and night.” Had God not already divided between light and darkness, and called the light day and the darkness night? From this it appears that he had divided between day and night. What, then, is meant now by the statement concerning the luminaries, “and let them divide between day and night”?

Or is this division now effected through the luminaries in such a way that it is known even to human beings who use their bodily eyes to contemplate these things, whereas God made the earlier division before the circuit of the luminaries, in such a way that it could be seen only by a few with sound spirit and serene reason?

Or did God divide between another day and another night—that is, between the form he was impressing upon that unformed matter and the unformed matter that still remained to be formed? For this day and this night are different: they are the alternation observed as the heaven revolves, which could not occur without the rising and setting of the sun.

## CHAPTER XIII

38. “And let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years.” It seems to me that by saying “for signs” he made clear what he meant by “for seasons,” lest the signs be understood as one thing and the seasons as another. For by “seasons” he now means those periods which, through the distinction of intervals, signify that unchanging eternity remains above them, so that time appears as a sign—that is, as a kind of trace—of eternity.

Likewise, when he adds, “and for days and years,” he shows what seasons he meant: days are produced by the revolutions of the fixed stars; years are evident when the sun completes the zodiacal circle, but more obscure when each of the wandering stars completes its own orbit. For he did not say, “and for months,” because perhaps a month is the year of the moon; just as twelve moons make a year, so the year of the star which the Greeks call *Phaéthōn* (Φαέθων) is elliptically indicated as consisting of such years, while thirty solar years constitute the year of the star called *Phaínōn* (Φαίνων). And perhaps when all the stars have returned to the same position, the great year is completed, about which many have said many things.

Or did he say “for signs” referring to the signs by which a definite route of navigation is indicated; and “for seasons” referring, for example, to spring, summer, autumn, and winter, since these too vary through the revolutions of the stars and preserve their own alternation and order? “For days and years” should then be understood as has already been explained.

39. “And let them be for brightness in the firmament of heaven, to give light upon the earth.” Earlier it had already been said, “Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven, to give light upon the earth.” Why do we think this was repeated?

Or, just as it was said of the plants that they should bear seed and that seed should be in them according to their kind and likeness, so here, conversely, was it said of the luminaries, “Let them be made and let them exist”—that is, let them be made, but not reproduce; let them themselves exist?

“And so it was made.” The same order is preserved.

40. “And God made two luminaries: the greater luminary for the beginning of day, and the lesser luminary for the beginning of night, and the stars.” What he means by “the beginning of day” and “the beginning of night” will soon become clear. Whether the stars he added belong to the beginning of night is uncertain.

Some wish this to signify that the moon was first made full, because a full moon rises at the beginning of night—that is, immediately after sunset. But it is absurd to suppose that we should begin counting not from the first day but from the sixteenth or fifteenth.

Nor should it disturb us that the luminary made ought to have been made perfect. It is perfect every day, but its perfection is not visible to human beings except when it is opposite the sun on the other side. For even when it is positioned with the sun, because it is beneath it, it appears to be diminished; yet even then it is full, because it is illuminated from the other side and cannot be seen by those below—that is, by the inhabitants of the earth. This can be taught not in a few words but through subtle discussions and demonstrations involving certain visible figures.

41. “And God placed them in the firmament of heaven, to give light upon the earth.” How did he say, “Let them be made in the firmament,” and now say, “God made the luminaries and placed them in the firmament,” as though they had been made outside it and afterward placed there, when he had already said that they should be made there?

Does this also repeatedly signify that God did not make things in the way human beings usually do, but that the account was narrated in the way human beings could understand? Among human beings, “he made” is one thing and “he placed” another; but with God both are the same, since by making he places and by placing he makes.

42. “And let them rule the day and the night, and let them divide between day and night.” It had said “the beginning of day” and “the beginning of night,” which it now explains by saying, “let them rule the day and the night.” We must therefore understand “beginning” to mean sovereignty, since in the day there is nothing visible more excellent than the sun, and in the night nothing more excellent than the moon or stars.

Accordingly, let the previous ambiguity no longer trouble us, and let us believe that the stars were placed so as to belong to the beginning of night—that is, to its sovereignty.

“And God saw that it was good.” The same order is preserved. Let us remember, however, that God did not name these either, although he could have said, “And God called the luminaries stars,” because not every luminary is a star.

43. “And evening came, and morning came, the fourth day.” If you consider these days as distinguished by sunrise and sunset, this is not the fourth day but perhaps the first, so that we might suppose the sun to have risen at the time when it was made and to have set before the other stars were made. But one who understands that the sun is elsewhere when it is night among us, and that night is elsewhere when the sun is with us, will investigate the enumeration of these days in a more exalted manner.

## CHAPTER XIV

44. “And God said, ‘Let the waters bring forth moving creatures having living souls, and flying creatures flying above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.’ And so it was made.”

The animals that swim have been called *reptilia*, “creeping things,” because they do not walk on feet. Or is it because there are other creatures that creep on the ground beneath the water? Or are there finned creatures in the waters, such as fish that have scales, or others that do not have scales but nevertheless move by means of fins? Whether these should be counted among the flying creatures in this passage may be questioned.

There is also a question why he assigned the flying creatures to the waters rather than to the air. For we cannot understand this passage as referring only to birds that are familiar with water, such as divers, ducks, and similar creatures. If he had meant only these, he would not have failed elsewhere to speak of other birds, among which some are so far removed from water that they do not even drink.

Unless perhaps he called this air contiguous with the earth “water” because it shows itself to be moist even on the clearest nights through dew and because it is also condensed into a cloud. A cloud is water, as all who happen to walk among clouds in the mountains, or even among mists in the plains, perceive.

Birds are said to fly in this air. They cannot fly in that higher and purer region which is truly called “air” by everyone, for its thinness cannot support their weight. Nor, it is asserted, do clouds condense or anything stormy arise there. Indeed, the wind is so entirely absent there that on the summit of Mount Olympus—which is said to rise beyond the reaches of this moist air—certain letters are reportedly sometimes traced in the dust and found intact and unharmed a year later by those who regularly climbed the mountain.

45. Therefore it may reasonably be thought that in Holy Scripture the firmament of heaven is called so as far as this region, so that even that calmest and clearest air may be believed to belong to the firmament. For by the name “firmament” this very tranquility, and a considerable part of created things, may be signified. Hence I think that the following is also said in several Psalms: “And your truth reaches to the clouds” (Ps. 35:6; 56:11). For nothing is firmer or clearer than truth. Clouds, however, form beneath this region of the clearest air.
