Although this is understood figuratively, it has nevertheless been written from things that bear some likeness to it, so that corporeal creation, more stable and purer, which extends from the summit of heaven to the clouds, may properly be seen as having the figure of truth—that is, extending as far as the dark, stormy, and humid air. Thus the flying creatures that fly over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven have appropriately been assigned to the waters, because this air is not inappropriately called “water.” From this it may also be understood that nothing was said about how or when the air was made, because this air is included under the name “waters,” while the other is included under the name “firmament”; and thus no element has been omitted.

46. But perhaps someone may say: If by the words “Let the water be gathered” we understand that water was made from that confusion of matter, and that God called this gathering “the sea,” how can we understand this air to have been made there, when it is not called “the sea,” even if it can be called “water”? Therefore it seems to me that in the words “Let the dry land appear” not only the form of the earth but also that of this denser air is indicated. Through it the earth is illuminated, so that it is visible to us. Thus, in the one word “appear,” everything without which it could not appear is implied: both its form, and its being uncovered from the waters, and the spreading of the air over it, through which light is transmitted to it from the higher part of the world.

Or is the form of this air rather commended in the words “Let the water be gathered,” because, when this air is condensed, it appears to produce this water? Perhaps he called its forcing into density a “gathering of the water,” so that the sea might be formed; while that which is not gathered—that is, not thickened—which is spread above, is water capable of supporting flying birds, so that the same substance may appropriately be called both thinner water and denser air.

But when the question is why this air was made, nothing is said. Or perhaps what some maintain is true: that these lower airs are produced by the moist exhalations of the sea and earth, becoming denser than that higher and fluid air, so that they are suited to carrying the flight of birds, yet thinner than the waters in which the body is washed, so that by comparison with those waters they seem dry and aerial? And since the earth and sea had already been mentioned, why was it necessary to speak of their exhalations—that is, of the waters belonging to the birds—once we have understood that the purest and calmest air was assigned to the firmament?

47. For it was not said how springs and rivers were made either. Those who investigate and discuss such matters more scrupulously say that, through the ethereal air passing above, a sweet vapor is invisibly drawn from the sea—through ascents that we cannot in any way perceive. From this vapor clouds are gathered; and thus, with the earth moistened by rains, it drips and sweats into more hidden caverns, only so much as, when collected and flowing through various channels, bursts forth into springs, whether small ones or those capable of giving rise to rivers.

They wish the evidence for this to be that when the vapor of boiled seawater is caught beneath a curved cover, it yields moisture that tastes sweet to those who drink it. It is also clear to almost everyone that springs diminish when rains are scarce. Divine history likewise bears witness to this, when Elijah, during a time of drought, sought rain: while he himself was praying, he ordered his servant to look toward the sea. When the servant saw a very small cloud rising, he announced to the anxious king that rain was coming; and soon even the fleeing man was refreshed by it (1 Kings 18:43–44).

And David says: “Lord, who calls the water of the sea and pours it over the face of the earth” (from Amos 5:8 and 9:6). Therefore, once the sea has been named, it would be superfluous to speak of the other waters, whether those that bear dew and by their thinness provide air for flying birds, or those of springs and rivers—if the former too are produced by exhalations, and the latter flow forth from recurring rains absorbed by the earth.

## CHAPTER XV

48. “Let the waters bring forth reptiles possessing living souls.” Why was “living” added? Can souls exist unless they live? Or did he wish to emphasize that more evident kind of life which exists in sentient animals, since plants lack it?

“And let flying creatures fly over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.” If flying creatures do not fly in that purest air where no clouds arise, it is clear from this that the air belongs to the firmament, because it is said that flying creatures fly over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.

“And it was so.” That order is preserved. Therefore this statement is added, as in the other cases, except in the case of light, which was made first.

49. “And God made the great sea creatures, and every living soul of the creeping animals, which the waters brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged flying creature according to its kind.”

Let us bear in mind that “according to its kind” is said of those creatures that are renewed by propagation through seed; for this has already been said of herbs and trees.

“And every winged flying creature.” Why was “winged” added? Can there be a flying creature without wings? But if there can be one, did God make this kind, since no place is found where it was made? Or can anything fly without wings? For bats, locusts, flies, and anything similar that lacks feathers do not lack wings.

“Winged” was added, however, so that we would not understand only birds, since fish are winged and fly over the earth beneath the waters. Therefore it does not say “birds,” but “flying creatures” in general, and “winged flying creatures.”

“And God saw that it was good.” Here too it is to be understood as in the other passages.

50. “And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let the flying creatures multiply upon the earth.”

He intended the blessing to serve fertility, which appears in the succession of offspring, so that, because these creatures were made weak and mortal, they might preserve their kind by being born. But since plants too preserve the likeness of things that pass away by being born, why did he not bless them? Is it because they lack sensation, which is near to reason?

Perhaps it is not without significance that God uses the second person when blessing, as though addressing these animals as listeners, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea.” Yet he does not continue in the same person to the end of the blessing. For it follows: “And let the flying creatures multiply upon the earth”; he did not say, “Multiply upon the earth.”

Unless perhaps this very fact signifies that the sensation of animals is not so close to reason that it can perfectly receive the command of one addressing it, as can those creatures that understand and are able to use reason.

51. “And it was so.” At this point even the slowest person ought to awaken and understand what sort of days are being enumerated. For since God gave living creatures determinate numbers of seeds, preserving a remarkable constancy in a fixed order, so that, according to each kind and within a definite number of days, they might both carry what had been conceived in the womb and warm the eggs they had laid—an ordering of nature preserved by the wisdom of God, which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)—how could they, in a single day, both conceive, become heavy with pregnancy, warm and nourish what had been produced, fill the waters of the sea, and multiply upon the earth?

For the text immediately adds, “And it was so,” before the coming of evening. But surely, when it says, “There was evening,” it recalls for us the formless matter; and when it says, “There was morning,” it recalls the form impressed upon the matter by that operation. For morning concludes the day that has passed after the operation.

Yet God did not say, “Let there be evening,” or “Let there be morning.” This is the briefest possible recollection of things that had been made, with matter and form signified by “evening” and “morning”; and it had already been said that God had made them. Nevertheless, although the defect itself—that is, the movement from form toward matter and nothingness—may, if we rightly think so, be indicated by the name “night,” he did not say that this was made. Yet he did say that it was ordered by God, when he stated earlier: “God divided the light from the darkness.”

Thus the word “evening” signifies formless matter, which, although it was made from nothing, nevertheless exists [Note: [Col. 0240] The Vatican manuscript reads: “although it was made, it nevertheless exists”; the second “is” is absent.] and possesses the capacity for forms and shapes. The name “darkness” may also be understood as signifying absolute nothingness, which God did not make, and from which he made whatever he graciously chose to make through his ineffable goodness, since he is omnipotent and made such great things even from nothing.

52. “And there was evening, and there was morning—the fifth day” [Col. 0241]. Here, after saying, “And it was so,” he did not add the execution of the command, as he usually does, as though things had been made again; for this had already been stated above. Nor was any new nature fashioned by the blessing pertaining to the production of offspring; rather, what had been made was preserved through succession.

Therefore it was not said either, “And God saw that it was good,” since the reality itself, which merely had to be preserved in the offspring, had already pleased him. Nothing, then, is repeated here except the statement, “And it was so,” immediately followed by the account of evening and morning. By naming these, the completed work was said to be signified: the work concerning formless matter and the form imposed upon it. Unless perhaps something better and more sublime occurs to those who inquire into these matters.

53. “And God said, Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind: quadrupeds, and reptiles, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and cattle according to their kinds. And it was so.”

Why “living” was added after “soul”; what “according to its kind” means; and the customary conclusion, “And it was so,” are matters to be considered and understood as discussed above.

Since in Latin the word “beasts” generally signifies every irrational animal, the species must nevertheless be distinguished here. By “quadrupeds” we should understand all beasts of burden; by “reptiles,” all creeping creatures; by “beasts” or “wild animals,” all untamed quadrupeds; and by “cattle,” quadrupeds that do not assist by their labor but provide some benefit to those who feed them.

## CHAPTER XVI

54. “And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and cattle according to their kinds, and every reptile of the earth according to its kind.”

This repetition of the words “And God made,” after it had already been said, “And it was so,” should be considered according to the rule given above.

Here, certainly, I think that by the name “cattle” all quadrupeds that live under human care are signified.

“And God saw that it was good”: this is to be understood in the customary way.

55. “And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

Here too certain conjunctions and distinctions among living creatures must be observed. Scripture says that man was made on the same day as the beasts. For all terrestrial living creatures are together; yet, because of the excellence of reason, according to which man is made in the image and likeness of God, man is mentioned separately, after the usual conclusion concerning the other terrestrial animals: “And God saw that it was good.”

56. It must also be considered that, in the case of the others, God did not say, “Let us make.” In this way too, perhaps, the Holy Spirit wished to indicate the preeminence of human nature.

To whom, however, is “Let us make” now said, if not to the one to whom “Let it be” was said in the other cases? For “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

But what do we think is meant by the difference between “Let it be” and “Let us make”? Is “Let it be” said so that he might make it at the Father’s command, while “Let us make” is said so that both might make it together? Or does the Father make all that he makes through the Son, and is “Let us make” now said so that, in man himself—for whose sake Scripture itself was written—it might be demonstrated that what the Son makes when the Father speaks, the Father himself also makes? Thus, whereas in the other cases it was said, “Let it be,” and it was made, here the words “Let us make” explain that the utterance and the execution were not separate, but occurred together.

57. “And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

Every image is like that whose image it is; yet not everything that is like something is also its image. Thus, a reflection in a mirror and a picture, because they are images, are also like their originals; nevertheless, unless one is derived from the other, neither can be called the image of the other. For something is an image when it is expressed from something else.

Why, then, after saying “in our image,” was “and likeness” added, as though an image could be unlike its original? It would have been sufficient to say “in our image.”

Or is one thing “like,” and another “likeness,” just as one thing is “chaste,” and another “chastity”; one thing “strong,” and another “strength”? Thus, just as whatever things are strong are strong through strength, and whatever things are chaste are chaste through chastity, so whatever things are like are like through likeness.

Yet our image is not properly said to be our likeness, although it is properly said to be like us. Thus likeness is that by which whatever things are like are like, just as chastity is that by which whatever things are chaste are chaste.

Chastity, however, is not chaste through participation in anything else; rather, through participation in it, whatever things are chaste are chaste. Chastity is found in God, where there is also that wisdom which is not wise by participation, but through participation in which every soul that is wise becomes wise.

Therefore the likeness of God, through which all things were made, is properly called likeness, because it is not like through participation in some other likeness. Rather, it is the first likeness, through participation in which those things are like that God made through it.

58. The addition of “in likeness,” after “in image” had already been said, may therefore perhaps be an explanation. It shows that what was called the image is not so like God as though it participated in some likeness, but that it is itself the likeness in which all things said to be like participate.

So too, God himself is chastity, through participation in which souls are chaste; wisdom, through participation in which souls are wise; and beauty, through participation in which whatever things are beautiful are beautiful.

For if he had said only “likeness,” he would not have signified that it was begotten from him. If he had said only “image,” he would have signified that it was indeed begotten from him, but would not have signified that it was so like him that it was not merely like him but was itself the likeness.

Just as nothing is chaster than chastity itself, nothing wiser than wisdom itself, and nothing more beautiful than beauty itself, so nothing can be said, thought, or exist that is more like likeness itself.

Hence it is understood that the likeness of the Father is so like the Father that it completely and perfectly fulfills his nature.

59. How much the likeness of God, through which all things were made, contributes to imposing form upon things greatly surpasses human thought; yet we may nevertheless form some conjecture if we consider that every nature, whether it is encountered by the senses or by reasoning, preserves an image of unity through parts that are like one another.

Rational souls are called wise from the wisdom of God, and this name is not extended further. For we cannot call any cattle—or, much less, trees, fire, air, water, or earth—wise, although all these things too exist insofar as they exist through the wisdom of God.

Yet we say that stones, animals, human beings, and angels are like one another.

Moreover, in individual things, the earth is earth because its parts are like one another; water, in every part whatsoever, is like its other parts, and could not otherwise be water; and however much air there may be, if it were unlike the rest, it could in no way be air. A particle of fire or light, because it is not unlike the remaining parts, is what it is [Note: [Col. 0243] The printed editions read, “because it is unlike the remaining parts.” The word “not” is absent from the Vatican manuscript.].

In the same way, with every stone, tree, or body of any living creature, it can be discerned and understood that such things would not exist—not only in relation to other things of their kind, but individually within themselves—unless they had parts like one another. And a body is more beautiful in proportion as its parts are more alike one another.

Furthermore, in souls, not only does the friendship of one soul with another arise from similar character, but also, within each soul, similar actions and virtues—without which stability cannot exist—indicate a blessed life.

All these things, however, we may call similar, but not likeness itself.

Therefore, if the universe consists of things that are like one another, so that each thing is what it is and all together complete the universe that God both created and governs, then through the likeness of the one who created all things—an exalted, unchangeable, and undefiled likeness—such things were made that they are beautiful through parts like one another. Yet not all things were made according to that likeness; only rational substance was.

Thus all things were made through it, but only the soul was made according to it [Note: [Col. 0243] The Vatican manuscript reads, “but not all things were made according to it.”].

60. Rational substance, then, was made both through it and according to it, for no other nature intervenes. For the human mind—which senses this only when it is most pure and blessed—clings to nothing except the truth itself, which is called the likeness and image of the Father and Wisdom.

Accordingly, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” is rightly understood according to what is inward and principal in man—that is, according to the mind. For man as a whole must be judged according to that which holds primacy in him and separates him from the beasts.

The other elements in him, although beautiful in their own kind, are shared with animals and therefore ought to be regarded as of little importance in man.

Unless perhaps the fact that the human body is upright so that it may look toward heaven has some significance, so that the body itself too may be believed to have been made in the likeness of God. Just as that likeness is not turned away from the Father, so the human body is not turned away from heaven, unlike the bodies of other animals, which are turned downward and prostrate upon their bellies.

Yet this must not be understood in every respect. For our body differs greatly from heaven; whereas in that likeness which is the Son, there can be nothing unlike the one whose likeness he is. Whatever other things are similar are also dissimilar to one another in some respect; likeness itself, however, is not dissimilar in any respect.

The Father, nevertheless, is the Father, and the Son is nothing other than the Son. For although, when he is called the likeness of the Father, this shows that no dissimilarity intervenes, the Father is not alone if he possesses a likeness [Note: [Col. 0244] The printed editions read, “but possesses a likeness.” The Vatican manuscript and others, as well as the first book of the *Retractions*, chapter 18, read, “if he possesses a likeness.”].

[Note: [Col. 0244] Augustine added the remainder many years later, when he published the books of the *Retractions*. See *Retractions* I, 18.]

61. “And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

What was said above sufficiently explains these words of Scripture, in which we read that God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” so that the likeness of God according to which man was made may be understood as the Word of God himself—that is, the only-begotten Son—not, of course, as though man himself were that same image and likeness equal to the Father.

Man too, however, is the image of God, as the Apostle most clearly shows when he says: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11:7).

But this image, made according to the image of God, is not equal or coeternal with the one whose image it is; nor would it be so even if it had never sinned at all.

Rather, this interpretation should be preferred in these divine words: we should understand that the statement was not made in the singular but in the plural—“Let us make man in our image and likeness”—because man was made not in the image of the Father alone, or of the Son alone, or of the Holy Spirit alone, but in the image of the Trinity itself.

The Trinity is such that it is one God; and it is one God in such a way that it is Trinity.

For God did not say to the Son, “Let us make man in your image,” or “in my image,” but said in the plural, “in our image and likeness.” Who would dare separate the Holy Spirit from this plurality?

Because this plurality does not signify three gods but one God, Scripture is accordingly understood to have subsequently used the singular and said: “And God made man in the image of God.” This must not be understood as though God the Father made man in the image of God, that is, of his Son. Otherwise, how is the statement “in our image” true if man was made only in the image of the Son?

Therefore, because what God said—“in our image”—is true, it is said, “God made man in the image of God,” as though it had said, “in his own image,” which is the Trinity itself.

62. Some, however, think that the likeness was not repeated, and that it was not said, “And God made man in the image and likeness of God,” because at that time he was made only according to the image, while the likeness was reserved for him later, in the resurrection of the dead. This is as though there could be an image in which likeness was absent.

For if something is not altogether like its original, it is certainly not an image either.

Yet, so that we may not seem to establish this by reason alone, the authority of the Apostle James must also be brought forward. Speaking of the human tongue, he says: “With it we bless God, and with it we curse human beings, who have been made according to the likeness of God” (James 3:9).

# [ON THE LITERAL MEANING OF GENESIS]

[Col. 0245]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOKS

Here now is Augustine’s third, or fourth, exposition of Genesis. While his conversion was still recent, he had set his hand to this book in order to treat Genesis, or defend it, against the Manichaeans. But, content to introduce an allegorical meaning in the more difficult passages, he passed over the literal meaning. Later, when as a presbyter he began to investigate the literal sense, he discovered that his strength was unequal to the task and left the work unfinished.

Around the year 400, therefore, the bishop took up the same subject again. First he treated it allegorically in the final three books of the *Confessions*; then, in this work, he treated it literally and composed the following twelve books on that subject.

In these books he narrates the history of Genesis from its beginning up to the verse in which Adam was expelled from Paradise. He passes over no detail and leaves nothing that he does not turn over and examine with every kind of reasoning and with the greatest scrutiny. Yet he makes no effort to explain the mysteries concealed beneath the coverings of figures, since he now places the entire value of the work in demonstrating that Genesis contains nothing that cannot be true literally, nothing contrary to reason or to the nature of things; and if anything appears superfluous or incongruous, it should be believed to be mystical and referred to a deeper meaning.

In passing, he also discusses certain matters: in Book II, against the astrologers; in Book IV, the perfection of the number six; in Book V, the knowledge and providence of God; in Book VI, Adam’s body; in Book VII, the soul, which he takes up again in Book X; then, in Book XI, the fall of the angels; and in Book XII, Paradise and the various kinds of visions. He treats other matters throughout, asserting and defending what is certain, while raising questions and doubts about what is uncertain.

Cassiodorus the senator praises this work at length in Book I, chapter 1, of his *Institutions*, and considers it far more elevated than the commentaries on Genesis by Basil and Ambrose.

Augustine assigned these books a place in the *Retractions* after certain shorter works composed around the year 400, arranging them, as he says, in the order in which he began them, not in the order in which he completed them. Although his friends repeatedly urged him to publish them, he kept them with him for a long time so that he might repeatedly revise them, as he says in Letter 143 to Marcellinus, written toward the end of the year 412.

He cites the twelfth book in Letter 159 to Evodius, which we have assigned to approximately the year 414. There he indicates that he was hastening the revision of the entire work so that he might make it public as soon as possible. Nevertheless, he had not yet published it when he wrote another letter to Evodius, namely Letter 162, as he testifies in its second section.

[Col. 0245]

[Note: [Col. 0245] See Book II, chapter 24, of the *Retractions*, col. 640, from the words “At the same time, concerning Genesis” up to the words “It was divided into two parts.” M.]

## THE TWELVE BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE LITERAL MEANING OF GENESIS

[Note: [Col. 0245] Begun around the year 401, completed around the year 415.]

[Note: [Col. 0245] We collated these books with twenty-six manuscripts: namely, three Vatican manuscripts; two from the Fathers of the Augustinian Order in the principal convent at Paris; two each from the College of Navarre and the Thuane Library; one from the library of the Church of Laon; one from the Abbey of Saint-Martin-des-Champs near Paris; and the Sorbonic, Colbertine, Bigotian, Cistercian, Albinian, Audoenian, Culturian, Gemmetic, Germanic, Lyran, Michaeline, Remigian, Theoderician, and Vendôme manuscripts, together with one from the Abbey of Saint Mary of Jehoshaphat at Chartres. We also consulted the variant readings of six Belgian codices excerpted by the Louvain theologians, as well as the earlier editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0245] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

## BOOK ONE

An examination of the beginning of Genesis, chapter 1, verse 1: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” up to verse 5: “And God called the light Day,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER ONE — What Must Be Considered in Scripture

1. All divine Scripture is divided into two parts, according to what the Lord signified when he said that a learned scribe in the kingdom of God is like a householder bringing forth from his treasure things new and old (Matt. 13:52). These are also called the two Testaments.

In all the holy books we must observe what eternal realities are indicated there, what events are narrated as having occurred, what future events are foretold, and what things are commanded or urged to be done.

In the narration of things that happened, therefore, the question is whether everything is to be understood only according to a figurative meaning, or whether it must also be asserted and defended according to the faith of historical events.

No Christian would dare say that these matters are not to be understood figuratively, attending to the Apostle’s statement: “Now all these things happened to them as a figure” (1 Cor. 10:11), and to the passage written in Genesis, “And the two shall become one flesh” (Gen. 2:24), which he commends as a great mystery in Christ and the Church (Eph. 5:32).

2. If, then, Scripture is to be investigated in both ways, let us ask how, beyond its allegorical significance, the statement “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” was spoken: whether “in the beginning” means at the beginning of time; or because these were made first of all; or whether “the beginning” is the Word of God, the only-begotten Son.

Let us also ask how God can be shown to have operated upon mutable and temporal things without any change in himself.

And what is signified by the names “heaven” and “earth”? Did spiritual and corporeal creation receive the names “heaven” and “earth,” or only corporeal creation? Perhaps the spiritual creation is passed over in silence in this book, and “heaven and earth” is said in such a way as to signify all corporeal creation, both higher and lower.

Or was the formless matter of both called “heaven and earth”? The spiritual life, that is, insofar as it can exist in itself without being turned toward the Creator—for it is formed and perfected by such turning, but if it is not turned, it is formless—and the corporeal creation, if it can be understood through the deprivation of every corporeal quality that appears in formed matter, once bodies possess forms perceptible either by sight or by any other bodily sense.

3. Or should heaven be understood as spiritual creation, perfect and always blessed from the beginning of its making, while earth is corporeal matter still imperfect? For it says, “The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss.” These words seem to signify the formlessness of corporeal substance.

Or is the formlessness of both also signified by these later words: corporeal formlessness by the statement “The earth was invisible and unformed,” and spiritual formlessness by the statement “Darkness was over the abyss”? Thus, by transferring the word, we may understand the dark abyss as the formless nature of life unless it is turned toward the Creator—the only way in which it can be formed so that it is no longer an abyss, and illuminated so that it is no longer dark.

And how should we understand the statement “Darkness was over the abyss”? Was it because there was no light? If light had been present, it would certainly have been above it, as though poured over it. This occurs in spiritual creation when it is turned toward the unchangeable and incorporeal light that is God [Note: [Col. 0247] Thus several manuscripts of excellent quality. The printed editions read “incomparable” instead of “incorporeal.”]

## CHAPTER TWO — How God Said, “Let There Be Light”: Through Creation or through the Eternal Word

4. And how did God say, “Let there be light”? Was this said temporally, or in the eternity of the Word?

If temporally, then certainly mutably. How, then, can God be understood to say this except through creation? For he himself is unchangeable.

And if God said through creation, “Let there be light,” how is light the first creation, if there was already a creation through which God could say, “Let there be light”?

Or is light not the first creation, because it had already been said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” and a voice could be produced temporally and mutably through heavenly creation, saying, “Let there be light”?

If this is so, the corporeal light that we see with corporeal eyes was made when God, through the spiritual creation that he had already made when, in the beginning, he made heaven and earth, said, “Let there be light.” This happened through the inward and hidden movement of such a creation, by divine command, when it was able to say, “Let there be light.”

5. Or did the voice of God saying “Let there be light” also sound corporeally, just as the voice of God saying “You are my beloved Son” sounded corporeally (Matt. 3:17)? And did this occur through corporeal creation, which God had made when, in the beginning, he made heaven and earth, before light was made—the light that came into being in this sounding voice?

If so, in what language did that voice sound when God said, “Let there be light”? For there was not yet the diversity of languages that later arose in the building of the tower after the Flood (Gen. 11:7). What language was that one and only language in which God spoke, “Let there be light”? And who was there who needed to hear and understand it, to whom such a voice would be addressed?

Or is this an absurd and carnal thought and supposition?

6. What, then, shall we say? Is it properly understood as the voice of God not the bodily sound itself, but what is understood in the sound of the voice when it is said, “Let there be light”?

And does this itself belong to the nature of his Word, of whom it is said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”?

For when it is said of him, “All things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3), it is sufficiently shown that light too was made through him when God said, “Let there be light.”

If this is so, what God said—“Let there be light”—is eternal, because the Word of God, God with God, the only Son of God, is coeternal with the Father, although a temporal creation was made when God spoke this in the eternal Word.

For words belong to time when we say “when” and “at some time.” Yet in the Word of God it is eternal when something ought to come into being. And it comes into being at the time when, in that Word, it is present as having ought to come into being—that Word in which there is no “when” or “at some time,” because the whole Word is eternal.

## CHAPTER THREE — What That Light Is; Why It Was Not Said, “Let There Be Heaven,” and So Forth, as It Was Said, “Let There Be Light”: First Answer

7. And what is the light itself that was made? Is it something spiritual or corporeal?

For if it is spiritual, it may itself be the first creation, perfected by this very command. It was already called “heaven” when it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Thus, when God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made, its turning and illumination may be understood as the Creator’s calling it back to himself.

8. And why was it said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” rather than, “In the beginning God said, Let there be heaven and earth, and heaven and earth were made,” as the account of light says, “God said, Let there be light,” and light was made?

Was it necessary first to include and proclaim universally, under the name “heaven and earth,” what God made, and then to carry out the account in its parts, explaining how he made it, since in each case it is said, “God said”—that is, because through his Word he made whatever he made?

## CHAPTER FOUR — A Second Answer to the Earlier Question
9. Or, when the formlessness of matter—whether spiritual or corporeal—was first coming into being, was it not appropriate to say, “God said, Let it come to be,” because imperfection does not imitate the form of the Word, which is always united to the Father and by which God eternally speaks all things—not through the sound of a voice or through thought unfolding the temporal sequence of sounds, but by the coeternal light of the Wisdom begotten from him—when, being unlike that which supremely and primarily is, it tends toward nothingness through a certain formlessness? Rather, does it then imitate the form of the Word, always and unchangeably united to the Father, when it too, according to the turning proper to its kind, turns toward that which truly and eternally is—that is, toward the Creator of its substance—takes on form, and becomes a perfect creature? Thus, when Scripture says, “God said, Let it come to be,” are we to understand God’s incorporeal utterance in the nature of his coeternal Word, calling the imperfection of creation back to himself, so that it may not remain formless but may be formed according to the individual things which he brings forth in sequence?

In this turning and formation, because it imitates God the Word in its own manner—that is, the Son of God, always united to the Father, equal in full likeness and essence, by which he and the Father are one (John 10:30)—it does not imitate the form of the Word if, turned away from the Creator, it remains formless and imperfect. Therefore the Son is not mentioned here so much because he is the Word, but only [Note: [Col. 0249] In earlier editions, “but also.” In the manuscripts, “but only.”] because he is the Beginning, when it is said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” For the beginning of creation is indicated, still existing in the formlessness of imperfection. But the Son is mentioned as also being the Word in the words, “God said, Let it come to be,” so that by what he is as Beginning he may indicate the beginning of creation, which, though still imperfect, existed from him, and by what he is as Word he may indicate the perfection of creation recalled to him, so that it might be formed by cleaving to the Creator and, according to its kind, imitating the form eternally and unchangeably united to the Father, from whom it immediately receives its being.

## CHAPTER V — That intellectual creation is formless unless it is perfected by turning toward the divine Word. Why the Holy Spirit is said to have been borne over the water before it was narrated that God said, “Let there be light.”

10. For the Word, the Son, does not possess a formless life. In him, being is not merely the same as living; rather, living is the same as living wisely and happily. But a creature, even if spiritual and intellectual or rational, which seems to be nearer to that Word, can possess a formless life. For, just as being is not the same for it as living, so living is not the same as living wisely and happily. [Note: [Col. 0250] The printed editions read: “For just as being is not the same for it as living, so neither is living the same as …” But the manuscripts, in strong agreement, read: “It is not the case that being is the same for it as living, while living is the same as …” This is also more consistent with Augustine’s teaching: in *On the Immortality of the Soul*, chapter 8, section 15, he says that the soul cannot exist unless it lives, and shortly afterward, in chapter 9: “No thing,” he says, “is without itself. But the soul is a kind of life.”]

For, turned away from unchangeable Wisdom, it lives foolishly and miserably; this is its formlessness. But it is formed when it turns toward the unchangeable light of Wisdom, the Word of God. From him it received its existence and its partial life; toward him it turns so that it may live wisely and happily. The eternal Wisdom is the Beginning of intellectual creation. That Beginning, remaining unchangeably in itself, never ceases to speak, by a hidden inspiration of calling, to the creature for which it is the Beginning, so that it may turn toward that from which it exists, since otherwise it cannot be formed and perfected. Therefore, when asked who he was, he replied, “The Beginning, because I also speak to you” (John 8:25).

11. But when the Son speaks, the Father speaks, because, when the Father speaks, the Word is uttered, and the Word is the Son—according to the eternal manner, if it is proper to call it a manner, in which God speaks the coeternal Word. [Note: [Col. 0250] What follows, through the end of chapter 7, was transferred into the book *Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, answer to question 8, sections 2 and 3.]

For there is in God the highest goodness, holy and just; and indeed [Note: [Col. 0250] Lov. reads *quidam*, “a certain.” Nearly all the manuscripts read *quidem*, “indeed.”] love for his works that comes not from need but from beneficence. Therefore, before it was written, “God said, Let there be light,” Scripture first said, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the water.” For either he wished to call the whole corporeal matter “water,” thereby indicating from what all things were made and formed—calling it water because we see that everything on earth is formed and grows together in various shapes from a moist nature—or he wished to indicate a certain spiritual life, as yet fluid and without form before its turning. In either case, the Spirit of God was borne over it, because whatever it was that had begun to be formed and perfected lay subject to the good will of the Creator. Thus, when God said in his Word, “Let there be light,” what was made remained in the good will—that is, in his good pleasure—according to the measure of its kind; and therefore it is right [Note: [Col. 0250] Six manuscripts read, “and therefore it was read.” The Vindobonensis manuscript reads, “and therefore it was said.” But the other manuscripts and the printed editions have *rectum est*, “it is right,” both here and in the book addressed to Dulcitius. Shortly afterward, the printed editions begin chapter 6 with “And just as,” and below read, “so also in the turning … is indicated.” In these places we follow the manuscripts.] that which pleased God was made, Scripture saying, “And there was light; and God saw that the light was good.”

## CHAPTER VI — The Trinity indicated both in the beginning and in the perfection of creation.

12. Thus, just as at the very beginning of creation, which had been begun and was mentioned under the name of heaven and earth because of what was to be perfected from it, the Trinity of the Creator is indicated—for when Scripture says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” we understand the Father under the name of God and the Son under the name of Beginning, who is the beginning not of the Father but of the spiritual creation first and above all created through him, and consequently also of the whole creation; while, when Scripture says, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the water,” we recognize the complete mention of the Trinity—so also in the turning and perfection of creation, as the kinds of things are arranged, the same Trinity is indicated: namely, the Word of God and the begetter of the Word, when it says, “God said”; and the holy goodness in which whatever is perfected according to the measure of its nature pleases God, when it says, “God saw that it was good.”

## CHAPTER VII — Why the Spirit of God is said to have been borne over the water.

13. But why, after the imperfect creation had first been mentioned, is the Spirit of God mentioned afterward? Scripture first says, “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss” [Note: [Col. 0251] So read the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The printed editions read, “and darkness was over the face of the abyss.”] and then adds, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the water.”

Was it because needy and impoverished love loves in such a way that it subjects itself to the things it loves? Therefore, when the Spirit of God is mentioned—as signifying his holy goodwill and love—he is said to be borne over them, so that God might not be thought to love his works through the necessity of need rather than through the abundance of beneficence? With this in mind, when the Apostle is about to speak of love and to demonstrate the way that surpasses all others, he says that he will show it (1 Cor. 12:31); and elsewhere he says, “the love of Christ surpassing knowledge” (Eph. 3:19).

Since, then, it was necessary to indicate the Spirit of God in such a way that he would be said to be borne over the waters, it was more suitably done by first indicating something begun, over which he could be said to be borne—not in place, but by a power surpassing and transcending all things.

## CHAPTER VIII — The love of God grants creatures that they exist and that they remain.

14. Thus also, after the things that had been perfected and formed from that beginning, “God saw that it was good.” For what had been made pleased him in that goodness by which it had pleased him that it should be made. There are two reasons for which God loves his creation: that it may exist and that it may remain. Therefore, so that what was to remain might exist, the Spirit of God was borne over the water; but so that it might remain, “God saw that it was good.” What is said of the light applies to everything. Some things remain, having transcended all temporal change, in the most extensive holiness under God; others remain according to the modes proper to their time, while the beauty of the ages is woven together through the passing and succession of things.

## CHAPTER IX — Whether “Let there be light” was said in time or without time.

15. When God therefore said, “Let there be light,” and there was light, did he say it on some day, or before every day? If he said it through the Word coeternal with himself, then he certainly said it timelessly, for time does not apply to the Word. But if he said it temporally, then he did not say it through the Word coeternal with himself, but through some temporal creature; and consequently light will not be the first creature, since there already existed something through which it could temporally be said, “Let there be light.”

What is said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” is understood to have been done before every day, so that by the name of heaven we understand the spiritual creation already made and formed, as though it were the heaven of this heaven, which is supreme among corporeal things. On the second day the firmament was made, which he again called heaven. By the name of earth—“invisible and unformed”—and of the dark abyss, the imperfection of corporeal substance is signified, from which those temporal things were to be made whose first element would be light.

16. But how could a temporal command, “Let there be light,” have been given through a creature that he made before time? It is difficult to discover. We do not understand the command to have been uttered by the sound of a voice, for whatever is such is corporeal. Did he make some corporeal voice from that imperfection of corporeal substance, so that it might sound, “Let there be light”? Then some vocal body was created and formed before the light. But if that is so, time already existed, through which the voice could travel and the successive intervals of sounds could pass away. [Note: [Col. 0252] Most manuscripts read *succedentium*, “of things succeeding,” rather than *succedentia*, “succeeding.”]

If time already existed before the light was made—the time in which the voice that resounded “Let there be light” was made—to which day did that time belong? For the one day, the first day, begins to be counted from the moment when the light was made. Or does the whole extent of time belong to that same day: both the time in which the vocal body was made, through which “Let there be light” would sound, and the time in which the light itself was made?

But every such voice is produced by a speaker for the bodily sense of a hearer. For hearing was made in such a way that it perceives when the air is struck. [Note: [Col. 0252] The common editions read, “for it was made so that it might be perceived when the air was struck.” But the manuscripts more correctly read, “it was made so that it might perceive …,” namely, the sense of hearing.] Did that invisible and unformed thing, whatever it was, therefore already possess such hearing, so that God could speak to it in this way and say, “Let there be light”? Let this absurdity depart from the mind of anyone considering the matter.

17. Was it therefore a spiritual movement, but nevertheless a temporal one, by which we understand “Let there be light” to have been uttered—expressed by the eternal God through the coeternal Word in the spiritual creature that he had already made when it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, in that heaven of heaven? Or is this utterance to be understood not only without any sound but also without any temporal movement of the spiritual creature, fixed in a certain manner in its mind and reason by the Word coeternal with the Father, and in a certain manner impressed upon it, according to which the lower, dark imperfection of corporeal nature would be moved and turned toward form, and would become light?

It is very difficult—indeed exceedingly difficult—to grasp how, when God does not command temporally and the creature, which through contemplation of truth transcends all times, does not hear temporally, it could transmit to what lies below it the reasons intellectually impressed upon it by the unchangeable Wisdom of God, as intelligible utterances, so that temporal movements might arise in temporal things, whether they were being formed or governed.

But if the light that was first commanded to come into being, and did come into being, is also to be understood as holding the primacy of creation, then it is intellectual life. Unless it turned toward the Creator to be illuminated, it would drift about formlessly. But when it turned and was illuminated, what had been said in the Word of God came to pass: “Let there be light.”

## CHAPTER X — How the one day was completed, whether in the creation or after the creation of the light. The first manner of explanation is rejected. The second manner of speaking is entangled in difficulties.

18. Nevertheless, just as it was said without time—for time does not apply to the Word coeternal with the Father—someone may perhaps ask whether it was also made without time. But how can this be understood, when, after the light had been made and divided from the darkness, and the names of day and night had been assigned, Scripture says, “There was evening and there was morning, one day”? It therefore seems that this work of God was made over the course of a day, and that, when the day had run its course, evening was reached, which is the beginning of night. Likewise, when the period of night had ended, the whole day was completed, so that morning came for the second day, on which God would next perform another work.

19. Rather, the truly astonishing thing is this: since God said “Let there be light” through the eternal reasoning of his Word, without any interval of syllables, why was the light made to last so long, until the day’s span had passed and evening came? Or was the light indeed made quickly, but could the duration of the day have been consumed while it was being distinguished from the darkness and each was marked by its own name?

It would be strange if even this could have taken as long for God as it is said to take for us. For the separation of light and darkness necessarily followed in the very act by which the light came to be; light could not exist unless it were distinguished from darkness.

20. As for God’s calling the light day and the darkness night, how long could this have taken—even if he had carried it out syllable by syllable through the sound of a voice—except as long as it takes us to say, “Let the light be called day, and let the darkness be called night”? Unless someone is so foolish as to think that, because God is great above all things, the very few syllables spoken by God’s mouth could have been stretched out over the entire span of a day.

Moreover, God called the light day and the darkness night through his coeternal Word—that is, through the inward and eternal reasons of unchangeable Wisdom—not through the bodily sound of a voice. Again, then, the question arises: if he called them by the words we use, in what language did he call them? And what need was there for passing sounds where there was no bodily hearing at all? No answer is found.

21. Should we say, then, that once this work of God had quickly been completed, the light remained for as long as necessary without night following it, until the duration of the day had been completed; and that the night remained for as long as necessary after the light, until the duration of the night had passed and morning came for the following day, with the one first day having elapsed?

But if I say this, I fear that I will be mocked both by those who know with complete certainty and by those who can easily observe that, when it is night here, those parts of the world where the sun returns from setting to rising are illuminated by the sun’s presence. Consequently, throughout all twenty-four hours, somewhere in the complete circuit of the globe there is day and somewhere else night.

Are we therefore going to place God in some particular region, where evening would occur for him when the light withdrew from that region to another? For in the book called Ecclesiastes it is written: “The sun rises, and the sun sets, and it is led [Note: [Col. 0254] The Colbertinus manuscript and three other manuscripts of excellent quality read, “it leads.” Jerome cites the same passage in this form and testifies that he followed the edition current in his time.] to its place”—that is, to the place from which it rose. It continues and says: “Rising there, it goes toward the south and circles toward the north” (Eccles. 1:5–6).

Thus, when the sun is in the southern region, it is day for us; but when, circling around, it reaches the northern region, it is night for us. Nevertheless, it is not not day in another region where the sun is present—unless we must bend our minds toward poetic fictions and believe that the sun plunges into the sea and, washed there, rises again in the morning from another side.

Even if that were so, the abyss itself would be illuminated by the sun’s presence, and day would exist there. For the sun could even illuminate the waters, since they could not extinguish it. But it is monstrous to suppose this. And what of the fact that the sun did not yet exist?

22. Therefore, if spiritual light was made on the first day, did it set so that night could follow it? But if the light was corporeal, what light was it that we cannot see after the setting of the sun, since neither the moon nor any stars yet existed?

Or, if it was always in that part of heaven in which the sun is, so that it was not the sun’s light but, as it were, its companion—so closely joined to it that it could not be distinguished or recognized—we return to the same difficulty in resolving this question. For this light too, in the same way as the sun, would circle from setting to rising as its companion and return; and it would be in another part of the world at the time when the region in which we are grew dark into night.

This would force us—God forbid—to believe that God was in one region, the region that this light abandoned, so that evening could occur for him. Or had he perhaps made the light in the region where he was going to make human beings? Thus, when the light withdrew from that region, evening is said to have occurred, even though that light was in another region, from which it would return in the morning after completing its circuit?

## CHAPTER XI — A new difficulty concerning the sun’s function in the preceding manner of explanation.

23. Why, then, was the sun made to rule the day (Ps. 135:8), so that it might shine upon the earth, if that light which was also called day had been sufficient to make day? Did the earlier light illuminate regions high above and distant from the earth, so that it could not be perceived on earth, and was it therefore necessary for the sun to be made, through which day would appear in the lower regions of the world?

This too may be said: that the brightness of the day was increased by the addition of the sun, so that day may be thought to have been less bright through that earlier light than it is now.

I also know that someone has said that the nature of light was first introduced into the Creator’s work when it was said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. Later, when the luminaries are mentioned, the text is said to recall what had been made from that light, according to the sequence of days in which it seemed good to the Creator that all things should be made. But where that nature of light went when evening was made, so that night in turn might pass, neither does he say nor, I think, can it easily be discovered.

For it must not be believed that the light was extinguished so that the darkness of night might follow [Col. 0255] and then kindled again so that morning might come, before this function was performed by the sun. Scripture itself testifies that this began on the fourth day.

## CHAPTER XII — Another difficulty concerning the succession of three days and nights before the creation of the sun. How the gathering of the waters occurred.

24. Before the sun was made, it is difficult both to discover and to explain by what circuit three days and nights could have succeeded one another while the nature of the light first made remained—if that light is to be understood as corporeal.

Unless someone should say that God called the mass of earth and water “darkness” before the two had been separated from each other, as is written to have happened on the third day, because of its denser bulk, which the light could not penetrate, or because of the very dark shadow cast by so great a mass; for a body must have a shadow on the opposite side whenever it is illuminated on one side by light.

Wherever the bulk of any body prevents light from reaching, there is shadow. A place without that light by which it would otherwise be illuminated, if an intervening body did not obstruct it, is precisely what is called shadow. If the shadow is as great as the mass of the body and occupies as much space as day occupies on the other side, it is called night.

Not all darkness, however, is night. In large caves, too, where light is prevented from breaking into the recesses by the intervening mass, there is darkness, because light is not there and the whole space is a place without light. Yet such darkness did not receive the name “night”; that name belongs to the darkness that succeeds in that part of the earth from which day withdraws.

Likewise, not all light is called day. There is the light of the moon, of the stars, of lamps, of flashes of lightning, and of all sorts of shining things. But that light is called day which is followed by, and gives way to, night.

25. But if that original light had surrounded and enveloped the mass of the earth on every side, whether it stood still or circled around, there would have been no side from which it could allow night to follow it, since it never withdrew anywhere to make room for night.

Or had it been made on one side, so that, while it circled around, it would also allow night to follow successively on the other side? For since water still covered the whole earth, nothing prevented the watery and spherical mass [Note: [Col. 0255] Several manuscripts read, “spherical.”] from producing day on one side through the presence of light and night on the other through the absence of light, with the night succeeding from the time of evening on the side from which the light declined toward the other.

26. Where, then, were the waters gathered, if they had previously occupied the whole earth? Those waters that were withdrawn so that the earth might be exposed—toward what region were they gathered?

If there was some bare part of earth into which they could be gathered, then the dry land was already visible, and the abyss did not occupy everything. But if they had covered everything, where was there a place into which they could be gathered so that the dryness of the earth might appear?

Were they gathered upward, as happens when threshed grain is raised on a threshing floor to be winnowed and piled into a heap, uncovering the place that it had covered while spread out? Who could say this, when he saw the plains of the sea spread out evenly everywhere—plains that, even when some mountains of moving water rise like hills, are again flattened when the storms have subsided?

And if some shores are exposed more broadly, it cannot be said that there are no other stretches of land toward which what withdraws from one place might move, so that it could later return to the place from which it had withdrawn. But when the watery nature entirely covered the whole earth, where could it withdraw in order to uncover some regions?

Or perhaps the more tenuous water covered the earth like a mist, and was thickened by being gathered together, so that it uncovered many regions in which dry land could appear? Moreover, the earth, sinking in various places over a wide area, could have provided hollow regions into which the waters flowing and falling together might be received, while dry land appeared in the regions from which the moisture withdrew.

27. Yet matter is not entirely formless when even a mist-like appearance is visible:

## CHAPTER XIII — When the water and the earth were created.

And therefore it may still be asked when God created these visible forms and qualities of the waters and the earth, for this is found nowhere in the six days. Thus, if he made them before every day, as is written before the mention of those first days, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” we may understand by “earth” an already formed earthly appearance, with the waters poured over it already made visible in the appearance proper to their kind.

Accordingly, when Scripture goes on to say, “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss; and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters,” let us not suppose any formlessness of matter, but understand that the earth and water had been created with their already familiar qualities, without the light that had not yet been made.

The earth is therefore called invisible because, being covered by the waters, it could not be seen even if there were someone able to see it. It is called unformed because it had not yet been distinguished from the sea, enclosed by shores, and adorned with its offspring and animals.

If this is so, why were these appearances, which are undoubtedly corporeal, made before every day? Why is it not written, “God said, Let earth come to be, and earth came to be”; likewise, “God said, Let water come to be, and water came to be”? Or, if they are contained together under one law as belonging to the lowest region, why not, “God said, Let earth and water come to be,” and so it happened?

## CHAPTER XIV — The reason why formless matter is understood in the first verse of Genesis.

Why was it not said, after this had been made, “God saw that it was good”?

28. This consideration led to the following conclusion. It is clear that everything mutable is formed from some formlessness. At the same time, both the catholic faith prescribes this and the most certain reasoning teaches that there could have been no matter belonging to any nature except from God, the originator and Creator of all things—not only of things already formed but also of things capable of being formed. Scripture also says of him, “You made the world from formless matter” (Wis. 11:18).

This matter, Scripture indicates in words suited, through spiritual prudence, even to slower readers and hearers [Note: [Col. 0256] Several manuscripts read *congrueretur*, “might be made suitable,” rather than *congrueret*, “might suit.”], when, before the enumeration of the days, it says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” and so on, until it says, “And God said” [Col. 0257], after which the order of formed things follows.

## CHAPTER XV — Matter precedes form in origin, not in time.

29. This is not because formless matter is earlier in time than formed things, since both were created together: both that from which something was made and that which was made. Just as the voice is the matter of words, while words indicate a formed voice, the speaker does not first emit a formless voice and afterward gather it together and form it into words. Similarly, God the Creator did not first make formless matter in time and afterward form it, as it were, through a second consideration, in the sequence of its various natures; rather, he created matter already formed.

But because that from which something is made, although not earlier in time, is nevertheless earlier in a certain origin than that which is made from it, Scripture could divide in the times of its narration what God did not divide in the times of making.

If it is asked whether we make a voice from words or words from a voice, no one of such sluggish understanding is easily found who would not answer that words are made from a voice. Thus, although the speaker makes both simultaneously, it is sufficiently clear, by natural attention, what he makes from what.

Therefore, since God made both simultaneously—the matter that he formed and the things into which he formed it—and Scripture had to mention both, yet could not mention both simultaneously, who would doubt that it ought to mention first that from which something was made and afterward that which was made from it?

For even when we say “matter and form,” we understand that both exist simultaneously, but we cannot utter both simultaneously. Just as, in the brevity of time, when we pronounce these two words, we happen to pronounce one before the other, so in the extended length of a narrative one had to be narrated before the other, although, as has been said, God made both simultaneously. Thus what is earlier only in origin in the making is also earlier in the narration, because two things—one of which is in no way earlier than the other—cannot be named simultaneously, and even less can they be narrated simultaneously.

There is therefore no doubt that this formless matter was, in some manner, close to nothing, so that it was made only by God and was created together with the things made from it.

30. But if it is credibly said that it is signified by the words, “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss; and the Spirit of God was borne over the water,” then, except for what is said there about the Spirit of God, we should understand the remaining terms to be names of visible things, but to have been spoken in order to indicate, as far as slower minds could grasp it, that formlessness.

For these two elements—earth and water—are more tractable than the others to the hands of craftsmen when something is to be made; and therefore that formlessness was more suitably indicated by these names.

## CHAPTER XVI — Another explanation of how day and night came to be, namely by the emission and contraction of light, is rejected.

If this is said with some probability, then there was no formed mass which, when illuminated by light on one side, produced darkness on the other, from which night could follow when day withdrew.

31. But if we wish to understand day and night as the emission and contraction of that light, we see no reason why this should have happened. For there were not yet animals for whom this alternation could beneficially be provided, as we see it provided for animals after they had appeared through the circuit of the sun.

Nor does any example present itself by which we could establish this emission and contraction of light as producing the alternation of day and night. The projection of rays from our eyes is indeed a projection of a kind of light. [Note: [Col. 0258] The printed editions read, “is clearly a projection of light.” All the manuscripts disagree; some have, “is indeed a projection of light,” while others omit the middle word and read, “is a projection of light.”] It can be contracted when we look at the air close to our eyes, and emitted when we direct our attention along the same line toward things that are far away.

When it is contracted, the gaze does not cease entirely to see distant things; but it certainly sees them more obscurely than when it is extended toward them. Nevertheless, that light which exists in the sense of the observer is shown to be so slight [Note: [Col. 0258] The printed editions read, “then it appears so slight.” The manuscripts read, “it is shown to be slight”; and six of them, instead of *adjuvemur*, “we are helped,” have *adjuvetur*, “it is helped.”] that, unless we are aided by an external light, we can see nothing. And since it cannot be distinguished from that external light, it is difficult to find an example by which the emission of light into day and its contraction into night could be demonstrated, as I have said.

## CHAPTER XVII — A difficulty concerning spiritual light: how evening and morning, and its division from darkness, can exist in it.

32. But if spiritual light was made when God said, “Let there be light,” this must not be understood as the true light coeternal with the Father, through which all things were made and which illuminates every human being. Rather, it is the light of which it could be said, “Wisdom was created before all other things” (Ecclus. 1:4).

For when that eternal and unchangeable Wisdom—which was not made but begotten—transfers itself into spiritual and rational creatures, as into holy souls (Wis. 7:27), so that, once illuminated, they may shine, there arises in them a certain affection of lucid reason. This can be understood as the light made when God said, “Let there be light.”

If the spiritual creature already existed, signified by the name “heaven” in the words, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” then it was not a corporeal heaven but the incorporeal heaven of the corporeal heaven [Note: [Col. 0258] The printed editions read, “the heavens of the corporeal heavens.” We have no doubt that the reading preserved by nearly all the manuscripts is more correct: “the incorporeal heaven of the corporeal heaven.” Here Augustine, in his customary manner, alludes to Psalm 113:16, “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord.” Compare above, sections 15 and 17, as well as *Confessions*, book 12, chapters 2, 8, and 9.], that is, placed above every body—not by degrees of place but by the sublimity of its nature.

How, then, that which was illuminated and the illumination itself could have been made simultaneously, and yet had to be narrated at different times, was explained shortly before when we were discussing matter.

33. But how are we to understand night succeeding this light, so that evening might occur? From what sort of darkness could such a light have been divided, when Scripture says, “And God divided between the light and the darkness”?

Were there already sinners and fools falling away from the light of truth, so that God might divide between them and those who remained in the same light, as between light and darkness? And, calling the light day and the darkness night, was he showing himself not to be the maker of sinners but the arranger of the distribution of merits? [Note: [Col. 0258] So read all the manuscripts. In Am., Er., and Lov., the conjunction *et*, “and,” had been removed from this place and inserted immediately before *ostenderet*, “might show.” A little later, those editions read *distribuendorum*, “of things to be distributed,” instead of the reading found in many manuscripts, *distributione*, “by distribution,” and in others, *distributionum meritorum*, “of distributions of merits.”] Or is this day the name of the whole of time, including all the cycles of the ages under this name? Is that why it was not called “the first” but “one day”? “There was evening and there was morning,” he says, “one day,” so that by the evening the sin of rational creation might be signified, while by the morning its renewal might be understood.

34. But this is an interpretation belonging to prophetic allegory, which we have not undertaken in this work. We have undertaken to speak now about the Scriptures according to the proper meaning of the events narrated, not according to the riddles of figures. [Note: [Col. 0259] Seven manuscripts read, “the riddles of things to come.”]

How, then, according to the account of the natures that were made and created, do we find evening and morning in spiritual light?

Could the division of light from darkness be the distinction between an already formed thing and one that was formless, while the naming of day and night indicates the distribution [Note: [Col. 0259] Six manuscripts read, “the distinction,” instead of “the distribution.”] by which it is signified that God leaves nothing disordered, and that formlessness itself—through which things pass in a certain manner from one form to another and change—is not without arrangement? Nor are the declines and advances of creation, through which temporal things succeed one another, without contributing to the beauty of the whole.

For night is darkness set in order.

35. Therefore, when the light had been made, it is said, “God saw the light, that it was good,” although He could have said this after everything belonging to that day, that is, after He had set forth:

[Note: Col. 0259. The printed editions read, “after He had set forth heaven.” The word “heaven” is redundant and absent from the manuscripts.] “God said, Let there be light”; “and light was made”; “and God divided between the light and the darkness”; “and God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night.” Then He could have said, “And God saw that it was good,” and thereafter added, “And evening was made, and morning was made,” as He does with the other works, to which He assigns names.

He did not act in this way here for the following reason: that formlessness was distinguished from the formed thing precisely so that the formlessness would not be an end in itself, but would still remain to be formed through the other, now bodily, creatures. Thus, if after that division and the assignment of names it had been said, “God saw that it was good,” we would have understood these completed things to be signified, to which nothing further in their own kind would need to be added.

But because He had thus completed the light alone, “God saw,” it says, “the light, that it was good,” and by division and names He distinguished it from the darkness. Even then He did not say, “God saw that it was good,” for that formlessness had been distinguished for the purpose that other things might still be formed from it.

For this night, which is most familiar to us—for the circuit of the sun produces it over the earth—when it is divided from day by the distribution of the heavenly lights, is said, after the division of day and night, to be good in God’s sight. This night was not some formless substance from which other things were still to be formed; it was rather a region filled with air and deprived of daylight. Nothing further needed to be added to this night in its own kind, so as to make it more beautiful or more distinct.

Evening, however, throughout those three days, before the heavenly lights were made, may perhaps reasonably be understood as the termination of a completed work; morning, on the other hand, as a sign of a work yet to come.

## CHAPTER XVIII — How God Works

36. Above all, let us remember what we have already said at length: God does not work through temporal movements, as though of His mind or body, in the manner in which a human being or an angel works; rather, He works through the eternal, immutable, and stable principles of His coeternal Word and, so to speak, through the fostering warmth (*fotu*) of His equally coeternal Holy Spirit.

[Note: Col. 0260. The printed editions read *flatu* (“breath”); manuscripts of better quality read *fotu* (“fostering warmth”). This accords better with the interpretive explanation of a certain Syrian cited here by Augustine, after Basil, Homily 2 on the Hexaemeron.]

For what was said in Greek and Latin about the Spirit of God—that He “was borne over the waters”—is, according to the meaning of the Syriac language, which is close to Hebrew, said to mean not that He was borne over them, but rather that He cherished them. This explanation is reported to have been given by a learned Christian who was a Syrian. It is not meant in the sense in which swellings or wounds in the body are fomented with water, whether cold or suitably warmed; it is rather like birds brooding over eggs, where the warmth of the mother’s body in some way assists in forming the chicks, through a certain affection of love appropriate to its kind.

Let us therefore not imagine that, on each successive day of these divine works, God uttered temporal words in a bodily manner. For the Wisdom of God itself did not come, having assumed our weakness, to gather the children of Jerusalem beneath His wings as a hen gathers her chicks (Matt. 23:37), so that we might remain perpetually childish; rather, it came so that we might cease to be infants in malice and become children in understanding (1 Cor. 14:20).

37. In matters that are obscure and most remote from our eyes, if we read something written about them in the divine Scriptures that, without violating the faith in which we have been instructed, can give rise to various interpretations, let us not throw ourselves precipitately into any one of them by an assertion so rash that, if more careful investigation should rightly undermine it, we fall with it. Let us not fight for our own opinion as though it were the opinion of the divine Scriptures, wishing our own view to be that of Scripture; rather, we ought to wish the view that belongs to Scripture to become our own.

## CHAPTER XIX — Nothing Rashly to Be Asserted in Obscure Passages of Scripture

38. Let us suppose, then, that concerning what is written, “God said, Let there be light; and light was made,” one person understood bodily light to have been made, while another understood spiritual light. Our faith has no doubt that spiritual light exists in a spiritual creature.

[Note: Col. 0260. Thus we emend in accordance with manuscripts of better quality. Earlier editions read: “One person understood bodily light to have been made, and another that spiritual light exists in a spiritual creature, which our faith does not doubt.”] But whether there was bodily light, heavenly or even above the heavens, or before the heavens, which could be followed by night, may be held without opposition to the faith until it is refuted by absolutely certain truth.

If that should happen, the divine Scripture did not contain this meaning; rather, human ignorance had understood it so. But if certain reasoning should demonstrate that this is true, it will still remain uncertain whether the writer of those holy books intended that meaning to be understood in these words, or some other meaning that is no less true.

If the rest of the context proves that he did not intend this meaning, that does not make false the other meaning that he did intend to be understood; it may be both true and more useful to know. If, however, the context of Scripture does not contradict the supposition that the writer intended this meaning, it will still remain to be asked whether he could not also have intended another.
