If we discover that he could have intended another as well, it will be uncertain which of these meanings he intended; and it is not unreasonable to believe that he intended both, if the surrounding context gives firm support to both interpretations.

39. It often happens that a non-Christian possesses such certain knowledge, through reliable evidence or experience, of matters concerning the earth, the heavens, and the other elements of this world; concerning the movement, revolution, magnitude, or distances of the stars; concerning particular eclipses of the sun and moon; concerning the cycles of years and seasons; concerning the natures of animals, plants, stones, and other such things, that he knows them with complete certainty.

It is therefore exceedingly disgraceful, harmful, and above all to be avoided that a non-believer should hear a Christian, allegedly speaking according to the Christian Scriptures about such matters, uttering such nonsense that, seeing him err as they say “by the whole heavens,” he can scarcely restrain his laughter. The harm is not merely that an erring person is mocked; rather, our authors are believed by outsiders to have held such views, and they are criticized and rejected as ignorant—to the great loss of those whose salvation we are striving to secure.

For when they catch one of the Christians mistaken in a matter that they themselves know extremely well, and asserting his empty opinion on the authority of our books, how will they believe those books when they speak of the resurrection of the dead, the hope of eternal life, and the kingdom of heaven? When, regarding matters that they have already been able to test or grasp through indisputable calculations, they think those books were deceptively written, what confidence will they place in them concerning things they cannot experience or understand?

The annoyance and sorrow that reckless presumptuous people cause their prudent brothers cannot adequately be expressed. Whenever they begin to be criticized and refuted for their perverse and false opinion by those who are not bound by the authority of our books, they try to produce those same holy books as proof of what they have said with the greatest frivolity and the most obvious falsehood. They may even recite from memory many words that they think will serve as testimony, not understanding either what they are saying or the matters about which they make assertions (1 Tim. 1:7).

## CHAPTER XX — Why He Interprets Genesis by Offering Various Meanings Rather Than Asserting a Single One

40. For this reason I have examined the book of Genesis in multiple ways, as far as I was able, and have brought forward interpretations of passages obscurely expressed for the sake of our exercise. I have not rashly asserted one particular meaning to the prejudice of another exposition that might perhaps be better, so that each person may choose, according to his capacity, what he is able to grasp. Where he cannot understand, let him honor God’s Scripture and fear for himself.

But since the words of Scripture that we have discussed can be explained in so many ways, let those who are inflated with secular learning finally restrain themselves from attacking them as though they were something ignorant and uncultivated, even though they were set down in this way to nourish every devout heart. Such people crawl upon the earth without wings and mock the nests of birds with the flight of frogs.

[Note: Col. 0262. The Louvain edition reads *volaturarum* (“of creatures about to fly”); the other editions and a large part of the manuscripts read *volatu ranarum* (“with the flight of frogs”).]

[Note: Col. 0261. Edition B reads “books”; the other printed editions read “book,” more aptly.]

Some weak brothers, however, fall into a more dangerous error. When they hear these impious men discoursing subtly and copiously about the measurements of heavenly bodies or about any of the questions concerning the elements of this world, they lose heart. With a sigh they prefer these men to themselves and regard them as great; they return with disdain to the books of the most wholesome piety and scarcely touch with patience what they ought to drink in sweetly. They shrink from the roughness of the grain and gape after the flowers of thorns.

They do not take the trouble to see how gracious the Lord is (Ps. 33:9), nor do they hunger on the Sabbath. Therefore they are too sluggish to pluck the ears of grain, having received from the Lord of the Sabbath the authority to do so, and to work them in their hands, rubbing and cleaning them until they reach the food (Matt. 12:1).

## CHAPTER XXI — The Benefit of This Kind of Interpretation, in Which Nothing Is Rashly Asserted

41. Someone may say: “What have you stripped away by all this threshing of discussion? What have you winnowed from the grains? Why does almost everything still remain hidden in questions? Assert something from among the many things you have argued can be understood in different ways.”

I reply that I have reached that very food with delight: I have learned not to be at a loss when replying in accordance with the faith to those who seek to disparage the books of our salvation. Whatever they can demonstrate about the nature of things by truthful proofs, we should show not to be contrary to our Scriptures.

But whatever they may bring forward from any of their books as contrary to these Scriptures of ours—that is, to the Catholic faith—we should either demonstrate by some means to be false, or believe without hesitation to be utterly false. Thus let us hold fast to our Mediator, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3), so that we may be led astray neither by the verbosity of false philosophy nor terrified by the superstition of false religion.

When we read the divine books amid such a multitude of true meanings that can be drawn from a few words and defended by the soundness of the Catholic faith, let us select above all what appears certain to have been intended by the author whom we are reading. If that remains hidden, let us select at least what the context of Scripture does not obstruct and what agrees with sound faith. If even the context of Scripture cannot be examined and investigated, let us hold at least that which sound faith prescribes.

It is one thing not to discern what the writer intended above all; it is another to depart from the rule of piety. If both errors are avoided, the reader’s benefit is complete. But if both cannot be avoided, then even if the writer’s intention remains uncertain, it is not useless to extract a meaning that agrees with sound faith.  
[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *tenuisse* (“to have held”) instead of *eruisse* (“to have extracted”).]

# BOOK TWO

Concerning what is written in chapter 1, verse 6: “And God said, Let there be a firmament,” etc., up to verse 19: “And evening was made,” etc. At the end, some remarks against the astrologers.

[Col. 0263]

## CHAPTER I — What the Firmament in the Midst of the Waters Is; Some Deny That There Are Waters above the Starry Heaven

1. “And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide between water and water; and so it was made. And God made the firmament, and God divided between the water that was beneath the firmament and the water that was above the firmament. And God called the firmament Heaven. And God saw that it was good. And evening was made, and morning was made—the second day.”

There is no need here to discuss again, in the same way, the word of God by which He said, “Let there be a firmament,” and so forth; nor His approval, by which He saw that it was good; nor evening and morning. We point out that whenever these things are repeated hereafter, they are to be considered provisionally according to the preceding inquiry.

But whether this is now the heaven that exceeds all the spaces of the air and all its height, where the heavenly lights and stars are also established on the fourth day; or whether the air itself is called the firmament, may reasonably be questioned.

2. Many assert that the nature of these waters cannot exist above the starry heaven, because their weight is so ordered that they either float upon the earth or are carried vapor-like in the air near the earth.

No one should refute them by saying that, according to the omnipotence of God, for whom all things are possible, we ought to believe that waters as heavy as those we know and feel have been poured over the heavenly body in which the stars are located. For now it is appropriate for us to inquire, according to His Scriptures, how God established the natures of things—not what He might wish to do in them or through them as a miracle of His power.

If God wished oil at some time to remain beneath water, it would indeed happen; yet from this we would not have an incorrect understanding of the nature of oil, which was made in such a way that, seeking its proper place, even if it had been poured beneath water, it breaks through the water and places itself above it.

We are therefore asking whether the Creator of things, who arranged all things “in measure and number and weight” (Wis. 11:21), assigned the waters not merely one proper place around the earth according to their weight, but also a place above the heaven that is spread around and solidified beyond the limit of the air.

3. Those who deny that this should be believed argue from the weights of the elements. They deny that the heaven could in any way be solidified above, like a kind of pavement, so as to support the weight of waters. Such solidity, they say, can belong only to the earth; and whatever has such solidity is not heaven but earth.

For, they argue, the elements are distinguished not only by their places but also by their proper qualities, so that in accordance with their proper qualities they receive their proper places: water, for example, above the earth. Even when water stands or flows beneath the earth, as in hidden caves and caverns, it is not contained by that part of the earth which is above it, but by the part beneath it.

For if any portion of earth falls from above, it does not remain upon the water; it breaks through it, sinks, and continues toward the earth. When it reaches it, it comes to rest as in its proper place, so that water is above and earth below.

From this it is understood that, even when the earth was above the waters, it was not supported by the waters themselves, but held in place by the structure of the earth, as is the case with the roofs of caverns.

4. Here we should warn against an error that I warned against in the first book: because it is written in the Psalms, “He founded the earth upon the waters,” someone might suppose that, against those who argue subtly from the weights of the elements, we ought to rely upon this testimony of Scripture.

Those people are not held back by the authority of our Scriptures, and, not knowing how the statement was made, they will more readily ridicule the holy books than reject what they have grasped through certain reasoning or proved by the clearest experiments.

That statement in the Psalms can rightly be understood figuratively. Since the names “heaven” and “earth” often signify spiritual and carnal people in the Church, the Psalm may indicate that the heavens belong to serene understanding of the truth when it says, “He made the heavens in understanding” (Ps. 135:5–6); and that the earth belongs to the simple faith of little ones—not a faith uncertain and deceptive because of fabulous opinions, but one made utterly firm by prophetic and evangelical preaching, and solidified through Baptism. For this reason it adds, “He founded the earth upon the waters.”

Or, if someone insists on understanding the statement literally, it may reasonably refer either to the elevated parts of the earth—whether mainland or islands—which are above the waters, or to the roofs of caves themselves, whose suspended solidity is supported above the waters.

Accordingly, no one can understand literally the statement, “He founded the earth upon the waters,” in such a way as to suppose that the weight of water is, according to the natural order, placed beneath the weight of earth in order to support it.

## CHAPTER II — Air Is Above the Earth

5. That air is above water, although on account of its greater expanses it also covers the dry land, is understood from the fact that no vessel can be filled with water when its mouth is pressed downward. This sufficiently indicates that the nature of air seeks a higher place.

A vessel appears empty, but is shown to be full of air when it is plunged mouth-first into water. Since through its upper part it finds no place by which to escape, and since nature does not permit it to move downward beneath the water by breaking through it, the air, by its fullness, repels the water and does not allow it to enter the vessel.

But when the vessel is placed so that its mouth is not downward but tilted to the side, water enters below while air escapes above. Likewise, if the mouth of an upright vessel is open toward the sky, when water is poured in, the air escapes upward through the other parts where the water is not being poured, and space is made for the water to enter from below.

If the vessel is forced downward with greater pressure, so that water suddenly rushes in from the side or from above and covers the vessel’s mouth on every side, the air, pressing upward, breaks through the water so as to make room for it below. This breaking through produces the gurgling of vessels, as the air escapes in portions, since it cannot all escape so quickly because of the narrowness of the mouth.

Thus, if air is forced to move above the water, it also disperses the water as it gathers, when the waters, driven by its force, leap up and boil, sending the air out amid bursting bubbles as it hastens toward its proper place and giving the waters access to descend below.

But if air is forced to move beneath the water from within a vessel, so that, as the air yields, one wishes the vessel to be filled from its mouth pressed downward, the vessel is more easily covered by water on every side than a small drop can find a place to enter through its mouth from below.

## CHAPTER III — Fire Is Above the Air

6. Who does not perceive that fire, flashing upward, also seeks to transcend the nature of the air itself? If anyone holds a burning torch with its head downward, nevertheless the hair-like flame strives toward the heights.

But because the surrounding and overlying air eventually extinguishes the fire through its greater density, and because the fire is repeatedly overcome by the abundance of air and changed into its quality, it cannot persist in leaping across the whole height of the air.

Thus the pure fire above the air is said to be heaven, and from this they infer that the stars and heavenly lights were made: the nature of that fiery light was gathered together and arranged into the forms that we see in heaven.

Accordingly, just as air and water yield to the weight of earth so that they reach the earth, so air itself yields to the weight of water so that it reaches either earth or water. Hence they wish to infer that, in the same way, if someone could release a particle of air in those lofty spaces of heaven, it would fall by its own weight until it reached the air below.

Consequently, they conclude that there can be even less room for waters above that fiery heaven, since air, which is much lighter than water, cannot remain there.

## CHAPTER IV — Someone Has Observed That There Are Waters above the Aerial Heaven Called the Firmament

7. Yielding to arguments of this kind, someone made a praiseworthy attempt to demonstrate that there are waters above the heavens, in order to support the credibility of Scripture by appealing to visible and observable natures.

First, and most easily, he showed that this air is called heaven—not only in ordinary speech, according to which we speak of a clear or cloudy heaven, but also according to the usage of our own Scriptures. They speak of “the birds of heaven” (Matt. 6:26), although it is evident that birds fly in this air; and when the Lord spoke of clouds, He said, “You can discern the face of heaven” (Matt. 16:4).

We often see clouds gathered in the air near the earth, resting along the slopes of ridges so that they frequently rise even above the mountain peaks. Having therefore established that this air is also called heaven, he wished it to be understood that it was called the firmament for no other reason than that its interval divides between certain vapors of water and those waters that flow more substantially upon the earth.

Clouds, as those who have walked among them in the mountains have discovered, produce such an appearance through the gathering and clustering of exceedingly small drops. If they become denser, so that many small drops join into one large drop, the air does not allow it to remain suspended within it, but yields space below to its weight; and this is rain.

Thus, from the air that lies between the moist vapors—where the clouds are gathered above—and the seas spread out below, he wished to show that there is a heaven between water and water.

I judge this diligence and consideration highly worthy of praise. What he said is not contrary to the faith, and it can be believed on the basis of an evident piece of evidence.

8. Nevertheless, it might appear that the proper weights of the elements do not prevent waters from existing even above that lofty heaven, in the form of the tiny particles through which they were able to exist above this expanse of air.

Although the air is heavier and lower than the highest heaven, it is undoubtedly lighter than water; yet its weight does not prevent those vapors from existing above it. In the same way, a lighter vapor of moisture might be spread above that heaven in smaller drops, without being forced to fall by its weight.

They themselves persuade us by exceedingly subtle reasoning that there is no bodily particle, however small, in which division comes to an end, but that all things can be divided infinitely. Every part of a body is itself a body, and every body must possess half of its own quantity.

Therefore, if water can, as we see, be reduced to such tiny drops that it is carried in vapor above this air, which by nature is lighter than water, why could not a vapor remain above that lighter heaven in still smaller drops and lighter forms?

## CHAPTER V — Waters above the Starry Heaven as Well

9. Some of our own people try to refute, by arguments drawn from the qualities and courses of the stars themselves, those who deny that waters can exist above the starry heaven because of the weights of the elements.

They assert that the star they call Saturn is extremely cold and that it traverses the zodiacal circle in thirty years, because it is higher and therefore moves through a larger circuit. The sun completes the same circle in one year, and the moon in one month—so much more quickly, they say, the lower each is, so that the extent of time corresponds to the extent of place.

They are therefore asked where that star derives its coldness, since it ought to be hotter in proportion to the greater height of the heaven through which it is carried.

For undoubtedly, when a rounded mass is driven in circular motion, its inner portions move more slowly and its outer portions more quickly, so that the larger spaces meet the same circuits at the same time as the shorter spaces. Whatever moves more quickly is necessarily hotter.

Accordingly, the star in question ought to be hot rather than cold. Although, on account of its own motion and the great distance it travels, it completes the whole circuit in thirty years, it is nevertheless rotated more rapidly in the opposite direction by the motion of heaven—a motion which it must undergo daily, since, as they say, each revolution of heaven produces a single day. It ought therefore to receive greater heat from a heaven driven more rapidly.

It is evidently the proximity of the waters established above the heaven that makes it cold—waters which those who argue about the motion of heaven and the stars in the manner I have briefly described refuse to believe in.

Some of our people use these conjectures against those who refuse to believe that there are waters above the heaven and who wish that star, which circles near the highest heaven, to be cold. In this way they seek to compel them to judge that the nature of the waters is there not in vaporous thinness but in icy solidity.

[Note: Col. 0267. After “compel them to judge the nature of the waters,” the printed editions add *credere* (“to believe”). The word is absent from the manuscripts and should be absent if *pendere* at the end of the sentence is understood not as “to hang” (*pendeo*), but as “to assess” (*pendo*).]

However these waters may be and whatever their nature there, let us have no doubt that they are there. The authority of this Scripture is greater than the capacity of every human intellect.

## CHAPTER VI — Whether the Addition “And God Made” Declares the Person of the Son of God

10. Some have observed something that I too do not think should be concealed: after God had said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let there be a division between water and water,” it apparently seemed insufficient to add merely, “And so it was made,” unless the further words were added: “And God made the firmament, and God divided between the water that was above the firmament and the water that was beneath the firmament.”

They understand this in such a way as to say that the person of the Father is declared in what is written: “And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let there be a division between water and water; and so it was made.” Then, so that it may be understood that the Son made what the Father had said should be made, they think the following was added: “And God made the firmament, and God divided,” and so forth.

11. But when we read earlier, “And so it was made,” from whom do we understand it to have been made? If from the Son, what need was there already to say, “And God made,” and what follows? But if we understand that what is written, “And so it was made,” was made by the Father, then it is no longer the Father who speaks and the Son who makes. The Father could then make something without the Son, so that afterward the Son might make not this but something else in the same way. This is contrary to the Catholic faith.

If the thing of which it is said, “And so it was made,” is the very thing that is made when it is likewise said, “And God made,” what prevents us from understanding the one who said that it should be made to be the one who made what He said?

Or do they wish the persons of the Father and the Son to be understood only in those words where it is said, “And God said, Let there be,” and later, “And God made,” excluding what is written, “And so it was made”?

12. But it may still be asked whether we ought to understand the Father as having commanded the Son, as it were, in what is written, “And God said, Let there be.” Yet why did Scripture not also take care to indicate the person of the Holy Spirit?

Or is the Trinity understood in this way: “And God said, Let there be”; “and God made”; “and God saw that it was good”? But this does not accord with the unity of the Trinity, as though the Son were understood to have made something under command, while the Holy Spirit, without anyone commanding Him, freely saw that what had been made was good.

With what words would the Father command the Son to make something, when the Son Himself is the principal Word of the Father, through whom all things were made?

Or is the very expression, “Let there be a firmament,” itself the Word of the Father, the only-begotten Son, in whom are all things that are created, even before they are created, and whatever is in Him is life? For whatever was made through Him is life in Him, and life is surely creative, while beneath it is the creature.

Things that were made through Him are in Him in one way, because He rules and contains them; things that He Himself is are in Him in another way. For He Himself is life, which is in Him in such a way that He Himself is it, since He Himself, life, is the light of men (John 1:3–4).

Since, therefore, nothing could be created—whether before time, though nothing is coeternal with the Creator; or at the beginning of time; or at any point in time—unless the principle of its creation, if it is properly called a principle, lived as coeternal life in the Word of God, coeternal with the Father, Scripture, before introducing each creature according to the order in which it says that it was made, turns its attention to the Word of God. It first says, “And God said, Let that be.”

For it did not find any cause for the creation of a thing that it did not find in the Word of God as something that ought to be created.

13. God therefore did not say, “Let this or that creature be,” as many times as this book repeats, “And God said.” He begot one Word, in which He said all things before each of them was made. But the language of the writer descends to the capacity of little ones. As it introduces the various kinds of creatures one by one, it refers each kind to its eternal principle in the Word of God; and although that principle was not repeated, the writer repeats, “And God said.”

If he wished first to say, “The firmament was made in the midst of the waters, so that there might be a division between water and water,” and someone asked him how it was made, he would rightly answer, “God said, Let there be”—that is, in the eternal Word of God it was ordained to be made.

Thus he begins to narrate each thing as made; and after narrating its making, if someone asked how it was made, he ought to answer by giving the reason.

14. When therefore we hear, “And God said, Let there be,” we understand that it was ordained in the Word of God that the thing should be made.

When we hear, “And so it was made,” we understand that the creature which was made did not exceed the limits of its kind prescribed in the Word of God.

When we hear, “And God saw that it was good,” we understand that, in the goodness of His Spirit, the thing did not please Him as something recognized only after it had been made; rather, it pleased Him in that goodness so that it should remain made, in which it had pleased Him that it should be made.

## CHAPTER VII — The Same Matter

15. The reason for inquiry therefore still remains: after He had said, “And so it was made,” by which the completion of the work is already indicated, why did He add, “And God made,” when the words, “And God said, Let that be,” together with “And so it was made,” already imply that God said it in His Word and that it was made through His Word?

At that point not only the person of the Father but also that of the Son might already appear.

For if “And God made” is repeated in order to display the person of the Son, did He not then gather the waters on the third day so that the dry land might appear through the Son, since there it is not said, “And God made the water to be gathered,” or “God gathered the water”?

Yet even there, after He had said, “And it was made so,” He repeated the account by saying, “And the water that is under heaven was gathered together.”

Was light not also made through the Son, where He did not repeat the phrase at all? For there too He could have said, “And God said, Let there be light; and so it was made; and God made the light; and He saw that it was good.”

Or, as in the gathering of the waters, He could have omitted “And God made” and simply repeated, “And God said, Let there be light; and so it was made; and light was made; and God saw the light, that it was good.”

But after introducing, “And God said, Let there be light,” He made no repetition at all. He added nothing except, “And light was made.” Thereafter he narrated, without any repetition, the light’s being pleasing, its division from the darkness, and the assignment of names to both.

## CHAPTER VIII — Why “And God Made” Was Not Added for the Light, as It Is Usually Said of the Other Creatures

16. What, then, does that repetition in the case of the other creatures mean?

Could it be that on the first day, when the light was made, the condition of the spiritual and intellectual creature is intimated under the name of light? In that nature all the holy angels and powers are understood to exist.

For this reason, after saying, “Light was made,” he did not repeat that it was made. The rational creature did not first know its own formation and then become formed; rather, in its very formation it came to know it—that is, through the illumination of truth, toward which it was turned and formed.

The other things below, however, are created in such a way that they first come to be in the knowledge of the rational creature and then in their own kind.

Therefore the creation of light exists first in the Word of God according to the principle by which it was created—that is, in the Wisdom coeternal with the Father—and then in the creation of light itself according to the nature in which it was created.

There it was not made but begotten; here it was made, because it was formed from formlessness. Hence God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made, so that what existed there in the Word might exist here in the work.

The creation of heaven, however, existed first in the Word of God according to the begotten Wisdom; then it came to be in the spiritual creature, that is, in the angels’ knowledge, according to the created wisdom brought about in them; and then heaven was made, so that the creature of heaven itself might exist in its own kind.

The same applies to the division or appearance of the waters and the lands; to the natures of trees and plants; to the heavenly lights; and to the living creatures that arose from the waters and the earth.

17. The angels do not see these sensible things merely through bodily sense, as cattle do. If they use such a sense at all, they rather recognize through it what they know better inwardly in the Word of God, by which they are illuminated so that they may live wisely.

There is in them the light that was made first, if we understand spiritual light to have been made on that day.

Just as the principle according to which a creature is made exists prior in the Word of God to the creature itself, so the knowledge of that same principle first comes to be in the intellectual creature that has not been darkened by sin; and thereafter the creature itself is made.

For the angels did not progress toward wisdom as we do, so that they might behold the invisible things of God understood through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20). From the moment they were created, they have enjoyed the holy and devout contemplation of the very eternity of the Word. From that vision they look down upon these things and, according to what they see inwardly, either rightly approve them as made or disapprove them as sins.

18. Nor is it surprising that God first showed His holy angels, formed in the first creation of light, what He was afterward going to create. For they would not have known the understanding of God except insofar as He Himself revealed it. “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor? Or who has first given to Him, and it shall be repaid him? For from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things” (Rom. XI, 34–36). From Him, therefore, the angels learned, when the knowledge of the creature subsequently to be made came to be formed in them, and afterward the creature itself came to be made in its proper kind.

19. Therefore, once the light had been made—in which we understand the rational creature to have been formed from the eternal Light—whenever, in the creation of the other things, we hear, “And God said, Let it be made,” we should understand Scripture’s intention as returning to the eternity of the Word of God. But whenever we hear, “And so it was made,” we should understand that, in the intellectual creature, there came to be the knowledge of the rational principle of the creature to be created, a principle that is in the Word of God [Note: [Col. 0270] Several manuscripts read *conditae* (“created”) rather than *condendae* (“to be created”).], so that in a certain manner it was first made in that nature which, by a kind of prior movement, first knew in the very Word of God that it was to be made. Finally, when we hear repeated the words, “And God made,” we should understand that the creature itself was then made in its proper kind. Further, when we hear, “And God saw that it was good,” we should understand that what had been made pleased the goodness of God, so that what He was pleased should be made might remain according to the measure of its own kind, while the Spirit of God was borne over the water.

## CHAPTER IX — The Form of Heaven

20. It is also customary to ask what form and shape heaven should be believed to have according to our Scriptures. Many people engage in extensive discussions about matters that our authors, with greater prudence, omitted because they would contribute nothing to the blessed life of those who learned them; and, what is worse, they occupy with them much precious time that ought to be devoted to salutary matters. For what does it concern me whether heaven, like a sphere, encloses the earth on every side, with the earth balanced in the middle of the universe, or whether it covers the earth from above on one side, like a disk? But since the authority of Scripture is at issue, for the reason I have mentioned more than once—lest someone, failing to understand the divine utterances, should find in our Books or hear from them something about these matters that appears contrary to the reasoning he has grasped [Note: [Col. 0270] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read *assertionibus* (“assertions”).], and should therefore refuse to believe anything else that they teach, relate, or proclaim for his benefit—it must briefly be said that our authors knew concerning the form of heaven what the truth contains; but that the Spirit of God, who spoke through them, did not wish to teach human beings anything that would contribute nothing to salvation.

[Col. 0271] 21. But, someone may say, how is it not contrary to those who attribute the shape of a sphere to heaven that it is written in our Scriptures, “Who stretches out heaven like a skin” (Ps. CIII, 2)? Let it indeed be contrary, if what they say is false; for what divine authority says is true, rather than what human weakness conjectures. But if perhaps they can prove their view by such arguments that it ought not to be doubted, then it must be demonstrated that what is said among us concerning a skin is not contrary to those true arguments. Otherwise, it will also be contrary to our Scriptures in another passage, where heaven is said to be suspended like a vaulted chamber (Isa. XL, 22, according to the Septuagint). For what is so different and mutually opposed as the flat extension of a skin and the curved convexity of a vaulted chamber? Yet if these two statements must be understood—as indeed they must—in such a way that both are found to agree and not contradict one another, then either of them must likewise be shown not to oppose those arguments, should sound reasoning happen to establish them as true, by which it is taught that heaven is convex on every side in the shape of a sphere, if that is in fact proved.

22. Now the likeness of a vaulted chamber found among us, even when taken literally, does not hinder those who speak of a sphere. For it is rightly believed that Scripture wished to speak of the shape of heaven according to that part which is above us. If, then, heaven is not a sphere, it is a vaulted chamber on the side from which heaven covers the earth; but if it is a sphere, it is a vaulted chamber on every side. Yet what is said of a skin presses the matter more strongly, lest it prove contrary not to the sphere—which may perhaps be a human invention—but to our own vaulted chamber. What I have understood allegorically from this is set out in the thirteenth book of my *Confessions* (ch. 15). Whether, then, heaven stretched out like a skin is to be understood as I explained there, or in some other way, I say this—for the sake of troublesome and excessively exacting interpreters of the literal sense—which, I think, is evident to everyone: perhaps both expressions, “skin” and “vaulted chamber,” can be understood figuratively; but how both can be understood literally must be considered. For if a vaulted chamber is rightly called not only curved but also flat, then surely a skin is extended not only into a plane but also into a rounded hollow. A wineskin, like a bladder, is in fact a skin.

## CHAPTER X — The Movement of Heaven

23. Some of the brethren also raise the question whether heaven stands still or moves. “For if it moves,” they say, “how is it a firmament? But if it stands still, how do the stars, which are believed to be fixed in it, travel around from east to west, while those near the north perform shorter circuits close to the pole—so that heaven appears to rotate like a sphere, if there is another pole hidden from us at the opposite vertex, but like a disk, if there is no other pole?” To them I reply that these matters are investigated by very subtle and laborious reasoning, so that it may truly be perceived whether they are so or not. I have no time now to undertake and examine such investigations, nor should those have time for them whom we wish to instruct for their salvation and for the necessary benefit of holy Church. Let them know this at least: the name “firmament” does not compel us to think that heaven stands still—for it may be understood to have been called firmament not because of standing, but because of firmness, or because it is an impassable boundary between the upper and lower waters. Nor, if truth should persuade us that heaven stands still, are we prevented by the circuits of the stars from understanding this. For even those who investigated these matters with the greatest curiosity and leisure discovered that, even if heaven did not move, everything observed and comprehended in the revolutions of the stars could have occurred if the stars alone were turning [Note: [Col. 0272] Twelve manuscripts read *moverentur* (“were moving”) instead of *verterentur* (“were turning”).].

## CHAPTER XI — On Verses 9 and 10, Where He Explains What Is to Be Understood by the Earth’s Formlessness

24. “And God said, Let the water under heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear. And so it was made; and the water under heaven was gathered into one gathering, and the dry land appeared. And God called the dry land Earth, and He called the gatherings of waters Sea. And God saw that it was good.”

We have already treated this work of God sufficiently in our first volume, because of the need to investigate another matter (Book I, chs. 12 and 13). Here, therefore, we briefly point out that anyone who is not moved to ask when the form of the waters and the earth was created may understand that on this day nothing was done except that these two lower elements were separated.

But whoever asks why light and heaven were made within the days, while water and earth existed outside or before all the days; and why those things were made at God’s word, with God saying, “Let it be made,” whereas these are found to have been separated when God spoke, but not to have been made at God’s command, has something he may understand without endangering the faith. Namely, when Scripture said, before enumerating the days, “The earth was invisible and unformed,” while indicating what sort of earth God had made—for it had already said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”—it wished to suggest by these words nothing other than the formlessness of corporeal matter, choosing to call it by a more customary name rather than a more obscure one.

This is provided that a slow understanding does not slip into separating matter and form in time merely because Scripture separates them in words, attempting to make these two things temporally distinct as well, as though matter had existed first and form had afterward been added to it after an interval of time. God created these things simultaneously and established matter as formed; Scripture, as I have said, referred beforehand to its formlessness by the customary names “earth” or “water.” For although earth and water, by their own qualities, exist as what we see, they are nevertheless nearer to that same formlessness because of their ease of corruption than are the heavenly bodies.

And since, through the enumeration of the days, various things are counted as having been formed from the formless, and Scripture had already narrated that heaven was made from this corporeal matter—whose form differs greatly from earthly things—it did not wish [Note: [Col. 0272] The printed editions read *voluit* (“wished”); all the manuscripts read *noluit* (“did not wish”). We adopt the latter, since the reason is given why the author of Genesis did not relate the formation of water and earth under the words “Let water be made; let earth be made,” as he narrates concerning heaven, “Let the firmament be made.” Compare chapter 13 of the preceding book.] to insert what remained to be formed from it, in the lowest part of the created order, under the words “Let it be made.” This residue was not going to receive a form such as heaven had received, but one already lower and weaker and nearer to formlessness. Therefore, when it says instead, “Let the waters be gathered,” and, “Let the dry land appear,” these two elements received their own familiar and perceptible forms: water, mobile; earth, immobile. Hence “let it be gathered” was said of the former, and “let it appear” of the latter. Water flows with instability; earth is fixed with stability.

## CHAPTER XII — On Verses 11–13: Why It Is Said Separately of the Herbs and Trees, “And So It Was Made,” and So Forth

25. “And God said, Let the earth bring forth vegetation producing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and a fruit-bearing tree producing fruit whose seed is in itself according to its likeness upon the earth. And so it was made. And the earth brought forth vegetation producing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness, and a fruit-bearing tree producing fruit whose seed was in it according to its kind upon the earth. And God saw that it was good. And evening was made, and morning was made: the third day.”

Here we should observe the ordering discretion of the Organizer. Since the creation of herbs and trees is distinct from the form of earth and water, so that they cannot be counted among the elements, it was said of them separately that they should come forth from the earth. The customary formula was also separately applied to them, so that it might be said, “And so it was made,” and then what had been made was repeated. It was likewise separately indicated that God saw that it was good. Nevertheless, because they are joined to and connected with the earth by their fixed roots, He wished these also to belong to the same day.

## CHAPTER XIII — On Verses 14, 15, and Following: Why the Luminaries Were Created on the Fourth Day

26. “And God said, Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven [Note: [Col. 0273] A large number of manuscripts consistently read here and below, “in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine”], so that they may shine upon the earth, for the beginning of day and night, and so that they may divide between day and night; and let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years, and let them be for brightness in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth. And so it was made. And God made two great luminaries: the greater luminary for the beginning of day, and the lesser luminary for the beginning of night; and the stars. And God placed them in the firmament of heaven [Note: [Col. 0273] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read *eas* (“them,” feminine), whereas the manuscripts have *ea* (“them,” neuter], so that they may shine upon the earth, and so that they may be for the beginning of day and night, and so that they may divide between light and darkness. And God saw that it was good. And evening was made, and morning was made: the fourth day.”

On this fourth day we must ask what this ordering means: that water and earth were first made or separated, and that the earth first brought forth vegetation, before the stars were made in heaven. For we cannot say that the better things were selected so that the sequence of the days might be arranged in such a way that the beginning and the middle would stand out as especially ornamented: the fourth is the middle of the seven days. One consideration presents itself: no creature was made on the seventh day. Or perhaps the light of the first day corresponds more closely to the rest of the seventh day, so that the order may be woven together by endings that harmonize in this way, with the lights of heaven standing out from the middle?

But if the first day harmonizes with the seventh, then the second ought also to harmonize with the sixth. What similarity, however, does the firmament of heaven have with a human being made in the image of God? Is it because heaven occupies the whole upper part of the world, while the power of ruling over the whole lower part was granted to the human being? But what shall we do about the cattle and beasts that the earth produced according to their kind on that very sixth day? What comparison can they have with heaven?

27. Or rather, since the formation of the spiritual creature is understood to have first been made under the name of light, it was fitting that the corporeal creature also—that is, this visible world—should be made. It was made in two days on account of its two greatest parts, of which the whole consists: heaven, namely, and earth. This follows the comparison of reason by which the entire spiritual and corporeal creation itself is often called “heaven and earth.” Thus this globe of more turbulent air is also assigned to the earthly part, since it is thickened by moist exhalations. But whatever calm air there is, where windy and stormy movements cannot exist, belongs to the heavenly part.

After this entire mass of corporeal nature had been fashioned—which is wholly in one place, the place where the world has been established—it was fitting that it should be filled with parts within the universe that would be moved from place to place by appropriate motions. Herbs and trees, however, are not of this kind. They are fixed in the earth by their roots; and although they possess the movements of their growth, they do not move from their proper places by their own efforts. Where they are fixed, there they are nourished and grow. For this reason they belong more to the earth than to the kinds of things that move in the waters and upon the earth.

Since, therefore, two days were assigned to the establishment of the visible world—that is, heaven and earth—it remains that the other three days be assigned to those mobile and visible parts that are created within it. And since, just as heaven was made first, it must also first be adorned with its corresponding parts, on the fourth day the stars were made. By shining upon the earth, they would illuminate the lower habitation as well, so that its inhabitants would not be brought into a dark dwelling.

And because the frail bodies of the lower inhabitants are restored by rest following their activities, it was arranged that, as the sun made its circuit, they would enjoy the alternation of day and night, corresponding to the alternation of sleeping and waking. Night, moreover, would not remain without adornment: by the light of the moon and stars it would comfort human beings, who often have need to work at night as well, and it would provide a moderated sufficiency for certain animals that cannot endure the light of the sun.

## CHAPTER XIV — How the Luminaries Are for Signs and Seasons, for Days and Years

28. But who does not see how obscurely the statement has been made, “And let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years,” if times are said to have begun on the fourth day, as though the preceding three days could have passed without time? Who, then, can penetrate in thought how those three days passed before times began, which are said to begin on the fourth day? Or did those days pass at all?

Or was the day named in relation to the form of the thing made, and night in relation to its privation, so that, before matter had been formed, the matter from which the remaining things were to be formed was called night? In this way, even amid formed things, the formlessness of matter can nevertheless be understood as existing in mutability itself [Col. 0275]—for it cannot be distinguished by intervals as though it were more remote in place or earlier in time.

Or rather, was mutability itself in the thing made and formed—that is, the possibility, so to speak, of failing—called night, because it is present in made things even if they do not change, in that they are capable of changing? And was evening and morning named not as though through the passing and arrival of time, but through a certain boundary by which it is understood how far the proper mode [Note: [Col. 0275] Almost all manuscripts read *propriae* (“of its own nature”) rather than *proprius* (“proper”).] of one nature extends and from where the beginning of another nature consequently arises? Or is some other account of these words to be investigated more carefully?

29. Who can easily break into so great a secret? And what signs does he mean when, speaking of the stars, he says, “And let them be for signs”? For he does not mean those signs whose observation is an act of vanity, but useful signs, necessary for the purposes of this life—signs that sailors observe in navigation, or that all people observe in order to anticipate the qualities of the air through summer and winter and the temperate conditions of autumn and spring.

And surely by “seasons” he means those that are produced through the stars, not intervals of delay, but changes in the conditions of this atmosphere. For if some bodily or spiritual movement preceded the establishment of these luminaries, so that something passed from future expectation through the present into the past, it could not have been without time. And who can maintain that there was no time except from the beginning when the stars were created?

But the definite hours, days, and years that we ordinarily know would not exist without the movements of the stars. Therefore, if we understand “seasons,” “days,” and “years” in this way [Note: [Col. 0275] The Louvain edition reads “as certain divisions,” omitting *tempora* (“seasons/times”), which is found in the other books.]—as certain divisions that we calculate by clocks, or divisions most clearly marked in heaven, when the sun rises from the east to its midday height and then declines from there again toward the west, so that afterward the moon or some star may be observed to emerge from the east immediately after sunset; and when it reaches the middle height of heaven, it indicates midnight, setting, as morning occurs with the returning sun; if “days” means the complete circuit of the sun from east to east [Note: [Col. 0275] The printed editions read “to the west.” The manuscripts, more correctly, read “to the east.”]; and if “years” means either the sun’s familiar circuits—not when it returns to the east, as it does daily, but when it returns to the same places among the stars, which it does only after 365 days and six hours, that is, one quarter of a whole day, which portion, taken four times, requires the insertion of one day, called by the Romans a leap day, so that it may return to the same circuit—or even longer and more hidden years, for larger years are said to be completed according to the periods of other stars—then, if we understand seasons, days, and years in this way, no one doubts that they are produced by the stars and luminaries.

The wording, however, leaves it uncertain whether the statement, “Let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years,” pertains to all the stars, or whether “signs and seasons” pertain to the others, while “days and years” pertain only to the sun.

## CHAPTER XV — What Kind of Moon Was Created

30. Many people also inquire very talkatively what kind of moon was made [Col. 0276]—if only, while inquiring, they would speak as investigators rather than attempting to teach! They say that it was made full because it was not fitting for God to make anything imperfect among the stars on the day when Scripture says that the stars were made.

Those who resist them say: “Then it ought to have been called the first moon, not the fourteenth; for who begins counting in that way?” I, however, stand between these positions in such a way that I assert neither, but plainly say that whether God made the first moon or the full moon, He made it perfect.

For God is the author and creator of these very natures. Whatever a thing gradually brings forth and unfolds in the course of nature, at the appropriate times, it already contained secretly beforehand—not in the form or mass of its body, but in the rational principle of its nature [Note: [Col. 0276] Three manuscripts read, “not in the body, but nevertheless in the power and rational principle of its nature.”]. Otherwise, perhaps a tree that during winter is empty of fruit and stripped of leaves should be called imperfect at that time; or perhaps that nature was imperfect even in its beginnings, when it had not yet produced any fruit. Yet this could not rightly be said merely of the tree, nor even of its seed, in which all the things that later emerge in the course of time lie hidden in invisible ways.

Although, if it were said that God had made something imperfect which He would afterward perfect Himself, what fault would there be in such a view? It would rightly be displeasing only if what had been begun by Him were said to have been perfected by another.

31. Those who do not complain about the earth that God made—when, in the beginning, God made heaven and earth—because it was invisible and unformed and afterward, on the third day, was made visible and ordered: why do they create shadows of questions concerning the moon?

Or if they understand what is said of the earth not as referring to an interval of time, since God created matter together with the things themselves [Note: [Col. 0276] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “God created the things themselves together with matter.”], but as referring to the arrangement of the narrative, why do they not observe, in the case of something that can also be seen with the eyes, that the moon possesses a complete body and is perfect in all its roundness even when it shines with horn-shaped light, whether it is beginning to shine upon the earth or is ceasing to shine?

If its light therefore increases, reaches fullness, or diminishes, it is not the luminary itself that changes, but that which is kindled. If, however, it always shines from one part of its little sphere, but appears to grow as it turns that part toward the earth until it has turned the whole of it—which occurs from the first to the fourteenth day—then it is always full, but does not always appear so to the inhabitants of earth.

The same reasoning applies if it is illuminated by the rays of the sun. For even then, when it is near the sun, it cannot appear except with luminous horns, since the remaining part, which is illuminated throughout its circle, is not turned toward the earth so that it can be seen, except when it is opposite the sun, so that the whole of what is illuminated in it appears to the earth.

32. There are nevertheless some who say that they do not believe the moon was first made by God as a fourteenth-day moon because it should be believed to have been made full, but because the words of God in Scripture say that the moon was made for the beginning of night. It appears at the beginning of night when it is full; at other times, however, it begins to be visible during the day before fullness, and as the night progresses it appears at an increasingly later point as it wanes.

But whoever understands “for the beginning of night” to mean nothing other than authority or dominion—for the Greek word indicates this more clearly when it says *archēn* (ἀρχήν, “beginning” or “authority”), and the Psalms state it more explicitly: “The sun for authority over the day, the moon and stars for authority over the night” (Ps. CXXXV, 8–9)—is not compelled to begin counting from the fourteenth day, or to believe that the moon was made first without being the first moon.

## CHAPTER XVI — Whether the Stars Shine Equally

33. It is also customary to ask whether these visible luminaries of heaven—that is, the sun, moon, and stars—shine equally, but appear to our eyes with greater or lesser brightness because they are at different distances from the earth.

Those who say this do not doubt, in the case of the moon, that it shines less brightly than the sun, by which they also say that it is illuminated. They dare to say that many stars are equal to the sun or even larger, but appear small because they are farther away.

For our part, perhaps it may be enough, however this matter stands, that the stars were created by God the artisan. Yet we hold to the statement made by apostolic authority: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. XV, 41).

But they may still say—even without resisting the Apostle—“They differ in glory, but only in relation to the eyes of earthly beings”; or, “Because the Apostle was speaking with reference to the likeness of those who rise again, who will not be one thing to the eyes and another in themselves, the stars differ in glory in themselves as well, but some are nevertheless larger than the sun.”

Let them decide how they can attribute such great authority to the sun that they say it overcomes by its rays certain stars—and indeed the principal stars, to which they pray more than to the others—and that it can hold them back and force them to move backward from their proper course. For it is not plausible that larger stars, or even stars equal to it, could be overcome by the force of its rays.

Or if they assert that the stars of the signs, or the stars near the north, are larger and that they suffer no such thing from the sun, why do they honor them more as they travel through the signs? Why do they call them the rulers of the signs? Even if someone maintains that the backward movements of those stars—or perhaps their delays—are not caused by the sun but by other, more hidden causes, it is nevertheless plainly evident from their books that they attribute supreme power to the sun in their delusions, by which they deviate from the truth and suppose that the power of fate governs events.

34. Let those who are alien to the Father who is in heaven say what they wish about heaven. For us, however, to investigate something more subtle concerning the distances and sizes of the stars, and to devote to such an inquiry time that is necessary for more serious and better matters, is neither useful nor fitting.

We more readily believe that the two luminaries commended by Holy Scripture are larger than the others: “And God made two great luminaries.” Yet they are not equal. For after placing them above the others, Scripture consequently says that they differ from one another. It says, “The greater luminary for the beginning of day, and the lesser luminary for the beginning of night.”

Surely they will at least concede this to our eyes: it is evident that these shine upon the earth more brightly than the others; that the day is not bright except by the light of the sun; and that, even when all the stars appear, the night does not shine as it does when the moon is present.

## CHAPTER XVII — Against the Genethliacs

[Col. 0278]

35. As for the fates of the stars, let us utterly reject from the soundness of our faith all their various sophistries and what they call astrological “results” (*apotelesmata*, ἀποτελέσματα), as though they were experimental demonstrations of the art of astrology. For by such arguments they also attempt to take away from us the grounds for prayer, and in their impious perversity, concerning evil deeds that are rightly condemned, they introduce the claim that God, the creator of the stars, should be accused rather than the human being responsible for crimes [Note: [Col. 0278] The printed editions read, “human crimes.” The manuscripts read, “the human being responsible for crimes.”].

Let them also hear from their own philosophers that our souls are not by nature subject even to bodily things, much less to heavenly bodies. And that those superior bodies are not more powerful than earthly bodies in the matters they themselves discuss, let them at least recognize from this: when many bodies of different kinds—whether animals, herbs, or shrubs—are sown at the same moment of time, and innumerably many are born at the same moment, not only in different places but even in the same places on earth, such differences occur in their development, actions, and experiences that, if these people consider the matter, they truly “lose the stars,” as the saying goes.

36. What could be more foolish and dull than to say, when they are refuted by these facts, that the fatal influence of the stars applies only to human beings who are subject to them? Yet even in the case of human beings they are refuted by twins, who, although they live differently, have different fortunes and misfortunes, and die differently, usually receive the same constellations.

For even if there was some difference when they were brought forth from the womb, in some cases the difference is nevertheless so slight that it cannot be grasped by these people’s calculations. The hand of Jacob, who followed his brother while they were being born, was found holding the heel of the brother who preceded him; they were born so closely together that it seemed as though one infant, twice as long, were being born (Gen. XXV, 25).

Their so-called constellations certainly could not have been different in any way. What, then, could be more absurd than for an astrologer, observing those constellations, at the same horoscope and under the same moon, to say that one of them was loved by his mother and the other was not loved? If he said something else, he would certainly speak falsely; but if he said this, he would speak truly, though not according to the foolish little songs of his books.

If they refuse to believe this history because it comes from our Scriptures, can they nevertheless erase the nature of things? Since they claim that they are not deceived if they discover the hour of conception, let them at least, as human beings, not disdain to consider the conception of twins.

37. Therefore, when these people say things that are true, it must be admitted that they speak by some exceedingly hidden impulse, which human minds undergo without knowing it. When this occurs in order to deceive human beings, it is the activity of seducing spirits. They are permitted to know certain truths concerning temporal matters, partly because of the sharpness of a more subtle perception, partly because they are strong in more subtle bodies, partly because of their more practiced experience resulting from their very great length of life, and partly because the holy angels reveal to them what they themselves learn from almighty God—even at His command—who distributes human merits with the unsearchable sincerity of His justice [Col. 0279].

At times, however, those same wicked spirits also foretell, as though by divination, what they themselves are going to do. Therefore, whether they are astrologers or any other impious diviners—especially when they say what is true—the good Christian must beware of them, lest, through fellowship with demons, they entangle the deceived soul in some pact of association.

## CHAPTER XVIII — The Difficulty Concerning the Stars: Whether They Are Governed and Animated by Spirits

38. It is also customary to ask whether these visible luminaries of heaven are merely bodies, or whether they have certain spirits as their rulers; and, if they do, whether they are also given life by them, as flesh is animated by the souls of animals, or whether their spirits are present alone, without any commingling.

Although this may not easily be grasped at present, I nevertheless believe that, as we proceed in treating the Scriptures, more suitable passages may arise in which, according to the rules of holy authority, we may be permitted concerning this matter—not to demonstrate something certain, but at least to believe.

For now, however, while always preserving the moderation of reverent seriousness, we should not rashly believe anything concerning an obscure matter, lest perhaps we come to hate what the truth later reveals—even though it could in no way be contrary to the holy books, whether of the Old or the New Testament—because of our attachment to our error.

Now let us proceed to the third book of our work.

# BOOK THREE

## On Verse 20: “And God Said, Let the Waters Bring Forth,” and the Remaining Verses to the End of the First Chapter

[Col. 0279]

## CHAPTER I — The Production of Animals from the Waters Is Narrated Before That of Animals from the Earth, Because Water Is the Element Nearest to Air, and Air to Heaven

1. “And God said, Let the waters bring forth creeping things having living souls, and winged creatures above the earth, according to the firmament of heaven. And so it was made. And God made the great sea creatures and every creeping animal, which the waters brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged creature according to its kind. And God saw that they were good, and God blessed them, saying, Increase and multiply, and fill the waters in the sea, and let the winged creatures multiply upon the earth. And evening was made, and morning was made: the fifth day.”

Now, in the lower part of the world, those things that are moved by the spirit of life are made, and first those of the waters, since water is the element nearest in quality to air. For air is so close to this heaven in which the luminaries are situated that it too has received the name “heaven,” although I do not know whether it can also be called the firmament.

The heavens are spoken of in the plural in reference to one and the same thing, which is called one heaven. For while in this book heaven is spoken of in the singular as that which divides the waters above from those below, in that psalm it says, “And you waters that are above the heavens, praise the name of the Lord.” And if we rightly understand “heavens of heavens” as the sidereal heavens and “heavens of air” as the lower heavens—like the higher in relation to the lower—we also find these in the same psalm, where it says, “Praise Him, heavens of heavens” (Ps. CXLVIII, 4–5).

It is sufficiently clear that this air is called not only heaven but also heavens, just as earths are spoken of in the plural, while nothing other than what is singularly called earth is signified when we say “the globe of the earths” or “the globe of the earth.”

## CHAPTER II — That the Heavens of Air Perished in the Flood, and That the Air Passed into the Nature of Water

2. We also read in one of those letters called canonical that these heavens of air once perished in the flood (II Pet. III, 6). For that moist substance, which had accumulated to such an extent that it rose fifteen cubits above the peaks of the highest mountains (Gen. VII, 20), could not have reached the stars.

But because it had filled all or nearly all the space of this moister air in which birds fly, that letter says that the heavens which had existed perished [Col. 0280]. I do not know how this can be understood unless the quality of this denser air was transformed into the nature of water. Otherwise, those heavens did not then perish but were raised higher when water occupied their place.

Thus, in accordance with the authority of that letter, we more readily believe that they perished and that others were stored up, as it says there (II Pet. III, 5–7), namely, after the exhalations had been thinned [Note: [Col. 0280] Almost all manuscripts read *extentis* (“having been extended”) rather than *extenuatis* (“having been thinned”)] than that they were raised so high that the nature of the higher heaven had to yield its place to them.

3. It was therefore fitting that, in creating the inhabitants of this lower part of the world—which is often referred to in its entirety by the name “earth”—animals should first be produced from the waters, and afterward from the earth. For the air is so similar to water that it is shown to be enriched by its exhalations: it produces the breath of storms, that is, wind; gathers clouds; and is able to support the flight of birds. Therefore, even if a certain secular poet spoke truly when he wrote, “Olympus rises above the clouds, / and the heights possess peace” (Lucan, *Book 2*), because it is said that at the summit of Olympus the air is so thin that it is neither shadowed by clouds nor disturbed by wind, cannot support birds in flight, and cannot nourish human beings who might happen to ascend there with the breath of denser air, as they are accustomed to be nourished by this air—nevertheless, that too is air, diffused from a neighboring quality of water; and for that reason it too is believed to have been transformed into a watery nature at the time of the Flood. For we must not suppose that it took anything from the spaces of the starry heaven, since the water had risen above even all the highest mountains.

## CHAPTER III — On the Opinions Concerning the Transformation of the Elements. The Air Was Not Omitted in the Genesis Narrative

4. Yet there is considerable disagreement concerning the transformation of the elements, even among those who have examined these matters with the greatest subtlety and idle diligence. Some say that everything can be changed and transformed into everything else; others maintain that each element has something wholly proper to itself, which in no way changes into the quality of another element. Perhaps, if the Lord wills, we shall discuss this more carefully in its proper place. For the present discussion, however, I have thought it necessary to mention these matters so that we may understand that the order of things was preserved: animals of the waters had to be narrated as created before animals of the earth.

5. Nor should we suppose in any way that any element of this world was omitted in this Scripture, since it is generally accepted that the world consists of four well-known elements. Here heaven, water, and earth appear to be mentioned, while air is passed over in silence. For it is customary in our Scriptures either to call the world by the names “heaven and earth,” or sometimes to add “and the sea.” Air, then, is understood either to belong to heaven, if there are in its upper regions spaces of complete tranquility and calm; or to belong to earth, because of this turbulent and dark region, which is enriched by moist exhalation, although it too is often called by the name “heaven.” Consequently, it was not written, “Let the waters produce reptiles possessing living souls, and let the air produce winged creatures flying over the earth”; rather, both kinds of animals are narrated as having been produced from the waters. Whatever, therefore, is watery—whether it is fluid and waves in liquid motion, or has been thinned and suspended in vaporous form—belongs in either case to the watery nature, so that the former appears to have been assigned to reptiles possessing living souls, and the latter to winged creatures.

## CHAPTER IV — The Five Senses Referred to the Four Elements

6. Accordingly, there are also those who, with the most subtle consideration, distinguish these five most evident bodily senses according to the four customary elements, saying that the eyes belong to fire and the ears to air. They attribute the senses of smell and taste to the watery nature: smell, indeed, to those moist exhalations by which this region, in which birds fly, is thickened; and taste to those flowing and substantial fluids. For whatever has a flavor in the mouth is mixed with the moisture of the mouth so that it may be tasted, even if it appears to have been dry when it was received. Fire, however, penetrates everything in order to produce motion in it. Moisture freezes through the deprivation of heat; and although the other elements can become hot, fire cannot become cold. It is more easily extinguished, so that it ceases to be fire, than it remains cold or becomes warmer through contact with something cold.

[Note: The printed editions read *frigescere* (“become cold”); most manuscripts read *fervescere* (“become hot”).]

Touch, which is the fifth of the senses, corresponds more closely to the earthly element. Accordingly, touch, which is especially associated with the whole body of the animal, itself chiefly derived from earth, perceives whatever is touched. They also say that nothing can be seen without fire, nor touched without earth. Thus all the elements are present in all things, but each thing has received its name from the element that it possesses in greater measure. The sense is dulled through deprivation of heat when the body becomes excessively cold because the motion that heat produces in the body grows sluggish, while fire affects air, air affects moisture, and moisture affects earthly things; the more subtle elements penetrate the denser ones.

7. The more subtle anything is in bodily nature, the closer it is to spiritual nature—although the difference of kind is very great, since one is body and the other is not.

## CHAPTER V — How the Faculty of Sensation in the Five Senses Relates Differently to the Four Elements

Since sensation belongs not to the body but to the soul through the body, one may argue with precision, according to the diversity of bodily elements, that the senses are distributed through the body. Yet the soul, in which the faculty of sensation resides, is not bodily; through the more subtle body it activates the power of sensation.

The movement therefore begins in all the senses from the subtlety of fire, but does not reach the same point in all of them. In sight, restrained heat reaches as far as light. In hearing, the heat of fire penetrates as far as the more fluid air. In smell, it passes through pure air and reaches the moist exhalation from which this denser atmosphere subsists. In taste, it passes through this as well and reaches the more substantial moisture. Once this too has been penetrated and traversed, when it reaches earthly heaviness, it produces the final sense, that of touch.

## CHAPTER VI — The Element of Air Was Not Omitted by the Writer of Genesis

8. The writer who, when introducing the creation of visible things that move within the world according to the elements, narrated first the heavenly luminaries, then the animals of the waters, and finally those of the earth, was therefore not ignorant of the natures of the elements or of their order. He did not omit air; rather, any spaces belonging to the purest and most tranquil air, where birds are said to be unable to fly, are joined to the higher heaven and, in Scripture’s use of the name “heaven,” are understood to belong to the upper part of the world.

Thus the name “earth” universally signifies the whole region beginning from the point where things descend downward: “fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind, and all the abysses,” until one reaches the dry land that is called “earth” by its proper name. That higher air, whether because it belongs to the heavenly part of the world or because it has no visible inhabitant—the sort of inhabitants of which the narrator is now speaking—was neither omitted when heaven was named nor counted among the elements in the creation of animals.

This lower air, however, which receives the moist exhalations of sea and land and is in a sense thickened so as to support birds, receives animals only from the waters. For its moisture carries the bodies of birds, which in flight rely upon their wings, just as fish swim by means of certain fins of their own.

## CHAPTER VII — It Is Not Without Reason That Flying Creatures Are Said to Have Been Created from the Waters

9. The Spirit of God, who was present with the writer, therefore wisely says that the flying creatures were produced from the waters. Their nature has been allotted a divided region: a lower region in the flowing wave and an upper region in the moving air—the former assigned to swimmers, the latter to flyers.

We likewise see that two senses corresponding to this element have been given to animals: smell for investigating vapors, and taste for investigating liquids. The fact that we also perceive waters and winds by touch is due to the solid element of earth, which is mixed into all the elements; but it is perceived more strongly in these denser elements, so that they can even be handled by touch.

[Note: Five manuscripts read, “For the nature of the waters.” The same reading is found in the Amiatine and Erfurt manuscripts.]

For this reason, too, these two regions of the world are generally included under the name “earth,” as that psalm shows. It enumerates all the upper things beginning with, “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” and all the lower things beginning with, “Praise the Lord from the earth.” There “the storm wind” and “all the abysses” are named, as well as that fire which burns the one who touches it (Psalm 148:1–8), because it arises from earthly and moist movements in such a way that it is continually transformed into another element.

Although fire indicates its upward inclination by striving upward according to its nature, it cannot escape into the higher, heavenly tranquility. Overcome by a great quantity of air and transformed into it, it is extinguished. Thus, in this more corruptible and sluggish region of things, it is driven by turbulent movements, both to moderate its intensity and for the uses and terrors of mortals.

10. Since, then, even the sense of touch—which properly belongs to earth—can perceive both the waves of waters and the breaths of winds, the bodies of aquatic animals themselves also feed on earthly things, and birds especially do so. They rest on the earth and propagate their offspring there; for the portion of moisture exhaled in vaporous form also extends above the earth.

Accordingly, after Scripture had said, “Let the waters produce reptiles possessing living souls,” it added, “and flying creatures,” and then said, “over the earth, according to the firmament of heaven.” Here what had previously seemed obscure can appear somewhat more clearly.
