It did not say, “in the firmament of heaven,” as it says concerning the luminaries; rather, it says “flying over the earth, according to the firmament of heaven,” that is, “near the firmament of heaven.” For this dark and moist region in which birds fly is adjacent to that region where they cannot fly, which, by reason of its tranquility and rest, properly belongs to the firmament of heaven.

Birds therefore fly in heaven, but in that heaven which the psalm also includes under the name “earth.” For this reason, in many places flying creatures are called “birds of heaven.” Yet they do not fly in the firmament, but according to the firmament.

## CHAPTER VIII — Why Fish Are Called “Reptiles Possessing Living Souls”

11. Some think that fish are called not “a living soul” but “reptiles possessing living souls” because of the sluggishness of their senses. But if they were so called for that reason, birds would have been given the name “living soul.” Since the flying creatures too are called “flying creatures,” just as the others are called “reptiles,” with “possessing living souls” understood, we must admit, I think, that the expression was used as though it said: “The reptiles or flying creatures that are among living souls.” One might similarly say, “the ignoble among human beings,” meaning all those who are ignoble among human beings.

Although there are also terrestrial animals that crawl upon the earth, most of them move by means of feet, and perhaps as few crawl on land as walk in the waters.

12. Others have thought that fish were called not “a living soul” but “reptiles possessing living souls” because they have no memory and no form of life that is, as it were, closer to reason. But their limited experience deceives them. Some have written about many remarkable things they were able to observe in fishponds. Even if they happened to write falsehoods, however, it is absolutely certain that fish possess memory. I have discovered this by experience myself, and those who can and wish to do so may test it.

There is a certain large spring at Bulla Regia, almost full of fish. People customarily look down into it from above and throw something to the fish, which either rush together to seize it for themselves or fight among themselves to snatch it away. Accustomed to this food, when people walk along the edge of the spring, the fish too gather and swim back and forth with them, waiting for something to be thrown, since they perceive the people’s presence.

It therefore does not seem to me that aquatic animals were called “reptiles” without reason, just as birds were called “flying creatures.” For if either a complete lack of memory or a duller sense had disqualified fish from bearing the name “living souls,” it would certainly have been applied to flying creatures, whose life is plainly before our eyes: they possess memory, are talkative, and are most skillful in building nests and raising their young.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “is memorably talkative.”]

## CHAPTER IX — How Certain Philosophers Assigned Animals to Each Element

13. I am not unaware that certain philosophers distributed animals among the elements in such a way that they called terrestrial not only those that crawl and walk upon the earth, but also birds, because they too rest on the earth when fatigued by flying. They called demons aerial animals; heavenly animals, gods—some of whom we call luminaries and some angels.

They assign fish and creatures of their own kind to the waters, so that no element may be without its animals. But it is as though the earth were not beneath the waters, or as though they could prove that fish do not rest upon it and recover their strength for swimming, just as birds recover their strength for flying. And even if fish perhaps do this less often, because water is stronger than air for carrying bodies, so that it bears even terrestrial animals when they swim—whether taught by practice, as human beings, or by nature, as quadrupeds and serpents—this does not alter the point.

If they think otherwise because fish have no feet, then seals do not belong to the waters, nor snakes and snails to the earth. The former have feet, while these latter creatures, though entirely without feet, not only rest on the earth but scarcely ever or never leave it.

Dragons, however, although without feet, are said both to rest in caves and to rise into the air. Although they are not easily known, writings—not only ours but also those of the Gentiles—have by no means been silent about this class of animals.

## CHAPTER X — Even If Demons Are Aerial Animals, Nothing Is Taken Away from Scripture’s Teaching That Flying Creatures Were Produced from the Waters. Winds, Thunder, Clouds, Rain, Snow, Hail, and Clear Weather

14. Therefore, even if demons are aerial animals, since they exist through the nature of aerial bodies and consequently are not dissolved by death—for the element that is more suited to acting than to being acted upon prevails in them—this does not conflict with our Scripture’s indication that flying creatures were produced not from air but from the waters.

There are two elements placed below—water and earth—and one placed above—the starry fire. The elements are distributed so that two are suited to being acted upon, moisture and soil, while the other two are suited to acting, air and fire. If these things are so, this distinction does not hinder our Scripture, which indicates that flying creatures were produced from the waters, because a region of thinner moisture, exhaled and spread into the air, was assigned to flying creatures.

Air extends from the boundary of the luminous heaven down to the fluid waters and exposed earth. Yet moist exhalations do not darken its entire extent; they reach only as far as the point from which earth too begins to be named, according to the psalm in which it is said, “Praise the Lord from the earth” (Psalm 148:7). The higher part of the air, because of its pure tranquility, is joined in common peace to the heaven bordering upon it and is called by its name.

Perhaps it was in this region that the angels who transgressed with their prince—now the devil, then an archangel—were situated before their transgression. For some among our people do not think that they were celestial or supercelestial angels. It is therefore not surprising if, after their sin, they were thrust into this darkness, where there is nevertheless air, thinly woven with moisture. When this moisture is disturbed, it produces winds; when stirred more violently, fires and thunder; when drawn together, clouds; when thickened, rain; when clouds freeze, snow; when thicker clouds freeze with greater turbulence, hail; and when spread out, clear weather—all through hidden commands and by the work of God, who governs everything he created from the highest to the lowest.

Accordingly, when that psalm had mentioned fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm wind, so that no one might think that such things occur and move without divine providence, it immediately added, “which fulfill his word” (ibid., verse 8).

15. If those transgressors, before they transgressed, possessed celestial bodies, it is likewise no wonder if, as a punishment, these were transformed into an aerial quality, so that they could now suffer something from fire, that is, from the element of the higher nature. They were not even permitted to occupy the upper and purer regions of the air, but were confined to these dark regions, which, in accordance with their nature, serve them as a kind of prison until the time of judgment.

If anything more needs to be investigated carefully concerning these transgressing angels, another passage of Scripture will be more appropriate. For the present, it is enough to say that, if these turbulent and stormy regions can support aerial bodies because the nature of the air extends as far as the waters and the earth,

[Note: The editions read *porrecta*; we emend to *porrectam* on manuscript authority.]

they can also support birds, which were produced from the waters, because of the waters’ subtle vapors.

These vapors are inserted in vaporous form into the same air that surrounds the waters and the earth and is therefore assigned to the lowest and earthly region; they weave themselves through the air, which, weighed down by the chills of night, also drips with clear dew. When the cold is more intense, they whiten further into brighter frost.

## CHAPTER XI — The Meaning of Verses 24 and 25, Where the Various Kinds of Animals Created from the Earth Are Discussed

16. “And God said, ‘Let the earth produce a living soul according to its kind: quadrupeds, reptiles, and beasts of the earth according to their kind, and cattle according to their kind.’ And it was so. And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kind, and cattle according to their kind, and every reptile of the earth according to its kind. And God saw that they were good.”

It was now fitting that the other part—the part properly called earth, the lowest region of this place, which Scripture elsewhere embraces universally under the name “earth,” together with all the abysses and the misty air—should be adorned with its animals.

The kinds of animals that the word of God caused the earth to produce are clear enough. But because “cattle” and “beasts” are often used to mean all animals lacking reason, it is rightly asked which creatures Scripture now specifically calls beasts and which it calls cattle.

As for crawling or creeping terrestrial creatures, there is no doubt that it intended all serpents to be understood.

[Note: Several manuscripts read *repentes*, “creeping creatures.”]

Although serpents can also be called beasts, the name “cattle” is not customarily applied to them. Again, lions, leopards, tigers, wolves, foxes, dogs, monkeys, and the other animals of that kind are customarily called beasts. The name “cattle,” however, is more suitably applied to animals used by human beings, whether for assisting with labor, such as oxen and horses and similar animals, or for wool production—or, as the manuscripts generally read, “for wool-making”—or for food, such as sheep and swine.

17. What, then, are the quadrupeds? Although all these creatures, apart from certain serpentine animals, walk on four feet, unless Scripture wished certain creatures to be understood specifically by this name, it would not have mentioned quadrupeds here as well, even though it says nothing of them in the repetition.

Were deer, does, wild asses, and boars specifically called quadrupeds because they cannot be grouped with those beasts among which lions are found—for they are similar to cattle, yet are not under human care—as though these were the remaining animals to which this general name was assigned, along with many others, because of the number of their feet, but with a special meaning?

Or, because the phrase “according to their kind” is said three times, does it invite us to attend to three particular classes?

First, “according to their kind,” quadrupeds and reptiles: here, I think, the creatures called quadrupeds are those belonging to the class of reptiles, such as lizards, geckos, and anything of that sort. For this reason the name quadrupeds is not repeated in the later account, since it may have been included under the term reptiles. Hence the text does not simply say “reptiles,” but adds “all the reptiles of the earth.” “Of the earth,” because there are also reptiles of the waters; and “all,” so that those creatures that also move by means of four feet may be understood there—the creatures previously designated specifically by the name quadrupeds.

The beasts of which it likewise says “according to their kind” are whatever is fierce with its mouth or even with its claws, excepting serpents. The cattle of which it says “according to their kind” for the third time are those that tear neither with mouth nor claws, but either with horns or not even with these.

As I said earlier, the breadth of the name quadrupeds can readily be recognized from the number of feet itself, and the name cattle or beasts sometimes includes every irrational animal. The term “wild animals” likewise commonly has the same force in Latin. Nevertheless, we must not neglect to consider how these names—which were not placed in this passage of Scripture without reason—can also be distinguished by a specific classification, something that can easily be observed in everyday speech.

## CHAPTER XII — What “According to Its Kind” Means When Said of Certain Creatures, but Not of Man

18. The reader is also rightly prompted to ask whether the phrase “according to its kind” is used randomly and almost accidentally, or according to some reason—as though kinds had existed previously, when the creatures were first narrated as created—or whether their kind is to be understood in the higher principles, namely the spiritual principles according to which lower things are created.

[Note: In most and best manuscripts, *narrarentur* (“were narrated”) is read.]

But if that were the case, the phrase would also be used of light, heaven, the waters and the earth, and the luminaries of heaven. For what of these lacks an eternal and unchangeable principle existing in the very Wisdom of God, which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1)?

The phrase begins to be used, however, of herbs and trees and continues through these terrestrial animals. For even with respect to the creatures made from the waters, although it was not said in the first account, it was said in the repetition: “And God made the great sea creatures and every living soul of the reptiles which the waters brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged creature according to its kind.”

19. Is it because these creatures arose in such a way that other creatures would be born from them, preserving the form of their origin through succession, that they are said to be “according to their kind,” on account of the propagation of offspring, through which they were created to continue?

But why is it said not only of herbs and trees, “according to their kind,” but also “according to their likeness,” when animals, whether of the waters or of the earth, likewise reproduce according to their likeness? Perhaps, because likeness follows kind, Scripture did not wish to repeat it everywhere. Nor did it repeat “seed” everywhere, although seed exists in herbs and trees as well as in animals, though not in all animals.

For it has been observed that certain creatures arise from the waters or the earth in such a way that they have no sex; and therefore their seed is not in them but in the elements from which they arise.

“According to their kind,” then, refers to the power of seed and to the likeness of those succeeding those who depart.

[Note: Thirteen manuscripts read, “of those succeeding those who have succeeded.”]

Nothing was created in such a way that it would exist only once, either continuing forever or departing without anything succeeding it.

20. Why, then, was it not said of man as well, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness, according to his kind,” since the propagation of the human race is evident?

Is it because God had not made man in such a way that he would die if he wished to keep the commandment, and therefore no successor to one departing was necessary? But after sin he was compared with senseless cattle and made like them (Psalm 48:13), so that now the children of this age beget and are begotten, allowing the race of mortals to continue through succession.

What, then, does that blessing after the creation of man mean: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” which could certainly be accomplished by begetting? Or should nothing be rashly said about this until we reach the passage of Scripture where these matters must be investigated and treated more carefully?

For the present it may perhaps be enough to say that “according to its kind” was not spoken of man because one man was made, from whom the woman too was made. There were not many kinds of human beings, as there are kinds of herbs, trees, fish, flying creatures, serpents, cattle, and beasts. Thus we may understand the expression “according to its kind” as though it said “by kinds,” distinguishing creatures that are similar to one another and belong to a single origin of seed from the rest.

## CHAPTER XIII — Why the Blessing Was Given to Aquatic Creatures Alone, as to Man. The Function of Begetting

21. It is also asked what the aquatic animals had done to deserve so much from the Creator that they alone were blessed, as human beings were. For God also blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea, and let the flying creatures multiply upon the earth.”

Was it necessary to say this of one class of creatures so that it might consequently be understood of the others that increase through generation? If so, it would first have been said of the first thing of that kind created, namely the herb and the tree.

Or did he perhaps judge creatures that had no desire to propagate offspring and reproduced without any sensation unworthy of the words of blessing, “Increase and multiply”? Wherever such a desire existed, he first spoke these words, so that they might also be understood as applying to terrestrial animals even though they were not repeated there.

It was necessary, however, to repeat this concerning man, lest anyone should say that there was any sin in the function of begetting children, as there is in lust—whether the lust of fornication or the excessive abuse of marriage itself.

## CHAPTER XIV — The Creation of Insects

22. There is also a question concerning certain very small animals: were they created in the first ordering of things, or did they arise from the subsequent corruptions of mortal things?

For many of them are generated from the defects, excretions, or exhalations of living bodies, or from the decay of corpses. Some arise from the corruption of wood and plants, and some from the corruption of fruits. We cannot rightly say of all these that God is not their creator.

For each possesses a certain beauty of its own nature, so that the thoughtful observer finds greater wonder in them and offers more abundant praise to the omnipotent craftsman who made all things in wisdom (Psalm 103:24). His wisdom, extending from end to end and arranging everything sweetly (Wisdom 8:1), does not leave even those latest things in the order of creation that dissolve according to their kind, whose dissolution we dread as a consequence of our mortal condition, without form. Rather, he creates animals that are tiny in body but keen in sense, so that we may marvel more attentively at the agility of a flying fly than at the size of a walking beast, and admire the works of ants more than the burdens of camels.

23. But the question is whether, as I said, these smallest creatures were also established in the first ordering of things—those creatures said to have been created in the sequence of the six days—or whether they arose afterward through the subsequent dissolution of corruptible bodies.

It can indeed be said that the very smallest creatures that arise from the waters or the earth were created then. Among them may also reasonably be understood those born from the things that arose when the earth sprouted; for those things had preceded the creation not only of animals but also of the luminaries, and are joined to the earth through the connection of their roots. Since they arose on the day when the dry land appeared, they are to be understood as belonging more to the furnishing of the dwelling-place than to the number of its inhabitants.

But it is utterly absurd to say that the other creatures generated from the bodies of animals, especially dead animals, were created at the time when the animals themselves were created. Unless, that is, there already existed in all animate bodies a certain natural power—primordia of future animals, as it were pre-seeded and in some fashion “threaded”—which, through the ineffable administration of the unchangeable Creator who moves all things, were destined to arise from the corruptions of such bodies, each according to its own kind and distinctions.

[Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “pre-seeded matter, and beginnings in some fashion initiated.” The manuscripts lack the word “matter” and, instead of *initiata*, read *liciata*, as does the Amiatine edition. The meaning of this word can be understood from *The City of God*, book 22, chapter 14, where Augustine teaches that all the members are secretly present in the seed and that, at birth, the measure of perfection already exists not in bulk but in rational form: “Within that rational form,” he says, “the bodily matter of each thing already appears to contain, in a certain fashion, as I may put it, something ‘threaded’—what does not yet exist, or rather what lies hidden, but in the course of time will exist, or rather will appear.”]

## CHAPTER XV — The Creation of Poisonous Animals

24. It is also customary to ask concerning the kinds of poisonous and harmful animals whether they were created after the sin of man as a punishment, or whether, having already been created harmless, they only later began to harm sinners.

Nor is this surprising, since even during the times of this laborious and sorrowful life—when no one is so righteous that he dares to call himself perfect, as the Apostle faithfully testifies when he says, “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect” (Philippians 3:12)—bodily trials and troubles are still necessary for virtue to be exercised and perfected in weakness.

The same Apostle makes this clear when he says that, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations, there was given to him “a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet him.” He says that he pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from him, and that the Lord answered him, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

Yet holy Daniel also lived safely and fearlessly among lions (Daniel 6:22; 14:38). In his prayer he confessed not only the sins of his people but also his own, and thus certainly did not lie to God (ibid. 9:4–19). A deadly viper fastened upon the hand of the Apostle himself, but did him no harm (Acts 28:5).

These creatures, therefore, could have been created without causing harm if there had been no reason either to terrify and punish vices or to test and perfect virtue. For examples of endurance must be displayed for the progress of others; and in temptations a person comes to know himself more certainly. Moreover, that eternal salvation which was shamefully lost through pleasure is rightly recovered through suffering.

[Note: The printed editions read “through the will”; the manuscripts read “through pleasure.”]

## CHAPTER XVI — Why Beasts Were Created to Harm One Another

25. Someone may ask: Why, then, do beasts harm one another, when they have no sins for this harm to be called a punishment and gain no virtue from such an exercise?

The answer is plainly that some are food for others. Nor can we rightly say, “There should not be some for others to eat.” For as long as all things exist, they possess their own measures, numbers, and orders. When all these are rightly considered, they are praised; and even as they pass from one thing into another, they are not changed without a hidden regulation of temporal beauty appropriate to their kind. This is hidden from fools, faintly visible to those making progress, and clear to the perfected.

Certainly, all such movements of lower creation provide human beings with salutary reminders. A person should see how much effort must be devoted to spiritual and eternal salvation, by which he surpasses all irrational animals, when he observes that—from the largest elephants to the smallest worms—animals do everything they can to preserve the bodily and temporal life allotted to them according to the lower order of their kind, whether by resistance or by caution.

This becomes apparent when some seek bodily nourishment from the bodies of others, while others defend themselves either by the power of resistance, by the protection of flight, or by the shelter of hiding places.

Even bodily pain in any animal is a great and wondrous power of the soul. Through an ineffable mingling it keeps that bodily structure alive and gathers it into a unity of its own measure, while it suffers corruption and dissolution not indifferently but, so to speak, with indignation.

## CHAPTER XVII — A Difficulty Concerning the Devouring of Dead Bodies

26. Someone may perhaps also be troubled by this question: if harmful animals injure living human beings either as a punishment, or exercise them beneficially, or test them usefully, or teach them unknowingly, why do they tear apart and devour even the dead bodies of human beings for food?

As though it made any difference to our usefulness through what passages this lifeless flesh now travels into the deep secrets of nature, from which, by the wondrous omnipotence of the Creator, it will once again be brought forth for restoration.

Yet even this provides a certain admonition to the prudent: they should entrust themselves to the faithful Creator, who governs all things, great and small, by his hidden will, and whose care extends even to the numbering of our hairs (Luke 12:7). Thus they should not, because of empty anxieties, dread any form of death for their lifeless bodies, but should not hesitate to prepare the sinews of devout courage for every eventuality.

## CHAPTER XVIII — Why and When Thorns, Thistles, and Fruitless Trees Were Created

27. A similar question is commonly raised concerning thorns and thistles and certain fruitless trees: why or when were they created, since God said, “Let the earth produce fodder-bearing grass, sowing seed, and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit”? 

But those who are troubled by this do not understand, even from the customary expressions of human law, how the term “usufruct” is used. For a certain usefulness enjoyed by those who make use of something is considered under the name “fruit.” Let them observe for themselves how great are the uses—whether manifest or hidden—of all the things that the earth, producing them, nourishes from their roots, and let them inquire from those with experience about the rest.

28. As for thorns and thistles, a more straightforward answer can be given, because after the sin it was said to the man concerning the earth, “Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Gen. 3:18). Yet it is not easy to say that these first began to arise from the earth at that time. For perhaps, since many uses are also found in these kinds of plants, they could have had their proper place without being any punishment for man. But that they should also grow in the fields in which he was already laboring under punishment may be believed to have contributed to the accumulation of his penalty, although they could have grown elsewhere, either for the feeding of birds and livestock or for certain uses of human beings themselves.

Nevertheless, the interpretation is also not incompatible with these words according to which “Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” is understood in this way: although the earth had previously brought forth these things, it did not bring them forth for man’s labor, but as food suitable for various animals. There are animals that feed conveniently and pleasantly on these kinds of plants, both softer and drier. But it then began to bring them forth for man as a burdensome task, when, after the sin, he began to labor upon the earth.

This does not mean that these plants had previously grown in other places and afterward in the fields which man cultivated to obtain crops; rather, they grew both before and afterward in the same places—before, however, not for man, and afterward for man. This is signified by the addition of the word “for you”: it was not said, “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles,” but “it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you”—that is, these things would now begin to grow for you as labor, although previously they grew only for the nourishment of other animals.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On verses 26 and 27, and so forth: Why, in the creation of man alone, it was said, “Let us make”

29. “And God said, ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness; and let him rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, and over all the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.’ And God made man; according to the image of God he made him: male and female he made them. And God blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and rule it; and exercise authority over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and all the livestock, and all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.’ And God said, ‘Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant that sows seed, which is upon all the earth, and every tree that has within itself the fruit of seed-bearing produce; it shall be food for you, and for all the beasts of the earth, and for all the birds of the air, and for every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth, which has within itself the breath of life; and every green plant for food.’ And it was so. And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And evening came, and morning came: the sixth day.”

There will later be a fuller opportunity to consider and discuss more carefully the nature of man. For the present, however, to conclude our inquiry and treatment of the works of the six days, we say this first and briefly: it should not be understood indifferently that in the other works it is said, “God said, ‘Let it be,’” whereas here it is said, “God said, ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness.’” This was, so to speak, intended to suggest a plurality of persons, because of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Yet the unity of the Godhead is immediately indicated when it says, “And God made man according to the image of God.” It is not as though the Father made man according to the image of the Son, or the Son according to the image of the Father. Otherwise “according to our image” would not truly have been said if man had been made according to the image of the Father alone or of the Son alone. Rather, “God made him according to the image of God” is said as though it were said, “God made him according to his own image.”

When it now says “according to the image of God,” although above it had said “according to our image,” it signifies that the plurality of persons does not entail that we should say, believe, or understand that there are several gods. Instead, because of that Trinity, for which reason “according to our image” was said, we are to understand one God, for which reason “according to the image of God” was said.

## CHAPTER XX  
### In what respect man was made according to the image of God; why, concerning the creation of man, it is not said, “And so it was made”

30. Here too the following must not be passed over. After saying “according to our image,” Scripture immediately added, “and let him have authority over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and the other animals lacking reason,” so that we may understand that man was made according to the image of God in that respect in which he surpasses irrational living creatures. This is reason itself, or mind, or intelligence, or whatever other term may more suitably be used.

Hence the Apostle also says, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man” (Eph. 4:23–24), “who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him” (Col. 3:10). He sufficiently shows where man was made according to the image of God: not in bodily features, but in a certain intelligible form of the illumined mind.

31. Accordingly, just as with that first light—if it is correctly understood by that name as intellectual light made a participant in the eternal and unchangeable wisdom of God—it was not said, “And so it was made,” to be followed by “And God made,” because, as we have already discussed as far as we could, there was no cognition of the Word of God in the first creature such that, after that cognition, what was being created in the Word would be created below it. Rather, the first light itself was created, in which there would be cognition of the Word of God through which it was created, and that cognition would be for it a turning from its formlessness toward the God who forms it, and thus its being created and formed.

But in the other creatures it is said, “And so it was made.” This signifies that in that light—that is, in the intellectual creature—the cognition of the Word first took place; and then, when it says “And God made,” the kind of creature itself is shown to have come into being, the creature that had been commanded in the Word of God to come into being.

The same pattern is preserved in the creation of man. For God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” and so forth. Then it does not say, “And so it was made,” but immediately adds, “And God made man according to the image of God,” because this nature too is intellectual, like that light; and therefore for it to be made is the same as for it to recognize the Word of God through which it is made.

32. For if it had said, “And so it was made,” and afterward added, “And God made,” it would seem that it was first made in the cognition of a rational creature and afterward in some creature that was not rational. But because it is itself a rational creature, it is perfected by that same cognition.

For just as, after the fall into sin, man is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him, so he was created in that very knowledge before he grew old through sin, so that he might afterward be renewed in the same knowledge.

Those things, however, that were not created in that cognition—because bodies or irrational souls were being created—were first known in the intellectual creature by the Word through which it was said that they should come into being. It is because of this cognition that it was first said, “And so it was made”: to show that the cognition itself had been made in that nature which could first know this in the Word of God. Then the bodily and irrational creatures themselves came into being; for this reason “And God made” was added afterward.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### The difficulty concerning man’s immortality arising from the food provided for him

33. How man was made immortal, and yet received food, along with the other animals, consisting of seed-bearing plants, fruit-bearing trees, and green plants, is difficult to say. For if he became mortal through sin, then before sin he certainly did not need such food. That body could not have been corrupted by hunger.

As for what was said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” although this seems unable to take place except through the intercourse of male and female—and from this too there arose an indication of mortal bodies—it can nevertheless be said that there could have been another mode in immortal bodies, so that, through the affection of holy love alone and without any desire for corruption, children might be born, neither destined to succeed deceased parents nor destined themselves to die. The earth would thus be filled with immortal human beings, and then, once a just and holy people had been established, such as we believe will exist after the resurrection, a mode of begetting would also come about.

This may indeed be said, and how it may be said is a matter for separate consideration. But no one will dare to say that the need for foods by which bodies are restored can exist except in mortal bodies.

[Note: [Col. 0293] The printed editions read: “by which they were restored, can exist only in mortal bodies.” The manuscript reading, which we present in the text, is truer.]

## CHAPTER XXII  
### The opinion of certain persons that the creation of the soul is signified by the words “And he made,” and that of the body by “And God formed”

34. Some have also conjectured that the inner man was made at this point, while the human body was made later, when Scripture says, “And God formed man from the clay of the earth”: so that what is said “made” pertains to the spirit, whereas “formed” pertains to the body.

They do not observe that male and female could have been made only according to the body. For although it may be argued with the greatest subtlety that the human mind itself, in which man was made according to the image of God—that is, a certain rational life—is divided between the truth of eternal contemplation and the administration of temporal affairs [Note: [Col. 0293] The printed editions read, “and into a certain … administration”; “a certain” is absent from the manuscripts.], and that in this way it is made, as it were, male and female, with one part giving counsel and the other obeying, nevertheless in this division the image of God is properly attributed only to that which cleaves to the contemplation of unchangeable truth.

In a figure of this matter, the Apostle Paul speaks of the man alone as the image and glory of God: “But the woman,” he says, “is the glory of the man” (1 Cor. 11:7). Thus, although this has been outwardly represented in two human beings of different sexes according to the body, it is also understood inwardly in the single human mind. Yet the woman who is female in body is herself also renewed in the spirit of her mind in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created her, where there is neither male nor female.

Just as women are not excluded from this grace of renewal and restoration according to the image of God, although something else has been represented in the sex of their bodies, because of which the man alone is said to be the image and glory of God, so also in the first creation of man, insofar as the woman too was a human being, she certainly possessed her own mind, and that mind was rational, according to which she too was made according to the image of God.

But because of the unity of their union, Scripture says, “God made man according to the image of God.” And lest anyone should think that only the spirit of man was made, although he was made according to the image of God only with respect to the spirit, Scripture says, “He made him male and female,” so that the body too may now be understood to have been made.

Again, lest anyone should suppose that he was made in such a way that both sexes were expressed in a single human being, as sometimes happens in those whom they call *androgynes*, Scripture shows that it used the singular number because of the unity of their union and because the woman was made from the man, as will be made clear later, when what has here been stated briefly begins to be explained more carefully. For this reason it immediately added the plural number, saying, “He made them, and he blessed them.”

But, as I have already said, we shall inquire more carefully into the creation of man in what follows of Scripture.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### What is intended by verse 30, “And so it was made”

35. We must now observe that after saying, “And so it was made,” Scripture immediately added, “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” Here the power and capacity given to human nature to take the produce of the field and the fruit of the tree as food are understood.

For this reason it added, “And so it was made,” referring back to the point at which it had begun to speak, where it says, “And God said, ‘Behold, I have given you seed-bearing plants,’” and so forth.

For if we refer the words “And so it was made” to everything said above, it will follow that we must admit that they had already increased, multiplied, and filled the earth on that same sixth day—something which, as the same Scripture testifies, we find happened only after many years.

Therefore, when this capacity for eating had been given, and man had learned of it through God’s declaration, it is said, “And so it was made”—that is, in the respect that man came to know it through God’s declaration.

For if he had also carried it out at that time—that is, if he had actually taken and eaten as food the things that had been given—Scripture’s customary manner of expression would have been preserved. After saying “And so it was made,” which pertains to expressing the preceding cognition, it would then have added the actual action and said, “And they took and ate.” This could have been said even without naming God again.

Similarly, after Scripture says, “Let the water that is under the heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear,” it adds, “And so it was made.” Then it does not say, “And God made,” but it nevertheless repeats the matter in this way: “And the water was gathered into its gatherings,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### Why it was not said of man individually, as it was of the others, “God saw that it was good”

36. It is worth asking why, as with the other creatures, Scripture did not say individually of the human creature, “And God saw that it was good,” but, after man had been made and had been given the power either to rule or to eat, added concerning everything, “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.”

It could first have given to man individually what it had given individually to the other things that had previously been made, and then finally have said concerning everything that God had made, “Behold, they were very good.”

Or perhaps, because everything was completed on the sixth day, it was necessary to say of everything, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good,” rather than to say this individually of the things made on that day. Why, then, was it said of the livestock, the beasts, and the reptiles of the earth, which belong to that same sixth day? Perhaps those creatures deserved to be called good both individually, each in its own kind, and universally together with the others, whereas man, made according to the image of God, deserved to be called good only together with the others.

Or was it because he was not yet perfect, since he had not yet been established in paradise? As though, after he had been established there, Scripture had said what it had omitted here.

37. What, then, shall we say? Was it because God foreknew that man would sin and would not remain in the perfection of his image that he chose to call him good not individually but together with the others, thereby hinting at what would happen?

For while those things that have been made remain in the condition in which they were made, according to what they received—whether those that did not sin or those that cannot sin—each is good individually, and all together are very good. The word “very” was not added without reason. For even if the members of a body are individually beautiful, they are nevertheless much more beautiful in the structure of the whole body.

For example, although an eye may be pleasing and praised, if we saw it separated from the body, we would not call it as beautiful as when we saw it in that connection of the limbs, placed in its proper location within the whole body.

Those things, however, that lose their proper beauty through sin nevertheless in no way cause the whole, when rightly ordered, to cease to be good together with them.

Thus, before sin, man was good in his own kind; but Scripture omitted saying this so that it might instead say something that would foretell a future event. What was said about him was not false. For whoever is good individually is certainly more good together with all. But when someone is good together with all, it does not follow that he is also good individually.

It was therefore fitting that Scripture should say what was true in the present and signified foreknowledge of the future. For God is the best creator of natures, but the most just governor of those who sin, so that even if some things become individually deformed through wrongdoing, the whole universe may nevertheless always be beautiful together with them.

But let us treat what follows in the following volume.

# BOOK FOUR

The beginning of Genesis, chapter 2, is treated. After some discussion of the perfection of the number six, a question is raised again concerning verse 5 of chapter 1: namely, how, after the creation of light, evening and morning came to be, and how the days were thus numbered up to the sixth and seventh.

[Col. 0295]

## CHAPTER I  
### How the six days are to be understood

1. “And heaven and earth were completed, and all their adornment. And God completed on the sixth day his works that he had made; and God rested on the seventh day from all his works that he had made. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he rested from all his works that God began to make.”

It is indeed arduous and exceedingly difficult, given the powers of our attention, to penetrate with the liveliness of the mind the author’s intention in these six days: whether those days have passed and, with the seventh added, are now repeated through the succession of ages—not in reality but in name.

For throughout time many days come, similar to those that have passed, but none returns as the same in reality. Did those days, then, pass away? Or do those days which are designated by their names and number, passing daily in the sequence of time, remain in the very conditions of created things, so that the name “day” may be understood not only in those first three days before the luminaries were made, but also in the remaining three, as referring to the form of the thing that was created, and its night to deprivation or defect—or by whatever other name this may better be signified—when the form is lost, through some change by which it declines and tends from form toward formlessness?

This change is present in every creature, whether as a possibility even when it does not occur in actuality, as in the higher heavenly things, or as something carried out to complete the temporal beauty of lower things through the ordered alternation of the departures and successions of mutable things [Note: [Col. 0296] The manuscripts read “cessions” (*cessionibus*)], as is evident in earthly and mortal things.

Evening, however, may be a kind of limit of every completed condition, while morning is the beginning of one that is starting. For every created nature is contained within its own definite beginnings and ends. How this should be investigated is difficult.

But whether this interpretation, or that one, or even some third interpretation that is more probable, can be found—and this may perhaps become apparent in the course of the discussion—to explain how day, night, evening, and morning are to be understood in those days, it is nevertheless not beside the point to consider the perfection of the number six in the inward nature of numbers themselves. By contemplating it with the mind, we count and arrange numerically those things that also lie before the bodily senses.

## CHAPTER II  
### On the perfection of the number six

2. We find, then, that six is the first perfect number, for the reason that it is completed by its own parts. There are also other numbers that are perfect for other causes and reasons. We have therefore called six perfect for this reason: it is completed by its own parts, specifically by such parts as, when multiplied, can complete the number whose parts they are.

For a part of a number may be said to indicate what fraction it is. The number three, for example, may be called a part not only of six, of which it is one-half, but also of every number greater than three itself. For three is also a part of four and of five: four can be divided into three and one, and five into three and two.

Three is also a part of seven, eight, nine, and every number beyond them—not a greater part or a half, but a smaller part. Seven can be divided into three and four, eight into three and five, and nine into three and six. But three can be said to be a specified fraction of none of these except nine, of which it is one-third, just as it is one-half of six.

Thus, of all the numbers I have mentioned, none is completed by a certain number of threes except six and nine. The former consists of two threes, while the latter consists of three.

3. The number six, then, as I had begun to say, is completed within itself when its parts are counted together and added into a sum. For some numbers have parts which, when added together, produce a smaller sum, while others have parts producing a larger one. Only a small number, found at definite intervals, are completed by their own parts: their sum neither falls short nor exceeds, but reaches exactly the amount of the number whose parts they are. Six is the first of these.

The number one has no parts among numbers, for one is spoken of in the numbers by which we count in such a way that it has neither a half nor any part, but is truly, purely, and simply one.

The number two has one part, namely one, and that part is its half; it has no other. Three has two parts: one that can be said to indicate its fraction, namely one, since one is its third; and another, larger part, which cannot be said to indicate its fraction, namely two. Therefore its parts of the kind under discussion—that is, those that can be said to be specified fractions—cannot both be counted.

Four has two such parts: one, which is its fourth, and two, which is its half. But when both are added together—one and two—they make three, not four. Therefore its own parts do not complete it, since their sum remains smaller.

Five has only one such part, namely one, which is its fifth. For although two is a smaller part of it and three a larger part, neither can be said to be a specified fraction of it.

Six, however, has three such parts: its sixth, its third, and its half. Its sixth is one; its third is two; its half is three. When these parts are added together—one, two, and three—they complete and perfect the same number six.

4. Seven has no such part except its seventh, which is one. Eight has three: its eighth, its fourth, and its half—that is, one, two, and four. But when these are added together, they make seven, which falls short; therefore they do not complete eight.

Nine has two: its ninth, which is one, and its third, which is three. Together they make four, far smaller than nine.

Ten has three such parts: one, its tenth; two, its fifth; and five, its half. When these numbers are added together, they reach eight, not ten.

Eleven has only its eleventh, just as seven has only its seventh, five only its fifth, three only its third, and two only its half, which is one in every case.

Twelve, when its such parts are added together, is not itself completed but exceeded; they produce a number greater than twelve, reaching as far as sixteen. For it has five such parts: its twelfth, sixth, fourth, third, and half. Its twelfth is one, its sixth two, its fourth three, its third four, and its half six. One, two, three, four, and six, added together, make sixteen.

5. Not to delay with too much detail, in the infinite series of numbers many numbers are found which either have only one such part, like three, five, and the others of that kind, or have several such parts which, when taken together and reduced to a sum, either fall short, as eight, nine, and many others do, or exceed, as twelve, eighteen, and many of the same kind do.

There are therefore more of each of these kinds than of those called perfect, because they are completed when their such parts are added together. For after six, twenty-eight is found, which likewise consists of its such parts. It has five of them: its twenty-eighth, fourteenth, seventh, fourth, and half—that is, one, two, four, seven, and fourteen. When these are added together, they complete the same twenty-eight, for they amount to twenty-eight.

And as the order of numbers proceeds, these numbers that, when their such parts are reduced to a sum, reach exactly themselves are found at increasingly longer intervals in due proportion [Note: [Col. 0298] The manuscripts read “in due ratio” (*pro rata portione*); the printed editions, “in due proportion” (*pro rata proportione*)], and they are called perfect.

Numbers whose such parts, when added together, do not complete the numbers whose parts they are are called imperfect; those whose parts even exceed them are called more than perfect.

6. Thus, with the number of days completed—that is, with six—God completed the works that he had made. For it is written, “And God completed on the sixth day the works that he had made.” [Note: [Col. 0298] The printed editions read “on the seventh,” following the Vulgate; the manuscripts read “on the sixth,” following the Septuagint, which Augustine follows above and regularly cites.]

I am all the more drawn to consider this number when I also reflect on the order of the works themselves. Just as this same number rises gradually through its parts into a triangle—for one, two, and three follow in such a way that no other number can be placed between them, and each is a part of six, namely one its sixth, two its third, and three its half—so light was made in one day, while in the next two days the structure of this world was made: on one day its upper part, namely the firmament, and on the other its lower part, namely the sea and the earth.

He did not fill the upper part with any kinds of bodily nourishment, because he was not going to place there bodies requiring such refreshment. But he first enriched the lower part, which he was going to adorn with animals suited to it, with the foods necessary for their needs.

During the remaining three days, therefore, those things were created which, within the world—that is, within this whole visible universe made from all the elements—were to be set in motion visibly through movements suited to them.

First, the luminaries were placed in the firmament, because the firmament had been made first. Then came the living creatures in the lower region, as the order itself required: on one day, those of the waters; on another, those of the earth.

No one is so foolish as to dare say that God could not have made everything in one day, if he had wished; or, if he had wished, in two days—on one day the spiritual creature and on the other the bodily creature; or on one day heaven with everything belonging to it and on the other earth with everything in it; or whenever he wished, for however long he wished, and in whatever manner he wished. Who is there who can say that anything could have resisted his will?

## CHAPTER III  
### On what is written in Wisdom 11:21, “You have ordered all things in measure,” and so forth

7. Therefore, when we read that he completed everything in six days, and, considering the number six, find it to be perfect, and see the order of creatures proceeding in such a way that even among the parts by which this number is perfected there appears to be a kind of graded distinction, let us also call to mind what is said to him elsewhere in Scripture: “You have ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight” (Wis. 11:21).

Then let the soul that is capable of it, having invoked God for help and received and been inspired with strength, consider whether these three things—measure, number, and weight—in which Scripture says that God ordered all things existed somewhere before the whole creation was made, or whether they too were created; and, if they existed beforehand, where they were.

For before creation there was nothing except the Creator. Therefore they were in him. But how? We also read that the things that were created are in him (Rom. 11:36). Were those things in him as he himself is, while these are in him as in the one by whom they are ruled and governed?

And how are those things himself? For God is not measure, or number, or weight, or all these things. Or, in the sense in which we know measure in the things we measure, number in the things we count, and weight in the things we weigh, is he not these things; but in the sense that measure sets a limit for every thing, number gives form to every thing, and weight draws every thing toward rest and stability, is he first, truly, and uniquely these things—the one who limits everything, forms everything, and orders everything?

What else can be understood by the words, as they could be expressed through the human heart and tongue, “You have ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight,” except, “You have ordered all things in yourself”?

8. It is a great thing, granted to few, to surpass everything that can be measured, so that measure without measure may appear; to surpass everything that can be counted, so that number without number may appear; and to surpass everything that can be weighed, so that weight without weight may appear.

## CHAPTER IV  
### That in God there is measure without measure, number without number, and weight without weight

For measure, number, and weight cannot be observed and contemplated only in stones, wood, and masses of this kind, however large, whether bodily, earthly, or heavenly. There is also measure in action, so that its progress may not be irreversible and excessive. There is also number in the affections of the soul and in the virtues, by which one is gathered from the deformity of folly into the form and beauty of wisdom. And there is weight in the will and in love, where it becomes apparent how much each thing is weighed when it is desired, avoided, preferred, or postponed.

But the measure of these souls and minds is restrained by another measure; their number is formed by another number; and their weight is carried along by another weight.

Measure without measure is that to which what comes from it is made equal, while it itself does not come from elsewhere. Number without number is that by which all things are formed, while it itself is not formed. Weight without weight is that by which things are brought to rest, whose rest is pure joy, while that weight itself is no longer directed toward anything else.

9. But whoever knows the names “measure,” “number,” and “weight” only in a visible sense knows them in a servile manner. Let him therefore transcend everything that he knows in this way; or, if he is not yet able to do so, let him not cling even to the names, since he cannot think of them without degrading them.

For these higher realities are dearer to each person in proportion as he himself is less attached to lower things. If someone does not wish to transfer to sublime realities the terms he learned from the lowest and most contemptible things, in order to contemplate those realities and brighten his mind, he should not be compelled to do so. So long as what must be understood is understood, it is not of great importance what it is called.

Nevertheless, we must know what sort of likeness there is between lower things and higher things. For reason cannot properly extend and strive from here to there in any other way.

10. But if someone says that measure, number, and weight were created—the things in which Scripture testifies that God ordered everything—then, if he ordered everything in them, where did he order those very things? If he ordered them in other things, how then is everything in them, when they themselves are in other things?

There is therefore no doubt that they are outside those things which have been ordered, and that all things have been ordered in them.

## CHAPTER V  
### That in God himself there exists the principle of measure, number, and weight, according to which all things have been ordered

11. Or should we perhaps understand the words, “You have ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight,” as though they meant, “You have ordered all things in such a way that they would have measure, number, and weight”?

For even if it were said, “You have ordered all bodies in colors,” it would not follow that the Wisdom of God itself, through which all things were made, must be understood to have first possessed colors within itself, in which it made bodies. Rather, “You have ordered all bodies in colors” would be understood as if it meant, “You have ordered all bodies in such a way that they would have colors.”

For how could bodies ordered by God the Creator in colors—that is, ordered so that they would be colored—be understood otherwise than by recognizing that a certain principle for assigning colors to each kind of body was not lacking in the wisdom of the one who ordered them, even though color itself is not said to be present there?

This is what I meant: once the matter is understood, we need not struggle over the words.

[Note: [Col. 0300] The printed editions read, “Let us confess”; the manuscripts read, “Let us suppose.”]

12. Let us therefore understand the words, “You have ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight,” as though they meant, “You have ordered them in such a way that they would have their own measures, their own numbers, and their own weight,” which would change in them according to the mutability of each kind, through increases and decreases, multiplicity and scarcity, lightness and heaviness, in accordance with God’s ordering.

But do we therefore say that God’s own plan, in which he ordered these things, is mutable in the same way that they are mutable? May he himself avert such madness.

## CHAPTER VI  
### Where God saw the source from which he ordered all things

When, then, these things were ordered in such a way that they would have their own measures, numbers, and weights, where did he himself, the one ordering them, see them?

He did not see them outside himself, as we see bodies with our eyes—bodies which certainly did not yet exist when they were being ordered so that they might come into being. Nor did he see them within himself as we see, in the mind, images of bodies that are not present to the eyes, imagining and thinking of them from things we have seen or from things derived from what we have seen.

How, then, did he see these things so as to order them? Where else but in that way in which he alone can see them?

[Note: [Col. 0301] The manuscripts read “nevertheless” (*verumtamen*).]

13. Yet even we mortals and sinners, whose souls are weighed down by corruptible bodies and whose thought, occupied with many earthly things, is depressed by its earthly dwelling (Wis. 9:15)—even if we possessed the purest hearts and simplest minds, and were already equal to the holy angels—the divine substance would still not be known to us in the way it is known to itself.

## CHAPTER VII  
### How we contemplate the perfection of the number six
Nevertheless, we do not discern this perfection of the number six outside ourselves, as we do bodies with our eyes; nor do we discern it within ourselves in the same way as the phantasies of bodies and images of visible things, but in another, altogether different, manner. For although, when the composition, order, or division of the number six is considered, certain likenesses of little bodies seem to present themselves to the mind’s gaze, the stronger and more powerful reason from above does not assent to them, but gazes inwardly upon the force of the number. Through this contemplation it confidently declares that what is called one in numbers cannot be divided into any parts, whereas all bodies can be divided into innumerable parts; and that heaven and earth, which were fashioned according to the number six, could more easily pass away than the number six be made not to be completed by its own parts. Let the human mind therefore always give thanks to the Creator, by whom it was so created that it can see what no bird and no beast can see, although they see with us heaven, earth, the heavenly bodies, the sea, the dry land, and all that is in them.

14. For this reason we cannot say that the number six is perfect because God completed all his works in six days; rather, God completed his works in six days because the number six is perfect. Thus, even if these things did not exist, that number would still be perfect; but if it were not perfect, these things would not have been made perfect according to it.

## CHAPTER VIII — How God’s Rest on the Seventh Day Is to Be Understood

15. Now, with regard to what is written—that God rested on the seventh day from all the works he had made, and that he therefore blessed and sanctified that same day because on it he rested—we should first drive from our minds the carnal suspicions of human beings [Col. 0302], so that we may attempt, as far as we can and with whatever understanding he grants us, to grasp the meaning. For is it permissible to say or believe that God labored in working when he established the things written above, when he spoke and they came to be? A human being, too, does not labor if, as soon as he has said that something is to be made, it is done. Although human words are uttered with the support of sounds, and a prolonged speech may weary the speaker, nevertheless, since the words are as few as those we read in the account—“Let there be light,” “Let there be a firmament,” and the rest through the completion of the works, which he consummated on the sixth day—it is the height of absurd madness to regard this as labor, whether human, much less divine.

16. Or perhaps someone might say that God did not labor by commanding the things that were immediately made, but that he may have labored by considering what ought to be made; and that, as though released from this care by the perfection of his works, he rested, and for that reason wished to bless and sanctify the day on which he was first freed from this mental activity. But if to think such things is to think very foolishly—for with God the capacity and ease of creating things are incomparable and ineffable.

## CHAPTER IX — In What Sense God Is Said to Rest. Laudable Sorrow

What remains for us to understand, unless it is that he provided rest in himself for the rational creature, in which he also created humanity, after its perfection, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts (Rom. 5:5), so that we may be carried by the desire of longing to that place where, when we arrive, we shall rest—that is, seek nothing further? For just as God is rightly said to do whatever we do with him working in us, so God is rightly said to rest when we rest through his gift.

17. We understand this correctly, because it is true and requires no great effort of concentration to see that God is said to rest when he causes others to rest, just as he is said to know when he causes us to know. For God does not come to know in time what he previously did not know; and yet he says to Abraham, “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12). What else do we understand by this except, “Now I have caused it to be known”? In these modes of expression, when we speak of things that do not happen to God as though they happened to him, we acknowledge that he causes them to happen to us—provided that they are things deserving praise, and only insofar as the usage of Scripture permits this. For we ought not rashly say anything of this kind about God that we do not read in his Scripture.

18. I think that the Apostle’s statement was made in this mode of expression: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30). For the substance of the Holy Spirit itself, whatever he is in himself, cannot be grieved, since he possesses eternal and unchangeable blessedness, or rather, since he himself is eternal and unchangeable blessedness. But because he dwells in the saints in such a way as to fill them with the love by which human beings must rejoice, in the course of time, at the progress of the faithful and at their good works, they must therefore also grieve at their falling away or sins—those whose faith and devotion had been a source of joy to them. Such sorrow is laudable, because it arises from the love which the Holy Spirit pours into them. [Col. 0303] For this reason the Spirit himself is said to be grieved by those who act in such a way that the saints are grieved by their deeds—not for any other reason than that they possess the Holy Spirit. Through this gift they are so good that the wicked cause them sorrow, especially those whom they either know or believe to have been good. Such sorrow is certainly not merely free from blame, but especially deserving of praise and commendation.

19. The same Apostle again used this mode of expression wonderfully when he said: “Now, knowing God—or rather, being known by God” (Gal. 4:9). God had not first come to know them then, since they had been foreknown before the foundation of the world (1 Pet. 1:10); but because they had then come to know him through his gift, not through their own merit or ability, he preferred to speak figuratively, saying that they were then known by him when he made himself known to them. He corrected the expression, as though what he had said literally were less precise, rather than allow them to claim for themselves that they had been able to do what he had granted them the ability to do.

## CHAPTER X — Whether God Himself Could Properly Be Said to Rest

20. This understanding—that in the statement that God rested from all his works, which he had made very good, the meaning is that he causes us to rest when we have done good works—may perhaps suffice for some. But after undertaking to consider the testimony of Scripture concerning this interpretation, we are compelled to ask how he himself could also have rested, although by intimating to us his rest he has urged us to hope that our rest will be in him. For just as he himself made heaven and earth and all that is in them, and completed everything on the sixth day—and nothing in these works can be said to have been created by us, even though he granted us the ability to create, so that it was said, “God completed on the sixth day the works that he had made” because he enabled us to complete them—so also, when it is said, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works that he had made,” we must first understand not our rest, which we shall attain with his permission, but his own rest, by which he rested on the seventh day after completing his works. First, therefore, everything written must be shown to have taken place; only afterward, if necessary, should it be taught that it signified something further. It is rightly said that just as God rested after his good works, so we shall rest after our good works. But for this very reason it is rightly demanded that, just as we have discussed the works of God, which plainly appear to be his own, so we should sufficiently discuss God’s rest, and demonstrate that it properly belongs to him [Note: [Col. 0303] Most manuscripts read “properly” (*proprie*).].

## CHAPTER XI — How Both Statements Are True: That God Rested on the Seventh Day and That He Continues to Work

21. Therefore, with the greatest justice, we are compelled to investigate, if we are able, and to explain how both statements can be true: that God rested on the seventh day from his works, which he had made, as is written here; and that he himself, through whom all things were made, says in the Gospel, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). He said this in response to those who complained that, because of God’s rest, he did not observe the Sabbath commended from ancient times by the authority of this Scripture [Col. 0304]. It can reasonably be said that the Jews were commanded to observe the Sabbath as a shadow of things to come, signifying the spiritual rest that God, through the hidden meaning of his own rest, promised to the faithful who do good works. The Lord Christ himself—who suffered only when he wished—also confirmed the mystery of this rest by his burial. On that very Sabbath day [Note: [Col. 0304] Lov. reads “therefore indeed” (*ideo quippe*); the other editions and manuscripts read “on that very day” (*ipso*).] he rested in the tomb, and he kept the whole day as a holy cessation, after completing all his works on the sixth day, that is, the preparation day, which they call the sixth of the Sabbath, when the things written concerning him were fulfilled on the wood of the cross. For he also used this word when he said, “It is finished”; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30). Why, then, should it be surprising if God, wishing also in this way to foretell the day on which Christ would rest in the tomb, rested from his works for one day, and thereafter continued to work out the sequence of the ages, so that it would also truly be said, “My Father is working until now”?

## CHAPTER XII — Another Way of Reconciling Scripture Concerning God’s Rest and His Continual Work

22. It can also be understood that God rested from creating kinds of creatures, because thereafter he created no new kinds; but that from then until now, and into the future, he has continued to work by governing those same kinds, which were established at that time. This does not mean that on the seventh day his power ceased to govern heaven and earth and all the things he had created; otherwise they would immediately dissolve. For the power of the Creator, the power of the omnipotent and all-sustaining one, is the cause of existence for every creature. If that power were ever to cease governing what has been created, their form would cease at the same time, and all nature would collapse. The world cannot remain standing even for the blink of an eye if God withdraws from it the governance by which he sustains it, any more than a builder, after constructing a house, can depart and leave his work standing merely because he has ceased to work on it.

23. Accordingly, when the Lord says, “My Father is working until now,” he indicates a certain continuation of God’s work, by which he sustains and governs the whole creation. The meaning could be different if he had said, “And now he is working,” where it would not be necessary for us to understand a continuation of the work. But when he says, “Until now,” he compels us to understand that it extends from the time when he worked while creating all things. And what is written about his Wisdom—“She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)—and what is likewise written, that her motion is more agile and swift than all motions (ibid. 7:24), becomes sufficiently clear to those who look upon it rightly: this very incomparable, ineffable, and, if it can be understood, stable motion provides creatures with the gentle ordering by which they are arranged. If it were withdrawn, and she ceased from this work, they would immediately perish. The Apostle’s statement, made when he was preaching God to the Athenians—“In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28)—also supports this view as far as the human mind, with God’s help, is able to grasp it [Col. 0305]. We believe and say that God works without ceasing in the things he created. We are not in him as though we were his substance, in the way that it is said that he has life in himself (John 5:26). Rather, since we are something other than he is, we are in him for no other reason than that he works this, and this is his work: he sustains all things, and through his Wisdom he reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. Through this ordering we live, move, and are. Hence it follows that if he withdrew this work from things, we would neither live, nor move, nor exist. It is therefore clear that God did not cease for even one day from the work of governing what he had created. Otherwise created things would immediately lose their natural motions, by which they are moved and enlivened, so that they are altogether natures and remain, each according to its kind, what it is; and they would cease entirely to be anything if that motion of God’s Wisdom, by which he orders all things sweetly, were withdrawn from them. Accordingly, we understand God to have rested from all his works that he had made in this sense: he no longer created any new nature, but he did not cease to sustain and govern what he had created. Thus both statements are true: that God rested on the seventh day, and that he continues to work until now.

## CHAPTER XIII — On Observance of the Sabbath. The Christian Sabbath

24. We see his works to be good; but we shall see his rest after our good works. To signify this, he commanded the Hebrew people to observe one day (Exod. 20:8). They observed it so carnally that, when they saw the Lord working our salvation on that day, they accused him, as though he were rightly answering them concerning the work of the Father, with whom he himself also worked equally—not only in governing the whole creation, but also in accomplishing our salvation. Now, in the time of revealed grace, that observance of the Sabbath, which was signified by the cessation of one day, has been removed from the observance required of the faithful. For the person who works whatever good he does in hope of future rest already observes an everlasting Sabbath in that grace, and does not boast in his good works as though he possessed a good that he had not received. Thus, receiving and understanding the sacrament of Baptism as the Sabbath day—that is, the cessation of the Lord in the tomb—he rests from his former works, so that, now walking in newness of life (Rom. 6:4), he may recognize God working in him: God who both works and rests, providing the fitting governance of creation and possessing eternal tranquility in himself.

## CHAPTER XIV — Why God Sanctified the Day of His Rest

25. In conclusion, God was not exhausted when he created, nor was he refreshed when he ceased; rather, through his Scripture he wished to exhort us to desire rest, by telling us that he sanctified the day on which he rested from all his works. For nowhere in the account of the six days during which all things were created do we read that he sanctified anything; nor, before those six days, where it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), is the statement “and he sanctified” added. But he wished to sanctify this day [Col. 0306], on which he rested from all the works he had made, as though, even for him who does not labor in his work, rest were of greater value than activity. The Gospel indicates this to us in the case of human beings, where our Savior says that Mary chose the better part because, sitting at his feet, she rested in his word, rather than Martha, who, though occupied with many tasks in the service she was rendering him, was nevertheless doing a good work (Luke 10:39–42). But how this applies to God, or how it is to be understood, is difficult to state, even though it can be touched upon to some extent in thought: why God sanctified the day of his rest, when he sanctified none of his work, not even the sixth day on which he made humanity and completed all things. And first, what is the nature of God’s resting, which the acuity of the human mind can grasp? Yet unless this were so, Scripture would not have stated it at all.
