I shall say what I think, first asserting two things beyond doubt: God was not pleased by a temporal rest as though he desired it after labor or the completion of his task; nor did these Scriptures, which rightly hold such great authority, say falsely or pointlessly that God rested on the seventh day from all the works he had made, and that for this reason he sanctified that same day.

## CHAPTER XV — The Previously Proposed Question Is Resolved

26. Clearly, then, because it is a defect and weakness of the soul to take such pleasure in its works that it rests in them rather than in itself—for unquestionably there is something better in the soul, by which those works were made, than the works themselves—God is presented to us through this Scripture, which says that he rested from all the works he had made, as taking no pleasure in any work of his as though he had needed to make it, or would have been less without making it, or would have become happier after making it. Since everything that comes from him is what it is from him in such a way that it owes its existence to him, whereas he owes to nothing that comes from him the fact that he is blessed, he placed himself above the things he made by loving himself. He did not sanctify the day on which he began to make them, nor the day on which he completed them, lest his joy appear to have been increased either by making them or by having made them; rather, he sanctified the day on which he rested from them in himself. He himself, indeed, never lacked this rest, but he displayed it to us through the seventh day. Here too he signified that his rest is perceived only by perfected creatures, since he assigned no day to signify it except the day that followed the perfection of all things. For he who is always at rest rested for us when he showed that he had rested.

## CHAPTER XVI — God’s Rest from His Works on the Seventh Day

27. We must also observe that God’s rest, by which he is blessed in himself, had to be intimated to us so that we might understand how he is also said to rest in us—which is said only when he grants us rest in himself. Properly understood, therefore, God’s rest is that by which he needs no good; and for this reason it is certain for us in him, because we are made blessed by the good that he is, whereas he is not made blessed by the good that we are. We too are some good from him, who made all things very good, among which he also made us. But there is no other good besides him that he did not make; and therefore he, who does not need the good he made, needs no good besides himself [Col. 0307]. This is his rest from all the works he made.

But from what good things would he laudably not have needed anything, if he had made nothing? It could even be said in that case that he needed no good things—not by resting in himself from things made, but by making nothing at all. Yet if he could not make good things, there would be no power; and if he could but did not, there would be great envy. Because, then, he is omnipotent and good, he made all things very good; but because he is perfectly blessed in the good that he himself is, he rested in himself from the good things he made—that is, in the rest from which he never departed. If he were said to have rested from things to be made, this would mean nothing other than that he did not make them. But unless he were said to have rested from things made, his not needing the things he had made would be commended less clearly.

28. On what day, then, ought this to have been commended, if not the seventh? Anyone who recalls the perfection of the number six, about which we spoke above, and how fittingly it was applied to the perfection of creation, will understand this. If creation was to be completed according to the number six, as it was completed, and if God’s rest was to be commended to us in order to show that even perfected creatures are not themselves the source of blessedness, then clearly the day following the sixth had to be sanctified for this commendation. We were thereby to be raised up to desire this rest, so that we too might rest in him.

## CHAPTER XVII — Our Rest in God

29. For it is not a pious likeness if we wish to be like God in such a way that we too rest from our works in ourselves, just as he rested in himself from his works. We ought to rest in an unchangeable good, which is what he is for us, since he made us. This, then, will be our highest, entirely humble, and truly pious rest: just as he rested from all his works because his works are not his good, but he himself is his own good, by which he is blessed, so we too should hope to rest from all works—not only our own, but even his—in no one but him. We should desire this after our good works, which we recognize in ourselves to belong to him rather than to us. In this way he also rests after his good works, when, after the good works that we perform as people justified by him, he grants us rest in himself [Note: [Col. 0307] The printed editions add “in us,” which is absent from the manuscripts.].

It is a great thing for us to have come into existence from him, but it will be greater to have rested in him. He himself is not blessed because he made these things, but because, needing nothing that had been made, he rested in himself rather than in them. Hence he sanctified not the day of work but the day of rest, because he revealed himself to be blessed not by making these things, but by not needing the things he had made.

30. What, then, is so humble and easy to say, and what so sublime and difficult to grasp in thought, as God resting from all the works he had made? And where could he rest except in himself, since he is blessed only in himself? When could he rest except always? But in the days during which the completion of the things he created is narrated, and the order of God’s rest is distinguished from them, when could this be except on the seventh day, which follows their perfection? For he rests from perfected things [Col. 0308], since he does not need even the perfected in order to become more blessed.

## CHAPTER XVIII — Why the Seventh Day Had a Morning but No Evening

31. With God there is neither morning nor evening for his rest, since it is neither opened by a beginning nor closed by an end. But for his completed works it has a morning and no evening. For perfected creation has a certain beginning in its conversion toward the rest of its Creator, but that rest has no end as the termination of its perfection, as do the things that have been made. Accordingly, God’s rest begins not for God himself but for the perfection of the things created by him, so that what is perfected by him may begin to rest in him and have its morning in him. In its own kind it has been terminated as though by an evening; but in God it can no longer have an evening, because nothing will be more perfect than that perfection.

32. In those days during which all things were being created, we understood the evening as the end of the creature created, and the morning as the beginning of another creature to be created. Accordingly, the evening of the fifth day is the end of the creature created on the fifth day; and the morning that came after that evening is the beginning of the creature to be created on the sixth day. Once that creature had been made, evening became its end. Since nothing else remained to be created, morning came after that evening, but it was not the beginning of another creature to be created. Rather, it was the beginning of the rest of the whole creation in the rest of the Creator.

For heaven and earth and all that is in them—the whole spiritual and bodily creation—do not remain in themselves, but in him of whom it is said, “In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). Although each part can exist in the whole of which it is a part, the whole itself exists only in him by whom it was created. Therefore it is not absurd to understand that, after the completion of the sixth day and its evening, morning came—not to signify the beginning of another creature to be created, as on the other days, but to signify the beginning of the whole created order’s remaining and resting in the rest of him who created it.

This rest [Note: [Col. 0308] The printed editions read “God’s” (*Dei*); the manuscripts read “for God” (*Deo*).] has neither beginning nor end for God, but for creation it has a beginning and no end. Thus the seventh day began for creation with morning, but it is terminated by no evening.

33. For if the evening and morning on the other days signify the alternations of such periods as now pass through these daily intervals, I do not see what would have prevented the seventh day from having an evening and its night from concluding in a morning, so that it might likewise be said, “And there was evening, and there was morning, the seventh day.” After all, it too is one of the days, and all seven are days whose recurrence carries months, years, and ages forward. The morning that would have been placed after the evening of the seventh day would then have been the beginning of an eighth day, about which Scripture would thereafter have had to remain silent, because it is the same as the first, to which the cycle returns [Col. 0309] and from which the sequence of the weeks begins again [Note: The manuscripts read *octo*, “eight,” and *ordinatur*, “is ordered”; the printed editions read *octavi*, “of the eighth,” and *ordiatur*, “begins.”].

It is therefore more probable that these seven days, by their names and number, represent temporal intervals that follow one another in succession as they run their course; whereas the first six days were unfolded in the very creation of things in a form unknown and unfamiliar to us. In those days evening and morning, like light and darkness—that is, day and night—did not produce the alternation that they produce now through the courses of the sun. We are compelled to admit this at least concerning those three days that are mentioned and numbered before the heavenly bodies were created.

34. Whatever the evening and morning of those days may have been, we must nevertheless in no way suppose that God’s rest began with the morning that came after the evening of the sixth day. Otherwise, in reckless vanity, we would imagine that some temporal good had accrued to that eternity and immutability. Rather, God’s rest—the rest by which he rests in himself and is blessed by the good that he himself is—has neither beginning nor end in God himself; but for perfected creation it has a beginning. For the perfection of each thing is established, according to the measure of its kind, not so much in the whole of which it is a part as in him from whom it comes, in whom the whole itself also exists, so that it may rest—that is, preserve the order proper to its being.

Accordingly, the whole creation, which was completed in six days [Note: [Col. 0309] Four manuscripts read: “was completed in its own nature, has another [condition] in its own nature.”], has one condition in its own nature and another in the order by which it exists in God. It is not God, but it is so ordered that its rest of proper stability is found only in the rest of him who desires nothing besides himself, in attaining whom he rests. And so, while he remains in himself, he turns back to himself everything that comes from him, so that every creature may have in itself the limit of its nature, by which it is not what he is, but may have in him the place of rest by which it preserves what it is.

I know that I have not used the word “place” in its strict sense, for properly a place is spoken of in relation to spaces occupied by bodies. But since bodies themselves do not remain in a place except where they arrive, as though driven by the appetite of their weight, and, having reached it, rest there, the word is not improperly transferred from bodily to spiritual things, so that we speak of a “place,” even though the reality itself is very different.

35. I therefore think that the beginning of creation in the rest of the Creator was signified by the morning that came after the evening of the sixth day. For it could not rest in him unless it were perfected. Accordingly, when everything had been completed on the sixth day and evening had occurred, morning also came, so that perfected creation might begin to rest in him from whom it had been made. With this beginning it found God resting in himself, in whom it too could rest, all the more stably and firmly because it needed him, whereas he did not need it, for his own rest.

But whatever the whole creation may become through its various changes, it will certainly not become nothing. Therefore the whole creation will always remain in its Creator; and consequently, after that morning there was no subsequent evening.

36. This is why we said [Note: [Col. 0309] The printed editions add “so that it may be understood,” words omitted by all the manuscripts.] that the seventh day, on which God rested [Col. 0310] from all his works, had a morning after the evening of the sixth day but had no evening.

## CHAPTER XIX — Another Explanation of How the Seventh Day Had a Morning without an Evening

There is another interpretation of this matter which, in my judgment, is more precise and better, although somewhat more difficult to explain: the rest of God on the seventh day had a morning without an evening—that is, a beginning without an end—not only for creation but also in relation to God himself [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, omitting the word *Dei*, “of God,” read “the rest of the seventh day.”].

For if it were said simply, “God rested on the seventh day,” and the words “from all his works that he had made” were not added, we would search in vain for the beginning of this rest. God does not begin to rest, since his rest is eternal, without beginning and without end. But because he rested from all his works that he had made, needing none of them, God’s rest itself is understood neither to have begun nor to have ended; whereas his rest from all the works he had made began from the time when he completed them. For he would not have rested by not needing his works before they existed, since he would not have needed them even when perfected. And because he never needed them at all, neither will this blessedness, by which he does not need them, be perfected as though he were making progress. Therefore no evening followed the seventh day.

## CHAPTER XX — Whether the Seventh Day Was Created

37. But it may certainly be asked—and the question deserves consideration [Col. 0311]—how we are to understand that God rested in himself from all the works he had made, when it is written, “And God rested on the seventh day.” It does not say, “in himself,” but “on the seventh day.” What, then, is the seventh day? Is it some creature, or merely a period of time?

But a period of time was also created together with temporal creation; and therefore it too is undoubtedly a creature. For no times exist, or could have existed, or will be able to exist, whose creator is not God. Accordingly, if this seventh day is time, who created it except the Creator of all times?

The earlier passage of Holy Scripture indicates with which creatures or within which creatures those six days were created. Therefore, among these seven days, whose form is familiar to us—days that pass in reality but, by succeeding one another, somehow hand on their names so that they may be called the six days—we know when the first of them was created. But we do not see when the seventh day, called by the name “Sabbath,” was created. On that day God did not make anything; rather, on it he rested from the things he had made during the six days.

How, then, did he rest on a day he had not created? Or how did he create it immediately after the six days, when on the sixth day he had completed everything he created, and on the seventh day he created nothing but rather rested from everything he had created? Or did God create only one day, so that through its repetition the many days called days might pass and run their course, and was there no need for him to create the seventh day because the seventh recurrence of the day he had created necessarily produced it?

God separated the light of which it is written, “And God said, ‘Let there be light’; and there was light” (Gen. 1:3), from the darkness, and he called the light “day,” while he called the darkness “night.” God therefore made the day whose recurrence Scripture calls the second day, then the third, and onward to the sixth, on which God completed his works. From that point, the seventh recurrence of the day first created received the name of the seventh day, on which God rested. Accordingly, the seventh day is not a creature, except insofar as it is that same day returning seven times—the day created when God called the light “day” and the darkness “night.”

## CHAPTER XXI — On the Light That Existed before the Heavenly Bodies for the Alternation of Day and Night

38. We therefore return again to the question from which we seemed to have emerged in the first book, and ask once more how the light could have revolved so as to provide the alternation of day and night—not only before the heavenly bodies were made, but before the heaven itself, which was called the firmament, was made, and even before there was any form of earth or sea that could receive the circuit of the light and from which it could pass when night followed.

Compelled by the difficulty of this question, we ventured to bring our discussion, as it were, to this conclusion: that the light first created was the formation of spiritual creation, while night was the still-unformed material of the remaining works of creation, the matter that had been established when, in the beginning, God made heaven and earth, before he made the day by his word [Note: The printed editions add here, “in which he rested”; this is absent from the manuscripts.].

But now, prompted by consideration of the seventh day, it is easier for us to admit that we do not know—something beyond the reach of our senses—in what way that light which was called “day” carried out the alternation of day and night, whether by its revolution or, if it was bodily, by its contraction and emission; or, if it was spiritual, how it was presented to all creatures as they were being made, so that by its presence it produced day and by its absence night, with evening being the beginning of its absence and morning the beginning of its presence. It is easier to confess our ignorance of this than to attempt, contrary to the words of divine Scripture, to assert that the seventh day was something other than the seventh recurrence of that day which God made.

Otherwise, either God did not create the seventh day, or he created something after those six days—namely, the seventh day itself. In that case, the statement that he completed all his works on the sixth day and rested on the seventh from all his works would be false. But since this cannot be false, it remains that the presence of that light which God made “day” was repeated throughout all his works whenever “day” is mentioned, including the seventh day, on which he rested from his works.

## CHAPTER XXII — How the Spiritual Light Is Understood to Have Produced the Alternation of Day and Night
39. But since we do not find by what circuit, or by what advance and retreat, corporeal light could have produced the alternation of day and night before the firmament called heaven had been made, in which the luminaries too were created, we ought not to leave this question without expressing some opinion of our own. If that light which was first created is not corporeal but spiritual, as it was made after the darkness, when it is understood to have been turned from a certain formlessness toward its Creator and formed by him, then likewise morning may have come after evening when, after recognizing its own nature—for it is not what God is—it turns back to praise the Light, which is God himself, by contemplation of whom it is formed.

And since the other creatures, which are made beneath it, are not made without its knowledge, the same day is therefore repeated everywhere, so that by its repetition as many days may be made as there are distinctions among the kinds of created things, to be brought to completion by the perfection of the number six. Thus the evening of the first day is also its knowledge of itself—not being what God is [Note: [Col. 0312] The passage has been corrected in accordance with the manuscripts; the printed editions had *cognitione*, “by knowledge,” and shortly afterward *conversio fit ejus*, “its turning takes place.”]. But morning, after this evening, by which one day is concluded and the second begun, is its turning by which, because it is a creature, it refers itself to the praise of the Creator and receives from the Word of God knowledge of the creature that is made after it, namely, the firmament.

This happens first in its knowledge when it is said, “And so it was made”; then in the nature of the firmament itself, which is created, when, after the already-mentioned “And so it was made,” it is added, “And God made the firmament.” Next comes the evening of that light, when it recognizes the firmament itself, no longer in the Word of God as before, but in the firmament’s own nature. Since this knowledge is lesser, it is rightly signified by the name “evening.” After this comes morning, by which the second day is concluded and the third begins. On this day likewise morning is the turning of this light—that is, of this day—toward praising God for having made the firmament and toward receiving from his Word knowledge of the creature that is to be made after the firmament.

Accordingly, when God says, “Let the water beneath the heaven be gathered into one collection, and let the dry land appear,” that light recognizes this in the Word of God, by which it is said; and therefore there follows, “And so it was made”—that is, it was made in its knowledge through the Word of God. Then, when it is added, “And the water was gathered,” and so forth (Gen. I, 9–10), after “And so it was made” had already been said, the creature itself is made in its own kind. When it is likewise recognized as made in its own kind by that light which had already known in the Word of God that it was to be made, a third evening occurs. From that point onward the remaining things proceed in this manner until the morning after the evening of the sixth day.

## CHAPTER XXIII — Knowledge of things in the Word of God and in themselves

40. There is a great difference between knowledge of any thing in the Word of God and knowledge of it in its own nature; the former properly belongs to day, the latter to evening. In comparison with that light which is perceived in the Word of God, every knowledge by which we know any creature in itself may rightly be called night. Yet it differs so greatly from the error or ignorance of those who do not even know the creature itself that, in comparison with them, it may appropriately be called day.

Thus the very life of the faithful, lived in this flesh and in this age, is reasonably called light and day in comparison with the life of the unbelieving and ungodly, as the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8); and again: “Let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light; let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. XIII, 12–13). Yet this day too would itself be night in comparison with that day when, made equal to the angels, we shall see God as he is; otherwise we would not need the lamp of prophecy. Hence the Apostle Peter says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, and you do well to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (II Pet. I, 19) [Note: [Col. 0313] The manuscripts omit *lucenti*, “shining.”].

## CHAPTER XXIV — The knowledge of the angels

41. Therefore, since the holy angels, to whom we shall be made equal after the resurrection (Matt. XXII, 30), if we hold fast to the way—which Christ became for us—to the end, always behold the face of God and enjoy his only-begotten Son, the Word, who is equal to the Father, and since in them wisdom was first created before all else, they undoubtedly first knew the whole creation, in which they themselves were principally created, in the Word of God. In that Word are the eternal principles of all things, including those made in time, as in the one through whom all things were made.

Then they know creation itself, which they thus know as though looking down upon it as lying below them, and refer it to the praise of him in whose unchangeable truth they principally behold the principles according to which it was made. There, therefore, as though through day—for the most harmonious unity of the angels, created first by participation in that same truth, is day—there; but here, as though through evening.

Yet immediately morning comes, as may be observed on all six days, because angelic knowledge does not remain in what has been created without immediately referring it to the praise and love of him in whom it is recognized that this was not made but was to be made; by standing in this truth, it is day. For if the angelic nature were to turn even toward itself and take greater delight in itself than in him through participation in whom it is blessed, it would fall, swollen with pride, like the devil. We shall speak of him in his proper place, when the subject properly demands discussion of the serpent who deceived the human being.

## CHAPTER XXV — Why night is not added to the six days

42. Since, therefore, the angels know creation in the creature itself in such a way that, through choice and love, they prefer to that knowledge the knowledge of it in the Truth through whom all things were made, having become participants in him, night is not named throughout the six days. Instead, after evening and morning comes one day; likewise, after evening and morning, the second day; then, after evening and morning, the third day; and so on until the morning of the sixth day, from which God’s seventh-day rest begins. Although the days are accompanied by their nights, the narrative speaks of days, not nights.

For night belongs to day, not day to night, when the exalted and holy angels refer what they know of creation in the creature itself to the honor and love of him in whom they contemplate the eternal principles according to which it was created. Through this most harmonious contemplation they are one day—the day that the Lord made, to which the Church, freed from this pilgrimage, will be joined, so that we too may rejoice and be glad in it (Ps. CXVII, 24).

## CHAPTER XXVI — How the number of the days is to be understood

[Col. 0314]

43. Thus, when the sixth repetition of that day had been completed—a day whose evening and morning can be understood according to the explanation given above—the whole of creation was completed. Morning came, by which the sixth day would end, and from which the seventh would begin, having no evening, because God’s rest is not a creature.

While creation was being made through the other days, it was known as made in itself in one way, and in another way in him in whose truth it was seen as destined to be made; the appearance of this knowledge, as it were a faded one, constituted evening. Therefore, in this account of created things, we must not understand the day to be the form of one work, evening its completion, and morning the beginning of another work. Otherwise we would be forced to say, contrary to Scripture, either that the creature of the seventh day was created in addition to the six days, or that the seventh day itself is no creature.

Rather, that day which God made is itself repeated through his works—not by a bodily circuit but by spiritual knowledge—when that blessed company of angels first contemplates the works in the Word of God, by which God says, “Let it be,” and therefore they are first made in its knowledge when it is said, “And so it was made.” Later, they recognize the thing itself as made, in the thing itself; this is signified by evening. Then they refer their knowledge of the made thing to the praise of that truth in which they had seen the principle according to which it was to be made; this is signified by morning.

Thus throughout all those days there is one day. It is not to be understood according to the ordinary usage of these days, which we see determined and counted by the circuit of the sun, but according to another mode—one from which the three days mentioned before the creation of these luminaries cannot be excluded. For this mode did not extend only to the fourth day, so that we would then begin thinking of the ordinary days; it extended through the sixth and seventh as well.

Accordingly, “day” and “night,” between which God divided, must be understood in one way, and this day and night, between which he said that the luminaries he created should divide, in another, when he said, “Let them divide between day and night” (Gen. I, 14). For he created this day when he created the sun, whose presence displays that same day. But that day which was first created had already completed three days when these luminaries were created at the fourth repetition of that day.

## CHAPTER XXVII — The ordinary days of the week are utterly different from the seven days of Genesis

44. Since, therefore, we cannot experience or perceive in this earthly mortality of ours that day—or those days counted by its repetition—and since, if we can make any effort to understand them, we ought not rashly to pronounce a judgment as though no other interpretation could be more fitting or probable, let us believe that these seven days, which serve in place of those days as the week whose course and return carry time along, in which one day is the circuit from sunrise to sunrise, provide some sort of representation of them. Yet we should have no doubt that they are not similar to those days but greatly unlike them.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — The interpretation given concerning spiritual light and day should not be considered improper or figurative

45. No one should suppose that what I said about spiritual light, the spiritual day that was created, the angelic creature, the contemplation it possesses in the Word of God, the knowledge by which the creature is known in itself, and its reference to the praise of unchangeable truth—in which the principle of the thing to be made was first seen, and which is recognized as made—applies to the understanding of day, evening, and morning not properly but only figuratively and allegorically.

It applies differently from the customary daily course of this corporeal light, but not as though it were proper here and figurative there. For where the light is better and more certain, there too the day is more truly day. Why, then, should there not also be a truer evening and a truer morning?

If in these days light has a certain decline toward its setting, which we call evening, and returns again toward its rising, which we call morning, why should we not also speak there of evening when the creature is looked down upon from contemplation of the Creator [Note: [Col. 0315] The Bigotian manuscript has *dispicitur*, “is looked at”; others have *despicitur*, “is looked down upon,” as though “looked at from above,” a usage employed by Augustine above, no. 41, and in Book 2, no. 17, and by Virgil, *Aeneid* I.228:

> Looking down upon the sail-bearing sea and the lands lying below.]

and of morning when, from knowledge of the creature, one rises up in praise of the Creator?

Christ is not called light in the same way that he is called a stone (John VIII, 12; Acts IV, 11): the former is said properly, the latter certainly figuratively. Whoever, therefore, seeks in the enumeration of those days an interpretation other than the one we have been able, according to our capacity, either to investigate or suppose—an interpretation that could be understood more properly and better in this account of the creation of things, not figuratively in prophecy—should seek it and, with divine assistance, discover it.

It may happen that I too shall perhaps find another interpretation more consonant with these words of divine Scripture. For I do not affirm this interpretation in such a way as to claim that another, which ought to be preferred, cannot be found, any more than I affirm that Scripture’s account of God’s rest was intended to suggest to us rest after weariness or the burden of anxiety.

## CHAPTER XXIX — Day, evening, and morning in angelic knowledge

46. For this reason someone may perhaps contend with me in argument and say that the angels of the higher heavens do not behold in succession, first, the principles of creatures unchangeably in the unchangeable truth of God’s Word; then the creatures themselves; and, third, their knowledge of those creatures in themselves, referring it to the praise of the Creator. Rather, he may say, their minds can possess all these things simultaneously with marvelous ease.

Yet would he say—or, if anyone said it, should he be heard—that the heavenly city among the angelic multitudes either does not contemplate the eternity of the Creator, or is ignorant of the mutability of creation, or does not praise the Creator on the basis of that lower knowledge as well? They can do all this simultaneously; they do all this simultaneously. Therefore they possess simultaneously day, evening, and morning.

## CHAPTER XXX — Angelic knowledge is no less noble, although it contains evening and morning

47. Nor need we fear that someone who is already capable of perceiving those realities may therefore think that this cannot happen there, because it cannot happen in these days that are completed by the circuit of this sun.

Even here, in the same parts of the earth, all these things cannot occur simultaneously. But who would not see, if he wished to attend to it, that the whole world simultaneously possesses day where the sun is, night where it is not, evening where it departs, and morning where it approaches?

We plainly cannot possess all these things simultaneously on earth. Yet we should not therefore equate this earthly condition and the temporal and spatial circuit of corporeal light with that spiritual homeland, where there is always day in the contemplation of unchangeable truth, always evening in knowledge of the creature in itself, and always morning even from that knowledge in praise of the Creator.

For there evening is produced not by the departure of a higher light but by the distinction of a lower knowledge; nor does morning follow night as morning knowledge follows the night of ignorance. Rather, it elevates even the evening knowledge to the glory of the Creator.

Finally, without mentioning night, he says: “In the evening, and morning, and at midday I will recount and announce, and he will hear my voice” (Ps. LIV, 18). Here perhaps the reference is to the alternation of times, but, as I think, it nevertheless signifies what would be done without alternation of times in the homeland for which his pilgrimage longed.

## CHAPTER XXXI — Why, at the beginning of creation, day, evening, and morning were not simultaneous in angelic knowledge

48. But if that angelic society and unity of the day that God first created now performs and possesses all these things simultaneously, did it also possess them simultaneously when these things were being created?

Throughout the six days, when the things that God chose to create on each day were being made, did it not first receive them in the Word of God, so that they were first made in its knowledge when it was said, “And so it was made”? Then, when they had been made in their own nature and had pleased God because they were good, did it not likewise know them through a certain lower knowledge, signified by the name “evening”? And then, after evening had occurred, did morning not come when God was praised for his work and knowledge was received, from God’s Word, of the next creature that was to be made, before it was made?

Therefore at that time day, evening, and morning were not all simultaneous, but occurred individually, in the order recalled by Scripture.

## CHAPTER XXXII — If all these things were then simultaneous in the angels’ knowledge, they were nevertheless not without a certain order

49. Or were all things even then simultaneous, not according to temporal delays, as these days occur when the sun rises and sets and returns to its place in order to rise again, but according to the spiritual power of the angelic mind, which comprehends simultaneously, with the greatest ease, everything it wishes to know?

Yet even then they were not without an order, in which the connection of preceding and succeeding causes appears. Knowledge cannot take place unless the things to be known precede it; and these things are prior in the Word through which all things were made rather than in all the things that have been made.

The human mind first experiences created things through the bodily senses and receives knowledge of them according to the measure of human weakness. It then seeks their causes, if somehow it can reach those causes that abide principally and unchangeably in the Word of God, and thus perceive his invisible things, understood through the things that have been made (Rom. I, 20).

Who does not know how slowly and with what difficulty it does this, and how much time is required because of the corruptible body that weighs down the soul (Wis. IX, 15), even when it is carried along by the most ardent zeal to do this promptly and perseveringly?

The angelic mind, however, clinging to the Word of God in pure love, after it had been created in such an order as to precede the other creatures, first saw them in the Word of God as things to be made, before they were made. Thus they first came to be in its knowledge when God said that they should be made, before they came to be in their own nature. Once made, it likewise recognized them in themselves, through that lesser knowledge which was called evening.

The things that were being made naturally preceded this knowledge, because whatever can be known precedes knowledge. Unless something first exists to be known, it cannot be known. After this, if the angelic mind took delight in itself in such a way that it delighted more in itself than in its Creator, morning would not occur—that is, it would not rise from its knowledge to the praise of the Creator.

But when morning had occurred [Note: [Col. 0317] Most and better manuscripts lack *mane*, “morning.”], another thing had to be made and known, when God said, “Let it be,” so that it would likewise first come to be in the knowledge of the angelic mind, and “And so it was made” could again be said; then it would come to be in its own nature, where it would be recognized in the succeeding evening.

50. Accordingly, even if there are here no intervals of temporal delay, the principle of the creature to be made nevertheless preceded in the Word of God when he said, “Let there be light.” Then the light itself followed, by which the angelic mind was formed and which came to be in its own nature; it did not follow elsewhere that it should be made. Therefore it was not first said, “And so it was made,” and afterward, “And God made the light.” Rather, immediately after the Word of God, light was made, and created light adhered to the creating Light, seeing that Light and seeing itself in it—that is, the principle according to which it was made.

It also saw itself in itself—that is, it saw the distinction between what had been made and him who made it [Note: [Col. 0317] The Sorbonne manuscript has *distare*, “to be distinct.”]. Therefore, when what had been made pleased God, and the light, seeing that it was good, was separated from the darkness, and the light was called day and the darkness night, evening also occurred. This knowledge was necessary, by which the creature was distinguished from the Creator and was known in itself in a different way from how it was known in him.

From this point morning came, so that another thing might be known beforehand—something that was to be made by the Word of God, first in the knowledge of the angelic mind and afterward in the nature of the firmament itself. Therefore God said, “Let there be a firmament,” and “so it was made” in the knowledge of the spiritual creature, which knew it beforehand before it came to be in itself.

Then God made the firmament—that is, he now made the nature of the firmament itself, whose knowledge was lesser, as it were an evening knowledge. In this way the process continued until the completion of all the works and until God’s rest, which has no evening, because it was not made as a creature, so that its knowledge too could be doubled—as prior and greater in the Word of God, like day, and later and lesser in itself, like evening.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — Whether all things were created simultaneously or through intervals of days

51. But if the angelic mind can possess simultaneously all the things that discourse distinguishes individually according to the order of their connected causes, were the things that were being made—the firmament itself, the gathering of the waters, the appearance of the uncovered lands, the sprouting of shrubs and trees, the formation of the luminaries and stars, and the aquatic and terrestrial animals—all made simultaneously?

Or were they made rather through intervals of time according to predetermined days? Or perhaps we should not think of them as having been instituted in the same way that we now experience their natural movements, but according to the wonderful and ineffable power of God’s Wisdom, which reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly (Wis. VIII, 1)?

Wisdom itself does not reach things by steps or arrive as though by walking. Therefore, as its movement is easy and most effective, so God easily created all things, since they were created through it. The fact that we now see them moved through temporal intervals to accomplish what is appropriate to each kind proceeds from those implanted principles which God scattered as seeds in the instant of creation, when he spoke and they were made, commanded and they were created (Ps. XXXII, 9).

52. It was not therefore instituted slowly so that things that are slow might be slow, nor were the ages created with the delay by which they pass. For time brings about those numbers which things did not receive temporally when they were created.

Otherwise, if we imagine that the natural movements of things and the ordinary spans of these days that we know were already present when these things were first made by the Word of God, not one day but several would have been required. Things that sprout from roots and cover the earth would first have to germinate beneath the soil; then, over a definite number of days, each according to its kind, they would have to burst into the air—even if this continued in the manner that Scripture says occurred in the creation of their nature on one day, namely the third.

Then how many days would have been needed for birds to fly, if, existing from their beginnings, they reached feathers and wings through the natural stages proper to them? Or were only eggs created when, on the fifth day, it was said that the waters brought forth every winged creature according to its kind?

If this could rightly be said because, in the moisture of the eggs, all the things were already present that grow together and unfold through definite numerical stages, because those numerical principles were already immaterially woven into corporeal things, why could the same thing not rightly be said even before the eggs, when those same principles were already being formed in the moist element, by which birds could arise and reach completion through the temporal delays proper to each kind?

For the Creator of whom Scripture has related that he completed all his works in six days is the one of whom it is also written elsewhere, without contradiction, that he created all things simultaneously (Ecclus. XVIII, 1). Accordingly, he who created all things simultaneously also made these six or seven days—or rather, one day repeated six or seven times—simultaneously.

Why, then, was it necessary for the six days to be narrated so distinctly and orderly? Clearly, because those who cannot see what is meant by “He created all things simultaneously” unless discourse proceeds with them more slowly cannot reach the point to which it leads them.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — All things were made both simultaneously and nevertheless over six days

[Col. 0319]

53. How, then, do we say that the presence of that light was repeated six times, from evening to morning, through angelic knowledge, when it was enough for it to possess the three things simultaneously—that is, day, evening, and morning—once, since it contemplated the whole creation simultaneously, just as it was made simultaneously: in the first and unchangeable principles through which it was created, for the sake of day; in its own nature, for the sake of evening; and, on the basis even of that lower knowledge, praised the Creator, for the sake of morning?

Or how did morning precede, so that it might know in the Word what God was afterward going to make, which it would subsequently know in the evening, if nothing was made earlier or later because all things were made simultaneously?

On the contrary, the things recalled over the six days were made both earlier and later, and all things were made simultaneously. The Scripture that narrates God’s works through the days mentioned, and the Scripture that says he made all things simultaneously, are both truthful; and both are one, because they were written under the inspiration of the one Spirit of truth.

54. In matters where intervals of time do not demonstrate what is earlier or later, although both may be said—simultaneous, and earlier and later—what is said to be simultaneous is nevertheless more easily understood than what is said to be earlier and later.

For example, when we look at the rising sun, it is certainly clear that our sight could not reach it unless it crossed the entire expanse of air and sky between us and it. Who could adequately estimate the distance involved?

Our sight, or the ray of our eyes, would not reach the air above the sea unless it had first passed through the air above the land, wherever inland region we may occupy between where we are and the seashore. Then, if along the same line of our gaze land adjoining the sea still lies beyond the sea, our sight cannot cross the air spread above those transmarine lands unless it has first traversed the expanse of air extending above the sea that it encountered first.

Let us suppose that beyond those lands across the sea nothing remains but Ocean. Can our sight cross the air spread above Ocean unless it has first crossed all the air on this side of Ocean above the land? Ocean is said to be of immeasurable size. But however great it is, the rays of our eyes must first pass through the air above it, and afterward through whatever lies beyond, before finally reaching the sun that we see.

Since, then, we have said “first” and “afterward” so many times, does our gaze for that reason not cross all these things simultaneously, in one stroke? If, with our eyes closed, we turn our face toward the sun we are about to see, then as soon as we open them, will we not think that our sight found itself there rather than carried itself there, so that even our eyes do not seem to have been opened before our gaze reached the place toward which it was directed [Note: [Col. 0320] The American and Erfurt editions have *quam illo quo intenderant pervenisse*, “than having reached the place toward which they were directed.” Lovaniensis has *pervenissent*, “they would have reached.” The manuscript reads *quam illa quo intenderat pervenisse*—that is, “than that the sharpness of the eyes had reached the place toward which it was directed.”]?

And certainly this is a ray of corporeal light, flashing from our eyes and touching something so far away with such speed that it cannot be estimated or compared. It is therefore clear that both all those vast and immense spaces are crossed simultaneously in a single stroke, and that they are nevertheless crossed in an earlier-and-later order.

55. When the Apostle wished to express the swiftness of our resurrection, he said that it would occur “in the twinkling of an eye” (I Cor. XV, 52). Nothing in the movements or strokes of corporeal things can be found swifter than this.

If the sight of bodily eyes can accomplish so much through speed, what can the sight of the mind do—especially the angelic mind? What should we say of the speed of God’s supreme Wisdom, which reaches everywhere because of its purity, and into which nothing defiled enters (Wis. VII, 24)?

In things therefore that were made simultaneously, no one sees what ought to have happened earlier or later except in that Wisdom through which all things were made simultaneously and in an ordered manner.

## CHAPTER XXXV — Conclusion concerning the days of Genesis

56. If, then, that day which God first made is a spiritual and rational creature—that is, the angels and heavenly powers—it was presented to all God’s works according to an order of presence that was also an order of knowledge [Note: [Col. 0320] Several manuscripts have *praescientiae*, “of foreknowledge.”]. Through this knowledge it would know beforehand in the Word of God the things that were to be made and would know them in the creature once made—not through the delays of temporal intervals, but possessing an earlier and later order in the connection of creatures, while, in the efficacy of the Creator, all things were simultaneous.

For he made things that were to be future in such a way that he did not make temporal things temporally; rather, times proceeded from the things made by him. Accordingly, these seven days, which the light of the heavenly body unfolds and repeats by circling around, admonish us, by a certain shadow of signification, to seek those days in which created spiritual light could be presented to all God’s works through the perfection of the number six. And then it could have God’s seventh rest as morning, and no evening.

Thus God’s resting on the seventh day does not mean that he needed the seventh day for his rest. Rather, he rested from all his works that he had made in the sight of his angels—and certainly only in himself, who was not made. That is, his angelic creature, which was presented as day with evening for knowing all his works both in him and in themselves, could know nothing better, after all his very good works, than that he rested from them all in himself, needing none of them in order to be more blessed.

# BOOK FIVE

Concerning what is written in Genesis, chapter 2, verse 4: “This is the book of the creation of heaven,” and so forth, up to verse 6: “But a spring rose from the earth,” and so forth

[Col. 0321]

## CHAPTER ONE — The six or seven days of Genesis could have been counted by the repetition of one day

1. “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth. When day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field before it was upon the earth, and every grass of the field before it sprang up. For God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no human being to work the earth. But a spring rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth.”

The interpretation that God made one day, from the repetition of which the six or seven days could then have been counted, now becomes more firmly established. Holy Scripture now says this more openly, as it were concluding all that it had said from the beginning up to this point, and adding: “This is the book of the creation,” or “making,” “of heaven and earth, when day was made.”

No one will say that heaven and earth are mentioned here in the same way as when it was said, before the creation of day was indicated, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1). If that passage is understood to mean that God made something without day, before he made day, I have explained in its proper place how it can be understood, as I thought necessary to explain, without preventing anyone from finding a better interpretation.

But now Scripture says: “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when day was made.” It sufficiently shows, in my opinion, that it is not here mentioning heaven and earth in the same way as at the beginning, before day was made, when darkness was over the abyss. Rather, it is speaking of how heaven and earth were made when day was made—that is, once the parts and kinds of things had already been formed and distinguished, by which the whole of creation was ordered and composed into the appearance called the world.

2. The heaven mentioned here, then, is that which, when God had created it, he called the firmament, together with all that is in it; and the earth is that which, together with the abyss, occupies the lowest place, with all that is in it.

For the text continues and adds: “God made heaven and earth.” By mentioning heaven and earth both before the reference to the making of day and again after that reference, it does not allow us to suppose that it is now naming heaven and earth as it did at the beginning, before day existed.

The words are arranged as follows: “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when day was made; God made heaven and earth.” If anyone should wish to understand the earlier expression, “the book of the creation of heaven and earth,” in the same way as the statement, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” before he created day—because heaven and earth are mentioned here first and day was made afterward—he is corrected by the words that follow. For after the making of day has been mentioned, the name of heaven and earth is again added.

3. Moreover, even the fact that the word “when” is inserted and thus joined to “day was made” compels any contentious person to admit that no other interpretation is possible.

If the sentence had been arranged so as to read, “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth; day was made; God made heaven and earth,” someone might perhaps think that the book of the creation of heaven and earth was named in the same way as heaven and earth were named at the beginning, before day was created. Then “day was made” would have been added, just as it was afterward narrated there that God made day; and immediately afterward it would again say, “God made heaven and earth,” as though these things had been made after day was created.

But because the phrase is placed so as to say, “when day was made”—whether you connect it with the preceding words, making the sentence read, “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth when day was made,” or with what follows, so that the complete sentence reads, “When day was made, God made heaven and earth”—it undoubtedly compels us to understand that heaven and earth are being mentioned as having been made when day was made.

Then, after it had said, “God made heaven and earth,” it added, “and every green plant of the field,” which was certainly made on the third day. From this it becomes even clearer that this is the same one day that God made, by whose repetition the second, third, and remaining days were made, up to the seventh day.

## CHAPTER II — Why “the green plant of the field” was added

4. Since, in accordance with the customary usage of Scripture, he now wished the name “heaven and earth” to be understood as referring to the whole creation, one may ask why he added, “and every green plant of the field.”

It seems to me that he included this in order to indicate more meaningfully which day he was commending when he said, “when day was made.” Someone might quickly suppose that this referred to the day of corporeal light, whose circuit displays for us the alternation of daytime and nighttime.

But when we recall the order of the created things and find that every green plant of the field was created on the third day, before the sun was made—which was made on the fourth day, and whose presence produces this ordinary daily day—when we hear, “When day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field,” we are reminded to think about that day. Whether it was corporeal, produced by some light unknown to us, or spiritual, in the fellowship of the unity of the angels, we should nevertheless strive to investigate it by understanding, since it was not of the kind that we know here.

## CHAPTER III — From the Order of the Narrative It Is Understood That All Things Were Created Simultaneously

**5.** It will also not be irrelevant to observe that, although he could have said, “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when God made heaven and earth”—so that by “heaven and earth” we might understand whatever is in them, as Holy Scripture customarily speaks, often indicating the whole creation by the name “heaven and earth,” sometimes adding “and the sea,” and occasionally joining the words, “and all that is in them” (Ps. 145:6)—so that, whatever of these expressions he might have used, we would understand “the day” to be included, whether the day he created first or the day produced by the presence of the sun: he did not speak in this way. Rather, he inserted the word “day,” saying, “When day was made.”

Nor did he speak in such a way as to say, “This is the book of the creation of day, heaven, and earth,” as though following the order in which the things are narrated as having been made. Nor did he say, “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when day and heaven and earth were made, when God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field.” Nor did he say, “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when God made day, heaven and earth, and every green plant of the field.” For ordinary usage of speech would have favored these forms of expression more strongly.

Rather, he says: “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth: when day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field”—as though indicating that, when day was made, God then made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field.

**6.** The earlier narrative, moreover, first indicates that day was made, and counts it as one day. After it, it numbers a second day, on which the firmament was made; and a third, on which the forms of the earth and the sea were ordered, and the earth produced trees and grass.

Or is this perhaps what we were attempting to demonstrate in the preceding book: that God made all things simultaneously, since, after the continuity of the narrative had recalled that all things were created and completed in the order of six days, everything is now reduced to a single day under the name of heaven and earth, with the kind of shrubs also included?

This was surely the reason for what I said above: if, perhaps, from our customary understanding the word “day” were taken in its ordinary sense, the reader would be corrected when he recalled that God had said that the green plant of the field was to be produced before this solar day.

Thus the testimony that God created all things simultaneously is not brought forth from another book of Holy Scripture (Ecclus. 18:1); rather, the testimony immediately following on the page admonishes us concerning this matter when it says: “When day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field.” Thus you should understand this day to have been repeated seven times, so that seven days came to be. And when you hear that all things were made “when day was made,” grasp—if you are able—that the sixfold or sevenfold repetition took place without intervals of delays or temporal stretches. If you are not yet able, leave these matters to be contemplated by those who are capable.

But as you make progress, with Scripture not abandoning your weakness and walking beside you more slowly with a mother’s step, it speaks in such a way that by its loftiness it mocks the proud, by its profundity terrifies the attentive, by its truth nourishes the great, and by its gracious familiarity feeds the little ones.

[Note: Older manuscripts of the highest quality read, “it feeds lambs.”]

## CHAPTER IV — Why the Grass Is Said to Have Been Made Before It Sprouted

**7.** What, then, does the following also mean? For the discourse is joined together in this way: “When day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field, before it was upon the earth, and every grass of the field, before it sprang up.”

What does this mean? Must we not ask where he made these things, before they were upon the earth and before they sprang up? Who would not more readily believe that God made them when they sprang up, rather than before they sprang up, unless he were warned by this divine utterance that God made them before they sprang up? Thus, if he cannot discover where they were made, anyone who piously believes this Scripture may nevertheless believe that they were made before they sprang up; for whoever believes it impiously does not believe it.

**8.** What, then, shall we say? Is it what some have thought: that all things were made in the very Word of God before they sprang up on the earth?

But if they were made in this way, they were made not when day was made, but before day was made. Scripture, however, plainly says: “When day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field before it was upon the earth, and every grass before it sprang up.”

Therefore, if they were made when day was made, they were certainly not made before day was made. Consequently, they were not made in the Word, which is coeternal with the Father, before day—or rather, before anything at all—was made; they were made when day was made.

For those things that are in the Word of God before the whole creation were certainly not made.

[Note: Lovaniensis reads, “they were certainly not made when day was made.” M.]

These things, however, were made when day was made, as the words of Scripture declare. Yet they were made before they were upon the earth and before they sprang up—this is said concerning the green plants and grass of the field.

**9.** Where, then? Was it causally and rationally in the earth itself, just as everything is already present in seeds before, so to speak, unfolding and displaying its growth and forms through the sequence of times?

But the seeds that we see are already upon the earth; they have already sprung up. Were they not upon the earth, but beneath the earth? And for this reason were they made before they sprang up: because they sprang up when the seeds germinated and, through the advance of growth, burst forth into the open air—a process that we now see occurring over intervals of time assigned to each kind?

Were the seeds, then, made when day was made, with every green plant of the field and every grass of the field already contained in them—not yet in the form in which they have sprung up upon the earth, but in the power that they possess in the principles of the seeds?

Did the earth, then, first produce the seeds? But Scripture did not speak in this way when it said: “And the earth produced grass for fodder, or grass for hay, bearing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness; and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit, whose seed is in itself according to its kind upon the earth” (Gen. 1:11–12).

These words rather make it appear that the seeds arose from the grasses and trees, not that the latter arose from the seeds, but from the earth—especially since the very words of God have this meaning. For he did not say, “Let seeds germinate in the earth, producing grass and fruit-bearing trees”; rather, he said, “Let the earth germinate grass bearing seed,” indicating that the seed came from the grass, not the grass from the seed.

“And so it was done, and the earth produced” (Gen. 1:11–12)—that is, first it was so made in the knowledge of that day, and then the earth produced it, so that this might also occur in the creation itself, which had been established.

**10.** How, then, were they made before they were upon the earth and before they sprang up? It is as though there were one kind of making for them together with heaven and earth, when that unusual and unknown day was made which God made first, and another kind of springing up upon the earth, which occurs only through these days produced by the sun’s circuit, through intervals of time suited to each kind.

If this is so, and if that day is the fellowship and unity of the heavenly angels and powers, then undoubtedly God’s creation is known to the angels in a very different way from that in which it is known to us. Apart from the fact that they know it in the Word of God, through whom all things were made, I mean that they know it in itself in a very different way from us.

To them it was known primordially, or, so to speak, originally, as God first established it, and after that establishment rested from his works, creating nothing further. To us, however, it is known according to the administration of things previously created, already through the order of times, according to which God, after completing those things through the perfection of the sixfold work, continues to operate even now.

**11.** Thus it was causally that the earth was then said to have produced grass and trees—that is, it received the power to produce them. For in it, as though in roots, if I may put it so, of time, those things had already been made which were destined to exist through time.

For afterward God planted a paradise toward the east and brought forth there from the earth every tree beautiful to look upon and good for food (Gen. 2:8–9). Yet it must not be said that he then added something to creation which he had not made previously, as though something had subsequently to be added to that perfection in which he completed all things as very good on the sixth day.

Rather, because all the natures of shrubs and trees had already been made in the first creation—from which creation God rested—he subsequently moves and administers through temporal courses the very things that he created and from whose creation he rested. He therefore not only planted paradise then, but also now creates all things that come into being.

For who else creates these things even now except the one who continues to work until now? Yet now he creates them from things that already exist. Then, however, when absolutely nothing existed, he created them—when that day was made which itself also absolutely did not exist.

[Note: The printed editions read, “which was wholly spiritual,” omitting the negative particle; we restore it here from the manuscripts.]

That day was, of course, a spiritual and intellectual creation.

## CHAPTER V — The Order of the Creation of Things Through Six Days: Not by Intervals of Time but by the Connection of Causes

**12.** Once creation had been made, times began to run through its movements. Therefore it is pointless to seek times before creation, as though times could be found before time.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and the edition of Amerbach. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “times before creation.”]

For if there were no movement, whether of a spiritual or bodily creation, by which the future succeeded the past through the present, there would be no time at all. Creation, however, could not move if it did not exist.

Time therefore began from creation rather than creation from time; yet both are from God. For from him, through him, and in him are all things (Rom. 11:36).

Nor should the statement “time began from creation” be understood as though time were not itself a creation, since it is the movement of creation from one thing to another, with things following one another according to the ordering of God, who administers all that he created.

Therefore, when we consider the first creation of things, from which works God rested on the seventh day, we must think neither of those days as solar days such as these nor of that work in the manner in which God now works something in time. Rather, we must consider how he worked that from which times would begin; how he worked all things simultaneously, granting them an order not by intervals of time but by the connection of causes, so that the things made simultaneously might also be completed through the presentation of the number six belonging to that day.

**13.** Thus, in causal rather than temporal order, shapeless and formable matter was made first, both spiritual and bodily, from which what was to be made would come to be, although matter itself had not existed before it was established.

Nor was it established except by that supreme and true God, from whom all things are. This matter may have been signified by the term “heaven and earth”—having been made by God in the beginning before that one day which he created, and already so called because heaven and earth were made from it; or it may have been signified by the terms “invisible and unformed earth” and “dark abyss,” as was discussed in the first book.

**14.** Among those things that had already been formed from formlessness and that are more explicitly called created, made, or established, day was made first. For it was fitting that the primacy of creation should belong to that nature which could recognize creation through the Creator, rather than the Creator through creation.

Second came the firmament, from which the bodily world begins.

Third came the forms of the sea and the earth, and upon the earth, potentially, so to speak, the nature of grasses and trees. For in this way the earth produced them at God’s word before they sprang up, receiving all the numbers belonging to them, which it would bring forth through time according to their kind.

Then, after this habitation of things had been established, on the fourth day the lights and stars were created, so that the higher part of the world might first be adorned with visible things that move within the world.

On the fifth day the nature of the waters, because it is joined to the sky and air, produced at God’s word its native creatures—namely, all things that swim and fly—and these too potentially, in the numbers that would be brought forth through the suitable movements of time.

On the sixth day, similarly, came the terrestrial animals, as the last things from the world’s final element—nevertheless potentially, with their numbers to be visibly unfolded by time afterward.

**15.** That day knew this entire order of creation. Through this knowledge it was, in a certain sense, presented six times and exhibited as six days, although it is one day: it recognized the things that were made first in the Creator and afterward in themselves, without remaining in them, but referring even their later knowledge back to the love of God.

It provided evening, morning, and midday in all things—not through delays of time, but on account of the order of created things. Finally, by representing the knowledge of its Creator’s rest—his rest in himself from all his works—it merited to be blessed and sanctified, for that rest has no evening.

For this reason Scripture in a certain manner dedicates the number seven itself to the Holy Spirit (Isa. 11:2–3), and the Church recognizes this.

**16.** This, then, is the book of the creation of heaven and earth: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”—according to a certain formability of matter, so to speak, which was destined to be formed subsequently by his word, preceding its formation not in time but in origin.

For when it was being formed, day was made first. “When day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field before it was upon the earth, and every grass of the field before it sprang up,” as we have discussed—or in whatever clearer and more suitable way this may be seen or expressed.

## CHAPTER VI — Concerning the Verse “For God Had Not Rained,” and Whether It Is Thereby Understood That All Things Were Created Simultaneously

**17.** What follows, however—“For God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no human being to work the earth”—is difficult to investigate: what it refers to and what it suggests to us.

It is as though God made the grass of the field before it sprang up for this reason: because it had not yet rained upon the earth. For if he had made the grass after the rain, it would appear to have sprung up more through the rain than to have been made by him.

But what of this? What springs up after the rain is made by someone other than the same God? And why was there no human being to work the earth? Had he not already made the human being on the sixth day and rested on the seventh from all his works?

Or does he mention this by recapitulation, because when God made every green plant of the field and every grass, it had not yet rained upon the earth and there was not yet a human being? For he made these things on the third day, but the human being on the sixth.

Yet when God made every green plant and every grass of the field before it sprang up upon the earth, not only was there no human being to work the earth, but the grass itself was not yet upon the earth—although he says that it was made before it sprang up.

Or did God make these things on the third day because there was not yet a human being whose cultivation of the earth would cause them to grow? As though so many trees and so many kinds of grasses did not grow from the earth without any human labor at all.

**18.** Or were both statements included for this reason: both because it had not yet rained upon the earth and because there was not yet a human being to work the earth?

Where there is no human labor, these things grow through rain. There are also some things that do not grow through rain unless human labor is added. Thus both forms of assistance are now necessary for everything to grow. Then, however, both were lacking; therefore God made these things by the power of his Word, without rain and without human labor.

Even now it is he who makes them, but now through rain and through human hands—although neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God, who gives the growth, is everything (1 Cor. 3:7).

**19.** What, then, does he add when he says, “But a spring rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth”?

That spring, flowing with such abundance as the Nile flows for Egypt, could have served as rain for the whole earth. Why, then, is it commended as something great that God made these growing things before it rained, when a spring watering the earth could provide as much assistance as rain?

Even if it provided somewhat less, perhaps smaller things would have grown, though they would not have failed to grow altogether.

Or does Scripture here also, according to its custom, speak in a manner adapted to the weak, and yet suggest something that whoever is capable may understand?

For just as earlier, in connection with this day, it indicated that one day had been made by God, and that God made heaven and earth when day was made—so that we might in some way think that God made everything simultaneously, although the preceding enumeration of six days seemed to indicate intervals of time—so, after saying that God made every green plant of the field together with heaven and earth before it was upon the earth, and every grass of the field before it sprang up, it added:

“For God had not yet rained upon the earth, and there was no human being to work the earth.”

It was as though it were saying: “God did not make these things in the way he now makes such things, when he sends rain and when human beings work.” For these things now come to be through intervals of time, whereas at that time there were no intervals of time, when he made everything simultaneously and from that simultaneous creation time itself would begin.

## CHAPTER VII — Concerning the Spring That Watered the Whole Earth, and Related Matters

**20.** What follows—“But a spring rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth”—now indicates, as I think, what comes to be according to intervals of time from that first creation of things in which all things were made simultaneously.

And rightly he began with the element from which all kinds of animals, grasses, and trees arise, so that they might carry out their temporal cycles distributed according to their proper natures.

For all the beginnings of seeds, whether those from which all flesh or those from which all shrubs arise, are moist and grow together from moisture. Yet within them are highly effective numbers, drawing along with them the derivative powers from those perfect works of God from which he rested on the seventh day.

**21.** Nevertheless, it is rightly asked what sort of spring this was, capable of watering the whole face of the earth.

For if it existed and was blocked or dried up, the cause must be sought. Now we see that there is no spring by which the whole face of the earth is watered.

Perhaps, then, human sin also merited this punishment: that the great abundance of that spring should be restrained, removing from the earth its easiest fertility and increasing the labor of its inhabitants.

Human conjecture could affirm this, although Scripture has narrated nothing of the sort, except that the following consideration arises: the human sin upon which the punishment of labor was imposed occurred after the delights of paradise; but paradise had its own very great spring, concerning which we shall speak more carefully in its proper place. From one head of this spring, four great rivers known to the nations are said to flow.

Where, then, were this spring or these rivers when that single, greatest spring rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth?

Certainly it was not then the Gihon, which is called the Nile and is one of the four, that watered Egypt, when the spring rose up from the earth and satisfied not Egypt alone but the whole face of the earth.

**22.** Or should we believe that at first God willed one greatest spring to water the whole earth, so that the things he had established in it principally might, after receiving the assistance of moisture, also come forth through temporal intervals, according to the diversity of their kinds and through different numbers of days?

And afterward, once paradise had been planted, did he restrain that spring and fill the earth with many springs, as we now see? Did he divide the four great rivers from the one spring of paradise, so that the rest of the earth, filled with the kinds of God’s creatures and carrying out the appropriate numbers of their times, might also have its own springs and rivers, while paradise, planted in a more distinguished place, sent forth those four rivers from the head of its spring?

Or did that one spring of paradise, overflowing much more abundantly, first water the whole earth and make it fertile for producing, through the numbers of time, the kinds that he had created in it without intervals of time; and afterward did he restrain the immense eruption of water in that place, so that rivers and springs might then flow from different sources throughout the earth?
