And then, in the region of that spring—which no longer watered the whole earth but sent forth only those four memorable rivers—did he plant paradise, where he placed the human being whom he had made?

## CHAPTER VIII — How Far It Is Helpful to Bring Forward by Conjecture What Scripture Leaves Unstated

**23.** Since not everything has been written concerning how time proceeded after that first creation of things, or how the administrations of created things that were first made and completed on that sixth day followed one another, but only as much as the Spirit who was present in the writer judged sufficient—things that serve not only for knowledge of what was made but also for the prefiguration of what was to come—we conjecture, without knowing, what may have happened—what he, not being ignorant, passed over.

We attempt this only insofar as our capacity permits and as we are assisted, so that no absurdity or contradiction may be thought to exist in the Holy Scriptures, offending the reader’s judgment. Otherwise, while supposing that the things Scripture records as having happened could not have happened, a person might either recoil from faith or fail to approach it.

## CHAPTER IX — The Difficulty Concerning the Spring That Watered the Whole Earth

**24.** Therefore, when we ask about this spring—how the statement “It rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth” may not appear impossible—if what we have said seems impossible to anyone, let him seek another explanation by which this truthful Scripture may nevertheless be shown to be true. It is unquestionably true even if its truth is not demonstrated.

For if he wishes to argue in such a way as to prove it false, then either he himself will say nothing true about the creation and administration of created things, or, if he says something true, he will judge this passage false because he does not understand it.

For example, he might contend that one spring, however large, could not have watered the whole face of the earth, because if it did not water the mountains, it did not water the whole face of the earth; but if it watered the mountains as well, then this was no longer a distribution of nourishment but an inundation like the Flood. And if the earth was then like that, it was entirely sea, and the dry land had not yet been separated.

## CHAPTER X — How That Spring, Which Watered the Whole Earth, Is to Be Understood

**25.** The answer to him is that this could have happened in alternating periods of time, just as at a certain season the Nile spreads over the plains of Egypt and at another season returns to its banks.

Or if the spring is believed to gather annual increases from the waters and winter frosts of some unknown and distant region of the world, what can be said of the alternating tides of the Ocean, or of certain shores that are widely exposed when the waves withdraw and are covered again when they return?

I omit what is reported about the remarkable alternation of certain springs: at fixed intervals of years they overflow so greatly that they water the entire region, while at another time they scarcely provide enough water for drinking from deep wells.

Why, then, should it be incredible that the whole earth was once watered by an alternating flood and ebb flowing from one source of the abyss?

But if Scripture wished to call “the spring,” rather than “the springs,” that part of the abyss which is distinct from what is called the sea—which surrounds the lands with its evident vastness and bitter waves—and which lies solely in that part contained by the earth in hidden recesses, from which all springs and rivers are distributed through different channels and veins and emerge in their several places, then it may have used the singular because of the unity of nature.

This spring, ascending from the earth through innumerable passages of caverns and cracks and watering the whole face of the earth, as though with scattered locks of hair, did not water it in a continuous expanse like the sea or a pond, but as we see water moving through the channels of rivers and winding streams and, when they overflow, soaking the neighboring ground.

Who would not accept this explanation, unless he were afflicted by a contentious spirit?

The whole face of the earth can indeed be understood to have been watered in this way, just as we say that the whole surface of a garment is colored even when the coloring is not continuous but spotted.

This is especially plausible because, at the beginning of the earth’s existence, although not everything was level, it is credible that much of it was, so that the streams bursting forth could spread and extend more widely.

[Note: The printed editions read, “the waters of the sea with waves,” and shortly afterward, “springs and all waters through different courses.” At these places we reproduce the manuscript reading.]

**26.** Accordingly, whether this spring was one that had a single eruption from somewhere, or whether, because of some unity in the earth’s hidden recesses from which all the waters above the earth gush forth—the source of all large and small springs—it was called one spring, ascending from the earth through all its divisions and watering the whole face of the earth; or whether, as is more credible, because Scripture does not say, “One spring rose up,” but says, “A spring rose up from the earth,” it used the singular for the plural—

so that we may understand many springs, watering their own places or regions throughout the earth, just as “a soldier” may be said when many are understood, or as “the locust” and “the frog” are mentioned in the plagues (Ps. 105:34) by which the Egyptians were struck, although the number of locusts and frogs was innumerable—

we need not labor over the matter any longer.

## CHAPTER XI — The First Creation of Things Took Place Without an Interval of Time; Their Administration Did Not

**27.** But let us consider again and again whether the position we have stated can be maintained throughout: that God worked all creatures differently in their first creation, from which works he rested on the seventh day, and differently in their administration, through which he continues to work until now.

That is, then he made everything simultaneously, without any intervals of temporal delay; now, however, he works through intervals of time, in which we see the stars move from rising to setting, the heavens change from summer to winter, and shoots sprout, grow large, become green, and wither at fixed moments of days.

We also see animals conceive, develop, and be born at appointed limits and courses of time, and pass through the stages of life into old age and death, along with other temporal processes of this kind.

For who works these things except God, even without any such movement on his part? Time does not happen to him as it happens to creation.

Between those works of God from which he rested on the seventh day and those which he continues to work until now, Scripture inserted a certain section of its narrative, indicating that it had explained the former and beginning now to join together the latter.

The explanation of those completed works was given in this way:

“This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth. When day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field before it was upon the earth, and every grass of the field before it sprang up. For God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no human being to work the earth.”

The account of the latter works began in this way:

“But a spring rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth.”

From this mention of the spring onward, the things that are narrated came to be through intervals of time, not all simultaneously.

## CHAPTER XII — The Works of God Under Three Considerations

**28.** Since, then, the unchangeable principles of all creatures in the Word of God are one thing; his works, from which he rested on the seventh day, another; and the things that he continues to work from those works until now, a third—the last of these, which I have placed third, is in some measure known to us through bodily senses and through the ordinary course of this life.

The other two, however, are remote from the senses and from the customary activity of human thought. They must first be believed on the authority of God; then, through these things that are known, they must be understood as far as each person can, more or less, according to the measure of his capacity, with divine assistance through inward and eternal principles.

[Note: Thus the printed editions. The manuscripts of the highest quality lack the words “through inward and eternal principles”; they may be removed without damage to the sense.]

## CHAPTER XIII — All Things Were in the Wisdom of God Before They Were Made

**29.** Concerning those first divine, unchangeable, and eternal principles, since the Wisdom of God itself, through which all things were made, knew them before they were made, Scripture testifies as follows:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3).

Who, then, could be so foolish as to say that God did not make the things he knew?

Moreover, if he knew them, where did he know them except with himself, with whom the Word was, through whom all things were made? For if he knew them outside himself, who had taught him? “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, so that it might be repaid to him? For from him, through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:34–36).

**30.** What follows in the Gospel also sufficiently supports this position. For the Evangelist adds and says: “What was made, in him is life, and the life was the light of human beings” (John 1:4).

The meaning is that rational minds—the kind in which the human being was made according to the image of God—have no true light except the Word of God himself, through whom all things were made, and whose participants they can become once purified from every iniquity and error.

## CHAPTER XIV — How the Passage from John, “What Was Made,” Is to Be Punctuated

**31.** The passage should not, then, be pronounced in this way: “What was made in him was life,” as though we should make a subordinate division after “what was made in him” and then continue, “was life.”

For what was not made in him, when, after many earthly creatures had been mentioned, the Psalm says, “You made all things in Wisdom” (Ps. 104:24), and the Apostle says, “For in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” (Col. 1:16)?

If we make the division in that way, it will follow that the earth itself and everything that is in it are life. Since it is absurd to say that all things live, how much more absurd would it be to say that they are life?

This is especially so because the passage specifies what kind of life it means when it adds, “And the life was the light of human beings.”

The division should therefore be made so that, after saying “What was made,” we continue, “in him was life.” This does not mean that in itself—that is, in its own nature, by which it was made a created thing and a creature—it is life; but that in him it is life, because he knew all things that were made through him before they were made.

Thus it is life in him not in the manner of the creature he made, but in the manner of life and the light of human beings—that is, Wisdom itself, the only-begotten Son of God, who is the Word himself.

Thus what was made is life in him in the same way that it is said: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26).

**32.** Nor should it be passed over that the more accurate manuscripts read, “What was made, in him was life,” so that “was life” is understood in the same way as “In the beginning was the Word,” and “the Word was with God,” and “God was the Word.”

[Note: The manuscripts of the highest quality and most others read, “In him was life, as it was in the beginning,” and do not contain the words, “so that ‘was life’ may be understood.”]

Therefore what was made was already life in him, and not just any kind of life. For animals too are said to live, although they cannot participate in wisdom. But this was “life that was the light of human beings.”

Rational minds, purified by his grace, can attain a vision of such a kind that nothing is higher and nothing is more blessed.

## CHAPTER XV — What Kind of Life All Things Are in God

**33.** But even if we read and understand the passage as, “What was made is life in him,” the same meaning remains: what was made through him is understood to be life in him, in which life he saw all things when he made them; and as he saw them, so he made them.

He did not see them outside himself, but in himself he numbered all the things he made. His vision and that of the Father are not different, but one, just as their substance is one.

The Wisdom through which all things were made is also proclaimed in the Book of Job:

“But Wisdom,” it says, “where was she found? Or what is the place of understanding? Mortal humanity does not know her way, nor is she found among human beings.”

And shortly afterward:

“We have heard,” it says, “of her glory. The Lord established her way, and he himself knows her place. For he completed everything that is under heaven, and he knows the things that are upon the earth, all that he made: the balancing of the winds and the measures of the waters. When he made them, he enumerated them as he saw them” (Job 28:12, 22–25).

By these and similar testimonies it is proved that all these things were, before they were made, in the knowledge of the one who made them.

And certainly they were better there, where they were truer, where they were eternal and unchangeable.

It ought to be sufficient for anyone to know—or to believe without hesitation—that God made all these things. I do not think anyone could be so witless as to suppose that God made things he did not know.

Moreover, if he knew them before he made them, then before they were made they were certainly known to him in the manner in which they live eternally and unchangeably and are life. Once made, however, they existed in the manner proper to each creature according to its kind.

## CHAPTER XVI — We Perceive God More Easily with the Mind Than Creatures

[The supplied source ends here.]

34. Although, then, that eternal and unchangeable nature which is God possesses in itself the fact of its existence, as was said to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14)—plainly in a manner altogether different from the things that have been made, since that truly and primarily exists which is always in the same condition, and which not only is not changed but cannot be changed at all—although, I say, it exists without any of the things it has made, while possessing all things primarily, just as it is itself: for it would not make them unless it knew them before making them; nor would it know them unless it saw them; nor would it see them unless it possessed them; nor would it possess things not yet made unless it possessed them in the manner in which it itself exists, unmade; although, then, that ineffable substance cannot be spoken of by a human being through a human being except by employing certain words belonging to place and time, even though it precedes all times and all places, nevertheless the one who made us is nearer to us than are many things that have been made. For “in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). But most of those things are far removed from our mind because of the dissimilarity of their kind, since they are bodily; nor is our mind itself capable, in the very principles according to which they were made, of seeing them with God, so as thereby to know how many they are, how great, and of what sort, even if we do not perceive them through the bodily senses. They are also removed from the senses of our body, since they are far away, or are separated from our sight and touch by other things interposed or placed in the way [Note: [Col. 0333] Nearly all manuscripts read, “and touch” (actuque).]. Consequently, the labor required to discover them is greater than that required to discover him by whom they were made, although it is incomparably more blessed to perceive him with a pious mind, however small its capacity, than to comprehend all those things. Hence the investigators of this world are rightly reproved in the Book of Wisdom: “For if they were able to know so much that they could estimate the world, how did they not more easily find its Lord?” (Wis. 13:9). The foundations of the earth, then, are unknown to our eyes, but the one who founded the earth is near to our minds.

## CHAPTER XVII — Before the ages, from the age, in the age

35. Let us now consider the things that God made all together, from which, when they had been completed on the sixth day, he rested on the seventh; afterward we shall consider his works in which he continues to work until now. He himself is before the ages; we speak of things as being “from the age” from the time when the age began, as with the world itself; and “in the age,” as with the things that are born in the world. When Scripture therefore had said, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” [Col. 0334], shortly afterward it says, “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:3, 10). Elsewhere it is written of this work of God: “You who made the world out of formless matter” (Wis. 11:18). This world is usually designated by the name of heaven and earth, as we have already mentioned; Scripture says that God made these when day was made. We have discussed these words as far as seemed appropriate: how they accord with the creation of this world, how it was completed in six days together with all that is in it, and how it was made when day was made, so that the statement “he created all things together” might also accord with them (Ecclus. 18:1).

## CHAPTER XVIII — Many creatures are unknown to us; how they are known by God and by the angels; morning and evening knowledge

36. We do not know many things belonging to the whole of God’s creation, whether those in the heavens that are too high for our sense to reach; or those perhaps in regions of the earth that are uninhabitable; or those that lie below, either in the depth of the abyss or in the hidden recesses of the earth. These things, then, before they were made, certainly did not exist. How, then, were things that did not exist known to God? And again, how could he make things that were not known to him? For he did not make anything in ignorance. He therefore made them known; he did not come to know them after they had been made. Accordingly, before they were made, they both were and were not: they were in God’s knowledge, but they were not in their own nature. Thus that day was made in which they would become known in both ways, both in God and in themselves: in the one manner, as though by morning or daytime knowledge; in the other, as though by evening knowledge. Yet I would not dare say that they became known to God in a different way when he made them from the way in which he knew them in order to make them, since with him there is no change, nor “shadow caused by turning” (James 1:17).

## CHAPTER XIX — The angels, God’s messengers, have known the mystery of the kingdom of heaven from the ages

37. Certainly he does not need messengers on account of knowledge of inferior things, as though he became more knowledgeable through them; rather, in that simple and wondrous manner he knows all things stably and unchangeably. But he has messengers for our sake and for their own, because it is good for them, according to the order of their proper nature and substance, to obey and attend upon God in such a way that they consult him concerning inferior things and obey his commands and orders from above. Messengers are called *angeli* in Greek, ἄγγελοι; by this general name that entire heavenly city is designated, and we believe that it was created on the first day.

38. For the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, which was revealed at the proper time for our salvation, did not escape them either—the mystery that, once freed from this pilgrimage, we may be joined to their company [Note: [Col. 0334] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read *quo* (“by which”).]. For they could not have been ignorant of this, since the seed itself, which came at the proper time [Note: [Col. 0334] See *Retractations* II, chapter 24, section 2.], was arranged through them in the hand of the mediator (Gal. 3:19), that is, in the power of the one who is their Lord both in the form of God and in the form of a servant. The Apostle also says:

> To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to announce among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all concerning the administration of the mystery that was hidden from the ages in God, who created all things; so that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the Principalities and Powers in the heavenly places, according to the plan of the ages, which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord (Eph. 3:8–11).

Thus this mystery was hidden from the ages in God, yet in such a way that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known through the Church to the Principalities and Powers in the heavenly places; for the Church was first there, where after the resurrection this Church also is to be gathered, so that “we may be equal to the angels of God” (Matt. 22:30). It became known to them from the ages because every creature is not before the ages but from the ages. For the ages arose from it, and it itself is from the ages, since its beginning is the beginning of the ages. But the Only-Begotten is before the ages, through whom the ages were made (Heb. 1:2). Therefore, speaking in the person of Wisdom, he says, “Before the ages he established me” (Prov. 8:23, according to the Septuagint), so that he might make all things in her, to whom it was said, “You made all things in Wisdom” (Ps. 103:24).

39. That what is hidden becomes known to the angels not only in God but also here, when it is brought about and disclosed, is likewise attested by the same Apostle:

> And undoubtedly great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory (1 Tim. 3:16).

And, unless I am mistaken, it is remarkable that whenever God is said to know something as though in the present time, this is not said because he comes to know it then, but because he causes it to be known, whether by angels or by human beings. For this mode of expression, in which what is accomplished is signified through the one who accomplishes it, is frequent in the Holy Scriptures—especially when something is said of God that Truth itself, presiding over our minds, cries out does not properly apply to him according to the literal force of the expression.

## CHAPTER XX — God continues to work

40. Let us now distinguish the works of God that he continues to perform until now from those works from which he rested on the seventh day. For there are some who think [Note: [Col. 0335] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain have *arbitrantur* (“think”). M.] that God made only the world itself, while all other things are now made by the world itself, according to the order and command he gave it; but that God himself now performs no work. Against them is brought the Lord’s statement: “My Father is working until now.” And lest anyone should think that he works something within himself but not in this world, he says, “The Father who remains in me does his works”; and, “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wishes” (John 5:17, 20–21). Furthermore, because he himself works not only great and pre-eminent things but also these earthly and lowly ones, the Apostle says:

> Fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it dies; and what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each seed its own body (1 Cor. 15:36–38).

Let us therefore believe—or, if we can, also understand—that God continues to work until now, so that if his operation were withdrawn from the things he created, they would perish.

[Col. 0336] 41. But plainly, if we suppose that he is now instituting some creature in such a way that he has not included its kind in its original creation, we openly contradict Scripture, which says that he completed all his works on the sixth day (Gen. 2:2). For it is evident that, according to the kinds of things he first created, he now makes many new things that he did not make then. But it cannot rightly be believed that he institutes a new kind, since he completed everything then. Therefore, by a hidden power he moves his entire creation; and as it is set in motion by that movement—while the angels carry out his commands, while the stars revolve, while the winds alternate, while the abyss of waters is stirred by its flows and by various formations gathered also through the air, while the green places [Note: [Col. 0336] The ancient codices consistently read *virecta*.] put forth shoots, unfolding their seeds, while animals are born and live their proper lives with varied appetites, while the wicked are permitted to exercise the righteous—he unfolds the ages that he had implanted, as it were, folded up [Note: [Col. 0336] The printed editions read, “which were established as though enfolded.” But all the manuscripts read, “which was established,” clearly referring to the whole creation. Some continue, “as though pleasing”; others, more faithfully, read *plicita*, from the verb *plico*, “I fold.”] within it when it was first created. Yet these things would not unfold into their appointed courses if the one who created them ceased to govern them by his provident movement.

## CHAPTER XXI — All things are governed by divine providence

42. We must be instructed by the things that are formed and born in time concerning how we ought to consider these matters. For it is not without reason that it is written of Wisdom that “she shows herself to her lovers graciously in her ways and meets them in every providence” (Wis. 6:17). Nor should we listen at all to those who have thought that the higher regions of the world—that is, from the boundary of the denser air upward—are governed by divine providence, but that this lowest earthly and watery region, together with the neighboring air made moist by the exhalations of earth and waters, in which winds and clouds arise, is driven rather by chance and accidental movements.

Against them the Psalm speaks. Having proclaimed the praise of heavenly things, it also turns to these lower things, saying:

> Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all abysses; fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm wind, which perform his word (Ps. 148:7–8).

Nothing seems more subject to chance than all these stormy and turbulent conditions, by which the face of this lower heaven—rightly also assigned the name “earth”—is varied and changed. But when the Psalm adds, “which perform his word,” it sufficiently shows that the order of these things too is subject to divine command; rather, it is hidden from us than absent from the nature of the universe.

Moreover, when the Savior himself says that not one sparrow falls to the ground without the will of God (Matt. 10:29), and that although the grass of the field is shortly to be thrown into the furnace, he himself nevertheless clothes it (Matt. 6:30), does he not confirm that divine providence governs not only this entire region of the world, assigned to mortal and corruptible things, but also its most worthless and insignificant parts?

## CHAPTER XXII — Arguments for divine providence

[Col. 0337]

43. Certainly, if those who deny this and do not submit to the authority of the sacred utterances, but think that this region of the world is disturbed by accidental movements rather than governed by the wisdom of the divine summit, use as evidence either the inconsistency of storms, which I mentioned above, or the fact that human happiness and unhappiness do not occur according to the merits of one’s life, they should observe the order that appears in the limbs of any living creature—not merely physicians, who have carefully laid open and examined these things because of the needs of their art, but any person of ordinary intelligence and reflection. Would they not cry out that God, from whom comes every measure of dimensions, every equality of numbers, and every order of weights, does not cease for even a moment from his governance?

What, then, can be thought more absurd or more foolish than that the whole of that realm should be empty of the direction and governance of providence, when you see its outermost and smallest parts formed with such arrangement that, if considered somewhat more attentively, they inspire an ineffable awe of wonder? And since the nature of the soul surpasses the nature of the body, what could be more senseless than to suppose that divine providence makes no judgment concerning human conduct, when such clear indications of its skill shine forth and are demonstrated in their flesh?

But because these smallest things are readily available to our senses, and we investigate them easily, the order of things is evident in them. Those who do not think that anything exists except what they can see, however, judge the things whose order they cannot see to be disorderly; or, if they think such things exist, they imagine them to be of the sort they are accustomed to see.

## CHAPTER XXIII — How God created all things together and continues to work until now

44. We, however, whose steps are guided by the same divine providence through Holy Scripture lest we fall into that perversity, should try, with its assistance, to investigate from the works of God themselves where he created these things together, when he rested from his completed works, whose visible forms he continues to work out through the succession of time until now.

Let us consider the beauty of any tree—in its trunk, branches, leaves, and fruits. This visible form certainly did not suddenly arise so great and of such a kind, but arose in an order that we also know. It sprang from a root, which the earth first fixed as a shoot; and from that root all those things were formed, distinguished, and grew. That shoot, in turn, came from a seed. All those things therefore existed originally in the seed, not as a mass of bodily size but in causal force and power. For that size is a mass gathered from earth and moisture. But there is a more wondrous and excellent power in the tiny grain: by it the moisture lying beside it, mixed with earth as with matter, was able to be transformed into the quality of that wood, the spreading of its branches, the greenness and form of its leaves, the shapes and abundance of its fruits, and the most orderly distinction of all its parts [Col. 0338]. For what rises or hangs from that tree that has not been drawn out and brought forth from some hidden treasury of that seed?

Yet the seed came from a tree, though not that one but another; and that tree in turn from another seed. Sometimes, too, a tree comes from a tree, when a shoot is taken and planted. Thus there is seed from a tree, a tree from a seed, and a tree from a tree. But seed never comes from seed unless a tree intervenes first. A tree, however, can come from a tree even if no seed intervenes. Thus, by alternating successions, one comes from the other, but both come from the earth, and not from the things themselves: the earth, then, is the first parent of both. The same is true of animals. It may be uncertain whether the seeds come from the animals themselves or the animals from the seeds; whichever of these came first, however, it is absolutely certain that it came from the earth.

45. Just as all the things that would arise through time into a tree were invisibly present together in the grain itself, so the world itself must be understood to have had together, when God created all things together, all the things that were made in it and along with it, when day was made. This includes not only heaven with the sun, moon, and stars, whose form remains in revolving motion, and the earth and abysses, which undergo movements that seem unstable and, being joined below, contribute another part to the world; it also includes those things that water and earth produced potentially and causally, before they emerged through the delays of time in the manner in which they are now known to us in those works that God continues to perform until now.

46. Since this is so, the statement, “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth: when day was made, God made heaven and earth, and every green plant of the field before it was upon the earth, and every grass of the field before it arose,” must be understood not in the manner in which he makes them by the work through which he continues to work until now, through rain and human cultivation—for this is why it was added, “For God had not rained upon the earth, nor was there a man to work the earth”—but in the manner in which he created all things together and completed them in the sixfold number of days, presenting the day he made six times to the things he made, not through a temporal succession of intervals but through an ordered causal knowledge.

From those works he rested on the seventh day, also graciously offering his own rest to the knowledge and joy of that same day; and therefore he blessed and sanctified him not in any individual work but in his rest. Hence, instituting no further creature, but governing and moving all the things he made together by an administrative act, he works without cessation, both resting and working at the same time, as has already been discussed.

Taking the beginning of the narration of these works of his, which he continues to perform until now, as they unfold through the volumes of time, Scripture says: “But a spring rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth.” Since we have said what we thought should be said about this spring, let us consider what follows from another beginning.

# BOOK SIX

In the words of Genesis 2:7, “And God formed man, dust from the earth,” and so forth, the question is investigated how, or when, man was formed from clay; then, with consideration of the soul deferred for a little while, the discussion concerns the body of Adam.

[Col. 0339]

## CHAPTER I — Whether “And God formed,” and so forth, is to be understood of the first formation of man, made on the sixth day, or of another formation made afterward in the course of time

1. “And God formed man, dust from the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul.” We must first see whether this is a recapitulation, so that it is now explained how the man was made whom we read was made on that sixth day; or whether, when he made all things together, he also secretly made man among them, just as he made the grass of the earth before it arose. In that case, although he had already been made in some hidden condition of nature, he too would later, with the passage of time, come to exist in this manner, in which he lives in this visible form, whether well or badly, just as the grass, which was made before it arose upon the earth, arose after time had passed and after that spring had watered it, so that it might be upon the earth.

2. Let us therefore first try to understand it as a recapitulation. Perhaps man was made on the sixth day in the same way as the day itself was first made, and as the firmament, the earth, and the sea were made. For we must not say that these things had already been made beforehand in certain beginnings, hidden there, and that afterward, with the passage of time, they emerged and shone forth in the form in which the world was constructed; rather, from the beginning of the age, when day was made, the world was created, and within its elements were created together those things that would later arise with the passage of time—whether plants or animals, each according to its kind.

Nor should we believe that the stars themselves were first made and stored within the elements of the world, then later came forth with the passage of time and developed into these forms that shine from heaven. Rather, all things were created together in that sixfold number of perfection, when day was made.

Was man therefore also created then in the form in which he now lives and acts, whether doing good or evil? Or was he himself hidden, like the grass of the field before it arose, so that what later emerged for him with the passage of time was his being made from the dust?

## CHAPTER II — The question is examined from the context of Scripture

3. Let us therefore take him as having been formed on that very sixth day in this visible and perceptible form from clay [Note: [Col. 0339] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain read here and elsewhere *factum*, “made.” M.], but as not having been mentioned then, since what is now indicated is presented by recapitulation. Let us see whether Scripture itself agrees with us.

This is certainly how it is written, while the works of the sixth day were still being narrated:

> And God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness; and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and all cattle, and the whole earth, and all creeping things that creep upon the earth.” And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them, and God blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and rule it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and all cattle, and the whole earth, and all creeping things that creep upon the earth” (Gen. 1:26–28).

Man had therefore already been formed from clay, and a woman had already been made from his side while he slept, but this had not then been mentioned; it is now mentioned by recapitulation. For the male was not made on the sixth day and the female made afterward with the passage of time; rather, Scripture says, “He made him; male and female he made them, and he blessed them.”

How, then, was a woman made for him after the man had already been placed in paradise? Did Scripture recall something it had previously omitted? For on that sixth day paradise too was planted, and the man was placed there, and he was put into a sleep so that Eve might be formed; once she had been formed, he awoke and gave her a name. But these things could not have taken place except through temporal intervals. They were therefore not made in the same way as all things were created together.

## CHAPTER III — The same question is examined from other passages of Scripture

4. However easily a person may imagine that God made even these things together with the rest, we certainly know that human speech cannot be uttered aloud except through temporal intervals. When, therefore, we hear the words of the man—whether when he gave names to the animals, or when he gave a name to the woman, or when he then went on to say, “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24) [Note: [Col. 0340] Nearly all manuscripts read, “and both shall be one flesh.”]—however many syllables these words contained, two syllables of them could not sound simultaneously. How much less, then, could all these things take place together with those that were created together?

Accordingly, either all those things too were not made together from the very beginning of the ages, but were made through temporal delays and intervals, and that day, being first created not as a spiritual but as a bodily substance, produced morning and evening either by some sort of circuit of light or by its emission and contraction; or, if a plausible account has persuaded us, in view of everything discussed in the preceding books, that that spiritual day was sublimely and originally created as a certain wise light called “day,” whose presence was offered to the creation of things through an ordered knowledge in the number six, then the words of Scripture agree with this view when it later says:

> When day was made, God made heaven and earth, and every green plant of the field before it was upon the earth, and every grass of the field before it arose (Gen. 2:4–5).

This is also confirmed by what is written elsewhere: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1).

There is no doubt, then [Col. 0341], that this matter of the man formed from the dust of the earth, and of his wife formed from his side, no longer belongs to the creation in which all things were made together, from which God rested when they had been completed; rather, it belongs to that operation which takes place through the succession of the ages and through which he continues to work until now.

5. In addition, the very words in which it is narrated how God planted paradise, placed there the man whom he had made, brought to him the animals for him to name, and, when no helper like him was found among them, formed a woman for him from a rib taken from his side, sufficiently warn us that these things do not belong to that operation of God from which he rested on the seventh day, but rather to this operation through which he continues to work until now in the course of time.

For when paradise was planted, the account runs as follows:

> And God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the east, and there he placed the man whom he had formed. And God further caused every tree that was beautiful to look upon and good for food to spring up from the earth (Gen. 2:8–9).

## CHAPTER IV — The same matter is considered in Genesis 2:8–9

When he says, “He caused every tree that was beautiful to look upon to spring up from the earth,” he clearly shows that he caused the tree to spring up from the earth in one way now and in another way then, when on the third day the earth produced vegetation bearing seed according to its kind and fruit-bearing trees according to their kind. For “he caused it to spring up further” means above what he had already caused to spring up. Then, certainly, it was produced potentially and causally in the work belonging to the creation of all things together, from which he rested on the seventh day; now, however, it is produced visibly in the work belonging to the course of time, through which he continues to work until now.

6. Unless perhaps someone should say that not every kind of tree was created on the third day, but that something was postponed to be created on the sixth day, when man was made and placed in paradise. But Scripture most plainly declares what was created on the sixth day: living souls according to their several kinds—quadrupeds, creeping things, and beasts—and man himself, male and female, in the image of God.

Accordingly, Scripture could have omitted how man was made, although it narrated that he was made on that very day, so that it might afterward explain by recapitulation how he was also made—that is, from the dust of the earth, and the woman from his side. It could not, however, omit any kind of creature, whether in the statement “God said, ‘Let it be made,’” or “Let us make,” or in the statement “So it was made,” or “God made.”

Otherwise, it would be pointless for everything to have been so carefully distinguished by individual days if any suspicion of mixing the days could remain—so that, although grass and trees were assigned to the third day, we might believe that certain trees were also created on the sixth day, which Scripture had passed over on that sixth day.

## CHAPTER V — On the same matter

7. Finally, what shall we answer concerning the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven that God brought to Adam so that he might see what he would call them? The text is as follows:

> And the Lord God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make him a helper corresponding to him.” And God formed further from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of heaven, and brought them to Adam to see what he would call them; and whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name. And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to all the birds of heaven, and to all the beasts of the field. But for Adam no helper corresponding to him was found. And God cast a trance upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs and filled its place with flesh; and the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman (Gen. 2:18–22).

If, then, after no helper corresponding to the man had been found among the cattle, beasts of the field, and birds of heaven, God made for him a corresponding helper from a rib taken from his side—and this happened after he had again formed those same beasts of the field and birds of heaven from the earth and brought them to him—how can this be understood as having happened on the sixth day, since on that day the earth produced a living soul according to the word of God, while on the fifth day the waters similarly produced the birds according to the word of God?

The text would not say here, “And God formed further from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of heaven,” unless the earth had already produced all the beasts of the field on the sixth day and the water all the birds of heaven on the fifth day.

At that time, therefore, the process was one way—that is, potentially and causally, as suited the work by which he created all things together and from which he rested on the seventh day. Now it is another way, as we see the things that he creates through temporal intervals, in the manner in which he continues to work until now.

Accordingly, during those familiar days of bodily light, produced by the circuit of the sun, Eve was made from the side of her husband. At that time God formed the beasts of the field and the birds further from the earth; and when no helper corresponding to Adam was found among them, she was formed. During such days, therefore, God also formed the man himself from clay.

8. For we must not say that the male was made on the sixth day but the female on later days, since it is expressly said on the sixth day, “Male and female he made them, and he blessed them,” together with the other statements made about both and addressed to both.

At that time, then, both were made in one way, and now both in another way: then, according to the power that had been imparted to the world in a seminal manner through the word of God, when he created all things together and rested from them on the seventh day, so that from them all things might thereafter come into being at their proper times in the order of the ages; now, according to the operation to be supplied to the times, through which he continues to work until now. Thus Adam had to be made in his own time from the clay of the earth, and his woman from the man’s side.

## CHAPTER VI — He explains his position more clearly, lest it be misunderstood

9. In this distribution of God’s works—some belonging to those invisible days in which he created all things together, and others belonging to these subsequent days in which he daily works whatever unfolds in time from those primordial coverings—if we have followed the words of Scripture neither improperly nor absurdly, which led us to distinguish these matters, we must take care that, because the perception of the things themselves is somewhat difficult and the slower among us are unable to grasp them, we are not thought to hold or say something that we know we neither hold nor say.

Although in the preceding discussions I have prepared the reader as far as I could, I nevertheless think that many are confused at these passages and suppose that man existed previously in that work of God in which all things were created together in such a way that he lived some kind of life, and that he discerned, believed, and understood God’s speech addressed to him when God said, “Behold, I have given you every plant bearing seed for food.” Let anyone who thinks this know, then, that this is not what I have thought or said.

10. But again, if I say that man did not exist in that first creation of things in which God created all things together in the way in which he exists—not merely as a man of mature age, but not even as an infant, and not merely as an infant, but not even as a fetus in his mother’s womb, and not even as a visible human seed—he will think that man did not exist at all.

Let him return, then, to Scripture. He will find that on the sixth day man was made in the image of God, and that male and female were made. Let him also ask when the female was made. He will find that she was made outside those six days, for she was made when God formed further from the earth the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven—not when the waters produced the birds and the earth produced a living soul, which includes the beasts.

At that time, however, man was made both male and female. Therefore he was made both then and afterward. Not then but not afterward, nor afterward but not then; nor were different persons made afterward, but the very same persons were made one way then and another way afterward.

He will ask me how. I shall answer: afterward, visibly, in the manner in which the form of human constitution is known to us—not, however, through parents generating them, but the man from clay and the woman from his rib.

He will then ask how they existed at that time. I shall answer: invisibly, potentially, and causally, as future things exist before they are made.

11. Perhaps he will not understand this. For everything he knows is removed from him, even down to the bodily substance of seeds themselves. Man did not yet exist in even such a form when he was made in that first creation of the six days. Some comparison with seeds may indeed be offered for this matter, because the things that will be in them are stored together in them; nevertheless, those causes precede all visible seeds. But he does not understand.

What, then, shall I do except, as far as I can, offer the salutary warning that he should believe God’s Scripture: that man was made then, when, as day was made, God made heaven and earth, of which Scripture says elsewhere, “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1); and also that he was made then when God no longer created all things together but, creating each in its proper time, formed him from the clay of the earth and the woman from his bone?

For Scripture permits us neither to understand that they were made in this latter manner on that sixth day nor to understand that they were not made on that sixth day.

## CHAPTER VII — That souls cannot have been created before bodies

12. Were their souls, then, perhaps made on that sixth day, where the image of God may also rightly be understood to exist in the spirit of their mind, so that their bodies were formed afterward?

But the same Scripture does not permit us to believe this. First, there is the completion of the works, which I do not see how it could be understood if something had been lacking then—something not causally created—that was afterward to be created visibly.

Moreover, the very distinction of male and female [Col. 0344] cannot exist except in bodies. If someone should think that, according to understanding and action, both sexes are to be understood as present in one soul, what will he do with the foods that God gave on that very day from the fruits of the trees? Such food is certainly not appropriate except to a human being possessing a body. For if someone should wish to take this food figuratively as well, he will depart from the literal character of the events, which in narratives of this kind must be established at the outset with every care.

## CHAPTER VIII — The difficulty concerning God’s speech addressed to man on the sixth day
13. “How, then,” he says, “was he speaking to those who did not yet hear or understand, since there were not yet any who could receive the words?” I could answer that God addressed them in the same way that Christ addressed us, though we were not yet born and were still far in the future—not only us, but also all who are to come after us. For he was speaking to all whom he saw would become his own: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). So too the prophet was known to God, to whom he said, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. 1:5); and Levi was tithed while he was still in Abraham’s loins (Heb. 7:9–10). Why, then, should Abraham himself not likewise have been in Adam, and Adam himself in those first works of the world, which God created all at once?

Yet the words of the Lord through the mouth of his flesh, and the words of God through the mouths of the Prophets, are uttered with the temporal voice of the body; and with all their syllables they assume and expend corresponding intervals of time. But when God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and all cattle, and all the earth, and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth”; and, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and rule it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and all cattle, and all the earth, and all the things that creep upon the earth”; and, “Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant, sowing seed upon all the earth, and every fruit-bearing tree that has in itself the fruit of seed-bearing produce, which shall be for your food” (Gen. 1:26–29)—his Word itself, before every sound of air, before every voice of flesh or cloud, in that highest Wisdom of his through which all things were made, was not resounding as though in human ears. Rather, upon the things made he inscribed the causes of the things to be made, and by his omnipotent power he made future things; when he established the things from which the ages would begin, he deposited man, who was to be formed in his own time, in the seed, as it were, or root of the times—those things having been established by him who is before the ages.

Other creatures precede other creatures: some precede them in time, others in their causes. But he precedes all that he made not only in excellence—for he is also the maker of their causes—but in eternity. This, however, may perhaps be discussed more fully later, in more suitable passages of Scripture.

## CHAPTER IX — How Jeremiah was known to God before he was formed; the merits of the unborn

14. Let us now bring to an end what has been begun concerning man, preserving this restraint: in the profound meaning of Scripture, let us devote ourselves more to the diligence of inquiry than to the rashness of assertion. Since God knew Jeremiah before he formed him in the womb, there can be no legitimate doubt; for he says most plainly, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.” But where he knew him before forming him in this way—although for our weakness this may be either difficult or impossible to grasp—whether in some nearer causes, as Levi was tithed while in Abraham’s loins; or in Adam himself, in whom the human race was established as though at its root; and, in Adam himself, whether when he had already been formed from the clay, or when he had been made causally in those works that God created all at once; or rather before every creature, as he chose and predestined his saints before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4); or rather in all the preceding causes, whether those I have mentioned or those I have not mentioned, before he was formed in the womb—I do not think it necessary to inquire with excessive minuteness, provided that it is certain that Jeremiah, from the time he was brought forth by his parents into this light, lived his own life, in which, as he advanced in age, he could live either well or badly; but before that, in no way—not only before he was formed in the womb, but even after he had been formed there, before he was born.

For that apostolic statement concerning the twins who had not yet been born and had not yet done anything good or evil in Rebecca’s womb (Rom. 9:11) admits no hesitation.

15. Yet it was not written without purpose that an infant is not clean from sin, whose life upon the earth is but one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint); nor what is said in the Psalm: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me” (Ps. 50:7) in the womb; nor that all die in Adam, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12).

Let us now hold this clearly: whatever merits of parents are transmitted to their offspring, and whatever grace of God sanctifies a person before he is born, there is neither iniquity with God nor anyone’s doing of good or evil that pertains to his own person before he has been born. Therefore, the opinion held by some—that souls sinned elsewhere to a greater or lesser degree and, according to the varying merits of their sins, were thrust into different bodies—does not agree with the apostolic statement, since it is said most plainly that those not yet born had done nothing, whether good or evil.

16. Accordingly, a certain question must be reconsidered in its proper place: what did the entire human race, like a mass of dough, contract from the sin of the first parents, who were only two? [Note: [Col. 0345] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read conspersio, “mass” or “mixture.” M. has the reading consparsio.] Yet there is no question that a human being could possess no such merits before he had been fashioned from the dust of the earth and before he had lived his own life in his own time.

For just as we could not say that Esau and Jacob, whom the Apostle says had done nothing good or evil while not yet born (Rom. 9:11), had inherited any merit from their parents if the parents themselves had done nothing good or evil; and just as the human race would not have sinned in Adam if Adam himself had not sinned; and Adam would not have sinned unless he had already been living in his own time, in which he could live either well or badly—so it is pointless to seek Adam’s sin or righteous action while he was still causally established among the things created all at once, when he was not yet living his own life and was not present in parents living in such a way.

In that first creation of the world, when God created all things simultaneously, man was made who was to be; it was the principle of man’s creation, not the action of the man created.

## CHAPTER X — Things existing in various ways

17. These things exist in one way in the Word of God, where they are not made but eternal; in another way in the elements of the world, where all things were made simultaneously as future realities; in another way in things that are created according to causes created simultaneously, but are not themselves created simultaneously, each being created in its own time—among these is Adam, already formed from clay and animated by God’s breath, just as grass springs up; and in yet another way in seeds, in which the primordial causes are, as it were, repeated, derived from things that came into existence according to the causes he first established, like grass from the earth and seed from grass.

In all these things, those realities that have already received the forms and activities proper to their time have emerged from the hidden and invisible principles that lie causally within creation into manifest forms and natures: for example, grass springing up upon the earth, man becoming a living soul, and other things of this kind, whether plants or living creatures, which belong to that work of God that he continues to perform until now.

But these things also carry within themselves, as though invisibly reproducing themselves again, a certain hidden generative power that they drew from the primordial sources of their causes. Those causes were implanted when the world was created and day came into being, before they emerged into the visible form of their own kind.

## CHAPTER XI — How the works of creation on the sixth day were both completed and still begun

18. For if those first works of God, when he created all things simultaneously, had not been perfect in their own mode, then without doubt those things that were lacking for their completion would have been added later, so that some perfection of the universe would have been composed from both—each being like a half, as though they were parts of some whole whose parts, when joined together, completed the whole of which they had been parts.

Conversely, if those works had been perfect in the same way that things are perfected when each is brought forth in its own time into manifest forms and activities, then either nothing would subsequently come from them through the course of time, or what would come from them would be precisely what God does not cease to work from those things that arise in their respective times.

But now, because those very things that God first created all at once when he made the world were, in one respect, already completed and, in another, still begun—completed because, in their proper natures, by which they proceed through the courses of their times, they contain nothing that had not already been made causally in those first works; begun, because some of them were like seeds of future things, to be brought forth at suitable places through the course of the ages from hiddenness into manifestation—the words of Scripture itself stand out as a sufficient and powerful reminder of this, if one is attentive to them.

For Scripture says both that they were completed and that they were begun. If they had not been completed, it would not have been written: “And the heaven and the earth were completed, and all their arrangement”; and, “God completed on the sixth day his works that he had made; and God rested on the seventh day from all his works that he had made”; and, “God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.” Again, if they had not been begun, it would not have followed that on that day he rested from all his works that God began to make.

19. If someone therefore asks here how he completed them and how he began them—for he did not complete some things and begin others, but the very same things, from which he rested on the seventh day—the answer is clear from what we have said above.

We understand that God completed these things when he created all things simultaneously and so perfectly that nothing still remained for him to create in the order of time which had not already been created by him here in the order of causes. But he began them in the sense that what he had established here in causes he would afterward bring to completion in effects.

Accordingly, “God formed man,” dust or clay of the earth—that is, from the dust or clay of the earth—“and breathed,” or blew, “into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.” He was not then predestined; that had occurred before the age, in the foreknowledge of the Creator. Nor was he then causally or in a completed manner begun, or in a begun manner completed; that had occurred from the age onward in the primordial principles, when all things were created simultaneously. Rather, he was created in his own time, visibly in body and invisibly in soul, consisting of soul and body.

## CHAPTER XII — Whether the human body was formed by God in a unique manner

20. Let us now see how God made him, first his body from the earth; afterward we shall consider the soul, if we are able to say anything about it.

To suppose that God fashioned man from clay with bodily hands is an excessively childish notion. If Scripture had said this, we should rather believe that the writer had used a metaphorical expression than that God was defined by such outlines of limbs as we see in our bodies.

For it is said, “Your hand scattered the nations” (Ps. 43:3); and, “You brought out your people with a strong hand and an exalted arm” (Ps. 135:11–12). Who could be so foolish as not to understand that the name of this bodily member is used to signify God’s power and might?

21. Nor should we accept the view held by some that man is for this reason God’s pre-eminent work: because he said of the other things, “and they were made,” whereas he himself made man. Rather, man is pre-eminent because God made him in his own image.

For of those things that he spoke and that were made, Scripture says this (Ps. 148:5) because they were made through his Word, just as human beings could speak to other human beings through words conceived in time and uttered by the voice. God does not speak in this way except when he speaks through a bodily creature, as to Abraham, as to Moses, or through the cloud concerning his Son.

Before every creature, so that the creature itself might exist, it was spoken by that Word which in the beginning was God with God. And because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1, 3), man too was certainly made through him.

Certainly God made heaven by the word, because he spoke and it was made; yet it is written, “The heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. 101:26). And concerning this, as it were, lowest foundation of the world, it is written: “For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land” (Ps. 94:5).

Let this therefore not be counted to man’s honor, as though God spoke all the other things and they were made, but made this one himself; or as though he made the others by his word but this one with his hands. What is pre-eminent in man is that God made man in his image, because he gave him an intellectual mind by which he surpasses the beasts; we discussed this above.

If, placed in such honor, he does not understand so as to act rightly, he will be compared with the very beasts over which he was set. For it is written: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). God made the beasts as well, but not in his image.

22. Nor should it be said, “He himself made man, but merely commanded the beasts, and they were made.” He made both man and the beasts through his Word, through which all things were made (John 1:3).

But because that same Word is also his Wisdom and Power, it is called his hand—not a visible bodily member, but the power of bringing things into being.

For the same Scripture that says God fashioned man from the clay of the earth also says that he fashioned the beasts of the field from the earth, when he brought them, together with the birds of the sky, to Adam to see what he would call them. For it is written: “And God formed all the beasts from the earth” (Gen. 1:25).

If, then, he himself formed both man from the earth and the beasts from the earth, what superiority does man possess in this respect except that he was created in the image of God? Yet this is not according to the body, but according to the understanding of the mind, about which we shall speak later.

Nevertheless, even in his body he possesses a certain characteristic that points to this: he was made with an upright posture, so that by this very fact he might be admonished not to pursue earthly things like the beasts, whose entire pleasure is from the earth, and for that reason all their limbs are directed and prostrated toward the belly.

Thus his body too corresponds to his rational soul—not according to the outlines and shapes of the limbs, but rather according to the fact that it is raised toward heaven, to contemplate the heavenly realities present in the body of the world itself. In the same way, the rational soul ought to rise toward those realities that are most excellent in spiritual nature, so that it may set its mind on the things above, not on the things upon the earth (Col. 3:2).

## CHAPTER XIII — At what age or stature Adam was created

23. But how did God make him from the clay of the earth? Was it suddenly, in a perfected age—that is, in manhood and youthful maturity—or as he still forms human beings in their mothers’ wombs? For no one other than the one who said, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. 1:5), does this.

Was Adam’s only distinctive feature, then, that he was not born from parents but made from the earth—yet in such a way that, in being perfected and growing through the stages of life, the periods of time that we see assigned to the nature of the human race would be completed?

Or should this question not be asked at all? Whichever way he did it, he did what it was fitting for God, both omnipotent and wise, to be able and willing to do. For he assigned definite laws of time to the kinds and qualities of things that are brought forth from hiddenness into manifestation, in such a way that his will remains sovereign over all.

By his power he gave numbers to creation; he did not bind his power to those same numbers. For his Spirit moved over the world as he made it (Gen. 1:2), so that he might also move over it when it was made—not in bodily places, but in the excellence of his power.

24. Who does not know that water absorbed by the earth, when it reaches the roots of a vine, is drawn into the nourishment of that wood, and there takes on the quality by which it gradually proceeds into a grape? As the grape grows, it becomes wine; when ripe, it becomes sweet; while still fermenting after being pressed, and strengthened by a certain aging, it arrives at the use of drinking both more suitably and more pleasantly.

Did the Lord therefore need wood or earth or these intervals of time when he changed water into wine by a marvelous shortcut—and wine of such quality that even a drunken guest would praise it (John 2:9–10)? Did the creator of time need time’s assistance?

Does not the nature of every serpent grow, take shape, come to birth, and grow strong according to definite numbers of days suited to each kind? Were those days awaited so that the staff might be changed into a serpent from the hand of Moses and Aaron (Exod. 7:10)?

When such things happen, they do not happen contrary to nature except for us, who have come to know the course of nature in another way; but not for God, for whom what he has made is nature.

## CHAPTER XIV — Of what kind were the causal principles first implanted in the world

25. It may rightly be asked how those causal principles that God implanted in the world when he first created all things simultaneously were established.

Were they established so that, just as we see all things that are born—whether plants or animals—pass through different periods of time according to the diversity of their kinds in their formation and growth, they too would pass through such periods? Or were they established so that, as Adam is believed to have been made without any gradual growth, in mature manhood, they would be formed immediately?

But why should we not believe that they possessed both capacities, so that what would proceed from them would be whatever pleased their maker? If we say that they were established in the former manner, not only the transformation of water into wine but all miracles that occur contrary to the customary course of nature will begin to appear to have been done against them. If we say that they were established in the latter manner, it will be far more absurd to suppose that the ordinary forms and kinds of nature themselves pass through their periods contrary to those primary causal principles of all things that are born.

It remains, therefore, that they were created capable of both modes: either the mode by which temporal things most commonly proceed, or the mode by which rare and marvelous things occur, according as God chooses to do what is appropriate to the time.

## CHAPTER XV — The first man was formed according to the primordial causes

26. Nevertheless, man was made in the manner in which those first causes had established that the first man should be made. He was not to be born from parents, since none had preceded him, but was to be formed from clay according to the causal principle in which he had first been made.

For if he was made otherwise, God had not made him among the works of those six days. When Scripture says that he was made among them, God had made the cause itself by which man was to be in his own time, and according to which he was to be made by him who had both completed the things begun, for the perfection of the causal principles, and begun the things to be completed, for the order of times.

[Note: [Col. 0350] Thus in all the manuscripts. But in the printed editions, with a conspicuous gloss, the passage reads: “Who at once both completed them, producing these manifest forms, having begun them for the perfection of the causal principles; and began them, impressing upon the world the causal principles of things to be made, having completed them for the order of times.”]

If, therefore, in those first causes of things that the Creator initially implanted in the world, he placed not only the fact that he would form man from clay but also the manner in which he would form him—whether as in the mother’s womb or in the form of a young man—then without doubt he made him in the way he had established there; for he would not act contrary to his own arrangement.

But if he placed there only the power of possibility, so that man would come to be in whatever manner he came to be, so that he could come to be in either way—that is, so that this possibility too was there because he could come to be in either way—and if he reserved the particular manner in which he would make him to his own will and did not weave it into the world’s creation, then it is evident that even in this case man was not made contrary to what existed in that first condition of causes. For there too was the possibility of his being made in this way, although it was not there that he had necessarily to be made in precisely this way. This necessity was not in the condition of creation but in the decision of the Creator, whose will is the necessity of things.

## CHAPTER XVI — In the nature of a thing lies what it can be; that it will be lies only in God’s will

27. We too, within the limits of human weakness, can know what exists in the nature of things that have already emerged in time, insofar as we have learned it by experience; but we do not know whether it will actually occur.

For in the nature of a young man there is, for example, the possibility that he may grow old; but whether this is also in God’s will, we do not know. Yet it would not be in his nature unless it had first been in the will of God, who created all things.

There is, to be sure, a hidden principle of old age in the body of a young man, just as there is a hidden principle of youth in the body of a child. It is not visible to the eyes, as childhood itself is visible in a child and youth in a young man; rather, by another kind of knowledge we infer that something hidden exists in nature by which the hidden numbers of youth from childhood, or of old age from youth, are brought into the open.

This principle, then, by which it comes about that something can exist, is hidden from the eyes but not from the mind. Whether it is also necessary that it occur, however, we do not know at all. We know that the principle by which it can occur exists in the nature of the body itself; but it is evident that the principle by which it must occur is not there.

## CHAPTER XVII — Which things among future things are truly future

28. Perhaps, however, it is in the world that this particular man must grow old. But if it is not in the world, it is in God. For that will necessarily happen which he wills, and those things are truly future which he foreknew.

Many things are future according to lower causes; but if they are also so in God’s foreknowledge, they are truly future. If they are otherwise there, they will rather be future in the manner in which they exist there—in the place where the one who foreknows cannot be deceived.

Old age is said to be future in a young man; yet it is not future if he is going to die beforehand. What occurs will depend on the other causes, whether woven into the world or reserved in God’s foreknowledge.

According to certain causes of future events, Hezekiah was going to die, but God added fifteen years to his life (Isa. 33:5). In doing this, God did what he knew before the foundation of the world that he would do and had reserved in his own will.

He therefore did not do what was not future. Rather, that was more truly future which he foreknew he would do. Yet those years would not rightly be called “added” unless something was added [Note: [Col. 0351] Several manuscripts of good authority read, “unless they were added to something.”] that had existed differently according to other causes.

According to certain lower causes, then, Hezekiah’s life had already come to an end. But according to those causes that exist in the will and foreknowledge of God, who from eternity knew what he would do at that time—and this was truly future—he was then to end his life when he actually ended it.

For even if his life was granted in response to his prayer, God certainly foreknew that he would pray in such a way that such a prayer ought to be granted. His foreknowledge could not be deceived; and therefore what he foreknew was necessarily future.

## CHAPTER XVIII — It follows that Adam was not formed contrary to what had been established in the primordial causes

29. Therefore, if the causes of all future things were implanted in the world when day came into being, at the time when God created all things simultaneously, Adam was not made otherwise when he was formed from clay than was more probably established in those causes—namely, as already possessing mature manhood—when God made man among the works of the six days.

For there it was established not merely that he could be made in this way, but also that he must be made in this way. God did not act against the cause that he had unquestionably established by his will, any more than he acts against his own will.

But if he did not establish all causes in the creature first created, and reserved some in his own will, then those which he reserved in his will do not depend by necessity upon those which he created. Nevertheless, they cannot be contrary to those which he established by his will, because God’s will cannot be contrary to itself.

He established these causes in such a way that from them the thing whose causes they are could come to be, but need not come to be. He concealed the others in such a way that from them it was necessary for that to come to be which he had made possible through the former causes.

## CHAPTER XIX — God formed Adam with an animal, not a spiritual, body

30. It is also commonly asked whether an animal body was first formed for man from clay, such as we now have, or a spiritual body, such as we shall have when we rise.
