Although this body will be changed into that one—for “an animal body is sown, a spiritual body will rise”—the question of what was first made for man is debated because, if an animal body was made, then we shall not receive what we lost in Adam, but something much better, since the spiritual body is superior to the animal body, when we shall be equal to the angels of God (Matt. 22:30).

But angels may be placed above others in righteousness; surely not above the Lord? Yet of him it is said: “You made him a little less than the angels” (Ps. 8:6). Why, except on account of the weakness of the flesh that he took from the Virgin, accepting the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), in which, by dying, he would redeem us from servitude?

But why should we discuss this at greater length? The Apostle’s statement on this matter is not obscure. When he wished to provide testimony proving that there is an animal body, he recalled and employed not so much the body of himself or of any human being that was visible in the present as this very passage of Scripture, saying:

“If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual body. Thus it is written: ‘The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.’ Yet the spiritual was not first, but the animal; afterward, the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:44–49).

What can be said against this? We now bear the image of the heavenly man by faith, and in the resurrection we shall have what we believe. But we have borne the image of the earthly man from the very beginning of human generation.

## CHAPTER XX — A difficulty against the preceding view; the opinion that Adam’s body was first animal and afterward spiritual in paradise

31. Here another question arises: how are we renewed if through Christ we are not restored to what we first were in Adam? Although many things are renewed not to their former state but to something better, they are nevertheless renewed from a lower state than that in which they previously were.

How, then, was that son dead and came to life again; was lost and was found (Luke 15:32)? From where is the first robe brought out for him, if he does not receive the immortality that Adam lost? But how did he lose immortality if he had an animal body? For it will not be an animal body but a spiritual one when “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53).

Some, constrained by these difficulties, wished both to preserve the statement in which an example is drawn from an animal body—“The first man Adam was made a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit”—and to maintain, without absurdity, that this renewal and recovery of immortality will be a restoration to the former state, namely, to what Adam lost.

They therefore supposed that man first possessed an animal body; but when he was placed in paradise, he was changed, just as we too shall be changed by the resurrection. The Book of Genesis does not mention this; but they believed that this must necessarily follow if the two Scriptural testimonies were to agree with each other: both the statement made about the animal body and the many passages found in the sacred Scriptures concerning our renewal.

## CHAPTER XXI — That opinion is rejected

32. But if this is so, we try in vain to understand paradise and its trees and fruits according to the literal reality of the events, apart from their figurative meaning. For who could believe that such foods from the fruits of trees were already necessary for immortal and spiritual bodies?

Nevertheless, if nothing else can be found, we prefer to understand paradise spiritually rather than either suppose that man is not renewed, although Scripture mentions this so often, or believe that he receives what is not shown to have been lost.

Moreover, the very death of man, which many divine testimonies declare that he incurred through sin, indicates that he would have been without death if he had not sinned. How, then, could he have been mortal without death? Or how could he not have been mortal if he had an animal body?

## CHAPTER XXII — Some wrongly suppose that Adam deserved the death of the soul, not of the body, through sin

33. For this reason some believe that he did not deserve bodily death through sin, but the death of the soul, which iniquity brings about. They think that, because of his animal body, he would have departed from this body—namely, to the rest now enjoyed by the saints who have already fallen asleep—and that at the end of the age he would have received the same members back in immortality [Note: [Col. 0353] The printed editions have recepturi, “they who will receive.” We restore recepturum, “he who will receive,” from the manuscripts.]. Thus bodily death would appear to have occurred not because of sin but naturally, as with the other animals.

But the Apostle again contradicts them and says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:10–11).

Accordingly, bodily death too results from sin. If Adam had not sinned, he would not have died in body either, and therefore he would have had an immortal body as well. How, then, could it have been immortal if it was animal?

## CHAPTER XXIII — Against those who say that Adam’s animal body became spiritual in paradise

34. But again those who think that his body was changed in paradise, so that it became spiritual from animal, fail to see that, if he had not sinned, nothing would have prevented him from receiving the same bodily transformation after the life in paradise that he would have lived justly and obediently—in eternal life, where he would no longer have needed bodily foods.

Why, then, is it necessary on this account to be forced to understand paradise figuratively rather than literally, on the ground that a body could not die except through sin? It is true that he would not have died bodily if he had not sinned; for the Apostle plainly says, “The body is dead because of sin.” Yet it could have been animal before sin and, after a life of righteousness, have become spiritual when God willed.

## CHAPTER XXIV — How, in renewal, we receive what Adam lost

35. “How, then,” they ask, “are we said to be renewed if we do not receive what the first man lost, in whom all die?”

In one respect we certainly receive it, and in another respect we do not receive it. We do not receive the immortality of a spiritual body, which man had not yet possessed; but we receive the righteousness from which man fell through sin.

We are therefore renewed from the oldness of sin—not into the former animal body in which Adam existed, but into something better, that is, into a spiritual body, when we shall become equal to the angels of God (Matt. 22:30), suited to a heavenly habitation, where we shall not need food that decays.

We are therefore renewed in the spirit of our mind (Eph. 4:23), according to the image of the one who created us, which Adam lost through sin. We shall also be renewed in the flesh when this corruptible body puts on incorruption, so that it becomes a spiritual body. Adam had not yet been changed into this body, but was going to be changed, unless by sin he had deserved the death even of his animal body.

36. Finally, the Apostle does not say, “The body is mortal because of sin,” but, “The body is dead because of sin.”

## CHAPTER XXV — Adam’s body both mortal and immortal

Before sin, Adam’s body could be called mortal in one respect and immortal in another: mortal because it could die; immortal because it could refrain from dying.

It is one thing to be unable to die, as God created certain natures immortal; it is another thing to be able not to die. In this latter sense the first man was created immortal. This was granted to him from the tree of life, not from the constitution of his nature. He was separated from that tree when he sinned, so that he could die—whereas, if he had not sinned, he could have refrained from dying.

He was therefore mortal by the condition of his animal body, but immortal by the benefit of the Creator. If his body was animal, then it was certainly mortal, because it could die; yet it was also immortal, because it could refrain from dying.

For that which cannot die at all will be immortal only if it is spiritual, and this is what is promised to us in the resurrection. Accordingly, that animal body—and for this reason mortal—which would have become spiritual through righteousness and thus altogether immortal, became through sin not mortal, since it had been mortal beforehand, but dead—something that would not have happened if man had not sinned.

[Note: [Col. 0354] The printed editions have here mortale, “mortal,” with the following punctuation: “It would become spiritual; and for this reason it became altogether mortal because of sin.” We have emended the text in accordance with the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XXVI — Adam’s body and ours are different
37. How, then, does the Apostle call our body “dead” while he was still speaking of the living, unless it is because the very condition of dying, arising from the sin of our parents, has already clung to their offspring? This body too is animal, just as the body of the first man was; but in the class of animal bodies it is now much worse, for it has the necessity of dying, which that body did not have. Although it still remained for it to be changed and, having become spiritual, to receive complete immortality, where it would no longer need corruptible food, nevertheless, if man had lived justly and his body had been changed into a spiritual condition, he would not have gone into death. In our case, however, even when we live justly, the body is destined to die. On account of this necessity, which comes from the sin of that first man, the Apostle called our body not mortal but dead, because we all die in Adam (Rom. 5:12; and 1 Cor. 15:22). He says likewise: “As the truth is in Jesus, put off, with respect to your former way of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of deceit”; that is, Adam, who was made such through sin. See, then, what follows: “But be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God in the justice and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:21–24). Behold what Adam lost through sin.

## CHAPTER XXVII — How we are renewed in mind and body to that which Adam lost

[Col. 0355]

In this, then, we are renewed according to what Adam lost—that is, according to the spirit of our mind. But with respect to the body, which is sown an animal body and will rise a spiritual body, we shall be renewed into something better, something Adam had not yet been.

38. The Apostle likewise says: “Stripping off the old man with his deeds, put on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him” (Col. 3:9–10). Adam lost this image, impressed upon the spirit of his mind, through sin [Note: [Col. 0355] *Retractationes* II, chapter 24, no. 2.]; we receive it through the grace of righteousness—not the spiritual and immortal body, in which Adam had not yet been and in which all the saints will be when they rise from the dead; for this is the reward of the merit that he lost. Accordingly, that first robe (Luke 15:22) either is the very righteousness from which he fell, or, if it signifies the garment of bodily immortality, he lost this as well, since through sin he could not attain to it. For a person is said to have lost a wife, and to have lost an honor, when he did not receive what he had hoped for because the one from whom he hoped had been offended.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Although spiritual in mind, Adam was animal in body even in paradise

39. According to this view, then, Adam had an animal body not only before being placed in paradise but also while he was in paradise, although in the inner man he was spiritual, according to the image of him who created him. He lost this by sin and thereby merited bodily death; whereas, had he not sinned, he would have merited a change into a spiritual body. For if he lived as an animal even inwardly, we cannot be said to be renewed toward what he was. When it is said to such people, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind,” this is said so that they may become spiritual. But if he was not spiritual even in his mind, how are we renewed toward something that man never was? The Apostles and all righteous people still had animal bodies, certainly, yet inwardly they lived spiritually: they had been renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created them. Nevertheless, they could still sin if they consented to iniquity. For the Apostle shows that spiritual people can fall into the temptation [Note: [Col. 0356] Several manuscripts read *in tentationem*, “into temptation.”] of sin, when he says: “Brothers, if a man is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in the spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1). I have said this so that no one may think it impossible that Adam sinned if he was spiritual in mind, although he was animal in body. Nevertheless, since matters stand thus, we do not yet hastily affirm anything; rather, we await whether the rest of Scripture also does not impede this understanding.

## CHAPTER XXIX — The soul is to be discussed in the following book

40. For there follows a very difficult question concerning the soul, on which many have labored and have left us laboring as well. Either I have not been able to read everything written on this subject by those who, in accordance with the truth of our Scriptures, were able to arrive at something clear and entirely free from doubt; or the question is so great that even those who solve it truthfully are not easily understood by people such as myself. I confess that no one has yet persuaded me to hold such a view of the soul that I should think nothing further needs to be sought. Whether I shall now discover and settle anything certain, I do not know. Whatever I can do, if the Lord assists my effort, I shall undertake to explain in the following volume [Note: [Col. 0356] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *conabor*, “I shall endeavor.”].

# BOOK SEVEN

In which the passage of Genesis, chapter 2, verse 7—“And he breathed into his face the breath of life,” etc.—is illuminated by an exceedingly full treatment of the soul.

[Col. 0355]

## CHAPTER I — A treatment of the soul is undertaken

1. “And God formed man dust from the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.” We proposed these words of Scripture for consideration at the beginning of the preceding book as well, and we discussed the man who was made, especially his body, as far as we thought sufficient and as far as seemed appropriate according to the Scriptures. But because the question concerning the human soul is considerable, we thought it should be deferred to this book, not knowing how much the Lord would assist us, who desire to speak correctly; yet knowing this: unless he assisted us, we would not speak correctly.

To speak correctly means to speak truthfully and appropriately, refuting nothing boldly and affirming nothing rashly while it remains uncertain whether something is true or false, whether in matters of faith or of Christian knowledge; but whatever can be taught either by the clearest reasoning about things or by the most certain authority of Scripture should be asserted without hesitation.

[Col. 0356]

2. First, let us examine what is written: “He breathed,” or “He blew into his face the breath of life.” For some manuscripts have “He breathed” or “He inspired into his face.” But since the Greeks have *ἐνεφύσησεν* (*enephysēsen*), there is no doubt that it should be rendered “he blew” or “he breathed into.” In the preceding discussion, when we were considering God’s hands and the formation of man from clay, we asked what should be understood by this. What, then, are we to say now concerning the statement, “God breathed,” except that, just as he did not form man with bodily hands, so he did not blow with a throat and lips?

3. Nevertheless, in this extremely difficult question Scripture greatly assists us, as I believe.

## CHAPTER II — From the passage of Scripture under discussion it is argued that the soul is not of the same nature as God

For since some, on the basis of this expression, have believed that the soul is something from God’s own substance—that is, of the same nature as he is—thinking this because, when a man blows, he expels something of himself in his breath, we should rather be warned by this to reject a view hostile to the catholic faith. We believe that God’s nature and substance, in which the Trinity is believed by many but understood by few, is altogether immutable. But who can doubt that the soul’s nature can be changed either for the worse or for the better? Therefore it is a sacrilegious opinion to believe that it and God are of one substance. For what else is believed in this way than that God too is changeable? We must therefore believe and understand, without any doubt, what the right faith holds: that the soul is from God as something he made, not as something from the nature that he himself is, whether he generated it or brought it forth in any manner whatsoever.

## CHAPTER III — The same argument is pressed

4. “How, then,” they ask, “is it written, ‘He breathed into his face, and man became a living soul,’ if the soul is not a part of God or God’s substance altogether?”

On the contrary, this expression sufficiently shows that it is not so. For when a man blows, the soul itself moves the bodily nature subject to it and produces breath from that nature, not from itself. Perhaps these people are so dull that they do not know that by this reciprocal breath, which we draw in and expel from the air surrounding us, breath is also produced when we blow voluntarily.

Even if we expelled something by blowing not from this external air that lies nearby and is drawn in and released, but from the nature of our own body, of which we consist, the nature of the body and of the soul would still not be the same; and they themselves certainly agree with this. Therefore, even in this case, the substance of the soul, which governs and moves the body, is one thing, and the breath that it produces by governing or moving the body subject to it is another. Since, then, the soul governs its subject body in a manner indeed vastly and incomparably different from the way God governs the creation subject to him, why should we not rather understand that God made the soul from the creation subject to him in the act described as his breathing, since the soul itself, although it does not rule its body in the way God rules the universe that he created, nevertheless produces breath by the body’s movement, not from its own substance, to which the body is subject?

5. We could indeed say that God’s breath itself is not the soul of man, but that by breathing God made the soul in man. But lest anyone think that what he made by his word is better than what he made by his breath—for in us, too, a word is better than breath—for the present, according to the reasoning stated above, there is no reason why we should hesitate to call the soul itself God’s breath, provided that it is understood not to be God’s nature and substance, but that “to breathe” means precisely “to make breath,” and that “to make breath” means “to make the soul.”

This agrees with what God says through Isaiah: “For the spirit shall go forth from me, and I have made every breath.” That he is not speaking of just any bodily breath is shown by what follows. For after saying, “I have made every breath,” he adds: “And because of sin, I have grieved him a little, and struck him” (Isa. 57:16–17, according to the Septuagint). What, then, does he call “breath” except the soul, which because of sin has been struck and grieved? What, then, is “I have made every breath” except “I have made every soul”?

## CHAPTER IV — By breathing, God did not make the soul from himself or from the elements

[Col. 0358]

6. If, then, we were to call God the soul of this bodily world, with the world itself as the body of a single living being, we would rightly say that by breathing he made man’s soul only if it were bodily, made from the air subject to him and proceeding from his body. Yet we should not think that by breathing he had given something from himself; rather, he would have given it from the air of his body subject to him, just as the soul similarly produces breath from something of this kind that lies nearby—that is, from the body, not from itself.

But since we say not merely that the world’s body is subject to God, but that he is above every creature, whether bodily or spiritual, we must not believe that by breathing he made the soul either from himself or from bodily elements.

## CHAPTER V — Whether the soul is from nothing

7. It is reasonably asked whether the soul was made from what absolutely did not exist—that is, from nothing—or from some thing that had already been made spiritually by him but was not yet a soul. For if we do not believe that God still creates anything from nothing after he created all things simultaneously, and therefore believe that, after all his works had been completed, he rested from the works he began, so that whatever he subsequently made he made from those things, I do not see how we can understand him still to make souls from nothing.

Or should we say that, among the works of those first six days, he made that hidden day—as though this should rather be understood as the spiritual and intellectual nature, namely the angelic unity—and the world, that is, heaven and earth? And that in those already existing natures he created the principles of other things that were to come, not the natures themselves? For if the latter had already been created there just as they were going to be, they would not still be future.

If this is so, there was not yet in created things any nature of the human soul; it began to exist when God made it by breathing and placed it in man.

8. But this does not remove the question of whether he created from nothing the nature called the soul, since perhaps his breath itself was made not from some underlying substance, as we said of the breath that the soul produces from its body, but was made altogether from nothing when God wished to blow, and became the soul of man; or whether something spiritual already existed, although whatever it was had not yet been the nature of the soul, and from this God’s breath was made, which would be the nature of the soul—just as the nature of the human body did not yet exist before God formed it from the clay or dust of the earth.

For human flesh was not dust or clay; nevertheless, there was something from which it could be made, although it was not yet flesh.

## CHAPTER VI — Whether, as with the body, some matter preceded the soul

9. Is it therefore credible that, in those first six days’ works, God created not only the causal principle of the future human body but also the matter from which it would be made—that is, the earth, from whose clay or dust it would be formed—while for the soul he created there only the principle according to which it would be made, and not also some matter of its own kind from which it would be made?

For if the soul were something immutable, we should in no way seek something like its matter. But now its mutability sufficiently indicates that it can meanwhile be disfigured by vices and falsehoods, and formed by virtues and the teaching of truth, while remaining within the nature that is already its nature as a soul. Flesh too, within its nature as flesh, is adorned by health and disfigured by diseases and wounds.

But just as flesh, apart from being already flesh—a nature in which it may improve so as to be beautiful or decline so as to be deformed—also had matter, namely earth, from which it was made so that it might altogether be flesh, so perhaps the soul, before it became that very nature called the soul, whose beauty is virtue and whose deformity is vice, could have had some matter of its own kind, spiritual matter that was not yet a soul. Thus the earth from which flesh was made already was something, although it was not flesh.

10. Yet the earth already occupied the lowest part of the world before the human body was made from it, contributing its own part to the universe, so that even if no flesh of any living creature were made from it, it would nevertheless by its appearance complete the structure and mass of the world, according to which the world is called heaven and earth.

## CHAPTER VII — It cannot be said what that matter would have been like

But if there was, or is, some spiritual matter from which the soul was, or is, made, what is it itself? What name does it have, what form, what function does it possess among created things? Does it live, or does it not? If it lives, what does it do? What does it contribute to the effects of the universe? Does it live a blessed life, a miserable one, or neither? Does it give life to something? Or is it free even from this work, resting idle in some hidden part of the universe without vigilant awareness or vital movement?

For if there was not yet any life at all, how could there be some incorporeal but lifeless matter destined for life? Either this is false, or it is excessively obscure. But if it already lived neither blessedly nor miserably, how was it rational? And if it became rational when the nature of the human soul was made from that matter, then was the matter of the rational—that is, human—soul an irrational life? What, then, distinguished it from the soul of an animal? Or was it rational in potential, though not yet in capacity?

For if we see that an infant’s soul—already certainly a human soul—has not yet begun to use reason, and yet we call it rational, why should we not believe that in the matter from which the soul was made there was likewise a quiet movement of sensation, just as in an infant, which is already certainly a human soul, the movement of reasoning is still quiet?

## CHAPTER VIII — It cannot be admitted that that matter was blessed

11. For if the life from which the human soul was made was already blessed, then it became worse; and therefore this was not the matter of the soul, but the soul was a decline from that blessed life. For when any matter is formed, especially by God, it is without doubt formed into something better.

But even if the human soul could be understood as a decline from some life made by God in a state of blessedness, it still should not be believed to have begun in any act of its own merits, except from the time when it began to live its own life, when it became a soul animating flesh and, using its senses as messengers, sensing itself to live within itself through its will, understanding, and memory.

For if there is something from which God could inspire this decline into formed flesh, as though by breathing he were making a soul, and if that something is itself blessed, then it is in no way moved or changed or deprived of anything when something proceeds from it from which the soul is made.

## CHAPTER IX — Nor is that matter some irrational soul

For it is not a body, so that it could be diminished as if by exhalation.

12. But if an irrational soul is in some way the matter from which a rational soul—that is, a human soul—is made, the question arises again: from what is the irrational soul itself made? For it too is made only by the creator of all natures.

Is it made from bodily matter? Why, then, not the rational soul as well? Unless perhaps someone will deny that what is granted to occur gradually can be done by God in a shorter way. Accordingly, whatever intermediate stage is introduced, if body is the matter of the irrational soul and the irrational soul is the matter of the rational soul, then without doubt body is the matter of the rational soul. I know of no one who has ever dared to hold this, except one who places the soul itself in the category of some kind of body.

13. Furthermore, we must beware lest a transmigration of the soul from an animal into a human being be thought possible—a belief altogether contrary to truth and the catholic faith—if we grant that an irrational soul lies beneath as matter from which a rational soul is made. For then, if the former is changed for the better, it will become human; and if the latter is changed for the worse, it will become an animal.

The descendants of certain philosophers were even ashamed of this mockery of theirs and said that the philosophers had not held this view but had been misunderstood. And I believe that this is so, as though someone were to hold such a view even on the basis of our Scriptures, where it is said: “Man, when placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless animals and became like them” (Ps. 48:13); or where we likewise read: “Do not give over to the beasts the soul that confesses you” (Ps. 73:19).

For not all heretics fail to read the catholic Scriptures; nor are they heretics for any other reason than that, not understanding them correctly, they obstinately assert their false opinions against the truth of those Scriptures. But however the philosophers’ opinion concerning the revolutions of souls may stand—or may not stand—it does not accord with the catholic faith to believe that the souls of animals transmigrate into human beings, or those of human beings into animals.

## CHAPTER X — Similarity of conduct does not make the human soul pass into an animal

14. That human beings become like animals in their manner of life is proclaimed by human affairs themselves and attested by the Scriptures. Hence the passage I mentioned: “Man, when placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts of burden and became like them.” But this occurs in the present life, certainly, not after death.

Accordingly, the person who said, “Do not give over to the beasts the soul that confesses you,” did not want his soul to be placed in the power of such beasts—or perhaps of those whom the Lord signifies when he says that they are clothed in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matt. 7:15)—or of the devil and his angels; for he too is called a lion and a dragon (Ps. 90:13).

15. What argument, then, do the philosophers who think that human souls can pass after death into animals, or animal souls into human beings, offer? Certainly this: that similarity of conduct draws them into such transformations, as though the greedy became ants, the predatory became kites, the savage and proud became lions, and those who pursue filthy pleasure became swine, and so on with similar examples.

They offer these examples but do not notice that, on this reasoning, it is in no way possible for an animal’s soul after death to pass into a human being. A pig will in no way be more like a human being than like a pig; and when lions become tame, they become more like dogs or even sheep than like human beings.

Since animals do not depart from the behavior of animals, and those that become somewhat unlike the others are nevertheless more like their own kind than like the human race, differing far more from human beings than from animals, they will never become human souls if those things that are more similar are what draw them across.

But if this argument is false, how will the opinion be true, since they offer nothing else by which it might be regarded as at least plausible, even if not true? Hence I would more readily believe that their later followers too understood the men who first set these ideas down in their books as intending that, in this life, through a perversity and depravity of conduct, human beings become like animals and thus in a certain manner are changed into animals—so that, by presenting this disgrace, they might recall people from the crookedness of their desires.

## CHAPTER XI — Imaginary transmigrations of certain souls; the Manichaean opinion is worse than that of the philosophers

16. As for the stories that are told of certain people seeming to remember the bodies of which animals they had been, they are either false accounts, or this was brought about in their minds by the deceptions of demons. For if it happens in dreams that, through a deceptive memory, a person seems to remember having been what he was not or having done what he did not do, what wonder is it if, by some just and hidden judgment of God, demons are permitted to produce something of this kind even in the hearts of those who are awake?

17. The Manichaeans, who either consider themselves Christians or wish to be considered Christians, are worse and more detestable than those Gentile philosophers—or any other foolish people who hold this view—in their belief concerning the transmigration or revolutions of souls. The philosophers distinguish the nature of the soul from the nature of God; the Manichaeans, however, since they say that the soul is nothing other than God’s own substance and altogether what God is, do not hesitate to call it shamefully changeable, so that, in an astonishing madness, they think it is mixed into every kind of grass or worm, or capable of revolving into any one of them.

Yet if they remove from their minds the questions concerning exceedingly obscure matters, which, as they turn them over with a carnal mind, necessarily cause them to slip and roll headlong into false, harmful, and monstrous opinions, and if they hold with complete firmness the one thing naturally and truly implanted in every rational soul without the winding paths of dispute—namely, that God is altogether immutable and incorruptible—their entire fable of a thousand forms suddenly collapses. In their vain and sacrilegious minds they fabricated it solely from the utterly shameful mutability of God.

18. Therefore, an irrational soul is not the matter of the human soul.

## CHAPTER XII — The soul is not from a bodily element

What, then, is the source from which the soul was made by God’s breath? Was it some body, earthly and moist? By no means; for from this the flesh was made. For what else is clay than moist earth? Nor should the soul be believed to have been made from moisture alone, as though flesh were made from earth and the soul from water.

It is exceedingly absurd to think that the human soul was made from what produced the flesh of fish and birds.

19. Then perhaps it was made from air? Breath does indeed belong to this element, but our breath, not God’s. As we said above, this could coherently be supposed if we believed God to be the soul of the world as of one immense living being, so that he breathed the soul from the air of his body just as our soul breathes from the air of its body.

But since it is established that God is above every bodily thing in the world and above every spirit that he created, at an altogether incomparable distance, how can this rightly be said? Or perhaps, the more God is present to all his creation through his unique omnipotence, the more was he able to make from air the breath that would be the human soul?

But since the soul is not bodily, whereas whatever is made from the bodily elements of the world must be bodily, and since air too is numbered among the elements of the world, it should not be believed even if the soul were said to have been made from the element of that pure and heavenly fire.

Some have asserted that every body can be changed into every other body. But I know of no one who has held that some body, whether earthly or heavenly, can be changed into a soul and become an incorporeal nature; nor does the faith hold this.

## CHAPTER XIII — The physicians’ view concerning the human body

20. Furthermore, if what physicians not only say but also claim to prove should not be dismissed, then although all flesh plainly possesses earthly solidity, it nevertheless contains something of air within it. This air is contained in the lungs and is distributed from the heart through the veins they call arteries.

It also contains fire—not only the hot quality whose seat is in the liver [Note: [Col. 0362] The printed editions add “and in the brain,” which is absent from the manuscripts.] but also a luminous quality, which they show as though it were liquefied and rising upward to the elevated region of the brain, like the heaven of our body. From there rays shine forth from the eyes, and from its center, as from a kind of central point, thin channels are led not only to the eyes but also to the other senses—to the ears, nostrils, and palate—for hearing, smelling, and tasting.

They say that the sense of touch itself, which is spread throughout the whole body, is directed from that same brain through the marrow of the neck and through what is contained within the bones joined together by the spine of the back, so that from there certain very fine streams, which produce the sense of touch, are distributed through all the limbs.

## CHAPTER XIV — The soul is not from the elements

Since, then, the soul receives through these messengers whatever bodily things are not hidden from it, while it itself is so entirely something else that, when it wishes to understand either divine things, God, or even itself and its own virtues, in order to grasp something true and certain, it turns away from even the light of the eyes themselves and, recognizing that light as not merely useless but even somewhat obstructive for this task, raises itself to the gaze of the mind—how can it belong to that class of things whose highest member is nothing but the light that shines from the eyes?

That light assists the soul only in perceiving bodily forms and colors, whereas the soul itself possesses innumerable things profoundly unlike the whole class of bodies, things that it sees only through understanding and reason, to which no sense of the flesh reaches.

## CHAPTER XV — The soul is incorporeal

21. Therefore the nature of the human soul is not from earth, water, air, or any kind of fire. Nevertheless, it administers the matter of its coarser body—that is, a certain moist earth, which has been changed into the quality of flesh—through the nature of a more subtle body, namely through light and air.

For without these two there is neither any sense in the body nor any spontaneous movement of the body by the soul. Just as one must first know before acting, so sensing precedes moving. Since, then, the soul is an incorporeal thing, it first acts upon the body that is near to the incorporeal, such as fire, or rather light and air; and through these it acts upon the other, coarser parts of the body, such as moisture and earth, from which the solidity of the flesh is compacted. These are more subject to being acted upon than endowed with the power to act.

## CHAPTER XVI — Why it is said, “Man became a living soul”

22. It does not seem to me, then, that “Man became a living soul” was said for any other reason than that he began to sense in the body; and this is the most certain indication of animated and living flesh.

Plants too are moved—not only by a force pushing them from outside, as when they are shaken by winds, but by that movement through which everything that contributes to the growth and appearance of a tree is moved inwardly, by which sap is drawn into the root and transformed into the substances that constitute the nature of grass or wood. None of this occurs without inward movement.

But this movement is not spontaneous, as is the movement joined to sensation for the administration of the body, as occurs in every kind of animal, which Scripture calls a living soul (Gen. 1:21).

For unless that movement also existed in us, our bodies would not grow, nor would our nails and hair grow out. But if only this existed in us, without that spontaneous movement of sensation and motion, man would not be said to have become a living soul.

## CHAPTER XVII — Why God is said to have breathed into man’s face

[Col. 0364]

23. Since, then, the front part of the brain, from which all the senses are distributed, is located toward the forehead, and since the organs of sensation themselves are situated in the face—except for the sense of touch, which is spread throughout the whole body—yet even this sense is shown to have its pathway from that same front part of the brain, running backward through the crown and neck to the marrow of the spine, of which we spoke shortly before, so that the face too has the sense of touch, as does the whole body, except for the senses of sight, hearing, smell, and taste, which are located in the face alone. I therefore think it was written that God breathed the breath of life into man’s face when he became a living soul.

For the front part is rightly placed before the rear: the former leads, while the latter follows; and sensation proceeds from the former, movement from the latter, just as deliberation precedes action.

## CHAPTER XVIII — The three chambers of the brain

24. Since bodily movement, which follows sensation, cannot occur without intervals of time, and since we cannot perform actions involving intervals of time by spontaneous movement except with the assistance of memory, three chambers of the brain are accordingly identified.

One is in front, toward the face, and from it comes all sensation. Another is behind, toward the neck, and from it comes all movement. The third lies between the two; they show that memory operates there, so that when movement follows sensation, a person does not fail to connect what must be done because he has forgotten what he has done.

They say these facts have been established by reliable indications. When the individual parts are affected by some disease or defect and the functions of sensing, moving the limbs, or remembering bodily movements have failed, each part sufficiently demonstrates what it can do, and it has been determined what sort of treatment applied to it has helped restore the relevant function.

But the soul acts in these parts as in organs; none of these is the soul itself. Rather, the soul gives life to and governs all things, and through them cares for the body and for this life in which man became a living soul.

## CHAPTER XIX — The superiority of the soul over bodily things

25. Since we are asking, then, from what the soul itself comes—that is, from what matter, so to speak, God made this breath called the soul—nothing bodily ought to present itself as the answer.

For just as God surpasses every creature, so the soul surpasses every bodily creature in the dignity of its nature. Nevertheless, through light and air, which are also the superior bodies in the world and have greater excellence for acting than the corporeal density of moisture and earth has, the soul administers the body as through things more akin to spirit.

Bodily light announces something; but the one to whom it announces is not the same as what announces it. The soul is the one to whom it announces, not the thing that announces. When the soul painfully senses bodily afflictions, it is distressed because its action—by which it is present to govern the body—is hindered by the body’s disturbed condition; this distress is called pain.

The air infused into the nerves obeys the will so that it may move the limbs, but it is not itself the will. That middle part announces the movement of the limbs so that it may be retained in memory [Note: [Col. 0364] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “so that the things remembered may be retained.”]; it is not itself memory.

Finally, when these things that serve the soul as ministers fail altogether through some defect or disturbance, when the messengers of sensation and the servants of movement cease, the soul withdraws, as though it had no reason to remain present. But if they do not fail to the extent that ordinarily occurs in death, the soul’s attention is disturbed, as though it were trying to restore what is collapsing but unable to do so. From the things by which it is disturbed, one can determine which part of its services is at fault, so that medicine may come to its aid if possible.

## CHAPTER XX — The soul is one thing, the organs of the body another

26. That the soul itself is one thing and these bodily services, vessels, or organs of its own—whatever the most suitable term may be—are another is clearly shown by the fact that it often turns its attention away from everything through intense concentration on thought, so that, although its eyes are open and functioning properly, it is unaware of many things placed before them.

If its concentration is greater, while it is walking it suddenly stops, evidently turning the command to move away from the service of movement by which its feet were being carried. But if its concentration on thought is not so great that it fixes the walker in place, yet is still great enough that it does not have leisure to attend to that middle part of the brain which announces bodily movements, it sometimes forgets both where it came from and where it is going, and unwittingly passes beyond the village toward which it had been heading. The nature of its body is sound, but its attention has been diverted elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0365] The printed editions have “by its own force.” The word *force* is absent from nearly all the manuscripts.].

Therefore, whether God mixed or joined to the body of the living being these bodily particles of the bodily heaven—that is, light and air, which first receive the impulses of the life-giving soul because they are nearer to an incorporeal nature than moisture and earth are—taking them from this surrounding and overarching heaven, or whether he made them from clay just as he made flesh, is not a question relevant to the matter at hand.

For it is credible that every body can be changed into every other body; but it is absurd to believe that any body can be changed into a soul.

## CHAPTER XXI — The soul is neither from any body nor itself a body
27. Therefore neither should we accept the view held by certain people that there is a fifth kind of body from which the soul comes [Note: [Col. 0365] Most manuscripts read “from which souls come.”], one that is neither earth, nor water, nor air, nor fire—whether the latter be the more turbulent and earthly fire, or that pure and luminous heavenly fire—but some other thing lacking its customary name, though nevertheless being a body (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book 1). For if those who hold this view call “body” what we do—that is, any nature occupying a spatial extension in length, breadth, and height—then neither is the soul this, nor should it be believed to have been made from it. For whatever is of this kind can, not to mention many other properties, be divided or bounded in any part of itself by lines. If the soul were subject to this, it could in no way know such lines, which cannot be cut lengthwise; yet it knows that such lines cannot be found in a body.

28. Nor does anything of this kind present itself to the soul itself, since it cannot fail to know itself, even when it searches in order to know itself. For when it seeks itself, it knows that it is seeking itself; and it could not know this if it did not know itself. It does not seek itself from elsewhere, but from itself. Since, then, it knows itself as the seeker, it certainly knows itself; and whatever it knows, it knows wholly. Therefore, since it knows itself as the seeker, it knows itself wholly, and thus knows its whole self. For it does not know anything else, but knows itself wholly [Note: [Col. 0366] A few manuscripts read, “but knows itself wholly,” which, we think, is an error.]. Why, then, does it still seek itself, if it knows itself as the seeker? For if it did not know itself, it could not know that it was seeking itself. But this concerns the present; what it asks about itself is what it was before, or what it will be in the future. Let it therefore cease for the moment to suspect that it is a body. For if it were something of that kind, it would know itself to be such—yet it knows itself more than it knows heaven and earth, which it knows through the eyes of its body.

29. I pass over the fact that that faculty of it which even animals are understood to possess, or the birds of heaven when they return to their dwellings or nests—the faculty by which images of all bodily things are apprehended—is in no way similar to any body. And surely this faculty ought rather to be similar to a body in which the likenesses of bodily things are contained. But if this faculty is not a body, as is certain, although the likenesses of bodies are not only retained there in memory but also fashioned innumerably at will, how much less can the soul, by any power of its own, be similar to a body?

30. If, however, they call everything that exists a body in some other sense—that is, every nature and substance—then this way of speaking should not indeed be admitted, lest we fail to find a way, when speaking, to distinguish things that are not bodies from bodies. Yet we should not labor too much over the word. For we too say that whatever the soul is, it is not any of those four well-known elements that are manifestly bodies; but neither is it what God is. What it is cannot be better expressed than by “soul” or “spirit of life.” The word “of life” is added because air, too, is often called spirit. Indeed, some have called the soul that same air, so that no name can now be found by which this nature may be properly distinguished: it is neither body, nor God, nor life without sensation, such as may be believed to exist in trees, nor life without a rational mind, such as exists in animals; rather, it is life now inferior to that of the angels, but destined to become like the angels if here it lives according to the command of its Creator.

31. As to where it comes from—that is, from what sort of matter it was made, or from what perfect and blessed nature it flowed, or whether it was made altogether from nothing—even if this is doubtful and subject to inquiry, one thing nevertheless ought not to be doubted: if anything existed beforehand, what existed was made by God, and the soul is now made by God so that it may be a living soul. For either nothing existed, or what now exists did not exist. But the question concerning that part which we were investigating as its material, from which it was made, has already been treated sufficiently.

## CHAPTER XXII  
Whether the causal principle of the soul was created during the days of Genesis.

32. Now, if the soul did not exist at all beforehand, we must ask how it can be understood that its causal principle was said to have existed in the first six days of God’s works, when God made man in his own image—something that cannot rightly be understood except with reference to the soul. There is a danger, however, that when we say that at that time God did not create the very natures and substances that were going to exist, while creating all things simultaneously, but rather certain causal principles of those future things, we may appear to be saying something empty. For what are these causal principles, according to which it could already be said that God made man in his own image, although he had not yet formed his body from the earth, nor made him a living being by breathing a soul into him?

Even if there was some hidden principle of the human body by which it was destined to be formed, there was also matter from which it would be formed—that is, earth—in which that principle may be understood to have lain hidden, as it were, in a seed. But with regard to the soul that was to be made—that is, the breath that was to become the human soul—what causal principle was first established there when God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (something that cannot rightly be understood except with reference to the soul), if there was no nature in which it could be established? [Note: [Col. 0367] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “from which.” Ambrosianus and the manuscripts read “in which.”]

33. For if this principle was in God and not in a creature, then it had not yet been created. How, then, was it said, “God made man in the image of God” (Gen. I, 26–27)? But if it was already in a creature—that is, in those things which God created all together—in what creature was it? Was it in a spiritual or a bodily creature? If in a spiritual one, was it active in the bodies of the world, whether heavenly or earthly? Or was it lying inactive in that creature until man was created in his own proper nature, just as in a human being who is already living his own life there lies secretly and idly a generative principle that does not operate except through intercourse and conception?

Or was that spiritual creature, in which this principle lay hidden, itself doing none of its own work? And why had it been created? Was it to contain the principle of the future human soul, or of future souls, as though they could not exist in themselves but only in some creature already living its own life, just as the principle of generation can exist only in certain natures that already exist and are complete?

Thus some creature would have been appointed as the parent of the soul—a spiritual creature in which the principle of the future soul might exist, though the soul would not proceed from it until God caused it to be breathed into a human being. For God alone creates and forms even the fetus from a human being, whether from seed or from offspring already born, through Wisdom, which reaches everywhere by reason of its purity, so that nothing defiled enters into it (Wis. VII, 24–25), “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (ibid. VIII, 1).

But I do not know how one could understand that some spiritual creature was created solely for this purpose, although it is not mentioned among God’s works made during those six days. God is said to have made man on the sixth day, though he had not yet made him in his proper nature, but only in a causal principle within that unmentioned creature. That creature ought rather to have been mentioned, since it had been so completed that it no longer had to be made according to the preceding principle of its own cause.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
Whether that causal principle of the soul was implanted in the angelic nature.

[Col. 0368]

34. Or perhaps God implanted the causal principle for making the soul in the nature of that day which he created first, if that day is rightly understood as an intellectual spirit, when on the sixth day he made man in his own image—establishing, that is, the cause and principle according to which he would make him after those seven days—so that the causal principle of his body may be believed to have been created in the nature of earth, but that of his soul in the nature of that day?

But what else is being said by this than that an angelic spirit is, as it were, the parent of the human soul, if the pre-established principle for creating the human soul exists in that spirit just as the principle of future offspring exists in a human being? On this view, human beings would be the parents of human bodies, but angels the parents of souls; God, however, would be the creator both of souls and of bodies—of bodies through human beings, of souls through angels—or, in the case of the first body, through earth, and in the case of the first soul, through the angelic nature in which he had established their causal principles when he first made man among those things he created simultaneously; thereafter, human beings would come from human beings, body from body, soul from soul.

It is difficult to say that the soul is the daughter of an angel or of angels; but it is much more difficult to say that it is the daughter of the corporeal heaven—and how much more difficult, then, of the sea and the earth? Therefore the causal principle of the soul was much less pre-established in any bodily creature when God made man in his own image, before he animated him at the appointed time by forming him from earth and breathing into him, if it is absurd to believe that he established the soul causally in the angelic nature.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
Whether the soul was created before it was inserted into the body.

35. Let us therefore consider whether the following might perhaps be true—which certainly seems to me more tolerable to human opinion: that God, in those first works in which he created all things simultaneously, also created the human soul, to breathe it at the appointed time into the limbs of a body formed from earth, while he had created causally, among those things made simultaneously, the principle of that body, according to which the human body would be formed when it had to be made.

For we rightly understand neither the statement “in his own image” except with reference to the soul, nor the statement “male and female” except with reference to the body. Let it therefore be believed, if no authority of Scripture or reasoning from truth contradicts it, that man was made on the sixth day in such a way that the causal principle of the human body was in the elements of the world, while the soul itself had already been created, just as the day was created at the beginning, and lay hidden among God’s works until, at the appointed time, he inserted it by breathing— that is, by inspiration—into the body formed from earth.

## CHAPTER XXV  
Whether, if the soul existed outside the body, it came to the body by its own will.

36. But here another question arises that must not be dismissed. If the soul had already been made and was lying hidden, where could it have been better for it than there? What, then, was the reason that an innocent soul, living harmlessly, was inserted into this life of the flesh, in which, by sinning, it would offend the one who created it, so that it would deservedly be followed by the misery of labor and the torment of condemnation? [Col. 0369]

Should we say that it inclined by its own will toward the administration of the body, and that, since one may live either justly or unjustly in this bodily life, it would have what it chose—either the reward of justice or the punishment of iniquity—so that this would not contradict the apostolic statement that those not yet born had done nothing good or evil (Rom. IX, 11)?

For that inclination of the will toward the body is not yet an act either of justice or of iniquity, for which an account must be rendered at God’s judgment, when each person will receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil (II Cor. V, 10).

Why, then, should we not also believe that the soul came to the body by God’s will, so that, if it chose to act according to his command, it would receive the reward of eternal life and the company of the angels [Note: [Col. 0369] The printed editions read “the company”; the manuscripts have “of the company.”], but, if it rejected that command, would pay the most just penalties, whether of prolonged labor or of eternal fire? Or is the very fact of obeying God’s will already a good action, so that this would conflict with the statement that those not yet born had done nothing either good or evil?

## CHAPTER XXVI  
Whether, if the soul was inserted into the body by its own will, it had no foreknowledge of the future. Free will.

37. If this is so, we shall also have to acknowledge that the soul was not originally created in such a class of things that it had foreknowledge of its future action, whether just or unjust. For it is utterly incredible that it could have been inclined by its own will toward bodily life if it foresaw that it would sin in such ways as to be justly punished with everlasting punishment.

The Creator is rightly praised in all that he made, since everything was very good. He is not to be praised only for those creatures to which he gave foreknowledge; he is also rightly praised for creating animals, to which human nature is superior even in human beings who sin. For human nature is from God, not the iniquity by which a person entangles himself through misuse of free will. Yet if he did not possess free will, he would be less excellent within the order of nature.

We must contemplate a human being living justly without foreknowledge of future things, and see there how the excellence of a good will is not prevented from living rightly and pleasing God by the fact that, ignorant of the future, he lives by faith. Whoever would not want such a creature to exist among created things contradicts God’s goodness. Whoever does not want it to suffer penalties for its sins is an enemy of equity.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
That the soul is carried toward the body by a natural appetite.

38. But if the soul is made for this purpose, that it may be sent into a body, one may ask whether it is compelled if it does not wish to go. It is better, however, to believe that it naturally wills this—that is, that it is created with a nature such that it wills it—just as it is natural for us to wish to live. But to live badly is no longer a matter of nature, but of a perverse will, which is justly followed by punishment.

39. It is therefore pointless now to ask from what sort of matter the soul was made, if it can rightly be understood to have been made among those first works when the day was made. For just as those things that did not exist were made, so too was the soul made among them.

But if there was some matter capable of being formed, both bodily and spiritual, it too was established by God, from whom all things come. That matter would precede its formation not in time but in origin, as the voice precedes the song. What, then, is more fitting to believe than that the soul was made from spiritual matter?

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
The difficulties arising when it is said that Adam’s soul was not created before it was breathed into his body.

40. But if someone does not wish to think that the soul was made until it was breathed into an already formed body, let him consider what answer he will give when asked from what it was made. Either he will say that God made or makes something from nothing after the completion of his works; and he must consider how he can explain the statement that man was made on the sixth day in the image of God—a statement that cannot rightly be understood except with reference to the soul—that is, in what nature the causal principle of something that did not yet exist was made.

Or he will say that the soul was made not from nothing but from something already existing; and he will have to investigate what that nature was, whether bodily or spiritual, in accordance with the questions we examined above. There will remain the further difficulty of asking in what substance among the creatures first established during the six days God made that causal principle of the soul, which he had not yet made either from nothing or from something.

41. If he wishes to avoid this by saying that man was also made from earth on the sixth day, but that this was mentioned later by way of recapitulation, let him consider what he will say about the woman. For Scripture says, “Male and female he made them, and he blessed them” (Gen. I, 27–28).

If he answers that she too was made on that day from the man’s bone, let him consider how he will maintain that the birds brought to Adam were made on the sixth day, when Scripture indicates that every kind of bird was created from the waters on the fifth day. Likewise, he must consider how the trees planted in paradise were made on the sixth day, when the same Scripture assigns this kind of creature to the third day.

Let him also consider the meaning of the very words: “God again caused every tree pleasant to the sight and good for food to spring up from the earth,” as though those trees that the earth had brought forth on the third day had not been pleasant to the sight and good for food, although they belonged among the works that God made all very good.

What, too, is meant by: “God formed from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky” (ibid. II, 19)? It sounds as though those were not all the creatures that had first been brought forth—or rather, as though none had been brought forth before. For it does not say, “God formed from the earth the remaining beasts of the field and the remaining birds of the sky,” as though the earth on the sixth day or the water on the fifth had produced something less than all; rather, it says, “all the beasts” and “all the birds.”

Let him also consider how God made everything in six days: first, the day itself; second, the firmament; third, the appearance of the sea and the earth, together with grass and trees from the earth; fourth, the lights and stars; fifth, the animals of the waters; sixth, those of the earth. Yet afterward it is said: “When the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field.” For when the day was made, he made nothing except the day itself.

How, moreover, did he make every green plant of the field before it was upon the earth, and every grass before it sprang up (Gen. II, 4–5)? If it was made when it sprang up, and not before it sprang up, who would say otherwise unless the words of Scripture compelled him to reconsider?

Let him also remember that it is written, “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. XVIII, 1), and let him see how those things can be said to have been created together whose creation is separated by intervals of time—not merely by hours, but even by days.

Let him also take care to show how both statements can be true, although they may seem contrary: that God rested on the seventh day from all his works, as the book of Genesis says (Gen. II, 2), and that he works until now, as the Lord says (John V, 17). Let him also examine what is said to have been completed and how the same things are said to have been begun.

42. Guided by all these testimonies of divine Scripture—which no one doubts to be truthful except an unbeliever or an impious person—we have been led to say that at the beginning of the world God created all things simultaneously: some as already established natures, others as pre-established causes. Thus the Almighty made not only present things but also future things [Note: [Col. 0371] This is the reading of the ancient codices. The printed editions have: “so that he made not only present things but also future things.” A little later they read, “that he rested and thereafter their …,” and so on.], and, having made them, rested from them, so that thereafter, through their administration and governance, he might also create the orders of times and temporal things.

He had both completed them, because of the termination of all kinds of things, and begun them, because of the propagation of the ages: so that he might rest on account of what was completed, and work until now on account of what was begun. But if these matters can be understood better, I not only do not resist, but even gladly accept it.

43. For the present, however, concerning the soul that God made by breathing into the human face, I affirm nothing except that it is from God in such a way that it is not God’s substance; that it is incorporeal—that is, not a body [Note: [Col. 0372] The printed editions had: “so that it is not God’s substance, and is incorporeal in such a way that it is not a body.” The manuscripts read: “so that it is not God’s substance, and is incorporeal, that is, not a body.”]; that it is spirit; that it is not begotten from God’s substance, nor proceeds from God’s substance, but is made by God; and that it was not made in such a way that any bodily nature or irrational soul was changed into its nature. Accordingly, it was made from nothing.

As for its being immortal, this may be understood according to one mode of life, which it cannot in any way lose; but according to another kind of mutability, by which it can become either worse or better, it may not unreasonably also be understood as mortal. For only the one of whom it is properly said, “He alone has immortality” (I Tim. VI, 16), possesses true immortality.

Let the other things that I have said in disputation throughout this book serve the reader either to understand how matters that Scripture does not state openly should be investigated without rash affirmation, or, if this method of inquiry does not please him, to know how I myself have sought them. If he can teach me, let him not refuse to do so; and if he cannot, let him join me in seeking the one from whom both of us may learn.

# BOOK EIGHT

Concerning the passage read at Genesis 2:8, “And God planted a paradise in Eden,” and so forth, up to verse 17, “But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat of it,” and so forth.

[Col. 0371]

## CHAPTER I  
Paradise, planted in Eden, is to be understood both literally and figuratively.

1. “And God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had formed.” I am not unaware that many people have said many things about paradise. Three general views, however, may be distinguished concerning it. One belongs to those who wish paradise to be understood only bodily; another to those who wish it to be understood only spiritually; and a third to those who accept paradise in both ways—sometimes bodily, sometimes spiritually.

To put the matter briefly, I confess that I prefer the third view. In accordance with it, I have now undertaken to speak about paradise, trusting that the Lord will grant that the man made from earth—which certainly means a human body—may be understood to have been placed in a bodily paradise. Just as Adam himself, although he signifies something else in accordance with what the Apostle says, that he was “a figure of the one to come” (Rom. V, 14), is nevertheless understood as a human being represented in his own nature—one who lived for a definite number of years and died after producing a numerous offspring, as other human beings die, although he was not born from parents as other human beings are, but was made from the earth as was necessary at the beginning—so too the paradise in which God placed him should be understood as nothing other than a certain place, namely, a region where the earthly human being would dwell.

[Col. 0372]

2. For the narrative in these books is not, in its manner of expression, a narrative of figurative things, as in the *Song of Songs*, but of things that actually happened, as in the books of Kings and other works of this kind. But because those books speak of matters familiar from ordinary human experience, they are initially understood literally—not merely with difficulty, but most readily—and only afterward are the events themselves examined to discover what they signified concerning future things.

Here, however, because things are said that do not occur to those who observe the ordinary course of nature, some people do not wish them to be understood literally, but figuratively. They want history—that is, a narrative of things literally done—to begin from the point at which Adam and Eve, having been sent out of paradise, came together and produced children. As if it were familiar to us that they lived for so many years, or that Enoch was taken away, or that an old and barren woman gave birth, and other things of this kind.

3. “But,” they say, “one narrative concerns miraculous events, and another concerns created natures. In the former, the very unusual things show that there are certain modes of nature and certain modes of miracles, which are called mighty works; here, however, the establishment of natures themselves is being indicated.”

They are answered: those things too are unusual precisely because they are first. For what event in the establishment of worldly things was so without example and without equal as the world itself? Should we therefore believe that God did not make the world because he no longer makes worlds, or that he did not make the sun because he no longer makes suns?

And this answer ought indeed to have been given not concerning paradise but concerning the man himself. But if they believe that the man himself was made by God in a way in which no other man has been made, why do they refuse to believe that paradise was made in the way in which they now see forests being made?

4. I am speaking to those who follow the authority of these Scriptures, for some of them do not wish paradise to be understood literally, but figuratively. As for those who wholly oppose these writings, we have dealt with them elsewhere and in another manner (*On Genesis against the Manichaeans*). Yet even in this present work we defend these matters, as far as we can, literally, so that those who refuse to believe them—not because they have been moved by reason, but because of a stubborn or dull mind—will nevertheless find no argument by which they can prove them false.

But these people of ours, who have faith in these divine books and do not want paradise to be understood according to the literal meaning—that is, as a most pleasant place shaded by fruitful groves, both extensive and abundantly watered by a great spring—see that no human work can cause so many and such great green things to flourish through God’s hidden activity. I wonder how they can believe that the man himself was made in a manner they have never seen.

Or if he too must be understood figuratively, who fathered Cain, Abel, and Seth? Were they also merely figures, and not human beings born from human beings? Let them therefore observe where this presumption leads, and let them try with us to understand all the events first narrated according to the expression of their literal reality.

For who would not afterward favor them when they understand what these events also admonish us of through their figurative meaning—whether concerning spiritual natures or dispositions, or even concerning future things?

Certainly, if the things named bodily here could in no way, without endangering faith in the truth, also be understood bodily, what would remain except to understand them as spoken figuratively rather than impiously to accuse Holy Scripture? But if understanding them bodily not only causes no difficulty but also establishes the narrative of divine speech more firmly, then, I think, no one will be so stubbornly unbelieving that, when he sees it expounded literally according to the rule of faith, he will prefer to remain in his former opinion, if he had happened to think that these things could be understood only figuratively.

## CHAPTER II  
Why he previously expounded Genesis allegorically against the Manichaeans.

5. For I too, against the Manichaeans, who err by failing to accept the writings of the Old Testament in the manner they ought to be accepted, and who blaspheme by wholly refusing and detesting them, wrote two books soon after my conversion. I wished quickly either to refute their ravings or to raise their attention toward seeking in the writings they hate the Christian and evangelical faith.

At that time, not everything occurred to me as to how these matters could be understood literally; indeed, many seemed incapable of being understood in that way, or scarcely capable, or difficult to understand. So that I would not be delayed, I explained with as much brevity and clarity as I could what figurative meanings belonged to those things that I could not find a literal way to understand. I did this lest they, deterred either by the length of the reading or by the obscurity of the argument, fail to take the books in hand at all.

Nevertheless, remembering what I had most wanted but had not been able to achieve—that everything should initially be understood not figuratively but literally—and by no means despairing that it might also be understood in this way, I wrote the following in the first part of the second book:

“Certainly,” I said, “whoever wishes to accept everything that has been said according to the letter—that is, not to understand it otherwise than the letter sounds—and can avoid blasphemies while proclaiming everything consistent with the Catholic faith, is not merely someone who should not be envied; he should be regarded as an exceptional and highly praiseworthy interpreter.

“But if there is no way for the written words to be understood piously and worthily of God unless we believe that these things have been set forth figuratively and in riddles, then, possessing the apostolic authority through which so many riddles from the books of the Old Testament are resolved, let us follow the method we have undertaken, with the help of the one who urges us to ask, seek, and knock (Matt. VII, 7). Let us explain all these figures of things according to the Catholic faith, whether they pertain to history or to prophecy, without prejudging a better and more careful treatment, whether by ourselves or by others to whom the Lord may choose to reveal it” (*On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book 2, chapter 2).

This is what I said then. But now, since the Lord has willed that, by looking at and considering these matters more carefully, I should not without reason, as I think, believe that it can also be shown by me that these writings are expressed according to their proper, rather than allegorical, meaning, let us investigate what follows concerning paradise in the same way as what we were previously able to establish.

## CHAPTER III  
On verses 8 and 9, where the creation of the tree is again mentioned.

6. “Therefore God planted a paradise of delights”—for this is what *Eden* means—“toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had formed.” For it is written in this way because it happened in this way.

Then the narrative recapitulates, in order to show how what it had briefly stated was done—namely, how God planted paradise and established there the man whom he had formed. For it continues:

“And God again caused every tree pleasant to the sight and good for food to spring up from the earth.”

It did not say, “God caused another tree or the remaining tree to spring up from the earth,” but, it says, “he caused every tree pleasant to the sight and good for food to spring up from the earth.”

Therefore the earth had already produced every tree pleasant to the sight and good for food—namely, on the third day. For on the sixth day he had said, “Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant, sowing seed, which is upon all the earth, and every fruit-bearing tree that has in itself the fruit of seed-bearing produce, which shall be for your food” (Gen. I, 29).

Did he therefore give them something different then and wish to give them something different now? I do not think so. Rather, since the trees established in paradise belonged to those kinds that the earth had already produced on the third day, it produced them again at their proper time.

For at that earlier time, when Scripture says that the earth produced them, this had been accomplished causally in the earth.
