That is, the earth had then secretly received the power to produce them, and by that power it comes about that even now the earth brings forth such things openly and at their proper time.

[Col. 0375]

7. Therefore the words of God spoken on the sixth day—“Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant, sowing seed, which is upon all the earth,” and so forth—were not words uttered with an audible or temporal voice, but words in which the power of creation exists in his Word.

But what God said without temporal sounds could be spoken to human beings only through temporal sounds. For it was destined that the human being, once formed from earth and animated by his breath, and whatever should arise from him as the human race, would use for food those things that were to spring up upon the earth through the generative power the earth had already received.

Creating the causal principles of this future reality in the creature, he spoke as though it already existed, through the inward and innermost truth that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard,” but which his Spirit revealed to the one who wrote it.

## CHAPTER IV  
On the second part of verse 9: the tree of life was truly created and also signified Wisdom.

8. What follows must be considered more carefully: “And the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of discerning good and evil.” Otherwise it might compel us to interpret the passage allegorically, so that these were not actually trees but something else signified by the name “tree.”

For it is said of Wisdom, “She is a tree of life to all who embrace her” (Prov. III, 18). Nevertheless, although there is an eternal Jerusalem in heaven, a city was also established on earth to signify it. And although Sarah and Hagar signified the two Testaments, they were nevertheless also two women (Gal. IV, 24–26). Likewise, although Christ waters us with a spiritual stream through the suffering of the wood, there was also a rock which, struck with a piece of wood, poured forth water for the thirsty people; of it it was said, “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4).

All those things signified something other than what they were, but they also existed bodily. And when they were mentioned by the narrator, the expression was not figurative, but a straightforward account of things whose earlier occurrence had a figurative significance.

Thus there was also a tree of life, just as there was a rock that signified Christ. Nor did God wish human beings to live in paradise without the bodily presence of signs of spiritual realities. Therefore the other trees provided him with food, but that tree provided him with a sacrament. What did it signify except Wisdom, of whom it is said, “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her,” just as it might be said of Christ, “The rock that flows forth is for those who thirst for it”?

It is rightly called by the name of what preceded it in order to signify him. He is the sheep that is sacrificed at Passover; yet that event was represented not only by words but also by an action. For that sheep was truly a sheep: it was killed and eaten (Exod. XII, 3–11). Yet through that true event something else was also represented.

This is unlike the fattened calf that was killed for the feast when the younger son returned (Luke XV, 23). There the narrative itself is a narrative of figures, not a figurative representation of events that actually occurred. For it was not the evangelist who narrated this, but the Lord himself. The evangelist narrated that the Lord had narrated it.

Therefore what the evangelist narrated also happened—namely, that the Lord spoke such things. But the Lord’s own narrative was a parable, and no one ever requires that the things spoken in it be shown to have occurred literally.

Christ is also the stone anointed by Jacob (Gen. XXVIII, 18), and the stone rejected by the builders that became the cornerstone (Ps. CXVII, 22). But the former also occurred in actual events, whereas the latter was foretold only in figures. The former was written by a narrator of past events; the latter by one who merely foretold future events.

## CHAPTER V  
On the same tree of life: it was both a figure and nevertheless a real thing.

9. Thus Wisdom, Christ himself, is the tree of life in the spiritual paradise, into which he sent the thief from the cross (Luke 23:43). But in the bodily paradise the tree of life too was created, to signify it; for this was said by that Scripture which, narrating events accomplished in their own times, also narrated that the human being had been bodily formed and placed there, living in a body.

[Note: [Col. 0376] The printed editions read *certum* (“certain”); ten manuscripts read *creatum* (“created”).]

Or, if anyone thinks that souls, after departing from the body, are contained in bodily visible places, although they are without bodies, let him state his view. There will be people enough to support him, even to the point of asserting that the rich man who was thirsting was in a bodily place and that the soul itself is altogether corporeal, on account of the burning tongue and the drop of water desired from Lazarus’s finger (Luke 16:24). I do not hesitate to say that I am not rashly entering into conflict with them over so great a question. For it is better to be uncertain about hidden matters than to quarrel about uncertain ones.

I have no doubt that that rich man is to be understood as being in the heat of punishments, and that the poor man is in the refreshment of joys. But how that flame of hell, that bosom of Abraham, that tongue of the rich man, that finger of the poor man, that thirst of torment, and that drop of refreshment are to be understood—this is perhaps scarcely discovered by those who inquire meekly, and never by those who contend arrogantly.

A brief answer must be given, lest this profound question, which requires many words, delay us. If souls are contained in bodily places even after they have been stripped of their bodies, the thief could have been brought into that paradise where the body of the first man had been. If necessity should demand it, we may at the appropriate place in Scripture inquire or express, as best we can, what we should think about this matter.

10. Now, that wisdom is not a body, and therefore is not a tree, I neither doubt nor, I think, expect anyone else to doubt. But the person who does not think that wisdom could have been signified in the bodily paradise through a tree—that is, through a bodily creature—as through a kind of sacrament, must be regarded as failing either to see the many bodily sacraments of spiritual realities in Scripture or as contending that the first human being ought not to have lived with some such sacrament.

The Apostle says that even what he said about the woman whom we believe was made for him from his side—“For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24)—is “a great sacrament” in Christ and in the Church (Ephesians 5:31–32).

[Col. 0377]

It is astonishing, and scarcely tolerable, that people should want paradise to have been spoken of figuratively, yet should not want it also to have been made figuratively. If they allow that, as with Hagar and Sarah, and as with Ishmael and Isaac, these things both happened and nevertheless were also figurative, I do not see why they should not also admit that the tree of life was truly some tree and yet signified wisdom.

11. I add this as well: although that tree supplied bodily food, it supplied food of such a kind that the human body would be firmly established in lasting health—not as with other food, but through some hidden impartation of health. Ordinary bread, certainly, had something more in it, by which God rescued a man from the need for food for forty days with a single cake of bread (1 Kings 19:8).[^c0036-1] Shall we perhaps hesitate to believe that, for the sake of some higher signification, God supplied human beings with food from a tree so that their bodies would not deteriorate through either weakness or age, or even fall into dissolution—he who gave ordinary human food such a marvelous power that, in earthen vessels, the flour and oil were replenished and did not fail? (1 Kings 17:16)

Let some contentious person now appear and say that God ought to have performed such miracles in our lands, but ought not to have done so in paradise—as though he had not there performed a greater miracle by making a human being from dust and a woman from a man’s side than by raising the dead here.

[^c0036-1]: A *collyris* was a cake of bread baked under ashes; it was also called *colluran*.

## CHAPTER VI

### The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was a real and harmless tree. Obedience and disobedience.

12. We must now consider the tree of the knowledge of discerning good and evil. This too was plainly visible and bodily, like the other trees. There is no doubt, therefore, that it was a tree; but we must inquire why it received this name.

As I consider the matter again and again, I cannot say how much I appreciate the view that this tree was not harmful as food. For he who had made all things “very good” (Genesis 1:31) had not established anything evil in paradise. Rather, the evil was the transgression of the command.

It was necessary that the human being, placed under the Lord God, should be prohibited from something, so that obedience itself would be the means by which he merited the Lord’s favor. I can say with complete truth that obedience is the sole virtue of every rational creature acting under God’s authority. The first and greatest vice is the swelling desire to use one’s own power independently, and the name of this vice is disobedience.

There would have been no basis for the human being to think and feel that he had a Lord unless something had been commanded him. That tree, therefore, was not evil; but it was called the tree of the knowledge of discerning good and evil because, if the human being ate from it after the prohibition, the transgression of the command would follow in that act. Through the experience of punishment, he would then learn the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience.

Accordingly, this too is to be understood not as having been spoken figuratively, but as a real tree. Its name was given not from the fruit or apple that grew from it, but from what would follow when it was touched contrary to the prohibition.

## CHAPTER VII

### On verses 10, 11, 13, and 14: the rivers there are to be understood as real rivers. The Tiber was formerly the Abula; the Nile was formerly the Gihon; the Ganges was formerly the Pishon.

[Col. 0378]

13. A river went out from Eden to water the paradise, and from there it divided into four branches. The name of one is Pishon; it is the river that encircles the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. The gold of that land is good; there too are a carbuncle and a green stone (*lapis prasinus*). The name of the second river is Gihon; it is the river that encircles the whole land of Ethiopia. The third river is the Tigris; it is the river that flows toward Assyria. The fourth river is the Euphrates.

What more need I do concerning these rivers to establish that they are real rivers, and not figuratively spoken of as things which do not exist, as though their names merely signified something? They are well known in the regions through which they flow and famous among nearly all peoples.

Indeed, since it is certain that these are real rivers—for antiquity changed the names of two of them, just as the river now called the Tiber was formerly called the Abula; the Gihon is the river now called the Nile; and the Pishon was the one now called the Ganges, while the other two, the Tigris and Euphrates, have retained their ancient names—we ought to be warned to understand the other matters also, first of all, according to the literal meaning. We should not suppose that figurative speech is being used in them, but should understand that the things narrated both existed and also signified something.

This does not mean that a parable could not take something from a subject which is not also known to exist literally [Note: The word *non* is absent in Erasmus and M.], as when the Lord speaks of the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers (Luke 10:30). Who does not recognize and plainly see that this is a parable and that the whole account is figurative? Yet the two cities named there are still shown in their proper locations today.

We would understand these four rivers in the same way if some necessity compelled us to interpret the other matters narrated about paradise not literally but figuratively. But now, since no reasoning prevents us from first understanding the things themselves literally, why should we not simply follow the authority of Scripture in its narration of accomplished events—understanding first that the events truly happened, and then investigating whatever else they signify?

14. Shall we be troubled by the fact that the sources of some of these rivers are said to be known, while those of others are completely unknown, and therefore conclude that it cannot be taken literally that they divide from a single river in paradise? On the contrary, we should believe that, since the place of paradise is most remote from human knowledge, four branches of water were divided there, just as the most trustworthy Scripture testifies.

The rivers whose sources are said to be known may have run underground somewhere and, after traversing lengthy regions, emerged in other places where they are reported to be known as though at their own sources. Who does not know that some waters commonly behave in this way? It is simply known where they do not run underground for long.

Thus a river went out from Eden—that is, from the place of delights—and watered the paradise—that is, all the beautiful and fruitful trees that shaded the whole land of that region.

## CHAPTER VIII

### On verse 15: whether the human being was placed in paradise to work at agriculture.

[Col. 0379]

15. “The Lord God took the human being whom he had made and placed him in paradise, to work it and to guard it. And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: ‘From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat from it. On the day when you eat from it, you shall die by death.’”

[Note: Here and shortly below, all the Louvain manuscripts read *escam edes* (“you shall eat food”). Conversely, Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice variously read *escam edes*, *esca edes*, and *edes ad escam*.]

After saying briefly above that God planted the paradise and placed there the human being whom he had formed, the text recapitulates in order to explain how the paradise was established. Now, by recapitulating, it has also recalled how God placed there the human being whom he had made.

Let us therefore see what is meant by the words “to work it and to guard it.” What was he to work, and what was he to guard? Did the Lord perhaps intend the first human being to practice agriculture? Or is it not believable that before sin he had condemned him to labor?

We might indeed think so, unless we saw some people cultivating the soil with such delight of spirit that it is a great punishment for them to be called away from it to something else. Whatever delight agriculture possesses, therefore, was surely much greater then, when nothing adverse occurred either from the earth or from the sky.

It was not an affliction of labor, but an exhilaration of the will, when the things God had created came forth more happily and abundantly with the assistance of human work. Thus the Creator himself would be praised more richly, since he had given the soul, established in an animal body, both the reason to work and the ability to work as much as a willing spirit found satisfying, not as much as bodily need compelled an unwilling one.

16. What spectacle is greater or more marvelous, or where can human reason speak more intimately, in a manner of speaking, with the nature of things, than when seeds have been sown, shoots planted, little trees transplanted, and slips grafted, and the power of each root and sprout is as though questioned: what can it do, and what can it not do? From where can it do it, and from where can it not? What does the invisible and inward power of numbers accomplish in it, and what does diligence applied from outside accomplish?

In this very contemplation one can perceive that “neither he who plants is anything nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7). For even the work added from outside comes through him whom God nonetheless created, and whom he invisibly governs and orders.

## CHAPTER IX

### The work of agriculture allegorically understood.

17. From this point the eye of thought is raised toward the world itself, as toward a kind of great tree of things. In the world too, a twofold operation of providence is found: partly natural and partly voluntary.

The natural operation occurs through God’s hidden administration, by which he also gives growth to trees and grasses. The voluntary operation occurs through the works of angels and human beings.

According to the first, the heavenly things above and the earthly things below are ordered; the lights and stars shine; the alternations of day and night proceed; the earth, founded upon the waters, is washed and surrounded by them; the air is spread above; trees and animals are conceived and [Col. 0380] born, grow and grow old, die, and undergo whatever else is accomplished in things through an inward and natural motion.

According to the second, signs are given, instruction is offered and received,[^c0036-2] fields are cultivated, communities are governed, arts are practiced, and whatever else is done either in the society above or in this earthly and mortal society takes place, so that the good may be cared for even through evil people who do not know it.

In the human being himself this same twofold power of providence is active. It operates naturally with regard to the body—that is, through the motion by which the body comes to be, grows, and ages—and voluntarily with regard to the measures taken for its food, clothing, and healing. Similarly, with regard to the soul, it operates naturally so that the soul may live and perceive, but voluntarily so that it may learn and consent.

[^c0036-2]: Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain editions read *discere*, “to learn,” rather than *doceri et disci*, “to be taught and learned.”

18. As agriculture acts externally upon a tree so that what is being accomplished inwardly may prosper, so, with respect to the body, medicine serves externally what nature accomplishes inwardly. Likewise, with respect to the soul, instruction is supplied externally so that nature may be made blessed inwardly.

What negligence in cultivating is to a tree, carelessness in healing is to the body, and sluggishness in learning is to the soul. What useless moisture is to a tree, destructive food is to the body, and an iniquitous persuasion is to the soul.

God, therefore, who is above all things, who created all things and governs all things, creates every nature good and orders every will justly.

What is contrary to the truth, then, if we believe that the human being was placed in paradise to practice agriculture—not through servile labor, but through an honorable delight of the spirit? For what occupation is more innocent than this for those who are at leisure, and what is more full of great reflection for the wise?

## CHAPTER X

### What is meant by “to work it and to guard it.”

19. But what was he to guard? The paradise itself? Against whom? Certainly no neighboring invader was feared, no disturber of boundaries, no thief, no assailant.

How, then, are we to understand that a bodily paradise could have been guarded bodily by a human being? Yet Scripture did not say, “to work the paradise and to guard it”; it said, “to work it and to guard it.”

Although, if the Greek is rendered more carefully word for word, it is written as follows: “And the Lord God took the human being whom he had made and placed him in paradise, to work it and to guard it.” But whether the phrase means that he placed the human being to work—that is, as the translator understood it, “to work it”—or that he placed him to work the paradise, that is, for the human being to work the paradise, the wording is ambiguous. The construction seems rather to require that one should not say, “to work the paradise,” but “in the paradise.”

20. Nevertheless, lest perhaps it was said in the sense “to work the paradise,” just as it was said above, “There was no human being to work the ground”—for “to work the ground” is the same construction as “to work the paradise”—let us examine the ambiguous statement in both ways.

If it is not necessary to understand “to guard the paradise,” but rather “to guard in the paradise,” what was he to guard in the paradise? We have already discussed, as far as seemed appropriate, what he was to work in the paradise.

Was he perhaps to guard within himself through discipline what he worked on the earth through agriculture? That is, just as the field obeyed him when he cultivated it, so he too [Col. 0381] was to obey the Lord who commanded him. Having received the command of obedience, he was to return the fruit of obedience, not the thorns of disobedience.

Finally, because he refused, as a subject, to preserve in himself the likeness of the paradise cultivated by him, he received, after his condemnation, a field like himself: “Thorns and thistles it shall produce for you” (Genesis 3:18).

21. But if we understand the words to mean that he was to work the paradise and guard the paradise, he could indeed work the paradise, as we said above, through agriculture. He could guard it, however, not against wicked or hostile beings, for there were none, but perhaps against wild animals.

How would that be, and why? Were the wild animals already raging against the human being, something that would not happen except through sin? He himself gave names to all the animals when they were brought to him, as is mentioned later. He also received, on the sixth day, together with all the animals, the common foods by the word of God.

Or, if there was already something to fear from the wild animals, how could one human being have fortified that paradise? It was not a small place, for so great a spring watered it.

He ought indeed to have guarded it if he could enclose the paradise with a wall so great and so strong that the serpent could not enter it. But it would be astonishing if, before building such a wall, he could have excluded all the serpents from it.

22. Why, then, do we overlook the meaning that lies before our eyes? The human being was placed in paradise to work that same paradise, as was argued above, through agriculture—not laborious but delightful, and one that brought great and useful reminders to a prudent mind. He was to guard that same paradise for himself, so that he would not do anything deserving of expulsion from it.

Finally, he also received a command, so that he might have the means by which to guard the paradise for himself—that is, by preserving the command, he would not be cast out from it. Someone is rightly said not to have guarded his own property if he acted in such a way as to lose it, even if it remains safe for another who either found it or deserved to receive it.

23. There is another sense in these words which, I think, ought reasonably to be preferred: that God himself was to work the human being and guard him.[^c0036-3]

Just as a human being works the earth not in order to make it earth, but to make it cultivated and fruitful, so God works the human being much more profoundly. God created him to be human, and he works him so that he may be just, provided that the human being does not depart from him through pride.

For this is what it means to apostatize from God, which Scripture calls the beginning of pride: “The beginning of human pride is to apostatize from God” (Sirach 10:14).

Since God is the unchangeable good, whereas the human being, both in soul and in body, is changeable, he cannot be formed as just and blessed unless he turns toward the unchangeable good, which is God, and remains established in it.

Thus the same God who creates the human being so that he may be human also works the human being and guards him so that he may be good and blessed as well.

Accordingly, in the same way that one says that a human being works the earth, which was already earth, so that it may be cultivated and fruitful, one [Col. 0382] says that God works the human being, who was already human, so that he may be devout and wise; and that God guards him, because a human being cannot be safe through his own power when he takes delight in himself and despises the dominion of the one above him.

[^c0036-3]: The alternative interpretation nevertheless accords better with the Hebrew, in which the pronoun “it” refers to the paradise, agreeing with the feminine gender of the word.

## CHAPTER XI

### Why the designation “Lord” is added here. The true Lord.

24. I therefore think that it is by no means without purpose, but that it gives us a significant warning, that from the beginning of this divine book—where it begins, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”—up to this point, the words “Lord God” have nowhere appeared, but only “God.”

Now, however, when the text has reached the point at which God placed the human being in paradise and was to work and guard him through a command, Scripture speaks in this way: “And the Lord God took the human being whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work him and to guard him.”

This is not because God was not Lord over the creatures mentioned above, but because this was written not on account of angels or any other created things, but on account of the human being, to warn him how beneficial it is for him to have the Lord God—that is, to live obediently under his dominion rather than licentiously abuse his own power.

For this reason Scripture did not wish to use the expression earlier, until it reached the point at which the human being was placed in paradise to be worked and guarded. It did not say, as it had said of all the other things above, “And God took the human being whom he had made,” but said, “And the Lord God took the human being whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work him”—so that he might be just—and to guard him—so that he might be safe—by that very dominion of God, which is not useful to God but to us.

He does not need our service, but we need his dominion, so that he may work and guard us. Therefore he alone is truly Lord, because we serve him not for his benefit but for ours, for our salvation.

If he needed us, he would not thereby be a true Lord, since his need would be assisted by us, and under that need he too would be serving.

Rightly does he say in the Psalm: “I have said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods’” (Psalm 15:2).

Nor should what we have said—that we serve him for our benefit and salvation—be understood as though we expected something other than him himself from him, since he himself is our supreme benefit and salvation. Thus we love him freely, in accordance with the saying: “But for me, clinging to God is good” (Psalm 73:28).

## CHAPTER XII

### The human being cannot do anything good without God. Departure from God.

25. The human being is not such that, once made, he can do anything well as though from himself if the one who made him should abandon him. Rather, his entire good action consists in turning toward the one by whom he was made and continually becoming just, devout, wise, and blessed through him.

This is not like being healed by a bodily physician and then departing. A bodily physician was an external worker serving the nature that works inwardly under God, who brings about every healing through the twofold work of providence about which we spoke above (Chapter 9).

The human being must not therefore turn toward the Lord in such a way that, once he has been made just [Col. 0383] by him, he departs from him. He must turn in such a way that he is always being made by him.

Indeed, by the very fact that he does not depart from God, he is justified, illuminated, and blessed by God’s presence, while God works and guards him as he exercises dominion over one who obeys and submits.

26. As we were saying, this is not like a human being working the earth so that it may be cultivated and fruitful, then departing after he has worked it, leaving behind the work that has been done—plowed, sown, watered, or whatever else—while the work remains after the worker has gone away.

Rather, God works the human being as a just person—that is, by justifying him—not so that, if God departs, what he has done remains in the one from whom he has departed. Instead, it is like air: in the presence of light it is not made luminous once and for all, but continually becomes luminous. For if it had been made luminous rather than continually becoming so, it would remain luminous even when the light was absent.

In the same way, the human being is illuminated when God is present to him, but immediately becomes dark when God is absent. One departs from God not through intervals of place but through an aversion of the will.

27. Let him, therefore, work the good human being and guard him who is unchangeably good. We must always be made by him and always be perfected by him, clinging to him and remaining in that turning toward him of which it is said, “For me, clinging to God is good,” and to whom it is said, “I will guard my strength toward you” (Psalm 59:10).

We are his workmanship not only so that we may be human beings, but also so that we may be good.

When the Apostle was commending to the faithful who had turned from impiety the grace by which we have been saved (Ephesians 2:8–10), he said: “For by grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God; not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them.”

And elsewhere, after saying, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling,” lest they should think that this was to be attributed to themselves, as though they made themselves just and good, he immediately added: “For it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13).

Thus “the Lord God took the human being whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work him”—that is, to work in him—and to guard him.

## CHAPTER XIII

### Why the human being was forbidden the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

28. “And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: ‘From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat from it. On the day when you eat from it, you shall die by death.’”

If that tree from which God prohibited the human being had been evil, its very nature would have appeared to be poisoned for death. But God, who made all things very good, had planted all the trees in paradise as good (Genesis 1:12), and there was no nature of evil there, because there is nowhere any nature of evil—a matter we shall discuss more carefully, if the Lord wills, when we begin to speak about that serpent.

The human being was therefore prohibited from that tree, which was not evil, so that the preservation of the command itself would be his good and the transgression itself his evil.

29. The extent of the evil that disobedience alone is could not have been commended more clearly or carefully. The human being became guilty of iniquity because he touched the thing contrary to the prohibition; if he had touched it without being prohibited, he would certainly not have sinned.

For example, if someone says, “Do not touch this plant,” because it is poisonous and threatens death, death does indeed follow if he touches it in contempt [Col. 0384] of the command. But even if no one had prohibited him and he had touched it, he would nonetheless die. That thing would be contrary to his health and life whether he was forbidden to touch it or not.

Likewise, when someone prohibits another from touching something that would not harm the person who touches it, but would harm the one who issued the prohibition—for example, if someone reached his hand into another person’s money and was forbidden by the owner to do so—the prohibited person would sin because the act could be damaging to the one who issued the prohibition.

But when something is touched that would harm neither the person touching it, if it had not been prohibited, nor anyone else whenever it might be touched, why was it prohibited unless to demonstrate the good of obedience in itself and the evil of disobedience in itself?

30. In the end, the sinner desired nothing other than not to be under God’s dominion, when he committed the act in which he ought to have attended solely to the command of the one who ruled, so that he would not commit it.

If he had attended solely to that command, what else would he have attended to but God’s will? What else would he have loved but God’s will? What else would he have placed above the human will but God’s will?

Let the Lord see to why he commanded it. The servant must do what he commanded, and perhaps only afterward should the person who has earned his favor consider why he commanded it.

Nevertheless, so that we do not inquire too long into the reason for this command: if it is itself a great benefit to the human being that he serves God, then by commanding God makes beneficial whatever he wishes to command. There is no reason to fear that he could command something useless.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Through contempt of the divine command, the experience of evil.

31. It is impossible that the self-will should not fall upon the human being with the weight of a great ruin if, by exalting itself, it places itself above the will of the one superior to it.

The human being experienced this when he despised God’s command, and through this experience learned the difference between good and evil: the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience—that is, of pride and defiance, of perverse imitation of God, and of harmful liberty.

The tree in which this occurred received its name from the event itself, as was said above (Chapter 6).

We would not recognize evil through experience unless we had done it, for evil would not exist if we had not committed it. There is no nature of evil; rather, the loss of good has received that name.

God is the unchangeable good. The human being, insofar as he belongs to the nature in which God created him, is indeed good, but he is not unchangeable as God is. Mutable good, which comes after unchangeable good, becomes a better good when it clings to the unchangeable good by loving and serving it with rational and proper will.

This nature is itself therefore also a great good, because it has received the capacity to cling to the nature of the supreme good. If it does not wish to do so, it deprives itself of good, and this is evil for it; hence, by God’s justice, punishment also follows.

For what is more unjust than that it should go well with one who abandons the good? That can never happen. Yet sometimes the evil of having lost a higher good is not felt when an inferior good is possessed and [Col. 0385] loved.

But it is divine justice that one who voluntarily lost what he ought to have loved should lose with pain what he did love, while the Creator of natures is praised everywhere.

Even the good that feels the loss of good remains, for if some good had not remained in the nature, there would be no pain over lost good in the punishment.

32. But the person who delights in good without experiencing evil—that is, who chooses to hold on to the good before feeling its loss, so that he may not lose it—must be praised above all human beings.

Yet if this had not been an extraordinary distinction, it would not have been attributed to that child who, born from the race of Israel, became “Emmanuel, God with us” (Matthew 1:23), reconciled us to God as the mediator, the human being Christ between human beings and God (1 Timothy 2:5), the Word with God and flesh among us (John 1:1, 14), the Word, flesh between God and us.

Concerning him the prophet says: “Before the child knows good or evil, he will reject wickedness in order to choose the good” (Isaiah 7:16, according to the Septuagint).

How can someone who does not know something reject or choose it, unless good and evil are known in two different ways: good through prudent understanding, and evil through experience?

Through prudent understanding of good, evil is known even if it is not felt. Good is held fast so that its loss will not be experienced as evil.

Likewise, through the experience of evil, good is known, because the person who suffers from the loss of good feels what he has lost.

Before, then, the child knew through experience either the good of which he would be deprived or the evil that he would feel through the loss of good, he rejected evil in order to choose good. That is, he did not wish to lose what he possessed, lest, by losing it, he should experience the loss of what he ought not to lose.

This is the singular example of obedience: he came not to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him (John 6:38), unlike the one who chose to do his own will rather than the will of the one by whom he was made.

Therefore, just as through the disobedience of one many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many are made righteous (Romans 5:19). For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ (1 Corinthians 15:22).

## CHAPTER XV

### Why the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was so called.

33. Some people are pointlessly clever and obtuse when they ask how the tree could have been called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil before the human being transgressed the command through it and, through that very experience, discerned the difference between the good he lost and the evil he committed.[^c0036-4]

The tree received such a name so that, when it was not touched in accordance with the prohibition, people would be on their guard against what would be felt when it was touched contrary to the prohibition.

It did not become the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because they ate from it contrary to the command. Rather, even if they had been obedient and had taken nothing from it contrary to the command, it would rightly have been called by that name, because what happened to them there would have happened if they had taken from it.

For example, suppose it were called the tree of satiety because people could be satisfied from it. If no one had approached it, would that name therefore be inappropriate? Certainly not, since when they approached it and were satisfied, they would then prove how rightly that tree was called the tree of satiety.

[^c0036-4]: The ancient manuscripts consistently read *obtunsi sunt*, “have been blunted,” rather than *obtusi sunt*, “are obtuse.” The same reading occurs in *On Christian Doctrine* 4.7.

## CHAPTER XVI

### How the human being could understand what evil was before experiencing evil.

[Col. 0386]

34. “And how,” they say, “could the human being understand what was being said to him when the tree was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, when he had no knowledge at all of what evil was?”

Those who think this way pay too little attention to how many unknown things are understood from familiar opposites. Even when words for things that do not exist are inserted into speech, no listener is left confused.

That which does not exist at all is called “nothing.” Anyone who hears and speaks Latin understands these two syllables. From what else does this come except that, when the mind perceives what exists, it also recognizes through its absence what does not exist?

Likewise, when “empty” is said, we understand what is meant by looking at the fullness of a body and recognizing the emptiness as its contrary through the absence of that fullness. In the same way, through the sense of hearing we judge not only voices but also silence.

So, from the life that was present in the human being, he could guard against its contrary—that is, the deprivation of life called death. He could also understand, by whatever syllables it might be named, the cause by which he would lose what he loved: any act of his by which he would bring about the loss of life. When it was called “sin” or “evil” in Latin, he would understand it as a sign of what he discerned in his mind.

How do we understand what is meant when “resurrection” is said, although we have never experienced it? Is it not because we perceive what it is to live, call the deprivation of that state death, and call the return to the state we perceive resurrection?

Whatever name is given to the same thing in any language, a sign is introduced into the mind through the voice of the speaker. When that sound is made, the mind recognizes what it could also think about without the sign.

It is astonishing how nature avoids even an unexperienced loss of things it possesses. Who taught animals to avoid death except the sense of life? Who taught a little child to cling to the person carrying him when that person threatens to throw him down from a height? This behavior begins at a certain point, yet it occurs before the child has experienced anything of that kind.

35. Thus, for those first human beings, life was already sweet, and they certainly avoided losing it; and they could understand God signifying this very thing by whatever means or sounds He used. Nor could they otherwise have been induced to sin unless they had first been persuaded that, as a result of that act, they would not die—that is, that they would not lose what they possessed and rejoiced to possess. The matter will be discussed in its proper place. Let those who are troubled by this consider how they could have understood God naming or threatening things they had not experienced; and let them observe that we recognize the names of all things we have not experienced only from things we already know, when they are privations, or from similar things, when they are kinds or forms, without any agitation of doubt. Unless, perhaps, someone is troubled by how they could have spoken, or understood one who spoke, when they had not learned either by growing up among speakers or through some instruction—just as though it were a great thing for God to teach speech to those whom He had made in such a way that they could also learn it from human beings, if there were any from whom they could learn.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Whether the command was given to both Adam and Eve

[Col. 0387]

36. It is rightly asked whether God gave this command to the man alone, or also to the woman. But it has not yet been related how the woman was made. Or perhaps she had already been made? Yet the manner in which what had happened earlier took place was narrated later by way of recapitulation. For the words of Scripture are as follows: “And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying”; it does not say, “He commanded them.” Then it continues: “From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food”; it does not say, “You shall eat” in the plural. Then it adds: “But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat of it.” Here He seems already to be speaking to both in the plural, and He concludes the command in the plural, saying: “On the day on which you eat from it, you shall surely die.” Did He, knowing that He was going to make the woman for him, give the command in such an orderly way that the Lord’s command would reach the woman through the man? This is the discipline that the Apostle preserves in the Church when he says: “If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home” (1 Cor. 14:35).

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### How God spoke to man

37. It may likewise be asked how God now spoke to the man whom He had made, who certainly already possessed both sensation and understanding, so that he was able to hear and understand one who spoke. For he could not otherwise have received a command whose transgression would make him guilty [Note: [Col. 0387] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “by transgressing which he would be its transgressor.”], unless he understood what he had received. How, then, did God speak to him? Was it inwardly, in the mind according to understanding—that is, so that he might wisely understand God’s will and command without any bodily sounds or likenesses of bodily things? But I do not think that God spoke to the first man in this way. Scripture relates such things that we should rather believe God spoke to man in paradise as He later spoke to the patriarchs, such as Abraham and Moses—that is, in some bodily form. For this is why they “heard the sound of the Lord God walking in the garden toward evening, and they hid themselves” (Gen. 3:8).

## CHAPTER XIX  
### So that God’s activity in creatures may be understood: what must first be thought concerning God Himself

38. A great subject, therefore, and one that must not be passed over, is set before us: to contemplate, as far as we can and as far as He Himself deigns to help and grant us understanding, the twofold work of divine providence. Earlier, when we were speaking about agriculture, we touched on this briefly as an incidental matter, so that the reader’s mind might already begin to grow accustomed to contemplating what greatly helps prevent us from forming any unworthy conception of God’s own substance.

We therefore affirm that the highest, true, one and only God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, that is, God, His Word, and the Spirit of both; the Trinity itself, neither confused nor separated—is the God who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, “whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). He is contained neither by the finite nor by the infinite extent of places, nor does He vary through the finite or infinite succession of times. For in His substance, insofar as He is God, there is nothing that is shorter in a part than in the whole, as must be the case with things that move in places around a fixed axis: so the whole palm moves from the joint; nor was there in His substance something that now is not, or will be something that is not yet, as occurs in natures capable of undergoing temporal change.

## CHAPTER XX  
### Bodily creation exists in place and time, spiritual creation in time alone; the Creator Himself is changeable in neither respect

39. Living, therefore, in unchangeable eternity, He created all things simultaneously—from them times would proceed, places would be filled, and the ages would revolve through the temporal and local movements of things. Among these things He made some spiritual and some bodily, forming matter that no other being, and no being at all except Himself, established as formless yet formable, so that its formation would be preceded by it not in time but in origin.

He placed spiritual creation above bodily creation, because the spiritual could be changed only through time, whereas the bodily could be changed through both time and place. By way of example, the mind moves through time, whether by remembering what it had forgotten, learning what it did not know, or willing what it did not will; the body moves through place, whether from earth to heaven, from heaven to earth, from east to west, or in some other similar manner. Everything that moves through place must also move simultaneously through time; but not everything that moves through time must also move through place.

Therefore, just as the substance that moves through time and place is preceded by the substance that moves only through time, so that substance is preceded by the one that moves neither through place nor through time. Accordingly, just as the created spirit, which moves through time, itself moves the body through time and place, so the Creator Spirit, who moves neither through time nor through place, Himself moves the created spirit through time: the created spirit moves itself through time and moves the body through time and place; but the Creator Spirit moves Himself without time or place, moves the created spirit through time without place, and moves the body through time and place.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### How God, remaining unmoved, moves creatures may be discerned from the example of the soul

40. Whoever therefore attempts to understand how the truly eternal, truly immortal, and unchangeable God—who is Himself moved neither through time nor through place—moves His creature temporally and locally, cannot, I think, attain this unless he first understands how the soul, that is, a created spirit, moved not through place but only through time, moves the body through time and place. For if he is not yet able to grasp what takes place in himself, how much less will he grasp what is above him?

41. For the soul, affected by the habit of bodily senses, thinks that it too is moved through place together with the body while it moves the body through place. But if it could examine carefully, as though they were the hinges of its bodily members, how these are arranged joint by joint, and from which the beginnings of movements arise, it would discover that things moved through the distances of places are moved only by things fixed in place.

The finger alone is not moved unless the hand is fixed; from its joint, as from the elbow, the elbow is moved from the joint of the shoulder, and the shoulder from the shoulder blade. While these are moved, the hinges on which the movement rests remain fixed, and the thing that is moved travels through the space of a place. Thus the joint of the sole is in the ankle, and, when it remains fixed, the sole is moved; likewise the joint of the leg is in the knee, and that of the whole foot in the hip. No movement of any member that the will moves takes place unless it proceeds from some joint or hinge [Note: [Col. 0389] The printed editions have *articulrai*; the manuscripts have *atriculi*.] which the motion of that same will first fixes, so that what is moved can be driven by what does not move through the space of a place.

Indeed, even in walking, one foot is not lifted unless the other remains fixed and bears the whole body until the foot that has moved from the place where it stood comes to rest upon the place toward which it is moving, supported by the unmoving joint of its hinge.

42. Further, if in the body the will moves no member through place except from that member’s joint which it does not move—and if both the bodily part that is moved and the part by which it is fixed so that it may be moved possess their bodily quantities, by which they occupy the spaces of their respective places—how much more is this true of the soul’s own impulse, to which the members are subject, so that whatever pleases it may be fixed, providing the point from which what must be moved takes its support?

The soul is not a corporeal nature, nor does it fill a body in local space as water fills either a vessel or a sponge; rather, in wondrous ways it is joined to the body by its very incorporeal impulse, giving it life. By a kind of intention, not by bulk, it commands the body. How much more, then, does the impulse of its will itself move not through place in order to move the body through place, when it moves the whole body through its parts, and moves no parts through place except through those which it does not move through place?

## CHAPTER XXII  
### How God moves, and how the soul moves

43. If this is difficult to understand, let both propositions be believed: that spiritual creation, not moved through place, moves the body through place; and that God, not moved through time, moves spiritual creation through time. If someone does not wish to believe this concerning the soul—a truth that he would undoubtedly not only believe but also understand if he were able to conceive of it as it is, incorporeal—who would not easily recognize that what is not extended through the spaces of a place is not moved through place? Whatever is extended through the spaces of a place is a body; consequently, if the soul is believed not to be a body, it follows that it should not be thought to move through place.

But, as I began to say, if someone does not wish to believe this concerning the soul, he should not be pressed too hard. If, however, he does not believe that God’s substance is moved neither through time nor through place, he does not yet perfectly believe that it is unchangeable.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### God is always at rest, yet accomplishes everything

44. But because that nature of the Trinity is altogether unchangeable, and therefore eternal in such a way that nothing can be coeternal with it, it moves, while remaining with and within itself without any time or place, the creature subject to it through time and place. It creates natures by goodness and orders wills by power, so that among natures there is none that is not from Him; while among wills there is no good will that is not under His governance, and no evil will that He cannot use well.

But because He has not given every nature freedom of will, whereas those to which He has given it are more powerful and superior, those natures that do not possess will must be subject to those that do, by the ordering of the Creator, who never punishes an evil will in such a way as to destroy the dignity of its nature.

Since, therefore, no body and no irrational soul possesses freedom of will, these are subject to natures endowed with freedom of will—not all to all, but according to the distribution of the Creator’s justice. Thus God’s providence, ruling and administering the whole creation, both natures and wills—natures so that they may exist, and wills so that good wills may not be fruitless and evil wills may not go unpunished—first subjects everything to Himself; then bodily creation to spiritual creation, irrational creation to rational, earthly to heavenly, female to male, the weaker to the stronger, and the more needy to the more abundant.

Among wills, it subjects good wills to Himself and the others to those that serve Him, so that the evil will suffers what the good will has done at God’s command, whether through itself or through an evil will, at least in things that are naturally subject even to evil wills—that is, in bodies. For evil wills have their own inward punishment in themselves: their very iniquity.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### What creatures are subject to the blessed angels

45. Accordingly, the whole bodily nature, every irrational life, and every will that is either weak or depraved is subject to the exalted angels, who are subject to God, enjoy Him, and blessedly serve Him. Thus they act concerning the things subject to them, or together with them, in whatever way the order of nature requires in all things, at the command of Him to whom all things are subject.

They see unchangeable truth in Him and direct their wills according to it. They therefore become partakers of His eternity, truth, and will, always [Note: [Col. 0390] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “always doing His will.”] without time or place. Yet they are moved by His command temporally, while He is not moved temporally. They do not do so by springing away from or flowing down from His contemplation; rather, they contemplate Him simultaneously without place or time and carry out His commands in lower things, moving themselves through time and the body through time and place, insofar as their activity requires.

Therefore God presides over the whole creation through the twofold work of His providence: over natures, so that they may come into being; and over wills, so that they may do nothing without His command or permission.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### The nature of the universe, and how its parts are administered by God

46. The bodily nature of the universe as a whole is not helped bodily from outside. For there is no body outside it; otherwise it would not be the universe. But it is helped incorporeally from within, God causing it to be nature altogether, because “from Him and through Him and in Him are all things” (Rom. 11:36).

The parts of this same universe are also helped, or rather brought into being, incorporeally from within, so that they may be natures; and they are helped bodily from outside so that they may be maintained in better condition, as by food, agriculture, medicine, and whatever else is done for adornment, so that they may be not only sound and more fertile but also more comely.

47. But if created spiritual nature is perfect and blessed, as is that of the holy angels, then, insofar as it concerns its own existence, wisdom, and blessedness, it is helped only incorporeally from within. God speaks inwardly to it in a marvelous and ineffable manner—not through writing fixed by bodily instruments, nor through voices sounding in bodily ears, nor through likenesses of bodies formed imaginatively in the spirit, as happens in dreams or in some ecstasy, which in Greek is called *ἔκστασις* (*ekstasis*), a word that we too now use in place of the Latin term.

For although this kind of vision occurs more inwardly than those things announced to the mind through the bodily senses, nevertheless, because it resembles them—so that when it occurs it either cannot be distinguished from them at all, or can be distinguished only with difficulty and very rarely—and because it is more external than what the rational and intellectual mind beholds in unchangeable truth itself, by whose light it judges all these things, I think it should be reckoned among the things that occur externally.

Perfect and blessed spiritual and intellectual creation, therefore, such as the angels are, is, as I have said, helped, insofar as its own existence, wisdom, and blessedness are concerned, only inwardly by the eternity, truth, and love of the Creator. If it is to be said to be helped outwardly, it is perhaps helped only by the fact that the angels see one another, rejoice in their fellowship in God, and, having also observed all creatures in them, give thanks everywhere and praise the Creator.

But insofar as the activity of angelic creation is concerned—the activity by which God’s providence cares for every kind of thing, and especially for the human race—it does help from outside, both through those visions that resemble bodily things and through the bodies themselves that are subject to angelic power.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### God, always the same and unmoved, administers everything

48. Since these things are so, and since almighty and all-sustaining God, always the same in unchangeable eternity, truth, and will, moved neither through time nor through place, moves spiritual creation through time and bodily creation through time and place, He administers externally, through that movement, the natures that He established inwardly. He does this through wills subject to Him, which He moves through time, and through bodies subject both to Him and to those wills, which He moves through time and place—at the time and in the place whose ordering is life in God Himself, without time or place.

When God does such a thing, therefore, we must not suppose that His substance, insofar as He is God, is changeable in times and places or mobile through times and places. Rather, we must recognize these things in the work of divine providence—not in the work by which He creates natures, but in the work by which He also administers externally the natures created inwardly. He Himself is present without any interval or extent of places, by an unchangeable and surpassing power: He is more inward than every thing, because all things are in Him, and more outward than every thing, because He is above all things.

Likewise, without any interval or extent of times, He is older than all things, by His unchangeable eternity, because He is before all things; and He is newer than all things, because He Himself is after all things.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### How God spoke to Adam

49. Therefore, when we hear Scripture saying, “And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat of it. On the day on which you eat from it, you shall surely die,” if we ask how God spoke these words, the precise manner cannot properly be comprehended by us. Nevertheless, we must hold with complete certainty that God speaks either through His own substance or through a creature subject to Him.

Through His own substance He speaks only in creating all natures, and in creating and also illuminating spiritual and intellectual natures once they are capable of receiving His speech—such as that speech which is in His Word, “which in the beginning was with God, and the Word was God,” through whom all things were made (John 1:1–3).

But when God speaks to those who cannot receive such speech, He speaks only through a creature: either through a spiritual creature alone, whether in dreams or in ecstasy, in the likeness of bodily things; or also through a bodily creature, when some form appears to the bodily senses or voices sound.

50. If Adam was such that he could receive that speech of God which He offers to angelic minds through His own substance, there is no doubt that God moved Adam’s mind through time in a marvelous and ineffable manner, although He Himself was not moved through time; that He impressed upon him a useful and salutary command of truth; and that He showed him, by that same ineffable truth, what punishment was owed to the transgressor.

Thus all good commands are heard or seen in unchangeable Wisdom itself, which “transfers itself into holy souls” (Wis. 7:27), at some point in time, although it itself undergoes no movement in time.

But if Adam was righteous in such a way that he still needed the authority of another, holier and wiser creature through whom he might know God’s will and command—as we need the prophets, and as the prophets themselves need the angels—why should we doubt that God spoke to him through some such creature, by signs of speech that he could understand?

No one who understands the Catholic faith doubts that what was later written—that, after they had sinned, they heard “the sound of the Lord God walking in the garden” (Gen. 3:8)—took place not through God’s own substance but through a creature subject to Him.

I have wished to discuss this matter at somewhat greater length because certain heretics [Note: [Col. 0392] Arians.] think that the substance of the Son of God is visible in itself without assuming any body, and therefore suppose that, before He received a body from the Virgin, He Himself appeared to the patriarchs. They reason as though the statement “whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:16) were spoken only of God the Father, because the Son was seen before receiving the form of a servant, even through His own substance. This impiety must be driven far from Catholic minds.

But we shall discuss this more fully elsewhere, if it pleases the Lord. Now that this volume has been brought to an end, what follows must be prepared: how the woman was created from the side of her husband.

# BOOK NINE  
### On what is read in Genesis, chapter 2, verse 18: “And the Lord God said: It is not good for man to be alone,” etc., up to verse 24: “And the two shall be one flesh”

[Col. 0393]

## CHAPTER I  
### Why it is said, “And God fashioned further from the earth,” etc.; concerning the term “earth”

1. “And the Lord God said: It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper corresponding to him. And God fashioned further from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of heaven, and brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them. And whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name. And Adam gave names to all the cattle, and to all the birds of heaven, and to all the beasts of the field. But for Adam there was not found a helper corresponding to him. And God cast Adam into an ecstasy, and he fell asleep. And He took one of his ribs and filled in flesh in its place; and the Lord God built the rib which He had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam. And Adam said: ‘This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man.”’ And for this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

If the matters considered and written down in the preceding books are of any help to the reader, we ought not to linger long over the statement that God “fashioned further from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of heaven.” Why “further” was said—that is, with reference to the first creation of creatures, completed in six days, in which all things were both perfected causally and begun simultaneously, so that afterward their causes might be brought to their effects—we have already explained as far as we could in the preceding discussions (Book 6, chapter 5).

And if anyone thinks that this must be disentangled in another way, let him carefully attend to all those matters to which we attended in order to arrive at this understanding. If he can derive from them a more probable interpretation, we ought not merely not to resist it; we ought also to rejoice.

2. If someone is troubled because Scripture did not say, “God fashioned further from the earth all the beasts of the field and from the waters all the birds of heaven,” but, as though He had fashioned both kinds from the earth, says, “And God fashioned further from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of heaven,” let him see that this may be understood in two ways.

Either Scripture has now omitted to say from what He fashioned the birds of heaven, because it could be understood even without being stated that God did not fashion both from the earth, but only the beasts of the field; and although Scripture is silent, we may understand from what He fashioned the birds of heaven, since we know that, in the first creation of causal principles, they were produced from the waters.

Or “earth” is used here universally together with the waters, just as it is used in the psalm where, after the praises of heavenly things have been completed, the discourse turns to the earth and says: “Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all deeps, etc.” (Ps. 148:7); and afterward it does not say, “Praise the Lord from the waters.” For all the deeps are there, and yet they praise the Lord from the earth; there too are the creeping things and winged birds, which likewise praise the Lord from the earth.

According to this universal use of “earth,” by which the whole world is also meant when it is said, “God who made heaven and earth,” whatever was created either from dry land or from the waters may truthfully be understood as having been created from the earth.

## CHAPTER II  
### How God said, “It is not good,” etc.

3. Let us now see how we should understand what God said: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper corresponding to him.” Did God say this at a particular time, uttering sounds and syllables? Or is the reason here recalled that was principally present in the Word of God, according to which the woman was to be made—the same reason Scripture had in mind when it said, “And God said, Let this or that be,” at the time when all things were first created?

Or perhaps God said this in the mind of the man himself, as He speaks to certain servants of His within those very servants? Among this kind of servant was the one who said in the psalm: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9).

Or was a revelation concerning this matter made to the man himself, within the man himself, through an angel, in likenesses of bodily speech, although Scripture has not said whether it occurred in a dream or in an ecstasy? For this is usually how such things happen.

Or was it made known to him in some other way, as it is revealed to the prophets—whence: “And the angel who spoke in me said to me” (Zech. 2:3)? Or did the voice itself sound through a bodily creature, as the voice from the cloud said, “This is my Son” (Matt. 3:17)? Which of all these things took place, we cannot determine with precision. Nevertheless, let us hold with complete certainty both that God said this and that, if He expressed it in a bodily voice or through a temporally displayed bodily likeness, He did not say it through His own substance but through some creature subject to His command, as we discussed in the preceding book (chapter 27).

4. God was also later seen by holy men, at one time with a head white like wool, at another with the lower part of His body like brass (Rev. 1:14–15), and at other times in various ways. Yet it is absolutely certain to those who either faithfully believe or excellently understand that the substance of the Trinity is eternally unchangeable, moved neither through time nor through place, and moving things through time and place, that He did not offer those visions to human beings through the substance that He Himself is, but through what He had created and subjected to Himself, and that through likenesses of bodily forms and sounds He showed and said what He willed.

Let us therefore no longer ask how He said this, but rather understand what He said. The eternal truth itself, through which all things were created, knows that a helper corresponding to man was to be made; and whoever can know in that truth why each thing was created hears this there.

## CHAPTER III  
### The woman was made as a helper for the sake of offspring

5. If it is asked for what purpose this helper ought to have been made, nothing else reasonably presents itself except the procreation of children, just as the earth is a helper to the seed, so that a plant may arise from both. For this too had been said in the first creation of things: “He made them male and female, and God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and rule over it” (Gen. 1:27–28).

This purpose of the creation and union of male and female, together with the blessing, did not fail even after the human being’s sin and punishment. For it is according to this purpose that the earth is now filled with human beings who rule over it.

6. Although it is mentioned that, after they had been sent out from paradise, they came together and had children, I do not see what could have prevented their marriage from being honorable and their marital bed undefiled even in paradise (Heb. 13:4). If God had granted them to live faithfully and justly, obediently and holily serving Him, offspring could have been generated from their seed without any restless ardor of lust and without any labor or pain of childbirth.

The children would not have succeeded their dying parents; rather, while those who had begotten them remained in some fixed condition of bodily form, and drew bodily vigor from the tree of life planted there, those who were born would also have been brought to the same condition. Then, when the predetermined number had been completed, if all had lived justly and obediently, that transformation would have taken place in which, without any death, animal bodies would be changed into another quality because they would serve the spirit governing them at every command. Living solely through the spirit that gave them life, without any bodily means of nourishment, they would be called spiritual bodies. This could have happened if the transgression of the command had not deserved the punishment of death.

7. Those who do not believe that this could have happened attend to nothing but the customary course of nature as it now proceeds after sin and human punishment. But we must not be among those who believe only what they are accustomed to see. Who, after all, would doubt that what we have described could have been granted to a human being living obediently and piously, when he does not doubt that the Israelites’ clothing was granted a particular condition of its kind, so that for forty years it suffered no deterioration from age (Deut. 29:5)?

## CHAPTER IV  
### Why the first parents did not have intercourse in paradise

8. Why, then, did they not have intercourse except after they had left paradise? The answer may quickly be given: because, as soon as the woman had been created, before they came together, the transgression occurred. By its merit they were sentenced to death and also left that place of happiness.

Scripture did not specify how much time elapsed between their creation and the birth of Cain from them. It may also be said that God had not yet commanded them to come together. Why should divine authority not have been awaited for this matter, where no concupiscence pressed upon them like a stimulus of disobedient flesh?

God had not commanded this because, according to His foreknowledge, He was arranging all things; and in that foreknowledge He undoubtedly also foresaw their fall, from which the human race was already destined to be propagated.

## CHAPTER V  
### The woman was made as a helper for no other purpose than offspring

9. Or, if the woman was not made for the man as a helper for begetting children, for what other assistance was she made? If she were to work the earth together with him, there was not yet any labor requiring assistance; and if assistance were needed, a male would make a better helper. The same may be said of companionship, if solitude perhaps wearied him. How much more fitting would it be for two friends of the same sex to live together for companionship and conversation than a man and a woman?

And if one had to live by commanding and the other by obeying, lest contrary wills disturb the peace of those living together, the proper order for retaining this arrangement would not have been lacking: one would be first and the other later, especially if the later were created from the earlier, as the woman was created.

Could anyone say that God, if He had wished, could have made a male from the man’s rib, and not only a female? Therefore I do not find for what assistance the woman was made for the man, if the purpose of giving birth is excluded.

## CHAPTER VI  
### What the succession of children would have been if Adam had not sinned

10. For if parents had to yield their place to their children by departing from this life, so that the whole human race might be filled through departures and successions according to a fixed number, human beings could also, after begetting children and completing the proper fulfillment of human duty, have been transferred from here to better things—not through death, but through some transformation.

They might have received either that supreme transformation by which, after receiving their bodies, the saints will be like the angels in heaven (Matt. 22:30), or, if that transformation ought to be granted only to all together at the end of the age, some lower state than that one, though it would still have a better condition than either this body or those bodies first created—the man from the clay of the earth and the woman from the man’s flesh.

11. We must not suppose that Elijah is already either as the saints will be when, after the day’s work has been completed, they will all receive the denarius together (Matt. 20:10), or as are human beings who have not yet departed from this life, from which he nevertheless departed not by death but by being taken away (2 Kings 2:11).

He therefore already possesses something better than he could have possessed in this life, although he does not yet possess what he will receive at the end as the reward of a rightly conducted life. “For they provided something better for us” [Note: [Col. 0396] Three manuscripts read, “something better was provided.” Others have, “they provided,” as Augustine often writes in accordance with Hebrews 2, to which passage he alludes here.] “so that they should not be made perfect without us” (Heb. 11:40).

Or if someone thinks that Elijah could not have deserved this if he had taken a wife and fathered children—for it is believed that he had none because Scripture does not say so, although it also says nothing about his celibacy—what will he answer concerning Enoch? After fathering children and pleasing God, Enoch was not dead but was taken away [Note: [Col. 0397] The printed editions have, “but was taken away alive.” “Alive” is absent from the manuscripts.] (Gen. 5:24).

Why, then, could Adam and Eve not likewise, if they had lived justly and chastely and had begotten children, yield their place to them through being taken away rather than through death? For if Enoch and Elijah, who died in Adam and bear in the flesh the inheritance of death—an obligation which they are believed also to return to this life in order to discharge, and, after so long a postponement, to die (Mal. 4:5; Rev. 11:3–7)—are nevertheless now in another life, where, before the resurrection of the flesh and before the animal body is changed into a spiritual one, they suffer neither disease nor old age, how much more justly and plausibly would it have been granted to those first human beings, living without any sin of their own or of their parents, to yield to their children after begetting them a place in some better condition? Then, when the age had ended, they and all the posterity of the saints would be changed into the angelic form—not through the death of the flesh, but through the power of God, and with far greater happiness.

## CHAPTER VII  
### The woman for the sake of childbearing; the excellence of virginity and marriage; the threefold good of marriage
12. I therefore do not see for what other assistance woman was made for man, if the purpose of generation is removed—though why that purpose should be removed, I do not know. For why would faithful and devout virginity possess great and highly honoured merit before God, unless, now that at this time an abundant supply from all nations is available to complete the number of the saints, the desire for sordid pleasure did not claim for itself what the necessity of sufficient offspring no longer demands? Thus the weakness of either sex, inclining toward the ruin of disgrace, is rightly received within the honor of marriage, so that what could be an obligation for the healthy may be a remedy for the sick. For although incontinence is an evil, it does not follow that marriage, or the union by which the incontinent are joined, is not good. On the contrary, this good is not blameworthy because of that evil; rather, that evil is pardonable because of this good, since what marriage possesses as good, and by which marriage is good, can never be sin.

This good is threefold: fidelity, offspring, and the sacrament.
