In fidelity, the concern is that no one have intercourse with another man or woman outside the marriage bond; in offspring, that the child be received with affection, nourished with kindness, and raised with religious care; in the sacrament, that the marriage not be dissolved and that neither the divorced man nor the divorced woman enter another union, even for the sake of having children. This is, as it were, the rule of marriage, by which either the beauty of nature’s fecundity is adorned, or the perversity of incontinence is governed. Since we have discussed these matters sufficiently in the book that we recently published on the Good of Marriage, where we also distinguished widowhood’s continence and virginity’s excellence according to the dignity proper to each state, our pen need not be occupied here any longer.

## CHAPTER VIII — The Flight from Vices into Their Opposites

13. For now we are asking for what assistance woman was made for man, if they were not permitted to unite with one another in paradise for the begetting of children. Those who hold this view perhaps [Col. 0398] think that every act of intercourse is sinful. It is difficult, when people perversely avoid vices, for them not to rush headlong into their opposites. Thus, just as someone who detests avarice becomes spendthrift, or someone who detests luxury becomes miserly; someone becomes restless whose laziness you have criticized, or lazy whose restlessness you have criticized; someone who, after being reproached, begins to hate his own boldness flees into timidity; or someone who tries not to be timid, as though the bond had been broken, becomes reckless—because they measure offenses not by reason but by opinion—so, when people do not know what divine law condemns in adultery and fornication, they detest marital intercourse even when undertaken for the sake of procreation.

## CHAPTER IX — Woman Was Made for the Begetting of Children, Even if the Necessity of Dying Had Not Resulted from Sin

14. Those who do not do this, but nevertheless understand the fecundity of the flesh as divinely bestowed for the succession of mortal beings, do not themselves think that those first human beings could have had intercourse unless, because they were destined to die on account of the sin they had committed, they sought successors by begetting them. Nor do they consider that, if successors could rightly be sought for those who were destined to die, companions could have been sought much more rightly for those who were destined to live.

For once the earth had been filled with the human race, it would rightly have been necessary to seek offspring only to succeed those who were dying. But, in order for the earth to be filled by two human beings, how could they fulfill the duty of companionship except by begetting? Is anyone so blind in mind that he does not see how greatly the human race adorns the earth, even when only a few live rightly and honorably; and how powerful is the order of the state, which restrains even sinners within the bond of a certain earthly peace? Human beings are not so depraved that even in such a condition they do not surpass cattle and birds. Yet who would not take pleasure in contemplating all their kinds, by which this lowest part of the world is adorned according to the allotment of its place? Who, then, is so senseless as to think that it could not have been adorned more fully if it had been filled by righteous people who did not die?

15. Since the heavenly city of the angels is exceedingly numerous, human beings would not rightly have been joined in marriage unless they were destined to die. The Lord, foreseeing that this perfect number would also be joined to the angels in the resurrection of the saints, said: “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they will not begin to die, but will be equal to the angels of God” (Matt. 22:30). Here, however, when the earth was to be filled with human beings, and when, because of the closer bond of kinship and the bond of unity that especially needed to be commended, it was necessary for it to be filled from one human being, for what other reason was the assistance of the female sex sought for him except that, like the fertility of the earth, female nature might assist the sowing of the human race?

## CHAPTER X — The Disease of Lust Resulting from Sin

16. Although it is more honorably and more reasonably believed that, while those human beings were then in paradise, their animal bodies had not yet been condemned under the law of death, and therefore did not possess the appetite for carnal pleasure that these bodies now possess, since they have already been derived through the succession of death. For something certainly happened to them when they ate from the forbidden tree, since God [Col. 0399] had said not, “If you eat, you will die,” but, “On the day when you eat, you will die” (Gen. 2:17). Thus that day itself brought about in them what the Apostle laments when he says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward man; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:22, 25).

It would not have been enough for him to say, “Who will deliver me from this mortal body?” Rather, he says, “from the body of this death.” Likewise, when he says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (ibid. 8:10), he does not say “mortal,” but “dead,” although it is certainly also mortal because it is destined to die. Those bodies should not be thought to have been like this. Though they were animal bodies and not yet spiritual, they were nevertheless not dead—that is, they were not such as necessarily had to die. This happened on the day when they touched the tree against the prohibition.

[Note: [Col. 0399] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have, “on the day when they touched the forbidden tree.”]

17. In our own bodies, a certain degree of health is spoken of as belonging to them. If that health is so disturbed that a fatal disease is already consuming the viscera, and doctors, upon examining the condition, declare death imminent, the body is still called mortal, but in a different sense from when it was healthy, although it was certainly destined to die at some point. So those human beings, though bearing animal bodies that would not have died unless they sinned, and that were destined to receive an angelic form and heavenly quality, immediately after transgressing the command conceived death itself in their members, as though it were a fatal illness; and the quality by which they had so governed their bodies that they did not say, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind,” was changed.

For although the body was not yet spiritual but animal, it was not yet the body of this death, the death from which and with which we were born. For what else did we begin—not merely when born, but altogether when conceived—except a certain illness through which we are necessarily to die? For it is not as necessary for one who has become dropsical, dysenteric, or elephantine to die from that very disease as it is for one who has begun to possess this body, in which all human beings are by nature children of wrath (Eph. 2:3), because nothing but the punishment of sin produced this condition.

18. Since this is so, why should we not believe that before sin those human beings could have governed their generative members for the begetting of children just as they governed the other members that the soul moves in any activity without disturbance or, as it were, the tickling of pleasure? For if the omnipotent Creator, who is ineffably worthy of praise and is great even in his smallest works, granted bees the ability to carry out the generation of offspring in the manner in which they produce the form of wax and the liquid of honey, why should it seem incredible that he made the bodies of the first human beings in such a way that, if they had not sinned and had not immediately conceived a certain illness by which they would die, they could command the members from which offspring arise by the same act of will by which they command their feet when walking? In that case, seed would be sown neither with burning desire nor would childbirth occur with pain.

But now, by transgressing the command, they deserved to possess in their members the movement of that law which wars against the law of the mind, the movement of death conceived [Col. 0400] in them. Marriage orders it; continence restrains and curbs it, so that just as punishment came from sin, merit may likewise come from punishment.

## CHAPTER XI — The Female Sex Was Formed for Offspring, Though Not for Procreation with Lust Unless Man Had Sinned. Obedience

19. Since, then, woman was made for man, from man, in that sex and in that form and distinction of members by which women are recognized—she who bore Cain and Abel and all their brothers, from whom all human beings were to be born, and who also bore Seth (Gen. 4:1 and 25), through whom the line came down to Abraham and to the people of Israel, a nation already well known among all nations, and, through Noah’s sons, to all nations—anyone who doubts this should be driven far from the minds of the faithful, for he would force everything we believe to totter.

When, therefore, we ask for what assistance that sex was made for man, nothing presents itself to one who considers everything carefully, insofar as I am able, except the purpose of offspring, so that the earth might be filled through their stock. But offspring was not generated in the manner in which human beings are now generated, when the law of sin is present in the members, warring against the law of the mind, even though it is overcome by the power of God’s grace. This, we must believe, could not have existed except in the body of this death, the body that is dead because of sin.

And what punishment could be more just than that the body—that is, its servant to the soul—should not obey every command, just as the soul itself had refused to serve its Lord? This is so whether God creates both from the parents, body from body and soul from soul, or creates souls in some other way. It is not, in any case, for an impossible task or for a small reward: when the soul, submitting to God in devotion, overcomes by grace that law of sin which is in the members of this body of death, the law that the first human being received as punishment, it receives the heavenly reward with greater glory, demonstrating how great is the praise of obedience, which by its power could overcome the punishment of another’s disobedience.

## CHAPTER XII — The Animals Were Truly Brought to Adam So That He Might Give Them Names; but Something Was Signified by This Action

20. Since, then, we have investigated sufficiently, as I think, for what assistance woman was made for man, let us now consider why it happened that all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the air were brought to Adam so that he might give them names. In this way, something like a necessity would arise for creating woman for him from his side, since no similar assistance had been found for him among those animals.

It seems to me that this was done for some prophetic signification, but it was nevertheless done, so that, once the event had been established, the interpretation of the figure might remain open. For what is the meaning of the fact that Adam gave names to the terrestrial animals and birds, but not also to the fish and all the creatures that swim? If human languages are consulted, all these things are called what human beings have named them by speaking. Not only the things that are in the waters and on the earth, but the earth itself, the water, the heaven, the things seen in heaven, and the things not seen but believed, are called by different names according to the diversity of the languages of the Gentiles.

[Col. 0401] We have learned that originally there was one language, before the pride involved in building that tower after the flood divided human society into the various sounds of signs (Gen. 11:1–8). Whatever that language was, what benefit is there in asking? Adam certainly spoke it then, and in that language—if it still survives—these articulated sounds exist by which the first human being gave names to the terrestrial animals and birds.

Is it in any way credible, then, that in that same language the names of fish were instituted not by human beings but divinely, so that human beings would afterward learn them by God’s instruction? If that too had happened, there would undoubtedly be a mystical signification in why it happened. But we should believe that names were imposed as the kinds of fish were gradually recognized. At that time, however, when cattle, beasts, and birds were brought to the human being so that, after they had been gathered to him and distinguished according to their kinds, he might give them names—names that he could impose gradually, and much more quickly than he could have imposed them on fish if this had not happened—what reason was there except a principle of signification that would serve as a foreshadowing of future events? The order of this narrative is especially concerned with this matter.

21. Moreover, was God unaware that he had created nothing among the natures of animals that could serve as a similar companion for man? Was it necessary for man himself also to learn this, and thereby to esteem his wife all the more because, among every living creature created under heaven and living from this same air as he did, he had found nothing like himself? It would be astonishing if he could not know this except after all the animals had been brought to him and inspected.

If he believed God, he could have said this to him in the same way in which God gave him the command, questioned him when he sinned, and judged him. But if he did not believe, he certainly could not know whether the one in whom he did not believe had brought everything to him, or whether perhaps he had concealed from him, in some more distant regions of the earth, beings resembling him that he had not displayed.

I therefore do not think it should be doubted that this was done for the sake of some prophetic signification; but it was nevertheless done.

22. In this work we have not undertaken to investigate prophetic enigmas, but to commend the truth of the events according to the literal meaning of the history. What may seem impossible to the vain and unbelieving, or may seem to resist the authority of Holy Scripture as though it contradicted its testimony, I will demonstrate, insofar as my abilities permit and God assists me, by discussion to be neither impossible nor contradictory. What appears possible and has no appearance of contradiction, but may nevertheless seem superfluous or even foolish to some, I will demonstrate through discussion to have occurred not according to the natural or customary order of events, so that, with the most faithful authority of the holy Scriptures set before our hearts, it may be believed mystical, since it cannot be foolish, although we have either already supplied its exposition or investigation elsewhere, or defer it to another time.

[Note: [Col. 0401] We restore the negation here from the manuscripts; in the printed editions it had wrongly been relegated to the margin.]

## CHAPTER XIII — The Formation of Woman Occurred in the Manner Narrated So That Something Might Be Foreshadowed

[Col. 0402]

23. What, then, is the meaning of the fact that woman was made for man from his side? Let us grant that we believe this had to happen in that way in order to commend the force of their union. But did the same reason or necessity also demand that it happen while he was sleeping, and finally that a bone be removed, with flesh supplied in its place? Could the flesh itself not have been removed, so that woman, who is the weaker sex, might be formed from it more suitably? Or could God, after adding so many things, build a rib into a woman, but not flesh or tissue—he who made man himself from dust? Or, if a rib was already to be removed, why was another rib not put back in its place? Why was it not said, “He fashioned,” or “He made,” as in all the works mentioned above, but, “The Lord God built the rib,” as though it were not a human body but a house?

There is no doubt, therefore, that since these things happened and cannot be foolish, they happened in order to signify something. From the very beginning of the human race, God, who foresaw the future age, was mercifully proclaiming it through his own works, so that, once revealed and written down at the appointed time for his servants—whether through the succession of human beings, through his Spirit, or through the ministry of angels—these works might bear witness both to the promises of future events and to the recognition of events already fulfilled. This will become increasingly clear in what follows.

## CHAPTER XIV — How the Animals Were Brought to Adam

24. Let us therefore consider, as we have undertaken in this work, not according to the foreshadowing of future events, but according to the non-allegorical, literal meaning of the events themselves, how these things can be understood:

“And God fashioned,” he says, “from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the air.” We have already discussed what seemed appropriate, and as much as seemed appropriate. “And he brought them all to Adam, to see what he would call them.”

How God brought these creatures to Adam should not be understood carnally. What ought to help us is what we discussed in the preceding book concerning the twofold operation of divine providence (Book I, ch. 9, §§19–26). We should not believe that this happened as hunters or fowlers track and drive whatever animals they catch into nets; nor that some voice of command came from a cloud in words that rational souls, upon hearing them, would ordinarily understand and obey. Beasts and birds have not received the capacity to do this. Yet they obey God within their own kind—not by the rational judgment of the will, but in the manner in which he moves all things at suitable times, while he himself is not moved temporally, through the ministry of angels. The angels perceive in his word what must be done at what time; and, while he himself is not moved temporally, they move the creatures temporally so that his commands may be carried out in the things subject to them.

25. Every living soul is moved by things seen—not only the rational soul, as in human beings, but also the irrational soul, as in cattle, birds, and fish. The rational soul, by the judgment of its will, either consents to what it sees or does not consent; the irrational soul does not possess this judgment. Yet, according to its kind and nature, when touched by something seen, it is driven onward.

Nor is it in the power of any soul to determine what things appear to it, whether they enter through the bodily senses or arise inwardly in the spirit—things by which the appetite of any living creature is moved. Thus, when such sights are supplied from above through the obedience of angels, God’s command reaches not only human beings, nor only birds and cattle, but also those creatures that lie beneath the waters, as it reached the whale that swallowed Jonah (Jonah 2:1). It reaches not only larger creatures, but even a little worm; for we read that this too was divinely commanded to gnaw the root of the gourd under whose shade the prophet had rested (ibid. 4:6–7).

If God granted a human being such capacity, forming him so that, even while bearing the flesh of sin, he could not only bring cattle and beasts of burden under his uses, and not only domestic birds, but also any birds flying freely,

[Note: [Col. 0403] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have, “birds of free will.”]

and even savage beasts, capture them, tame them, and wonderfully command them by the power of reason rather than of the body—capturing their appetites and pains, gradually enticing, pressing, and relaxing them, stripping them of their wild habit and clothing them, as it were, in human manners—how much more can angels do this? By God’s command they behold his unchangeable truth, which they eternally contemplate; moving themselves through time, and the bodies subject to them through time and place, with marvelous agility, they can produce the sights by which a living soul is moved

[Note: [Col. 0403] In Lovanius these words are absent: “and the bodies subject to them through time.” They are present in the other manuscripts.]

and the appetite of bodily need, so that every living soul may be brought, without knowing it, to wherever it is necessary for it to go?

[Note: [Col. 0403] The printed editions have, “and the commands by which they are moved.” Not all the manuscripts read “sights,” but all read “may be moved,” evidently referring to the living soul.]

## CHAPTER XV — The Formation of Woman Was Accomplished by God and No One Else

26. Let us now see how the formation of woman, which is also mystically called a building, took place. The nature of woman was created, although from the already existing nature of man, not by some movement of already existing natures.

[Note: [Col. 0403] Here the manuscripts, with great agreement, read “not some movement.” Perhaps “were” is to be understood.]

Angels, however, cannot create any nature at all. For the one Creator of every nature, whether great or small, is God alone—that is, the Trinity itself, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The question, then, is of another kind: how was Adam put to sleep, and how was his rib removed from the structure of his body without any sensation of pain? These things perhaps could have been done by angels. But to form or build the rib so that it became a woman could only be done by God, from whom every nature subsists. Indeed, I do not believe that even the flesh-supplement in the man’s body, which replaced the rib, was made by angels, any more than man himself was made from the dust of the earth.

This is not because there is no work of angels by which something is created, but because they are not thereby creators. We do not call farmers creators of crops and trees. “Neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7). This growth also includes what occurred in the human body when, after the bone was removed, the place was filled with flesh: it was accomplished by that work of God by which he establishes natures so that they exist, the same work by which he also created the angels themselves.

27. It is therefore the farmer’s work to conduct water when he irrigates; but it is not his work that the water should run down the slopes. That belongs to the one who has arranged all things according to measure, number, and weight [Col. 0404] (Wis. 11:21). Likewise, it is the farmer’s work to detach a shoot from a tree and commit it to the earth; but it is not his work that the shoot should absorb sap, send forth a bud, fasten one part into the soil to establish a root, advance another into the air to nourish its strength, and spread out branches. That belongs to the one who gives growth.

A physician also applies food to a sick body and medicine to a wounded one. First, he does not use things he himself has created, but things he has found already created through the work of the Creator. Second, he can prepare and administer food or drink, form a plaster, coat it with medicine, and apply it. But can he also produce and create strength or flesh from the things he applies? Nature accomplishes that through an inward and most hidden movement. Yet if God withdraws from nature the inward operation by which he establishes and makes it, it will immediately remain as though extinguished, and nothing will remain.

[Note: [Col. 0404] The printed editions have, “medicines immediately.” The manuscripts read, “coated with medicine.”]

28. Therefore, since God administers his entire creation through a certain twofold operation of providence, which we discussed in the preceding book, both in natural movements and in voluntary movements, no angel can create a nature any more than an angel can create himself. But the angelic will, obediently subject to God and carrying out his command, can, by natural movements, furnish material from things subject to it, so that something may be created in time according either to those principal ideas in the Word of God that were not themselves created, or according to those ideas that were created causally in the works of the first six days—just as a farmer or physician works.

What ministry, then, did the angels perform for God in the formation of that woman? Who would dare to assert it? Yet I would say with complete certainty that the supplement of flesh in place of the rib, and the body and soul of the woman herself, the formation of her members, all her viscera, all her senses, and everything by which she was at once creature, human being, and woman, were accomplished only in that work of God which God performs not through angels but by himself. He did not perform it and then abandon it; rather, he operates in it continually, so that neither the nature of any other things nor that of the angels themselves could subsist unless he were at work.

## CHAPTER XVI — The Slowness of the Human Intellect Does Not Attain to God’s Works

29. Since, insofar as we have been able to investigate the nature of things according to human understanding, we do not know animated and sentient flesh to be born except either from these elements as materials—that is, water and earth—or from shrubs and the fruits of trees, or even from the flesh of animals, as in the countless kinds of worms and reptiles, or certainly from the intercourse of parents; and since we know of no flesh born [Col. 0405] from the flesh of any living creature that would be so similar to it that they differed only in sex, we seek in the works of creation some likeness by which woman was made from man’s side, but we cannot find one.

The reason is only that we know how human beings work upon this earth, but we do not know how angels, in a certain sense, cultivate this world. For if, apart from human industry, the course of nature produced the kinds of shrubs, we would know nothing except that trees and grasses arise from the earth, and from their seeds, which likewise fall from them into the earth. Would we thereby come to know the power of grafting, by which a tree of another kind bears foreign fruit upon its own root and, once the parts grow together into a unity, bears fruit that is already its own?

We learned these things through the work of farmers, although they are in no way creators of trees; rather, they provide the course of nature, created by God, with a certain office and ministry of its own. Nothing would exist through their work if the innermost principle of nature did not possess this within God’s work.

Why, then, is it surprising that we do not know how a human being could be made from a human bone, when we do not know how angels serve God the Creator? We could not know how a tree is made from a tree-shoot in the strength of another tree either, if we likewise did not know how farmers serve God the Creator in this matter.

30. Nevertheless, we have no doubt at all that God alone is the Creator of both human beings and trees. We faithfully believe that woman was made from man without any intervening intercourse, even if perhaps the rib of the man was supplied through angels in the work of the Creator. In the same way, we faithfully believe that man was made from woman without any intervening intercourse, when the seed of Abraham was arranged through angels in the hand of the mediator (Gal. 3:19).

[Note: [Col. 0405] See *Retractions* II, ch. 24, §2.]

Both events are incredible to unbelievers. But why should believers find it credible that what happened concerning Christ occurred according to the literal truth of the event, while what is written about Eve occurred only for the sake of a figurative meaning?

[Note: [Col. 0405] The printed editions have, “should not seem credible.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts.]

Could a man indeed be made from a woman without anyone’s intercourse, but a woman not be made from a man? And did the virgin womb have a source from which a man could be made, while the man’s side did not have a source from which a woman could be made, when in the one case the Lord was born from a female servant, and in the other a female servant was formed from a male servant?

The Lord could also have created his flesh from a rib or from some other member of the Virgin. But he who could show in his own body that he had again done what had been done more usefully showed, in his mother’s body, that nothing shameful is involved in what is chaste.

## CHAPTER XVII — Whether the Reason for Forming Woman Already Pre-existed in the Causal Condition of Man on the Sixth Day

31. If it is asked how that causal condition should be understood in which God first made man in his own image and likeness—for there too it was said, “Male and female he made them” (Gen. 1:27)—whether the reason that God created and incorporated in the first works of the world already included the necessity that, according to it, woman should be made from the man’s side; or whether it included only the possibility that this could happen, while the fact that it had to happen in this way was not then established there but remained hidden in God—if this is the question, I will say what seems to me to be the case, without the rashness of asserting it. Yet, once I have said it, those who consider these matters prudently and have already been instructed in the Christian faith may judge that there is no doubt about it, even if they are learning these things for the first time now.

32. The ordinary course of nature has certain natural laws of its own. According to them, the spirit of life, which is itself a creature, has certain appetites determined in a certain way, which even an evil will cannot exceed. The elements of this corporeal world also have a defined power and quality: what each thing can or cannot do, and what can or cannot be made from each thing.

From these beginnings, as it were, of things, everything that is generated receives its own arising and development at its proper time, as well as the limits and decline proper to its kind. Thus wheat does not arise from a bean, nor a bean from wheat, nor a human being from cattle, nor cattle from a human being.

Above this natural movement [Note: [Col. 0406] Six manuscripts read “order.”] and course of things, the Creator’s power possesses within itself the ability to make something other than what their quasi-seminal principles contain. Yet it cannot make something that he did not place in them so that it could be made from them or by him.

[Note: [Col. 0406] All the manuscripts read this way. The printed editions, improperly removing the negation, had: “What he placed in them, so that it could be made from them or even without him.”]

For he is omnipotent not through reckless power but through the strength of wisdom. With respect to each thing, he does in its proper time what he previously made it capable of doing.

There is therefore one order of things by which one plant sprouts in one way and another in another; one age gives birth and another does not; a human being can speak and an animal cannot. The principles of these and similar orders are not only in God, but were also placed and incorporated by him in created things.

[Note: [Col. 0406] The manuscripts read, “incorporated.”]

But that a piece of wood cut from the earth, dry and polished, without any root, soil, or water, should suddenly flower and produce fruit (Num. 17:8); that a barren woman should give birth in old age after her reproductive years (Gen. 18:11 and 21:2); that a she-donkey should speak (Num. 22:28); and whatever else is of this kind—God did grant to the natures he created that these things could arise from them. For he could not make from them something that he himself had predetermined could not be made from them, since he himself is not more powerful than himself.

Nevertheless, he granted this in another manner, so that these things would not possess it in their natural movement, but in the manner in which they were created such that their nature was more fully subject to a will more powerful than itself.

## CHAPTER XVIII — The Reason for Forming Woman Pre-existed in a Manner Appropriate to the Mystery

33. God therefore has hidden within himself the causes of certain actions, which he did not implant in created things. He fulfills these causes not through that work of providence by which he establishes natures so that they exist, but through that work by which he administers them according to his will—he who created them according to his will.

There too is grace, through which sinners are saved. For as regards nature, corrupted by its own unrighteous will, it has no return to itself by itself, but returns through God’s grace, by which it is helped [Col. 0407] and restored. Nor should people despair because of the statement in which it is written: “All who walk in her will not return” (Prov. 2:19). This was said according to the weight of their iniquity, so that whoever returns should attribute the return not to himself but to God’s grace, “not from works, lest he should boast” (Eph. 2:9).

34. For this reason the Apostle called this mystery of grace hidden—not in the world, where the causal principles of all things that would arise naturally are hidden, just as Levi was hidden in Abraham’s loins when he too paid tithes (Heb. 7:9–10), but in God, who created all things.

Therefore, all the things that were done not by the natural movement of things but marvelously, in order to signify this grace, likewise had their hidden causes in God. One of these was that woman was made from the man’s side, and from the side of a sleeping man. She was thereby made strong through him, as though established by his bone, while he was made weak on her account, because flesh rather than another rib was supplied in the rib’s place.

The original condition of things, when it was said on the sixth day, “Male and female he made them,” did not contain the necessity that woman should be made in precisely this way. It contained only the possibility that this could happen, so that nothing might occur through a changeable will contrary to the causes that God had established by his will. But what would happen, so that something else entirely would not happen instead, was hidden in God, who created all things.

35. Since he said that this was hidden in such a way that the manifold wisdom of God might become known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places (Eph. 3:9–10), it is reasonably believed that, just as the seed to which the promise was made was arranged through angels in the hand of the mediator, so all the things that were done marvelously in nature [Col. 0408], outside the ordinary course of nature, either to foreshadow or to announce the coming of that seed, were done through the ministry of angels.

Nevertheless, everywhere the Creator or Restorer of creatures is none other than the one God who alone gives the growth, whether there is a planter or a waterer (1 Cor. 3:7).

## CHAPTER XIX — Adam’s Ecstasy
36. Accordingly, that ecstasy which God sent upon Adam, so that he fell into a sleep, is rightly understood to have been sent for this purpose: that his mind also, through ecstasy, might become a participant, as it were, in the angelic court, and, entering into the sanctuary of God, might understand “the last things” (Psalm 72:17). [Note: [Col. 0408] The printed editions read, “he might understand the last things.” But the manuscripts read, “in the last things,” as Augustine commonly does in Psalm 72:17, following the Greek Septuagint rendering, *sunō eis ta eschata* [the first word is corrupt in the supplied text; “until I enter into the last things”].]

Finally, when he awoke as though filled with prophecy, and saw the rib, brought to him as his wife, he immediately uttered forth—[Note: [Col. 0408] Some codices omit “the rib.” A little later, the very old manuscripts have *eructuavit* (“he cried out” or “uttered forth”).]—a great mystery commended by the Apostle (Ephesians 5:31–32):

> This now is bone of my bones,  
> and flesh of my flesh.  
> She shall be called Woman,  
> because she was taken from her man.  
> And for this reason a man shall leave his father and mother  
> and cling to his wife,  
> and the two shall be one flesh.

Although Scripture itself attests that these words belonged to the first man, the Lord nevertheless declared in the Gospel that God had spoken them. For he says:

> Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh”? (Matthew 19:4)

[Note: [Col. 0408] The Vulgate version in the Gospel adds here “a man” (*hominem*), but this word is absent from the Greek text and also from the Latin in the Germanic manuscript Bibles, as well as from all the books of Augustine’s present work.]

Thus we may understand that, because of the ecstasy which had preceded in Adam, he was able to speak this as a prophet under divine inspiration. But now it pleases us to bring this book to an end, so that what follows may renew the readers’ attention from another beginning.

# BOOK TEN

In which the origin of souls is discussed.

[Col. 0407]

## CHAPTER I.—The opinion of some that the woman’s soul was made from the man’s soul

1. The order of discussion itself now seems to demand that we speak about the sin of the first man. But since Scripture narrated how the woman’s flesh was made while remaining silent about her soul, it has made us all the more intent on investigating this matter carefully: namely, how those who believe that soul is made from soul, just as flesh is made from flesh, with the seeds of both being transmitted from parents to children, may—or may not—be refuted.

They are first led to this position by saying that God made one soul by breathing into the face of the man whom he had formed from dust, so that all the other human souls would be created from that one, just as all human flesh is derived from his flesh. For Adam was formed first and then Eve. [Col. 0408] It is said from what he received his body and from what he received his soul: his body, namely, from the dust of the earth, and his soul from God’s breath. But since she is said to have been made from his side, it is not said that God likewise animated her by breathing, as though both body and soul had been derived from him, who had already been animated.

“Either,” they say, “Scripture ought also to have remained silent about the man’s soul, so that we might understand—or at least believe—that it too had been given by God; or, if Scripture did not remain silent about this for the reason that we might not suppose that the soul, like the man’s flesh, had been made from earth, then it ought not to have remained silent about the woman’s soul, lest it be supposed to have been transmitted, if that is not true. Therefore,” they say, “the reason it is not said that God breathed into her face is that it is true that her soul too was propagated from man.”

2. This suspicion is easily answered. [Col. 0409] If they think that the woman’s soul was made from the man’s soul because it is not written that God breathed into the woman’s face, why do they believe that the woman was animated from the man when not even that is written?

If, therefore, God makes all the souls of human beings who are born, just as he made the first, Scripture was silent about the others because what is recorded as having happened in the case of one could prudently be understood also of the others.

Accordingly, if Scripture had to give us some warning about this matter, then, if something else was happening in the woman that had not happened in the man—namely, that her soul was derived from animated flesh, whereas the man’s body came from one source and his soul from another—Scripture ought rather not to have been silent about this very thing, lest we suppose that what we had already learned about him had happened in her as well.

Therefore, since it did not say that the woman’s soul was made from the man’s soul, it is more fitting to believe that by this very omission it wished to warn us not to suppose anything here other than what we had learned about the man’s soul: that is, that it likewise was given to the woman. This is especially so because there was an exceedingly clear opportunity for saying so, if not at the time when she was formed, then certainly afterward, when Adam said:

> This now is bone of my bones,  
> and flesh of my flesh (Genesis 2:23).

How much more warmly and lovingly would he have said, “And soul from my soul”! Yet the great question has not thereby been so completely resolved that we can hold one of these alternatives as manifest and certain.

## CHAPTER II.—What was investigated in the preceding books concerning the origin of the soul

3. We must therefore first see whether the holy Scripture of this book, which has been expounded from its beginning, allows us to remain uncertain about this matter. Then perhaps we may properly inquire either which position ought rather to be chosen or what method we should follow amid uncertainty about the matter.

Certainly, on the sixth day God made man in his own image; and it was also said, “Male and female he made them” (Genesis 1:27). We understood the former statement, where God’s image is mentioned, according to the soul, but the latter, where the distinction of sex is mentioned, according to the flesh (Books 6 and 7).

And because so many and such weighty testimonies, considered and discussed there, did not allow us to understand that the man formed from clay and the woman made from his side were formed on that same sixth day, but required us to understand that this happened afterward, following those first works of God in which he created all things together (Sirach 18:1), we asked what we ought to believe about the human soul.

After examining every aspect of our discussion, the more credible, or at least more tolerable, position seemed to be that the human soul itself was made in those works, while the causal principle of his body existed in the corporeal world as in a seed. Thus we would not be forced either to say, contrary to the words of Scripture, that the whole human being was made on the sixth day—that is, both the man from clay and the woman from his side—or to say that no human being was made at all in those six days of works; or to say that only the causal principle of the human body was made, but none of the soul, although it is rather according to the soul that the human being is made in the image of God.

Alternatively, even if we did not openly speak contrary to the words of Scripture, we would speak harshly and intolerably if we said that the causal principle of the [Col. 0410] human soul was made either in that spiritual creature which had been created solely for this purpose, although that creature itself was not mentioned among God’s works; or in some creature that was mentioned among those works—for example, in human beings who already exist, in whom the causal principle of begetting children lies hidden. [Note: [Col. 0410] The printed editions read: “For example, in all who have already been made, the causal principle.” The manuscripts read more aptly: “For example, in human beings who already exist, the causal principle made.”]

In that case we would believe the soul to be either the offspring of angels or, what is still more intolerable, the offspring of some corporeal element.

## CHAPTER III.—Three possible origins of souls

4. But now, if the woman is said to have received a soul made by God not from the man but, like his, directly from God, because God makes each soul individually, then the woman’s soul was not made in those first works. Or, if the general causal principle of all souls had been made, just as the causal principle of begetting exists in human beings, we return to that harsh and troublesome conclusion that we must say human souls are the offspring either of angels or, what is most unworthy, of the corporeal heaven or of some still lower element.

Accordingly, although what is true remains hidden, we must see what can at least be said more tolerably: whether the position I have just stated is preferable; or whether, in those first works of God, one soul was made—the soul of the first man—from whose stock all human souls would be created; or whether new souls are made successively, none of whose causal principle had previously been made in those first six days of God’s works.

Of these three possibilities, the first two do not conflict with those initial acts of creation in which all things were created together. For either the causal principle of the soul was made in some creature as in a parent, so that all souls would be generated from it, although created by God when they are given to individual human beings, just as bodies are generated from parents; or the soul itself, not merely its causal principle as offspring in a parent, was made altogether when the day was made, just as the day itself, heaven and earth, and the lights of heaven were made. In either case, the statement “God made man in his own image” is fitting.

5. But how the third possibility does not conflict with the view that man was made in God’s image on the sixth day and visibly created after the seventh day is not so easily understood.

If we say that new souls are made even though neither they nor their causal principle, as the offspring’s principle in a parent, was made on that sixth day together with the works whose completion God rested from on the seventh day, we must be careful lest Scripture’s careful assertion that God completed all his works in six days—works that he made very good—become pointless, if he was still going to create additional natures whose causal principles he had made neither in themselves nor in that creation.

This difficulty can be avoided if we understand that God possesses within himself the causal principle for making each individual soul and giving it to each person at birth, rather than having established it in some creature. Since the soul is not a different kind of creature from that according to which man was made in God’s image on the sixth day, it is not rightly said that God is now making a soul which he did not complete then.

For he had already made a soul of the kind he also makes now. Therefore he is not now making some new kind of creature which he did not create then in his completed works. Nor is this activity contrary to the causal principles of future things which he then implanted in the universe; rather, it accords with them. For human bodies, whose propagation is extended through an unbroken succession from those first works, appropriately receive souls of the kind he now makes and implants in them.

6. Therefore, fearing no longer that we may seem to hold an opinion contrary to the words of this book concerning that first creation of the six days, let us undertake a more careful treatment of this question, insofar as God helps us.

Perhaps it may be possible for us to arrive, if not at a fully clear position about which no further doubt is possible, at least at one so acceptable that it would not be absurd to hold it until something certain becomes evident.

But if we cannot even achieve this, with the weight of the evidence wavering in every direction alike, at least our uncertainty will not seem to have avoided the labor of inquiry, but rather the rashness of affirmation. Thus, if anyone is already rightly certain, may he kindly instruct me; and if anyone has been made certain not by the authority of divine speech or evident reason but by his own presumption, may he not disdain to doubt along with me.

## CHAPTER IV.—What is certain concerning the nature and origin of the soul

7. First, let us hold with the greatest firmness that the nature of the soul cannot be changed into the nature of body, so that what was already a soul becomes a body; nor into the nature of an irrational soul, so that what was a human soul becomes the soul of an animal; nor into the nature of God, so that what was a soul becomes what God is.

Conversely, neither body, nor an irrational soul, nor the substance that is God can be changed and become a human soul.

This too must be no less certain: the soul is nothing other than a creature of God. Therefore, if God did not make the human soul from body, from an irrational soul, or from himself, it remains that he either makes it from nothing or from some spiritual but rational creature.

But it is forceful to insist that something was made from nothing after the completion of those works in which he created all things together; and I do not know whether this can be established by clear evidence.

Nor should what man cannot comprehend be demanded of us—or, if he can now comprehend it, it is astonishing if he can persuade anyone of it except someone who, even without any human teacher attempting to instruct him, is himself able to understand such a thing.

It is therefore safer in matters of this kind not to proceed by human conjectures but to search the divine testimonies.

## CHAPTER V.—The soul is neither from angels, nor from the elements, nor from God’s substance

8. As for the idea that God creates souls from angels as from parents, I find no authority for it in the canonical books. Much less, then, does he create them from the corporeal elements of the world—unless perhaps one is influenced by the passage in the prophet Ezekiel where, in portraying the resurrection of the dead, the bodies are restored and the spirit is summoned from the four winds of heaven; when it breathes upon them, they are brought to life and rise.

For it is written:

> And the Lord said to me, “Prophesy concerning the spirit; prophesy, son of man, and say to the spirit, ‘Thus says the Lord: Come from the four quarters [Col. 0412] of the winds of heaven and breathe upon these dead, and let them live.’” And I prophesied as the Lord commanded me, and the spirit of life entered into them, and they came to life and stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great assembly (Ezekiel 37:9–10).

Here I think it was prophetically signified—not only from that field where the event itself was displayed, but from the whole world—that human beings would rise again, and that this was represented by the breath from the four regions of the world.

For that breath which came from the Lord’s body was not the substance of the Holy Spirit when he breathed and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Rather, it was certainly signified that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him in the same manner as that breath proceeded from his body.

But because the world is not joined to God in the unity of person in the way that that flesh was joined to his only-begotten Son, the Word, we cannot say that the soul is from God’s substance in the same way as that breath was made from the nature of the world through the four winds.

Nevertheless, I think that the breath was one thing and signified another. This can rightly be understood by the example of the breath proceeding from the Lord’s body, even if the prophet Ezekiel, in that passage, did not foresee by a figurative revelation the resurrection of the flesh as it will properly occur, but rather the unexpected restoration of a despairing people through the Spirit of the Lord, who has filled the world (Wisdom 1:7).

## CHAPTER VI.—Two opinions about the soul to be examined in relation to the testimonies of Scripture

9. Let us now see which opinion the divine testimonies support more strongly: the opinion that God made one soul and gave it to the first man, from which he would make the others just as he made the other human bodies from his body; or the opinion that he makes each soul individually for each person, just as he made that one, and does not make the others from it.

The statement made through Isaiah, “I have made every breath” (Isaiah 57:16), can be understood in either way, since what follows sufficiently shows that he is speaking about the soul. For whether he makes all souls from the one soul of the first man or from some hidden source of his own, he unquestionably makes them all.

10. The statement, “He who formed their hearts one by one” (Psalm 32:15), likewise does not conflict with either of the two positions about which we are now uncertain, if we wish to understand “hearts” as souls.

For whether God forms each soul from that one which he breathed into the face of the first man, just as he also forms bodies; or whether he forms and sends each one individually, or forms them in the very beings to whom he sends them, the statement remains compatible with both views.

Yet this does not seem to me to have been said except with reference to the way our souls are formed by grace through renewal in the image of God. Thus the Apostle says:

> For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:8–10).

We cannot understand our bodies to have been created or formed through this grace of faith. Rather, the reference is like that in the Psalm: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 50:12).

11. I also think the following passage refers to this: “He who formed the spirit of man within him” (Zechariah 12:1). It is as though sending the soul once it has been made is one thing, while making it within the human being is another—[Col. 0413] that is, restoring and renewing it.

But even if we understand this not of the grace by which we are renewed but of the nature in which we are born, it can be applied to either position. For God either forms within the human being, as though drawing the soul’s seed from that one first man, the soul which gives life to the body; or, not from that stock but from elsewhere, he likewise forms the spirit of life infused into the body through the mortal senses of the flesh, so that the human being becomes a living soul.

## CHAPTER VII.—Which opinion is favored by the statement, “I received a good soul,” and so forth

12. The passage in the Book of Wisdom, where it says, “I received a good soul, and, being more good, I came into an undefiled body” (Wisdom 8:19–20), demands more careful consideration.

It seems rather to support the opinion that souls do not propagate from one soul but come down from above into bodies. Yet what does “I received a good soul” mean? Is it as though, in that fountain of souls—if there is such a fountain—some souls were good and others not good, and that by a kind of lot each soul emerged, determining which soul would be assigned to which human being? Or does God make some souls good and others not good at the time of conception or birth, so that each person receives by lot whichever one happens to fall to him?

It is surprising if this at least helps those who believe that souls are made elsewhere and sent individually by God into each individual human body, rather than helping those who say that souls are sent into bodies according to the merits of deeds performed before embodiment.

For on what basis could some souls be thought to come into bodies good and others not good, except according to their deeds? Certainly not according to the nature in which they are made by the one who makes all natures good.

But let us not contradict the Apostle, who says that those not yet born had done nothing good or evil. In speaking of the twins still in Rebecca’s womb, he confirms that it could not have been said on the basis of works but on the basis of the one who calls: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Romans 9:10–13).

Let us therefore set aside for a little while this testimony from the Book of Wisdom. Those who think it was said specifically and uniquely about that soul of the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, should not be neglected, whether they are mistaken or understand the truth.

If necessary, we shall later consider what this interpretation amounts to. If it cannot apply to Christ, we shall seek how we ought to understand the passage, so that we do not oppose the apostolic faith by supposing that souls possess some merits from their own works before they begin to live in bodies.

## CHAPTER VIII.—How the statement, “You take away their spirit,” and so forth, is opposed to neither opinion

13. Let us now consider how the following words are to be understood:

> You take away their spirit, and they fail,  
> and they return to their dust.  
> You send forth your spirit, and they are created,  
> and you renew the face of the earth (Psalm 103:29–30).

Those who think that souls are created from parents just as bodies are may interpret this as seeming to support their view, if “their spirit” is understood to mean that which human beings have received from human beings. When they die, it cannot be returned to them by human beings so that they may rise again, because it is not again derived from parents in the way it was when they were born. Rather, God will return it, he [Col. 0414] who raises the dead (2 Maccabees 7:23).

Accordingly, the Psalm calls it “their spirit” when they die, but “God’s spirit” when they rise again.

Those who assert that souls come not from parents but from God’s sending may understand the testimony in accordance with their own view: the spirit is called “theirs” when they die because it was in them and departs from them; but it is called “God’s” when they rise because it is sent and restored by him.

Thus this testimony is opposed to neither position.

14. I myself think the passage is better understood of God’s grace, by which we are inwardly renewed.

For the spirit of all proud people who live according to the earthly human being and presume upon their own vanity is, in a certain sense, taken away when they strip off the old human being and are weakened so that they may be perfected after pride has been expelled. They then say to the Lord in humble confession, “Remember that we are dust” (Psalm 102:14). [Note: [Col. 0414] This follows the Greek *mnēsthēti* (“remember”). The old Psalter and the Roman, Arabic, and Ethiopic versions likewise read “remember.” The Vulgate, however, has “he remembered.”]

They gaze through the eye of faith upon God’s righteousness, so that they do not wish to establish their own (Romans 10:3). They despise themselves, as Job says, waste away, and consider themselves earth and ashes. This is the meaning of “they will return to their dust.”

After receiving God’s Spirit, however, they say:

> Yet I live—not I, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20).

Thus the face of the earth is renewed through the grace of the New Testament, by the multitude of the saints.

## CHAPTER IX.—The statement, “And let it return,” likewise stands between the two opinions

15. The statement written in Ecclesiastes, “And let the dust return to the earth as it was, and let the spirit return to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7), does not support one opinion against the other but stands between both.

When those who say that the soul is given not by parents but by God argue that the spirit returns to God who gave it when the dust returns to its own earth—that is, when the flesh made from dust returns to it—the others reply: “Certainly that is so. The spirit returns to God who gave it to the first man when he breathed into his face (Genesis 2:7), while the dust—that is, the human body—returns to the earth from which it was first made (Genesis 3:19).

“For the spirit would not return to the parents, even though it was created from them, having been transmitted from that one soul which was given to the first man. In the same way, the flesh itself does not return after death to the parents from whom it was certainly propagated.

“Just as the flesh does not return to the human beings from whom it was created but to the earth from which it was formed for the first man, so the spirit does not return to the human beings from whom it was transmitted but to God, by whom it was given to that first flesh.”

16. This testimony does, however, sufficiently warn us that God made the soul he gave to the first man from nothing, not from some creature already made, as he made the body from earth.

Therefore, when the soul returns, it has nowhere to return except to its creator, who gave it; it does not return to the creature from which it was made, as the body returns to the earth.

For there is no creature from which it was made, since it was made from nothing. [Col. 0415] Thus what returns returns to its maker, by whom it was made from nothing.

But not all souls return, since there are those of whom it is said, “A spirit that passes on and does not return” (Psalm 77:30).

## CHAPTER X.—The question concerning the soul is not easily resolved from Scripture

17. It is therefore difficult to gather all the testimonies of the holy Scriptures concerning this matter. Even if it were possible not merely to mention them but also to discuss them, they would lead to a very lengthy treatment.

Nevertheless, unless something can be brought forward as certain as the propositions established with certainty—namely, that God made the soul or that he gave it to the first man—I do not know how this question can be resolved by the testimony of divine speech.

If it had been written that God likewise breathed into the face of the woman after she had been formed, and that she became a living soul, this would certainly have added a great deal of light, leading us to believe that a soul was given to each human body after its formation, not from parents.

Yet we would still await a clear statement about what specifically takes place in offspring, since the ordinary process familiar to us is that one human being comes from another.

The first woman, however, was made in another way, and therefore it could still be said that Eve’s soul was not given to her divinely from Adam for the reason that she did not arise from him as offspring.

But if Scripture had recorded that the soul was given from above to the first human being born from those parents, rather than being derived from them, then this would have to be understood of all the others as well, even if Scripture remained silent.

## CHAPTER XI.—Whether the statement, “Through one man,” and so forth, can be applied to both opinions; the baptism of infants

18. Let us now consider whether the following passage confirms neither opinion but can be applied to both:

> Through one man sin entered this world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.

And shortly afterward:

> As through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of justification justification unto life came upon all human beings. For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:12, 18–19).

Those who defend the propagation of souls attempt to establish their position from these words of the Apostle as follows:

“If ‘sin’ or ‘sinner’ can be understood according to the flesh alone,” they say, “we are not compelled by these words to believe that the soul comes from parents. But if, although sin is occasioned by the enticement of the flesh, it is nevertheless the soul alone that sins, how are we to understand the words ‘in whom all sinned’ unless the soul too was propagated from Adam, just as the flesh was? Or how were they made sinners through his disobedience if they were in him only according to the flesh, which was created from him, and not also according to the soul?”

19. We must be careful lest God appear to be the author of sin if he gives a soul to flesh in which it must necessarily sin. Or lest there be any soul, apart from Christ himself, for whose liberation from sin Christian grace is unnecessary, because it did not sin in Adam, [Col. 0416] if the statement that all sinned in him is understood to refer only to the flesh created from him and not also to the soul.

This is so contrary to the faith of the Church that parents hasten to receive the grace of holy Baptism even with their little children and infants. If in them the bond of sin being loosed is only the bond of the flesh and not also that of the soul, it is rightly asked what harm would come to them if they left the body at that age without Baptism.

For if this sacrament benefits their body but not their soul, then the dead ought also to be baptized. But since we see that the Church universally maintains the practice of bringing the living to Baptism and assisting the living, lest, once they are dead, anything beneficial can still be done for them, we do not see what else can be understood except that every infant is Adam both in body and in soul, and therefore needs the grace of Christ.

That age has itself done nothing either good or evil. Therefore the soul would be entirely innocent if it had not been propagated from Adam. How, then, could it justly go into condemnation if it departed from the body without Baptism? Anyone who holds this position concerning the soul and can demonstrate it would be a wonder.

## CHAPTER XII.—The cause of carnal concupiscence is not in the flesh alone but also in the soul

20. It is written most truly and faithfully, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). Nevertheless, I think that no one, learned or unlearned, doubts that the flesh can desire nothing without the soul.

Accordingly, the cause of carnal concupiscence is not in the soul alone, but much less is it in the flesh alone. It arises from both: from the soul, because without it no pleasure is felt; and from the flesh, because without it carnal pleasure is not felt.

When the Apostle says that the flesh desires against the spirit, he is unquestionably referring to the carnal pleasure which the spirit experiences from and with the flesh against the pleasure which the spirit possesses alone.

For, unless I am mistaken, the spirit alone possesses that desire—not mixed with the pleasure of the flesh or the desire for carnal things—by which the soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord (Psalm 83:3).

It alone also possesses the desire of which it is told, “You have desired wisdom; keep the commandment, and the Lord will provide it for you” (Sirach 1:33).

When the spirit commands the bodily members to serve this desire, by which it alone is inflamed—as when a book is taken up, something is written, read, discussed, or heard, or when bread is finally broken for the hungry, and other services of humanity and mercy are performed—the flesh offers obedience; it does not arouse desire.

When something that delights the same soul according to the flesh opposes these and similar good desires, by which the soul alone desires, then the flesh is said to desire against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh.

21. The flesh is spoken of in this way according to what the soul does through it, just as it is said, “The ear hears, and the eye sees.” For who does not know that it is rather the soul that hears through the ear [Col. 0417] and sees through the eye?

We speak in the same way when we say, “Your hand has helped a person,” when something is given with an outstretched hand by which someone is assisted.

And if the statement, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6), refers even to the eye of faith, to which belief in what is not seen through the flesh belongs, then it must certainly refer to the soul, through which the flesh lives.

Even when, through this flesh of ours, we devoutly see Christ—that is, the form with which he clothed himself for our sake—this does not belong to concupiscence but to the service of the flesh.

For otherwise someone might wish to understand the words “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” in this way.

How much more appropriately, then, is the flesh said to desire when the soul not only gives animal life to the flesh but also desires something according to the flesh—something it cannot prevent itself from desiring as long as sin remains in its members?

This is a certain violent enticement of the flesh in this body of death, arising as punishment for that sin from which we derive our stock, according to which all are children of wrath before grace (Ephesians 2:3).

Those who live under grace wage war against this sin—not so that it may not exist in their body as long as that body is mortal enough to be rightly called dead, but so that sin may not reign.

It does not reign when its desires—that is, those things desired according to the flesh against the spirit—are not obeyed.

Accordingly, does the Apostle say, “Let sin not exist in your mortal body”? He knew, of course, that the pleasure of sin was present there, which he calls sin because nature had been corrupted through the first transgression.

Rather, he says:

> Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires; and do not present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness (Romans 6:12–13).

## CHAPTER XIII.—How straightforward that opinion concerning the concupiscence of the flesh is; the sins of children

22. According to this position, we neither assert the most absurd proposition that the flesh can desire without the soul, nor do we agree with the Manichaeans. When they saw that the flesh could not desire without the soul, they supposed that the flesh possessed another soul, from another nature opposed to God, from which it desired against the spirit.

Nor are we forced to say that Christ’s grace is unnecessary for any soul, when we are asked:

“What merit did an infant’s soul possess that it would be harmful for it to leave the body without receiving the sacrament of Christian Baptism, if it committed no personal sin and did not come from that soul which first sinned in Adam?”

23. We are not speaking here about somewhat older children. Some people do not wish to attribute personal sin to them until the threshold of their fourteenth year, when they begin to reach puberty.

We might rightly believe this if there were no sins except those committed with the genital members. But who would dare to assert that thefts, lies, and perjuries are not sins, except someone who wishes to commit such things with impunity?

Yet childhood is full of these faults, although they do not appear to deserve punishment in children to the same degree as in adults, because it is hoped that with advancing years, when reason grows stronger, they will be able to understand salutary commands better and obey them more willingly.

But we are not now speaking about children who, if truth and justice assail their carnal and childish pleasure, whether of body [Col. 0418] or mind, resist them with whatever powers of speech and action they can. What, in support of that pleasure, will seem to aid them except falsehood and injustice, whether in obtaining what attracts them or avoiding what offends them?

We are speaking about infants—not because they are for the most part born from adulteries [Note: [Col. 0418] In very many manuscripts, “from adulterers”]—for nature’s gifts are not to be blamed because of wicked customs; nor should grain have failed to sprout because the hand of a thief sowed it; nor will the parents’ wickedness harm the parents themselves if they correct themselves by turning to God, much less will it harm their children if the children live rightly.

## CHAPTER XIV.—An argument for the opinion that souls are transmitted, drawn from the guilt and baptism of infants, is examined

But that age raises a powerful question. Since an infant’s soul possesses no sin arising from its own exercise of will, it is asked how it can be justified through the obedience of that one man if it is not guilty through the disobedience of the other one man.

This is the position of those who wish human souls to be created from human parents—not indeed except by God the Creator, but in the same way as bodies.

For parents do not create bodies either; rather, it is he who says, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5).

24. To this it is replied that God does indeed give souls individually, newly created, to human bodies, so that by living rightly in sinful flesh, which comes from original sin, and by subduing carnal desires under God’s grace, they may acquire merit whereby, together with the body itself, they may be transferred to a better state at the resurrection and live eternally with the angels in Christ. But it is necessary that, when they are wonderfully joined to earthly and mortal members—especially members propagated from sinful flesh—they should first be fitted to give them life [Note: [Col. 0418] Lovaniensian edition, with all manuscripts, omits “that” (*ut*). M.] and afterward, as age advances, to govern them, as though they were weighed down by forgetfulness. If this forgetfulness were somehow indigestible, it would be attributed to the Creator. But since the soul, gradually recovering from the torpor of this forgetfulness, can turn to its God and earn his mercy and truth—first through the very piety of its conversion, and then through perseverance in keeping his commandment—what harm does it do for it to be briefly immersed, as it were, in that sleep, from which it can gradually awaken into the light of understanding, for the sake of which the rational soul was made, and by a good will choose the good life? This, however, it cannot do unless the grace of God assists it through the Mediator. If a person neglects this, he will be Adam not only according to the flesh but also according to the spirit. But if he takes care, he will be Adam according to the flesh alone; while, living rightly according to the spirit, he will deserve, in that transformation which the resurrection promises to the saints, to receive even that which was culpably drawn from Adam, cleansed from the stain of sin.

25. But before a person can live according to the spirit through maturity of age, he needs the sacrament of the Mediator, so that what he cannot yet accomplish through his own faith may be accomplished through the faith of those who love him. For through the Mediator’s sacrament even in infancy the original penalty of sin is removed. Without his help, even as a young man, a person will not subdue carnal desire; and, unless it has been subdued, he will not attain the merit of eternal life except by the gift of the one whom he strives to please. Therefore even an infant must be baptized while alive, lest the soul’s association with sinful flesh harm it, since, by being joined to that flesh, the infant’s soul is rendered incapable of any understanding according to the spirit. For this very disposition weighs down the soul even when it has been stripped of the body, unless, while it is still in the body, it is cleansed by the one sacrifice of the Mediator, the true priest.  
[Note: [Col. 0419] The word “Mediator” is absent from most manuscripts and from the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus.]

CHAPTER XV.—The same argument is examined more closely.

26. “What, then,” someone says, “if the child’s relatives fail to take care of this, whether through unbelief or negligence?” The same can indeed be said of adults. They may die suddenly, or they may fall ill among people where no one is available to help them obtain baptism. “But,” he says, “they also have sins of their own, for which they need forgiveness; and if these are not forgiven, no one will rightly say that they are punished undeservedly for things they have committed by their own will during their lives. But that soul, which has contracted a certain contamination from sinful flesh—if it was not created from that first sinful soul—cannot in any way be held accountable for it. For it is not accountable through any sin, but through the nature with which it was made and which, by God’s giving, was given to the flesh. Why, then, will it be excluded from eternal life if no one comes to the aid of the infant by baptizing it? Or will this perhaps do it no harm? What, then, does it profit the one who receives help, if it harms nothing that the one who does not receive help is left without it?”

27. I confess that I have not yet heard or read anywhere what those who, according to the holy Scriptures—or according to what is found in them or does not conflict with them—try to assert, namely, that newly created souls are given to bodies not from their parents, might answer in their own defense. Yet the case of the absent should not therefore be abandoned if something occurs to me by which it may seem capable of assistance. They may still say that God, knowing in advance how each soul would live if it continued longer in the body, arranges for it to receive the ministry of saving baptism, foreseeing that it would one day have possessed piety when it reached the years capable of faith, if it had not been necessary for it to be overtaken by death for some hidden reason.

The reason, then, why an infant is born only to die immediately or soon afterward is hidden, and is certainly most remote from human understanding—or at least from mine. But it is so hidden that it helps neither side whose opinions we are now discussing. For once the opinion has been rejected that souls are thrust into bodies on account of the merits of a previous life, so that the one who had committed few sins might appear to have deserved to be released from the body more quickly—lest we contradict the Apostle, who testifies that those not yet born had done neither good nor evil (Rom. 9:11)—neither can those who assert that souls are propagated explain in their own favor why the death of some is hastened and that of others delayed; nor can those who maintain that souls are newly given individually explain it. This cause, then, is hidden, and, so far as I judge, it equally neither supports nor opposes either side.

CHAPTER XVI.—The same argument.

[Col. 0420]

28. Accordingly, those who were pressed by the question of infants’ deaths—why the sacrament of baptism is necessary for all, when their souls were not derived from the one whose disobedience made many sinners—reply that all are indeed constituted sinners according to the flesh, but according to the soul only those who lived wickedly at a time when they could also have lived rightly. They say that all souls, including those of infants, therefore need the sacrament of baptism, without which it is not advantageous for them to depart from this life even at that age, because the contamination of sin from sinful flesh, by which the soul is overwhelmed when it is joined to these members, will harm it after death unless it is cleansed, while still in the flesh itself, through the Mediator’s sacrament.
