They further say that this help is divinely arranged for the soul which God foreknew would have lived piously if it had remained here until the fitting years of faith, but which, for some reason known to him, he both willed to be born in a body and soon withdrew from the body.

When they give this answer, what can be said against them except that we would thereby be made uncertain about the salvation of those who, after having lived this life well, have died in the peace of the Church? For if each person is to be judged not only according to how he lived but also according to how he would have lived if he had been able to live longer, then evil merits—not only of past but also of future sins—have force before God; and death does not free a person from the guilt of those sins if it comes before they have been committed. Nor has anything been gained for the one who was taken away “lest wickedness change his understanding” (Wis. 4:11). For since God foreknew that person’s future wickedness, why would he not judge him rather according to that wickedness, if he judged that a dying infant should be helped through baptism because he foresaw that, had the child lived, it would have lived piously and faithfully, lest the filth contracted from participation in sinful flesh harm it?

29. Or can this proposal be refuted for the very reason that it is mine, while those who assert that they are certain of this opinion perhaps bring forward other scriptural testimonies or rational arguments by which they remove this ambiguity? Or can they at least show that the Apostle’s statement is not contrary to what they hold? In commending with great emphasis the grace by which we are saved, he says: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22); and: “As through the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one man many shall be constituted righteous.” Wishing the same “many sinners” to be understood as all, not as some with exceptions, he had said earlier of Adam: “In whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:19, 12). Hence those who understand souls to be derived from one ancestor reasonably believe that the souls of infants cannot be separated from the meaning both of the word “all” and of the fact that they are helped through baptism—unless they are refuted by some manifest and clear argument that does not conflict with the holy Scriptures, or by the authority of those very Scriptures.

CHAPTER XVII.—The testimony from the Book of Wisdom is considered on both sides.

30. Let us now see, so far as the necessity of this undertaking permits, what is to be made of the passage which we postponed a little earlier. For it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “I was a gifted child, and I received a good soul; and, being more good, I came into an undefiled body” (Wis. 8:19–20).

This testimony appears to support those who say that souls are not created from parents but come to, or descend into, the body when God sends them. Yet it again obstructs their opinion in what it says: “I received a good soul.” For surely they believe that the souls God sends into bodies flow, as it were, from one source like streams, or are made with an equal nature—not that some are good or better, and others not good or less good. From where, then, would souls be good or better, or not good or less good, unless through moral character according to the free choice of the will, or through differences in the constitution of bodies, some being burdened more and others less by the body, which is corrupted and weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15)?

But there was no action on the part of any individual soul by which their characters could be distinguished before they came into bodies. Nor could this person have called his soul good because it came from a body that burdened it less, since he says, “I received a good soul; and, being more good, I came into an undefiled body.” He says that something was added to the goodness he already possessed: namely, having received a good soul, he also came into an undefiled body. Therefore he was good for another reason before he came into the body. But it was not because of a difference in character, since he had no previous merit from a life already lived; nor because of a difference in body, since he was good before he came into the body. From where, then?

31. Although the words “I came into a body” do not seem to support those who assert that souls are created through the propagation of the soul of the transgressor, the rest of the passage can be fitted to their view without incongruity. When he had said, “I was a gifted child,” he may immediately have explained the causes of his giftedness by adding, “And I received a good soul”—that is, from his father’s natural ability or bodily constitution. Then he says, “Being more good, I came into an undefiled body.” If this is understood of his mother’s body, not even the statement “I came into a body” will conflict with this opinion, since he may be understood to have come from his father’s soul and body into an undefiled maternal body—undefiled either by menstrual blood, for people are said to be burdened by this, or by adulterous contamination.

Thus these words of the book either favor more strongly those who speak of the propagation of souls, or, if the others can also interpret them in their own favor, they remain balanced between the two sides.

CHAPTER XVIII.—Concerning Christ’s soul: whether the statement “I was a gifted child,” and so forth, can apply to him.

32. If we wish to understand these words of the Lord as referring to his human creature, assumed by the Word, there are nevertheless features in the surrounding passage that do not suit his excellence. Most notably, the same person who speaks these words in the same book confessed somewhat earlier than the words now under discussion that he had been “formed from the seed of a man in blood” (Wis. 7:2). The birth of the Virgin is plainly foreign to such a mode of birth, since no Christian doubts that Christ’s flesh was conceived not from the seed of a man.

Yet in the Psalms we find the words: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked and saw me; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots”—words that properly fit that one person. There he also said: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me? The words of my sins are far from my salvation” (Ps. 21:17–19, 2)—words that again do not fit him, unless he was representing in himself the body of our humiliation, since we are members of his body. And because in the Gospel itself the child advanced in age and wisdom [Note: [Col. 0422] Thus all manuscripts. The printed editions read: “and wisdom, thus if they can.”], if the statements that occur around this passage in the Book of Wisdom can also be fitted to the same Lord on account of the humble form of a servant and the unity of the Church’s body with its head, then what child was more gifted than the one whose wisdom, at twelve years of age, astonished the elders (Luke 2:42–52)?

And what soul was better than that soul? Even if those who assert the propagation of souls prevail—not by contention but by proof—it would not follow that this soul too should be believed to have come through the propagation of that transgressor, lest through that man’s disobedience he also be constituted a sinner, through whose one obedience many are freed from that guilt and constituted righteous.

And what was more undefiled than the Virgin’s womb? Although her flesh came from the propagation of sinful flesh, it did not conceive from the propagation of sin. Thus even Christ’s body was not sown in Mary’s womb by the law which, placed in the members of the body of death, conflicts with the law of the mind. Holy married fathers, restraining that law, relaxed it into intercourse only as far as was permitted; yet they did not merely endure its impulse only to the extent that was permitted. Accordingly, although Christ’s body was assumed from the flesh of a woman who had been conceived from that propagation of sinful flesh, because he was not conceived in her in the same manner in which she herself had been conceived, it too was not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh.

He did not receive from it the guilt that makes death due, which appears in the involuntary movement of the flesh, though it is overcome by the will and against which “the spirit desires” (Gal. 5:17). Rather, he received from it what was sufficient not for participation in the contamination of transgression but for undergoing an undeserved death and displaying the promised resurrection—one of these being useful to us so that we would not fear, and the other so that we would hope.

33. Finally, if I were asked from where Jesus Christ received his soul, I would certainly prefer to hear better and more learned men on the subject. Nevertheless, within the limits of my understanding, I would more readily answer, “from where Adam did,” rather than “from Adam.” [Note: [Col. 0422] The printed editions read “not from Adam”; all manuscripts read “from where Adam did.”] If dust taken from the earth, on which no human being had worked, deserved to be divinely animated, how much more did the body assumed from flesh on which likewise no human being had worked receive a good soul—when in the former case one who was to fall was raised up, and in the latter one who would raise others up descended?

Perhaps for this reason he said, “I received a good soul”—if indeed this ought to be understood of him—because things given by lot are customarily understood to be given divinely. Or, as must be said confidently, lest that soul be thought to have been raised to such a height by some preceding works or merits that the Word could become flesh and dwell among us with it (John 1:14), the name “lot” was introduced to remove suspicion of preceding merits.

CHAPTER XIX.—Christ’s soul was not in Abraham’s loins, and therefore is not propagated.

34. There is a passage in the Epistle entitled “To the Hebrews” that deserves careful consideration. The author, distinguishing Christ’s priesthood from the priesthood of Levi through Melchizedek, in whom a figure of what was to come had gone before, says:

“See, then, how great this man was, to whom even the patriarch Abraham gave a tenth of the first fruits. Those indeed who are of the sons of Levi, receiving the priesthood, have a commandment according to the Law to take tithes from the people—that is, from their brothers—even though they themselves came forth from Abraham’s loins. But he who is not of their lineage received tithes from Abraham and blessed the one who had the promise. Without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the greater. Here mortal men receive tithes; there, one who testifies that he lives. And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, was tithed, for he was still in the loins of his father” (Heb. 7:4–10).

If this also contributes to the distinction by which Christ’s priesthood surpasses the Levitical priesthood—for Christ was prefigured by the priest who tithed Abraham, in whom Levi himself was tithed—then Christ certainly was not tithed by him. But if Levi was tithed because he was in Abraham’s loins, Christ was not tithed because he was not in Abraham’s loins.

Now, if we understand Levi to have been in Abraham not according to the soul but only according to the flesh, then Christ too was there, since Christ also descended from Abraham’s seed according to the flesh; and he too was therefore tithed. What, then, is the meaning of the great difference between Christ’s priesthood and Levi’s, namely, that Levi was tithed by Melchizedek while he was in Abraham’s loins, when Christ too was there and therefore both were equally tithed? It can only be that we must understand Christ not to have been there in some respect.

Who, however, would deny that he was there according to the flesh? Therefore he was not there according to the soul. Christ’s soul, then, is not derived through the propagation of Adam’s transgression; otherwise it too would have been there.

CHAPTER XX.—What should now be answered on behalf of those who defend the propagation of souls?

35. At this point [Note: [Col. 0423] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read “Hence” (*Hinc*). M.] those who defend the propagation of souls come forward and say that their opinion is confirmed if Levi is understood to have been in Abraham’s loins also according to the soul, since Melchizedek tithed him while he was in Abraham, so that Christ can be distinguished from him in this tithing. Since Christ was not tithed, although he was in Abraham’s loins according to the flesh, it follows that he was not there according to the soul, and therefore Levi must have been there according to the soul.

This does not greatly concern me, since I remain more ready to hear a comparison of the two views than to confirm either one of them. For the present, I wished by this testimony to distinguish Christ’s soul from the origin of this propagation. Those who hold this view may find others to answer them on the remaining points and may say something that also moves me considerably: although no human soul is in the loins of its father, Levi, constituted according to the flesh in Abraham’s loins, was tithed, whereas Christ, who was likewise constituted there according to the flesh, was not tithed.

For Levi was there according to that seminal principle by which, through intercourse, he was destined to enter his mother; but Christ’s flesh was not there according to that principle, although Mary’s flesh was there according to it. Therefore neither Levi nor Christ was in Abraham’s loins according to the soul; according to the flesh, both Levi and Christ were there—but Levi according to carnal desire, Christ according to bodily substance alone.

Since seed contains both visible corporeal matter and an invisible principle, both proceeded from Abraham, and indeed from Adam himself, down to Mary’s body, because Mary’s body too was conceived and came forth in that manner. But Christ took the visible substance of his flesh from the Virgin’s flesh; the principle of his conception, however, came not from male seed but in a wholly different manner, from above. Accordingly, in respect of what he received from his mother, he too was in Abraham’s loins.

36. The one who was tithed in Abraham, then, is the one who, although only according to the flesh, was nevertheless in his loins in the same way as Abraham himself was in the loins of his own father. That is, he was born from Father Abraham in the same way that Abraham was born from his own father: through the law in the members that conflicts with the law of the mind, and through the invisible desire that, although chaste and good marriage rights do not allow it to prevail beyond what is necessary for the propagation of the race, nevertheless remains present.

But the one whose flesh derived from that source not the heat of a wound but the material of a remedy was not tithed there. For since the tithing pertained to the prefiguring of a cure, what was being tithed in Abraham’s flesh was what was being healed, not that from which it was being healed.

That same flesh—not only Abraham’s but also that of the first earthly human being—simultaneously possessed both the wound of transgression and the remedy for the wound. The wound of transgression lay in the law of the members conflicting with the law of the mind, which is, through the principle of generation, as it were, copied into all flesh propagated from that source. The remedy for the wound lay in what was assumed from that source, without the operation of desire, solely in bodily matter, from the Virgin through the divine principle of conception and formation, for the purpose of sharing in death without guilt and providing an example of resurrection without falsehood.

Therefore, I think that even those who defend the propagation of souls will agree that Christ’s soul was not propagated from the soul of that first transgressor. For they wish the soul’s seed also to be transmitted through the seed of the father who engages in intercourse, and Christ is excluded from that mode of conception. They will also agree that, if Christ had been in Abraham according to the soul, he too would have been tithed; but Scripture testifies that he was not tithed, and on this basis as well distinguishes his priesthood from the Levitical priesthood.

CHAPTER XXI.—If Christ had been in Abraham according to the soul, he could not have failed to be tithed.

[Col. 0425]

37. Or will they perhaps say: “Just as he could be there according to the flesh without being tithed, why could he not also have been there according to the soul without being tithed?” The answer is: because even those who think that the soul is a body did not suppose that the simple substance of the soul is increased by bodily additions—although those who believe that souls are created from parents are especially among their number.

Accordingly, in bodily seed there can be an invisible power that operates through incorporeal numbers, to be distinguished by the intellect, not by the eyes, from the corporeal matter perceived by sight and touch. The quantity of the human body itself—which incomparably exceeds the small measure of the seed—sufficiently shows that something can be taken from the seed that does not possess that seminal power but only bodily substance, which was divinely, not through the propagation of those engaging in intercourse, assumed and formed into Christ’s flesh.

But who could assert this concerning the soul—that it possesses both manifest seminal matter and a hidden seminal principle? Yet why should I labor over a matter that perhaps cannot be persuaded to anyone by words, unless the person’s intellectual capacity is such that it can fly ahead of the speaker’s attempt and not wait for the whole argument to be completed?

I shall therefore summarize briefly. If this could also happen with respect to the soul—which, when we were speaking of the flesh, may perhaps have been understood—then Christ’s soul is propagated in such a way that it did not draw the stain of transgression along with it. But if it could not come from that source without this guilt, then it does not come from that source.

As for the origin of other souls—whether they come from parents or from above—let those who can prevail prevail. I am still uncertain between the two views and am moved now one way, now the other, provided only that I do not believe the soul to be a body or some corporeal quality or arrangement—if that is the right word for it—which the Greeks call ἁρμονία (“harmony”); nor do I expect that anyone’s chatter will make me believe this, with God aiding my mind.

CHAPTER XXII.—The passage in John, “That which is born,” and so forth, is adapted to both opinions concerning the origin of the soul.

38. There is another testimony that should not be neglected, which those who believe that souls come from above can bring forward. The Lord himself says: “That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the spirit is spirit” (John 3:6).

“What statement,” they say, “could be more decisive in showing that a soul cannot be born from flesh? For what else is the soul than the spirit of life, created but certainly not the Creator?”

Against them the others reply: “What else do we mean when we say that flesh comes from flesh and soul from soul? A human being consists of both, and we understand both to come from their respective sources: flesh from the flesh of the one who generates, and spirit from the spirit of the one who desires.” For the moment they set aside the fact that the Lord was speaking not of carnal generation but of spiritual regeneration.

CHAPTER XXIII.—Which of the two opinions concerning the soul has greater weight. The Church’s practice regarding the baptism of infants.

39. Having dealt with these matters as far as we could for the present, I would declare the considerations of reason and testimony on both sides equal or nearly equal, were it not that the opinion of those who believe souls to be created from parents is outweighed by the baptism of infants.

In the meantime I have not yet found what answer can be given to them. If God should afterward grant me anything, and grant students of such matters the opportunity to write, I shall not be reluctant to do so. For now, however, I first declare that the testimony supplied by infants must not be despised, so that, if the truth lies on the other side, it is not neglected as though it could be refuted.

Either nothing should be sought concerning this matter, so that it is sufficient for our faith to know the way by which we shall arrive through holy living, even if we do not know from where we have come; or, if the rational soul does not rashly burn with the desire to know this also about itself, let there be no obstinacy in arguing, but diligence in seeking, humility in asking, and perseverance in knocking. Then, if the one who knows better than we do what is advantageous for us knows that this knowledge is useful to us, he will also grant it—the one who gives good gifts to his children (Matt. 7:7, 11).

Nevertheless, the practice of Mother Church in baptizing infants must by no means be despised or regarded as superfluous, nor should it be believed to have been instituted unless it were an apostolic tradition. That little age itself carries great weight as a testimony: it was the first to deserve to shed blood for Christ.

CHAPTER XXIV.—What those who believe souls are propagated must guard against.

40. I urge, so far as I am able, those whom this opinion has preoccupied—those who believe that souls are propagated from parents—to examine themselves as much as possible and, for the present, to understand that their bodies are not their souls.

There is no nature closer to the likeness of God—if it is carefully examined—from which God, who remains immutable above all his creation, can be conceived incorporeally. Nothing is nearer, or perhaps nothing follows more necessarily, than that once the soul is believed to be a body, God too will be believed to be a body.

For those accustomed and attached to bodily sensations do not wish to believe that the soul is anything other than a body, lest, if it is not a body, it should be nothing. Consequently, the more they fear believing that the soul is not a body, the more they fear believing that God is not a body, because they fear believing that God is nothing.

Thus they are carried toward fantasies, or phantasms of images, which thought turns over in relation to bodies, and, when these are removed, they dread that they will perish as though into a void. Necessarily, then, they paint justice and wisdom, so to speak, in their hearts with forms and colors, since they cannot conceive of them as incorporeal. Yet they do not say, when justice or wisdom moves them to praise them or to act according to them, what color, stature, features, or forms they have seen.

We have already said much about these matters elsewhere, and, if God wills, we shall speak further when circumstances seem to require it. For now, let us return to what we began to say: if some people either do not doubt that souls are propagated from parents or doubt whether this is so, they must not dare to believe or say that the soul is a body. This is especially necessary for the reason I mentioned: lest they also suppose that God himself is nothing other than a body—although an exceedingly excellent body, and one belonging to a particular nature surpassing all others, yet still a body.

CHAPTER XXV.—Tertullian’s error concerning the soul.

41. Tertullian believed that the soul is a body for no other reason than that he could not conceive of it as incorporeal and therefore feared that, if it were not a body, it would be nothing. For the same reason he was unable to think differently concerning God. Yet because he is acute, he is sometimes overcome by the truth he perceives, contrary to his own opinion.

What could he have said more truly than what he says in one place: “Everything corporeal is susceptible to suffering” (Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 7)? He should therefore have changed the opinion he had expressed shortly before, that God too is a body. For I do not think that he was so senseless as to believe that God’s nature is susceptible to suffering, so that Christ would then be believed to be susceptible to suffering and change not only in the flesh, or in flesh and soul, but in the very Word through whom all things were made. May such a belief be far from a Christian heart.

Again, when he had assigned the soul an airy and luminous color, he came to the senses and attempted to furnish it limb by limb, as though it were a body. He says:

“Here will be the inner man, another outer man, one man in two, and he too will have his own eyes and ears, by which the people were to hear and see the Lord; he will have the remaining limbs as well, through which he operates in his thoughts and functions in dreams” (*ibid.*, chapter 9).

42. Behold the ears and eyes with which the people were supposed to hear and see God, and which the soul uses in dreams. If someone saw Tertullian himself in a dream, he would never say that he had been seen by Tertullian or had spoken with him while Tertullian, in turn, had not seen him.

Finally, if the soul sees itself in dreams, while its bodily members are certainly lying in one place and it itself wanders among various images that it sees, who has ever seen it in a dream with an airy and luminous color—unless perhaps in the same way as it falsely sees other things? It can indeed see even this. But when it awakens, may it not believe itself to be such. Otherwise, whenever it sees itself differently, either its soul will have changed, or even then the substance of the soul will not be seen, but an incorporeal image of the body, which is formed in a marvelous way just as it is formed in thought.

For what Ethiopian has not almost always seen himself as black in dreams? Or, if he saw himself in another color, was he not more surprised if he remembered it? Yet I do not know whether he would ever have seen himself in an airy and luminous color if he had never read or heard of this.

43. What of the fact that people are led astray by such visions and wish to prescribe to us from the Scriptures that something of this kind applies not to the soul but to God himself, as he was figuratively shown to the spirits of the saints and as he is presented in allegorical speech? Such visions are indeed similar to such statements.

And so they err, establishing in their hearts images of a vain opinion, and failing to understand that the saints judged such visions of theirs in the same way as they would have judged them if they had read or heard such things divinely expressed in figures. Thus, “the seven ears of grain and the seven cows are seven years” (Gen. 41:26); and the sheet fastened by its four corners, like a dish filled with various animals, is the whole world with all its nations (Acts 10:11). So too with all the other things—and especially those that concern incorporeal realities—which are signified not by bodily realities but by images.

CHAPTER XXVI.—Tertullian’s view concerning the growth of the soul.

44. Nevertheless, Tertullian did not wish the soul to grow in substance as the body does. He even supplied the reason for his fear: “Lest,” he says, “it should also be said to diminish in substance, and thus be believed capable of decay.”

Yet because he extends it locally through the body, he finds no way to explain its growth, although he wishes it, from a tiny seed, to become equal to the size of the body. He says:

“But its power, in which its natural properties are implanted and preserved, while the measure of its substance remains unchanged—the measure with which it was inflated from the beginning—is gradually produced along with the flesh” (*On the Soul*, chapter 37).  
[Note: [Col. 0428] Tertullian reads “in which” (*in qua*) rather than “in which” (*in quo*).]
[Note: [Col. 0428] The printed editions add “in the members,” which is absent from the manuscripts and from Tertullian.]

We might not understand this unless he made his meaning clear by comparing it with things we see. He says:

“Suppose a fixed weight of gold or silver in an as-yet-unworked mass. Its form is gathered together, and for the time being it is smaller, yet it contains within the bounds of its measure all that belongs by nature to the gold or silver. Then, when the mass is spread into a sheet, it becomes larger than it was at first through the expansion of its fixed weight, not through addition: it is extended, not increased—although in this way too it is increased, as it is extended. For it is permitted to increase in form, though not in its fixed state.

Then the very brilliance of the gold or silver is advanced, which previously had indeed been present in the mass, but more obscurely—not entirely absent. Then one form after another is added according to the pliability of the material, wherever the one who works it draws it, contributing nothing to its measure except shape. So the growth of the soul must be understood as not substantive but developmental” (*On the Soul*, chapter 37).

45. Who would have believed that a man with such a mind could be so eloquent? Yet these matters are dreadful, not laughable. Would he have been driven to this if he had been able to conceive of something that exists but is not a body?

What, however, is more absurd than to think that a mass of some metal can grow in one part while it is hammered unless it diminishes in another; or that it can increase in breadth unless it decreases in thickness; or that any body can grow in every direction while retaining its natural quantity unless it becomes more rarefied?

How, then, will the soul fill the size of the body it animates from that drop of seed, if it too is a body whose substance does not grow through any addition? How, I ask, will it fill the flesh it gives life to, unless it becomes as much more rarefied as the thing it animates becomes larger?

Apparently he feared that it would decay even by diminishing if it grew, but did not fear that it would decay by becoming more rarefied when it grew.

But why should I linger any longer, when the discussion is proceeding at greater length than the need to bring it to an end requires, and my position is already sufficiently known—both what I hold with certainty and where I remain uncertain, and why I am uncertain? Let this volume therefore now be concluded, so that we may afterward examine what follows.

BOOK ELEVEN. On Genesis, chapter 2, verse 25: “And they were naked,” and on the whole of chapter 3, in which, for the purpose of its exposition, the condition and fall of the devil are discussed.

[Col. 0429]

CHAPTER ONE.—After the text of Genesis has been recited, chapter 2, verse 25, is explained.

1. And both were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed. Now the serpent was the most cunning of all the beasts that are upon the earth, which the Lord God had made. And the serpent said to the woman, “Why—because God said, ‘You shall not eat from every tree of paradise’?” [Note: [Col. 0429] The printed editions read “from that one”; but the manuscripts, as in the sacred Scriptures, read “from every.”] And the woman said to the serpent, “We shall eat from the fruit of the tree that is in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise, God said, ‘You shall not eat from it, nor touch it, lest you die.’” And the serpent said to the woman, “You shall not die by death. For God knew that on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, that it was pleasing to the eyes to look upon, and beautiful to know. And she took of its fruit and ate, and gave some also to her husband who was with her, and they ate. And the eyes of both were opened, and they recognized that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves coverings. And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the paradise in the evening, and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord God among the trees of paradise.

And the Lord God called Adam and said to him, “Where are you?” And he said to him, “I heard your voice walking in the paradise, and I was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid myself.” And he said to him, “Who told you that you were naked, unless it was from the tree concerning which I commanded you alone not to eat from it? You have eaten from it.” And Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me—she gave me some of the tree, and I ate.” And the Lord God said to the woman, “What have you done?” And the woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

And the Lord God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, you are cursed above all cattle and above all the beasts that are upon the earth. You shall walk upon your breast and your belly, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. And I shall place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed: she shall watch over your head, and you shall watch over her heel.”

And he said to the woman, “Multiplying, I shall multiply your sorrows and your groaning. In sorrows you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.”

But to Adam he said, “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you, ordering you alone not to eat from it, cursed is the earth in your works. In sorrows you shall eat it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall produce for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go.”

And Adam called the name of his wife Life [Note: [Col. 0429] The printed editions read “Adam called the name of his wife Eve, that is, Life.” But all the manuscripts lack the words “Eve, that is”; these words are not found among the interpreters of the Septuagint either], because she is the mother of all the living.

And the Lord God made garments of skins for Adam [Col. 0430] and his wife, and clothed them. And the Lord God said, “Behold, Adam has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. And now, lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever”—and the Lord God sent him forth from the paradise of delight to work the earth from which he had been taken. And he expelled Adam and placed him opposite the paradise of delight; and he appointed cherubim and a flaming, turning sword to guard the way to the tree of life.

2. Before we deal systematically with the text of the Scripture set before us, I think we should be reminded of what I remember having stated elsewhere in this work: we must insist that what the writer himself narrates as having happened be defended according to the literal sense. If, however, something is said in the words of God or of any person taken up into the prophetic office that cannot be understood literally without absurdity, it must unquestionably be received as spoken figuratively on account of some signification. Yet it is not permissible to doubt that it was said: this is required by the faithfulness of the narrator and by the expositor’s pledge (Book 8, chapters 1–7).

3. Thus they were both naked: it is true that the bodies of the two human beings living in paradise were altogether naked. And they were not ashamed: for what would they have been ashamed of, when they had felt no law in their members resisting the law of their mind (Rom. 7:23)? That law followed them as the punishment of sin after the transgression had been committed, when disobedience appropriated what had been forbidden and justice punished what had been done. Before this occurred, they were naked, as has been said, and were not ashamed: there was no movement in the body to which shame was owed; they thought nothing needed to be covered, because they had felt nothing that needed to be restrained.

How they were to propagate children has already been discussed above (Book 9, chapters 3–11). Yet we must not believe that they would have propagated in the same manner in which they did after the crime had been committed and the foretold punishment had followed—when, before they died, the tumult of disobedient members was already moving within the bodies of disobedient human beings through a most just reciprocal process. Adam and Eve were not yet such as they became when both were naked and were not ashamed.

## CHAPTER II.—What the serpent’s wisdom was, and whence it came.

4. Now the serpent was there indeed the most cunning, but of all the beasts that were upon the earth, which the Lord God had made. For the word has been translated as “cunning,” or, as more Latin manuscripts have it, “the wisest”; but not with that proper wisdom by which wisdom is usually understood in a good sense—whether the wisdom of God, of angels, or of a rational soul—as when we call bees and ants “wise” because of their works, which seem to imitate wisdom.

Nevertheless, this serpent could be called the wisest of all the beasts not by its irrational soul [Col. 0431], but by the alien spirit already within it, that is, the diabolical spirit. For however much the transgressing angels, on account of their perversity and pride, have deservedly been cast down from their heavenly seats, they are nevertheless by nature superior to all beasts because of the eminence of reason.

What wonder, then, if the devil, already filling the serpent and mingling his own spirit with it—in the manner in which he is accustomed to fill the prophets of demons—had made it the wisest of all the beasts, according to the living and irrational soul of those creatures? [Note: [Col. 0431] In most manuscripts, “the prophets of demons are accustomed to be filled.”]

By an abuse of the term, wisdom is thus spoken of in an evil sense, just as cunning (*astutia*) is spoken of in a good sense; whereas, properly and more customarily, at least in the Latin language, the wise are called wise laudably, while the cunning are understood to be evil-hearted. Hence some, as we find in many manuscripts, transferring not the word but rather the sense into ordinary Latin usage, preferred to call this serpent “more cunning than all the beasts” rather than “wiser.”

What the Hebrew usage contains, however—whether there too people can be called and understood as wise in an evil sense, not abusively but properly—let those who know it thoroughly determine. We nevertheless read plainly in another place of the Scriptures that people are “wise for evil, not for good” (Jer. 4:22); and the Lord says that the children of this age are wiser than the children of light in providing for themselves in the future, though by fraud rather than by justice (Luke 16:8).

## CHAPTER III.—The devil was permitted to tempt only through the serpent.

5. We certainly ought not to suppose that the devil chose the serpent for himself, through which he might tempt and persuade the human being to sin. Rather, since the devil had a desire to deceive because of his perverse and envious will, he could act only through that animal through which he was permitted to act. The will to harm can indeed arise from the mind of any creature; but power comes only from God, and this by a hidden and profound justice, because there is no iniquity with God.

## CHAPTER IV.—Why the temptation of the human being was permitted.

6. If, then, it is asked why God permitted the human being to be tempted, when he foreknew that he would consent to the tempter, I cannot penetrate the profundity of his counsel, and I confess that this lies far above my powers. There may therefore be some more hidden reason reserved for better and holier persons, on account of his grace rather than their merits.

Yet, insofar as he grants us understanding or permits us to speak, it does not seem to me that the human being would have been worthy of great praise if he could live rightly for no other reason than that no one persuaded him to live wrongly—when he both had the natural capacity and possessed the power to will not to consent to the one who persuaded him, with the assistance, nevertheless, of him who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). [Note: [Col. 0431] Some manuscripts read “to have.” Some then continue, “if he wished not to consent.” Most others read, “that he has the will not to consent.” So also the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus. The Louvain edition reads, “that he has the will and does not consent.”]

Why, then, would he not permit the one whom he foreknew would consent to be tempted, when that person would act by his own will and thus incur guilt, while by God’s justice he would be ordered through punishment? [Col. 0432] It was also to show the proud soul, for the instruction of those who would later become holy, how rightly God makes use even of the wills of evil beings, when those beings make perverse use of good natures.

## CHAPTER V.—The human being was overthrown by the tempter because he was proud.

7. We should not suppose that this tempter would have overthrown the human being if a certain elation had not first arisen in the human soul and needed to be restrained, so that through the humiliation of sin he might learn what he had falsely presumed about himself. For it was most truly said: “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. 16:18).

Perhaps this is also the voice of this human being in the Psalm: “In my abundance I said, ‘I shall not be moved forever’” [Note: [Col. 0432] The ancient manuscripts read “unto the age.” Augustine sometimes does likewise, because of the ambiguity of the Greek reading among the Septuagint, *eis ton aiōna*.] Then, having experienced what evil there is in the proud presumption of one’s own power, and what good there is in the assistance of God’s grace: “Lord,” he says, “by your will you granted strength to my beauty; but you turned away your face, and I became troubled” (Ps. 29:7–8).

But whether this was said of this human being or of another, it nevertheless had to be shown, even by the experience of punishment, to a soul that exalted itself and trusted excessively as though in its own strength, how badly a created nature fares when it withdraws from its creator. For this especially commends what a good God is: no one who withdraws from him fares well. Those who rejoice in deadly pleasures cannot be without fear of pains; and those who do not feel at all the evil of their abandonment, because of an even greater dullness born of pride, appear utterly more wretched to those who know how to discern such things. Thus, if they refuse to receive the medicine that would make them avoid such conditions, they may at least serve as an example by which such conditions can be avoided.

For, as the apostle James says: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire; then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, produces death” (James 1:14–15). Thus, once the swelling of pride has been healed, one rises again if the will that was absent before the experience—so that one might remain with God—is present at least after the experience, so that one may return to God.

## CHAPTER VI.—Why God permitted the human being to be tempted.

8. Some people are disturbed by the temptation of the first human being, because God permitted it to occur, as though they did not now see the entire human race being ceaselessly tempted by the devil’s snares. Why does God permit this also? Is it because virtue is tested and exercised, and the palm of victory is more glorious for one who has not consented when tempted than for one who could not be tempted?

Indeed, even those who abandon the Creator and follow the tempter increasingly tempt those who remain in the word of God. They provide them with an example for avoiding desire and instill in them a reverent fear of pride. Hence the Apostle says: “Pay attention to yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1).

It is remarkable how greatly this humility—by which we submit to the Creator, lest we presume upon our own powers as though we did not need his assistance—is commended throughout all the divine Scriptures by continual exhortation. Since, then, even through the unjust the just advance, and through the impious the godly advance, it is futile to say: “God should not have created those whom he foreknew would become evil.” Why should he not have created those whom he foreknew would benefit the good, so that they might both arise as useful means for exercising and admonishing the good wills of others, and be justly punished for their own evil will?

## CHAPTER VII.—Why God did not create the human being such that he would never wish to sin.

9. “He should have made the human being such,” they say, “that he would not wish to sin at all.” We grant that the nature that does not wish to sin at all is better; let them also grant that the nature made such that it could refrain from sinning if it wished is not evil, and that the sentence by which it was punished is just, since it sinned by will, not by necessity.

As true reason teaches that the nature which is absolutely not delighted by anything unlawful is better, so true reason likewise teaches that the other nature is good: it has the power, if unlawful pleasure arises, to restrain it so that it rejoices not only in other lawful and rightly performed acts, but also in restraining that very perverse pleasure.

Since, then, this nature is good and the other is better, why would God make only the one and not both? Accordingly, those who were prepared [Note: [Col. 0433] The manuscripts read “had prepared.”] to praise God for the one alone ought to praise him more abundantly for both. The one exists in the holy angels, the other in holy human beings.

Those, however, who chose the portion of iniquity and corrupted a praiseworthy nature by a blameworthy will should not, for that reason—because they were foreknown—have been left uncreated. They too have their place, which they fill in the order of things for the benefit of the holy. For God does not need the justice of any upright person; how much less does he need the iniquity of the perverse?

## CHAPTER VIII.—Why those who were foreknown to become evil were created.

10. Who, with sober consideration, would say: “It was better not to create one whom he foreknew could be corrected through another’s iniquity than to create even one whom he foreknew ought to be condemned for his own iniquity”? For this is to say that it would be better for there not to be one who, by mercifully making good use of another’s evil, would be crowned, than for there to be even an evil person who would be justly punished according to his deserts.

When sound reasoning clearly demonstrates two goods that are not equal, one superior and the other inferior, dull-hearted people do not understand that, when they say, “Let both be such,” they are saying nothing other than, “Let only the one exist.” Thus, when they wish to equalize kinds of goods, they reduce their number; and by immoderately increasing one kind, they eliminate the other.

Who would listen to them if they said: “Since the sense of sight is superior to that of hearing, let there be four eyes and no ears”? So, if that rational creature is superior which submits to God without any comparison with punishment and without any pride, while some human beings were created in such a way that they cannot recognize God’s beneficence in themselves except by seeing another’s punishment, so that they may not be high-minded but fear (Rom. 11:20)—that is, may not trust in themselves but trust in God—who, understanding rightly, would say, “Let this be such as that,” and fail to see that he is saying nothing other than, “Let this not exist, but let that alone exist”?

If this is said ignorantly and foolishly, why, then, did God not also create those whom he foreknew would become evil, wishing to show his wrath and demonstrate his power, and for this reason enduring with great patience the vessels of wrath, which have been prepared for destruction, so that he might make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory (Rom. 9:22–23)?

Thus, the one who boasts boasts only in the Lord (2 Cor. 10:17), when he recognizes that it is not his own but God’s—not only that he exists, but also that it is well with him only through the one from whom he has existence.

11. It is therefore said with excessive impropriety: “There would be no people to whom God could grant such great beneficence of his mercy if they could not exist otherwise than with others in whom he would demonstrate the justice of vengeance.”

## CHAPTER IX.—On the same difficulty.

Why, then, should both not exist, when in both the goodness and the equity of God are rightly proclaimed?

12. “But,” they say, “if God had wished it, these too would have been good.” How much better did God will that they should be what they wished to be—good not without fruit, and evil not without punishment, and in that very respect useful to others! But he foreknew that their will would be evil. He certainly foreknew it; and because his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, the evil will is not his but theirs.

Why, then, did he create those whom he foreknew would become such? Because, just as he foresaw what evil they would do, so he also foresaw what good he himself would bring about from their evil deeds. For he made them in such a way as to leave them something that they themselves could do, so that whatever they might choose—even culpably—they would find him working laudably through them. From themselves they have an evil will; from him, however, they have both a good nature and a just punishment: for themselves, their deserved place; for others, an aid to discipline and an example for fear.

## CHAPTER X.—God can turn the will of the wicked to good; why he does not do so.

13. “But,” they say, “he could also turn their will to good, since he is omnipotent.” Certainly he could. Why, then, did he not do so? Because he did not wish to. Why he did not wish to is his concern. For we ought not to be wiser than we ought to be (Rom. 12:3).

I think, however, that shortly before we showed sufficiently that it is no small good for a rational creature—even this kind that avoids evil by comparison with the wicked—to exist. This kind of good creature would certainly not exist if God had turned all evil wills to good and inflicted on no one the punishment due to iniquity. In that case there would be only the one kind, which would make no progress through comparison with the sin or punishment of the wicked. Thus, as the number of the superior kind were apparently increased, the number of kinds of good would be diminished.

## CHAPTER XI.—God does not need the punishments of the wicked, but through them he provides for the salvation of the good.

14. “Then,” they say, “is there something in God’s works that needs another’s evil in order to advance toward good?” Have people become so deaf and blind, I do not know through what zeal for contention, that they neither hear nor see how, when some are punished, very many are corrected? What pagan, what Jew, what heretic does not prove this daily in his own household?

Yet when the discussion and investigation of truth are reached, people do not wish to turn their attention to their own perceptions, from which work of divine providence the agitation involved in imposing discipline comes upon them. Thus, even if those who are punished are not corrected, the others may nevertheless fear because of their example, and the just destruction of some may contribute to the salvation of others.

Is God the author of the wickedness or depravity of those whose just punishment he uses for the benefit of others, having determined that they should be aided in this way? Certainly not. But although he foreknew that they would become evil through their own vices, he did not cease to create them; he assigned them to the benefit of those whom he created in this category, so that they could advance toward good only by comparison with the wicked. [Note: [Col. 0435] The printed editions here read “through cooperation”; the manuscripts consistently read “by comparison.”]

For if they did not exist, they would certainly be useful to nothing. Is it not a great good that they have been brought into existence, since they are certainly useful to that category? Whoever does not want that category to exist is doing nothing other than ensuring that he himself will not belong to it.

15. “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. 111:2). He foresees who will be good and creates them; he foresees who will be evil and creates them. He offers himself for enjoyment to the good, bestows many of his gifts even upon the evil, mercifully forgiving and justly avenging; likewise, mercifully avenging and justly forgiving. He fears nothing from anyone’s evil, and needs nothing from anyone’s justice. He does nothing for his own benefit from the works of the good, yet benefits the good even through the punishments of the wicked.

Why, then, would he not permit the human being to be tempted by that temptation by which he would be tested [Note: [Col. 0435] In the manuscripts: “of good character”; the printed editions read “to be exposed”], convicted, and punished, when the proud desire for his own power would give birth to what it had conceived and be confounded by its own offspring, and when, through a just punishment, it would deter later generations from the evil of pride and disobedience—generations for whom these events were being prepared to be written down and proclaimed?

## CHAPTER XII.—Why the temptation was permitted to occur through the serpent.

16. If it is asked why the devil was permitted to tempt particularly through the serpent, who would not be reminded that this was done for the sake of signification by the Scripture, which acts in prophecy with such great authority and with such abundant demonstrations of divinity, as the world has already been filled with through its effects?

This is not because the devil wished to signify something for our instruction; but since he could not approach in order to tempt except by permission, could he approach by anything other than that through which he was permitted to approach?

Whatever, therefore, that serpent signified must be attributed to the providence under which the devil himself possesses a desire to harm, but has no power except what is granted—whether for overthrowing and destroying the vessels of wrath, or for humbling or testing the vessels of mercy.

We know, then, whence the nature of the serpent comes: the earth brought forth, at the word of God, all cattle, beasts, and serpents. All this creation, possessing within itself a living and irrational soul, is subject by the law of the divine order to every rational creature, whether of good or evil will (Gen. 1:20–26).

What wonder, then, if the devil was permitted to accomplish something through the serpent, when Christ himself permitted demons to enter pigs (Matt. 8:32)?

## CHAPTER XIII.—Against the Manichaeans, who do not wish the devil to be counted among God’s creatures.

[Col. 0436]

17. It is more often with particular care that people inquire into the nature of the devil, which certain heretics, offended and distressed by the evil of his will, attempt to alienate entirely from the creation of the supreme and true God, assigning him another principle that is opposed to God.

For they are unable to understand that everything that exists—insofar as it is some substance—is also good, and cannot exist except from that true God from whom every good comes. An evil will, however, moves disorderly, preferring lower goods to higher ones. Thus it came about that the spirit of a rational creature, delighting in its own power because of its excellence, swelled with pride, through which it fell from the blessedness of the spiritual paradise and wasted away through envy.

Yet even in this there is something good: the fact that it lives and gives life to a body, whether an airy body, as in the spirit of the devil himself or of demons, or an earthly body, as in the human soul—even the soul of any malicious and perverse person.

Thus, while they refuse to allow anything made by God to sin through its own will, they say that the very substance of God was first corrupted by necessity and afterward by an inexpiable will, becoming perverse. But we have already spoken elsewhere at length about this most insane error of theirs.

## CHAPTER XIV.—The cause of the angelic fall: pride and envy.

18. In this work, however, we must inquire, according to Holy Scripture, what should be said about the devil. First, whether from the beginning of the world, delighting in his own power, he withdrew from that fellowship and love in which the angels who enjoy God are blessed, or whether at some time he belonged to the holy company of the angels, himself likewise just and likewise blessed.

Some say that his fall from the heavenly seats occurred because he envied the human being made in the image of God. But envy follows pride; it does not precede it. For envy is not the cause of becoming proud; pride is the cause of becoming envious.

Since pride is love of one’s own excellence, while envy is hatred of another’s happiness, it is sufficiently clear which gives birth to which. By loving his own excellence, a person either envies equals because they are made equal to him, inferiors lest they become equal to him, or superiors because he is not made equal to them. Thus, by becoming proud one becomes envious; one does not become proud by becoming envious.

## CHAPTER XV.—Pride and private love, the sources of evils. The two loves. The two cities. A promise to discuss *The City of God*.

19. Scripture rightly defines pride as the beginning of every sin, saying: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. 10:15). To this testimony may also be appropriately joined what the Apostle says: “The root of all evils is avarice” (1 Tim. 6:10), if we understand avarice in a general sense, by which each person desires something more than is fitting, on account of his own excellence and a certain love of what belongs to himself.

The Latin language wisely gave this the name *privatum* (“private”), a word that clearly derives from loss rather than increase. For every deprivation diminishes. Therefore, from the very point at which pride wishes to rise above others, it is forced into straitness and poverty, when it is reduced from what is common to what is private through a destructive love of itself.

There is also a particular avarice, more commonly called love of money. By using its name to signify the species as a genus, the Apostle intended general avarice to be understood when he said, “The root of all evils is avarice.” For the devil too fell through this avarice: he certainly did not love money, but his own power.

Thus, a perverse love of self deprives the swollen spirit of holy fellowship and constricts it in misery, while it now desires to be satisfied through iniquity. Hence, in another passage, after saying, “People will be lovers of themselves,” he immediately added, “lovers of money” (2 Tim. 3:2), descending from that general avarice whose head is pride to this particular form that belongs properly to human beings. For human beings would not be lovers of money unless they thought themselves more excellent in proportion as they were richer.

The charity opposed to this disease does not seek what is its own; that is, it does not rejoice in private excellence. Therefore it is rightly said also that it “is not puffed up” (1 Cor. 13:5, 4).

20. These two loves—one holy, the other impure; one social, the other private; one concerned with the common good for the sake of heavenly fellowship, the other reducing even what is common to private power for the sake of arrogant domination; one submissive, the other rivaling God; one tranquil, the other turbulent; one peaceful, the other seditious; one preferring truth to the praises of those who err, the other hungry for praise by any means; one friendly [Note: [Col. 0437] Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “affable”; Amerbach and the manuscripts read “friendly.”], the other envious; one wishing for one’s neighbor what one wishes for oneself, the other wishing to subject one’s neighbor to oneself; one ruling one’s neighbor for the neighbor’s benefit, the other for its own benefit—preceded among the angels, one in the good and the other in the evil.

They distinguished the two cities founded among the human race under the wondrous and ineffable providence of God, who administers and orders all created things: one city of the just, the other of the unjust. Through a certain temporal intermingling, their history proceeds until the final judgment separates them. Then one, joined to the good angels under its king, will receive eternal life; the other, joined to the evil angels under its king, will be sent into eternal fire.

Concerning these two cities we shall perhaps discuss at greater length elsewhere, if the Lord wills.

## CHAPTER XVI.—When the devil fell.

21. When, then, pride cast down the devil, so that he perverted his good nature by an evil will, Scripture does not say. Yet reason plainly declares that this happened first, and that from this he envied the human being.

It is evident to all who observe these things that pride does not arise from envy; rather, envy arises from pride. It cannot, however, be thought without reason that the devil fell through pride at the beginning of time, and that there was no earlier period in which he lived peacefully and blessedly with the holy angels, but that from the very beginning of creation he apostatized from his creator.

Thus we may understand both elements in what the Lord says: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44)—not only that he was a murderer from the beginning, but also that he did not stand in the truth from the beginning [Col. 0438].

He was a murderer from the beginning at which a human being could be killed; for no one could be killed before there was someone to be killed. The devil was therefore a murderer from the beginning because he himself killed the first human being, before whom there had been no human beings.

But he did not stand in the truth from the beginning at which he himself was created—for he would have stood if he had wished to stand.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Whether the devil was blessed before his sin.

22. For how can it be believed that he led a blessed life among the blessed angels when he was not foreknowing of his future sin and punishment—that is, of abandonment and eternal fire? If he was not foreknowing, it is rightly asked why he was not. [Note: [Col. 0438] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venice edition read: “that is, of abandonment and eternal fire; if he was not foreknowing, it is rightly asked why he was not.” Manuscript M has this reading.]

For the holy angels are not uncertain of their eternal life and blessedness. For how could they be blessed if uncertain? Shall we say that God did not wish to reveal to the devil, while he was still a good angel, either what he would do or what he would suffer, while he revealed to the others that they would remain forever in his truth?

If this is so, then he was already not equally blessed—or rather, he was not fully blessed at all—for those who are fully blessed are certain of their blessedness, so that no fear disturbs it. On account of what evil desert, then, was he distinguished from the others, so that God did not reveal to him even what concerned his own future? Was he perhaps an avenger before he was a sinner? Far from it: God does not condemn the innocent.

Or perhaps he belonged to another order of angels, to whom God did not grant foreknowledge even of their own future? I do not see how those can be blessed whose very blessedness is uncertain.

Some have also held that the devil did not belong to that sublime nature of the angels which is heavenly, but to those who were made somewhat lower in the world and assigned different offices. Such beings might perhaps take pleasure in something unlawful; yet, if they did not wish to sin, they could restrain that pleasure by free choice—just as the human being could, especially the first human being, who did not yet have the punishment of sin in his members, since even that punishment is overcome through God’s grace by holy men subject to God.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—How the human being was blessed before sin.

23. This question concerning the blessed life—whether someone should be said already to possess it when it is uncertain whether it will remain with him or misery will one day follow [Note: [Col. 0438] The manuscripts read, “whose uncertainty is whether,” etc.]—can also arise concerning the first human being himself. For if he was foreknowing of his future sin and of the divine vengeance, how could he be blessed? Therefore he was in paradise but not blessed.

But was he not foreknowing of his future sin? Then, through this ignorance, was he either uncertain of that same blessedness—and how was he truly blessed already?—or certain through a false hope rather than through knowledge—and how was he not foolish?

24. Nevertheless, we can understand the blessed life in a certain sense as belonging to the human being while he was still established in an animal body, living obediently and still destined to receive the fellowship of angels and the transformation of his body from animal to spiritual, even if he was not foreknowing of his future sin.

For those to whom the Apostle says, “You who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1), were not foreknowing either. Yet we may say, neither absurdly nor improperly, that they were already blessed precisely because they were spiritual—not in body, but in the righteousness of faith, rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation (Rom. 12:12).

How much more, then, and in a greater manner, was the human being blessed in paradise before sin, although uncertain of his future fall? He rejoiced in hope because of the reward of a future transformation, and there was no tribulation for which patience would have to contend.

Although he was not certain of what was uncertain through a vain presumption, like a fool, but was not faithless in his hope, he could rejoice before he attained that life in which he would be utterly certain of his eternal life—rejoice, as it is written, “with trembling” (Ps. 2:11). Through this rejoicing he could be blessed in paradise far more abundantly than the saints on earth, though in a manner inferior to that eternal life of the holy and heavenly angels, but not without blessedness altogether.

## CHAPTER XIX.—The condition of the angels.

25. To say of certain angels that they could be blessed in their own order while uncertain of their future iniquity and condemnation, or at least of their perpetual salvation, without even possessing the hope that at some point they themselves would become certain of this through some transformation for the better, is a presumption scarcely tolerable.

Unless perhaps it is said that these angels were created and assigned to worldly ministries under other, higher, and more blessed beings, so that, under their superiors who directed them rightly, they might receive that blessed and more exalted life of which they could be certain—and that, rejoicing in the hope of it, they could appropriately already be called blessed.

If the devil fell from this number together with the companions of his iniquity, this would resemble the fall of human beings from the righteousness of faith: they too transgress through a similar pride, either deceiving themselves or consenting to that deceiver.

26. Let those who can establish it assert, according to Scripture, that there were these two orders of good angels: one heavenly, among whom was never found the one who by falling became the devil; the other worldly, among whom he was found.

For myself, I confess that I do not presently find from Scripture a basis for asserting this second view. But, constrained by the question whether he was foreknowing of his fall before he fell—for otherwise I would have to say that the angels were or had once been uncertain of their own blessedness—I said that it could reasonably be thought that the devil fell from the very beginning of creation, that is, from the very beginning either of time or of his own condition, and that he never stood in the truth.

## CHAPTER XX.—The opinion that the devil was created in wickedness.

27. Hence some maintain that he did not turn aside into this wickedness by the free choice of his will, but that he was created altogether in this condition, although by the Lord God, supreme and true Creator of all natures. They adduce as testimony the Book of Job, since it is written there, when the discussion concerns him: “This is the beginning of the Lord’s work, which he made in order to be mocked by his angels” (Job 40:14, according to the Septuagint). To this agrees what is written in the Psalm [Col. 0440]: “This dragon whom you formed to mock him” (Ps. 103:26), except that here it says “whom you formed,” whereas there it does not say, “This is the beginning of the Lord’s work”—as though at the beginning he had formed him in such a way that he would be evil, envious, a deceiver, altogether the devil: not corrupted by his will, but created so.

## CHAPTER XXI — This Opinion Refuted

28. How, then, is this opinion not opposed to what is written, “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1:31), although they try to demonstrate it? It is not foolish or unlearned to assert that not only in its original condition, but even now, despite so many corrupted wills, everything that has been created—that is, the whole of creation—is nevertheless very good. This does not mean that the evil beings in it are good, but that by their malice they do not cause the beauty and order of the universe to be disfigured or disturbed in any part under the rule, power, and wisdom of God its governor. For to each will, even evil wills, are assigned determinate and appropriate limits of power and weights of merit, so that, with all things—including those wills—fittingly and justly ordered, the universe is beautiful.

Nevertheless, since any person may perceive, and it is true and evident, that it is contrary to justice for God, without any preceding merit, to condemn in anyone the very thing that he himself had created in that person; and since the definite and manifest condemnation of the devil and his angels is proclaimed in the Gospel, where the Lord foretold that he would say to those on his left, “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41), we must by no means believe that the nature created by God is punished by the penalty of eternal fire. Rather, it is the evil of his own will that is punished.

*[Note: In the printed editions and manuscripts, after “very good” some add: “Where is the devil found not to have been corrupted by his own will, but to have been made very evil by the Lord God himself?” A censor, neither imprudent nor recent, noted in the Colbertine manuscript that this is a gloss. Soon afterward the printed editions read: “Although they try to demonstrate this absurdly”; but the manuscripts have “not absurdly.”]*

## CHAPTER XXII — The Foundations of the Same Opinion Overturned

29. Nor does the statement, “This is the beginning of the Lord’s work, which he made in order to be mocked by his angels,” signify his nature. It signifies either the ethereal body which he fitted suitably to such a will; or the ordering by which he made him useful to the good even against his will; or the fact that, foreknowing that he would become evil by his own will, God nevertheless created him, not withholding his goodness in granting life and substance even to a future harmful will *[Note: Several manuscripts have “of the future will.”]*, while at the same time foreseeing how many good things he would bring about through him by his wondrous goodness and power.

He is called “the beginning of the Lord’s work, which he made in order to be mocked by his angels,” not because God first created him, or created him evil at the beginning, but because, knowing that he would become evil by his own will in order to harm the good, he created him so that he himself might benefit the good through him. This is what is meant by “in order to be mocked by his angels”: he is mocked when his temptations benefit the holy, though he attempts through them to corrupt them, so that the wickedness in which he chose to exist becomes useful, against his will, to God’s servants. God formed him with this foreknowledge.

Therefore he is called [Col. 0441] “the beginning” of mockery because he precedes those others both in antiquity of time and in primacy of wickedness. God does this to him through the holy angels, by that work of providence through which he governs created natures: namely, by subjecting evil angels to good angels, so that the wickedness of the evil may accomplish not as much as it strives to accomplish, but only as much as it is permitted to accomplish. This applies not only to evil angels but also to human beings, until even that justice “by which one lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), now patiently exercised in human beings, is turned into judgment (Ps. 93:15), so that they too may judge not only the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19:28), but also angels (1 Cor. 6:3).

## CHAPTER XXIII — How the Devil Is to Be Understood Never to Have Stood in the Truth

30. The belief, then, that the devil never stood in the truth and never led a blessed life with the angels, but fell from the very beginning of his creation, must not be understood as though he were thought to have been created evil by the good God, rather than corrupted by his own will. Otherwise he would not be said to have fallen from the beginning, for he did not fall if he was made such.

Rather, as soon as he was made, he turned himself away from the light of truth, swollen with pride and corrupted by delight in his own power. Thus he did not taste the sweetness of the blessed and angelic life; he did not disdain it after receiving it, but abandoned and lost it by refusing to receive it. Consequently, he could not have foreknown his own fall, since wisdom is the fruit of piety.

But being immediately impious, and consequently blind in mind, he did not fall from what he had received, but from what he would have received had he been willing to submit to God. Because he refused, he fell from what he would have received, yet he did not escape the power of the one under whom he refused to exist. The weight of his merits was therefore established in him, so that he could neither delight in the light of justice nor be freed from its judgment.

## CHAPTER XXIV — The Statement “How He Fell” Is to Be Understood of the Devil’s Mystical Body

31. What is said of him through the prophet Isaiah—“How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, he who rose at dawn? He has been crushed to the earth, who sent forth to all the nations? But you said in your mind, ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will place my throne; I will sit on the high mountain, above the high mountains that are toward the north; I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’ But now you will descend to the underworld” (Isa. 14:12–14)—and the other statements that, under the figure of the king of Babylon, are understood to have been spoken against the devil, apply in many respects to his body, which he also gathers from the human race, and especially to those who cling to him through pride by apostatizing from the commandments [Col. 0442] of God.

For just as the one who was the devil is called a human being, as in the Gospel: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. 13:28), so one who was a human being is called the devil, as again in the Gospel: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71).

And just as the body of Christ, which is the Church, is called Christ—as in the statement, “You are Abraham’s seed,” when a little earlier he had said, “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed”; he does not say, “and to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one, “and to your seed,” which is Christ (Gal. 3:29, 16)—and again, “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Cor. 12:12): so, in the same way, the body of the devil, whose head is the devil—that is, the multitude of the impious, and especially those who fall from Christ or from the Church as from heaven—is called the devil. Many things are figuratively said of this body that apply not so much to the head as to the body and its members.

Thus Lucifer, who rose at dawn and fell, may be understood as the race of apostates, whether from Christ or from the Church. This race is turned to darkness after losing the light that it bore, just as those who turn to God pass from darkness to light—that is, those who were darkness become light.

## CHAPTER XXV — The Statement “You Are the Seal” Is Also Spoken of the Same Body of the Devil; Paradise Is the Church

32. Likewise, what is understood to have been spoken through the prophet Ezekiel against the devil under the figure of the prince of Tyre—“You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God; you were adorned with every precious stone” (Ezek. 28:12–13)—and the other statements, apply not so much to the prince himself, the spirit of wickedness, as to his body.

For the Church is called paradise, as it is written in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, a sealed fountain, a well of living water, a paradise with the fruit of apple trees” (Song 4:12–13).

From this paradise all heretics have fallen, either through open and bodily separation, or through hidden and spiritual separation—even though they appear bodily to remain in it—all who have returned to their vomit after having walked for a little while in the way of righteousness following the remission of all their sins. In them, “the last state has become worse than the first,” and for them it would have been better not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them (Prov. 26:11; 2 Pet. 2:21–22).

The Lord describes this most wicked generation when he says that an unclean spirit goes out from a person, then returns with seven other spirits more wicked than itself and enters the house it had found cleansed, so that “the last state of that person is worse than the first” (Matt. 12:43–45).
