To such a human race, which has now become the body of the devil, these words may apply: “From the day on which you were created, you were with the cherub”—that is, with the throne of God, whose interpretation is “increased knowledge”—“and I placed you on the holy mountain of God,” that is, in the Church. Hence the Psalm says, “He heard me from his holy mountain” (Ps. 3:5).

“You were among fiery stones,” that is, among saints burning with the Spirit, living stones. “You walked without fault in your days, from the day on which you were created until iniquities were found in you” (Ezek. 28:14–15).

*[Col. 0443]* These matters may be treated with greater care, so that it may perhaps be shown not only that this interpretation can be present in these words, but that no entirely different interpretation is possible.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Conclusion Concerning the Devil’s Creation and Fall

33. But because this is lengthy and requires another discourse devoted solely to this question, let this summary suffice for now: either the devil fell through impious pride from the blessedness that he would have obtained had he wished to receive it from the beginning of his creation; or there were other angels of a lower ministry in this world, among whom he lived according to a certain blessedness that did not include foreknowledge, and from whose fellowship he fell, together with the angels subject to him, as an archangel, through proud impiety—if this can in any way be maintained, which would indeed be remarkable if it could *[Note: Erasmus and Louvain have “through the impiety of pride”; but this cannot in any way be maintained, whereas the other reading would be remarkable if it could. It seemed preferable to restore the reading of the manuscripts.]*; or else we must seek an explanation of how all the holy angels, if the devil once lived blessedly among them with his angels, did not themselves yet possess certain foreknowledge of their own perpetual happiness, but received it after his fall; or on what merit, before his sin, the devil with his companions was separated from the other angels, so that he was ignorant of his future fall while they were certain of their perseverance.

Nevertheless, we must have no doubt that the sinful angels have been thrust down as into a prison, into this dark air around the earth, and are being kept for punishment at the judgment, according to apostolic faith (2 Pet. 2:4). Nor is there any uncertain eternal life in the heavenly blessedness of the holy angels; and, according to God’s mercy, grace, and most faithful promise, our future life will not be uncertain when we have been joined to them after the resurrection and the transformation of these bodies.

For this hope we live, and by the grace of that promise we are restored. Whatever else may be said concerning why God created the devil, knowing that he would become such, and why the Almighty does not turn his will toward the good, may be understood, believed, or discovered in some better way, in accordance with what we discussed when we considered the same question concerning evil human beings.

## CHAPTER XXVII — The Devil’s Temptation through the Serpent

34. Therefore, by the one whose power is supreme over all that he has created, and through the holy angels by whom the devil is mocked, even when the Church of God makes use of his own malevolence *[Note: Louvain has “is consoled.” Other manuscripts have “is consulted,” or “is taken into consultation.”]*, he was not permitted to tempt the woman except through the serpent, nor the man except through the woman.

In the serpent he himself spoke, using it as an instrument and moving its nature in the manner in which it could move and be moved, so as to produce the sounds of words and bodily signs by which the woman could understand the will of the one persuading her.

But in the woman herself, since she was a rational creature capable of using her own movement to produce words, he did not speak. Rather, it was his operation and persuasion, although by a hidden impulse he inwardly assisted [Col. 0444] what he had outwardly done through the serpent.

If he had acted only by a more hidden impulse, as he acted in Judas so that he might betray Christ (John 13:2), he could have effected this in a soul induced by proud love of its own power. But, as I have already said, the devil has the will to tempt; he has neither the power to carry out whatever he wishes nor to determine how he will carry it out.

Since he was therefore permitted, he tempted; and in the manner in which he was permitted, he tempted. He neither knew nor desired what benefit his action would bring to what class of human beings; and by that very fact he was mocked by the angels.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Whether the Serpent Understood the Words Spoken

35. The serpent did not understand the sounds of the words that came from it to the woman. We must not believe that its soul was transformed into a rational nature. Even human beings, whose nature is rational, do not know what they are saying when a demon speaks within them through that condition for which an exorcist is required; how much less could the serpent understand the sounds of the words that the devil produced through it and from it in that manner? For the serpent would not understand a human being speaking if it heard him while he was free from demonic affliction.

It is also believed that serpents hear and understand the words of the Marsi, so that when these people chant their spells the serpents often leap from their hiding places. Even there, too, a demonic power is at work, in order that divine providence may be recognized everywhere: providence that subjects each thing to whatever natural order is appropriate to it, and that, by its supremely wise power, permits evil wills to do certain things. Thus custom has come to associate serpents being moved by human incantations more than any other kind of living creature.

This too is no small testimony that human nature was originally seduced through conversation with the serpent. Demons rejoice that this power is granted to them, so that by human incantations they may move serpents and deceive people in whatever way they can. They are permitted to do this in order to commemorate the first deed, because there is a certain familiarity between them and this kind of creature.

Moreover, the first deed itself was permitted so that, through the nature of the serpent, the likeness of every demonic temptation might be signified to the human race, for whose instruction these events had to be written down. This will become evident when the divine sentence begins to be pronounced against the serpent.

## CHAPTER XXIX — Why the Serpent Is Called the Most Prudent

36. The serpent is therefore called the most prudent of all the beasts—that is, the most cunning—because of the cunning of the devil, who was acting deceitfully in it and through it. In the same way, a tongue is called prudent or cunning when a prudent or cunning person moves it to persuade someone prudently or cunningly.

This power or virtue does not belong to the bodily member called the tongue, but to the mind that uses it. So too the “lying stylus of the scribes” is called lying. For lying belongs only to a living and perceptive being; the stylus is called lying because through it a liar acts deceitfully. In the same way, this serpent could be called lying because the devil used it as a stylus for deception.

37. I have thought it necessary to emphasize this, lest anyone, supposing that creatures without reason possess human understanding or are suddenly transformed into rational animals, [Col. 0445] be led astray into that ridiculous and harmful opinion of the transmigration of souls—whether of human beings into beasts or of beasts into human beings.

Thus the serpent spoke to the human being just as the donkey on which Balaam sat spoke to a human being (Num. 22:28), except that the former was a work of the devil and the latter of an angel. For good and evil angels have certain similar works, as Moses and the magicians of Pharaoh did (Exod. 7:10–11).

Yet even in such matters the good angels are more powerful. Evil angels cannot perform even such works except insofar as God permits them through the good angels, so that each person may receive according to his heart or according to the grace of God. Both are done justly and kindly through “the depth of the riches of the wisdom of God” (Rom. 11:33).

## CHAPTER XXX — The Serpent’s Conversation with the Woman

38. The serpent therefore said to the woman, “Why has God said, ‘You shall not eat from every tree of the paradise’?” And the woman said to the serpent, “We shall eat from the fruit of the tree that is in the paradise. But concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the paradise, God said, ‘You shall not eat from it, nor touch it, lest you die.’”

The serpent first asked, and the woman answered, so that her transgression would be inexcusable and it could not in any way be said that the woman had forgotten what God had commanded. Even forgetfulness of a command—especially a single and so necessary command—would belong to the greatest culpable negligence and would deserve condemnation. Yet her transgression is more evident when she retains the command in her memory and, as though God were present and standing before her in that command, nevertheless despises him.

Thus it was necessary that, when the Psalm said, “and to those who remember his commandments,” it should add, “to do them” (Ps. 102:18). For many remember them in order to despise them; this is a greater sin of transgression, where forgetfulness offers no excuse.

39. The serpent therefore said to the woman, “You shall not surely die. For God knows that on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

Would the woman have believed from these words that she had been forbidden by God to do something good and beneficial, unless there had already been in her mind that love of her own power and a certain proud presumption concerning herself, which that temptation was intended to expose and humble?

Finally, not content with the serpent’s words, she looked at the tree and saw that it was good for food and attractive to the eyes. Not believing that she could die from it, I suppose she thought that God had said, “If you eat, you will die,” for some symbolic reason. Therefore she took its fruit and ate, and also gave it to her husband who was with her—perhaps even with a persuasive word, which Scripture leaves unstated but invites us to understand.

Or perhaps the man no longer needed persuasion, since he saw that she had not died from eating it.

## CHAPTER XXXI — Why the Eyes of Adam and Eve Were Opened

40. They therefore ate, and the eyes of both were opened. Opened for what, except to desire one another, as a punishment for sin conceived in the death of the flesh itself? Their body was no longer merely an animal body, which, if they had preserved obedience, could have been changed without death into a better and spiritual condition. It had now become a body of death, in which “the law [Col. 0446] in the members” fought against “the law of the mind” (Rom. 7:23).

They had not been made with closed eyes, nor had they wandered blindly and gropingly through the paradise of delights, so that they touched the forbidden tree without knowing it and, groping among the fruits, plucked the forbidden ones in ignorance.

How, then, were the animals and birds brought to Adam so that he could see what he should call them, if he could not see? And how was the woman herself brought to the man when she was made, so that, seeing her, he could say, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” and so forth (Gen. 2:19, 22–23), if he did not see her?

Finally, how did the woman see that the tree was good for food, pleasing to the eyes, and attractive to behold, if their eyes were closed?

41. Nevertheless, the whole passage should not for that reason be taken figuratively because of the translation of a single word. Let the reader determine how the serpent meant the words, “Your eyes will be opened.” The writer of the book reported that the serpent said this; in what sense or with what meaning he said it, he left for the reader to consider.

But what is written—“The eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked”—is written in the same manner as all the events that are narrated. Nor should it therefore lead us into an allegorical narrative.

The evangelist narrator, for example, did not insert figurative words spoken by someone else as though they were his own, but narrated from his own standpoint what had happened when he said of the two men, one of whom was Cleopas, that when the Lord had broken bread for them, “their eyes were opened, and they recognized him,” whom they had not recognized on the road (Luke 24:13–31). They had not been walking with closed eyes, but were unable to recognize him.

Thus, in that passage as well as here, the narrative is not figurative, even though Scripture uses a transferred expression when it says that eyes were opened which had already been open: they were opened to see and consider something to which they had never before paid attention.

For when bold curiosity was aroused to transgress the command—eager to test what would follow from touching what was forbidden—and when they took pleasure in breaking through the restraints of prohibition with a harmful freedom, judging it more likely that death would not follow than that the death they had feared would follow, we should reasonably believe that the fruit of that tree was of the same kind as fruits they had already experienced harmlessly on other trees.

Thus they believed all the more that God could easily forgive sinners than they were willing patiently to remain ignorant of what the thing was or why he had forbidden them to take food from it.

As soon, therefore, as they transgressed the command, having been completely stripped inwardly when grace departed—the grace they had offended by a certain arrogance and proud love of their own power—they turned their eyes upon their own members and desired them with the movement they had not previously known.

Their eyes were therefore opened to what had not previously been visible to them, although they had been open to other things.

## CHAPTER XXXII — The Origin of Mortality and Lust; Fig-Leaf Coverings

42. This death occurred on the very day on which the act forbidden by God was committed. For when they lost their wondrous condition, the body [Col. 0447] itself—which had also been sustained in that condition by the mystical power of the tree of life, so that they could neither be afflicted by disease nor altered by age, and in whose flesh, although it was still animal and would later be changed for the better, the food of the tree of life already signified that which comes to the angels from that spiritual nourishment, wisdom, whose sacrament that tree was—by participation in eternity, so that they are not changed for the worse: when, I say, they lost this condition, their bodies acquired a diseased and deadly quality, such as is also present in the flesh of animals.

Consequently, they also acquired the movement by which the desire for sexual intercourse arises in animals, so that those being born might replace those who die. Yet even in this punishment, the rational soul, an indicator of its noble origin, blushed at the animal movement in the members of its flesh and was struck with shame not only because they experienced it in a place where they had never before felt anything of the kind, but also because that shameful movement arose from the transgression of the command.

There they perceived the grace with which they had previously been clothed, when in their nakedness they suffered nothing indecent. There was fulfilled the Psalm: “You granted strength to my beauty according to your will; but you turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (Ps. 29:8).

Finally, in that disturbance they ran to the leaves of a fig tree, sewed coverings for themselves, and because they had abandoned what was worthy of glory, they covered what was shameful.

I do not think they consciously considered that those leaves were suitable for covering members that had now begun to itch. Rather, they were driven to this by a hidden impulse in their disturbance, so that, without knowing it, they would also produce a sign of their punishment—one that would convict the sinner through what had been done and instruct the reader through what had been written.

*[Note: Thus the manuscripts. In the printed editions it read: “which would convict the sinner through a false deed and instruct the reader through Scripture.”]*

## CHAPTER XXXIII — The Voice of God Walking in the Paradise

43. “And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the paradise toward evening.”

At that hour he had come to visit those who had fallen away from the light of truth. Perhaps before this God spoke with them inwardly in other ways, whether expressible or ineffable, just as he also speaks with the angels by the unchangeable truth itself, illuminating their minds. There the understanding is to know simultaneously all things that do not themselves occur simultaneously in time.

Perhaps, I say, he spoke with them in this way, though not with as great a participation in divine wisdom as the angels receive; nevertheless, he spoke according to the human measure, however much less that might be, but through the same kind of visitation and speech.

Perhaps he also spoke through the mode that occurs by means of a creature, whether in an ecstasy of the spirit through bodily images, or through some form presented to the bodily senses, either for seeing or hearing, just as God is accustomed to appear or sound through a cloud in his angels.

Now, however, when they heard the voice of God walking in the paradise toward evening, this occurred visibly only through a creature, lest that invisible substance—which is wholly everywhere and belongs to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—be believed to have appeared to their bodily senses through local and temporal movement.

44. “And Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face [Col. 0448] of the Lord God amid the tree that is in the paradise.”

When God turns his face away inwardly and a human being becomes troubled, we should not be surprised that things occur which resemble madness through excessive shame and fear. The hidden impulse also continued, driving them unknowingly to do things that would signify something to their descendants, who would one day learn of them and for whose sake these events were written down.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — Adam, Hiding Because of His Nakedness, Is Questioned by God

45. “And the Lord God called Adam and said to him, ‘Where are you?’”

This is the voice of one reproving, not of one who is ignorant. It also has a certain symbolic significance that, just as the command was given to the man through whom it would reach the woman, so the man is questioned first.

The command came from the Lord through the man to the woman; but sin came from the devil through the woman to the man. These events are full of mystical meanings, although the agents in whom they occurred were not acting to produce those meanings; rather, the exceedingly powerful wisdom of God was acting through them.

For the present, however, we are not disclosing the meanings signified, but defending the historic events.

46. Adam therefore replied, “I heard your voice in the paradise, and I was afraid because I am naked, and I hid myself.”

It is sufficiently probable that God was accustomed to appear to those first human beings through a creature suited to such an action, in human form. Yet he never allowed them to notice their nakedness, lifting their attention toward higher things, until after the sin they felt the shameful movement in their members through the punitive law imposed upon those members.

They were therefore affected as people commonly are when they are under the eyes of other people. Such an affectation was part of the punishment of sin: they wished to hide from one whom nothing can hide, and to conceal their flesh from the one who examines the heart.

But why should we be surprised if, in their pride, wishing to be like gods, they “became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened”? Claiming to be wise in their own abundance, they became fools when he turned his face away (Rom. 1:21–22).

What they were already ashamed of before one another, and for which they had made coverings, they were much more afraid to be seen wearing by him who, as though with a familiar adaptation, brought visible eyes through a creature in order to see them as human beings.

If he appeared in this way so that human beings might speak with him as with a human being, as Abraham did by the oak of Mamre (Gen. 18:1), that very semblance of friendship, which had given them confidence before sin, burdened them with shame afterward. They no longer dared to expose their nakedness to such eyes, since it displeased even their own eyes.

## CHAPTER XXXV — Adam’s and Eve’s Excuses

47. The Lord therefore wished to punish the sinners, now questioned according to the manner of justice, with a punishment greater than the one by which they had already been compelled to feel shame:

“Who told you,” he said, “that you were naked, unless it was because you ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you not to eat from it?”

For death had been conceived there, and because of the sentence of God who had threatened it, their members were perceived in concupiscent movement; their eyes were said [Col. 0449] to have been opened, and what caused shame followed.

Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me—she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.”

What pride! Did he say, “I have sinned” *[Note: Thus the manuscripts of good reputation. In other codices: “and I ate. Did he say, ‘I have sinned?’ Pride has it.”]*? Pride has the deformity of confusion, but not the humility of confession.

These things were written down because the questions themselves were surely made so that they might be written truthfully and usefully. If they had been written falsely, they would not have been useful. We are meant to notice what disease of pride afflicts people today: when they do anything evil, they try to attribute it only to the Creator, while wishing to have anything good they do attributed to themselves.

“The woman whom you gave to be with me”—that is, whom you gave so that she might be with me—“she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate,” as though she had been given for this purpose, rather than so that she herself should obey the man and both should obey God.

48. And the Lord God said to the woman, “What have you done?” And the woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

She too does not confess her sin, but shifts the blame to another: unequal in sex, equal in arrogance.

Nevertheless, from these two was born one who did not imitate them, but, exercised by many evils, said—and will say to the end of the age—“I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you’” (Ps. 40:5).

How much better would it have been if these two had spoken in the same way! But the Lord had not yet broken the necks of sinners (Ps. 128:4). There remained labors, the pains of death, and every affliction of the age, as well as the grace of God, by which he comes to the aid of human beings at the appointed time and teaches the afflicted that they must not presume upon themselves.

“The serpent deceived me, and I ate,” as though the persuasion of anyone ought to have been placed before the command of God.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — The Serpent’s Curse

49. And the Lord God said to the serpent:

“Because you have done this, you are cursed above all cattle and above all the beasts that are upon the earth. Upon your breast and your belly you shall walk, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. And I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall watch over your head, and you shall watch over her heel.”

The whole of this sentence is figurative. The faith of the writer and the truth of the narrative require nothing else of it except that we not doubt that it was spoken.

The words “And the Lord God said to the serpent” are merely the words of the writer; these must be understood literally. It is therefore true that something was said to the serpent.

The remaining words are the words of God. It is left to the reader’s free understanding to decide whether they should be taken literally or figuratively, as we stated at the beginning of this work.

Since, then, the serpent was not questioned about why it had done this, it may be understood that it had not done it through its own nature and will. Rather, the devil had acted from it, through it, and in it—the devil who, because of the sin of his impiety and pride, had already been destined for everlasting fire.

What is now said to the serpent, therefore, and plainly refers also to the one who acted through the serpent, is undoubtedly figurative. For in these words that tempter is described as he would be toward the human race. The human race began to be propagated at the time when this sentence was pronounced against the devil as against [Col. 0450] the serpent.

We have explained elsewhere how these words are to be understood when their figures are interpreted: in the two books on Genesis published against the Manichaeans, insofar as we were able. If at another time God should assist us to do so more carefully and appropriately, we will do it. For now, however, our purpose must not be diverted to something other than what we have undertaken, since nothing requires it.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — The Woman’s Punishment
50. And to the woman he said: “Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groaning; in sorrow you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.” These words of God concerning the woman are much more suitably understood figuratively and prophetically. Nevertheless, since the woman had not yet given birth, and since the pain and groaning of childbirth arise only from the body of death—which was conceived through that transgression of the commandment—this punishment may also be referred to the literal sense. The woman did indeed already possess animal limbs, but, had the human being not sinned, those limbs would certainly not have been destined to die; rather, they would have lived under another and happier condition until, after a life well lived, they deserved to be transformed into something better, as we have already indicated in several places above.

The only difficulty is determining how the words “And your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” can be understood literally. For it is not fitting to believe that, even before the sin, the woman was made otherwise than so that the man would rule over her and she would turn toward him in service. Yet this servitude can rightly be understood as having been signified—a condition arising more from subjection than from love—so that even that kind of servitude by which human beings later began to be servants of other human beings may be found to have arisen as a punishment for sin. The Apostle indeed said, “Through love serve one another” (Gal. 5:13); but he would certainly not have said, “Rule over one another.” Thus husbands and wives may serve one another through love; but the Apostle does not permit a woman to rule over a man (1 Tim. 2:12). For God’s sentence assigned this authority rather to the man, and the woman deserved to have a husband as her lord, not by nature but by fault. Yet unless this arrangement is maintained, nature will be further corrupted and guilt increased.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII—Adam’s Punishment and the Name Given to the Woman

51. Then he said also to her husband: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I had commanded you alone not to eat from it, cursed is the earth in your works. In sorrow you shall eat it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall produce for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and into earth you shall go.”

Who does not know that these are the labors of the human race on earth? And since they would not exist if the happiness that had been in paradise had been preserved, there can be no doubt that these words should first be understood literally as well. Nevertheless, the prophetic meaning must also be retained and awaited, for it is chiefly this that God’s intention in speaking here has in view.

Nor was it without reason that Adam himself, moved by some marvelous instinct, then called his wife’s name “Life,” adding, “For she is the mother of all the living.” These words too should be understood as those of the first man himself—not of the narrator who reports or affirms them—when he said, “For she is the mother of all the living,” as though he were supplying the reason for the name he had given her, explaining why he had called her “Life.”

### CHAPTER XXXIX—Garments of Skin; Rebuke of Pride

52. “And the Lord God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.” This too was done for the sake of signification, but it was nevertheless done, just as those things that were spoken for the sake of signification were nevertheless spoken. For this point, which I have often made and am not reluctant to make again, must be required of a narrator of events that actually occurred: he must narrate that things were done which were done, and that things were said which were said. Just as, in the case of deeds, one asks both what was done and what it signifies, so in the case of words one asks both what was said and what it signifies. Whether what is reported to have been said was spoken figuratively or literally, it must nevertheless not be thought that the fact of its having been said is figurative.

53. “And God said, ‘Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.’” However this may have been said, and in whatever manner, since God nevertheless said it, what he meant by “one of us” must be understood in no other way than as a plural referring to the Trinity, just as it was said, “Let us make the human being” (Gen. 1:26), and as the Lord said of himself and the Father, “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Thus the outcome desired by the proud one was turned back upon his head: he had coveted what the serpent suggested, “You shall be like gods.” “Behold,” he says, “Adam has become like one of us.” These are God’s words, intended not so much to mock him as to deter the others for whose sake these things were written, so that they would not become proud in the same way. “He has become,” he says, “like one of us, knowing good and evil.” What else should be understood here than that an example was intended to instill fear: he not only failed to become what he wished to become, but did not preserve even what he had been made?

### CHAPTER XL—Expulsion from Paradise; Excommunication

54. “And now,” God said, “lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.” And the Lord God sent him out from the paradise of delight to work the earth from which he had been taken.

The preceding words are God’s; what followed was an action carried out because of those words. Since he had been alienated from the life that he would have received with the angels had he kept the commandment, and even from the life he had been leading in paradise in a certain happy condition of the body, he necessarily had to be separated from the tree of life—whether that happy condition of the body continued to exist through the tree itself, from a visible thing by an invisible power, or whether the tree also contained a visible sacrament of invisible wisdom. He had to be removed from it, whether because he was already going to die or because he was, as it were, excommunicated, just as in this paradise—that is, the Church—people are customarily removed from the visible sacraments of the altar by ecclesiastical discipline.

55. “And he cast out Adam, and placed him opposite the paradise of delight.” This too was done for the sake of signification, but it was nevertheless done, so that the sinner would dwell opposite paradise, by which the blessed life was also signified spiritually, and would dwell in misery.

“And he appointed cherubim and a flaming sword, which turns, to guard the way to the tree of life.” This must certainly be believed to have been done by the heavenly powers even in the visible paradise, so that through angelic ministry a kind of fiery guardianship would be present there. Yet it must also be beyond doubt that this was not done without signifying something concerning the spiritual paradise.

### CHAPTER XLI—Opinions Concerning Humanity’s Sin: What Its Nature Was

56. I am not unaware that some have thought that those human beings’ desire for knowledge of good and evil had rushed ahead prematurely, and that they wished to acquire at an immature time what had been deferred and more suitably preserved for them. They think that the tempter brought this about so that, by seizing prematurely [Note: Most manuscripts read “by plucking prematurely” (*praecerpendo*).] what was not yet appropriate for beings of their condition, they would offend God, and, being excluded and condemned, would be deprived of the benefit of that thing—which, if they approached it at the proper time, as God intended, they could enjoy profitably.

If they happen to wish to understand that tree not literally, as a real tree with real fruit, but figuratively, this interpretation may have some outcome that is compatible with right faith and credible to the truth.

57. Some have also thought that the first two human beings stole their own marriage and had intercourse before the one who created them had joined them together. They suppose that this matter was signified by the tree from which they had been forbidden to eat until they should be joined at the proper time.

As though they should be believed to have been made at an age when the maturity of puberty had to be awaited! Or as though that union would have been legitimate when it could first take place, but would not take place when it could not yet take place—unless, perhaps, the bride had to be handed over by her father, and the solemnity of the vows, the celebration of the wedding feast, the assessment of the dowry, and the drawing up of the documents had to be awaited.

This is ridiculous. Besides, it departs from the literal account of events, which we have undertaken to uphold and have upheld insofar as God has chosen to grant us the ability.

### CHAPTER XLII—Whether Adam Believed the Serpent, and How He Was Led into Sin

58. What raises the greater difficulty is this: if Adam was already spiritual, though in mind and not in body, how could he have believed what was said through the serpent—that God had forbidden them to eat the fruit of that tree because he knew that, if they did so, they would become like gods through their knowledge of good and evil, as though the Creator had begrudged his creature this one good? It is remarkable if a human being endowed with a spiritual mind could have believed this.

Or was the woman added because Adam himself could not have believed it—because she had a limited understanding and perhaps still lived according to the sense of the flesh rather than according to the spirit of the mind?

[Note: All the books read “was added” (*addita est*), except the Remigian codex, in which the first hand wrote “was approached” (*adita est*); this is not altogether bad if “by the serpent” is understood.] Is this what the Apostle means by not attributing to her the image of God? For he says: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man” (1 Cor. 11:7).

This does not mean that a woman’s mind cannot receive that same image, since he says that in this grace there is neither male nor female (Gal. 3:27–28). Rather, perhaps she had not yet apprehended what comes about through the knowledge of God, and would gradually have apprehended it under the man’s direction and administration.

For it is not without reason that the Apostle says, “Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was made into transgression” (1 Tim. 2:13–14).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “into transgression” (*in praevaricationem*) rather than “in transgression” (*in praevaricatione*). This is not inappropriate if one considers the explanation that follows immediately; nevertheless, the Greek text of the Apostle has *en parabasei* (“in transgression”), which compels us to retain the reading found in the other manuscripts.]

That is, through her the man also transgressed. For the Apostle likewise calls him a transgressor when he says, “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come” (Rom. 5:14). Yet he denies that Adam was deceived. For when questioned, Adam did not say, “The woman whom you gave me deceived me, and I ate”; rather, he said, “She gave me some of the tree, and I ate.” But she said, “The serpent deceived me.”

59. Consider Solomon, a man of such great wisdom. Are we to believe that, in worshiping idols, he thought there was some benefit in it? Yet he was unable to resist the love of women, which was drawing him toward this evil. He did what he knew ought not to be done, lest he grieve those for whose deadly delights he was pining and wasting away (1 Kings 11:4).

So too Adam, after the woman had been deceived and had eaten from the forbidden tree, and had given some to him so that they might eat together, did not wish to grieve her. He believed that she might waste away without his consolation if he alienated himself from her affection, and that their disagreement might bring about her complete destruction.

He was not overcome by the desire of the flesh, which he had not yet experienced as resisting the law of his members against the law of his mind. Rather, he was overcome by a certain friendly goodwill, through which it often happens that a person offends God lest a friend become an enemy. The just outcome of the divine judgment showed that he ought not to have done this.

60. Therefore he too was deceived in another way; but by the serpentine deception through which the woman was deceived, I do not think that he could in any way have been deceived in the same manner in which she could.

The Apostle properly called this “deception”: that what was being suggested, although false, was thought to be true—namely, that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that, if they touched it, they would become like gods, as though he begrudged them divinity, having made them human beings.

But even if some desire for experimentation had troubled the man on account of a certain elevation of mind—which could not escape God, the searcher of inward things—when he saw that the woman had not died after receiving and eating that food, according to what we discussed above, nevertheless, if he already possessed a spiritual mind, I do not think that he could in any way have believed that God had forbidden them that food out of envy.

But why say more? That sin, then, was persuaded upon them in the manner in which such beings could be persuaded; it was nevertheless written down in the manner in which it ought to be read by everyone, even though only a few would understand it as they ought.

# BOOK TWELVE

In this book the discussion concerns paradise, the third heaven to which Paul was caught up, and the various kinds of visions.

[Col. 0453]

### CHAPTER I—The Apostle’s Passage Concerning Paradise to Be Examined

1. From the beginning of the sacred Scripture called Genesis until the first human being was sent out of paradise, throughout eleven books, we have discussed and written down whatever we could and in whatever way we could—whether asserting and defending what is certain to us, or investigating and expressing uncertainty about what is uncertain.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “investigating, conjecturing, and expressing uncertainty.”]

We have not so much prescribed to each person what he should think concerning obscure matters as shown that we ourselves need to be taught in matters about which we have had doubts, removing from the reader the rashness of affirming wherever we have been unable to provide certainty for an opinion.

[Note: Most manuscripts read “the certainty of knowledge” (*scientiae firmitatem*).]

This twelfth book, now freed from the concern that occupied us while we were treating the text of the sacred Scriptures, will discuss the question of paradise more freely and at greater length. We must not be thought to have avoided what the Apostle appears to imply concerning paradise in the third heaven, where he says:

“I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—such a one was caught up to the third heaven. And I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak” (2 Cor. 12:2–4).

2. In these words people ordinarily ask first what he means by “the third heaven.” Then they ask whether he intended paradise to be understood as being there, or whether, after he had been caught up to the third heaven, he was also caught up into paradise, wherever paradise may be located—not as though being caught up to the third heaven were the same as being caught up into paradise, but as though he were first caught up to the third heaven and afterward from there into paradise.

This is so ambiguous that I do not think it can be resolved unless someone finds, not in the Apostle’s present words but perhaps in other passages of Scripture or through clear reasoning, something by which to show either that paradise is in the third heaven or that it is not. For it is not even clear what the third heaven itself is, or whether it should be understood in terms of bodily things or perhaps spiritual things.

One might indeed say that a human being, together with his body, could have been caught up only into some bodily place. But since the Apostle put the matter in such a way that he said he did not know whether he had been caught up in the body or outside the body, who would dare say that he knows what the Apostle said he did not know?

Nevertheless, if neither a spirit without a body can be caught up into bodily places nor a body into spiritual places, this very uncertainty of his seems to compel us to understand—since no one doubts that he wrote these things about himself—that what he was caught up into was of such a nature that it could not be recognized or distinguished as either bodily or spiritual.

### CHAPTER II—How the Apostle Could Have Been Uncertain Whether He Saw Paradise Outside the Body, If He Saw It in Ecstasy

3. When images of bodies are represented either in dreams or in ecstasy, they are not at all distinguished from bodies until a person has been restored to the bodily senses and recognizes that he had been among images that he had not received through bodily sensation.

For when someone awakens from sleep, who does not immediately realize that the things he was seeing were imaginary, although while he was asleep and seeing them he could not distinguish them from the bodily things seen by those who are awake?

I know, however, that something of this sort has happened to me, and therefore I do not doubt that it could or can happen to others: while seeing in a dream, I felt that I was seeing in a dream; and I firmly held and perceived, even while asleep, that those images which are accustomed to deceive our very assent [Note: The printed editions read “our habit” (*consuetudinem*); the manuscripts read “our assent” (*consensionem*).] were not real bodies but were being presented in a dream.

Yet I was sometimes deceived in this respect: I tried to persuade a friend whom I was likewise seeing in a dream that those bodies we were seeing were not bodies but images belonging to dreamers, even though he himself appeared to me among them in the same way as they did. I also told him that what we were saying together was not true, but that he too, while asleep, was seeing something else, and that he did not know at all whether I was seeing these things.

But when I tried to persuade that very person that he did not exist, I was partly led to believe that he did exist—for certainly I would not have spoken to him if I had been affected in every way by the conviction that he did not exist. Thus the soul of a sleeping person, although remarkably awake, could not avoid being led by images of bodies as though they were the bodies themselves.

4. In ecstasy, however, I was once able to hear a certain man speak—a rustic who could scarcely express what he was experiencing—who knew that he was awake and yet saw something not with the eyes of his body. To use his words, as far as I can remember, he said: “My soul was seeing him, not my eyes.”

Yet he did not know whether it was a body or an image of a body. He was not the sort of person to distinguish such matters, but was so straightforwardly faithful that I heard him as though I myself had seen what he said he had seen.

5. Accordingly, if Paul saw paradise in the way that the disk lowered from heaven appeared to Peter (Acts 10:11), or in the way that whatever he wrote he had seen in the Apocalypse appeared to John (Rev. 1:12, etc.), or in the way that the plain with the bones of the dead and their resurrection appeared to Ezekiel (Ezek. 37:1–10), or in the way that God seated, with the seraphim before him and the altar from which a coal was taken to cleanse the Prophet’s lips, appeared to Isaiah (Isa. 6:1–7), it is clear that he could have been ignorant whether he saw these things in the body or outside the body.

### CHAPTER III—The Apostle Was Certain That He Saw the Third Heaven, but Uncertain How He Saw It

6. But if the things were seen outside the body and were not bodies, it may still be asked whether they were images of bodies or that substance which bears no likeness to a body—such as God, the human mind itself, understanding, reason, and the virtues: prudence, justice, chastity, love, piety, and whatever other things there are that we enumerate, distinguish, and define by understanding and thinking.

In contemplating these things, we do not observe their outlines or colors, how they sound, what they smell like, what taste they have in the mouth, or what they report to those who touch them concerning heat or cold, softness or hardness, smoothness or roughness. Rather, we perceive them by another kind of vision, another light, and another evidence of things—one far superior and more certain than the others.

7. Let us therefore return once more to the Apostle’s own words and examine them more carefully, having first established without doubt that the Apostle knew far more, and incomparably more, concerning incorporeal and corporeal nature than we are trying, in whatever way we can, to know.

If, then, he knew that spiritual things cannot be seen through the body and bodily things outside the body, why did he not distinguish, from the things he saw, how he was able to see them? If he was certain that they were spiritual, why was he not consequently also certain that he had seen them outside the body? But if he knew that they were bodily, why did he not also know that they could be seen only through the body?

Why, then, is he uncertain whether he saw them in the body or outside the body, unless perhaps he is likewise uncertain whether they were bodies or likenesses of bodies? Let us first see what there is in the context of these words about which he is not uncertain; then, when what he is uncertain about remains, perhaps it will become apparent from what he is certain about how he can also be uncertain about that.

8. “I know,” he says, “a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—such a one was caught up to the third heaven.”

He therefore knows that fourteen years earlier a man in Christ was caught up to the third heaven; about this he has no doubt, and therefore neither should we doubt it. But he is uncertain whether it was in the body or outside the body. Since he is uncertain, who among us would dare to be certain?

Could this perhaps also entail that we should doubt whether there was a third heaven to which he said the man had been caught up? If the reality itself was shown, then the third heaven was shown. But if some image resembling bodily things was produced, then that was not the third heaven; rather, the apparition was arranged in such a way that he seemed to ascend through a first heaven, above which he saw another, and then, ascending again, saw another above it; when he reached that one, he could say that he had been caught up to the third heaven.

But he neither doubted nor wished us to doubt that the place to which he was caught up was the third heaven. For he prefaced it with the words, “I know,” and began there, so that the only person who does not believe what the Apostle says he knows to be true is the one who does not believe the Apostle.

### CHAPTER IV—That the Place to Which the Apostle Was Caught Up Was Truly the Third Heaven; The Difficulty of How He Could Be Certain of the Heaven Seen and Uncertain of the Manner in Which It Was Seen

9. He knows, then, that a man was caught up to the third heaven. Therefore the place to which he was caught up truly is the third heaven—not some bodily sign which, when it was shown to Moses, he perceived so clearly to be one thing, while the very substance of God was another, that he said, “Show me yourself” (Exod. 33:13); nor some image of a bodily thing which, when John saw it in the spirit, he asked what it was and received the answer, “It is a city,” or “They are peoples,” or something else, when he saw a beast, a woman, waters, or something of that sort (Rev. 13:1; 17:15, 18).

Rather, he says, “I know that a man was caught up to the third heaven.”

10. If he had wished to call a spiritual image resembling a bodily heaven “heaven,” then the image of his body in which he had ascended to that place would likewise have been his body. He would therefore have called it his body, though it was an image of his body, just as he called that heaven heaven, though it was an image of heaven.

He would not have taken care to distinguish what he knew from what he did not know—that is, to say that he knew that a man had been caught up to the third heaven but did not know whether this was in the body or outside the body. He would simply have narrated the vision, calling the things he saw by the names of the things to which they were similar.

For we too say, when we narrate our dreams or some revelation in them, “I saw a mountain; I saw a river; I saw three men,” and so forth, assigning those names to images that resemble the things themselves. But the Apostle says, “I know that one thing; I do not know the other.”

11. Yet if both appeared imaginally, both are known or both are unknown in the same way. But if the heaven was literal, and for that reason is known, how could the body of that man have appeared imaginally?

12. For if a bodily heaven was seen, why was it concealed whether it was seen with bodily eyes? But if it was uncertain whether it was seen with bodily eyes or in the spirit, and therefore he said, “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know,” how was it not also uncertain whether a bodily heaven was truly seen or was displayed imaginally?

Again, if an incorporeal substance was seen—not in some image of a body, but in the way that justice, wisdom, and things of that sort are seen—and if this was heaven, it is also clear that something of this kind cannot be seen with the eyes of this body. Accordingly, if he knew that he had seen something of this kind, he could not be uncertain whether he had seen it through the body.

“I know,” he says, “a man in Christ fourteen years ago.” Let no one who believes me doubt this. “But whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows.”

### CHAPTER V—The Same Difficulty Resolved

13. What, then, do you know—what do you distinguish from what you do not know—so that those who believe are not deceived?

“I know,” he says, “that the same man was caught up to the third heaven.” But that heaven was either a body or a spirit. If it was a body and was seen with bodily eyes, why is it known that it was heaven while it is unknown that it was seen in the body?

But if it was a spirit, then either it presented an image of a body, in which case it is as uncertain whether it was a body as it is uncertain whether it was seen in the body; or it was seen in the way that wisdom is seen by the mind, without any images of bodies, in which case it is nevertheless certain that it could not have been seen through the body.

Therefore either both are certain or both are uncertain. Or how can what was seen be certain while the means by which it was seen is uncertain? For it is clear that an incorporeal nature could not have been seen by him through the body.

As for bodies, even if they can be seen without the body, they are not seen through the body in that way; if such a mode exists, it is entirely different. It is therefore remarkable if it could have deceived the Apostle, or driven him into uncertainty, as though he had seen a bodily heaven with non-bodily eyes and therefore said that he was uncertain whether he had seen it in the body or outside the body.

14. It remains, therefore, perhaps that, since the Apostle could not have lied—he took such care to distinguish what he knew from what he did not know—we should understand that he did not know whether, when he was caught up to the third heaven, he was in the body, in the way that the soul is in the body when the body is said to be alive, whether awake, asleep, or separated from bodily sensations in ecstasy; or whether he had entirely departed from the body, so that the dead body lay there until, after that revelation had been completed, the soul was restored to its dead limbs—not as though it were awakening from sleep or returning once again to its senses after being separated from them in ecstasy, but as though it were wholly dead and came back to life.

Accordingly, what he saw when he was caught up to the third heaven—and what he confirms that he knows—he saw literally, not imaginally. But because he himself was separated from the body, it was uncertain whether he had left behind a completely dead body or whether, according to some condition of a living body, his soul was there while his mind had been seized for the purpose of seeing or hearing the ineffable things of that vision. For this reason, perhaps, he said, “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows.”

### CHAPTER VI—Three Kinds of Vision

15. What is seen literally, rather than imaginally, and is not seen through the body, is seen by that vision which surpasses all the others. I shall explain its kinds and distinctions as far as the Lord assists me.

In this one commandment, when we read, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39), three kinds of vision present themselves. One is through the eyes, by which the letters themselves are seen; the second is through the human spirit, by which an absent neighbor is thought of; the third is through the mind’s contemplation, by which love itself, once understood, is perceived.

Of these three kinds, the first is evident to everyone. Through it heaven and earth and everything visible in them are seen by our eyes. Nor is the second difficult to explain, by which absent bodily things are thought of. We can think of heaven and earth, and of the things we are able to see in them, even while we are in darkness. Although we see nothing with the eyes of the body, we nevertheless contemplate bodily images in the mind, whether real images, as when we see the bodies themselves and retain them in memory, or fabricated images, such as thought is able to form.

[Note: The manuscripts read “form” (*formare*); the printed editions read “imagine” (*imaginari*).]

For we think of Carthage, which we know, in one way, and of Alexandria, which we do not know, in another.

The third kind, by which understood love is perceived, contains things that do not possess images resembling themselves and that are not themselves. A human being, a tree, the sun, and any other bodies—whether heavenly or earthly—are seen when present in their own forms and thought of when absent through images impressed upon the mind. They produce two kinds of visions: one through the bodily senses, and the other through the spirit, which contains those images.

But is love seen one way when present, in the form in which it exists, and another way when absent, in some image resembling it? Certainly not. Rather, insofar as it can be discerned by the mind, it is discerned more by one person and less by another. If some bodily image is thought of, however, love itself is not perceived.

### CHAPTER VII—Kinds of Vision: Bodily, Spiritual, Intellectual; Bodily Vision Literally and Figuratively; The Many Meanings of “Spiritual”

16. These are the three kinds of vision about which we also said something in the preceding books, as the subject required, although we did not then mention their number. Now that we have briefly introduced them, since the question we have undertaken demands that we discuss them somewhat more fully, we ought to designate them with precise and appropriate names, lest we waste time by continual circumlocution.

Let us therefore call the first bodily, because it is perceived through the body and presented to the bodily senses. Let us call the second spiritual. Whatever is not a body and yet is something is rightly called a spirit. An image of an absent body is certainly not a body, although it resembles a body; nor is it the very act of sight by which the image is perceived. Let us call the third intellectual, from “intellect,” because it would be excessively awkward, merely on account of the novelty of the word, to call it “mental,” from “mind.”

17. If I were to explain the rationale of these terms more subtly, my discourse would become both longer and more involved, while there is little or certainly not so much necessity for doing so. It is enough to know that “bodily” may be used literally when bodies are under discussion, or figuratively, as when it is said, “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.”

Divinity is not a body. But because he calls the sacraments of the Old Testament shadows of what was to come, he said that the fullness of divinity dwells in Christ bodily by comparison with those shadows: everything signified in those shadows is fulfilled in him, and thus, in a certain sense, he himself is the body of those shadows (Col. 2:9, 17)—that is, he himself is the reality of those figures and significations.

Thus, just as the figures themselves were called “shadows” figuratively rather than literally, so when he said that the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, he used the word figuratively.

18. “Spiritual,” however, is said in several ways. The Apostle calls the body that will exist in the resurrection of the saints “spiritual” when he says, “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:44). He means that it will be subjected to the spirit in marvelous ways, with complete facility and incorruption, and will be given life by the spirit alone, without any need for bodily nourishment—not that it will possess an incorporeal substance.

For the body we now have does not possess the substance of the soul either, and this is why it is called “animal,” from *anima* (“soul”).

The air, or its breath—that is, its movement—is also called “spirit,” as it is said: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, and the spirit of the storm” (Ps. 148:8).

The soul of an animal or of a human being is also called “spirit,” as it is written: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam goes upward, and whether the spirit of the animal goes downward into the earth?” (Eccl. 3:21).

The rational mind itself is also called “spirit,” for there is in it something like the eye of the soul, to which the image and knowledge of God belong. Hence the Apostle says, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who has been created according to God” (Eph. 4:23–24), while elsewhere he says of the inner person, “who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him” (Col. 3:10).

Again, after saying, “I myself serve the law of God with the mind, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25), he recalls the same thought elsewhere: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Gal. 5:17). What he had called “mind,” he also called “spirit.”

God himself is also called “spirit,” as the Lord says in the Gospel: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

### CHAPTER VIII—Why the Second Kind of Vision Is Called “Spiritual”

19. We did not derive the term by which we called this kind of vision “spiritual” from any of the meanings of “spirit” that we have mentioned, but from one particular usage found in the Epistle to the Corinthians, where spirit is distinguished from mind by the clearest testimony.

“For if I pray in a tongue,” he says, “my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.”

When he is understood in this passage to mean by “tongue” obscure and mystical significations, from which the mind’s understanding is removed, no one is edified by hearing what he does not understand.

[Note: The Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions read “tongue” (*lingua*). M.] Hence he also says, “For one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to human beings but to God; for no one hears, although in the spirit he speaks mysteries.”

This sufficiently indicates that here he calls “tongue” the place where there are signs, as it were images and likenesses of things, which require the mind’s contemplation in order to be understood. When they are not understood, he says that they are in the spirit, not in the mind.

Thus he says more plainly: “If you bless in the spirit, how will the one who occupies the place of the uninitiated say ‘Amen’ over your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?”

Since signs of things are also given through the tongue—that is, through the bodily member we move in the mouth when we speak—and not the things themselves, he used “tongue” figuratively for any utterance of signs before they are understood. When understanding, which properly belongs to the mind, is added, there is revelation, knowledge, prophecy, or teaching.

Accordingly, he says, “If I come to you speaking in tongues, what good will I do you unless I speak to you in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching?” (1 Cor. 14:14, 2, 16, 6). That is, signs must be accompanied by understanding: the intellect must be added to the tongue, so that what is being done may be done not only in the spirit but also in the mind.

### CHAPTER IX—Prophecy Belongs to the Mind
20. Therefore, when signs were displayed in the spirit through certain likenesses of bodily things, prophecy had not yet occurred unless the activity of the mind had been added, so that they might also be understood; indeed, the one who interpreted what another had seen was more truly a prophet than the one who had seen it. Hence it appears that prophecy pertains more to the mind than to that spirit which, in a particular sense, is called “spirit”—a certain power of the soul inferior to the mind, in which likenesses of bodily things are represented. Thus Joseph was more a prophet, because he understood what the seven ears of grain and the seven cows signified, than Pharaoh, who saw them in a dream (Gen. 41:1–32). For the spirit of the one was fashioned so that he might see; the mind of the other was enlightened so that he might understand. Accordingly, in the one there was “tongue,” in the other prophecy: in the one, the imagining of things; in the other, the interpretation of those imaginings.

The one who sees in the spirit only the signs of the things signified, through images of bodily things, is therefore a lesser prophet; greater is the one endowed only with their understanding. But greatest of all is the prophet who excels in both respects: who sees in the spirit the significant likenesses of bodily things and understands them through the liveliness of the mind, as Daniel’s excellence was tested and proved when he both told the king the dream he had seen and disclosed what it signified (Dan. 2:27–45; 4:16–24). For the bodily images themselves had been impressed upon his spirit, and their meaning had been revealed in his mind.

Accordingly, in accordance with this mode in which “spirit” is used in the distinction expressed by the Apostle—“I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15)—so that signs of things might be formed in the spirit and their meaning shine forth in the mind, I say that, in accordance with this distinction, we have now called “spiritual” that kind of vision in which we think of images even of absent bodies.

## CHAPTER X — The intellectual kind of vision

21. The intellectual kind, however, is the more excellent kind, properly belonging to the mind. I do not at all see how “understanding” can be said in as many ways as we have found “spirit” to be called in many ways. Whether we call it “intellectual” or “intelligible,” we mean the same thing. Some, however, have wished to distinguish the terms somewhat, so that an intelligible thing is that which can be perceived by the intellect alone, whereas an intellectual thing is the mind that understands. But whether there can be a thing that can be discerned by the intellect alone and yet does not itself understand is a great and difficult question. I do not think anyone would either suppose or say that there is a thing which perceives through the intellect but cannot itself be perceived through the intellect; for the mind is perceived only by the mind. Since, therefore, it can be seen, it is intelligible; since it can also see, it is intellectual, according to that distinction. Accordingly, setting aside that extremely difficult question—whether there is something that is only understood but does not understand—we now use “intellectual” and “intelligible” with the same meaning.

## CHAPTER XI — Bodily vision is referred to spiritual vision, and spiritual vision to intellectual vision

[Col. 0462]

22. These three kinds of vision—bodily, spiritual, and intellectual—must therefore be considered separately, so that reason may ascend from the lower to the higher. We have already proposed an example above in which all three kinds appear in a single sentence. When we read, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39), the letters are seen bodily, the neighbor is thought of spiritually, and love is perceived intellectually.

Yet absent letters can also be thought of spiritually, and a present neighbor can be seen bodily. Love, however, cannot be seen by the eyes of the body through its own substance, nor can it be thought of in the spirit through an image resembling a body; it can be known and perceived only by the mind, that is, by the intellect.

Bodily vision is not set over any of these kinds as their ruler; rather, what is perceived through it is reported to spiritual vision as to its ruler. For when something is seen by the eyes, an image of it is immediately formed in the spirit; but the fact that it has been formed is not recognized until, after the eyes have been withdrawn from what we were seeing through them, we find its image in the mind.

If the spirit is irrational, as in an animal, the eyes report only this much. But if the soul is rational, the perception is also reported to the intellect, which presides over the spirit. Thus, if what the eyes have taken in and reported to the spirit, so that its image might be formed there, is a sign of something, either what it signifies is immediately understood or it is sought; for neither understanding nor inquiry is possible except through the activity of the mind.

23. King Belshazzar saw the fingers of a hand writing on the wall. Immediately, through bodily sensation, the image of the bodily event was impressed upon his spirit; and once the event had been seen and had passed, that image remained in his thought. It was seen in the spirit, but was not yet understood. Nor had the sign been understood at the time when it was being made bodily and appearing to bodily eyes. Yet it was already understood to be a sign, and it had this character from the activity of the mind. Since the question was what it signified, the mind was certainly also engaged in the inquiry.

When this was not discovered, Daniel arrived and, with his spirit enlightened by prophetic insight, disclosed to the troubled king what that sign foretold (Dan. 5:5–28). Through this kind of vision, which properly belongs to the mind, Daniel was more truly a prophet than the man who had seen both the bodily sign bodily and its image in the spirit through the thought of what had passed, but who could do nothing intellectually except recognize that it was a sign and inquire what it signified.

24. Peter, in an ecstasy, saw a vessel bound at its four corners being lowered from heaven, filled with various animals, and he heard a voice: “Kill and eat.” When he had returned to his senses and was discussing the vision, behold, the spirit announced to him those whom Cornelius had sent, saying: “Behold, men are seeking you; but rise, go down, and go with them, because I have sent them.” When he came to Cornelius, he himself indicated what he had understood in that vision, in which he had heard, “What God has cleansed, you must not call common,” saying: “God has shown me that I should call no person common or unclean” (Acts 10:10–28).

When, therefore, he saw that dish while alienated from his bodily senses, and heard in the spirit the words “Kill and eat” and “What God has cleansed, you must not call common,” he was hearing them spiritually. After he had returned to his bodily senses, he saw in the same spirit, by thinking, the very thing that memory had retained from what he had seen and heard. All these things were not bodies but images of bodies, both when they were first seen in the ecstasy itself and when later they were remembered and thought about.

But when he was discussing them and searching for the meaning of those signs, the mind was engaged in the effort to understand, but the result was lacking [Note: [Col. 0463] The manuscripts, with great agreement, read *affectus* (“the result” or “the effect”); this may perhaps be preferable, namely in the sense in which the word *affectionis* is used below in §26.] until those sent by Cornelius were announced. When bodily vision was added—while the Holy Spirit again said to him in the spirit, “Go with them,” in the place where he had also shown that sign and impressed those words upon him—the mind, aided by divine intervention, understood what all those signs together meant.

When these and similar matters are carefully considered, it becomes sufficiently clear that bodily vision is referred to spiritual vision, and that spiritual vision is referred to intellectual vision.

## CHAPTER XII — Bodily and spiritual vision

25. But when we are awake and are in bodily vision, with the mind not alienated from the bodily senses, we distinguish from it spiritual vision, by which we think imaginatively of absent bodies—whether remembering what we know by memory, or somehow forming in the thought of the spirit things that we do not know but that nevertheless exist, or inventing things that exist nowhere at all according to our choice or supposition.

We distinguish all these from the bodily things that we see and in which our bodily senses are present, so clearly that we do not doubt that these are bodies, while those are images of bodies.

But when, whether through excessive concentration of thought, or through some force of illness—as happens to the delirious during fever—or through the involvement of some other spirit, whether evil or good, images of bodily things are represented in the spirit as though bodies were presented to the bodily senses themselves, while the mind’s attention nevertheless remains engaged in the bodily senses, then the images formed in the spirit are seen in the same way as bodies themselves are seen through the body. Thus a person who is bodily present may be seen by the eyes at the same time as another who is absent is seen by the spirit as though by the eyes.

We have ourselves encountered people in this condition and spoken both with those who were truly present and with others who were not present, as though they were present. When they recover, some report what they had seen, while others cannot. In the same way, some forget their dreams and some remember them.

When the mind’s attention is completely turned away and carried off from the bodily senses, this is more commonly called ecstasy. Then, whatever bodies may be present—even when the eyes are open—they are not seen, and no voices at all are heard. The entire attention of the mind is either in images of bodies through spiritual vision, or in incorporeal things represented without any bodily image through intellectual vision.

[Col. 0464]

26. But when spiritual vision, with the mind completely alienated from the bodily senses, is occupied with images of bodily things, whether in dreams or in ecstasy, then, if the things seen signify nothing, they are merely the imaginings of the soul. Even when awake and healthy, and moved by no alienation, people turn over in thought images of many bodies that are not present to the bodily senses.

The difference is that they distinguish these images from present and real bodies with a settled awareness. But if the images signify something—whether they are presented to people who are asleep, or to those who are awake, when they see present bodies with their eyes and perceive images of absent things in the spirit as though they were present to the eyes, or in what is called ecstasy, when the mind is entirely alienated from the bodily senses—the manner is extraordinary.

Nevertheless, through the involvement of another spirit, it can happen that the other spirit displays what it knows to the person with whom it is mingled through such images, whether to someone who understands them or so that they may be disclosed as understood by another. For if these things are demonstrated, and certainly cannot be demonstrated by the body, what remains except that they are demonstrated by some spirit?

## CHAPTER XIII — Whether the power of divination exists in the soul

27. Some indeed wish the human soul to possess within itself a certain power of divination. But if this is so, why cannot it exercise that power whenever it wishes, since it always wishes? Is it because it is not always aided so that it can? When it is aided, is it aided by no one, or can it be aided by the body for this purpose? It follows that it must be aided by a spirit.

Next, how is it aided? Does something happen in the body so that the soul’s attention is, as it were, released from it and springs forth, arriving at a place where it sees within itself significant likenesses that were already there but were not seen, just as we possess many things in memory that we do not always look upon? Or are things formed there that had not existed before, or do they exist in some spirit, so that the soul, bursting forth and emerging, may see them there?

But if they were already in the soul as its own proper possessions, why does it not consequently understand them as well? For sometimes, indeed most often, it does not understand them. Is it that, just as its spirit was aided so that it might see them within itself, so the mind, unless it is aided, cannot understand what the spirit possesses?

Or perhaps bodily impediments are not removed or, as it were, relaxed so that the soul may thrust itself forward by its own impulse toward what is to be seen; rather, the soul itself is entirely taken up into these things, whether they are to be perceived only spiritually or also to be known intellectually. Or does it sometimes see these things within itself and sometimes through the involvement of another spirit?

Whatever the case may be, it ought not to be asserted rashly. This, however, should not be doubtful: the bodily images perceived in the spirit are not always signs of other things, whether in those who are awake, asleep, or ill. It would nevertheless be extraordinary if ecstasy could sometimes occur without those likenesses of bodily things signifying something.

28. It is certainly not surprising if people who are possessed by a demon sometimes tell the truth about things absent from the senses of those present. This evidently occurs through some hidden mingling of that spirit, so that it is as though the spirit of the sufferer and that of the one tormenting him were one.

But when a good spirit takes up or carries away the human spirit into such visions, there can be no doubt that the images are signs of other things, and of things that it is useful for us to know; for this is a gift of God.

Discernment is exceedingly difficult when an evil spirit acts as though tranquil and, after taking up the human spirit without any bodily disturbance, says what it can. This is so even when it speaks the truth and proclaims useful things, disguising itself, as it is written, “as an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14), in order that, once it has been trusted in manifestly good matters, it may lead the person astray toward its own purposes.

I do not think that it can be distinguished except by that gift of which the Apostle speaks when discussing the various gifts of God: “To another, the discernment of spirits” (1 Cor. 12:10).

## CHAPTER XIV — Intellectual vision does not deceive; in the other kinds, error is not always harmful

For it is not difficult to recognize it when it has reached or led someone to things contrary to good morals or the rule of faith; then it is recognized by many. But through that gift, at the very beginning, when it still appears good to many, it is immediately judged whether it is evil.

29. Through bodily vision, through images of bodily things displayed in the spirit, both good spirits instruct and evil spirits deceive. Intellectual vision, however, is not deceived. For either a person does not understand, if he supposes something other than what it is; or, if he does understand, it is immediately true.

What can the eyes do when they see a body resembling another and cannot distinguish it from that other body? Or what can the mind’s attention do when an image of a body has been formed in the spirit and cannot be distinguished from a body?
