But the intellect is brought in, seeking what those things signify or usefully teach. If it discovers the meaning, it reaches its proper benefit; if it does not discover it, it remains in inquiry, lest through some destructive rashness it slide into ruinous error.

30. With divine assistance, sober understanding judges what and how great those matters are in which supposing something other than what it is would not be harmful to the soul. For no one becomes good, even if secretly evil, to the peril—or rather destruction—of those who think him good, provided that there is no error concerning the things themselves, that is, concerning the very good by which a person becomes good.

Nor does it harm all people that, when they sleep, they suppose the bodies whose likenesses they see in dreams to be real bodies. Nor did it harm Peter that, when he had been released from his chains and was being led by an angel, a sudden miracle occurred so that he supposed he was seeing a vision (Acts 12:7–9). Nor did it harm him when, in that ecstasy, he replied, “By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean,” supposing that the very things displayed in the vessel were real animals (Acts 10:11–14).

When such things are later discovered to be other than they seemed while they were being seen, we do not regret that they appeared to us in that way, provided that neither stubborn unbelief nor a vain or sacrilegious opinion is exposed. Therefore, even when the devil deceives through bodily visions, it does not matter that the eyes are misled, provided there is no error concerning the truth of the faith or the soundness of understanding by which God teaches those subject to him.

Or if he deceives the soul through spiritual vision by means of images of bodies, so that it supposes something to be a body that is not a body, this does not harm the soul provided that it does not consent to the destructive suggestion.

## CHAPTER XV — Erotic dreams can occur without sin

31. Hence a question sometimes arises about the consent of those who dream, when they seem to have sexual intercourse, either against their own purpose or even against lawful conduct. This occurs only because things that we also think about when awake are brought before us in dreams—not with the consent of deliberate approval, but just as we speak of such things for some reason, so they are introduced and represented in dreams. The flesh is thereby moved naturally, and what it naturally gathers is emitted through the genital passages.

I could not even say this unless I were also thinking about it. Moreover, if the images of bodily things that I necessarily had to think about in order to say this were presented in dreams with the same vividness with which bodies are presented to those who are awake, what could not occur without sin in a waking person would occur. For who, even while speaking, when necessity of speech requires him to say something about his own intercourse, could avoid thinking about what he says?

When the very phantasy produced in the thought of someone speaking is represented in the dream vision with such vividness that it cannot be distinguished from actual bodily intercourse, the flesh is immediately moved, and what ordinarily follows that movement follows as well. This occurs as innocently as a waking person innocently says what, in order to say it, he undoubtedly had to think about.

Nevertheless, because of the soul’s good disposition—which, through a better desire, has been purified and destroys many desires that do not belong to the natural movement of the flesh, a movement that the chaste restrain and curb while awake, but cannot control while asleep because they do not have power over whether a bodily image will be presented with such vividness that it cannot be distinguished from a body—even in dreams certain merits of that good disposition of the soul shine forth.

For Solomon, while asleep, preferred wisdom to all other things and, neglecting the rest, asked it from the Lord. As Scripture testifies, this pleased the Lord, and he did not delay a good recompense for the good desire (1 Kings 3:5–15).

## CHAPTER XVI — The spirit forms likenesses of bodily things within itself

32. Since these things are so, bodily sensation pertains to bodily visions. It is distributed through five channels, as it were, which are separated according to their capacities. The most subtle thing in the body, and therefore closer to the soul than the rest—that is, light—is first diffused by itself through the eyes and flashes forth in the rays of the eyes for the contemplation of visible things. Then, through a kind of mixture—first with pure air, second with dark and cloudy air, third with denser moisture, and fourth with earthly thickness—it produces, together with that element in which it alone excels, the five senses, including the sense of the eyes, which excels among them. I recall having discussed this in the fourth book and likewise in the seventh.

This, then, is the heaven visible to the eyes, from which the lights and stars shine forth. It is more excellent than all bodily elements, just as the sense of sight excels in the body. Since every spirit is unquestionably superior to every body, it follows that spiritual nature is superior—not by the position of its place but by the dignity of its nature—to this bodily heaven, including that part of it in which images of bodily things are represented.

33. Here something remarkable occurs. Although the spirit is prior to the body and the image of the body comes after the body, nevertheless, because what is later in time is formed in what is earlier by nature, the image of the body in the spirit is more excellent than the body itself in its own substance.

We must certainly not suppose that a body acts upon the spirit as though the spirit that is acted upon by the body were subjected to it as matter. In every respect, the one who makes something is superior to the thing from which he makes it; and in no respect is a body superior to the spirit—indeed, the spirit is manifestly superior to the body.

Although, therefore, we first see some body that we had not previously seen, and from this its image begins to exist in our spirit, by which we remember it when it is absent, it is not the body that makes that same image in the spirit. Rather, the spirit itself makes it within itself, with a marvelous swiftness that is ineffably far removed from the slowness of the body. As soon as the body has been seen by the eyes, its image is formed in the spirit of the one seeing it without any intervening temporal interval.

The same is true of hearing. Unless the spirit immediately formed within itself the image of the voice perceived by the ears and retained it in memory, it would not be known whether the second syllable was second, since the first would already be nonexistent, having passed after striking the ear. Thus all use of speech, all the sweetness of singing, and finally every bodily movement in our actions would dissolve and perish; nor could any action advance if the spirit did not retain in memory the bodily movements that had passed, by which it connects those that follow in action.

The spirit retains these movements only by making images of them within itself. Even images of future movements anticipate the ends of our actions. For what do we do through the body that the spirit has not first anticipated in thought, seeing within itself the likenesses of all visible works and, in a certain way, arranging them?

## CHAPTER XVII — How likenesses impressed upon the mind become known to demons; certain extraordinary visions; the delirious; a sick boy

34. How these spiritual likenesses of bodily things in our mind become known even to unclean spirits, or what obstacle our soul suffers from this earthly body so that we cannot see them reciprocally in our spirit, is difficult to discover and explain.

Nevertheless, the clearest indications have established among us that thoughts of human beings are announced by demons [Note: [Col. 0467] *Against the Academics*, Book 1, chapters 6 and 7.] Yet if they could see the inward form of virtue in human beings, they would not attempt such things. Certainly, if the devil had been able to see Job’s noble and remarkable patience, he would not have wished to be defeated by the man he tempted.

Nor is it surprising that they announce something that has already happened far away and that is later confirmed as true after several days. They can accomplish this not only through a keenness of perception incomparably greater than ours, even with respect to bodily things, but also through the marvelous speed of bodies themselves, which are certainly far subtler than ours.

35. We also learned that, while a sick man was staying in a house, an unclean spirit within him used to say when a presbyter, twelve miles away, had begun to come to him, and through every place along the route where he was, how near he was, and when he was entering the estate, the house, and the room, until he stood before him.

Although that sick man did not see all these things with his eyes, he must nevertheless have perceived them in some way, since otherwise he would not have announced them so truthfully. He was suffering from fever and said these things as though in delirium. Perhaps he really was delirious, but because of these phenomena he was thought to be possessed by a demon.

He accepted no restorative food from his family, but only from the presbyter. He resisted his family violently, as far as he could; when that presbyter alone came, he became calm, was submissive only to him, and answered him obediently.

Yet neither the mental alienation nor the demon yielded even to that presbyter, except when he had recovered from the fever, as delirious people are accustomed to recover; nor did he ever afterward suffer anything of this kind.

36. We also certainly know that a delirious man foretold the future death of a certain woman—not in the manner of one divining, but as though remembering something already done and past. When she was mentioned in his presence, he said, “She is dead. I saw her being carried out; she passed through here with her body,” although she was alive and unharmed. A few days later she suddenly died and was carried out through the place he had indicated.

37. There was also among us a boy who, at the beginning of puberty, suffered extremely severe pain in his genitals. The physicians were entirely unable to discover what it was, except that the nerve itself was hidden inwardly, so that it could not be seen even after the foreskin, which hung down to an excessive length, had been cut away; only later was it found with difficulty.

A viscous and sharp fluid oozed out and burned his testicles and groin. Yet he did not suffer the acute pain continuously. When he did suffer it, he wailed violently and tossed his limbs about with a perfectly sound mind, as usually happens in the torments of bodily pain.

Then, amid his cries, he was suddenly carried away from all his senses and lay there with his eyes open, seeing none of those standing around him and not moving in response to any pinching. After a while, as though awakening, and no longer in pain, he reported what he had seen. After a few days the same thing happened again.

In all, or nearly all, of his visions, he said that he saw two persons: one more advanced in age and the other a boy. They either told him or showed him things that he reported having heard and seen.

38. One day he saw a choir of devout people singing psalms and rejoicing in a marvelous light, and the diverse and most dreadful punishments of the impious in darkness. Those figures led him and showed him these things, indicating the merit of the happiness of some and the unhappiness of others.

He saw this on Easter Sunday, although throughout the whole of Lent he had felt no pain, whereas previously he had scarcely been granted an interval of three days without it. At the very beginning of Lent he had seen those figures promise him that for forty days he would feel no pain. Later they gave him what was like medical advice: that the excessive length of his foreskin should be cut away. After this was done, he remained free from pain for a long time.

When he again suffered similar pain and began to see similar things, he once more received advice from them: he was to enter the sea up to his pubic region and, after remaining there for some time, leave it. They promised that thereafter he would no longer suffer that severe pain, but only the discomfort of the viscous fluid. This happened as they had said. Never afterward did he experience such an alienation of mind from the senses or see anything like what he had seen previously, when, amid the worst pain and terrifying cries, he had suddenly fallen silent and been carried away.

Later, however, although the physicians treated and cured his other ailments, he did not persevere in his intention of holiness.

## CHAPTER XVIII — The causes of visions

39. If anyone can investigate and securely comprehend the causes and modes of these visions and acts of divination, I would rather listen to him than have people expect me to discuss them myself. Nevertheless, I will not conceal what I think—not so that the learned may laugh at me as though I were asserting it, nor so that the unlearned may accept it as instruction, but so that both may understand that I am discussing and seeking rather than claiming knowledge.

I compare all these visions with the visions of dreamers. For just as dreams are sometimes false and sometimes true, sometimes confused and sometimes tranquil—and even those that are true are sometimes entirely like future events or openly stated, while at other times they are foretold through obscure signs and figurative expressions—so too are all those visions.

But people enjoy examining what they have not experienced and searching out the causes of unusual things, while they generally do not trouble themselves to know the origins, often even more hidden, of everyday occurrences. For just as, in the case of words—that is, the signs we use in speaking—when they hear an unfamiliar word, they first ask what it is, that is, what it signifies; then, once they know this, they ask where the word came from, even though they do not carefully inquire into the origins of many familiar words used in speech, so, when something unusual happens in either bodily or spiritual matters, they anxiously investigate its causes and explanation and demand that teachers provide them.

40. When someone asks me, for example, what *catus* means, and I answer, “Prudent” or “sharp,” but he is not satisfied and goes on to ask where *catus* came from, I in turn refer him to and ask where *sharp* came from—something he likewise did not know, but whose origin he had patiently left unknown because it was a familiar word. When something new sounds in his ears, however, he thinks it insufficient to know what it means unless he also investigates where it comes from.

Therefore, whenever someone asks me where, in ecstasy, visions resembling bodily things come from—something that rarely happens to the soul—I in turn ask where the visions that appear to those who are asleep come from, something the soul experiences every day, yet no one, or scarcely anyone, cares to investigate.

As though the nature of such visions were less marvelous because they occur daily, or less worthy of inquiry because they are common to everyone. Or, if those who do not investigate such things are right to refrain, they would not be more right if they were equally incurious about those other visions.

For my part, I am much more astonished, and I am especially amazed, at the speed and ease with which the soul constructs within itself images of the bodies it has seen through the eyes of the body than at the visions of dreamers or even those in ecstasy.

Whatever the nature of those visions may be, it is certainly not bodily. If knowing this is not enough for someone, let him ask others where they also arise from. I confess that I do not know.

## CHAPTER XIX — Where visions arise from

41. The examples and experiences clearly allow us to infer that, just as pallor, blushing, trembling, and even illness sometimes have bodily causes and sometimes causes in the soul—bodily causes when fluid is poured over the body, or when food or something else has been introduced into the body from outside; causes in the soul when it is disturbed by fear, confused by shame, angered, in love, or in some similar condition, since what animates and governs the body, when more violently moved, also agitates it more violently—so too it sometimes happens to the soul itself that it proceeds toward visions that are not reported to it through the bodily senses but through an incorporeal substance, and proceeds in such a way that it does not distinguish whether they are bodies or likenesses of bodies.

This sometimes occurs through the body and sometimes through the spirit. Through the body, either by a natural alternation, as in the visions of dreamers—for sleeping belongs to the body—or through some illness that disturbs the senses, as when delirious people see both bodies and visions resembling bodies as though they themselves were present before their eyes; or when the senses are entirely blocked, as often happens to people severely affected by illness who, while bodies are present, remain absent for a long time, and then, restored to those around them, say that they have seen many things.

Through the spirit it occurs when, with the body entirely sound and unimpaired, people are carried away into alienation—either in such a way that they see bodies through the bodily senses while also seeing in the spirit certain likenesses that they cannot distinguish from bodies, or when they are entirely turned away from the bodily senses and, perceiving nothing at all through them, dwell in likenesses of bodies through spiritual vision.

But when an evil spirit seizes them into these states, it makes them demoniacs, possessed persons, or false prophets. When the spirit is good, it produces faithful people speaking mysteries; or, when understanding is also added, true prophets; or it makes them, for the time required that something be shown through them, see and report what must be displayed through them.

## CHAPTER XX — Visions that have their occasion from the body are nevertheless not presented by the body

42. But when the cause of such visions lies in the body, the body does not present them. For the body does not possess the power to form something spiritual. Rather, when the pathway of attention from the brain—by which the movement of sensation is directed—has been put to sleep, disturbed, or even blocked, the soul itself, which cannot cease from this activity by its own movement because the body does not allow it, or does not fully allow it, to perceive bodily things, directs the power of its attention toward bodily things through the spirit and acts upon or observes likenesses of bodily things presented to it.

If it itself produces them, they are merely phantasies; but if it observes them as presented, they are apparitions.

Finally, when the eyes are painful or extinguished, because the cause is not located in the seat of the brain from which the attention of sensation is directed, visions of this kind do not occur, although the body presents an obstacle to seeing bodily things. For blind people see more when asleep than when awake.

When they are asleep, the pathway of sensation in the brain, which leads attention to the eyes, is lulled; therefore the attention, turned elsewhere, sees dream visions as though bodily forms were present. The sleeper thus seems to himself to be awake and supposes that he is looking not at things resembling bodies but at bodies themselves.

When blind people are awake, however, the attention of seeing is led along those pathways. When it reaches the region of the eyes, it does not extend outward but remains there, so that they feel themselves awake and feel that they are in darkness while awake, even during the day, rather than asleep, whether by day or by night.

Indeed, many people who are not blind sleep with their eyes open, seeing nothing through them; yet they do not for that reason see nothing, since they perceive dream visions with the spirit. But if they remain awake with their eyes closed, neither the visions of sleepers nor those of waking people are present to them.

Nevertheless, the fact that the pathway of sensation reaching their eyes from the brain is neither lulled, disturbed, nor blocked, and leads the soul’s attention right up to the very doors of the body, even though those doors are closed, has such force that images of bodies are indeed thought of, but are in no way taken for the bodies perceived through the eyes.

43. The only distinction is where the impediment to perceiving bodily things occurs, when it occurs in the body. For if it occurs only at the very entrances, so to speak, and at the doors of the senses—as in the eyes, ears, and the other bodily senses—then only the perception of bodily things is impeded; the mind’s attention is not thereby diverted elsewhere in such a way that it takes images of bodies for bodies themselves. But if the cause is within the brain, from which the pathways are directed toward the things outside to be perceived, then the very vessels of attention are put to sleep, disturbed, or blocked—those by which the soul strives to look upon or perceive what is outside.

Since the soul does not lose this striving, it forms likenesses with such force that, being unable to distinguish images of bodily things from the bodies themselves, it does not know whether it is among the former or the latter. And when it does know, it knows in a very different way from when likenesses of bodies are present to it in thought or arise before it. This distinction cannot really be grasped except by those who have experienced it. For this was the situation: while asleep, I knew that I was seeing in dreams, yet I did not distinguish the likenesses of bodily things that I saw from the bodily things themselves in the way we ordinarily distinguish them when thinking about them, even with our eyes closed or while in darkness.

So powerful is the mind’s attention—whether it is carried all the way to the senses, even though they are closed, or whether, because of some cause existing in the brain, from which it strives toward these things, it is diverted elsewhere—that, although at times a person may know that he is seeing not bodies but likenesses of bodies, or, being less instructed, may even think that these likenesses are bodies themselves, he nevertheless feels that he sees them not with the body but with the spirit. Yet he is far removed from the condition in which something is presented to his own body. Hence even the blind know that they are awake, when they distinguish by a definite awareness the likenesses of bodies conceived in thought from the bodies themselves, which they cannot see.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### Likenesses resembling bodily things, toward which the soul is carried away, are not therefore of a different nature

[Col. 0472]

44. When, however, the body is healthy and the senses are not lulled by sleep, and the soul is carried away by some hidden spiritual operation toward visions resembling bodily things, the nature of the visions is not for that reason different merely because the mode is different. There is indeed a difference, and sometimes an opposite one, among the causes that arise from the body itself.

For people suffering from frenzy have their perceptive pathways in the head disturbed while they are awake, so that they see things like those seen by dreamers, whose attention is diverted from the perception proper to waking while they sleep and is turned toward seeing such things. Thus, although in one case this occurs without sleep and in the other during sleep, the things seen nevertheless do not belong to a different kind, but arise from the nature of the spirit in which or through which likenesses of bodies are formed.

Accordingly, although the cause of the diverted attention is different when, in a healthy body and while awake, the soul is carried away by some hidden spiritual force so that it sees in the spirit likenesses of bodily things expressed in place of bodies, the nature of the visions is nevertheless the same. For one cannot say that, when the cause lies in the body, the soul then turns images of bodies from itself without any foreknowledge of future events, just as it habitually does when thinking; but that, when the spirit takes it up into the seeing of such things, they are divinely shown. Scripture plainly says: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams” (Joel 2:28), attributing both to divine operation. Likewise: “An angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife”; and again: “Take the child and go into Egypt” (Matthew 1:20; 2:13).

## CHAPTER XXII  
### How those visions occur from which divinations are made through hidden inspiration or by chance

45. I therefore do not think that a human spirit is taken up by a good spirit to see such images unless they signify something. But when there is a bodily cause that makes the human spirit concentrate more intensely on looking at them, this should not always be regarded as signifying something. They signify something when they are inspired by a spirit that is showing them—whether to someone asleep or to someone undergoing some other bodily condition by which he is separated from the senses of the flesh.

We know that thoughts have also been secretly implanted in people who were awake, afflicted by no illness, and agitated by no madness, so that, by expressing them, they foretold something—not only while doing something else, as when the high priest Caiaphas prophesied (John 11:51), although his attention had no intention of prophesying, but also while deliberately undertaking to say something in the manner of divination.

46. For some young men, joking in order to deceive people where travelers were making their journey, pretended to be astrologers, although they did not know at all whether there were said to be twelve signs. When they saw their host marveling at what they said and affirming that it was all entirely true, they proceeded more boldly to say still more. He continued to affirm everything and to marvel at it all.

At last he asked them about the safety of his son, whom he had long been longing for because he was absent, and about whose unexpected delay he was anxious, fearing that something might have happened to him. The young men, unconcerned about what would later be discovered to be true once they had departed, and wishing meanwhile to make the man happy, replied that his son was safe and close at hand, and that he would arrive that very day. They were not afraid that, once the whole day had passed, he would follow them the next day to reproach them. What more need be said? Just as they were preparing to leave, behold, while they were still there, the son suddenly arrived.

47. Likewise, another man danced before a musical performer at a pagan festival where many idols were present. He had not been seized by any spirit; rather, in playful imitation, he imitated those possessed by spirits, while the people standing around and watching knew what he was doing. It was customary, after the sacrifices had been completed before the meal and the frenzied rites had been performed, that if any young men wished to play in that manner after the meal, no one prevented them.

While he was dancing, after making silence for himself, jokingly and surrounded by a laughing crowd, he foretold that during the coming night, in the nearby forest, a man would be killed by a lion; and that at daybreak a crowd would flock to see the corpse and would abandon the site of that festival. It happened as he had said. It was perfectly clear to everyone present, from all his movements, that he had said this while playing and joking, with his mind never disturbed or diverted. He himself was all the more astonished at what occurred because he knew better than anyone with what state of mind and with what words he had uttered it.

48. In what manner do such visions enter the human spirit? Are they first formed there, or are they brought in already formed and perceived through some conjunction, so that angels may thus show human beings their thoughts and the likenesses of bodily things which, through their knowledge of the future, they preform in their own spirit? In the same way, angels themselves see our thoughts—not, of course, with the eyes, since they are not bodily, but with the spirit.

There is, however, this difference: they know our thoughts even if we do not wish them to, whereas we cannot know theirs unless they show them to us. For, as I think, they have the power to conceal these thoughts in spiritual ways, just as we hide our bodies from the eyes of others by placing certain obstacles between them.

What occurs in our spirit so that sometimes only images that signify something are seen, while it is not known whether they signify anything; sometimes they are perceived to signify something, but what they signify is not known; and sometimes, as though through a fuller revelation, the human soul sees both the images themselves and, with its spirit and mind, what they signify—this is extremely difficult to know, and, even if we already know it, exceedingly laborious to discuss and explain.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### A spiritual nature exists in us in which likenesses of bodily things are formed through so many causes

49. What I now think it sufficient to indicate is this: it is certain that there is in us a certain spiritual nature in which likenesses of bodily things are formed.

This occurs when we touch some body with the bodily sense, and its likeness is immediately formed in the spirit and stored in the memory; or when we think about bodies that are absent but already known, so that a certain spiritual appearance is formed from them, although they already existed in the spirit before we thought about them; or when we look upon the likenesses of bodies that we do not know, although we do not doubt that they exist—not as those bodies actually are, but as they happen to present themselves to us; or when we think, by choice or conjecture, about things that either do not exist or are not known to exist; or when various forms of likenesses of bodily things move about in the mind, arising from who knows where, while we neither intend nor wish this to happen.

It occurs also when, intending to do something bodily, we arrange in advance the very things that will occur in that action and anticipate all of them in thought; or when, in the action itself—whether we are speaking or doing something—all bodily movements are preceded internally in the spirit by their likenesses, so that they may be brought forth. For not even the briefest syllable would have sounded in its proper order unless it had first been anticipated.

It occurs when dreams are seen by those who sleep, signifying either nothing or something; or when, because bodily health has disturbed the perceptive pathways internally, the spirit mingles images of bodies with real bodies so that they can scarcely, or not at all, be distinguished from one another, and so that they either signify something or arise without any significance.

It occurs also when some illness or bodily pain becomes more severe and blocks internally the pathways through which the soul’s attention was extended and directed through the flesh in order to perceive. Then, with the spirit withdrawn more deeply than in sleep, images of bodily things arise or are shown, either signifying something or appearing without any significance.

It occurs when, with no bodily cause present, some spirit takes up and carries away the soul so that it may see such likenesses of bodies, mingling bodily visions with them while the soul at the same time uses the bodily senses; or when the spirit takes it up in such a way that it is separated from every bodily sense and turned away from it, so that it is held by the likenesses of bodies alone in spiritual vision. I do not know whether, in that condition, some things that signify nothing can be seen.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### Intellectual vision surpasses spiritual vision, and spiritual vision surpasses bodily vision

50. This spiritual nature, then, in which not bodies but likenesses of bodies are expressed, has visions of a lower kind than that light of the mind and understanding by which these lower things are judged and by which things are seen that are neither bodies nor bear any forms resembling bodies. Such things include the mind itself and every good affection of the soul, whose opposites are its vices, rightly blamed and condemned in human beings.

For in what other way is understanding itself perceived except by understanding? The same applies to love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, and the other things of this kind by which one draws near to God (Galatians 5:22–23); and to God himself, from whom all things come, through whom all things exist, and in whom all things are (Romans 11:36).

51. Although, therefore, visions occur in the same soul—visions perceived through the body, such as this bodily heaven, the earth, and whatever things in them can be known, insofar as they can be known; visions of likenesses of bodies seen by the spirit, about which we have already said much; and visions in which the mind understands things that are neither bodies nor likenesses of bodies—they nevertheless have their proper order, and one is superior to another.

Spiritual vision is superior to bodily vision, and intellectual vision is again superior to spiritual vision. Bodily vision cannot exist without spiritual vision. At the very moment when a body is touched by the bodily sense, something of the same kind is also formed in the mind—not that it is the body itself, but that it is similar to it. If this did not happen, there would be no sense by which things lying outside us could be perceived.

For it is not the body that perceives, but the soul through the body, which it uses as a messenger to form within itself what is announced from outside. Bodily vision therefore cannot occur unless spiritual vision occurs at the same time. But this spiritual vision is not distinguished until the sense has been withdrawn from the body, so that what was seen through the body is found to exist in the spirit.

Spiritual vision, however, can occur without bodily vision, when likenesses of absent bodies appear in the spirit, and many others are fashioned either according to the will or apart from the will, or are shown to us. Spiritual vision also needs intellectual vision in order to be judged, whereas intellectual vision does not need this lower spiritual vision. Thus bodily vision is subject to spiritual vision, and both are subject to intellectual vision.

When we read, “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2:15), we should understand this not according to the spirit by which the mind is distinguished—as in the statement, “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind” (ibid. 14:15)—but according to that meaning expressed by the words, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23). For we have already shown above that the mind itself is also called “spirit” in another sense, according to which the spiritual person judges all things.

Therefore, I think it neither absurd nor inappropriate to regard spiritual vision as occupying something like a middle position between intellectual and bodily vision. For it is not incongruous to call that intermediate which is not a body but resembles a body, standing between what is truly a body and what is neither a body nor like a body.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### Only intellectual vision does not deceive

52. The soul is deceived by likenesses of things—not through any defect in those likenesses, but through its own opinion, when, failing in understanding, it approves things that are similar as though they were the things to which they are similar.

It is therefore deceived in bodily vision when it thinks that what occurs in the bodily senses occurs in the bodies themselves. Thus, to sailors, things that are stationary seem to move on land; to those looking at the sky, stars that are moving seem to stand still; with the eyes’ rays spread apart, two appearances of a single lamp seem to be present; an oar in water appears bent; and many similar things occur.

It is also deceived when it thinks that something is the same as what is similarly colored, or that sounds, smells, tastes, or tactile sensations identify the thing itself. Thus a waxed medicine cooked in a pot is thought to be a vegetable; the sound of a passing vehicle is thought to be thunder; and, if it is examined by no other senses but is presented only to smell, the herb called apiastrum is thought to be a citron. Food affected by some sweetish juice is thought to have been prepared with honey; and an unfamiliar ring handled in the darkness is thought to be gold when it is bronze or silver.

The soul is also deceived when, disturbed by sudden and unexpected bodily appearances, it thinks that it is seeing them in a dream or is being affected by some vision of the same kind in the spirit. Hence, in all bodily visions, the testimony of the other senses and, above all, that of the mind and reason itself is brought to bear, so that what is true in this realm of things may be discovered as far as it can be discovered.

In spiritual vision—that is, in the likenesses of bodies seen by the spirit—the soul is deceived when it thinks that the things it sees in this way are the bodies themselves; or when it thinks that something it has fashioned for itself through suspicion and false conjecture is actually present in the bodies it conjectures without seeing.

In intellectual visions, however, the soul is not deceived. Either it understands, and what it understands is true; or, if it is not true, it does not understand it. Hence it is one thing to err about what one sees, and another to err because one does not see.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### The soul’s twofold rapture: through spiritual and intellectual vision

53. Therefore, when the soul is carried away toward those visions that are perceived by the spirit and resemble bodily things, so that it is turned away from the bodily senses altogether—more than ordinarily happens in sleep, but less than in death—this is already a matter of divine admonition and assistance, so that it may know that it is seeing spiritually not bodies but visions resembling bodies, just as those who know, even before they awaken, that they are seeing things in dreams.

If future events are also seen there, so that they are recognized as wholly future while their images appear present—whether the mind of the person himself is divinely assisted, or whether someone among the visions explains what they signify, as it was explained to John in the Apocalypse (Revelation 1:10 ff.)—then this is a great revelation. Even if the person to whom these things are shown does not know whether he has left the body or is still in the body and sees them while separated in spirit from the bodily senses, he may be carried away in such a way that he does not know this, if it is not also shown to him.

54. If, moreover, just as he is carried away from the bodily senses so as to be among these likenesses of bodies seen by the spirit, he is also carried away from those likenesses themselves and transported, as it were, into that region of intellectual or intelligible things where perspicuous truth is seen without any likeness of a body, then he is not clouded by the mists of false opinions. There the virtues of the soul are not laborious and burdensome.

For there, temperance does not restrain desire by an effort; fortitude does not endure adversity by an effort; justice does not punish what is unjust by an effort; and prudence does not avoid what is evil by an effort. There the whole and only virtue is to love what one sees, and the highest happiness is to possess what one loves.

There the blessed life is drunk from its own source; from there something is sprinkled upon this human life, so that amid the temptations of this age one may live temperately, courageously, justly, and prudently. For the sake of attaining that state, where there will be secure rest and the ineffable vision of truth, labor is undertaken: labor to restrain oneself from pleasure, to endure adversities, to assist those in need, and to resist those who deceive.

There the glory of the Lord is seen—not through a vision that signifies something, whether bodily, as it was seen on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18), or spiritual, as Isaiah saw it (Isaiah 6:1), or John in the Apocalypse—but through direct appearance, not through riddles, insofar as the human mind can receive it according to the grace of God who takes it up, so that God may speak mouth to mouth with the one whom he has judged worthy of such an intercourse—not with the mouth of the body, but with that of the mind.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### The kind of vision in which God was seen by Moses

[Col. 0477]

This, I think, is how what is written about Moses should be understood (Numbers 12:8).

55. For, as we read in Exodus, he had desired to see God—not in the manner in which he had seen him on the mountain, nor in the manner in which he saw him in the tabernacle (Exodus 19:18; 33:9), but in that substance in which God is, without any bodily creature being assumed and presented to the senses of mortal flesh; nor through likenesses of bodies formed in the spirit, but through God’s own appearance, insofar as a rational and intellectual creature can receive it, with the spirit withdrawn from every bodily sense and from every symbolic riddle.

For this is what is written: “If, then, I have found grace in your sight, show me yourself openly, so that I may see you,” although shortly before we read that the Lord spoke to Moses “face to face, as one speaks to his friend.” Moses therefore perceived what he was seeing, and desired what he was not seeing.

A little later, when God had said to him, “You have found grace in my sight, and I know you above all,” he replied, “Show me your glory.” At that point he received from the Lord a figurative answer, whose interpretation would take too long to discuss here, when he said to him:

“You cannot see my face and live. For no human being shall see my face and live.” Then he continued and said to him: “Behold, there is a place beside me; you shall stand upon the rock as soon as my majesty has passed by, and I shall place you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I have passed by. Then I shall remove my hand, and you shall see my back; for my face shall not appear to you” (ibid. 33:11–23).

The subsequent narrative of Scripture did not, however, say that this also happened bodily, and it sufficiently demonstrates by this that the words were spoken figuratively, with reference to the Church. For “the place beside the Lord” is the Church, since it is his temple, and it was built upon the rock. The other things said there also correspond to this interpretation.

Yet unless Moses had been worthy to see the glory of God that he had desired and longed for, God would not have said in the Book of Numbers to Aaron and Miriam, his brothers and sister:

“Hear my words: If there is a prophet among you belonging to the Lord, I shall make myself known to him in a vision.”

[Note: [Col. 0477] Several manuscripts of good quality read: “If there is your prophet, the Lord shall make himself known to him in a vision.”]

“And I shall speak to him in a dream; not so with my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house. I shall speak mouth to mouth with him, in direct appearance and not through riddles, and he saw the glory of the Lord” (Numbers 12:6–8).

This should not be understood according to the bodily substance presented to the senses of the flesh. For in that bodily manner he was indeed speaking to Moses face to face, directly opposite him, when Moses nevertheless said, “Show me yourself.” And even now he was speaking in that same way to those whom he was rebuking and to whom he was commending Moses’ merit, through a bodily creature presented to the senses of the flesh.

In the other manner, however—in that appearance in which God is—he speaks through an ineffable utterance, far more secretly and more immediately, where no one who sees him will live with this life by which one lives mortally through the bodily senses.

But unless a person in some way dies to this life—either by departing from the body altogether or by being so turned away and separated from the bodily senses that, as the Apostle says, he does not know whether he is in the body or outside the body (2 Corinthians 12:3)—he cannot be carried away and transported into that vision.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### The third heaven and the paradise of which the Apostle speaks may be understood as a third kind of vision

56. Therefore, if the Apostle called this third kind of vision—the higher kind—not only a third heaven, above every bodily vision by which bodies are perceived through the bodily senses, but also above every spiritual vision by which likenesses of bodies are seen by the spirit rather than by the mind, then in this vision the glory of God is seen, for the sight of which hearts are purified. Hence it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

This is not through some bodily or spiritual symbolic representation, as through a mirror in a riddle, but face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12)—the same as what was said of Moses, “mouth to mouth.” It is through the direct appearance by which God is whatever he is, insofar as the mind—which is not what God is—can receive him, however little, even when purified from every earthly stain and withdrawn and carried away from every body and likeness of a body.

From this condition we are exiled, burdened by a mortal and corruptible weight, so long as we walk by faith and not by direct appearance (2 Corinthians 5:6–7), while living justly here.

Why should we not believe that God wished to show so great an apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, when he was carried away into this most excellent vision, the life in which one must live eternally after this life? And why should this not be called paradise, apart from that paradise in which Adam lived bodily among trees of the forest and trees bearing fruit?

For the Church, which gathers us into the embrace of charity, has also been called a paradise with the fruit of apples (Song of Songs 4:13). But this was said figuratively, as though the Church were signified by that paradise in which Adam was originally present, as a representation of what was to come.

Yet perhaps, for those who consider the matter more carefully, it may occur to them that the bodily paradise in which Adam was bodily present signified both this life of the saints, which is now lived in the Church, and the life that will exist eternally after this one.

So Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “Vision of peace,” is nevertheless shown as a certain earthly city and signifies Jerusalem our eternal mother in heaven—either in those who have been saved in hope and patiently await what they do not see (Romans 8:24–25), according to whom there are “more children of the deserted woman than of her who has a husband” (Galatians 4:26–27); or in the holy angels themselves, to whom, through the Church, the manifold wisdom of God is made known (Ephesians 3:10), and with whom we shall live after this pilgrimage, without labor and without end.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### Whether, just as there are many heavens, there are also many levels in spiritual and intellectual vision

57. But if we understand the third heaven to which the Apostle was carried away in such a way that we believe there are also a fourth heaven and several higher heavens beyond it, beneath which this third heaven is situated—as some assert that there are seven, others eight, others nine, or even ten heavens, and affirm that within the one called the firmament there are many heavens arranged in degrees—and if, accordingly, they reason or suppose that these heavens are bodily, it would take too long to discuss their reasoning or supposition here.

It may also be that someone argues, or is able to show, that there are many levels in spiritual or intellectual things, distinguished according to some progress in revelations that are more or less glorious.

[Note: [Col. 0479] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions read *autem* (“however”) here.]

However these matters may be, and however they may be received—one person in one way, another in another—I cannot yet know or teach of any visions or kinds of vision beyond these three: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual. But how many and how great are the differences within each of these kinds, so that within each one thing is progressively superior to another, I confess that I do not know.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### In the spiritual kind of vision, some visions are apparently divine and others human

58. Just as, in this bodily light, there is the heaven that we look up at above the earth, from which the luminaries and stars shine—bodies far superior to earthly bodies—so, in that spiritual kind of vision in which likenesses of bodies are seen by a certain incorporeal light belonging to them, there are certain visions of excellence and, in their character, divine. Angels display these in marvelous ways.

Whether they make their own visions ours as well through some easy and overpowering joining or mingling, or whether they somehow know how to shape our vision within our spirit, is difficult to perceive and even more difficult to express.

There are other visions, however, that are ordinary and human. They either arise in many ways from our own spirit or are somehow suggested to the spirit by the body, according to the condition in which we are affected in flesh or mind.

For people do not merely turn their concerns over in thought while awake through likenesses of bodies; they also often dream while asleep about what they need. They pursue their affairs out of desire of mind, and, if they happen to have gone to sleep hungry and thirsty, they occupy themselves with longing for food and drink.

I think that all these things, compared with those angelic revelations, should be regarded as earthly bodies are regarded in comparison with heavenly bodies in the bodily realm.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### In intellectual vision, some things are seen in the soul, while there is another light by which the soul itself is illuminated; God is the soul’s light

59. Likewise, in that kind of intellectual vision, there are things that are seen in the soul itself, such as the virtues opposed to vices. Some of these will remain, such as piety; others are useful for this life but will not exist afterward, such as faith, by which we believe what we do not yet see; hope, by which we patiently await what is to come; and patience itself, by which we endure all adversities until we reach the place to which we wish to come.

These and similar virtues are now greatly necessary for completing this pilgrimage. They will not exist in that life for the attainment of which they are necessary. Yet they too are seen intellectually, for they are neither bodies nor forms resembling bodies.

The light itself, however, by which the soul is illuminated so that it may truly understand and behold all things either in itself or in that light, is something else. For that light is God himself; but the soul is a creature, though rational and intellectual, made in his image. When the soul tries to look upon that light, it falters through weakness and is less capable of doing so.

Nevertheless, whatever it understands, it understands from that light, insofar as it is capable. When it is carried away to that light and, withdrawn from bodily senses, is presented more fully to that vision, it sees—not through local distances but in a certain mode proper to itself—that light which, with its aid, enables it to see whatever it sees by understanding, even within itself.

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### Where the soul goes when separated from the body

60. If it is asked, when the soul has departed from the body, whether it is carried to some bodily places, or to incorporeal places resembling bodily ones, or even to something beyond these, which is superior both to bodies and to likenesses of bodies, I would quickly reply that it is either not carried to bodily places except with some body, or is not carried there locally.

Let whoever can show whether the soul has some body when it departs from this body. I do not think that it does. For I think that it is spiritual, not bodily.

[Note: [Col. 0480] Several manuscripts of the highest quality lack the words “For I think that it is spiritual, not bodily,” which occur again at the end of section 61. They may have been transferred here from that passage, since in several manuscripts there is a notable transposition of nearly fifty lines.]

According to its merits, it is carried to spiritual places, or to places of punishment resembling bodies. Such places have often been shown to those who have been carried away from the bodily senses, have lain as though dead, and have seen infernal punishments. They too possessed within themselves a certain likeness of their body, through which they could be carried to those places and experience such things through likenesses of the senses.

For I do not see why the soul should have a likeness of its body when the body itself lies without sensation, though not yet completely dead, and it sees things of the kind that many restored to life after such a withdrawal have reported—yet should not have such a likeness when, in complete death, it has entirely departed from the body.

It is therefore either carried to those places of punishment, or likewise to places resembling bodily places, though not places of punishment but of rest and joy.

61. For it cannot rightly be said either that those punishments are false or that that rest and joy are false. Things are false when, through an error of opinion, one thing is taken for another.

Thus Peter was deceived not only when he saw that sheet and thought that there were bodies in it rather than likenesses of bodies (Acts 10:11–12)—for in this he was certainly mistaken—but also when, at another time, having been released by an angel from his chains, he walked bodily and was presented with bodily forms, thinking that he was seeing a vision (Acts 12:7–9). He was deceived then as well.

For the forms in the sheet were spiritual forms resembling bodily forms; and the bodily appearance of one released from his chains was, because of the miracle, similar to a spiritual appearance. In both cases the soul was deceived only when it approved one thing in place of another.

Although, therefore, the things affecting souls separated from their bodies are not bodily but resemble bodily things—whether the effect is good or bad—and although those souls themselves appear similar to their bodies, the joy and distress produced from the spiritual substance are nevertheless real.

In dreams also it makes a great difference whether we are in joyful or sorrowful circumstances. Thus some people, finding themselves in the midst of things they had desired, have regretted waking; while others, tormented and harassed by severe terrors and sufferings, have been afraid to sleep after awakening, lest they should be brought back into the same evils.

There can certainly be no doubt that the things called infernal are more vivid, and therefore are felt more intensely. Those who have been withdrawn from the bodily senses have reported seeing things more vividly than if they had reported dreams—less vividly, indeed, than if they had died altogether, but more vividly than if they had been asleep.

There is therefore certainly a substance of the infernal regions; but I think that it is spiritual, not bodily.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### The question of the infernal regions; the soul is incorporeal; the bosom of Abraham

62. Nor should we listen to those who assert that the infernal regions are explained in this life and do not exist after death. Let them determine how they interpret poetic fictions; we must not depart from the authority of the divine Scriptures, which alone are to be trusted concerning this matter.

We may, moreover, show that even the wise men among those people had no doubt at all about the substance of the infernal regions, which receives the souls of the dead after this life.

It is rightly asked, however, how the infernal regions are said to be beneath the earth if they are not bodily places, or how they are called “infernal” if they are not beneath the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0481] See *Two Books of Retractions*, chapter 24, section 2.]

I dare to profess that I do not merely think but plainly know that the soul is not bodily. Yet whoever denies that it can possess a likeness of a body and of bodily limbs in every respect can deny that there is a soul which, in dreams, sees itself walking, sitting, moving and being moved here and there on foot or even in flight—for this does not occur without some likeness of a body.

Therefore, if it also bears this likeness in the infernal regions—not bodily, but resembling a body—then it likewise appears to exist in places that are not bodily but resemble bodily places, whether in rest or in suffering.

63. Although I also confess that I have not yet found the infernal regions called the place where the souls of the righteous rest. And it is not without reason believed that Christ’s soul came even to those places where sinners are tormented, in order to release from their sufferings those whom, according to his hidden justice, he judged to be destined for release. For how else are we to understand what is said: “Whom God raised from the dead, having loosed the pains of hell, because it was not possible for him to be held by them” (Acts 2:24), unless we understand that he released the pains of certain persons in hell, by that power in which he is Lord, before whom every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2:10)—by which power he could not be held even by those pains that he loosed?

For Abraham, or that poor man in his bosom—that is, in the hidden place of his rest—was not in torment, between whose rest and those torments of hell we read that a great chasm [Note: [Col. 0481] The manuscripts, with great agreement: “and those infernal torments.”] had been fixed [Note: [Col. 0481] Most manuscripts: “chasm” (chasma).]. Nor are they said to have been in hell. “It happened,” he says, “that the poor man died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom; but the rich man also died and was buried; and when he was in hell in torments” (Luke 16:22–26), and so forth. We therefore see that hell is not mentioned in connection with the poor man’s rest, but in connection with the rich man’s punishment.

64. Moreover, when Jacob says to his sons, “You will bring my old age down with sorrow to hell” (Gen. 44:29), it seems that he feared rather that he might be so disturbed by excessive sorrow that he would not go to the rest of the blessed, but to the hell of sinners. For sorrow is no small evil of the soul, since the Apostle himself was so deeply concerned lest someone be swallowed up by excessive sorrow (2 Cor. 2:7).

Therefore, as I said, I have not yet found—and am still seeking, without its occurring to me—that canonical Scripture anywhere places hell among good things. But I do not know whether anyone could tolerate Abraham’s bosom, and that rest to which the devout poor man was carried by the angels, being understood otherwise than as good. And so I do not see how we are to believe that it is in hell [Note: [Col. 0482] The printed editions have “him” (*eum*); but all our manuscripts have “it” (*eam*), referring to “rest.”].

CHAPTER XXXIV—On Paradise and the Third Heaven to Which Paul Was Caught Up

65. Yet while we are investigating this matter, whether we find the answer or do not find it, the length of this work presses us to bring it to a conclusion at some point. Since, therefore, we have begun to speak of paradise because the Apostle says that he knows a man who was caught up to the third heaven, but does not know whether in the body or outside the body, and that he was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak, we do not rashly assert whether paradise is in the third heaven, or whether he was caught up into the third heaven and from there again into paradise.

For if, in the proper sense, paradise is a wooded place, but, by a transferred use of the word, every spiritual region, so to speak, where the soul is well can also rightly be called paradise, then not only the third heaven—whatever it is, and it is certainly something great and sublimely splendid—but even in the human being himself, a certain joy arising from a good conscience is paradise. Hence the Church, in the saints who live temperately, justly, and devoutly, is rightly called paradise (Eccli. 40:28), flourishing with an abundance of graces and chaste delights. For even amid tribulations it greatly rejoices in that very patience, because “according to the multitude of sorrows in the heart, the consolations of God delight its soul” (Ps. 93:19).

How much more, then, after this life can that bosom of Abraham be called paradise, where there is now no temptation, and such rest after all the sorrows of this life? For surely there is also there a certain light, proper to that place and of its own kind, and certainly a great one. The rich man, from his torments and the darkness of hell, saw it from so great a distance—although a great chasm lay between them—that he nevertheless recognized there the poor man whom he had once despised.

66. If this is so, hell is said or believed to be beneath the earth because, through those likenesses of bodily things, it is suitably represented in the spirit. Since the souls of the dead who deserve hell sinned through love of the flesh, what is displayed to them through those likenesses of bodily things is what ordinarily happens to the dead flesh itself: that it is buried beneath the earth.

Finally, hell is called *inferi* in Latin because it is below (*infra*). Just as, according to the body, if all things retain the order of their own weight, the lower things are all heavier, so according to the spirit all lower things are sadder. Hence in the Greek language too, the origin of the name by which hell is called is said to echo the idea that it contains nothing pleasant.

Yet our Savior did not disdain, after dying for us, to visit that region of reality itself, in order to release from it those whom, according to the hidden and divine justice, he could not fail to know were destined for release. Therefore he did not assign the soul of the thief to whom he said, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), to hell, where the punishments of sinners are found. Rather, he assigned it either to that rest which is Abraham’s bosom—for Christ is nowhere absent, since he himself is the Wisdom of God, reaching everywhere because of his purity (Wis. 7:24)—or to that paradise, whether it is in the third heaven or wherever else it may be, to which the Apostle was caught up after the third heaven, if indeed it is not one and the same place called by different names, where the souls of the blessed are.

67. If, then, we rightly understand the first heaven as everything corporeal, under that general name, which is above the waters and the earth; the second as what is seen in bodily likeness by the spirit, such as that object from which the sheet full of animals was lowered to Peter in ecstasy (Acts 10:10–12); and the third as what is seen by the mind, so hidden, remote, and wholly withdrawn from and purified of the senses of the flesh that what is in that heaven—and the very substance of God, the Word who is God, through whom all things were made—can be ineffably seen and heard in the love of the Holy Spirit: then we do not unreasonably suppose both that the Apostle was caught up there (2 Cor. 12:2–4), and that perhaps paradise is there, better than all others; or, if one must say so, the paradise of paradises.

For if the joy of a good soul in good things is found throughout every creature, what joy is superior to that which is in the Word of God, through whom all things were made?

CHAPTER XXXV—Why the Resurrection of Bodies Is Necessary for the Soul’s Perfect Blessedness

68. But if someone is troubled by the question why the spirits of the dead need to receive their bodies again in the resurrection, if that supreme blessedness can be granted to them even without bodies, the question is indeed too difficult to be brought to a complete conclusion in this discourse. Nevertheless, there must be no doubt that the mind of a human being, once it has been snatched away from the senses of the flesh, and after death has laid aside the flesh itself, even after transcending the likenesses of bodily things, cannot see the unchangeable substance in the same way as the holy angels see it.

This may be either because of some more hidden cause, or because there is in the soul a natural appetite to govern a body. By this appetite it is held back, in a certain way, from proceeding with its whole attention toward that highest heaven, so long as the body whose governance would quiet that appetite is not present.

Moreover, if the body is of such a kind that its governance is difficult and burdensome, like this flesh which is subject to corruption and weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15), being descended from transgression, the mind is still more turned away from the vision of the highest heaven. Hence it had necessarily to be snatched away from the senses of that same flesh [Col. 0484], so that what it was capable of grasping might be shown to it.

Therefore, when it has received this body—not now an animal body, but, through the future transformation, a spiritual body—made equal to the angels, it will possess the complete condition proper to its nature: obedient and commanding, made alive and giving life, with an ineffable facility, so that what had been a burden to it will be its glory.

CHAPTER XXXVI—How There Will Be Three Kinds of Vision in the Blessed

69. Certainly those three kinds of vision will exist then as well, but no falsehood will be accepted as one thing in place of another, whether in bodily or spiritual visions—much less in intellectual visions. The blessed will enjoy these latter as things presented and made clear [Note: [Col. 0484] The printed editions have *perfructur*; all the manuscripts have *perfruitur*.], whereas the bodily forms that now lie before us, which we reach through the sense of the flesh, are present to us with far less clarity. Many people are so devoted to them that they suppose them to be the only things that exist, and believe that whatever is not of this kind does not exist at all.

The wise, however, are so situated with respect to these bodily visions that, although such things seem more immediate to them, they are nevertheless more certain about those things which, beyond bodily appearance and beyond bodily likeness, they perceive to some extent by understanding, even though they cannot behold them in the mind as they behold bodily things with the bodily sense.

The holy angels, on the other hand, preside over the judgment and administration even of these bodily things, and do not incline toward them more familiarly as though they were more immediate. They so distinguish their significant likenesses in the spirit, and in a certain way handle them with such power, that they can also mingle them with human spirits by revealing them. And they contemplate the unchangeable substance of the Creator in such a way that, by vision and love, they both place it above all things and judge all things according to it; they are directed toward it in order to be guided, and from it they direct whatever they do.

Finally, although the Apostle was snatched away from the senses of the flesh into the third heaven and paradise, one thing certainly remained lacking for full and perfect knowledge of the realities possessed by the angels: whether he was in the body or outside the body, he did not know. This will certainly not be lacking when, after bodies have been received in the resurrection of the dead, “this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53).

For then all things—corporeal, spiritual, and intellectual—will be evident without any falsehood or ignorance, distributed according to their proper orders, in an unimpaired nature and perfect blessedness.

CHAPTER XXXVII—The Opinion of Certain Persons Concerning the Third Heaven

70. I know that some of those who are praised for having treated the holy Scriptures in the Catholic faith before us have also explained what the Apostle says about the third heaven in this way: they wished the distinctions of the corporeal, animal, and spiritual human being to be understood here, and believed that the Apostle was caught up to contemplate, with exceptional clarity, that class of incorporeal realities which spiritual people in this life love above other things and desire to enjoy.

Why I have preferred to speak of the spiritual and intellectual—whereas they perhaps spoke of the animal and spiritual—in order merely to use different names for the same realities, I have already explained sufficiently in the earlier parts of this work. If we have discussed these matters correctly [Col. 0485], according to the measure of our ability, the spiritual reader will either approve them, or, with the help of the Holy Spirit, will gain something from this reading so as to become spiritual.

But now we finally bring to a close this entire work, contained in twelve volumes.

[LOCUTIONS IN THE HEPTATEUCH.]

[Col. 0485]

CONCERNING THE SUBSEQUENT WORK ON LOCUTIONS

BOOK II OF THE RETRACTATIONS, CHAPTER LIV

I composed seven books on the seven books of the divine Scriptures—that is, five on Moses, one on Joshua son of Nun, and another on Judges—in which I noted the locutions that are less customary in our language. Readers who pay too little attention seek the meaning of these expressions in the divine utterances, although they are merely a type of locution; and sometimes they extract something that indeed does not depart from the truth, but which the author of the text is not found to have intended, while it appears more credible that he said it as a feature of expression.

Many obscure passages in the holy Scriptures become clear once the type of locution is recognized. For this reason, these same types of locution should be learned where the meaning is evident, so that, where the meaning is hidden, the knowledge itself may come to our aid and open them to the reader’s understanding.

The title of this work is *Locutions on Genesis*, and likewise for each of the individual books. But in the first book I wrote that it is said: “And Noah did all the words that the Lord commanded him; so he did” (*Locutions on Genesis* 6:22), and I said that this locution resembles what occurs in the account of the creation of the creature: after it is said, “And so it was made,” there is added, “and God made” (Gen. 1). This does not now seem to me entirely similar. Indeed, in the former passage the meaning too is hidden; here there is only a locution.

This work begins as follows: “Locutions of the Scriptures.”

[Col. 0485]

SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, SEVEN BOOKS OF LOCUTIONS ON THE HEPTATEUCH

[Note: [Col. 0485] It seemed appropriate to assign this work approximately to the year 419 because in the *Retractions* it occupies the place immediately after the books *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, which were evidently written at about that time.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] These seven books have been newly corrected against two Victorine manuscripts; the Vatican, Sorbonic, Cistercian, Beccensian, and Michaelinian manuscripts; one manuscript of the Bernardine Fathers’ College in Paris; the ancient and excellent Corbie manuscript; the variant readings of the Louvain editions from four Belgian manuscripts; and finally the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

BOOK ONE—Locutions on Genesis

Locutions of the Scriptures that appear to follow the peculiarities—called *idiomata* in Greek—of the Hebrew or Greek language.

[Gen. ch. 1, v. 14.] “And let them divide between the middle of the day and between the middle of the night.”

[Ib. 20, 26.] “Flying creatures flying over the earth according to the firmament of heaven.” The question is how “according to the firmament” should be understood. Likewise: “Let us make a human being according to image and according to likeness,” which many Latin manuscripts have as “in image and likeness.”

[Col. 0486] [Ib. 28.] “Fill the earth and rule it.” For the Latin expression is “Rule over it.”

[Ib. 2:5.] “And a human being was not there to work the earth.” Latin manuscripts have: “who would work the earth.”

[Ib. 8.] “God planted a paradise toward the east.” Latin manuscripts have: “toward the east” with the preposition *ad*.

[Ib. 9.] Many Latin manuscripts have: “And the tree of knowing good and evil,” or “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil,” or “the tree of knowing good and evil”; and if there are other variations among the translators concerning this matter, the Greek has: “and the tree for knowing the knowable good and evil.” I do not know whether this is a feature of locution, rather than an indication of some more definite meaning.

[Ib. 16.] Latin manuscripts have: “From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food.” The words should not be punctuated as “in paradise, for food,” but as “you shall eat for food.” For the Latin expression permits *esca edes* (“you shall eat food”), since in such expressions they customarily use the ablative—or what they call the seventh case—in place of the Greek dative. Or else the order of the words is: “From every tree, for food.”

[Ib. 3:1.] “The serpent was the most prudent of all the beasts,” as many Latin manuscripts have. In Greek it is written *φρονιμώτατος* (*phronimōtatos*, “most prudent”), not *σοφώτατος* (*sophōtatos*, “wisest”) [Note: [Col. 0487] All manuscripts have written *sophrôtatos*.].

[Ib. 7.] What is written about Adam and Eve—“Their eyes were opened”—is a locution, since it would be absurd to believe that they had previously wandered about in paradise blind or with their eyes closed. The same expression is used of Hagar: “He opened her eyes, and she saw a well” (Gen. 21:19); for she had not previously been sitting there with her eyes closed. Likewise, when the eyes of those who recognized the Lord after the resurrection were opened in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:31), they had not been walking along the road with their eyes closed.

[Ib. 15.] Many manuscripts have: “I will place enmity between you and the woman.” The Greek has: “in the midst of you and in the midst of the woman,” which is a locution; for it means exactly the same as “between you and the woman.” The same applies to what follows: “in the midst of your seed and in the midst of her seed.”

[Ib. 17.] Many Latin manuscripts have: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree from which I had commanded you, from that alone not to eat.” The Greek has: “You ate from the tree from which I had commanded you, from that alone not to eat from it.” Other Greek translators, however, have “you ate” or “you consumed,” so that according to them the sense is: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree from which I had commanded you not to eat from it alone, from it you ate.”

[Ib. 4:2.] “And she added to bear his brother Abel.” This is a frequent locution in the Scriptures: “added to say.”

[Ib. 8.] “And it happened, while they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel and killed him.” This is a locution; for even without “and it happened,” the complete meaning could be expressed: “when they were in the field.”

[Ib. 6:6.] Some Latin manuscripts have: “And God repented, and said, ‘I will wipe out the human being whom I made from the face of the earth.’” In Greek one finds *διενοήθη* (*dienoēthē*), which is said to signify “he reconsidered” more than “he repented.” Some Latin manuscripts also have this verb.

[Ib. 14.] Most Latin manuscripts have: “You shall make nests in the ark,” although the Latin expression is not “in the ark” but “in the ark” with the locative sense. The Greek has neither “in the ark” nor “in the ark” in that form, but: “You shall make nests—the ark,” which is understood to mean that the ark itself was to be nests.

[Ib. 16.] Most manuscripts have: “You shall make a door of the ark on the side”; some have: “across,” for this is how they wished to translate what is said in Greek, *ἐκ πλαγίων* (“from the side”).

[Ib. 7:4.] What is written as: “For after seven more days I will bring a flood of water upon the earth”—some Latin manuscripts have “I will bring rain upon the earth”—is found in Greek as: “I will bring rain upon the earth.” The Greek expression has the genitive case, not the accusative, so that if we expressed it in Latin it would read: “For after seven days’ [time] I will bring rain upon the earth.”

[Ib. 5.] What is written—“And Noah did everything that the Lord God commanded him; so he did”—is a locution resembling what occurs in the account of the creation of the creature: after “And so it was made,” there is added, “And God made.”

[Ib. 4.] What is written—“I will wipe out every *suscitatio*”—should be noted as saying not “creation,” but “rising” or “arising.” For the Greek has *ἀνάστασιν* (*anastasin*), a noun that is also regularly used for “resurrection” in the Greek Scriptures, although *ἐξανάστασις* (*exanastasis*) could have been used, so that *anastasis* would mean “arising” and *exanastasis* “resurrection.” The Apostle also used the latter word: “If somehow I may attain to the resurrection of the dead” (Phil. 3:11). There the Greeks have not *ἀνάστασιν* but *ἐξανάστασιν*.

[Ib. 14.] What is written—“And all the beasts according to their kind, and all the cattle according to their kind, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth according to its kind, and every flying creature according to its kind entered to Noah into the ark, two by two of every flesh in which there is the breath of life”—the phrase “in which” does not refer to anything unless one supplies “kind,” that is, “in which kind.” For if “flesh” were supplied, it should have been “in which,” feminine; Symmachus alone rendered it that way.
