[Ib. 23.] What is again written—“And every *suscitatio* that was upon the face of the whole earth was wiped out”—should be noted as a locution, as though it said “the condition or creature of flesh.” After it had said, “And every *suscitatio* that was upon the face of the whole earth was wiped out, from human being to cattle [Note: [Col. 0488] The printed editions have “cattle” in the plural (*pecudum*); the manuscripts have the singular (*pecudem*), in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, *heōs ktēnous*.] and creeping things and the birds of heaven,” it then added, “And they were wiped out from the earth.” It should be noted that the former expression is a repetition, a device the Scripture commonly uses [Note: [Col. 0488] We follow the readings of Lyon, Venice, and Louvain B, which have “uses.” M.].

[Ib. 8:6–7.] What is written—“He sent out the raven to see whether the water had ceased, and it went out and did not return until the water had dried from the earth”—is a customary locution in the Scriptures, which should now begin to be noticed. For it did return afterward; the statement that it did not return until the water had dried does not mean that it did not return thereafter.

[Ib. 9.] What is written—“And he stretched out his hand, took her, and brought her to himself into the ark”—is a locution that I think is Hebrew, because it is also extremely familiar in the Punic language, in which we find many expressions corresponding to Hebrew words. For surely “And he stretched out his hand” would have been sufficient, even if “his” had not been added. The same applies to what he says shortly afterward: “It had olive leaves, a shoot in its mouth.”

[Ib. 12.] “And he did not continue to return to him any longer.” This is a locution extremely familiar in the Scriptures.

[Ib. 21.] What is written—“And I will not continue any longer to curse the earth”—is similar to the preceding expression, “And he did not continue to return to him.”

[Ib. 21.] “And I will not continue to strike every living flesh.” The locution itself is the same.

[Ib. 9:5.] “For your blood, the blood of your souls” [Col. 0489], although either “your blood” or “the blood of your souls” would have been sufficient.

[Ib. 12.] “This is the sign of the covenant that I shall place between my midst and your midst,” that is, “between me and you.”

[Ib. 10:9.] “He was a giant” [Note: [Col. 0489] In the ancient manuscripts consistently, “giant” (gigans).] “a hunter against the Lord God.” It is uncertain whether this can be understood as “before the Lord God,” since what is said in Greek, *ἐναντίον* (“opposite,” “before”), is also customarily understood in that way.

[Ib. 14.] “From where the Philistines went out from there,” although “From where the Philistines went out” would have been sufficient.

[Ib. 11:1.] “And the whole earth was one lip,” which we ordinarily express as “one language.” “And the whole earth was one lip”: it should be noted that “the whole earth” refers to all the human beings who existed at that time, although they did not yet inhabit the whole earth.

[Ib. 3.] “And bricks became for them in place of stone.” The Greek has: “And bricks became for them into stone,” which, if said in Latin, would be less intelligible.

[Ib. 4.] “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose top will reach to heaven.” This is said hyperbolically, if a type of locution is to be understood here. But if “up to heaven” is taken literally, it should be considered among the questions.

[Ib. 10.] Some Latin manuscripts have: “Shem, the son of Noah, was one hundred years old when he fathered Arphaxad.” The Greek has: “Shem, a son of one hundred years, when he fathered Arphaxad,” where there is an ellipsis, because “was” is lacking. But the fact that they do not have “son of Noah,” but only “son,” is a new locution.

[Ib. 30.] “And Sarah was barren, and she did not give birth,” although “And Sarah was barren” would have been sufficient.

[Ib. 12:12.] “Therefore, when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife.’” The word “because” has been added as a feature of locution; “This is his wife” would have been sufficient.

[Ib. 14.] What the Scripture says—“And it happened immediately when Abram entered Egypt”—could have been sufficiently expressed as: “Immediately when Abram entered Egypt.”

[Ib. 18.] “What have you done to me, because you did not announce to me that she is your wife?” “You did not announce” would have been sufficient. The expression “you announced” is itself according to the usage of the Scriptures; for most Latin manuscripts have “you did not tell.”

[Ib. 13:1.] “Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that belonged to him, and Lot with him, into the desert.” “They went up” is understood. Yet it is not properly said that what he had that was lifeless—such as gold, silver, and all his household goods—went up with him. Hence this is understood as the locution called in Greek *ζεῦγμα κατ’ ἔλλειψιν* (“zeugma by ellipsis”).

[Ib. 7.] “And there was strife between the midst of the shepherds of Abram’s cattle and the cattle of Lot.” Almost all Latin manuscripts did not translate this locution, but speak as our usage requires. We therefore did not wish to note it further, since it occurs throughout the Greek Scripture wherever something of this kind is said.

[Ib. 8.] “For we are human beings who are brothers,” Abram said to Lot. From this it is understood that it is the custom of Scripture to speak in such a way that persons of one kindred are called brothers, even if they differ in degree of blood relationship, one being in the higher and the other in the lower degree, as here; for Abram was his uncle [Note: [Col. 0490] The printed editions had omitted “his”; we restored it from the Corbie and other manuscripts of excellent quality.].

[Ib. 14:1.] “And it happened in the reign of Amraphel, king of Shinar.” According to our customary expression, it would have been sufficient to begin: “In the reign of Amraphel.” Therefore, when the Scripture says “And it happened,” it has spoken according to its own usage.

[Ib. 5.] “In the fourteenth year, however, Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him”—“were” is understood, and some Latin manuscripts have added it.

[Ib. 6.] “And the Horites who were in the mountains of Seir”—“were” is understood.

[Ib. 13.] “And one of those who had escaped came and announced to Abram the Hebrew; he himself was dwelling by the oak of Mamre, son of an Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aunan, who were Abram’s confederates.” This is an obscure hyperbaton. The order is: “One of those who had escaped, an Amorite, the brother of Eshcol and the brother of Aunan, who were confederates, came and announced to Abram the Hebrew; he himself was dwelling by the oak.”

This hyperbaton is made still more obscure by an ellipsis. For when it had said “an Amorite, the brother of Aunan,” it did not say “what relation of Aunan,” but “son” is understood, just as when one says “James of Alphaeus,” although “son” is not stated, nothing else is understood. There are many such locutions in the Scriptures in which “son” is omitted but understood.

[Ib. 22.] Some Latin manuscripts have: “And Abram said to the king of Sodom, ‘I stretch out my hand to God Most High, who created heaven and earth: from a cord to a sandal strap.’” The translator was misled by the Greek, which has *σπαρτίου* (*spartiou*), which in Latin is understood as “a cord.” Thus the Scriptural locution is: “I stretch out my hand to God Most High, who created heaven and earth, if I take anything of all that is yours.”

For if he said “I stretch out my hand to God Most High” as though he were saying “I swear,” this is not a customary Latin expression unless it is stated in this way: “I stretch out my hand to God Most High that I will take nothing of all that is yours.”

[Ib. 15:13.] “Knowing, you shall know that your seed will be a stranger in a land.” This is indeed a very common locution of the Scriptures, but the Greek has: “Knowing, you shall know,” which is almost equivalent.

[Ib. 16:3.] “And he gave her to Abram, her husband, to him as wife.” The word “to him” is additional.

[Ib. 4.] “But when she saw that she had conceived, I was despised before her.” The Greek has here a participle, which the Latin language does not possess, namely *ἰδοῦσα* (*idousa*, “having seen”). But as though one were to say, “Seeing that she had conceived, I was despised before her,” it sounds like a solecism. The same is true of the participle *idousa*, for which we say “seeing.”

[Ib. 17:6.] Latin manuscripts have: “I will increase you exceedingly greatly.” The Greek has: “very, very greatly.”

[Ib. 8.] “And I will give to you and to your seed after you the land in which you dwell, all the land of Canaan, as an eternal possession.” It must be considered whether “eternal” is a locution; the Greek has *αἰώνιον* (*aiōnion*, “eternal”). And when it says “and to your seed after you,” it intended there to be understood what it had said earlier: “to you” [Col. 0491].

[Ib. 17:9.] “But you shall keep my covenant, and your seed after you throughout their generations.” “You shall keep” is used instead of “keep”; a promissive (future) form has been used in place of the imperative mood.

[Ib. 12.] “And a male of eight days shall be circumcised, every masculine thing,” instead of “every male,” as though anything but a male could be circumcised.

[Ib. 17.] “And Abraham fell on his face and spoke in his heart, saying, ‘If a man who is one hundred years old is to have a child, and if Sarah, being ninety years old, is to give birth?’” There is no doubt that this is the locution of one expressing amazement, not doubt.

[Ib. 24.] “Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised, the flesh of his foreskin.” It does not say “in the flesh” or “with the flesh.”

[Ib. 18:7.] “And Abraham ran toward the cattle.” It does not say “to the cattle.”

[Ib. 11.] “Now Abraham and Sarah were advanced in their days.” The Greek has: “advanced in days.”

[Ib. 20.] “And the Lord said, ‘The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has been filled, and their sins are exceedingly great.’” Scripture commonly uses “outcry” for such shamelessness and freedom in iniquity that it is hidden neither by modesty nor by fear.

[Ib. 28.] “And he said, ‘Because I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there.’” The word “because” seems superfluous, and for that reason it is not found in some Latin manuscripts.

[Ib. 30.] “Will you, Lord, if I speak”—“be angry,” or something of that sort, is understood.

[Ib. 19:29.] “When the Lord was overthrowing the cities in which he was dwelling in them” [Note: [Col. 0491] The printed editions have “in which they were dwelling in them,” but the manuscripts have “he was dwelling,” namely Lot, in accordance with the Greek.].

[Ib. 20:13.] “In every place where we enter there.”

[Ib. 21:19.] “And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water.” This is a locution; she was not, in fact, there with her eyes closed. We therefore spoke about it at the beginning of the book, where it is written: “And their eyes were opened.”

[Ib. 23.] “And the land in which you dwelt in it.”

[Ib. 27.] “And the two of them arranged a covenant,” or “the two of them made a covenant.” Scripture likes to call an agreement by the name of “covenant.”

[Ib. 22:2.] “Take your beloved son.” This is said with the same locution as the command concerning Hagar’s son: “Take.”

[Ib. 4.] “And Abraham, looking with his eyes.” “Looking” would have been sufficient.

[Ib. 16.] “By myself I have sworn: surely, blessing I will bless you,” as though it said: “By myself I have sworn that, blessing, I will bless you”; or, with no word added, simply: “By myself I have sworn; blessing, I will bless you.”

[Ib. 17.] “And multiplying, I will multiply your seed,” although “I will multiply” would have been sufficient.

[Ib. 20.] “And it was announced to Abraham, saying,” whereas ordinary usage has: “They announced to Abraham, saying,” or “It was announced by those who were speaking.”

[Ib. 23:3–4.] “And Abraham rose from his dead person.” It does not say “from his dead woman.” And again concerning the same woman: “And I will bury,” he says, “my dead person.” The Greek Scripture demonstrates that this is not said in the neuter, as though referring to a dead body, but in the masculine gender.

[Ib. 24:3.] “And I will adjure you by the Lord God of heaven and the God of earth.” The Greek does not have “by,” but: “I will adjure the Lord God of heaven.”

[Ib. 3.] “Among whom I dwell in them.”

[In 5.] “Lest at some time the woman should not wish to go with me.” To call a female person a “woman” is characteristic of that language.

[Ib. 5.] “To the land from which you went out from it.”

[Ib. 6.] “Pay attention to yourself, lest you bring my son back there.” Such words ordinarily express a threat.

[Ib. 9, 8.] “And the servant placed his hand under Abraham’s thigh, and swore to him concerning this word.” Therefore this is a locution corresponding to what Abraham had said, “I adjure you,” as though he had said, “Swear to me.” We do not ordinarily speak in this way, but it should be observed whether there are other similar locutions in the Scriptures. For when Abraham said, “If the woman should not wish to come with you, you will be free from this oath,” he showed that by saying “I adjure you” he meant “swear to me.”

[Ib. 16.] What is written about Rebekah—“The virgin was very beautiful; she was a virgin, and a man had not known her”—the repetition indicates praise of her virginity. But why “a man had not known her” was added, unless this is a locution, it is remarkable if it can be understood in such a way that “virgin” denotes age rather than bodily integrity. The Greeks, however, do not have “had known,” but “knew,” which seems inconsistent.

[Ib. 26.] “He worshiped to the Lord,” whereas our customary expression is “He worshiped the Lord.”

[Ib. 27.] “Because he has not abandoned justice and truth from my lord,” that is, “the justice and truth that are from my lord,” as though he said, “which my lord has done.”

[Ib. 28.] “And the girl ran and announced it to her mother’s house,” as though it were not also her father’s house.

[Ib. 32.] “And water to wash his feet, and the feet of the men who were with him.”

[Ib. 40.] “The Lord, before whom I have found favor, he himself will send his angel with you,” as though “before whom I have found favor” were not sufficient. For could he have found favor with him except before him?

[Ib. 42.] “If you prosper my way, by which I am now entering into it.”

[Ib. 43–44.] When Abraham’s servant recounted his words—what he had said when he was approaching the spring—he narrated them as follows: “And it will be the virgin to whom I say, ‘Give me a little water to drink from your jar,’ and she says to me, ‘You drink too, and I will draw water for your camels’: this is the woman whom the Lord has prepared for his servant Isaac.” These words make it sufficiently clear that, according to the Hebrew locution, women were also called those who were virgins.

[Ib. 48.] “And I blessed the Lord God of my lord Abraham.” This is a locution of honor and one extremely familiar in the Scriptures, as in “the God of Elijah.”

[Ib. 49.] “Tell me, so that I may return to the right or to the left.” By “right” he signified prosperity, and by “left” adversity—that is, the right if they granted his request, the left if they did not. For he was certainly going to return by the road on which he had come. Other passages of the Scriptures will also indicate this locution [Col. 0493], because “right” is named in all good things and “left” in evil things, whether happiness and unhappiness, or justice and injustice; and sometimes “right” refers to eternal things, “left” to temporal things.

[Ib. 25:13.] “These are the names of the sons of Ishmael according to the names of their generations,” as though it said: “according to the names by which their generations were called.”

[Ib. 20.] “He took Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Syrian from Mesopotamia, sister of Laban the Syrian, for himself as wife,” although it could have said merely “as wife,” or “for himself as wife.”

[Ib. 24.] “And she had twins in her womb,” although the added word “her” could have been omitted.

[Ib. 27.] “And the young men grew up.” There is a similar locution among secular authors, such as: “And they conceal the hidden shields” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.237), that is, “by concealing them, they make them hidden.” So here too, “The young men grew up,” although they were infants, is understood to mean that by growing they became young men.

[Ib. 31.] Jacob said to Esau: “Sell me today your birthright to me.” This is how the Greek manuscripts have it.

[Ib. 26:28.] “Seeing, we have seen that the Lord is with you.”

[Ib. 28.] “And we shall make a covenant with you”: Scripture likes to use *covenant* (*testamentum*) for an agreement, that is, διαθήκην (*diathēkēn*). The Latin reads, “And we shall make a covenant with you, that you may do us no harm,” as though it said, “so that you may agree not to harm us.”

[Ib. XXVII, 1.] “And he called his elder son Esau and said”: here the term *elder* does not indicate advanced age, but the older one by comparison.

[Ib. 3.] “Now then take your vessel, your quiver, and your bow”: he did not say *vessels*, but *vessel*. What he intended to be understood is not apparent, unless perhaps this is an expression in which he wanted *vessel* to mean *quiver* and, by explaining what he meant by *vessel*, added “your quiver and bow,” as though he had said, “Take your vessel and your quiver”; or as if he had said, “Take your vessel, that is, your quiver,” and then added something else, “and your bow,” which would not belong to that vessel, namely the quiver. Or perhaps he wanted to call the quiver and bow a single *vessel*, using the singular number for the plural—as if he said, “Take your garment,” by which we would understand several garments, just as we use *soldier* for *soldiers*. There are many such expressions.

[Ib. 3.] “Go out into the field and hunt game for me.”

[Ib. 9.] “Go to the sheep and take for me two tender and good kids”: by the name *sheep* he indicated the kind of both flocks, since they were together in the same pastures.

[Ib. XXVIII, 4.] “And may he give you the blessing of your father Abraham”: Isaac speaks to his son about his grandfather, his own father.

[Ib. 5.] “And he went out into Mesopotamia of Syria”: as though Mesopotamia could be called anything other than Syria, although it is reported that the Septuagint does not have *of Syria*, except where it is written with an asterisk.

[Ib. 15.] God says to Jacob, “I will not abandon you until I have done everything that I have spoken to you”: this sounds as though he would abandon him once he had done so; but that is not intended—it is simply an expression.

[Ib. XXVIII, 16.] “Jacob arose from his sleep and said, ‘For the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it’”: the meaning is complete even without the *for*. “The Lord is in this place”—as though he had said, “Here is a manifestation of the Lord”; for the meaning is not that the Lord is confined to a place.

[Ib. XXIX, 5.] Jacob asks, “Do you know Laban, the son of Nahor?” although Laban was the son of Bethuel. We must understand that Nahor was the more distinguished person, and that his dignity made it appropriate to ask about Laban through him. It is a very common expression to call someone the son of his grandfather, great-grandfather, or any still more remote ancestor from whom he is descended. This is why Isaac also called Abraham the father of his son, as I mentioned shortly before.

[Ib. 7.] “It is still broad daylight; it is not yet time to gather the flocks.”

[Ib. XXX, 4.] “And she gave him Bilhah, her maidservant, as a wife to him”: the sentence would be complete even without *to him*.

[Ib. 27.] “If I have found favor before you, I would have divined; for God has blessed me at your coming”: this does not seem logically consistent, since it should have said, “If I had found favor before you, I would have divined”; but it says, “If I have found.” The order is: “If I have found favor before you, permit me to divine.” Thus he says, “I would have divined,” as though he were saying, “Oh, if only I had divined!”—that is, “I would have had you in my house as a favorable omen.”

[Ib. 33.] “And my righteousness will answer me tomorrow”: that is, “It will cause me to be answered.”

[Ib. XXXI, 2.] “And Jacob saw Laban’s face, and behold, it was not toward him as on yesterday and the day before yesterday”: this is a very familiar scriptural expression. *Yesterday and the day before yesterday* is used for past time in general.

[Ib. 10.] “And I saw with my eyes in a dream,” although in sleep the bodily eyes are closed.

[Ib. 13.] “I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God”: this is an expression. Is “in the place of God” to be understood in the same way as “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Gen. XIX, 24), that is, the Son from the Father?

[Ib. 31.] “But Jacob answered and said to Laban, ‘For I said, lest you should take your daughters away from me, and all that is mine.’”

[Ib. 33.] “But Laban entered and searched in Leah’s house”: we should observe how it calls it the wife’s house, since Laban caught them on the journey—unless perhaps Scripture customarily uses *house* for a chamber or tent, just as it also speaks of the maidservants’ houses.

[Ib. 37.] Jacob says to Laban, “Because you searched all the vessels of my house”: here he speaks of one house, whose parts were the houses of his wives and concubines. Thus the “houses” are to be understood as chambers or tents, which are also called pavilions.

[Ib. 42.] “Unless the God of my father Abraham and the Fear of Isaac had been with me” [Note: In the manuscripts, *esset*; according to the Greek Septuagint, *en moi* (“in me”).]: he calls his grandfather his father, just as Isaac, his father, had called him.

[Ib. XXXII, 3–5.] “Jacob sent messengers before him to Esau his brother, into the land of Seir, into the region of Edom, and commanded them, saying, ‘Thus you shall say to my lord Esau: Thus says your servant Jacob: I have lived with Laban and stayed there until now; and I have acquired oxen and asses and sheep and male and female servants; and I have sent to inform my lord Esau.’” He did not say, “I have sent to inform you.”

[Ib. XXXII, 17.] “If Esau asks you, saying, ‘Whose are you? And where are you going? And whose are these things that go before you?’ you shall say, ‘Your servant Jacob’s’”: the sentence would be full and complete even without *and*.

[Ib. 18.] “I have sent gifts to my lord Esau, and behold, he himself is behind us”: in the customary form of speech it should have said, “To my lord, to you,” or “To his lord, to you.”

[Ib. 22.] “He arose that same night and took his two wives and his two maidservants”: here the maidservants are distinguished from the wives, whom Scripture had previously called wives. “And he took two wives and two maidservants”: we should note the scriptural custom in the expression *he took*. He did not marry them then, nor did he then receive them from his father-in-law.

[Ib. XXXIII, 13.] The Latin manuscripts read, “And the sheep and cattle are giving birth”; the Greek reads, “The sheep and cattle are giving birth upon me.” This was said in the sense that they are under my concern or care, just as we ordinarily speak when we say that something is “upon our head,” meaning that we take the greatest care of it.

[Ib. XXXIV, 7.] “And Jacob’s sons came from the field, and when they heard, the men were pierced with grief, and it was exceedingly grievous to them that he had done a shameful thing in Israel, that he had slept with Jacob’s daughter—and it shall not be so.” Expressions of this kind are difficult to find in Scripture when the writer inserts the words of the speakers without introducing them as speech. For it does not say, “and they said,” but, with this omitted, it gives their words. Who else could have said, “and it shall not be so,” except those who were gravely indignant and were plotting vengeance?

[Ib. 8.] We should note that Hamor, speaking about Dinah to Jacob and his sons, says “your daughter,” not “your daughter, the sister of these men.”

[Ib. 15, 16.] “In this we shall be like you, and we shall dwell in you”: that is, among you.

[Ib. 19.] “For he was attached to Jacob’s daughter”: that is, he loved her.

[Ib. 26.] “And they killed his son Shechem with the edge of the sword”: as though it said, “with a sword.”

[Ib. 28, 29.] What Jacob’s sons took from the city of the Shechemites, Salem, after they had conquered it, is enumerated as follows: “Their sheep and their cattle and their asses, whatever was in the city and whatever was in the field, they took; and they captured all their bodies, and plundered whatever was in the city and whatever was in the houses.” Among all this, it is not sufficiently clear what he meant by “their bodies.” We should not suppose that they took the bodies of those who had been killed; rather, things that are possessed bodily are intended. Thus the continuation—“and their household goods and everything else”—would explain it, just as in legal language one speaks of the transfer of *bodies*. Nevertheless, the Greeks very commonly call slaves σωμάτια (*sōmatia*); but since the word used here is not σωμάτια but σώματα (*sōmata*), we should not rashly assert that slaves are meant. Still, this may in fact be the more likely meaning.

[Ib. XXXVI, 40.] After Scripture has mentioned the nation of Edom—that is, the Idumaeans—and those who had reigned in it, it later says, “These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their places, in their regions and in their nations.” It calls the families *nations*, although there was one nation, because its generations had multiplied; Edom himself was also called by that name. Hence the nation that he propagated was likewise named after him, whose father he certainly was.

[Ib. XXXVII, 21.] “When Reuben heard this, he delivered him from their hands and said, ‘Let us not strike him in his life.’” He did not first deliver him and then say this; rather, by saying this he delivered him. Thus the text first says that he delivered him, and then briefly indicates how he delivered him.

[Ib. 22.] “Let us not strike him in his life”: here *life* means the life of an animated body, using the cause for what is caused. In this sense, it may also be understood that the devil was told concerning Job, “Do not touch his life” (Job II, 6)—that is, “Do not kill him.” But in the sense in which the nature of the soul is mentioned, the Lord says, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X, 28).

[Ib. 27.] What Judah says, “Let our hands not be upon him,” is what we ordinarily say as, “Let us not lay hands on him.”

[Ib. 27.] “For he is our brother and our flesh”: this is not two different things, but the same thing said twice, as though explaining what “our brother” means—namely, “our flesh,” because they had been born from the same flesh.

[Ib. 31.] “They killed the kid of the goats”: Scripture customarily speaks this way, as in the Psalm, “Like lambs of sheep” (Ps. CXIII, 4). It is as though a kid could be anything other than a goat’s, or a lamb anything other than a sheep’s.

[Ib. XXXVIII, 13.] “And it was announced to his daughter-in-law Tamar, saying”: it should have said, “They announced it, saying.”

[Ib. 14.] “And having removed from herself the garments of her widowhood”: how much less would have been said if *from herself* had not been added?

[Ib. 26.] “And he did not continue to know her”: this means “to have intercourse with her.”

[Ib. XXXIX, 4.] “And Joseph found favor in the sight of his lord”: this expression is familiar throughout Scripture.

[Ib. 6.] “And he knew nothing of the things that were around him at all” [Note: The printed editions have “the things that were around him” and do not add *at all*. We have restored it from the manuscripts, since Augustine mentions this expression because of this word.]: among the Greeks this is a common expression, but it is not correct in our language. We say, “He knew nothing.”

[Ib. 6.] “Except the bread that he himself ate”: by *bread* he intended everything pertaining to his food; hence, in the Lord’s Prayer, bread alone is understood as the daily nourishment: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. VI, 11).

[Ib. 7.] “And his lord’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph”: this is also a familiar expression among us, meaning “she loved him.”

[Col. 0497] [Ib. XXXIX, 7.] “And she said, ‘Sleep with me’”: this too is a familiar expression, meaning “Lie with me.”

[Ib. 22.] “And the keeper of the prison gave the prison into Joseph’s hand”: this means “into Joseph’s hands,” signifying “under his authority.”

[Ib. XL, 8.] “And they said, ‘We have seen a dream, and there is no one to interpret it’”: although each of them had seen his own dream, they did not say, “We have seen dreams,” but, “We have seen a dream.”

[Ib. 12.] “The three branches are three days”: he did not say, “They signify three days.” This expression should be carefully noted wherever things that signify something are called by the name of the things they signify. Hence the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4); he does not say, “The rock signified Christ.”

[Ib. 13.] “And you shall give the cup into his hand”: the sentence would be complete even without *into his hand*.

[Ib. 19.] “And Pharaoh shall take your head away from you”: the sentence would be complete even without *from you*.

[Ib. 19.] “And the birds of the sky shall eat your flesh from you”: this is similar to the preceding expression.

[Ib. XLI, 1.] “And it came to pass after two years of days”: what would be lacking if *of days* were omitted?

[Ib. 7.] “And Pharaoh arose, and it was a dream”: Scripture likes to speak this way of dreams after a person has awakened, as though, when the truth of wakefulness has been restored, the thing that had seemed like reality while it was being seen then appears as a dream.

[Ib. 9.] “I remember my sin today. Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put us in prison”: he speaks of Pharaoh as though of someone else.

[Ib. 11.] “And we both saw a dream in one night, I and he”: as though it were not enough to say *we both*. Then here too he says, “We saw a dream,” not “We saw dreams,” as though both had seen one dream.

[Ib. 13.] “And it happened just as he interpreted for us; so it also came to pass.” *And it happened* is a customary scriptural expression; the sentence would be complete with, “Just as he interpreted for us, so it also came to pass.”

[Ib. 19.] “Such as I have never seen, more ugly, throughout all the land of Egypt”: in our manner of speaking it could be said, “Ugliers than whom I have never seen”; or, “Such as I have never seen”; or, “I have never seen such.” “Rising, he slept”: *rising* means “waking.”

[Ib. 25.] “He shows Pharaoh the things God does”: although he is speaking to Pharaoh, he speaks of God as someone else.

[Ib. 30.] “And famine will consume the land”: *land* is used for the people who are in the land.

[Ib. 33.] “Now therefore look for a prudent and intelligent man and set him over the land of Egypt; and let Pharaoh act and appoint officials over the land”: it is as though the person to whom he says, “Provide a prudent man,” were different from the one of whom he says, “Let Pharaoh appoint.”

[Ib. 35.] “And let the grain be gathered under Pharaoh’s hand”: that is, under his authority.

[Ib. 40.] “Nevertheless, I shall precede you in the throne”: these are the words Pharaoh spoke to Joseph according to the Greek. *I shall precede you* is a customary expression among the Greeks, whereas we say, “I shall precede you.” But “I shall precede you in the throne” is reportedly not customary even among the Greeks. They say, “I shall precede you from the throne,” that is, in the honor of the seat. This is understood to mean, “I shall precede you in kingship”; and this is what he says to him afterward.

[Ib. XLI, 44.] “I am Pharaoh; without you no one shall lift his hand over all the land of Egypt”: as though he said, “I am the king, but you are the governor or prefect of Egypt.” *Pharaoh* is not the name of a man, but of royal authority.

[Ib. XLII, 1, 2.] “When Jacob saw that there was grain for sale in Egypt, he said to his sons, ‘Why are you idle? Behold, I have heard that there is grain for sale in Egypt’”: we should note that Scripture says he saw what he says he had heard.

[Ib. 2.] “Buy us a little food, so that we may live and not die”: one of these expressions would have been sufficient—either “so that we may live” or “so that we may not die.”

[Ib. 11.] “We are peaceful men; your servants are not spies”: they speak as though about others, saying “your servants are not spies,” although they could have said, “We are not spies.” This was chiefly a matter of respectful speech.

[Ib. 13.] “We are twelve brothers, your servants, in the land of Canaan”: later they say that one of them is no longer present, thinking that Joseph himself is absent—that is, dead. The same expression occurs in, “These are the sons of Jacob who were born in Mesopotamia” (Gen. XXXV, 26), although Benjamin was not born there. As for their saying, “We are in the land of Canaan,” although at the time they were speaking they were in Egypt, *we are* means “we live.” They had come from there and intended to return immediately, having merely stayed there temporarily.

[Ib. 14.] “This is what I said to you, saying that you are spies”: what would be lacking if *saying* were omitted?

[Ib. 19.] “You yourselves go and carry away the purchase of your grain”: *carry* means “bring,” because animals are led when they carry something, and therefore what is carried is also said to be led.

[Ib. 22.] “Did I not speak to you, saying, ‘Do not harm the boy,’ and you did not heed me?” We should note that *being heeded* is not used only of God’s hearing and answering.

[Ib. 23.] “But they did not know that Joseph heard”: *heard* means “understood.” Even someone who does not understand a language hears its sounds with his ears. The same expression is repeated when they tell their father what had happened to them in Egypt and what they had said to Joseph.

[Ib. 32.] “We are twelve brothers, sons of our father; one is no more, and the youngest is today with our father in the land of Canaan.” Many kinds of expression occur in these few words. There is the point I mentioned shortly before: “We are twelve,” although they say, “One is no more.” There is also, “We are sons of our father,” as though they could be sons of anyone other than their father. Then, “The youngest is with our father today in the land of Canaan,” without their saying *is* or anything similar.

We should also note something especially necessary in connection with the Evangelists’ narratives: when they report that certain things were said, they do not always repeat them in exactly the same words. Nevertheless, no truth of meaning is lost through the difference in wording. They said that Joseph had told them, “Trade in the land,” but this is not found among his words. Yet they did not lie, because from the words he had spoken they had understood his intention. Words are necessary only to express an intention and, as far as possible, convey it to the knowledge of those who hear.

[Ib. XLII, 35.] “And each man’s bundle of silver was in their sack”: he did not say, “in his sack,” or “in their sacks,” but spoke as though they all had one sack.

[Ib. 36.] “All these things have come upon me”: that is, “They burden me with misery.”

[Ib. XLIII, 3.] “But Judah said to him, saying”: the sentence could be complete even without *saying*.

[Ib. 3.] “The man questioned us with questioning”: this is a frequent scriptural expression—“the man questioned us with questioning,” or “he questioned us by questioning,” and similar forms.

[Ib. 16.] “For the men shall eat loaves with me at noon”: surely he does not mean loaves alone; rather, the expression includes everything else under the name of what is prominent. “For the men shall eat loaves with me at noon”: *noon* signifies the midday meal, which takes place in the middle of the day; that is what *noon* means.

[Ib. 18.] “So that you may take us and our asses as servants”: *servants* is not to be supplied with *asses*. Although the Latin manuscripts have *servants*, the Greek reads παῖδας (*paidas*), which cannot possibly refer to asses. Therefore only “take our asses” is to be understood.

[Ib. 21.] “We opened our sacks, and each man’s silver was in his sack”: he did not add *was found*, *appeared*, *was there*, or anything similar.

[Ib. 23.] “May you have God’s favor; do not be afraid”: in the words translated “May you have God’s favor,” two words are understood, *may he be* and *God*. The complete expression is, “May God be favorable to you,” which is entirely customary in Greek.

[Ib. 28.] “Your servant, our father, is safe; he is still alive”: here it is shown more explicitly that the word *boy* can signify a servant. It could not refer to age in that old man.

[Ib. 32.] “For the Egyptians could not eat bread with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to the Egyptians”: this expression is used so that all kinds of food are understood by *bread*.

[Ib. 34.] “Benjamin’s portion was made greater than the portions of all the others, fivefold in comparison with theirs”: since “greater than the portions of all” had already been said, *in comparison with theirs* need not have been added.

[Ib. XLIV, 6, 7.] “When he found them, he spoke according to these words”: he could have said, “He spoke these words to them.” Or is this not merely a kind of expression, but does the meaning also differ? It is one thing to say the very words themselves, and another to speak according to them, so that whatever other words are spoken, the same meaning contained in those words is retained. This is *according to them*, even if they are not the very words themselves. But since the response follows, “Why does my lord speak according to these words?”—where they surely should have said in the customary manner, “Why does my lord speak these words?”—it is clear that this is a kind of expression.

[Ib. XLIV, 7.] “Far be it from your servants to do according to this word”: they could have said, “Far be it from us,” but Scripture customarily uses this respectful form, speaking as though about others. *Servants* here means slaves.

[Ib. 9.] “And we too shall be servants to our lord”: here also the Greek has παῖδες (*paides*), that is, *boys*, which Scripture uses so constantly for servants that it is difficult to find it calling servants by any other name.

[Ib. 34.] “How shall I go up to my father, when the boy is not with us, so that I may not see the evils that will find my father?” The customary form of speech more properly required, “So that I may see the evils that will find my father” [Note: In the printed editions, the words “The customary form of speech more properly required, ‘So that I may see the evils that will find my father’” had been omitted. The passage has been restored from the manuscripts.]; that is, “How shall I go up so that I may see?” Thus, in an unusual form of speech, what he says has the force of saying *not*. The customary order of the words is: “I shall not go up to my father, when the boy is not with us, so that I may not see the evils that will find my father.”

[Ib. XLV, 2, 4.] When Joseph wept as he was recognized by his brothers, Scripture says, “All the Egyptians heard, and it was heard in Pharaoh’s house.” It then continues with the narrative: “Joseph said to his brothers.” Scripture therefore first stated what happened afterward; this occurred because the matter became widely known among all the Egyptians. Then, in a brief recapitulation, the narrative returned to what was being said.

[Ib. 16.] “And the report was spread in Pharaoh’s house, saying, ‘Joseph’s brothers have come’”: *saying* is used for *those who were saying it*. The report of those who said, “Joseph’s brothers have come,” was spread.

[Ib. XLVI, 2.] “But he answered, ‘What is it, saying?’” The order is: “But he answered, saying, ‘What is it?’”

[Ib. 4.] God says to Jacob, “I shall descend with you into Egypt, and I shall bring you up at the end”: this is how the Greek reads, whereas the Latin has, “And I shall lead you to the end.”

[Ib. 28.] “He sent Judah before him to Joseph, to come to meet him near the city of Heroum”: I do not know whether the name *Heroum* is readily found elsewhere in Scripture.

[Ib. 31, 32.] In Joseph’s words to his brothers—“I shall go up and announce to Pharaoh and say to him, ‘My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me; and they are shepherds’”—the parenthetical statement “for they were keepers of livestock” is inserted by the author in his own voice. He then returns to Joseph’s words by adding, “and they have brought their animals and sheep and all that is theirs.” Thus Joseph’s words are ordered as follows: “They are shepherds, and they have brought their animals and sheep and all that is theirs.”

[Ib. XLVII, 8.] “Pharaoh said to Jacob, ‘How many are the years of the days of your life?’” The words *there are* are understood.

[Ib. 9.] “Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life.” *Few* is used for *a small number*. The days of one person’s life cannot literally be shorter in duration than those of others. Jacob said this in comparison with the lives of his ancestors. For surely no one now lives to the age of one hundred and thirty years, which he had already reached.

[Ib. XLVII, 12.] “Grain according to the body”: that is, according to the number of bodies. By *body* he means the number of bodies, and by the number of bodies, the number of people.

[Ib. 13.] “The famine had become exceedingly severe, and the land of Egypt failed”: *land* is used for the people who were in the land.

[Ib. 15.] “All the Egyptians came to Joseph, saying, ‘Give us bread’”: by *bread* he means grain, using the product for the thing that produces it.

[Ib. 20.] “And the land became Pharaoh’s”: he did not say *Pharaoh’s land*. Scripture likes to speak in this way, as it says in the Psalm, “I kept your law; it became mine, because I sought your ordinances” (Ps. CXVIII, 55–56). Speaking of God’s law, he says, “It became mine,” that is, “for my benefit.”

[Ib. 22.] “Except the land of the priests alone, Joseph did not possess”: this is as though he had said, “Except the land of the priests alone, Joseph possessed all the land.”

[Ib. 26.] “And Joseph made it a statute for them, continuing to the present day in the land of Egypt, that they should give a fifth to Pharaoh”: from this it is understood that *Pharaoh* was the name of royal authority, since the text says “continuing to the present day.” The Egyptians who lived at that time could not have continued to pay until the day on which this was written, since that Pharaoh was already dead.

[Ib. 28.] “And the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were”: Scripture often says *the days of the years* when it could simply say *the years*.

[Ib. XLVIII, 1.] The text reads, “It was announced to Joseph that your father was troubled.” Some manuscripts have *afflicted*, some *distressed*, and others use different words, according to how the Latin translators rendered the Greek ἐνοχλεῖται (*enochleitai*). *Troubled* seems the more suitable translation because this is said of people who are shaken by bodily affliction as death approaches. From the same root comes the Greek word ὄχλος (*ochlos*), meaning *crowd*. A crowd is an unorganized multitude, unlike a people, which is called δῆμος (*dēmos*), or the common populace, which is called λαός (*laos*), but like ὄχλος, which means *crowd*.

[Ib. 16.] Jacob, blessing the sons of Joseph, his grandsons, says among other things, “And my name and the name of my fathers shall be invoked over them.” We should therefore note that not only *hearing and answering* but also *invocation* can sometimes be spoken of when the object is not God but human beings.

[Ib. 18.] “For this is the firstborn”: according to the Greek manuscripts, the sentence lacks *is*.

[Col. 0502] [Ib. XLIX, 24.] In Jacob’s blessing of Joseph he says, among other things, “From there comes the one who strengthened Israel.” It would be surprising if *is* were not understood, so that the complete sentence would be, “From there is the one who strengthened Israel.”

[Ib. L, 2, 3.] The text reads, “Joseph said to his servants, the buriers, to bury his father.” The Latin language has no way to designate ἐνταφιαστάς (*entaphiastas*). For they do not themselves bury the bodies of the dead—that is, commit them to the earth—which in Greek is not ἐνταφιάσαι (*entaphiasai*) but θάψαι (*thapsai*). The ἐνταφιασταί (*entaphiastai*) perform the work done for human bodies: preserving, drying, wrapping, and binding them. In this work the Egyptians are especially distinguished for their care. Therefore, when the text says, “They also buried him,” we should understand, “They cared for him.” And when it speaks of forty days for the burial, these should be understood as forty days for the preservation of the body. He was not actually buried until the place where he had ordered himself to be buried.

[Ib. 4.] “Speak in Pharaoh’s ears”: this is a customary scriptural expression.

[Ib. 6.] “And Pharaoh said to Joseph, ‘Go down and bury your father’”: even if Pharaoh spoke through the powerful men whom Joseph had sent to him, telling them to convey his words to Joseph, he nevertheless spoke to Joseph himself. This is like the passage in the Gospel where one Evangelist says that the centurion came to the Lord and said to him, “My boy lies at home paralyzed” (Matt. VIII, 5–6), while another, recounting the matter more fully, says that he sent friends to the Lord to say this to him (Luke VII, 3). In those friends he himself came, since his intention was present in them. Hence the saying, “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (Matt. X, 40).

[Ib. 10.] “They mourned him with a great and very powerful mourning”: it says *they mourned a mourning*, not *they mourned with mourning*. This is a recognized expression in Latin, as in “he served a servitude,” “he served a military service,” and similar forms.

[Ib. 15.] “And by repaying he will repay us all the evils that we showed him.” From this expression the Apostle also says, “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils” (II Tim. IV, 14). *We showed* and *he showed* mean “we did” and “he did.”

[Ib. 17.] “Receive the iniquity of the servants of the God of your father”: *Receive the iniquity* is a novel expression meaning “forgive,” “pardon,” or “forget.” But I think *receive* was used as though it said, “Bear it with equanimity”—that is, “Do not take offense at it.”

[Ib. 18.] “And they came to him and said”: they did not come a second time; rather, something that had been said is said again. Scripture often does this.

# BOOK TWO: Expressions from Exodus

[Col. 0501]

[EXOD. chap. I, vv. 7–12.] “And they grew exceedingly, exceedingly strong.”

[Ib. 21.] What is meant by the statement about the midwives, “And they made houses for themselves, because they feared God”? It had already been said, “God dealt well with the midwives.” [Col. 0502] The words “they made houses for themselves by fearing God” seem to belong to this, as though God’s benefits to them enabled them to make houses for themselves. Are we to understand that previously they had no houses? Or does the word refer to wealth, or rather to some resources sufficient for maintaining a household? This seems similar to what Jacob said to his father-in-law after fourteen years of service, when his father-in-law wished to keep him with him longer: “Now when shall I also make a house for myself?” He had said that Laban’s livestock had increased under his care, just as Laban himself had acknowledged by saying, “God has blessed me at your coming” (Gen. XXX, 29–31). When Jacob therefore says, “When shall I also make a house for myself?” the words “as you have” are understood. This seems to be the force of *also*, and the proposed arrangement of wages that follows with Laban appears to pertain to the making of that house.

[Ib. I, 22.] “And every female child you shall keep alive”: this is what the Greek has; the Latin does not have *it*.

[Ib. II, 1.] “There was a certain man from the tribe of Levi, and he took for himself one of the daughters of Levi”: a wife is understood, which some Latin translators thought should also be added. The text continues, “And he had her, and she conceived.”

[Ib. 3.] What *thibin* may mean is difficult to know because neither the Greek translator from the Hebrew nor the Latin translator from the Greek translated the word; each transferred it as he found it.

[Ib. 14.] “Moses was afraid and said, ‘If this matter has become known.’” Two things should be observed in this expression. First, the sentence is left hanging and is dismissed in that form. Second, *word* is used for *deed*.

[Ib. 25.] “And he looked upon the children of Israel, and it became known to them”: *became known* is used for what God did among them, so that they might understand God’s care for them.

[Ib. III, 7.] “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt.”

[Ib. 11, 12.] “And Moses said to God, ‘Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt?’ But he said, ‘Because I shall be with you.’” This is how the Greek reads. The Latin, however, has, “And who am I? he said,” and does not say, “that I should go” and “that I should bring out,” but “that I may go” and “that I may bring out.” The Greek’s “But he said, ‘Because I shall be with you’” is naturally understood as something he said to Moses. The Latin added all the rest, saying, “And God said to Moses.”

[Ib. 16.] God tells Moses what he should say to the children of Israel: “Visiting, I have visited you, and whatever has happened to you in Egypt.” The Greek has, “With a visitation I have visited you.”

[Ib. 18.] God says to Moses concerning the children of Israel, “And they shall hear your voice”: the Greek has, “And they shall heed your voice,” since *heeding* can also be said of a human being.

[Ib. 22.] The Latin reads, “The woman shall ask her neighbor and her fellow resident for vessels of silver and gold and clothing”; the Greek has *from her cohabitant*, that is, σύσκηνος (*syskēnos*) [Note: The printed editions have *sunoikou*. The manuscripts have *suskēnou*, as in the Septuagint.], which some Latin translators rendered “from her fellow cell-dweller.”

[Ib. IV, 1.] Moses says, “What if they do not believe me or heed my voice?” The Latin translated this as “hear my voice.”

[Ib. 4.] “Stretch out your hand and seize its tail,” as the Greek has. The Latin, however, translated, “Your hand and its tail.” “And he stretched out his hand and seized its tail, and it became a staff in his hand.”

[Ib. 5.] “And he said to him, ‘So that they may believe you, because the Lord God of their fathers appeared to you’”: the Greek does not have “And he said to him,” but immediately adds, “so that they may believe you”—that is, the words of God after the miraculous deed. It is as though he were still speaking and had just completed the thought of his words. The order of the words is: “Stretch out your hand and seize its tail, so that they may believe you.” But the narrative of the deed is inserted, and afterward the words “so that they may believe you” are resumed.

[Ib. IV, 6.] The Latin reads, “And his hand became leprous like snow”; the Greek does not have *leprous*, but only, “It became like snow.”

[Ib. 8.] “But if they do not hear the voice of the first sign”: this is how the Greek reads. The Latin, however, has, “the voice of your first sign.” The same follows: “They shall believe you because of the voice of the next sign.”

[Ib. 9.] “And the water that you take from the river shall become blood upon the dry”: or rather, “upon the dry thing,” that is, upon what is dry. The Latin said, “blood upon the earth.”

[Ib. 10.] Moses says, “I beg you, Lord; I am not eloquent from yesterday or the day before yesterday.”

[Ib. 17.] “And you shall take this staff in your hand, with which you shall make signs in it”: he could have said, “with which you shall make signs,” or, “You shall take this staff in your hand and make signs with it.” But here both expressions are used according to Scripture’s customary manner of speaking.

[Ib. 18, 19.] “After those many days, the king of Egypt died. And the Lord said to Moses in Midian, ‘Go, proceed to Egypt, for all who sought your life have died.’” Many kinds of expression should be noted in these words. First, “Go, proceed to Egypt,” as though either *go* or *proceed* alone were insufficient. Then, “All who sought your life have died,” although Scripture had said only that the king of Egypt had died, and earlier had said only of him that he was seeking to kill Moses. Did he die last, after the other enemies? If so, this is not an expression but a matter of meaning.

Likewise, “those who sought your life” is used in Scripture not only in a bad sense but also in a good one. In the bad sense, as here, it is also found in the Psalms: “Let those who seek my life be confounded and put to shame” (Ps. XXXIX, 15). In the good sense: “My escape has perished, and there is no one who seeks my life” (Ps. CXLI, 5). Unless perhaps a distinction is made between *those who seek* and *those who seek out*, so that the former is understood in a bad sense and the latter in a good one.

### [Book V, 10]

“And they said to the people, saying, ‘Thus says Pharaoh.’” This expression the Latin translator was reluctant to render.

### [Book V, 21]

“May God see you and judge, because you have made our odor offensive before Pharaoh and before his servants, by putting a sword into their hands to kill us.” Thus the Greek reads. But the Latin says, “so that you might give a sword into his hands,” which we used to read as the best version. This solecism was introduced without any necessity of translation, since it is not present in the Greek.

### [Book VI, 4]

“I established my covenant with them, so as to give them the land of the Canaanites, and the land in which they dwelt, in which also they dwelt in it.” Thus the Greek reads, which certainly appears absurd even in the Greek language; yet the authority of the Seventy translators is so great that they were not reluctant to speak in this way. What then? Is some meaning concealed here? If there is none, the expression itself should be noted, lest, when found elsewhere, it impede the meaning or compel someone to seek something where nothing ought to be sought.

### [Book VI, 5]

The Latin reads, “I heard the groaning of the children of Israel, how the Egyptians were oppressing them”; the Greek has καταδουλοῦνται, which could be translated “they reduce them to slavery,” since it cannot be rendered by a single word.

### [Book VI, 9]

“And Moses spoke thus to the children of Israel, and they did not hear Moses because of discouragement and because of harsh labors.” It says “they heard,” not “they listened.”

### [Book VI, 12]

“For I am ineloquent”—what Moses said to the Lord. The Greek has ἄλογος, not “unskilled,” as though it were ἀμαθής or ἀπαίδευτος.

### [Book VI, 26]

“These are Aaron and Moses, to whom God said that they should bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt.” Thus the Greek reads.

### [Book VI, 30]

“Behold, I am weak of voice, and how will Pharaoh hear me?” It should be noted that it says “will hear,” not “will listen.”

### [Book VII, 6]

“And Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded them; so they did.” What would be lacking if “so they did” were not said?

### [Book VII, 9]

“If Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, ‘Give us a sign or portent,’ then you shall say to Aaron your brother, ‘Take the staff.’” Did not the customary usage of our language, and a certain completeness of the expression, require it to be said in this way: “If Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, ‘Give us a sign or portent,’ you shall say to Aaron your brother, ‘Take the staff’”? Why, then, was “then” added, unless because of some characteristic feature of Hebrew expression? For it is reportedly not Greek either.

### [Book VII, 11]

The Latin translators do not seem to have rendered Φαραώ σοφιστάς—“Pharaoh’s sophists”—quite appropriately when they said “wise men.” For σοφοί means “wise men.” The Latin translator could have said *sophists*, since there is no equivalent way of saying this in Latin; and we already use this word as Latin, just as we say *philosophia* not only in Greek but also in Latin. The most eloquent authors of Latin literature called them [Note: So the manuscripts read. But the printed editions have: “sophists, however, are called …”] *sophists*.

### [Book VII, 12]

“And Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs”—as though it said, “Aaron’s dragon.”

### [Book VII, 15]

Regarding Pharaoh it says, “Behold, he has gone out to the water”; the Greek has “upon the water.”

### [Book VII, 16]

“Let my people go, so that they may serve me, and behold, you have not heard even until now.” How often is “you have heard” said when it is addressed to a human being?

### [Book VII, 22]

“And the Egyptian magicians likewise acted by their enchantments. And Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not hear them, as the Lord had said.” It is characteristic of scriptural usage to say “he heard” even when the subject is a human being.

### [Book VIII, 1]

“Let my people go, so that they may serve me”—not “so that it may serve me.” This manner of speaking is scarcely found except where the thing itself is singular but consists of many parts. “People” is a singular noun, but it consists of many persons. Likewise: “Let all the earth worship you” (Psalm 65:4), because “all the earth” is said of the people who are on the earth.

### [Book VIII, 2]

“Behold, I am striking all your borders with frogs.” Thus the Greek reads, in a most elegant expression, so that the frogs themselves are understood as the plague by which the land of Egypt is struck.

### [Book VIII, 3–4]

“And the river shall spew out frogs, and, coming up, they shall enter your houses and the storerooms of your chambers, upon your beds, and into the houses of your servants and your people, and into your kneading-troughs and your ovens; and upon you, your people, and your servants the frogs shall come up.”

It should be noted that, after saying “into the houses,” and so forth, the text retained the accusative case; and after saying “upon the beds,” and so forth, it likewise retained the accusative with “upon.” But in “in the kneading-troughs” and “in the ovens” it shifted to the ablative. The Greek also changes the preposition, whereas the Latin does not. For the Greek has εἰς τοὺς οἴκους, “into the houses,” but for “in the kneading-troughs” it has ἐν τοῖς φυράμασιν. It would be surprising if this were not also a matter of meaning rather than expression: perhaps it wishes the frogs that arose in the kneading-troughs and ovens to be understood, not frogs that came up or burst in from outside. Since it predicts that the river will spew them out, it is from there that they will fill everything.

### [Book VIII, 6]

“And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt and brought out the frogs, and the frog came out and covered the land.” A repetition has shifted from the plural to the singular: clearly “the frog” is used for the multitude of frogs. Yet, through the customary manner of speech that has formed people’s perceptions, something often seems greater when said in the singular than when said in the plural. For example, “there is a soldier there” is taken as more emphatic than “there are soldiers there”; “there is a fish there” than “there are fish there.”

### [Book VIII, 14]

“And they gathered them into heaps, heaps.” This repetition signifies a multitude of heaps and is familiar in Scripture.

### [Book VIII, 16]

The Latin reads, “Stretch out the staff with your hand and strike earth,” not “strike the earth.” The Greek has “the mound of the earth,” if τὸ χῶμα τῆς γῆς has been correctly translated by this expression.

### [Book VIII, 18]

“And the magicians likewise acted by their enchantments, to bring out gnats, and they could not.”

It should be noted that “they acted” is said instead of “they attempted to act.” For if they acted likewise, they certainly brought out gnats. But since the text continues, “to bring them out, and they could not,” they did not therefore act in the same way, but attempted to act in the same way. Or perhaps, although they too acted by enchantments, they extended a staff in the same manner of acting—something the Scripture did not state explicitly—and “they acted likewise” should be referred to this.

### [Book VIII, 21–22]

“And upon the land on which they are upon it. And I will glorify the land of Goshen on that day, in which my people are upon it.”

### [Book VIII, 29]

“And Moses said, ‘I will go out from you, and I will pray to God, and the dog-fly will go out from Pharaoh and from his servants.’” It is as though he said to one person, “I will go out from you,” and then referred to another Pharaoh from whom the dog-fly would go out.

### [Book IX, 1]

“Let my people go, so that they may serve me.”

### [Book IX, 18, 24]

“Behold, at this hour tomorrow I will rain much hail.” The hail, however, is “very, very great.”

### [Book IX, 29, 28]

“And the voices and the hail shall cease.” It should be noted that Scripture commonly calls thunder “voices.” Pharaoh himself previously called these the voices of God, saying, “Pray to the Lord for me, so that the voices of God may cease.” Here too there is the expression “that voices may come to an end.”

### [Book X, 2]

“So that you may tell your sons and your sons’ sons in their hearing all the things with which I mocked the Egyptians.” It should be noted how “I mocked” is said, lest the phrase perhaps be understood in the sense of “This is the dragon whom you formed for mockery” (Psalm 103:26), and the passage in Job, “This is the beginning of the Lord’s creation, which he made for mockery by his angels” (Job 40:14).

### [Book X, 4]

“Behold, at this time tomorrow I will bring a great locust.” Observe how above it said “the frog,” where we noted that something of this kind, when said in the singular, is often understood more fully than if it were said in the plural. For it plainly has greater force to say “a great locust” than “many locusts.”

### [Book X, 8]

“But who are those who will go?” In familiar usage we say every day, “Who are those who will go?”

### [Book X, 15]

“No green thing was left on the trees.” According to our customary manner of speaking, it should have been said, “Something green was not left on the trees.”

### [Book X, 16–17]

Pharaoh said to Moses, “I have sinned before the Lord your God and against you; therefore receive my sin.” His brothers used the same expression to Joseph when they said, “Accept the iniquity of the servants of the God of your father” (Genesis 50:17).

### [Book X, 23]

The Latin reads, “And no one saw his brother for three days”; the Greek has, “And no one saw no one his brother.” It should also be noted that “brother” may mean any human being.

### [Book X, 24]

Pharaoh says to Moses and Aaron, “Go and serve the Lord your God; apart from the sheep and cattle, leave them.” Thus the Greek reads. This is a very unusual expression, unless “leave them” is supplied after a pause, with “these things” understood, so that the sense is: “Go, apart from the sheep and cattle, and leave these things.” Such ellipsis frequently occurs in scriptural expressions.

### [Book X, 26]

“And we shall not leave a hoof”—as though, when the animals were taken away, a hoof could remain behind. For what else does “we shall not leave a hoof” mean except “we shall not leave even a hoof”?

### [Book X, 28]

Pharaoh said to Moses, “Take care not to add any more to seeing my face,” instead of “Take care that you do not see my face any more.”

### [Book XI, 2]

“And let each one ask his neighbor, and the woman her neighbor, for vessels of silver and gold and clothing.” It should be noted that the Egyptians too are called neighbors of the Hebrews.

### [Book XI, 6–7]

“And there shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has not been and such as shall not be added again; but among the children of Israel not even a dog shall move its tongue, from human being to cattle.”

This is a most elegant expression. By “dog” it signified the extreme case both of human beings and of cattle, thereby emphasizing how profound the quiet would be among the Hebrews while the Egyptians cried out amid bitter bereavement.

### [Column 0508] [Book XII, 3]

“Let each household take a sheep according to its ancestral houses.” It is not easy to understand what “ancestral houses” means here: whether the cities in which they lived, or rather the numerous families descended from each person’s supposed fatherhood. The latter, it is reported, is more clearly signified in the Greek.

### [Book XII, 4]

“But if there are few in the house, so that they are not sufficient for a sheep”—that is, so that the small number is not sufficient to consume a sheep—“he shall take with him his nearest neighbor”; that is, the household shall take a neighbor. A person is put for a person, and the singular for the plural. For it does not mean one person, but as many as are sufficient. When Scripture was speaking of consuming the sheep, it says, “According to the number of souls, each shall take what is sufficient.” “Souls” is used for persons: the whole is signified by a part.

### [Book XII, 7]

“They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the threshold, in the houses in which they will eat them in them.” After saying “in which,” it also said “in them,” in a very familiar manner. But “they will eat them” raises the question: what does “them” refer to? It is understood to mean “the meats,” for the text continues, “And they shall eat the meats roasted with fire this night.” The Latin manuscripts read “they shall eat the flesh”; the Greek has κρέας, “flesh,” but in the neuter gender. Hence the Greek has, “in the houses in which they shall eat it in them.” The expression is one in which the text first says “them” before stating in what follows what it means by “them.” It resembles the expression that we explained concerning Moses’ son (Book II of the *Questions on Exodus*, question 11), when the angel wished to kill him, and we cited the Psalm as an example: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion” (Psalm 86:1–2). We understand what “its foundations” refers to only from what follows. So here, “in which they will eat them in them”—that is, “in which houses they will eat them”—is understood to mean the meats of which the text subsequently speaks.

### [Book XII, 22]

“You shall take for yourselves a bundle of hyssop, dip it in the blood that is beside the door, and smear the threshold and both doorposts with the blood.” Here too “a bundle of hyssop” signifies several bundles, just as “the frog” signifies several frogs and “the locust” several locusts. This figure creates obscurity when it occurs with things that we do not ordinarily express in this way.

### [Book XII, 26–27]

“And it shall be, when your sons say to you, ‘What is this service?’ that you shall say to them, ‘This is the sacrifice of the Passover to the Lord.’” Even without “that,” the expression would be complete: “You shall say to them.”

### [Book XII, 28]

“And the children of Israel came and did as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron; so they did.” It would not have added “so they did” unless this were a customary feature of Scripture.

### [Book XII, 51]

“And it came to pass that on that day the Lord brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt.”

### [Book XIII, 1]

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying.”

### [Book XIII, 12]

“Everything that opens the womb, male.” The plural number is introduced into a singular expression, because “everything that opens” is understood not of one thing but of many. The expression resembles, “Attend, my people” (Psalm 77:1).

The same applies to what follows shortly afterward: “Everything that opens the womb among cattle and among sheep, whatever is born to you.” “Everything, whatever is born to you,” is the same manner of expression.

### [Book XIII, 13]

“Everything that opens the womb of a female donkey.” The Greek has “of a male donkey,” according to the manner of expression that we already noted in Genesis, where, in speaking of Sarah’s death, Scripture says, “Abraham rose from the dead man,” and “I will bury my dead man” (Genesis 23:3–4). Similar expressions concerning a dead woman occur there frequently.

### [Book XIII, 15]

“Therefore I sacrifice to the Lord everything that opens the womb, male.” This is an expression like the preceding one.

### [Book XIII, 16]

“And it shall be for a sign upon your hand,” that is, upon your works. Here perhaps the meaning is more important than the expression.

### [Book XIV, 27]

“And the Lord shook the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.” The Greek has, “And the Lord shook the Egyptians, the midst of the sea.”

### [Book XIV, 31]

“And Israel saw the great hand which the Lord wrought against the Egyptians.”

### [Book XV, 1]

“Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the Lord, and they said to say.” Thus the Greek reads: καὶ εἶπαν λέγειν.

### [Book XV, 22]

“And they did not find water, that they might drink.” It could have omitted “that they might drink.”

### [Book XV, 24]

“And the people murmured against Moses, saying.” It does not say “saying” in the singular, but “saying” in the plural, because the people consist of many persons.

### [Book XVI, 1]

“And the whole congregation of the children of Israel came into the wilderness.” It does not say “came” in the singular, because the Latin has the plural, “they came,” and the congregation consists of many persons.

### [Book XVI, 2]

“The whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron.” This is the same expression.

### [Book XVI, 4]

“And the Lord said to Moses, ‘Behold, I will rain bread for you from heaven.’” When he was about to rain manna, he promised bread. This is an expression in which “bread” is used for food. Scripture also prefers to say “breads” in the plural rather than “bread” in the singular.

### [Book XVI, 7]

“In the morning you shall see,” he says, “the glory, when he hears your murmuring against God”—that is, because you murmur against God, which has the same force as if he had said, “against God.” Further, it should be noted that here “hearing” is used in a new way, not of those who pray but of those who murmur, although Scripture clearly censures their murmuring. It is as though the text meant that God recognized their murmuring, and called God’s recognition “hearing.”

### [Book XVI, 9, 12]

“Draw near before God, for he has heard your murmuring.” Again, “hearing” signifies not prayers and requests but also the murmuring of the wicked. God says the same thing afterward: “I have heard the murmuring of the children of Israel.”

### [Book XVI, 14]

“And behold, on the face of the wilderness was something small, like coriander.” Since God so often says “the face of the earth,” as here “the face of the wilderness,” it is surprising that people, when they hear “face,” should make such a mistake as to imagine something like the face of a human being or of some living creature.

### [Book XVI, 16]

“According to the number of your souls, each of you shall gather for those who dwell with you.” How often Scripture calls human beings “souls,” using a part for the whole. It does not readily use “flesh” for human beings, but rather “flesh,” as in, “I will not fear what flesh can do to me”; and in the same Psalm it says more plainly, “What can a human being do to me?” (Psalm 56:5, 11). It would not say, “According to the number of your flesh,” as it says, “According to the number of your souls.”

### [Book XVI, 21]

“And they gathered it morning by morning.” Just as “wells, wells” and “heaps, heaps,” so it says “morning by morning.”

### [Book XVI, 29]

“Let none of you go out, each from his place, on the seventh day.” The insertion of “each” could have been omitted.

### [Book XVII, 1]

“But there was no water for the people to drink,” that is, for drinking.

### [Book XVII, 2]

“And the people cursed Moses,” that is, they dealt with Moses by curses; in other words, they cursed him. For he himself says in what follows, “Why do you curse me?”

### [Book XVII, 3]

“And the people murmured against Moses, saying.”

### [Book XVII, 5]

“Take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river.” “With which you struck” is said instead of what we say, “with which you struck”; this is an extremely common expression in Scripture.

### [Book XVIII, 12]

“And Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took burnt offerings and sacrifices for God.” “Took” is used instead of “offered.” Or perhaps this is a matter of meaning rather than expression, so that he is understood to have taken what Moses had offered. Yet Moses is not previously said to have sacrificed, nor Aaron, nor any of the Hebrews who were brought out of the land of Egypt. It is only written above that Moses built an altar and called it “The Lord is my refuge” (Exodus 17:15). We read that this Jethro was a priest of Midian, that is, of the nation of Midian. It is surprising if Moses began to sacrifice at his arrival, rather than Jethro himself, who was already a priest.

### [Book XVIII, 18]

“This word is too burdensome for you.” The verb “is” is understood.

### [Book XVIII, 20]

“And you shall show them the ways in which they shall walk in them.”

### [Book XVIII, 26]

“But they brought the difficult matter before Moses.” Thus the Greek reads; the Latin translators rendered it “to Moses.” That expression also signifies the very care indicated by “before Moses,” as though a burden were shown to have been placed upon him. “Difficult matter” means a difficult question; hence the text continues, “But every light matter they shall judge themselves.”

### [Book XX, 24]

The Greek has ἐπονομάσω. “I will give a further name” or “I will add a name” expresses it more precisely; some translators rendered it by the more usual “I will surname.” But “I will surname” does not have the necessary meaning. “I will add a name” is closer to the sense than “I will name,” although some translators have also used the latter.

### [Book XX, 24]

“And I will come to you and bless you.” Though the preceding verbs were plural—“you shall make” and “you shall sacrifice”—it says, “I will come to you,” as though speaking to Israel itself, that is, to the people.

### [Book XXI, 1]

“And these are the judgments that you shall set before them. If you buy a Hebrew slave,” and so forth.

This expression should be noted: although the first statement was addressed to Moses—“These are the judgments that you shall set before them”—everything that follows is spoken to the people themselves as though to Moses: “If you buy a Hebrew slave.” This was not said to Moses personally; rather, because he was to speak to the people, it was spoken to the people themselves.

### [Book XXI, 6]

“The Lord shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him forever,” or “for the age”: this is what the Greek has, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. Observe how in many passages Scripture, following this Greek expression, says “forever” or “eternally.” Here the eternity is not understood in the sense in which eternal things are promised to us, or in which the wicked are burned in everlasting fire. For this slave, who could not live forever, could not serve forever. Rather, “forever” means a period whose end is not specified; or certainly something eternal is signified by this sacrament.

### [Book XXI, 13]

“I will give you a place to which the one who kills may flee.”

### [Book XXI, 20]

“If someone strikes his male or female slave with a rod”—that is, “with the rod.”

### [Book XXI, 28]

“The ox shall be stoned with stones,” as though it could be stoned by anything other than stones. This expression differs somewhat from the scriptural manner in which one might say, “He shall be stoned with a stoning,” but it is nevertheless similar.

### [Book XXI, 29]

“But if the ox was horned yesterday and the day before yesterday.” A part is put for the whole to designate past time, however long that time may have been, according to scriptural usage.

### [Book XXI, 33]

“If anyone opens a pit, or digs a pit, and does not cover it, and a calf or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restitution.” This too is to be understood as a part for the whole. If a horse or a sheep fell into the pit, he would not for that reason fail to make restitution merely because this was not written.

### [Book XXI, 34]

“But whatever is dead shall belong to him,” instead of “shall be his.”

### [Book XXII, 5]

“But if someone grazes a field or vineyard, and lets his livestock graze another field”—that is, someone else’s.

### [Book XXII, 26]

“But if you take your neighbor’s garment as a pledge, you shall return it to him before sunset.” A general term is used for a specific one. It is said as though someone had given every garment as a pledge, whereas the context shows that the reference is specifically to the person who has no other garment with which to cover himself at night.

### [Book XXIII, 20–21]

“Behold, I am sending my angel before your face, to guard you on the way and bring you into the land that I have prepared for you. He will go before you” [Note: The old Corbie manuscript, of excellent quality, reads *ante ibi*, “before there”; perhaps the translator read *anti* for *ekei* in the Greek. In the Septuagint now, however, the reading is προσέχε σεαυτῷ, “pay attention to yourself.” In the Vulgate: “Observe him.”] “and hear him.”

God commands the people to hear his angel—not, of course, because the angel is asking something, but because he is commanding.

### [Book XXIII, 28]

“And I will send hornets before you, and he will drive out the Amorites.” The expression shifts from the plural to the singular. It is understood as “the hornet will drive out the Amorites,” just as “the frog” and “the locust” are used—not because there is only one, but because the singular signifies the plural.

### [Book XXIII, 30]

“I will drive them out from you in stages.”

### [Column 0512] [Book XXIII, 32–33]

“You shall not make a covenant with them or with their gods; and they shall not remain in your land, lest they cause you to sin against me.” It does not say “in me,” but the meaning is the same.

### [Book XXIV, 3]

“And all the people answered with one voice, saying.”

### [Book XXIV, 10]

“And they saw the place where the God of Israel had stood there.” “Where he had stood” would have been sufficient, but such expressions are characteristic of Hebrew.

### [Book XXV, 13]

“And you shall overlay them with gold.” This is an expression like “he shall be stoned with stones.”

### [Book XXV, 29]

“Cups in which they shall make offerings in them.”

### [Book XXVI, 19]
