“Two bases for one column on both its sides, and two bases for one column on both its sides.” Instead of speaking of all of them, it speaks of two, according to its customary repetition, as in “wells, wells,” “heaps, heaps,” “generations and generations,” and similar expressions.

### [Book XXVI, 29]

“And you shall overlay the columns with gold, and you shall overlay the bars with gold.”

### [Book XXVII, 6]

“And you shall overlay them with bronze.” This is the same kind of expression as “you shall overlay them with gold.”

### [Book XXVII, 21]

“Outside the veil that is over the testimony.” Speaking of the lamp that was to be lit, it means the lamp that was to be lit outside, where the Holy Place is, not within the veil that is over the testimony—that is, the Holy of Holies.

Thus “over” is not used as though something were a roof, chamber, the firmament of heaven, or the cover of an ark. It also refers to something placed opposite like a wall: just as we say that one person sits or stands “above” another, not necessarily that one is carried by the other.

### [Book XXVII, 21]

“A perpetual ordinance throughout your generations.” “Perpetual” is used in the sense explained in many passages above.

### [Book XXVIII, 22] [Note: According to the Septuagint. In the Vulgate, verse 29.]

“And Aaron shall take the names of the children of Israel upon the breastplate of judgment, upon his breast, as he enters the sanctuary” [Note: So the manuscripts of better quality read. But the printed editions have: “as he enters into the sanctuary,” that is, and so forth.]

It would have been natural to say, “as he enters the Holy Place,” that is, “Aaron shall take them as he enters.” Some Latin translators rendered it this way to avoid the solecism. But since the Greek also has “as he enters,” and some Latin manuscripts agree, I thought the expression should be noted rather than corrected.

### [Book XXVIII, 24] [Note: According to the Septuagint. In the Vulgate, verse 30.]

“And you shall place upon the breastplate of judgment fringes, chainwork.” Here too some Latin translators, avoiding the solecism, rendered it “chainworked fringes.” But the Greek has τοὺς κρωσσούς τὰ ἁλυσιδωτά. We usually call this an absolute expression, when the neuter is applied to a masculine or feminine noun, as if we were to say, “Earthly justices are not stable.”

### [Book XXVIII, 35]

“And when Aaron begins to perform the priesthood, his voice shall be heard as he enters the Holy Place before the Lord and as he goes out.” The text calls the sound of the bells “his voice,” although it is more properly his sound. “As he enters” and “as he goes out” use the dative instead of the genitive: “of the one entering” and “of the one going out.”

### [Book XXIX, 13]

“And the two kidneys and the fat that is over them”—“is” is understood; some translators added it.

### [Book XXIX, 26]

“And you shall set it apart with a setting-apart.”

### [Book XXX, 8]

“And when Aaron lights the lamps, he shall light it late upon it.” “Late” is used for “in the evening,” and therefore the expression should be noted. The Greek has ὀψέ. Properly speaking, *late* is ordinarily used only when the time at which something ought to have been done has passed, and thus something is said to have been done late.

### [Book XXX, 12–13]

“When you take a census of the children of Israel at their registration, each shall give the redemption of his soul to the Lord, and there shall be no destruction among them at their registration; and this is what they shall give you.”

This expression is suspended because a coordinating conjunction has been inserted. If it were removed, the sentence would not be suspended. It occurs in three places, and removing it from any one of them makes the sentence complete.

Again, where it says, “When you take a census of the children of Israel at their registration, and each shall give the redemption of his soul to the Lord,” if it had not said “and each shall give,” but merely “each shall give,” the sentence would end without suspension. It would read: “When you take a census of the children of Israel at their registration, each shall give the redemption of his soul to the Lord.”

But if the conjunction is retained here, it must be removed below, so that the sentence reads: “When you take a census of the children of Israel at their registration, and each shall give the redemption of his soul to the Lord, and there shall be no destruction among them at their registration; this is what they shall give.”

Or again, if the conjunction is removed in the middle, where it says, “and there shall be no destruction among them,” the sentence will not be suspended. The sense would be: “When you take a census of the children of Israel at their registration, and each shall give the redemption of his soul to the Lord, there shall be no destruction among them.”

But because the same conjunction is placed everywhere, it makes the expression suspended. For this reason we thought it should be noted.

### [Book XXXII, 1]

“The people rose up against Aaron, and they said to him.” This is a customary expression because the people consist of many persons. Further, the whole is put for a part. The Apostle, stating what was actually the case, says that some of them did this, not the whole people, when he says, “Nor should we serve idols, as some of them did” (1 Corinthians 10:7).

### [Book XXXII, 1]

“Rise up and make gods for us who shall go before us.” Were they speaking to someone who was seated? Or should this expression instead be noted because Scripture often says, “Arise, Lord” (Psalm 44:26), or “Arise, God, judge the earth” (Psalm 82:8)?

### [Book XXXII, 10]

“And now leave me, and let me be angry with anger.” As in “he shall surely die,” Scripture likes to speak in this way.

### [Book XXXII, 24]

“Those who have gold, remove it.” It did not say what the golden things were; hence the Latin translators said, “Let the one who has gold remove it.”

### [Book XXXII, 26]

“Whoever is for the Lord, let him come to me.”

### [Book XXXII, 31]

“They made golden gods for themselves”—from one calf. Thus the plural is put for the singular. Hence also the phrase, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

Such expressions are not ordinarily found where the plural is used for the singular except in a category of things in which several could also be made or understood. The fact that there was one calf does not mean that several could not have been made, or that it was not like many idols.

By this expression Scripture says that the robbers insulted the Lord (Matthew 27:44), although it testifies that only one did this (Luke 23:39); but he was not the only robber. Indeed, when this expression occurs with proper names, although we have not yet found it used in Scripture in that way, several are understood. Thus some people have said “Phaedras” and “Medeas,” although there was one Phaedra and one Medea; they called all those like Phaedra and Medea “Phaedras” and “Medeas.”

These expressions therefore are not introduced without reason, nor randomly and indiscriminately, as ignorant people use them incorrectly, but according to a definite manner and definite rules.

### [Book XXXIII, 1]

“Go up from here, you and your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt.” It does not say “whom you brought out” in the singular, but in the plural; this is so customary that the alternative is rarely used.

### [Book XXXIII, 5]

“And the Lord said, ‘Remove the garments of your glory and your adornment, and I will show what I shall do to you.’” The expression concludes with a shift from the plural to the singular because they were many and constituted a people, as he had said to them, “You are a stiff-necked people.” He did not say, “You are a people” with the singular pronoun, but “you are a people” with the plural pronoun, although “you” is plural and “people” singular.

### [Book XXXIV, 9]

“If I have found favor in your sight, let my Lord walk together with us.” It sounds as though he were speaking of someone else. Such expressions are frequent, but when they are addressed to God, people think that the Son is being spoken of to the Father. When similar things are said in many places to Pharaoh, Joseph, and others, however, the kind of expression is understood.

### [Book XXXIV, 15]

“Lest you make a covenant with those who sit upon the land,” as though it said, “who have seats,” that is, “who dwell.”

### [Book XXXIV, 17]

“And you shall not make cast gods for yourself.” This expression signifies the whole by a part. It does not mean that, because it mentioned cast images, it permitted carved, beaten, molded, or any other kind of image, or gods made in any fashion.

### [Book XXXIV, 19]

“Everything that opens the womb, male.” That is, “everything that opens the womb shall be mine among those that are male.”

### [Book XXXIV, 20]

“You shall redeem the firstborn of a beast of burden with a sheep.” This too signifies the whole by a part. If an animal were not a beast of burden, and its flesh were rejected as unclean, it would not for that reason fail to require redemption or require redemption by anything other than a sheep.

### [Book XXXIV, 25]

“You shall not kill upon leaven the blood of my sacrifices.” This is certainly an expression in which “you shall kill blood” means “you shall pour it out by killing.”

### [Book XXXIV, 25]

“And the sacrifice of the feast of Passover shall not remain until morning.” “Shall remain” is expressed as “shall sleep.” For how could the flesh of a slaughtered and cooked animal sleep? Thus when it says, “Why do you sleep, Lord?” (Psalm 44:24), this kind of expression means, “Why do you cease?”—that is, “Why do you not avenge?”

### [Book XXXIV, 28]

Regarding Moses’ forty-day fast, Scripture says, “He did not eat bread and did not drink water.” A part signifies the whole: “bread” signifies all food and “water” all drink.

### [Book XXXIV, 1]

“Cut for yourself two tablets, as the first ones”—“were” is understood. For this reason our translators thought this verb should even be suppressed, since such ellipsis is unusual in the Latin language.

### [Book XXXV, 4]

“And Moses said to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, saying.” The expression would be complete even without “saying.”

### [Book XXXV, 21]

“And each brought what their heart was bringing.” It could have been said more conventionally, “And each brought what his heart was bringing.”

### [Book XXXV, 21]

“And those whose soul was willing brought an offering” [Note: The printed editions have *redemptionem*, “redemption”; the manuscripts consistently have *demptionem*, “an offering,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, ἀφαίρεμα.]

It does not say, “And as their soul was willing.”

### [Book XXXV, 23]

“And everyone with whom red-dyed rams’ skins were found.” More conventionally, this would be, “All those with whom red-dyed rams’ skins were found.”

### [Book XXXV, 24]

“Everyone bringing an offering, they brought silver and bronze offerings to the Lord.” More conventionally, it would say, “Everyone brought,” rather than “everyone brought” with the plural verb.

### [Book XXXV, 24]

“And with whom imperishable wood was found, with them.” “With them” has been added according to scriptural usage, for without it the sentence would be complete.

### [Book XXXV, 25]

“And every woman wise in mind, with her hands, spun.” As though spinning could be done without the hands. “Wise, she spun” is an elegant and unusual expression.

Then follows, “Every woman, they brought,” where the singular is concluded with a plural verb, according to the preceding examples. More conventionally, it would say, “Every woman brought.”

### [Book XXXV, 26]

“And all the women whose minds were willing spun goat hair with wisdom.” It should be noted that Scripture often calls skill in these arts “wisdom,” that is, σοφία.

### [Book XXXV, 28]

“And the compositions, and the oil of anointing, and the composition of the incense.” We should not understand “compositions” to refer to additional compositions. After saying “compositions,” the text adds nothing different through the coordinating conjunction, but explains what it had said, so that we understand which compositions: “the oil,” it says, “of anointing, and the composition of the incense.” It calls them “compositions” because they were made from many ingredients.

### [Book XXXV, 29]

“And every man and woman whose understanding moved them to enter and to do every work whatsoever the Lord commanded to be done through Moses brought an offering to the Lord.” Therefore “every man and woman” is understood as “the children of Israel.” The remaining expressions resemble those noted above.

### [Book XXXV, 32–33]

“To make gold and silver and bronze,” instead of “to make from gold, silver, and bronze.” For they were not making gold itself, but making things from gold. The same applies to what it says shortly afterward: “And to work wood,” that is, to make things from wood.

[Ib. 35.] To make all the holy textile works, and to weave variegated work in scarlet and fine linen, to make every architectural work of variety. Behold, even in textile matters he calls the work “architectural”: unless perhaps for this reason: the tabernacle was being made, which resembled a building and was erected like a house. What, however, he means by “holy works” is not clearly apparent: whether the works of the holy priest, since these things are also said concerning his robe or robes; or the works of holy God, for whose worship these things were made; or holy works, as “the Holy Place” and “the Holy of Holies” were so called.

[Ib. XXXVI, 8 [Note: [Col. 0516] According to the Septuagint.].] Connecting shoulder-pieces from both its sides: he did not say “from both sides of them,” although he had used the plural “shoulder-pieces,” not “shoulder-piece,” just as he usually says “shoulder-piece.” For he himself called it “shoulder-pieces” in the plural, just as “robe” and “those same robes.”

[Ib. 37 [Note: [Col. 0516] According to the Septuagint; but in the Vulgate, chapter 38, verse 23.].] And Eliab son of Achisamach, of the tribe of Dan, who worked as an architect on textiles and embroidered work and multicolored work, weaving with scarlet and fine linen. In a novel manner, textiles are said to be worked architecturally. That statement also, “to weave with scarlet and fine linen,” must be understood as referring to the whole from a part; for from these we understand the remaining materials as well, namely purple and violet.

[Ib. XXXIX, 31.] And the children of Israel did just as the Lord commanded Moses; so they did: the statement would be complete even if “so they did” were not added.

[Ib. XL, 14.] And Moses did everything that the Lord commanded him; so he did: similarly to what was said concerning the children of Israel.

# BOOK THREE. Expressions from Leviticus

[Col. 0515]

[Note: [Col. 0515] Several manuscripts, and all editions published until now, lack these first thirty-one expressions; they are now published for the first time from the Cistercian manuscript and also from the excellent Corbie manuscript, written more than eight hundred years ago.]

[LEVITICUS, chapter I, verse 2.] If anyone among you brings an offering to the Lord, you shall offer it from the livestock, from cattle and from sheep: that is, if you offer from the livestock, you shall offer from cattle and from sheep. By the name “sheep” he also included the species of goats, as he commonly does elsewhere.

[Ib. II, 6.] And you shall break it into fragments: that is, by breaking it you shall make it into fragments.

[Ib. IV, 23.] And the sin that he committed shall have become known to him in it. Two modes of expression must here be noted: “he sinned a sin,” and the addition “in it.” In what else, indeed, except in the thing itself—that is, in the sin?

[Ib. V, 1.] But if a person sins and hears the voice of the oath, and he himself is a witness, or has seen, or has knowledge of it, if he does not report it, he shall also receive sin: the conjunction “and” appears to be superfluous; for when it is removed, the sentence follows perfectly: “he shall receive sin.”

[Ib. 1.] But if a person sins and hears the voice of the oath, and he himself is a witness, or has seen, or has knowledge of it, he does not report it: “and” has been placed in the sense of “that is.” For in accordance with our customary manner of speaking it could be said: “But if a person sins—that is, hears the voice of the oath—and so forth.”

[Ib. 3.] Or touches something unclean from a human being, from all his uncleanness; if he touches it, he is defiled, and it was hidden from him; but afterward he realizes it and commits an offense: the proper order would have been, “and commits an offense, but afterward realizes it.”

[Col. 0517] [Ib. XV, 16.] If a soul is hidden from him through forgetfulness, and he sins unwillingly: he does not say, “if it has been hidden from her,” because he uses “soul” for a human being, just as he does elsewhere, where he first uses *anima* (“soul”), which is feminine in gender, and afterward introduces the masculine gender, referring to a man. But here the expression is much more compressed, since both genders are placed consecutively, so that it says, “If a soul has escaped him.” This expression frightened the Latin translators, and they refused to translate it; instead they rendered it, “If any soul has escaped, and has sinned unwillingly.” Yet it is one thing for a soul to be hidden, and another for something to be hidden from a soul. Scripture says here, “if it has escaped her,” not “if she herself has been hidden.”

In another Greek manuscript, however, we find, “If a soul has escaped her through forgetfulness” [Note: [Col. 0517] Thus the old Corbie manuscript. But the Cistercian manuscript has “a soul.”]. Yet even that manuscript introduces the masculine gender in what follows, saying, “The priest shall make expiation for him, and it shall be forgiven him,” where the Greek has αὐτῷ (*autō*, “for him”). Hence it is apparent that the scribe feared a solecism, but nevertheless could not persist in the feminine gender, overcome by the evidence of the Scripture that follows.

[Ib. VI, 9.] This is the burnt offering upon its burning on the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn upon it: it could have omitted “and,” so that it would read, “all night until morning the fire of the altar shall burn.” But the conjunction that has been added creates obscurity for those who are not accustomed to such expressions in Scripture.

[Ib. 14.] This is the law of the sacrifice that the sons of Aaron, the priests, should offer before the Lord: nothing would be lacking if it did not contain “it.”

[Ib. 17.] It is Holy of Holies. The Greek also has this, but it is a Greek expression. Some of our translators, unwilling to render it, said, “They are Holy Things of Holy Things.”

[Ib. 32 [Note: [Col. 0517] According to the Septuagint; but in the Vulgate, chapter 7, verse 2.].] They shall slaughter the ram that is for the offense before the Lord. The Latin translators added “is” and said, “that is for the offense,” which the Greek does not have.

[Ib. VII, 6 [Note: [Col. 0517] According to the Septuagint; but in the Vulgate, verse 16.].] And if he offers his vow or voluntary offering as a sacrifice, on whatever day he offers the sacrifice, it shall be eaten on the morrow: that is, “on the following day.” Hence others translated it “on the next day.”

[Ib. VIII, 31.] Boil the meat in the court of the tabernacle of testimony, in the holy place, and there you shall eat it, and the loaves that are in the basket of consecration, as it was commanded me, saying, “Aaron and his sons shall eat it.” Some, unwilling to translate this expression, said, “as he commanded me, saying,” because that appears to be the logical consequence; but in accordance with our customary manner of speaking it is a solecism.

[Ib. 35.] And you shall sit at the door of the tabernacle of testimony for seven days, day and night: that is, “you shall dwell there.”

[Ib. IX, 7.] And Moses said to Aaron, “Approach the altar, and make [the offering] for your sin and the burnt offering; make expiation for yourself and your household, and make the offerings of the people, and make expiation for them, as the Lord commanded Moses.” He did not say, “as the Lord commanded me”; rather, he spoke as though there had been one Moses to whom the Lord gave the command, and another Moses who was speaking these words to Aaron.

[Col. 0518] [Ib. X, 8, 9.] And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying, “You shall not drink wine or strong drink,” and so forth. He concludes this speech of the Lord with, “All the ordinances that the Lord spoke to them through the hand of Moses.” When the Lord was speaking, he did not say, “which I spoke to them through the hand of Moses”; instead, he used the expression that Moses himself had used above.

[Ib. 9.] An everlasting ordinance throughout your generations, to distinguish between the midst of the clean and the defiled, and so forth. Notice how he says “everlasting,” although it certainly will not be without end.

[Ib. 14.] Moses, speaking to Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar his sons, says among other things: “From the sacrifices of the peace offerings of the children of Israel they shall offer the shoulder of the offering and the breast of separation upon the sacrifices of fat, to separate the separation before God. And it shall be an everlasting ordinance for you and for your sons and your daughters with you”—although all this was destined to have an end.

[Ib. XI, 9.] When he was giving instructions concerning the creatures that are in the waters, specifying which of them are clean or unclean, he says, “In the waters, and in the sea, and in the streams.” But in Latin manuscripts the phrase “in the sea” is found because it was exceedingly unusual to translate the plural from the Greek and say “in the seas,” especially because of the ambiguity, lest “males” be understood rather than “seas”—that is, males. For it is no less unusual, but it has nevertheless been translated from *sanguines* (“bloods”), since the Latin language does not accept the plural of *sanguis* (“blood”), not even in the nominative case. For although no one says *maribus* from *mare* (“sea”), people do say *maria* (“seas”), whereas they do not say *sanguines*; nevertheless it is written, “Deliver me from bloods” (Psalm 50:16), and, “I will not gather their assemblies from bloods” (Psalm 15:4). Thus one could also say *maribus*, unless, as I have said, ambiguity were being avoided.

In this passage, however, Scripture uses “streams” for rivers, although properly “streams” are winter torrents that dry up in summer and therefore cannot contain fish. Consequently, some of our translators preferred to translate not “streams” but “rivers.” That Scripture uses “streams” for rivers is sufficiently shown by the passage of the Psalm where we read, “You shall give them drink from the stream of your delight.” For by the name “stream” it did not intend anything that would flow for a time and then dry up, since it continues, “For with you is the fountain of life” (Psalm 35:9–10), which is certainly eternal and unfailing.

[Ib. 21.] But these you shall eat among the winged creeping things that walk on four, which have the upper legs of their feet: he did not say, “of their own feet.”

[Ib. 44.] And you shall be holy, for I am holy: “I am” is understood. Hence most of our translators rendered it, “for I am holy.”

[Ib. XII, 1.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying. This is an extremely common and frequent expression in Scripture: “he spoke, saying.” But the expression that follows is found more rarely and constricts the poverty of the Latin language. For the Greek has καὶ ἐρεῖς πρὸς αὐτοὺς λέγων (*kai ereis pros autous legōn*), which could be expressed in Latin as, “and you shall say to them, saying.” It is less offensive if one says, “and you shall tell them, saying”; and it is more similar to the Greek, since the Greek also did not say λέξεις πρὸς αὐτοὺς λέγων (*lexeis pros autous legōn*), but ἐρεῖς πρὸς αὐτοὺς λέγων (*ereis pros autous legōn*).

[Ib. XII, 2.] Any woman who receives seed and gives birth to a male shall also be unclean for seven days: most of our translators refused to render this literally and instead said, “Any woman who receives seed and gives birth to a male shall be unclean for seven days.” Since this expression is unusual even in Greek, it could have been left untranslated in the Greek; but since the Greeks did not shrink from translating it, I do not know why the Latins should have shrunk from doing so.

[Ib. 4.] She shall sit for thirty-three days [Note: [Col. 0519] The manuscripts have “six days.” But it is clear that here, in accordance with the Septuagint, “three days” should be read.] in the blood of her purification. Similarly, concerning the woman who gives birth to a female, it is said, “she shall sit in the blood of her purification,” but with the same number of days doubled, namely sixty-six days. “She shall sit,” therefore, means “she shall remain”; for she was not forbidden to rise from her seat for all those days.

[Ib. XIII, 2.] If a bright scar of a mark appears on anyone’s bodily skin. It must be noted that Scripture calls a scar not only a wound but also a mark consisting merely of a color.

[Ib. 2.] And there is on his skin a leprous-colored mark: “mark” refers to the spot itself, as though the man had been touched by leprosy.

[Ib. 3.] And the priest shall see him and defile him: that is, “shall pronounce him defiled.”

[Ib. 3.] And the hair that is in the mark shall turn white: that is, “shall turn into white.”

[Ib. 6.] And the priest shall cleanse him; for it is a sign: he shall pronounce him cleansed, just as “he shall defile,” stated above, means “he shall pronounce defiled.”

[Ib. 7, 8.] And the priest sees him, and behold, the mark on the skin has changed, and the priest shall defile him: the conjunction “and” is superfluous. For when that conjunction is removed, the complete sense is as follows: “But if the mark has changed on the skin after the priest saw him in order to cleanse him, and he is seen again by the priest, and the priest sees him, and behold, the mark on the skin has changed, the priest shall defile him.”

[Ib. 9, 10.] And a mark of leprosy, if it is on a man, shall come before the priest; and the priest shall see, and behold, a white scar on the skin, and it has changed the hair to white, and [there is something] from sound living flesh in the scar: that is, it has changed the hair to a white colour in the scar; it has changed it from the sound state of living flesh, that is, because it does not have such hair as is sound in living flesh.

[Ib. 45, 46 [Note: [Col. 0519] In earlier editions, Book Three begins here.].] Speaking about the leper, he says, “And ‘unclean, unclean’ shall he be called,” as though it were not sufficient to say “he shall be called unclean” once. Although some manuscripts have this wording, in another Greek manuscript we find “he shall be called unclean” stated only once.

Likewise, shortly afterward he says, “Since he is unclean, he shall be unclean.” This could not be expressed in Latin from the Greek exactly as it stands. For the Greek says, ἀκάθαρτος ὢν ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται (*akathartos ōn akathartos estai*), as though it said, “being unclean, he shall be unclean.” But *being* is not equivalent to the Greek ὢν (*ōn*). If it could be said, one would need a form meaning “essent,” derived from *esse* (“to be”), not from *existere* (“to exist”).

[Ib. XIII, 47.] And if there is on a garment a mark of leprosy: it could have customarily been said, “And if there is a mark of leprosy on a garment.”

[Ib. 51.] Or in any leather vessel, in whatever there is a mark in it: it would have been sufficient to say, “in whatever there is a mark.”

[Ib. 55.] And behold, the mark has not changed its appearance: that is, the color at which one looks, not the appearance with which it itself looks. For by “mark” he means the spot itself.

[Ib. XIV, 15.] And the priest, taking some of the *hemina* of oil, shall pour it upon the priest’s left hand: he did not say “upon his own left hand,” although naturally he will pour it upon his own.

[Ib. XV, 2.] A man, a man, anyone in whom there is a discharge.

[Ib. 16.] And a man from whom there has issued an emission of semen.

[Ib. 21.] And everything on which he sleeps, upon it; and everything on which he sits, upon it, shall be unclean.

[Ib. XVI, 21.] And he shall send it away by the hand of a man prepared for the wilderness: that is, “he shall send it into the wilderness by the hand of a man prepared for this purpose.” He was speaking of the scapegoat when he said this. Notice, however, how Scripture says “by the hand.”

[Ib. XVII, 3.] A man, a man of the children of Israel: that is, “from the children of Israel.” This repetition appears to signify any man whatsoever—that is, this man or that man.

[Ib. XVIII, 7.] You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father or the nakedness of your mother: by this expression he prohibited intercourse with these persons.

[Ib. 14.] You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s brother, and you shall not approach his wife: for she is your relative. Here “and” has been used in the sense of “that is”; for he calls the nakedness of his father’s brother—that is, the nakedness of his uncle—the private parts of his uncle’s wife.

[Ib. 25.] And the land vomited out those who sit upon it: that is, those who have settlements, which means “those who dwell.”

[Ib. XIX, 9.] And when you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not finish reaping the harvest of your field. What begins with the plural and ends with the singular, most Latin translators did not wish to translate, but said “your field,” where “your field” occurs, as though the Greek could not say this. The expression, therefore, should have been noted rather than corrected.

[Ib. XX, 17.] Whoever takes his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees his nakedness, has uncovered the nakedness of his sister; they shall receive their sin: “sin” is used for the punishment of sin.

[Ib. 25.] And you shall separate yourselves among the clean animals and among the unclean animals, and among the clean birds and the unclean. He said, “You shall separate yourselves among the clean and the unclean,” because the clean are separated from the unclean, or the unclean from the clean. This is altogether a new expression. For one thing is, “You shall separate among the clean animals and among the unclean animals,” as Scripture very often speaks; another is what it says here, “You shall separate yourselves,” as though, while separating those things from one another, they themselves separated themselves from both, as though judging between the two.

[Ib. XXI, 1.] Say to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them: They shall not defile themselves among their people except for a close relative who is nearest to them. He speaks of mourning, which is owed to the souls of the dead; for this is why mourning takes place: because they have departed.

[Ib. 5.] And you shall not shave your head for the dead, and they shall not cut their flesh with cuts: the customary expression would have been, “they shall not cut their flesh with cuts.”

[Ib. 7, 8.] They shall not take a prostitute or a profane woman, nor a woman cast out by her husband, because he is holy to the Lord his God: he did not say, “because they are holy,” but spoke as though of one person, although he had begun with the plural. Then he continues in the singular: “He shall sanctify him” [Note: [Col. 0521] Printed editions have “I sanctified.” Manuscripts have “He shall sanctify”; according to the Septuagint, *hagiaseis*, “you shall sanctify.”], “this man shall offer the offerings of the Lord your God; he is holy, for I am the Lord who sanctify them.” Again he concludes in the plural.

[Ib. XXII, 11.] But if a priest has acquired a person bought with money, he shall eat of his bread: he did not say “she shall eat,” although he had used *anima* (“person,” literally “soul”), which is feminine in gender; rather, he looked to what he intended to signify by “person,” namely, a human being.

[Ib. 12.] And if the daughter of a priest has become the wife of a foreign man: that is, “if she has married a foreign man.”

[Ib. 26, 27.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, “A calf, or a sheep, or a goat, when it has been born, shall be seven days under its mother”: the conjunction “and” appears to be superfluous, according to the very common expressions in Scripture that most Latin translators refused to render.

[Ib. 32.] And I shall be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel: that is, “I shall be held holy.” For the Lord is not holy only among the children of Israel and not elsewhere. The same sense is found in the Lord’s Prayer, “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9), that is, “may it be held holy by human beings.”

[Col. 0522] [Ib. XXIII, 2.] Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: “The festivals of the Lord which you shall proclaim as holy convocations—these are my festivals: for six days you shall perform work.” Although he had spoken to several people, afterward he speaks as though to one.

[Ib. 15 and 16.] And you shall count for yourselves from the day after the Sabbath, on which you offered the sheaf of the offering; you shall count seven complete weeks: he did not say “you shall count,” although he had previously been speaking to several people.

[Ib. XXIV, 11.] And when the son of the Israelite woman had pronounced the name, he cursed: although he did not add “of God,” it is nevertheless evident that the name of God, whom he cursed, is to be understood.

[Ib. 15.] A man, a man—if he curses his God, he shall receive his sin. Here it is sufficiently clear that this is an expression: when it says “a man, a man,” it is as though it said, “that man or that man,” that is, “any man whatsoever.” It is not to be understood as some have thought, namely, that “a man, a man” is said as a term of praise, as though it meant, “a man, but a man”—that is, not just any creature, like an animal, but one who is truly a human being. That this interpretation is not correct, and that this is a scriptural expression, is clearly shown here, since it is said of one who is blamed, not of one who is praised.

[Ib. XXV, 46.] When he was speaking about the slaves whom the Israelites were permitted to possess, he says, “And they shall be for you as a possession forever,” although, since they were mortal, neither masters nor slaves could be eternal. He therefore used “forever” where no fixed limit of time is prescribed for how long they should serve, unlike those whom he commands to be released into their own freedom at the remission.

[Ib. XXVI, 3.] If you walk in my ordinances, and observe my commandments, and perform them, I shall give you rain in its season: the conjunction “and” is superfluous according to our customary manner of speaking, but it has been added according to the usage of Scripture. The sentence would continue, “I shall give you.”

[Ib. 18.] And if even until now you do not obey me, I shall add to chastise you sevenfold for your sins: here also “and” is superfluous; the sentence would continue, “I shall add to chastise you.” The word “sevenfold” is to be understood as signifying every number.

# BOOK FOUR. Expressions from Numbers

[Col. 0521]

[Numbers, chapter I, verse 4.] And with you there shall be each one according to the head of each of the leaders.

[Ib. 22, 20.] For the sons of Simeon, according to their kindreds, according to their peoples, according to their ancestral houses, according to the number of their names, according to their heads, every male from twenty years old and above, everyone who goes forth in strength: their registration. This expression—he does not say “the sons of Simeon” or “from the sons of Simeon,” but “for the sons of Simeon,” in the dative case—is not translated by the Latin interpreters whom we have been able to consult; and he preserves it thereafter in the other tribes. In the tribe of Reuben alone, which was counted first, this expression is absent. For he does not say, “For the sons of Reuben, according to their kindreds,” and so forth, but says, “And the sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, were according to their kindreds”; and afterward [the wording is] as in the other tribes.

[Ib. 54.] And the children of Israel did according to everything that the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron; so they did.

[Ib. III, 3.] The priests who were anointed, whose hands they completed to perform the priesthood.

[Ib. IV, 14.] And they shall place upon it all its vessels with which they minister in them.

[Ib. V, 7.] And he shall repay the one against whom he committed the offense: some, unwilling to translate this expression, transferred the words in corrected order [Col. 0523], saying, “And he shall repay him against whom he committed the offense.”

[Ib. 6.] A man or woman, whoever commits any of all human sins: he does not say “whatever she commits”; rather, it is an expression in which the masculine gender has claimed the pronoun, although the feminine gender is placed afterward. This expression is not customary.

[Ib. 12.] Men, men, if his wife transgresses: the expression must be noted not only because he doubled the noun, saying “men, men,” but also because he added “his.”

[Ib. 14.] If a spirit of jealousy comes upon him, but she has not been defiled, and the man brings his wife to the priest: “and” is superfluous, but this is an expression customary in Scripture.

[Ib. 18.] It shall be water of accusation, which is accursed—this: the order of the words makes this expression unusual. It could have been customarily said, “This shall be the water of accusation that is accursed,” or, “This shall be the water of accusation that is accursed,” or in whatever other way the customary arrangement of the words permits it to be said.

[Ib. 19.] Stand innocent from the water of accusation, which is accursed—this. In this expression not only does the order of the words sound unusual, but the case has also been changed. It would be complete and customary to say, “Stand innocent from this water of accusation, which is accursed,” or “from this water of accusation, which is accursed.”

[Ib. 27.] And she shall swell as to her belly: instead of “her belly shall swell.” This expression is also frequent among Latin authors; but our translators, unwilling to render it, said, “And her belly shall swell.”

[Ib. VI, 2.] A man or woman who makes a great vow: he did not say “whatever woman.”

[Ib. 9.] And he shall be shaved as to his head: this is an expression like the one above, “she shall swell as to her belly.”

[Ib. VII, 3.] Six covered wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon from two leaders, and a calf from each individual: in this expression I thought it worth noting that the same animals are called “calves” which he had called “oxen.” But this is also said to be a Greek idiom.

[Ib. 11.] One leader each day, a leader each day shall offer their offerings: instead of saying, “on each day, each leader.”

[Ib. 15.] One calf for the oxen, and one goat from the goats.

[Ib. VIII, 19.] And there shall be no one among the children of Israel approaching, of the children of Israel, to the holy things: it appears that it would have been sufficient to say, “And there shall be no one among the children of Israel approaching the holy things,” or at least, “There shall be no one of the children of Israel approaching the holy things.”

[Ib. 20.] And Moses and Aaron and the whole assembly of the children of Israel did for the Levites according to what the Lord commanded Moses concerning the Levites; so the children of Israel did for them.

[Ib. IX, 13.] And a man, a man, whoever is clean and is not on a distant journey, and fails to make the Passover, that person shall be cut off from his people: therefore “a man, a man” is an expression, as though he said, “any man whatsoever, this one or that one.”

[Ib. 17.] And when the cloud had gone up from the tabernacle, afterward the children of Israel moved on: the sentence could have been complete as, “And when the cloud had gone up from the tabernacle, the children of Israel moved on.”

[Col. 0524] [Ib. X, 14.] And the order of the camp of the children of Judah shall move on first.

[Ib. 17.] And the children of Gershon and the children of Merari shall move on: he used a future-tense verb while narrating a past event, just as above, when he was speaking about the cloud, at whose movement or stopping the camps moved on or halted (Exodus 12:21–22); and thereafter he uses this verb in the movements of the various groups.

[Ib. 29.] And Moses said to Obeth, the son of Raguel the Midianite, Moses’ son-in-law: he does not say “his son-in-law.”

[Ib. 30.] And he said to him, “I will not go, but to my land and to my kindred”: “I will go” is understood.

[Ib. XI, 4.] And the mixed multitude that was among them conceived a desire: he used the singular for the plural, saying “the mixed multitude,” not “the mixed multitudes” in the plural; yet he rendered the verb in the plural when he said, “they conceived a desire.”

[Ib. 6.] But now our soul is dry; our eyes are upon nothing except the manna: the verbs “is” and “are” are absent. The sentence would be complete as, “Our soul is dry; our eyes are upon nothing except the manna.” For some translators rendered it in this way and added words that are not in the Greek.

[Ib. 8.] And they ground it in a mill.

[Ib. 21.] Six hundred thousand foot soldiers, among whom I am among them.

[Ib. 25.] And he took from the spirit that was upon him: “or was,” or “will be,” is understood. But Latin translators were reluctant to render this expression, called an ellipsis, which is extremely familiar in Greek—and, as I think, also in Hebrew—although it occurs in Latin as well, though less frequently than in Greek.

[Ib. 33.] And the Lord struck a very great plague: the expression “he struck a plague” must be noted; it does not say “the plague struck,” which is customary.

[Ib. XII, 3.] And the man Moses was exceedingly meek: “he was” is understood.

[Ib. 9.] And the anger of the Lord’s spirit was upon them: “came to be” is understood.

[Ib. 10.] And behold, Mary became leprous like snow: here also “became” is understood.

[Ib. XIII, 20.] And what is the land in which these men sit upon it? And what are the cities in which these men dwell in them?

[Ib. 25.] The very place which they called the Valley of Botri [Note: [Col. 0524] The manuscripts consistently have “Botrui.”]: whereas above he had said, “They came into the Valley of Botri,” it is therefore spoken by anticipation—not because it was already called this when they arrived, but because when this book was written it was already so called.

[Ib. 32.] For he is much stronger than we: the expression would be customary if it did not contain “much.”

[Ib. 33.] And they brought forth the fear of the land that they had explored.

[Ib. 33.] The land which we crossed to explore it, the land that devours those who dwell upon it, is: the customary wording would have been, “the land which we crossed to explore.”

[Ib. XIV, 7.] The land which we explored, it is very, very good.

[Ib. 10.] And the whole assembly said to stone them with stones: it does not say “with stones”; the verb “to stone” itself could have sufficed in customary usage.

[Col. 0525] [Ib. 11.] And how long will they not believe me in all the signs that I performed among them? He does not say, “which I performed among them.”

[Ib. 24.] But my servant Caleb, because another spirit is in him and he followed me, I shall bring him into the land: the expression would be customary if it did not contain “and.”

[Ib. 24.] And I shall bring him into the land into which he entered there: in customary usage, “into which he entered” would be sufficient.

[Ib. 26.] And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: this was introduced while the Lord was also speaking above. Scripture often does this when it wishes to say something else: it again introduces the speaker who had already been speaking.

[Ib. 29.] All those who murmured over me: he does not say “about me” or “against me.”

[Ib. 31.] And they shall inherit as a possession the land which you withdrew from: customary usage would be, “from which you withdrew”; but here, in a novel manner, it says “the land which you withdrew,” and adds “from it,” as Scripture is accustomed to speak. Thus we have, “You approached the deeply resounding crags” (Aeneid 1.200–201; 6.638), where it does not say “to the crags”; and, “They reached places,” where it does not say “to the places.” So here also it says “the land which you withdrew,” not “from which you withdrew.”

[Ib. 35.] I, the Lord, have spoken: unless I do this to this wicked assembly. It must indeed be investigated what the Greek expression ἦ μὴν (*ē mēn*) means [Note: [Col. 0525] Printed editions have *ekei*. The manuscripts mostly have the form found in the Septuagint, *ē mēn*, which in Numbers chapters 28 and 35 and elsewhere is translated “unless.”]. For our translators have translated this almost everywhere as “unless.”

[Ib. XV, 18.] Into the land into which I am bringing you there.

[Ib. 27, 28.] But if one soul sins involuntarily, she shall offer one year-old she-goat for sin, and the priest shall make expiation for the unwilling soul—the one that sinned unintentionally before the Lord—to make expiation for him; and it shall be forgiven him. In this sentence that expression also had to be noted: it says “the priest shall make expiation,” and afterward “to make expiation”; both could have been said together as “he shall make expiation to make expiation.” The sentence also begins with the feminine gender and ends with the masculine. For after saying, “If one soul has sinned,” it concludes, “to make expiation for him,” where “for that man” is understood. The addition “and it shall be forgiven him” is not apparent in Latin, because this pronoun has the same form for every gender; but the masculine is clear in Greek, where it has αὐτῷ (*autō*), “to him,” which is rendered here by “him.”

As for the phrase “for the unwilling person,” it means “for the person who has sinned unwillingly,” not that he is unwilling for the offering to be made on his behalf. For Scripture explains this afterward when it says, “who has sinned unintentionally.” Therefore *invita* (“unwilling”) is used because Latin could not express what the Greek says, ἀκουσιασθείσης (*akousiastheisēs*). It could not say *nolentata*, “made unwilling,” or anything else derived from the idea of doing something unwillingly.

[Ib. 30.] And any person who acts with a hand of pride: “sin” is understood. It must also be noted that he says “with a hand of pride,” using “hand” for an action or power.

[Ib. 35.] The man shall surely die; let the whole assembly stone him with stones: “he shall die by death,” “stone him with stones,” and “the whole assembly shall stone him” are expressions unusual to us.

[Ib. XVI, 17.] And each shall take his own censer.

[Col. 0526] [Ib. 33.] And they descended, they themselves and everything that is with them: he used the present for the past, “are” for “were” or “had been.”

[Ib. 34.] And all Israel that was around them fled at their cry: “was” is understood; that is, “all Israel that was around them.”

[Ib. 37.] For they sanctified the censers of these sinners in their souls: he did not say, “because these sinners sanctified the censers in their souls”; rather, when asked whose censers they were, instead of saying “their own,” he said, “of these sinners.” As for who sanctified them, he left it to be understood: namely, “because they themselves did so.”

[Ib. XVII, 8.] And behold, Aaron’s staff had budded into the house of Levi: Latin usage would require it to be said, “in the house of Levi.”

[Ib. XVIII, 6.] And I have taken your brothers, the Levites, from among the children of Israel, a thing given, given to the Lord: this expression was necessarily translated into Latin in this way. For the Greek has δόμα δεδομένον (*doma dedomenon*), which, if anyone wished to express it in Latin, would have to say *datum datum* (“a thing given, given”), since δόμα means “a thing given,” as the Apostle says, “Not because I seek a thing given, but I seek fruit” (Philippians 4:17), where the Greek has δόμα.

Likewise, in Genesis, “Abraham gave things given to his sons” (Genesis 25:6), the Greek has δόματα; and in the Gospel, “You know how to give good things given to your children” (Matthew 7:11), where the Greek has δόματα. And δεδομένον (*dedomenon*) means “given” and is not a noun but a participle. Accordingly, *datum datum* could be said, as though meaning “a thing given which is given,” unless ambiguity had to be avoided.

Some of our translators, seeking to avoid this ambiguity, said *donum datum* (“a gift given”); but “gift” in Greek is δῶρον (*dōron*), not δόμα. Therefore it would not properly be said here, because God does not say that this was given to him as a gift by the children of Israel, but that it was rendered to him in place of the firstborn owed to him. Hence both things returned and things bestowed may be called things given; and therefore every gift is also a thing given, but not every thing given is also a gift, because not everything that is given is thereby bestowed.

[Ib. XVIII, 12.] Every firstfruit of oil, and every firstfruit of wine and grain, their firstfruit—whatever they shall give to the Lord—I have given them to you. He did not say, “I have given every firstling to you,” using the masculine form; rather, after saying “every firstfruit” and listing the things from which it came, he added, “I have given them to you.” Nor did he even say, “I have given it to you” or “I have given them to you,” referring to the firstfruits; instead, he introduced the neuter gender. This can indeed occur as a complete expression even in Latin.

The word *primitia* itself does not appear to be Latin. For *primitiae* (“firstfruits”) is ordinarily used only in the plural. But if our translators could translate what they found in Greek as “I will not gather their assemblies from bloods” (Psalm 15:4), and elsewhere, “The Lord will abhor a man of bloods and deceit” (Psalm 5:7), although *sanguis* (“blood”) has only the singular number in Latin, why should they have been reluctant here also to express the singular *primitia*, as the Greek has it? Some translators nevertheless rendered it *primitias* (“firstfruits”) and used the accusative case, saying, “I will give you all the firstfruits.” Thus they were unwilling to translate either of the two expressions unusual to us in the form in which they found them in Greek.

[Ib. XIX, 2.] Speak to the children of Israel, and let them take from you a red heifer: this is as though he said, “let them bring to you”; or, in customary usage, both could be said: “let them take and bring to you a red heifer.”

[Ib. 7.] And he shall wash his body with water: this would be understood even if “water” were not present.

[Ib. 9.] And he shall place it outside the camp to a clean place: he did not say “in a clean place,” which is the Latin expression.

[Ib. 15.] Every open vessel—whatever vessels do not have a fastening tied upon them.

[Book of Numbers, ch. XX, v. 9.] “And Moses took the rod that was before the Lord”: “was” is understood.

[Ib. v. 12.] “Because you did not believe so as to sanctify me in the sight of the children of Israel”: that is, to declare my holiness. According to this expression it is said, “And for their sake I sanctify myself” (John 17:19), and in the Lord’s Prayer, “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9).

[Ib. v. 15.] “And we dwelt in Egypt for many days”: meaning, for many years.

[Ib. v. 18.] “And Edom said to him”: that is, the nation itself; for Edom, who was Esau, was no longer living. Similarly, those who sent the messengers were called Israel, although that had formerly been the name of one man.

[Ib. v. 19.] “And the children of Israel said to him, ‘We will pass by the mountain; but if I and my cattle drink from your water, I will give you the price.’” The passage moves quite elegantly from the plural to the singular, as though Israel had said this after beginning with “the children of Israel” and using plural verbs—“we will pass” and “we will drink.”

[Ib. v. 30.] “And all the congregation saw that Aaron had been dismissed.” This word, “dismissed,” is not easily found in Scripture in the sense of “dead.” It also occurs in the Gospel, where Simeon says, “Now dismiss your servant in peace” (Luke 2:29). The Greek, however, has ἀπολύεις (*apolyeis*), which sounds more like “release” than “dismissal”; for it does not say ἄφεις (*apheis*), which unquestionably means “you dismiss.”

[Ib. v. 30.] “And all the house of Israel mourned Aaron for thirty days.” It does not say “mourned” in the singular, nor does it say “the whole” or “the entire,” but “all,” as though there were several. This is like “every human being,” which is said of all people and is altogether different from “the whole human being,” which is said of one person. Scripture, however, continually uses *all* for *whole*.

[Ib. XXI, v. 5.] “And the people spoke disparagingly toward God and against Moses.” It does not say “of God,” but “toward God.” Some translators, unwilling to preserve this expression, rendered it “they spoke disparagingly of God.”

[Ib. v. 7.] “Pray, therefore, to God, that he may take away the serpent from us.” So also in Exodus it says “the frog” (Exodus 8:6), using the singular for the plural.

[Ib. XXI, v. 9.] “And it happened that when the serpent bit a person, he looked at the bronze serpent, and he lived.” This expression has not only the feature that it changes the tense of the verb, concluding with the imperfect instead of the perfect past tense; it also contains the additional word “and.”

[Ib. v. 11.] “And setting out from Oboth, they encamped at Achalgai, beyond the wilderness”: that is, in the farther wilderness.

[Ib. XXII, v. 23.] “And he struck the she-ass with the rod.” It does not say “with a rod,” but “in the rod.”

[Ib. XXIII, v. 11.] “I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have uttered [Col. 0528] a blessing.” It does not say “with a blessing,” but as though he were saying, “Behold, you have spoken a blessing.”

[Ib. v. 12.] “Whatever God puts into my mouth, this I shall observe to speak.” It does not say “these things I shall observe.”

[Ib. v. 13.] “Come with me still to another place, from which you will not see him from there.”

[Ib. XXV, v. 4.] “And the Lord said to Moses, ‘Take the leaders of the people and display them before the Lord opposite the sun, and the anger of the Lord’s indignation will be turned away from Israel.’” Although the Lord was speaking, he did not say, “Display them before me, and my anger will be turned away from Israel.”

[Ib. v. 15.] “The family-house is of Midian.” He said this of the woman who was killed together with the adulterous Israelite. By these words, I think, he wished it to be understood that she was of noble birth, calling her “the family-house,” just as among ordinary people, as a mark of wealth, one says “master of the household” and “mistress of the household.”

[Ib. XXVI, v. 1.] “And the Lord spoke to Moses and to Eleazar the priest, saying, ‘Take the beginning of the whole congregation of the children of Israel, from twenty years old and upward.’” It should be noted what he called the “beginning”: namely, the strength of maturity among the people.

[Ib. XXVII, vv. 20–21.] “So that the children of Israel may obey him”; and, “At his word they shall go out”; and, “At his word they shall go in”—that is, when he commands.

[Ib. v. 22.] “And Moses did according to what the Lord commanded him; and he took Joshua and set him before Eleazar the priest,” and so forth. Here this should be noted: after already saying, “And Moses did according to what the Lord commanded him,” he repeats the same words.

[Ib. v. 23.] “And he commended him according to what the Lord commanded Moses.” He does not say, “according to what the Lord commanded him.”

[Ib. XXVIII, v. 13.] “A tenth, a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil for one lamb”: that is, individual tenths for individual lambs. By saying “a tenth, a tenth,” he indicated that the tenths were to be repeated for each lamb.

[Ib. vv. 16–17.] “And in the first month, on the fourteenth day of this month, there shall be a festival; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread.” It should be noted that the festival is celebrated over several days, and yet it is called “the festival,” not “the festivals,” referring to the celebration of the same feast, however many days it lasts.

[Ib. XXIX, v. 1.] “And in the seventh month, one of the month.” According to this expression it is said in Genesis, “And there was evening, and there was morning, one day” (Genesis 1:5). For there also, as here, the Greek has ἡμέρα μία (*hēmera mia*), “one day.” Hence some translators here rendered it “on the first day of the month,” and omitted the necessary expression, although they did not depart from the meaning of the words.

[Ib. v. 2.] “One bull from the cattle, one ram.” It does not say “from the sheep,” as it says “from the cattle,” although the passage would be complete even if that expression were absent.

[Ib. v. 2.] “Seven one-year-old lambs without blemish.” The qualification “without blemish,” which is applied to the lambs, is understood throughout—namely, also with the bull and the ram.

[Ib. v. 4.] “A tenth, a tenth for one lamb, for the seven lambs”: that is, one for each.

[Ib. v. 39.] “Besides your vows, and your freewill offerings, and your burnt offerings, your sacrifices, your libations, and your offerings of well-being.” I would not note this expression if it were even Greek [Col. 0529]. For it does not say, “Besides your vows and your freewill offerings,” and so forth, as it had begun; nor does it say *excepta vota vestra* (“excepted vows”), so as to begin with a kind of solecism. Rather, after first saying correctly, in ordinary usage, “Besides your vows,” it then adds the remaining items in another case, where *exceptis* cannot be understood, but rather *excepta*—an expression admitted by neither Greek nor Latin usage.

[Ib. XXX, v. 3.] “A man, a man, whoever makes a vow to the Lord”: meaning, every man.

[Ib. v. 4.] “But when a woman makes a vow to the Lord, or makes a declaration in her father’s house in her youth.” Here Scripture calls a woman *femina* even if she is a virgin, according to its customary usage. Hence the Apostle also says of Christ, “Born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4).

[Ib. v. 4.] “And her father hears her vows and her declarations that she has declared.” “Declarations that she has declared” is an expression of this kind.

[Ib. v. 4.] “She has declared against her own life”: that is, against the pleasures of her own soul.

[Ib. v. 4.] “And her father is silent, and all her vows shall stand.” Here there is an additional “and.” The complete sense is: “If her father hears and is silent, all her vows shall stand.”

[Ib. v. 7.] “But if she has become a man’s”: “has married” is understood; Scripture speaks in this way.

[Ib. v. 7.] “And her vows are upon her”: “are” is understood, although some translators also added it.

[Ib. v. 13.] “Everything that has proceeded from her lips, according to her vows and according to the declarations that are against her soul, shall not remain for her.” Although a plural verb might have been expected—“shall not remain for her”—it says “shall not remain,” in the singular. Some translators rendered it that way, avoiding this supposed solecism.

[Ib. XXXI, v. 4.] “A thousand from a tribe, a thousand from a tribe, from all the tribes of Israel.” Did he say “a thousand” twelve times? Yet this repetition signifies a thousand from each tribe.

[Ib. v. 8.] “They killed with the sword”: in ordinary usage one would say, “They killed by the sword.”

[Ib. v. 10.] “And all their cities that were in their settlements”: “were” is understood.

[Ib. v. 10.] “And they burned their villages in the fire”: in ordinary usage one would say, “They burned them with fire.”

[Ib. v. 18.] “And preserve alive the whole multitude of the women who have not known the intercourse of a male.” Nowhere does it appear more clearly that, in Hebrew usage, women are also customarily called virgins.

[Ib. vv. 28–29.] “And from their half you shall take, and you shall give them to Eleazar the priest as the Lord’s firstfruits.” It does not say “you [plural] shall give.”

[Ib. v. 35.] “And the human beings among the women who have not known the intercourse of a man: every person, thirty-two thousand.” Here too the preceding expression is confirmed: women are also called those who have not known the intercourse of a man—that is, virgins.

[Ib. v. 54.] “And Moses and Eleazar the priest took the gold from the chiliarchs and the centurions, and brought them into the tent of testimony.” It seems that he ought to have said, “and brought it into the tent of testimony,” since he had stated that gold had been received, and many Latin manuscripts [Col. 0530] read this way. But it seems to have been brought in in the plural—“he brought them”—because many vessels had been mentioned above, and this gold was in them.

[Ib. XXXII, v. 1.] “And livestock: there was a multitude belonging to the children of Reuben and the children of Gad, a very great multitude.” It does not say, “And there was a multitude of livestock.”

[Ib. v. 1.] “And they saw the region of Jazer and the region of Gilead, and the place was a place for livestock.” In pronunciation, the two occurrences of “place” should not be joined; rather, one should pause: “And the place was,” and then continue, “a place for livestock.” Since one might expect a description of what kind of place it was, the repetition is introduced elegantly.

[Ib. v. 2.] “And the children of Reuben and the children of Gad approached and said to Moses and Eleazar the priest, and to the leaders of the congregation, saying.” “They said, saying” is neither a Greek nor a Latin expression; it appears to be Hebrew.

[Ib. v. 5.] “Let this land be given to your servants as a possession.” They speak as though they were referring to others, although they were asking it for themselves.

[Ib. v. 12.] “For they did not follow after me, except Caleb son of Jephunneh.” He seems to have ought to say, “except Caleb son of Jephunneh” with *son* in the accusative; but he used the nominative because “they followed” preceded it. This expression also exists in Latin, although it is rare.

[Ib. v. 13.] “Until the whole generation that did evil in the sight of the Lord was consumed.” It does not say “doing evil,” nor “of those doing evil.”

[Ib. v. 16.] “And they approached him and said.” It does not use the ordinary expression, “They approached him.”

[Ib. v. 24.] “And you shall build cities for yourselves for your baggage.” It is as though he said, “You shall build cities for yourselves because of your baggage.”

[Ib. vv. 26–27.] “Our baggage and our wives and all our livestock shall be there in the cities of Gilead; but your servants shall all cross over armed.” They did not say, “But we shall all cross over armed”; rather, they spoke as though they were referring to others.

[Ib. v. 28.] “And Moses commissioned Eleazar the priest, and Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders of the families of the tribes of Israel.” He does not say, “Moses commissioned them to Eleazar the priest,” although the order of ordinary expression would require this. For these men were the ones through whom the Israelites were brought into the land they were requesting. Accordingly, Eleazar and Joshua seem rather to have been commended to those by whom they were to be brought into the requested land than those who were to bring them in to those whom they were bringing in.

[Ib. v. 30.] “But if they do not cross over armed with you into battle in the sight of the Lord, and transfer their baggage.” The additional “and” is present.

[Ib. v. 33.] “And Moses gave to them, to the children of Gad and to the children of Reuben.” It contains the additional “to them.”

[Ib. XXXIII, v. 14.] “And there was no water there for the people to drink”: meaning, for drinking.

[Ib. v. 51.] “Speak to the children of Israel, and you shall say to them.” “Speak to the children of Israel” would seem sufficient.

[Ib. v. 52.] “And you shall destroy all their cast idols; destroy them.” It contains the additional “them.”

[Ib. XXXIV, v. 6.] “This shall be your boundary of the sea.” It does not say, “These shall be.”

[Col. 0531] [Ib. v. 7.] “And this shall be your boundary toward the north.” The same expression is repeated.

[Ib. XXXV, v. 3.] “And the cities shall be theirs for dwelling”: meaning, for habitation.

[Ib. v. 11.] “They shall be places of refuge for you, for the murderer to flee there.” In ordinary usage one could say, “So that the murderer may flee there.”

[Col. 0532] [Ib. v. 15.] “And the inhabitants who are among you: these cities shall be for refuge.” *Inhabitants* is placed in the singular, meaning, “for this inhabitant who is among you,” since the expression lacks *is*. It does not say, in the familiar expression, “who is among you,” but uses a rarer construction in Latin than in Greek.

# BOOK FIVE. Expressions in Deuteronomy

[Col. 0531]

[Deuteronomy, ch. I, v. 7.] “As far as the great river, the river Euphrates.” It does not say, “as far as the great river Euphrates.”

[Ib. v. 17.] “And whatever judgment is too difficult for you, you shall bring it to me.” It does not say “too difficult for you,” but “from you”—that is, so difficult that it cannot be judged by you.

[Ib. v. 35.] “If any of these men sees this good land that I swore to their fathers, except Caleb son of Jephunneh, he shall see it.” In the Book of Numbers we noted this expression, because it does not say “except Caleb son of Jephunneh,” but “except Caleb, son of Jephunneh,” with *son* in the nominative.

[Ib. II, v. 7.] “For the Lord your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands.” It does not say “has blessed you all” in the plural, “in all the work of your hands,” although it had previously said “your,” not “thy.”

[Ib. v. 24.] “Now therefore rise up, set out, and cross over the valley of Arnon; behold, I have given into your hands Sihon king of Heshbon.” It does not say “into your hands” in the plural, but moves from the plural to the singular.

[Ib. IV, v. 7.] ““For what great nation is there to which there is for it a God drawing near to them?” Two things should be noted here: the expression “to which there is for it,” and the fact that it does not say “drawing near to it,” but “drawing near to them.”

[Ib. v. 12.] “And you saw no likeness, but a voice.” Since a voice cannot be seen, he used this verb generally, as though seeing pertained to every bodily sense.

[Ib. vv. 5 and 14.] “Into which you are entering there, to inherit it.” The sentence would be complete even without the addition of “there.”

[Ib. v. 20.] “And he brought you out of the iron furnace, from Egypt.” By the iron furnace he wished a harsh tribulation to be understood. In accordance with this, the Psalms also say of Joseph, “Iron passed through his soul” (Psalm 104:18).

[Ib. v. 22.] “And I shall not cross this Jordan.” It is as though there were another Jordan. From this expression I think that “this world” is also often said, as though there were another world.

[Ib. v. 25.] “But if you beget sons and sons of your sons.” The expression should be noted, in which grandfathers are also said to beget grandchildren.

[Ib. v. 29.] “And you shall seek the Lord your God there, and you shall find him when you seek him with all your heart and with all your soul in your tribulation.” It does not say “with all your hearts and with all your souls, in your tribulations.”

[Col. 0532] [Ib. v. 32.] “Ask about the former days, which were before you.” “Days” is not meant; people are to be understood. Similarly, it should be noted that although he had earlier said “ask” in the plural, he added the singular *te* (“you”), not the plural *vobis* (“you”).

[Ib. v. 34.] “Whether God also attempted, by entering, to take for himself a nation from the midst of a nation.” “Attempted” is used for “wished,” or for something similar. But “from the midst of a nation” is to be understood as “from the midst of nations,” the singular being used for the plural. Thus we read “the serpent,” “the frog,” and “the locust” for “the serpents,” “the frogs,” and “the locusts.”

[Ib. v. 34.] “According to all that the Lord your God did in Egypt before your eyes.” Nothing is lacking, even if “before your eyes” is omitted.

[Ib. V, v. 5.] “And I stood at that time between the Lord and you, to announce to you the words of the Lord, because you were afraid before the fire and did not go up the mountain, saying, ‘I am the Lord your God,’” and so forth. “Saying” is used for “when he said.”

[Ib. v. 14.] “And the resident alien who dwells among you.” This should be understood as spoken to the people, not as though to one man, since the resident alien dwells among the people.

[Ib. v. 15.] “For this reason the Lord your God appointed for you to observe the Sabbath day and to sanctify it.” If the “and” were absent, the expression would not seem unusual: “to observe the Sabbath day, to sanctify it.” Or it could have been expressed, “to observe the Sabbath day and to sanctify it”; or, “for this reason the Lord your God appointed you to observe the Sabbath day and to sanctify it.” But as it stands—“to observe the Sabbath day, and to sanctify it”—it is an unusual and noteworthy expression.

[Ib. VI, v. 13.] “Take heed for yourself, lest your heart be enlarged and you forget the Lord your God.” It should also be noted that enlargement of the heart can be spoken of in a bad sense. Exultation is understood in enlargement, and its opposite is distress, that is, sadness. Both, however, can be understood in either a good or a bad sense.

[Ib. v. 20.] “And it shall be, when your son asks you tomorrow, saying.” “Tomorrow” is used for any future time.

[Ib. VII, v. 1.] “Seven great and numerous nations.” How can they be numerous if there are seven? He called them numerous because they had a large population.

[Ib. v. 2.] “You shall not make a covenant with them.” Since he was speaking about nations, he used *covenant* for *agreement*.

[Col. 0533] [Ib. vv. 3–4.] “And you shall not take his daughter for your son; for she will cause your son to depart from me, and he will serve other gods, and the Lord will be angry with you in indignation.” He does not say “I shall be angry,” but speaks as though referring to someone else.

[Ib. IX, v. 1.] “Great and fortified cities up to heaven.” This is said hyperbolically.

[Ib. v. 4.] “Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has destroyed these nations before your face, saying, ‘Because of my righteousness the Lord brought me in to inherit this good land.’” The order is: “Do not say in your heart, saying.”

[Ib. v. 28.] “Lest the inhabitants of the land should say, ‘From where you brought us out, from there.’” The additional “from there” is inserted according to scriptural usage.

[Ib. XI, v. 3.] “What he did to the power of Egypt.” Some Latin translators, not understanding this, refused to say “power,” and rendered it “to the force” or “to the army,” because they understood the Greek word δύναμις (*dynamis*) as “army.” But “what he did to their power” is an elegant expression. One must understand what he did to it: he reduced it to nothing. Yet because it is expressed in the plural, it is somewhat obscure.

[Ib. v. 6.] “When the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, and their houses and their tents.” Two expressions should be noted here: first, the added “them,” although the earlier “whom” would have been sufficient; and second, “their houses,” after which he adds “and their tents,” as though they had other houses in the wilderness besides tents. Certainly he wished the people belonging to them to be understood as their “houses,” just as it is said to the people themselves, “And now you, house of Jacob” (Isaiah 2:5). This expression is not foreign to Latin either; for the Romans are called “the house of Assaracus” (*Aeneid* 1.284), because they derived their origin from the Trojan Assaracus.

[Ib. v. 7.] “For your eyes have seen all the great works of the Lord that he did among you today.” Although he was speaking of those works that were performed in the wilderness during the time when they were led about there for forty years, he said “today,” intending this present period to be understood—however many years that same period might have lasted.

[Ib. v. 9.] “The land that the Lord swore to your fathers to give to them and to their seed after them.” It is as though he said, “that is, to their seed after them.” For he did not give it to the fathers themselves, but gave it to them in the sense that he gave it to their seed.

[Ib. v. 13.] “But if by hearing you hear all his commandments that I command you today.” “By hearing” seems superfluous, but it is an expression very familiar in Holy Scripture.

[Ib. v. 14.] “And he will give rain to your land in its season, early and late.”

[Note: [Col. 0533] Five manuscripts have here only *matutinam et serotinam*, “early rain and late rain,” in the feminine.]

Since “early” may refer to the daytime, did he perhaps intend the first season of the year? “Late” is less idiomatic in Latin, but the Greek term ὄψιμον (*opsimon*) could not be rendered more precisely. It is nevertheless common in Latin usage to speak of something as “late,” meaning something done later than it ought to have been done. Here, however, he intended a season of the year to be understood.

[Col. 0534] [Ib. vv. 15–16.] “And when you have eaten and been satisfied, take heed to yourself lest your heart be enlarged, and you transgress and serve other gods.” We have already noted such expressions above, whether because he moves from the singular to the plural, or because he intended “let your heart be enlarged” in a bad sense, signifying harmful prosperity.

[Ib. v. 24.] “And the great river, the river Euphrates.” Such repetitions are customary in Scripture and suitably emphasize the matter.

[Ib. v. 25.] “The Lord your God will place your fear and your trembling upon the face of the whole earth.” This does not mean the fear and trembling by which they themselves fear and tremble, but that by which they are feared and cause others to tremble.

[Ib. XII, v. 17.] “You will not be able to eat the tithe of your grain in your cities.” This means, “you shall not be permitted to.”

[Ib. XIII, v. 16.] “And you shall burn the city with fire.” We would more ordinarily say, “with fire.”

[Ib. XIV, v. 24.] “But if the way is far from you.” It is as though he said, “if the way is long”; an adverb is used in place of an adjective.

[Ib. XV, v. 6.] “And you shall lend to many nations.” Scripture calls money given on loan *lending*, even when no interest is received. Hence the Psalm says, “Blessed is the one who shows mercy and lends” (Psalm 111:5). Our translators preferred to render the sense rather than the words, for the Greek has δανείζει (*daneizei*), “lends at interest.”

[Ib. v. 6.] “And you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you.” It is as though he said, “They shall not rule over you”—that is, the nations. For *tui* is the singular genitive of the pronoun whose dative is *tibi*; it is not the plural nominative, whose genitive is *tuorum*.

[Ib. v. 7.] “But if there is among you a poor person among your brothers.” This is not said to one man, but to the people; hence the expression “among you.”

[Ib. vv. 7–8.] “But if there is among you a poor person among your brothers, in one of your cities, in the land that the Lord your God is giving you, you shall not turn your heart away, nor shall you close your hand from your poor brother; opening, you shall open your hands to him; lending, you shall lend to him as much as he asks and as much as he needs.” Here, although he commands works of mercy, the cruelty of interest-taking is certainly not to be accepted. Accordingly, by saying “lending, you shall lend to him,” he wished a loan of whatever he asked to be understood. The expression “opening, you shall open your hands” is like what follows, “lending, you shall lend”; it is a customary expression in Holy Scripture.

[Ib. v. 17.] After commanding that the servant’s ear be pierced, he says, “You shall do likewise to your maidservant,” placing the accusative for the dative. He does not say, “You shall do to your maidservant,” as the normal usage of our language would require.

[Ib. v. 21.] “But if there is a defect in it, lame or blind, or any evil defect.” He does not say “lameness” or “blindness,” which are the defects themselves, but “lame” and “blind,” which are not defects but animals possessing defects. It should also be noted that he says “an evil defect,” as though a defect could be good.

[Ib. XVI, v. 4.] “And none of the meat from what [Col. 0535] you sacrifice on the first day shall remain overnight until morning.” Instead of saying “it shall not remain that night,” he says “it shall not sleep.”

[Ib. XVII, v. 1.] “You shall not offer to the Lord your God a bull or a sheep in which there is a defect in it.” Ordinary usage would say, “in which there is a defect,” but this form is more customary in Scripture.

[Ib. v. 5.] “And you shall stone them with stones, and they shall die.” In our usage one would say, “with stones,” not “in stones.”

[Ib. v. 16.] “He shall not multiply a horse for himself.” He uses “horse” for “horses” or “cavalry”; hence some translators rendered it “cavalry.”

[Ib. v. 15.] “You shall not be able to set over yourself a foreign man, because he is not your brother.” “You shall not be able” is used for “you shall not be permitted.”

[Ib. XVIII, v. 16.] “According to all that you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb, on the day of the assembly, saying.” After previously using “you asked,” he adds “saying” in the plural, not in the singular.

[Ib. XX, v. 4.] “For the Lord our God, who goes before with you.” It does not say “you.”

[Ib. XXII, v. 6.] “If you encounter a bird’s nest before your face on the road.” It should be noted that he says “you encounter” even of someone who is not walking.

[Ib. v. 8.] “But if you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, and you shall not make bloodshed in your house if the one who falls should fall from it.” That is, “so that the one who falls may fall from the roof.” This is a highly unusual expression.

[Ib. XXIV, vv. 2–3.] “And she goes away and becomes another man’s, and the last husband hates her.” It should be noted that, of two men, the later one is called “the last.” The same expression occurs in the Gospel when the question is asked which of two brothers did the father’s will, and the answer is “the last,” although there were two of them (Matthew 21:31).

[Ib. v. 6.] “You shall not take a millstone as a pledge, nor the upper stone of the mill, because it pledges a soul.” This means, “because you pledge a soul, if you do so.” It should further be noted that he says “a soul” for the life possessed by the soul in the body.
