From the same expression comes the saying in the Gospel, “Is not the soul more than food?” (Matthew 6:25).

[Ib. v. 7.] “But if a man is caught stealing a soul from among his brothers, the children of Israel.” He uses “soul” for “person.” The passage continues, “and, having oppressed him, sells him.” This expression is no less noteworthy: he did not say “and, having oppressed it,” which would have followed more naturally from the preceding word “soul,” but “him”—that is, the human being for whom he had used “soul.”

[Ib. v. 10.] “If there is a debt owed by your neighbor, any debt whatsoever.” The repetition of the word makes the expression noteworthy.

[Ib. XXV, v. 7.] “But if the man does not wish to take his brother’s wife, the woman shall go up to the gate to the council and say, ‘My husband’s brother does not wish to raise up his brother’s name in Israel; my husband’s brother does not wish to.’” Although Scripture favors repetitions of words, this repetition is more unusual. Yet it displays the emotion of the woman’s complaint more elegantly.

[Ib. XXVII, v. 21.] “Cursed is everyone who sleeps with [Col. 0536] every animal.” This means, “who has intercourse with it.” Further, “with every animal” means, “with any animal whatsoever.”

[Ib. XXVIII, v. 48.] “And you shall serve your enemies whom the Lord your God sends against you.” The Greek has λατρεύσεις (*latreuseis*), which the Latin translator rendered *you shall serve*. Scripture ordinarily uses this verb for the service owed to God; hence idolaters are called *idol-worshipers*, because they render that service to idols. Therefore the verb is used unusually here. It could, however, also have this meaning: the things he has described may be so severe that they will be compelled to serve their enemies, who will become excessively proud, as though they were gods.

[Ib. v. 49.] “A nation whose voice you will not hear.” This too should be noted: he says both “whose” and “its,” as Scripture commonly does. In saying “whose voice you will not hear,” he means, “whose language you will not understand.”

[Ib. vv. 54–55.] “The man among you who is soft and exceedingly tender will look with an evil eye upon his brother, and upon the wife in his bosom, and upon any of the remaining children who are left to him, so that he will give to one of them some of the flesh of his children, which he is eating, because nothing has been left to him amid the distress and tribulation with which your enemies will afflict you in all your cities.” It should be noted how the text says “will look with an evil eye” in the sense of “will envy,” as though this were left as the reason why he must give some of his children’s flesh, which necessity compels parents to take as food. In Proverbs too, where the Latin manuscripts have, “You shall not dine with an envious man” (Proverbs 23:6), the Greek has ἀνδρὶ βασκάνῳ (*andri baskano*). The Greek *baskanos* denotes an envious or bewitching person; Augustine here glosses it with Latin *fascinus*, ‘the evil eye’ or ‘bewitchment.’

[Ib. v. 63.] “And it shall be as the Lord rejoiced over you, to benefit you.” The Greek has “to benefit you” with the accusative, and this does not seem even to be Greek usage. Nevertheless, the accusative is understood in place of the dative. Hence the Latin translators preferred to say “to you” rather than “you.”

[Ib. XXIX, v. 2.] “You saw all that the Lord your God did in the land of Egypt before you: to Pharaoh and all his servants and all his land, great trials, which your eyes saw.” It should be noted that those plagues are also called “trials.”

[Ib. XXX, v. 4.] “If your dispersion is from the summit of heaven to the summit of heaven, from there the Lord your God will gather you.” It is surprising if this does not mean “from the summit of heaven to the summit of heaven,” as he is also accustomed to say “from the summit of the earth to the summit of the earth.” Perhaps this is because, according to the fact that the air itself is also called heaven, it is joined to the earth.

[Ib. vv. 12–13.] “It is not in heaven, saying, ‘Who will ascend into heaven for us and take it for us, so that we may hear it and do it?’ Nor is it beyond the sea, saying, ‘Who will cross the sea for us and take it for us, so that we may hear it and do it?’” He uses “saying” for “so that you may say.” This is a new expression.

[Ib. XXXI, v. 8.] “And the Lord who accompanies you, with you.”

[Ib. v. 16.] “And the Lord said to Moses, ‘Behold, you shall sleep with your fathers.’” By this expression he signified his death.

[Ib. v. 27.] “You were embittering what belongs to God”: that is, “you were embittering the things that belong to God.”

[Col. 0537] [Ib. v. 29.] “For I know that after my death you will commit iniquity upon iniquity.” In Greek this is expressed by one verb, ἀνομήσετε (*anomēsēte*), “you will commit iniquity.”

[Ib. v. 29.] “And evils will meet you at the last of the days.” Thus the Greek reads, meaning “in the last days” or “at the end of the days.”

[Ib. XXXII, v. 6.] “Is not this very one your father who possessed you, and made you, and created you?” The order should be noted. He seems first to have ought to say, “who created you and made you,” and then, “possessed you.” For how can one who does not exist be understood to be possessed?

[Ib. v. 14.] “With the fat of the kidneys of wheat.” This metaphor is highly unusual: the “kidneys of wheat” are understood as the inner parts of wheat, from which flour is extracted. He also called this “fat,” for the Greeks commonly use this name for flour as well. Thus in Exodus, where it is written, “Lifting the flour upon their shoulders” (Exodus 12:34), the Greek translator used στέατα (*steata*), which means “fats.”

[Col. 0538] [Ib. v. 20.] “Children in whom there is no faith in them.” This is an expression customary in Scripture.

[Ib. v. 36.] “For the Lord will judge his people, and in his servants he will be comforted.” This means, “he will comfort his servants,” unless perhaps “to be comforted” is used metaphorically of his withdrawal from the indignation and offense with which the wicked offend him. His consolation must be understood in this way, not according to human custom, just as neither “anger” nor “jealousy” nor other such expressions are to be understood according to human custom.

[Ib. v. 37.] “Where are their gods, in whom they trusted in them?” The sentence would be complete without “in them.”

[Ib. v. 40.] “And I shall swear by my right hand”: that is, “by my right hand.”

[Ib. v. 42 [Note: [Col. 0538] According to the Septuagint].] “Rejoice, heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him.” Other manuscripts have, “and let all the sons of God worship him.” It is not easily found in Holy Scripture that those who are angels in heaven are called “sons of God.”

# BOOK SIX. Expressions in Joshua

[Col. 0537]

[Col. 0537] [Joshua, ch. I, v. 14.] “But you shall cross over more fully equipped than your brothers, every strong man.” That is, everyone among you who is strong.

[Ib. III, v. 4.] “So that you may know the way by which you will go, it.” The sentence would be complete even without “it.”

[Ib. V, v. 13.] “And it happened, when Joshua was in Jericho.” This expression should be noted. They were not yet in the city itself, whose gates had been shut against them, so that they could not enter it unless its walls fell as the ark of the Lord was carried around them. Therefore “in Jericho” means in the territory belonging to Jericho.

[Ib. VI, v. 1.] Concerning Jericho, when it was shut, it is said, “No one went out from it, nor did anyone enter.” “Into it,” rather than “from it,” is understood in the latter clause. In Greek this is called ζεῦγμα κατ’ ἔλλειψιν (*zeugma kat’ elleipsin*), “a zeugma by ellipsis.”

[Ib. v. 21.] “The Lord says to Joshua: ‘Behold, I deliver Jericho, subjugated, into your hands, and its king who is in it, powerful in strength.’” It is surprising that he does not here place the coordinating conjunction and say, “and powerful in strength,” which Scripture uses so constantly that it is even found where it obstructs the sense of its customary expression. Or are both Jericho and its king said to be powerful in strength?

[Ib. vv. 25 and IV, v. 9.] “And Joshua preserved Rahab the prostitute and her father’s household alive, and she dwelt in Israel until this day.” It should be noted [Col. 0538] how Scripture says “until this day,” an expression it uses constantly. Thus it is said also of the twelve stones that were placed where the Jordan had flowed down from below and stood still above, when the ark or the people crossed over, that they were there “until this day.” This seems to sound as though these things were being narrated long after the event by means of this Scripture, and that the books were not composed at the time when these events were still recent. But whoever thinks this, what will he say about this prostitute? Certainly she lived for as long as the span of one human life, and yet she is said to remain “until this day.” Accordingly, this is said of things that were not established in such a way that those who established them would later alter them. Thus someone is said to have been sent into perpetual exile because he is punished by this penalty without a fixed term—not because anyone can be perpetual in exile, since a human being himself cannot be perpetual. In the same way, this prostitute was not commanded to dwell in Israel for a fixed period; therefore it is said, “until this day.”

[Ib. VII, v. 11.] The Lord says to Joshua: “The people have sinned and transgressed my covenant, which I ordained for them.” It should be noted how he calls “covenant” what he had commanded: that Jericho should be under the ban and that no one should take anything from it for himself.

[On Joshua VIII.1 and 2.] The Lord, speaking to Joshua, said among other things: “Behold, I have delivered into your hands the king of Ai and his land; and you shall deal with Ai and its king as you dealt with Jericho, and you shall plunder its livestock for yourself.” The wording especially deserves notice, not only because he said “you shall plunder for yourself,” as though that plunder were to belong to one person, when it was to belong to everyone—for such expressions are extremely common when God speaks as though to one person of what he says to the people—but also because something new occurs here. Scripture had said, “And the Lord said to Joshua,” and it is clear that Joshua was one man; yet it says, “you shall plunder for yourself.” This was not said in such a way that the plunder was commanded to belong to this one man, but to the whole people.

[On Joshua 8.12.] “And ambushes were against the city from the sea.” Anyone who does not know the usage might think that this was a maritime city. But it is customary in Scripture to call the western region “from the sea,” or “toward the sea,” because, from the part of the land where these events took place, the sea is nearer than from the other sides.

[On Joshua 8.18.] “Stretch out your hand toward the spear that is in your hand against the city.” This expression would not need to be noted were it not for the obscure noun, unfamiliar to those among whom it is not customary. For what *gaeson* means is not readily understood; Symmachus is said to have called it a shield. But I wonder whether the translators of the Septuagint, whose version we are discussing and who retained *gaeson*, intended the Greek word to mean a Gallic spear or lance. For such weapons are called *gaesa*, which Virgil also mentions when he describes the Gauls depicted on Aeneas’ shield:

> Each brandished in either hand his Alpine *gaesa*  
> (*Aeneid* 8.661–662).

[On Joshua 8.22.] “And they were made to stand in the midst of the camp, these on one side and those on the other.” Two things should be noted in this expression. First, although the defeated enemies were in the middle, it is as though the words “these on one side and those on the other” referred to them, whereas in fact it was the Israelites who had placed them in the middle to be struck down. Second, Scripture says that they were made to stand “in the midst of the camp,” calling even battle lines drawn up for combat “camps,” although *camp* is ordinarily used only where an army settles in order to remain there—unless perhaps they were called camps because they were advancing with all their possessions.

[On Joshua 8.27.] “Except for the livestock and the spoils that were in the city, the Israelites plundered them according to the Lord’s command, as the Lord had instructed Joshua.” Thus it says, “Except for the livestock and the spoils, they plundered,” as though those things themselves had not been plundered, when in fact they were precisely what was plundered; they are called “excepted” because they alone were not consumed in that battle.

[On Joshua 9.7.] The Israelites answered the Gibeonites: “Take care that you do not dwell with me. And how shall I make a covenant with you?” We have already noted similar expressions above. “Take care that you do not dwell with me” means “with me,” that is, in the land which God had promised them. Here too they seem to speak to one man, although the delegation that came to them was not a single person. But in their customary manner, when answering a nation and people, they use the singular number, just as God or their leader often does when speaking to them. It should also be noted that Scripture calls a pact of peace a covenant, following its customary usage, for it frequently speaks in this way.

[On Joshua 10.17.] “And it was reported to Joshua, saying, ‘Five kings have been found hidden in the cave’”—instead of “they reported, saying.”

[On Joshua 10.25.] “Thus the Lord will deal with all your enemies whom you will defeat.” Nothing would be lacking from this sentence even if it did not contain “them.”

[On Joshua 11.19 and 20.] “And he captured them all in battle, because it was brought about by the Lord that their hearts were strengthened, so that they went out to meet Israel in battle, in order to be exterminated.” It should be noted that “their hearts were strengthened” is not always to be understood in a good sense.

[On Joshua 14.6.] “You know the word that the Lord spoke to Moses, the man of God, concerning me and you.” It does not say “his man.”

[On Joshua 17.16.] The descendants of Joseph said: “The mountain is not enough for us, nor the chosen horse, and the iron belonging to the Canaanite who dwells in Beth-shean.” He said “the chosen horse” instead of “the chosen horses,” an expression not customary in our speech. Hence some Latin translators did not wish to translate it as “horse,” but as “cavalry.” Thus “chosen horse” is used for “horses,” just as in our usage *soldier* may be used for *soldiers*.

[On Joshua 19.33 and 34.] “And their boundaries were the Jordan, and they will return to the sea.” He did not say “they returned,” or at least “they return,” as is customary when boundaries are mentioned, but “they will return,” as though this were still future, although the narrative concerns the past. In nearly all these divisions of the land, Scripture speaks to each tribe using verbs in the future tense.

[On Joshua 20.9.] “Let him flee there who has struck a person unintentionally.” Here “person” (*soul*) should be understood either as a human being or as the life of the flesh, which exists through the soul. The same expression occurs when Joseph’s brothers said, “Let us not strike his soul” (Gen. 37.22), that is, “Let us not kill him.” For if the soul could be struck by the slayer, the Lord would not say, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10.28).

[On Joshua 21.2.] “The Lord commanded through Moses.” This is an expression very familiar in Scripture. Thus it says, “The word that came through the hand of this or that prophet,” meaning that the power to speak was given through him.

[On Joshua 21.40 [according to the Septuagint].] “And Joshua took stone knives with which he circumcised the Israelites.” It does not say “with which he circumcised,” but “in which.”

[On Joshua 22.7.] “And when Joshua sent them to their homes and blessed them, saying…” Here the conjunction *and* appears superfluous. The sentence could have been stated: “And when he sent them to their homes, he blessed them, saying…”

[On Joshua 22.8.] Another expression deserves notice. Scripture had said, “And Joshua blessed them, saying,” thereby directing their attention to what Joshua said in blessing them. Yet it then added only this: “They went to their homes with great riches, very much livestock, silver and gold, and very much clothing; they divided the spoils of their enemies with their brothers.” This clearly appears to be the statement of a narrator rather than of one giving a blessing.

[On Joshua 22.10.] “They built there an altar by the Jordan, a great altar to look at.” This expression is also familiar in Latin speech.

[On Joshua 22.11.] “And the Israelites heard those saying…” It does not say “the one saying” or “those saying.”

[On Joshua 22.27.] “To serve the service of the Lord.” Two things should be noted in this expression: first, “to serve the service,” which is also found as a Latin expression; and second, “the service of the Lord,” that is, the service owed or rendered to the Lord.

[On Joshua 22.30.] “And when Phinehas the priest and all the leaders of the assembly who were with him heard the words spoken by the descendants of Reuben, the descendants of Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, they were pleased.” *Hearing* is used instead of *they heard*; or the *and* is superfluous here, since the complete sense is: “Hearing these words, they were pleased.” Yet even this is not entirely consistent, because, since they had heard, it ought to have said “when they had heard.”

[On Joshua 23.1.] “And Joshua, advanced in age and far along in days…” We have noted this concerning Abraham: in Scripture *the older man* does not refer only to one who is below the age of old age, but also to one who is very old. Thus not every older man is an old man, although every old man may be called older.

[On Joshua 24.7.] “And he brought the sea upon them, and it covered over them.” It does not say “it covered them,” although some translators preferred to say this.

[On Joshua 24.17.] “Among all the nations through which we passed, through them.” Such expressions are customary in Scripture and need not be noted as often as they occur.

# BOOK SEVEN

## Expressions from Judges

[Judges 1.1.] “And it came to pass, after Joshua died, that the Israelites inquired in the Lord.” It does not say “the Lord,” as the usage of our language would require.

[On Judges 1.3.] “And let us wage war in the Canaanite.” It does not say “against the Canaanite,” or “contrary to the Canaanite,” or at least “into the Canaanite.”

[On Judges 2.8.] “And Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died, the son of one hundred and ten years.” This repetition is unusual: after saying “son of Nun,” it repeats “son” and then adds “of one hundred and ten years,” as though it preferred to say “the son of one hundred and ten years” rather than “a man of one hundred and ten years.” Yet the expression is also found elsewhere.

[On Judges 2.10.] “And every generation were added to their fathers.” The expression should be noted because it does not say “was added,” since they were many.

[On Judges 2.14.] “He delivered them into the hand of plunderers.” It does not say “into the hand” in the singular, although Latin usage seems to require that form.

[On Judges 2.18.] “And when the Lord raised up judges for them, the Lord was with the judge.” Here, in the customary expression, the *and* is superfluous. The complete sentence would be: “And when the Lord raised up judges for them, he was with the judge.” It should also be noted that, in passing from the plural to the singular, it does not say “with the judges,” but “with the judge,” that is, with each individual judge.

[On Judges 2.19.] “And it came to pass, when the judge died, that they returned and again acted corruptly beyond their fathers.” According to the usage of our language, the expression could properly have been: “And it happened, when the judge died, that they returned and again acted corruptly beyond their fathers.” If the *and* were omitted, the sentence would be complete: “When the judge died, they returned and again acted corruptly beyond their fathers,” that is, more than their fathers had done.

[On Judges 2.20.] “Because this nation so greatly abandoned my covenant.” *So greatly* is used for *so much*, a noun being employed as an adverb. This is also found, especially in poetic Latin expressions.

[On Judges 2.20.] “And they did not obey my voice.” This is more a Greek expression.

[On Judges 3.10.] “The Spirit of the Lord was made upon him.” The Spirit of the Lord was certainly not made or created; rather, “was made upon him” is expressed as though one had said, “It came about that it was upon him.” From the same usage we read in the Gospel, “He was made before me” (John 1.27), that is, “it came about that he was before me”; in another form, “He was preferred to me.”

[On Judges 3.21.] “And Ehud took the sword from above his right thigh.” This could be translated in accordance with the Greek, *apo anōthen* (“from above”), for the expression is less Latin.

[On Judges 3.17.] “Eglon was a very slender man.” This is said *kat’ antíphrasin*, that is, by an expression contrary to the intended meaning, as the following words show. When he was struck, it is said that the fat closed over the wound, because the sword was not drawn out from his belly.

[On Judges 3.31.] “And he struck six hundred men among the foreigners.” It does not say “six hundred men of the foreigners,” or at least “the foreigners in six hundred men.”

[On Judges 4.6.] “Has not the Lord God of Israel commanded you, and you will go up to Mount Tabor?” It does not say “that you should go,” which would seem to follow. Instead, in an unusual expression, it says, “Has he not commanded you, and you will go?” We must supply the verb used above, so that the sense is, “Has he not commanded you? Will you not go?” Or the *and* is superfluous according to ordinary usage. Removing it gives the sense: “Has not the Lord God of Israel commanded you: ‘Go up to Mount Tabor and take with you ten thousand men’?” and so forth.

[On Judges 4.8.] “For I do not know the day on which the Lord prospers the angel with me.” Does this mean, “the day on which he prospers the activity of his angel who is with me,” or “the day on which he brings prosperity to me through the angel”?

[On Judges 4.13.] “All his chariots, nine hundred iron chariots.” Wherever the division is placed, the repetition is elegant. Is the sense “all his chariots,” followed by “nine hundred iron chariots”? Or is it “all his nine hundred chariots,” followed by “iron chariots”?

[On Judges 4.15.] “And the Lord terrified Sisera, all his chariots, and all his army, with the edge of the sword before Barak.” How could he terrify the chariots, unless by “chariots” we understand those who were in the chariots? “The Lord terrified Sisera, all his chariots, and all his army, with the edge of the sword before Barak.” “He terrified with the edge of the sword” is as though it said, “He killed with the edge of the sword.” Thus he terrified them when they were being struck down with the sword.

[On Judges 4.16.] “And Sisera came down from above his chariot.” This could be expressed in Latin in accordance with the Greek *apo anōthen* (“from above”).

[On Judges 4.19.] “And she covered him in her skin.” It does not say “with skin” or “from skin.” This is how the Greek reads: *en tē derrhei autēs* (“in her skin”).

[On Judges 4.20.] “And it will happen that if anyone comes to you and says, ‘Is there a man here?’ you shall say, ‘There is not.’” If the conjunction were removed, the sense would be more direct: “If anyone comes to you and says, ‘Is there a man here?’ you shall say, ‘There is not.’”

[On Judges 4.24.] “And the hand of the Israelites continued, continuing.” This is an ordinary and common expression.

[On Judges 4.24.] “And it became hardened against Jabin king of Canaan.” The verb *became hardened* is used here in a new way, meaning “became strong and exceedingly powerful.”

[On Judges 5.26.] “She pierced his head and struck him,” that is, “she struck his head and pierced it.”

[On Judges 5.31.] “So may all your enemies perish, Lord; and may those who love him be like the rising of the sun in his power.” It does not say “those who love you,” although clearly the Lord is intended.

[On Judges 6.3.] “And it came to pass, whenever an Israelite sowed…” This does not refer to one man, but to the nation itself.

[On Judges 6.3.] “Midian and Amalek and the sons of the East came up, and they came up against him.” This repetition of the verb does not seem to possess its customary elegance or expressive force.

[On Judges 6.9.] “And I delivered you from the hand of Egypt.” “Hand” signifies power; “Egypt” signifies the Egyptians.

[On Judges 6.13.] Gideon said to him, “As for me, my lord…” The implied expression is “pay attention to me,” that is, “pay attention to me, my lord.” This is an expression very familiar in Scripture.

[On Judges 6.13.] “And if the Lord is with us, why have all these evils found us?” The conjunction *and* is superfluous, as Scripture often speaks. If it is removed, the sentence is complete: “If the Lord is with us, why have all these evils found us?” The preceding conjunction may also be omitted without affecting the sense. After “As for me, my lord,” the sentence may continue: “If the Lord is with us, why have all these evils found us?” This is more in accordance with the usage of our language.

[On Judges 6.25.] “And a seven-year-old bull.” Here it is clear how Scripture uses the word *calves*. For, according to our customary usage, a seven-year-old ox is not a calf. In accordance with this usage, it is said of Shamgar [Note: In the manuscripts, *Sagemar*.] that he killed six hundred men “besides calves of oxen” (Judg. 3.31), that is, besides oxen.

[On Judges 6.34.] “And he blew on the horn.” The trumpet is understood; the Greek does not contain the word “trumpet,” but only “horn.”

[On Judges 7.12.] “Their camels could not be numbered, and they were like the sand that is on the shore of the sea.” It is clear that this is said hyperbolically (*hyperbolikōs*). This translation, in which it uses “the lip of the sea” for “the shore,” is frequent in Scripture but rare in Latin manuscripts, because most translators rendered *lip* by *shore*, preferring to convey what “lip” meant rather than the word itself. For if the Septuagint translators had wished to say “shore,” the Greek language would not have lacked a word for it.

[On Judges 7.16.] “And he divided the three hundred men into three beginnings.” He used *beginnings* for *divisions*.

[On Judges 8.1.] “And the men of Ephraim said to Gideon,” that is, “the men of the tribe of Ephraim.”

[On Judges 8.1.] “What is this word that you have done to us, not calling us when you went out to fight against Midian?” He uses *word* for *deed*.

[On Judges 9.4.] “And they gave seventy pieces of silver.” *Pounds* or something similar is understood. The translation from the Hebrew has “seventy pounds.”

[On Judges 9.4.] “And Abimelech hired men with them.” He says “with them” instead of “from them,” that is, he hired men with the seventy pounds of silver.

[On Judges 9.4.] “Empty and disturbed men.” He uses *empty* for *light-minded*, the opposite of *weighty*. Hence it is said, “Among a weighty people I will praise you” (Ps. 34.18).

[On Judges 9.5.] “And he entered the house of his father at Ephrathah and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerobaal, seventy men, upon one stone.” Since he had already said that Jerobaal—that is, Gideon—had seventy sons, and now says that these seventy were killed, although two fewer were actually killed—namely, the killer himself and Jotham the youngest, who hid, concerning whom he adds, “And Jotham, the youngest son of Jerobaal, remained, because he hid himself”—the complete number is therefore used for almost the complete number.

[On Judges 9.23.] “And the men of Shechem despised in the house of Abimelech.” It does not say “they despised the house of Abimelech.”

[On Judges 9.34.] “And they lay in ambush against Shechem in four beginnings,” that is, in four divisions. We have already noted this expression above.

[On Judges 9.43.] “And he took the people and divided them into three beginnings.” *He took* refers to the people who were with him; and here too he uses *three beginnings* for *three divisions*.

[On Judges 9.55.] “And the men went to his place,” that is, each man went to his own place.

[On Judges 11.8.] “And you will be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.” It does not say “you will be our head.” Scripture commonly speaks in this way. Hence we read, “Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge” (Ps. 30.3), and many similar expressions.

[On Judges 11.34.] “And she was his only child, and he had no son or daughter besides her.” This is the meaning of “she was his only child”; but the sentence is repeated because of affection. “He had no son or daughter besides her”: “he has” is used for “he had,” since the events are narrated in the past.

[On Judges 13.2.] “And his wife was barren, and she did not bear children.” The word “barren” by itself could have sufficed.

[On Judges 13.8.] “And Manoah prayed to the Lord and said, ‘As for me, my lord, may the man of God whom you sent come to us again.’” “As for me” is expressed with “pay attention” understood.

[On Judges 15.8.] “And he struck them leg upon thigh.” This is an unusual expression, but it is an expression, not a particular place of injury on the body, as I explained in the *Questions*; it means that he struck them to the point of astonishment and stupefaction (*Questions on Judges*, question 55).

[On Judges 15.10.] “And the men of Judah said, ‘Why have you come up against us?’” The singular is used for the plural, for it was the men of Judah who spoke, not one man.

[On Judges 15.12.] “Lest perhaps you come upon me, you yourselves.” This means “lest you kill me.” The expression has also been explained in the *Questions* (*ibid.*, question 56).

[On Judges 15.13.] “And they brought him down from the rock, and he came as far as the Jaw.” This place was subsequently given that name because of what Samson himself did there, when, fighting with the jawbone of a donkey, he struck down a thousand men. The name is therefore stated by prolepsis, because the history was written after all those events had taken place.

[On Judges 15.14.] “As flax when it has smelled the fire.” This is a metaphor from an animate to an inanimate thing, for flax does not possess the sense of smell. It is as though one had said, “when it has sensed the fire.” Yet even the word “sensed” that I have used belongs to the same metaphor; the word “smelled” was chosen to express the speed of the action.

[On Judges 15.15.] “And he stretched out his hand and took it.” Even if it had not said “he stretched out his hand,” we would certainly understand that he took it with his hand extended.

[On Judges 16.2.] “And it was reported to the Gazites, saying…” It does not say “they reported, saying,” or “it was reported by those speaking.”

[On Judges 16.7.] “If they bind me with seven moist sinews that have not yet dried…” It does not say “with seven sinews,” but “in seven sinews.”

[On Judges 16.7.] “If they bind me with seven moist sinews that have not yet dried, I shall become weak.” The sentence would be complete even without the conjunction *and*.

[On Judges 16.9.] “And the ambush sat in the chamber.” Some translated this as “they surrounded him,” but the Greek has *ekathēto*, that is, “sat,” because *ambush* is expressed in the singular in Greek, and *ambush* cannot be used in the singular in Latin. The expression deserves notice because it says “the ambush sat” instead of “those who were lying in ambush”; it was the men themselves who sat.

[On Judges 16.10.] “Now tell me with what you will be bound.” It does not say “by what” or “from what” you will be bound.

[On Judges 16.11.] “If they bind me with new ropes.” It does not say “with ropes.”

[On Judges 16.11.] Likewise: “If they bind me with new cords, with which no work has been done, I shall become weak.” The sentence would be complete even if the conjunction *and* were not placed at the beginning.

[On Judges 16.15.] “And this third time you have deceived me.” He uses *third* for *the third time*, employing a noun as an adverb, something that can also be done elegantly in Latin expressions.

[On Judges 16.26.] “Let me go, and I shall feel the pillars on which the house is established upon them.”

# QUESTIONS ON THE HEPTATEUCH

## On the Work of the Following Questions

### Book II of the *Retractions*, Chapter 55

1. At the same time [Note: That is, at the time when the holy Doctor was compiling the preceding collection of *Expressions*, which is reviewed in Book II, chapter 54 of the *Retractions*, he completed this following book of *Questions on the Heptateuch*, as they are entitled in the ancient manuscripts. It is understood, however, from *Expressions on Exodus*, chapter 12, verse 7, and *Expressions on Judges*, chapters 15, verses 8 and 12, that he dictated the *Questions* first and then the *Expressions* on the same divine books, although in the *Retractions* he placed the collection of *Expressions* first, perhaps because he had either begun dictating it in that order or wished it to be read in that order.] I also wrote seven books of *Questions on the same divine books*. I wished to call them this because in them I proposed matters more as questions to be investigated than as questions already solved, although many more of them seem to me to have been treated in such a way that they may rightly be judged solved and explained.

We had also begun to examine the Books of Kings in the same way; but, having made little progress, we turned our attention to other matters that pressed more urgently upon us. In the first book, where the matter of the variegated rods that Jacob placed in the water is discussed, so that the sheep would see them while drinking when they conceived and would give birth to varied offspring (*Questions* 93), we did not explain properly why he did not place them again when they conceived—that is, when they conceived other offspring—but only during the first conception. For the explanation of another question (*ibid.*, 95), where it is asked why Jacob said to his father-in-law, “You have cheated me of my wages ten lambs” (Gen. 31.41), demonstrates truthfully that this question was not solved as it ought to have been.

2. Likewise, in the third book, where the high priest is discussed—how he could beget sons when he was required to enter the Holy of Holies twice a day, where the altar of incense was, to offer incense morning and evening (Exod. 30.7–8), and where, according to the Law, an unclean person could not enter—while the same Law says that a man also becomes unclean through marital intercourse, commanding him indeed to wash with water but also declaring that even after washing he remains unclean until evening (Lev. 15.16), I said, “It followed that he was either continent or that the incense was omitted on certain days” (*Questions* 82). I did not see that this did not necessarily follow. For the statement “He shall be unclean until evening” can be understood to mean that by evening he would no longer be unclean, but only until that time, so that he could offer incense as a clean man in the evening, having joined himself to his wife after the morning incense in order to beget children.

Likewise, when it was asked how the high priest could have been forbidden to enter upon the death of his father, even before the father’s burial (Lev. 21.11), when, since there was only one high priest, he ought not to become priest until after the death of his priestly father, I said, “For this reason it was necessary that, before his father had been buried, immediately after his death, his son should be appointed to succeed him; and also because of the uninterrupted offering of incense, which had to be offered twice a day” (*Questions* 83). Yet that priest was forbidden to enter upon the death of his father, who had not yet been buried.

I paid too little attention to the possibility that this command was intended especially for those who would become high priests without succeeding high-priest fathers, but nevertheless would be from their sons—that is, from the descendants of Aaron—if perhaps the high priest had no sons, or had sons so wicked that none of them ought to succeed their father. Thus Samuel succeeded the high priest Eli (1 Sam. 1), although Samuel himself was not the priest’s son, but was nevertheless from the sons—that is, the descendants—of Aaron.

3. Concerning the thief to whom it was said, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23.43), I stated as though certain that he had not been visibly baptized (*Questions* 84), although this is uncertain, and it is more credible that he had been baptized, as I later argued elsewhere.

Likewise, what I said in the fifth book, where the mothers in the Gospel genealogies are mentioned—that “they are not listed except together with the fathers” (*ibid.*, 46)—is true, but does not pertain to the issue under discussion. The issue concerned those who married the wives of their brothers or relatives who had died without children, because of Joseph’s two fathers, one of whom Matthew mentions and the other Luke. I discussed this question carefully in the present work when I was revising our work against Faustus the Manichaean.

This work begins as follows: “As we were reading through the holy Scriptures that are called canonical…”

# THE SEVEN BOOKS OF QUESTIONS ON THE HEPTATEUCH OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO

[Note: Written about the year 419 after Christ.]

[Note: These books were reviewed against two Vatican manuscript codices; one belonging to the college of Fuxensis at Toulouse; the Sorbonne manuscript, written about four hundred years ago; the Beccensis, which dates back six hundred years; the Remigianus and Michaelinus, of approximately the same age; the Thuaneus and Benignianus, which appear to have been written eight hundred years ago; the oldest and finest of all, the Corbeiensis; the variant readings of the Louvain theologians, gathered from five Belgian manuscripts; the excerpts of Abbot Eugippius contained in two manuscripts; and the handwritten collection of Florus. Finally, they were compared with the older editions: the Badius, or Ratisbon, edition—that is, the edition published at Lyons in 1497 from the recension of Augustine of Ratisbon, under the care of Jodocus Badius—the Amerbach edition, Erasmus’ Froben edition, and the Antwerp edition of the Louvain theologians.] [Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

# BOOK ONE

## Questions on Genesis

### Preface

As we were reading through the holy Scriptures that are called canonical, and comparing them with other copies according to the Septuagint translation, we decided to commit to writing the questions that occurred to us, whether merely proposing them by briefly mentioning them or also treating them at some length, or even solving them in some fashion, as though in haste, so that they would not escape our memory.

Our purpose was not to explain them adequately, but to enable us to consult them when necessary: either so that we might be reminded of what still needed investigation, or so that, from what already appeared to have been discovered, we might, as far as we could, be equipped for reflection and prepared to respond. Therefore, if anyone does not disdain to read these pages because of the unpolished language produced by our haste, and finds questions proposed but not solved, let him not think that nothing has been contributed to him for that reason. For a considerable part of discovery consists in knowing what one is seeking.

But if a solution to a question proves satisfactory, let him not despise the plainness of the expression in which it is given; rather, let him rejoice in having received some share of instruction. For it is not disputation that is sought through truth, but truth through disputation.

Except for those matters that can be treated in many ways from the beginning, where God is related to have made heaven and earth, up to the expulsion of the first two human beings from paradise—matters on which we have discussed elsewhere as much as we were able, in the books on Genesis—these are the points that occurred to us as we read and that we wished to preserve in writing [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain edition read *attingere*, “to touch upon.” Three older manuscripts read *attinere*. We, with the Ratisbon edition and two manuscripts, read *attineri*.].

### Question I

[Genesis 4.17.] How could Cain have founded a city, since a city is ordinarily established for a multitude of human beings, whereas only two parents and two sons are reported to have existed, and one of the sons was killed by the other, in whose place another son is said to have been born?

Or is this a question only because those who read the passage think that at that time there were no human beings except those whom divine Scripture mentions, and do not consider that the first two human beings who were created, or even those whom they begot, lived long enough to beget many others? Adam himself did not beget only those whose names are recorded, since Scripture, speaking of him, concludes by saying that he begot sons and daughters (Gen. 5.4).

Therefore, since they lived many more years than the Israelites spent in Egypt, who cannot see how many people could have been born from whom that city might be filled, if the Hebrews could multiply so greatly in a much shorter time?

### II

[Genesis 5.25.] It is customary to ask how Methuselah could have lived, according to the calculation of years, after the flood, since everyone except those who entered the ark is said to have perished.

But this question was produced by the corruption of many manuscripts [Note: Compare *The City of God*, book 15, chapter 11.]. For not only is the matter found differently in the Hebrew text; even in the Septuagint translation, the fewer but more reliable manuscripts show Methuselah to have died six years before the flood.

### III

[Genesis 6.4.] It is also asked how angels could have had intercourse with the daughters of men, from whom giants are said to have been born. Some Latin and Greek manuscripts, however, do not read “angels,” but “sons of God.” To resolve this question, some have believed that these were righteous men who could also be called by the name “angels.” For it is written concerning the man John, “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way” (Mal. 3.1).

But the difficulty is this: how could giants have been born from human intercourse, or how could the beings in question have had intercourse with women if they were not human beings but angels? As for giants—that is, men of extraordinary size and strength—I think there is nothing astonishing in their being born from human beings, since some such men are found even after the flood. In our own times too, some human bodies have existed of incredibly great size, not only among men but also among women.

It is therefore more credible that righteous men, called either angels or sons of God, fell through desire and sinned with women than that angels without flesh could have descended into such a sin. Nevertheless, many people say many things about certain demons who are lustful toward women, so that it is not easy to reach a definitive judgment concerning this matter.

### IV

[Genesis 6.15.] Concerning Noah’s ark it is customary to ask whether, with the capacity attributed to it, it could have carried all the animals said to have entered it, together with their food.

Origen resolves this question by means of the geometric cubit, asserting that Scripture did not say without reason that Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7.22), who devoted themselves to geometry. He says that a geometric cubit was worth as much as six of our cubits. If, therefore, we understand the cubits to have been so large, there is no difficulty in believing that the ark had sufficient capacity to contain all those things.

### V

[Genesis 6.15.] It is also asked whether such a large ark could have been built in one hundred years by four men, namely Noah and his three sons.

But if they could not build it, it would not have been difficult to employ other craftsmen—although, once they had received payment for their labor, they may not have cared whether Noah was building it wisely or foolishly. For this reason they did not enter it: they did not believe what he believed.

### VI

[Genesis 6.16.] What does he mean when, speaking of the construction of the ark, he says, “You shall make its lower parts with two chambers and three chambers” [Note: The printed editions read *ea*, “them”; the manuscripts read *eam*, “it,” in accordance with the Septuagint, *autēn*. The reference is to the ark.]?

The lower parts were not themselves to have two and three chambers. Rather, by this division he intended the entire internal arrangement of the ark [Note: The printed editions read “its structure.” All our manuscripts, however, read “its internal arrangement.”], so that it would have lower parts and also the upper parts of the lower sections [Note: Thus read several of the more numerous and better manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “so that it would have lower parts, middle parts, and upper parts, which are called three-chambered.”], which he called two-chambered; and it would also have the upper parts of the upper sections, which he called three-chambered.

In the first dwelling, that is, in the lower part, the ark had one level of chambers. In the second dwelling, above the lower one, it had two levels of chambers; and consequently, in the third, above the second, it undoubtedly had three levels of chambers.

### VII

[Genesis 6.21.] Since God said that the animals in the ark were not merely to live but also to be fed there, and commanded Noah to take for himself and for them food of every kind that would enter with him, the question arises how lions or eagles, which are accustomed to live on flesh, could have been fed there.

Were animals beyond the stated number brought in for the sake of feeding the others? Or—and this is more credible—did the wise man, perhaps with God showing him, provide something other than flesh that would be suitable as food even for animals of that kind?

### VIII

[Genesis 7.8–9.] It is written: “From clean birds and from unclean birds, and from clean cattle and from unclean cattle, and from all the creeping things upon the earth.” The word “clean” and “unclean” is understood again when it is not added, and the text continues: “Two by two” [Note: The printed editions read “two and two.” The conjunction *and* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek Septuagint.] “entered to Noah into the ark, male and female.”

The question is how the earlier passage distinguished “two by two” from the unclean animals, whereas here it says that two by two entered, whether clean or unclean. But this does not refer to the number of clean or unclean animals; it refers to the male and the female, because among all animals, whether clean or unclean, there are two: male and female.

### IX. [Ibid., VII, 15]

It should be noted that what is written, “in which is the spirit of life,” is said not only of human beings but also of cattle, on account of what some wish to understand of the Holy Spirit where it is written, “And God breathed into his face the spirit of life” (Gen. 2:7). Certain manuscripts more correctly read “the breath of life.”

### X. [Ibid., VII, 20]

With regard to the height of the mountains, which the text says the water entirely surpassed by fifteen cubits, a question arises because of the account of Mount Olympus. For if the earth could rise into that tranquil expanse of air where, it is said, neither clouds are seen nor winds felt, why could the water not likewise rise as it increased?

### XI. [Ibid., VII, 24]

It is written, “The water was raised above the earth for one hundred and fifty days.” The question is whether it continued to rise until that day, or whether it remained at the height to which it had risen throughout those days, since other translators seem to express this more clearly. Aquila said, “It prevailed”; Symmachus, “They prevailed”—that is, the waters.

[Note: The printed editions read “the waters prevailed,” omitting “that is,” which is found in all our manuscripts.]

### XII. [Ibid., VIII, 1]

[Note: The printed editions read: “What is written is that the water was raised after one hundred and fifty days and that the spirit was brought”; seven manuscripts of better quality oppose this reading, which we follow here.]

The text states that after one hundred and fifty days the spirit was brought over the earth, the water ceased, the fountains of the abyss and the cataracts of heaven were closed, and the rain from heaven was held back. The question is whether these things happened after one hundred and fifty days, or whether everything is mentioned by recapitulation—namely, the events that began after the forty days of rain—so that only this belongs to the one hundred and fifty days: that until then the water had remained elevated, either because the fountains of the abyss continued after the rain had ceased, or because it remained at its height while no wind dried it. The other things that have been mentioned, however, did not all happen after one hundred and fifty days; rather, all the events that began at the end of the forty days are recalled.

[Note: Am. Er. and Lov. read “while it was in that wind.” Rat. and all the manuscripts read “while no wind dried it.”]

### XIII. [Ibid., VIII, 6–9]

The text says that the raven was released and did not return, and that afterward the dove was released and returned because it had found no resting-place for its feet. A question commonly arises: did the raven die, or could it have survived in some way? For if there was land where it could rest, surely the dove too could have found a resting-place for its feet. Hence many infer that the raven could have perched on a corpse, which the dove naturally avoids.

### XIV. [Ibid., VIII, 9]

There is also the question of how the dove found no place on which to settle if, as the sequence of the narrative suggests, the summits of the mountains had already appeared. This question can apparently be resolved either by recapitulation, so that what happened earlier is understood to have been narrated later, or rather on the grounds that the mountains had not yet dried.

### XV. [Ibid., VIII, 21]

What does the Lord’s statement mean: “I will not again add to curse the earth because of human works, for the human mind is inclined to evil from youth”? “I will not again add to strike every living creature, as I have done.” He then adds the things that, according to the abundance of his goodness, he grants to human beings who are unworthy. Is the indulgence of the New Testament prefigured here, while the former punishment belongs to the Old Testament—that is, the former to the severity of the Law and the latter to the goodness of grace?

[Note: The printed editions read “inclined to wickedness from youth.” The manuscripts of Corbie and the two manuscripts of Eugippius read “inclined to evil,” in agreement with the Greek Septuagint, τὰ πονηρά, “the evil things.”]

### XVI. [Ibid., IX, 5]

What does “And from the hand of a human being, his brother, I will require the life of a human being” mean? Did he intend every human being to be understood as the brother of every other human being, according to the kinship derived from one ancestor?

[Note: The printed editions read “to be understood in the name of a human being.” The word “name” is absent from the manuscripts; two of them have “or of a human being” in its place.]

### XVII. [Ibid., IX, 25]

Why is Ham, who sinned by offending his father, cursed not in himself but in his son Canaan? Is it not because it was in a sense prophesied that the sons of Israel, who would come from the seed of Shem, would receive the land of Canaan after the Canaanites had been expelled and defeated?

### XVIII. [Ibid., X, 8]

The question arises how it was said of Nimrod, “He began to be a giant upon the earth,” when Scripture records that giants had been born earlier. Or perhaps, since after the Flood the renewal of the human race is being mentioned anew, he began to be a giant upon the earth in the novelty of this renewed race.

[Column 0552] ### XIX. [Ibid., X, 25]

The question arises what is meant by, “And two sons were born to Eber; the name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided.” Perhaps the diversity of languages arose in his days, through which the nations were divided.

### XX. [Ibid., XI, 1]

“And the whole earth had one language.” How can this be understood when it was stated above that the sons of Noah, or the sons of his sons, had been distributed throughout the earth according to their tribes, nations, and languages, unless this later statement recalls by recapitulation what had existed earlier? Yet the obscurity is increased by the fact that these matters are linked together in such a form of expression that the narrative seems to proceed as though it concerned events that happened later.

### XXI. [Ibid., XI, 4]

“Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose top will reach to heaven.” If they believed that they could accomplish this, their excessive foolish daring and impiety are exposed. And since God’s vengeance followed for this reason, so that their languages might be divided, it is not unreasonable to believe that they had conceived such a plan.

### XXII. [Ibid., XI, 7]

“Come, let us descend and confuse their language there, so that each one may not hear the voice of his neighbor.” Is this to be understood as something the Lord said to the angels? Or should it be understood according to the statement found at the beginning of the book, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26)? For just as the later statement uses the singular number, saying that “the Lord confused the languages of the earth,” so there too, although it had been said, “Let us make him in our image,” the subsequent text nevertheless does not say, “They made,” but “God made.”

[Note: The printed editions read “their languages.” Shortly afterward they also read “the Lord confused the language of the earth.” Following the Greek, we restore “their language” first, in accordance with the Corbie manuscript, and then, together with seven other manuscripts, “the languages of the earth.”]

### XXIII. [Ibid., XI, 12–13]

It is written, “Arphaxad was one hundred and thirty-five years old when he begot Cainan; and Arphaxad lived four hundred years after he begot Cainan”—or, as we find in the Greek, three hundred years. The question arises how God could have said to Noah, “The years of their life shall be one hundred and twenty.” Arphaxad had not yet been born when God said this, nor had he been in the ark with his parents. How, then, are the one hundred and twenty years subsequently understood as having been foretold as the duration of human life, when a human being is found to have lived more than four hundred years?

Unless the meaning is that God said this twenty years before the ark began to be built—which is found to have taken one hundred years—when he was already announcing to Noah that he would bring about the Flood; and that he did not foretell the future span of human life in those who would be born after the Flood, but the lifespan of the people whom he was going to destroy by the Flood.

### XXIV. [Ibid., X, 21]

The question arises why it is written, “Shem was the father of all the sons of Eber,” when Eber is found to be the fifth generation from Shem, the son of Noah. Is it because the Hebrews are said to have received their name from him? For through him the line of descent passed to Abraham. It is therefore rightly asked which is more probable: that the Hebrews were called Hebrews after Eber, or that they were called Hebrews as descendants of Abraham.

[Note: See *The City of God*, Book 16, chapter 3, and *Retractions*, Book 2, chapter 16.]

[Column 0553] ### XXV. [Ibid., XI, 26]

#### 1.

How are we to understand that when Terah—the manuscripts consistently have *Thara* or *Thara*, as does the Greek—was seventy years old, he begot Abraham; that afterward he remained with all his people in Harran, lived two hundred and five years in Harran, and died there; and that the Lord then told Abraham to depart from Harran, whereupon he left it when he was seventy-five years old?

Unless the meaning is shown by recapitulation: the Lord spoke to Abraham while Terah was still alive, and Abraham, while his father was alive, departed from Harran in obedience to the Lord’s command when he was seventy-five years old—that is, in the one hundred and forty-fifth year of his father’s life, if his father’s lifetime was two hundred and five years. Thus it is written that “the years of Terah’s life in Harran were two hundred and five” because he completed all the years of his entire life there.

The question is therefore resolved by recapitulation. It would remain insoluble if we supposed that the Lord spoke to Abraham to leave Harran only after Terah’s death, because Abraham could not still have been seventy-five years old after his father had died, when his father had begotten him in the seventieth year of his own life. Abraham would have been one hundred and thirty-five years old at his father’s death if his father’s entire lifetime had been two hundred and five years.

When this principle of recapitulation is observed in Scripture, it resolves many questions that may otherwise seem insoluble, as is also shown by the explanation of the preceding questions, which are resolved through the same recapitulation.

#### 2.

Some people resolve this question differently, reckoning the years of Abraham’s age from the time when he was rescued from the fire of the Chaldeans. He had been thrown into it to be burned because he refused to worship that same fire according to Chaldean superstition. Although this is not recorded in Scripture, it is handed down in Jewish tradition.

The question can also be resolved in this way: Scripture says, “When Terah was seventy years old, he begot Abraham and Nahor and Haran.” This does not necessarily mean that he begot all three in the seventieth year of his life; rather, Scripture mentioned the year in which he began to beget children. It is possible that Abraham was born later, but that, because of the excellence by which he is so highly commended in Scripture, he was named first.

The same occurs when the prophet names the younger first: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:2–3). Likewise, in Chronicles, although Judah is fourth in birth order, he is mentioned first (1 Chron. 4:1), because the Jewish people received their name from him, on account of the royal tribe. More conveniently, however, several explanations may be found by which difficult questions can be resolved.

#### 3.

Stephen’s account of this matter should certainly be considered, in order to see which of these explanations conflicts with it least. It compels us to understand that God did not speak to Abraham, as the account in Genesis seems to say (Gen. 12:1), after Terah’s death, telling him to leave his kindred and his father’s household. Rather, God spoke to him while he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Harran, after he had already departed from the land of the Chaldeans; thus God is to be understood as having spoken to him during that journey.

But what Stephen later says creates considerable difficulty for the explanation by recapitulation: “Then Abraham departed from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Harran; and from there, after his father died, God settled him in this land” (Acts 7:4).

It seems that Abraham had received the Lord’s command, spoken to him on the journey through Mesopotamia as he departed from the land of the Chaldeans and went toward Harran, and that he obediently fulfilled this command after his father’s death when it is said, “He lived in Harran.” Accordingly, the question remains: if, as the text of Genesis clearly states, Abraham was seventy-five years old when he departed from Harran, how can Stephen’s account be true?

Perhaps Stephen’s words, “Then Abraham departed from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Harran,” should not be understood to mean, “Then he departed after the Lord had spoken to him.” For he was already in Mesopotamia, as stated above, when he heard that command from the Lord. Rather, Stephen wished to link together, according to the rule of recapitulation, the point from which Abraham departed and the place where he lived when he said, “Then Abraham departed from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Harran.”

In the interval—that is, between his departure from the land of the Chaldeans and his residence in Harran—God spoke to him. Then, when Stephen adds, “And from there, after his father died, God settled him in this land,” we should observe that he did not say, “And after his father died, he departed from Harran,” but “From there God settled him in this land.” Thus Abraham was settled in the land of Canaan after his residence in Harran, not that he departed after his father’s death, but that after his father’s death he was settled in the land of Canaan.

The order of the words is therefore: “He lived in Harran, and from there God settled him in this land after his father died.” We should understand Abraham to have been settled and established in the land of Canaan when he received there the son of his nephew, whose entire offspring was destined to reign there, the inheritance having been granted by God’s promise.

For Ishmael was born from Abraham through Hagar, and other sons were born through Keturah, but the inheritance of that land did not belong to them. Esau was born from Isaac, and he likewise was excluded from that inheritance. But from Jacob, the son of Isaac, all the sons who were born—that is, his entire offspring—belonged to that inheritance.

Thus, if the matter is correctly understood, Abraham was settled and established in that land because he lived until Jacob was born, and the question is resolved according to recapitulation, although other explanations should not be disregarded.

### XXVI. [Ibid., XII, 12, 14]

“When the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife.’” It happened that as soon as Abraham entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw the woman because she was exceedingly beautiful.

How should we understand the fact that, when Abraham came into Egypt, he wished to conceal that Sarah was his wife, according to everything written about this matter? Was such conduct fitting for so holy a man, or should it be understood as a lapse in his faith, as some have thought?

I have already discussed this matter in my work against Faustus (*Against Faustus*, Book 22, chapters 33–34), and the presbyter Jerome has explained more carefully why it does not follow that, because Sarah remained for some days in the king of Egypt’s household, she should be thought to have been defiled by intercourse with him (*Jerome, Questions on Genesis*). It was the royal custom for women to be admitted to the king by turns, and no woman entered the king’s presence until her body had first been carefully prepared for a long time with lotions and perfumes.

[Note: The printed editions read “fomentations” (*fomentis*) in place of the manuscripts’ “cosmetics” (*lomentis*).]

While these preparations were taking place, Pharaoh was afflicted by the hand of God, so that he might return to her husband unharmed the woman whom her husband had entrusted to God, remaining silent about the fact that she was his wife but not lying when he said that she was his sister. Thus Abraham took whatever precautions he could, as far as a human being could, and entrusted to God what he could not protect. Otherwise, if he entrusted even what he could protect entirely to God, he might be found not to believe in God but rather to test God.

[Note: The manuscripts consistently have *Sarram*, with double *r*, as in the Septuagint.]

[Note: The printed editions read “in a lapse of faith.” The manuscripts read “a lapse of faith,” as again below in Book 6, Question 30.]

[Column 0555] [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts. The editions of Am., Er., and Lov. read, “lest if even she did what she could guard,” whereas the edition of Rat. reads, “lest if even he did what he could guard.”]

### XXVII. [Ibid., XIII, 10]

The fact that, before it was destroyed, the land of Sodom and Gomorrah is compared with the paradise of God because it was well watered, and with the land of Egypt watered by the Nile, sufficiently demonstrates, in my opinion, how that paradise should be understood which God planted and in which he placed Adam. I do not see what other paradise of God could be meant.

Indeed, if the fruit-bearing trees in paradise were to be understood as virtues of the soul, as some think, and no physical paradise on earth had been established with genuine kinds of trees, the text would not have said of that land that it was like the paradise of God.

[Note: The printed editions read “like the land of Egypt.” The manuscripts read “and the land of Egypt”; supply “it is compared.”]

### XXVIII. [Ibid., XIII, 14]

“Look with your eyes and see from the place where you now are, toward the north, the south, the east, and the sea, because I will give you and your seed forever all the land that you see.” The question arises how the promise of land made to Abraham and his seed is to be understood as extending as far as he could see while looking around toward the four quarters of the world. For how much land can the physical power of sight reach when looking upon the earth?

There is no difficulty if we observe that this was not the only thing promised. The text does not say, “I will give you as much land as you see,” but, “I will give you the land that you see.” Since land farther away was also being given in every direction, what was especially being given was the land that he saw.

Next, we should consider what follows. So that Abraham himself would not think that only the land he could see or survey was being promised, God says, “Rise and walk through the land in its length and breadth, because I will give it to you.” By walking through it, he would reach land that he could not see while standing in one place.

This signifies the land that the people of Israel first received, Abraham’s offspring according to the flesh—not the more extensive offspring according to faith. So that the latter would not be left unmentioned, God said that it would become like the sand of the sea: an expression indeed according to hyperbole, but denoting such a multitude that no one could count it.

[Note: The old Corbie manuscript reads “first.”]

[Column 0556] ### XXIX. [Ibid., XIV, 13]

“And he announced it to Abraham the Transfluvial.” The Greek copies sufficiently indicate that Abraham was called “the Transfluvial.” The reason for this designation seems to be that, coming from Mesopotamia, he crossed the river Euphrates and established his dwelling in the land of Canaan; he was called “the Transfluvial” from the region from which he had come.

Hence Jesus son of Nun says to the Israelites: “What? Do you wish to serve the gods of your fathers who are beyond the river?” (Josh. 24:15).

### XXX. [Ibid., XV, 12]

Concerning the statement, “Around sunset a dread fell upon Abraham, and behold, a great fear came upon him,” this question must be examined for the sake of those who insist that disturbances cannot befall the mind of a wise person.

Is this like what Agellius—whose name appears everywhere in the manuscripts of highest quality, whereas the printed editions have Aulus Gellius—reports in the books of the *Attic Nights*? He tells of a certain philosopher who was disturbed during a great storm at sea while he was on a ship. A dissolute young man noticed this and, after the danger had passed, mocked him because the philosopher had quickly become agitated, while the young man himself had neither been afraid nor grown pale.

The philosopher replied that the young man had not been disturbed because he had nothing to fear for his utterly depraved soul—nothing worthy of fear could happen to a soul such as his (Gellius, Book 19, chapter 1; *The City of God*, Book 9, chapter 4).

To the other students who were on the ship and waiting, he produced a book of the Stoic Epictetus. In it, it was stated that the Stoics did not hold that no such disturbance could befall the mind of a wise person, as though no such thing appeared among their affections. Rather, they defined disturbance as occurring when reason yielded to such movements; when reason did not yield, they did not call it disturbance.

But we must consider how Agellius expresses this, and insert it carefully.

[Note: Am., Er., and Lov. read “and discuss it carefully.” The Rat. edition reads “and compassionately consider it.” Twelve manuscripts read “and insert it carefully.”]

### XXXI. [Ibid., XVII, 8]

“I will give to you and to your seed after you the land in which you dwell, the whole cultivated land, as an everlasting possession.”

[Note: The Septuagint and Vulgate have “the land of Canaan.” The Corbie manuscript has “the uncultivated land.”]

The question is how he could have called it everlasting when it was given to the Israelites only temporarily. Is “everlasting” used here in reference to this age, so that the Greek word αἰώνιον (*aionion*), derived from αἰών (*aion*), which means “age,” is like what could be called in Latin *saeculare*, “age-long”? Or are we compelled to understand here something according to the spiritual promise, so that it is called everlasting because something everlasting is signified by it?

Or is this rather a characteristic expression of Scripture, by which it calls something everlasting when no limit has been set for it, or when it is not done in such a way that it need not continue to be done thereafter, insofar as this pertains to the care or authority of the one who acts? Thus Horace says:

> He will serve forever who does not know how to use little.  
> (*Horace, Book 1, Letter 10*)

For he cannot serve forever whose very life, during which he serves, cannot be everlasting. I would not cite this testimony unless it concerned a mode of expression. Horace is an authority for us concerning words, not concerning realities or doctrines.

If the Scriptures are defended according to their proper expressions, which are called idioms, how much more should they be defended according to expressions they share with other languages?

### XXXII. [Ibid., XVIII, 16]

The question arises how the statement made to Abraham about his son is to be understood: “And kings of nations shall come from him.” Since this did not occur according to earthly kingdoms, should it be understood according to the Church? Or did it also occur literally on account of Esau?

### XXXIII. [Ibid., XVIII, 2]

“And seeing them, he ran to meet them from the doorway of his tent, bowed with his face toward the ground, and said, ‘Lord, if I have found favor before you, do not pass by your servant.’”

Since the men who appeared to him were three, how does he address the Lord in the singular, saying, “Lord, if I have found favor before you”? Did he understand one of them to be the Lord and the others to be angels? Or, rather, sensing the Lord in the angels, did he choose to speak to the Lord rather than to the angels?

For afterward, when one of the three remained with Abraham and two were sent to Sodom, Lot likewise speaks to them as to the Lord.

### XXXIV. [Ibid., XVIII, 4]

“Let water be brought, and wash your feet; rest beneath the tree, and I will bring bread, and eat.”

If Abraham understood them to be angels, the question arises how he could invite them to such human hospitality, since refreshment is necessary for mortal flesh, not for the immortality of angels.

[Note: The better manuscripts read “which is necessary for the refreshment of mortal flesh.”]

### XXXV. [Ibid., XVIII, 11]

“Abraham and Sarah were advanced in days; and Sarah’s womanly functions had ceased.”

The age of the *seniores* is less advanced than that of the *senes*, although the *seniores* are also called *senes*. Therefore, if what some physicians assert is true—that an older man cannot beget children with an older woman, even if she still menstruates—we may understand Abraham’s astonishment at the promise of a son (Gen. 17:17), as well as the Apostle’s description of the miracle, where he says that Abraham’s body was “as good as dead” (Rom. 4:19).

The expression “as good as dead” should not be understood as though Abraham had no power at all to beget a child if the woman had been of youthful age. Rather, his body was “as good as dead” in the sense that he could not beget a child even with a woman of advanced age. This is why he was able to beget children through Keturah: he found her still of youthful age.

For physicians teach that a man whose body has declined to the point that he cannot beget a child with a woman of advanced age, even though she still menstruates, can beget one with a young woman. Likewise, a woman who is already advanced in age, even if she still menstruates and therefore cannot give birth to a child by an older man, can give birth to one by a young man.

The miracle therefore occurred because, according to what we have said, Abraham’s body was as good as dead while the woman too was advanced in age, so that her womanly functions had ceased. If someone presses the Apostle’s words because he said “as good as dead,” then Abraham would have to be understood as no longer having a soul, but as having been a corpse—an utterly absurd falsehood.

This, then, is how the question is resolved. Otherwise, it is rightly puzzling how Abraham, who was still nearly middle-aged by the standards of the lifespan of people in those days and afterward fathered children through Keturah, could be described by the Apostle as having a body “as good as dead,” and how his begetting a child could be proclaimed as a miracle.

[Note: The ancient manuscripts consistently read *juvenalis*.]

[Column 0558] ### XXXVI. [Ibid., XVIII, 13]

“And the Lord said to Abraham, ‘Why did Sarah laugh within herself, saying, “Shall I indeed give birth?” I, who have grown old?’”

The question arises why the Lord reproves her when Abraham also laughed. The reason is that his laughter expressed wonder and joy, whereas Sarah’s expressed doubt. This could be judged by the one who knows the human heart.

[Note: The manuscripts have this wording in agreement with the Greek Septuagint. The printed editions read, “Shall I indeed give birth, even I?”]

### XXXVII. [Ibid., XVIII, 15]

“Sarah denied it, saying, ‘I did not laugh,’ for she was afraid.”

How did they understand that it was God who was speaking, when Sarah even dared to deny that she had laughed, as though he could be unaware of it? Perhaps Sarah thought they were human beings, while Abraham understood that they were God.

Yet Abraham himself, by offering the services of hospitality mentioned above—which could not be necessary except for weak flesh—seems initially to have thought that they were human beings. Perhaps, however, he understood that God was speaking through them because certain signs of divine majesty were present and manifested in them, just as Scripture often testifies that God appeared through human beings.

But the question arises again: if this was the case, how did they later learn that they were angels? Perhaps they learned it when, in their sight, the angels went up into heaven.

[Note: The printed editions read “God.” The manuscripts read “of God.”]

### XXXVIII. [Ibid., XVIII, 19]

“For I know that he will direct his children and his household after him, and they will keep the ways of the Lord and practice justice and judgment, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham all that he has spoken to him.”

Here the Lord promises Abraham not only rewards but also the obedience of his sons in righteousness, so that the promised rewards may likewise be fulfilled with respect to them.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek Septuagint. The printed editions read, “so that they may keep the ways of the Lord and practice justice and judgment.”]

### XXXIX. [Ibid., XVIII, 21]

“Therefore, descending, I will see whether they are brought to completion according to the outcry that has come to me; and if not, I will know.”

If we understand these words not as those of someone uncertain which of two outcomes will occur, but as the words of one who is angry and threatening, there is no difficulty. In Scripture, God speaks to human beings in a human manner, and those who understand know how to interpret his anger without attributing disturbance to him.

We commonly speak threateningly in this way as well: “Let us see whether I do not do this to you,” or “Let us see whether I do not do this to him,” or “whether I will not be able to do this to you”; or, “I will know,” meaning, “I will test this very matter, to see whether I am unable to do it.” When such words are spoken as a threat, not because of ignorance, they reveal an angry disposition; yet disturbance does not befall God.

This manner of human speech is customary and suited to human weakness, to which God accommodates his manner of speaking.

[Note: The manuscripts read *congruit*, “is suited,” rather than *coaptat*, “accommodates.”]

### XL. [Ibid., XVIII, 32]

It is commonly asked whether God’s statement concerning Sodom—that he would not destroy the place if ten righteous people were found there—was a special judgment concerning that city, or whether it is to be understood generally of all places: that God spares any place in which even ten righteous people are found.

In this question, we are not compelled to understand it as applying to every place. Nevertheless, it could also have been said of Sodom in this sense, because God knew that not even ten righteous people were there. The answer given to Abraham therefore signified that not even that number could be found there, in order to heighten the demonstration of their wickedness.

God was not obliged to spare such criminal people merely to avoid destroying the righteous with them. Once the righteous had been rescued from their midst, he could impose on the wicked the punishment they deserved. But, as I have said, in order to display the wickedness of that multitude, he said, “If I find ten there, I will spare the whole city,” as though he were saying: “Certainly I can neither destroy the righteous together with the wicked nor, for that reason, spare the wicked. Once the righteous have been rescued and separated from them, I can impose on the wicked the punishment they deserve.
