Nevertheless, if ten are found there, I will spare it”—that is, because not even that many could be found there.

Something similar occurs in Jeremiah, where he says: “Go around the streets of Jerusalem, look, and search its squares, and see whether you will find a person practicing justice and seeking faith, and I will be merciful toward their sins” (Jer. 5:1). That is: “Find even one, and I will spare the rest”—to heighten and demonstrate that not even one could be found there.

### XLI. [Ibid., XIX, 1]

Lot met the angels and bowed with his face toward the ground, which suggests that he understood them to be angels. Yet when he invites them to refreshment—something necessary for mortal beings—he seems to have thought that they were human beings. The question is therefore resolved in the same way as it was in the case of the three who came to Abraham: through certain signs it became apparent that they had been sent by God, although they were believed to be human beings.

The Epistle to the Hebrews also says this when speaking of the virtue of hospitality: “Through it some, without knowing it, received angels as guests” (Heb. 13:2).

### XLII. [Ibid., XIX, 8]

Lot said to the Sodomites: “I have two daughters who have not yet known men. I will bring them out to you; use them as you please. Only do not do anything wrong to these men.”

He wished to prostitute his daughters as a compensatory offering, so that the Sodomites would do nothing of the same kind to his guests. It is therefore rightly asked whether a compensation of crimes or of any sins should be admitted—whether we may do something evil so that another person may not do something worse—or whether Lot’s statement should rather be attributed to his disturbance and not to deliberate judgment.

Such compensation is certainly admitted only with the greatest danger. If, however, the statement is attributed to human agitation and to a mind thrown into confusion by so great an evil, it should in no way be imitated.

### XLIII. [Ibid., XIX, 11]

“They struck the men who were at the doorway of the house with blindness.”

The Greek has ἀορασία (*aorasia*), which more nearly means, if one could put it so, “non-seeing”—a condition that prevents someone from seeing, not everything, but what is unnecessary.

For it is rightly puzzling how they could have become incapable of finding the doorway if they had been struck with a blindness that made them see absolutely nothing. In that case, overcome by their misfortune, they would no longer have searched for the doorway.

Those who were seeking Elisha were struck by this same ἀορασία (*aorasia*) (2 Kings 6:18). The same condition affected those who walked with the Lord after his resurrection and did not recognize him on the road (Luke 24:16), although this word is not used there and the reality itself is understood.

### XLIV. [Ibid., XIX, 18–19]

Lot said to them: “I beg you, Lord, because your servant has found mercy before you, and you have magnified your righteousness by what you are doing for me, so that my life may live. But I cannot be saved on the mountain, lest perhaps the evils overtake me and I die.”

In the disturbance of fear, he did not trust the Lord himself, whom he recognized in the angels. In the same disturbance he had also made the statement about prostituting his daughters. We should therefore understand that what he said concerning the shameful treatment of his daughters is not to be regarded as authoritative. Nor should it be regarded as authoritative that God is not to be trusted.

[Column 0560] ### XLV. [Ibid., XIX, 29]

“And God remembered Abraham, and rescued Lot from the midst of the overthrow.”

Scripture commends Lot as having been rescued especially through Abraham’s merits, so that we may understand Lot to have been called righteous in a certain sense—particularly because he worshiped the one true God and, by comparison with the crimes of the Sodomites among whom he lived, could not be bent toward a similar way of life.

### XLVI. [Ibid., XIX, 30]

“Lot went up from Zoar and settled in the mountain.”

It is difficult to believe that this was not the very mountain to which he went up of his own accord, although the Lord had urged him to ascend it and he had refused. Either there is no other mountain, or it is not apparent.

### XLVII. [Ibid., XIX, 30]

“For he was afraid to dwell in Zoar.”

The Lord had accommodated himself to Lot’s weakness and fear by granting him the city that Lot himself had chosen, and had promised him safety there, saying that he would spare the city on his account. Yet Lot was afraid even to remain there. Thus his faith was not of great strength.

### XLVIII. [Ibid., XX, 2]

“Abraham said of Sarah his wife, ‘She is my sister.’ For he was afraid to say, ‘She is my wife,’ lest perhaps the men of the city should kill him because of her.”

The question commonly arises how, at that age, Abraham could still fear for his life on account of Sarah’s beauty. But the greater wonder should be the power of her appearance, which could still inspire love, rather than the difficulty of the question.

### XLIX. [Ibid., XX, 6]

God said to Abimelech concerning Sarah: “I spared you so that you would not sin against me,” when he warned him that she was Abraham’s wife, although he had thought her to be Abraham’s sister.

It should be observed and noted that people sin against God when they commit acts that they think human beings should regard lightly, as though they were merely sins of the flesh.

God also said to him, “Behold, you shall die.” This too should be noted: God speaks as though predicting without doubt what will happen, even though he says it as a warning, so that the person may guard himself by refraining from sin.

### L. [Ibid., XXI, 8]

It is rightly asked why Abraham held a feast neither on the day his son was born nor on the day he was circumcised, but on the day he was weaned.

Unless this is referred to some spiritual significance, there is no resolution to the question. The great spiritual joy should occur when a person has reached spiritual maturity—when he has become a new spiritual human being, no longer like those of whom the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able; indeed, you are not yet able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:2).

### LI. [Book XXI, 10]

When Sarah says, “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac,” it is asked why Abraham was distressed, since this was a prophecy which he himself ought certainly to have understood better than Sarah. We must understand either that Sarah said this by revelation, because it had first been revealed to her, while Abraham—whom the Lord afterward instructed concerning it—was moved by paternal affection for his son; or that both of them had previously been unaware of what it signified, and that it was prophetically spoken through Sarah, although she had been stirred by a woman’s feelings on account of the slave woman’s arrogance.

### LII. [Book XXI, 13]

It should be noted that Ishmael too was called by God Abraham’s offspring, because the Apostle teaches that the statement “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” is to be understood in this way: “the children of the flesh” are not counted as the offspring, but “the children of the promise” (Rom. 9:7–8). Properly speaking, therefore, this applies to Isaac, who was not a child of the flesh but a child of the promise, where the promise concerns all the nations.

### LIII. [Book XXI, 14]

“Abraham rose early, took bread and a skin of water, gave them to Hagar, and placed them on her shoulders, along with the boy, and sent her away.” It is commonly asked how he could have placed on her shoulders a boy so large. Ishmael had been circumcised at thirteen, before Isaac was born, when Abraham was ninety-nine; and Ishmael was playing with Isaac when Sarah was provoked—plainly with a fairly grown child, who had already been weaned. Thus Ishmael must have been more than sixteen when he was expelled from his father’s house with his mother.

But even if we understand the statement that he played with the little child as having been given by recapitulation, before Isaac was weaned, it is still exceedingly absurd to believe that a boy more than thirteen years old was placed upon his mother’s shoulders together with the skin and the bread.

How easily, however, the difficulty is resolved if we do not supply “he placed [them]” but “he gave [them].” Abraham gave his son’s mother, as it is written, the bread and the skin, and she placed them on her own shoulders. When “and the boy” is added, we supply “he gave,” since he had given the bread and the skin—not “he placed [the boy] on her shoulders.”

### LIV. [Book XXI, 15–18]

“The water in the skin was exhausted, and she cast the boy under one of the fir trees, and went away and sat opposite him, at a distance as far as a bowshot; for she said, ‘I shall not see the death of my son.’ And she sat opposite him. The boy cried aloud and wept; and God heard the voice of the boy from the place where he was. And the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, ‘What is the matter, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of your son from the place where he is. Rise, take the boy, and hold him by the hand, for I shall make him into a great nation.’”

It is commonly asked how, when the boy was more than fifteen years old, his mother could have cast him under a tree and gone away as far as a bowshot so that she would not see him die. The wording seems to suggest that she cast down someone whom she had been carrying, especially since it follows that “the boy wept.”

We must understand that he was not cast down by the woman who was carrying him, but that he was cast down, as people say, in spirit, as one who was about to die. For the person who said, “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” (Ps. 30:23), was not being carried. In ordinary speech, moreover, someone is said to be “cast away” from another when he is separated from one with whom he had been, so that he may neither be seen by that person nor remain with him.

We must understand that Scripture has omitted the fact that the mother went away from her son in such a way that the boy did not know where she had gone, and that she hid among the wooded growth so as not to see her son failing from thirst. At that age, what is surprising if, after not seeing his mother for some time and supposing her lost, he wept in the place where he had been left alone?

Thus, when it is later said, “Take the boy,” this was not said so that she might lift him from the ground as though he were lying there, but so that she might join him and henceforth hold him by the hand as her companion, as he was. People of every age commonly do this when walking together.

### LV. [Book XXI, 22]

“It came to pass at that time, and Abimelech said,” and so forth. It may be asked when Abraham made his covenant with this Abimelech, and how it accords with the truth that the well which he dug was called “the Well of the Oath.” Hagar, after being expelled from Abraham’s household with her son, was wandering near the well, as the text says, of the oath—a well which is said to have been made by Abraham much later. For Abimelech and Abraham swore there, and this had certainly not yet happened when Hagar and her son were expelled from Abraham’s household.

How, then, was she wandering near the Well of the Oath? Should we understand that it had already been made, and that what Abraham did with Abimelech was later recalled by recapitulation?

Unless perhaps the writer, who composed the book much later, called the region in which the mother wandered with her son by the name of the well, as though he were saying, “She was wandering in that region where the Well of the Oath was made.” Although the well was made later, it was made long before the writer’s time; and when the book was written the well was called by that name, retaining the ancient name Abraham had given it.

But if this is the same well which Hagar saw with open eyes, nothing remains except to resolve the difficulty by recapitulation. Nor should it be troubling that Hagar did not know of the well Abraham had dug, if it had been dug before she was expelled. It could very easily have been that, for the sake of his livestock, Abraham dug a well far from the house in which he lived with his household, and that she did not know of it.

### LVI. [Book XXI, 33]

It may be asked how Abraham had planted a grove at the Well of the Oath if, in that land, as Stephen says, he had received no inheritance, “not even room for a foot” (Acts 7:5).

The inheritance must be understood as that which God was to give by his gift, not what was purchased for a price. The area around the well is understood to have belonged to that purchase agreement in which the seven ewe-lambs had been given, when Abimelech and Abraham also swore an oath to one another.

[Note: The Beccensis and Michaelinus manuscripts read “grove.”]

### LVII. [Book XXII, 1]

“And God tested Abraham.” It is commonly asked how this can be true, since James says in his Epistle that God tests no one (Jas. 1:13). The answer is that, in the idiom of Scripture, “he tests” is commonly said for “he proves.”

The testing of which James speaks, however, is understood only as that by which a person becomes entangled in sin. Hence the Apostle says, “Lest perhaps the tempter should have tempted you” (1 Thess. 3:5).

Elsewhere too it is written, “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13:3). Here also the expression “to know” is used in this idiom, as though it said, “to make you know,” since the strength of a person’s love is hidden from him unless, through a divine trial, it is also made known to him.

### LVIII. [Book XXII, 12]

The angel’s voice from heaven to Abraham said, “Do not lay your hand on the boy, nor do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God.” This question too is resolved by a similar idiom. “Now I know that you fear God” means, “Now I have made you know.”

The same kind of expression appears clearly in what follows, where it is said, “And Abraham called the name of that place, ‘The Lord saw,’” so that they say today, “On the mountain the Lord appeared.” “He saw” is used for “he appeared,” that is, “he saw” for “he caused himself to be seen,” signifying through the agent the thing effected, as with “inert cold,” which makes people inert.

### LIX. [Book XXII, 12]

“And you did not spare your beloved son for my sake.” Did Abraham not spare his son for the angel’s sake and not for God’s?

Either, therefore, the Lord Christ is signified by the name “angel”—and he is certainly God, and is expressly called by the prophet “the Angel of Great Counsel” (Isa. 9:6, according to the Septuagint)—or God was in the angel, and the angel spoke in the person of God, as often happens also in the Prophets.

This seems even clearer in what follows, where we read, “And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying, ‘By myself I have sworn, says the Lord.’” It is not easy to find the Lord Christ calling the Father “Lord” as though he were his own Lord, especially at that time, before he assumed flesh. Insofar as he took the form of a servant, however, this does not seem inappropriate. For according to the prophecy of this future event it is said in the Psalm, “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son’” (Ps. 2:7).

Nor do we easily find in the Gospel itself that Christ called God the Father “Lord” as though he were his Lord, although we do find him calling him God in the passage where he says, “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17).

But what is written, “The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. 109:1), refers to the one who was speaking. That is, “The Lord said to my Lord”—the Father to the Son. Likewise, “The Lord rained from the Lord,” as the one who wrote it said (Gen. 19:24), is to be understood as “our Lord rained from our Lord,” the Son from the Father.

### LX. [Book XXII, 21]

Among those whom they announced to Abraham as sons born to Milcah, Chemuel is also named “the father of the Syrians.” Those who brought the announcement could not have announced him as the father of the Syrians, for the nation of the Syrians was propagated from his lineage much later.

Rather, this was said from the perspective of the writer, who narrated these events in writing after all that time had passed, just as we said above concerning the Well of the Oath (above, question 55).

### LXI. [Book XXIII, 7]

“Abraham rose and worshiped the people of the land.” It is asked how it can be written, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. 6:13; 10:20), when Abraham honored a certain people of the nations so greatly that he even worshiped them.

We must observe that the same command does not say, “You shall worship the Lord your God alone,” as it says, “You shall serve him alone”—which in Greek is λατρεύσεις (*latreuseis*). Such service is owed to God alone. Hence idolaters are condemned: that is, those who offer idols the kind of service that is owed to God.

Nor should it be troubling that elsewhere, in a certain passage of Scripture, an angel forbids a person to worship him and urges him instead to worship the Lord (Rev. 19:10). The angel had appeared in such a form that he could be worshiped as God; therefore the worshiper had to be corrected.

### LXII. [Book XXIV, 3]

Abraham orders his servant to place his hand beneath Abraham’s thigh, and in this way adjures him by the Lord God of heaven and the Lord of earth. This commonly perplexes the inexperienced, who do not notice that it was a great prophecy concerning Christ: the Lord God of heaven and Lord of earth himself was to come in that flesh which was propagated from that thigh.

### LXIII. [Book XXIV, 12–14]

It must be asked how unlawful auguries differ from the request for a sign made by Abraham’s servant, when he asked God to show him that the woman who, when he requested a drink from her, would say to him, “Drink, and I will water your camels until they stop drinking,” was to be his master Isaac’s future wife.

For it is one thing to request something marvelous that, by the very miracle, may serve as a sign; it is another to observe things that happen in such a way that they are not marvelous, but are interpreted by diviners through superstitious folly.

Even the request for something marvelous by which what someone wishes to know may be signified is itself a substantial question: whether such a request should be made. This belongs to the matter concerning those who do this wrongly and are said to tempt the Lord. For when the Lord himself was tempted by the devil, he cited the testimony of Scripture: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:16; Matt. 4:7).

The devil was suggesting to him, as though he were merely a human being, that he should test by some sign how great he was—that is, how much power he had with God. It is wrong when this is done.

This is distinguished from what Gideon did when danger in battle was imminent (Judg. 6:17), for that request was consultation rather than a tempting of God.

Hence Ahaz is afraid to ask for a sign in Isaiah, lest he appear to tempt God, although the Lord urges him through the prophet to do so (Isa. 6:11–12). I believe that he thought the prophet was testing whether he remembered the commandment forbidding us to tempt God.

### LXIV. [Book XXIV, 37–38]

Abraham’s servant, recounting the instructions his master had given him, says that Abraham told him, “You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell in their land; but you shall go to the house of my father and to my tribe, and from there you shall take a wife for my son.” If the rest is read as Abraham instructed him, the same meaning is found; but the words are not all identical, nor are they necessarily expressed in precisely that form.

I thought this should be pointed out on account of foolish and uneducated people who criticize the Evangelists on this basis: that in some words they do not agree in every respect, although they do not differ at all in events or meaning.

Certainly, this book was written by one man. When Abraham gave the instructions described above, the writer could have reproduced them again in the same form if he had judged that this was relevant, since the truth of the narrative is required—unless it is the truth of the events and meanings that is required, through which the intention for whose communication the words are spoken is sufficiently evident.

[Note: The printed editions read *non exigitur* (“is not required”). The manuscripts lack the negation, which was inserted here because of the following *nisi* (“unless”); but it was inserted incorrectly, since, with the negation removed, this is a very elegant manner of expression: “if he judged it relevant, unless it is the truth of the events and meanings that is required in the narrative.”]

### LXV. [Book XXIV, 41]

The Latin manuscripts, in the servant’s account of what his master had commanded him, read: “Then you shall be innocent of my oath,” or “of my swearing.” The Greek manuscripts read, “of my curse”: for ὅρκος (*horkos*) means “an oath,” while ἀρά (*ara*) means “a curse.” Hence κατάρατος (*katáratos*) or ἐπικατάρατος (*epikatáratos*) means “cursed.”

The question therefore arises how that oath can be understood as a curse—unless it is because the person who acts against an oath is cursed.

### LXVI. [Book XXIV, 49]

“If, then, you will show mercy and justice toward my master, tell me.”

Those two qualities, which are repeatedly set forth in the other Holy Scriptures, and especially in the Psalms—mercy and justice, for “mercy” and “truth” have the same force—are beginning to appear here.

### LXVII. [Book XXIV, 51]

“Here is Rebecca before you; take her, go back, and let her be the wife of your master’s son, as the Lord has spoken.”

It is asked when the Lord spoke, unless either they knew Abraham to be a prophet and recognized as spoken by the Lord prophetically what had been spoken through him, or they called the sign that his servant had reported to them the Lord’s speech. The latter interpretation is more clearly applicable to Rebecca.

For what Abraham had said did not concern Rebecca, but some woman from his tribe or kindred. It also served the double purpose of freeing the servant from his oath if he did not succeed. Such a qualification is not made when something is prophesied, for prophecy ought to be certain.

### LXVIII. [Book XXIV, 60]

Rebecca’s brothers said to her as she departed, “Our sister, may you become thousands upon thousands, and may your offspring possess the cities of their enemies.”

They were not prophets, nor did they make so great a wish merely at random; rather, what God had promised to Abraham could not have been hidden from them.

### LXIX. [Book XXIV, 63]

It is written, “Isaac went out into the field at midday to exercise.” Those who do not know the Greek word used here think that this refers to bodily exercise. But the Greek text reads ἀδολεσχῆσαι (*adoleschēsai*). The verb ἀδολεσχεῖν (*adoleschein*) pertains to exercise of the mind and is often counted as a fault; nevertheless, in the manner of Scripture it is frequently used in a good sense.

For this word some translators have rendered “exercise,” while others have rendered it “talkativeness,” as though it meant excessive verbalizing—a sense that, in Latin usage, is scarcely or never found as a positive quality. Yet, as I have said, in Scripture it is frequently used in a good sense.

It seems to me to signify the mind’s devotion to thinking about something with the greatest diligence and with pleasure in the act of thought—unless those who understand these Greek words better perceive something else.

### LXX. [Book XXV, 1]

“Abraham, continuing, took a wife named Keturah.”

This would be a question if it were a sin, especially among ancient people who devoted themselves to producing offspring. Whatever should be suspected here, it is more appropriate to suspect anything other than incontinence in so great a man, particularly at that age.

Why he had sons by her, although he had produced Isaac from Sarah by a miracle, has been said above (Question 35). Some, however, maintain that the gift Abraham received, as though his body had come back to life for the procreation of children, remained with him for a long time, so that he could produce other children as well.

But it is much more straightforward to understand that an older man could have children by a young woman, whereas an old man could not have children by an old woman unless God had provided a miracle there—especially on account not only of Sarah’s age but also of her barrenness.

It can also be understood from this that a man of advanced age, and one who, in the language of Scripture, is “full of days,” may be called an elder, that is, a presbyter, since Abraham was called this when he died.

Consequently, every old man is also a presbyter, but not every presbyter is also an old man. For this word often designates an age that is below old age but close to it, and for this reason it too took its name from old age in the Latin language, so that a presbyter is called *senior*, “older.”

Among the Greeks, especially as Scripture speaks, πρεσβύτεροι (*presbyteroi*) and νεώτεροι (*neōteroi*) are used even when the ages of young men are being compared; we would say “older” and “younger.”

Nevertheless, what Abraham did—having sons by Keturah after Sarah’s death—should not be understood as though it happened merely according to human custom and reasoning, for the purpose of replacing a more numerous offspring. People could also understand what was done with Hagar in this way unless the Apostle warned us that those events happened prophetically, so that, in the persons of both women and their sons, the two Testaments were represented by an allegorical sign for the prediction of future things (Gal. 4:22–24).

Accordingly, something of this kind must also be sought in what Abraham did here, even if it does not readily present itself. For the moment, I will state what occurs to me: the gifts received by the sons of the concubines seem to me to signify certain gifts of God, given either in the sacraments or in various signs even to the carnal Jewish people and to heretics, as to sons of concubines. The gift of the inheritance, however—which is charity and eternal life—belongs only to Isaac, that is, to the children of the promise.

### LXXI. [Book XXV, 13]

What is meant by the statement, “These are the names of the sons of Ishmael according to the names of their generations”? It is not sufficiently clear why “according to the names of their generations” was added, since only those whom he himself begot are named, not those who were begotten by them.

Unless perhaps, because nations were propagated from them and called by their names, this was signified when it said, “according to the names of their generations.” Yet in this case those nations are rather “according to the names of these men,” not these names “according to those nations,” since the nations came into existence later.

The expression should therefore be noted, since it is later also said of them, “twelve princes according to their nations.”

### LXXII. [Book XXV, 22]

It is written concerning Rebecca that she went to inquire of the Lord when the children struggled in her womb. It is asked where she went. At that time there were no prophets, nor priests according to the order of the Lord’s tabernacle or temple.

Where, then, did she go? The question is reasonable, unless perhaps she went to the place where Abraham had established an altar. But how she heard the answer there, Scripture is entirely silent.

Was it through some priest? That is incredible, since, if there had been one, it would be strange for him not to be named, and Scripture makes no mention at all of any priests there.

Or perhaps, after they had expressed their desires in prayer, they slept in that place so that they might be instructed through a dream?

Or was Melchizedek still alive, whose excellence was so great that some have doubted whether he was a human being or an angel?

Or were there at that time other such men of God, through whom God could be consulted?

Whatever the answer may be—and even if there is some other possibility that has escaped me and therefore remains unmentioned—Scripture nevertheless cannot lie. It says that Rebecca went to inquire of the Lord and that the Lord answered her.

[Note: The Beccensis and Michaelinus manuscripts read *responsa audierit* (“how she heard the answers”). The others read *responsa dentur* (“how answers were given”).]

### LXXIII. [Book XXV, 23]

In the Lord’s answer to Rebecca—“Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be separated from your body; one people shall prevail over the other, and the elder shall serve the younger”—those who are carnal within the people of God are signified spiritually by the elder son, and those who are spiritual by the younger. For, as the Apostle says, “It is not the spiritual that is first but the animal; afterward, the spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46).

This statement is also commonly understood in such a way that Esau represents the elder people of God, namely Israel according to the flesh, while Jacob represents Jacob himself according to his spiritual descendants.

But this answer is also found to have been fulfilled in its historical sense, when the people of Israel—that is, Jacob, the younger son—prevailed over the Idumaeans, the nation descended from Esau, and made them tributary through David. This continued for a long time, until the reign of Joram, under whom the Idumaeans rebelled and cast the yoke of the Israelites from their neck, in accordance with Isaac’s own prophecy when he blessed the younger instead of the elder. For he said this to that same elder when he later blessed him also (Gen. 27:40).

[Note: The words “namely, Joram” are absent from the manuscripts.]

### LXXIV. [Book XXV, 27]

“Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in a house.” The Greek word is ἄπλαστος (*aplastos*), which the Latins translated as “simple.” Properly, however, ἄπλαστος means “not feigned.” Hence some Latin translators rendered it “without deceit,” saying, “Jacob was without deceit, dwelling in a house.”

This creates a serious question: how could one who was without deceit have obtained the blessing by deceit?

But Scripture prefaced this statement in order to signify something important. It is precisely because the one who committed the deceit was without deceit that we are compelled above all to understand spiritual realities in that passage.

What we thought about this matter we explained sufficiently in a sermon delivered to the people (Sermon 4, §§16–24).

[Note: The manuscripts followed here read “to signify something important, Scripture prefaced this.” Am., Er., and Lov. read “to signify something important that Scripture omitted.” Rat. reads “to signify something that Scripture prefaced.”]

### LXXV. [Book XXVI, 1]

It is written, “There was a famine in the land, besides the former famine that had occurred in the time of Abraham; and Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerar.” It is asked when this happened.

Did it happen after Esau sold his birthright for a meal of lentils? For the account begins to narrate this after that story. Or, as often happens, did the narrator return by recapitulation to an earlier event after, having progressed from the story of Isaac’s sons, he had reached the passage concerning the lentils?

The matter is troubling because the Abimelech who appears here seems to be the same one who had desired Sarah. The same paranymphus (bridegroom’s attendant) and commander of the army who were mentioned there are mentioned here as well. Could they have lived so long?

When Abraham became Abimelech’s friend, Isaac had not yet been born, although he had already been promised. Let us suppose that the earlier event took place one year before Isaac was born. Isaac then had sons when he was sixty years old; and they were young men when Esau sold his birthright. Let us suppose that they were about twenty years old. Isaac would therefore have been about eighty when this event involving his sons occurred.

If we suppose that Abimelech was a young man when he desired Isaac’s mother and became Abraham’s friend, he could already have been approximately a hundred years old when Isaac went to that famine-stricken land after the event involving his sons.

Therefore, no necessity compels us to think that Isaac’s journey to Gerar was narrated by recapitulation. But since Isaac is said to have remained there for a long time, to have dug wells, disputed over them, and become wealthy, it is surprising if these events were not recalled by recapitulation. They had been omitted so that the narrative might first proceed from his sons to the passage concerning the lentils.

[Note: The manuscripts read “one year before he was born.” The printed editions read “before Isaac was born.”]

### LXXVI. [Book XXVI, 12–13]

The reason the following statement about Isaac is written—“The Lord blessed him, and the man became great, and continued to advance until he became exceedingly great”—is shown by what follows: it refers to earthly prosperity.

The narrator goes on to describe the same wealth by which he became great. Abimelech was moved by this and feared that Isaac’s presence there might become hostile to him because of Isaac’s power.

Although these things signify something spiritual, nevertheless, according to the events as they occurred, the statement “The Lord blessed him” was placed first so that, with sound faith, we might understand that even temporal gifts can neither be given nor hoped for—although they are sought by weaker people—except from the one God.

Thus, whoever is faithful in what is least may also be faithful in what is great; and whoever is found faithful in unrighteous mammon may deserve to receive what is true, as the Lord says in the Gospel (Luke 16:10).

Similar statements are made concerning Abraham, namely, that such prosperity came to him as a gift from God. Accordingly, this narrative greatly strengthens sound faith in those who understand it devoutly, even if no allegorical meaning could be drawn from these matters.

[Note: Three reliable manuscripts read *excludi* (“excluded”) instead of *exsculpi* (“drawn out” or “elicited”).]

### LXXVII. [Book XXVI, 28]

“Let there be an oath between us and between you”—that is, an oath binding by curses, which would fall upon the person who swore falsely.

In light of this, we should understand what Abraham’s servant also mentioned when recounting the matter to those from whom he obtained a wife for his master Isaac.

### LXXVIII. [Book XXVI, 32]

What is meant by the statement that, when Isaac’s servants came and said, “We dug a well and found no water,” Isaac called the same well “the Oath”?

Or, although this event happened, must it certainly be directed toward some spiritual meaning, since, according to the literal sense, it makes no sense for him to have called the well “the Oath” because no water had been found there?

Some translators, however, have said that Isaac’s servants reported instead that they had found water. But even then, why was it called “the Oath,” when no oath had been sworn there?

### LXXIX. [Book XXVII, 1–17]

Since the great patriarch Isaac, before his death, asks his son to obtain the kind of game and food he loves as though it were a great favor, and promises him a blessing—and especially since his wife hastens to ensure that the younger son whom she loved receives that blessing—we certainly think that this cannot be devoid of prophetic significance. Other details in the same narrative also strongly urge us to understand or seek meanings of greater importance.

### LXXX. [Book XXVII, 33]

The Latin manuscripts read, “Isaac was struck with great fear, exceedingly.” The Greek manuscripts read, ἐξέστη δὲ Ἰσαὰκ ἔκστασιν μεγάλην σφόδρα (*exestē de Isaak ekstasin megalēn sphodra*), “Isaac entered into a very great ecstasy,” indicating such intense agitation that it was followed by a kind of alienation of mind.

This state is properly called *ecstasy*. Since it commonly occurs in revelations of great matters, we should understand that a spiritual admonition took place here, so that Isaac might confirm his blessing upon the younger son, even though he ought rather to have been angry with him for deceiving his father.

Likewise, in the passage concerning Adam, when the great sacrament is prophesied—that which the Apostle says concerns Christ and the Church, “The two shall be one flesh”—it is said that an ecstasy preceded it (Gen. 2:21–24; Eph. 5:31–32).

### LXXXI. [Book XXVII, 42]

How were Esau’s words, in which he threatened to kill his brother, announced or reported to Rebecca, when Scripture says that he spoke them in his own thoughts?

The answer is that this gives us to understand that everything was revealed to them by God. Hence it belongs to a great mystery that Isaac wished his younger son to be blessed in place of the elder.

### LXXXII. [Book XXVIII, 2]

The Latin manuscripts read that Isaac said to his son, “Go to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father, and take a wife for yourself from there.” The Greek manuscripts do not read “go,” but “flee”—that is, ἀπόδραθι (*apodrathi*).

From this it is understood that Isaac too knew what his son Esau had said in his thoughts concerning his brother.

### LXXXIII. [Book XXVIII, 16–17]

“Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, ‘Indeed, the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.’ And he was afraid and said, ‘How fearful this place is! This is nothing other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.’”

These words pertain to prophecy, because the tabernacle that the Lord established among human beings in his first people was destined to be there.

We should understand “the gate of heaven” as meaning that from there access is granted to believers so that they may obtain the kingdom of heaven.

[Note: The printed editions read, “This is nothing other than the house of God.” The manuscripts read *hoc*, “this,” corresponding to the Greek τοῦτο.]

### LXXXIV. [Book XXVIII, 18]

Jacob set up the stone that he had placed beneath his head and established it as a pillar, pouring oil over it. He did not do anything resembling idolatry. Neither then nor later did he regularly worship the stone or sacrifice to it.

Rather, it was a sign established in an especially clear prophecy, one that pertains to anointing, from which the name “Christ” derives from *chrism*.

### LXXXV. [Book XXVIII, 19]

“Jacob called the name of that place ‘House of God,’ and Ulammaus had previously been the name of the city.”

If we understand that he slept near the city, there is no difficulty. But if he slept in the city, it seems surprising that he could have established the pillar.

Moreover, the vow he made—that, if he prospered in going out and returning, he would promise tithes to the future house of God in that place—is a prophecy concerning the house of God, where, on his return, he himself also offered sacrifice to God.

He did not call that stone God, but called the place “the house of God,” that is, because the house of God was destined to be there.

### LXXXVI. [Book XXIX, 10]

Rachel came with her father’s sheep, and Scripture says that, when Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, he approached and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well.

Rather than raising any question, we should note that Scripture has omitted something we ought to understand. The men with whom Jacob had first been speaking were asked who the woman was who was coming with the sheep, and they themselves said that she was Laban’s daughter, whom Jacob did not know. Scripture has omitted their question and answer but intended them to be understood.

### LXXXVII. [Book XXIX, 11–12]

It is written, “Jacob kissed Rachel, raised his voice, and wept. And he told her that he was her brother and that he was Rebecca’s son.”

It was customary, especially in the simplicity of ancient times, for relatives to kiss one another, and this is still done in many places today. But it may be asked how she accepted a kiss from a stranger if Jacob only afterward revealed their relationship.

We must therefore understand either that Jacob, who had already learned who she was, confidently rushed to kiss her, or that Scripture later narrated by recapitulation what had happened first—namely, that Jacob had told her who he was.

The same kind of recapitulation appears in the later account of paradise, where it is said how God established it, although it had already been stated that God planted the paradise and placed there the man whom he had formed. Many other passages are similarly understood as having been narrated by recapitulation.

### LXXXVIII. [Book XXIX, 20]

It is written, “Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him like a few days because he loved her.” It must be asked how this was said, since even a short period of time usually seems long to lovers.

It was said, therefore, with reference to the labor of servitude, which love made easy and light.

### LXXXIX. [Book XXIX, 27–31]

If the narrative is not carefully considered, it will be thought that, after Jacob took Leah as his wife, he then served another seven years for Rachel and only afterward took her as his wife.

But this is not what happened. Laban said to him, “Complete this week, and I will give you this one also for the work that you will perform for me for another seven years.”

When he says, “Complete this week,” he refers to the celebration of the wedding, which was customarily held for seven days. Thus he said, “Complete the seven days of the wedding belonging to the woman whom you have taken, and I will give you this one also in return for the work that you will perform for me for another seven years.”

Then it follows: “Jacob did so and completed her week”—that is, Leah’s seven wedding days—“and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife. Laban also gave his daughter Rachel his slave woman Bilhah as her slave woman, and he went in to Rachel. He loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served him another seven years.”

It is entirely clear that Jacob served another seven years for Rachel after he had taken her as his wife. It would have been excessively harsh and wholly unjust for Laban, after deceiving him, to make him wait another seven years and only then give him the woman whom he ought to have given him first.

That weddings were customarily celebrated for seven days is also shown by the Book of Judges in the account of Samson, when he held a drinking feast for seven days (Judg. 14:10). Scripture adds that this was the custom of young men; he did this on account of his wedding.

[Note: Nine manuscripts consistently read *septima*; Am. and Rat. do likewise.]

[Note: The printed editions read *Balam*. The manuscripts spell it *Ballam* with a double *l*, as in the Greek.]

[Note: Lov. reads *convivium* (“banquet”), while Rat., Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *potum* (“drinking feast”). This word is used from the Book of Judges, chapter 14, verse 10, where the Septuagint has ἐποίησε πότον (*epoiēse poton*).]

## XC. [On Genesis 30:3, 9]

It is not easy to determine which women Scripture calls concubines and which it calls wives, since Hagar too is called a wife, although afterward she is called a concubine, as is Keturah (Gen. 16:3; 25:1, 6), and likewise the maidservants whom Rachel and Leah gave to their husband (ibid. 30:3, 4, 9). Unless perhaps, according to the manner of speaking found in Scripture, every concubine is a wife, but not every wife is called a concubine: that is, Sarah, Rebekah, Leah, and Rachel cannot be called concubines, whereas Hagar, Keturah, Bilhah, and Zilpah may be called both wives and concubines.

## XCI. [On Genesis 30:11]

Where the Latin has, concerning the son born to Leah by Zilpah, that she said, “I have become Blessed” or “Happy,” the Greek has εὐτύχη (*eutychē*), which more specifically signifies “good fortune.” This seems to provide an opportunity for those who do not understand the matter properly to suppose that these people worshiped Fortune, or that the authority of the divine Scriptures admitted this word into its usage. But either “fortune” should be understood as referring to things that seem to happen by chance—not because there is some divinity called Fortune, since even those things that seem accidental are nevertheless given by God through hidden causes. Hence words that no one can remove from ordinary speech are also ready to hand: *forte* (“perhaps”), *fortasse* (“possibly”), *forsitan* (“perhaps”), and *fortuito* (“by chance”). Thus the Greek expression may also seem to have the same resonance in the word τάχα (*tacha*), as if derived from τύχη (*tyche*). Or certainly Leah spoke in this way because she still retained the customary manner of speech of the Gentiles. For Jacob did not say this, so that authority might thereby be thought to have been given to the word.

## XCII. [On Genesis 30:30]

When Jacob says, “The Lord blessed you at my foot,” the meaning of Scripture must be carefully observed and noted, lest, when someone speaks in this way, he seem almost to be practicing augury. There is a great difference in what he added: “The Lord blessed you at my foot.” He wanted this to be understood as referring to my entrance, giving thanks to God from that point onward.

## XCIII. [On Genesis 30:37, 42]

In Jacob’s action, when he peeled the rods by stripping away the green so that the white appeared in varied patterns, and thus caused the offspring of the flocks to be marked differently when their mothers drank at the watering troughs and saw the rods, many things are said to occur similarly in the offspring of animals. It is also reported to have happened to a woman, and is recorded in the books of the very ancient and highly skilled physician Hippocrates. A woman was about to be punished on suspicion of adultery because she had given birth to a very beautiful child unlike both parents and the family, unless the physician mentioned had resolved the question by advising them to investigate whether perhaps some such picture was present in the bedroom. When one was found, the woman was freed from suspicion.

But as for the action performed by Jacob, it is not at all apparent what usefulness the joining of rods from three different kinds of trees contributed to the multiplication of various types of livestock. Nor does it matter for this purpose whether the rods were varied from wood of one kind or whether several kinds of wood were used, since only the variety of the wood was relevant. Accordingly, this matter compels us to seek a prophecy and some figurative meaning in the action, which Jacob undoubtedly performed as a prophet; and therefore he must not be accused of fraud. For it should not be believed that he did anything of this sort except through spiritual revelation.

As for what concerned justice, other interpreters explain it more clearly: he did not place the rods during the second conception of the sheep. This is expressed more obscurely because the Septuagint stated it more briefly: “When they had given birth, he did not place them.” This is understood to mean “when they had given birth the first time,” so that he is understood no longer to have placed them when they were about to give birth a second time, lest he take away all the offspring—an unjust arrangement.

[Note: *Retractations* II, chapter 55, no. 1.]

## XCIV. [On Genesis 31:30]

When Laban says, “Why have you stolen my gods?” this perhaps relates to the fact that he had also said that he practiced divination and that his daughter had spoken of good fortune. It should also be noted that this is the first time in the book that we encounter the gods of the nations. In the earlier passages of Scripture, they named God.

## XCV. [On Genesis 31:41, 7]

What does Jacob mean when he says to his father-in-law, “You have cheated me of my wages ten lambs”? Scripture does not relate when or how this happened. Nevertheless, what he recalls certainly happened, for he said the same thing to his wives when he summoned them to the field. Complaining about their father, he said, among other things, “He changed my wages ten lambs.”

The meaning, then, is that at each period of the sheep’s giving birth, when Laban saw that offspring had been born of the kind that had been agreed to belong to Jacob, he fraudulently changed the agreement and decreed that in the next birth other colors of livestock should constitute Jacob’s wages. At that point Jacob did not place the various rods, and the offspring were not varied but of one color, which Jacob took away according to the new agreement. When Laban saw this, he again fraudulently changed the agreement so that the varied offspring would belong to Jacob; then, when the varied rods had been placed, varied offspring were born.

Therefore, when Jacob said to his wives, “He changed my wages ten lambs,” and later said to Laban himself, “You have cheated me of my wages ten lambs,” he did not speak as though the fraud itself had benefited his father-in-law. Rather, he said that God had been on his side against him. He used “ten lambs,” whether males or females, for ten periods during which the sheep he tended gave birth over the six years. They gave birth twice a year. It happened that in the first year, when they made their agreement and he undertook their care in return for this wage, they gave birth only once at the end of the year, since when he began they had already given birth once. Likewise, in the sixth and final year, after they had given birth once, the necessity of his departure arose, and he left before they gave birth again. Thus the first and final years together contained two births of the sheep under his care, one in each year, while the four middle years contained two births each, making ten in all.

Nor is it surprising that he called these ten periods “lambs,” since lambs were born during those periods. It is as if someone were to say, “Through so many grape harvests,” or “through so many harvests,” meaning a number of years. Hence a certain poet says, “After several ears of grain” (Virgil, *Eclogue* 1.70), meaning by “ears” harvests and by “harvests” years. The fertility of the livestock in that region, like that of Italy, is said to be so great that they give birth twice a year.

[Note: *Retractations* II, chapter 55, no. 1.]

## XCVI. [On Genesis 31:45]

“Jacob took a stone and set it up as a monument.” We must carefully observe how they set up such monuments as testimony in each matter—not in order to worship them as gods, but so that they might signify something to them.

## XCVII. [On Genesis 31:47, 48]

Laban and Jacob called the heap of stones that they had established between them by somewhat different names: Laban called it “Heap of Testimony,” while Jacob called it “Heap of the Witness.” Those who know both the Syrian and Hebrew languages report that this occurred because of the particular character of each language. It often happens that something expressed by one word in one language cannot be expressed by a single word in another, and that it is named through a similarity of meaning.

For afterward it is said, “For this reason its name was called ‘The Heap Testifies.’” This expression was placed in the middle because it suited both parties: the one who had said “Heap of Testimony” and the one who had said “Heap of the Witness.”

## XCVIII. [On Genesis 31:48, 49]

What does Laban mean when, speaking to Jacob, he says, “This heap testifies, and this monument testifies. For this reason its name is called ‘The Heap Testifies’”? And what of the vision he mentioned: “May God look between me and you”? Unless perhaps the order is, “And may God, who spoke in the vision, look between me and you,” for God had told him in a vision not to harm Jacob.

## XCIX. [On Genesis 31:50]

What does Laban mean in what follows when he says, “See, no one is with us”? Unless perhaps he means “no outsider,” or because, in view of God’s testimony, they ought to conduct themselves as though no one were with them whom they could add as a witness to God’s testimony.

## C. [On Genesis 31:53, 42]

“Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.” This certainly means the fear with which he feared God—a fear that he had also commended earlier when he said, “The God of my father Abraham and the Fear of my father Isaac.”

## CI. [On Genesis 32:2]

There is no doubt that the “camp of God” which Jacob saw on the journey was a multitude of angels, since in Scripture it is called the host of heaven.

## CII. [On Genesis 32:6–12]

When Jacob was informed that his brother was coming to meet him with four hundred men, he was disturbed and confused in mind, because he was greatly afraid. As seemed appropriate to a frightened man, he divided his people and arranged them into two camps.

It may be asked how he retained faith in God’s promises, since he said, “If my brother Esau comes upon the first camp and destroys it, the second will be left for safety.” But it could also happen that Esau overthrew his camp and that God nevertheless came to his aid after that affliction, delivered him, and fulfilled what he had promised. We are also instructed by this example that, although we trust in God, we should nevertheless do what human beings ought to do for the protection of their safety, lest by neglecting such measures we appear to tempt God.

Finally, we must consider what Jacob himself says afterward:

“O God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, O Lord, who said to me, ‘Return to the land of your birth, and I will do you good,’ I am not worthy of all the righteousness and all the truth that you have shown your servant. For with this staff of mine I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps. Deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau, because I fear him, lest when he comes he strike me and the mothers with their children. Yet you said, ‘I will do you good, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted because of its multitude.’”

These words sufficiently display both human weakness and the faith of devotion.

## CIII. [On Genesis 32:20]

The Latin manuscripts have, concerning Jacob, “For he said, ‘I will appease his face with the gifts going before him.’” The writer of the book, who narrates the matter by saying, “For he said, ‘I will appease his face,’” is understood to have reported Jacob’s words only up to this point; what follows is supplied in the narrator’s own words: “with the gifts going before him,” as though he were saying, “With the gifts that went before Jacob, I will appease my brother’s face.”

The order of Jacob’s words, therefore, is: “I will appease his face, and afterward I will see his face; perhaps he will receive my face.” The narrator’s words, “with the gifts going before him,” have been inserted between them.

## CIV. [On Genesis 32:26]

That Jacob desired to be blessed by the angel whom he overcame by wrestling is a great prophecy concerning Christ. The event itself admonishes us that it contains a mystical meaning, because every human being wishes to be blessed by one who is greater. How, then, did this man wish to be blessed by one whom he had overcome in wrestling?

Jacob prevailed over Christ—or rather appeared to prevail—through those Israelites by whom Christ was crucified. Yet he was blessed by Christ through those Israelites who believed in Christ, among whom was the one who said, “For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. 11:1).

Thus one and the same Jacob is both lame and blessed: lame in the breadth of his thigh, as though in the multitude of his descendants, concerning whom it was said, “They have gone astray from their paths” (Ps. 17:46); but blessed in those concerning whom it was said, “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11:5).

[Note: The manuscripts and the editions of Rat., Am., and Er. read “of the stock” (*ex genere*) instead of “of the seed” (*ex semine*).]

## CV. [On Genesis 33:10]

What does Jacob mean when he says to his brother, “For this reason I have seen your face as though someone were seeing the face of God”? Did words arising from a fearful and disturbed mind burst forth into such flattery? Or can they be understood as spoken without sin according to some interpretation?

Perhaps, since the gods of the nations are also called gods, though they are demons, these words should not be used to prejudice the man of God. He did not say, “As though I were seeing the face of God,” but, “As though someone were seeing it.” It is uncertain whom this “someone” could signify. The words may therefore have been carefully framed so that Esau himself would gratefully accept the great honor shown him, while those who could understand the words in another way would not accuse the speaker of any crime of impiety.

Even if these fraternal words were spoken with a kindly intention, since Jacob’s fear had passed after his brother’s favorable reception, the expression could have been used in the same way that Moses is called the god of Pharaoh (Exod. 7:1), in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, just as there are many gods and many lords” (1 Cor. 8:5).

This is especially so because the Greek has no article. It did not say πρόσωπον τοῦ Θεοῦ (*prosōpon tou Theou*, “the face of God”), but πρόσωπον θεοῦ (*prosōpon theou*, “the face of a god”). Those who are accustomed to hearing and understanding Greek readily perceive the distinction conveyed by the presence or absence of the article.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “who can also understand it properly” (*etiam rite intelligere*).]

## CVI. [On Genesis 33:14]

The question is whether Jacob falsely promised his brother that, following the footsteps of his people and delaying his journey because of them, he would come to him at Seir. For, as Scripture afterward narrates, he did not do this, but proceeded by the route that led toward his own.

Or perhaps he made the promise sincerely but later chose another course after reconsidering the matter?

[Note: In Lov., “because of whom he would thus delay” (*propter quos sic moraretur*).]

## CVII. [On Genesis 34:2, 3]

How does Scripture say that Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, saw Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, “and took her, and slept with her, and humbled her”; and then that he “set his heart on Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, and loved the maiden, and spoke according to the mind of the maiden”? How is she called a maiden if he had already slept with her and humbled her?

Unless perhaps “maiden” is an age designation according to Hebrew usage. Or is it rather a case of recapitulation, in which what happened first is mentioned afterward? For he could first have set his heart on her, loved the maiden, and spoken according to the maiden’s mind, and then slept with her and humbled her.

[Note: Eight manuscripts read “Hamor the Horrite, prince of the land.”]

[Note: Am., Er., and Lov. read *ipsius* (“of the maiden herself”); Rat. and the better manuscripts read *ipsi* (“to the maiden”), in accordance with the Septuagint’s αὐτῇ (*autē*).]

## CVIII. [On Genesis 33:5 and 34:25]

Since, shortly before, when Jacob was speaking with his brother Esau, he indicated that his sons were infants—called παιδία (*paidia*) in Greek—it may be asked how they could have carried out such a great slaughter and plunder of the city, killing men who were still suffering from circumcision, on behalf of their sister Dinah.

We must understand that Jacob had lived there for a long time, until his daughter had become a maiden and his sons young men. For it is written:

“Jacob came to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, in the land of Canaan, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria, and encamped before the city. And he bought a portion of the field where he had pitched his tent from Hamor, the father of Shechem, for one hundred lambs. And he set up an altar there and invoked the God of Israel. Then Dinah, the daughter of Leah, whom Leah bore to Jacob, went out to learn with the daughters of the land” (Gen. 33:18–20; 34:1), and so forth.

These words clearly show that Jacob did not remain there merely in passing, as a traveler normally does, but bought a field, established a tent, and built an altar. He therefore lived there for a considerable time. When his daughter had reached the age at which she could already have companions, she wished to learn with the daughters of the citizens of the place. Thus the extremely bloody slaughter and plunder were carried out on her behalf; and, as I think, the question no longer presents any difficulty.

Jacob had a considerable multitude with him, since he had become exceedingly wealthy. His sons, however, are named in connection with this act because they were its leaders and instigators.

[Note: Five better manuscripts read, “where he had pitched his tent beside Hamor, the father of Shechem.” The Latin edition of the Septuagint likewise has this reading.]

## CIX. [On Genesis 34:30]

When Jacob, fearing wars with the neighboring peoples around the city of Salem—which his sons had conquered—says, “I am few in number, and they will gather against me and kill me,” he said that he was few in number because of the many wars that could arise, not because he had fewer men than would have been sufficient to conquer that city. He had, after all, divided his people into two camps during the journey.

## CX. [On Genesis 35:1]

God said to Jacob, “Rise and go up to the place Bethel, and live there; and make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from the face of your brother Esau.”

Why did he not say, “Make an altar there to me, who appeared to you,” but rather God says, “Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you”? Did the Son appear there, while God the Father says this? Or should it be classified under some form of expression?

## CXI. [On Genesis 35:2]

When Jacob was about to go up to Bethel, where he had been commanded to make an altar, he said to his household and to all who were with him, “Remove the foreign gods who are among you from your midst,” and so forth. It is then said, “And they gave Jacob the foreign gods that were in their hands, and the earrings that were in their ears.”

The question is why the earrings were included. If they were ornaments, they did not belong to idolatry—unless we are to understand that they were amulets of the foreign gods. For Scripture testifies that Rebekah received earrings from Abraham’s servant; this would not have happened if it had not been permissible for her to wear earrings as an ornament.

Therefore, those earrings that were given along with the idols were, as has been said, amulets of the idols.

## CXII. [On Genesis 35:5]

“And the fear of God fell upon the cities that surrounded them, and they did not pursue the sons of Israel.”

Let us begin to observe how God works in the minds of human beings. From whom did the fear of God arise in those cities, except from the one who was protecting his promises in Jacob and his sons?

## CXIII. [On Genesis 35:6]

“Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, which is Bethel.”

It should be observed that three names of this city have now been mentioned: Ulammaus, which it was previously said to have been called when Jacob first came there while traveling to Mesopotamia (Gen. 28:19); Bethel, the name he himself gave it (ibid. 35:15), interpreted as “House of God”; and Luz, which has just been mentioned.

This should not seem strange. In many places this has happened, both with cities and rivers and with various regions of the earth: names have been added or changed for different reasons, just as happens with people themselves.

## CXIV. [On Genesis 35:9, 10]

Again God appeared to Jacob at Luz and said to him, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.”

Here God says this to him again in a blessing, and the repetition confirms the great promise contained in this name. For it is remarkable that, in the case of those to whom it was said even once that they would no longer be called what they had been called, but that a new name would be imposed upon them, they were thereafter never called anything except the name imposed upon them.

But this man continued to be called Jacob throughout his life and afterward, although God had said to him not once, “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (ibid. 32:28).

Clearly, therefore, this name should be understood as referring to that promise in which God will be seen in a manner unlike anything by which he was previously seen by the patriarchs. There the old name will not remain, because nothing of old age will remain even in the body itself, and the vision of God will be the supreme reward.

[Note: Er. reads “to whom God had said more than once,” which is better, as the sequence of the context shows. D. reads “to whom God had said once,” with this note added in the margin: “Perhaps, ‘not once.’”]

## CXV. [On Genesis 35:11]

In the promises made to Jacob it is said, “Nations and assemblies of nations shall come from you.” The question is whether “nations” refers to those according to the flesh, while “assemblies of nations” refers to those according to faith; or whether both expressions were spoken on account of the faith of the nations, if the one nation of Israel according to the flesh cannot be called “nations.”

## CXVI. [On Genesis 35:13–15]

“God went up from the place where he had spoken with him. Jacob set up a monument in the place where he had spoken with him, a stone monument; and he poured a libation upon it and poured oil upon it. Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him there Bethel.”

Was what had happened earlier repeated in this place, or is it merely being mentioned again? Whichever of these is the case, Jacob poured the libation upon the stone, not to the stone. Therefore he did not act as idolaters do, who set up altars before stones and pour libations to stones as though to gods.

## CXVII. [On Genesis 35:26]

### 1

Twelve sons are counted as belonging to Israel, those who were born to him, and it is said, “These are the sons of Israel who were born to him in Mesopotamia,” although Benjamin was born much later, after Jacob had already passed Bethel and was approaching Bethlehem.

Some have tried in vain to resolve this question by saying that the reading should not be “were born,” as most Latin manuscripts have it, but “were made,” since the Greek reads ἐγένοντο (*egenonto*). They therefore wish Benjamin to be understood as included because, although he was not born there, he was made there: he had already been conceived in the womb, so that Rachel may be understood to have left that place pregnant.

Even if the reading were “were born,” they could argue in the same way that he had already been born in the womb because he had been conceived, just as it is said concerning holy Mary to Joseph, “That which has been born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20).

### 2

But another consideration prevents this solution of the question. If Benjamin had already been conceived there, when Jacob’s other sons left that place as grown men they could scarcely have been twelve years old.

Jacob completed twenty years there. During the first seven he had no wife, until he obtained one by serving for her. Thus, if a son was born to him in the first year in which he took a wife, his firstborn could have been twelve years old when he left that place.

Therefore, if Benjamin had already been conceived, the entire journey, and everything Scripture records about Jacob along the way, would have taken place within ten months. It would then follow that his sons were so young that they carried out such a great slaughter on behalf of their sister Dinah, killed so many people, and conquered the city in this way.

Among them, Simeon and Levi, who first entered those men with swords and killed them, would have been eleven and ten years old respectively, even if Rachel had given birth every year without interruption. This is surely incredible: that children of that age could have done all these things, even if she had given birth every year without interruption, especially since Dinah herself would scarcely yet have been six years old.

### 3

The question must therefore be resolved differently. When the twelve sons are mentioned and it is said, “These are the sons of Jacob who were made for him in Mesopotamia of Syria,” this is to be understood because, among the very many who were there, only one had not been born there—although he nevertheless derived the cause of his birth from that place, since his mother had there been joined to his father.

This solution must be supported by some comparable example of such a manner of speaking.

[Note: After “must be supported,” the very old Corbie manuscript has, in the middle of the text, “From this point it should be written.” From this it may be understood that this manuscript was perhaps copied from the exemplar in which Eugippius, who excerpted this passage, had written that note in his own hand. The conjecture is strengthened by the fact that it usually agrees with Eugippius’s excerpts in variant readings.]

### 4

Nevertheless, there is no easier solution to this question than to understand the statement as an instance of synecdoche. Where the greater or more important part is present, what does not properly belong to the name is often included under that name as well.

Thus Judas no longer belonged to the twelve Apostles—indeed, he was already dead when the Lord rose from the dead—yet the Apostle retained the name of that twelvefold number in his Epistle when he said that Christ “appeared to the twelve” (1 Cor. 15:5). The Greek manuscripts have the article here, τοῖς δώδεκα (*tois dōdeka*), so that the expression cannot mean any twelve whatsoever, but those distinguished by belonging to that number.

I think the Lord spoke in the same manner when he said, “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71), so that the one who was a devil does not appear to belong to the election. For the name “elect” is not easily found in a bad sense, except when the wicked are chosen by the wicked.

If we should think that Judas too was chosen so that through his betrayal the Lord’s Passion might be fulfilled—that is, that his wickedness was chosen for some purpose, with God making good use even of the wicked—we should consider another passage in which the Lord says, “I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen” (ibid. 13:18). There he makes clear that only the good belong to the election.

Accordingly, the statement “I chose you twelve” is spoken by synecdoche, so that, under the name of the greater and better part, even what does not properly belong to that name is included.

### 5

The same manner of speaking appears in this very book. Hamor went out to speak with Jacob on behalf of his son Shechem, asking that he receive Dinah, Jacob’s daughter; Jacob’s sons, who had been absent, also came. Hamor said to them all, “My son Shechem has set his heart on your daughter; therefore give her to him as a wife” (Gen. 34:6–8).

Because the father’s person was the more important, by synecdoche Hamor used the expression “your daughter,” thereby including the brothers under that designation, although she was not their daughter.

The same is true of the statement, “Go to the sheep and fetch me two young goats from there” (ibid. 27:9). The sheep and the goats were being pastured together; and because sheep are the more important animals, he included the goats under the name of the sheep.

Likewise, because the number of Jacob’s eleven sons who had been born in Mesopotamia was the more important part, Scripture included Benjamin, who had not been born there, in its mention of them. Thus it says, “These are the sons of Jacob who were made for him in Mesopotamia of Syria.”

## CXVIII. [On Genesis 36:1]

After the account of Isaac’s death, Scripture narrates which wives Esau took and which children he fathered. This must be understood as a recapitulation. These things did not begin to happen after Isaac’s death, since Esau and Jacob were then already one hundred and twenty years old. Isaac had fathered them when he was sixty and lived to the age of one hundred and eighty.

## CXIX. [On Genesis 36:6, 7]

The question is how Scripture can say that, after the death of his father Isaac, Esau departed from the land of Canaan and lived on Mount Seir, when it is recorded that he was already living there when his brother Jacob returned from Mesopotamia.

It is easy to consider what could have happened so that Scripture should neither be thought to have been mistaken nor to have misled us. After his brother had departed for Mesopotamia, Esau may have been unwilling to live with his parents, either because of the resentment caused by his grief at having been deprived of the blessing, or because of some matter concerning his wives, whom he saw to be hateful to his parents, or for some other reason. He then began to live on Mount Seir.

After his brother Jacob returned and peace had been established between them, Esau himself returned to his parents. When they had buried their father together, the land, as Scripture says, could not contain them because they had become exceedingly wealthy. Esau therefore departed again for Seir and there established the nation of the Idumaeans.

## CXX. [On Genesis 36:21]

“This is the list of the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom.”

The writer is speaking according to the time in which he lived. When Seir, who fathered these men, lived there, Esau had not yet come to that land, and it was not yet called the land of Edom.

The land received its name from Esau himself, since he was called both Esau and Edom. From him the Idumaeans were descended—that is, the nation of Edom.

## CXXI. [On Genesis 36:31, 32]

What is written—“These are the kings who reigned in Edom before a king reigned over Israel”—should not be understood as though all the kings mentioned were listed up to the time when the kings of Israel began, the first of whom was Saul.

There were many kings in Edom up to the time of Saul, including during the period of the Judges, whose time preceded the kings. But from among the many, Moses could mention only those who lived before his own death.

Nor is it surprising that, when one counts from Abraham through Esau, the father of the Edomite nation, and through Reuel, the son of Esau, and Zerah, the son of Reuel, and Jobab, the son of Zerah, followed in the kingdom by Balac, who is recorded as having been the first king in the land of Edom, more generations are found up to the last king Moses could name than are counted from Abraham through Jacob to Moses.

In the former line there are found approximately twelve generations, while in the latter there are about seven up to Moses. It could happen that more were named in the former line because they died sooner and succeeded one another more rapidly.

The same thing happened when Matthew, following a different order, counted forty-two generations from Abraham to Joseph (Matt. 1:1–17), while Luke, counting the generations in another order—not through Solomon, as Matthew did, but through Nathan—mentioned fifty-five generations from Abraham to Joseph (Luke 3:23–38). In the line where more generations are counted, people died sooner than in the line where fewer are counted.

Lest anyone be troubled by the fact that Balac, the son of Beor, is mentioned among the kings of Edom and, because of the similarity of the name, suppose him to be the Balac who opposed Moses when he led the people of Israel, let him know that the latter Balac was a Moabite, not an Idumaean. He was the son of Sephor, not the son of Beor. But at that time there was also a son of Beor named Balaam, not Balac; Balaam was hired by that same Balac to curse the people of Israel (Num. 22:2–6).

## CXXII. [On Genesis 35:29 and 37:2]

However one turns the matter, it is difficult to discover how Isaac’s death could have found Joseph, his grandson, seventeen years old, as Scripture seems to narrate if read in sequence.

I do not wish to say that it cannot be discovered, lest perhaps I overlook what someone else has noticed. If Joseph was seventeen years old after the death of his grandfather Isaac, when his brothers sold him into Egypt, then undoubtedly his father Jacob was one hundred and twenty years old in the seventeenth year of Joseph’s life.

Isaac fathered Jacob and Esau when he was sixty years old, as it is written (Gen. 25:26). Isaac therefore lived another one hundred and twenty years, since he died at the age of one hundred and eighty. Thus he left his sons one hundred and twenty years old and Joseph seventeen.

Joseph, however, was thirty years old when he appeared before Pharaoh. Then seven years of abundance and two years of famine followed before his father came to him with his brothers. Joseph was therefore thirty-nine years old when Jacob entered Egypt.

At that time Jacob himself said to Pharaoh that he was one hundred and thirty years old (Gen. 47:9). Yet Jacob was one hundred and twenty when Joseph was seventeen. This cannot possibly be correct. If Jacob was one hundred and twenty in the seventeenth year of Joseph’s life, then in Joseph’s thirty-ninth year Jacob would necessarily have been one hundred and forty-two, not one hundred and thirty.

If Joseph was not yet seventeen on the day Isaac died, but reached the age of seventeen some time after his grandfather’s death—the year in which Scripture says he was sold into Egypt by his brothers—then his father should have been more than one hundred and forty-two years old when he came to his son in Egypt.

After Scripture had related Isaac’s final year, his one hundred and eightieth, and his death and burial (ibid. 35:28, 29), it then recounted how Esau departed from his brother from the land of Canaan to Mount Seir and included the account of the kings and chiefs of the nation that Esau established or propagated. After this it introduced the account of Joseph in the following way (ibid. 36:6–43):

“Jacob lived in the land of Canaan. These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph was seventeen years old, tending the sheep with his brothers.”

It then narrates the cause of his dreams, how he became hated by his brothers, and how he was sold (ibid. 37:1–28).

Either he came to Egypt in that same seventeenth year, or even somewhat older. In either case the question remains.

For if he was seventeen after the death of his grandfather, when his father was one hundred and twenty, then in Joseph’s thirty-ninth year, when Jacob came to Egypt, Jacob ought to have been one hundred and forty-two. Yet he was then one hundred and thirty. Therefore, if Joseph was sold into Egypt at the age of seventeen, he is found to have been sold twelve years before his grandfather died.
