He could not have been seventeen unless, twelve years before Isaac’s death, he was in the one hundred and eighth year of the life of his father Jacob. When the twenty-two years that Joseph spent in Egypt before his father’s arrival are added to these figures, Joseph’s age is thirty-nine and Jacob’s is one hundred and thirty, and no difficulty remains.

But because Scripture narrated these events after Isaac’s death, Joseph is thought to have been seventeen after the death of that grandfather of his. We should therefore understand that, when Scripture began speaking about Jacob and his sons, it passed over Isaac’s life as though he were already a very old man. Yet while Isaac was still alive, Joseph began to be seventeen years old.

### CXXIII. [On Genesis XXXVII, 10]

When Jacob says to Joseph, “What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come and bow down to you upon the earth?”—unless this is understood as having been said with reference to some mystery, how can it be understood of Joseph’s mother, who was already dead? Accordingly, this should not be thought to have been fulfilled in Egypt, when Joseph was exalted: for neither did his father bow down to him when he came to him in Egypt, nor could his mother, who had long been dead, do so. In the person of Christ, therefore, it can easily be understood even of the dead, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “He bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians II, 9–10).

### CXXIV. [On Genesis XXXVII, 28]

It is asked why Scripture also calls the Ishmaelites—to whom Joseph was sold by his brothers—Midianites, since Ishmael was the son of Abraham by Hagar, whereas the Midianites were descended from Keturah. Is it because Scripture had said of Abraham that he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines, namely Hagar and Keturah, and sent them away from his son Isaac toward the land of the East (Genesis XXV, 6), so that they are to be understood as having formed one nation?

**Note:** Three manuscripts read *diviserit* (“divided”); other codices read *dimiserit* (“sent away”). The latter is taken from the Septuagint, *ἐξαπέστειλεν* (“he sent away”); the former agrees with the Vulgate, *separavit* (“he separated”).

### CXXV. [On Genesis XXXVII, 35]

It is written of Jacob, when he was mourning Joseph: “All his sons and daughters gathered together and came to comfort him.” What daughters were these besides Dinah? Or does he call them sons and daughters while counting grandchildren and granddaughters as well? For his older sons could already have had children.

### CXXVI. [On Genesis XXXVII, 35]

“And he refused to be comforted, saying, ‘For I shall go down mourning to my son in the underworld.’” It is commonly a serious question how the underworld is to be understood: whether only the wicked, or also the righteous dead, are accustomed to descend there. If only the wicked go there, how can Jacob say that he wishes to descend there mourning for his son? For he does not believe that Joseph is in punishments. Or are these the words of a troubled and grieving man, exaggerating his misfortunes even in this way?

### CXXVII. [On Genesis XXXVII, 36]

“And they sold Joseph into Egypt to Potiphar, the eunuch of Pharaoh, chief of the cooks.” Some do not wish to interpret “chief of the cooks”—which in Greek is called *ἀρχιμάγειρος* (“chief cook”)—but rather “chief of the army,” who possessed the power of execution. For that is also what the man whom Nebuchadnezzar sent was called; and in his case the primacy of the army is more clearly found.

### CXXVIII. [On Genesis XXXVIII, 1–3]

“Now it happened at that time that Judah went down from his brothers to a certain Odollamite man, whose name was Iras. And Judah saw there the daughter of a Canaanite man, whose name was Sava, and he took her, and went in to her, and she conceived, and bore a son,” and so forth.

**Note:** Thus the manuscripts, following the Septuagint. The printed editions, as in the Vulgate, read *Sue*.

It is asked when these events could have taken place. For if they occurred after Joseph came to Egypt, how could it have happened within approximately twenty-two years—for after that length of time they are understood to have come to the same Joseph, their brother, in Egypt with their father—that Judah’s sons could all have reached an age at which they were able to take wives? Tamar, his daughter-in-law, was given to another son after her firstborn had died; when that son also died, she waited for the third to grow up; and when he had grown up, Judah did not give him to her, fearing that he too might die. Consequently, she offered herself to her father-in-law.

How, then, could all these events have occurred within so few years? The question is reasonable, unless Scripture intends us to understand—as it sometimes does—that, by recapitulation, this began several years before Joseph was sold, since the narrative is arranged as though it said, “Now it happened at that time.” Yet another question arises: if Joseph was seventeen years old when he was sold, how old could Judah, Jacob’s fourth son, have been? His firstborn, Reuben, could at most have preceded his brother Joseph by five or six years in age.

Scripture clearly says that Joseph was thirty years old when he became known to Pharaoh (Genesis XLI, 46). If, therefore, he is believed to have been sold in the seventeenth year of his life, he had spent thirteen years in Egypt without being known to Pharaoh. To these thirteen years were added seven years of abundance, making twenty years; two more are added because Jacob entered Egypt with his sons in the second year of the famine, yielding twenty-two years during which Joseph was absent from his father and brothers. During this interval, it is difficult to discover how all that is narrated concerning Judah’s wife, sons, and daughter-in-law could have occurred—unless perhaps we believe (and this too could have happened) that as soon as Judah began to reach manhood, he fell in love with the woman whom he married, before Joseph had been sold into Egypt.

### CXXIX. [On Genesis XXXVIII, 14]

“And she removed from herself the garments of her widowhood.” This indicates that even in the time of the patriarchs widows had their own distinctive garments, evidently unlike those of married women.

### CXXX. [On Genesis XXXIX, 1]

When it is said again, “Joseph was brought down into Egypt, and Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch, acquired him,” Scripture returns to the point from which it had departed, in order to relate what it had arranged above.

### CXXXI. [On Genesis XL, 16]

Some Latin codices read, “three baskets of *alica*,” whereas the Greek has *χονδριτῶν*, which those familiar with that language interpret as ordinary loaves. But the question arises how Pharaoh could have had coarse bread among his foods. For it says that in the upper basket were all the things that Pharaoh ate, the work of bakers.

**Note:** The Cerbeian manuscript reads *opus pistorium* (“the work of baking”), and shortly afterward *operis pistorii* (“of baking work”).

Nevertheless, it is to be understood that the basket itself also contained coarse loaves, since it says, “three baskets of *χονδριτῶν*,” and that above them, in the same upper basket, were items of every kind of baked preparation.

### CXXXII. [On Genesis XLI, 1]

Pharaoh thought that he was standing beside the river, just as Abraham’s servant said, “Behold, I am standing beside the spring of water” (Genesis XXIV, 13). For in that passage too the Greek has *ἐπὶ τῆς πηγῆς* (“beside the spring”), just as here it has *ἐπὶ τοῦ ποταμοῦ* (“beside the river”).

If this expression is understood in the Psalm where it is written, “He founded the earth upon the waters” (Psalm XXIII, 2), people are not forced to suppose that the earth floated upon the water like a ship. According to this expression, it is correctly understood that the earth is higher than the water: it is raised above the waters, where earthly animals dwell.

### CXXXIII. [On Genesis XLI, 30]

When it is written, “They shall forget the coming abundance throughout the whole land of Egypt,” this does not mean that those who will suffer hunger will forget an abundance that will come to them later. Rather, the abundance was future at the time when he spoke, as though he had said: “In that famine, which the bad cows and bad ears signified, people will forget this abundance, which the good cows and good ears signified as future.”

### CXXXIV. [On Genesis XLI, 38]

“Shall we find such a man, who has the Spirit of God in him?” Behold, unless I am mistaken, this is already the third time in this book that the Holy Spirit—that is, the Spirit of God—is intimated to us.

First, where it is said, “And the Spirit of God was moving over the water” (Genesis I, 2); second, where God says, “My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Genesis VI, 3); and third, here, when Pharaoh says of Joseph that the Spirit of God is in him. Yet we have not so far read the words “Holy Spirit.”

**Note:** The printed editions read *caro sunt* (“they are flesh”), but the better manuscripts, here and below in Book II, Question 55, read *carnes sunt* (“they are flesh”). This is also the reading in the Septuagint.

### CXXXV. [On Genesis XLI, 45]

“And Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Psonthomphanech.” This name is said to be interpreted as “He has revealed hidden things,” evidently because Joseph disclosed the king’s dreams. In the Egyptian language, however, they claim that by this name he was called “Savior of the world.”

### CXXXVI. [On Genesis XLI, 45]

“And he gave him Aseneth, the daughter of Potiphar, priest of the city of the Sun, as his wife.”

It is commonly asked whose Potiphar this was: whether the man whose servant Joseph had been, or another. It is considered more credible that he was another. For there are many considerations that make it difficult to believe that he was the former.

First, Scripture would surely have mentioned this, since it could scarcely have passed over the fact that it contributed substantially to the young man’s honor that he married the daughter of the man whose servant he had been. Further, how could a eunuch have had a daughter?

The answer is: “How could he have had a wife?” For it is believed that he was castrated afterward, either through an accidental injury or by his own choice. Moreover, the honor that is mentioned is not the one usually attributed to him—that is, that he was *ἀρχιμάγειρος*, whom the Latin translators rendered “chief of the cooks,” while some wish to understand him as “chief of the army.”

Here too, however, it may be answered that he held two honors: the priesthood of the Sun and the command of the army. Elsewhere, the honor appropriate to such activities was fittingly mentioned; here, after Joseph’s remarkable divine power had appeared, his father-in-law’s honor ought to be named in relation to a comparable divinity, according to the Egyptians’ view of the priesthood of the Sun.

Yet in all this, since he was also chief of the prison guards, it is exceedingly incredible that a priest should have been placed over this office.

**Note:** The manuscripts and the edition of Badius read “that a priest was placed over this office.” Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain instead read “that this man was placed over the office of priests.”

Furthermore, Scripture does not simply say that he was a priest of the Sun, but that he was priest of the city of the Sun, which is called Heliopolis. It is said to be more than twenty miles from Memphis, where the Pharaohs—that is, the kings—chiefly resided. How, then, could he have served the king energetically in command of the army while abandoning his priestly office?

It is also reported that Egyptian priests did not ordinarily serve anywhere except in the temples of their gods and did not hold any other office. But if matters were different at that time, let each person believe what seems right. The question nevertheless has no decisive outcome, whether there was one Potiphar or two: whichever view one holds, it is not dangerous to the faith and is not contrary to the truth of God’s Scriptures.

**Note:** The printed editions read *in sacerdote* (“in the priest”), whereas the manuscripts read *in sacerdotio* (“in the priesthood”).

### CXXXVII. [On Genesis XLI, 49]

“And Joseph gathered grain like the sand of the sea, very abundantly, until it could not be counted; for there was no number.” The statement “for there was no number” means that the quantity exceeded every ordinary designation of number, and no name could be found for it. For how can it be that a number does not exist for a multitude, however great, that is nevertheless finite? Still, this may also have been said by way of hyperbole.

### CXXXVIII. [On Genesis XLII, 9]

“And Joseph remembered his dreams, which he himself had seen; for his brothers had bowed down to him.” Something more exalted must be sought in those dreams. For what was seen concerning the sun and the moon cannot be fulfilled in the same way with regard to his father and mother, since his mother was already dead, although his father, who was alive, rebuked him when he heard it (Genesis XXXVII, 10).

**Note:** Two manuscripts read “who had seen it.”

### CXXXIX. [On Genesis XLII, 15–16]

What are we to make of Joseph, a man so wise and praised not only by the testimony of the people among whom he lived but also by Scripture itself, swearing by Pharaoh’s life that his brothers would not leave Egypt unless their younger brother came? Was Pharaoh’s life of so little value even to a good and faithful man, to whom Joseph preserved fidelity in everything, just as he had originally done toward his master? How much more would he have preserved it toward the man who had placed him in such honor, if he had preserved it toward the man who possessed him as a purchased slave?

But if he did not care about Pharaoh’s life, should he not nevertheless have avoided perjury for the sake of any human being? Or is it not perjury? He detained one of them until Benjamin came, and what he had said proved true: “You shall not leave here unless your brother comes.” This could not have applied to all of them; for how could Benjamin have come unless some had returned to bring him?

But what follows presses the question more strongly, where he again swore, saying: “Send one of you, and bring your brother; but you shall be led away”—

**Note:** The printed editions read *non educemini* (“you shall not be led out”). The manuscripts, without the negation, read *ducemini* (“you shall be led”), with “into prison” understood; the Vulgate expresses it as “you shall be in bonds.” The Septuagint has *ὑμεῖς δὲ ἀπαχθῆτε* (“but you shall be led away”).

—“until your words are made clear, whether you speak the truth or not. Otherwise, by Pharaoh’s life, you are spies”—that is, if you do not speak the truth, you are spies.

He inserted an oath into this statement because, if they had not spoken the truth, they would be spies—that is, worthy of the punishment of spies—although he knew that they were speaking the truth. A person is not perjured if, knowing someone to be entirely chaste, he says to him, “If you committed the adultery of which you are accused, God condemns you,” and adds an oath to these words. He is swearing truthfully, because the statement contains a condition: “If you did it,” although he is certain that the person did not do it.

Someone may object: “It is true that if he committed adultery, God condemns him. But how is this statement true—‘If you do not speak the truth, you are spies’—when, even if they were lying, they would not be spies?”

This is what I meant: “You are spies” is stated as though it meant, “You are worthy of the punishment of spies”; that is, “You will rightly be considered and judged spies because of your lie.” That *estis* (“you are”) can be used for “you will be considered” and “you will be judged” is shown by countless similar expressions. Thus Elijah says: “Whoever is answered by fire, he shall be God” (1 Kings XVIII, 24). He will not then become God, but will then be regarded as God.

### CXL. [On Genesis XLII, 23]

When the sons of Israel, repenting, spoke among themselves about their brother Joseph—how they had treated him badly, and how divine judgment was repaying them by making them see themselves in danger—why does Scripture add: “They did not know that Joseph understood, for there was an interpreter between them”?

This is to be understood as meaning that they supposed Joseph did not hear because they saw that the interpreter who stood between them was not telling him what they were saying. They thought that no other reason had been given for the interpreter’s presence except that Joseph did not know their language; and the interpreter had no concern to tell Joseph what they were saying to one another rather than to him, the person by whom he had been appointed.

### CXLI. [On Genesis XLII, 24]

“And he again approached them and spoke to them.” Scripture does not add what he said to them. Hence it is understood that he said the same things he had said before.

### CXLII. [On Genesis XLII, 38]

“And you will bring down my old age with sorrow to the underworld.” Does he say “to the underworld” because he is going there with sorrow? Or does he speak this way because, even if sorrow were absent, he would descend to the underworld by dying?

For the underworld is a major question, and wherever Scripture happens to mention it, we must carefully observe what view Scripture expresses concerning it.

### CXLIII. [On Genesis XLIII, 28]

The steward of the house said to them, “Your God and the God of your fathers has given you treasures in your sacks; as for your silver, I have received it as tested.” This appears to be false, but it must be believed to signify something.

For the silver that is both given and not diminished, since it is also called “tested,” evidently refers to what we read elsewhere: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm XI, 7)—that is, perfectly purified.

**Note:** All the manuscripts here read *probum* (“good” or “honest”); the Greek Septuagint has *εὐδοκιμοῦν* (“approved” or “well-pleasing”).

### CXLIV. [On Genesis XLIII, 34]

“And they drank, and became drunk with him.” Drunkards commonly invoke this as supporting evidence—not on behalf of those sons of Israel, but on behalf of Joseph, who is commended as exceedingly wise. Yet anyone who pays close attention will find in many passages that this word is also used to mean satiety.

Thus we read: “You visited the earth and made it drunk; you multiplied it to enrich it” (Psalm LXIV, 10). Since this occurs in praise of blessing and commemorates a gift of God, it is evident that this drunkenness signifies fullness. For to become drunk in the manner of drunkards is not even useful to the earth: it is corrupted by an excess of moisture beyond what suffices for satiety, just as the life of drunkards is not filled by satiety but submerged in a flood.

### CXLV. [On Genesis XLIV, 15]

Joseph said to his brothers:

**Note:** Seven manuscripts read *tantae* (“of such a great…”).

“Did you not know that a man such as I am practices divination?” He also commanded his servant to say this to them concerning the divination. It is commonly asked what this action means. Since it was not said seriously but in jest, as the outcome showed, is it therefore not to be counted as a lie?

Lies are seriously practiced by liars, not in jest; but when things that are not true are said as a joke, they are not counted as lies.

What is more troubling is the meaning of Joseph’s conduct in repeatedly deceiving his brothers and keeping them in suspense until he revealed who he was. Although the story is all the more pleasing to read because what is done is all the more unexpected for those involved, nevertheless, unless something great were signified by this apparent game, it would neither have been done by Joseph nor been included in Scripture, which possesses such great authority of holiness and such great concern with prophesying future things.

We have not undertaken to pursue that matter here by interpretation, but have wished merely to indicate what ought to be investigated. For I do not think it is without significance that he does not say, “I practice divination,” but, “A man such as I am practices divination.” If this is a type of expression, something similar ought to be found in the body of Scripture.

### CXLVI. [On Genesis XLIV]

I think it should not be considered carelessly how Joseph, during the disturbance of his brothers, kept them in such misery for as long as he wished and prolonged the delay as much as he wished. He was not actually making them wretched, since he was thinking of the outcome of their future joy; and everything he did to delay their happiness he did in order that the same delay might increase it.

It was as though their sufferings during the entire time in which they were distressed were not worthy of the future glory of rejoicing that would be revealed in them when they recognized the brother whom they thought they had lost.

### CXLVII. [On Genesis XLIV, 19]

Many things in Judah’s account are stated differently from the way Joseph had dealt with them, although he was speaking to Joseph; in particular, nothing at all is said about the accusation that they were spies. Whether this was deliberately omitted, or whether forgetfulness caused him to overlook that episode in his agitation, is not evident.

It is also remarkable that they said they had been questioned by Joseph himself about their father and brother, and that they had given him the information when he asked. It is difficult to see how this account can even reach the level of coherence necessary for it to be considered truthful.

Nevertheless, even if there are some falsehoods in it, he could have been mistaken through forgetfulness rather than daring to lie—especially before someone to whom he inserted into his account, in order to bend his mercy, not as though he were ignorant, but even matters which they knew that he knew.

### CXLVIII. [On Genesis XLV, 7]

What does Joseph mean when he says, “For God sent me before you, to preserve your remnants upon the earth and to nourish for you a great *reliquiarium* [remnant]”?

**Note:** Erasmus and Louvain read, “and to nourish your remnant,” which is strange; “for this….” Ratramnus and Amerbach read, “to nourish the remnant of you”; “it is strange. For this….” The Vatican manuscripts read, “to nourish your great remnant-seed.” The Thuaneus, Benignianus, and other ancient manuscripts of excellent quality have, “your great remnant,” in agreement with the Septuagint, *ὑμῶν κατάλειψιν μεγάλην* (“a great remnant of you”).

The scribes’ opportunity for error was the word *reliquiarium*, a barbarous term, though Augustine used it without hesitation after the sacred Scriptures in Book V of the *Confessions*, chapter 8, section 15.

This does not entirely fit if we understand “remnant” or “remnant-seed” as Jacob and his sons, since they are all safe and sound. Or does it perhaps signify, in a profound and hidden mystery, what the Apostle says: “A remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Romans XI, 5)? For the prophet had foretold: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isaiah X, 22).

For this reason Christ was killed by the Jews and handed over to the Gentiles, just as Joseph was handed over to the Egyptians by his brothers, so that the remnant of Israel might also be saved. Hence the Apostle says, “For I too am an Israelite,” and, “Until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel is saved” (Romans XI, 1, 25)—that is, from the remnant of Israel according to the flesh, and from the fullness of the Gentiles who, according to the spirit, are Israel through faith in Christ.

Or, if the fullness of faith still remains for that Israelite nation from which the remnant came—the remnant in which the Apostles were then also saved—this may signify that fullness of Israel’s deliverance by which they were freed from Egypt through Moses.

### CXLIX. [On Genesis XLVI, 6–7]

“Jacob and all his offspring entered Egypt with him: his sons and his grandsons, his daughters and the daughters of his granddaughters.” It must be asked how Scripture can say that his daughters and the daughters of his daughters were with him, when he is read to have had only one daughter.

Above, we said that his daughters could be understood as his granddaughters, just as all the Israelites are called the entire people propagated from him. But here, when it says “the daughters of his granddaughters,” because of the one Dinah, the plural number has been used for the singular, just as the singular is sometimes used for the plural. Unless someone maintains that his daughters-in-law could have been called his daughters.

### CL. [On Genesis XLVI, 15]

When Scripture says that Leah bore so many persons, or that so many persons came forth from Jacob’s loins, we must consider what answer should be given to those who attempt to confirm by this testimony that souls are propagated from parents together with bodies.

No one doubts that “souls” is used for “human beings,” by an expression in which a part signifies the whole. But how are we to detach the very part by which the whole is commemorated—that is, the soul, by whose name the whole human being is signified—from the statement that they “came forth from his loins,” so that we understand only flesh to have been born from him, although only souls are named? We must investigate the kinds of expression found in Scripture.

### CLI. [On Genesis XLVI, 15]

“These are the sons of Leah whom she bore to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria, and Dinah his daughter. All the souls of his sons and daughters were thirty-three.”

**Note:** All the books read, “But certainly [there were] sons,” except one Vatican manuscript, which reads, “Six.” The former is better, as Scripture supports it.

Were all these thirty-three persons born from Leah in Mesopotamia of Syria? Certainly six sons and one daughter were born there, from whom the grandsons are also mentioned.

If, therefore, a question had arisen concerning Benjamin when, after Jacob’s twelve sons had been counted and individually named, it was said, “These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria” (above, Question 117), how much greater is the question now: how were thirty-three persons born from Leah in Mesopotamia of Syria?

The answer is that the expression is confirmed as meaning that all were born there because their parents were born there. Furthermore, it is now no longer doubtful that, because of the one daughter, “daughters” is used in the plural for the singular.

### CLII. [On Genesis XLVI, 26–27]

It is read that sixty-six persons entered Egypt with Jacob, excluding Joseph’s sons; and then, after those sons have been counted, Scripture adds: “There were seventy-five persons who entered Egypt with Jacob.” This must be understood as referring to those who were in Jacob’s household when he entered Egypt. For obviously those whom he found there did not enter with him.

Yet, after a more careful examination, it is found that two had already been born when he entered: Ephraim and Manasseh. Not only are the Hebrew codices said to have this reading in this passage, but the version according to the Septuagint itself makes this clear in Exodus. Nor do I think that the Septuagint translators erred here. Rather, because of some mystical significance, they wished, with a kind of prophetic freedom, to complete the number, if, while Jacob was still alive, persons had descended from the two sons of Manasseh and Ephraim, whom they judged ought to be added to the number of Jacob’s household.

But since Jacob is found to have lived seventeen years in Egypt (Genesis XLVII, 28), it cannot be discovered how Joseph’s sons could have had grandsons while he was still alive. Jacob entered Egypt in the second year of the famine (Genesis XLV, 6), whereas Joseph’s sons were born during the years of abundance (Genesis XLI, 50). However many of the years of abundance in which they are believed to have been born, from the first year of abundance to the second year of famine, when Jacob entered Egypt, there were nine years. When the seventeen years Jacob lived there are added, the total is twenty-six years.

How, then, could young men who were less than twenty-six years old have had grandsons? Nor is this question resolved by any Hebrew reading. For how could it have been fulfilled that Jacob received so many grandsons before entering Egypt, including descendants of Benjamin, who came to his brother at that age?

Scripture not only records that Benjamin had sons, but also grandsons and a great-grandson, all of whom are counted among the sixty-six persons with whom Jacob is said to have entered Egypt, even according to the Hebrew text.

We must also consider what is meant by the fact that, although Joseph and his sons are counted as no more than eight persons, while Benjamin and his sons together number eleven, the total is reported as eighteen rather than nineteen, which would result from eight and eleven. Later Joseph and his sons are said to have been not eight persons but nine, although eight are found in the text (Genesis XLVI, 21, 22, 27).

All these matters, which appear insoluble, unquestionably contain a profound meaning. But I do not know whether everything can be made to agree literally, especially in the case of numbers, which we rightly believe to be most sacred and full of mysteries in Scripture, as we have been able to learn from certain examples.

### CLIII. [On Genesis XLVI, 32]

The patriarchs are commended because they were keepers of flocks from their youth, as were their parents. And rightly so, for this is without doubt just servitude and just dominion: cattle serve human beings, and human beings rule over cattle.

Thus it was said when humanity was created: “Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all the cattle that are upon the earth” (Genesis I, 26). This indicates that reason ought to rule irrational life.

Human servitude to human beings was produced either by iniquity or by adversity.

**Note:** Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read *dominari fecit* (“made [one] rule”); this is absent from all the manuscripts and from the Ratramnus edition. By iniquity, as it is said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Genesis IX, 25). By adversity, as happened to Joseph himself, so that, having been sold by his brothers, he became the slave of a foreigner (Genesis XXXVII, 28, 36).

Thus wars made the first slaves, to whom this name was given in the Latin language. A man who had been defeated by another in war could justly be killed; because he was spared, he was called a *servus* (“slave”). Hence also *mancipia* (“slaves”), because they were captured by hand.

There is also a natural order among human beings, according to which women serve men and children their parents, because even there justice consists in the weaker reason serving the stronger.

Thus in dominion and servitude there is a clear justice: those who excel in reason should excel in authority. When this order is disturbed in the present age by human iniquity or by the bodily diversity of human natures, the righteous endure the temporary perversity, destined at the end to possess an utterly ordered and eternal happiness.

### CLIV. [On Genesis XLVI, 34]

“For every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians.” Rightly is every shepherd of flocks an abomination to the Egyptians, in whom there is a figure of the present age, in which iniquity abounds. For a righteous man is an abomination to an iniquitous man.

### CLV. [On Genesis XLVII, 5–6]

“Jacob and his sons came to Joseph in Egypt. And Pharaoh, king of Egypt, heard, and Pharaoh said to Joseph: ‘Your father and your brothers have come to you. Behold, the land of Egypt is before you; settle your father and your brothers in the best land.’”

This repetition does not concern an omitted matter to which the narrative often returns obscurely through recapitulation; rather, it is entirely explicit. Scripture had already said how Joseph’s brothers came to Pharaoh and what he said to them or heard from them (Genesis XLV, 16–20). But now it repeats the matter as though from the beginning, in order to continue the narrative from the words that Pharaoh addressed to Joseph alone.

In the Greek codices written by more careful scribes, some of these passages bear obeli. These indicate passages found in the Septuagint but not in the Hebrew text. Others bear asterisks, indicating passages found in the Hebrew text but not in the Septuagint.

### CLVI. [On Genesis XLVII, 9]

What did Jacob mean when he said to Pharaoh, “The days of the years of my life, which I sojourn”?

The Greek has this wording, whereas the Latin has “which I live,” “which I possess,” or something similar. Did he say “which I sojourn” because he was born in a land that the people had not yet received as an inheritance through the divine promise? Living there, he was therefore in a foreign land—not only when he was traveling abroad, as in Mesopotamia, but even when he was in the place where he had been born?

Or should it rather be understood according to what the Apostle says: “As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians V, 6)? According to this, the statement in the Psalm is also understood: “I am a sojourner in the earth and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Psalm XXXVIII, 13).

For Jacob again speaks of those same days of his life: “They did not attain the days of the years of my fathers’ lives, the days during which they sojourned.” Here he did not wish anything other than what the Latin codices have—“they lived”—and thus signified that this life is a sojourn upon the earth, that is, a dwelling in pilgrimage.

I believe that this is appropriate to the saints, to whom the Lord promises another, eternal homeland. We must therefore examine how the statement about the wicked is to be understood: “They will sojourn and hide; they themselves will watch my heel” (Psalm LV, 7). This is more appropriately understood of those who sojourn in order to hide—that is, in order to plot against the sons—and do not remain in the house forever.

### CLVII. [On Genesis XLVII, 11]

“And he gave them a possession in the best land, in the land of Rameses, just as Pharaoh had commanded.” It must be asked whether the land of Rameses is itself Goshen. For they had requested that land, and Pharaoh had commanded that it be given to them.

### CLVIII. [On Genesis XLVII, 12]

“And Joseph measured out grain for his father.” Yet his father neither bowed down to him when he saw him nor when he was receiving grain from him. How, then, should we think that Joseph’s dream was fulfilled at this point (Genesis XXXVII, 9), rather than that it contained a prophecy of something greater?

### CLIX. [On Genesis XLVII, 14]

“And Joseph brought all the money into Pharaoh’s house.” In this matter too Scripture intended to commend the faithfulness of God’s servant.

**Note:** The old Corbeian manuscript reads *famulis Dei* (“God’s servants”) rather than *famuli Dei* (“God’s servant”).

### CLX. [On Genesis XLVII, 16, 4]

Joseph said to them: “Bring your cattle, and I will give you bread in exchange for your cattle, if your silver has failed.”

**Note:** The printed editions read *deficit* (“has failed” in the present tense), but the manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek, read *defecit* (“has failed” in the past tense).

It may be asked: since Joseph had gathered grain from which human beings could live, on what did the cattle live when the famine became so severe? This is especially difficult because Joseph’s brothers had said to Pharaoh, “There is no pasture for the cattle of your servants, for the famine has prevailed in the land of Canaan,” and had stated that they had come because of this very lack of pasture.

Therefore, if pasture had failed in the land of Canaan because of the famine, why had it not failed in Egypt, when the same famine was then prevailing everywhere?

Or, as those familiar with the regions report, could pasture have remained available in the many marshes of Egypt even when there was a famine of grain, grain ordinarily being produced by the inundation of the Nile? For those marshes are said to produce more fertile pasture when the water of the Nile rises less high.

**Note:** Fifteen manuscripts read *feracius* (“more fertile”) rather than *feracia* (“fertile”).

### CLXI. [Book 1, 47:29]

As Jacob was dying, he said to his son Joseph: “If I have found favor in your sight, put your hand beneath my thigh, and show me mercy and truth.” By this oath he binds his son as Abraham bound his servant (Gen. 24:2): the former, charging his servant from where a wife should be brought for his son; the latter, entrusting the burial of his body. In both cases, however, those two things are named that are to be highly valued and carefully considered throughout the Scriptures, wherever they are scattered: mercy and justice, or mercy and judgment, or mercy and truth. For in one place it is written: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Thus these two qualities, so strongly commended, are to be given very serious consideration.

Abraham’s servant had said: “If you will show mercy and justice to my master” (Gen. 24:49); and this man likewise says to his son: “That you may show me mercy and truth.” But what this very great man intended by so anxious a concern for his body—that it should not be buried in Egypt but in the land of Canaan beside his fathers—seems strange, even absurd, and inconsistent with the greatness of his prophetic mind, if we judge it by human custom. If, however, mysteries are sought in all these things, the person who discovers them will experience a joy of still greater wonder.

There can be no doubt that the bodies of the dead signify sins in the Law, since people are commanded, after handling them or coming into any kind of contact with them, to be purified as from uncleanness. From this comes the statement: “He who is baptized because of the dead, and again touches him, what does his washing profit? So also he who fasts for his sins and then goes and does the same things again” (Sir. 34:30–31). The burial of the dead therefore signifies the remission of sins, corresponding to the statement: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31:1). Where, then, were the bodies signifying these things to be buried, except in that land where he was crucified whose blood brought about the remission of sins? For the deaths of the Patriarchs prefigured human sins.

The place called Abrahamium, where these bodies lie, is said to be nearly thirty miles from the place where the Lord was crucified. Thus even this number is to be understood as signifying the one who appeared in baptism at approximately thirty years of age. And if anything further concerning so great a matter can be understood in this way, or in a still more exalted manner, let it at least remain certain that we should not suppose that such great and holy men of God took so much care over the burial of their bodies without reason. For the security of the faithful is, and ought to be, that wherever their bodies are buried—or even if, through the fury of their enemies, they are left unburied, or are torn apart and consumed according to their enemies’ desire—their resurrection will not therefore be less whole or less glorious.

### CLXII. [Book 1, 47:31]

What the Latin manuscripts have—“And he worshiped over the head of his staff”—some manuscripts give more correctly as: “He worshiped over the head of his own staff,” or “on the head of his own staff,” or “at the top” [Note: Most manuscripts have *sive in cacumen*, “or at the top,” instead of *in cacumine*, “at the top.”], or “above the top.” The readers are misled by the Greek word, which is written with the same letters whether it means “his” or “his own.” But the accents are different, and those who understand such matters do not disregard them in manuscripts; they are important for making a significant distinction. It could also have one additional letter if the meaning were “his own,” so that the word would not be αὐτοῦ but ἑαυτοῦ.

Accordingly, the question rightly arises as to what the statement means. It would easily be understood that the old man, who carried a staff in the customary manner of the aged, did this over the top of his own staff when he bent down to worship God—carrying it in such a way that, by bending his head over it, he worshiped God upon it.

What, then, does “He worshiped above the top of his staff,” that is, the staff of his son Joseph, mean? Or perhaps he had taken the staff from Joseph when that same son made him swear the oath; and while holding it, after the words of the one who had sworn—and before it had been returned—he immediately worshiped God? He was not ashamed, for that brief time, to carry the emblem of his son’s authority, since a figure of a great future reality was being prefigured. Nevertheless, it is said that in Hebrew the question has a very easy solution: they report that it reads, “Israel worshiped toward the head of the bed.” The old man was lying on the bed, which was positioned so that he could pray there without difficulty whenever he wished. Yet it should not for that reason be thought that what the Seventy translated has no meaning, or even no slight meaning.

### CLXIII. [Book 1, 48:4]

Here also, when Jacob recalls the promises of God made to him, he says that God told him: “I will make you into assemblies of peoples.” By these words he signifies the calling of the faithful more than the propagation of a carnal lineage.

### CLXIV. [Book 1, 48:5–6]

The passage in which Jacob speaks of Ephraim and Manasseh says: “Now therefore your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine as Reuben and Simeon are. But any children whom you beget afterward shall be yours; they shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance.”

This sometimes misleads readers, so that they suppose Jacob to have said that, if Joseph had other sons, he ordered them to be called by the names of these two. But that is not the meaning. The order of the words is as follows: “Now therefore your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine as Reuben and Simeon are; they shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance.” That is, they shall receive an inheritance together with their brothers, so that they may together be called sons of Israel.

These two tribes were added so that, apart from the tribe of Levi, which was priestly, there would be twelve tribes to divide the land and provide the tithes. The intervening statement concerns the other sons whom Joseph might beget.

### CLXV. [Book 1, 48:7]

Jacob wished to point out to his son Joseph, as though Joseph did not know it, where and when he had buried Joseph’s mother, even though Joseph himself had been there with his brothers. Yet even if Joseph had been so young that he could neither care about nor retain the matter in his memory, what compelled Jacob to mention it now? Unless perhaps it was relevant to recall that Joseph’s mother had been buried there where Christ was to be born.

### CLXVI. [Book 1, 48:14, 19]

Israel blesses his grandsons in such a way that he places his right hand on the younger and his left hand on the elder. When his son Joseph wishes to correct him as though he were mistaken and unaware, he replies: “I know, my son, I know. He too shall become a people, and he too shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations.”

This is to be understood of Christ insofar as the statement made concerning Jacob himself and his brother also applies: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23). By this prophetic action, Israel signified something: the later people who would come through Christ by spiritual generation would surpass the earlier people who gloried in their carnal descent from the fathers.

### CLXVII. [Book 1, 48:22]

Jacob says that he gives Shechem as a special possession to his son Joseph, adding that he acquired it “with his sword and bow.” It may be asked how this can be reconciled with the literal account. He bought that possession for one hundred lambs (Gen. 33:19); he did not take it by the right of military victory.

Or was it because his sons stormed Salem, the city of the Shechemites (Gen. 34:25), and it could have become his by right of war, since it might seem that a just war had been waged against those who had first inflicted so great an injury by violating his daughter? Why, then, did he not give that land to the men who had carried out the deed—that is, to his elder sons?

Moreover, if he now gives that land to his son Joseph because he is boasting of that victory, why were the sons who had committed the deed displeasing to him at that time? And why, when he blessed them even now, did he recall the deed reproachfully in his account of their actions (Gen. 49:5)?

There is therefore undoubtedly some prophetic mystery hidden here. Joseph, by a certain special signification, prefigured Christ; and that land is given to him in which Jacob had destroyed and buried foreign gods. Thus Christ is understood to possess the nations that renounce the gods of their fathers and believe in him.

### CLXVIII. [Book 1, 49:32]

We should examine how Scripture speaks of the dead, repeatedly saying: “He was gathered to his fathers,” or “He was gathered to his people.” For Jacob is said to have been gathered to his people when he was already dead but not yet buried; and it is not immediately apparent to what people he could have been gathered.

From him arose the earlier people called the people of Israel. Those who preceded him, however, are so few righteous people that we hesitate to call them a people. If it had said, “He was gathered to his fathers,” there would be no question.

Or is the people not only the people of holy human beings but also of the angels—the people of that city of which Hebrews says: “But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to thousands of rejoicing angels” (Heb. 12:22)? Those who end this life pleasing God are gathered to this people [Note: The printed editions have: “who become pleasing to God after this life.” We correct the passage on the authority of the manuscripts, supported by the collection of Abbot Eugippius both in the printed editions and in two Corbie manuscripts.].

They are said to be gathered then, when no anxiety from temptations and no danger from sins remains. With this in view Scripture says: “Before death, praise no one” (Sir. 11:30).

### CLXIX. [Book 1, 50:3]

The forty days of burial mentioned by Scripture perhaps signify something concerning repentance, by which sins are buried. For it was not without reason that forty days of fasting were also established, during which Moses (Exod. 34:28), Elijah (1 Kings 19:8), and the Lord himself fasted (Matt. 4:2); and the Church calls its special observance of fasting Lent.

Accordingly, they report that in Hebrew the prophet Jonah’s account of the Ninevites reads: “Forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4). Thus, during those days—obviously suited to the humiliation of penitents—they are understood to have mourned their sins in fasting and obtained God’s mercy.

Yet this number should not be thought appropriate only to the mourning of penitents. Otherwise the Lord would not have spent forty days with his disciples after the resurrection, entering and leaving with them, eating and drinking; and those days were certainly days of great joy.

Nor should we think that the Seventy interpreters, whom the Church customarily reads, erred by saying not “Forty days” but “Three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown.” For, endowed with an authority greater than that belonging to the task of translators, they placed “three days” by the prophetic Spirit. It is also firmly attested that, in their translations, they harmonized with one voice—a great miracle—even though they knew that the Hebrew manuscripts read forty days.

They did this so that, in the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ, sins might be understood to be dissolved and abolished; of him it is said: “He was delivered up for our offenses and raised for our justification” (Rom. 4:25). The Lord’s glorification is recognized in his resurrection and ascension into heaven.

For this reason he gave the Holy Spirit twice, although it was one and the same Spirit: first, after he had risen (John 20:22), and again after he had ascended into heaven (Acts 2:2–4). Since he rose after three days but ascended after forty days, the Hebrew manuscripts signify by the number of days the one event that occurred later. The Seventy, however, wished to mention the other event—the three days, which also pertained to the same matter—not in servile adherence to translation, but with prophetic authority.

Let us therefore not say that one of these statements is false, and let us not quarrel, on behalf of one set of translators, against another. Those who translate from the Hebrew should prove to us that what they translate is written there; while the authority of the Seventy translators—commended by so great a divinely wrought miracle and established by such antiquity in the churches—should also be upheld.

### CLXX. [Book 1, 50:5]

Joseph commanded the Egyptian officials to say to Pharaoh on his behalf: “My father made me swear, saying, ‘In the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan, there you shall bury me.’” It may be asked how this is true, since these words of his father are not recorded when he gave instructions about his burial.

We must refer the words to the meaning, as we have similarly pointed out above concerning repeated words or narratives. Words ought to serve the expression and communication of the will. Nowhere earlier in Scripture is Jacob said to have dug a grave for himself. But unless he had done so while he was still in those same lands, the statement would not now have been made.

### CLXXI. [Book 1, 50:10]

What is meant by the statement that, when they went to bury Jacob, Scripture says: “They came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan”?

They had passed beyond the place where the dead man was to be buried by more than fifty miles, as those familiar with the region report. That, approximately, is the distance from the place where the Patriarchs—including Jacob—were buried to the place at which they are said to have arrived.

After mourning and lamenting there at length, they returned to the place they had passed, crossing the Jordan again.

Unless perhaps someone says that, to avoid certain enemies, they came with the body through the wilderness, along the route by which the people of Israel were later led by Moses after being liberated from Egypt. Along that route there is a considerable detour, and one reaches Abrahamium by way of the Jordan [Note: The Ratian manuscript has “to Abraham”; the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis have “to Mamre.” The reading “to Abrahamium,” found in the manuscripts, should be retained, as above in Question 161.], where the bodies of the Patriarchs are located—that is, the land of Canaan.

However this may have happened, whether they went so far beyond those places toward the east and then came to them by way of the Jordan, it should be believed that this occurred for the sake of signification: Israel would later come to those lands in his descendants by way of the Jordan.

### CLXXII. [Book 1, 50:10, 3]

“And he mourned for his father seven days.”

I do not know whether Scripture records that any of the saints observed nine days of mourning, which the Latins call a *Novemdial* [Note: The manuscripts of Eugippius’s collection have *Novemdialia*]. Hence it seems to me that Christians who observe this number of days for their dead should be prohibited from doing so, since the practice belongs more properly to pagan custom.

The seventh day, however, has authority in Scripture. Thus it is written elsewhere: “The mourning for the dead lasts seven days, but for the fool all the days of his life” (Sir. 22:13). The number seven, because of the mystery of the Sabbath, chiefly signifies rest; and therefore it is appropriately offered to the dead as to those who are resting.

The Egyptians, however, multiplied this number tenfold in Jacob’s mourning, mourning him for seventy days.

### CLXXIII. [Book 1, 50:22]

“And Joseph lived one hundred and ten years. And Joseph saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation, and the children of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s knees.”

Since Scripture says that Joseph lived to see these sons of sons, or grandsons, how does it include them among the seventy-five people with whom Jacob is said to have entered Egypt (Gen. 46:27)? Joseph had grown old enough to see them born, whereas Jacob, when he entered Egypt, found Joseph still a young man; and when Jacob died, he left Joseph at approximately fifty-six years of age.

It is therefore clear that Scripture wished to commend that number—seventy-five—for the sake of a certain mystery.

If anyone asks how it can also be historically true that Jacob entered Egypt with seventy-five persons, his entry should not be understood as occurring on the single day when he arrived. Since Jacob is often named in his sons, that is, in his descendants, and since it is clear that he entered Egypt through Joseph, his entry should be understood as lasting as long as Joseph lived, through whom his entry took place.

Throughout that entire period all those who are mentioned could have been born and lived, so that the seventy-five persons could be counted down to Benjamin’s grandsons. For Scripture says: “These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria” (Gen. 46:15), speaking even of those who had not yet been born. Their parents, from whom they were born, had been born there; Scripture declares that the children were born there because the cause of their birth—their parents, whom Leah bore there—was born there.

Similarly, since Jacob had the cause of his entry into Egypt in Joseph, the whole time Joseph lived in Egypt was Jacob’s entry into Egypt through his descendants. Those descendants continued to multiply while Joseph was alive, through whom it had come about that Jacob entered.

## BOOK TWO

### Questions on Exodus, and at the end a description of the Tabernacle

[Col. 0597]

### QUESTION I. [Exod. 1:19–20]

Concerning the lie of the midwives, by which they deceived Pharaoh so that they would not kill the Israelite males when they were born, saying that Hebrew women did not give birth as Egyptian women did: it is often asked whether such lies were approved by divine authority, since Scripture says that God dealt well with the midwives. But whether he forgave the lie on account of their mercy, or whether he judged the lie itself worthy of reward, is uncertain.

For the midwives were doing one thing by preserving the infants alive and another by lying to Pharaoh. In preserving them alive, they were performing an act of mercy; but by that lie they were protecting themselves so that Pharaoh would not harm them. This may have pertained not to praise but to pardon.

Nor does it seem to me that authority to lie is thereby offered to those of whom it is said: “No lie was found in their mouth” (Rev. 14:5). The life of persons far inferior to the profession of the saints, if it has these sins of lying, is tolerated on account of its very progress and natural disposition, especially if they do not yet know how to await heavenly benefits from God but are occupied with earthly things.

But those who live in such a way that, as the Apostle says, their conduct is in heaven (Phil. 3:20), should not, I think, shape the regulation of their speech—so far as expressing truth and avoiding falsehood are concerned—according to the example of the midwives. This question nevertheless requires more careful discussion because of other examples found in Scripture.

### II. [Book 2, 2:12]

Concerning Moses’s action, when he killed the Egyptian in defense of his brothers, we have discussed sufficiently in the work we wrote against Faustus on the life of the Patriarchs: whether there was in him a praiseworthy natural disposition by which he committed this sin, just as the fertility of the earth is sometimes praised even before useful seed, because of the abundance of its otherwise useless plants; or whether the deed itself should altogether be justified (*Against Faustus*, book 22, chapters 60 and following).

The latter does not seem possible because he did not yet possess any legitimate authority, either divinely bestowed or established by human society. Nevertheless, as Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles, Moses “supposed that his brothers understood that God was giving them salvation through him” (Acts 7:25). By this testimony Moses appears already to have been divinely prompted—although Scripture is silent about it at that point—to dare the deed.

### III. [Book 2, 3:4]

“The Lord called him from the bush” [Note: The printed editions have “The Lord called to him.” The manuscripts have “The Lord called him,” that is, “summoned him,” as in the Vulgate. In the Septuagint: ἐκάλεσεν αὐτόν, *ekalesen auton*.].

Was the Lord in the angel? Or was the Lord that angel who is called “the Angel of the Great Counsel” (Isa. 9:6), and is understood to be Christ? For earlier it says: “The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the bush.”

### IV. [Book 2, 3:8]

“To lead them out of that land into a good and spacious land, into a land flowing with milk and honey”: should we understand spiritually the land flowing with milk and honey, since, literally speaking, the land given to the people of Israel was not such? Or is this a manner of speech referring to the richness and sweetness of the land as praise?

### V. [Book 2, 3:9]

“And now, behold, the cry of the children of Israel has come to me”: not like the cry of Sodom (Gen. 18:20), by which iniquity without fear or shame is signified.

### VI. [Book 2, 3:22]

Concerning the Lord’s command to the Hebrews through Moses that they should receive from the Egyptians vessels of gold and silver and clothing, with the addition, “And you shall plunder them”: the judgment of this command cannot be unjust. It was God’s command, concerning which one ought not to pass judgment but to obey. He knows how justly he gave the command; it is the servant’s duty to do obediently what he commanded.

### VII. [Book 2, 4:10]

When Moses says to the Lord: “I pray, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither from yesterday nor from the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant,” he is understood to be saying that he could believe himself suddenly made eloquent by God’s will, since he says, “nor since you began to speak to your servant.” It is as though he were indicating that, although he had not been eloquent before yesterday or the day before, he could suddenly have become so from the time when the Lord began to speak with him.

### VIII. [Book 2, 4:11]

“Who made the mute and the one who hears, the one who sees and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?”

There are people who bring accusations against God—or rather against the Old Testament Scriptures—because God is said to have made the blind and the mute. What, then, do they say about the Lord Christ, who plainly says in the Gospel: “I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39)?

Who but a fool would believe that anything could happen to a person, in relation to bodily defects, which God did not will? Yet no one doubts that he justly wills the whole of it.

### IX. [Book 2, 4:12]

When the Lord says to Moses: “But now go, and I will open your mouth and instruct you in what you are to say,” it is sufficiently clear here that not only the instruction of the mouth but its very opening belongs to God’s will and grace.

He does not say, “Open your mouth, and I will instruct you,” but promises both himself: “I will open it, and I will instruct you.” Elsewhere he says in the Psalm: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11). There he signifies the human will to receive what God gives to one who is willing: “Open your mouth wide” belongs to the beginning of the will, while “I will fill it” belongs to God’s grace. Here, however, he says: “I will open your mouth, and I will instruct you.”

### X. [Book 2, 4:14–16]

“And the Lord, being angry with anger, said” [Col. 0599].

Whenever Scripture speaks in this way of God’s anger, we must understand how God can be angry—not as a human being is angry through irrational disturbance. This must be maintained throughout, so that it need not be said repeatedly whenever Scripture uses such language.

Yet it is rightly asked why, while angry, he said here concerning Moses’ brother that Aaron himself would speak to the people. For it seems that, as though Moses were distrustful, God did not grant him the fullest ability he was going to give him; and that he wished what could have been done through one person to be done through two, if Moses had believed.

Nevertheless, when all the words are examined more carefully, they do not signify that the Lord gave Aaron to Moses as a punishment in anger. For he says: “Is not Aaron your brother, the Levite? I know that he will surely speak” [Note: The manuscripts have this according to the Septuagint, ὅτι λαλῶν λαλήσει αὐτός, *hoti lalōn lalēsei autos*. The editions have: “For he is eloquent; he will speak.”].

By these words God rather shows that he rebuked Moses for fearing to go because he was less capable, when he had a brother through whom he could say to the people whatever he wished. Moses himself was weak-voiced and slow of tongue, although he ought to have hoped for everything from God.

Then God repeats the very promises he had made shortly before, even after becoming angry. He had said: “I will open your mouth and instruct you”; now he says: “I will open your mouth and his mouth, and I will instruct you both in what you are to do.” But since he added, “He himself will speak to you to the people,” the opening of the mouth appears to have been granted with reference to what Moses says about being slow of tongue.

As for weakness of voice, the Lord did not wish to remedy it in Moses; instead, for that reason he added his brother as a helper, who could use a voice sufficient for teaching the people. Therefore, when he says: “You shall put my words into his mouth,” he shows that he would give him words to speak. If they were merely words to be heard, as in the case of the people, he would have said that he was putting them into his ears.

Furthermore, when he says shortly afterward: “He himself will speak to you to the people, and he will be your mouth,” “to the people” is again understood. And when he says, “He will speak to you to the people,” he clearly indicates Moses’ primacy and Aaron’s ministry.

Then, when he says: “You shall be to him in matters relating to God” [Note: The manuscripts preserve the Greek expression, ἔσῃ τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, *esē ta pros ton Theon*. In the printed editions this has sometimes been retained and sometimes changed to: “You shall be to him in those matters that relate to God.”], a great mystery may perhaps be examined here: what figure is represented by Moses as a kind of mediator between God and Aaron, and Aaron as a mediator between Moses and the people?

### XI. [Book 2, 4:24–25]

In the passage that says: “And it happened that, on the way, at the lodging-place, an angel met him and sought to kill him. And Zipporah, taking a flint, circumcised the foreskin of her son; and she fell at his feet and said, ‘The blood of circumcision of my child has stopped.’ And he withdrew from him; therefore she said, ‘The blood of circumcision has ceased,’” the first question is whom the angel wished to kill.

Was it Moses, since it says that the angel met him and sought to kill him? For whom would he be thought to have met except the one who presided over his entire company and from whom the others were led?

Or did he seek to kill the child, whom the mother saved by circumcising him? On this view, the angel is understood to have wished to kill the infant because he was uncircumcised, thereby enforcing the command of circumcision through the severity of punishment.

If this is so, it is uncertain of whom the statement was first made: “He sought to kill him,” since the identity is not known until it is discovered from what follows. It is certainly a remarkable and unusual manner of expression that the text first says, “He met him and sought to kill him,” without having previously said anything about the person concerned.

Yet there is a similar construction in the Psalm: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion” (Ps. 86:1–2). The Psalm begins there, without having said anything earlier about the person or place whose foundations he intended to indicate when he said, “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.”

But because it follows, “The Lord loves the gates of Zion,” the foundations must be understood either as the Lord’s or Zion’s; and for easier understanding, more probably Zion’s, so that they are taken as the foundations of the city.

Since, however, the pronoun *ejus* (“its”) has an ambiguous gender—for the pronoun is used in all genders, masculine, feminine, and neuter—whereas in Greek it is feminine as αὐτῆς, but masculine and neuter as αὐτοῦ, and the Greek manuscript has αὐτοῦ, this compels us to understand not the foundations of Zion but the foundations of the Lord—that is, those established by the Lord. Of him it is said: “The Lord builds Jerusalem” (Ps. 146:2).

Yet neither Zion nor the Lord had been mentioned earlier when it said, “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” So here too, although the infant had not yet been named, it says, “He met him and sought to kill him,” so that we may recognize from what follows whom the statement concerns.

Even if someone wishes to understand it of Moses, there is no great need to resist that interpretation. Rather, if possible, we should understand what the following passage means: why did the angel withdraw from killing either of them because the woman said, “The blood of circumcision of my child has stopped”?

For it does not say, “He withdrew from him because she circumcised the child,” but because “the blood of circumcision stopped”—not because it flowed, but because it stopped. This, unless I am mistaken, involves a great mystery.

### XII. [Book 2, 4:20]

Earlier it was said that Moses put his wife and children on pack animals so that he could travel with them to Egypt. Later, however, his father-in-law Jethro [Note: The printed editions have *Jethro*. The manuscripts, as in the Septuagint, have *Jothor*.] came to meet him with them after Moses had led the people out of Egypt (Exod. 18:1–5). It may be asked how both statements can be true.

It should be understood that, after the event in which the angel was about to kill Moses or the child, Zipporah returned with the children. Some have thought that the angel caused this terror so that the female sex would not accompany Moses as an impediment to the ministry divinely entrusted to him.

### XIII. [Book 2, 5:1–3]

It is asked how the people are told that God commanded that he would lead them out of Egypt into the land of Canaan, while Pharaoh is told that they wished to go out into the wilderness for a three-day journey in order to sacrifice to their God, at his command.

It should be understood that, although God knew what he was going to do—since he foresaw that Pharaoh would not consent to release the people—what was first said was also what would first have happened if Pharaoh had released them.

For the fact that everything happened as the subsequent Scripture testifies was brought about by the obstinacy of Pharaoh and his people. God does not command deceitfully when he commands something he knows the person commanded will not do, so that a just judgment may follow.

### XIV. [Book 2, 5:22–23]

The words Moses says to the Lord—“Why have you afflicted this people? And why did you send me? From the time I entered to speak to Pharaoh in your name, to this people, you have not delivered your people”—are not words of defiance or indignation, but of inquiry and prayer. This is clear from what the Lord answered him.

He did not rebuke Moses for unbelief but revealed what he was going to do.

### XV. [Book 2, 6:14–28]

There is no doubt that this passage contains a mystery. Scripture wishes to demonstrate Moses’ ancestry, since his action was already approaching, and therefore begins with the firstborn of Jacob, Reuben, then proceeds to Simeon, and then to Levi. It does not go farther because Moses came from Levi.

Those are mentioned who had already been included among the seventy-five with whom Israel entered Egypt. God did not wish the first or second tribe but the third tribe, the Levitical tribe, to be priestly.

### XVI. [Book 2, 6:30]

When Moses says: “Behold, I am weak-voiced, and how will Pharaoh hear me?” he does not seem to excuse himself from weakness of voice merely because of the size of the people, but also because of one man.

It would be strange if his voice were so weak that he could not be heard even by one person. Or perhaps royal arrogance did not allow people to speak to Pharaoh at close range?

He is then told: “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet” (Exod. 7:1).

### XVII. [Book 2, 4:16]

It should be noted that, when Moses was sent to the people, he was not told: “Behold, I have made you a god to the people, and your brother shall be your prophet.” Rather, he was told: “Your brother will speak to you to the people.”

It was also said: “He shall be your mouth, and you shall be to him in matters relating to God”; it was not said, “You shall be his god.”

To Pharaoh, however, Moses is said to have been given as a god, and by analogy Aaron was the prophet of Moses—but in relation to Pharaoh.

Here we are shown that the prophets of God speak the things they hear from him, and that a prophet of God is nothing other than one who declares God’s words to human beings, who either cannot or do not deserve to hear God directly.

### XVIII. [Book 2, 7:3]

God repeatedly says: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart.” He even seems to give a reason for doing so: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and I will multiply my signs and wonders in Egypt,” as though the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart had been necessary for God’s signs to be multiplied or fulfilled in Egypt.

God therefore makes use of evil hearts for what he wishes to show the good, or for what he is going to do for the good [Note: The old Corbie manuscript and the collection of Eugippius in two manuscripts have: “or for what he is going to make the good.”].

Although the quality of each person’s heart in evil—that is, the kind of heart one has toward evil—comes about through that person’s own fault, formed by the choice of the will, nevertheless, that a person should be moved in one direction or another by that evil quality—though moved badly either way—comes about through causes by which the mind is driven.

Whether those causes exist or do not exist is not within human power; they arise from the hidden providence of God, wholly just and wise, who orders and governs the entire universe he created.

Thus, for Pharaoh to have a heart that God’s patience would not move toward piety but rather toward impiety was the fault of Pharaoh’s own vice. But the fact that events occurred by which his heart, already so malignant through its own vice, resisted God’s commands—that is what is meant by its being hardened, since it did not consent flexibly but resisted inflexibly—belonged to the divine dispensation.

Through that dispensation, a punishment was being prepared for such a heart that was not only just but manifestly just, so that those who feared God might be corrected.

For example, if profit is proposed as the reason for committing murder, a miser is moved differently from someone who despises money: the former is moved to commit the crime, while the latter is moved to avoid it. Yet the proposal of profit itself was not within the power of either person.

In the same way, causes come to evil people that are not indeed within their power, but these causes make of them what they find them already to be, formed by their own vices through their former will.

It should certainly be considered whether “I will harden” can also be understood as though God were saying: “I will demonstrate how hard he is.”

### XIX. [Book 2, 7:9]

“If Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, ‘Give us a sign or wonder,’ then you shall say to your brother Aaron, ‘Take the staff and throw it down before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it shall become a serpent.’”

Here the ministry of speech was certainly not required, for Aaron seemed to have been assigned almost out of necessity because of Moses’ weakness of voice. But the staff had to be thrown down so that it might become a serpent.

Why, then, did Moses himself not do this, unless Aaron’s mediation between Moses and Pharaoh represents a figure of some great reality?

### XX. [The same, VII, 10]

This too should be noted: when the sign was performed before Pharaoh, it is written, “And Aaron threw down his rod.” For perhaps, if it had said, “He threw down the rod,” there would have been no question; but since it added “his,” although Moses had given it to him, perhaps this was not said without reason. Or was that rod common to both of them, so that whichever of them it was called “his,” it would truly be called so?

### XXI. [The same, VII, 12]

“And Aaron’s rod swallowed their rods.” If it had been said, “Aaron’s dragon swallowed their rods,” it would be understood that Aaron’s real dragon did not swallow those illusory fabrications, but rods. For it could swallow what they were, not what they appeared to be and were not. But since it says, “Aaron’s rod swallowed their rods,” a dragon could certainly swallow rods, but not a rod. Yet the object is called by the name of what it was changed from, not of what it was changed into, because it was also changed back into that former state; and therefore it had to be called what it principally was.

What, then, are we to say about the magicians’ rods? Had they too become real dragons, but were called rods for the same reason that Aaron’s was? Or rather, by magical deception, did they appear to be what they were not? Why, then, are they called both rods and dragons on either side, so that the manner of speaking differs in no respect with regard to those fabrications?

It is difficult to demonstrate how, even if real dragons were made from the magicians’ rods, neither the magicians nor the evil angels through whose ministry those things were done were nevertheless creators of the dragons. For throughout the elements of the world there exist in bodily things certain hidden seminal principles, by which, when a temporal and causal opportunity has been given, they break forth into the forms appropriate to them, according to their own modes and limits. Thus the angels who bring these things about are not called creators of animals, just as farmers are not to be called creators of crops, trees, or any things that grow from the earth, although they know how to provide certain visible opportunities and causes for those things to be born.

What those men do visibly, the angels do invisibly; but God alone [Note: [Col. 0603] Fifteen manuscripts: “one.”] is the true Creator, who implanted in things their causes and seminal principles. The matter has been stated briefly; if it were explained with examples and an extensive discussion, so that it might be more easily understood, a lengthy treatment would be required—a requirement from which the necessity of our haste excuses us.

### XXII. [The same, VII, 22]

“But the Egyptian magicians likewise did this by their enchantments; and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.”

When this is said, Pharaoh’s heart seems to have been hardened for this reason: the Egyptian magicians also performed similar acts. But what follows will show how great that hardening was, even after the magicians had failed.

### XXIII. [The same, VIII, 7]

“But the Egyptian magicians likewise did this by their enchantments, and they brought frogs up over the land of Egypt.”

The question is: from where, if this had already happened everywhere? But the same question arises concerning where they obtained water to turn into blood, if all the water of Egypt had already been turned into blood. Accordingly, we must understand that the region where the children of Israel lived had not been struck by such plagues. From there the magicians could either draw water which they would turn into blood, or bring out some frogs as a mere demonstration of magical power. Yet they could also have done this after those things had been suppressed; the Scripture, by narrating rapidly, joined together what could have happened later as well.

### XXIV. [The same, VIII, 15]

“And Pharaoh saw that there was relief, and his heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.”

Here it becomes evident that the causes of the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart were not only the fact that his magicians were doing similar things, but also God’s very patience, by which he was sparing him. God’s patience, in relation to human hearts, is useful for some in bringing them to repentance, but useless for others, leading them to resist God and persist in evil. Yet it is not useless in itself, but according to the evil heart, as we have already said.

The Apostle says the same thing: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each according to his works” (Rom. II, 4–6).

Elsewhere, too, when he had said, “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place,” he added, “both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (II Cor. II, 15). He did not say that he was the good fragrance of Christ to those who are being saved, but an evil fragrance to those who are perishing; he simply called himself a good fragrance. Yet they are such that they perish even through the good fragrance, according to the quality of their hearts—as has often been said—which must be changed by a good will through God’s grace, so that God’s judgments, which harm evil hearts, may begin to benefit them.
