Hence, after his heart had been changed for the better, that man sang: “My soul shall live, and it shall praise you; and your judgments shall help me” (Ps. CXVIII, 175). He did not say, “Your gifts,” or “Your rewards,” but “Your judgments.”

It is a great thing that one can say with sincere confidence, “Prove me, Lord, and test me; burn my reins and my heart.” And lest he seem to have attributed anything to his own powers, he immediately added: “For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleasing in your truth” (Ps. XXV, 2–3). He recalls that mercy was shown toward him, so that he might take pleasure in the truth, “for all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).

### XXV. [The same, VIII, 19]

When the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God” [Note: [Col. 0604] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek interpretation of the Septuagint. The printed editions have, “This finger is.”], because they could not bring forth the gnats, they certainly perceived—although they knew the power of their wicked arts—that their efforts had been thwarted, not by arts of the same kind, as though Moses were more powerful in them, but by the finger of God, which was evidently working through Moses.

The finger of God, as the Gospel most clearly states, is understood to be the Holy Spirit. For while one Evangelist records the Lord’s words as saying, “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI, 20), another Evangelist, narrating the same event, wished to explain what the finger of God is, and says, “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. XII, 28).

Thus, although the magicians—on whose power Pharaoh relied—acknowledged that the finger of God was in Moses, by whom they were defeated and whose magic was frustrated, Pharaoh’s heart was nevertheless hardened—now with an altogether astonishing hardness.

But why the magicians failed at this third plague—for the plagues began when the water was turned into blood—is difficult both to perceive and to explain. They could also have failed at the first sign, when the rod was changed into a serpent; and at the first plague, when the water was changed into blood; and at the second, concerning the frogs, if the finger of God—that is, the Spirit of God—had willed it.

For who, however insane, would say that the finger of God could have hindered the magicians’ efforts in this sign but could not have done so in the earlier ones? There is therefore certainly a reason why they were permitted to perform those things up to this point. Perhaps the Trinity is being commended; and what is true is that the foremost philosophers among the nations, insofar as one can investigate this in their writings, philosophized without the Holy Spirit, although they did not remain silent about the Father and the Son. Didymus also mentions this in his book which he wrote on the Holy Spirit (Didymus, *On the Holy Spirit*, book 1).

### XXVI. [The same, VIII, 21–23]

“Behold, I shall send against you, against your servants, against your people, and against your houses, the dog-fly; and the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with the dog-fly, so that you may know that I am the Lord God of all the earth. And I shall set a division between my people and your people.”

Since Scripture makes this explicit here, we should understand that the same thing also occurred in the later and earlier signs: the land in which God’s people lived was not afflicted by any such plagues.

It was appropriate for this to be stated openly at the point where the signs begin which the magicians neither attempted nor even tried to imitate. For, since the gnats had certainly been everywhere in Pharaoh’s kingdom but had not been in the land of Goshen, the magicians attempted to do something similar there and were completely unable. Until they failed, nothing had been said about the separation of that land; but from the time when those signs began—signs which they no longer dared even to attempt to imitate—it was stated.

### XXVII. [The same, VIII, 25]

Where the Latin text has, “Go and sacrifice to the Lord your God in the land” [Note: [Col. 0605] The printed editions have, “in this land.” The demonstrative particle is absent from the manuscripts, and is likewise absent from the Septuagint translation; this is why Augustine has no difficulty in explaining the passage.], the Greek has, “Coming” [Note: [Col. 0605] *Elthontes*.], “sacrifice to the Lord your God in the land.”

For he did not want them to go where they said they would go; rather, he wanted them to sacrifice there, in Egypt. This is shown by Moses’ words that follow, where he says that it cannot be done because of the Egyptians’ abominations.

### XXVIII. [The same, VIII, 26]

When Moses says, “It cannot be done so, for we shall sacrifice to the Lord our God the abominations of the Egyptians,” the meaning is: “We are going to sacrifice those things which the Egyptians abominate, and for that reason we cannot do so in Egypt.” The words he adds make this clear: “For if we sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians in their sight, we shall be stoned.”

Some of our interpreters, not understanding this, translated it as though it said: “It cannot be done so: shall we sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God?” Yet Scripture has said rather that they are going to sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians.

Other Latin versions have: “It cannot be done so, because we shall not sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God.” The added negative particle produces the opposite sense, whereas Moses said: “It cannot be done so: we shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God.” For this reason they said that they wished to go into the wilderness, where the Egyptians would not see their abominations.

This should be understood as having a mystical significance, as we also say concerning the shepherds, who were abominable to the Egyptians (Gen. XLVI, 34); and for this reason the Israelites received a separate land when they came into Egypt. In the same way, the Israelites’ sacrifices are abominations to the Egyptians, just as the lives of the righteous are abominations to the wicked.

### XXIX. [The same, VIII, 32]

When the locust had been removed, it was said of Pharaoh: “And Pharaoh hardened his heart even at this time, and he was unwilling to let the people go.”

Certainly it is not now said, “Pharaoh’s heart was hardened,” but, “Pharaoh hardened his heart.” This is likewise the case in all the plagues. The origin of vices comes from the human will; but human hearts are moved by causes—some in one way, others in another—and often by the same causes in different ways, according to their particular qualities, which arise from their wills.

### XXX. [The same, IX, 7]

“But Pharaoh, seeing that none of the livestock of the children of Israel had died, had his heart hardened.”

How did this hardening of Pharaoh’s heart arise from contrary causes? If the Israelites’ livestock had also died, there would then seem to be an appropriate reason for his heart to be hardened in contempt of God—as if his magicians too had caused the Israelites’ livestock to die. But now, seeing that not one animal from the Hebrews’ livestock had died—a fact by which he ought to have been moved to fear or believe—his heart was hardened from this; that is, that hardening progressed even to this point.

### XXXI. [The same, IX, 8]

What does God’s command to Aaron and Moses mean: “Take full handfuls of ashes from the furnace, and let Moses scatter them toward heaven before Pharaoh and before his servants, and let the dust become throughout the whole land of Egypt”?

In the earlier signs, the rod was used: Aaron, not Moses, either extended it over the water or struck the earth with it. Now, however, after the two signs concerning the dog-fly and the deaths of the livestock—during which neither Aaron nor Moses did anything with his hand—it is said that Moses should scatter ashes from the furnace toward heaven. Both are commanded to take them, but Moses is commanded to scatter them not toward the earth but toward heaven. It is as though Aaron, who had been given for the people, ought to strike the earth or extend his hand over the earth or the water; but Moses, of whom it was said, “He shall be to you in matters pertaining to God” (Exod. IV, 16), is commanded to scatter the ashes toward heaven.

What, then, do those two earlier signs mean, in which neither Moses nor Aaron performs anything with his hand? What is the significance of this difference? Surely it is not without meaning.

### XXXII. [The same, IX, 16]

“And for this very reason you have been preserved, so that I may show my power in you and so that my name may be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.”

The Apostle also quoted these words of Scripture when he was dealing with the same exceedingly difficult passage. There he says: “But if God, wishing to show wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath” —that is, sparing those whom he had foreknown would become evil—“which,” he says, “he made ready for destruction; and that he might make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy” (Rom. IX, 22–23).

Hence, in the Psalms, the voice of the vessels of mercy says: “My God, his mercy shall prevent me; my God has shown me among my enemies” (Ps. LVIII, 11–12).

God therefore knows how to use the wicked well. In creating human nature, he does not create it for wickedness, but bears with the wicked patiently for as long as he knows is appropriate—not pointlessly, but using them for the instruction or exercise of the good.

For behold, that the name of God might be proclaimed throughout the whole earth is certainly beneficial to the vessels of mercy. Pharaoh was therefore preserved for their benefit, as Scripture itself testifies and the outcome demonstrates.

### XXXIII. [The same, IX, 19, 6, 20]

What does it mean that, when God threatened that he would produce a great hailstorm, he commanded Pharaoh to hasten to gather his livestock and whatever he had in the field, lest they perish in the hail? This seems to be an admonition given not so much in anger as in mercy.

But this creates no difficulty, since even when God is angry he moderates the punishment. The point that rightly causes concern is: what livestock is now being protected, if all of it had died in the preceding plague? There it is written that God distinguished between the livestock of the Hebrews and that of the Egyptians, so that none of the former died, while all the Egyptian livestock died.

Is the question resolved by the fact that he had foretold that those animals which were in the field would die, so that “all” should be understood to mean all those animals? Those which were in the houses may be understood to have escaped; perhaps even people who were doubtful gathered them and kept them in the house, lest what Moses had foretold the Lord would do prove true. From these animals there could again have been some in the fields, which he now warns them to gather into the houses so that they might not perish in the hail—especially since Scripture continues and says:

“He who feared the word of the Lord among Pharaoh’s servants gathered his livestock into the houses; but whoever did not direct his mind to the word of the Lord left his livestock in the field.”

This could therefore have happened even when God threatened the death of the livestock, although Scripture did not mention it.

### XXXIV. [The same, IX, 22]

“And the Lord said to Moses, ‘Extend your hand toward heaven, and there shall be hail throughout the whole land of Egypt.’”

Here again Moses is commanded to extend his hand not toward the earth but toward heaven, as earlier with the ashes.

### XXXV. [The same, IX, 27, 30]

Amid the crash of heaven, which was violent in the hailstorm, Pharaoh was terrified and asked Moses to pray for him, confessing his own iniquity and that of his people. Moses said to him: “I know that you and your servants still do not fear the Lord.”

What kind of fear was he seeking, for whom this fear was not yet the fear of the Lord? It is easy to fear punishment, but that is not the fear of God—the fear of devotion, namely, which Jacob recalls when he says: “Unless the God of my father Abraham and the Fear of Isaac had been with me, you would now have sent me away empty” (Gen. XXXI, 42).

### XXXVI. [The same, X, 1]

The Lord said to Moses: “Enter to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants, so that these signs of mine may come upon them in due order” [Note: [Col. 0607] After “upon them,” the Corbie manuscript adds: “Thus he says: ‘For I have hardened his heart, so that these signs of mine may come upon them in due order.’”].

This sounds as though God needed someone’s wickedness. But it should be understood as if he had said: “I was patient toward him and his servants, so that I would not remove them, so that my signs might come upon them in due order.” Because God’s patience made the evil disposition more obstinate, “I was patient toward him” is expressed as “I hardened his heart.”

### XXXVII. [The same, X, 19]

“And not one locust was left in the whole land of Egypt; and the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart.”

Scripture certainly recalled God’s benefaction, by which he removed the locusts; and afterward it said that the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart—by his benefaction, certainly, and by his patience, through which Pharaoh became more obstinate while he was being spared. In this way all evil human hearts become hardened by misusing God’s patience.

### XXXVIII. [The same, X, 21, 12]

For the third time Moses is told, “Extend your hand toward heaven,” so that the plague of darkness might also occur. But Aaron his brother is never told to extend his hand toward heaven.

As for what was said to Moses, “Extend your hand over the land of Egypt, and let the locust rise over the land,” I believe this signified that one who can do less can also do what one who can do more can do; but it does not follow that one to whom lesser things are granted can also do greater things.

### XXXIX. [The same, XI, 2]

God said to Moses: “Speak secretly in the ears of the people, and let each man ask his neighbor, and each woman her neighbor, for gold and silver vessels and clothing.”

No one should think that an example is being given here for stripping one’s neighbor in this way. God commanded this, and he knew what each person ought to suffer. Nor did the Israelites commit theft; they rendered service to God’s command.

In the same way, when a judge’s minister kills someone whom the judge has ordered to be killed, if he does so of his own accord he is a murderer, even if he kills someone whom he knows ought to be killed by the judge.

There is also this question: if the Hebrews lived separately in the land of Goshen, where the plagues afflicting Pharaoh’s kingdom did not occur, how could each man ask his neighbor, or each woman her neighbor, for gold, silver, and clothing? This is especially puzzling because, when the command is first given through Moses, it is phrased: “and each woman from her neighbor, and from her fellow-dweller, or fellow-resident—or *cohabitator*, if that is the proper word” [Note: [Col. 0608] In Greek: *para geitonos kai suskēnou autēs*.].

We must therefore understand that not only Hebrews lived in the land of Goshen, but that some Egyptians also lived there with them. On account of the Hebrews’ merits, those divine benefits could reach these Egyptians as well, so that the Egyptian residents both loved them and readily lent them what they requested.

Nevertheless, God did not judge them to have been so alien to the injuries and afflictions endured by God’s people that they should not also be struck by this loss, since they had not been struck by those plagues precisely because that land had been spared.

### XL. [The same, XI, 9]

“But the Lord said to Moses, ‘Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I may multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt.’”

This sounds as though Pharaoh’s disobedience had been necessary for those signs to be multiplied, although they were beneficially performed to terrify God’s people and, by that very distinction, to form them in devotion.

But this was God’s doing: he made good use of the wickedness of Pharaoh’s heart, rather than Pharaoh’s doing, since Pharaoh was misusing God’s patience.

### XLI. [The same, XII, 10, 46]

“But whatever remains of it until morning you shall burn with fire.”

One may ask how anything could remain, since they had first been warned that, if a household did not have a sufficient number of people to consume the animal, neighbors were to be invited. But since it was said, “You shall not break a bone of it,” it is understood that bones would necessarily remain, to be burned with fire.

### XLII. [The same, XII, 5]

“It shall be a perfect lamb for you, a male, a year old.”

This expression may cause difficulty, as though a lamb could be something other than male, for someone unaware of the reason why it was translated in this way. The word should have been translated as *sheep*, since the Greek has πρόβατον (*probaton*); but *probaton* is neuter in Greek, and everything that follows could fit, as though it said: “It shall be a perfect animal for you, a male, a year old.”

In Latin one could say “a male animal,” just as one says *mascula thura* (“male frankincense”), with a neuter noun. But one could not say *ovis masculus* (“male sheep”), because *ovis* (“sheep”) is feminine in gender. Likewise, if one said *ovis mascula* (“female sheep”), it would be more absurd.

If *pecus* (“animal” or “livestock”) were used, it would also be understood as something else, and the sacramental meaning would not be preserved. For although Scripture speaks of a sheep, it afterward says, “You shall take it from the lambs and the kids.” In this matter Christ is rightly understood to be signified. For what need would there be to instruct that a sheep or lamb be taken from lambs and kids, unless the one were being represented whose flesh was propagated not only from the righteous but also from sinners?

Although the Jews try to understand this as commanding that a kid also be taken for the celebration of Passover, and think that “take it from the lambs and the kids” means that either a lamb from lambs or a kid from kids should be taken if the former is unavailable, nevertheless, once these things have been fulfilled in Christ, it is evident what was signified by that command.

### XLIII. [The same, XII, 14]

What is written—“And you shall make this day a legal ordinance for your generations, eternal or everlasting,” which in Greek is called αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*)—should not be understood as though the day of these passing things could itself be eternal. Rather, what this day signifies is eternal. It is like saying that God himself is eternal: we do not, of course, call these two syllables eternal, but what they signify.

Nevertheless, one must carefully investigate how Scripture ordinarily calls something eternal, lest it have called that observance eternal in the sense that they must not dare to omit or change it of their own accord.

For one thing is commanded only until it is completed, as when the ark was commanded to circle the walls of Jericho seven times (Josh. VI, 3–4). Another thing is commanded to be observed in such a way that no limit to the observance is specified—whether solemnly every day, every month, or every year, or at fixed intervals of many or several years.

Thus it either called it eternal because they were not to cease celebrating it of their own accord, or, as I said, so that not the signs themselves, but the eternal realities signified by them, should be understood as eternal.

### XLIV. [The same, XII, 30]

“And there arose a great cry in the land of Egypt, for there was no house in which there was not a dead person.”

Could there not have been some house that had no firstborn? Since only the firstborn were dying, how was there no house that did not have a dead person?

Or had God’s foreknowledge providentially arranged this as well, so that absolutely every house contained firstborn sons whom the Egyptians would lose?

Certainly the Egyptians who lived in the land of Goshen should not be thought to have been exempt from this plague. The plague concerned human beings or animals, not the land: that is, firstborn humans and animals died through a hidden, angelic blow. Nothing occurred in the earth or in the sky by which its inhabitants would be afflicted, as happened with the frogs, locusts, or darkness.

Since the land of Goshen had been exempt from such plagues, the benefit undoubtedly reached those Egyptians who lived in that same land with the Hebrews. But in this plague all their firstborn were struck.

### XLV. [The same, XII, 35–36]

“The children of Israel did as Moses had commanded them, and they asked the Egyptians for gold and silver vessels and clothing. And the Lord gave favor to his people before the Egyptians, and they lent them these things, and they despoiled the Egyptians.”

This had already happened before the deaths of the Egyptians’ firstborn, but it is now repeated by recapitulation. For it was narrated when it happened. How could it now have happened, when, amid such mourning over the deaths of their own people, the Egyptians would lend these things to the children of Israel?

Unless perhaps someone says that the Egyptians who inhabited the land of Goshen with the Hebrews were not struck by this plague either.

### XLVI. [The same, XII, 22]

What does he mean when he says: “You shall take a bundle of hyssop, and dipping it in the blood which is beside the door, you shall smear it on the lintel and on both doorposts”?

The question is what blood he means by “which is beside the door,” since he evidently means the blood of that lamb by whose sacrifice the Passover is celebrated. Did he consequently command—although he did not state it—that the same lamb be killed beside the door?

Or, more plausibly, did he say “from the blood which is beside the door” because the person who was going to smear it on the lintel and the doorposts would place beside the door the vessel itself in which he had caught the blood, so that he would have it at hand when dipping the hyssop?

### XLVII. [The same, XII, 37, 40]

“The children of Israel departed from Rameses for Succoth, six hundred thousand men on foot, besides their equipment, or their possessions.” If the Greek word ἀποσκευή (*aposkeuē*) can rightly be translated in this way, Scripture indicates that the word signifies not only movable goods but also living beings who move. Thus Judas says to his father: “Send the boy with me, and we will rise and go, so that both we and you and our substance may live and not die” (Gen. XLIII, 8).

There the Greek has *aposkeuē* where the Latin translator has “substance.” Our translators sometimes render it “possessions.” Here we have chosen “equipment,” provided that this word is understood to include human beings, beasts of burden, or all livestock. I do not know whether wives may also be included.

Nevertheless, since Scripture mentions six hundred thousand men on foot and adds, “apart from the equipment,” or “possessions,” or “substance,” or whatever other word may better translate *aposkeuē*, it is clear that people are also signified—whether slaves, women, or those ages that were not suited for military service—so that the six hundred thousand men on foot may be understood to mean only those capable of being armed in a military formation.

It is often asked whether the Hebrews could have reached such a number during the years they spent in Egypt, as the reckoning of the years found in Scripture seems to show. The first question is how many those years were.

For God says to Abraham, when the sacrifice involving a three-year-old heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove, and a pigeon had been made—before not only Isaac but even Ishmael had been born: “Know with certainty that your seed shall be a sojourner in a land that is not its own, and they shall reduce them to slavery and harm them for four hundred years” (Gen. XV, 13).

If we understand these four hundred years as the time they were in servitude under the Egyptians, it was not a short period in which the people could have multiplied so greatly. But Scripture gives unmistakable evidence that they did not spend so many years there.

Some think that the four hundred and thirty years should be reckoned from the time Jacob entered Egypt until the people were liberated from it through Moses, because Exodus says: “The sojourning of the children of Israel, which they sojourned in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, was four hundred and thirty years.”

They want the years of their servitude to be four hundred, on the grounds that Genesis says: “Know with certainty that your seed shall be a sojourner in a land that is not its own, and they shall reduce them to slavery and harm them for four hundred years.”

But since the years of servitude are reckoned after Joseph’s death—for while he was alive they not only did not serve there but even exercised authority—there is no way to count four hundred and thirty years in Egypt.

Jacob entered in the thirty-ninth year of his son’s life, since Joseph was thirty years old when he appeared before Pharaoh (Gen. XLI, 46) and began to reign under him. After seven years of abundance had passed, Jacob entered Egypt with his other sons in the second year of the famine (Gen. XLV, 6). Joseph was therefore then thirty-nine years old. After completing the years of his life—one hundred and ten—he died (Gen. L, 22, 25). Thus, after his father entered Egypt, Joseph lived there seventy-one years.

If we subtract those years from four hundred and thirty, the years of servitude—that is, the years after Joseph’s death—will amount not to four hundred but to three hundred and fifty-nine.

If we think that we should reckon from the time Joseph began to reign under Pharaoh, so that Israel is in a sense understood to have entered Egypt when his son had been raised there to such power, there would still be three hundred and fifty years. Tychonius wants these to be understood as four hundred, with a part taken for the whole: that is, fifty years as a part of the whole hundred. He proves that Scripture customarily uses this manner of speaking (Tychonius, *On the Rules*, book 5).

But if, as can be said with somewhat greater probability, we consider Israel to have entered Egypt when Joseph began to be sold there, we must subtract another thirteen years, so that we accept three hundred and thirty-seven years in place of four hundred.

Yet Scripture states that Caath, the son of Levi and the grandfather of Moses, entered Egypt with his grandfather Jacob (Gen. XLVI, 11), and says that Caath lived one hundred and thirty years (Exod. VI, 18, 20) [Note: [Col. 0611] Exodus VI, 18 now reports that Caath lived one hundred and thirty-three years, both in the Vulgate and in the Septuagint.]. It says that his son, Moses’ father, Ambram [Note: [Col. 0611] The printed editions have “Caath, Amram.” But the manuscripts consistently read “Cath, Ambram.” The Greek Septuagint has “Ambram,” not “Cath.” “Cath” does appear in Genesis 46, but in Exodus 6 it is written with the doubled *a*, “Kaath.”], lived one hundred and thirty-seven years; and that Moses was eighty years old when he liberated the people from Egypt (Exod. VII, 7).

Even if Caath had begotten the father of Moses in the year in which he died, and Ambram had likewise begotten Moses in the final year of his own life, the combined years—one hundred and thirty, one hundred and thirty-seven, and eighty—would amount to three hundred and forty-seven years, not four hundred and thirty.

If someone says that Caath, the son of Levi, was born in the final year of Joseph’s life [Note: [Col. 0611] The printed editions have “Jacob’s life.” It should be read, with the best manuscripts, “Joseph’s life.”], nearly seventy years can be added to that total, since Joseph lived approximately seventy-one years in Egypt after his father’s entry.

Accordingly, even in this case, the seventy years of Joseph’s life from Jacob’s entry into Egypt until Caath’s birth—if Caath is asserted to have been born then—together with Caath’s one hundred and thirty years, his son Ambram’s one hundred and thirty-seven years, and Moses’ eighty years, amount to four hundred and seventeen years, not four hundred and thirty.

Therefore, the reckoning followed by Eusebius in his *Chronicle* is evidently founded on clear truth. He reckons the four hundred and thirty years from the promise by which God called Abraham to leave his land and go into the land of Canaan (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 3260 from the creation of the world).

For when the Apostle praises and commends Abraham’s faith, referring to the promise in which he wishes Christ to be understood as having been prophesied—that is, the promise in which God promised Abraham that all the tribes of the earth would be blessed in him—he says: “I say this: the Law, which was made four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul a covenant confirmed by God, so as to abolish the promises” (Gal. III, 17).

Thus, the Apostle says that the Law was made four hundred and thirty years after the promise by which Abraham was called and believed God, not from the time when Jacob entered Egypt.

Moreover, Scripture itself in Exodus made this sufficiently clear. It did not say, “The sojourning of the children of Israel, which they sojourned in the land of Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years,” but expressly said, “which they sojourned in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers.”

It is therefore clear that the time of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob must also be included in the reckoning—from the time when Abraham began to sojourn in the land of Canaan; that is, from the promise in which the Apostle praises his faith, until the time when Israel entered Egypt.

Throughout that entire period the fathers sojourned in the land of Canaan, and afterward the seed of Israel in Egypt. Thus the four hundred and thirty years were completed from the promise until Israel’s departure from Egypt, when the Law was given on Mount Sinai—a Law that does not annul the covenant so as to abolish the promises.

Abraham, therefore, in the seventy-fifth year of his life, as Scripture says, went out into the land of Canaan (Gen. XII, 4), and he begot Isaac when he was one hundred years old (ibid. XXI, 5). Thus twenty-five years elapsed from the promise to the birth of Isaac. To these are added all the years of Isaac’s life, namely, one hundred and eighty (ibid. XXXV, 28), making two hundred and five. Jacob was then one hundred and twenty years old; for he and Esau, the twins, were born when their father was sixty (ibid. XXV, 26). Ten years later Jacob entered Egypt, when he was one hundred and thirty years old (ibid. XLVII, 9). Joseph, however, was thirty-nine. Thus from the promise to Jacob’s entry into Egypt there were two hundred and fifteen years.

Joseph, from that thirty-ninth year of his life, in which his father found him in Egypt, lived seventy-one years, since all the years of his life amounted to one hundred and ten (ibid. L, 22). When, therefore, seventy-one years are added to the two hundred and fifteen, the total is two hundred and eighty-six years. There remain one hundred and forty-four or forty-five years, during which the people of Israel are understood to have served in Egypt after Joseph’s death. Considering how greatly they could have multiplied if human fertility is taken into account, with the aid of the One who wished to multiply them exceedingly, it is found not to be surprising that the people went out of Egypt numbering six hundred thousand infantry, apart from the rest of their equipment and company, which included servants, women, and those of noncombatant age. [Col. 0613]

When God therefore said to Abraham, “Know assuredly that your offspring will be a sojourner in a land that is not its own; and they will reduce them to servitude, and they will harm them for four hundred years,” this should not be understood as though the people of God had been in that most oppressive servitude for four hundred years. Rather, because it is written, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (ibid. XXI, 12), from the year of Isaac’s birth to the year of the exodus from Egypt there are reckoned four hundred and five years. When, therefore, twenty-five years—the period from the promise to the birth of Isaac—are subtracted from the four hundred and thirty, it is not surprising that Scripture chose to call the solid total of four hundred and five years four hundred, since it commonly designates periods in such a way that what slightly exceeds or falls short of the total of a more complete number is not counted.

Thus the words, “They will reduce them to servitude, and they will harm them,” are not to be referred to four hundred years, as though they had held them in servitude for that entire period. Rather, the four hundred years are to be referred to the statement, “Your offspring will be a sojourner in a land that is not its own.” For whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt, that offspring was a sojourner before they received the land as an inheritance through God’s promise—which happened after they had been freed from Egypt. A hyperbaton is therefore to be understood here, and the order of the words is: “Know assuredly that your offspring will be a sojourner in a land that is not its own for four hundred years”; while the intervening words, “And they will reduce them to servitude, and they will harm them,” are to be understood as inserted, so that this insertion does not belong to the four hundred years. For it was toward the end of this total period of years—that is, after Joseph’s death—that the people of God came to endure harsh servitude in Egypt.

### XLVIII. [On XIII, 9]

What does it mean when, giving the command concerning Passover, he says, “It shall be for you as a sign upon your hand”? Is it to be understood as meaning “upon your works,” that is, something you ought to place before your works? Passover, on account of the slaughter of the sheep, pertains to faith in Christ and to the blood by which we were redeemed. This faith must be placed before works, so that it may in some manner be “upon the hand,” against those who gloried in works of the Law. The Apostle speaks at length about this matter [Note: [Col. 0613] Thus the manuscripts. Earlier printed editions have, “and no one can please God without faith,” and so on. Shortly afterward, Am., Er., and Lov. had placed *pertinent* (“they pertain”) instead of *pertinet* (“it pertains”), which certainly refers to faith and ought therefore to have been restored by us, on the authority of the manuscripts, with which the edition of Regensburg agrees.]; he wishes faith to be placed before works in such a way that good works depend upon it and proceed from it, not so that faith itself appears to be repaid as though it were earned by good works (Gal. III; Heb. XI). Faith belongs to grace; but if it is grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace (Rom. XI, 6).

### XLIX. [On XIII, 17]

“When Pharaoh sent the people away, God did not lead them by the road of the land of the Philistines, because it was near.” For God said, “Lest the people repent when they see battle and return to Egypt.” [Note: [Col. 0613] The printed editions have *per viam*, “by way of the road.” The word *per* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek Septuagint. Shortly afterward Am., Er., and Lov. have *quae prope erat*, “which was near.” The manuscripts and Regensburg, in agreement with the Septuagint (*hoti eggus ēn*), have *quia*, “because.”]

Here it is shown that everything which can rightly be done with prudence ought to be done in order to avoid adversity, even when God is manifestly the helper. [Col. 0614]

### L. [On XIII, 18]

“And in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt.” Is “generation” to be reckoned as one hundred years, so that it is called the fifth generation because it occurred after four hundred and thirty years? Or should this rather be understood in terms of human generations, from Jacob, who entered Egypt, to Moses, who went out with the people? Jacob is found to be the first, Levi the second, Kohath the third, Amram the fourth, and Moses the fifth. The Latin translator calls these *generations*, which the Greeks call *geneai* (γενεαί), the term used in the Gospel for generations. They are counted only through human succession, not by a number of years.

### LI. [On XIV, 13]

Moses said: “Take courage, stand firm [Note: [Col. 0614] The Vatican manuscripts have, “Take courage, stand,” omitting *et*, “and”; the Greek also lacks it.], and see the salvation that is from the Lord, which he will accomplish for you today. For as you have seen the Egyptians today, you will never see them again for all eternity.”

How are these words to be understood, since the Israelites afterward saw the Egyptians? Or is the meaning that those who were then seeing them did not see them again, because both those who pursued them died and each of these Israelites died on his own day, while their descendants saw the descendants of the Egyptians? Or should “You will not see them as you do today” be understood to mean, “not as you see them today pursuing you as enemies and advancing behind you in such a great column,” so that there is no difficulty at all, not even concerning the eternal time mentioned here? For even if the two groups will see one another at the time of the resurrection, they will certainly not see one another as they do today.

### LII. [On XIV, 15]

What does the Lord’s saying to Moses mean: “Why are you crying out to me?” Scripture has not mentioned anything about Moses’ cries, nor recorded him as praying. The meaning must be that he did this in the silence of his voice, crying out in his heart.

### LIII. [On XIV, 16]

“And you, lift up your rod and stretch out your hand over the sea.” This is the rod with which miracles were performed. Here it is said to be Moses’ rod; earlier, however, it was said to belong to his brother, since Aaron himself worked through it.

### LIV. [On XV, 12]

“You stretched out your right hand [Note: [Col. 0614] The printed editions have, “your hand.” The manuscripts have, “your right hand,” in agreement with the Septuagint, *tēn dexian sou*. Moreover, before *transvoravit* (“swallowed up”), the particle *et* (“and”), which was added in the printed editions, is absent.], and the earth swallowed them up.”

It is not surprising that “earth” is used for “water.” For the whole of this lower or outermost region of the world is designated by the name “earth,” in accordance with the frequent expression, “God who made heaven and earth.” In the distribution of that psalm, after the heavenly bodies have been mentioned, it says, “Praise the Lord from the earth,” and then includes in its praise things that also pertain to the waters (Ps. CXLVIII, 7).

### LV. [On XV, 10, 8]

“You sent your Spirit, and the sea covered them.” Here the Spirit of God is already mentioned for the fifth time, so that we should understand as belonging to this number also the statement, “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII, 19). First, where it is written, “The Spirit of God was hovering over the waters” (Gen. I, 2); second, where it is said, “My Spirit will not remain in these people, because they are flesh” [Note: [Col. 0615] Am., Er., and Lov. have, “because they are flesh,” singular. The edition of Regensburg, supported by our manuscripts, has *carnes*, plural, as in the Greek Septuagint.] (ibid. VI, 3); third, where Pharaoh says to Joseph, “Because the Spirit of God is in you” (ibid. XLI, 38); fourth, where the Egyptian magicians say, “This is the finger of God”; fifth, in this song, “You sent your Spirit, and the sea covered them.”

Let us remember that the Spirit of God is mentioned not only in connection with benefits but also in connection with vengeance. For what else did he say above: “By the Spirit of your wrath the water was divided”? This Spirit of God, therefore, was the Spirit of his wrath toward the Egyptians, whom the division of the waters harmed, since it enabled them to enter and then be overwhelmed when the waters returned. [Note: Most manuscripts read: “This Spirit of God upon the Egyptians; for the Spirit of his wrath harmed them.” Here *for* is added and *was* omitted.] But toward the children of Israel, who benefited from the division of the water, that Spirit was not the Spirit of God’s wrath.

Thus it is signified that, because of different operations and effects, the Spirit of God is called in different ways, although he is one and the same Spirit, namely, the one who is also understood as the Holy Spirit in the unity of the Trinity. Accordingly, I do not think that anyone other than this same Spirit is signified when the Apostle says, “For you did not receive the Spirit of slavery again unto fear [Note: [Col. 0615] The manuscripts of the best quality have, “unto fear,” in agreement with the Greek, *eis phobon*. This was also the reading of the Vulgate version in the ancient Corbie Bibles.]; but you received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII, 15). For by the same Spirit of God—that is, by the finger of God—with which the Law was written on the stone tablets (Exod. XXXI, 18), fear was instilled in those who did not yet understand grace, so that through the Law they might be convicted of their weakness and sins, and the Law might become their pedagogue, leading them to the grace that is in faith in Jesus Christ (Gal. III, 22–26).

Of this Spirit of adoption and grace—that is, of this work of the Spirit of God by which grace and rebirth unto eternal life are imparted—it is said, “The Spirit gives life,” whereas it was said above, “The letter kills” (II Cor. III, 6), that is, the written Law, which merely commands without the assistance of grace [Note: [Col. 0615] Several manuscripts have, “the written Law merely,” without the assistance of grace.].

### LVI. [On XV, 23, 24]

“They came to Marah, and they could not drink from Marah [Note: [Col. 0615] The printed editions have, “drink water from Mesra.” The manuscripts have, “drink from Marah,” as does the Septuagint.], because it was bitter.”

If the place received this name, meaning “bitterness,” because they could not drink water there on account of its bitterness—for *Marah* is interpreted as “Bitterness”—how did they come to Marah, unless Scripture called the place by the name it already bore when these things were written? The account was certainly written later than the events themselves.

### LVII. [On XV, 25]

“The Lord showed him a piece of wood, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet.”

Was this a kind of wood possessing such power, or could God, who performed such great miracles, have done this with any piece of wood? Yet the statement “he showed him” appears to indicate [Col. 0616] that the wood was already of such a kind that this could be done with it. Unless perhaps the place was one where wood could not be found at all, so that the divine assistance consisted precisely in the Lord showing him a piece of wood where none existed, and making the waters sweet through the wood, prefiguring the glory and grace of the cross. But even in the nature of such wood, whom should one praise except the Creator and the One who displayed it?

### LVIII. [On XVI, 4]

“The Lord said to Moses, ‘Behold, I will rain down bread for you from heaven. The people shall go out and gather enough for one day at a time, that I may test them, whether they will walk [Note: [Col. 0616] The printed editions have *si ambulent*, “whether they walk.” The manuscripts have *si ambulabunt*, “whether they will walk,” as does the Septuagint, *ei poreusontai*.] in my law or not.’”

This testing is a proving, not a seduction into sin. Nor is it a proving so that God might come to know something, but so that he might show it to the people themselves [Note: [Col. 0616] The printed editions have *sed ut ipse ipsis*, “but so that he himself might show it to them.” The manuscripts more correctly have *ipsos ipsis*, “so that he might show it to the people themselves.”], so that they might become more humble in asking for help and acknowledging God’s grace.

### LIX. [On XVI, 8]

Among other things, Moses and Aaron said to the people: “Because the Lord has heard your grumbling, with which you grumble against us. But what are we? Your grumbling is not against us, but against God.”

They did not wish to claim for themselves an authority equal to God’s. For they said, “What are we?” so that the people might understand that they had grumbled against the One who had sent Moses and Aaron and who worked through them.

This is not like the statement in which Peter says to Ananias: “How have you dared to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (Acts V, 3, 4). He did not say, “How have you dared to lie to me? You have not lied to me, but to God”; had he said that, the expression would have been similar. Nor did he say, “How have you dared to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to the Holy Spirit, but to God,” for by speaking in that way he would have denied that the Holy Spirit is God. Instead, after saying, “How have you dared to lie to the Holy Spirit?”—when Ananias thought that he had lied to human beings—Peter demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is God by adding, “You have not lied to human beings, but to God.”

### LX. [On XVI, 12]

God commands the people through Moses: “In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread.”

Here “bread” does not designate every kind of food. If it did, meat too would be included under that name, since meat is also food. Yet Moses does not call only what is made from grain “bread”; that is what we ordinarily call bread in the proper sense. He calls manna by the name of bread.

It is not without significance that he says he will give meat in the evening and bread in the morning. Something similar was signified in Elijah, when a raven brought him food (III Kings XVII, 6). Or perhaps the meat in the evening and bread in the morning signify the One who was handed over because of our offenses and raised because of our justification (Rom. IV, 25). In the evening he died from weakness and was buried; in the morning he appeared to the disciples, having risen in power.

### LXI. [On XVI, 33]

“Moses said to Aaron, ‘Take one golden vessel, put in it a full *gomer* of manna, and place it before God, so that it may be preserved for generations, as the Lord commanded.’”

It may be asked where Aaron was to place it before God, since there was neither an image nor yet an ark of the covenant. Or did he perhaps use the future tense—“you shall place it”—so that it might be understood that it could be placed before God at the time when the ark was to exist? Or does “before God” rather refer to something done through the very devotion of offering, wherever it might be placed? For where is God not present?

Yet the statement that follows, “And Aaron placed it before the testimony, to be kept,” supports the former interpretation. In this way Scripture spoke by prolepsis of what happened later, when the tabernacle of testimony came into existence.

### LXII. [On XVI, 35]

“The children of Israel ate manna for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They ate manna until they came into the territory of Phoenicia.”

Scripture has spoken by prolepsis—that is, by mentioning here something that also happened later—to indicate that the children of Israel ate nothing in the wilderness except manna. This is the meaning of “until they came to an inhabited land,” that is, a land that was no longer wilderness. It does not mean that as soon as they came to an inhabitable land they ceased to eat manna, but that they did not cease before then.

For the cessation of manna is signified after the Jordan had been crossed, when they ate the bread of the land. Thus, when they entered the inhabitable land, before crossing the Jordan, they could have eaten either only manna or both kinds of food; this is what may be understood, since manna is not said to have ceased until after the crossing of the Jordan.

Why, however, did they desire meat amid the scarcity of that wilderness, when they had gone out of Egypt with very large numbers of livestock? This is a difficult question. Perhaps it may be said that, since there were not enough pastures throughout the wilderness and the fertility of the herds seemed likely to diminish, they spared their animals, lest, when all the livestock had perished, they should also lack what was necessary for sacrifices—or whatever other explanation may resolve the question.

Nevertheless, it is more plausibly believed that they did not desire meat that they could have obtained from their livestock, but the meat that was lacking from the waters. For they did not find this in that wilderness. Hence they were given *ortygometra*, that is, birds, which many have translated into Latin as “quail,” although *ortygometra* is another kind of bird, even though it is not entirely unlike quail. God knew what they desired and with what kind of meat to satisfy their desire. But because Scripture had said that they desired meat and had not specified what kind of meat, the question arose.

### LXIII. [On XVI, 35]

“They ate manna until they came into the territory of Phoenicia.”

He had already said, “until they came to an inhabited land.” But because he had not specified precisely which land he meant, he appears to have expressed a certain precision by repeating the statement and saying, “into the territory of Phoenicia.” At that time, however, that land should be believed to have been called by this name; for it is not now called by that name.

There is another region called Phoenicia, belonging to Tyre and Sidon, and Israel’s having passed through it is not recorded. Yet perhaps Scripture could have called the land “Phoenicia” because palm trees had begun to appear there after the desolation of the wilderness, since “palm” is called *phoenix* in Greek. At the beginning of their journey they found a place where there had been seventy palm trees and twelve springs; afterward, however, they encountered the great expanse of the wilderness, where [Col. 0618] nothing of that kind existed, until they came to cultivated regions.

The more probable interpretation, however, is that we should believe the land was then called by this name. The names of many lands and places, like those of rivers and cities, have changed over the course of antiquity for specific reasons.

### LXIV. [On XVII, 5]

“The Lord said to Moses, ‘Go ahead of the people; take with you some of the elders of the people, and take in your hand the rod with which you struck the river.’”

The river is said to have been struck by Aaron, not Moses. Moses divided the sea with the same rod, but not the river. What, then, does “Take the rod with which you struck the river” mean? Or did he perhaps call the sea a river? If so, an example of this manner of expression must be sought.

Or is what Aaron did attributed rather to Moses because God commanded through Moses what Aaron was to do? Authority was in Moses, while the ministry was in Aaron. Indeed, in his very first words concerning his brother, God said this to Moses: “He shall be for you to the people, and you shall be for him in matters pertaining to God” (Exod. IV, 16).

### LXV. [On XVII, 9]

“Behold, I stand upon the top of the hill, and the rod of God is in my hand,” Moses says to Joshua son of Nun when he commanded that battle be waged against Amalek.

The rod is now called the rod of God, although it was first called Aaron’s rod and afterward Moses’ rod. In the same way, the spirit of Elijah is called the Spirit of God (Luke I, 17), because Elijah became a participant in it; so that rod could also be called God’s.

God’s righteousness is likewise called ours, although it is given by God. Speaking of it, the Apostle rebukes the Jews, saying, “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own righteousness” (Rom. X, 3), that is, as though it had been prepared by themselves for themselves. Against such people he says, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

### LXVI. [On XVIII, 12]

Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law before God—or, as other books have it, “in the presence of God”; in Greek it is written *enantion tou Theou* (ἐναντίον τοῦ Θεοῦ).

The question is where they could be before God, since there was neither a tabernacle nor an ark of the covenant, which were instituted only afterward. Nor can we understand this here as referring to the future, as we did with the manna that was placed in the golden vessel (above, Question 61). Therefore, we should understand “before God” as referring to something done in God’s honor. For where is God not present?

### LXVII. [On XVIII, 15]

Moses said to his father-in-law: “Because the people come to me to seek judgment from God; whenever they have a dispute and come to me, I judge each one and make known to them the ordinances of God and his law.”

How could Moses have said this when no law of God had yet been written down? Unless the law of God is eternal, which all devout minds consult, so that whatever they find in it they may do, command, or forbid, in accordance with what it has prescribed in its unchanging truth [Note: [Col. 0618] The printed editions have, “in accordance with what they have perceived in its unchanging truth,” except for the edition of Regensburg, which, together with our manuscripts, has, “in accordance with what it has prescribed.”].

For surely, although God spoke with Moses, we should not believe that he habitually consulted God about each individual matter whenever some dispute arose among the vast multitude that kept him occupied in judging cases from morning until evening. Yet unless he consulted the Lord presiding over his mind and wisely attended to his eternal law, he could not discover what was most just to decide among those engaged in disputes. [Col. 0619]

### LXVIII. [On XVIII, 18, 19]

In Jethro’s advice to his son-in-law Moses—not to let himself and the people be consumed by an intolerable exhaustion through being occupied with judging the people—the first question is why God allowed his servant, with whom he himself spoke about such great and important matters, to be admonished by a foreigner.

Through this, Scripture admonishes us that whenever counsel of truth is offered by any human being, it ought not to be despised. We must also consider whether God perhaps wished Moses to be admonished by a foreigner precisely where pride might tempt him: for Moses sat alone in judicial eminence while the entire people stood. Jethro’s own instruction indicates this interpretation, when he ordered that men who hated pride be chosen to judge the people’s cases.

Furthermore, how carefully the statement elsewhere in Scripture should be observed—“My son, do not let your affairs be numerous” (Eccli. XI, 10)—is sufficiently apparent here as well.

The words of Jethro giving Moses advice should also be considered. He says, “Now therefore listen to me, and I will give you counsel, and God will be with you.” Here it seems to me that an intellect excessively absorbed in human affairs is in some manner emptied of God; it becomes so much fuller as it extends more freely toward things above and eternal.

### LXIX. [On XVIII, 19, 20]

When he adds, “You shall be for the people in matters pertaining to God, and you shall refer their words to God; and you shall testify to them the ordinances of God and his law; and you shall show them the ways in which they shall walk and the works they shall do,” he shows that these duties are to be performed for the people as a whole.

For he does not say, “You shall refer each person’s words to God,” but “their words,” having said above, “You shall be for the people in matters pertaining to God.” After this he gives instructions that the individual matters they have among themselves should not be neglected. Men who were capable, worshiped God, were just, and hated pride were to be chosen and placed over thousands, others over hundreds, others over fifties, and others over tens.

In this way he removed from Moses himself burdensome and dangerous occupations, without burdening the others. For each thousand would have one man over them, beneath him ten others, beneath these twenty, and beneath those one hundred, so that scarcely anything would reach each individual official that required his judgment.

An example of humility is also presented here: Moses, with whom God spoke, did not disdain or reject the counsel of his foreign father-in-law. Yet concerning Jethro himself, since he had not been an Israelite, it is reasonably asked whether he should be counted, like Job, among men who worshiped the true God and were religiously wise, although he did not belong to that people. Indeed, this is the more credible view.

The words are ambiguous as to whether Jethro offered sacrifice to the true God among his people when he saw his son-in-law, or whether Moses himself worshiped him. Even if worship had been explicitly mentioned, it could be understood as honor rendered to a father-in-law, in the manner in which honor is ordinarily shown to human beings by way of respect. Thus it is written of Abraham that he worshiped the sons of Heth (Gen. XXIII, 7).

It is not easy to determine whom he calls *grammatoeisagogeis* (γραμματοεισαγωγεῖς) after the officials, since we have no use for this term either among offices or among teaching positions. Some learned interpreters have understood it to mean teachers, specifically of letters, who introduce people to literacy, as the Greek word suggests. This indicates that the Hebrews possessed writing before the Law was given. I do not know whether it can be discovered when writing first began. Some think that it began with the first human beings, was transmitted to Noah, then to Abraham’s ancestors, and from them to the people of Israel; but I do not know how this can be proved.

### LXX. [On XIX, 1–11]

“In the third month after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. They departed from Rephidim and came into the wilderness of Sinai, and Israel encamped there opposite the mountain. Moses went up to the mountain of God, and the Lord called him from the mountain, saying, ‘Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and declare to the children of Israel,’” and so forth.

A little later: “Go down and testify to the people, and purify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will descend upon Mount Sinai before all the people.”

On this day the Law is found to have been given, written on stone tablets by the finger of God, as the subsequent passage shows (Exod. XXXI, 18). This third day appears to be the third day of the third month after Israel’s departure from Egypt.

From the day on which they celebrated Passover—that is, sacrificed and ate the lamb, which was the fourteenth day of the first month (ibid. XII, 6)—until the day on which the Law was given, fifty days are counted: seventeen days of the first month, counting the days remaining after the fourteenth; then all thirty days of the second month, making forty-seven; and the third day of the third month, which is the fiftieth day from the feast of the slaughtered lamb.

Thus, in this shadow of what was to come, just as the Law written by the finger of God was given on the fiftieth day after the feast of the slaughtered lamb, so in the very reality of the New Testament fifty days are counted from the feast of the immaculate Lamb, Christ Jesus, and the Holy Spirit was given from on high [Note: [Col. 0620] Er. and Lov. have, “when the Holy Spirit was given.” Would it not be better to read “and”? This conjecture is supported by another passage of Saint Augustine, namely Sermon 8, §§13–14, where these same words are repeated. M.] (Acts II, 2–4). We have already said above, on the testimony of the Gospel, that the finger of God is the Holy Spirit (above, Question 25).

### LXXI. [On XX, 1–17]

The question is how the Ten Commandments of the Law should be divided. Are there four commandments up to and including the commandment concerning the Sabbath, which pertain to God himself, and six remaining commandments, the first of which is “Honor your father and your mother,” which pertain to human beings? Or are there rather three commandments in the former group and seven in the latter?

Those who say that the first group contains four separate the statement, “You shall have no other gods besides me,” so that “You shall not make for yourself an idol,” and so forth, is a different commandment, in which the worship of images is prohibited. They wish to treat as one commandment “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house,” together with everything that follows to the end.

Those who say that the first group contains three and the second seven wish to treat as one commandment everything prescribed concerning the worship of the one God, so that nothing else besides him may be worshiped as God. They divide the final commandments into two, so that “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” is one and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house” is another.

Neither group, however, doubts that there are ten commandments, since Scripture testifies to this.

It seems to me, nevertheless, more appropriate to understand the first group as three and the second as seven, because, to those who look more carefully, the three pertaining to God appear to signify the Trinity more explicitly.

Indeed, the statement “You shall have no other gods besides me” is explained more fully when the worship of images is forbidden. The coveting of another man’s wife and the coveting of another man’s house differ so greatly in the act of sinning that to the statement “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house” Scripture adds, “nor his field, nor his servant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his beast of burden, nor any of his livestock, nor anything that belongs to your neighbor.”

The coveting of another man’s wife appears to have been distinguished from the coveting of any other foreign possession, since the two statements begin separately: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house.” To the latter it then adds the other things.

For when it had said, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” it did not connect the other things to that commandment by saying, “nor his house, nor his field, nor his servant,” and so forth. Rather, these things plainly appear to be joined together and to be contained under one commandment, distinct from the commandment in which the wife is named.

As for the statement, “You shall have no other gods besides me,” what follows plainly constitutes a more detailed exposition of it. For to what else do the words refer—“You shall not make for yourself an idol or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the water beneath the earth; you shall not worship them or serve them”—except to the statement, “You shall have no other gods besides me”?

Yet another question arises: how does “You shall not steal” differ from the commandment given shortly afterward concerning not coveting the possessions of one’s neighbor? Not everyone who covets another person’s possession steals; but if everyone who steals covets another person’s possession, then what pertains to theft could have been included in the general commandment forbidding the coveting of another’s property.

Similarly, how does “You shall not commit adultery” differ from what is said shortly afterward, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”? The latter could also have been understood in the statement “You shall not commit adultery.”

Unless perhaps, in those two commandments—against adultery and against theft—the acts themselves are marked, while in these final commandments the coveting itself is marked. These differ so greatly that someone may at times commit adultery without coveting his neighbor’s wife, when some other motive is involved; at another time he may covet her without committing adultery, because he fears the punishment. Perhaps the Law wished to show that both are sins.

It is also customary to ask whether fornication is included under the term “adultery.” This is a Greek word, which Scripture now uses in place of the Latin term. The Greeks, however, call only adulterers *moichoi*.

But this Law was certainly given not only to the men of the people but also to the women. A woman should not think that, because it says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” nothing here is commanded of her, and that she may therefore licitly covet the husband of her neighbor.

If, then, from what was said to the man, this is understood to apply also to the woman, although it was not stated in words that explicitly include her, how much more does the commandment “You shall not commit adultery” bind both sexes, since the commandment itself can be referred to both, just as “You shall not kill,” “You shall not steal,” and other similar commandments, when one sex is not explicitly named, appear to be commonly addressed to both?

Nevertheless, when one sex is expressly named, the more honored sex is named—that is, the male—so that from this the woman may also understand what is commanded to her.

Accordingly, if a woman who has a husband is an adulteress when she has intercourse with a man who is not her husband, even if that man has no wife, then surely a man who has a wife is also an adulterer when he has intercourse with a woman who is not his wife, even if she has no husband.

But whether, if a man who has no wife has intercourse with a woman who has no husband, both are held liable for transgressing this commandment is rightly questioned. For if they are not held liable, fornication is not prohibited in the Decalogue, but only adultery—although every adultery is also understood to be fornication, as Scripture speaks.

For the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery” (Matt. V, 32). Here he certainly called it fornication if a woman who has a husband sins with another man, which is adultery. Thus every adultery is also called fornication in Scripture.

But whether every fornication can also be called adultery, I do not at present encounter an example of such usage in the same Scriptures. If not every fornication can also be called adultery, I do not know whether it can be discovered where in the Decalogue that fornication is prohibited which is committed by men who have no wives with women who have no husbands.

But if the term “theft” is rightly understood to include every unlawful appropriation of another’s property—for the one who prohibited theft did not permit robbery, but plainly wished the whole to be understood from the part, namely, whatever is unlawfully taken from another’s possessions—then surely the term “adultery” must also be understood to prohibit every unlawful intercourse and every illegitimate use of those bodily members.

And when it is said, “You shall not kill,” it should not be thought that this commandment is violated when the Law kills or when God commands someone to be killed. The one who commands does this, since it is not permissible to refuse the ministry.

In the statement, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor,” it is commonly asked whether every lie is prohibited—for perhaps this commandment is not directed against those who say that one ought to lie when the lie benefits someone and harms no one to whom one lies. Such a lie is not, after all, “against your neighbor,” so that Scripture may seem to have added this qualification, whereas it could have said simply, “You shall not bear false witness,” just as it said, “You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery,” [Col. 0623] “You shall not steal.” But this is a major question, and cannot suitably be explained by those in a hurry: how are we to understand, “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7), and “Do not desire to utter any lie” (Ecclus. 7:14), and other statements of this kind?

### LXXII. [Book II, 20:18]

“And all the people saw the voice, and the lamps, and the voice of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking.”

It is customary to ask how the people “saw the voice,” since a voice seems to belong not to sight but rather to hearing. But just as I said a little earlier—“Let it be seen,” concerning all the things I have said—so “to see” is commonly used in a general sense, not only of the bodily faculty but also of the mind. Hence we read, “When Jacob saw that there was food in Egypt” (Gen. 42:1, according to the Septuagint), although he was absent from Egypt.

Some, however, have thought that “to see the voice” means nothing other than “to understand,” since understanding is the sight of the mind. Yet if it had been necessary here to say briefly that the people saw the voice and the lamps, and the voice of the trumpet and the smoking mountain, a greater difficulty would have arisen: how did they hear the lamps and the smoking mountain, which belong to the sense of sight? Unless one says that it should not have been stated so briefly, but that the whole sentence should have read: “They heard the voice and saw the lamps, and heard the voice of the trumpet and saw the smoking mountain.”

There were, in fact, two kinds of voice: one from the clouds, like thunder, and one from the trumpet—if indeed he called “voice” the sound that came from the clouds. Consequently, it is better that, in the matters belonging to the sense of hearing, a general sense—namely, that of seeing—was used, since Scripture wished to include everything briefly, than that in matters belonging to the sense of sight hearing should be understood implicitly; for we do not ordinarily speak in that manner. We commonly say, “See what is making that sound”; we do not commonly say, “Hear what is shining.”

### LXXIII. [Book II, 20:19]

“Speak to us yourself, and let God not speak to us, lest we die.”

This very clearly signifies that fear belongs rather to the Old Testament, just as love belongs to the New—although the New is concealed in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New. Yet it is not sufficiently clear how a people of this kind can be said to see the voice of God, if “seeing” is to be understood as “understanding,” when they are afraid that God may speak to them lest they die.

### LXXIV. [Book II, 20:20]

“And Moses said to them, ‘Be steadfast, for God has come to you in order to test you, so that his fear may be in you and you may not sin.’”

They had to be restrained from sins by fearing that they might suffer tangible punishments, since they were not yet able to love righteousness. In this consisted their testing by the Lord, by which they were proved, so that it might become evident what sort of people they were—not so that they might become known to God, from whom nothing about them was hidden, but so that they might become known to one another and to themselves.

Yet the difference of the Old Testament is strongly commended by these terrors, as is also stated most openly in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb. 12:24–28).

### LXXV. [Book II, 20:21]

“But Moses entered into the cloud where God was”—that is, where the signs by which God might be recognized became more explicit. For how could he be in the cloud, whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain, unless in the sense that he is nowhere absent, since he is in no place [Note: [Col. 0623] The editions read *deest* (“is lacking”); all the manuscripts instead have *est* (“is”).]?

[Col. 0624]

### LXXVI. [Book II, 20:23]

“You shall not make for yourselves gods of silver, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold.”

What was inculcated in the first commandment is repeated. By “gods of silver and gold,” therefore, all images are understood together, just as in that psalm: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold” (Ps. 113:4; 135:15).

### LXXVII. [Book II, 21:2]

As for what is prescribed concerning the Hebrew slave—that he serve six years and then be released freely—the apostolic authority commands Christian slaves to be subject to their masters, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be blasphemed (Eph. 6:5; 1 Tim. 6:1), lest Christian slaves demand this from their masters. It is sufficiently clear that the former command was given in a mystical sense, since God also commanded that the ear of the slave who refused that freedom should be pierced with an awl at the doorpost.

### LXXVIII. [Book II, 21:7–11]

“But if someone sells his daughter as a maidservant [Note: [Col. 0624] Thus consistently in the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The editions, however, read *in famulam* (“as a maidservant”).], she shall not depart as the maidservants depart. But if she does not please her master, who did not designate her for himself, he shall compensate her. He shall not have the authority to sell her to a foreign nation, because he has rejected her. But if he designates her for his son, he shall treat her according to the rights of daughters. But if he takes another for him, he shall not deprive her of what is necessary—clothing, and her marital relations. If he does not do these three things for her, she shall depart freely, without payment.”

These exceedingly obscure words and expressions have made this passage so difficult that our interpreters scarcely found how to explain it. What is said here is also very obscure in the Greek wording. Nevertheless, I shall explain, as best I can, what it seems to mean.

“If someone,” he says, “sells his daughter as a maidservant”—that is, so that she may be a maidservant, whom the Greeks call *οἰκέτην* (*oikétēn*, a household servant)—“she shall not depart as the maidservants depart.” This should be understood to mean that she will not depart in the manner in which Hebrew maidservants depart after six years. The law must indeed be understood to have been given also concerning the Hebrew female slave, since it is observed with regard to males.

Why, then, will this woman not depart in that manner? Because in that servitude she is understood to have been humiliated by the fact that her master has had intercourse with her. This becomes somewhat clearer in what follows. For the text continues: “But if she does not please her master, who did not designate her for himself”—that is, did not make her his wife—“he shall compensate her.” This is the meaning of what it said above: she shall not depart as maidservants depart. It is just [Note: [Col. 0624] The manuscripts read *iussa est* (“she is ordered”);] that she receive something in return for having been humiliated, since he did not have intercourse with her in such a way as to make her his wife—that is, to designate her for himself.

Some interpreters, however, have said that “he shall compensate her” means “he shall redeem her.” If the Greek had said *ἀπολυτρώσεται* (*apolytrṓsetai*, “he shall redeem”), it would have been written as it is written, “He himself will redeem Israel” (Ps. 129:8); for *ἀπολυτρώσεται* is indeed written there. In this passage, however, one reads *ἀπολυτρώσει* (*apolytrṓsei*), which is understood to mean that she receives something, rather than that something is given for her redemption. To whom would her master give payment in order to redeem a woman whom he himself possesses as a maidservant?

“He shall not have the authority to sell her to a foreign nation, because he has rejected her”: that is, it does not follow from his having rejected her that he has authority to sell her—namely, that he may exercise such dominion over her as to sell her lawfully even to a foreign nation. “He has rejected her” is equivalent to “he has rejected her”;” he rejected her by humiliating her, that is, by having intercourse with her without making her his wife. The Greek says *ἠθέτησεν* (*ēthétēsen*), which we translated “he rejected.” Scripture uses this verb in Jeremiah: “As a woman rejects the man with whom she has had intercourse” (Jer. 3:20).

The text then continues: “But if he designates her for his son, he shall treat her according to the rights of daughters.” Here it begins to become clear what was meant above by “who did not designate her for himself.” For what else can “if he designates her for his son” mean than that he joins her to his son as a wife? For it says, “he shall treat her according to the rights of daughters”—that is, he shall give her over as a daughter, furnishing her with a dowry.

It then adds: “But if he takes another for him”—that is, if he does not regard this woman as wife for his son, but takes another for him—“he shall not deprive her of what is due: food, clothing, and her marital relations.” He shall give her what is appropriate under the same law, since she did not remain the wife of his son, just as he would have given her had he not designated her for himself, although he had humiliated her by having intercourse with her.

What we translated as “her marital relations,” the Greek has *ὁμιλίαν* (*homilían*), literally “conversation” or “association.” Scripture uses this term as a more decorous designation for sexual intercourse. But what does “he shall not deprive her of intercourse” mean except that he shall give her compensation for intercourse?

For in Daniel, when the elders bore false witness against Susanna, they said: “A young man came to her, who was hiding in a concealed place, and he had intercourse with her.” But Daniel, questioning them about this very matter, said: “Under what tree did you see them conversing?”—referring to what they had said, namely, that he had intercourse with her. Then, reproving and convicting the other, he said: “Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty deceived you, and desire perverted your heart. Thus you used to act toward the daughters of Israel; but they, fearing, submitted to you” (Dan. 13:37, 54–58).

The Greek has *ὡμίλουν ὑμῖν* (*hōmíloun hymin*), which could be rendered word for word in Latin as “they were speaking with you”; by this, intercourse is signified. For where it says, “Under what tree did you seize them?”, the Greek has, “You seized them conversing with one another”; and there too intercourse is signified.

Therefore, when Scripture adds concerning the woman under discussion, “But if he does not do these three things for her, she shall depart freely,” this is understood as follows: if he has not humiliated her by intercourse, nor joined her to his son, nor expelled her after taking another woman for his son, she shall depart freely—that is, it is enough for her not to be held in servitude. She shall depart without receiving anything, like the Hebrew male slave.
