For her master is not permitted to marry her to a non-Hebrew man, since she may not be handed over to a foreign nation. But if he joins her to a Hebrew male slave, this is understood to mean that she will depart freely with him, never separated from her husband.

### LXXIX. [Book II, 21:12–13]

“If someone strikes another and he dies, he shall be put to death. But if he did not intend it, and God delivered him into his hands, I will give you a place to which he may flee.”

The question is how this was said: “If he did not intend it, and God delivered him into his hands,” as though, even if he killed intentionally, he could have killed only if God delivered the victim into his hands.

It is therefore understood that God alone caused the death when someone is killed by an unwilling agent; and because God alone caused it, the text says, “But God delivered him into his hands.” When someone kills intentionally, however, both he himself kills and God delivers the victim into his hands. The difference, then, is that in the former case God alone acts, whereas in the latter both God and the human being act, because of the killer’s will. Yet the human being does not act as God does: God acts only justly, whereas the human being is worthy of punishment—not because he killed someone whom God did not wish to be killed, but because he acted through iniquity. He did not provide service to God who commanded it; he served his own wicked desire.

Thus, in one and the same deed, God is praised for his hidden justice, while the human being is punished for his own iniquity. The fact that God did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all (Rom. 8:32) does not excuse Judas, who likewise delivered Christ over to death (Matt. 26:48).

### LXXX. [Book II, 21:22–25]

“But if two men quarrel and strike a pregnant woman [Note: [Col. 0626] So the manuscripts of better quality, in accordance with the Septuagint and the Syriac, Chaldaic, Samaritan, and Arabic versions. The editions, however, read: ‘and if someone strikes a woman carrying a fetus in her womb.’], and her child comes out not yet formed, he shall suffer loss according to what the woman’s husband imposes, and he shall pay with a demand. But if it is formed, he shall give life for life.”

It seems to me that this is said for the sake of some symbolic meaning, rather than because Scripture is concerned with such occurrences in themselves. For if it were concerned with preventing a pregnant woman who had been struck from being forced into miscarriage, it would not have specified two men quarreling, since this could also be done by one man who quarreled with the woman—or even by one who did not quarrel with her but did it out of a desire to harm another’s offspring.

The fact that it did not wish the unformed child to be treated as homicide certainly shows that it did not regard what is carried in the womb in that condition as a human being. Here the question concerning the soul is usually raised: whether what is not formed can even be understood as animated, and whether therefore it is not homicide because it cannot be said to have been deprived of life if it did not yet possess a soul.

The text continues: “But if it is formed, he shall give life for life.” What else can this mean except that he himself shall die? For in the other cases as well the law commands on this occasion: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, bruise for bruise”—plainly according to the equity of retaliation.

The Law established these penalties in order to show what vengeance is due. For unless the Law made known what vengeance was due, how would it be known what forgiveness should cancel, so that we might say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12)? The Law therefore reveals who are debtors, so that when forgiveness is granted it may become clear what is being forgiven. For we would not forgive debts unless we learned from the Law what was owed to us.

If, then, that unformed child already existed, but was in some manner still formlessly animated—since the great question concerning the soul must not be rushed into by the rashness of an unexamined judgment—the Law did not wish this to pertain to homicide because a living soul cannot yet be said to exist in a body that lacks sensation, if it is in such a state of unformed flesh and therefore not yet endowed with the senses.

But what he said—“And he shall pay with a demand,” whatever the woman’s husband should determine ought to be paid for the unformed child—is not easy to understand. For the Greek term *ἀξίωμα* (*axíōma*) has several possible meanings, and “with a demand” is a more tolerable rendering than some alternative would be. Perhaps the husband will demand that he pay, so that in this way [Note: [Col. 0627] The editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read: *postulabit ut de eo modo* (“he will demand that in this way”). Ratramnus and seven manuscripts read: *postulavit ut det eo modo* (“he demanded that he pay in this way”). Five other reliable manuscripts read: *postulabit ut det, ut eo modo* (“he will demand that he pay, so that in this way”). Perhaps the text should read: “the judge will demand that he pay in this way.” Or perhaps, with a prefixed negation: “he will not demand that he pay in this way,” and so forth.] he may satisfy God, even if neither the husband nor the wife seeks it.

### LXXXI. [Book II, 21:28]

“But if a bull gores a man or a woman and the person dies, the bull shall be stoned with stones, and its flesh shall not be eaten; but the bull’s owner shall be innocent.”

It belongs to justice that an animal harmful to human beings should be killed. What is said about the bull should be understood as a part standing for the whole—that is, whatever among domesticated animals subject to human use is dangerous to human beings.

But if it must be killed, why must it be stoned? For what difference does it make by what death an animal that must be removed is removed? Moreover, why did he add that its flesh was not to be eaten, unless all these things signify something—which is what Scripture is especially accustomed to consider?

### LXXXII. [Book II, 21:35]

“But if one man’s bull gores his neighbor’s bull and it dies, they shall sell the living bull and divide its price, and they shall divide the bull that died.”

Is this legal provision to be observed only with regard to a bull, and not with regard to every animal in a similar case? Here too, a part must be understood as standing for the whole. Yet this cannot be done with the flesh of the slaughtered animal, since such flesh is not eaten.

### LXXXIII. [Book II, 22:1]

What is the reason for returning five for one calf, but four for one sheep, unless this is understood to signify something?

### LXXXIV. [Book II, 22:2]

“But if a thief is found breaking in and is struck and dies, he is not guilty of homicide. But if the sun rises over him, he is guilty; he shall die in return for the death” [Note: [Col. 0627] The printed editions have *et morte morietur* (“and he shall die by death”). The manuscripts have *pro morte morietur* (“he shall die in return for the death”), that is, correspondingly, according to the Greek Septuagint *antapothaneitai*.].

It is therefore understood that it does not count as homicide if a thief is killed at night, but that it does count as homicide if he is killed by day. This is the meaning of “if the sun rises over him.” For it could then be discerned that he had come to steal, not to kill, and therefore ought not to be killed.

The same rule is found in the ancient secular laws [Note: [Col. 0627] Namely, in the Twelve Tables, from which Cicero quotes this very law in his *Oration for Milo*], although those laws are later than this one: a nocturnal thief may be killed with impunity by any means, but a daytime thief only if he defends himself with a weapon—for by then he is more than a thief.

### LXXXV. [Book II, 22:9]

What does “the one who is convicted by God shall repay double” mean, unless God sometimes wishes, by giving a sign, to expose the perjurer?

### LXXXVI. [Book II, 22:28]

“You shall not curse the gods.”

The question is whom he called “gods”: whether the rulers who judge the people, as it was said of Moses that he had been appointed “a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1), so that the following words explain the expression by showing whom he called gods: “You shall not curse the ruler of your people.” The Greek has, “You shall not speak evil.”

Or should it be understood according to what the Apostle says: “For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, just as there are many gods and many lords” (1 Cor. 8:5)? By adding “just as there are,” he wished those gods to be understood who are rightly called gods. Yet *λατρεία* (*latreía*), which is the Greek term translated into Latin as *servitus* (“service”), in the sense of service belonging to religion, is owed only to the one true God, who is our God.

Those who are called gods—even if there are some who are rightly so called—are forbidden to be cursed; they are not commanded to be honored with sacrifices or with any acts of *latria*.

### LXXXVII. [Book II, 23:2]

“You shall not join the many in evil.”

Let no one defend himself on the grounds that he acted with many others, or therefore suppose that it is not a sin.

### LXXXVIII. [Book II, 23:3]

“And you shall not have pity on the poor in judgment.”

If he had not added “in judgment,” there would have been a major difficulty. Yet it would have been understood even if it had not been written. For above he had said, “You shall not join the multitude in declining with the many, so as to pervert judgment”; and therefore “you shall not have pity on the poor” could have been understood as referring to judgment.

But since the words are added, there is no question that this is the command: lest, when we judge, we should see that justice favors the rich against the poor, and think that we are acting rightly if, out of compassion, we favor the poor against justice. Mercy is good, therefore, but it must not be contrary to judgment. Scripture calls “judgment” that which is just.

Yet lest anyone, because of this statement, think that God prohibits mercy, what follows is most appropriately added: “But if you meet your enemy’s ox, or his beast of burden, wandering, you shall lead it back and return it to him.” Thus you know that you are not prohibited from showing mercy; indeed, show mercy even toward your enemies when you have freedom from judging. For when you lead back your enemy’s wandering ox and return it to him, you are not sitting as a judge between litigants.

### LXXXIX. [Book II, 23:10–11]

“For six years you shall sow your land and gather its produce; but in the seventh year you shall grant it release and give it rest. The poor of your nation shall eat, and the wild beasts shall eat what remains. You shall do the same with your vineyard and your olive grove.”

It may be asked what the poor gather if, in the seventh year, the land is spared to such an extent that it is not even sown. For the statement “the poor of your nation shall eat” does not concern the vineyard and olive grove, since from unsown land they can take nothing, where crops cannot grow. Concerning the vineyard and olive grove, it later says that the same thing is to be done; consequently, the earlier statement is understood to concern fields used for grain.

Or should it be understood as follows: “For six years you shall sow your land and gather its produce”—that is, “you shall sow for six years and gather”—but in the seventh year you shall not gather, with “you shall sow” understood even though it is not stated, so that sowing and gathering belong to the six years, while in the seventh the crop that has been sown is left?

For what will the poor have from it, when what remains is also given to wild beasts—namely, those that can feed on such crops, such as boars, deer, and animals of that kind? Yet this would not be said unless for the sake of some symbolic meaning.

For if, with regard to the commandments given to human beings, “God does not care about oxen” (1 Cor. 9:9)—which is not understood to mean that he does not himself feed those that neither sow nor reap nor gather into a barn, but rather that he does not consider it his concern to instruct human beings by a command about how they should provide for their ox—how much less is it his concern to command concerning wild beasts how human beings should provide for them, since he himself feeds them with the riches of nature, fruitful everywhere, and feeds them during the other six years as well, when what has been sown is gathered?

### XC. [Book II, 23:19]

“You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk.”

I do not know whether the literal meaning of these words can be discovered. If we understand that the boiling of a lamb in milk was prohibited for the sake of some symbolic meaning, there is no customary practice of boiling it in that way. If, however, the command concerns the days during which it is suckled, which Jew ever observed the rule of not boiling a lamb until it had ceased to suck?

What does “in its mother’s milk” mean? Even if this is the intended meaning, could it not be boiled without transgressing the command if, after the lamb was born, its mother died and it was suckled by another ewe? No one doubts that the command was given to signify something. But even those things that can be carried out as a matter of observance were not commanded without reason; they signify something. How this command is to be observed according to the literal meaning of the words is either impossible or not clear.

Nevertheless, I approve the interpretation concerning Christ: that this prophecy foretold that the Lamb would not be killed by the Jews, since Herod, seeking him in order to kill him, did not find him (Matt. 2:13–16). The words “you shall boil” would then refer to the fire of the Passion, that is, to tribulation. Hence it is said: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation in tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27:6).

Since the infant did not then suffer, although when Herod sought him such danger appeared imminent, this was foretold in the words, “You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk.”

It may perhaps also be appropriate that others say this command was given through the Prophet so that good Israelites would not associate with the wicked Jews by whom Christ suffered as a lamb in its mother’s milk—that is, at the time when he was conceived. For women are said to begin producing milk from the time they conceive. That Christ was conceived and suffered in the same month is shown both by the observance of Passover and by the date of his birth, which is well known to the churches.

He who was born in the ninth month, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, was certainly conceived in the first month, around the eighth day before the Kalends of April; and this was also the season of his Passion. Thus he was “in his mother’s milk,” that is, in the days of his mother [Note: [Col. 0629] The following additional interpretation was found in a copy of the *Questions* written approximately eight hundred years ago at Corbie, in these words:

“There is another, easier sense: ‘You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk.’ Do not send the little ones, still suckling, of whom the Apostle says, ‘I gave you milk to drink, not food,’ into a premature Passion, as though this had been said of Christ, who spared such disciples while they were still at that stage. Offering himself on their behalf, he said, ‘If therefore you seek me, let these go away.’ And so that it might be understood that they were still weak and less fit for the Passion, like lambs in their mother’s milk, the Evangelist continued: ‘That the saying might be fulfilled which he had spoken: Those whom you gave me I have not lost any of them.’ From this it is evident that, had they suffered then, they would have perished. What they did not suffer then, they suffered later—not still lambs in milk, but rams already in the flock.’

Some other material concerning this interpretation precedes it in the same manuscript, but it was evidently all transferred by the copyist from the margin into the text. For it is entirely absent from the other manuscripts of the *Questions* [Col. 0630], but it exists in two of our manuscripts of Eugippius’s collection: in one in continuous sequence, and in the other with the following prefatory notice: ‘From this point the following material from another work of St. Augustine has been added.’

We therefore suspect that the copy of the *Questions* used by the scribe of the first-mentioned Corbie manuscript contained material that Eugippius the abbot, nearly Augustine’s contemporary, had written in his own hand as marginal notes. Thus, in Book 1 on Genesis, Question 117, section 3, before the words “Yet there is no easier [interpretation],” he inserted in the middle of the text: “From here it should be written.” We suppose this was a note by Eugippius instructing that what follows should be copied; the same material is still found in his collection today.]

[Col. 0630]

### XCI. [Book II, 23:20–21]

“Behold, I am sending my angel before your face, to guard you on the way and to bring you into the land that I have prepared for you. Pay attention to yourself and listen to him; do not disbelieve him, for he will not withhold anything from you, since my name is upon him.”

This is clearly understood of the one whose name was changed so that he might be called Jesus [Note: [Col. 0630] Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read “Israel,” but the manuscripts and Ratramnus more correctly read “Jesus”: that is, Joshua.], for he brought the people into the promised land.

### XCII. [Book II, 23:25–27]

“And you shall serve the Lord your God; and I will bless your bread, your wine, and your water, and I will remove sickness from you. There shall be none who fails to bear children, nor shall there be barrenness in your land. I will fill up the number of your days. And I will send fear before you, and I will drive mad all the nations into which you enter,” and so forth.

Although these promises can also be understood spiritually, when they are understood according to the temporal happiness of human beings they belong to the Old Testament. There, although the commandments—including those that do not signify something in a sacramental sense—are likewise directed toward good conduct, the promises are nevertheless carnal and earthly.

Thus, in Psalm 72, the man of God says that his steps had nearly slipped and been poured out when he was jealous of sinners and observed the peace of sinners. For he saw the wicked enjoying in abundance the very things that, according to the Old Testament, he himself expected from the Lord God, whom he served in the hope of this reward.

When an impious thought began to creep over him from this circumstance, so that he supposed God did not care about human affairs, he says that he was corrected. He did not dare to condemn the authority of the saints, and he began to understand, saying: “This is labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their end” (Ps. 72:2–17).

There the rewards belonging to the New Testament will be given, which the wicked will not receive; and then there will be punishments for the wicked, which none of the godly will experience.

### XCIII. [Book II, 23:28]

“And I will send wasps before you, and he will drive out [Note: [Col. 0630] Erasmus and Louvain read *ejiciam* (“I will drive out”); the manuscripts, as well as Ratramnus and Amerbach, read *ejiciet* (“he will drive out”), referring to the wasp. Here there is a transition from the plural to the singular, as explained in *Locutions*, Book 2, locution 107.] the Amorites, the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites from before you.”

The question concerns what is to be understood by these wasps. God both promises this and the Book of Wisdom says that it was fulfilled, where it states: “He sent wasps ahead of his army” (Wis. 12:8).

Yet we do not read that this happened, either in the time of Moses, or under Joshua son of Nun, or under the judges, or under the kings. Consequently, these wasps may perhaps be understood as the stings of fear by which the aforementioned nations were driven and compelled to yield to the children of Israel.

For God is speaking, and if something is said figuratively in his speech and is not fulfilled literally, this does not impede the historical truth of the narrative, in which the truth of the account is discerned. Nor is the narrative of the Evangelists impeded in its literal sense if something is said figuratively by Christ.

### XCIV. [Book II, 23:33]

“If you serve their gods, they will be a stumbling block to you.”

Here the Greek has *δουλεύσῃς* (*douleúsēs*, “you serve”), not *λατρεύσῃς* (*latreúsēs*, “you worship”). From this it is understood that *δουλεία* (“service,” servitude) is owed to God as Lord, whereas *λατρεία* (“worship”) is owed only to God as God.

### XCV. [Book II, 24:1–3]

“And he said to Moses, ‘Go up to the Lord, you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and they shall worship the Lord from afar. Moses alone shall draw near to the Lord, but they shall not draw near, and the people shall not go up with them.’ Moses entered and related to the people all the words of God and the ordinances. And all the people answered with one voice, saying, ‘All the words that the Lord has spoken we shall do, and we shall hear.’”

Up to this point in Scripture, the “ordinances” are understood to be those given to the people for observance. Beginning here, as the very wording of Scripture indicates, is the source of the name “ordinances”—from the Hebrew slave whose ear is pierced at the doorpost.

In all these ordinances, we must consider what may be derived from them for the conduct of life and the preservation of good morals. For many of them signify sacraments rather than instructing our life. The Latin translators called these ordinances *justificationes*, corresponding to what the Greeks call *δικαιώματα* (*dikaiṓmata*).

### XCVI. [Book II, 24:3]

It should be noted that the people again answer in this manner: “All the words that the Lord has spoken we shall do, and we shall hear,” although the order would seem to require: “We shall hear, and we shall do.” It would be surprising if some meaning were not hidden here.

For if “we shall hear” is used in place of “we shall understand,” then one must first render obedience in action to the words of God, so that he himself may lead us to an understanding of the things done at his command by the merit of that devotion through which they were not despised but performed.

Yet it must be considered whether this people is found to resemble the son who said to his father when commanded, “I will go into the vineyard,” but did not go (Matt. 21:30). For the nations that had utterly despised the Lord were later justified through the obedience of one man; though they were not pursuing righteousness, they attained righteousness (Rom. 9:30).

### XCVII. [Book II, 24:4]

It should be noted that Moses built an altar beneath the mountain, together with twelve stones for the twelve tribes of Israel. The altar’s construction from twelve stones is understood to signify that the people themselves are the altar of God, just as they are the temple of God (2 Cor. 6:16).

### XCVIII. [Book II, 24:5]

“And they sacrificed a sacrifice of salvation to God.”

He did not say “a saving sacrifice,” but “a sacrifice of salvation,” which the Greek has *σωτηρίου* (*sōtēriou*). Hence in the Psalm: “I will take the cup of salvation” (Ps. 115:13); it does not say “a saving cup.”

We must consider whether perhaps the one is signified of whom Simeon said, “For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30). The Psalm also commends him where it says, “Announce his salvation from day to day” (Ps. 95:2). For what else does “from day to day” mean, if we attend more carefully, than “light from light”—that is, “God from God,” namely, the only-begotten Son?

### XCIX. [Book II, 24:6–7]

“Moses took half of the blood and poured it into a bowl, and he poured the remaining blood upon the altar. And he took the book of the covenant and read it aloud to the people.”

It should be noted that Scripture now says explicitly for the first time that Moses offered sacrifice since the people were led out of Egypt. Earlier, it had been said concerning Jethro, his father-in-law—although with some ambiguity—that he sacrificed to God (Exod. 18:12).

It should also be observed that the book of the covenant was read together with the blood of the sacrifice. In this book we should understand the ordinances to have been written. For it is subsequently made clear that the Decalogue of the Law was written on tablets of stone.

### C. [Book II, 24:7]

“And they said, ‘All that the Lord has spoken we shall do, and we shall hear.’”

They respond in this way for the third time already.

### CI. [Book II, 24:9]

“And Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up, and they saw the place where the God of Israel had stood.”

It is agreed among those who understand correctly that God is contained in no place and does not assign bodily members to himself according to some bodily position, as our bodies do in sitting, lying, standing, and the like. Such things belong only to bodies, whereas God is spirit (John 4:24).

Therefore, when he displays himself in a bodily appearance or through bodily expressed signs, it is not his substance that appears—the substance by which he is himself what he is—but rather the assumption of visible forms, which is subject to his omnipotence.

## CII. [Ib. XXIV, 11, 10.]

“And from the chosen men of Israel not one disagreed; and they appeared in the place of God, and ate and drank.” Who could doubt that those whom he expressly names—the seventy elders—are here called the chosen men of Israel? They undoubtedly represented those who are chosen in the people of God. “For faith is not possessed by all” (II Thess. III, 2), and “the Lord knows those who are his.” “In a great house there are vessels not only for honor but also for dishonor” (II Tim. II, 19–20). Since, therefore, “those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 30), certainly not one of the chosen men of Israel disagreed.

They are signified by the number four in Moses, Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, because of the four Gospels and the promise concerning the whole world, which is divided into four parts. The seventy elders of Israel signify, by the number seven multiplied by ten, that which pertains to the signification of the Holy Spirit. Sapphire signifies the heavenly life, especially because it is said to be “like the appearance of the firmament.” Who does not know that the firmament is called heaven? The form of a brick in the same sapphire represents the square itself, or stability, or the mystery of that same number four.

That they eat and drink in the place of God signifies sweetness and satiety in that kingdom of eternity. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V, 6). Hence the Lord also says that many will come—whom could he mean except the chosen, foreknown, predestined, called, justified, and glorified?—and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. VIII, 11). Elsewhere he himself promises this to his faithful: that he will make them recline, pass by, and serve them (Luke XII, 37).

## CIII. [Ib. XXIV, 13.]

What does it mean that Joshua son of Nun, who was not mentioned among those four, suddenly appears with Moses and ascends with him onto the mountain to receive the tablets of the Law, and then suddenly disappears again—that is, is no longer mentioned—while Moses receives the Law on the two tablets, and Joshua again appears with him? Does it perhaps signify the New Testament under the name of Jesus, and that it was hidden in the Law but at some point appears to those who understand?

That Jesus is already called by this name, although Scripture testifies in the Book of Numbers that he received it only when they were already close to entering the promised land (Num. XIII, 17), is an instance of prolepsis, that is, of anticipatory reference: Scripture anticipates what happened later. For all these things were written after they had happened; consequently, when the event now being mentioned occurred, he was not yet called Jesus, but when it was written down, he was already called by that name.

## CIV. [Ib. XXV, 11, 12.]

“And you shall make golden mouldings for it, turned, all around.” He called *cymatia* those projections that extend on all four sides of a square, as square tables are usually made. We should not understand “turned” to mean movable. They are fixed, as I have said such things on tables ordinarily are. Rather, he called them turned or twisted—what the Greeks call στρεπτά (*strepta*)—either because they are grooved, as twisted columns are, or because two rods are intertwined in the manner of a rope, as necklaces are also made.

When he says, “And you shall make for it four golden rings, and put them on its four sides: two rings on one side and two rings on the second side,” the four rings meet at the four corners, one at each corner. By counting the corners, what is placed on two sides is thus placed on all four. For one corner is common to two sides. Otherwise, two rings would not be placed along each of the four sides when there are only four rings; there would have to be eight if the arrangement were understood otherwise than according to the number of corners.

The rings are placed at the corners so that carrying poles or shafts may be inserted into them, by which the ark may be carried by four men, two on each side.

## CV. [Ib. XXV, 17.]

It is often asked what he means by the mercy seat, which he commands to be placed over the ark. But since he orders it to be made of gold and gives its length and breadth as equal to those specified for the ark itself, he undoubtedly commands that a golden plate of that size and shape be made to cover the ark. On the mercy seat itself there were to be two cherubim, facing one another from either side, with their faces turned toward the mercy seat and their wings overshadowing it. This is a great mystery.

Gold signifies wisdom; the ark signifies the secret of God. The Law, manna, and Aaron’s rod were commanded to be placed in the ark. The commandments are signified in the Law, power in the rod, and grace in the manna, because power to perform the commandments does not exist without grace.

Yet because the Law is not fulfilled in every respect by anyone who is making progress, the mercy seat is above it. For this is necessary so that God may be merciful; and it is placed above because “mercy rejoices over judgment” (James II, 13).

The two cherubim overshadow the mercy seat with their wings—that is, they honor it by veiling it—because these mysteries are located there. They face one another because they are in agreement; the two Testaments are represented there. Their faces are turned toward the mercy seat because they strongly commend the mercy of God, in which alone there is hope. Finally, God promised to speak to Moses from above the mercy seat, from between the cherubim.

Moreover, if rational creation, in the multiplicity of knowledge—for this is the interpretation of “cherubim”—is signified by those two living beings, there are two of them to commend the fellowship of love. They overshadow the mercy seat with their wings because they attribute their wings not to themselves but to God—that is, they honor God by the virtues in which they excel. Their faces are directed only toward the mercy seat because, for anyone progressing toward a multiplicity of knowledge, hope exists only in the mercy of God.

## CVI. [Ib. XXV, 27.]

What he says—“The rings shall be in the cases”—

> [Note: Among the Septuagint, *eis thêkas tois anaphoreûsei* occurs. It should therefore be read “into the cases,” although all the manuscripts have “in the carrying cases”; this is evidently a familiar error of scribes, who later thought that the same words should be made to agree with one another in case and gender. For in the editions published thus far one read “as carrying cases,” whereas from several manuscripts we have restored “of the carrying poles.”]

—must be understood as meaning that the rings were like cases for the carrying poles, so that the carrying poles could be inserted into them as into cases. “They shall be in the cases” was said as though it meant, “They shall serve as cases.”

## CVII. [Ib. XXVI, 1.]

He commands ten curtains to be made for the tabernacle, since the Law contains the Decalogue. The curtains signify breadth, because of ease. For love is the fullness of the Law (Rom. XIII, 10), and the commandments are easy only through love. Hence that expansion is commended when it is said, “You have enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footsteps have not weakened” (Ps. XVII, 37).

But since this enlargement comes about through the grace of God—for “the love of God has been poured into our hearts,” not through ourselves, but “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 5)—the number itself is also mystically commended here, since it pertains to the Holy Spirit, through whom the Law can be fulfilled.

The curtain is said to be twenty-eight cubits long. This number, because it must be divided by seven, is signified when he says that the curtain is to be four cubits wide. Four times seven makes twenty-eight. This number is also perfect, because, like the number six, it is composed of its own parts.

But when he so often says, “You shall make cherubim on them by the work of a weaver,” what else is being commended in all these things than the multiplicity of knowledge, which “cherubim” signifies?

## CVIII. [Ib. XXVI, 7.]

“And you shall make haircloth coverings over the tabernacle; you shall make eleven coverings.” These are haircloth coverings—that is, coverings of sackcloth—and they are said to number eleven. In sins there is transgression. Transgression is signified by the number eleven, because it goes beyond ten, that is, beyond the Law. Therefore these eleven, multiplied by seven, make seventy-seven. In this the Lord signified the complete forgiveness of sins when he said, “Not only seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matt. XVIII, 22)—as many generations as are found when Luke, reckoning upward from the baptism of the Lord, reaches through Adam to God (Luke III, 23–38).

The sins are signified in these coverings so that they may be expressed through confession and abolished—or covered—through the grace given to the Church. Hence it is said, “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1).

Then he commands these coverings to be covered with reddened rams’ skins. Who would not recognize in the reddened ram Christ bloodied in his passion? The holy martyrs are also signified by these, through whose prayers God is appeased for the sins of his people. Finally, blue skins are thrown over them, signifying eternal life in its greenness, as though in perpetual vigor.

## CIX. [Ib. XXVI, 17.]

“You shall make two *anconisci* standing opposite one another for one column”—that is, one on this side and one on that side, on the sides of the column. By *anconisci* he means what we commonly call *ancones*, such as those on the columns of wine cellars, on which the timbers supporting the casks rest. The likeness of the word is drawn from the elbows, where the arms bend and on which reclining persons lean; in Greek these are called ἀγκῶνες (*ankōnes*).

## CX. [Ib. XXVI, 21.]

“Two bases for one.” Scripture appears to call bases not only those by which columns are supported from below, but also the upper ones that we call capitals. Hence it says, “Two bases for one column, on both its sides.” For what are the two sides except the lower and the upper?

## CXI. [Ib. XXVI, 25.]

When Scripture says that there are eight columns and sixteen bases at the rear of the tabernacle according to the foregoing arrangement, although it earlier said six, it is understood that, once the two corner columns are counted, there are eight.

## CXII. [Ib. XXVI, 33.]

“And the veil shall divide for you between the holy place and the holy of holies”—that is, this veil, of which he is now speaking, is to be stretched between the holy place and the holy of holies on four columns.

The Epistle to the Hebrews speaks of this distinction between the holy place and the holy of holies (Heb. IX, 1–12). Where the ark of the testimony is, there is the holy of holies—that is, inside, beyond the veil. Outside are the table, the lampstand, and the other things whose construction he described shortly before; these are called holy, not holy of holies.

The outside signifies the Old Testament, while the inside signifies the New, although both are found in the reading of the Old Testament, expressed in its works and represented in its signs. Consequently, in the holy place there is the figure of a figure, because it is a figure of the Old Testament; but in the holy of holies there is the figure of the truth itself, because it is a figure of the New Testament. For the whole Old Testament, in the things and observances that it commands to be kept in this manner, is a figure.

## CXIII. [Ib. XXVII, 1, 2.]

Concerning the altar, it is asked why he wished it to be three cubits high, when that is almost the height of a man. How, then, was service performed at the altar, when elsewhere he forbids the altar to have steps? “You shall not uncover your nakedness upon it,” he says (Exod. XX, 26).

There he was speaking of an altar that was to be constructed of earth or stones, where the steps themselves, being built together with the altar, would necessarily belong to the body of the altar. But here he commands an altar to be made of boards. If, for the time of service, something were placed beside it on which the minister of the altar could stand and which was removed when the service was completed, it would not belong to the body of the altar.

It is likewise asked how a sacrifice placed upon a wooden altar could be burned, especially since he commands it to be made hollow and a grating to be lowered to its middle—that is, to the middle of its hollow interior—in a latticework construction. Or, since he says, “And you shall make horns at its four corners; its horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall cover them with bronze,” should “you shall cover them with bronze” be referred not only to the horns but to everything of which he was speaking when he commanded the altar to be made?

## CXIV. [Ib. XXVIII, 3.]

“And you shall speak to all who are wise in mind, whom I have filled with the spirit of understanding.” The Greek has αἴσθησις (*aisthēsis*), which we usually render in Latin as “sense,” not “understanding.” But Scripture commonly speaks of the inner sense, which we call understanding, as in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Solid food belongs to the mature, who by practice have their faculties trained to distinguish good and evil” (Heb. V, 14). There, the word translated “faculties” is αἴσθησις in Greek. What spirit, then, should we understand this to be except the Holy Spirit?

### [Ib. XXVIII, 4.]

“And the garments which they shall make are a breastpiece, an ephod, a long tunic, and a tunic with *corymbi*.”

> [Note: The published editions read “a tunic with horns”; likewise below they preferred “with horns” as more dignified, and so forth. It is surprising if anyone thought that expression more dignified. The manuscripts consistently have “with *corymbi*.” This word properly denotes clusters of ivy berries, as in Pliny, Book 16, chapter 34, and Servius on Virgil, *Eclogue* 3, line 39: “Pale ivy clothes the spreading corymbs.” The Greek version of the Septuagint has here *chitōna corymbōton*, that is, “a fringed garment,” or rather “a curled garment” or “one with curls,” as Augustine suggests.]

It should be noted that these are called garments in the plural, although above he had proposed that one garment be made. Latin interpreters thought it more decorous to say “a tunic with *corymbi*” than “with curls,” which, when properly arranged, commonly serve as an adornment for garments.

## CXV. [Ib. XXVIII, 4, 16, 9, 10.]

What are the *aspidiscas* that he mentions in the priestly garment? Are they small shields, called *scutulae* in Latin from *scutum*, since the Greeks likewise call a shield ἀσπίς (*aspis*)? Or does he call them *aspidiscas* because they are carefully fastened, taking the name from the asp serpent, just as *muraenulae* are also named?

> [Note: In Ratbertus and the older manuscripts, *muraenae*.]

A span in length and a span in width. Some Latin translators rendered this as the measure of an outstretched palm, from the end of the thumb to the end of the little finger.

> [Note: The manuscripts have this form. The printed editions have *spithamus*, although the Septuagint has the genitive *spithamēs*. They use the same word in Isaiah, chapter 40, verse 12, which Jerome interprets there as follows: “*Spithamē*, he says, that is, a palm, signifies an outstretched hand from the thumb to the tip of the finger.”]

Likewise, when it says, “Take two onyx stones and engrave upon them the names of the sons of Israel: six names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, according to the order of their birth,” should this be understood to mean:

> [Note: In the manuscripts, immediately after the word “little finger,” the following occurs: “And let the stones be of the names of the sons of Israel according to their births.” This is found in Exodus, chapter 28, verse 21, except that the Septuagint has *kata onomata* (“according to the names”), where Augustine seems to have read *kata gennēmata* (“according to the births”).]

—that the stones should bear the names of the sons of Israel according to their births, that is, according to the order in which they were born?

## CXVI. [Ib. XXVIII, 22.]

“And you shall make upon the breastpiece fringes forming a chainwork of pure gold.” What the Latins translated as *rationale* was due to the poverty of the language. The Greek has λόγιον (*logion*), not λογικόν (*logikon*). We usually call *rationale* what the Greeks call λογικόν. But since λόγος in Greek is ambiguous—it may mean “word” or “reason,” because it is the name of both—when it was thought that *logion* derived from “word,” our translators rendered it *eloquia* (“utterances”). Thus, where we have “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances” (Ps. XI, 7), the Greeks have λόγια (*logia*).

Here, however, in the priestly garment, the item commanded to be made of gold, blue, purple, double-twisted scarlet, and double-twisted fine linen was a square, doubled piece placed on the priest’s breast and called λόγιον. It is uncertain whether the name was derived from “reason” or from “word.” Our translators, thinking it was derived from “reason,” called it *rationale*.

## CXVII. [Ib. XXVIII, 30.]

“And you shall place upon the breastpiece of judgment the manifestation and the truth.” It is difficult to discover what this means, or what object or metal the “manifestation and truth” were to be placed upon the breastpiece, since he speaks of things that are made physically in the priest’s garment.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript has *ut fiunt*, “as they are made.”]

Nevertheless, some tell a story that there was a stone whose color changed either toward adversity or toward prosperity when the priest entered the holy place. They say that this is what is meant by, “And Aaron shall bear the judgments of the sons of Israel upon his breast,” displaying in that manifestation and truth what judgment the Lord had made concerning them.

It may also be understood that the manifestation and truth were inscribed in letters upon the λόγιον.

## CXVIII. [Ib. XXVIII, 31.]

“And you shall make a long blue tunic,” that is, one hanging down to the ankles. “And it shall have a *peristomion* in its middle,” that is, an opening through which the head is put forth; this is what the Greeks call περιστόμιον (*peristomion*).

“It shall have a border around the *peristomion*, the work of a weaver, a woven seam”—that is, so that the border itself is not sewn on from the outside. This seems to be what “a woven seam” means. Hence he also added, “from itself,” so that it would not be torn; that is, so that the border itself would be woven together with the garment from the garment itself.

## CXIX. [Ib. XXVIII, 35.]

“And Aaron shall wear it when he begins to perform the priestly office; its sound shall be heard when he enters the holy place before the Lord and when he comes out, so that he may not die.” He said that the sound of the one entering and leaving was to be heard from the bells, and he gave such weight to this observance that he added, “so that he may not die.”

He therefore wished certain testimonies to be signified in the priestly garment—which itself certainly signifies the Church—through these bells, so that the priest’s conduct might be known, as the Apostle says: “In all things present yourself as an example of good works” (Tit. II, 7); or, “What you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust to faithful people who will be able to teach others also” (II Tim. II, 2).

Or does it mean something else? Whatever it is, it is nevertheless something great. “When he enters and when he leaves” is a manner of expression meaning “of the one entering and leaving.” “Voice” means sound, for the sound of bells is more properly called a sound than a voice.

## CXX. [Ib. XXVIII, 36–38.]

“And you shall make a pure golden plate, and you shall form upon it the form of a sign: ‘Holiness of the Lord.’”

> [Note: The editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read: “And you shall form upon the same formation ‘Holiness of the Lord.’” Five manuscripts have: “upon it, a deformation of the sign, ‘Holiness …’”; two others and Ratbertus have: “upon it, a deformation of the signs, ‘Holiness …’”; several have: “upon the same, the formation of the sign …” The Septuagint reads: *kai ektupōseis en autō ektupōma hagiasma Kyriou* (“and you shall impress upon it an impressed work, ‘Holiness of the Lord’”).]

“And you shall put it upon a twice-twisted blue cord; and it shall be upon the turban. According to the appearance of the turban it shall be; and it shall be above Aaron’s forehead. And Aaron shall take away the sins of the holy things, whatever the sons of Israel shall sanctify, every gift of their holy things.”

How the holiness of the Lord was to be formed upon the plate, I do not see, unless by certain letters, which some say were four Hebrew letters—the name of God called by the Greeks the τετραγράμματον (*tetragrammaton*, “four-lettered” name), which they believe was and still is ineffable. Whatever those letters were, and whatever their form, as I have said, I believe that “Holiness of the Lord”—or “sanctification,” if that is the better expression, since the Greek has ἁγίασμα (*hagiasma*)—could have been formed in the gold only by letters.

It says there that the priest takes away the sins of the holy things: “Whatever,” he says, “the sons of Israel shall sanctify, every gift of their holy things.” I think this refers to the sacrifices they offer for their sins. We should therefore understand not the holy people, but the holy things, because those offerings are holy and are offered for sins.

After speaking of the plate, he adds: “And Aaron shall take away the sins of the holy things, whatever the sons of Israel shall sanctify, every gift of their holy things.” That is, the priest shall take away whatever they offer for their sins, things called both holy because they are sanctified and sins because they are offered for sins. Scripture clearly recalls this very point in many places.

When he adds, “And it shall be upon Aaron’s forehead, always accepted for them before the Lord,” he returns to the plate. It is understood as an ornament for the forehead.

> [Note: We removed here certain words not found in the better manuscripts. In the editions it read: “He returns to that plate. From this it should be observed, if it can be discovered, who has no need to offer for his own sins except Christ, who alone can take away the sins of all. It is understood as an ornament for the forehead.”]

The ornament signifies confidence in a good life. The one who truly and perfectly possesses this—not merely in sign but in reality—is the only priest who can take away sins and has no need to offer for his own.

## CXXI. [Ib. XXVIII, 41.]

When he commanded Moses concerning Aaron and Aaron’s sons, telling him how they were to be clothed and anointed, what does he mean when he says, “And you shall fill their hands, so that they may serve as priests for me”? Does he perhaps mean with the gifts that are to be offered to God?

## CXXII. [Ib. XXVIII, 42.]

“And you shall make linen undergarments for them to cover the shame of their body; from the loins to the thighs they shall be.” Since such a garment covers the whole body, what does he mean by saying, “You shall make linen undergarments to cover the shame of their body,” as though it could be visible beneath so extensive an outer garment?

Perhaps he wished this to be a sign of chastity or continence. It is signified by the garment so that it may be understood not as possessed from oneself but as given.

> [Note: Our manuscripts consistently have *coloris* (“of color”); the Greek version of the Septuagint has χρωτός (*chrōtos*, “of the body”).]

## CXXIII. [Ib. XXIX, 8, 9.]

When he was speaking of Aaron’s sons, he says: “And you shall put tunics on them, gird them with belts, and wrap turbans around them.” What he calls *cidaris* or *cidarae* is unknown, since it has not been translated and is no longer in use. I nevertheless think it is not a head covering, as some have supposed. For he would not say “you shall wrap them around them” unless it were something useful not to the head but to the body.

## CXXIV. [Ib. XXIX, 9.]

“And their priesthood shall be mine forever.” We have often explained above how “forever” is said of these things that signify something else. For this priesthood was certainly changed so that the one according to the order of Melchizedek might be eternal, not the one according to the order of Aaron.

In the former there are both an oath and no repentance on God’s part, by which the change is signified. “The Lord has sworn,” he says, “and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

The priesthood according to the order of Aaron was indeed called “forever,” either because no time was prescribed for how long it was to be observed, or because it signified eternal realities. Yet nowhere is it said of Aaron’s priesthood that “the Lord has sworn and will not repent.” Therefore, in speaking of the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, it says, “He will not repent,” to signify that he did repent of the priesthood of Aaron—that is, he changed it.

## CXXV. [Ib. XXIX, 9.]

What does “And you shall complete the hands of Aaron and the hands of his sons” mean? Does he perhaps signify power by the hands, so that they too might consecrate something? And was that power itself completed by the sanctification through which Moses was commanded to sanctify them?

## CXXVI. [Ib. XXIX, 10.]

“And you shall bring the bull to the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands upon the head of the bull before the Lord.”

Here is the basis for what was said above, that their hands were to be completed—that is, that their power was to be perfected—so that they too might sanctify. This takes place when they lay their hands upon the bull that is to be sacrificed.

## CXXVII. [Ib. XXIX, 18.]

When Scripture often calls the sacrifice of animal victims “an odor of sweetness to the Lord,” it certainly does not mean that God is pleased by the smell of smoke. Rather, God is pleased by what these things signify spiritually when it is offered spiritually, since the odor of God itself is to be understood spiritually. He does not draw in an odor through bodily nostrils as we do. Just as he smells that, so these things signify this.

## CXXVIII. [Ib. XXIX, 26.]

“And you shall take the breast from the ram of consecration, which is Aaron”—that is, “of this Aaron.”

> [Note: The editions have “that is, of Aaron himself.” The manuscripts have *hujus* (“of this one”), by which Augustine indicates that the name Aaron is placed in the genitive case in this passage of Exodus.]

He wished this to pertain to the high priest.

## CXXIX. [Ib. XXIX, 28–30.]

“And it shall be an everlasting statute for Aaron and his sons from the sons of Israel,” when he was speaking of the breast and the arm of the victims. He therefore used “everlasting” in the sense we have often mentioned above.

“And the holy garment, which belongs to Aaron, shall belong to his sons after him, to anoint them in it and to complete their hands. For seven days the priest who succeeds him from among his sons, who enters the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy things, shall wear it.”

These words raise many questions. First, it should be noted that after calling it “the holy garment,” he later speaks in the plural, saying “to anoint them in them,” as though there were garments. Above too he had called them many garments, although one consisted of them.

It is uncertain, however, whether “in them” refers to the word in its neuter form, meaning whatever things complete that garment—that is, the priestly clothing. This is more likely because he says in what follows, “For seven days the priest who succeeds him shall wear it,” meaning all the things he mentioned when describing the priestly garment.

He repeats what he had said above, “to complete their hands,” concerning which I explained what seemed to me the meaning (above, question 125).

But when he says, “For seven days the priest shall wear it,” does he mean that he will not wear it on other days? Rather, he wished those seven consecutive days to be understood, during which his priesthood is in a certain sense dedicated and a festival is held at its beginning for the week.

He calls the successor of Aaron the one who enters the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy things. He is signifying one who could be only a single individual, not men such as Aaron’s sons were while their father was alive, but one who is Aaron’s successor.

How, then, does he say that it belongs specifically to this one to enter the tabernacle of the testimony and minister in the holy things, when the things outside the veil that covers the holy of holies are also called holy, and when the tabernacle of the testimony is also the place where the holy things are—the table and the lampstand? Since later priests also minister at the table, the lampstand, and the altar, how does he call Aaron’s successor one who enters the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy things?

If he had said, “to minister in the holy of holies,” there would be no question. For only one person, the high priest, entered the place where the ark of the testimony was. This is also very carefully commended in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

Perhaps, by saying that one person enters the tabernacle of the testimony to minister in the holy things, he does not intend anything other than the holy of holies, since it too is certainly called holy. Not everything that is holy can also be called the holy of holies, but whatever is the holy of holies is undoubtedly holy.

This one person, who entered the holy of holies once a year, signified Christ the Lord; the Epistle to the Hebrews makes this completely clear (Heb. IX, 7–11).

What was prefigured in the holy of holies—namely, that over the ark containing the Law there should be a mercy seat, in which the mercy of God was to be understood as signified, by which he is merciful toward the sins of those who do not fulfill the Law—seems to me to be signified also in the priest’s garment itself. For what else does it signify than the sacraments of the Church?

In the λόγιον, that is, the *rationale* placed upon the priest’s breast, he established judgments; but in the plate he established sanctification and the taking away of sins.

> [Note: The editions have “offering.” Several manuscripts have “abolition”; others, “taking away.”]

Thus the *rationale* on the breast is like the ark in which the Law was kept, while the plate on the forehead is like the mercy seat that was above the ark, so that in both places what is written might be preserved: “Mercy rejoices over judgment” (James II, 13).

## CXXX. [Ib. XXIX, 37.]

What does it mean that he calls the altar, purified and sanctified for seven days, “holy of the holy”? He does not call the altar the holy of holies, as is the altar separated by the veil, where the ark of the testimony is. Nevertheless, he says that this altar, placed outside the veil, becomes holy of the holy through the sanctification of seven days rather than through anointing.

> [Note: Most manuscripts omit *quam* (“rather than”). Some read: “it could have been said to become holy through anointing.”]

And he adds, “Everyone who touches the altar shall be sanctified.”

## CXXXI. [Ib. XXX, 3, 4.]

When he was speaking of the rings of the altar of incense—which he commanded to be gilded, not covered with bronze—he says: “And you shall make two pure golden rings beneath its twisted crown; you shall make them on the two sides, on the two sides.” The Greek has: εἰς τὰ δύο κλίτη ποιήσεις ἐν τοῖς δυσὶ πλευροῖς.

For κλίτη (*klitē*) means “sides,” and πλευρά (*pleura*) also means “sides.” Hence some Latin translators rendered it: “You shall make them on two parts, on the two sides.” But the Greek does not say μέρη (*merē*), which means “parts”; it says κλίτη, “sides.”

This word occurs in the psalm where it is written: “Your wife is like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house” (Ps. CXXVII, 3). Thus the only difference is one of case: first he used the accusative, then the ablative—“You shall make them on two sides, on two sides.”

It is difficult to determine the meaning, unless perhaps, as Scripture often favors ellipsis, something is omitted and understood here as well: “they shall be.” The meaning would then be: “You shall make them on two sides; on two sides they shall be”—that is, you shall make rings for the two sides, because they shall be on the two sides.

## CXXXII. [Ib. XXX, 4.]

“And the rings shall be arches for the carrying poles, so that the thing may be carried by them.”

The rings that he had mentioned he now calls arches. He used “rings” for rounded handles. For what else is a ring or circle than an arch extending all around?

Therefore some, unwilling to say “arches,” translated the word as “cases,” into which the carrying poles were to be inserted, saying, “And they shall be cases for the carrying poles.” But the Greek could have expressed this, since “case” is itself a Greek word. Instead, it says ψαλίδες (*psalides*), which is translated “arches.”

## CXXXIII. [Ib. XXX, 8, 10.]

“He shall burn upon it incense of continuation before the Lord throughout their generations.” He calls it “incense of continuation” because it was to be made continually, with no day omitted.

When he gave instructions concerning the altar of incense—that is, the altar on which incense alone was to be placed, not a burnt offering, sacrifice, or libation—he had already stated that this same incense was to be placed there every day. But now he says, “And Aaron shall make atonement”—or “shall make propitiation”—upon its horns once a year, with the blood of purification from sins.

“Make propitiation” derives from the word *propitiation*, which in Greek is called ἐξιλασμός (*exilasmos*). From this it should be understood that what he commands to be done once a year in order to propitiate God upon the horns of the altar of incense—that is, that the horns of the altar of incense be touched once a year with the blood of purification from sins, namely, of victims offered for sins—does not pertain to the placing of incense that he commanded to be done daily.

The daily rite was performed with spices, not blood, and every day, not once a year. We should therefore not understand that the priest ordinarily entered the holy of holies only once a year, but that he entered with blood once a year. He did, indeed, enter daily without blood in order to place the incense, but with blood once a year.

This is especially clear because he continues: “Once a year he shall purify it; it is holy of holies to the Lord.” Thus he does not place incense there once a year, since that was commanded to be done daily; rather, once a year he purifies it, which was commanded to be done with blood.

After this he adds, “It is holy of holies to the Lord.” Therefore, if the holy of holies was not outside but inside the veil, then the altar of which he is now speaking, which he commanded to be placed opposite the veil, was also commanded to be inside.

## CXXXIV. [Ib. XXX, 12.]

What does he mean when he says, “If you take a census of the sons of Israel at their visitation,” except that he commands them at some time to be visited and counted, that is, numbered? This must be understood as the reason David was punished: God had not commanded it (II Sam. XXIV).

### CXXXV. [On Exodus 30:26–33]

It should also be observed and noted how he commanded everything to be anointed with the oil of chrism: namely, the tabernacle and the things that were in it, and thereafter the holy of holies. Once everything has been anointed, everything will be the holy of holies. What, then, will now distinguish those inner things that are covered by the veil from the other things, if everything, once anointed, will be the holy of holies? This must be investigated more carefully; nevertheless, we have thought these points worth noting.

Here too we should remember that, just as concerning the altar of sacrifices—which after its anointing he wished to be called “the holy of the holy”—it was immediately said, “Everyone who touches it shall be sanctified,” so likewise concerning all the things subsequently mentioned as having been anointed with that oil and called “the holy of holies,” the same statement follows: “Everyone who touches them shall be sanctified.” This can be understood in two ways: either that one will be sanctified by touching them, or that one will be sanctified so as to be permitted to touch them.

This is so, however, only if the people were not permitted to touch the tabernacle when they brought sacrifices, or whatever things brought by them were offered to God. For consequently, the statement is not to be addressed only to the priests or only to the Levites. He says to Moses, “And you shall speak to the children of Israel, saying”—the children of Israel were, of course, the whole people. He commands that they be told: “This shall be holy oil of anointing for you throughout your generations. It shall not be applied to the flesh of any human being, and according to this composition you shall not make any for yourselves in the same way. It is holy, and it shall be holiness for you. Whoever makes anything like it, and whoever gives any of it to a foreign nation, shall be cut off from his people.”

He therefore commands not only the priests but the whole people of Israel not to make such an ointment for human uses. This is what he means by saying, “It shall not be applied to the flesh of any human being.” He therefore forbids its being made similarly for their own uses, and threatens destruction if anyone makes anything like it—that is, if anyone prepares a similar ointment for his own uses—or gives any of it to a foreign nation.

Accordingly, when he says, “It shall be holiness for you,” and commands this to be said to the whole people of Israel, I do not see how it can be understood except that they were permitted, whenever each person came with his own offerings, to touch the tabernacle; and by touching it they were sanctified because of the oil with which all things had been anointed. Hence it was said, “Everyone who touches it shall be sanctified.” They were not sanctified in the same manner as the priests, who were also anointed with it so that they might exercise the priesthood.

### CXXXVI. [On Exodus 30:34]

When he prescribes with which spices the *thymiama*, that is, the incense, is to be made, and says that it is to be prepared according to the art of the perfumer, as the work of a perfumer, we must not therefore think that an ointment is being made—that is, something with which a person is to be anointed—but, as has been said, *thymiama*, or incense, which is to be placed upon the altar of incense, where sacrifice was not permitted and which was inside the holy of holies.

[Note: Thus the better-quality manuscripts. But the printed editions have: “which was inside the holy of holies.”]

### CXXXVII. [On Exodus 30:36]

“And you shall pound some of it finely, and place it before the testimony in the tabernacle of the testimony, where I shall make myself known to you. It shall be most holy incense for you.”

Here again this incense, because it was placed inside, on the altar of incense that was inside, is called “the holy of holies.” And “the tabernacle of the testimony” properly designates that inner part itself where the ark was, with the distinction added when he says, “Where I shall make myself known to you.” For he had first said this concerning the mercy seat, which is certainly inside—that is, within the veil, above the ark.

### CXXXVIII. [On Exodus 31:2–5]

What does it mean that, when he commanded Bezalel to be appointed for the work of making the tabernacle, he said that he had filled him with the divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every kind of work, “to devise and to construct,” and so forth? Are these works, which appear to belong to craftsmanship, also to be attributed to the gift of the Holy Spirit? Or was this also said figuratively, so that the things signified by these works might be understood to belong to the divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge? Nevertheless, here too, although this man is said to have been filled with the divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, the Holy Spirit is not yet mentioned by name.

### CXXXIX. [On Exodus 31:13]

What does it mean that, when he was commanding the observance of the sabbath, he said, “An eternal covenant in me and in the children of Israel,” rather than, “between me and the children of Israel”? Is it because the sabbath signifies rest, and our rest is nowhere except in him?

For he certainly calls the whole people his children of Israel—that is, the seed of Abraham—and there is an Israel according to the flesh and an Israel according to the spirit. If Israel were not to be understood except as those descended according to the flesh, the Apostle would not say, “Behold Israel according to the flesh” (1 Corinthians 10:18), where he clearly indicates that there is also an Israel according to the spirit, who is a Jew inwardly and circumcised in heart (Romans 2:29).

Thus the passage may perhaps be more appropriately distinguished as follows: “An eternal covenant in me”; then the meaning is, “And for the children of Israel it is an eternal sign,” that is, a sign of an eternal reality—just as “the rock was Christ,” because the rock signified Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). It should not therefore be joined as though the covenant were “in God and in the children of Israel,” but rather: “An eternal covenant in me,” because in him eternal rest was promised; “and for the children of Israel it is an eternal sign,” because the children of Israel received a sign to observe, by which eternal rest is signified for true Israelites, that is, for the children of promise and those who will see God face to face as he is.

### CXL. [On Exodus 31:18]

“And he gave Moses, as soon as he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets written with the finger of God.”

[Note: Read, as the manuscripts and the more carefully corrected printed editions have it: “the tablets of the testimony, stone tablets.” [“Of the testimony, stone.”]]

Although God spoke so many things, only two stone tablets are given to Moses, which are called tablets of the testimony and are destined to be placed in the ark. Clearly, if they are carefully sought out and rightly understood, all the other things that God commanded are understood to depend upon those ten commandments written on the two tablets—just as these same ten commandments in turn depend upon those two commandments, namely, the love of God and of one’s neighbor, upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matthew 22:37–40).

### CXLI. [On Exodus 32:2]

When Aaron commands that the earrings be removed from the ears of their wives and daughters, so that he might make gods from them, it is not absurd to understand that he wished to give them a difficult command in order by this means to turn them back from that intention. Nevertheless, I thought the difficulty of gold being available for making the idol should be noted for the sake of those who are distressed if something of this kind is divinely commanded, or tolerated with equanimity, for the sake of eternal life.

### CXLII. [On Exodus 32:8]

The Lord, indicating to Moses what the people had done with the calf—that is, with the idol they had made from their gold—says that they declared, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.” It is not recorded that they actually said this, but God shows that this was the disposition of their minds. They carried in their hearts the meaning of these words, which could not be hidden from God.

### CXLIII. [On Exodus 32:14]

“And the Lord was appeased concerning the evil which he had said he would do to his people.”

Here he wished “evil” to be understood as punishment, as in the passage, “Their departure was regarded as evil” (Wisdom 3:2). In this sense it is said that good and evil come from God (Sirach 11:14), not in the sense of the evil by which human beings are wicked. God is not evil; rather, because he is just, he inflicts evil upon the wicked.

### CXLIV. [On Exodus 32:19]

Moses certainly appears to have been angry when he struck and broke the tablets of the testimony written with the finger of God. Nevertheless, by a great mystery the repetition of the covenant was prefigured, since the Old Covenant had to be abolished and the New established.

It should also be noted how much he labored in supplication to God on behalf of the people, although he had shown such severity in punishing them. But what the crushing of the cast image of the calf, after it had been thrown into the fire, and the scattering of it upon the water that he gave the people to drink, seems to signify for us, we have already written elsewhere, in the work against Faustus the Manichaean (Book 22, chapter 93).

### CXLV. [On Exodus 32:24]

“And they gave it to me, and I threw it into the fire, and this calf came out.”

He spoke concisely, without saying that he himself had fashioned it so that the cast calf came out. Or did he lie through fear as an excuse—as though he had thrown the gold into the fire, expecting it to be destroyed, and the calf’s form had emerged without his intending it?

This should not be believed to have been said with such an intention, because Moses could not have failed to know what was in the man with whom God was speaking, and he did not rebuke his brother for lying.

[Note: The manuscripts have *in vero* (“in truth”).]

### CXLVI. [On Exodus 32:25]

“And when Moses saw the people, that they were scattered—for Aaron had scattered them, so that they might become a joy to their adversaries.”

It should be noted how the whole evil that the people committed is attributed to Aaron, because he consented to their doing what they had wrongly demanded. For it is said more properly, “Aaron scattered them,” since he yielded to them, than that they scattered themselves, though they had demanded so great an evil.

### CXLVII. [On Exodus 32:31–32]

When Moses says to God, “I beg you, this people has committed a great sin, and they have made gods of gold for themselves. And now, if indeed you forgive their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of the book you have written,” he certainly spoke with confidence, so that the reasoning might be concluded from what follows: namely, because God would not blot Moses out of his book, he would forgive the people that sin.

Nevertheless, it should be observed how great an evil Moses perceived in that sin, since he believed it had to be expiated by such slaughter, though he loved them so greatly that he poured out those words before God on their behalf.

### CXLVIII. [On Exodus 32:35]

It is rightly asked: since Aaron was previously said to have scattered the people, why did no punishment fall upon him—neither when Moses ordered every person who met the Levites as they went to and returned from the gate, armed, to be killed, nor when what Scripture says happened afterward: “And the Lord struck the people because of the calf which Aaron made”? This is especially puzzling because the same point is emphasized here by repetition. It does not say, “And the Lord struck the people because of the calf which they made,” but “which Aaron made.” Yet Aaron was not struck; indeed, what God had commanded concerning his priesthood before his sin was fulfilled.

He commanded both Aaron and his sons to be washed, and thus they were established in the priesthood. So he knows whom to spare until a change for the better; whom to spare for a time, although he foreknew that the person would not be changed for the better; whom he does not spare so that the person may be changed for the better; and whom he does not spare, without even awaiting his change.

The whole matter returns to what the Apostle says in exclamation: “How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions, omitting the negation, have: “so that he awaits a change of life,” and so forth.]

### CXLIX. [On Exodus 33:1]

“Go up from here, you and your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt.”

God appears to speak in anger when he says, “You and your people, whom you brought up,” since otherwise he would have said, “You and my people, whom I brought up out of the land of Egypt.” But when they demanded the idol, they had spoken in this way: “This Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt—we do not know what has happened to him.” By placing their deliverance in a human being, they had fallen away from it.

This is now thrown back at them when it is said, “You and your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt”—something that is a crime against them, not against Moses. For Moses wanted nothing else than that they should place their hope not in him but in the Lord, and should believe that they had been freed from that slavery by the Lord’s mercy, with thanksgiving.

Nevertheless, through the grace of God, Moses had such merit before God as his most faithful servant that God said to him, “Let me alone, and in my anger I will destroy them” (Exodus 32:1, 23, 10).

Whether the words “Let me alone” are a command or a request seems absurd either way. For if God was commanding him, the servant was disobedient in not obeying; and it was not fitting for God to ask this of his servant as though for a favor, especially since he could destroy them even against Moses’ will.

The meaning that readily presents itself is therefore that, by these words, God signified how greatly that people benefited in his sight from being loved by the man whom the Lord loved. In this way we are admonished that, when our own merits weigh against us so that we are not loved by God, we can be lifted up before him by the merits of those whom he loves.

For when the Almighty says to a man, “Let me alone, and I will destroy them,” what else is he saying than, “I would destroy them if they were not loved by you”? Thus “Let me alone” was said as though he were saying, “Do not love them, and I will destroy them,” because your love for them intervenes to prevent me from doing so.

One ought to obey the Lord commanding, “Do not love them,” if he had said this as a command and not rather as an admonition expressing what restrained him from punishing them. Yet even while Moses interceded, God did not leave the people without the scourge of discipline.

Somehow, although Moses loved them in this way, God loved them more secretly, while visibly terrifying them with his voice.

### CL. [On Exodus 33:1–3]

When God says to Moses, “Go, go up from here, you and your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, into the land which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to your seed,’” he immediately, as though still speaking to Moses himself, turns covertly—an alteration called in Greek *ἀποστροφή* (*apostrophē*)—and now speaks to the people themselves, saying:

“And at the same time I will send my angel before you, and he will drive out the Canaanite, the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite; and he will bring you into a land flowing with milk and honey. For I will not go up with you, because you are a stiff-necked people, lest I destroy you on the way.”

There is here a great and wondrous depth of mystery, as though an angel could have greater mercy than God: the angel would spare a stiff-necked people, whereas God, if he were with them, would not spare them. Yet he says that, even through his angel, and in a certain sense while absent from them—although he can be absent nowhere—he will fulfill what he swore to their fathers, as though also showing here that he does this because he promised it to those righteous fathers, not because these people were worthy.

What, then, does this signify, unless perhaps that he is not with them because they are stiff-necked, since only humility and devotion receive him as gracious and saving? For God’s being with stiff-necked people means nothing other than being present by punishing and chastising them. Thus, when he is not present with the wicked in that manner, he spares them.

This is the sense of the saying, “Turn your face away from my sins” (Psalm 50:11), because if he turns his face toward them, he overturns them.

For just as wax melts before the face of fire, so sinners perish before the face of God (Psalm 67:3).

[Note: The editions of Ratisbon, Amerbach, and Erasm. have: “because unless he turns away, he turns toward them.” Louvain and seven manuscripts have: “because unless he turns away, he overturns them.” We have preferred the reading of the manuscripts of the best quality, those of Corbie, Michaelstein, and others.]

### CLI. [On Exodus 33:12–13]

“And Moses said to the Lord, ‘Behold, you say to me, “Lead this people.” But you have not shown me whom you will send with me.
