Yet you said to me, “I know you above all others, and you have found favor with me.” If therefore I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself plainly, so that I may see you, so that I may continue to find favor before you, and so that I may know that this nation is your people.’”

What the Greek has as *γνωστῶς* (*gnōstōs*), certain Latin translators rendered as “plainly,” although Scripture did not say *φανερῶς* (*phanerōs*, “openly” or “manifestly”). It could perhaps more suitably be rendered: “If I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself, so that I may see you knowingly.” By these words Moses sufficiently shows that, despite the great familiarity of their encounter, he did not yet see God in the manner he desired to see him.

For all those visions of God that were presented to mortal eyes, and from which a sound was produced to reach mortal hearing, were displayed by means of a form assumed as God willed and in whatever form he willed. In them the divine nature itself was not perceived by any bodily sense. That nature is wholly invisible everywhere and contained in no place.

And because the whole Law depends upon two commandments, namely the love of God and of one’s neighbor (Matthew 22:37–40), Moses therefore expressed his desire in both respects: in love of God, when he said, “If I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself plainly, so that I may see you, so that I may continue to find favor in your sight”; and in love of his neighbor, when he said, “And so that I may know that this nation is your people.”

### CLII. [On Exodus 33:17]

What does God mean when he says to Moses, “Because I know you above all others”? Does God know some things more and some less? Or is this like what is said to certain people in the Gospel, “I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12)?

According to this kind of knowledge, by which God is said to know what pleases him and not to know what displeases him—not because he is ignorant of these things, but because he does not approve them, just as an art is rightly said not to know defects when it rejects defects—God knew Moses above all others because Moses pleased God above all others.

### CLIII. [On Exodus 33:12, 17]

Should we note that Moses had first said to God, “You said to me, ‘I know you above all others’,” and that God is subsequently recorded as saying this to Moses only after Moses himself had said it to God, whereas it is not recorded earlier? Are we therefore to understand that not everything God spoke with him was written down?

This must, however, be investigated more carefully in the earlier parts of Scripture, to determine whether this is really so.

[Note: The editions of Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain make this annotation there: “It should be noted that Moses himself had first said to God, ‘You said to me, “I know you above all others”’; and that God is recorded as saying this to him after he himself had said it, whereas it is not recorded earlier, so that we may understand that not everything God spoke with him was written down. But it must be more carefully investigated in the earlier parts of Scripture whether this is truly so.” —M.]

### CLIV. [On Exodus 33:14–23]

When Moses had said to the Lord, “Show me your glory,” the Lord answered him, “I will pass before you in my glory”; and, “I will call in the name of the Lord in your sight.” I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.” Shortly before he had said, “I myself will go before you, and I will give you rest.” Moses seems to have understood this as, “I will go before you,” as though he would not be with the people who would be present on the journey. Therefore he said, “If you yourself do not come with us, do not bring me up from here,” and so forth.

God did not deny him this, saying, “I will also do this word that you have spoken.” How, then, after Moses had said to him, “Show me your glory,” does God again seem to say, as though he would go ahead and not be with them, “I will pass before you,” unless this means something else?

The one understood to be speaking and saying, “I will pass before you,” is the one of whom the Gospel says, “When the hour had come for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13:1). This passing is also said to be interpreted as the Passover.

This, then, is altogether a great prophecy. He himself passes before all the saints from this world to the Father, to prepare for them the dwelling places of the kingdom of heaven, which he will give them at the resurrection of the dead, since, passing before all, he became the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18).

He strongly commends his grace in the very words, “And I will call upon the name of the Lord in your sight,” as though this were in the sight of the people of Israel, whose type Moses represented while he heard these things. In the sight of that nation, scattered throughout the world, Christ the Lord is called among all the nations.

He said, “I will call,” not “I will be called,” using an active verb in place of a passive one, in an unusual form of expression in which a profound meaning is concealed. For perhaps he wished to signify that he himself brings this about: that is, that by his grace it comes to pass that the Lord is called upon among all the nations.

But when he added, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion,” he clearly expressed more explicitly the calling by which he called us into his kingdom and glory—not according to our merits, but according to his mercy.

Since he was promising to bring in the nations, saying, “I will call in the name of the Lord in your sight,” he commended this as something he would do mercifully, just as the Apostle says: “For I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers; but that the Gentiles should glorify God for his mercy” (Romans 15:8–9).

This, then, was foretold: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.” By these words he prevented human beings from boasting as though they had merited mercy through the merits of their own virtues, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10:17).

For he did not say, “I will have mercy on such and such people,” but, “on whom I am merciful,” thereby showing that no one had merited the mercy of so great a calling by preceding good works. Indeed, “Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).

Whether he wished to repeat this same thing when he added, “I will show compassion to whom I show compassion,” or whether there is some distinction, I do not know. What was said in Greek with two words, *ἐλεήσω* (*eleēsō*) and *οἰκτειρήσω* (*oikteirēsō*), which seem to signify one and the same thing, could not be rendered by the Latin translator with two different words except by repeating the same mercy in different forms.

If it were said, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy,” the expression would not seem sufficiently suitable. Yet the meaning expressed there is nevertheless stronger: either God showed by this repetition the firmness of his mercy—as with “Amen, amen,” “Let it be, let it be,” and Pharaoh’s repeated dream, along with many similar examples—or in this way God foretold that he would show mercy to both peoples, that is, to the Gentiles and to the Hebrews.

The Apostle expresses this as follows: “For just as you were once disobedient to God, but now have received mercy through their disobedience, so they too have now been disobedient through your mercy, in order that they also may receive mercy. For God has shut up all in disobedience, so that he may have mercy on all” (Romans 11:30–32).

Then, after this commendation of his mercy, he answers what had been said to him, “Show me your glory,” or what Moses had requested earlier when he said, “Show me yourself plainly, so that I may see you.”

“You will not be able,” he says, “to see my face. For no human being shall see my face and live.” By this he shows that God as he is cannot appear to this life, which is lived amid the senses of mortal and corruptible flesh—that is, he cannot be seen as he can be seen in the life in which, in order to live, this life must be died to.

Again, after an intervening clause in which Scripture says, “And the Lord said,” it continues: “Behold, there is a place beside me.” For what place is not beside God, who is absent nowhere? But by saying, “Behold, there is a place beside me,” he signifies the Church, as though commending his temple.

“And you shall stand,” he says, “upon the rock”—for the Lord says, “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18)—“as soon as my glory passes by.” That is: “As soon as my glory passes by, you shall stand upon the rock,” because after Christ’s passing—that is, after Christ’s passion and resurrection—the faithful people stood upon the rock.

“And I will place you,” he says, “in a cleft of the rock,” signifying the firmest protection. Others have translated it, “in a watchtower of the rock,” but the Greek has *ὀπήν* (*opēn*). We more correctly understand this as a hole or a cavern.

“And I will cover you with my hand until I pass by; and I will remove my hand, and then you shall see my back; but my face shall not be seen by you.”

Since he had already said, “You shall stand upon the rock as soon as my glory passes by,” where he is understood to have promised stability upon the rock after his passing, how should we understand his saying, “I will place you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand until I pass by; and I will remove my hand, and then you shall see my back,” as though, once Moses had already been placed upon the rock, God would cover him with his hand and then pass by, when he cannot be upon the rock except after God’s passing?

A recapitulation of an omitted event must be understood here, such as Scripture often uses in many places. It subsequently states what occurred earlier in temporal order. The order is therefore this:

“I will cover you with my hand until I pass by, and then you shall see my back; for my face shall not be seen by you. And you shall stand upon the rock as soon as my glory passes by, and I will place you in a cleft of the rock.”

This took place in those whom Moses’ person then signified, namely the Israelites, who later believed in the Lord Jesus, as the Acts of the Apostles indicate—as soon as his glory passed by.

After he had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, and the Apostles spoke in the tongues of all nations after the Holy Spirit had been sent down from above, many of those who had crucified Christ were cut to the heart. Because they had not recognized him, and had crucified the Lord of glory, blindness had come upon Israel in part (Romans 11:25), just as it had been said, “I will cover you with my hand until I pass by.”

[Note: The Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain editions omit the negative particle, which we have restored from the manuscripts and the Ratisbon edition.]

Hence the Psalm says, “For day and night your hand was heavy upon me,” calling “day” the time when Christ was performing divine miracles, and “night” the time when he died as a human being, when even those who had believed during the day stumbled.

This is therefore what is meant by, “When I have passed by, then you shall see my back”: “When I have passed from this world to the Father, those whose type you bear will afterward believe in me.” Then they were cut to the heart and said, “What shall we do?” The Apostles ordered them to repent and to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, so that their sins might be forgiven (Acts 2:37–38).

The Psalm continues after saying, “Day and night your hand was heavy upon me”—that is, so that I would not recognize him. “For if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). It continues and joins the following words: “I turned in my distress when the thorn was fixed”—that is, when I was cut to the heart.

Then it adds, “I acknowledged my sin, and I did not conceal my transgression,” after they had seen the enormity of the crime in which they had crucified Christ. And because they received the counsel to repent and to receive forgiveness of sins in baptism, he says, “I declared my transgression against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Psalm 31:4–5).

That this was a prophecy rather than a literal account of what the Lord said to Moses is sufficiently shown by the event itself, since no visible deed is afterward recorded concerning the rock or its cavern, the covering of his hand, or the vision of his back.

For immediately Scripture adds, with an intervening clause, “And the Lord said to Moses,” although the Lord himself was certainly speaking even in the preceding words. It then continues with what the Lord says next: “Cut for yourself two stone tablets, like the first ones,” and so forth.

[Note: The printed editions have *ante te in gloria mea* (“before you in my glory”). The phrase *in gloria* is absent from one manuscript and from the Septuagint.]

### CLV. [On Exodus 34:7]

What does it mean that it is said of the Lord, “And he will not purify the guilty,” except that it means, “He will not declare him innocent”?

### CLVI. [On Exodus 34:10]

When God speaks to Moses, who is to write two new stone tablets, he says among other things, “Before all your people I will do glorious things.” He still does not deign to say, “Before all my people.”

Did he say “your people” as one might say to any individual belonging to that people, namely, “The people from which you come”? It is like saying, “Your city,” not of a city over which you rule or which you founded, but of the city of which you are a citizen.

For shortly afterward he likewise says, “All the people among whom you are.” What else could “your people” mean in another form? But the fact that he did not say, “Among whom you are,” is simply a customary form of expression.

### CLVII. [On Exodus 34:12]

What does it mean when Moses is told, “Take heed for yourself, lest at any time he make a covenant with those who dwell in the land”?

The Greek does not have “lest you make,” but “lest he make.” Could he perhaps have wished to speak of the people, whose leader Moses was? Yet Moses himself did not bring the people into that land where he forbids a covenant from being made with those who lived there.

It is therefore a remarkable and as yet untested or unnoticed kind of expression—if indeed it is an expression and not some other meaning.

[Note: The printed editions have *ponas* (“you make”). All the manuscripts have *ponat* (“he make”), as do most copies in the *Locutions*, Book 2, chapter 135. In the Greek Septuagint, some books have *thes*, while others, according to Nobilius, have *thē*.]

### CLVIII. [On Exodus 34:13, 15]

When God, speaking to Moses, commanded that, once the land had been given into their possession, every form of idolatry should be destroyed and that foreign gods should not be worshiped, he said, “For the Lord God is a jealous name, a jealous God.” That is, the very name by which he is called “Lord God” is jealous, because God is a jealous God.

God does not do this through the defect of human agitation, since he is always and in every way unchangeable and tranquil. Rather, by this word he indicates that his people will not commit fornication with foreign gods without punishment.

The expression is drawn metaphorically from marital jealousy, which guards the chastity of a wife. This benefits us, not God. For who could harm God by such a kind of fornication? It harms the fornicator greatly, so that he may perish.

God forbids this with the gravest warning, calling himself jealous. To him the Psalm says, “You destroyed everyone who fornicates away from you; but it is good for me to cling to God” (Psalm 72:27–28).

Finally, it follows: “Lest you make a covenant with those who dwell in the land, and they fornicate after their gods.”

### CLIX. [On Exodus 34:20]

When he says, “You shall not appear empty before me,” the surrounding circumstances indicate that he is speaking of appearing before him. God said this in relation to his tabernacle.

The meaning is: “You shall not appear there empty-handed; you shall never enter without some offering.” Understood spiritually, this is a great mystery. Yet these statements were spoken concerning shadows of things signified.

### CLX. [On Exodus 34:21]

When he had commanded the sabbath, what does he mean by adding, “In sowing and in harvest you shall rest”?

He seems to be saying, “At the time of sowing and harvest.” Or did he perhaps command the sabbath rest to be observed in such a way that even those periods would have no excuse, although they are extremely necessary to farmers for food and livelihood?

It was therefore commanded that even during the time of sowing and harvest, when agricultural labor is especially pressing, people should rest on the sabbath. Thus, through these periods that demand extensive labor, it was signified that work must cease on the sabbath at all times.

[Note: The printed editions have “At the time of sowing.” Our manuscripts omit *de* (“at the time of”), and one or another has *requies* (“rest”) instead of *requiesces* (“you shall rest”), as does the Septuagint.]

### CLXI. [On Exodus 34:24]

When he says, “No one shall covet your land when you go up to appear before the Lord your God three times a year,” this is to be understood as meaning that everyone could go up without fear and need not be anxious about his land, since God promised to guard it: no one would covet anything from it because of the one who had gone up, so that he would not fear for his absence from it.

Here too he sufficiently shows what he had said earlier, “You shall not appear empty before the Lord your God,” because he said it in the place where God was going to have the tabernacle or temple.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and the Greek Septuagint. The printed editions have “for three times of the year.”]

### CLXII. [On Exodus 34:25]

What does he mean by saying, “You shall not slaughter the blood of my sacrifices over leaven”?

Does he here call those sacrifices his own which are slaughtered at Passover, and command that there be no leaven in the house at that time, since these are the days of unleavened bread?

### CLXIII. [On Exodus 34:25]

What does he mean by saying, “And the sacrifice of the feast of Passover shall not remain until morning,” except what he expressly commanded above: that nothing of the flesh of the animal that is sacrificed should remain until morning?

The obscurity is caused by the form of expression. He said “shall not sleep” in place of “shall not remain.”

### CLXIV. [On Exodus 34:26]

“You shall not boil a lamb in the milk of its mother.”

Here he has said again something whose meaning I do not know how to determine. Nevertheless, it is a great prophecy concerning Christ, even if it can be carried out literally—how much more so if it cannot!

For not everything in the words of God is to be reduced to the literal performance of the acts, just as neither is the statement concerning the rock, its cavern, and the covering of the hand (Exodus 33:22). But the faithfulness of the narrator is certainly to be required: what he says happened must truly have happened, and what he says was said must truly have been said.

The same is required of the Gospel narrators. For although they report that Christ said certain things in parables, their account that he said these things is not itself a parable but a historical narrative.

### CLXV. [On Exodus 34:28]

“And Moses was there with the Lord for forty days and forty nights; he did not eat bread and he did not drink water.”

He had also said this earlier, when Moses received the tablets that he broke, and he repeats it here. He is not recapitulating what happened, but emphasizing that it happened again. We have already explained what the repetition of the Law signifies.

When he says, “He did not eat bread and he did not drink water,” this is understood to mean that he fasted: the whole is expressed by a part, since Scripture uses the word “bread” to signify every kind of food and the word “water” to signify every kind of drink.

### CLXVI. [Ibid. XXXIV, 28, 27, 1.]

“And he wrote on the tablets the words [Note: [Col. 0652] In the printed editions *hic, verba* is omitted here. It is found in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint.] of the Covenant, ten words.” It is said of Moses that he himself wrote them; God had also said to him shortly before, “Write these words for yourself.” But when he first received the Law, whose tablets he threw down and broke, he is not said to have carved the stone tablets himself; whereas now it is said, “Carve for yourself two stone tablets.” Nor was he then told to write, as he is told now; nor is he narrated to have written them himself, as Scripture now narrates and says, “He wrote on the tablets the words of the Covenant, ten words.” But at that time it was said: “And he gave to Moses, as soon as he ceased speaking with him on Mount Sinai, two tablets of testimony, stone tablets written with the finger of God” (Exod. XXXI, 18). Then shortly afterward: “And Moses turned and went down from the mountain,” it says, “and the two tablets of testimony were in his hands; stone tablets written on both their sides, written on this side and on that side. And the tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets” (ibid. XXXII, 15–16).

A major question therefore arises: how is it that those tablets, which Moses was certainly going to break, God knowing this beforehand, are said not to be the work of man but of God, and not to have been written by man but with the finger of God; whereas the later tablets, which were to remain for so long and to be kept in God’s tabernacle and temple, were, although commanded by God, carved by man and written by man? Or perhaps God’s grace was signified in those earlier tablets—not the work of man—which grace they became unworthy of when they turned back in heart toward Egypt and made an idol; thus they were deprived of that benefit, and for that reason Moses broke the tablets. But by these later tablets were signified those who glory in their own works; hence the Apostle says, “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X, 3). Therefore tablets carved by human work and written by human work were given to them, remaining with them to signify those who would glory in their own works, and not in the finger of God—that is, in the Spirit of God.

Certainly, then, the repetition of the Law signifies the New Testament; whereas the former signified the Old, and therefore was broken and abolished. This is especially so because when the Law is given a second time, it is given without any terror, unlike the first occasion, amid such a great tumult of fires, clouds, and trumpets. Then the people, terrified, said, “Let God not speak to us, lest we die” (Exod. XX, 19). This signifies that fear belongs to the Old Testament, and love to the New.

How, then, is the question resolved—why were the former tablets the work of God, and these the work of man; why were the former written with the finger of God, and these written by man? Perhaps the Old Testament was signified more particularly in the earlier tablets because God commanded there, but man did not do it. For the Law was established in the Old Testament to convict transgressors; it entered in so that the offense might abound (Rom. V, 20). It was not fulfilled through fear, since it is fulfilled only through love. And therefore it is called the work of God, because God established the Law and God wrote it: there is no work of man, because man did not obey God, and the Law rather made him guilty. For he says, “Sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death for me through what is good” (ibid. VII, 12–13).

But on the second tablets, by God’s help, man makes and writes the tablets, because the love of the New Testament fulfills the Law. Hence the Lord says, “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17); and the Apostle says, “Love is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. XIII, 10), and, “Faith working through love” (Gal. [Col. 0654] V, 6). Thus in the New Testament what had been difficult in the Old became easy for a person who has faith working through love, while that finger of God—that is, the Spirit of God—writes it inwardly in the heart, not outwardly on stone. Hence the Apostle says, “Not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (II Cor. III, 3), because the love of God, by which the commandment is truly fulfilled, has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V, 5). This, then, is the Law first given—where the Old Testament is signified, which is solely God’s work and the writing of God’s finger—of which the Apostle says: “So the Law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.” The Law, then, being holy and good, is God’s work: there man does nothing, because he does not obey; rather, he is burdened with guilt by the Law that threatens and condemns.

But a person is blessed when this holy, just, and good commandment is also his work [Note: [Col. 0654] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “and does what is good, this too being his work.”], though through the grace of God.

### CLXVII. [Ibid. XXV, 1.]

After Moses had descended from the mountain, bearing other tablets of the Law and covering himself with a veil because of the glory of his face, which the children of Israel could not look upon, he said: “These are the words which the Lord has spoken to do them.” The expression is ambiguous: does “to do them” refer to the Lord himself or to them? It is nevertheless clear that it refers to them, for he commanded what was to be done.

Perhaps, however, it was phrased in this way so that it might be understood in both senses, because the Lord also acts when he assists those who act, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Philipp. II, 12–13).

### CLXVIII. [Ibid. XXXV, 24.]

“All who brought an offering brought silver and bronze as an offering to the Lord,” as though he were saying: everyone who brought something brought this and that, mentioning silver and bronze among the other things he was describing. The Latins have translated the word as *demptio* (“deduction,” “offering set apart”), corresponding to the Greek ἀφαίρεμα (*aphaírema*). It is called *demptio* because the person who brings something to the Lord takes it away from himself.

### CLXIX. [Ibid. XXXV, 29.]

In Moses’ account it is mentioned that God spoke to him about Bezalel in the same words and with the same number of words: that he had filled him with the divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, for carrying out the works of the tabernacle belonging to the crafts of artisans [Note: [Col. 0654] The old Corbeiensis manuscript has: “which belong to the craft of artisans.” Perhaps one should read *opificium* (“workmanship”) instead.]. We have already stated above what seemed to us concerning this (above, question 138). But I thought the same matter ought to be mentioned again now, because it was certainly not without reason that it was repeated in exactly the same words in which the Lord had previously made it known to Moses.

Here, moreover, the art of architecture is described in an unusual manner as the work of craftsmen in gold, silver, and every kind of metal, whereas *architectonica* is ordinarily used of the art concerned with the construction of buildings.

### CLXX. [Ibid. XXXVI, 2–3.]

“And all who were willing to go to the work, to complete it, received from Moses all the offerings” [Note: [Col. 0655] The printed editions and manuscripts have *demptum aes* (“bronze taken away”). Nobilius notes that the passage is corrupt and should read *omnes demptiones* (“all the offerings”), in accordance with the Septuagint, πάντα τὰ ἀφαιρέματα (*panta ta aphairemata*), and with the Vulgate, *universa donaria* (“all the gifts”).].

Moses had merely made known what works the Lord had commanded to be carried out—namely, the tabernacle with everything that was to be in it, and the priestly garments [Note: [Col. 0655] Manuscripts of better quality have “and the priestly garment,” singular.]. He also mentioned certain persons to whom he said that the Spirit had been divinely given, so that they could make these things. Nevertheless, many others are understood to have come willingly to the same works, although they had not been commanded to do so, nor had their names been mentioned by the Lord as having been spoken to Moses.

Therefore those who are mentioned by name were not the only ones who possessed this divinely given gift, but perhaps they possessed it in a special and more excellent degree. In all these people, what should be praised is not a mind drawn servilely to the work, but one devoted to it freely and willingly.

### CLXXI. [Ibid. XXXVI, 4–5.]

It should be noted that those who are called wise, the skilled workers of the holy works, were also such in character that, when they themselves received everything the people offered—thinking that these things were necessary for completing all the works—they saw that more was being offered than was needed. They told Moses, and he prohibited the people by proclamation from offering anything further.

They could have taken away many things if they had wished, but modesty restrained them, or religious scruple frightened them.

### CLXXII. [Ibid. XXXV, 2.]

After Moses descended from the mountain, the construction of the tabernacle and the priestly garment are prescribed. Before he commanded anything concerning their manufacture, however, he spoke to the people about observing the Sabbath.

This raises a not insignificant question. Since he had again received the ten words of the Law on stone tablets, which he himself had carved and written, why, after descending, did he admonish the people only about the Sabbath? If it was superfluous for the people to hear the ten commandments of the Law again, why was it not also superfluous for them to hear about the Sabbath, since this too is read among those same ten commandments?

Or is this also analogous to the veil with which he covered his face, because the children of Israel could not look upon the brightness of his face? Of the ten commandments, this was the only one he prescribed to the people in a figurative sense. We have no doubt that the other nine, as they are commandments there, are also to be observed in the New Testament. But that one concerning the Sabbath was so veiled among the Israelites by the figurative observance of the seventh day, and was prescribed as a mystery and represented by a certain sacramental sign, that it is not observed by us today; we contemplate only what it signified.

In that rest in which the cessation of servile works is commanded, there is a profound greatness of God’s grace. For good works are performed in rest when faith works through love (Galat. V, 6). But fear has torment; and where there is torment, what rest is there? Hence, “There is no fear in love” (I John IV, 18). “But God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 5).

Therefore the Sabbath is “holy rest to the Lord”: it is to be attributed to God’s grace, not to us as though it came from ourselves. Otherwise our works will be human, or sins [Note: [Col. 0655] The printed editions have “or with sin.” The manuscripts have “or sins.”], or performed with fear rather than with love; and therefore they will be servile, without rest [Col. 0656]. The fullness of the Sabbath, however, will be in everlasting rest. For the “Sabbath of Sabbaths” was not instituted without reason (Lev. XXV).

### CLXXIII. [Ibid. XL, 9–10.]

[Note: [Col. 0656] Here we begin to depart from the divisions of the questions found in the printed editions, in order to follow the manuscripts.]

Earlier, when God first spoke of anointing the tabernacle, he said that all those things were to be sanctified by the same anointing and made “holy of holies.” But he had said that the altar of burnt offering, sanctified by the same anointing, was to be made “holy of the holy.” The difference seemed to be that he had called nothing “holy of holies” except what was separated from the holy place by the veil—that is, where the ark of the covenant and the altar of incense were (Exod. XXX, 26–38).

Now, however, when he repeated the same instructions, he said of the anointed tabernacle and the things that were in it that they were to be sanctified by the same anointing and made “holy.” But of the altar of burnt offering, of which he had previously said that it was to be made “holy of the holy,” he now said that by the same anointing it was to be made “holy of holies.”

This gives us to understand that what had been called “holy of the holy” has the same force as what is called “holy of holies.” Consequently, all those anointed things—that is, the whole tabernacle and everything in it—which he had previously called “holy of holies,” have the same force as what he now calls “holy.” Nor is each of them, after this anointing, called merely “holy of the holy”; it is also called “holy of holies,” as is the altar of burnt offering.

Thus, as far as this designation is concerned, there is no longer any difference between those things that had been inside the veil—where the ark of testimony was—and the other things outside it, except that the interior objects were called “holy of holies” or “holy of the holy” [Note: [Col. 0656] So the manuscripts and the Regensburg edition. Other editions read “or holy of the holy.”] even before the anointing, whereas the others were sanctified by the anointing so that they might receive this name. What these things signify remains to be examined at leisure.

### CLXXIV. [Ibid. XL, 19.]

When Scripture narrated how Moses set up the tabernacle, it said: “He spread the curtains over the tabernacle.” This does not mean that he covered it from above like a roof, but that he encircled the columns, since he had said that he set up the tabernacle with columns.

### CLXXV. [Ibid. XL, 29.]

When it said, “And over the court around the tabernacle and the altar,” it makes clear that the altar of burnt offering was outside, at the entrance of the tabernacle, so that the whole was surrounded by the court and the altar stood within the court, between the gate of the court and the entrance of the tabernacle.

### CLXXVI. [Ibid. XL, 34–35.]

A very remarkable circumstance must be noted: when the cloud descended and filled the tabernacle—although it is called the glory of the Lord—Moses could not enter the tabernacle, even though on Mount Sinai, when he first received the Law, he entered the cloud where God was (ibid. XIX, 20).

Without doubt, therefore, he represented one person then and another now. Then he represented those who become participants in the innermost truth of God; now he represented the Jews, to whom the glory of the Lord that is in the tabernacle—which is the grace of Christ—is presented like a cloud, because they do not understand it, and therefore do not enter [Col. 0657] the tabernacle of testimony [Note: [Col. 0657] The printed editions have “he entered.” The manuscripts have “they enter.”].

It should be believed that this happened once, immediately after the tabernacle had been established, either for the sake of this symbolism or for some other reason. For the cloud was not always over the tabernacle in such a way that Moses could not enter it. The cloud was not removed except when the people were given the sign to depart—that is, to move their camp from the place where they were—and to proceed where the cloud led by day and the flame by night (Exod. XIII, 21). These two signs also remained over the tabernacle in turn when they had set up camp: the cloud by day and the flame by night.

## QUESTION CLXXVII. On the Tabernacle

### 1.

Since the book called Exodus concludes with the establishment of the tabernacle, and since much has also been said about this tabernacle in the preceding portions of the same book—things that create difficulty for understanding, as every *topographia* (τοπογραφία), that is, the description of some place, commonly does in any historical narrative—it seemed good to me to discuss the whole tabernacle separately. In this way, if possible, we may understand what it was like and what it signified, while for the present examining the literal sense of the narrative [Note: [Col. 0657] Several manuscripts have “while for the present attending to the literal sense of the narrative,” or “expecting it,” and continue with “and postponing the figurative meaning to another time.” Two Vatican manuscripts read: “while for the present considering what pertains to the literal sense of the narrative, and postponing it to another time.”], postponing its figurative meaning to another time.

For nothing there should be thought to have been established at God’s command without signifying some great reality, the knowledge of which builds up faith and the form of godliness.

### 2. [Ibid. XXVI, 1, 6.]

God therefore commands Moses to make a tabernacle of ten curtains, from twisted fine linen, hyacinth-blue, purple, and twisted scarlet, with Cherubim in the work of a weaver. The things which the Greeks call αὐλαίας (*aulaias*) the Latins call *aulaea*, and ordinary usage calls curtains. He therefore did not command ten courts to be made, as some have carelessly translated; for he said not αὐλὰς (*aulas*), but αὐλαίας (*aulaias*).

He commanded Cherubim to be made in the curtains by woven workmanship. He prescribed that the length of each curtain should be twenty-eight cubits and its width four cubits. He also commanded that the curtains be joined and connected to one another, five on one side and five on the other, so that the space enclosed by them would be the space of the tabernacle.

As for how these groups of five curtains were to be connected with one another, he commanded as follows: “You shall make,” he said, “loops of hyacinth-blue on the edge of one curtain, at the joining, on one side; and so you shall make the uppermost loops [Note: [Col. 0657] Thus in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint. The printed editions have “you shall make the top.” In B., “you shall make them above the upper edge.” M.] at the second joining.” That is, where one curtain is joined to another—the third to the second, which has already been joined and connected to the first—the loops are to stand opposite one another, each facing its counterpart.

Whether the space enclosed by these curtains was square or round is not yet apparent; it will become clear when he begins to speak of the columns by which the curtains are extended.

He did not intend to speak of more than three curtains joined together, a joining made at two connections: the second to the first and the third to the second. From this kind of rule the others would be joined.

He therefore commanded that fifty loops be made on the first curtain, on the side where it was to be joined to the second; and fifty loops on the third curtain, on the side where it was joined to the second. But he wished the second curtain itself, situated between the two sets of fifty loops, to have fifty golden clasps, on one side, by which it would be joined to the fifty loops of the first curtain. Consequently, it followed that on the other side it would also have the same number of clasps, by which it would be joined to the loops of the third curtain.

Scripture expressed this briefly as follows: “You shall make fifty golden clasps and join curtain to curtain with the clasps, and the tabernacle shall be one.” The fifty golden clasps of the second curtain were therefore inserted into the fifty hyacinth-blue loops of the first curtain; fifty clasps were also inserted into the fifty loops of the third curtain; and the remaining curtains were connected in the same way, so that five were embraced together, and on the opposite side another five likewise.

### 3. [Ibid. VII–XI.]

Then he says: “You shall make curtains of goats’ hair as a covering over the tabernacle”—that is, curtains which would come over it, not as a roof but by encircling it. For we also say that something is placed over another thing in this sense, not like the roof of a house but like plaster over a wall, as though over a strip laid across it.

“You shall make,” he says, “eleven curtains. The length of one curtain shall be thirty cubits, and the width of one curtain four cubits; the same measure shall apply to the eleven curtains. You shall join five curtains together and six curtains together.”

Just as he wished the earlier curtains to be joined in groups of five, so these curtains, which numbered eleven rather than ten, were to be joined in groups of five and six.

“And you shall double,” he says, “the sixth curtain at the front of the tabernacle”—so that it would not cause difficulty because the six and the five did not correspond evenly with each other [Note: [Col. 0658] The printed editions have “so that it would not be moved.” The manuscripts have “so that it would not cause difficulty.”].

Then he also says how these goats’ hair curtains were to be joined to one another. He repeats the instruction, perhaps more clearly: “You shall make,” he says, “fifty loops on the edge of one curtain which is opposite the middle one”—that is, opposite the second, since it will be the middle curtain between the first and the third—“at the second joining,” that is, at the connection.

“And you shall make fifty loops on the edge of the curtain which is joined to the second curtain”—that is, on the edge of the third curtain where it is joined to the second. “And you shall make fifty bronze clasps, and join the clasps to the loops; and you shall join the curtains together, and they shall be one.”

He therefore wished the clasps to be attached to the middle curtain, that is, the second, by means of which it would be joined to the first and third through the fifty loops. There is no other difference here except that he now commanded the clasps to be made not of gold but of bronze.

He had said that the loops on the earlier curtains were to be hyacinth-blue. But since he did not say of what kind the loops on the goats’ hair curtains were to be, what is more plausible than to understand them as being of goats’ hair?

### 4. [Ibid. XII–XIV.]

What follows is so difficult to understand that I fear explaining it may make it more obscure. He says:

“And you shall place upon the curtains of the tabernacle the half of the curtain that remains; you shall cover what is left over from the curtains of the tabernacle; you shall cover the rear of the tabernacle. A cubit on this side and a cubit on that side, from what remains of the length of the curtains of the tabernacle, shall be a covering over the sides of the tabernacle, on this side and on that side, so that it may cover it.”

Since he commanded the sixth curtain to be doubled at the front of the tabernacle, what does he mean by saying that half a curtain remains among the curtains? And what does he mean by “a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side,” when half a curtain amounts to fifteen cubits, since he commanded one curtain to be thirty cubits long? Who could easily understand this?

Or, if the curtains are said to exceed the others in length because he prescribed that the first curtains, made of fine linen, scarlet, purple, and hyacinth-blue, should be twenty-eight cubits long, while he wished the goats’ hair curtains to be thirty cubits long, then each goats’ hair curtain exceeds each earlier curtain by two cubits. Multiplied together, except for the eleventh, which he commanded to be doubled, these make twenty cubits by which the circumference of the goats’ hair curtains exceeds the circumference of the earlier curtains.

For ten curtains, each two cubits longer, make twenty cubits. Ten cubits on this side and ten on that side could exceed the others, not “a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side,” as Scripture says.

Therefore, it seems to me that the explanation of this passage should be postponed until the tabernacle has been established with all its columns, together with the court that surrounds it, on every side. Perhaps he is anticipating something about these goats’ hair curtains that is relevant to those of which he has not yet spoken.

For when he says, “You shall make curtains of goats’ hair as a covering over the tabernacle,” it is uncertain whether he wishes the entire tabernacle to be covered with these curtains, including the court, about which he later speaks as being placed around it, or whether he means only the inner tabernacle, which he commanded to be made from the ten curtains.

He continues and says: “And you shall make a covering for the tabernacle, skins of rams dyed red.” Here too it is uncertain whether he commanded this covering to be made around the entire tabernacle or only around the inner one.

But when he adds, “And coverings of hyacinth-blue skins above,” this should be understood not as being around it but as forming a roof, like a vaulted ceiling.

### 5. [Ibid. XV–XXI.]

“And you shall make,” he says, “columns for the tabernacle from incorruptible wood: one column ten cubits high and one and a half cubits wide; two projections belonging to one column, standing opposite one another. So shall you make all the columns [Note: [Col. 0659] The printed editions have “all the columns.” The manuscripts and the Septuagint have “all the columns” in the dative construction.] of the tabernacle.”

Why he commanded these projections to be made, concerning which I previously explained what they were (above, question 109), is not sufficiently clear to me. If they were made for carrying the columns, there would have to be at least four [Note: [Col. 0659] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, except the Batavian edition, have: “If they were made for carrying the columns, there would be four, so that they might become one.”]. But if they were places on which the bars rested, there would have to be even more, since he assigned five bars to each column.

Unless perhaps these projections have no practical use but only symbolic significance, as does the eleventh goats’ hair curtain. For a column extending two projections like arms on either side presents the figure of a cross.

Let us now examine the number of columns, from which the shape of the tabernacle may also be discerned: whether it is square, round, or has an elongated quadrangular shape, with longer sides and shorter fronts, as most basilicas are constructed. For the latter is what is more clearly expressed here.

He says: “You shall make columns for the tabernacle, twenty columns on the side facing north. And you shall make forty silver bases for the twenty columns, two bases for one column, on both its sides. And on the second side, toward the south, twenty columns, and forty silver bases for them; two bases for one column, on both its sides, and two bases for one column, on both its sides.”

The repetition should not trouble us. It is a feature of the expression, so that all the things about which he does not speak may be understood in the same way.

We have already explained the bases: why one column has two, because at this point he also calls the capitals bases (above, question 110).

### 6. [Ibid. XXII–XXV.]

We therefore see that the two sides of the tabernacle, toward the north and the south, were extended by twenty columns each. The two remaining sides were the eastern and western sides; if they had possessed the same number of columns, the tabernacle would undoubtedly have been square.

The number of columns on the western side is not omitted, but the eastern side is not mentioned. Whether this is because it had none, and the curtains were extended there without columns from the outermost column of one side to the outermost column of the other, or whether they are omitted for some reason but are nevertheless to be understood, I do not know.

Later, ten columns are mentioned on the eastern side itself, but these belong to the court, of which he speaks afterward and which he commands to be placed around this tabernacle.

After mentioning the north and south sides of the tabernacle with their twenty columns each, he continues and adds:

“And at the rear of the tabernacle, on the side facing the sea, you shall make six columns; and you shall make two columns at the corners of the tabernacle at the rear. And they shall be equal below and joined together; they shall be equal at the tops, toward one joining. So shall you make them at both the two corners [Note: [Col. 0660] The printed editions have: “So shall you make the corners for the two corners.” The manuscripts have “at both the two corners,” in accordance with the Septuagint, ἀμφοτέραις ταῖς δυσὶ γωνίαις.]; they shall be equal. And there shall be eight columns, and their silver bases sixteen: two bases for one column, so that there may be two bases for one column on both its sides.”

The same reasoning and the same expression apply to the bases.

Thus the western side—for this is the side toward the sea—is extended by eight columns: six in the middle and two at the corners, which he says should be equal toward a single joining. I believe this means that a corner joins two sides to each other, and that a corner column is common to both sides: one to the western and northern sides, and the other to the western and southern sides.

When he also says that they are to be equal below, he means that they should be balanced according to the perpendicular, so that they would not be thicker below than above, as most columns are.

### 7. [Ibid. XXVI–XXIX.]

Then he says:

“You shall make bars of incorruptible wood: five for one column on one side of the tabernacle; and five bars for the column on the second side of the tabernacle; and five bars for the column on the rear side of the tabernacle, which is toward the sea.”

It would be surprising to doubt that the eastern side had no columns in this inner tabernacle, around which the court was afterward placed. He therefore commands that each of the columns on all three sides have five bars.

“And the middle bar,” he says, “shall pass through the middle of the columns, from one side to the other side.”

This seems to mean that a bar reached from one column to the next and extended across the interval between the columns, from the side of one to the side of the other [Col. 0661]. Consequently, one of all these columns would not have five bars of its own, since five bars arriving from the neighboring column would reach the outermost column.

“And you shall overlay the columns with gold, and make bronze rings into which you shall insert the bars, and you shall overlay the bars with gold.”

So that the columns would not have holes bored into them for the bars to enter, he commanded rings to be made, by which the ends of the bars would be held on both sides. These rings are therefore understood to have hung from loops fixed in the wood, so that they could receive and hold the ends of the bars.

### 8. [Ibid. XXX–XXXVII.]

“And you shall erect,” he says, “the tabernacle according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.

“And you shall make a veil of hyacinth-blue, purple, twisted scarlet, and fine twined linen; you shall make it a woven work with Cherubim [Note: [Col. 0661] The printed editions have “with Cherubim above.” In the manuscripts and in the Septuagint, the particle “above” is absent: “you shall make it a woven work with Cherubim.” This is a Hebraism by which the veil is commanded to be made through the skill of the craftsman, that is, adorned with winged figures, or rather, as the Vulgate version has it, woven with beautiful variety.]. And you shall place it upon four incorruptible columns overlaid with gold, with their golden capitals and their four silver bases.

“And you shall place the veil upon the columns, and you shall bring in there, inside the veil [Note: [Col. 0661] Thus the manuscripts according to the Greek Septuagint: καὶ εἰσοίσεις ἐκεῖ ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος. Therefore the earlier printed editions are wrong to read, “and you shall bring it inside where the veil is.”], the ark of testimony. And the veil shall divide for you between the midst of the holy place and the midst of the holy of holies. And you shall cover the ark of testimony with the veil in the holy of holies [Note: [Col. 0661] The printed editions have “in the holy places of the holy places.” The Vatican manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek, have “in the holy of holies.”].”

All this is clear. The ark of testimony was placed inside, behind the veil, which rested upon four columns. He did not command the veil to cover it in such a way that it lay over the cover of the ark, but that it should stand opposite it [Note: [Col. 0661] The printed editions have “that it should stand opposite the table.” The word “table” is absent from the manuscripts.].

Then he says:

“And you shall place the table outside, beyond the veil; and the lampstand opposite the table, on the side of the tabernacle facing south; and you shall place the table on the side of the tabernacle facing north.”

This too is clear.

But what follows—“And you shall make a screen of hyacinth-blue, purple, twisted scarlet, and twisted fine linen, the work of an embroiderer. And you shall make five columns for the screen, and overlay them with gold, and their capitals shall be gold; and you shall cast five bronze bases for them”—does not yet reveal what purpose this screen, stretched across five columns, serves. That will appear later. He intends it to be the screen of the entrance to the tabernacle, namely, to this inner tabernacle around which the court is placed.

Then he commands the altar of sacrifice, the altar of burnt offering, to be made, and explains how it is to be made. He does not yet say where it is to be placed; but this too will appear later.

### 9. [Ibid. XXVII, 9–13.]

From this point he speaks of the court until the end—the court that is to be placed around that tabernacle whose construction he previously described.

“And you shall make,” he says, “the court”—which in Greek is called αὐλὴν (*aulēn*), not αὐλαίαν (*aulaian*). Some of our translators, failing to distinguish these terms, translated both this word and the curtains—which the Greeks call αὐλαίας (*aulaias*), not αὐλάς (*aulas*)—as “courts,” saying, “You shall make a tabernacle of ten courts,” where they should have said, “of ten curtains.”

Some translators, much more ignorant, translated both αὐλὰς and αὐλαίας as “doors.”

Just as in Latin we find *aulaea*, which the Greeks call αὐλαίας, so the term they call αὐλὴν was rendered by our people as *aula*. But in Latin this word no longer signifies a court; it signifies a royal residence, whereas among the Greeks it signifies a court.

“Therefore,” he says, “you shall make the court for the tabernacle on the side facing south; and the hangings of the court shall be of twisted fine linen. Its length shall be one hundred cubits for one side; its columns twenty, and their bases twenty of bronze; their rings and their hooks of silver.

“Likewise for the side facing north, hangings one hundred cubits long; their columns twenty, and their bases twenty of bronze, and their rings, and the hooks of the columns, and their bases overlaid with silver.

“But the width of the court on the side facing the sea shall be fifty cubits; its columns ten, and their bases ten.

“And the width of the court on the east shall be fifty cubits; its columns ten, and their bases ten.”

### 10

Here we now see columns on the eastern side mentioned, when he speaks of the court and says that there are ten of them with bronze bases, just as he also said concerning the western side—where a very difficult question arises. For it is easy enough to suppose that on the eastern side there was a single row of columns belonging to the court, by which the inner tabernacle was enclosed on all four sides, since the inner tabernacle had no columns on that side. But on the western side, where there were already eight columns of the inner tabernacle, how are we to understand these ten also, which he mentions as belonging to the outer court—as though on the western side there were two rows of columns, eight inner ones and ten outer ones?

If this is so, the sides of the outer court will also be longer than those of the inner tabernacle, so that there is room for another row of columns to be drawn from one end to the other without running into the earlier row belonging to the inner tabernacle. And if this is the case, it will follow that the twenty columns of the two sides of the inner tabernacle, south and north, must be separated by shorter intervals than the twenty columns possessed by the outer court on those same sides. Since those outer rows of twenty columns, as Scripture says, occupy one hundred cubits, while the inner rows contain the same number of columns but occupy fewer cubits, because Scripture does not specify this, it will follow that the eight columns of the inner tabernacle on the western side are more sparsely placed than the twenty southern and northern columns of the same tabernacle, so that they can enclose a space sufficient for stretching around it the ten curtains with which he first said that this tabernacle was to be made.

For each of those curtains measures twenty-eight cubits, making two hundred and eighty altogether. If one hundred cubits were assigned to each of the two sides, south and north, where the rows of twenty columns are located, then forty cubits would necessarily extend along the other two sides, east and west; and, in proportion, forty cubits would correspond to the eight columns just as one hundred cubits correspond to the twenty columns. But the sides of the outer court would not be longer, since they are defined as one hundred cubits; and therefore there would be no way for that row of ten columns to enclose, from the southern corner [Col. 0663] to the northern corner, the row of eight inner columns.

Accordingly, in order that the inner tabernacle may be surrounded by the court on every side, it must also be shorter in length. Thus its twenty columns on the two sides along which it extends lengthwise must necessarily be placed more closely together than the twenty columns of the outer court, while the eight columns of the inner tabernacle on the western side must be more widely spaced than the ten on the same side of the outer court. Whatever number of cubits is lacking from those curtains along the two sides of twenty columns, south and north, must be made up by the breadth of the eastern and western sides, so that the two hundred and eighty cubits of curtains may be fully used. For, unlike the hairy curtains, where one was made double, he did not command that anything be doubled in the case of these curtains.

Therefore, if the length of the inner tabernacle is shortened by as much as could be enclosed by the outer court—so that its twenty columns do not stretch curtains for one hundred cubits, but, for example, at the least ninety-six, four cubits shorter—then those same four cubits, that is, eight cubits, must necessarily be extended along the other two sides, east and west. Thus, along the eight western columns of the inner tabernacle, not forty cubits but forty-four will be extended, and another forty-four on the eastern side.

When, therefore, fifty cubits are stretched along the ten columns of the outer court, while forty-four cubits are stretched along the eight columns of the inner tabernacle, the intervals between the eight inner columns are found to be wider than those between the ten outer columns. For if the intervals were equal, forty cubits would be stretched along eight columns just as fifty are stretched along ten, since eight is to ten as forty is to fifty. The number five is contained eight times in forty and ten times in fifty.

### 11. [Book 14–16]

Nor would the unequal intervals between the columns trouble us—the columns being placed more closely together along the longer sides, where there are twenty, and more sparsely along the breadth, where there are eight—unless something else arose that compelled us to alter this interpretation.

For after mentioning that the length of the court toward the sea was fifty cubits, with ten columns and ten bases, and that the breadth of the court toward the east was likewise fifty cubits, with ten columns and ten bases, so that the form of the tabernacle with its surrounding court seemed complete, he added something whose meaning and placement are extremely difficult to determine:

“Fifteen cubits shall be the height of the curtains for one side: their columns three, and their bases three. And for the second side, fifteen cubits shall be the height of the curtains: their columns three, and their bases three. And for the gate of the court, a covering twenty cubits high, of violet, purple, scarlet, and twisted linen, embroidered in variegated needlework: its columns four and its bases four.”

When these elements are placed, I do not see the previously established form of the tabernacle completed. But I clearly see the same total number of ten columns, consisting of three, three, and four—namely, three on each side [Col. 0664] and four in the middle. Consequently, those curtains of fifty cubits cannot be continuous, lest there be no entrance into the court. Rather, the middle twenty cubits will be separated by the two sections of fifteen cubits, so as to form the covering of the tabernacle gate—that is, a curtain hanging as an ornament and covering, occupying the space assigned and set apart for the four columns of the court gate.

For this reason he also wished the covering itself, divided and separated from the two fifteen-cubit sides, to be distinguished in appearance, so that it might be varied by embroidered needlework in those four colors.

But if those fifteen-cubit sides, each having three columns, are joined to the court gate in the same straight line, there will be no space between the ten columns of the outer court and the eight of the inner tabernacle where the five-cubit square altar could stand, together with the space in front of it where service was performed at the altar, and the space between it and the entrance of the inner tabernacle where the bronze basin was placed.

For it was commanded that the priests wash their hands and feet there when they entered the tabernacle or approached to minister at the altar. Unless we understand this basin as being outside the tabernacle, in the court, how could they wash their hands and feet first and then enter the tabernacle? Yet we cannot place the altar outside the court, since he commanded that both the tabernacle and the altar be enclosed by the court.

It remains, therefore, that we understand those two fifteen-cubit sides, each with three columns, as extending from the sides in such a way that they themselves create an interval of the same number of cubits between the court gate and the entrance of the inner tabernacle:

[Note: [Col. 0664] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read “of some number of cubits.”]

the gate being open for twenty cubits between four columns and having a twenty-cubit curtain varied by embroidered work; and the inner entrance of the tabernacle being the place where that curtain was stretched between five columns. We must understand that this curtain was placed not within the row of eight columns but outside, toward the court.

Then there would be the curtain of the tabernacle entrance, whose opening functioned like doors, at the place where the curtains were not joined to one another by rings and loops.

Or perhaps, within that row of eight columns of the inner tabernacle, this curtain was set before the entrance of the tabernacle on five columns, so that, when it was opened, the interior would not be exposed or visible to those looking in. Whether this curtain was placed inside that row of columns or outside it is not sufficiently clear. But undoubtedly it stood at a moderate distance from that row, lest the five columns, packed more closely together than the four columns, block the entrance rather than veil it.

### 12

According to this arrangement, then, and according to this form of the tabernacle, there is no longer any need to place the twenty columns of the inner tabernacle’s southern and northern sides more closely together, or to make the eight columns on the western side more widely spaced. Those ten columns of the outer court on the same western side do not form a long row of columns enclosing the eight inner ones. Rather, three are placed on each side and four at the gate,

[Note: [Col. 0665] Rat. and Lov. read “unequal”; Am., Er., and five manuscripts, “into the gate”; other manuscripts, “at the gate.”]

enclosing the space in which there was the altar of burnt offering within the court gate, before the entrance of the tabernacle; the basin between the entrance of the tabernacle and the altar; and the interval necessary for the ministry between the altar and the court gate.

Thus the entire space of the court is enclosed by ten columns: three to the north, three to the south, and four to the west, as though one were making the Greek letter Π (pi).

This same space was joined to the longer row of columns of the inner tabernacle as though, to the aforementioned letter, on the side where it has none, one added the extension of the letter called iota. Thus it is enclosed on that side by its middle portion, while the remaining parts of the iota extend on either side.

The ten columns in that long row of the western part of the inner tabernacle could therefore be counted, but two of them were added to the eight: those two had been the final columns in the rows of the northern and southern sides of the court.

For those ten columns which properly belonged to the court on the western side, from which one entered the tabernacle, had three on each side and four at the front, where the gate was; and thus they enclosed within the court, before the tabernacle, the space necessary for the sacrificial rites. Along the three columns on the sides there were linen curtains fifteen cubits long; while on the four columns where the gate was, there was a twenty-cubit curtain varied with embroidered needlework.

### 13. [Book XXXVIII, 9–18]

Nor should it trouble us that Scripture says:

“Fifteen cubits shall be the height of the curtains for one side: their columns three, and their bases three. And for the second side, fifteen cubits shall be the height of the curtains: their columns three, and their bases three. And for the gate of the court, a covering twenty cubits high.”

For it gives the same dimension as height that had previously been given as the length of the curtains. The height is the same when they are woven as the length when they are stretched out.

Lest this seem merely conjectural, Scripture mentions the same matter elsewhere, saying:

“And they made the court that is toward the south: the curtains of the court of twisted linen, one hundred by one hundred”—that is, one hundred cubits of curtains by one hundred cubits of the space occupied by the twenty columns.

Then it continues:

“And their columns twenty, and their bases twenty, [Col. 0665] of bronze. And the side toward the north, one hundred by one hundred, and their columns twenty.”

[Note: The editions, except Rat., read “twenty bronze ones.” The word “bronze” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Septuagint.]

“And their bases twenty, of bronze. And the side toward the sea, curtains fifty cubits long: their columns ten and their bases ten.”

It calls the curtains the same thing as the hangings. Then:

“And the side toward the east, curtains fifty cubits.”

After this it returns to the rear of the tabernacle, to show how those ten columns enclosed the space of the court of which he was speaking:

“Fifteen cubits,” he says, “which is from the rear.”

He calls it the rear because it was the back of the tabernacle, that is, the western side.

“And their columns,” he says, “three, and their bases three. And from the second rear, on this side and on that side according to the gate of the court, curtains fifteen [Col. 0666] cubits: their columns three, and their bases three.”

[Note: The editions read “side” instead of the manuscripts’ “gate.” The Septuagint likewise has “gate.”]

It is certainly clear that this passage calls the same two sections “rears” when all the features are mentioned as having been made—features which had been called “sides” when the instructions for making them were given. They were called sides because, joined on either side, they enclosed the space of the western gate of the court;

[Note: [Col. 0666] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “joined on the western side.”]

they are called rears because this part of the court lay behind the tabernacle, that is, on the western side.

It continues:

“All the curtains of the court of twisted linen, and the bases of the columns bronze, and their loops silver, and their capitals overlaid with silver; and the columns of the court, all of them overlaid with silver.”

Then it adds something not yet mentioned in this passage:

“And the curtain of the court gate, the work of a weaver, of violet, purple, scarlet, and twisted linen: twenty cubits in length and breadth.”

[Note: The Septuagint reads, in Exodus 37, “the curtain of the court gate.” Compare the Vulgate, Exodus 38:18.]

Here it becomes clear that the height mentioned above was the length of the stretched curtains. Finally it adds:

“And its breadth five cubits.”

For the curtains of the outer court were raised to a height of five cubits, just as those of the inner tabernacle were raised to four cubits.

Thus he had also said above:

“The length of the court was one hundred by one hundred, and its breadth fifty by fifty, and its height five cubits, of twisted linen.”

He calls this dimension the breadth, which he later calls the height, because what is the breadth of things lying flat is the height of things erected. Likewise, as I mentioned shortly before, the dimension that is the height when they are woven is the length when they are stretched.

### 14. [Book XXVI, 12, 9, 13]

Let us now examine what I postponed: how, from this form of the entire tabernacle—which I have set before the eyes as best I could—that difficulty concerning the hairy curtains may be resolved.

Perhaps the matter was more obscure because something was stated there in anticipation, something that would contribute to the work about which he was later going to speak, when he described the court as being placed around the tabernacle.

Let us now examine the actual words:

“And you shall lay down that which remains over in the curtains of the tabernacle; you shall cover the half-curtain which remains over; you shall cover behind the tabernacle that which is in excess in the curtains of the tabernacle.”

Everything said here has one meaning: the half of the curtain that remains over—that is, whatever exceeds the curtains of the tabernacle—is to be covered behind the tabernacle.

How, then, does half a curtain remain over, that is, exceed and be left over? This must be determined from the series of curtains joined together, since he wished five to be joined to one another and six to one another, as he had said above, ordering the sixth curtain to be doubled at the front of the tabernacle, that is, on the eastern side. For he repeatedly indicated that the rear of the tabernacle was on the western side, toward the sea.

What, then, is meant by “the front of the tabernacle,” except that part which is toward the east?

The section in which five curtains were joined together therefore has one hundred and fifty cubits, that is, five times thirty, since each curtain measured thirty cubits, as God had commanded them to be made. The section in which there were not five but six curtains similarly joined had one hundred and eighty cubits, that is, six times thirty.

Accordingly, when one of these was doubled, as commanded, at the front of the tabernacle, fifteen cubits were removed [Col. 0667] by that doubling. After this subtraction, one hundred and sixty-five cubits remained. Therefore, after the one hundred and fifty cubits by which the section of six curtains was made equal to the section of five curtains, fifteen cubits remained and exceeded it.

On the one side, the section of five curtains had one hundred and fifty cubits; on the other side, the section of six curtains, after one curtain was doubled at the front of the tabernacle, had one hundred and sixty-five cubits. Thus this section had fifteen cubits more.

This is the half of the curtain which he commands to be covered behind the tabernacle: since one half was doubled at the front, the excess half at the rear of the tabernacle was not to be doubled but covered over. That is, all those fifteen cubits were to be let down and covered. In this way they too were subtracted from that length, just as the fifteen cubits at the front of the tabernacle were removed by doubling one curtain. Thus the one hundred and fifty cubits of the five curtains would correspond on the other side to one hundred and fifty cubits of the six curtains: thirty cubits having been removed from the one hundred and eighty by doubling a curtain at the front of the tabernacle and covering half a curtain at its rear.

### 15

What follows is something different and raises another question. This is why I thought it best to postpone the exposition of this passage until we had first examined both the form of the tabernacle’s construction and what is written about placing the court around it.

The text continues:

“An additional cubit on this side and an additional cubit on that side, from what exceeds in the curtains in the length of the curtains of the tabernacle, shall be a covering over the sides of the tabernacle on this side and on that side, to cover it.”

One thing is the amount by which one section of six curtains exceeds the other section of five, because of the greater number of curtains; we have already discussed that. Another is what exceeds in the length of the curtains, which is what is now being mentioned.

Here one section is not compared with another, nor is one found to exceed the other—the section with six curtains exceeding the section with five. To make the two equal, one curtain was doubled at the front of the tabernacle and half was covered at the rear.

Rather, the hairy curtains themselves, when compared with the curtains from which he commanded the inner tabernacle to be made, woven in four colors, are found to be two cubits longer. Each of those curtains measured twenty-eight cubits, whereas these measured thirty. For that reason he does not say here, “from what exceeds in the curtains,” but “from what exceeds in the curtains in the length of the curtains.”

What, then, does “an additional cubit on this side and an additional cubit on that side shall be a covering over the sides of the tabernacle” mean, except that the length by which the hairy curtains are two cubits longer than the curtains—one cubit for each—is not to be gathered wholly to one side, so that whatever exceeds is collected at the rear of the tabernacle. Instead, it is to be distributed equally, with as much assigned to the front of the tabernacle as to the rear.

That is, since the two cubits by which each curtain exceeds the others produce the excess length, one cubit is to be taken from one side and one cubit from the other. Thus from their individual excess cubits this side will have ten cubits and the other side ten [Col. 0668] cubits, since ten curtains, each two cubits longer, produce a total excess of twenty cubits by which their series appears to exceed the series of the curtains.

### 16

Next we must determine what space these twenty excess cubits serve to enclose.

If the inner tabernacle is surrounded by the hairy curtains, they exceed by so much that there seems to be no part for them to cover at all. It therefore remains that these too must be covered and, by being covered, subtracted—a point Scripture does not state.

The ten curtains, each measuring twenty-eight cubits, by which the inner tabernacle is stretched, enclose as much space as two hundred and eighty cubits can enclose. The two longer sides, southern and northern, each having twenty columns, take one hundred cubits from this total; eighty remain, to be distributed by the two shorter sides, east and west, forty each. The western side had eight columns; the eastern side had no row of columns.

Accordingly, in the hairy curtains, since after thirty cubits had been removed three hundred remained, if the two hundred and eighty cubits of the inner curtains are covered by the three hundred cubits of the hairy curtains, twenty cubits will remain, with nothing for them to cover.

Therefore those two cubits which each hairy curtain has in excess, producing a total of twenty cubits, are to be distributed in this way: “an additional cubit on this side and an additional cubit on that side.” That is, they are not all to be gathered to one side so as to serve for covering the sides of the tabernacle, but the entire three hundred cubits of the hairy curtains are to surround the tabernacle on the outside—that is, the outer court.

For, when the one-hundred-cubit sides of the outer court, south and north, are added, fifty cubits remain for each of east and west.

[Note: [Col. 0668] Lov. reads “one hundred cubits, that is”; and a little later “fifty cubits” for “fifty each,” undoubtedly through a serious printers’ error.]

Together these make three hundred cubits, and the three hundred cubits of hairy curtains are sufficient to cover them.

This is what he means by “an additional cubit on this side and an additional cubit on that side”: the distribution of the two cubits by which each hairy curtain is longer, that is, “from what exceeds in the curtains in the length of the curtains, shall be a covering over the sides of the tabernacle, on this side and on that side, to cover it.” These are the outer sides belonging to the court.

He does not mean the sides of the court itself, which extend one hundred cubits and have twenty columns. Those sides have not been made longer than the sides of the inner tabernacle, which are stretched by ten curtains and likewise have twenty columns each. For just as the two sides of the inner tabernacle, north and south, extend one hundred cubits, so do those of the outer court.

The greater length of the hairy curtains beyond the length of the curtains therefore does not serve to cover those outer sides having the same number of columns. It gives to the outer sides no more than it would give to the inner sides—one hundred cubits each, making two hundred in all.

But because forty-cubit sides would have been sufficient for the eastern and western sides if only the inner tabernacle had been surrounded by hairy curtains, the addition of the court increased the breadth of the tabernacle.
