Thus, for covering the eastern and western sides, [Col. 0669] not forty but fifty cubits were now required. The greater length of the hairy curtains than of the curtains could serve to cover them, so that the two excess cubits by which each was longer were not expended entirely on one side, but one cubit on this side and one on that. Thus the eastern side received ten cubits from the excess, and the western side another ten.

For two times ten makes twenty, since the thirty cubits of the eleventh curtain are reduced from this circuit by doubling and covering.

[Note: The editions read “eleven”; several manuscripts more correctly read “of the eleventh.”]

### 17

But because what has been translated into Latin as “an additional cubit on this side and an additional cubit on that side, from what exceeds in the curtains in the length of the curtains of the tabernacle, shall be a covering over the sides of the tabernacle” has in Greek *πλάγια*, which some Latins translated not as *sides* but as *oblique parts*, the question rightly arises.

For although nothing here may appear oblique, since all four corners of the four sides are right angles, nevertheless those parts cannot be called *πλάγια* which consist of one at the front and another at the rear, that is, the eastern and western sides. Rather, *πλάγια* can refer to the right and left sides, that is, the northern and southern sides.

Since, then, the *πλάγια* are not the sides measuring fifty cubits—the sides which, as we have said, could have been covered by the excess length of the hairy curtains—how can it be true that “an additional cubit on this side and an additional cubit on that side, from what exceeds in the curtains in the length of the curtains of the tabernacle, shall be a covering over the sides of the tabernacle”?

Clearly he is speaking of those sides which he also calls the rears: the fifteen-cubit sides with three columns. Together with the court gate, which had twenty cubits and four columns, they complete fifty cubits and ten columns.

These sides placed the court gate in the middle between their respective ends, while at their other ends they placed the entrance of the tabernacle. Between the court gate and the entrance of the tabernacle there lies a space enclosed by those dimensions: twenty cubits from the gate, and fifteen cubits on the right and fifteen on the left.

In that space was the altar of burnt offering, inside the court gate and before the entrance of the tabernacle; and between the altar and the entrance of the tabernacle was the bronze basin, where the priests washed their hands and feet.

[Note: This passage has been restored in full with the aid of one Vatican manuscript and the Corbeiensis and Thuaneus manuscripts. In the editions of Am., Er., and Lov. it appeared as follows: “In that space was the altar of the tabernacle, and between the altar of the tabernacle was the basin,” etc. In Bat. and several manuscripts: “In that space was the altar of the tabernacle, and between the altar and the entrance of the tabernacle was the basin.”]

On careful examination of the measurements, perhaps some obliquity is also found in these sides with three columns, which are called *πλάγια* in Greek. Thus our translators were not without reason when they rendered the Greek *πλάγια* as *oblique parts*.

For the hairy curtains, each fifteen cubits long, cannot cover the fifteen-cubit curtains on those sides unless, before turning toward those sides, they have contributed no more than ten cubits to the rear portions of the tabernacle.

Thus, from the straight line of the rear of the tabernacle—that is, the western side—which line had eight columns belonging to the inner tabernacle and then came to have ten when the sides of the outer court were added; and which had forty cubits belonging to the [Col. 0670] eight columns and then came to have fifty with ten columns—from this line, when ten cubits of hairy curtains extend from each corner, thirty cubits will remain in the middle uncovered by the hairy curtains and covered only by the curtains. In the middle of those thirty cubits, at whatever intervals they were stretched, was the entrance of the tabernacle.

Therefore those sides with three columns and fifteen cubits, from the ends at which they joined the court gate, opened toward one another by twenty cubits, since the gate separating them had that width. But at their other ends, where they were attached to the rear line of the tabernacle just mentioned, they opened toward one another by thirty cubits. They were therefore certainly oblique, since they opened more widely on the side where the middle interval was thirty cubits than on the side where it was twenty.

Thus the ten cubits of hairy curtains—which were half the excess length and served the rear part of the tabernacle, that is, the western side, just as the other ten served the front, or eastern, side—covered those sides, called *πλάγια* in Greek, five cubits from one direction and five from the other.

If those same five cubits had been absent, ten cubits would have been covered on those same sides and five would have remained bare.

Accordingly, as it seems to me, the passage is better understood as saying “an additional cubit on this side and an additional cubit on that side, from what exceeds in the curtains in the length of the curtains of the tabernacle,” not because there were five cubits on each side, but because the excess arose from the length in which the hairy curtains were two cubits longer than the curtains. Of those two cubits belonging to each curtain, one cubit served the eastern side; the other necessarily remained for the western side, so that the additional cubit on this side became a covering over the *πλάγια* of the tabernacle.

Hence it says “on this side and on that side, to cover,” because the whole would not have been covered if those five cubits on each side had been absent.

### 18

Now that we have sufficiently discussed how all those matters which seemed obscure in the construction of the tabernacle are to be understood, let us briefly attempt, if possible, to show what has been established by this discussion.

Entry was therefore from the west. The first entrance was the gate of the court, which opened for twenty cubits and had four columns, from which hung a curtain stretched over twenty cubits and raised to a height of five cubits. It was varied by embroidered needlework in the four colors repeatedly mentioned.

Those who entered through this gate were received by the court. Its right and left sides extended inward for fifteen cubits each on three columns each, so that the entrance of the inner tabernacle could be placed in the middle at the point where those sides reached it, just as the court gate was placed in the middle at the point from which the sides began.

This court was therefore broader than it was long. Its length, from its gate to the entrance of the inner tabernacle, was approximately fifteen cubits; its breadth was about twenty cubits at the gate and about thirty cubits at the entrance. Hence those sides on the right and left are understood to have been oblique, consisting of three columns and fifteen cubits.

In this court was the square altar of sacrifices, five cubits long [Col. 0671] and the same breadth.

Between the gate and the altar was a space in which those who placed the sacrifices upon the altar moved about. Inside, between the altar and the entrance of the tabernacle, was the place for the ashes before the altar.

[Note: The Batavian edition and four manuscripts omit “before the altar.”]

Then came the bronze basin, where the priests washed their hands and feet, whether they were about to minister at the altar in the court or enter the inner tabernacle.

The curtains of this court, along the sides having three columns, were of linen, stretched for fifteen cubits and raised to a height of five cubits.

### 19

From this court, therefore, one entered the entrance of the tabernacle after passing the altar and the bronze basin.

The entrance was made through openings in the curtains. Ten curtains—five on one side and five on the other, set opposite one another—surrounded the entire inner tabernacle.

As one entered, one encountered the curtain placed before the entrance, stretched on five columns and varied in the four colors. When he commanded this curtain to be made, he called it an *adductorium*, I believe because it moved back and forth, drawing and withdrawing as it covered and opened the entrance.

After passing through this curtain, one entered the central part of the tabernacle, lying between this curtain and the other inner curtain, which had been placed upon four columns, made in those same four colors, and separated the holy place outside from the Holy of Holies within.

In this central space between the two curtains stood the golden table, which held the loaves of the Presence on the northern side; opposite it stood the golden lampstand with seven lamps on the southern side.

Up to this point the subordinate priests were permitted to enter.

### 20

Further inside, that is, in the Holy of Holies beyond the curtain of four columns, stood the gilded ark of the testimony. In it were the stone tablets of the Law, Aaron’s rod, and a golden urn containing manna. Above it was the golden mercy seat, where two cherubim stood, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings and looking toward one another and toward the mercy seat itself.

Before the ark—that is, between the ark and the curtain—stood the altar of incense. Scripture sometimes calls it golden and sometimes gilded; it calls it golden because it was overlaid with gold.

No one except the high priest was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies every day, for the offering of incense. He entered once a year with blood to purify the altar, and whenever necessity required it because of the sin of the priest or of the whole congregation, as it is written in Leviticus 16.

Thus the tabernacle was entered from the west—from the gate of the court—

[Note: So reads the old Corbeiensis manuscript. The editions and several manuscripts have “from the southern gate.” The Vatican manuscript reads “from the southern gate of the court.”]

—inward as far as the eastern side, where the ark of the testimony stood.

### 21

This inner tabernacle, however, which began not at the court gate but at the entrance called the entrance of the tabernacle, and ended lengthwise at the eastern side where the ark of the testimony stood, was enclosed by ten curtains. Each measured twenty-eight cubits; five were joined to five by loops and rings and set opposite one another.

There were twenty columns along the longer northern and southern sides, and eight columns along the western side. Along the [Col. 0672] eastern side there were no columns, but only curtains.

These ten curtains were raised to a height of four cubits, and throughout their circuit were stretched for two hundred and eighty cubits: one hundred cubits along each of the longer southern and northern sides, by means of twenty columns; and forty cubits along each of the two shorter sides—one on the west, by means of eight columns, and the other on the east, where there were no columns but only curtains stretched from the two corner columns, with no columns in the middle.

These were ten curtains woven in four colors.

This inner tabernacle was therefore surrounded by the court: twenty columns on the south and twenty on the north. These two sides of the court had the same length as the sides of the inner tabernacle, since they too extended by twenty columns over the same number of cubits, namely one hundred.

On the eastern side the court was enclosed by ten columns over fifty cubits. This row of columns was straight and met the two corner columns of the inner tabernacle, which were the only columns belonging to its eastern side; thus, together with those two, the number was completed at ten.

On the western side the court did indeed have ten columns, but not in a straight row. Rather, as we have already shown, it was like a three-sided portico: four at the gate and three on each side.

22. Now the entire court surrounding the tabernacle was enclosed with linen hangings, which were erected to a height of five cubits. Over these were eleven curtains of goats’ hair, five joined to one another on one side and six on the other. Thus, in the joining of the five curtains, there were 150 cubits; on the other side, in the joining of the six curtains, there were 180 cubits, since each curtain was thirty cubits long. But so that one side might be made equal to the other, one curtain was doubled at the front of the tabernacle, that is, on the eastern side, and half a curtain was covered over at the rear, that is, on the western side. Thus thirty cubits were subtracted, the length of one curtain, and 150 remained, the same number as on the other side.

Therefore, the circuit of the goats’ hair curtains by which the court of the tabernacle was enclosed extended for 300 cubits, just as the circuit of the ten inner tabernacle hangings extended for 280 cubits. For each of the hangings had a length of twenty-eight cubits, whereas the goats’ hair curtains were thirty cubits long. Accordingly, of the circuit of the inner tabernacle hangings, which was 280 cubits, 100 cubits were on the longer southern and northern sides, and forty on the two shorter eastern and western sides. But of the circuit of the goats’ hair curtains, by which the outer court was covered, since the circuit was 300 cubits, 100 cubits were on the longer southern and northern sides, because these were equal to the sides of the inner tabernacle, while fifty were on the two remaining eastern and western sides.

Consequently, those two cubits by which the goats’ hair curtain was longer did not benefit the southern and northern sides, which were equal in length in the outer court and the inner tabernacle, but the eastern and western sides. For it was on those sides that the width of the tabernacle increased when the court was placed around it externally.

[Col. 0673] But the fifty cubits of goats’ hair curtains on the eastern side extended in a straight line through the ten columns; and one cubit of the two by which those curtains had the greater length contributed to them. The other fifty cubits, which belonged to the western side, and to which the other of those two cubits contributed, were not extended in a straight line through the order of the columns. For there was the structure resembling a three-sided portico, which enclosed the space of the court where the altar of sacrifices stood: four columns at the entrance and three on each side. Consequently, those fifty cubits could not enclose the entrance as well [Note: [Col. 0673] The printed editions omit “the entrance”; all manuscripts have it.], but extended as far as covering those oblique side-sections, which were fifteen cubits on each side, supported by three columns. The goats’ hair curtains, moreover, were erected to a height of four cubits, and by them the linen hangings of the court were covered; these had an erected height of five cubits.

23. Red-dyed skins, however, were placed over the goats’ hair curtains. Above, that is, on the roofing side, the tabernacle was covered with violet skins in place of a ceiling. Whether this included the court and that interior space is not apparent; but it is more credible that the spaces of the court between the outer and inner columns were open to the sky [Note: [Col. 0674] Am., Er., and Lov. read “a curtain”; Bat. and the manuscripts read “the sky.”], especially the western side, where the altar of sacrifices was located.

BOOK THREE. Questions on Leviticus.

[Col. 0673]

[Col. 0673] QUESTION I. [LEVITICUS, chap. V, verse 1.] “But if a person sins, or hears the voice of an oath, and is himself a witness, or has seen it, or is privy to it, if he does not report it, he shall bear the sin”: that is, “If he certainly does not report it, he shall bear the sin.” The conjunction “and” that has been added is a customary form of expression in Scripture.

Yet because this meaning is obscure, it seems that it should be explained. For it appears to say that a person sins if, in his hearing, someone swears falsely, and he knows that the person is swearing falsely, yet remains silent. He knows this when he has been a witness to the matter about which the oath is sworn, or has seen it, or has learned it from the person himself who swears—that is, he has come to know it in some way, either has seen it with his own eyes, or the person who swears has disclosed it to him. Thus he could be privy to it.

But between fear of this sin and fear of betraying people there is often no small temptation. We can recall someone prepared to commit perjury from so grave a sin by warning or restraining him. But if he does not listen and, in our presence, swears falsely concerning a matter known to us, whether he should be exposed—especially if, once exposed, he should incur the danger of death—is a very difficult question.

But since he did not specify to whom this should be disclosed—whether to the person to whom the oath is sworn, or to a priest, or to someone who not only cannot persecute him by inflicting punishment but can also pray for him—it seems to me that a person frees himself from the bond of sin if he reports it to those who are more able to help than to harm the perjurer, whether by correcting him or by appeasing God on his behalf, provided that he himself also applies the remedy of confession.

II. [Ibid. V, 2–6.] After this kind of sin, which he had mentioned concerning an unreported perjury, he did not order any sacrifice to be offered for it. Instead, he then added:

“Any person who touches any unclean thing, or the carcass of an unclean animal, or the carcass of an unclean animal taken by a wild beast, or the carcasses of unclean abominations, the carcasses of unclean cattle; or touches human uncleanness, any uncleanness of his by touching which he is defiled, though it has escaped his notice, and afterward he comes to know it and commits an offense.”

Here too he did not mention a sacrifice to be offered for this kind of sin [Col. 0674], but added further and said:

“Any person who swears, distinguishing with his lips whether to do evil or good, according to everything that a person may distinguish with an oath, though it has escaped him, and afterward he comes to know it, and sins in one of these matters, and confesses the sin for which he sinned against it.”

After connecting and explaining all these matters without any intervening mention of sacrifice, he adds and says:

“And he shall offer for the things in which he offended against the Lord, for the sin by which he sinned, a female lamb from the sheep or a she-goat from the goats as a sin-offering; and the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin, and his sin shall be forgiven.”

What, then, is the meaning of this? For tacit perjury, and for touching a carcass or something unclean, he mentioned no sacrifice; but for the sin in which someone unknowingly swore falsely, he said that a lamb or she-goat should be offered. Are we to understand that this sacrifice applies to all the matters mentioned above? For perhaps he first wished to enumerate everything and then indicate by what sacrifice they could be expiated.

But among all the kinds of sin mentioned above, some are expressed somewhat obscurely because of their forms of speech, such as “the carcass of beasts.” For the creatures whom the Greeks call κτήνη (*ktēnē*) most of our translators have rendered by “beasts of burden” (*jumenta*). In Latin usage this word denotes animals whose labor assists us, especially in carrying burdens, such as horses, asses, mules, camels, and anything of that kind. But the creatures whom the Greeks call κτήνη are understood so broadly that all, or almost all, livestock are included under that name.

Therefore, in a novel form of expression—or, as it were, by pleonasm—the word “unclean” was added in Greek when “beasts” was mentioned, since there are also clean livestock that are called κτήνη. But the animals that Latin usage calls *jumenta*, according to the distinction of the Law, are unclean only.

III. [Ibid. V, 2–6.] Likewise, when it says, “Any person who swears, distinguishing with his lips whether to do evil or good,” the question is what it means by “distinguishing.” Scripture uses this word repeatedly. Hence there is also the passage, “I shall fulfill my vows, which my lips distinguished” (Psalm LXV, 13–14). Likewise it is said to Ezekiel: “When I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you have not distinguished or spoken” (Ezekiel III, 18). It is also written: “If a woman, established in her father’s house, makes a vow, distinguishing with her lips against her own person” (Numbers XXX, 4).

This “distinguishing,” therefore, seems to be like a definition by which something is separated from other things that are not fixed by a mere statement. Thus it should be understood as though it said:

“Any person who swears, defining with his lips whether to do evil or good, according to everything that a person may define with an oath, though it has escaped him”—that is, not knowing that it ought or ought not to be done, he has sworn to do it—“and afterward comes to know it, and sins in one of these matters,” either because he swore before he knew, or because he did what he had sworn to do and afterward learned that it ought not to have been done or sworn to; “and confesses the sin for which he sinned”—that is, the sin which he committed. This is a form of expression.

But when it adds “against it,” what can be understood except that he confessed against the sin itself—that is, by confessing, he accused the sin? “And he shall offer for the things in which he offended against the Lord, for the sin by which he sinned, a female lamb from the sheep.” In customary speech he says “a female lamb,” as though there could be a lamb that was not female; or “a she-goat from the goats,” just as “a female lamb from the sheep,” as though there could be either a lamb that was not from sheep or a she-goat that was not from goats.

There is, however, a question—indeed, not a small one—about what he repeatedly means when he says, “Afterward he comes to know it, and commits an offense,” as though the offense occurred only when it became known. Or is it rather because satisfaction cannot be made except for what is known? Yet he does not say, “Afterward he comes to know it and repents.” What, then, is “Afterward he comes to know it and commits an offense,” except “after coming to know it, he commits an offense,” so that purification from the offense is owed when someone knowingly does what ought not to be done?

But he did not introduce the matter in that way. For he seems to be dealing with sins committed by those who are ignorant and consequently unwilling. Perhaps, then, “he commits an offense” is said by a certain form of expression for “he learns that it is an offense.” Or is the order perhaps reversed—as Scripture also has such forms of expression—so that what is said elsewhere in the proper order is here stated in the reverse order?

For whereas elsewhere it is so often written, “and he commits an offense, and it becomes known to him,” here, as I have said, the order is reversed: first “he comes to know,” and then “he commits an offense.” In its proper order it could be stated as follows:

“Any person who touches any unclean thing, or the carcass of an unclean animal, or the carcass of an unclean animal taken by a wild beast, or the carcasses of unclean abominations, the carcasses of unclean beasts, or touches human uncleanness, any of his uncleanness, by which he is defiled if he touches it; and if it has escaped him, and he commits an offense, and afterward comes to know it.”

IV. [Ibid. V, 7.] “But if his hand cannot provide what is sufficient for a sheep, he shall offer for the sin which he committed two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the Lord, one for sin and one as a burnt offering.”

Here he certainly clarifies the question about which we were uncertain above. For this is apparently why he says, “one for sin, the other as a burnt offering”: a sacrifice for sin was not offered without a burnt offering. Thus, when he previously spoke separately about burnt offerings, he mentioned a turtledove but did not say “two” (Leviticus I, 14). Now, however, he says “two” because a sacrifice for sin was not offered without a burnt offering.

Therefore, when he said above, “And he shall place it upon the burnt offering” (ibid. IV, 35), there is no doubt that the burnt offering came first and that the other sacrifice was placed upon it. But now, concerning the birds, he says something different: first one bird is to be offered for sin, and then the other as a burnt offering.

V. [Ibid. V, 15.] When it says, “If it has escaped him through forgetfulness,” this means: if it happened through forgetfulness that it escaped him—or “her,” if the reference is taken to “soul” (*anima*), since by saying “him” he referred it to the human being. For here he calls a human being a “soul.”

VI. [Ibid. V, 15–16.] “And he sins unknowingly against the holy things of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0676] The printed editions read: “And if he sins unknowingly against the Lord’s holy things.” But the manuscripts, agreeing with the Greek, lack “if” and have “of the Lord.” On the authority of the manuscripts, we have restored the Greek reading in so many frequent passages that we are reluctant to note all of them.].

This kind of sin seems to be expressed obscurely, but it is explained in what follows, where, after the sacrifice of a ram has been offered, it says: “He shall restore it, and add a fifth part.” From this it is understood that to sin unknowingly against holy things means to appropriate through forgetfulness something owed to holy things, whether to priests, offerings, first fruits, or anything of that kind.

VII. [Ibid. V, 17–19.] “And any person who sins and does one of all the commandments of the Lord that ought not to be done, and does not know it, and commits an offense, and does not know his sin” [Note: [Col. 0676] All the manuscripts have this reading here, although later, in Question 20, no. 5, they read “and has received his sin”; that reading is more correct, as is clear from the Greek Septuagint.], “shall bring to the priest a ram without blemish from the sheep, valued in silver, as a guilt-offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him because of his ignorance, through which he was ignorant and did not know; and it shall be forgiven him. For he has indeed committed an offense before the Lord.”

Apart from the unusual density of the expressions—which, because of their constant repetition, ought by now to be well known—the whole meaning is obscure, because it is asked how this kind of offense is distinguished from those that he previously included under a certain general category.

For reason seems to demand that particular kinds of sin should have particular kinds of sacrifices by which they are expiated. But this passage does not specify a particular sin; rather, it seems to remain within the general category in which, earlier, he prescribed a bull for the priest, and likewise a bull for the whole congregation, a he-goat for the ruler, and for any person—that is, for any human being—a she-goat, or, if he wished, a sheep, but still a female animal (Leviticus IV).

Then he began to make exceptions for certain kinds of sins and to specify by name what should be offered for them: for hearing and concealing another’s perjury, for touching a carcass or unclean thing, and for false swearing through ignorance, a female lamb from the sheep, or a she-goat from the goats, or a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons, or a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour; but for the person who, through forgetfulness, appropriated something belonging to holy things, a ram and restitution of the thing itself, with a fifth part added.

Now, without specifying the kind of sin, he adds generally: “Any person who commits an offense and does one of all the commandments of the Lord that ought not to be done”—just as in that general category he had said, “one of the commandments of the Lord that shall not be done”—“and does not know it,” that is, sins unknowingly and unwillingly. He orders a ram to be offered, not a she-goat or a female sheep, as he had earlier prescribed in such a general category of sins.

What, then, does this mixture mean? Perhaps when he says here, “He has committed an offense as an offense before the Lord,” by adding “before the Lord” he wished the offense to be understood as one committed in matters that take place before the Lord—that is, matters by which the Lord is served in the tabernacle. A little earlier he had said, “He sinned against holy things,” and we understood this to mean that he appropriated something belonging to holy things, since he had also ordered its restoration.

Accordingly, a person can sin in these matters not only by appropriating something from them through forgetfulness; one can also offend through ignorance in many other ways in matters presented for the service of the Lord. He wished to mention this kind of offense afterward in general terms, and therefore ordered a ram to be offered both there and here.

The Scriptures are full of passages in which “before the Lord” is said and means only what is offered to the Lord, such as a sacrifice, first fruits, or some service in sacred matters.

VIII. [Ibid. V, 7.] It is also asked whether what is said—if his hand cannot provide what is sufficient for a sheep, he must offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, and, if he cannot provide even this, a specified quantity of fine flour—is to be understood as applicable everywhere.

For if it is understood that this is permitted everywhere, it cannot reasonably be said that a priest does not possess a bull, or that the whole congregation does not possess one, or that a ruler does not possess a he-goat [Note: [Col. 0677] Er. and Lov. read “a she-goat.” Other manuscripts read “a he-goat.”] or a sheep. If that is so, why was it later necessary to say that concealed perjury, or touching something unclean, or perjury committed through ignorance, was to be purified by the sacrifice of a lamb and a she-goat, when these same sacrifices were prescribed also in that general category of sin, to which these matters could likewise have belonged?

But if these are distinguished from that category because in their case it was permitted to offer turtledoves and pigeons, or, if even those were unavailable, fine flour, whereas in the other case, where this was not stated, it was not permitted, then the poor do not seem to have been helped. For there could be many sins not specifically expressed that would belong to that general category, and the poor would be burdened if it were permitted to offer only a female she-goat, a female lamb from the sheep, those birds, and fine flour.

Unless perhaps someone says that these exceptional and expressly specified sins are distinguished from those mentioned generally because here he says “a lamb,” whereas there he says “a sheep,” so that the age of the animals makes some difference. Nevertheless, it must be understood that equal provision was made for the poor, so that if they had no four-footed animals, or the birds mentioned, or fine flour, they could offer these for the sins committed in ignorance.

But if it troubles anyone that, although he had included all sins of ignorance under a general category and had distinguished the sacrifices not according to differences among the sins—which he had not made—but according to differences among persons, he later wished also to distinguish sins and prescribe different sacrifices according to their variety, as though all did not belong to that general category, the later exception must be understood in this way: whatever remained after the sins he specifically and individually mentioned had been excepted, we should understand as included in the general category.

This mode of expression is not found elsewhere, but there is a comparable passage in the holy Scriptures where the Apostle says: “Every sin whatever a person commits is outside the body.” For here he seems to have omitted nothing sinful, since he says, “Every sin whatever a person commits.” Yet afterward he excepts fornication when he adds: “But whoever commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians VI, 18).

According to our customary form of speech, this would be expressed as follows: “Every sin whatever a person commits, except fornication, is outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body.” So too here, when he first said generally that all sins of ignorance were to be expiated by the sacrifices he had mentioned, he afterward nevertheless excepted those for which, once they had been expressly and distinctly set out, he prescribed a specific purification by sacrifices. Thus, apart from these, whatever other sins remained belonged to the general category.

IX. [Ibid. VI, 6–10.] “He shall offer a ram from the sheep without blemish, at a price, for the matter in which he has committed an offense.” This should not be parsed as though “at a price” qualified “the matter in which he has offended,” as though the price itself had offended. Rather, if he offers a ram, he should offer it at a price—that is, one purchased.

This too seems to have been intended to pertain to the sacramental significance of something, since he did not specify the price itself. For if he had specified it, he might have seemed to prescribe that an inferior animal should not be offered, so that even if the offerer did not purchase it, he would nevertheless offer one worth that amount.

But by adding not merely “at a price,” so that a purchased ram should be offered, but also “in holy shekels”—for he says, “at a price of silver, shekels, by the holy shekel” [Note: [Col. 0678] The printed editions read “of silver, holy shekels.” The manuscripts read “of silver, shekels, by the holy shekel.” The Septuagint reads *argyriou syklōn, tō syklō tōn hagiōn*; in some manuscripts, however, according to Nobilius, *tō syklō tō hygiō*.] (Leviticus V, 15)—he wished the ram to be bought for several shekels, not for one shekel.

What “holy shekel” means we have already discussed where the matter arose. But when, after saying, “And he shall offer to the Lord his chosen ram from the sheep without blemish, at a price,” he then adds, “according to what he offended,” this should be understood to mean that he should offer it for what he offended—that is, for, or on account of, that matter.

“And he shall remove the whole burnt offering that the fire has consumed, that burnt offering from the altar.” What will he remove if it has been consumed? For he ordered the priest, after the fire had burned throughout the night, to remove the whole burnt offering—that is, the sacrifice that the fire had consumed.

Or what does the added phrase “that burnt offering” mean, when *holocarpoma* and *holocaustosis* appear to signify the same thing? Perhaps the reading we found in a certain Greek text is correct. For it does not say, “He shall remove the *holocarposis*,” but “He shall remove the *katakarposis*” [Col. 0679]—that is, the remains of the burnt offering that the fire consumed.

These remains, such as ash and charcoal, he called *holocaustosis*, naming the remains of the consumption after the thing that had been consumed.

X. [Ibid. VI, 9.] When he said above, “This is the law of the burnt offering,” and then, explaining what that same law is, said, “This is the *holocaustosis*, upon its burning on the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn upon it; it shall not be extinguished,” the meaning would be clearer according to our customary form of speech if it did not contain the conjunction “and.” For with that conjunction removed, the sentence runs as follows:

“This is the *holocaustosis*: upon its burning on the altar all night until morning, the fire of the altar shall burn upon it”—that is, upon the altar. Then, to complete the expression of the thought, he adds, “it shall not be extinguished,” for this had already been stated by saying “all night.”

XI. [Ibid. VI, 11.] “And he shall put on another robe and carry the *holocarpoma* outside the camp to a clean place.” He calls the *holocarpoma* what has already been burned up. In the Greek this is read as *katakarposis*. Some Latin translators added “which has been burned” [Note: [Col. 0679] The manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions read “which has been consecrated.”], and translated it: “And he shall carry the *holocarpoma*, which has been burned, outside the camp to a clean place.”

XII. [Ibid. VI, 12.] “And the fire upon the altar [Note: [Col. 0679] The printed editions read “And the fire of the altar.” The manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint, read “upon the altar.”] shall always burn from it, and shall not be extinguished”—that is, from the fire in which the burnt offering burned until morning.

For he does not wish the fire to be completely extinguished. Rather, when the burnt offering has burned until morning, and the remains of the consumption have been removed, the fire is not even then to be extinguished, but is to be renewed from the same source, so that other things placed upon it may burn.

XIII. [Ibid. VI, 12–13.] What follows says: “And the priest shall burn wood upon it morning by morning” [Note: [Col. 0679] The printed editions have “morning” only once, here and below; the manuscripts and the Septuagint repeat it. The Vulgate version has “morning by morning.”], “and shall arrange the burnt offering upon it, and shall place the fat of the peace-offering upon it; and the fire shall always burn upon the altar; it shall not be extinguished.”

We must consider whether “morning by morning” is intended to mean every day, so that no day would pass on which the burnt offering and the fat of the peace-offering were not found there; or whether it means that on whatever day it was placed there, it was to be placed only in the morning.

For if we understand it as every day, what if no one brought anything? But if the priests provided the daily burnt offerings as public offerings or from their own resources, the things that he ordered to be brought by the people for sins were placed upon those offerings. It was not necessary for the person offering a sacrifice for sin also to offer a burnt offering upon which it could be placed, except when a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons was offered. For there it is expressly specified that one was to be offered for sin and the other as a burnt offering, first the one for sin and then the one as a burnt offering (Leviticus V, 7).

It may also be asked whether the burnt offering that he ordered to be placed morning by morning burned throughout the entire night until the following morning, or whether the burnt offering that he said should burn all night was the evening burnt offering, and whether he then began to speak about the law of the burnt offering by starting with the evening burnt offering. It would be surprising if he were silent about this and did not warn that such offerings ought to be made in the evening.

XIV. [Ibid. VI, 20.] “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘This is the gift of Aaron and his sons, which they shall offer to the Lord on the day when you anoint him.’”

There are other sacrifices, which he mentioned in Exodus, by which the priests are sanctified for seven days so that they may begin to perform their priestly office (Exodus XXIX, 1). The passage now under discussion concerns something else: what the high priest offers when he is appointed, that is, when he is anointed.

For it continues: “On whatever day you anoint him.” He did not say, “when you anoint them,” although he also commands the lesser priests to be anointed.

Then he says that the sacrifice itself is a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour, as an everlasting sacrifice. How can it be everlasting if it is offered by the one who has been anointed on the day on which the high priest is anointed? Unless it means that it is always to be offered on the day when the high priest is anointed—that is, through the succession of priests.

Even in the other sense it can be understood as everlasting—not in itself, but in what it signifies.

XV. [Ibid. VI, 20–21.] “Half of it,” he says, “in the morning, and half of it in the afternoon”—the Greek has *deilinon*. “In a frying pan,” he says, “it shall be made with oil; you shall offer it mixed, broken up,” that is, the fine flour.

Then he says “broken up,” if this has been correctly translated from the Greek *erikta* [Note: [Col. 0680] The printed editions and the Septuagint have *elicta*, “rolled up.” But the Corbie manuscript more correctly has *ericta*, that is, “broken up,” as Augustine interprets it. The same word occurs in Leviticus II, 14, *chidra ericta*, in Latin “ears of grain,” or “crushed grain.], using the word in the neuter plural. For he does not say *fresam*, as though referring to the same fine flour that he had called “mixed.”

This *fresa* is said to be a sacrifice made from fragments. Does *fresa*, then, refer to the fragments themselves, that is, things crushed up; or did he call the very finely crushed flour *fresa*? This is not clear.

XVI. [Ibid. VI, 21–22.] It continues and says: “A sacrifice for a pleasing fragrance to the Lord. The anointed priest who succeeds him from among his sons shall make it.”

Perhaps this is why he had called it everlasting: every high priest is to make it when he succeeds one who has died, on the day when he has been anointed. For he adds: “An eternal law,” although this too can be understood as everlasting according to what it signifies.

XVII. [Ibid. VI, 23.] It continues: “Everything shall be completed,” which the Greek has *epitelesthēsetai*, and some translators rendered, “Everything shall be placed.” Here he wishes it to be understood as a burnt offering, because nothing remains from it.

Finally, he adds: “And every sacrifice of the priest shall be a burnt offering; it shall not be eaten.” This, then, is what he meant by “Everything shall be completed.”

XVIII. [Ibid. VI, 26, 36.] Speaking of the sacrifice for sin, he says: “The priest who lays it on shall eat it.” He does not mean that he shall eat what he lays on, for that will be consumed by fire, but what remains from it; for it is not a burnt offering, so that the whole of it should burn on the altar.

But afterward he says: “Everything that is for sin, from which some of its blood has been brought into the tabernacle of testimony to make atonement in the sanctuary, shall not be eaten, but shall be burned in the fire.”

How, then, do the sacrifices for sins belong to the priests for eating [Col. 0681], when remains from them are left? It must therefore be understood that this is an exception concerning those sacrifices whose blood is brought to the altar of incense in the tabernacle of testimony.

For above he ordered this to be done with the bull that the priest was to offer for his own sin and with the bull that he was to offer for the sin of the whole congregation: the flesh that remained was to be burned outside, beyond the camp (Leviticus IV, 12 and 21). He has now briefly recalled the same rule.

XIX. [Ibid. VII, 1.] “And this is the law of the ram that is for a guilt-offering; they are holy of holies”: that is, they belong to the priests to be eaten.

XX. [Ibid. VII, 7.] After speaking of the ram for a guilt-offering and explaining the law of the sacrifice, why does he say: “As is the sacrifice for sin, so also is the sacrifice for guilt; there is one law for them”?

The question is what difference there is between sin and guilt, since, if there were none, Scripture would in no way say, “As is the sacrifice for sin, so also is the sacrifice for guilt.” Although their law and sacrifice do not differ, because there is one law for them, nevertheless, if the two things themselves—one of which is called sin and the other guilt—differed in no respect, and if they were merely two names for the same thing, Scripture would not take such care to commend that the sacrifice for both is one.

Perhaps, then, sin is the perpetration of evil, while guilt is the abandonment of good. Just as in a praiseworthy life it is one thing to turn away from evil and another to do good, as Scripture admonishes us, “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm XXXVI, 27), so in a blameworthy life it may be one thing to turn away from good and another to do evil. The former is guilt, the latter sin.

For if the word itself is examined, what else does *delictum* mean except “something abandoned” (*derelictum*)? And what does the person who commits a *delictum* abandon except the good?

The Greeks, too, have assigned two customary names to this evil. Among them guilt is called both παράπτωμα (*paraptōma*) and πλημμέλεια (*plēmmeleia*). In this very passage of Leviticus the word is πλημμέλεια. But where the Apostle says, “If a person is overtaken in any guilt” (Galatians VI, 1), the Greek has *paraptōmati*. If the origin of these words is examined, in *paraptōma* the person who commits guilt is understood as falling away. Hence what the Latins call a *cadaver*, deriving it from *cadere*, “to fall,” is called in Greek πτῶμα (*ptōma*), from πίπτειν (*piptein*), that is, “to fall.”

Therefore, whoever does evil by sinning first falls away from the good by committing guilt. *Plēmmeleia* is likewise a word resembling negligence. For negligence in Greek is ἀμέλεια (*ameleia*), because what is neglected is not cared for. Thus the Greek says, “I do not care,” οὐ μέλει μοι (*ou melei moi*).

The particle πλὴν (*plēn*), which is added to form πλημμέλεια, means “besides” or “beyond.” Thus ἀμέλεια, which is called negligence, seems to signify “without care,” while πλημμέλεια means “beyond care,” which is almost the same thing. For this reason some of our translators preferred to render πλημμέλεια not as “guilt” but as “negligence.”

In the Latin language, what is neglected except what is not read—that is, what is not chosen? Hence Latin authors have also said that *lex* (“law”) was named from *legere*, “to read,” that is, “to choose.”

From these traces, in a certain way, it may be gathered that the person who commits guilt is the one who abandons the good; and by abandoning it, falls away from the good because he neglects it—that is, does not choose it. But from where *peccatum*, the word corresponding to the Greek ἁμαρτία (*hamartia*), was derived, I do not for the moment recall in either language.

It may also be thought that guilt is what is committed imprudently, that is, unknowingly, while sin is what is committed knowingly. The following divine testimonies seem to support this distinction: “Who understands his offenses?” (Psalm XVIII, 13). And likewise: “For you knew my imprudence”; immediately he continues, “and my offenses are not hidden from you” (Psalm LXVIII, 6), as though repeating the same thought in another form.

Nor does the statement of the Apostle that I mentioned shortly before disagree with this reasoning: “If a person is overtaken in any guilt.” For by saying “overtaken” he signifies that the person has fallen unknowingly.

But that sin pertains to one who knows, the Apostle James seems to define when he says: “Therefore, for one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin” (James IV, 17).

Yet whether this or that, or some other, is the difference between sin and guilt, if there were no difference at all, Scripture would not speak in such a way as to say: “As is the sacrifice for sin, so also is the sacrifice for guilt; there is one law for them.”

Nevertheless, the terms are often used interchangeably, so that sin is called by the name of guilt and guilt by the name of sin. For when remission of sins is said to take place in Baptism, does remission of guilt not also take place? Yet both are not mentioned, because both are understood under the one name.

Likewise, the Lord says that he pours out his blood for many for the remission of sins (Matthew XXVI, 28). Since he did not say “and of guilt,” will anyone dare to claim that remission of guilt does not take place in his blood?

Again, when it is written in the Apostle: “Judgment indeed came from one offense to condemnation, but grace from many offenses to justification” (Romans V, 16), what else does this mean than that sins too are included under the name “offenses”?

In this very same book of Leviticus, by which we are compelled either to discover or to believe that there is some distinction between *delictum* and *peccatum*, it is written as follows, when God was speaking about the sacrifices that were commanded to be offered for sins:

“But if the whole assembly of the children of Israel errs, and the matter remains hidden from the eyes of the assembly, and they do one of all the commandments of the Lord which ought not to be done, and they commit an offense, and the sin which they committed in it becomes known to them.” Here, where he said, “and they commit an offense,” he immediately added, “the sin which they committed”—plainly the very thing in which they committed the offense.

A little later: “But if a ruler,” he says, “sins and does one of all the commandments of the Lord his God which ought not to be done, unintentionally [Note: [Col. 0682] So in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint; but in the printed editions, “and does it intentionally”], and commits an offense.”

Likewise, shortly afterward: “But if one soul,” he says, “of the people of the land sins unintentionally, in doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which ought not to be done, and commits an offense, and the sin which he committed becomes known to him” (Leviticus 4:13–14, 22, 27–28).

Elsewhere also: “Whatever soul swears, distinguishing with his lips whether to do evil or good, according to everything that a person has distinguished under oath, and it has escaped his notice, and afterward he recognizes it, and he has sinned in one of these matters: he shall confess the sin on account of which he sinned against it, and he shall offer for the things in which he committed an offense to the Lord, for the sin which he committed.”

And a little later: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: If a soul, through forgetfulness, is unaware of it and sins unintentionally against the holy things of the Lord, he shall offer to the Lord for his offense a ram without blemish from the sheep, valued at silver shekels according to the holy shekel, for the offense he committed; and for the holy thing against which he sinned he shall make restitution, and shall add a fifth to it, and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the offense, and it shall be forgiven him.”

It continues and says: “Whatever soul sins and does one of all the commandments of the Lord which ought not to be done, and does not know [Note: [Col. 0683] The word “not” was lacking in the printed editions; it is found in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint], and commits an offense, and bears his sin, he shall offer to the priest a ram from the sheep, valued in silver, as an offering for the offense. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his ignorance, through which he was ignorant and did not know, and it shall be forgiven him. For he has committed an offense—an offense before the Lord” (Leviticus 5:4–6, 14–19).

And it says further: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Whatever soul sins and, utterly despising, despises the commandments of the Lord, and lies concerning what belongs to his neighbor, whether about a deposit or a partnership, or commits robbery, or does his neighbor some injury, or finds something lost and lies about it, and swears falsely concerning any one of all the things that a person does, so that he sins in these matters—when he has sinned and committed an offense, he shall restore the robbery which he robbed, or the injury which he inflicted, or the deposit which was entrusted to him, or the lost property which he found, or anything concerning which he swore falsely. He shall restore it in full, and shall add a fifth to it; he shall give it to the person to whom it belongs on the day when he is convicted of his offense [Note: [Col. 0683] B. has, “on the day when he is convicted”; and “of his offense.” We follow the reading of Erasmus and Lovaniensis. M.]. And he shall offer to the Lord a ram from the sheep, without blemish, valued at the amount of the offense he committed. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord, and he shall be forgiven for any one of all the things that he did and in which he committed an offense” (the same, 6:1–7).

Thus, in almost all the acts which he calls sins, he also calls the same things offenses. Therefore it is clear that these terms are used indifferently in many passages of Scripture. Yet Scripture also testifies that they possess some distinction, since it says: “Just as the offering for sin, so also the offering for offense.”

## XXI. [On 7:23–25]

“You shall not eat any fat of cattle, sheep, or goats. The fat of animals that have died of themselves or have been torn by wild beasts may be used for any work, but it shall not be eaten. Whoever eats the fat of animals from which you offer an offering to the Lord—that person shall perish from his people.”

Earlier he had said concerning the fat: “All fat is the Lord’s” (the same, 3:16). We had asked whether this meant absolutely all the fat of clean animals only—for there is no question concerning unclean animals—and what was to be done with the fat which he forbade to be used as food. Now, however, he has said what is to be done with the fat of an animal that has died of itself or has been caught by a wild beast: it may be used for any work—that is, for whatever work requires such a thing.

The question therefore remains: what is to be done with the fat of the other animals which are clean for eating [Note: [Col. 0683] The printed editions have *immundae*, “unclean”; manuscripts of better quality have *munda*, “clean”]? But when he says that every person who eats the fat of those animals from which an offering is made to the Lord shall perish from his people, he seems to have defined that only the fat of clean animals from which sacrifice is made is forbidden to be eaten—although we have heard that the Jews do not take any fat at all as food.

[Col. 0684] But what Scripture intended must be sought, not what they may have supposed. Indeed, they do not discover what proper use to make of the fat from which they abstain, or how they should dispose of it, if “All fat is the Lord’s” is understood to refer not only to sacrificial fat but also to the fat of those animals which are not sacrificed, even if they are unclean.

## XXII. [On 7:29–34]

What does it mean that he again gives instruction concerning the sacrifices of well-being, and says that the person who offers the gift of his sacrifice of well-being must give the breast and the arm to the priests, yet in such a way that the fat of the breast is offered to the Lord together with the lobe of the liver [Note: [Col. 0684] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *penna jecoris*, “the lobe of the liver”; shortly afterward, *pennam jecoris*. B. has *pinna jocineris*, corruptly. M.]?

Earlier, when speaking about the sacrifices of well-being, he had commanded that the lobe of the liver be offered to the Lord together with the fat of the entrails, the kidneys, and the loins (Leviticus 4:9), but had said nothing about the fat of the breast. Does he here mention what he omitted there? Why, then, does he mention the lobe of the liver both there and here? Or perhaps there is some difference in that earlier he gave instructions concerning a sacrifice of well-being, whereas here he added “his,” as though one thing were a sacrifice of well-being and another the sacrifice of his well-being?

## XXIII. [On 4:3–7 and 8:2, 14, 15, 28]

When he first mentioned sacrifices for sins, Moses said that a bull-calf was to be offered for the sin of the priest who had caused the people to sin. Later, when Scripture narrated how the things commanded by the Lord were carried out concerning Aaron and his sons, it is again said that a bull-calf was offered for sin.

Earlier, however, concerning the blood of the bull-calf, he commanded that the horns of the altar of incense be touched with it; some of the blood was also to be sprinkled toward the holy veil, while the remaining blood was to be poured out at the base of the altar of burnt offerings. Later, when Aaron was consecrated, nothing is said about sprinkling blood toward the veil; the horns of the altar are mentioned, but “of incense” is not added. It is, however, added that the blood was to be poured out at the base of the altar. He did not say “at its base,” as though it were necessary to understand that altar whose horns had been touched with blood.

Accordingly, although the wording is ambiguous, it is nevertheless permissible to understand the matter as having been carried out as previously commanded concerning the bull-calf for sin: we should not understand the horns of the altar whose base received the blood to have been touched, but rather the horns of the altar of incense to have been touched, while the blood was poured out at the base of the altar of sacrifices.

Earlier, because he was giving a general command, if a priest sinned he ordered the priest himself—anointed and fully consecrated, whom he wishes to be understood as the high priest—to offer these sacrifices. But now, when Aaron is being consecrated, Moses offers the sacrifice, and himself receives the breast of presentation, which he had previously said was to be given to the priest.

I think the breast was called the breast of presentation because the fat was placed upon it, as he mentioned earlier concerning the sacrifice of well-being. Since the high priesthood appears to have begun with Aaron, what are we to think Moses was? If he was not a priest, how were all those things carried out through him? But if he was a priest, how do we determine that the high priesthood began with his brother?

Yet that psalm in which it is said, “Moses and Aaron among his priests” (Psalm 98:6), removes the doubt that Moses too was a priest. Nevertheless, Aaron is commanded to receive that priestly garment, which contains a great sacrament, as are his successors, the high priests (Exodus 28).

In Exodus, before any instruction at all is given about the consecration and, so to speak, ordination of priests, when Moses is ascending the mountain and the priests are commanded not to ascend (the same, 19:24), we can understand no others by “priests” than the sons of Aaron. This is not because they already existed as priests, but because they were going to exist; Scripture already called them this by anticipation, as occurs in many such expressions. Thus the son of Nun was also called Jesus (the same, 33:11), although Scripture reports that this name was given to him much later (Numbers 13:17).

Therefore were Moses and Aaron both high priests at that time? Or rather, was Moses the high priest and Aaron subordinate to him? Or was Aaron himself also high priest because of the pontifical garment, while Moses held the higher office because of his more excellent ministry? For from the beginning God says to Moses concerning Aaron: “He shall speak to you concerning the things that belong to the people, and you shall speak to him concerning the things that belong to God” (Exodus 4:16).

It may also be asked who anointed the successor of the high priest after Moses’ death, since no one could succeed him while he was still alive. Or was the successor already anointed among the ordinary priests—for the same oil was used to anoint both the high priest and the subordinate priests—and did that pontiff merely take up the garment by which his high rank would become apparent?

And if so, did he put it on himself, or did someone else clothe him, just as Moses clothed his brother’s son after his brother’s death? If he was clothed by another, could a subordinate priest not make someone a high priest, especially since the garment was such that he necessarily had to be dressed by another? Or was he first clothed in such a way that he could later put it on himself? For it was not the case that, once clothed, he never removed it, or that, once he had removed it, he did not put it on again. It could therefore perhaps have happened that the subordinate priests clothed the first priest as an act of service, not as an assertion of superiority.

But how was it apparent which of the high priest’s sons ought to succeed him? Scripture did not specify the firstborn or the elder, unless we understand that this was customarily determined by some divine sign, whether through a prophet or in whatever other manner God ordinarily gives counsel. Yet the matter appears to have arisen from contention, so that later there were several high priests because, when men of higher rank were contending, the honor itself was granted to several in order to bring the dispute to an end.

## XXIV. [On 8:35]

What does Moses say to Aaron and his sons when they are being consecrated to undertake the priesthood?

“You shall sit at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony for seven days, day and night, lest you die.”

Can it really be believed that they were commanded to sit in one place, in bodily posture, for seven days and nights, without moving at all? Yet we are not compelled to take this as though something were signified allegorically which did not happen but was merely to be understood [Note: [Col. 0685] The words “but was merely to be understood” are absent from Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Lovaniensis. M.]. Rather, we should recognize the Scriptural manner of expression by which it uses “sitting” for dwelling and remaining.

For when it is said of Shimei that he “sat in Jerusalem for three years” (1 Kings 2:38), we should not therefore suppose that he sat on a chair for the whole period without rising. Hence places where people dwell are also called “seats,” since the term has acquired the meaning of habitation.

## XXV. [On 9:1]

“And it came to pass, on the eighth day, that Moses called Aaron and his sons and the council of Israel.”

The Greek has *gerousia* (γερουσία), which some of our translators rendered “senate.” The translator therefore followed this sense, since “senate” (*senatus*) also appears to be derived from old age (*senium*). It would not, however, be idiomatic Latin to say, “He called the old age of Israel,” instead of “the old men” or “elders,” although the same expression would be acceptable if one said, “He called the youth of Israel,” meaning “the young men.” The latter is customary in Latin, whereas the former is not.

Properly speaking, one would say, “He called the old age of Israel,” only if that expression itself were intended. Accordingly, some, rather unusually supposing that the term “senate” could also be used, translated it as “the order of the elders.” For brevity, however, it might perhaps better be rendered: “He called the elders of Israel.”

## XXVI. [On 9:2–4]

Moses says to Aaron:

“And speak to the council of Israel, saying: Take one male goat from the goats for sin, and a ram and a bull-calf and a year-old lamb for a whole burnt offering, without blemish; and a bull from the cattle, and a ram for a sacrifice of well-being before the Lord, and fine flour mixed with oil, because today the Lord will appear among you.”

Earlier he had set forth four kinds of animal sacrifices: the burnt offering, the sacrifice for sin, the sacrifice of well-being, and the sacrifice of consecration. The sacrifice of consecration pertains to the consecration of the priest.

Here, therefore, the remaining three kinds are commanded to be offered, and this is said to the elders of Israel so that it may pertain to the whole people. But in this passage the sacrifice for sin includes three animals: a goat, a ram, and a bull-calf. The lamb belongs to the burnt offering, while the bull-calf and ram belong to the sacrifice of well-being.

Accordingly, the passage should not be divided in such a way that only the goat is understood as being for sin, while the other three—ram, bull-calf, and lamb—are assigned to the burnt offering. Rather, the first three are for sin: after the words, “Take one male goat from the goats for sin,” the words “and a ram and a bull-calf” should be understood as continuing, “for sin.” The remaining animal is the lamb for the whole burnt offering.

We had to point this out because the passage could also be divided in such a way that, once it had said, “Take one male goat from the goats for sin,” the remaining animals would be said to belong already to the whole burnt offering. The phrase “without blemish,” however, can be referred to them all.

Since the division is ambiguous, the following consideration leads us to understand the first three as offerings for sin: earlier he commanded that a goat be offered for the sin of a ruler (Leviticus 4:23); for the personal sin of any individual who sins before the Lord by doing one of the things that ought not to be done, he commanded a ram (the same, 5:18); and for the sin of the whole assembly, a bull-calf (the same, 4:14).

Therefore, when he was speaking to the council about what the whole people ought to offer, it was appropriate that a goat should be ordered on account of the rulers, a ram on account of each person’s individual sin, and a bull-calf on account of the sin of the whole assembly.

For it is one thing when each person in the people has his own individual sin—for all may have individual sins—and another thing when the sin is collective, committed with one mind and one will by a multitude united for some purpose.

[Col. 0687] The reason he commands a bull-calf and a ram for the sacrifices of well-being is that he commands those which are especially significant, since the matter concerns the whole people. Earlier, when giving instructions concerning sacrifices of well-being, he commanded that an animal of either sex might be offered, provided that the offerings came only from cattle, sheep, or goats (Leviticus 3).

If it is asked why he commanded two animals here, a bull-calf and a ram, it is difficult to determine—unless perhaps he intended the bull-calf as the sacrifice of well-being for the whole people, and the ram for each individual, as though for each person separately. For earlier also he seems to have commanded two kinds of sacrifice of well-being: one which, as though it belonged to everyone collectively, he called “the sacrifice of well-being”; and another where he said, “If anyone offers the sacrifice of his well-being.”

There too we found a distinction. In what he called simply “well-being,” he did not mention that the fat of the breast was to be offered to the Lord, nor that the breast itself and the right arm were to be given to the priest. But he ordered this to be done in the sacrifice which he later calls “the sacrifice of his well-being” (above, question 22). This perhaps is to be understood as the private sacrifice of each individual, not the public sacrifice of the whole community.

Moses too offered sacrifices of well-being, and it is not said there, “of his well-being”; I believe this is because he offered them on behalf of the whole people. Wherever the whole is concerned, individuals are included; but where individuals are concerned, the whole is not necessarily included. Individuals can exist without the whole, but the whole cannot exist except from all its individual members. For individuals gathered together, or reckoned as a totality, constitute the whole.

It should certainly be noted that, when sacrifices were offered on behalf of the people, sacrifices for sin, burnt offerings, and sacrifices of well-being were commanded; but for the priest, a sacrifice for sin, a burnt offering, and a sacrifice of consecration were offered, not a sacrifice of well-being.

The sacrifice of consecration was offered when the priests were consecrated so that they might perform the priesthood; Moses offered it on behalf of Aaron and his sons (Leviticus 8). Later, once Aaron had been consecrated and was exercising the priesthood, he was commanded to offer on his own behalf a bull-calf for sin and a ram as a burnt offering.

He was not commanded to offer a sacrifice of consecration for himself, because that sacrifice had then been offered so that he might be completed through consecration and be able to exercise the priesthood. Since he was already exercising it, there was no need for him to be consecrated again.

## XXVII. [On 9:7–21]

“And Moses said to Aaron: Approach the altar and perform what is for your sin and your burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself and your household.”

It is remarkable that he first says that what is for sin is to be performed, and then the burnt offering, whereas earlier he commands that sacrifices for sins be placed upon the burnt offerings (the same, 4:35), except in the case of the birds, concerning which he gave instructions separately (the same, 5:8–10).

Or perhaps here he mentioned later what was actually done first, namely the burnt offering? For he did not say, as he did concerning the birds, “Perform this first and that afterward,” but simply, “Perform this and that.” What was to be done first is indicated by the instruction given earlier, where he says that the sacrifice for sin is to be placed upon the burnt offering.

Nevertheless, it is very striking that Scripture also narrates Aaron as having done what he heard, mentioning first that he performed what was for sin and afterward the burnt offering. Whether he himself also did these things in that order, or whether Scripture narrated first what was done later, as it often does in many passages, would remain uncertain, unless what I mentioned above were read in the passage dealing with the sacrifice for sin.

For it is written:

“And the priest shall place it upon the altar, upon the burnt offering of the Lord, and the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he committed, and it shall be forgiven him” (Leviticus 4:35).

How, then, could this be placed upon the burnt offering unless the burnt offering had first been placed there?

He also gave this command concerning the sacrifice of well-being, that it be placed upon the burnt offering. But because he does not say this everywhere, perhaps it may be argued that it was not prescribed as a rule for every sacrifice of well-being or every sacrifice for sin. Rather, it was commanded only in those particular cases: in the sacrifice of well-being when the animal was from cattle, for there he gave the instruction; and in the sacrifice for sin when the animal was a female from the sheep [Note: [Col. 0688] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Lovaniensis read, “when it is”; M.]. In other cases, whether the sacrifice is one of well-being or one for sin, it may not be necessary for it to be placed upon the burnt offerings.

It is also striking that when Aaron performed the gifts of the people, which he had mentioned above, not all the animals previously specified are said to have been sacrificed. Only the goat for sin and the burnt offering are mentioned, although even the lamb is not explicitly named. The other two, which we said belonged more properly to the sacrifices for sin than to the burnt offering—the ram and the bull-calf—are passed over in silence.

Unless perhaps he wished the whole to be understood from a part, so that, by mentioning only the goat, we should also understand the animals that followed.

When he narrated how Aaron performed the people’s sacrifices of well-being, he said concerning the bull-calf and the ram:

“And he slaughtered the bull-calf and the ram of the people’s sacrifice of well-being, and the sons of Aaron brought the blood to him, and he poured it around the altar. And the fat from the bull-calf, and from the ram the loin, and the fat covering the entrails, and the two kidneys, and the fat upon them, and the lobe which is on the liver; and he placed the fat upon the breasts and placed the fats upon the altar. And Aaron took the breast and the right arm, an offering before the Lord, as the Lord commanded Moses” [Note: [Col. 0688] In the earlier printed editions three verses of Scripture had been displaced; we have restored them here from the manuscripts, namely, “And the fat which was from the bull-calf,” and so forth.]

He speaks now in the singular and now in the plural, although he is speaking of two animals, the bull-calf and the ram. Thus when he says “the two kidneys,” this is to be understood of each animal, making four altogether; and the same applies to the other items.

But what does he mean when he says, “And he placed the fats upon the breasts,” although he did not place the breasts themselves upon the altar? They were owed to the priest together with the right arms. Is it to be understood as, “And he placed the fats which are upon the breasts”? These are the fats which he placed, after removing them from the breasts, in order to put them on the altar. For he had given the same instruction earlier.

Finally, the text continues: “And he placed the fats upon the altar, and Aaron took the breast and the right arm as an offering before the Lord.” Here he again uses the singular, saying “the breast,” clearly meaning both breasts, one from each animal, which he had previously called “breasts.”

[Col. 0689]

## XXVIII. [On 9:22]

What does he mean when he says:

“When Aaron had raised his hands over the people, he blessed them, and descended, after performing what was for sin, and the burnt offerings, and the sacrifices of well-being”?

Where did he perform these things except upon the altar—that is, standing beside the altar and ministering to it? From there, therefore, he descended, from the place where he had been standing.

This testimony seems to assist in resolving the question which we had raised in Exodus: how could he minister at the altar, which was three cubits high? There we were forbidden to understand a step, because God had prohibited it, lest the minister’s nakedness be exposed above the altar. This would certainly happen if part of the altar itself were a step—that is, if the step were joined to it as an integral part (Questions on Exodus, 113).

There he prohibited this in speaking of an altar constructed of masonry, since the altar and the step would be one thing, with the step constituting part of it; for that reason it was forbidden. Here, however, where the altar was so high that a priest could not minister suitably unless he stood upon something, we must understand that whatever it was which was placed there for the moment of ministry and then removed was not part of the altar. It therefore did not violate the command prohibiting an altar with a step.

What this object may have been, Scripture does not say, and for that reason the question arose. But now, when Scripture says that the priest descended after performing the sacrifices—that is, after placing the slaughtered offerings upon the altar—it plainly shows that he had been standing somewhere from which he could descend. Since he had stood there, he was able to minister at the altar three cubits high.

## XXIX. [On 9:24]

“And all the people saw it and were beside themselves.”

Other translators rendered this as “were terrified,” attempting to translate the Greek word ἐξέστη (*exestē*), from which ἔκστασις (*ekstasis*) is derived. The latter is frequently rendered in Latin Scripture as *mentis excessus*, “an excess or rapture of mind.”

## XXX. [On 9:24]

“And fire went out from the Lord and devoured what was upon the altar, the burnt offerings and the fats.”

It may be asked what is meant by “from the Lord”: whether it happened because of the Lord’s command and will, or whether the fire came out from the place where the ark of testimony was. For the Lord is not located in one place in such a way that he is not elsewhere.

## XXXI. [On 10:1–3]

After fire went out from the Lord and consumed Aaron’s sons, who had dared to place incense in their censers after applying unauthorized fire—something they were not permitted to do because everything that had to be kindled in the tabernacle was thereafter to be lit from the fire that had come upon the altar by divine action and was carefully preserved—Moses said to them after their death:

“This is what the Lord said: ‘Among those who draw near to me I shall be sanctified, and before all the assembly I shall be glorified.’”

By those who draw near to the Lord he wished to be understood those who exercised the priesthood in the tabernacle; and by being sanctified in them, even through punishment, as happened here.

Was this so that it might be known how little he spares others if he does not spare them? In this sense it is said: “If the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Peter 4:18).

Or should it rather be understood according to the saying, “From the one to whom more is given, more is required”? And also: “The servant who did not know his master’s will and did things deserving blows shall be beaten few times; but the servant who knew his master’s will and did things deserving blows shall be beaten many times” (Luke 12:47–48). And again: “For the insignificant shall be shown mercy, but the powerful shall suffer more powerful torments” (Wisdom 6:7).

But where the Lord said what Moses is recorded as recalling, it is not found in the Scripture that precedes this passage. This is therefore like the passage in Exodus where Moses says to the Lord, “You said, ‘I know you above all others’” (Exodus 33:12). The Lord is indeed found to have said this to him, but only afterward. Since Moses would never have said it falsely, we understand that the Lord had said it to him earlier as well, although it was not written down. The same applies here.

Thus it becomes evident that not everything God spoke to those through whom his holy Scripture was supplied to us was written down.

## XXXII. [On 10:6–7]

What does Moses mean when, forbidding Aaron and his remaining sons to mourn the death of those two, he says:

“You shall not uncover the *cidara* on your head”?

This certainly shows that the *cidarae* were coverings for the head—unless the point is that mourners performed actions contrary to ordinary practices of adornment. For in our custom, since an uncovered head is considered more customary, it is covered in mourning. In their custom, however, since they adorned themselves with a covering of the head, mourners would have had to uncover it.

He forbids this so that they would not mourn those through whose punishment the Lord had been sanctified—that is, whose punishment had commended or demonstrated his fear. This does not mean that they were not to be mourned at all, for he permits others to mourn them. Rather, they were not to mourn them at that time, while the days of their consecration were being completed, before the seven days had ended during which he had commanded them not to leave the tabernacle.

Yet it may also appear that, because they had been consecrated with that oil, the command meant that they were never to mourn anyone. For he says:
