“But your brothers, the whole house of Israel, shall weep for the burning with which they were burned by the Lord. And you shall not go out from the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, lest you die, for the oil of anointing from the Lord is upon you.”

## XXXIII. [On 10:9–11]

“And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: You and your sons with you shall not drink wine or strong drink when you enter the tabernacle of testimony, or when you approach the altar, lest you die.”

When, then, were they permitted to drink, since it was necessary for them to enter the tabernacle and approach the altar every day because of their continual service?

If someone says that sacrifices were not ordinarily placed upon the altar every day, what will he say about entering the tabernacle, which was a daily necessity because of the lampstand and the bread of the Presence that had to be placed upon the table?

If the response is that by “the tabernacle of testimony” here he means the place where the ark of testimony was, it was still necessary for the high priest to enter there because of the continual incense. He did not enter only once a year: he entered once a year with the blood of purification, but because of the incense he entered daily.

Is the command to be understood as requiring them not to drink wine at all? Why, then, did he not give the command in a brief form by saying, “You shall not drink wine,” but added, “when you enter the tabernacle, or when you approach the altar”?

Or was the reason for abstaining from wine not to be passed over in silence, especially because God foresaw that afterward there would be many high priests at one time—that is, not one succeeding another—who would minister in turns at the tabernacle, the sacrifices, the incense, and all that service? In that case those whose turn it was to minister would not drink, while the others would drink.

Or is something else to be understood in this passage?

For when he prohibited the priests from drinking wine and strong drink, he continued:

“An eternal ordinance throughout your generations.”

It is ambiguous whether this is connected with the preceding sense, referring to the prohibition against drinking wine, or with what follows:

“To distinguish between the holy and the profane, and between the clean and the unclean, and to teach the children of Israel all the ordinances which the Lord spoke to them through the hand of Moses.”

On the latter interpretation, this would be the eternal ordinance of the priests throughout their generations.

We have often discussed how he can call it “eternal.” The phrase “to distinguish between the holy and the profane, and between the clean and the unclean” is also ambiguous. Does it refer to things that are holy and clean, or polluted and unclean? Or does it refer to people who are holy and clean, or polluted and unclean?

That is, did he wish the priests to distinguish among the sacred things themselves, according to whether they were performed properly or improperly? Or among human beings, to determine who was to be approved or rejected? Or should the statement rather be referred to both, whether persons or sacred rites?

## XXXIV. [On 10:14]

“You shall eat the breast of separation and the arm of removal in a holy place.”

Although the portions were given separately to separate recipients, both could certainly be called portions of separation, because both are set apart for the priest. Both could also be called portions of removal or taking-away—the Greek term is ἀφαίρεμα (*aphairema*)—because both are taken away and removed from those on whose behalf they are offered, in order to be given to the priest.

Earlier we read of the breast of presentation and the arm of removal, because nothing from the arm was placed upon the altar, whereas fat from the breast was placed upon it.

## XXXV. [On 10:14]

What does he mean when he says, “from the sacrifices of well-being,” when he says here the same things which elsewhere he called sacrifices of well-being, and when he uses the singular number, saying “the sacrifice of well-being,” although the same matter is being discussed [Note: [Col. 0691] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Lovaniensis, with altered punctuation, read as follows: “What does he mean when he says, ‘from the sacrifices of well-being,’ when he says here the same things which elsewhere he called sacrifices of well-being, although he used the singular number and said ‘the sacrifice of well-being,’ when the same matter was being discussed?” M.]?

Or perhaps in this passage, where he says “from the sacrifices of well-being,” it ought to have been understood as “from the sacrifices of salvations” or “healings.” For in the psalm where it is said, “Hear us, God of our salvations” (Psalm 64:6), the Greek has the same word as here, namely σωτηρίων (*sōtēriōn*).

This genitive plural in Greek is ambiguous: it may be derived either from *salvation* or from *the sacrifice of well-being*. For σωτηρία (*sōtēria*) means salvation or healing, and its genitive plural is τῶν σωτηριῶν (*tōn sōtēriōn*). But σωτήριον (*sōtērion*) means “a salutary thing,” and its genitive plural is exactly the same.

If, therefore, “sacrifice of salvation” can rightly be understood as “sacrifice of a salutary thing,” since salvation is given by what is salutary, and it is the salutary thing from which salvation is received, it is not necessary to understand the phrase “sacrifices of well-being” here as referring to sacrifices of many salutary things. Perhaps it refers instead to many salvations or healings, which nevertheless are received from one salutary thing.

What the salvation of God is, of which it is said, “I shall take up the cup of salvation” (Psalm 115:13), and of which Simeon says in the Gospel, “For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30), the Christian faith knows.

It is also possible, without absurdity, to understand or call these “sacrifices of well-being,” since they are sacrifices of salvation.

## XXXVI. [On 10:15–20]

“And it shall be an everlasting ordinance for you and for your sons and for your daughters.”

It was not without reason that “daughters” was added, since in some matters relating to the priests’ food he forbids women to partake, while he commands men to do so.

When Moses had sought the goat offered for the sins of the people and had not found it, because it had been burned, and had become angry because the Lord had ordained that the offerings made by the people for sin should be eaten by the priests after the fat and kidneys had been offered from them—angry, however, not with his brother but with his sons, since, I believe, the duty of bringing this to his attention belonged to them—Aaron answered him and said: “If today they have offered the things for their sin and their burnt offerings before the Lord, and such things have happened to me, and I eat today that which is for sin, will it be pleasing to the Lord?” Moses heard, and it pleased him.

[Col. 0692] Aaron appears to have said that, on the very day when the children of Israel had first offered a sacrifice for their sin, it ought not to have been eaten by the priests but wholly burned; yet he was not thereby establishing a rule for subsequent occasions, for thereafter they themselves ate the sacrifices for sins. But because this was the first offering made on that first day, we must believe that Aaron the priest said this by divine inspiration [Note: All our manuscripts read, “said this by divine breathing/inspiration” (*hoc divina aspiratione dixisse*).], so that thereafter both the provision which the Lord had commanded Moses concerning the priests might be observed and what Aaron had said, as though divinely spoken, might be approved by Moses.

What, then, are we to say about the other sacrifices of that same day, namely the ram and the calf, which we have said must also be understood as having been offered for sin? Is there no question concerning the calf, since it was necessary for things to be done in such a way that its blood should be brought inside as had been commanded, and the horns of the altar of incense should be touched with it, and consequently the whole animal should be burned? What, then, about the ram? Since Moses first sought the goat, is what was answered him concerning the goat also to be understood concerning the ram, which he would have sought next in order, had the priest’s answer not pleased him?

But what would he have sought concerning the calf, since it could have been dealt with according to the law that God had prescribed concerning the calf for the sin of the whole congregation, just as concerning the calf for the priest’s sin—that is, that it should be wholly burned outside the camp (Leviticus 4:12, 21)? For these are the words of Moses in his anger to the sons of his brother, when he had sought the goat for sin and had not found it because it had been wholly burned:

“Why did you not eat the thing that was for sin in the holy place? For since it is most holy, he gave it to you to eat, so that you might take away the sin of the congregation and make intercession for it before the Lord. For its blood was not brought into the sanctuary before the presence within. You shall eat it in the holy place, as the Lord has appointed for me.”

[Col. 0693] Certainly, when he says, “For its blood was not brought inside, before the presence of the Lord,” he plainly distinguishes it from what is done for the priest’s sin or for the sin of the whole congregation. Since the blood of the goat had not been commanded to be brought inside to touch the horns of the inner altar of incense, it ought not to have been wholly burned but eaten by the priests. Why, then, this was done—that is, why it too was wholly burned—Aaron explained, and Moses approved his explanation.

Furthermore, since six animals had been commanded to the elders of the people to be offered for the people, of which he first mentioned four—the goat, the ram, the calf, and the year-old lamb—it is clear that the goat was for sin, and it is also clear that the year-old lamb was for a burnt offering. But the two in between, the ram and the calf, we had seen to be ambiguously presented: whether they belonged to the sacrifice for sin and were to be joined to the goat, or rather whether they were to be offered with the lamb as a burnt offering. We explained in its proper place what seemed to us the case.

Afterward, however, in order to complete the number of six animals, he mentioned the calf and the ram as a sacrifice of salvation. Yet in the subsequent account, when they were sacrificed and mentioned again, there is no reference to those same animals—the ram and the calf—which he had placed between the goat and the lamb. Instead, only that calf and that ram are mentioned which he had commanded to be offered as a sacrifice of salvation. Thus they may be thought to have been not six animals but rather four.

Perhaps it can be understood that he named again the two which he had earlier placed between the goat and the lamb, and that there was not another calf and another ram for the sacrifice of salvation. In that case, after saying that the goat was for sin, and mentioning the ram and the calf without saying for what purpose—that is, for what they were to be used—and the year-old lamb for a burnt offering, he later wished to say what was to be done with the calf and the ram: namely, that they were not to be brought for sin like the goat, nor as a burnt offering like the lamb, but as a sacrifice of salvation.

But if we understand it in this way, the question remains why a goat was offered for the sin of the congregation, when, speaking from the beginning about sacrifices that were to be offered for sins, the Lord commanded a calf to be offered for the sin of the congregation, just as for the priest’s sin—not a goat but a calf. Concerning that calf, too, he commanded that its blood be brought in, just as for the priest’s sin, to touch the horns of the altar of incense (Leviticus 4:3–18).

What, moreover, was the reason that for Aaron’s sin Moses offered a calf (ibid. 8:14), and Aaron himself another calf (ibid. 9:8), just as a calf ought to be offered for a priest’s sin according to God’s command, whereas for the sin of the people a goat rather than a calf was offered, contrary to what had been commanded?

Since this troubled us, it seemed to us, as we said above, that not only the goat was commanded to be offered for the sin of the people, but also the ram and the calf, so that “for sin” should be understood with respect to all three. For there were also leaders among the people, for whom the goat was to be offered; each individual could have had personal sins, for which the ram was offered; and there was one sin belonging to all, for which the calf was offered, just as from the beginning God had commanded a calf to be offered for the sin of the whole congregation.

When the animals were sacrificed, only the goat is therefore named, so that the others might also be understood by implication through the figure in which the part signifies the whole, since all had been offered for sins.

### XXXVII. [Ibid. 11:33–34]

[Col. 0694] When he was speaking about the carcasses of unclean animals, he says: “And every earthen vessel into which any of them falls inside”—whatever is inside it will be unclean; and it itself shall be broken, that is, the vessel itself. “And every food that is eaten, upon which water comes,” will be unclean for you.

Not every kind of water that comes upon food is to be understood as making it unclean; rather, this applies if the water is in that vessel which has been made unclean by the carcasses of unclean animals.

### XXXVIII. [Ibid. 11:47]

“Instruct” [Note: Printed editions read *Instrue*. The manuscripts, however, have *Instruere*, which is how Nobilius conjectured that it should be read in his notes on Leviticus 2. He further observes that the words, “And to instruct the sons of Israel” (*Kai sumbibazein tous huious Israēl*), which are not presently found in the printed Septuagint, occur inserted in some manuscripts in verse 47, immediately after “among the living creatures.”] the children of Israel concerning the living creatures that are eaten and the living creatures that are not eaten.

The Greek has *zōogonounta* (ζωογονοῦντα). Some of our translators have preferred to render it “living creatures” (*vivificantia*), because, in whatever way, our usage has admitted this word rather than creating a new and unfamiliar one, if it could be said, “life-generating creatures” (*vivigignentia*). For the term does not mean things that give life—that is, that make things live—but things that produce living offspring: not eggs, but young. Such creatures are called *zōogonounta*.

### XXXIX. [Ibid. 12:4]

What does he mean when he says of the woman who has given birth, “She shall touch nothing holy, and she shall not enter into the sanctuary”? What sanctuary does he mean, when we read that only priests were accustomed to enter the tabernacle, and that only as far as the second inner veil, while beyond the veil itself, where the ark was, only the one high priest entered?

Or could the area before the tabernacle, where the altar of sacrifices stood, also be called the sanctuary? For the courtyard itself is often called a holy place, as when it is said, “They shall eat them in the holy place” (Leviticus 6:26). Perhaps women were accustomed to enter there when they offered their gifts to be placed upon the altar.

### XL. [Ibid. 12:2–8]

What does he mean when he says: “If a woman gives birth to a male child, she shall be unclean for seven days; according to the days of the separation of her purification she shall be unclean. And on the eighth day he shall circumcise the flesh of his foreskin; and she shall sit thirty-three days in the blood of her purification. She shall touch nothing holy, and she shall not enter the sanctuary”?

What difference is there between the seven days during which he says she is unclean and the thirty-three during which she shall sit in the blood of her purification? For if she is no longer unclean during the thirty-three days, why does she not touch what is holy?

Or is there still this distinction: that she is in blood, although purified, so that when she is unclean, wherever she sits she makes it unclean, whereas when she sits in purified blood, she is merely forbidden to touch what is holy and to enter the sanctuary?

This is what he means when he says, “according to the days of the separation of her purification.” In another passage he says that a woman’s uncleanness during menstruation lasts seven days, during which everything upon which she sits will be unclean (ibid. 15:19–23). He speaks of “separation” because she withdrew for a time, so as not to pollute everything while she completed those days.

[Col. 0695] The Law doubled these days of her uncleanness if she bore a female child and made them fourteen. The remaining days during which she sat in her purified blood were likewise commanded to be observed as double, namely sixty-six, so that the total would be forty days for the birth of a male and eighty for that of a female.

Some Greek manuscripts, however, do not read “in her purified blood” but “in her unclean blood.”

“And when the days of her purification have been completed, for a son or for a daughter she shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove” [Note: Most printed editions and many manuscripts read here and below, “and a turtledove.” The Corbie manuscript and one Vatican manuscript read, “or a turtledove.” This reading is supported by the Septuagint and the Vulgate; nor does Augustine contradict it, as Nobilius incorrectly thought. Later, the holy Doctor criticizes certain manuscripts not because they read “or a turtledove,” but because they read “or a young pigeon” instead of “and a young pigeon,” and so forth.], “for sin, at the door of the tabernacle of testimony, to the priest. And he shall offer it before the Lord, and the priest shall make intercession for her, and shall purify her from the source of her blood. This is the law for her who has borne a male or a female.

“But if her hand does not find what is sufficient for a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and one for sin. And the priest shall make intercession for her, and she shall be purified.”

Accordingly, the earlier passage should not be read, as some manuscripts have it: “She shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering, or a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin.” Rather, it should be read as stated above: “and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin.” For afterward it says: “If her hand does not find what is sufficient for a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves.” Here the conjunction *and* seems to be more fully present; once it is removed, the sentence proceeds coherently: “She shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons”—one bird, that is, for a burnt offering and the other for sin.

But for what sin? Is giving birth a sin? Or is that offspring here indicated which comes from Adam, concerning which the Apostle says, “From one, unto condemnation,” and, “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin, death, and so it passed into all human beings” (Romans 5:16, 12)? Here it becomes sufficiently clear how the words are to be understood: “For I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Psalm 50:7).

Why, then, does Scripture say that it is the woman who gave birth who is purified by this sacrifice, rather than the child who was born? Or was the purification referred to the woman herself, from whom that origin was transmitted, on account of the source of blood? Yet it could not take place without the purification of the offspring itself, which arose from that blood. For what else does the earlier statement mean: “For a son or for a daughter she shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin,” if this sacrifice accomplished nothing for those who were born?

[Col. 0696] If someone attempts to distinguish the passage in such a way as to say that “for a son or for a daughter she shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering, and a young pigeon for sin” should not be joined together, but that it should instead be read as follows: “And when the days of her purification have been completed for a son or for a daughter”—that is, when the days of purification have been completed for him or for her, namely the son or daughter—then the following sense begins: “She shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering and a young pigeon for sin,” that is, for her own sin, when the days of her purification for the son or daughter have been completed—whoever thinks that the passage should be divided in this way will be refuted by the Gospel.

For when the parents of the Lord, born of a virgin, did something of this kind, it is read that they did so more because of the custom of the Law than because of any need to expiate or purify sin in him: “And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law” (Luke 2:27). It does not say “for his mother,” but “for him,” although they did what is commanded in this passage concerning the two turtledoves or the two young pigeons.

Thus he also graciously consented to be baptized with the baptism of John, which was a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins (Matthew 3:13, 11), although he had no sin. Accordingly, some of our translators correctly interpreted this passage in Leviticus in such a way that they did not say “for a son or for a daughter” (*super filio aut super filia*) but “for the son or for the daughter” (*pro filio aut pro filia*). They understood this to be the force of the preposition in this passage, where the Greek reads *eph’ huiō ē epi thugatri* (ἐφ’ υἱῷ ἢ ἐπὶ θυγατρί).

It should certainly be noted how poor the Lord wished to be at his birth, so that not a lamb and a young pigeon or a turtledove were offered for him, but a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, as the Gospel records (Luke 2:24). The Law in Leviticus had commanded this to be offered when the hand of the one making the offering did not possess what was sufficient for a lamb.

### XLI. [Ibid. 13:20]

“If a scar of a shining mark appears on anyone in the skin of his body, and there is a touch of leprosy in the color of his skin.”

He explained the first expression as though interpreting it afterward, so that we might understand what he had initially said. For when he said, “If a scar of a shining mark appears on anyone in the skin of his body,” lest we understand “scar” in the way it is usually understood as the trace of a healed wound, he made clear that he was speaking of color when he added, “and there is a touch of leprosy in the color of his skin.”

Whatever that thing is, therefore, it is a defect of color which he calls by the name “scar.” But when he says “a touch of leprosy,” he does not mean that color is perceived by touch. Rather, he speaks of “a touch of leprosy” as though the man himself or his body had been touched by leprosy—that is, marked and disfigured—just as one commonly says, “The fever touched him,” or “The fever did not touch him.”

Finally, he calls the mark itself “a touch,” and always refers to it by this name. Hence some of our translators rendered it not “touch” but “mark.” This makes the wording sound clearer, but the Greek may also have used not *haphē* (ἁφή), meaning “touch,” but *mōmos* (μῶμος), meaning “blemish,” from which it calls something unblemished *amōmos* (ἄμωμος). Yet Scripture is accustomed to call not only what occurs in color but anything free from every defect *amōmos*. Thus the intention may be not a blemish of color but the mark of every kind of defect, which it calls *mōmos*.

If the reference were only to color, it could have used *spilos* (σπίλος), the word used by the Apostle when he says of the Church, “not having spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). But it used neither *mōmos* nor *spilos*, but *haphē*, that is, “touch,” a word used unusually in Greek of colors, yet one which the Septuagint translators did not hesitate to use in Greek. Why, then, should Latin translators have hesitated?

The expression “a scar of a mark” is used either because it signifies something or, rather, because it distinguishes the person himself by a certain mark from others—that is, makes him conspicuous.

### XLII. [Ibid. 13:3]

[Col. 0697] What does he mean when he says, “And the priest shall see him and declare him unclean,” when the person comes to him to be purified? “He shall declare him unclean” means that he shall pronounce him unclean if he sees in him the features which Scripture describes in connection with the mark of leprosy.

### XLIII. [Ibid. 13:4, 7, 2]

“But if there is a shining whiteness in the color of his skin” [Note: Am. Er. and Lov. read, “in the skin, his color.” Bat. and the manuscripts have “of his color.” The Greek has *tou chrōtos autou*, “of his color.”], “and its appearance is not lower than the skin.”

“Shining whiteness” is understood to refer to the touch, that is, to the mark of color, not to the hair. When he later says, “If the mark has changed and been altered in the skin,” he is referring by “mark” to what is read above in Latin as “sign.” For both above and here the Greek uses the same word, *sēmasia* (σημασία).

### XLIV. [Ibid. 13:5–6]

“And the priest shall isolate him for seven days a second time; and the priest shall examine him on the seventh day a second time. And behold, the touch is dark and the touch has not changed in the skin; and the priest shall purify him, for it is a mark.”

That is, he shall pronounce him purified. For it is not leprosy but a mark.

### XLV. [Ibid. 13:4–7]

“But if the mark has changed and been altered in the skin after the priest examined him in order to purify him; and he appears again before the priest, and the priest examines him, and behold, the mark has changed in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean: it is leprosy.”

Here too “he shall declare him unclean” means “he shall pronounce him unclean.” The word “and” is an addition arising from the customary manner of expression in Scripture.

This appears to have been intended as a warning that, when a color alone is seen to be white and shining, differing from the healthy color, it should still be examined by the priest. If he also sees that the hair has changed to a white color and that the place of the skin where the white color is found has become lower, then he should pronounce it leprosy—that is, he should declare the person unclean by pronouncing him a leper.

“But if,” he says, “there is a shining whiteness in the color of his skin,” that is, if that touch is shining white—the name by which he calls the same mark—“and its appearance is not lower than the skin; and the hair has not changed to white, but it is dark,” namely the hair itself, because it is not white—“the priest shall isolate the touch for seven days; and the priest shall examine the touch on the seventh day,” that is, the mark; “and behold, the touch remains before him; the touch has not changed in the skin,” that is, it has not been found discolored or unlike the skin.

Therefore what was defective has been healed. Yet he still commands that this same healing be tested for another seven days, and so the passage continues: “And the priest shall isolate him for seven days a second time,” that is, for another seven days; “and the priest shall examine him on the seventh day a second time; and behold, the touch is dark,” that is, because it is not white and shining and therefore is of the same color as healthy skin; “the touch has not changed in the skin,” as he also said shortly before—that is, it is not unlike the rest of the skin.

[Col. 0698] “And the priest shall purify him,” that is, shall pronounce him purified from the suspicion of leprosy—not because he had leprosy and no longer has it, but because it was not leprosy. The touch, that is, the mark which had appeared, had been shining and white while it was being observed to see whether the place would become lower and the hair there turn white. This did not happen. Rather, the touch which had previously been shining and white was found to be dark—that is, like the rest of the color, not shining.

It was therefore not leprosy, but a mark; for it had appeared in this way. Nevertheless, because of this, having been purified from suspicion of leprosy, he shall wash his clothes, since even in that mark there was something on account of which his clothes had to be washed; and he shall be clean.

### XLVI. [Ibid. 13:7–8]

Then the passage continues: “But if the mark has changed and been altered in the skin after the priest examined him to purify him”—that is, after the priest examined him on the seventh day, when he was previously healed, in order to purify him, the mark in the skin changed, that is, the sign in the skin—“and he appears a second time before the priest,” that is, after another seven days, “and the priest examines him, and behold, the mark has changed in the skin,” that is, it did not remain in the healthy state in which he had seen it after the first seven days, “the priest shall declare him unclean: it is leprosy.”

Since what had appeared healthy after the first seven days did not remain as it was but changed back into its former defect, it is pronounced leprosy. There is no longer any need to wait for the place to become lower or for the hair to turn white.

For since leprosy is conspicuous and defective only because of variation, this very change from a defective color to a healthy one and from a healthy one back to a defective one is so conspicuous that there is no need to wait for what he had commanded to be awaited at first—the lowering of the place and the whiteness of the hair. By this variation alone it is unquestionably leprosy.

### XLVII. [Ibid. 13:9–17]

Then the passage continues: “And if the touch of leprosy is in a person, he shall come to the priest; and the priest shall examine him, and behold, there is a white scar in the skin; and this has changed the hair to white, and from healthy living flesh in the scar.”

If we remove the conjunction *and*—for it has been inserted according to the customary expression of Scripture—the sense will be: “And the priest shall examine him; and behold, there is a white scar in the skin; and this has changed the hair to white from healthy living flesh in the scar.”

The order is: “It has changed the hair to white in the scar, in contrast to healthy living flesh”; that is, while living and healthy flesh has dark or black hair, this scar has white hair.

“It is an old leprosy in the color of his skin; and the priest shall declare him unclean,” that is, shall pronounce him unclean. “He shall not isolate him, because he is unclean.”

This appears to mean that, wherever hair is found to have changed to white and to be the same color as the white defect of the skin, he is no longer isolated for examination, nor is it necessary to wait to see whether the place will also become lower. From the mere fact that the skin is white and differs from the rest, and that it has hair differing in whiteness from the other hairs on living and healthy flesh, it is pronounced an old leprosy.

It is called old because it no longer needs to be tested through two periods of seven days.

“But if the healthy color is restored and becomes white”—since he had said that the whole skin had become white, and that for this very reason the person was already clean, because there would no longer be any variation—then he adds: “And on whatever day a living color appears in him, he shall be declared unclean.” Here he clearly shows that variation is rejected.

Accordingly, what he has just said is: “But if the healthy color is restored and becomes white, he shall come to the priest; and the priest shall examine him; and behold, the touch has become white; and the priest shall purify the touch: it is clean.”

We should not understand “the healthy color is restored” to mean that the color had become healthy, since it was precisely that color which had made him unclean because of its variation. He therefore called the color “restored” in the sense that it had become what it had been, namely white while the healthy color had disappeared. He would then become clean again when he was wholly white, because there would be no variation there.

But to understand “restored” as meaning “having disappeared” is a highly unusual expression. It would seem more appropriate to say, “But if the white color is restored.” Yet he now says, “restored and healthy, and it becomes white,” as though he were saying, “If the healthy color is restored as white.”

### XLVIII. [Ibid. 13:30]

[Col. 0699] Why, when he was speaking about leprosy of the head, did he also call it a “shaking” [Note: *Thrausma*.], although it occurs only in the color of the skin or hair, and its appearance is lower than that of the surrounding skin, yet without pain or any distress?

Or did he wish to call what is unclean a “shaking” in the sense of a wound, as though a person had been struck by this uncleanness?

### XLIX. [Ibid. 13:47–48]

What is meant by the fact that, when speaking of leprosy in clothing and other things used by human beings, he says: “Or in a woolen garment, or in a linen garment, or in the warp, or in the wool, or in linen things, or in woolen things,” when he had already said above, “in a woolen garment or in a linen garment”?

For linen cloth is certainly *stuppeum*. Or did he intend “garments” there, but here any woolen thing and any linen thing? For the straw coverings of animals are not garments, although they are woolen; nor are nets garments, although they are made of linen.

Therefore, in the first passage he wished to speak specifically about garments, and afterward generally about all woolen and linen things.

### L. [Ibid. 13:48]

It is asked what he meant by “in every worked leather,” which some have translated, “in every prepared leather.” But the Greek does not say *ergasmenō dermatī* (ἐργασμένῳ δέρματι); rather, it says *ergasimō* (ἐργασίμῳ), a word also used in the Book of Kings, where Jonathan says to David, “Be in the field on the working day” (1 Kings 20:19), that is, on the day when work is done.

Accordingly, here too we should understand “worked leather” to mean leather on which work is performed, that is, leather adapted to some task. For there are skins kept merely for ornament, not for use.

### LI. [Ibid. 13:48]

What else can he mean by “in every leather vessel for work” than something made from leather—that is, in every leather vessel?

Here the word “vessel” is the term which the Greeks call *skeuos* (σκεῦος), for this is a general name for all utensils. There is another term, *angeion* (ἀγγεῖον), which Latin also renders “vessel.” But *angeion* is more properly understood as a vessel that holds liquid.

### LII. [Ibid. 15:11]

[Col. 0700] What does he mean when he says, “And whomever the man suffering a discharge of semen touches” [Note: Printed editions have “whoever touches,” and below, “whoever does not wash.” The manuscripts consistently read “whomever he touches.” The Septuagint reads *hosōn ean hapsētai*, “whatever he touches”; perhaps scribes changed *hosou* into *hosōn*. The Vulgate likewise has, “Everyone whom he touches.”], “and has not washed his hands with water shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and he shall be unclean until evening”?

The wording “has not washed his hands with water” is ambiguous, as though it meant after he has touched someone. But it should be understood as: whoever he touches with unwashed hands, the person whom he has touched shall wash his clothes, and so forth.

### LIII. [Ibid. 16:16, 19]

[Col. 0701] Why, when he was prescribing how the high priest ought to enter the sanctuary that is within the veil, did he say, among other things: “And he shall make intercession for the holy persons, away from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel, and away from their injustices, concerning all their sins”?

How, then, can he make intercession “for the holy persons,” if they are away from the uncleannesses and injustices of the children of Israel, concerning all their sins? Or is the point that he does not say “for the uncleannesses of the children of Israel” but “away from the uncleannesses”? This would mean: “He shall make intercession for the holy persons, away from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel”—that is, for those who are holy because they are separated from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel and do not consent to their uncleannesses.

This does not mean that intercession was to be made only for them, but that it was also to be made for them, lest anyone think that they were so holy that there was nothing for which intercession should be made on their behalf, even though they were separated from the uncleannesses and injustices of the children of Israel.

“Concerning all their sins” means the injustices that arose from all their sins.

Another possible sense is: “He shall make intercession for the holy persons, away from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel,” that is, he shall make intercession for them so that they may be protected from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel.

But “make intercession” cannot be understood except in the sense expressed by another word, “make propitiation.” Hence the object is called the *propitiatory*, which others have rendered the *place of intercession*; in Greek it is called *hilastērion* (ἱλαστήριον).

What the Latin reads here as “he shall make intercession for the holy ones,” the Greek has *exilasetai* (ἐξιλάσεται), which can mean nothing other than making propitiation for sins. Thus it is written in the Psalm, “He who makes propitiation for all your iniquities” (Psalm 102:3).

The more suitable sense, therefore, is that the priest also makes propitiation for those who are holy because they are separated from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel. Although they are holy in such a way that they do not consent to the uncleannesses and injustices of the children of Israel, they nevertheless have something for which God’s propitiation is necessary.

In one Greek manuscript, however, we found, “And he shall make intercession for the holy thing,” not “for the holy things.” The word *holy thing* is neuter, *to hagion* (τὸ ἅγιον). It could be understood to mean, “He shall make intercession for the holy God,” and there would be no difficulty. But how it could mean, “He shall make intercession for this holy thing,” is difficult to say, unless perhaps that holy thing is whatever God is. For the Holy Spirit, who is certainly God, is also expressed in Greek in the neuter gender: *to Pneuma to hagion* (τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον), “the Holy Spirit.”

This may be the meaning, if that manuscript is the more reliable one, which appeared to be more carefully corrected: *exilasetai to hagion* (ἐξιλάσεται τὸ ἅγιον), that is, *to Pneuma to hagion*, “the Holy Spirit,” which cannot be expressed in Latin in the neuter gender.

Yet in three other manuscripts, one Greek and two Latin, we found only the reading given above: “He shall make intercession for the holy things.”

This can also be understood not of holy human beings but of things that are holy, namely the tabernacle itself and whatever within it had been sanctified to the Lord. The meaning would then be: “He shall make intercession for the holy things because of the uncleannesses of the children of Israel”—he shall make propitiation with God for what has been sanctified to the Lord, because of the uncleannesses of the children of Israel, since the tabernacle was situated in their midst.

The following words support this interpretation. For after saying, “He shall make intercession for the holy things because of the uncleannesses of the children of Israel, and because of their injustices, and because of all their sins,” he immediately adds: “And thus he shall do for the tabernacle of testimony, which has been established among them, in the midst of their uncleanness.”

The propitiation for the holy things—that is, for the tabernacle and all the things called holy within it—therefore appears to have been necessary for this reason. Shortly afterward he says the same thing about the altar: the priest was to cleanse it by sprinkling blood and sanctify it from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel.

### LIV. [Ibid. 16:20]

“And he shall complete, making intercession for the holy thing.”

Does this mean, “He shall complete the holy thing”? Or “making intercession for the holy thing,” according to what we said above? Here too the Greek has *to hagion* (τὸ ἅγιον) in the neuter gender.

Does it therefore mean that, by making intercession to the Lord, he shall complete the holy thing—that is, perfectly sanctify what he sanctifies? Or does “he shall complete” mean that, by making intercession, he shall complete the holy thing which is *to Pneuma to hagion*, “the Holy Spirit”?

### LV. [Ibid. 16:20, 27, 29, 33]

Concerning the two goats, one to be sacrificed and the other to be sent into the desert—the latter of which they call *apopompaios* (ἀποπομπαῖος) [Note: The “goat sent away,” Greek *apopompaios*, appears in the Septuagint at Leviticus 16:8 and 10. This accords with Theodoret’s observation in his *Questions on Leviticus*, question 22: *hōs apopempomenos eis tēn erēmon*, “as one sent into the desert.” He concludes that the name derives from the words of Leviticus 16:10, *aposteilai auton eis tēn apopompēn*, “to send it away into the sending-away.”—], there is often debate. Some understand the one to be sacrificed as representing the good and the one to be sent away as representing the evil.

This interpretation should not, however, be confirmed merely because the man in whose hand the goat is sent into the wilderness is ordered, when he returns, to wash his clothes and his body with water and then enter the camp, as though this were also an indication that the goat is to be understood in an evil sense, since the man must be cleansed from its contagion.

For the same cleansing is prescribed for the person who carries the flesh of the other goat and of the calf and burns it outside the camp, since he commands this to be done with the goat and the calf whose sacrificed blood is used for sprinkling and which are offered for sins. Accordingly, the distinction between these two goats must not be handled carelessly in its allegorical meaning.

Likewise, after he had appointed the tenth day of the seventh month [Note: Printed editions read, “the tenth day of the seventeenth month.” The manuscripts have “the tenth day of the seventh month,” which is more correct, as is clear from the Septuagint and the Vulgate.] as a Sabbath of Sabbaths, on which the purification described above was to be performed by that one priest who succeeds his father, speaking of the same priest he says: “He shall propitiate the holy place of the holy place.”

I do not know whether this should be understood in any other way than as, “He shall propitiate in the holy place of the holy place,” by a certain manner of expression—namely, in that holy place into which only the high priest himself entered, the place within the veil where the ark of the testimony and the altar of incense were.

He will not make intercession to that place as though it were God; rather, because he will make intercession to God there, the expression is, “He shall propitiate the holy place of the holy place.” Here too the Greek has the neuter expression *to hagion tou hagiou* (τὸ ἅγιον τοῦ ἁγίου).

Or does it perhaps mean the Holy Spirit of the holy God, *to hagion Pneuma tou hagiou Theou* (τὸ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα τοῦ ἁγίου Θεοῦ)?

Or should “he shall make intercession” be understood as “he shall purify by making intercession”? For the words proceed as follows: “And he shall make intercession for the holy thing of the holy thing, and for the tabernacle of testimony” [Note: Printed editions read “the tabernacle of testimonies.” The manuscripts, together with the Greek, read “of testimony.”], “and he shall make intercession for the altar, and for the priests and for the whole congregation he shall make intercession.”

[Col. 0702] How, then, could he propitiate the tabernacle and the altar unless we understand, as was said, that he shall purify them by making intercession?

### LVI. [On XVII, 3–4]

What does he mean when he says, “Whoever kills a calf, or a sheep, or a goat in the camp, and whoever kills one outside the camp and does not bring it to the door of the tabernacle of testimony,” and thereby declares it a sin and threatens the one who does this? He is not speaking of animals killed for eating or for some other purpose, but of sacrifices. For he prohibited private sacrifices, lest anyone should dare in some fashion to be his own priest; rather, each person was to bring the sacrifice there where it would be offered to God through the priest. Thus they would not sacrifice to empty vanities either; for he also warned that this practice had to be avoided.

Since, then, sacrifices were not permitted to be offered except in the tabernacle, which was later succeeded by the temple—and since King Jeroboam of Israel therefore dared to make calves for the people to sacrifice to, lest those under his rule be led away from him by the necessity of this law, while they went to Jerusalem to offer their sacrifices in God’s temple, an act for which he was condemned by the Lord (1 Kings XII, 28–30)—it is rightly asked how Elijah could lawfully sacrifice outside God’s temple, when he both obtained fire from heaven and defeated the prophets of the demons (ibid. XVIII, 36–39).

I see no way to defend this except by the argument with which Abraham’s action is also defended, when, commanded by God, he was willing to sacrifice his son to God (Gen. XXII, 3–10). For when the one who established the law commands something to be done that he prohibited in the law, the command itself is regarded as law, since he is the author of the law. Other miracles besides the sacrifice could certainly not have been lacking, by which the prophets of the groves might be overcome and refuted. But whatever the Spirit of God, who was in Elijah, did in this matter cannot be contrary to the law, because he is the giver of the law.

### LVII. [On XVII, 10–12]

What does he mean when, prohibiting the eating of blood, he says, “The soul of every flesh is its blood”? He explains the whole passage as follows:

“And any man, any one of the children of Israel, or of the foreigners who have joined themselves to you, whoever eats any blood, I will set my face against the soul that eats blood, and I will destroy it from its people. For the soul of every flesh is its blood. And I have given it to you upon the altar, to make expiation for your souls; for its blood shall make expiation for the soul. Therefore I said to the children of Israel, No soul among you shall eat blood; and the foreigner who has joined himself to you shall not eat blood.”

Surely, if we say that the soul of an animal is its blood, must the soul of a human being also be considered blood? Far from it. How, then, does he not say, “The soul of every flesh of cattle is its blood,” but instead say, “The soul of every flesh is its blood”? Every flesh certainly includes human flesh as well.

Is it because something vital is in the blood, since life is sustained especially through it in this flesh, and since it is diffused through all the veins throughout the body, that he called it the body’s life—“soul” not meaning the life that departs from the body, but the life that ends in death?

[Note: [Col. 0702] The editions read, “Is it because there is also something of such a kind,” and a little below, “which is in all the veins and the body’s joint.” We restore from nine manuscripts: “Is it because [there is] something vital … through all parts of the body.”]

By this usage we say that this life is temporal, not eternal; mortal, not immortal, while the nature of the soul is immortal—the soul that was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom (Luke XVI, 22), to which it is said, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid. XXIII, 43), and which was burning in the torments of hell (ibid. XVI, 23).

According to this meaning, by which even this temporal life is called “soul,” the apostle Paul said, “For I do not make my life more precious than myself” (Acts XX, 24), where he wished to show that he was prepared to die for the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0703] The Ratian edition has, “more precious to me.” The better manuscripts likewise have this, indeed all except one, which reads, “more precious than myself.” In the Greek text of Acts, chapter 20, verse 24, we read *timian emautō* (“precious to myself”), which supports those manuscripts.]

For according to the meaning in which “soul” refers to that which departs from the body, he was making it more precious by acquiring for it such great merit. There are other expressions of this kind as well.

Thus this temporal life is contained in the body chiefly through the blood. But what does he mean when he says, “I have given it to you upon God’s altar, to make expiation for your soul,” as though soul might make expiation for soul? Is it blood for blood, as though we were concerned about our own blood when we wish expiation to be made for our soul? This is absurd.

But it is much more absurd to suppose that the blood of an animal makes expiation for the soul of a human being, which cannot die, since Scripture plainly testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews that the blood of victims accomplished nothing toward making expiation to God for human sins, but signified something beneficial. “For it is impossible,” it says, “for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Heb. X, 4).

It remains, therefore, that since that Mediator makes expiation for our soul—the one prefigured by all those sacrifices that were offered for sins—the thing that signifies the soul is called “soul.”

It is customary for the thing that signifies something to be called by the name of the thing it signifies, as it is written, “The seven ears are seven years”; for he did not say, “signify seven years.” Likewise, “The seven cows are seven years” (Gen. XLI, 26), and many similar expressions.

This is why it is said, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X, 4). He did not say, “The rock signifies Christ,” but spoke as though it were this—although in substance it was not this, but was so by signification.

So too, since blood signifies the soul on account of a certain vitality of bodily substance, it is called “soul” in the sacraments.

But if anyone thinks that the soul of an animal is its blood, there is no need to struggle over this question. What must be very carefully avoided, and this error refuted in every way, is the supposition that the soul of a human being—which gives life to human flesh and is rational—is blood.

Expressions should also be sought in which what contains something signifies what is contained, so that, since the soul is held in the blood within the body—for when the blood has been poured out, the soul departs—it is appropriately signified through the blood, and the blood receives its name.

Thus “church” is used of the place in which the Church gathers. The Church consists of human beings, of whom it is said, “that he might present to himself a glorious Church” (Eph. V, 27). Yet the same apostle also testifies that the house of prayer itself is called by this name, when he says, “Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God?” (1 Cor. XI, 22).

Everyday speech has likewise established that to go out into the church, or to flee for refuge to the church, is said only of someone who has gone or fled to the very place and its walls within which the assembly of the Church is contained.

It is also written, “And he who sheds blood is one who cheats a hired laborer of his wages” (Sir. XXXIV, 27). He called the wages “blood,” because the life called by the name of blood is sustained by them.

But when the Lord says, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54), what does it mean that the people are so emphatically prohibited from the blood of sacrifices offered for sins, if those sacrifices signified this one sacrifice in which true remission of sins takes place? From the blood of that sacrifice, however, no one is prohibited from taking nourishment; rather, all who wish to have life are urged to drink it.

We must therefore ask what it signifies that a human being is prohibited by the Law from eating blood, while being commanded to pour it out to God. As for the nature of the soul, and why it has been signified by blood, we have said as much as seemed sufficient for the present.

### LVIII. [On XVIII, 7–8]

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father and the nakedness of your mother; for their nakedness is theirs.”

He prohibits intercourse with one’s mother; for in her lies the nakedness of father and mother. Later he also prohibits intercourse with a stepmother, where he says, “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife; for it is your father’s nakedness.” There he explained how, in the mother, there is the nakedness of both—father and mother—whereas in the stepmother there is only that of the father.

[Note: [Col. 0704] The manuscripts have, “their nakedness.” The editions have, “for their nakedness is theirs.” Neither reading agrees with the text of Scripture, in which, after “you shall not uncover,” there follows immediately, “She is your mother; you shall not uncover her nakedness.”]

### LIX. [On XVIII, 9, 11]

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, whether born of your father or of your mother, whether born at home or born outside; you shall not uncover their nakedness.”

The one born at home is understood to be born of the father; the one born outside is understood to be born of the mother, if perhaps the mother had conceived her from an earlier husband and brought her with her into the household when she married her father. Scripture warns him not to uncover the nakedness of his sister.

Here he seems not to have prohibited, and as though to have passed over, intercourse with a sister born of both parents. For he does not say, “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister born of your father and mother,” but “born of your father or of your mother.”

Yet who does not see that this too is most emphatically prohibited? If it is not lawful to uncover the nakedness of a sister born of either parent, how much more is it prohibited when she is born of both?

But what does it mean that, after inserting the prohibition of intercourse even with one’s own nieces, whether through a son or through a daughter, he continues and says, “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter”?

If he had stopped there, we would understand intercourse with the daughter of a stepmother to have been prohibited—if the stepmother had borne her to an earlier husband, so that she was not the sister of the one prohibited from intercourse with her, either through the father or through the mother.

But when he adds, “She is your sister, born of the same father; you shall not uncover her nakedness,” he makes it clear that the prohibition concerns a sister born of the father and the stepmother, about whom he had already spoken above.

Or did he wish to prohibit this again more explicitly because it had previously been obscure? Scripture often does this.

### LX. [On XVIII, 14]

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s brother, and you shall not approach his wife.”

He explained what he meant by “the nakedness of your father’s brother,” that is, of your paternal uncle: namely, “You shall not approach his wife.” In the wife of the paternal uncle he intended the nakedness of the paternal uncle to be understood, just as in the father’s wife he intended the nakedness of the father to be understood.

### LXI. [On XVIII, 16]

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife; it is your brother’s nakedness.”

It is asked whether this prohibition concerns a living brother or a dead one; and this is no small question.

If we say that Scripture is speaking of the wife of a living brother, then this is certainly included under the one general commandment by which a person is prohibited from approaching another man’s wife (Exod. XX, 14).

What, then, is the point of distinguishing these persons, whom it calls members of the household, from others by specific prohibitions so carefully? For the prohibition concerning one’s father’s wife—that is, one’s stepmother—should not be understood as applying only while the father is alive, but rather after his death. While the father is alive, surely no one fails to see that it is most emphatically prohibited, if the wife of any man whatsoever is forbidden to be defiled by adultery.

It therefore seems to be speaking of persons who, if they had no husbands, could marry one another were they not prohibited by the Law, as is reported to have been the custom among the Persians.

But again, if we understand it as prohibiting the taking of a brother’s wife after the brother’s death, we encounter the passage in which Scripture commands that it be done for the raising up of offspring if he died without children (Deut. XXV, 5).

When this prohibition is compared with that command, so that they do not contradict one another, an exception must be understood: namely, that no one may take the wife of a deceased brother if the deceased left descendants.

Or perhaps the prohibition is also that no one may take the wife of his brother even if she had separated from the living brother by divorce. For then, as the Lord says, Moses permitted the Jews, because of the hardness of their hearts, to give a certificate of divorce (Matt. XIX, 8), and after such a dismissal someone might think it lawful to marry his brother’s wife, since adultery would not be feared because she had departed by divorce.

### LXII. [On XVIII, 17]

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter”—that is, no one should think it lawful to take his wife’s daughter.

It is not lawful to uncover the nakedness of both the woman and her daughter, that is, to have intercourse with both mother and daughter.

### LXIII. [On XVIII, 17–18]

“You shall not take the daughter of her son or the daughter of her daughter.”

He also prohibited taking as a wife the wife’s granddaughter, whether through her son or through her daughter.

“You shall not take one wife in addition to her sister, to provoke jealousy.”

Here he did not prohibit taking an additional wife, which was permitted to the ancients because of the abundance of offspring; but he did not want one sister to be taken in addition to another. Jacob appears to have done this (Gen. XXX, 22–28), either because it had not yet been prohibited by the law, or because he was deceived by the fraud of the woman substituted for the other, and she came to him more by agreement than the one whom he later received. Yet it would have been unjust to dismiss the first, lest he cause her to commit adultery.

[Note: [Col. 0705] The manuscripts and the Septuagint have, “in addition to her sister.” The editions have, “a sister in addition to a wife,” and so on.]

But what does he mean by “to provoke jealousy”? Is this expression used so that there should be no jealousy between sisters, although jealousy between women who were not sisters would not have been contemptible?

[Note: [Col. 0706] Nearly all the manuscripts have the neuter form, *zelum* … *contemnendum*, “jealousy … not to be despised.”]

Or is it rather placed there to prohibit the action from being done for this reason—that is, so that one sister might be taken in addition to another with the intention of provoking the sister’s jealousy?

### LXIV. [On XVIII, 19]

“And you shall not approach a woman during the separation of her uncleanness, to uncover her nakedness”—that is, you shall not approach a menstruating woman.

According to the Law, she was separated because of her uncleanness. Since this had already been prohibited sufficiently above (Lev. XV, 19–27), what does it mean that he wished to add the same commandment here as well?

Or perhaps, because the matter had already been stated above, it was placed here lest anyone think it should be understood figuratively, since it appears here among prohibitions of the kind that must unquestionably be observed even in the time of the New Testament, after the removal of the observance of the ancient shadows.

This also seems to have been signified by the prophet Ezekiel, who, among sins that are not figurative but manifest iniquities, mentions someone approaching a menstruating woman, and among the merits of righteousness mentions not approaching her (Ezek. XVIII, 6; XXII, 10).

In this matter nature is not condemned; rather, the act is declared harmful to the conception of offspring.

[Note: [Col. 0706] The editions have, “the harm of offspring is prohibited.” The manuscripts have, “harmful to offspring,” and most of them, “is declared.”]

### LXV. [On XVIII, 20]

“And you shall not give the lying together of your seed to your neighbor’s wife, to be defiled with her.”

Here again he prohibits adultery committed with another man’s wife, which is also prohibited in the Decalogue (Exod. XX, 14).

It therefore appears that the women previously mentioned were prohibited in such a way that they were not to be taken as wives even after their husbands had died, since he prohibits uncovering their nakedness.

### LXVI. [On XVIII, 21]

“And you shall not give any of your seed to serve the ruler.”

I do not see what this can mean except serving a ruler who is worshiped in place of God.

For in Greek he does not say *douleuein* (δουλεύειν), but *latreuein* (λατρεύειν), which Latin writers ordinarily translate only by *servire*, “to serve,” although the distinction is very great.

Serving human beings as slaves serve them—which is not *latreuein* but *douleuein*—is not prohibited by Scripture. But serving in the sense of *latreuein* is not commanded to human beings, except to the one true God, as it is written, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. VI, 13).

Not only does the word *latreuein* sufficiently indicate what sort of ruler he means—that is, one to whom worship is offered as to God—but this is also shown by what he adds: “And you shall not profane the holy name,” whether the name of God, whose people are said in that way to serve the ruler, or the holy name of that people, Israel, on account of which it is said, “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. XI, 44; XIX, 2; and 1 Pet. I, 16).

He most appropriately adds here, “I am the Lord,” thereby reminding us that *latreia* (λατρεία), that is, the service by which God is served, is due to him alone.

### LXVII. [On XIX, 25]

When he says, “And the land was disgusted with those who dwell upon it,” because of the evil deeds he mentioned above, this should not be understood as though the earth has a sense by which it perceives and detests these things. Rather, by the name “earth” he signifies the human beings who are upon the earth.

Therefore, when human beings commit these evils, they defile the earth, because the human beings who imitate them are defiled; and the earth is disgusted because those who neither commit nor imitate them are disgusted.

### LXVIII. [On XIX, 11]

“You shall not steal, nor shall you lie, nor shall anyone slander his neighbor.”

The statement concerning theft is included in the Decalogue. As for what he says, “Nor shall you lie, nor shall anyone slander his neighbor,” it is surprising if this is not contained in the commandment stated there, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exod. XX, 15–16), since slander cannot occur without lying, which is included under the general category of false testimony.

But whether these things may be admitted under some form of compensation is a major question. In the case of lying, nearly everyone seems to hold that one ought to lie for the sake of someone’s safety when no one is harmed.

Does the same apply to theft? Or can theft not occur where no one is harmed?

Indeed, it can occur even when the person against whom it is committed is being helped, as when someone steals a sword from a man who wishes to kill himself.

But I do not know whether slander can be committed for anyone’s benefit, unless perhaps the matter concerning Joseph is an example: he slandered his brothers over the cup, and also charged them falsely with spying, in order to produce a greater joy which they would later enjoy (Gen. XLIV, 5; XLII, 9, 14).

Yet if we try to determine these matters by definitions, perhaps theft is not theft except when a neighbor is harmed by the secret removal of what belongs to another; and slander is not slander except when a neighbor is harmed by the accusation of a false crime.

But we cannot say that lying occurs only when a neighbor is harmed. When something false is knowingly said, it is certainly a lie, whether someone is harmed by it or no one is.

Thus the great question concerning lying—whether a lie can ever be just—might perhaps be easily resolved if we looked only at the commandments and not also at the examples.

For what commandment could be clearer than, “You shall not lie”? It is stated in the same way as, “You shall not make an idol for yourself,” and an act of that kind can never be just. It is also stated in the same way as, “You shall not commit adultery”; yet who would say that adultery could ever be just?

Likewise, “You shall not steal”: according to that definition of theft, theft can never be just.

And, “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX, 4, 14, 15, 13). For when a human being is justly killed, the law kills him, not you. Can one similarly say, “When a human being justly lies, the law lies”?

But the examples make the question exceedingly difficult. The Egyptian midwives lied, and God rewarded them with good (ibid. I, 19–20). Rahab lied on behalf of the spies of the land, and for that reason she was delivered (Josh. II, 4; VI, 23).

After the Law said, “You shall not lie,” should we therefore understand that lying is not permitted even in such a situation as that in which Rahab is recorded to have lied?

It is more credible, however, that lying was prohibited because it was unjust, rather than that it became unjust because it was prohibited.

Perhaps, therefore, as we said concerning the midwives, what was rewarded in them was not the fact that they lied, but that they delivered the Hebrew infants; so that, on account of this mercy, that sin became venial, though it should not be thought not to have been a sin.

The same should be understood of Rahab: her delivery of the spies was rewarded, so that, on account of that same deliverance, pardon was granted for the lie.

But wherever pardon is granted, it is evident that there is a sin.

This must be guarded against, however, lest anyone think that pardon can likewise be granted for other sins whenever they are committed for the sake of delivering human beings. Many intolerable and utterly detestable evils follow from this error.

### LXIX. [On XIX, 15]

“You shall not harm your neighbor.”

If it were clear to human beings what it means to harm and not to harm, this general commandment might perhaps be sufficient for preserving innocence.

For everything that is prohibited from being committed against one’s neighbor must be referred to this one principle: “You shall not harm your neighbor.”

As for what follows, “You shall not rob,” unless it is referred to the principle that one must not harm by robbing, it may sometimes happen that someone harms another by not robbing. A sword must be taken away from a madman; and if someone does not do what ought to be done,

[Note: [Col. 0708] The Michaelinus and Beccensis manuscripts have, “what he could have done.”]

he will cause greater harm.

### LXX. [On XIX, 17–18]

What does it mean that, after saying above, “You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall certainly rebuke your neighbor, and you shall not incur sin because of him,” he then adds, “And your hand shall not be avenged”?

Does this mean, “Your hand shall not be punished”? For you act with a good intention when you impose discipline on a neighbor who is sinning, so that you do not incur his sin by neglecting him. This is the purpose of what he placed earlier: “You shall not hate your neighbor in your heart.” The person being rebuked might think that you hate him, although hatred is not in your heart.

Or does “Your hand shall not be avenged” rather warn you not to seek vengeance with your hand, nor to be carried away by the desire for revenge?

For what else is it to wish to be avenged than to rejoice or find consolation in another’s misfortune? Therefore it is said, “You shall not be angry with the children of your people.” Anger has rightly been defined as the desire for revenge.

Some manuscripts, however, have, “And your hand shall not be avenged,” that is, do not wish to avenge yourself by rebuking him, but rather to benefit the one whom you rebuke.

### LXXI. [On XIX, 28]

“And you shall not make incisions upon the soul in your body.”

He said, “upon the soul,” meaning at the funeral of a dead person. For grief concerns the soul that has departed.

This grief includes mourning, during which certain nations have the custom of cutting their bodies. God prohibits this.

[Note: [Col. 0708] The editions have, “This is prohibited by God among the Jews.” The manuscripts do not have the words “among the Jews.”]

### LXXII. [On XX, 5]

“So that those of his people commit fornication with the rulers.”

[Note: [Col. 0708] The editions had omitted the particle *in*, “with,” which is restored from the manuscripts and from the Septuagint text. The printed Greek has *hōste ekporneuein auton*, “so that he may commit fornication,” or “so that he might commit fornication.” In other books, however—those followed here by Augustine—*autous* is read instead of *auton*, as Nobilius testifies in his notes on Leviticus, chapter 20. Thus we find the Vulgate represented in the Germanensis manuscripts as, “so that they might commit fornication,” although the editions have, “so that he might commit fornication.”]

It is not rulers who are of his people, but those of his people who commit fornication with the rulers.

By “rulers” he wishes those to be understood who were worshiped as gods, as the Apostle says, “according to the ruler of the authority of the air” (Eph. II, 2); and in the Gospel the Lord says, “Now the ruler of this world has been cast out” (John XII, 31), and, “The ruler of the world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (ibid. XIV, 30).

### LXXIII. [On XX, 10]

“Any man, any man who commits adultery with another man’s wife, or whoever commits adultery with his neighbor’s wife, shall die the death.”

He used the plural, “shall die the death,” meaning both the man who committed adultery and the woman with whom adultery was committed.

Here he wished to make some distinction between any man and one’s neighbor, although in many places he uses “neighbor” for every human being.

But what kind of expression is it that, after already speaking of “another man,” he repeats the same thing concerning “one’s neighbor,” when it follows that one must all the more abstain from one’s neighbor’s wife if one must abstain from the wife of any man?

For if he had first spoken of one’s neighbor, then, lest anyone think it permissible to commit adultery with the wife of someone who was not a neighbor, it would have been necessary to add “of any man.”

But now, if what is less is not permitted, how much less is what is the greater evil?

For if it is not permitted to commit adultery with the wife of any man, how much more is it forbidden with the wife of one’s neighbor?

Or perhaps this repetition explains what was said first, so that a person may understand how great an evil it is to commit adultery with another man’s wife: namely, because in doing so he commits adultery with his neighbor’s wife. For every human being is a neighbor to every other human being.

### LXXIV. [On XX, 16]

“And the woman who approaches any animal, to be mounted by it, you shall kill the woman and the animal; they shall die the death; they are guilty.”

It is asked how the animal can be guilty, since it is irrational and in no way capable of the law.

Or, just as words are transferred by a figure of speech—called *metaphora* (μεταφορά) in Greek—from an animate being to an inanimate one, as when we say “a wicked wind” or “an angry sea,” so here too the word has been transferred from a rational being to an irrational one.

The animals should be believed to have been ordered to be killed because, having been polluted by such a disgraceful act, they perpetuate the unworthy memory of what was done.

### LXXV. [On XX, 17]

“Whoever takes his sister, born of his father or of his mother, and sees her nakedness—it is a disgrace; they shall be exterminated in the sight of their people.”

“He has uncovered the nakedness of his sister; they shall bear his sin.”

[Note: [Col. 0709] Thus the editions read. At this point the manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint, omit “his.”]

What does “sees” mean here except that he has known her by intercourse? Thus in the Law it is said, “He knew his wife” (Gen. IV, 1, 17, 25), meaning that he joined himself to her.

And what does “they shall bear his sin” mean, when he was speaking of their punishment, except that he wished even the punishment of sin to be called “sin”?

### LXXVI. [On XX, 20, 25]

“Whoever sleeps with his kinswoman has uncovered the nakedness of his kinship; they shall die without children.”

It is asked how far this kinship is to be understood, since it is certainly permissible to take a wife from a distant degree of relationship, and always has been.

It must be understood as referring to the degrees that he prohibited. In accordance with these he said, “Whoever sleeps with his kinswoman.” Here he also left certain unmentioned cases to be understood, such as a sister born of both parents and the wife of one’s mother’s brother, that is, one’s maternal uncle.

He first prohibited the wife of one’s paternal uncle, although this is said to be not kinship but affinity.

But what does “they shall die without children” mean, when children have been born from such unions in the past and are born even today?

Should this be understood as a provision established by the Law of God, so that any children born from such unions are not counted as children—that is, do not lawfully succeed their parents?

[Note: [Col. 0710] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Lovaniensis omit “and.”]

“And you shall not make your souls abominable through cattle, birds, and all the reptiles of the earth, which I have separated for you as unclean.”

Here he seems to indicate that these things are not unclean by nature, but by some sacramental sign, since he says, “which I have separated for you as unclean,” as though they would not be unclean for them if they had not been separated for that purpose.

### LXXVII. [On XX, 27]

“And a man or woman, if there should be in him or her a ventriloquist, or an enchanter, both shall die; you shall stone them with stones; they are guilty.”

Does this mean “a man and a woman,” or “a man and a ventriloquist,” or “a woman and a ventriloquist or enchanter”?

The better interpretation is that it means both the one who has it and the one whom it has.

[Note: [Col. 0710] Nearly all the manuscripts have, “and the woman who has it.”]

### LXXVIII. [On XXI, 7–8]

“They shall not take a prostitute or a profane woman, nor a woman divorced by her husband, because he is holy to the Lord his God.”

Above he had said, “They shall not take”; here, however, he says, “because he is holy,” not “because they are holy.” He was speaking of several priests who existed at one time, and he said of each one of them, “He is holy,” in the manner of expression Scripture commonly uses.

Later he mentions that one great priest who entered the Holy of Holies. He also concluded in the plural, saying, “And you shall sanctify him: he shall offer the gifts of the Lord your God; he is holy, because I, the Lord who sanctify them, am holy.”

As far as the offerings are concerned, since he said, “He shall offer the gifts of the Lord your God,” it was not only that supreme priest who offered them, but also the lesser priests.

Therefore, when he says, “They shall not take a prostitute or a profane woman or a woman divorced by her husband,” this prohibition applies to the lesser priests as well. Concerning the supreme priest he later says that he was commanded to take only a virgin.

### LXXIX. [On XXI, 10]

“And the great priest from among his brothers”—

[Note: [Col. 0710] The editions read, “before his brothers.” The manuscripts read, “from among his brothers”; the Septuagint agrees with them.]

that is, the one who is great among his brothers, namely, the one and only great priest.

“Upon whose head the oil of the anointed one has been poured.”

Scripture calls the oil itself “the anointed one.”

### LXXX. [On XXI, 10]

“And, with his hands perfected, he shall put on the garments.”

These are, of course, the garments that are described with such elaborate detail in the priestly vesture.

### LXXXI. [On XXI, 10–11]

“He shall not uncover his head from the turban, and he shall not tear his garments, and he shall not enter over any dead soul.”

This is understood as referring to the mourning practices that he had prohibited above: uncovering the head from the turban and tearing the garments.

Tearing one’s garments was an ancient practice of mourners, as is written concerning Job, when he was told that his sons had been crushed in the collapse (Job I, 20).

Uncovering the head from the turban could likewise have been a sign of mourning because it involved the removal of an adornment.

But what he means by saying, “He shall not enter over any dead soul,” when he calls a dead body a “dead soul,” is difficult to understand. Nevertheless, this is a customary expression in Scripture, although it is extremely unusual for us.

Thus the soul gives its own name to the body that has been deprived of it, because the body will be restored to the soul in the resurrection. In the same way, a building called a church continues to be called a church even after the Church—that is, the human beings—has left it.

But since, in a living human being, the body is not called by the name of the soul, it is strange that it should then be called “soul” when it has been deprived of the soul.

Or, if we understand “dead soul” as separated from the body, so that he appears to have called the separation itself death—that is, so that the soul is “dead” because it has been separated from the body, not because it has lost its nature—then, when we are said to be “dead to sin” (Rom. VI, 2), this does not mean that our nature has perished, but that we no longer use sin, so that the soul may be understood to be “dead,” that is, dead to the body because it has ceased to use it, while continuing to live in its own nature.
