How, then, can anyone enter over a dead soul, which this priest is prohibited from doing, when anyone who enters enters over a dead body, not over the soul that has departed from the body?

Or did he call the temporal life the “soul,” since that life has indeed died in the dead body when the soul—which cannot die—has departed?

The life itself was not the soul; rather, it received the soul’s name through the presence of the soul by which it subsisted. We made this distinction when speaking about blood, explaining the statement, “The soul of every flesh is its blood” (above, question 57).

Even blood is dead in the body of a dead person; for it did not depart together with the departing soul.

Scripture therefore prohibited the supreme priest from entering even over the funeral of his father or mother, whereas it did not prohibit this from the lesser priest.

The passage continues, “He shall not be defiled over his father or over his mother.” The order of the words is: “He shall not be defiled over his father, nor over his mother.”

### LXXXII. [On XXI, 12]

“And he shall not go out from the holy places.”

This undoubtedly refers to the time when the funerals of his relatives were being conducted, just as he was prohibited from going out from the holy places during the seven days in which he was being sanctified (Lev. VIII, 33), but not at all times.

If, however, the high priests of that time were not prohibited from taking wives or begetting children, a serious question arises.

The Law calls a person unclean until evening even through marital intercourse, even after he has washed his body with water (ibid. XV, 16). Moreover, the high priest was commanded to enter within the veil twice every day for the continual offering of incense (Exod. XXX, 7–8), where the altar of incense was located, and no unclean person was permitted to approach the holy places.

How, then, did the high priest fulfill this daily duty if he was begetting children?

If illness had befallen him, one might ask who would perform his function in his place. It could be answered that, by God’s grace, he did not become ill. But can the same answer be given concerning the begetting of children?

It follows, therefore, either that he was continent, or that the incense was omitted on certain days;

[Note: [Col. 0712] See *Retractationes* II, 2, chapter 55, no. 9.]

or, if it could not be omitted—since it had necessarily to be offered by the high priest alone—that he did not become unclean through marital intercourse because of the exceptional sanctification of his office.

Or, if the statement that follows concerning all the sons of Aaron also applies to him—that none of them may approach the holy places if some uncleanness has happened to him—then the remaining possibility is certainly that the incense was not offered on certain days.

[Note: [Col. 0712] Thus the manuscripts read. The editions have, “if some uncleanness has happened to him because of sin, the remaining possibility is to understand.”]

### LXXXIII. [On XXI, 11]

Since the high priest is prohibited from entering over the funeral of his father, it may be asked how he could already be high priest while his father was not yet dead, since the Law commands them to succeed their fathers.

For this reason it was necessary that, before the high priest had been buried, another priest should immediately be appointed in his place, because of the continual incense, which had to be offered daily by the high priest.

[Note: [Col. 0712] See the same work.]

Yet the question concerning the illness of the high priest remains, if it was necessary for him to be ill for several days before dying. Unless perhaps this too can be resolved by saying that high priests ordinarily died suddenly, without a preceding illness, as Scripture testifies concerning Aaron himself (Num. XX, 26–29).

### LXXXIV. [On XXI, 15]

It should be noted how often he says, “I am the Lord who sanctifies him,” speaking of the priest, when he also said to Moses, “And you shall sanctify him” (Exod. XXIX, 24). How, then, do both Moses and the Lord sanctify? Moses does not act in place of the Lord: Moses sanctifies through visible sacraments by his ministry, whereas the Lord sanctifies through invisible grace by the Holy Spirit, in whom lies the entire fruit even of the visible sacraments. For without this sanctification of invisible grace, what benefit do the visible sacraments provide?

It is rightly asked, however, whether this invisible sanctification likewise provides no benefit without the visible sacraments by which a person is visibly sanctified. That is plainly absurd. Someone could more tolerably say that this sanctification does not exist without those sacraments than that, once present, it provides no benefit, since all their usefulness lies in it. Yet even the claim that this invisible sanctification cannot exist without them must be examined to see how it can rightly be stated.

The visible baptism profited Simon Magus nothing, because he lacked invisible sanctification; but those who received this invisible sanctification—and, because it was present, benefited from it—had likewise received the visible sacraments, having been baptized [Note: [Col. 0712] The manuscripts of Beccensis and Michaelinus read *percepere* (“received”).]. Nevertheless, it is not shown that Moses, who visibly sanctified the priests, was himself sanctified by those sacrifices or by oil. Would anyone dare deny that he was sanctified invisibly, when such great grace was preeminent in him?

The same can be said of John the Baptist: he appeared as a baptizer before he appeared as one baptized (Matt. III, 11, 14). Therefore we can by no means deny that he was sanctified; yet we do not find that this was done visibly in him before he came to the ministry of baptizing [Col. 0713]. The same applies to that thief to whom the Lord, crucified with him, said, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43) [Note: [Col. 0713] See *Retractationes*, book 2, chapter 55.]. For he was not granted such blessedness without invisible sanctification.

Accordingly, it follows that invisible sanctification was present and beneficial in some people without the visible sacraments, which have been changed according to the diversity of times, so that the sacraments were one thing then and another now. Visible sanctification, however, which takes place through visible sacraments, can exist without this invisible sanctification, but cannot provide benefit without it. Nevertheless, the visible sacrament should not for that reason be despised: one who despises it can in no way be sanctified invisibly. Thus Cornelius and those who were with him, although they had already appeared to be sanctified by the Holy Spirit invisibly poured out upon them, were nevertheless baptized (Acts X, 44–48); nor was the visible sanctification judged superfluous, even though invisible sanctification had preceded it.

### LXXXV. [Ibid. XXII, 1–2]

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Say to Aaron and his sons: Let them keep away from the holy things of the children of Israel, and they shall not profane my holy name, whatever things they themselves consecrate to me. I am the Lord. And you shall say to them: Throughout your generations, any man of all your descendants who approaches the holy things that the children of Israel sanctify for the Lord, when his uncleanness is upon him, that person shall be cut off from me. I am the Lord your God.’”

All doubt has been removed: no priest, whether a high priest or one of the secondary priests, was to approach the holy things if his uncleanness was upon him. It therefore followed that the priest had to abstain, lest on account of the procreation of children the continual incense should not be offered on certain days. This incense was customarily offered twice daily by the high priests alone, morning and evening (Exod. XXX, 7–8), even though after marital intercourse a man remained unclean until evening, despite having washed his whole body (Lev. XV, 16), and it was necessary for him to offer it.

When he says, “the things that the children of Israel sanctify,” this should be understood as referring to what they sanctify by offering it to the priests, so that it may be offered through them to the Lord. We should also note the kind of sanctification that takes place through the vow and devotion of the one making the offering. But whether, just as the things offered by human beings are sanctified in this way, human beings themselves are likewise said to sanctify themselves in the same way when they vow themselves in some matter must be examined in Scripture.

### LXXXVI. [Ibid. XXII, 4]

“And whoever touches any uncleanness of a soul”—that is, something dead, contact with which according to the Law defiles.

### LXXXVII. [Ibid. XXIV, 15–16]

“A man, a man, if he curses his God, shall bear his sin; but whoever names the name of the Lord shall surely die”—as though cursing his God were one thing and naming the name of the Lord another, with the former being a sin, but the latter such a great sacrilege that it deserves death as well.

Although in this passage “the name of the Lord” should be understood in such a way that it is accompanied by a curse—that is, he names it while cursing—what, then, is the difference between that sin and this crime of such enormity? Perhaps by repeating the matter he showed that it was not a slight sin but such a great crime that it was to be punished by death. Yet because he introduced this by a distinction, saying not “for whoever names” but “but whoever names,” the meaning has become somewhat obscure. Therefore, if this is correctly understood, we should also note the type of expression involved.

### LXXXVIII. [Ibid. XXIV, 17]

“And a man who strikes the soul of any human being, and he dies, shall surely die.” He does not say, “Whoever strikes a man and he dies,” but “the soul of a human being,” although it is rather the human body that is struck by the assailant, just as the Lord says, “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. X, 28).

Accordingly, in the manner customary in Scripture, he calls the life of the body, which comes about through the soul, “the soul,” and by this he intended to show that the murderer strikes the human soul—that is, by striking, he deprives the human being of life. Why, then, did he add, “and he dies,” if he had already indicated homicide by saying that he struck the human soul, meaning that the person was deprived of life by the one who struck him? Perhaps he wished to explain how “the human soul was struck” was to be understood, and therefore said, “and he dies,” as though he were saying, “that is, he dies.” For this is what it means for the human soul to have been struck.

### LXXXIX. [Ibid. XXV, 2–7]

“When you enter the land that I give you, and the land that I give you rests, there shall be sabbaths for the Lord. For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather its fruit; but in the seventh year there shall be a sabbath, a rest for the land, a sabbath for the Lord.”

How should we understand the wording, “When you enter the land that I give you, and the land rests; for six years you shall sow your field,” and so forth—as though the command were given when the land had rested, when in fact the land rests precisely because this is done? By the rest of the land he plainly means the seventh year, in which he commanded that no one work it by agriculture.

A very long hyperbaton, however, makes this meaning obscure. The order of the words therefore appears to be as follows: “When you enter the land that I give you, and the land that I give you rests, there shall be sabbaths for the Lord: you shall not harvest the growth that springs up of itself in your field, and you shall not gather the grapes of your consecration; it shall be a year of rest for the land. The sabbaths of the land shall be food for you, for your male servant, your female servant, your hired laborer, and the resident alien who has attached himself to you, and for your cattle and the wild animals that are in your land; everything that grows from it shall be food.”

He inserted an explanation of how the land is to rest, saying: “For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vine and gather its fruit; but in the seventh year there shall be a sabbath, a rest for the land, a sabbath for the Lord. You shall not sow your field, and you shall not prune your vineyard.”

By saying “you shall not prune,” we should understand that every kind of cultivation was prohibited in that year. For if it is not to be pruned, neither is it to be ploughed, supported with stakes, or subjected to anything else belonging to its cultivation. But just as the whole is often understood through one part, so here every kind of cultivation is signified by pruning.

And by “field” and “vineyard,” since he prohibited both sowing the former and pruning the latter, every kind of field is to be understood. For nothing is to be done in an olive grove or in a field of any other kind, although he remained silent about them [Col. 0715]. When he says, “The sabbaths of the land shall be food for you, for your male servant, your female servant,” and so forth, he makes it sufficiently clear that the owner of the field is not prohibited from eating what grows spontaneously that year without cultivation; rather, he is prohibited from gathering the produce. Thus he is permitted to take some of it for food, as someone passing by might take only what he would immediately consume by eating, not what he would store for later use.

### XC. [Ibid. XXV, 23]

“And the land shall not be sold for profanation.” Other manuscripts read, “for confirmation.” I think this error arose first in one or the other form of the Greek text because of the similar sound of the words: βεβήλωσις means “profanation,” whereas βεβαίωσις means “confirmation.”

The first meaning is clear: “The land shall not be sold for profanation”—that is, no one should dare to sell land received from God to profane people who would use it for impiety and the worship of foreign and false gods.

The other wording, “The land shall not be sold for confirmation,” is somewhat obscure. I think it should be understood only as meaning that the sale must not be confirmed in such a way that the seller does not receive the land back at the time of release, as has been commanded.

What follows can suit either meaning, whether we read, “The land shall not be sold for profanation,” or “for confirmation.” For he immediately adds, “For the land is mine,” on account of which “you are proselytes and resident aliens before me.”

### XCI. [Ibid. XXV, 24]

“And throughout all the land of your possession you shall give compensation to the land.” Other manuscripts read, “You shall give redemption to the land.”

The meaning, then, is this: “The land shall not be sold for profanation”—that is, to those who would use it as an insult to the Creator—or “for confirmation,” that is, so that the buyer might possess it perpetually and not restore it to the seller at the appointed interval of years according to God’s command.

“For the land is mine,” he says; therefore you must use it according to my command. And to show that it belonged to him and not to them, he consequently added what they themselves were in it, saying, “For you are proselytes and resident aliens before me.” That is: although proselytes—meaning foreigners who have been joined to your people—and resident aliens—meaning those who do not remain in their own land—you yourselves are nevertheless all foreigners and resident aliens before me.

God says this either to the Israelites, because he gave them the land of other nations whom he expelled; or to every human being, since before God, who always remains and, as it is written, fills heaven and earth (Jer. XXIII, 24), every human being is a foreigner by being born and a resident alien by living, because he is compelled to move away by dying [Note: [Col. 0715] Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions have: “the human being who always remains before God.”].

### XCII. [Ibid. XXV, 24]

Then he adds and says, “Throughout all the land of your possession you shall give compensation to the land,” as tenants—or “redemption.”

Unless I am mistaken, he intends this to mean that, by the cessation of every seventh year and of the fiftieth year, which he calls the year of release, they were in a certain sense returning what they had received. Thus the land’s being left fallow was like compensation for habitation, or redemption from him to whom it belongs—that is, from God its Creator [Col. 0716].

### XCIII. [Ibid. XXVI, 11]

“And I will place my tabernacle among you, and my soul will not abhor you.” God calls his will “his soul.” For he is not an animal possessing a body and a soul; nor is his substance of the kind possessed by his creature called the soul, which he made, as he himself testifies through Isaiah, saying, “And I made every breath” (Isa. LVII, 16). The context makes clear that he is speaking there of the human soul.

Therefore, just as when he speaks of his eyes, his lips, and the other names of bodily members, we certainly do not understand him to be defined by bodily form, but understand all those names of members only as the effects of his operations and powers [Note: [Col. 0716] The manuscript of Corbeiensis reads, “and the power.”], so when he says, “my soul,” we should understand his will.

That perfectly simple nature called God does not consist of body and spirit; nor is it mutable even in spirit, as the soul is. Rather, God is spirit, and he is always the same, with whom there is no change (James I, 17).

From this, however, the Apollinarists took an opportunity to claim that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (I Tim. II, 5), did not possess a soul, but was only the Word and flesh, when he said, “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38). Yet from the very action of Christ, which is made known to us through the history of the Gospel, the functions of a human soul are so clearly apparent that only a madman could doubt them.

### XCIV. [Ibid. XXVI, 33, 36]

What did God mean when, while threatening the punishments of disobedience, he said among other things, “And a sword passing through shall consume you,” and then added, “And your land shall be desolate, and your cities shall be deserted; then the land shall enjoy its sabbaths throughout all the days of its desolation, while you shall be in the land of your enemies”?

How, then, will the sword consume them if they are to be in the land of their enemies? Will it consume them in that very land, because after the slaughter of the dead they will not remain there? Or does “it will consume you” mean as though he had said, “It will kill you,” so that those who fall by the sword belong to this consumption, but not everyone, since shortly afterward he says, “And upon those of you who remain I will bring fear into their hearts”?

Or was “it will consume you” spoken hyperbolically, in the same manner in which their abundance is described as being “like the sand of the sea” (Gen. XXII, 17; XXXII, 12)? In this same manner we should understand what follows: “And the sound of a flying leaf will pursue them”—that is, they will be seized by such excessive fear that they will dread even the lightest things.

## BOOK FOUR. Questions on Numbers

[Col. 0717]

### QUESTION I. [Num. I, 1–44]

What does it mean that he commands leaders to be chosen individually from each tribe and calls them χιλίαρχοι (*chiliarchoi*)? Certain Latin interpreters have called them *tribunes*. But χιλίαρχοι appear to have been named from a thousand.

When Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, gave his son-in-law Moses the counsel—also approved by God—about organizing the people under leaders, so that the cases of everyone would not burden Moses beyond his strength, he called for the appointment of χιλίαρχοι over groups of a thousand men, ἑκατόνταρχοι over groups of a hundred, πεντηκόνταρχοι over groups of fifty, and δεκάδαρχοι over groups of ten; they were named from the numbers over which they presided (Exod. XVIII, 14–25).

Are the χιλίαρχοι here likewise to be understood as men each placed over a thousand? Certainly not. The entire people of Israel did not at that time consist of twelve thousand men. Rather, one man was chosen from each tribe, and the twelve tribes unquestionably contained not one thousand men each but many thousands.

The name, therefore, is shared with those who are called χιλίαρχοι in Exodus because each of those men was a leader of a thousand men. But in the present passage each of these men is a leader of the thousands, since whether the name is derived from “a thousand” or “thousands,” the same compound is heard in the word, and they are called χιλίαρχοι.

### II. [Ibid. I, 20–46]

It is rightly asked what is meant by the fact that throughout all the tribes, whenever the children of Israel are counted individually, each at military age, the text says: “according to their kinships, according to their peoples, according to their ancestral houses, according to the number of their names, according to their heads.” These five expressions are repeated in exactly the same way until all the tribes have been completed—as though “according to their kinships” meant one thing, “according to their peoples” another, “according to their ancestral houses” another, “according to the number of their names” another, and “according to their heads” another—when all these expressions rather seem to signify the same thing in different words.

The matter attracts our attention because the same wording is repeated so carefully throughout all the tribes that anyone would judge it was not done without purpose, even if he did not understand it. Surely, then, the number itself conveys some sacramental meaning, so that the same thing is repeated five times in various forms. For this number—the number five—is especially commended in the Old Testament, just as it appears in the five books of Moses.

The four expressions connected afterward—“male,” “from twenty years and upward,” “everyone who goes forth in strength,” and “their enrollment”—although likewise repeated in precisely the same way throughout all the tribes, possess a necessary distinction.

Since the total number of the multitude belonging to one tribe was being recorded, sex had to be distinguished; therefore it says, “all the males.” And so that children would not also be counted, it adds, “from twenty years and upward.” Again, so that the feeble age of old age would not be included, it adds, “everyone who goes forth in strength” [Col. 0718]. Everything is concluded by the word describing the work being carried out, namely, “their enrollment.” This enrollment was made so that the thousands of men could be counted.

Thus the five expressions—kinships, peoples, ancestral houses, number of names, and heads—and then the four—sex, age, strength, and enrollment—perhaps convey something through their numbers themselves. For if one of these two numbers, the five and the four, is multiplied by the other—if four is taken five times, or five four times—the result is twenty. This is also the number by which that age of young men is signified.

The number is also mentioned when they enter the promised land, and that age of twenty years is described as one that did not turn aside to the right or to the left. Here I think the holy faithful who hold the true faith from both Testaments are signified. For the Old Testament is especially distinguished by the five books of Moses, and the New by the four Gospels.

### III. [Ibid. I, 51]

Regarding what he says about stretching out, carrying, and erecting the tabernacle—“And the foreigner who approaches shall die”—the “foreigner” here should also be understood as one of the children of Israel who did not belong to that tribe which he commanded to serve the tabernacle, that is, one who was not from the tribe of Levi [Note: [Col. 0718] According to Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition, *fuerant* (“had been”); the manuscript reading is *fuerit* (“has been” or “is”).].

It is surprising that the word “foreigner” is used improperly here, since it more properly signifies a person of another race—that is, ἀλλογενής (*allogenēs*)—rather than ἀλλόφυλος (*allophylos*), which signifies a person of another tribe. Scripture more commonly uses the latter term for people of other nations, calling them *allophyli*, as though they were people belonging to other tribes.

### IV. [Ibid. III, 5–7]

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Take the tribe of Levi and set them before Aaron the priest, and they shall minister to him. They shall keep his watches and the watches of the children of Israel before the tabernacle of testimony.’”

The Greek term φυλακάς (*phylakas*) has been translated by our interpreters in different ways: some as “guards,” others as “watch duties.” But surely “watches” is the better term for those periods that are customarily observed in military camps in divisions of three hours. Hence it is written, “But in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea” (Matt. XIV, 25)—that is, after the ninth hour of the night, after three watches.

In many passages of Scripture our interpreters have translated as “watches” what the Greeks call φυλακάς. There is no doubt that periods of nighttime are signified; I think the word should be understood in that sense here as well.

For how are the Levites commanded to observe the watches of Aaron and the watches of the children of Israel—that is, the φυλακαί—unless perhaps this was said so that they would not think themselves exempt from observing the watches customarily kept in military camps, on account of the honor in which they served the tabernacle? They too had to observe in turn, on account of the tabernacle’s tasks, the watches that were observed in the other camps of the children of Israel all around them [Col. 0719].

### V. [Ibid. III, 10]

“The foreigner who touches it shall die.”

It must be asked how Leviticus says, “Whoever touches the tabernacle shall be sanctified” (Lev. VI, 18), when the present passage says, “The foreigner who touches it shall die,” intending “foreigners” to mean those who were not from the tribe of Levi.

Or perhaps “touches” here refers to undertaking the service of ministering, since he commanded that service to the tabernacle be performed by the Levites alone. This is what he was discussing.

### VI. [Ibid. III, 12–31]

What does it mean that God assigns the Levites to himself in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel, so that when the firstborn of the people were counted and were found to outnumber the Levites, they were redeemed with silver, five shekels being given for each one?

This was not done in the case of cattle, even though he wished the cattle of the Levites to belong to him in place of the firstborn cattle of Israel. How, then, did their firstborn, whether human or animal, thereafter belong to God, when he commanded unclean firstborn animals, or human firstborn, to be exchanged for sheep?

Why were the sons of the Levites not afterward also counted in place of these firstborn? The same tribe remained in their descendants, and it could have been counted in place of later firstborn. Was it not because this was just: those born from people who already belonged to the Lord’s portion—the portion given in place of the firstborn who came out of Egypt—were already God’s own, as his own from his own, and therefore could not rightly be counted in place of those firstborn who thereafter were owed to God?

For a portion was given to God from the entire people and from all the people’s cattle in place of the firstborn; this portion consisted of the Levites and their cattle. If they subsequently produced offspring, that offspring belonged to God. It could not be given as though it came from the people, since it was already alienated from them. Consequently, the firstborn thereafter owed to God had to be returned, and the descendants of the Levites or of their cattle could not be counted in their place.

### VII. [Ibid. IV, 7]

When he gave instructions about removing the table, he commanded that the loaves be removed along with it, saying: “And the loaves that will always be upon it.”

Those particular loaves would not always be upon it, but loaves like them would, because the loaves were removed and fresh ones were placed there every day, while the table was never left without loaves. Therefore he said, “that will always be upon it”—that is, because loaves would always be there, not because those same loaves would always remain.

### VIII. [Ibid. IV, 11]

“And over the golden altar they shall spread a violet-colored garment, and they shall cover it with a violet-colored leather covering.”

This expression might appear to be one that the Latin interpreters, regarding it as strange and incomplete, were unwilling to translate. It says, “Over the golden altar they shall spread a violet-colored garment,” as though it ought to have said, “They shall cover the golden altar with a violet-colored garment.” For “they shall spread a violet-colored garment” seems to mean that the garment itself was to be covered from elsewhere, not that the altar was to be covered with that garment [Note: [Col. 0719] The printed editions read, “the altar would be covered from elsewhere,” omitting the words “not that the altar would be covered with that garment,” which have been restored from the manuscripts.].

But it seems to me that this is not so much a type of expression as an obscure meaning. It can be understood as follows: “Over the golden altar they shall spread a violet-colored garment,” with the command that the violet-colored garment itself, which would already be over the altar, be covered with something else [Col. 0720]. In this way the sentence briefly encompasses both matters: the altar is to be covered with the violet-colored garment, and the violet-colored garment is to be covered with another covering.

Finally, he added what he wanted the violet-colored garment to be covered with when he said, “And they shall cover it with a violet-colored leather covering.”

### IX. [Ibid. V, 6–8]

“A man or a woman, whoever commits any of the sins of human beings, and, despising, despises and commits an offense, that person shall declare the sin that he has committed and shall restore the offense; he shall add its principal amount and its fifth part to it, and shall repay the one against whom he committed the offense. But if the person has no close relative, so that he may repay the offense to him personally, the offense that is repaid to the Lord shall belong to the priest, except for the ram of atonement by which he shall make expiation for him.”

Here we should understand sins committed in matters whose loss can be repaid with money. For otherwise he would not have said how they were to be repaid, unless they involved monetary losses. He commands that the principal and the fifth be repaid—that is, the entire amount, together with one-fifth of it—apart from the ram that was to be offered as a sacrifice to expiate the offense.

He commands that what is repaid should belong to the priest—that is, the principal and the fifth—if the person against whom the offense was committed has no close relative. Here it is clearly understood that what belongs to the priest is to be returned to the Lord if the person who suffered the loss is no longer alive, nor is his close relative. I think he intended an heir to be understood.

Scripture said nothing about the person himself. Nevertheless, when it says, “If he has no close relative,” it indicates briefly that his close relative is to be sought if he himself is not present. But if he has no close relative either, the amount is to be repaid to the Lord, so that what was committed may not remain unpunished; it is not, however, to be applied to a sacrifice, but is to belong to the priest.

The words of Scripture should accordingly be distinguished as follows: “But if he has no close relative, so that he may repay the offense to him personally.” The addition “personally” is a feature of the expression; or perhaps “personally” means “as belonging to him,” that is, “so that he himself may possess it.”

Then it continues: “The offense that is repaid to the Lord shall belong to the priest.” He calls it an “offense” when the thing that was taken through the offense is repaid [Note: [Col. 0720] The printed editions read, “he shall repay the offense and its fifth,” omitting “the principal.” Shortly afterward they read, “so that he may repay the offense itself to him,” omitting “to.” Both passages have been restored according to the manuscripts, which agree with the Greek.].

### X. [Ibid. V, 6–7]

It can also be asked how Exodus says that if someone steals a calf or a sheep, he must repay five calves or four sheep if he has killed or sold it; but if what he took is found alive in his possession, he must repay double (Exod. XXII, 1, 4), whereas here he is commanded to repay the principal and a fifth, which is far from double, and even more so from fourfold or fivefold repayment.

Perhaps because the passage says, “A man or a woman, whoever commits any of the sins of human beings,” it intends sins of ignorance—that is, human sins. It can happen that through insufficient attention a person, by negligence, transfers someone else’s property into his own possession. This is a sin because, if he had paid careful attention, he would not have committed it. Such a person is commanded to restore the principal and the fifth, not to be punished as a thief.

For if we understand this passage to concern thefts and frauds committed not through ignorant negligence but with the intention of stealing and defrauding—and therefore called “human” because they are committed against human beings—the solution to the question will be, unless I am mistaken, that the person who committed the act does not repay merely double because he is not detected or convicted; rather, while others do not know who committed the act or whether it was committed, he himself declares his offense.

For after Scripture had said, “A man or a woman, whoever commits any of the sins of human beings, and, despising, despises and commits an offense”—that is, commits these acts contemptuously—it added: “That person shall confess the sin that he has committed and shall restore the offense, the principal and its fifth.” Perhaps, then, this lighter penalty applies precisely because he himself confessed, and therefore he was not to be punished with the penalty appropriate to a thief who had been apprehended or convicted.

### XI. [Ibid. V, 21]

The words that Scripture says the priest must speak to the woman when her husband brings her under suspicion of adultery are: “May the Lord make you a curse and an oath.” The Greek has ἐνόρκιον (*enorkion*).

This word seems to signify an oath expressed through a curse, as when someone says, “May such-and-such not happen to me,” or certainly swears in this way: “May such-and-such happen to me if I have done, or have not done, this or that.”

Thus the words, “May the Lord make you a curse and an oath,” mean something like this: those who swear by imprecation will swear by you—“May this not happen to them,” or “May this happen to them, unless they have done this or that” [Note: [Col. 0721] Five manuscripts and the Rat. edition read, “unless they have done that.” Two other manuscripts read, “unless they have done that concerning you.” The Amiens and Erasmus editions read, “unless they have done this or that concerning you.”].

### XII. [Ibid. VI, 14–17]

“And he shall offer his offering to the Lord: a year-old male lamb without blemish as a burnt offering, and one year-old female lamb without blemish as a sin offering.”

Certain of our interpreters were unwilling to translate this wording, as though avoiding an unusual expression, and said “for sin” rather than “as sin,” although the sense contained in the expression should not have been disturbed.

It says “as sin” because what was offered for sin was itself called “sin.” Hence the Apostle’s statement concerning the Lord Christ: “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us” (II Cor. V, 21). God the Father made God the Son sin for us—that is, a sacrifice for sin.

Therefore, just as the lamb is “as a burnt offering,” so that the animal itself would be a burnt offering, so the female lamb is “as sin,” so that the animal itself would be sin—that is, so that it would become a sacrifice for sin. The same applies to what follows concerning the ram, which he calls “as a saving offering,” as though it itself were salvation, when it is in fact a sacrifice of salvation.

He makes this clear by repeating the matter later: he calls “for sin” what he had previously called “as sin,” and calls “a sacrifice of salvation” what he had previously called “as salvation.”

### XIII. [Ibid. VIII, 24]

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying, ‘This is concerning the Levites.’”

Some have interpreted this as, “This is the law concerning the Levites.” But what is written—“This is concerning the Levites”—is understood to mean, “This is what I establish concerning the Levites.”

[Col. 0722]

### XIV. [Ibid. VIII, 24–26]

Then the passage continues:

“From the age of twenty-five years and upward they shall enter to minister in the service, in the work of the tabernacle of testimony; and from the age of fifty he shall withdraw from the ministry and shall no longer work (and his brother shall minister): to keep watch in the tabernacle of testimony; but he shall not perform work.”

The hyperbaton makes this meaning obscure, because the sentence is so confused that it appears to say of the brother himself, “to keep watch,” when in fact this is said of the man who withdraws from the work. He will remain there, in the tabernacle of testimony, to keep watch; but he will not perform work. His brother, that is, the one who has not yet reached the age of fifty and begins to work at twenty-five, will perform the work.

The passage should therefore be punctuated as follows: “And from the age of fifty he shall withdraw from the ministry and shall no longer work, and his brother shall minister.” Then it returns to the fifty-year-old man under discussion and explains the remainder concerning him, saying: “In the tabernacle of testimony, to keep watch; but he shall not perform work.”

When it says “to keep watch,” “he shall begin” is understood, as though it were expressing in one word, “he shall keep watch.” It is common even in Latin expressions for an infinitive verb to be used in place of a finite verb.

### XV. [Ibid. IX, 6–12]

At the time of Passover, certain people who had become unclean through a human being—that is, through a corpse—asked how they could celebrate Passover, since according to the Law they had to be purified from uncleanness for seven days.

Moses consulted the Lord and received the answer that anyone to whom such a thing had happened, or who was situated on such a distant journey that he could not arrive in time, was to celebrate Passover in another month, observing the fourteenth day of the month, when the lunar reckoning was kept.

But if it is asked what they were to do if such uncleanness happened to occur even during the second month, I think that what was said concerning the second month was to be retained as a rule, so that they would observe it in the third month. Or perhaps, if they failed to celebrate Passover because of such a necessity, this would not count as guilt.

### XVI. [Ibid. IX, 15–23]

“And on the day when the tabernacle was established, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the house of testimony; and in the evening there was over the tabernacle something like the appearance of fire until morning. This happened continually: the cloud covered it by day, and the appearance of fire by night.

“And when the cloud rose from the tabernacle, the children of Israel then moved on; and wherever the cloud had stood, there the children of Israel set up camp.

“By the command of the Lord the children of Israel shall set up camp, and by the command of the Lord they shall move on. All the days during which the cloud overshadows the tabernacle, the children of Israel shall remain in camp; and when the cloud lingers over the tabernacle for many days, the children of Israel shall keep the watch of God and shall not move on.

“And when the cloud has been over the tabernacle for a number of days, at the word of the Lord they shall remain in camp, and at the command of the Lord they shall move on. And when the cloud is from evening until morning, and the cloud rises in the morning, they shall move on by day; or by night, and if the cloud rises, they shall move on.

“Whether for a day, or a month, or for many days, while the cloud abounds, overshadowing it, the children of Israel shall remain in camp and shall not move on. For at the command of the Lord they shall move on. They kept the watch of the Lord at the command of the Lord, by the hand of Moses.”

[Note: [Col. 0722] The printed editions read “when the cloud has sheltered it.” The manuscripts read “when the cloud has prolonged its stay,” in accordance with the Greek ἐπελκήται (*ephelkētai*).]

[Note: [Col. 0723] The manuscripts consistently read this way, and the printed editions agree with them below; only in this passage do they have “and when the cloud has risen in this way.”]

This entire passage must be expounded carefully, since it is obscured by unusual forms of expression. “And on the day,” he says, “on which the tabernacle was erected, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the house of testimony”; he called the same tabernacle the house of testimony. “And in the evening it was over the tabernacle like the appearance of fire until morning.” This always happened. Then he carefully explains what always happened: “The cloud,” he says, “covered it by day, and the appearance of fire by night.” “And when the cloud had risen from the tabernacle, then the children of Israel moved on.” This statement is not obscure except because of the conjunction *and* inserted there. For the complete order of the words follows even if the conjunction itself is absent, so that it reads: “And when the cloud had risen from the tabernacle, the children of Israel moved on”; indeed, even if the word “then” were absent, the sentence could still be complete. Then he continues, saying: “And in whatever place the cloud had stood, there the children of Israel would pitch camp.”

Referring all that they did to the Lord’s command, he sums it up as follows: “At the command,” he says, “of the Lord the children of Israel will pitch camp, and at the command of the Lord they will move on.” He calls the command of the Lord the very sign that appeared in the cloud, whether when it stood, overshadowing the tabernacle, so that they should remain in camp, or when it had risen and moved onward, so that they should follow it after breaking camp. In this statement, however, he changed the manner of the narrative and began to use future-tense words as though he were predicting and announcing what would happen. For he does not say, “At the command of the Lord the children of Israel pitched camp,” but “will pitch camp”; nor does he say, “At the command of the Lord they moved on,” but “will move on.” He also maintains this manner in what follows, a manner exceedingly unusual in Scripture. For we know that future events are often foretold with verbs in the past tense, as in: “They pierced my hands and feet” (Ps. XXI, 17), and: “Like a sheep he was led to be slaughtered” (Isa. LIII, 7), and innumerable passages of this kind. But for a narrator of accomplished events to use verbs in the future tense, as here, is found in Scripture only with the greatest difficulty.

Therefore, after he had spoken of day and night, and of the sign by which the people would move on or remain, lest anyone suppose that they walked by night and customarily settled down by day, and did this every day, he added what follows and said: “All the days during which the cloud overshadows the tabernacle, the children of Israel will be in camp; and when the cloud prolongs its stay over the tabernacle for many days.” Then, reminding us that this did not happen from their own necessity but from God’s will, he says: “And the children of Israel will keep the observance of God”—that is, the observance which God commanded—“and they will not move on.” And as though someone might ask, “When, then, will they move on?” [Col. 0724] he says: “And it will be when the cloud has covered the tabernacle for a stated number of days”—that is, for a definite number of days, a number which would of course please God—“at the word of the Lord they will remain in camp, and at the command of the Lord they will move on.” He seems to call the word of the Lord the sign that he gives through the standing and movement of the cloud, since the voice of one speaking is undoubtedly a sign of his will. Therefore, when he says “at the command,” I think the same sign is to be understood. Nevertheless, “the word and command of the Lord” could also be understood as what he spoke, as he usually did, to Moses, commanding that this should be done. For they would not have known that they were to move when the cloud moved and stand when the cloud stood, unless this had first been commanded to them.

In what has been said, it has not yet become clear whether they traveled only by day or also by night, according to the sign given by the movement of the cloud. For although they might remain in camp for many days while the cloud did not move on, someone might nevertheless suppose that the cloud did not usually rise from the camp and give the signal for travel except by day. He therefore continues and says: “And it will be when the cloud has been from evening until morning, and the cloud has risen in the morning, that they will move on by day.” Here the conjunction *and* has been placed according to the customary usage of Scripture. If it is removed, the meaning is complete as follows: “And it will be when the cloud has been from evening until morning, and the cloud has risen in the morning, they will move on by day.” Then, because they also moved on at night if the cloud rose, and undertook a night journey when they received that sign, he added and said: “Or at night, and if the cloud rises, they will move on.” But this is a more unusual form of expression. For not merely has *and* been inserted, but it has been inserted in a manner in which it is not ordinarily used. Hence it seems to me that the order of the words has been inverted, as often happens also in Latin expressions; this kind of arrangement is called *antistrophe*. Accordingly, if it is read, “or, even at night, if the cloud rises, they will move on,” or certainly, “if the cloud also rises at night, they will move on,” the meaning is perfectly clear.

As he continued to reflect, another question arose: just as it had become known that they customarily traveled by day and night, or remained in camp by day and night, in accordance with the sign of the cloud, whether they also customarily remained only during the days, even when they traveled during the nights. I think Scripture indicated this in what follows when it says: “By day, or for a month of days, while the cloud abides in abundance, overshadowing it, the children of Israel will remain in camp and will not move on.” Since he had said, “or at night, and if the cloud rises, they will move on,” it seemed to remain for him to say: “But by day, if it does not rise, they will not move on,” when they appeared as though they ought to move on. But because this also could happen for many days—that they might travel at night when the cloud moved on, and not travel during the days when it remained—he therefore said, “by day, or for a month of days.” He did not say simply “for a month,” lest the nights of that same month also be included; instead he said “for a month of days,” that is, for a month insofar as it was days, not insofar as it was night. “By day, or for a month of days, while the cloud abides in abundance, overshadowing”—that is, abundant in its overshadowing, or overshadowing more abundantly—“over it,” namely, over the tabernacle, “the children of Israel will remain in camp and will not move on.” Finally, he repeated that this was done by divine authority, which of course ought not to be resisted, adding: [Col. 0725] “For at the command of the Lord they will move on. They kept the observance of the Lord, at the command of the Lord, through the hand of Moses.” He returned to the past tense when he said, “They kept.” What he placed at the end—“through the hand of Moses”—is a very common expression in Scripture, because God gave these commands through Moses.

## XVII. [On X, 7]

“And when you assemble the assembly, you shall blow the trumpets, and not for a sign.” He does not therefore command the trumpets to be blown so that the assembly may be gathered; for if that were done, it would be a sign. Rather, once the assembly had already been gathered, he commands the trumpet to be blown, as though this already belonged to the song and not to the giving of a sign, by which, once given, they would be warned to undertake some action. Accordingly, when someone belonging to the New Testament interprets spiritually the fact that, after the assembly had been gathered, they blew the trumpets, this is a sign to the person who understands why it was done, not to those who did not understand, except when it was done for the purpose of announcing some action.

## XVIII. [On XI, 17]

“And I will take from the spirit that is in you and place it upon them; and they will bear with you the burden of the people, and you will not bear them alone.”

Most Latin interpreters did not translate this as it is in the Greek, but said: “I will take from your spirit which is in you, and I will place it upon them,” or “I will place it in them,” and they produced a meaning difficult to understand. For it may be thought that this refers to the spirit of the human being, by which human nature is completed when the body is joined to it; human nature consists of body and spirit, which they also call the soul. Concerning this the Apostle likewise says: “For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being, except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God.” And when he adds and says, “But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (I Cor. II, 11–12), he plainly shows that there is another Spirit of God, whose participant the human spirit becomes through the grace of God.

Yet it could also be understood, as others have interpreted it, as the Spirit of God in the phrase “from your spirit which is upon you”; so that it is called “your” because what belongs to God also becomes ours when we receive it, as it is said of John: “In the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke I, 17). For Elijah’s soul had not passed into him. If some people, in heretical perversity, suppose this, what will they say about what is written: “The spirit of Elijah rested upon Elisha” (IV Kings II, 15), when he certainly already possessed his own soul [Note: [Col. 0725] Compare Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 35.]? The only explanation is that it was said of the Spirit of God, so that through him Elisha might also perform works of the kind Elijah had performed—not because the Spirit departed from Elijah in order to fill Elisha, nor because it was diminished in Elijah by being divided, so that it could be partly in Elisha as well. For God is able to be fully present in all those in whom he wills to be present through that grace.

But now, since it is written, “And I will take from the spirit that is upon you,” and it does not say, “from your spirit,” the question has an easier solution: we understand that God wished to signify nothing other than that those men too would receive assistance from the same Spirit of grace from which Moses received his, so that they would have as much as God willed, but not so that Moses would thereby have less.

## XIX. [On XI, 21–23]

“And Moses said, ‘Six hundred thousand foot soldiers, among whom I am myself, and you have said, “I will give them meat [Col. 0726], and they will eat for a month of days.” Shall sheep and cattle be slaughtered for them, and will it be enough for them? Or shall all the fish be gathered for them, and will it be enough for them?’”

It is customary to ask whether Moses said this in distrust or in inquiry. But if we suppose that he said it in distrust, the question arises why the Lord did not rebuke him for it, as he rebuked him when, at the rock from which water flowed, he appeared to have doubted the Lord’s power. If, on the other hand, we say that he asked in order to learn how this would be accomplished, the Lord’s own response, when he said to him, “Will the Lord’s hand not be sufficient?” seems to rebuke him for not having believed this.

Nevertheless, I think it better understood that the Lord replied as though he did not wish to explain the manner in which the promised event would occur—the manner Moses was asking about—but preferred to demonstrate his power by the deed itself. For when Mary said, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” her accusers could likewise have charged her with insufficient faith, although she had asked about the manner and had not doubted God’s power. The answer given to her was: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” It could also have been answered in the same way as here: “Can it be impossible for the Holy Spirit, who will come upon you?” In this way the same meaning would have been preserved. But when Zechariah said something similar, he was accused of unbelief and punished by the suppression of his voice (Luke I, 34–35, 18–20). Why, unless because God judges not words but hearts?

Otherwise, Moses’ words at the rock from which water flowed could also have been excused, unless the divine judgment against him had clearly shown that he spoke them in distrust. For the words are these: “Hear me, you unbelievers; shall we bring water for you from this rock?” Then Scripture continues: “And Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with the rod, and abundant water came out, and the assembly and their cattle drank.” Certainly he had gathered the people for this purpose; for this purpose he had taken the rod with which he had performed so many miracles; he struck the rock with it and obtained the customary result of divine power.

The words, therefore, in which he said, “Shall we bring water for you from this rock?” could be understood as though he were saying: “Surely, according to your unbelief, water cannot be brought forth from this rock.” Thus, by striking the rock, it would finally be shown that what they did not believe could happen because of their unbelief could happen by divine power—especially since he had said, “Hear me, you unbelievers.” These words could indeed be understood in this way, unless God, who examines the heart, had revealed with what intention they were spoken. For Scripture continues and says: “And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron, ‘Because you did not believe so as to sanctify me in the sight of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land which I have given them’” (Num. XX, 10–12).

Accordingly, it is understood that Moses spoke those words as though he struck the rock uncertainly, so that, if the result had not followed, he would have appeared to have predicted this when he said, “Shall we bring water for you from this rock?” What lay hidden in his mind would have been entirely unknown unless the divine judgment had disclosed it.

By contrast, in the present passage we ought to understand Moses’ words about the promised meat as spoken rather to ask how it would happen than in distrust, since the Lord’s judgment did not follow in order to punish him, but rather to instruct him.

## XX. [On XII, 1]

[Col. 0727] Concerning Moses’ Ethiopian wife, it is customary to ask whether she was Jethro’s daughter, or whether he took another wife, or added another wife to the first. But it is credible that she was the same woman. For she was descended from the Midianites, who are found called Ethiopians in Chronicles, when Jehoshaphat fought against them. In these passages it is said that the people of Israel pursued them in the regions where the Midianites dwell (II Chron. XIV, 9–14); they are now called Saracens. But nowadays almost no one calls them Ethiopians, just as the names of places and peoples commonly change with the passage of time.

## XXI. [On XIII, 18–26]

“And he said to them, ‘Go up through this wilderness, and you shall go up into the mountain, and you shall see what the land is like, and the people who dwell upon it, whether they are strong or weak, whether they are few or many.’”

He is understood to have explained in what respect he said “whether they are strong or weak,” namely, “whether they are few or many.” For how could those looking out from the mountain perceive the strength of human forces? There can also be another meaning, much more consistent with the truth. When he says, “You shall go up into the mountain,” he meant the land itself which they wished to explore. For they could not easily be understood as explorers if they investigated everything as though they were strangers traveling through the land.

For if we suppose that they saw and explored the land from the summit of the mountain, how could they investigate everything that Moses commanded them to investigate? How could they enter the cities, which Scripture says they entered? How could they carry away from that valley the cluster of grapes on account of which the place itself was given the name “Valley of the Cluster” [Note: [Col. 0727] In the manuscripts consistently, *Botrui*. In the LXX at Num. XIII, *Botruos*.]?

The land was therefore explored on the mountain itself, because it was the land that was being explored; and there was there a somewhat lower place, from which the cluster was taken.

## XXII. [On XIII, 33]

“And they brought forth the terror of the land which they had explored.” He said “the terror of the land,” not the terror by which the land itself was afraid, but the terror which they had conceived from that land.

## XXIII. [On XIV, 9]

Caleb and Jesus son of Nave, speaking to the people of Israel so that they would not be afraid to enter the promised land, said among other things: “But do not fear the people of the land, for they are food for us. Their time has departed, but the Lord is with us; do not fear them.”

By the words “They are food for us,” they wished it to be understood: “We shall consume them.” But when they added, “Their time has departed, but the Lord is with us,” they very carefully did not say, “The Lord has departed from them.” For they had been impious from ancient times. But since, by the hidden dispensation of divine providence, even the impious are granted a time in which to flourish and rule, they said: “Their time has departed, but the Lord is with us.” They did not say, “Their time has departed, and ours has succeeded”; rather, “The Lord is with us,” not “time.”

For the former had time, while the latter had the Lord, God who created and orders time and distributes it to each person as he wills.

## XXIV. [On XV, 24–29]

When it is commanded how the sins that are committed unintentionally are to be expiated, it is rightly asked what those sins of unwilling persons are: whether they are sins committed by those who are unaware, or whether it can also correctly be called the sin of an unwilling person when he is compelled to do something. [Col. 0728] For this too is commonly said to be done against one’s will. Yet he certainly wishes the thing for the sake of which he acts. For example, someone may not wish to swear falsely, but does so [Note: [Col. 0728] The printed editions, and the manuscripts except for one Corbie manuscript, lack the words “for example, someone may not wish to swear falsely, but does so.”] because he wishes to live, if someone threatens him with death unless he does it. He therefore wishes to do it because he wishes to live; and so he does not desire in itself to swear falsely, but desires to live by swearing falsely.

If this is so, I do not know whether such acts can be called the sins of unwilling persons, of the kind that are said here to require expiation. For, if the matter is carefully considered, perhaps no one wishes to sin itself; rather, it is done for the sake of something else, which the sinner does desire. All human beings who knowingly do what is not permitted would wish it to be permitted. To such an extent does no one desire the sin for its own sake, but for the sake of what results from it. If this is so, they are not the sins of unwilling persons, except of the ignorant; and these are distinguished from the sins of willing persons.

## XXV. [On XV, 30–31]

“And every soul that sins with a hand of arrogance, whether native-born or among the proselytes, provokes God here, and that soul shall be cut off from its people, because it has despised the word of the Lord and destroyed his commandments. With crushing shall that soul be crushed; its sin is upon it.”

What sins are committed “with a hand of arrogance,” that is, committed through arrogance, Scripture itself sufficiently explains in what follows, where it says: “Because he has despised the word of the Lord.” It is one thing to despise the commandments, and another to hold them in high regard but act against them either through ignorance or because one has been overcome. These two kinds perhaps belong to the sins committed by unwilling persons, concerning which he previously instructed us how they could be expiated after God had been propitiated. He then added the sins of arrogance, when someone acts wrongly through pride—that is, by despising the commandment.

He did not say that this kind of sin ought to be cleansed by any kind of sacrifice, as though he judged it incurable by that particular remedy which was carried out through sacrifices, such as those whose performance is commanded in this Scripture. If these sacrifices are considered in themselves, they can heal no sin [Note: [Col. 0728] The printed editions read “by no means”; the manuscripts read “no sin.”]; but if the realities of which these sacraments are signs are investigated, purification from sins can be found in them.

The person of whom Scripture says, “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3), is therefore signified here by the one whom Scripture says sins “with a hand of arrogance.” This sin cannot be abolished without punishment for the one who commits it; consequently it cannot remain unpunished, even when it is healed through repentance. For the very affliction of the repentant person is the punishment of sin, although it is medicinal and salutary.

It is rightly judged a great sin when arrogance despises the commandment. But, conversely, so that it may be healed, “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L, 19). Nevertheless, because it does not occur without punishment, the following words are said here: “He provokes God,” because “God resists the proud” (James IV, 6). “And that soul shall be cut off from its people,” because such a person is in no way counted among those who belong to God.

“Because he has despised the word of the Lord and destroyed his commandments: with crushing shall that soul be crushed.” [Col. 0729] Why it will be crushed with crushing, he adds immediately, saying: “Its sin is upon it.” Therefore, if by repenting he himself applies to himself the crushing due to such a sin, God will not despise the contrite heart, as has been said.

In the Greek, however, it does not say here, “With crushing shall it be crushed,” but: “By wearing-away shall that soul be worn away” (*extritione exteretur anima illa*). This can be understood as though it were worn away by complete abrasion and ceased to exist. But the soul’s natural immortality first rejects this interpretation. Moreover, if whatever is worn away were thereby made wholly nonexistent, Scripture would not say of the wise person: “Let your foot wear away the steps of his doors” (Ecclus. VI, 36). Yet this distinction must be considered more and more carefully: whether no one sins except through ignorance, defeat, or contempt. It would take too long to discuss this here.

## XXVI. [On XVI, 13–14]

What does it mean that Dathan and Abiron, when they had risen up in rebellion and had been summoned by Moses, replied proudly and insultingly: “Is it a small thing that you have brought us up from a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, because you rule over us? You are a prince [Note: [Col. 0729] Thus in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint. Earlier printed editions read: “a prince rules over us; and you ...”]; and you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, nor given us a portion of field and vineyards. Would you have put out the eyes of those men? We will not go up.”

Whose eyes did they mean by “the eyes of those men”? Did they mean the people of Israel, as though they were saying: “If you had done these things, you would have put out the eyes of those men”—that is, they would have loved you so much that they would have torn out their own eyes and given them to you? The Apostle also calls this a great sign of love: “For if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me” (Gal. IV, 15).

Then they added a complete act of defiance: “We will not go up,” that is, “We will not come,” since he had summoned them. Or does “the eyes of those men” instead refer to the enemies, who had been reported to be exceedingly fierce and terrifying? As though they were saying: “Even if you had done this, we would not obey you,” except that one form of the verb has been put in place of another, so that they did not say, “We would not go up,” but, “We will not go up,” according to a certain form of expression?

## XXVII. [On XVI, 20–21]

“And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘Separate yourselves from the midst of this assembly.’”

It should be noted that the Lord commands bodily separation at the moment when punishment already threatens the wicked. Thus Noah and his household are separated from the others who were destined to perish in the flood (Gen. VII, 15); thus Lot and his household are separated from Sodom, which was to be consumed by heavenly fire (ibid. XIX, 12); thus the people themselves are separated from the Egyptians, who were to be overwhelmed by the waves of the sea (Exod. XIX, 20); and thus these men are now separated from the assembly of Korah, Abiron, and Dathan, who had first attempted to sever themselves through rebellion.

Yet before this, the holy people lived and associated with them, and, together with the others whom God rejects, they could not be defiled by them, in accordance with the words with which he rebukes them. Nor were they commanded to separate themselves when the Lord either postponed his vengeance or employed a form of punishment by which the innocent could neither perish nor be harmed—for example, through the bites of serpents or through a slaughter in which God struck whomever he wished, as he wished, while others remained untouched. This was not like the water [Col. 0730] of the flood, the rain of fire, the water of the sea, or the opening of the earth, which could consume the guilty and the innocent together—not because God could not preserve his own people there as well, but because, where separation could be made, what need was there to test the miracle, so that the water, fire, or chasm might carry away those whom it found?

So also at the end the wheat will be separated from the weeds, so that, while the wicked are burned by flames, the righteous may shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XIII, 30, 40–43).

## XXVIII. [On XVI, 30]

When Moses says concerning Korah, Abiron, and Dathan, “In a vision God will show it, and the earth will open its mouth and swallow them,” some have interpreted it as: “In a chasm the Lord will show it.” I believe they thought that the Greek word was *χάσματι* (*chasmati*), whereas the text has *φάσματι* (*phasmati*), which was used in that sense, as though it said, “In a manifestation”—something that would plainly appear to the eyes.

For it was not said “in a vision” in the way visions are usually spoken of, whether visions in dreams or figures appearing in ecstasy; rather, as I have said, it means “in a manifestation.” Others, however, holding a different opinion, wished to interpret it as “in a phantasm.” This is wholly foreign to our customary manner of expression, since *phantasm* is almost never used except where our senses are deceived by the false appearance of things seen. Although that word too derives from seeing, customary usage, as I have said, has assigned it another meaning.

## XXIX. [On XVI, 32–33]

“And they themselves descended, and all that belonged to them, alive into the underworld.”

It should be noted that “the underworld” is used here of an earthly place, that is, of the lower regions of the earth. In Scripture the name “underworld” is used in various ways and with several meanings, according to what the sense of the subject matter requires, and it is especially accustomed to refer to the dead.

But since these men are said to have descended alive into the underworld, and the narrative itself makes clear what happened, it is evident, as I have said, that the lower parts of the earth are here called the underworld in comparison with this upper earth, on whose surface human beings live. In the same way, in comparison with the higher heaven, where the holy angels dwell, Scripture says that the angels who sinned were cast into the darkness of this air and reserved as though in the prisons of the underworld to be punished.

“For if God,” he says, “did not spare the angels when they sinned, but thrust them into the prisons of the darkness of the underworld and handed them over to be reserved for punishment in the judgment” (II Pet. II, 4), while the Apostle Paul calls the devil “the ruler of the power of the air, who works in the children of disobedience” (Eph. II, 2).

## XXX. [On XVI, 36–40]

“And the Lord said to Moses and to Eleazar son of Aaron the priest: ‘Take the bronze censers from the midst of those who have been burned, and scatter this strange fire there, because they sanctified the censers of these sinners in their souls; and make them into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, because they were offered before the Lord and were sanctified, and they have become a sign for the children of Israel.’”

Why the Lord spoke here not to Moses and Aaron, as in the preceding passages, but to Moses and Eleazar son of Aaron, is explained to me for the present by the following consideration. The question concerned the priestly lineage—that is, what family the priests ought to come from. [Col. 0731] Those men perished in such a dreadful and wondrous punishment because they had dared to usurp the priesthood from another lineage. God therefore wished to speak not to Aaron, who was already the high priest, but to Eleazar, who was to succeed him and who was already serving in the second priesthood, in order in this way to commend the succession of the lineage that was to exist among the priests.

Hence he also says in what follows: “And Eleazar son of Aaron the priest took the bronze censers, as many [Note: [Col. 0731] The editions of Am., Er., and Lov. read “which had previously”; Rat. and the manuscripts read “as many,” following the Septuagint’s *hosa*.] as those who had been burned had offered, and he added them as a covering for the altar, as a memorial for the children of Israel, so that no foreigner who is not of the seed of Aaron might approach to burn incense before the Lord; and he shall not be like Korah and like his conspiracy, as the Lord spoke through the hand of Moses.”

In this way, therefore, God wished through Eleazar to commend not the priesthood, which already belonged to Aaron, but the lineage of the priestly succession.

When he says, “And scatter this strange fire there,” it is to be understood as “scatter it.” And when he adds, “Because they sanctified the censers of these sinners in their souls,” the sentence is expressed in an unusual manner. It should be noted that their punishment is said to have sanctified the censers in a new way, because through them an example was given to the others, so that they would be afraid.

Why he wished the plates to be made from these censers and placed around the altar, he explains by adding: “Because they were offered before the Lord and were sanctified, and have become a sign for the children of Israel.” He did not therefore wish what had been offered by such men to be rejected in the censers; rather, he wished people to consider and attend to before whom they had been offered—namely, because they had been offered before the Lord—so that the name of the Lord, before whom they had been offered, would have greater force in them than the very evil merit of those by whom they had been offered.

Scripture had already mentioned this in Exodus, when it says that the altar was constructed (Exod. XXVII, 2). From this it is understood that accounts of events have been distributed among the books, rather than arranged in a continuous chronological order. For in this book Scripture narrated how the matter of Aaron’s rod occurred, how it flowered and sprouted and thus divinely indicated his election to the priesthood (Num. XVII, 8). Yet Exodus speaks of that same rod when it commands that it be placed with the manna in the ark in the Holy of Holies, at the time when instructions were given for the construction of the tabernacle (Exod. XXVI). This command was of course given long before the tabernacle itself was constructed, completed, and set up. It stood in the first month of the second year after they had gone out from Egypt (ibid. XL, 15), whereas this book begins on the first day of the second month of that same second year.

It is therefore clear that, if we consider the order of the books, these events are recalled by recapitulation—that is, by remembrance of earlier events. Those who pay insufficient attention suppose that they happened in the same order in which they are narrated.

## XXXI. [On XVIII, 1]

“And the Lord said to Aaron: ‘You and your sons, and your father’s household with you, shall receive the sins of the holy things; and you and your sons shall receive the sins of your priesthood.’”

These are the sins that are called sacrifices for sins. Accordingly, “the sins of the holy things” does not mean the sins committed by holy people. Rather, the word “holy” is used [Col. 0732] because they are holy things and are offered among holy things; and they are called “sins” because they are sacrifices for sins. For this reason they are called “the sins of the holy things.”

“And the sins of your priesthood” means the very same offerings that are made for sins, as Leviticus also explains, saying that they ought to belong to the priest (Lev. VI, 25–26).

## XXVII. [On XVIII, 12]

“All the first products that are in their land, whatever they may bring to the Lord, however much they may bring, shall be yours.”

Here “first products” does not mean the first offspring of animals. The latter are called in Greek *πρωτότοκα* (*prōtotoka*), whereas these are called *πρωτογενήματα* (*prōtogenēmata*). But in Latin no two distinct words have been found for these two things. Therefore some have translated *πρωτογενήματα* as “firstfruits.” Yet “firstfruits” are called *ἀπαρχαί* (*aparchai*) in Greek, and they are something else.

These three terms are therefore distinguished as follows: *πρωτότοκα* are the first offspring of animals, including human beings; *πρωτογενήματα* are the first fruits taken from the earth, a tree, or a vine; while *ἀπαρχαί* are indeed fruits, but fruits already gathered from the field, such as those taken first from a mass of dough, a winepress, a jar, or a vat.

## XXXIII. [On XIX]

Concerning the red heifer, whose ashes the Law commanded to be useful for the water of sprinkling and for the purification of those who had touched a dead person, we are not permitted to remain silent [Note: [Col. 0732] Thus in the manuscripts. In the printed editions, *tangere*, “to touch.”]. For in it the clearest sign of the New Testament is prefigured, and we cannot speak with sufficient dignity, though we hasten to discuss so great a sacrament.

First, who would not be moved and made exceedingly attentive to the depth of the sacrament by the way Scripture begins to speak about this matter? “And the Lord,” it says, “spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘This is the distinction of the Law, whatever the Lord has established.’”

There is undoubtedly no distinction except between two things or more; for what is singular requires no distinction. Nor did he mention the distinction of just any matter, but added, “of the Law.” Nor did he mean just any law. For Scripture repeatedly says of each matter that is lawfully commanded, “This is the law of this or that matter”; it does not mean the universal Law that contains everything lawfully commanded.

Here, however, after saying, “This is the distinction of the Law,” he continued by adding, “whatever the Lord has established,” namely, by commanding, not by creating. Indeed, some translators rendered it, “whatever the Lord has commanded.” If, therefore, this is the distinction of the Law—whatever the Lord has commanded—then this is undoubtedly a great distinction, and it is rightly understood as distinguishing the two Testaments.

For the same things are found in the Old and in the New: there they are veiled, here they are revealed; there they are prefigured, here they are manifested. Not only are the sacraments different, but the promises also differ. In the Old Testament temporal things appear to be set forth, by which a spiritual reward is secretly signified; in the New, however, spiritual and eternal things are promised most plainly.

What clearer and more certain distinction is there between temporal and carnal goods on the one hand, and spiritual and eternal goods on the other, than the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ? In his death it was sufficiently established that this earthly and transitory happiness is not to be hoped for or desired from the Lord God as a great gift. For when he willed his only-begotten Son to endure such suffering, he made it perfectly clear, by this distinction, that something altogether different was to be sought and expected from him.

This passion, therefore, of our Lord Jesus Christ, as the distinction between the two Testaments, is fittingly prefigured by what is narrated here concerning the slaughter of the red heifer.
