The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, “This is the distinction of the Law, whatever the Lord has established.” Then he begins to give the command, adding these words: “Speak to the children of Israel.” It may also be punctuated this way: “And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the ordinance of the Law, whatever the Lord has established, saying”—not whatever the Lord established by creating, such as heaven and earth and all that is in them, but whatever the Lord established by speaking, namely, in the two Testaments. Then what follows is: “Speak to the children of Israel, and let them bring to you” [Note: The printed editions have *a te* (“to you”), but the manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint, have *ad te* (“to you”).] a red heifer without defect.

The red heifer signifies the flesh of Christ. Its female sex refers to carnal weakness; it is red on account of that bloody passion itself. When it says, “Let them bring it to you,” it shows in Moses himself the figure of the Law, since they seemed, according to the Law, to kill Christ because, in their view, he was abolishing the Sabbath and profaning the lawful observances.

That this heifer is said to be without defect is not surprising: this flesh was also represented by the other sacrifices, where animals likewise are commanded to be sacrificed without defect. For that flesh was “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VIII, 3), but it was not sinful flesh. Nevertheless, here, where God wished to commend the distinction of the Law more explicitly, it was not enough to say “without defect” unless it was added, “which has no defect in itself.” If this was said for the sake of repetition, perhaps it was not without purpose that the repetition itself confirmed the matter more firmly.

Yet it is also not contrary to the truth to understand the addition “which has no defect in itself” as having been made because, although it had already been said, “a heifer without defect,” Christ’s flesh had no defect in itself, whereas others who are his members did have defect. For what flesh in this life is without sin except that which has no defect in itself?

“And no yoke has been placed upon it.” For it was not subjected to iniquity. Finding those subjected to it, he set them free and broke their bonds, so that it might be said to him: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. CXV, 16–17). For no yoke was placed upon the flesh of the one who had power to lay down his life and take it up again (John X, 18).

“And you shall give it,” he says, “to Eleazar the priest.” Why not to Aaron, unless perhaps this was prefigured in such a way as to indicate that the Lord’s passion would come not to the priesthood of that present time but to its successors? “And they shall lead it outside the camp.” Thus also the Lord was led outside the city to suffer. When it says, “to a clean place,” this signifies that he had no evil cause. “And they shall kill it in his presence”: so Christ’s flesh was killed in the presence of those who were destined to be priests in the Lord’s new Testament.

“And Eleazar shall take some of its blood and sprinkle it toward the front of the tabernacle of testimony seven times from its blood” [Col. 0734]. This bears witness that Christ, according to the Scriptures, shed his blood for the remission of sins (Rom. III, 25; Eph. I, 7). It was sprinkled toward the front of the tabernacle of testimony because this was not otherwise declared than it had been foretold by divine testimony; and it was sprinkled seven times because this number pertains to spiritual cleansing.

“And they shall burn it in his presence.” I think that the burning pertains to the sign of resurrection. Fire by nature rises upward, and what is burned is transformed into it. Indeed, the word *cremare* (“to burn”) itself was brought from Greek into Latin from the idea of suspension [Note: *Kremeō*, “I suspend.”]. As for the addition “in his presence,” that is, in the priest’s presence, it seems to me to suggest that the resurrection of Christ appeared to those who were destined to be a royal priesthood.

What follows—“And its hide and its flesh and its blood, together with its dung, shall be burned”—explains how it would be burned. It signifies that not only the mortal substance of Christ’s body, indicated by the mention of hide, flesh, and blood, but also the disgrace and rejection of the people—which I think is signified by the word “dung”—would be transformed into glory, signified by the flame of the burning.

“And the priest shall take cedar wood and hyssop and scarlet, and shall cast them into the midst of the burning of the heifer.” Cedar wood is hope, which ought to dwell firmly in heavenly things. Hyssop is faith, which, although it is a lowly herb, clings with its roots to the rock. Scarlet is charity, which bears witness to the fervor of the spirit by its fiery color. These three we ought to cast into the resurrection of Christ, as into the midst of that burning, so that our life may be hidden with him, as the Apostle says: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3).

“And the priest shall wash his garments, and wash his body with water; then he shall enter the camp, and the priest shall be unclean until evening.” What is the washing of garments and body except the cleansing of outward and inward things? This concerns the priest.

Then it continues: “And the one who burns it shall wash his garments and wash his body with water, and he shall be unclean until evening.” In the one who burns it, I think those are represented who buried Christ’s flesh, committing it, as it were, to a conflagration—that is, to the resurrection.

“And a clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer and place them outside the camp in a clean place.” What do we mean by the ashes of the heifer—the remains, that is, of that killing and burning—except the report that followed Christ’s passion and resurrection? “For there are remains for the peaceful man” (Ps. XXXVI, 37). It was ashes because he was despised by unbelievers as though he were dead; yet it cleansed, because believers believed that he had risen.

And because this report became especially well known among those who lived among the other nations and did not belong to the fellowship of the Jews, I think it was therefore said: “And a clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer.” He was clean, certainly, from the killing of Christ, which had made the Jews guilty. “And he shall place them in a clean place,” that is, he shall treat them honorably; yet outside the camp, because evangelical honor became evident outside the celebration of Jewish custom [Col. 0735].

“And it shall be for the synagogue of the children of Israel for safekeeping.” The water of sprinkling is purification. Afterward Scripture explains more fully how the water of sprinkling was made from these ashes, by which they were cleansed from contact with the dead—a contact that certainly signifies cleansing from the iniquity of this dying, or rather death-filled, life.

But what follows is remarkable: “And the one who gathers,” it says, “the ashes of the heifer shall wash his garments, and he shall be unclean until evening.” How will one who approached clean become unclean through this, unless it is because even those who seem clean to themselves acknowledge in the Christian faith that all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely through his blood (Rom. III, 23–24)?

Yet he is told to wash his garments, not also his body. I believe that, if the gathering of those ashes and their placement in a clean place are understood spiritually, he is already understood to have been cleansed inwardly; just as Cornelius, hearing and believing what Peter preached, was so cleansed that, before visible baptism, he and those who were present with him received the gift of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, the visible sacrament could not be despised (Acts X, 44–48), so that, having also been washed outwardly, he might in a certain sense wash his garments [Note: The manuscripts of Michaelinus and Beccensis read: “Nor could the visible sacrament offered be despised, so that he might also wash outwardly,” and so forth.]

“And it shall be,” he says, “for the children of Israel and for the proselytes who are joined to them, a perpetual ordinance.” What else does this show except the baptism of Christ, which the water of sprinkling signified and which would benefit both Jews and Gentiles—that is, the children of Israel and the proselytes—as natural branches and the wild olive grafted into the richness of the root (Rom. XI, 16–24)?

Who would not be attentive to the fact that, after the washing of each individual, it is said: “And he shall be unclean until evening”? This is said not only here but in all, or nearly all, such cleansings. I do not know whether anything else can be understood by this except that every person, after the fullest remission of sins, contracts something by remaining in this life through which he is unclean until the end of that same life, when this day is, in a certain sense, closed for him—which is signified by evening.

Then Scripture begins to say, and explains, how people who have become unclean are purified by that water of sprinkling:

“Whoever touches a dead person,” it says, “every human soul shall be unclean for seven days. He shall be purified on the third day and on the seventh day, and he shall be clean. But if he is not purified on the third day and on the seventh day, he shall not be clean. Whoever touches a dead person, any human soul, and dies and is not purified—that is, dies before he has been purified after touching the dead person—has polluted the tabernacle of the Lord. That soul shall be removed from Israel” [Col. 0736].

It should be noted that it is extremely difficult to find anything more explicit in these books concerning the life of the soul after death. Here, then, when it says that if someone dies before purification, uncleanness remains in him and that the soul is removed from Israel—that is, from the fellowship of God’s people—what else does it wish to be understood except that punishment remains for the soul even after death if, while living, it was not cleansed by this sacrament, which prefigures Christ’s baptism?

“For the water of sprinkling,” it says, “was not sprinkled upon him; he is unclean; his uncleanness is still in him.” Still—that is, even after death. When it said above, “He has polluted the tabernacle of the Lord,” it certainly meant this insofar as it depended on him, just as the Apostle says, “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (I Thess. V, 19), although the Spirit cannot be extinguished. For if Scripture had wished it to be understood that the tabernacle had thereby been made unclean, it would certainly have commanded that it be cleansed.

Afterward it commands that those made unclean by the dead—that is, by dead works, which are all iniquities—be cleansed in this way:

“And they shall take for the unclean person,” it says, “some of the ashes of the purification that was burned, and they shall pour living water over it—that is, over those same ashes—in a vessel. And a clean man shall take hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle it around the house, over the vessels, and over the souls who may be there, and over the one who has touched a human bone, or a wounded person, or a dead person, or a tomb. And the clean person shall sprinkle the unclean on the third day and on the seventh day; and he shall purify him on the seventh day, and he shall wash his garments and bathe himself in water, and he shall be unclean until evening.”

There is one water of sprinkling, and clearly another water with which he washes his garments. “And he shall bathe himself in water”: I think this is to be understood spiritually by signification, not literally. For without doubt it was visible, like all those shadows of future things. Therefore, whoever is rightly washed by the sacrament of baptism, which that water of sprinkling prefigured, is cleansed spiritually—that is, invisibly—in both flesh and soul, so that he may be clean in body and spirit.

When it says that the water of sprinkling is sprinkled with hyssop, and we have said above that this herb signifies faith, what else comes to mind except what is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV, 9)? Baptism is of no benefit if faith is absent.

It says that this is done by a clean man, by whom ministers are signified, bearing the person of their Lord, who is truly a clean man [Note: The printed editions read: “Bearing the persons of their Lord, who is truly clean.” The manuscripts, however, read: “Bearing the person of their Lord, who is truly a clean man.”]

For concerning these ministers it also says in what follows: “And the one who sprinkles the water of sprinkling shall wash his garments”—that is, he shall observe it also in his body [Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions have: “and his body.”]—“And the one who touches the water of sprinkling shall be unclean until evening. And everything that the unclean person touches shall be unclean; and the soul that touches it shall be unclean until evening.” I have already said above what I think “until evening” signifies.

### XXXIV. [Book XIX, 16]

“Everyone who touches in the open field a wounded person, or a dead person, or a human bone, or a tomb.”

It may be asked what is meant by “wounded” or “dead.” If “wounded” means one thing and “dead” another, care must be taken lest it be thought that even someone who touched a wounded living person would be unclean, which is certainly absurd. But since the dead can also be wounded, it is understood that the dead themselves are being distinguished, so that “a wounded dead person” means one killed by a wound, or one who died without a wound.

### XXXV. [Book XX, 11]

What the drawing of water from the rock signified was explained by the Apostle when he said: “And they all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). Thus spiritual grace flowing from Christ was signified, by which the inner thirst was refreshed.

But the striking of the rock with the staff prefigures the cross of Christ. When wood approached the rock, grace flowed forth; and the fact that it was struck twice signifies the cross more clearly. For the cross consists of two pieces of wood.

### XXXVI. [Book XX, 13]

Concerning that water which flowed from the rock, it was said: “This is the water of contradiction,” because the children of Israel reviled the Lord, and he was sanctified among them. First they reviled him when they spoke against the Lord’s benefit by which they had been brought out of Egypt; afterward he was sanctified among them when, through that miracle of the flowing water, his holiness was declared.

Or did he perhaps indicate two kinds of people: those who contradict the grace of Christ and those who receive the grace of Christ, so that for the former it is the water of contradiction and for the latter the water of sanctification? For it is also written of the Lord himself in the Gospel: “And for a sign that will be contradicted” (Luke II, 34).

### XXXVII. [Book XX, 17, 19]

When Moses says to the king of Edom, among other things, “Nor will we drink water from your well,” it should be understood as meaning “without payment”—that is, “because we will not drink without payment.” He makes this clear afterward by saying: “But if we drink of your water, I and my cattle, I will give you the price.”

### XXXVIII. [Book XX, 17]

“We will not turn aside to the right or to the left”: this is expressed in the plural, meaning “toward the things that are on the right or toward the things that are on the left.”

### XXXIX. [Book XX, 24]

“You shall not enter the land that I have given to the children of Israel as a possession, because you provoked me over the water of cursing.” What he previously called the water of contradiction he here calls the water of cursing. For he does not say *antilogias* (ἀντιλογίας, “of contradiction”), but *loidōrias* (λοιδορίας, “of reviling”).

### XL. [Book XXI, 2]

“And Israel vowed a vow to the Lord and said: ‘If you deliver this people into my power’”—that is, “if by delivering them to me you subject them”—“I will devote them and their cities to destruction.”

Here it must be considered how what is vowed is called “devoting to destruction,” yet is placed in the sense of a curse, just as it is said of this people: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. I, 9). From this arose the common usage by which *devotatio* (“devotion” or “devoting”) is spoken of; for scarcely anyone says that a person “devotes himself” except when cursing.

### XLI. [Book XXI, 3]

“And he devoted it and its city to destruction; and the name of that place was called Anathema.”

From this it arose that *anathema* came to signify something detestable and abominable. For in order that the victor might take nothing from it for his own use but vow the whole of it to undergo punishment, this was to anathematize, which is commonly called to devote.

The origin of this word, however, is in the Greek language, from those things which, having been vowed and paid—that is, promised and delivered—were placed on high in temples: *apo tou anō tithenai* (ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄνω τιθέναι), that is, “to place on high,” either by fixing them in place or by hanging them.

### XLII. [Book XXI, 13–14]

In the account of the journey of the children of Israel, as they moved and established their camps, it is written among other things: “And from there they camped beyond the Arnon, in the wilderness” [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts had *in Hernon* here, corruptly instead of *in eremo* (“in the wilderness”), as is clear from the Septuagint and the Vulgate.]—which extends from the borders of the Amorites. For the Arnon is the boundary of Moab [Note: The printed editions omit *Moab* here and consistently have *Moab* below instead of *Zoob*. These errors are corrected from the manuscripts and the Septuagint.] between Moab and the Amorite.

Therefore it is said in the book: “The war of the Lord set Zoob aflame, and the torrents of Arnon; and he established the torrents to inhabit Er.” Scripture does not mention in what book this was written, and there is no such book among those that we call canonical divine Scriptures.

Those who seek to insert apocryphal books into the ears of the careless and the curious, in order to persuade them of fabulous impieties, find opportunities in passages of this kind. But here it says that it was written in a book; it does not say that it was written in the holy book of some prophet or patriarch.

Nor should it be denied that books already existed, whether among the Chaldeans, from whom Abraham came; among the Egyptians, where Moses had learned all their wisdom; or among any other people, in some book of whom this may have been written. Nevertheless, such a book should not for that reason be admitted among the Scriptures through which divine authority is commended. The same is true of the Cretan prophet whom the Apostle mentions (Titus I, 12), and of the Greek writers, philosophers, or poets whom that same Apostle, speaking to the Athenians, confirms to have said something of considerable importance and truth: “For in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts XVII, 28).

Divine authority may take testimony from wherever it wishes when it finds something true; but it does not thereby confirm that everything written there is to be accepted.

Why this was mentioned in this place is not evident, unless perhaps the boundaries between the two peoples were established there through war. Because of the magnitude of that war, the inhabitants of the place called it “the war of the Lord,” so that it was written in one of their books: “The war of the Lord set Zoob aflame.” Perhaps that city was burned in the same war, or was inflamed—that is, roused—to fight, or perhaps something else is concealed in the obscurity of this passage.

### XLIII. [Book XXI, 16]

“This is the well of which the Lord said to Moses: ‘Gather the people, and I will give them water freely’” [Col. 0739].

This is mentioned as though the Lord’s having said this to Moses had been recorded somewhere earlier. But because it is found nowhere, it must be understood that the people who were complaining of thirst drank here also.

### XLIV. [Book XXI, 24–25]

“And Israel struck him with the edge of the sword; and they took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the children of Ammon, because Jazer is the boundary of the children of Ammon. And Israel took all these cities. And Israel dwelt in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon.”

Here Israel certainly took possession of the cities of the Amorites that it conquered in war, because it did not devote them to destruction. For if it had devoted them to destruction, it would not have been permitted to possess them or to appropriate any spoil from them for its own use.

It is worth noting how just wars were conducted. An innocent passage was refused, although it ought to have been open by the most equitable right of human society. But since God was now bringing his promises to completion, he helped the Israelites, to whom the land of the Amorites was to be given.

When Edom likewise refused them passage, the Israelites—that is, the children of Jacob—did not fight that people, the children of Esau, the two brothers and twins, because God had not promised that land to the Israelites. Instead, they turned away from them.

### XLV. [Book XXI, 27]

“Therefore the enigma-makers will say: ‘Come to Heshbon,’” and so forth.

Who these “enigma-makers” were is not apparent, because the term is not customary in our literature and is scarcely found elsewhere in the divine Scriptures themselves. But since they seem to sing a song in which they celebrated the war fought between the Amorites and the Moabites, in which Sihon, king of the Amorites, defeated the Moabites, it is not implausible to think that these people were then called “enigma-makers” whom we call poets.

This is because it is customary and permitted for poets to mix into their songs the enigmas of myths, by which they are understood to signify something. For they would not otherwise be enigmas unless figurative speech were present, and once that speech had been examined one could arrive at the meaning hidden in the enigma.

### XLVI. [Book XXII, 4–6]

What Scripture says—that after Israel defeated the Amorites and took possession of all their cities, Balak, king of the Moabites, sent messengers to hire Balaam to curse Israel—clearly shows that not all the Moabites had come under the rule of Sihon, king of the Amorites, when he defeated them in war. For the Moabite people remained until the time when Balak was king of Moab.

When Moab said to the elders of Midian—that is, the Moabites said to the elders of the Midianites—“Now this assembly will lick up all those who are around us” [Note: The printed editions have *adjunget synagogae hae omnes*; the manuscripts have *ablinget synagoga haec*, which is the reading of the Septuagint.] it was not one people speaking about another, but neighbors speaking to neighbors about what they needed jointly to avoid.

For Moab was the son of Lot by one of his daughters (Gen. XIX, 37), whereas Midian was the son of Abraham by Keturah (ibid. XXV, 2). They were therefore not one people but two neighboring and contiguous peoples.

### XLVII. [Book XXII, 7–13]

What does it mean when it is written, “And divinations were in their hands,” concerning those whom Balak sent to hire Balaam to curse Israel? Were they themselves practicing divination? Or were they carrying something from which Balaam could make use in divining—perhaps things that would be burned in sacrifices or offered in some other way—and were these therefore called “divinations” because through them he could divine? Or does it mean something else? The statement is obscure.

It should certainly be noted that God came to Balaam and said to him, “Who are these men with you?” and so forth. It is not stated whether this happened in a dream, although the fact that it happened at night is sufficiently clear when Scripture afterward says, “And Balaam arose in the morning.”

It may be asked how God spoke with a very wicked man. Even if it were certain that this happened in a dream, the question would not thereby disappear, because of the man’s very unworthiness.

Likewise the Lord Jesus Christ speaks of that rich man who planned to destroy his old storehouses and fill larger new ones: “God said to him, ‘Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; whose will those things be that you have prepared?’” (Luke XII, 20). Let no one boast because God speaks to him in the manner in which he knows such people must be addressed, since this can also happen to the reprobate. For even when he speaks through an angel, it is he himself who speaks.

### XLVIII. [Book XXII, 12–38]

When Balaam said again to the more honored messengers sent to him, “If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not transgress the word of the Lord, to do anything small or great according to my own mind,” there is absolutely no sin in this statement. But what follows is not without grave sin.

Once he had heard the Lord say, “You shall not go with them, nor shall you curse the people, for they are blessed,” he ought to have remained steadfast. He ought not to have given them any hope that the Lord might change his decision against his own people, whom he had said were blessed, as though Balaam himself could bend him by gifts and honors.

He showed himself overcome by greed when he again wished the Lord to speak to him about a matter concerning which he already knew the Lord’s will. For what need was there to add what follows: “And now remain here tonight also, and I shall know what more the Lord will say to me”?

Accordingly, the Lord, seeing that his greed had been captured and overcome by gifts, permitted him to go, in order to restrain his avarice through the animal on which he rode. By this very act he put that madness to shame: the donkey did not dare to transgress the Lord’s prohibition, delivered through the angel, while Balaam tried to transgress it through greed, although he suppressed that same greed through fear.

For God came to Balaam at night and said to him: “If the men have come to call you, rise and follow them; but the word that I shall speak to you, that you shall do.” And Balaam arose in the morning, saddled his donkey, and went with the princes of Moab.

Why did he not consult God again after this permission, whereas after the earlier prohibition he had thought it necessary to consult him again, unless his evil greed was apparent, even though it was restrained by fear of the Lord?

Finally, Scripture continues: “And God was angry in wrath because he went; and the angel of God rose up to prevent him on the way,” and so forth, until the donkey spoke.

Nothing here seems more astonishing than that he was not terrified when the donkey spoke, but instead continued to answer it in anger, as though accustomed to such marvels. Afterward the angel also speaks to him, reproving and condemning his way; yet when he saw the angel, he was terrified and bowed down.

Then he was permitted to go, so that through him a very clear prophecy might be uttered. For he was not permitted at all to say what he wanted, but only what he was compelled to say by the power of the Spirit.

He himself nevertheless remained reprobate. For afterward Holy Scripture spoke of him in such a way that certain blameworthy and reprobate people were said to have followed his way: “They followed,” it says, “the way of Balaam the son of Beor, who loved the wages of iniquity” (II Pet. II, 15).

### XLIX. [Book XXII, 22, 32]

Concerning the angel who spoke to Balaam on the way, at whose sight his donkey did not dare to proceed, Scripture speaks as follows: “And God was angry in wrath because he went; and the angel of God rose up to delay him on the way.”

First, it should be noted how it says, “God was angry, and the angel of God rose up.” It does not say that God, being angry, sent the angel; rather, it signifies the angry God in the angel, because God’s truth and justice made the angel angry.

The expression “rose up” must certainly be understood as referring to movement. Then, when it says “to delay him on the way,” the Greek word is *diabalein* (διαβαλεῖν). The angel himself uses the same word later: “Behold, I have come out for your delay,” where the Greek has *diabolē* (διαβολή).

Perhaps “accusation” is the more suitable meaning, so that “to delay him on the way” should be understood as “to accuse him.” From this it is also believed that the devil was so called, as though he should be called “the accuser” in Latin—not because no one can accuse rightly and well, but because the devil loves to accuse, driven by the goads of envy, as the testimony concerning him in the Apocalypse shows (Rev. XII, 9–10).

This word is also used in a comedy, and there is no doubt that it is Latin, with the same or at least a closely related meaning, where an angry father is said to his son:

> He hopes he has found a speech  
> By which he may delay you.  
> *(Terence, Andria, act 2, scene 4.)*

Here *differat* is usually understood as meaning that he may carry you here and there in a storm of words, as though tearing you apart and scattering you—which he would certainly seem to be doing by accusing you.

But even if we understand “to delay him on the way” in this sense, that the angel delayed his haste by holding him back, so that he might both show and tell him what was necessary, the use of this word with that meaning is not unreasonable.

### L. [Book XXII, 23–29]

“And when the donkey saw the angel of God standing in the way, with a drawn sword in his hand, the donkey turned aside from the way and went into the field.” This field was still outside the walls of the vineyards.

“And he struck the donkey with a staff, to correct it on the way. And the angel of God stood in the furrows of the vineyards, with a wall on one side and a wall on the other.”

It is rightly asked: if walls stood on both sides and placed the road between them, as usually happens, how is the angel said to have stood in the furrows of the vineyards? There could not have been furrows of vineyards on the road between the walls.

But the order of the words is: “to correct it on the way, with a wall on one side and a wall on the other.” He therefore wished to correct Balaam’s donkey on this road, so that it would walk between the walls.

The intervening statement—“And the angel of God stood in the furrows of the vineyards”—means that he stood in one of the vineyards, which lay on one side of the road. “And when the donkey saw the angel of God, it pressed itself against the wall,” that is, against the wall of that vineyard in which the angel was not, since he was in the furrows on the other side.

“And it crushed Balaam’s foot against the wall, and he continued to beat it.” “And the angel of God went on and stood in a narrow place” [Note: The Septuagint has *kai apelthōn* (“and departing”).]—now no longer in the furrows of the vineyards but between the walls themselves, that is, on the road, where there was no room to turn either to the right [Note: Thus the manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint. The printed editions have: “where there was no room to turn to the right.”] or to the left.

“And when the donkey saw the angel of God, it sat down” [Note: The printed editions have *concidit* (“fell down”), but the manuscripts have *consedit* (“sat down”); the Septuagint has *suneekathisen* (“sat down together”).]

Since it had been beaten, it could not go backward; it did not press itself against the wall, because it was not frightened from the other side. The angel was in the middle of the road, in a narrow place. It therefore remained only for the donkey to sit down.

“And Balaam was angry, and he struck the donkey with his staff. And God opened the mouth of the donkey, and it said to Balaam: ‘What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?’ And Balaam said to the donkey: ‘Because you have mocked me; and if I had a sword in my hand, I would already have pierced you.’”

Clearly he was driven by such great greed that he was not terrified even by so great a miracle, but answered as though he were speaking to a human being. Yet God had not transformed the donkey’s soul into a rational nature; rather, he had made the words he wished to come from it in order to restrain Balaam’s madness.

Perhaps this prefigured the fact that God would choose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (I Cor. I, 27), in place of the spiritual and true Israel, that is, the children of the promise.

### LI. [Book XXIII, 5]

“And the Spirit of God came to be upon him”—that is, upon Balaam.

The Spirit of God did not “come to be” as though the Spirit of God were a created thing. Rather, it came to be upon him, that is, it came about that it was upon him.

This is like the statement, “He who comes after me has come before me”: that is, it came about that he was before me, that he was placed before me, because, as he says, “he was before me” (John I, 30).

It is also like: “The Lord became my helper” (Ps. XXIX, 11). The Lord did not become a created thing; rather, it came about that he helped me. Likewise: “The Lord became a refuge for the poor” (Ps. IX, 10), that is, it came about that the poor fled to him; and: “The hand of the Lord came upon me” (Ezek. I, 3; III, 22), that is, it came about that it was upon me. Many such expressions are found in the Scriptures.

### LII. [Book XXV, 4, 7–8]

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Take the leaders of the people and display them before the Lord opposite the sun; and the wrath of the Lord’s anger shall be turned away from Israel.’”

God was angry because of Israel’s fornications, both carnal and spiritual. They had joined themselves shamelessly to the daughters of Moab and had been consecrated to idols. He said this to Moses so that he might display the leaders of the people before the Lord opposite the sun.

In this expression it is understood that they were commanded to be crucified, so that “display them before the Lord opposite the sun” means “display them publicly, in the full view of this light.”

For the Greek says *paradeigmatison* (παραδειγμάτισον), which could be translated “make them examples,” since *paradeigma* (παράδειγμα) means “example.” Besides the Septuagint translators, Aquila is reported to have said “fix them,” or rather “fix them aloft,” corresponding to *anapēxon* (ἀνάπηξον); Symmachus, using a clearer word, has “hang them.”

It is remarkable that Scripture stops short of telling whether this was carried out according to the Lord’s command. I do not see how the command could have been disregarded without consequence—or, if it was disregarded, how it could have been disregarded with impunity.

But if it was carried out and simply left unmentioned, why does Scripture testify that the Lord was appeased when Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, pierced the adulterers, and that the plague ceased—as though, after the leaders had been crucified as the Lord had commanded, the continuing indignation still needed to be appeased in another way?

For surely what the Lord had foretold and promised could not be false when he said: “Take the leaders of the people and display them before the Lord opposite the sun; and the wrath of the Lord’s anger shall be turned away from Israel.” If this had therefore been done, who could doubt that the Lord’s anger had been turned away from Israel?

What need, then, was there for Phinehas still to avenge God in this way upon the adulterers, and for Scripture to testify that by this act he appeased the Lord?

Unless perhaps we understand the matter as follows: when Moses was preparing to carry out what the Lord had commanded concerning the leaders of the people, he wished also, in accordance with the Law, to punish such crimes and sacrilegious insolence by commanding each person to kill his neighbor who had been impiously consecrated to foreign gods. Meanwhile Phinehas also carried out his act; and thus, once the Lord’s anger had been appeased, it was no longer necessary for the leaders of the people to be crucified.

This severity was appropriate to that time, and it makes sufficiently clear to those of prudent faith how great an evil fornication and idolatry are.

### LIII. [Book of Numbers 27:13–14]

The Lord gives the same cause for Moses’ death as for his brother’s. For he had previously foretold to both of them that they would not enter with the people of God into the promised land, because they had not sanctified him before the people at the water of contradiction (Numbers 20:12)—that is, because they had doubted his gift, namely, that water could flow from the rock, as we explained at that very passage of Scripture above (Question 19).

The mystery of this is understood to be that neither the priesthood instituted earlier, represented by Aaron, nor the Law itself, represented by Moses, brings the people of God into the land of the eternal inheritance; rather, it is Jesus, in whom there was a type of the Lord Jesus Christ—that is, grace through faith. Aaron died before Israel entered any part of the promised land. While Moses was still alive, the land of the Amorites was captured and possessed, but he was not permitted to cross the Jordan with them.

For the Law is observed in the Christian faith in some respects. It contains commandments that Christians are still instructed to observe today. That priesthood, however, and those sacrifices have no place in the Christian faith today, except insofar as they were performed and completed as shadows of things to come.

When both brothers—that is, Aaron and Moses—are told to be gathered to their people, it is clear that God’s anger was not directed against them in a way that separated them from the peace of the holy and eternal fellowship. Thus it is shown that not only their offices but also their deaths were signs of things to come, not punishments inflicted by God’s indignation.

### LIV. [Book of Numbers 27:18–19] [Col. 0744]

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Take for yourself Jesus son of Nave, a man who has the Spirit in himself; and you shall lay your hands upon him, and set him before Eleazar the priest, and command him before all the assembly,’” and so forth.

It should be noted that although Jesus son of Nave already had the Spirit in himself, as Scripture testifies—and what other Spirit should we understand here than the Holy Spirit? For it would not say this of the human spirit, which no one lacked—Moses was nevertheless commanded to lay his hands upon him. This was so that no human being, however distinguished by exceptional grace, might dare to reject the sacraments of consecration.

[Note: The printed editions have *sacramentum*, “the sacrament.” The manuscripts have *sacramenta*, “the sacraments.”]

### LV. [Book of Numbers 27:20]

What does God mean when, among other things, he commands Moses concerning Jesus son of Nave: “And you shall give some of your glory upon him”?

The Greek expression has τῆς δόξης (*tēs doxēs*), which amounts to saying “from the glory,” that is, ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης (*apo tēs doxēs*). Some Latin translators, however, rendered it, “You shall give your glory,” rather than “some of your glory.”

But whether the wording was “your glory,” Moses would not therefore cease to possess it; nor, because it says “from the glory,” is what he possessed thereby diminished. It should be understood as though it said: “You shall make him a sharer in your glory.” Such things are not diminished as though they were divided into portions; rather, they are wholly possessed by all, and wholly possessed by each person who shares in them.

### LVI. [Book of Numbers 30:3]

“Man, any man who makes a vow to the Lord, or swears an oath, or makes a determination concerning his own life, shall not violate his word: he shall do everything that has gone out of his mouth.”

This does not apply to every oath, but to an oath in which someone vows, concerning his own life, to abstain from something that he was permitted by the Law to use, but which by his vow he makes impermissible for himself.

### LVII. [Book of Numbers 30:4–6]

“But if a woman makes a vow to the Lord, or makes a determination in her father’s house, in her youth, and her father hears her vows and her determinations, which she has determined against her own life, and her father remains silent, then all her vows and all her determinations, which she has determined against her own life, shall stand for her. But if her father expressly rejects them on the day when he hears all her vows and her determinations, which she has determined against her own life, they shall not stand; and the Lord shall cleanse her, because her father rejected them.”

Since he is speaking of a woman who is still young and in her father’s house, the question appropriately arises whether this also concerns a vow of virginity. It is well known that women who are virgins are also regularly called “women” in Scripture. The Apostle likewise seems to speak of a father when he says, “Let him keep his virgin,” and “Let him give his virgin in marriage” (1 Corinthians 7:37–38), and other things of this kind.

Some have understood “his virgin” to mean “his virginity.” Yet they do not demonstrate this by any similar scriptural usage, although such a usage is exceedingly uncommon.

When Scripture says “against her own life,” this should not be understood as though such vows harm the soul. Rather, “against the life” means against animal pleasure, just as, when commanding a fast, it says above: “And you shall afflict your souls” (Numbers 29:7).

### LVIII. [Book of Numbers 30:6] [Col. 0745]

When Scripture says, “And the Lord shall cleanse her, because her father rejected it,” “he shall cleanse” means that he will absolve her from the guilt of an unfulfilled vow. Thus in many passages it says, “The priest shall cleanse him,” meaning that he will regard him as clean and judge him clean. Likewise, “You shall not cleanse the guilty by cleansing” means, “You shall not declare someone clean who is unclean.”

### LIX. [Book of Numbers 30:7–16]

“But if she is married to a man, and her vows are upon her according to the distinction of her lips, whatever she has determined against her own life; and her husband hears it, and remains silent toward her on the day when he hears it, then her vows shall stand, and her determinations, which she has determined against her own life, shall stand.”

The Law did not wish a woman, whether still under her father before marriage or married and under her husband, to make a vow to God against her own life—that is, to abstain from things that are lawful and permitted—in such a way that the woman’s authority would prevail in those vows, rather than the man’s.

[Note: The Amiens, Erfurt, and Louvain editions read “would not prevail”; the Ratramnus edition, “would not be valid.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts, most of which read “would prevail.”]

Thus, if her father had permitted her to fulfill her vows while she was still unmarried, but she married before fulfilling them, and her husband, having learned of them, did not approve, she should not fulfill them and would be entirely without sin, because the Lord would cleanse her, as Scripture says—that is, he would judge her clean. This should not be thought to occur against God, since God himself commanded and willed it.

The text then proceeds to widows and women who have been cast out by their husbands—that is, women who are under the authority neither of a husband nor of a father—and says that their vows are free to be fulfilled, as follows: “The vow of a widow and of a woman who has been cast out, whatever she has vowed against her own life, shall stand for her.”

Then it speaks of a married woman who, already established in her husband’s house, makes such a vow. It had first spoken of the woman who had made a vow in her father’s house and then married before fulfilling it. Concerning the woman who makes a vow in her husband’s house, it says:

“But if, in her husband’s house, her vow or the determination which she has made against her own life with an oath is upon her, and her husband hears it, remains silent toward her, and does not reject it, then all her vows and all her determinations, which she has determined against her own life, shall stand against her. But if her husband expressly annuls them on the day when he hears all the things that have gone out from her lips, according to her vows and according to the determinations that she has made against her own life, they shall not remain for her. Her husband has annulled them, and the Lord shall cleanse her.

“Every vow and every oath that binds her by afflicting her life, her husband may establish for her, and her husband may annul. But if he remains completely silent toward her from day to day, and establishes for her all her vows and determinations that are upon her, he establishes them for her because he remained silent toward her on the day when he heard them. But if her husband expressly annuls them after the day on which he heard them, he shall bear his sin.”

It is clear that the Law wished a woman to be under her husband in such a way that none of the vows she made for the sake of abstinence would be fulfilled by her unless the man’s authority permitted it.

[Col. 0746]

For when the Law wished the matter to count as the husband’s sin—if he had first permitted the vow and afterward prohibited it—it nevertheless did not say that the woman should do what she had vowed, merely because her husband had earlier permitted it. It said that the sin belonged to the man, because he rejected what he had previously allowed. Yet it did not thereby give the woman permission to disregard him: although her husband had first permitted the vow, if he later prohibited it, she was not to despise his prohibition.

It is worth asking, however, whether these provisions also apply to vows of continence and abstinence from sexual intercourse, lest perhaps only those vows made concerning food and drink are meant by the expression “against her own life.”

This seems also to be suggested by the passage where the Lord says, “Is not the life more than food?” (Matthew 6:25), and where, in prescribing a fast, he says, “You shall afflict your lives” (Numbers 29:7). I do not know whether a vow concerning abstinence from intercourse can be found anywhere called a vow “against the life,” especially since here the Law grants authority to the husband, not to the wife who is subject to her husband, so that the woman’s vows are to be fulfilled if the husband approves, but need not be fulfilled if he refuses.

Yet when the Apostle speaks of marital intercourse, he does not grant greater authority to the husband than to the wife. Rather, he says: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband also does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (1 Corinthians 7:3–4).

Since, in this matter, he wished the authority of both to be equal, I think he suggests that we should understand this rule concerning intercourse or abstinence from intercourse not to apply to those vows in which the husband and wife do not have equal authority, but in which the husband’s authority is greater and belongs almost exclusively to him. For the Law does not say that the husband should not fulfill his vows if his wife prohibits him, but that the wife should not fulfill hers if her husband prohibits her.

Therefore, it does not seem to me that such vows, determinations, and obligations made “against the life” should include agreements between husband and wife concerning intercourse or abstinence from intercourse.

Furthermore, these are called “ordinances,” and we remember that among the ordinances mentioned under this name in Exodus there are many commands that cannot be observed literally and are not observed in the New Testament—for example, the piercing of a slave’s ear (Exodus 21:6), and anything similar.

Thus it is not unreasonable to understand something figurative here as well. Since there are many unreasonable practices of abstinence, sometimes even hostile to the truth, perhaps what is intended here is that they are valid when they are reasonable—that is, when reason approves them—reason which ought, in place of a husband, to govern every animal impulse, not only in desiring but also in abstaining. If the mind and reason determine that something should be done, then it should be done; but if the judgment of reason disapproves it, it should not be done.

If reason later disapproves what it had earlier and rightly determined should be done, then the sin belongs to the judgment. Even so, that impulse should consent only to reason.

### LX. [Book of Numbers 31:5–6] [Col. 0747]

What does the statement mean: “And Moses sent them, a thousand from each tribe and a thousand from each tribe, with their strength”?

Does “their strength” mean their leaders? Or the strength given to them by the Lord, or obtained for them through Moses? Or does “their strength” instead refer to the things by which their strength was sustained?

[Note: The printed editions read, “their strength, because he gave them those things by which strength…” We have adopted the manuscript reading, except that some manuscripts have “by which their food…”]

### LXI. [Book of Numbers 31:8]

A question may arise concerning how, when the Israelites defeated the Midianites, Scripture says that Balaam was killed—the man who had been hired to curse the people of Israel—since earlier, when he was compelled to bless them, Scripture concluded the same episode by saying: “And Balaam arose and departed, returning to his own place, and Balak went to himself” (Numbers 24:25).

If Balaam had returned to his own place, how was he killed here, since he had come from so far away, namely from Mesopotamia? Or perhaps he returned to Balak, though Scripture did not say so?

It is also possible to understand “he returned to his own place” as meaning that he returned from the place where he had been offering sacrifices to the place from which he had set out—that is, to the place where he had lodging as a foreigner. For Scripture does not say “to his own house” or “to his homeland,” but “to his own place.” Every foreigner also has a place of his own, where he dwells temporarily.

Concerning Balak, who had hired him, Scripture does not say that he went “to his own place,” but “to himself,” that is, to the place where he lived as a ruler. Thus both a ruler and a foreigner could be said to return to his own place; but I do not see how a foreigner could be said to return “to himself,” once he had gone to his lodging.

### LXII. [Book of Numbers 31:9]

“And they took captive the women of Midian, and their household goods, and their cattle, and everything that they possessed, and they plundered their strength.”

Since Scripture had already mentioned the women, the household goods, the cattle, and everything they possessed, why does it then add, “and they plundered their strength”?

Certainly this “strength” should be understood as the strength mentioned above, when it was said that Moses sent a thousand from each tribe “with their strength.”

Or perhaps the food by which they were sustained was called their strength, since when it is supplied, strength is available, and when it is taken away, strength fails? Thus God says through the prophet when threatening punishment: “I will take away the strength of bread and the strength of water” (Isaiah 3:1).

[Col. 0748]

Accordingly, Moses sent those thousand men with provisions, which is what is meant by the phrase “with their strength”; and after defeating the Midianites, they also plundered this among the other things belonging to them.

### LXIII. [Book of Numbers 31:15–16]

“Why have you kept every female alive? For these were for the children of Israel, according to the word of Balaam, to make them depart from and despise the word of the Lord because of Peor.”

Scripture does not say when Balaam gave this wicked counsel—that women should be placed before them as a temptation, through whom they would commit fornication not only bodily but also spiritually by worshiping an idol. Yet it is clear that this happened, since it is mentioned here.

Thus Balaam himself also could have returned, although he had already gone to his own place, if by “his place” we do not understand a lodging in a foreign land—although Scripture has kept this silent.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “so that only his place …” (*ut modo locum ejus*).]

### LXIV. [Book of Numbers 35:11–12]

What does the statement mean: “The cities shall be places of refuge for you from the avenger of blood, and the one who kills shall not die until he stands before the assembly for judgment,” when it is speaking of those who have killed unintentionally, while elsewhere it says that anyone who has fled to such a city may leave it freely when the high priest has died?

How, then, can it say here, “The one who kills shall not die until he stands before the assembly for judgment,” unless the reason is that he is judged so that he may then be permitted to remain in the city of refuge, if it becomes clear in the judgment that he killed unintentionally?

### LXV. [Book of Numbers 35:19, 12]

“The avenger of blood himself shall kill the murderer; when he encounters him, he shall kill him.”

To those who understand the passage badly, this sounds as though the avenger of a relative’s death had been given unrestricted permission to kill the person who killed him, without any judgment.

But the intended meaning is this: according to what was said above, the one who has killed should flee to one of the cities of refuge until he stands trial, so that he may not be killed beforehand if his relative finds him. For even if he killed unintentionally, he is killed if found outside those cities.

When, however, he has stood trial in one of those cities and has been judged a murderer, he is not permitted to remain in any of the cities to which he was allowed to flee. Only then, once he has been judged, may his relative kill him wherever he is found. There is no need to bring him to trial again, since he has already been judged a murderer and for that reason expelled from those cities.

# BOOK FIVE

## Questions on Deuteronomy

### I. [Deuteronomy 1:29–30] [Col. 0747]

In the passage where Moses recalls that he said to the people, who feared the enemies inhabiting the land into which they were to be brought, “Do not be afraid, and do not fear them. The Lord our God, who goes before your face, will himself fight them together with you,” it is sufficiently demonstrated that God is a helper in such a way that human beings also do something.

### II. [Deuteronomy 2:30] [Col. 0748]

“And Sihon king of Heshbon was unwilling to let us pass through him, because the Lord our God had hardened his spirit and strengthened his heart, so that he might be delivered into your hands, as on this day.”

In saying this while addressing the people, Moses recalls something like what is said in Exodus: “I have hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exodus 10:1), and what is read in the Psalms: “He turned their heart, so that they hated his people” (Psalm 104:25).

[Col. 0749]

Nor is the reason for this hardening omitted here, since it says, “so that he might be delivered into your hands, as on this day”—that is, so that he might be defeated by you. This would not happen unless he resisted; and he would not resist unless his heart had been hardened.

If we seek the justice of this, God’s judgments are inscrutable (Romans 11:33); but there is no iniquity with God (Romans 9:14). It should certainly be noted that a heart may be said to have been strengthened even in evil.

### III. [Deuteronomy 3:2]

“Yet Og king of Bashan was left over from the Rephaim.”

Those who know the Hebrew language say that the name *Rephaim* signifies giants. Thus, where most manuscripts read “he was left behind by the Rephaim,” the meaning is made clearer by the reading “he was left over from the Rephaim,” so that he himself is understood to have remained from among them.

The length and breadth of his iron bed are also subsequently mentioned in order to emphasize his great size.

### IV. [Deuteronomy 4:16]

“Do not commit iniquity, and make for yourselves a carved likeness, every image.”

It is often asked what difference there is between a “likeness” and an “image.” Here, however, I do not see what distinction was intended, unless Moses used the two words to signify one thing, or called something a likeness if, for example, a statue or representation were made with a human form, without reproducing the features of any particular person, as painters and sculptors do when they look at those whom they paint or model.

No one would doubt that this is called an image. According to this distinction, every image is also a likeness, but not every likeness is an image.

Thus, if two twins resemble each other, one may be said to possess the likeness of the other, but not the image of the other. If a son resembles his father, however, he is rightly also called an image, with the father as the prototype from which the image appears to have been expressed. Some such images are of the same substance, as the son is; others are not of the same substance, as a painting is not.

Accordingly, where Genesis says, “God made man in the image of God,” it is clear that the image made was not of the same substance. If it were of the same substance, it would be said to have been begotten, not made.

But because Genesis did not add “and likeness,” although it had earlier said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:27, 26), some have thought that likeness is something greater than image, something reserved for the later restoration of humanity through Christ’s grace.

I wonder, however, whether the reason it later wished to mention only the image was not that wherever there is an image, there is immediately also a likeness.

Thus Moses here prohibits the making of both likeness and image, perhaps according to the distinction we have described. In the Decalogue, however, the prohibition is stated generally: no likeness is to be made (Exodus 20:4); no image is mentioned. For when no likeness is made, certainly no image is made, since wherever there is an image, there is also a likeness. But when a likeness is made, an image does not necessarily follow; nevertheless, if there is no likeness, there can be no image.

Finally, when he prohibited the likeness and image of a human being, he intended a likeness in which a human being could be represented—not necessarily this or that person, but any human being—and an image, that is, specifically this person or that person.

[Col. 0750]

When he spoke of cattle and irrational animals, however, he mentioned only likeness. For who can be found who would select a particular dog, or something similar, as a model and, looking at it, paint or model its image? Such a practice is extremely common with human beings.

### V. [Deuteronomy 4:18]

“What does he mean by saying, ‘the likeness of every fish, whatever are in the waters beneath the earth’?”

Did he intend water also to be understood as earth, because of its tangible corporeal nature, and accordingly mean that in the statement “God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1) we should also understand the waters?

For Scripture frequently wishes the entire world to be understood when it mentions these two parts, as in the passage, “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 120:2), and countless similar passages.

Or was it said “beneath the earth” because, unless the earth were above the waters, it could not be inhabited by human beings or support terrestrial animals?

### VI. [Deuteronomy 4:19]

“Lest, when you look up to heaven and see the sun and moon and stars and all the array of heaven, going astray you worship them and serve them, which the Lord your God has distributed to all the nations that are under heaven.”

This is not said as though God commanded the nations to worship these things, while commanding only his own people not to worship them. Rather, it may mean either that God foreknew that the nations would offer worship to these heavenly bodies and nevertheless created them, while foreknowing that his own people would exist who would not worship them; or “distributed” was said so that their use might be understood.

That use is commended in Genesis: “Let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years” (Genesis 1:14). The people of God share this use of them with all nations, but not the worship that the other nations offer.

### VII. [Deuteronomy 4:23]

“Do not forget the covenant of the Lord your God, which he established with you, and make for yourselves a carved likeness of everything that the Lord your God has appointed for you.”

Here, speaking generally, he used the word “likeness” and omitted “image,” because if no likeness is made, certainly no image is made: wherever there is an image, there is immediately also a likeness, though wherever there is a likeness there is not necessarily an image.

### VIII. [Deuteronomy 4:32–33]

It should be asked how we are to understand the statement: “Question the former days, which were before you, from the day when God created man upon the earth, and from one end of heaven to the other.”

The word “question” is understood from the preceding clause. The passage seems to signify the whole inhabited world. But why it says “from one end of heaven to the other,” rather than “from one end of the earth to the other,” is not easy to determine.

A similar expression occurs in the Gospel, where the Lord says that his elect “will be gathered from the ends of the heavens to their boundaries” (Matthew 24:31).

Unless perhaps Scripture does not mean that this was heard either among human beings or among angels, but wishes to emphasize as unique what happened among this people. For it continues:

“If anything has ever happened according to this great word, or if anything like this has ever been heard: whether a nation has heard the voice of the living God speaking from the midst of the fire, as you heard it, and lived?”

[Note: The printed editions read “and saw.” The manuscripts read “and lived.” The same reading occurs in the Septuagint and the Vulgate.]

[Col. 0751]

If this is so, and the passage says that such a thing was heard neither among human beings nor among angels, what are we to make of the Gospel passage, “from the ends of the heavens to their boundaries,” since the Lord undoubtedly said this when speaking of the final gathering of his elect?

### IX. [Deuteronomy 5:2–4]

What does Moses mean when he says: “The Lord your God established a covenant with you at Horeb. The Lord did not establish this covenant with our fathers, but with you—all of you who are alive today. The Lord spoke with you face to face on the mountain from the midst of the fire”?

Is the reason that those who do not enter the promised land—for they all died—do not belong to this covenant, since they were counted at that time from the age of twenty years and upward, to fifty years, as fit for war?

How, then, did the Lord speak with those who are alive today? Perhaps because at that time there could have been many who were twenty years old or younger who remembered this well, since they were excluded from the punishment that God imposed upon those who were counted at that time, namely, that they should not enter the promised land.

Moses certainly calls those people “alive today” who, although they were not yet twenty years old or older when God spoke on the mountain and thus could not then be counted, might nevertheless have been nineteen years old or younger, down to an age still capable of seeing, hearing, and retaining in memory the things that were done and said.

But what does he mean by saying, “The Lord spoke with you face to face”?

[Note: Most manuscripts read “face to face” (*faciem ad faciem*), as does the Greek, πρόσωπον κατὰ πρόσωπον (*prosōpon kata prosōpon*).]

A little earlier, he had taken great care to remind them that they had seen no likeness, but had heard only a voice from the midst of the fire. Is he using these words because of the obviousness of the event and, so to speak, the presence of the divinity made manifest, about which no one could doubt?

If so, what prevents us from understanding the same thing concerning Moses, where it is said that the Lord spoke with him “face to face” (Exodus 33:11), so that even Moses himself saw nothing with his eyes except the fire?

Or is he understood to have seen something more because it is written that he entered the cloud or mist where God was (Exodus 24:18)? Even if he saw something more than they did, however, those words do not allow us to understand that he saw God’s substance with mortal eyes, since he said to God: “If I have found favor before you, show yourself to me, so that I may see you knowingly” (Exodus 33:15).

Nor should we suppose that this people, to whom Moses was speaking, saw God “face to face” when he spoke on the mountain from the midst of the fire in the same way that the Apostle says we shall see him at the end, where he says: “Now we see through a mirror in a mystery, but then face to face.” He then explained what this would be and how great it would be by adding: “Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

This statement too must be understood carefully, lest anyone suppose that human beings will possess as much knowledge of God as God now possesses of human beings. Rather, they will possess knowledge perfect in its own measure, so that nothing further will be expected to be added to it. Just as God now knows human beings perfectly, yet as God knows human beings, so then human beings will know God perfectly, yet as human beings know God.

[Col. 0752]

For when it is said, “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48), we should not therefore hope for the equality with the Father that the only-begotten Word possesses. Some, nevertheless, have thought that even this will occur—unless perhaps we understand too poorly what they mean.

[Note: Compare Letter 92, section 5, and Letter 147, section 36.]

### X. [Deuteronomy 5:5–6, 24]

What does Moses mean when he says: “And I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce to you the words of the Lord,” as though the Lord were located in a particular place—that is, on the mountain from which they heard the voices?

This should be understood in such a way that we do not infer from it that God’s substance exists in any bodily place. God is wholly everywhere; he does not approach or withdraw through intervals of space. Rather, his manifestations are presented to human senses in the creature that is not what he himself is.

Therefore, the Lord wished to remove our minds from such suspicions, by which God is thought to be confined to some place, when he said:

“The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:21–24).

Moses therefore said that he stood in the middle, not between God’s substance and the people with some intervening distance in space, but because God was pleased to have the people hear the rest of his words through Moses after they had been greatly terrified by hearing the voice of God from the midst of the fire as he spoke the Decalogue of the Law.

The question rightly arises, however, how these words in Deuteronomy should be understood when Moses says: “And I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce to you the words of the Lord, because you feared before the fire and did not ascend the mountain,” followed by, “saying, ‘I am the Lord your God,’” and so forth—words that are already the words of God and that comprise the Decalogue.

What, then, is intended by the addition “saying”? If we take it as a hyperbaton, arranging the words as follows—“And I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce to you the words of the Lord, saying, ‘I am the Lord your God’”—the result will not be true. For the people did not hear these words through Moses, but from the midst of the fire. When they could not endure this after hearing the Decalogue, they asked to hear the rest through Moses.

It remains, therefore, to understand the word “saying” as standing for “when he said,” so that the sense is:

“And I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce to you the words of the Lord, because you feared before the fire and did not ascend the mountain, when he said, ‘I am the Lord your God.’”

That is, “when the Lord was saying” this. For when the Lord spoke these words, which Moses subsequently recalls one by one from the Decalogue, the people feared before the fire, did not ascend the mountain, and asked that they should hear the words of the Lord through Moses instead (Exodus 20:18–19).

[Col. 0753]

Moses recalls in Deuteronomy the words that the people then spoke to him when they no longer wished to hear the voice of God but asked that, through him, they should be told what God was saying:

“Behold, the Lord our God has shown us his glory, and we have heard his voice from the midst of the fire,” and so forth.

The same words are not found in Exodus, where the event is first narrated, exactly as they are repeated here. From this we should understand something I have already mentioned several times: it should not be counted as falsehood if the same intention is expressed in different words.

This is also evident in the words of the Evangelists, which the ignorant and contentious criticize as though they contradicted one another. For it would not have been difficult for Moses to pay attention to what he had written in Exodus and repeat it in exactly the same words, unless our holy teachers wished to suggest this very lesson to their students: that in the words of speakers they should seek nothing other than the intention for which the words were established and spoken.

### XI. [Deuteronomy 5:29]

What does Moses mean when he says that the Lord spoke to him concerning the Hebrew people: “Who will grant that their heart may be such within them that they fear me and keep my commandments”?

Does he now intend it to be understood that, by his grace, this benefit is granted so that the righteousness of God may exist in human beings through faith, rather than as their own righteousness, as though it came from the Law?

The prophet also signifies this when he says: “I will take away from them the heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26). This is said with reference to the faculty of sensation, which flesh possesses and stone does not, using the word figuratively.

The same is said elsewhere:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant that I established with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. For this is the covenant that I will establish with them after those days, says the Lord: I will give my laws into their heart, and I will write them upon their mind, and I will no longer remember their iniquities and their sins” (Jeremiah 31:31–34).

This distinguishes the New Testament from the Old: in the Old, the Law was given on tablets of stone; in the New, it is given in hearts, which happens through grace.

Thus the Apostle also says, “Not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts”; and elsewhere: “He made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of writing but of spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:3, 6).

[Note: The manuscripts of the best quality, in agreement with the Greek of the Apostle, read “not of writing but of spirit” (*ou grammatos, alla pneumatos*). The printed editions read “not of the letter but by the spirit.”]

### XII. [Deuteronomy 6:13]

When Scripture says of the Lord, “And you shall swear by his name,” this command should not be understood as though it ordered people to swear. Rather, it prohibited swearing by the name of any other god.

It is better, however, if, according to the Gospel, you do not swear at all (Matthew 5:34)—not because a true oath is evil, but lest the ease of swearing lead to perjury. A person who swears can swear not only truthfully but also falsely; someone who does not swear at all keeps far away from perjury.

### XIII. [Deuteronomy 8:2]

“And you shall remember the whole way by which the Lord your God led you in the wilderness, in order to afflict you, test you, and make known what was in your heart, whether you would observe his commandments or not.”

[Note: The printed editions read “the way through which.” The word “through” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek Septuagint.]

[Col. 0754]

Here it is stated more clearly what elsewhere is expressed through an obscure form of speech, where we read: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13:3).

The expression “to know” is understood as standing for “to make known.” This is stated plainly here: “to test you and make known what was in your heart.” For it does not say “and know,” which, had it said that, would nevertheless have to be understood as “make known.”

### XIV. [Book IX, 6–8]

“And know today that it is not on account of your righteousnesses that the Lord your God is giving you this good land to inherit, for you are a stiff-necked people.” Surely these are the people who for that reason did not deserve to perish in the wilderness, because they did not know the right hand or the left [Note: [Col. 0754] The manuscripts here and below read “the right and the left,” that is, “good and evil,” as is found in Num. 14:23 and Deut. 1:39]; yet now they are called stiff-necked. Therefore we must see that this was said sacramentally, not because their merits had been commended.

For lest anyone suppose that those who had previously deserved praise suddenly became blameworthy, a little later they are told: “Remember; do not forget how greatly you provoked the Lord your God in the wilderness; from the day when you came out [Note: [Col. 0754] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The printed editions, except Rat., continue with singular forms: “you came out, you came, you persisted in unbelief”; and shortly afterward, “you provoked.”] from the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you persisted in unbelief toward the Lord.” But even if some of them were of this character while others were faithful and good, the land of promise is nevertheless not given to those who do not know the right hand or the left, as though we were to understand that they had not offended God.

Their fathers too, who died and were not permitted to enter that same land, are found to have included some who were good. For this reason the Apostle says that not all of them, but some, offended, and in these he recalls their sins (1 Cor. 10:5–10). This Scripture of Deuteronomy also teaches more clearly that these people were like their fathers, when it subsequently adds: “And at Horeb you provoked the Lord.” Certainly those who provoked him there were the ones who, on account of those same evil merits, were not brought into the land of promise.

### XV. [Book X, 1–4]

“At that time the Lord said to me: ‘Cut for yourself two stone tablets like the first ones, and go up to me on the mountain; and make yourself a wooden ark. I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke, and you shall put them into the ark.’ And I made an ark of imperishable wood, and cut two stone tablets like the first ones, and went up the mountain, with the two tablets in my two hands. And he wrote on the tablets, according to the former writing, the ten words that the Lord spoke to you on the mountain from the midst of the fire; and the Lord gave them to me.”

It is not without reason that the question is asked how these things can be said in Deuteronomy, where Moses recalls and repeats what happened, when in Exodus, where these words and events are first narrated, it is written as follows: “And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Write these words for yourself, for in accordance with these words I have established a covenant with you and Israel.’ And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water; and he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words.” Since Exodus therefore says that Moses himself wrote the ten words of the Law on the tablets, how is it that here in Deuteronomy God is recalled as having written those same words on the tablets?

Finally, when we briefly treated the matter in Exodus and committed to writing what seemed to us concerning this difference, we said that the two Testaments were signified by the distinction whereby the first tablets, which were broken, are reported to have been written by the finger of God, whereas Moses is said to have written the second tablets, which were to remain for so long in the ark and the tabernacle. Thus, in the Old Testament the Law was commended as the work of God, in which man had done nothing, because the Law could not be fulfilled through fear; for when the work of the Law is truly done, it is done through love, not fear, and this love is the grace of the New Testament. Therefore, in the second tablets man is read to have written the words of God, because through the love of righteousness man can do the work of the Law, which he cannot do through fear of punishment (Book of Questions on Exodus, question 166).

Now, however, when in Deuteronomy we read the following concerning the second tablets: “And I cut two stone tablets like the first ones, and went up the mountain, with the two tablets in my two hands. And he wrote on the tablets, according to the former writing, the ten words”—for it does not say, “And I wrote,” but “he wrote,” that is, God, just as shortly before it had said that the words of God were spoken to Moses: “Cut for yourself two stone tablets like the first ones, and go up to me on the mountain; and make yourself a wooden ark; and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets”—a question arises that must be examined: here God is read as having written both sets of tablets, the first and the second, not man.

But if in Exodus too the words of God are read in the passage where he commands Moses to cut out the second tablets, nothing else is found than that God himself promised that he would write those same words.
