For it is written as follows: “And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Cut for yourself two stone tablets like the first ones, and go up to me on the mountain; and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.’”

Apart from the book of Deuteronomy, therefore, Exodus alone contains this question: how could God say, “I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets,” when shortly afterward we read: “Write these words for yourself, for in accordance with these words I have established a covenant with you and Israel. And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water; and he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words” (Exod. 34:1, 27–28)?

For if what was said earlier—“Write these words for yourself, for in accordance with these words I have established a covenant with you and Israel”—refers to what precedes it, which God commanded in such a way that the words were not to be written on two stone tablets but in that book of the Law in which many things were written, then surely what follows—“And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water; and he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words”—makes it sufficiently clear that Moses himself wrote these ten words on the tablets, not God.

Unless, perhaps, we are compelled by a forceful but unavoidable interpretation, where it says, “And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words,” to understand not Moses implicitly but the Lord. For it has been stated above, “And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord”; thus these ten words may be understood to have been written on the tablets by the Lord, in whose presence Moses was, while he neither ate bread nor drank water for forty days and forty nights, just as the Lord had promised earlier.

But if this is so, the distinction between the two Testaments that seemed to us to be commended in these words cannot in fact be commended, since both the first and the second tablets were written by God, not man. Nevertheless, that difference certainly remains beyond doubt: God both made and wrote the first tablets. For it was not then said to Moses, “Cut for yourself two tablets,” but rather we read: “And Moses turned and descended from the mountain, and the two tablets of the testimony were in his hands. The tablets were stone, written on both sides; on this side and on that side they were written. And the tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets” (Exod. 32:15–16).

Earlier he had already said that these same tablets were written by the finger of God, speaking as follows: “And he gave Moses, as soon as he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone written by the finger of God” (Exod. 31:18). Thus there the tablets were the work of God, and their writing was made by the finger of God.

But Moses himself is commanded to cut out the second tablets, so that these at least may be understood to have been cut out by human work, although God himself wrote on them, just as he promised when he commanded them to be cut out.

Moreover, if we attend more carefully, both statements were made concerning the second tablets because God, through his grace, performs the work of the Law in man, while man, receiving God’s grace through his faith and belonging to the New Testament, cooperates with the God who assists him. In the first tablets only the work of God is mentioned because “the Law is spiritual,” and “the Law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (Rom. 7:12). No work of man is mentioned there because unbelievers do not conform themselves to the assistance of grace; rather, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3). Thus the Law serves for their condemnation, which the breaking of the tablets signifies.

We are therefore not compelled by a forced interpretation to understand that God wrote where Scripture says: “And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water, and he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant.” The wording strongly indicates that Moses wrote.

But God earlier promised that he would write, and in Deuteronomy he is narrated not only as having made this promise but also as having written, in order to signify what the Apostle says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13). This applies to those who receive grace through faith and do not seek to establish their own righteousness, but submit to the righteousness of God, so that they may be the righteousness of God in Christ.

The Apostle also says both things there: that God works and that they themselves work. For if they themselves were not working, how could he say to them, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12–13)? He works, therefore, and we cooperate; he does not remove the freedom of a good will, but assists it.

### XVI. [Book X, 8–9]

“At that time the Lord set apart the tribe of Levi, to carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord, to stand before the Lord, to minister, and to pray in his name, until this day. For this reason Levi has no portion or inheritance with his brothers; the Lord himself is his portion, as he said to him.”

Unless this tribe signified the entire royal priesthood belonging to the New Testament, a man who was not of that tribe would never have dared to say, “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 72:26), and in another psalm, “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15:5).

### XVII. [Book XI, 20]

What does Moses mean when, commending the words of the Lord, he commands and says, “You shall write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates,” when no Israelite is either remembered or read to have done this literally? For no one could do so unless, perhaps, he divided the words into many parts throughout his house. Is this a hyperbolic form of exhortation, as many things are said?

### XVIII. [Book XII, 11]

It must be asked how he commands that the tithes of all produce and the firstborn of cattle are not to be eaten except in the city where the temple will be, when in the Law he commanded that they be given to the Levites.

### XIX. [Book XIII, 1 and 3]

“But if a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or wonder, and the sign or wonder that he spoke to you comes to pass, saying, ‘Let us go and serve other gods whom you do not know,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams, for the Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul.”

Some Latin translators did not render this as “to know whether you love,” but as “so that he may know whether you love.” Although the meaning seems the same, the expression “to know” more readily refers to the people themselves. Thus we may understand “he tests you to know” as if it said, “by testing you, he makes you know.”

Here he clearly wished it to be understood that even those things spoken by diviners contrary to God, if what they say should happen, are not to be accepted in such a way that what they command is done or what they worship is worshiped. Nor does God show that these events occur outside his power. Rather, as though someone had asked why he permits them, he explained that their purpose is testing: to discover whether they love their God, though this knowledge is for them rather than for him, who knows all things before they happen.

### XX. [Book XIV, 28–29, and XV, 1]

“After three years you shall bring out every tithe of your produce, and in that year you shall place it in your cities. And the Levite shall come, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow who are in your cities; and they shall eat and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works that you do.”

Concerning this tithe he did not say that the offerer himself should eat it with his household—and consequently he commanded it to be spent on the Levites, resident aliens, orphans, and widows. But the wording is obscure because this tithe is not distinguished from the one that he wanted to be eaten with the Levites in the place that the Lord had chosen for his temple [Note: [Col. 0758] The printed editions and two manuscripts read “at the time.” The other manuscripts read “in the temple.”]

In the interpretation derived from the Hebrew, however, we find this distinction expressed more clearly. It says: “In the third year you shall separate another tithe from all that is produced for you at that time, and you shall store it within your gates. And the Levite shall come, who has no other portion or possession with you, and the stranger, the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates; and they shall eat and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands that you do.”

First, the statement “In the third year” is clearer; it is understood to mean after one intervening year. In the Septuagint, however, because it says “after three years,” it is uncertain whether the intervening years are intended, so that this would occur every fifth year.

Then, by saying “you shall separate another tithe,” he sufficiently shows that this is distinct from the tithe that he wanted the offerer himself to eat with his household and the Levites in the place that the Lord had chosen. This “other” tithe [Note: [Col. 0758] Am., Er., and Lov. read “and another.” The conjunction is absent from the manuscripts and from the Ratisbon edition.] he also commanded him to place within his gates, not to carry it to the place where the Lord wished himself to be invoked.

“And the Levite shall come,” he says, “who has no portion or possession with you, and the stranger, the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates, and they shall eat.” From this it is plainly evident that God did not wish this tithe to be held in common by the one who offered it and those for whom it was intended; rather, he commanded it to be distributed only to those who had nothing else, among whom he placed the Levite especially.

“After seven years you shall make a remission.” Here it is certainly shown how he also said above, “After three years.” For he did not intend these seven years to be intervening years either; he commanded it to be done every year, as though it were a sabbatical observance of years.

### XXI. [Book XV, 9]

“Take heed to yourself, lest there be a secret word in your heart, an iniquity saying, ‘The seventh year, the year of remission, is approaching,’ and your eye become evil toward your needy brother, and you do not give to him; and he will cry out against you to the Lord, and there will be great sin in you.”

He very appropriately called this a secret word, since no one who has been able to think it dares to say that a loan should not be given to a needy person because the year of remission is approaching, when God, out of mercy, commanded both that a loan be made whenever someone is in need and that it be remitted in the year of remission.

How, then, will he mercifully remit it in the year when it ought to be remitted, if he cruelly thinks that it ought not to be given at the time when it ought to be given?

### XXII. [Book XV, 12]

“But if your Hebrew brother or Hebrew sister is sold to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh you shall set him free from yourself.”

He did not intend these purchased slaves to be released in the year of remission, which every seventh year was to be observed by all, but in the seventh year of their purchase, whenever that seventh year of theirs occurred.

### XXIII. [Book XV, 19]

“Every firstborn that is born among your cattle and among your sheep, the male [Note: [Col. 0759] The printed editions read “the male one.” The manuscripts, together with the Greek, read “male.”] you shall sanctify to the Lord your God.”

It must be asked whether the things called in Greek *πρωτότοκα* (*prōtótoka*), which could only be rendered in Latin as *primogenita* (“firstborn”), are to be understood only of those born from mothers. For these are properly said to be brought forth rather than begotten. To bring forth is *τίκτειν* (*tíktein*), which is from a female, and from this *πρωτότοκον* (*prōtótokon*) is derived. To beget, however, is *γεννᾷν* (*gennân*), from which the Latin *primogenitus* (“first-begotten”) is properly derived.

The firstlings, that is, those brought forth first, were given from females; they were not those first begotten by males, if, for example, they were begotten from widows who had already borne children. Otherwise they would not be those that opened the womb, which the Law wished to be the defining characteristic of what was owed to the Lord as firstborn.

If, therefore, there is a definite distinction in these words, it is not without reason that the Lord is not called by the Father *μονότοκος* (*monótokos*), but *μονογενής* (*monogenḗs*), that is, “only-begotten,” meaning “unique.” From the dead, however, he is called *primogenitus* in Latin, “firstborn,” because the Latin word could not be formed in accordance with ordinary usage in another way; in Greek he is called *πρωτότοκος* (*prōtótokos*), not *πρωτογενής* (*prōtogenḗs*), as though the Father had begotten one equal to himself, while creation had brought him forth.

Likewise, what is said, “the firstborn of every creature” (Col. 1:15, 18), where the Greek reads *πρωτότοκος*, can be understood in relation to the new creation, of which the Apostle says, “If therefore anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation” (2 Cor. 5:17). He is the firstling of this creation because he rose first in such a way that he would no longer die and death would no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9). This is what is promised at the end concerning the new creation that is in him.

But this distinction should not be asserted rashly; it must be investigated more carefully in the Scriptures. For it raises the question how it could be said in Proverbs, “Firstborn, I say to you, son” (among the Septuagint, Prov. 24 or 31)—that is, from whose person the statement is to be understood.

For if it is spoken from the person of God the Father to Christ—though it is hardly possible to assert that the following context agrees with this—then it calls the same one both firstborn and only-begotten: firstborn because we too are sons of God, but only-begotten because he alone is of the substance of the Father and is equal and coeternal with the Father.

It is remarkable whether Sacred Scripture distinguishes “to bring forth” and “to beget” by unmistakably clear evidence.

### XXIV. [Book XVI, 2]

“And you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, sheep and cattle.”

What does the addition of “cattle” mean, when he commended the Passover sacrifice only from a sheep, which he commanded to be taken from sheep and goats or from kids? This is understood mystically on account of Christ, whose fleshly origin is from the righteous and from sinners.

For he did not say, “from sheep or goats,” although strictly speaking a sheep cannot be understood to come from goats. Rather, lest the Jews perhaps say that a goat should be understood if it had been said, “or from goats,” it was said, “from sheep and goats” (Exod. 12:5).

What, then, do cattle mean here? Is it on account of the other sacrifices that were to be offered on those days of Unleavened Bread?

### XXV. [Book XVI, 9–11]

It must be asked how he commanded the following to be observed: “You shall count seven complete weeks for yourself, beginning when you put the sickle to the standing grain; you shall begin to count seven weeks, and you shall celebrate the feast of weeks to the Lord your God according to what your hand can provide, whatever the Lord your God gives you, according to how the Lord your God blesses you; and you shall feast before the Lord your God.”

For if this Pentecost was commanded to be observed by the whole people, are we to believe that everyone was commanded to put the sickle into the harvest on the same day? But if each person observes this fiftieth day for himself, counting from the day on which he puts the sickle to the grain, then it is not one and the same day for the whole people. The one day, however, is that counted from the sacrifice of the Passover to the day on which the Law was given on Sinai.

### XXVI. [Book XVII, 14–15]

“But when you enter the land that the Lord your God is giving you as a possession, and inherit it and dwell in it, and say, ‘I will set a ruler over me, like all the other nations that are around me,’ you shall certainly set over yourself the ruler whom the Lord your God chooses. You shall set over yourself a ruler from among your brothers; you may not set over yourself a foreigner, who is not your brother.”

It may be asked why the people displeased God when they desired a king (1 Sam. 8:7), when here this is found to be permitted. Rather, this should be understood to mean that it was not according to God’s will, since he did not command it to be done but permitted it to those who desired it.

Nevertheless, he commanded that the king not be a foreigner but a brother, that is, a native of the same people, not an alien. When he says, “you may not,” this should be understood as “you must not.”

### XXVII. [Book XVII, 17]

Speaking about the king, he said: “He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away; and he shall not greatly multiply silver and gold for himself.”

Hence it is asked whether David acted contrary to this command, for he did not have only one wife (2 Sam. 5:13). In Solomon’s case it is clear that he transgressed this command, both with respect to women and with respect to gold and silver.

Rather, the passage should be understood to have permitted kings to have more than one wife, while forbidding them to multiply them. This prohibition is not transgressed if they are few, as they were in David’s case, but it is transgressed if they are many, as in Solomon’s case.

Although when he added, “lest his heart turn away,” he seems especially to have commanded that the king not multiply wives to the point of turning to foreign women. Through these women Solomon’s heart was turned away from God (1 Kings 11:1–4).

Nevertheless, multiplication in general was prohibited in such a way that even if he had multiplied wives from Hebrew women alone, he could rightly be accused of acting contrary to this command.

### XXVIII. [Book XVIII, 6–8]

“But if a Levite comes from one of your cities, from anywhere among the children of Israel where he dwells, according to the desire of his soul, to the place that the Lord will choose—that is, if he desires to go to the place where the Lord is invoked—and ministers in the name of the Lord his God, as all his fellow Levites do who stand there before the Lord, he shall eat an equal portion, apart from the sale according to the family.”

What sale he means is obscure. Perhaps it is because he commanded that tithes and firstborn animals be sold by those who lived far away, so that they would not be compelled to carry many things to the place of the Lord’s invocation or to lead the animals there, only to purchase them again there for the same price. He had also commanded that the Levite who remained in the city from which those tithes and firstborn animals were owed should have a portion there.

For this reason he said that this was owed to the Levite “according to the family,” since, by the succession through which he succeeds his parents, what was provided for his parents ought to be maintained in his case.

### XXIX. [Book XVIII, 11]

Since he forbids observers of omens to exist among the people of God, it must be asked how these omens, whose observation is forbidden, are distinguished from those given divinely in such a way that what they signify ought to be explained.

Examples include all the miracles found in Scripture that signify something belonging to the rule of faith. Thus we explain what was signified by the fleece that was dry while the threshing floor was wet, or wet while the threshing floor was dry [Judg. 6:37–40], or by Aaron’s rod that blossomed (Num. 17:8) and produced almonds, and other things of this kind.

Just as the divinations that he subsequently forbids are distinguished from the predictions or proclamations of the Prophets, so the observation of omens must be distinguished from the signs of divine miracles.

### XXX. [Book XX, 4]

“For the Lord your God, who goes before you, will himself fight together with you against your enemies and save you.”

Here we see how, in spiritual conflicts as well, God’s assistance must be hoped for and requested—not so that we do nothing, but so that, having been helped, we cooperate with him. For he says, “he will fight together with you,” thereby showing that they themselves would also do what had to be done.

### XXXI. [Book XX, 5–7]

“And the scribes shall speak to the people, saying: ‘Who is the man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man dedicate it. And who is the man who has planted a vineyard and has not enjoyed its produce? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man enjoy it. And who is the man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man take her.’”

These words may seem troubling, as though those who have already dedicated their buildings, already eaten the produce of their newly planted vines, and already taken their betrothed wives die in battle under better conditions than those who have not yet done so.

But since human affection is bound up with these things and people value them highly, the words should be understood as being addressed to those going out to war so that anyone whose heart is attached to these things may appear when he returns, lest he act less bravely because he fears dying before dedicating his house, drinking from his new vineyard, or taking his betrothed wife.

For certainly, as far as the woman is concerned, it is better for another man to marry her while she is untouched than as a widow. But these provisions, as I said, were established to test the courage of the men.

### XXXII. [Book XXII, 5]

“Men’s vessels shall not be upon a woman.”

He wants “vessels” to be understood as weapons, that is, arms. Some have interpreted it in this way as well.

### XXXIII. [Book XXII, 13–21]

“But if a man takes a wife and lives with her, and hates her, and brings charges against her, and gives her a bad name, and says, ‘I took this woman as my wife, and when I approached her I did not find her signs of virginity,’ then the girl’s father and mother shall bring the girl’s signs of virginity to the elders at the gate, and the girl’s father shall say to the elders, ‘I gave my daughter to this man as a wife, and because he hates her he is now bringing charges against her, saying, “I did not find the signs of virginity in your daughter.” But here are the signs of my daughter’s virginity.’ And they shall spread the garment before the elders of that city. Then the elders of that city shall take the man, chastise him, fine him one hundred shekels, and give them to the girl’s father, because he has brought a bad name upon an Israelite virgin; and she shall remain his wife, and he may not dismiss her for all time.

“But if this charge is true, and the signs of virginity are not found in the girl, they shall bring the young woman to the door of her father’s house, and the men of her city shall stone her with stones, and she shall die, because she has committed a disgraceful act in Israel by prostituting her father’s house; and you shall remove the evil from among yourselves.”

This makes sufficiently clear how the Law wished wives to be subject to their husbands and almost to be their servants. When a husband brought against his wife testimony by which she would be stoned if it were proved true, he himself nevertheless was not stoned if it was established that the charge was false. Instead, he was merely chastised and fined, and he was commanded to remain permanently attached to the woman of whom he had wished to rid himself.

In other cases, however, the man who harmed someone by false testimony is commanded to suffer the same punishment that the person he harmed would have suffered if the accusation had been true—when that person, if the accusation were proved, was to be put to death.

### XXXIV. [Book XXII, 28–29, 19]

“But if someone finds a virgin girl who is not betrothed, and by force lies with her, and they are discovered, the man who lay with her shall give the girl’s father fifty didrachmas of silver [Note: [Col. 0762] The printed editions read “fifty didrachmata.” Some manuscripts, as in the Greek, read “didrachma.” Others read “didrachmas.”], and she shall be his wife, because he humbled her; he may not dismiss her for all time.”

It is rightly asked whether the penalty is that he may not dismiss for all time the woman whom he violated in a disorderly and unlawful manner.

For if we wish to understand that she cannot—that is, ought not to—be dismissed for all time because she has become his wife, we are confronted by the fact that Moses permitted a man to give a bill of divorce and dismiss his wife (Deut. 24:1).

But in the case of those who unlawfully violate women, he did not wish this to be permitted, lest the man appear to have acted in mockery and to have pretended that he had taken her as his wife rather than to have taken her in truth and with proper consent.

The same command was given concerning the woman whose husband had falsely accused her of lacking the signs of virginity.

### XXXV. [Book XXIII, 3–4]

“No Ammonite or Moabite shall enter the assembly of the Lord; even to the tenth generation they shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, and not even forever.”

The question is how Ruth, who was a Moabite (Ruth 1:22), entered it, especially since the fleshly origin of the Lord also derives from her (Matt. 1:5).

Perhaps this prophetically signified that she would enter after the tenth generation, as the passage says. The generations are counted from Abraham, at whose time Lot was also living, and Lot begot the Moabites and Ammonites from his daughters (Gen. 19:37–38). Counting Abraham himself, ten generations are found to extend to Salmon, who begot Boaz, Ruth’s second husband.

They are Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, Aram, Amminadab, Nahshon, and Salmon. Salmon begot Boaz, who took the widow Ruth as his wife. Accordingly, it appears that after the tenth generation she produced offspring for the assembly of the Lord by bearing children to Boaz.

But why “and not even forever” was added remains rightly an additional question. Is it because thereafter no person from the Ammonites or Moabites entered that assembly of the Hebrew people, after this prophecy was fulfilled in the tenth generation?

Or was it rather said, “even to the tenth generation,” in such a way that he intended this always to be understood through a certain totality represented by the number ten, and that he explained this in a manner by adding, “and not even forever”? If so, Ruth appears to have been admitted contrary to the forbidden command.

Or did he prohibit Ammonite men, not Ammonite women—that is, men from that people, not women? This is especially possible because when the Israelites overthrew that nation, they were commanded to kill all the men but not the women, except those who had known sexual intercourse with a man (Num. 31:17–18), since they had seduced the people into fornication. They wished the virgins to be spared, not imputing to them the guilt for which that nation deserved to be destroyed.

This guilt was also mentioned here, as though someone might ask why he did not wish Moabites and Ammonites to be admitted into the assembly of the Lord. He added: “Because they did not meet you with bread and water on the way when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired Balaam son of Beor from Mesopotamia against you, to curse you.”

They did not impute these faults to the women even when that nation was conquered, for they preferred to preserve them alive.

### XXXVI. [Book XXIII, 15–16]

“You shall not hand over to his master a slave who has attached himself to you from his master.”

This does not mean that his master had attached him—that is, entrusted him—to you; for in that case the text would more properly say “deposited.” Rather, it says that he was attached to you by his master, that is, joined to this man after departing from him. Therefore, it prohibited not receiving but returning fugitives.

This might be supposed if we understood the command as addressed to one individual. But it is addressed to a nation and people. Therefore he prohibited a man who had fled from one nation to the nation to which he was speaking from being returned to his master, that is, to his king.

King Achish of Gath also observed this rule when David fled to him from the face of his master, that is, King Saul (1 Sam. 21:10).

The passage explains this most plainly when it says concerning the fugitive himself: “He shall dwell among you, in whatever place he chooses.”

### XXXVII. [Book XXIII, 17]

“There shall not be a prostitute among the daughters of Israel, and there shall not be a fornicator among the sons of Israel.”

Here he clearly prohibited both men and women from fornication, even with persons who were not married to someone else. He demonstrated that it is a sin to have intercourse with those who are not one’s spouses, since he prohibits both women from being prostitutes and men from approaching prostitutes, whose shameful conduct is publicly for sale.

In the Decalogue, however, he does not seem to have openly prohibited this under the name of adultery, since *moechia* is ordinarily understood to mean nothing other than adultery. We discussed what seemed to us concerning that passage elsewhere (Questions on Exodus, question 71).

### XXXVIII. [Book XXIII, 18, 17]

“You shall not offer the wages of a prostitute, nor an exchange for a dog, in the house of the Lord your God for any vow, because both are an abomination to the Lord your God.”

This should be understood as meaning: “because it is an abomination to the Lord your God, both this and that,” that is, not merely one of these things but both.

Concerning the dog, he forbids the exchange of firstborn animals to be made with it, although he commands such an exchange to be made with other unclean animals, namely horses and donkeys, and with whatever other animals assist human beings and are called in Latin *jumenta* from *juvare*, “to help.”

He did not wish this to be done with a dog. It must be asked whether he also prohibited it with a pig, and why he did so. If he prohibited it with all such animals, why did he single out the dog in this passage? [Note: [Col. 0764] The printed editions read “he wished.” We restore “he did not wish” from five manuscripts of better quality.]

As for the wages of a prostitute, the reason for mentioning them seems to be that he had earlier prohibited a woman from Israel from being a prostitute or any Israelite man from using a prostitute. Lest the thought arise that this sin could be expiated if something derived from it were offered in the temple, it had to be stated that it is an abomination to the Lord.

### XXXIX. [Ib. XXIV, 7.]

“That thief shall die,” that is, the one who has stolen a person; “and you shall remove the evil one from among yourselves.” Scripture says this repeatedly when it commands that wicked people be put to death. The Apostle also used this expression when he said: “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Is it not those who are within whom you judge? Remove the evil one from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:12–13).

For the Greek has τὸν πονηρόν, which is also written here; this is usually translated “the malignant one” rather than “the evil.” Nor does it say τὸ πονηρόν, that is, “this evil thing,” but τὸν πονηρόν, which means “this malignant person.” From this it is evident that he intended the one who had committed something such as to deserve excommunication. For excommunication now accomplishes in the Church what execution accomplished then.

The apostolic passage can nevertheless be understood in another way: each person is commanded to remove evil, or the malignant one, from himself. This interpretation would be more acceptable if the Greek had τὸ πονηρόν, “this evil thing,” or “this malignant thing,” rather than τὸν πονηρόν, “this malignant person.” As it stands, however, it is more credible that the reference is to a person than to a vice.

Yet it can also be elegantly understood as a command that a person remove an evil person from himself, just as it is said, “Put off the old person.” Explaining this, he says, “Let the one who was stealing steal no longer” (Eph. 4:22, 28).

### XL. [Ib. XXIV, 8.]

“According to every law concerning which the Levitical priests shall instruct you.” Here it appears that every priest was a Levite, although not every Levite was a priest.

### XLI. [Ib. XXIV, 10–13.]

“If your neighbor owes you any debt, whatever debt it may be, you shall not enter his house to take a pledge. You shall stand outside, and the man who owes you shall bring the pledge outside to you.” But if the man is needy, you shall not sleep in his pledge; at sunset you shall surely return his garment to him, and he shall sleep in his garment, and he shall bless you, and it shall be mercy for you before the Lord your God.”

It is not without reason that this seems to pertain to the work of mercy: the one taking a pledge is not to enter the house, lest the debtor be thrown into confusion. Yet by this very command the debtor is also admonished to bring the pledge outside to the creditor.

But when he commands that the pledge be returned to the needy person on that same day, so that one who has no other place to sleep may sleep in it, it reasonably prompts the question why he did not instead command the creditor not to take the pledge that he would have to return that same day. If this was intended to compel the debtor, how would it urge him to repay, when he knew that he would recover the pledge on the same day?

Or perhaps he wished this to be done as a reminder, so that the debtor may not forget to repay, and then fail to repay if he truly has nothing—especially since he is overcome by the mercy of his creditor, to whom he ought not to be ungrateful if he receives back the pledge in which he can sleep. At the same time, if the debtor does not repay, the creditor ought to believe that he lacks the means, since he needs this further mercy: the pledge is returned to him precisely because he has nothing else in which to sleep.

### XLII. [Ib. XXIV, 16.]

“Fathers shall not be put to death for their sons, nor sons for their fathers: each person shall die for his own sin.”

Behold, not only did the Prophets say this (Ezek. 18:17), but the Law also says that each person is to be put to death for his own fault, not for that of his father or his son. What, then, is meant by the statement elsewhere that God “repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons, to the third and fourth generation”?

Is this understood of sons not yet born, because of original sin, which the human race also drew from Adam, while here the distinction concerns sons already born, so that each person dies in his own sin? For one who was already born does not derive anything from his father when his father sinned.

But since that other passage also says, “upon those who hate me” (Exod. 20:5), it is clear that this condition too can be changed if the children do not imitate the deeds of their parents. The consequence inherited from Adam is also repaid temporally, since all people die because of it; but it is not repaid eternally to those who have been spiritually reborn through grace and have remained in that state to the end.

Nevertheless, it is reasonable to ask: if the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the children who hate God, why “to the third and fourth generation”—either with the first and second omitted, or without the consequence continuing into all the remaining generations when impiety and imitation of wicked parents persist?

Or did he intend by this number, since it is understood as seven, to signify the whole? And for that reason did he not state the number seven itself by saying “to the seventh generation,” so that the whole might be understood, because in this way he indicated more clearly the reason for the perfection of that number?

It is called perfect because it consists of these two numbers: three, the first complete odd number, and four, the first complete even number. Hence I think that prophetic statement also has this meaning, which is frequently repeated: “For three transgressions and for four I will not turn away” (Amos 1:3). By this he intended all transgressions to be understood, rather than merely three or four.

### XLIII. [Ib. XXIV, 17.]

“You shall not pervert the judgment of the resident alien, the orphan, or the widow. You shall not take a widow’s garment as a pledge.”

Why does he not say, “You shall not take their garment as a pledge”? What reason is there for forbidding the judgment of all three to be perverted, while forbidding a garment to be taken as a pledge only from the widow and not from the others?

Unless it is because he commended the judgment of all three as requiring protection precisely because they have no one to defend them: the resident alien, because he is in a foreign land; the orphan, that is, the minor, because he lacks parents; and the widow, because she has no husband.

But when he forbids a widow’s garment to be taken as a pledge, I think he rather elegantly admonishes us that those should truly be called widows who are also poor. The Apostle clearly shows this when he says: “If any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to manage her own household piously and to repay the care owed to her parents, for this is acceptable before the Lord. But the widow who is truly a widow and desolate has placed her hope in God and continues in prayers night and day.” He called her truly a widow because she has no one to support her: she is deprived not only of a husband but also of descendants and every form of assistance. For he would not call a rich woman “desolate.”

Therefore a poor woman’s garment must not be taken as a pledge. Indeed, by forbidding the garment itself to be taken, he shows that she is poor. A creditor would surely prefer to take money, or something else, rather than a garment.

But suppose the thought occurs: What if she has many garments, not necessary ones but superfluous ones? How can she be understood to be truly a widow—that is, not only desolate but also one who does not live in luxury? He added this when he said, “But she who lives in luxury is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:4–6). He set her in opposition, as it were, to the true widow, as though such a woman were not a true widow.

Those who, although rich, have refused to enter another marriage are praised for their continence, not commended for desolation. They have been widowed only of their husbands, not of other resources.

**Editorial note:** The printed editions read “who lives in luxury,” omitting the negative particle that appears in the better manuscripts: “who does not live in luxury.”

### XLIV. [Ib. XXIV, 19.]

The command that, during the harvest, no one should gather a sheaf that has been forgotten, and that no one should go back to collect more carefully an olive or grape that has been left behind, says that these things are to be left for the needy. Perhaps the thought occurs: What if the things left by the owners of the fields are gathered not by the needy but by dishonest people?

First, we must consider that the person who leaves them does so mercifully, with the intention that the needy should have what is left. Then, when these commands are given to the people, those who are not in need are simultaneously admonished not to seek such things. If they do seek them, what else should they be judged to be invading than the property of others—and, more seriously, the property of the poor?

Thus both groups are addressed by these commands: those whose fields they are, so that they may leave the produce mercifully; and those who are not needy, so that they may abstain from it. Both are mentioned because the passage says both from whom the produce is to be left and for whom it is to be left.

**Editorial note:** Erasmus reads “are admonished” instead of “are reminded.”

### XLV. [Ib. XXV, 1–3.]

“But if there is a dispute between people, and they come to judgment, and they judge and declare the righteous person righteous”—the judges are to be understood as the ones who judge, not those who are said to be engaged in the dispute.

Then it continues: “And they condemn the wicked person. And if the one who acts wickedly is worthy of blows, you shall set him before the judges, and they shall beat him before them according to his wickedness. They shall beat him with forty lashes; they shall not add to them. But if they add more lashes beyond these blows, your brother will be disfigured before you.”

It must be observed very carefully that, although he commanded those sins to be corrected by blows which are not worthy of being punished by death—and by so few blows—he nevertheless called the person being beaten “wicked” or “one who acts wickedly.”

Thus we learn that Scripture did not speak as most people speak when they read it carelessly. They suppose that adultery is not impiety because the person who commits it seems to have sinned against a human being, even though the Law commands that this sin be punished by death (Deut. 22:22). Yet we call impieties more serious than these sins, although some impieties are punished by forty lashes.

There is therefore a lesser impiety, worthy of beating, and a more serious one, worthy of death. Likewise, among the sins that seem to be committed not against God but against a human being, some are worthy of death, while others are subject to correction, beating, or easier forgiveness. It is clear that the Seventy translators spoke in this way, since they called even the person worthy of blows “impious.”

**Editorial note:** The editions read “punishment,” but the manuscripts have “forgiveness.”

### XLVI. [Ib. XXV, 5.]

“But if brothers dwell together, and one of them dies without having a son, the wife of the deceased shall not marry outside the family to one who is not a near relative; the brother of her husband shall enter her, take her as his wife, and dwell with her. And whatever child is born shall be established under the name of the deceased, and his name shall not be erased from Israel.”

**Editorial note:** The printed editions read, “the wife of the deceased brother shall not marry another who approaches.” The text is corrected from the manuscripts and the Septuagint.

The Law appears to have commanded that a man take his brother’s wife for no other reason than to raise up offspring for a brother who died childless. When it says, “He shall be established under the name of the deceased, and his name shall not be erased from Israel,” that is, the name of the deceased, it seems to mean that the one who is born should be called by the name by which the deceased was called, and should in some way perpetuate him.

For this reason it seemed to us more appropriate, according to the custom of adoption, to resolve in the Gospel the question concerning Joseph’s two fathers (*On the Harmony of the Gospels* 2.3). Matthew mentions one, namely the one who begot Joseph (Matt. 1:16); Luke mentions another, whose son Joseph was (Luke 3:23). Neither of them, however, gave Joseph his own name.

**Editorial note:** Two Vatican manuscripts read, “whose son Joseph was not.”

Unless perhaps the statement, “He shall be established under the name of the deceased,” does not mean that he is to receive the deceased’s name, but that, on the basis of his name—that is, as his son—he is to be established as heir, not of the one whose seed produced him but of the deceased for whom offspring was raised up.

The addition, “and his name shall not be erased from Israel,” can be understood not to mean that the child subsequently receives his name, but that the deceased will not appear to have died without descendants. Thus his name, that is, his memory, remains.

For even if he himself had begotten a son, he would not necessarily have given the son his own name so that his name would not be erased from Israel. Rather, his name would not be erased because he would have departed this life not without children. His brother is commanded to accomplish through the deceased man’s wife what the deceased himself could not.

Even if there had been no brother, a relative could marry the wife of a man who had died without children in order to raise up offspring for his brother. Thus Boaz took Ruth, so that he might raise up offspring for his relative, whose wife she had been and by whom she had borne no child. Yet the one born from her was established under the name of the deceased, because he was called his son; in this way the deceased’s name was not erased from Israel, although the child was not called by his name (Ruth 4:13–17).

## QUESTION CONCERNING JOSEPH’S TWO FATHERS

Matthew 2:16; Luke 3:23

Since this is so, the Gospel question can be resolved more fully in two ways. One of the men whom Matthew and Luke mention as different may have been related to the other in such a way that he took his wife, and therefore the two could have had different parents and ancestors extending upward.

For if they had been sons of brothers, they would have shared one grandfather. But that is not the case: according to Matthew, Mathan is Joseph’s grandfather, whereas according to Luke it is not Mathan but Mathath.

If someone thinks that the names are so similar that the scribes made an error in a single letter, producing such a small and almost negligible difference, what will he say about their fathers? According to Luke, Mathath was the son of Levi; according to Matthew, Mathan is found to have been descended from Eleazar. Thus, from that point upward, the fathers and grandfathers are different, and so are the ancestors all the way to Zerubbabel, who is approximately the twentieth ancestor upward from Joseph in Luke, but the eleventh in Matthew.

Zerubbabel is believed to be the same person in both genealogies because his father is found to be Salathiel in both Evangelists. Yet it could have happened that another man bore the same name and had a father of the same name, just as that other man did.

From that point upward they are again different: in Luke, Zerubbabel has a different grandfather, namely Neri; in Matthew, it is Jeconiah. From there upward there is no further agreement until David is reached—through Solomon in Matthew and through Nathan in Luke.

It seems most difficult to suppose that there was no nearer relative to take his brother’s wife than one who was related to David at so distant a degree, without being connected by some closer relationship below, since in Luke David is nearly the fortieth ancestor from Joseph, while in Matthew he is approximately the twenty-seventh.

Or, if relatives who were to take the wives of deceased men were sought even among those related through the female line, it could have happened that someone so closely related begot Joseph by the wife of a relative who had died childless. In this way Joseph would have had one father by nature and another according to the Law. Their fathers, grandfathers, and later ancestors would then show no relationship because the relationship would run not through males but through females.

Nevertheless, if that were the case, David would not at some point appear as one father in both genealogies.

Or if someone maintains that this could have happened, what shall we say about the fact that it is not the custom of Scripture to place women in genealogies in the position of men, just as no Evangelist inserted them? When mothers are mentioned, they are mentioned only together with fathers.

**Editorial note:** *Retractations* 2.55.3.

**Editorial note:** The printed editions read “from David”; “from” is to be deleted, as it is absent from the manuscripts.

Accordingly, either no closer relative was available to take the deceased man’s wife, so that the origin of the relationship had to be traced back to David; or adoption made one of the fathers whom Joseph could have.

### XLVII. [Ib. XXVI, 14.]

Among the things that a person is commanded to say when he has completed all the commandments concerning the giving of tithes and whatever else he has been ordered to give or expend, why is he also commanded to say, with praise and commendation of himself, “I have not given any of it to the dead”?

Does this forbid the funeral rites that the nations customarily observe?

### XLVIII. [Ib. XXVIII, 13–14.]

“You shall not depart from any of the words that I command you today, turning to the right or to the left, to go after foreign gods and serve them.”

**Editorial note:** The printed editions read “on the right”; “on” is absent from the manuscripts and the Septuagint.

The question can be raised how it can be understood as “turning to the right” when someone goes after foreign gods to serve them, since “the right” is used in a favorable sense, whereas this action can never be praiseworthy. For when the person who turns aside on the path of life to the right is censured, the things that are on the right are not being censured, but the one who turns toward them—that is, the one who arrogates to himself what belongs to God.

For this reason Proverbs says: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left; for he knows the ways that are on the right, but those on the left are perverse.” Thus the ways on the right are good, and the Lord knows them. “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous,” as it is written in the Psalm (Ps. 1:6).

Why, then, is it said, “Do not turn aside to the right”? The following words show this by adding, “For he himself will make your paths straight.” Far be it from us to deny that the right-hand ways known by the Lord are straight. Rather, as I said, to turn toward them means not to attribute what is right to God’s grace but to wish to claim it for oneself.

Finally, as I said, he adds: “For he himself will make your paths straight, and he will lead all your ways forward in peace” (Prov. 4:27).

Accordingly, the statement in this passage of Deuteronomy—“You shall not depart from any of the words that I command you today, turning to the right or to the left, to go after foreign gods and serve them”—does not mean that other gods can also be understood as being on the right. Rather, either earthly locations are indicated, because on both the right and the left there were nations worshiping other gods; or the words concerning the other gods should be pronounced separately, so that there are two meanings.

The first would be: “You shall not depart from any of the words that I command you today, to the right or to the left,” according to the interpretation explained above. The second would be: “To go after foreign gods and serve them,” with the words “You shall not depart from any of the words that I command you today” understood here as well.

If we wished to state the whole meaning, we would repeat the words common to both interpretations. Just as the passage says in the first instance, “You shall not depart from any of the words that I command you today, to the right or to the left,” so it would also say here: “You shall not depart from any of the words that I command you today, to go after foreign gods and serve them.”

For by departing from the words that have been commanded, a person also goes after foreign gods. The command is not only this one, nor does God wish people to depart only from the command not to go after foreign gods, but from all that he has commanded. Nevertheless, he wished to commend this particular matter separately after the general command by which he warned that one must not depart from any of his commandments.

**Editorial note:** These words—“so it would also say here: ‘You shall not depart from any of the words that I command you today’”—were missing here. We found them in the Sorbonic and Remigian manuscripts.

The phrase “to the right or to the left” can also be understood in this way: he commanded that one should not go after other gods either because of things sought for the sake of happiness or because of things avoided for the sake of unhappiness. That is, one must not seek help from other gods either for the things one loves or against the things one hates.

Or, at any rate, one must not worship them either to win their favor so that they may benefit one, or to appease them so that they may not cause harm.

For something similar is written in the Psalm: “Their mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” This is because they think that a person is made happy by things that both good and evil people can possess. Their right hand is therefore a right hand of iniquity, because those who regard it as a right hand are wicked.

It is not the true right hand, but the right hand of those whose mouth has spoken vanity. “They called the people blessed to whom these things belong,” whereas, as the Psalm immediately adds and teaches, “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. 143:8, 15). This is the true right hand, the right hand of righteousness, not of iniquity.

One must therefore not go after foreign gods, neither to the right, so that one may suppose that happiness comes from them, nor to the left, so that, supposing oneself made miserable by their opposition, one may worship them in order to turn them away.

Or, if we understand the right-hand things as eternal goods and the left-hand things as temporal goods, holy Scripture may be understood to warn here that they are not to be worshiped either for the sake of the former or for the sake of the latter.

**Editorial note:** The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have: “or as though they were consulted, that they might benefit.”

### XLIX. [Ib. XXIX, 1.]

“These are the words of the covenant that the Lord commanded Moses to establish with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant that he made with them at Horeb.”

This shows the origin of the name *Deuteronomy*, as though it were a second Law. It is more a repetition of the earlier Law than something else, for there are few things in it that are not contained in what was first given.

Yet these are not called two covenants, although the words may seem to say so. Both constitute one covenant, the one called the Old Covenant in the Church. For if these words required us to call them two covenants, there would already be more than two, apart from the New Covenant. Scripture speaks of a covenant in many places, such as the covenant made with Abraham concerning circumcision (Gen. 17:4), or the earlier one made with Noah (Gen. 9:9).

### L. [Ib. XXIX, 2–4.]

“And you saw everything that the Lord your God did in the land of Egypt before your eyes, against Pharaoh and all his servants and all his land: the great trials that your eyes saw, those great signs and wonders, and the mighty hand. Yet the Lord your God did not give you a heart to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear, until this day.”

How, then, did he say above, “You saw the great trials that your eyes saw,” if the Lord did not give them eyes to see or ears to hear? Unless it is because they saw with the body but did not see with the heart. For there are also said to be eyes of the heart. That is why he began with, “The Lord your God did not give you a heart to understand.”

The two expressions that follow—“eyes to see” and “ears to hear”—refer to understanding and obeying.

But when he says, “The Lord your God did not give you,” he would in no way have said this while rebuking and reproving them unless he intended it to be understood that this also pertained to their own guilt, so that no one might think himself excusable on this account.

At the same time, he shows both that without the help of the Lord God they cannot understand or obey with the eyes and ears of the heart, and that nevertheless, if God’s help is lacking, human fault is not thereby excusable, since God’s judgments, although hidden, are just.

### LI. [Ib. XXIX, 5–6.]

“And he led you for forty years in the wilderness. Your garments did not wear out, and your sandals were not worn away from your feet. You did not eat bread, and you did not drink wine or strong drink, so that you might know that he is the Lord your God.”

From this it appears that the Israelites were able to carry so much wine among their provisions when they departed from Egypt that they could consume it quickly. For if they had taken absolutely nothing with them, where would the wine have come from when it is said, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play”?

This could not have been said of water, since Moses’ own words make it perfectly clear that the sound was not the beginning of a battle but the beginning of wine (Exod. 32:6, 18).

### LII. [Ib. XXIX, 18–21.]

“Is there anyone among you, man or woman, family or tribe, whose mind has turned away from the Lord your God, to go and serve the gods of those nations? Is there among you a root sprouting upward in gall and bitterness?

**Editorial note:** The printed editions and most manuscripts read “or a servant”; a little later, “there is a wicked root in him.” Some better manuscripts restore this passage and bring it into agreement with the Septuagint. And when he hears the words of this curse, he will imagine in his heart, saying, ‘Let what is holy be mine, because I walk in the error of my heart,’ so that the sinner may not destroy together with himself the one who is without sin. The Lord will not be willing to show him mercy, but then the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will burn against that man, and all the curses of this covenant written in this book of the Law will cling to him.”

The wording “Is there anyone among you?” is expressed as though the speaker were searching to see whether such a person might perhaps exist.

If anyone did exist, he was strongly terrified, lest someone, hearing those curses, say in his heart, “Let what is holy be mine”—that is, “Let these curses be holy to me”—because “I walk in the error of my heart.” In other words: “May these things not happen to me; may these evils not be mine, but holy—that is, favorable and harmless—because I walk in the error of my heart,” going after the gods of the nations and serving them as though this could be done with impunity.

“No,” he says, “it will not be so. The sinner must not destroy together the one who is without sin,” as though he were saying: “Take care lest someone who thinks such things persuade any of you of them.”

God will not be willing to show mercy to either the one who thinks such things or the one to whom such things have been persuaded, as the person himself imagined when he said, “Let what is holy be mine,” attempting in this way to avert the force of the curse from himself.

But then the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will burn against that man, when he supposes that he can avert the curse by saying these things in his heart. “And all the curses of this covenant written in this book of the Law will cling to him.”

Not all of them can literally happen to one person, for no one can die as many times as there are kinds of death listed here. But he said “all” in the sense of “whatever ones may apply,” so that the person to whom some of the curses occur by which he perishes is not immune from all of them.

When he says, “So that the sinner may not destroy together the one who is without sin,” where the Greek has ἀναμάρτητον, “without sin,” this should not be understood as though he were speaking of someone completely cleansed and exempt from every sin. Rather, he means someone who was without that particular sin under discussion.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John 15:22). He does not mean every sin, but the sin by which they did not believe in him.

God also said to Abimelech concerning Sarah, Abraham’s wife, “I know that you did this with a pure heart” (Gen. 20:6). He did not mean that Abimelech’s heart was so pure that he was like those of whom it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Rather, his heart was pure from the particular sin in question, because, as far as he was concerned, he had not desired another man’s wife.

### LIII. [Ib. XXX, 6.]

“And the Lord will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, in order that you may live.”

This is an evident promise of grace. God promises that he will accomplish what he ordinarily commands to be done.

### LIV. [Ib. XXX, 11–14.]

“For this commandment that I command you today is not too difficult for you, nor is it far from you. It is not in heaven, so that you should say, ‘Who will ascend into heaven for us, take it for us, and, when we hear it, do it?’ Nor is it beyond the sea, so that you should say, ‘Who will cross the sea for us, take it for us, and, when we hear it, do it?’ The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart and in your hands, to do it.”

The Apostle says that this is the word of faith, which pertains to the New Covenant. But one may ask why the preceding passage calls those things commandments which are written in this book of the Law (Deut. 29:21), unless all those things signify spiritual realities pertaining to the New Covenant when they are rightly understood.

One may also ask why the Apostle rendered the phrase found here—“Nor is it beyond the sea, so that you should say, ‘Who will cross the sea for us and take it for us?’”—as “Or who will descend into the abyss?” He explains it by adding, “That is, to bring Christ back from the dead.”

This is because he called the whole of life in this age “the sea,” since it is crossed by death. In a certain sense, the sea comes to an end, and death itself is called “beyond the sea,” as though it lay beyond this life, which is signified by the name “sea.”

Furthermore, the words added here, “and in your hands,” are not stated by the Apostle, who says only, “in your mouth and in your heart.” He develops this point to the end by saying: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:7, 8, 10).

As far as we have been able to examine, the translation made from the Hebrew does not contain “in your hands.” Yet I do not think that the Seventy translators added this without reason, unless they intended us to understand that even the hands themselves—which signify works—must be understood in the heart, where faith is found, the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6).

For if the things God commands are done outwardly with the hands but are not done in the heart, no one is so foolish as to think that the commandments have been fulfilled. But if love, which is the fullness of the Law (Rom. 13:10), dwells in the heart, then even if someone is unable to act with the bodily hands, he nevertheless has peace with people of good will (Luke 2:14).

### LV. [Ib. XXXII, 5.]

“They sinned, not to him, children deserving blame.”

The Greek expression τέκνα μωμητά has been translated by some, as here, “children deserving blame”; by others, “defiled children”; and by others, “corrupt children.” Thus there is no substantial question here—or rather, no question at all.

But another matter rightly prompts inquiry. If the statement “They sinned, not to him” is general, because the one who sins does not sin against God—that is, he does not harm God but himself—how are we to understand what is written in the Psalm, “Against you alone I have sinned” (Ps. 50:6); and in Jeremiah, “We have sinned against you, O patience of Israel, Lord” (Jer. 14:7–8); and again in the Psalm, “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5)?

Is “sinning to God” the same as “sinning against God”? Hence the priest Eli says: “If a person should sin against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. 2:25).

For the present, then, I will say what seems to me at this moment. Perhaps those who understand these matters better will discover something better, or perhaps we ourselves will do so at another time, insofar as the Lord grants assistance.

To sin against God means to sin in matters that pertain to the worship of God. For the passage I mentioned indicates nothing else. Thus the sons of Eli were sinning, and their father said this to them.

We should also understand that people sin against human beings who belong to God. For God is read to have said to Abimelech concerning Sarah, “For this reason I spared you, so that you would not sin against me” (Gen. 20:6).

But those, I think, are rightly said to “sin to the Lord,” or rather to have “sinned to the Lord”—unless some passage is found elsewhere that contradicts this interpretation—who now undertake pious repentance for their sin, so that the forgiving Lord may be glorified.

For when David gives the reason why he said, “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you,” he adds: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” This may refer either to God’s saying, “Judge between me and my vineyard” (Isa. 5:3), or to the Lord Jesus Christ.

Christ alone could most truly say: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me”—that is, nothing sinful deserving death—“but so that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father commanded me, so I do. Rise, let us go from here” (John 14:30–31).

It is as though he were saying: “Even if the ruler of the world pursues the slightest sins with the punishment of death, he has nothing in me. But rise, let us go from here”—that is, let me suffer—for in what I suffer I fulfill the will of my Father; I do not pay the penalty for my own sin.

And when Jeremiah says, “We have sinned against you, O patience of Israel,” he is certainly speaking supplicatively in repentance, with hope of salvation through forgiveness.

Likewise, when it is said, “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you,” the same thing is being done: God is glorified by forgiving, because his mercy is great toward those who confess to him and return to him. He says that he does not desire the death of a sinner, but rather that he should turn back and live (Ezek. 33:11).

For this reason David himself, not only in the Psalm but also when God rebuked him through the prophet, replied, “I have sinned against the Lord” (2 Sam. 12:13), not without hope of the Lord’s mercy.

One who submits himself to a physician’s hands in order to be healed seems, in a certain sense, to have been wounded by the physician, so that the work of medicine may be accomplished in him.

In this song the Prophet foresaw that some people would sin by offending God through great iniquities, yet would refuse to repent and return to God to be healed. Concerning them it is also said elsewhere: “For they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77:39).

The statement “They sinned, not to him” can also be understood according to the sense that their sin did not harm him but themselves.

**Editorial notes:**

- The printed editions read “to sin against the Lord.” The manuscripts have “to have sinned to the Lord.” This is correct, although a little later the same manuscripts and all the printed editions incorrectly read “who do not practice a pious repentance for their sin,” whereas the text certainly must read “who now practice it,” or perhaps “who accomplish this through a pious repentance for their sin.”
- The manuscripts read “malignant” instead of “evil.”
- The manuscripts read “and through forgiveness”; other editions read “and through the forgiveness of sins.”
- The manuscripts read *quantum* (“insofar as”), in agreement with the Septuagint, ὡς ἀποστρέψαι (“that he should turn back”). The printed editions have *tantum ut revertatur* (“only that he should turn back”).

## LVI. [Book XXXIII, 1–3]

And this is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the sons of Israel before his death.

[Note: The printed editions have *qua benedixit* (“with which he blessed”), and below *the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob*, and shortly afterward *together with the tribes of Israel*. In these passages we follow the manuscripts, which agree with the Greek of the Septuagint.]

And he said:

“The Lord came from Sinai and dawned upon us from Seir; he hastened from Mount Paran with many thousands of Kadesh. At his right hand were angels with him, and he spared his people. And all the sanctified are under your hands, and these are under you. And he received from his words the Law, which Moses commanded us, the inheritance of the congregations of Jacob. And he shall be ruler in the Beloved, when the princes of the peoples are gathered together, together with the tribes of Israel.”

This prophecy must not be passed over carelessly. For it is evident that this blessing pertains to the new people whom the Lord Christ sanctified. These words are spoken by Moses in the person of that people, not in the person of Moses himself, as becomes clear in what follows.

For if it was said, “The Lord came from Sinai,” because the Law was given on Mount Sinai, what does the following phrase mean: “and dawned upon us from Seir,” since Seir is a mountain of Idumea where Esau reigned? Furthermore, when Moses blesses the sons of Israel in these words, as Scripture has foretold, how can he also say, “And he received from his words the Law, which Moses commanded us”? Clearly, then, this is a prophecy, as we said, foretelling the new people sanctified by Christ’s grace. They are called the sons of Israel because they are Abraham’s seed—that is, sons of the promise—and its interpretation is “Seeing God.”

The Lord, therefore, who came from Sinai, is to be understood as Christ, since *Sinai* is interpreted as “Temptation.” He came, therefore, from the temptation of his passion, cross, and death.

“And he dawned upon us from Seir.” *Seir* is interpreted as “Hairy,” which signifies the sinner; for Esau was born in this way and was hated [Gen. 25:25]. But because “upon those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, light has arisen” [Isa. 9:2], therefore he dawned from Seir.

At the same time, it is not absurdly understood as having been foretold that grace would come to the people of Israel from the nations signified by the name Seir, because the mountain belongs to Esau. Hence the Apostle says: “So they too now have not believed because of your mercy, so that they themselves also may obtain mercy” [Rom. 11:31].

They therefore say, “He dawned from Seir upon us, and he hastened from Mount Paran”—that is, from the fruitful mountain, for this is the interpretation of *Paran*, by which the Church is signified—“with many thousands of Kadesh.” *Kadesh* is interpreted both as “Changed” and as “Holiness.” Thus many thousands were changed and sanctified by grace, with whom Christ came to the Israelites who were afterward to be gathered.

It follows and says, “At his right hand were angels with him.” This requires no explanation.

“And he spared,” it says, “his people”—granting remission of sins.

From there he turns his speech to the people themselves and says: “And all the sanctified are under your hands, and these are under you”—not, certainly, proudly exalting themselves and wishing to establish their own righteousness, but acknowledging grace so that they may be subject to the righteousness of God [Rom. 10:3].

“And he received,” it says, “from his words the Law”—the people, namely, of whom he said, “And he spared his people.” He therefore received from his words the Law which, he says, “Moses commanded us.” That is, his people received the Law from his words, because from his teaching they understood the very Law that Moses commanded us.

For he himself says in the Gospel: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote about me” [John 5:46]. That people did not receive a Law which it failed to understand; rather, it received it when it understood it from his words, having cast off the old veil and turned to the Lord.

He calls this “the inheritance of the congregations of Jacob,” which is to be understood as heavenly, not earthly; eternal, not temporal.

“And he shall be,” he says, “ruler in the Beloved.” The Lord Jesus himself shall be ruler in the Beloved people, when the princes of the peoples—that is, of the nations—are gathered together, together with the tribes of Israel, so that what was said above may be fulfilled: “Rejoice, nations, together with his people”; because “a partial hardening has happened to Israel until the fullness of the nations should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” [Rom. 15:10; 11:25].

## LVII. [Book XXXIII, 17]

When he blessed Joseph, he said among other things: “The firstborn of the bull—his beauty.”

This should not be read as though he had said, “the firstborn of a bull”; rather, since he is the firstborn, “his beauty is that of a bull.” It is understood figuratively of the Lord, on account of the horns of the cross.

# BOOK SIX

## Questions on Joshua son of Nun

[Note: In the title of this book one should read *Joshua son of Nun*, as in the manuscripts, not *Josue*, as appears in the printed editions. [*Josue*.]]

[Col. 0775]

## QUESTION I. [Joshua 1:5]

The Lord says to Joshua son of Nun: “And as I was with Moses, so I shall be with you.”

Not only by this testimony, but also by many statements in Deuteronomy, it is proved that Moses died as God’s servant and pleasing to God, although that punishment was fulfilled in him which prevented him from entering the promised land [Deut. 32:48–52; 34:4–5].

From this it is understood that the Lord may be angry with his good servants in some respect and punish them temporarily, while nevertheless counting them among those who are vessels in his house, useful to the Lord for honor, to whom he will give the promises made to the saints [2 Tim. 2:21].

## II. [Joshua 1:11; 3:7]

The question is how, after the Lord had spoken to Joshua son of Nun, exhorting and strengthening him and promising that he would be with him, that same Joshua ordered the people through the scribes to prepare provisions because after three days they were to cross the Jordan, when they are found to have crossed the Jordan many more days later.

After giving this order to the people, he sent spies into Jericho, since, once the Jordan had been crossed, that city lay immediately ahead. They, however, turned aside to Rahab, a prostitute, and were hidden by her. When the king sought them and did not find them, she let them down through the window and advised them to hide in the hill country for three days. Four days therefore seem to have been used up.

Afterward, when they reported what had happened to them, Joshua set out at dawn with the entire people from the place where he was. When he came to the Jordan, he turned aside and stayed there. Then the people were again instructed to prepare themselves after three days to cross the Jordan, with the ark of the Lord going before them.

From this, therefore, it is understood that the arrangement which he announced to the people—that they should prepare provisions as though they were going to cross the river after three days—was a human plan. For he could, as a human being, have hoped that this would be possible if the spies returned quickly.

Because they were delayed, the rest was fulfilled by divine arrangement, although Scripture is silent about it, so that Joshua might already begin to be glorified among the people and it might be shown that the Lord was with him, as he had been with Moses.

For this too is said to him as he was about to cross the river, as it is written: “And the Lord said to Joshua: On this day I shall begin to exalt you before all the sons of Israel, so that they may know that as I was with Moses, so I shall be with you.”

Nor should it seem incredible that even those with whom God spoke wished to do something according to human planning, while nevertheless trusting that God was their governor, and that their plans were altered by the providence of him by whom they were governed.

[Note: Ten manuscripts and the Ratisbon edition read *viderent* (“might see”) in place of *fiderent* (“might trust”).]

Moses himself, surely, as a human being, had thought that he should hear the people’s cases in such a way that, by taking upon himself and them an intolerable burden, he would be unable to benefit them. His plan was changed by divine direction, when his father-in-law himself suggested and advised this, and God approved the advice [Exod. 18:14–26].

## III. [Joshua 3:3, 4, 15]

The scribes say to the people:

“When you see the ark of the testimony of the Lord our God, and our priests and Levites carrying it, set out from your places and follow it. But let there be a long interval between you and it: stand at a distance of about two thousand cubits; do not approach it, so that you may know the way by which you are to go, for you have not gone by this way yesterday or the day before.”

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have “the ark of the testimony of your God and your priests.”]

The ark was ordered to go far ahead so that it could be seen by the people. For if such a large column proceeded close behind it, it would not see the ark going before it and would not know which way to follow.

From this event it is to be understood that the pillar of cloud, which used to give the signal for moving the camps and to show them the way [Exod. 13:21], had now withdrawn and no longer appeared to them. Hence it happened that the three-day period too was announced according to human planning [above, Question 2].

Now, therefore, under the leadership of Joshua, they follow the ark of the Lord, the cloud having been removed as though the veil had been taken away.

The Jordan, however, was full along its entire bank, as it is during the days of the wheat harvest. This seems incredible in our regions; there, however, as those who know report, the wheat harvest occurs at the beginning of spring, and at that time the river is fuller than during winter.

## IV. [Joshua 4:7]

“And these stones shall be a memorial for you to the sons of Israel forever.”

How can this be “forever,” when heaven and earth pass away [Matt. 24:35]? Or is it because these stones signify something eternal, although the stones themselves cannot be eternal?

Although what is in Greek, **ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος** (*heōs tou aiōnos*), can be rendered in Latin as *usque in saeculum* (“unto the age”), it does not necessarily have to be understood as “eternal.”

## V. [Joshua 4:15–16]
