“And the Lord spoke to Joshua, saying: Command the priests who are carrying the ark of the covenant of the testimony.”

The ark is usually called either “the ark of the covenant” or “the ark of the testimony.” Here it is called “the ark of the covenant of the testimony,” so that not only the ark but also the covenant itself might be called the covenant of testimony.

For this is why the Apostle says: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, bearing witness through the Law and the Prophets” [Rom. 3:21]. That which is called the Old Testament had been given as a testimony to something else that was to come.

## VI. [Joshua 5:2–7]

The Lord said to Joshua: “Make sharp knives for yourself from stone,” or, as the Greek has it, “from sharp stone,” “and sit down and circumcise the sons of Israel again.”

In this command it is asked why he said “again.” One man was not to be circumcised twice. But because one people consisted partly of those who had been circumcised and partly of those who had not been circumcised, the word “again” was used: not so that a man, but so that the people, might be circumcised again.

The following words show this as well. Scripture says: “And Joshua made for himself sharp stone knives, and circumcised the sons of Israel at the place called the Hill of the Foreskins.”

In this way Joshua circumcised the sons of Israel who had at one time been on the journey and who had at one time been uncircumcised, the children of those who had come out of Egypt; Joshua circumcised all these. [The transmitted wording is syntactically uncertain.]

For Israel had dwelt forty-two years in the wilderness of Mabdaritis, and therefore many of the warriors who had come out of the land of Egypt were uncircumcised because they had disobeyed God’s commands. Among these the Lord had decreed that they should not see the land which he had sworn to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.

In their place he appointed their sons, whom Joshua circumcised because they had remained uncircumcised on the journey. It is therefore clear that not all were uncircumcised, but some.

For some of the sons of those who came out of Egypt were uncircumcised within that people, and Joshua could circumcise them—namely, the sons of those who had fathered children in the wilderness and had neglected to circumcise them because they were disobedient to the law of God.

There is therefore no reason why those who think that people possessing the sacrament of Christian baptism must be baptized again should suppose that this testimony of the Law supports them. No individual man was circumcised twice; rather, the people had already been circumcised in some members, while others were still uncircumcised.

And even if it could in some way happen that God ordered a man to be circumcised twice, could they say that this was commanded because they had been circumcised by Egyptians, or by certain heretics separated from the fellowship of the Israelites?

Since it is also sufficiently clear why God gave this command, people can find here no defense for their error.

## VII. [Joshua 5:15–13]

When Joshua saw a man standing opposite him with a drawn sword, and when the man answered that he was the commander of the army of the Lord’s power, Joshua fell upon the ground and said, “What do you command your servant?” It may be asked whether he prostrated himself before an angel and called him “lord,” or whether, understanding by whom the man had been sent, he called the Lord himself “Lord” and prostrated himself before him.

Joshua was, as we read, in Jericho—not in the city itself, certainly, whose walls had not yet fallen, though that was soon to happen so that they could enter it, but in the territory belonging to it. For the translation made from the Hebrew has this wording.

## VIII. [Joshua 7]

When Achar of the tribe of Judah stole from the things devoted to destruction in the city of Jericho, contrary to the Lord’s command, and because of his sin the three thousand who had been sent against Gai turned their backs to the enemy, thirty-six men among them being killed, and when the people were terrified, Joshua and the elders prostrated themselves before the Lord, who answered that this had happened because the people had sinned; and when God also threatened that he would not be with them unless they removed the devoted thing from among themselves; and when the perpetrator was exposed and was killed not alone but together with all that belonged to him—it is commonly asked how punishment can justly be inflicted on some for another’s sins, especially since in the Law the Lord said that neither fathers should be punished for the sins of their sons nor sons for the sins of their fathers [Deut. 24:16].

Is the command intended for human judges, who are to understand one thing, namely, that they must not punish anyone for another’s offense, while God’s judgments are not of this kind? In his high and hidden counsel he knows to what extent he should extend even a temporal punishment of human beings that is salutary as a warning.

For, as far as the administration of the whole world is concerned, nothing dire happens to mortals when they die, since they are destined to die at some time in any case.

[Note: The printed editions read *durum* (“harsh”) for *dirum* (“dire”).] Yet among those who fear such things, discipline is established, so that each person may care not only for himself within the people but also show diligence toward others, and so that, as members of one body and one person, they may be concerned for one another.

Nor should it be believed that, even in punishments inflicted after death, one person can be condemned in place of another. This punishment is inflicted only in matters that were destined to have an end, even if they did not end in that particular way.

At the same time, it is shown how closely the whole community is joined together in the society of the people, so that individuals are regarded not only as separate persons but also as parts within a whole.

Through the sin and death of one man, therefore, the whole people was admonished, as though the offense that had been committed had to be sought in the entire body.

At the same time, it was signified how great the evil would be if the whole assembly had sinned, since not even one man could be punished in such a way that the others would be secure from punishment.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads *vindicari* (“be punished”) for *judicari* (“be judged”).]

But if Achar had been discovered and seized by someone, and, charged with that crime, had been brought before Joshua for judgment, it should certainly not be thought that the human judge would have punished either him or anyone else who had not been implicated in his deed.

For the judge was not permitted to exceed the command of the Law given to human beings: by his own judgment, in matters in which human beings are commanded or permitted to judge other human beings, he must not consider one person punishable for another’s sin.

God, however, judges with a far more hidden justice. He is able, even after death, to free or destroy, which man cannot do.

Visible afflictions and deaths of human beings, since they can harm or benefit those upon whom they are inflicted, are distributed by the Lord according to the hidden manner of his providence, even when he appears to avenge the sins of some upon others.

Invisible punishments, however, which can do nothing but harm and cannot benefit, are not endured before God the judge by anyone for another’s sins, just as before a human judge no one ought to endure these visible punishments except for his own fault.

For God gave this command to the human judge concerning matters subject to human judgment: he himself carries out the vengeance in his own judgment, to which human power does not aspire.

[Note: Thus the Ratisbon edition and the manuscripts. But Am. Er. and Lov. have *judicanda* (“to be judged”).]

## IX. [Joshua 7:15, 25]

It is rightly asked why, when the Lord had commanded that the man who had been exposed as having stolen from the devoted thing should be burned with fire, Joshua instead had him exposed and stoned by the people.

Was he required to die in the manner understood by Joshua, who followed the Lord more closely and could understand the Lord’s words when he gave the command? Another person could not easily have understood them in this way.

It is therefore more appropriate to ask why the Lord called stoning “fire” than to believe that Joshua did something other than what the Lord commanded. No one could have been wiser in understanding the Lord’s words, nor more obedient in carrying them out.

That the name “fire” could signify punishment is attested by Scripture in Deuteronomy, where it says to the sons of Israel: “He brought you out from the iron furnace, from Egypt” [Deut. 4:20]. There he clearly wished a harsh tribulation to be understood.

Two explanations occur to me—not so that both should be accepted, but so that one of them should be accepted—for why he was not burned with his entire household by a visible fire.

If the Lord judged his sin to be of such a kind that, once expiated by that punishment, it would not be punished eternally, then, because of that expiation and purification, the punishment appropriately received the name “fire.”

No one would be prompted to seek this interpretation if a visible fire had literally consumed him. Everyone would remain with what he plainly saw fulfilled and would seek nothing further.

But now, since on account of the Lord’s words and Joshua’s action—by which those words could not be transgressed—it is rightly said that stoning too was fire, the meaning of that punishment is elegantly recognized: the man was purified so that he would not perish in the future because of that sin.

The vessels in Leviticus signify the same thing, since they are commanded to be purified by fire.

But if that sin was of such a kind that Gehenna would receive him even after this life, Joshua therefore wished him to be stoned, so that the statement of the Lord, “He shall be burned with fire,” would be understood as referring to what the Lord would do, not to what they themselves were required to do.

If the Lord had said, “You shall burn him and all that belongs to him with fire,” there would be no room for this interpretation. But since the wording is such that God appears rather to have foretold what would happen to him than to have commanded what should be done to him by human beings, Joshua could not have acted better. As so great a prophet, he understood the divine words and prophetically performed the very act: he killed the man with stones rather than flames, so that the Lord’s words would not appear to have been fulfilled in those fires, since the Lord intended them to be understood in another sense.

Nor should it trouble us that God foretold that not only the man himself but also everything belonging to him would be burned with fire. For he says: “He shall be burned with fire, and everything that belongs to him.”

“Everything that belongs to him” can be understood as his works, which he said would be burned together with him—not in the sense in which the Apostle speaks of certain works being consumed by fire while the person himself is saved [1 Cor. 3:15], if this man’s sin is to be understood as deserving punishment in eternal fire.

When the people punished him, they stoned his sons and daughters, together with his livestock and everything he possessed. Yet Joshua did this not by human judgment but by prophetic inspiration: either he understood “everything that belongs to him” in such a way that he did not consider his sons excluded, and inflicted the punishment of stoning in place of fire; or he signified through his children, as well as through the other things belonging to him, the works that God was going to burn in him after death.

Nor should it therefore be believed that they were burned with the punishment of hellfire after death for their father’s sin, from which they were innocent.

This death, which awaits everyone, although it comes from the first sin, is nevertheless useful when hastened for some, since we are born in such a condition that death is necessarily required. Hence we read concerning a certain person: “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding” [Wis. 4:11].

By what judgment, then, or mercy of God, this punishment was inflicted either upon his sons or upon the thirty-six men, when all were strangers to his sin, is hidden with him in whom there is no injustice [Rom. 9:14].

Yet this is clear: the people had to seek with terror what had been committed; and the others feared imitating his deed all the more intensely because human weakness greatly recoils from being subjected to so great and so just a hatred of the people, and from dying in such a way that those descendants whom he thought he would leave behind to extend the human race would be consumed together with him because of his sin.

## X. [Joshua 8:2]

When God speaks to Joshua and commands him to set ambushes behind the city—that is, ambushing warriors who would lie in wait for the enemy—we are taught that this is not unjustly done by those who wage a just war.

A just person ought to consider nothing more important in such matters than undertaking a just war, when it is lawful for him to fight; for it is not lawful for everyone.

Once he has undertaken a just war, whether he wins by open battle or by ambush makes no difference with regard to justice.

Wars are commonly defined as just when they avenge wrongs—if a nation or city against which war is to be waged has either failed to punish what its people have wickedly done or failed to restore what was taken through wrong.

But there is also no doubt that this kind of war is just which God commands, since there is no injustice with him and he knows what ought to happen to each person.

In such a war, the commander of the army or the people themselves should be regarded not so much as the author of the war as its minister.

## XI. [Joshua 8:4–8]

Joshua, sending thirty thousand warriors to fight against Gai, said to them:

“You shall lie in ambush behind the city, and you shall not be far from the city, and you shall all be ready. I and all the people who are with me shall approach the city. And when those who dwell in Gai come out to meet us, as before, we shall flee from their face. When they come out after us, we shall draw them away from the city, and they will say, ‘These men are fleeing from our face, as before.’ But you shall rise from the ambush and enter the city. According to this word you shall act. Behold, I command you.”

The question is whether every intention to deceive must be classified as a lie; and, if so, whether a lie can be just by which someone is deceived who deserves to be deceived.

If even this cannot be found to be a just lie, it remains that, according to some signification, what was done by the ambush must be referred to truth.

## XII. [Joshua 9:3–13]

The Gibeonites came to Joshua with old bread and sacks, so that they might be thought—as they had pretended—to have come from a distant land and thus be spared. For the Lord had decreed that they should spare no one inhabiting those lands into which they were entering.

Some Greek and Latin manuscripts have: “And taking old sacks upon their shoulders.” Others, which appear more reliable, do not have “upon their shoulders,” but “upon their asses.”

The similarity of the words in Greek easily caused the corruption, and therefore the Latin copies too have varied. For **ὤμων** (*ōmōn*) and **ὄνων** (*onōn*) do not differ greatly from one another: the former is the word for “shoulders,” the latter for “asses.”

It is more credible, however, that the reading concerns asses, since they said that they had been sent from their own distant people. It is therefore evident that they were envoys, and for that reason could have carried their necessary supplies on asses rather than on their shoulders. They could not have been numerous, and Scripture records that they carried not only sacks but also wineskins.

## XIII. [Joshua 9:19]

It may be asked how the Hebrews believed that their oath to the Gibeonites had to be kept, since they had sworn to them as though they had come from a distant land, just as the Gibeonites had lied.

They knew that they would be destroyed if the Hebrews discovered that they lived in the land which the Hebrews had been promised that they would possess after killing its inhabitants.

Thus, while the Gibeonites were lying that they had come to them from a distant land, the Israelites swore an oath to them. Afterward, when they learned that they lived in the very place where all whom they found had to be destroyed according to God’s command, they nevertheless did not wish to break their oath.

Although they had learned that the Gibeonites had lied, they preferred to spare them for the sake of the oath. They could certainly have said that they had sworn only to those whom they had believed the Gibeonites to be—that is, people coming from a distant land—and that, once they had learned otherwise, the Lord’s command concerning them had to be fulfilled, so that they should be conquered like the others.

God, however, approved this and was not angry with those who spared them, even though they had not asked who the Gibeonites were and had therefore allowed themselves to be deceived by them.

Accordingly, it is reasonable to believe that, although they wished to deceive human beings for the sake of their own safety, they nevertheless sincerely feared God in his people. For this reason the Lord was not angry with those who swore or spared them, to such an extent that afterward he avenged the Gibeonites themselves as members of his people against the house of Saul, as the history in the Books of Kings shows [2 Kings 21:1–9].

And since the oath was kept, although it was kept toward men who had lied, so that the judgment might be bent toward mercy, this did not displease God.

For if, conversely, they had sworn to kill certain people whom they had thought were Gibeonites living in the promised land, and afterward had learned that they were foreigners from that land and had come to them from far away, it should in no way be supposed that they would have destroyed them in order to fulfill their oath.

For holy David, moved by the mercy of sparing someone, preferred to spare Nabal even after he had sworn that he would kill him [1 Sam. 25:22, 33], although he certainly knew whom he had sworn to kill. He preferred not to fulfill the oath in this harsher matter, judging that he would please God more by not doing what he had sworn in anger to do to harm Nabal than by carrying it out.

## XIV. [Joshua 10:7–8]

When the Gibeonites, besieged by the kings of the Amorites, sent to Joshua for assistance, Scripture continues:

“And Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of warriors with him, every man mighty in strength. And the Lord said to Joshua, ‘Do not fear them, for I have handed them over into your hands; none of them shall stand before you.’”

Here the Lord was not consulted as to whether they should go to them; rather, when his people spontaneously wished to provide proper assistance, he foretold the future victory.

In the same way, although he was not consulted, he could have warned them about the Gibeonites—who they were, despite their claim to be from a distant land—unless he had approved the oath, which required them to spare those who had submitted to them.

For they had believed in God, having heard him promise his people that he would overthrow those nations and possess their land. In a certain sense, he rewarded their faith by not exposing them.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts, together with the Ratisbon edition and Am. But Er. and Lov. have *perdendo* (“by destroying”).]

## XV. [Joshua 10:5–6]

It is asked how Adonibezek, king of the city of Jerusalem, and the other four kings who besieged the Gibeonites are called, according to the Septuagint translators, first kings of the Jebusites when they assembled to besiege them, and afterward kings of the Amorites by the Gibeonites themselves when they sent messengers to Joshua to free them from the siege.

As far as we could examine in the translation made from the Hebrew, they are called Amorites in both places.

Yet it is certain that the king of the city of Jerusalem belonged to the Jebusites, because the city itself was called Jebus, as though it were the capital of that people. Scripture also very often mentions seven nations which God promised to exterminate from before his people, one of which is said to be the nation of the Amorites.

Unless perhaps this was a universal name for all of them, or rather for the greater part, so that not one but several of these seven were included under this name—although there was also one among the seven that was properly called Amorite—just as one part of the world is properly called Libya, although that name applies to all Africa, and one part is properly called Asia, although some have designated Asia as half the world and others as a third of the world.

For it is certain that the Canaanites too are mentioned as one nation among those seven, and yet that entire land is, in its original designation, called the land of Canaan.

## XVI. [Joshua 11:14–15]

“Joshua left nothing living in it, just as the Lord commanded Moses his servant; and Moses likewise commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He did not transgress anything of all that the Lord had commanded Moses.”

For this reason it should in no way be thought that this was cruelty: that Joshua left no living person in the cities handed over to him, since God had commanded it.

Those who therefore suppose that God himself was cruel on this account and refuse to believe that he was the true author of the Old Testament judge as perversely of God’s works as they do of human sins. They do not know what each person deserves to suffer and consider it a great evil when things destined to fall are thrown down and mortals die.

## XVII. [Joshua 11:19]

“And there was no city which was not handed over to the sons of Israel.”

It may be asked how this is true, since neither in the period of the Judges nor in the period of the Kings were the Hebrews able to capture all the cities of those seven nations.

Either it must be understood that Joshua approached no city in battle which he did not capture, or certainly that none of the cities in the regions mentioned above remained uncaptured.

For the regions in which the cities were located were enumerated, and concerning them this conclusion was made: “And he captured them all in battle.”

## XVIII. [Joshua 11:20]

“For it was brought about by the Lord that their hearts were strengthened to go out to battle against Israel, so that they might be exterminated; so that no mercy would be shown to them, but they would be exterminated, as the Lord had commanded Moses.”

The statement that the Lord strengthened their hearts—that is, hardened their hearts—as in the case of Pharaoh [Exod. 7:3, 22; 8:19], must unquestionably be understood as something justly done by a profound divine judgment, when God abandons a person and the enemy takes possession of him. It must be interpreted here as it is there.

But another issue arises: how can it be said that their hearts were strengthened for this purpose, namely, that they should rise up in battle against Israel, and that for this reason Israel should not show them mercy? It seems that mercy would have had to be shown if they had not fought, although God had commanded that none of them be spared.

The Gibeonites, however, were spared because, pretending to have come from a distant land, they had secured the Israelites’ oath.

Since the Israelites had spontaneously shown mercy to certain people, contrary to God’s command, the present passage must be understood to mean that these others fought in such a way that they would not be spared, and that the Israelites themselves would not be moved to mercy by them in disregard of God’s command.

It should not be believed that this could have happened under the leadership of Joshua, who carefully observed all the divine commands. Nevertheless, even he would not have destroyed them so quickly if they had not opposed him with such complete unanimity.

Thus it could have happened that those whom he had not conquered might have remained until a time when they could be spared after Joshua’s death, since those who carried out God’s commands with less care might then have spared them.

Even while Joshua was alive, the Israelites spared some of them, merely subjecting them to their authority; and they were unable to conquer others.

But these events did not occur under his leadership. They occurred when he was already old and had withdrawn from warfare, merely dividing the lands among them. Thus, once he no longer fought, they held the lands assigned to them, partly already free of enemies and partly captured in battle.

That they were unable to conquer certain peoples was also part of divine providence, as will appropriately become clear from definite passages of Scripture.

### XIX. [Ib. XVI, 10]

“And Ephraim did not dispossess the Canaanite who lived in Gezer; and the Canaanite lived in Ephraim to this day, until Pharaoh king of Egypt went up, captured the city, and burned it with fire; and he removed the Canaanites, the Perizzites, and those who lived in Gezer; and Pharaoh gave it as a dowry to his daughter.”

Regarding what is said here about Pharaoh king of Egypt, I wonder whether we ought to understand it as spoken prophetically, since this history is believed to have been written in the times when these events were still recent. What important thing could have been selected for prophetic prediction when past events are being narrated, while greater and especially necessary future events are left unmentioned? It is therefore more reasonable to suppose that the Septuagint translators—who are said to have interpreted the text with prophetic authority, by their remarkable agreement—added this, not as a prediction of the future, but because they themselves lived at the time when they remembered these events as having taken place and had read about them in the Books of Kings (3 Kings 4:34 in the Septuagint; 9:16 in the Vulgate). Indeed, it occurred in the time of the kings.

This seemed more credible to us because we examined the translation made from the Hebrew and did not find this passage there. The same is true of the statement about Jericho, namely, that Hozah, who rebuilt it, incurred the curse pronounced by Joshua. For the text reads:

“And Joshua adjured them on that day, saying: Cursed is the man who will raise up and build that city; on his firstborn he shall lay its foundation, and on his youngest he shall set up its gates” (Joshua 6:26).

This is as far as the passage is found in the translation from the Hebrew. But the following words are not there:

“And Hozah of Bethel did so: he founded it on Abiron his firstborn, and on his surviving [Note: [Col. 0784] Rat. and Lov. read “and on his saved one.” Two Vatican manuscripts, and two of ours, read “and on his surviving one.” In the Septuagint: καὶ ἐν τῷ διασωθέντι, “and on the one who was saved.” Nevertheless, an old Cistercian codex has here “and on his sesal[Col. 0785]nato.” When this reading is compared with 3 Kings 16:34, where the Vulgate reads “and on Segub his youngest,” and the Arabic reads “and on Sagub, the youngest,” it leads us to suspect that the Greek διασωθέντι arose from a corrupt Latin text, and that this addition was therefore inserted later by the Latins, not by the Septuagint translators, as Augustine believes.] youngest he set up its gates” (Vulgate, 3 Kings 16:34).

This is not found there. It therefore appears to have been inserted by the Septuagint translators, who knew that the event had taken place.

### XX. [Ib. XIX, 47. [Note: [Col. 0785] In the Septuagint.]]

“And the Amorite remained to live in Elom and in Salumin, and the hand of Ephraim was heavy upon them, and they became tributaries to them.”

This was already happening contrary to the Lord’s command. Joshua was still alive, but because of his old age he was no longer leading them in those battles. For this reason it is said that the Lord caused the heart of those who had united in going to war against Joshua to be strengthened, so that this mercy might not be shown them—even contrary to God’s command (Joshua 21:20)—if they remained unconquered and were left to be conquered by the Israelites after Joshua had grown old or died, since the Israelites might spare them contrary to the Lord’s command, whereas Joshua would not have done so.

### XXI. [Ib. XXI, 41–43]

It is rightly asked how it can be true that Israel did not uproot the nations occupying the Promised Land, not only until the day of Joshua’s death but even afterward, although they had conquered some of them and were settled in the same promised inheritance. How, then, should we understand the statement:

“And the Lord gave Israel all the land which he swore to give their fathers, and they inherited it and dwelt in it. And the Lord gave them rest on every side, as he swore to their fathers; none of all their enemies stood before them, but the Lord delivered all their enemies into their hands. Not one of all the good words that the Lord had spoken to the children of Israel failed; all came to pass”?

Everything must therefore be considered carefully. First, we must examine the fact that the land of the nations was promised to the Israelites. Seven nations in particular are repeatedly mentioned, as in Exodus:

“And the Lord said to Moses: Go up from here, you and your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, into the land which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to your seed’; and I will send my angel before you, and he will cast out the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, the Jebusite, and the Canaanite” (Exodus 33:1–2).

It therefore appears that God promised the land of these seven nations to the patriarchs. The matter is stated even more explicitly in Deuteronomy:

“But if you approach a city to attack it, and summon them with an offer of peace, then, if they answer you peacefully and open their gates to you, all the people found in the city shall become your tributaries and obey you. But if they do not obey you and wage war against you, and you besiege it, the Lord your God will deliver it into your hands, and you shall strike every male in it with the edge of the sword, except the women; and the goods, all the cattle, and everything else in the city, all its furnishings, you shall take as spoil for yourself, and you shall consume all the spoil of your enemies whom the Lord your God will give you. Thus you shall deal with all the cities that are very far from you, which are not among the cities of these nations.

“But in the cities of these peoples, which the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance of their land, you shall not preserve any living thing, but you shall devote them to destruction: the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite, as the Lord your God commanded you” (Deuteronomy 20:10–17).

Here too it is clear that the land of these seven nations was promised as an inheritance, which the Israelites were to possess after conquering and destroying those nations utterly. As for the others found farther away, beyond these nations, God willed them to become tributaries if they did not resist; but if they resisted, they too were to be killed and destroyed, except for the livestock and whatever could be taken as spoil.

Again, in another passage of Deuteronomy we read:

“And it shall be, when the Lord your God brings you into the land into which you are entering to inherit it, and removes many great nations from before you—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—seven nations greater and stronger than you; and when the Lord your God delivers them into your hands, you shall strike them down and utterly destroy them. You shall not make a covenant with them, nor show them mercy, nor intermarry with them: you shall not give your daughter to his son, nor take his daughter for your son, and so forth” (Deuteronomy 7:1–3).

Thus, in this and many other passages of Scripture, it is frequently shown that the children of Israel received the lands of these seven nations as an inheritance in such a way that they would dwell there in place of those who had occupied them, not alongside them. Yet in Genesis not only these seven nations but eleven are promised to Abraham’s seed. For it is written:

“On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abraham, saying: To your seed I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates: the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hivites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites” (Genesis 15:18–21).

The question is resolved by understanding this as an earlier prophecy that Solomon would extend and enlarge his kingdom to those boundaries. Concerning him it is written:

“And all Solomon’s plans, which he had determined to carry out in Jerusalem and Lebanon and throughout the whole land under his authority; all the people who remained from the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, who were not of Israel, but descendants of those who had remained with them in the land, whom the children of Israel had not destroyed—Solomon subjected them to tribute to this day” (3 Kings 10:22 in the Septuagint; Vulgate 9:19–21).

Behold: Solomon subjected to tribute the remnants of the peoples who, according to God’s command, were to be conquered and utterly destroyed. According to God’s command he ought to have destroyed them, yet they were subjected and possessed as tributaries.

A little later we read:

“And he ruled over all the kings from the river to the land of the Philistines and to the borders of Egypt” (3 Kings 10:26 in the Septuagint; 4 Kings 4:21 in the Vulgate).

Here is where what God foretold when speaking to Abraham in Genesis, promising these things, was fulfilled. “From the river” is understood here as meaning from the Euphrates; for in those regions “the great river” can be understood even without its proper name being added. It cannot mean the Jordan, since the Israelites had already occupied lands both on this side of the Jordan and beyond it before Solomon’s reign.

Thus the text in the Books of Kings says that Solomon’s kingdom extended from the Euphrates in the east to the borders of Egypt in the west. At that time, therefore, more territory was subjected than the seven nations had occupied; and consequently not seven but eleven nations were reduced to servitude.

What is written in the Books of Kings—“to the borders of Egypt from the river”—expresses the extent of the kingdom from east to west. The same matter is stated in Genesis in the reverse direction, defining the boundaries from west to east: “from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates.” The river of Egypt, which marks the boundary separating the kingdom of Israel from Egypt, is not the Nile. It is another, smaller river, which flows through the city of Rhinocorura [Note: [Col. 0787] Thus it is written in the old manuscripts and in the edition of Rat. Er. and Lov. have “Rhinocolura”; Am. has “Rhinocornia.”], from which the Promised Land begins toward the east.

This, then, had been established for the children of Israel: they were to inhabit the lands of the seven nations after those nations had been exterminated and destroyed; over the others they were to reign as subjects and tributaries as far as the Euphrates. Although they did not obey God in this matter—for they made some of those whom they ought to have exterminated obedient to them—God nevertheless fulfilled the promise he had made during the time of Solomon.

How, then, in the Book of Joshua, which we have undertaken to examine, can this be true:

“And God gave Israel all the land which he swore to give their fathers, and they inherited it”?

How could he have given them the whole land while Joshua was still alive, when they had not yet overcome even the remnants of those seven nations?

The statement that “they inherited it” is true, because they were already there and had settled there. The further statement, “And the Lord gave them rest on every side, as he had sworn to their fathers,” is also true: while Joshua was still alive, the remnants of those nations did not yield to them, but none of them dared to trouble them by war in the lands where they had settled.

For this reason the next statement is also made:

“None stood before them among all their enemies.”

The following words—“But the Lord delivered all their enemies into their hands”—refer to those enemies who dared to meet them in battle.

Finally, when it says, “Not one of all the good words that the Lord had spoken to the children of Israel failed; all came to pass,” this should be understood as follows: although they had already acted contrary to the Lord’s command by sparing some of those seven nations and making them obedient, the Israelites still remained safe among them. Therefore, after saying “of all the words,” the text adds “good,” because the curses established for contemptuous and transgressing people had not yet come to pass.

It remains, then, to understand the statement, “The Lord gave Israel all the land which he had sworn to give their fathers,” in this sense: although remnants of those nations still remained to be crushed and exterminated—and although the other nations as far as the Euphrates were either to be subjected if they did not resist or destroyed if they resisted—they were nevertheless left for the Israelites’ use, so that the Israelites might be exercised by them. Otherwise, being weak in their bodily affections and desires, they might not be able to bear with moderation and for their welfare a sudden prosperity in temporal things, but might be lifted up and perish more quickly. This will be demonstrated suitably elsewhere.

Thus the whole land was given to them, because even that part which had not yet been given into their possession had already been given for a certain purpose of exercise.

### XXII. [Ib. XXI, 42]

Regarding the statement, “None stood before them among all their enemies,” it may be asked how this can be true, since it was previously written concerning the tribe of Dan that their enemies did not allow them to descend into the valley but prevailed against them in the mountains (Joshua 19:48 in the Septuagint).

But what we said when Scripture mentioned the twelve sons of Jacob born in Mesopotamia, where Benjamin had not been born (Questions on Genesis, question 117), should also be understood here: the eleven tribes are counted for the whole people, according to a rule sufficiently familiar to us from other passages of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0788] The printed editions have “twelve.” But all our manuscripts have “eleven.”].

If it is asked why this tribe did not obtain sufficient land in the lot that fell to it, and why it was oppressed by those who held the land, we must believe that this lies within God’s secret counsel. Nevertheless, when Jacob blessed his sons, he said such things about this Dan that it is thought the Antichrist would arise from that tribe (Genesis 49:17). We do not undertake to say more about this now, since the question can also be resolved in this way: “None stood before them among all their enemies” refers to the time when they were waging war together under one commander, before the territories that each tribe had to defend were divided among the individual tribes.

### XXIII. [Ib. XXII, 23]

“And in the sacrifices of our salvations.”

Because “sacrifices” is expressed in the plural, “salvations” is also plural. Here we must consider more carefully how one ordinarily speaks of a “sacrifice of salvation.” For if we understand Christ to be meant—since he is called the Salvation of God (Luke 2:30)—it is not immediately apparent how this word can be understood in the plural.

For “there is one Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:6), although those who are his by grace are called “christs,” as it is written in the Psalm: “Do not touch my christs” (Psalm 104:15). But whether they can be called “salvations” or “saving ones” is not something one should readily dare to say [Note: [Col. 0788] The Vatican manuscripts read “should readily hear.”]. For he alone is the Savior of the body.

### XXIV. [Ib. XXIII, 14]

When Joshua speaks of his approaching death, he says:

“But I am returning along the way, as do all who are upon the earth.”

In the translation from the Hebrew we find, “I am entering the way.” Thus the Septuagint’s “I am returning” should be understood in accordance with what was said to the human being:

“Until you return to the earth from which you were taken” (Genesis 3:19),

so that it is understood as referring to the body.

With respect to the soul, however, if we wish to understand it as it is written in Ecclesiastes—“And the spirit will return to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7)—I do not think this can be said of everyone, but only of those who have lived in such a way that they deserve to return to God as their creator. It cannot rightly be understood of those of whom it is said:

“A spirit that passes away and does not return” (Psalm 77:39).

But if this holy man, Joshua son of Nun, had not added, “as do all who are upon the earth,” there would be no question. We would believe of him nothing other than what we read him to have deserved. But since the words “as do all who are upon the earth” have been added, it is surprising if what the Latin translator rendered “I am returning” should not rather be rendered “I am traversing” or “I am running through,” if this can be said of what the Greek has ἀποτρέχω (*apotréchō*), “I run away” or “I run off.” For all traverse or run through the way of this life when they reach its end.

But because this verb is used where Rebecca’s parents say to Abraham’s servant:

“Here is Rebecca; take her, run back, and let her be the wife of your master” (Genesis 24:51),

the same verb was translated in this way here as well.

### XXV. [Ib. XXIV, 3]

The Septuagint translators have:

“And I took your father Abraham from beyond the river and led him through the whole land.”

The translation from the Hebrew has:

“And I brought him into the land of Canaan.”

It is therefore surprising that the Septuagint translators wished to put “the whole land” instead of “the land of Canaan,” unless they were considering the prophecy, so that what was most certainly to be fulfilled in Christ and in the Church—the true seed of Abraham—might be understood as already accomplished through God’s promise, not in the children of the flesh but in the children of the promise.

### XXVI. [Ib. XXIV, 11]

“And those who lived in Jericho fought against you.”

It may be asked how this can be true, since they merely defended themselves by keeping the gates closed and remaining within the circuit of the walls. Yet the statement is correctly made, because closing one’s gates against an enemy also belongs to warfare. They did not send ambassadors to ask for peace.

Thus, if it had said, “They fought against you,” it would have been false. War does not consist of continuous fighting, but sometimes of frequent battles, sometimes of rare ones, and sometimes of none at all. It is still war, however, when there is in some sense an armed disagreement [Note: [Col. 0789] All the manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “when the gates are closed against the enemy, and a kind of armed defense.”].

### XXVII. [Ib. XXIV, 12]

What does Joshua son of Nun mean when, among the other things he recalls that the Lord did for the Israelites, he says:

“He sent wasps before you and drove them out from before you” [Note: [Col. 0789] After “and drove them out,” we add from the manuscripts “from before you.” The current Greek has ὑπὸ προσώπου ἡμῶν, “from before us.”]?

This is also read in the Book of Wisdom (Wisdom 12:8), yet nowhere among the recorded events do we find that it happened.

Perhaps, by a transferred expression, he intended “wasps” to mean the sharpest stings of fear, by which they were, as it were, pricked through rumors flying about, so that they fled. Or perhaps he meant aerial, hidden spirits, of which the Psalm says:

“Through evil angels” (Psalm 77:49).

Unless someone should say that not everything that happened was written down, and that this too happened visibly, so that actual wasps are to be understood.

### XXVIII. [Ib. XXIV, 19]

What does Joshua mean when he says to the people:

“You will not be able to serve the Lord, because he is a holy God”?

Is it because, for human weakness, it is impossible to conform oneself in some way through perfect service to his holiness?

After hearing this, they ought not merely to have chosen his service, but also to have relied upon his help and mercy. The one who understood this says in the Psalm:

“Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2).

But they preferred to rely upon themselves, believing that they could serve God without any offense. Thus they were already beginning to fulfill what the Apostle later expressed concerning them:

“For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3).

So the Law was already entering among them, in order that transgression might abound, and afterward grace might superabound through the Lord Christ (Romans 5:20–21), who is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4).

### XXIX. [Ib. XXIV, 23]

What does the same Joshua mean when he says to the people:

“And now remove the foreign gods that are among you, and direct your hearts to the Lord God of Israel”?

They should not be thought still to have possessed among them images of the nations, since earlier their obedience had been praised. Moreover, if they had possessed them, after so many threats of the Law, prosperity would not have followed them, since punishment had been inflicted upon them when one of their number stole something devoted to destruction.

Jacob said the same thing to those who had gone out with him from Mesopotamia, where idols were worshiped in such a way that Rachel even stole her father’s idols (Genesis 31:19). After Jacob’s warning, they gave up what they had (Genesis 35:2, 4). From this it became clear that he spoke to them in this way because he knew that they possessed such things.

But here, after Joshua son of Nun’s warning, no one brought anything forward. Nevertheless, we must not think that he gave the command without reason. He did not say, “Now remove the foreign gods, if there are any among you”; rather, speaking as one who knew that they were there, he said, “the foreign gods that are among you.”

The holy Prophet therefore saw that in their hearts there were thoughts about God that were alien to God, and he warned them to remove those thoughts. For whoever conceives of God as he is not conceives and carries within his thought a foreign and false god.

But who is able to conceive of God as he truly is? Consequently, while the faithful are absent from the Lord and live as pilgrims (2 Corinthians 5:6), they must remove from their hearts the vain phantasms that rush upon them and insinuate themselves into their thoughts, as though God were such-and-such a being, when he is not. They must direct their hearts faithfully toward him, so that he may reveal himself to them through his Spirit in the manner and measure that he knows to be beneficial to us, until all falsehood is taken away—that falsehood of which it is said:

“Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:11).

Then, when not only impious falsehood but also the mirror and the riddle have passed away, we shall know face to face, just as we have been known. As the Apostle says:

“Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I have been known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

### XXX. [Ib. XXIV, 25–27]

“And Joshua made a covenant with the people on that day, and gave them a law and a judgment in Shiloh before the tabernacle of the Lord God of Israel. And he wrote these words in the book of the Law of God. And he took a great stone, and Joshua set it up beneath the terebinth before the Lord. And Joshua said to the people: Behold, this stone shall be a witness for you, because it has heard all the things that the Lord said, whatever he spoke to you today; and it shall be a witness for you in the last days, when you have lied to the Lord your God.”

Those who do not hear these words merely superficially, but examine them somewhat more deeply, must not think that so great a man was so foolish as to believe that the words of God spoken to the people were heard by a lifeless stone. Even if it had been shaped by an artisan into the likeness of a human being, it would certainly have been counted among those of whom the Psalm says:

“They have ears, but they will not hear” (Psalm 113:6).

For it is not only idols of the nations made of gold and silver that do not hear; if they are made of stone, neither do they hear.

Through this stone, therefore, he surely signified the one who became a stone of offense to unbelieving Jews and a rock of stumbling. Though rejected by the builders, he became the cornerstone (Psalm 117:22; 1 Peter 2:7–8). He was also prefigured by that rock which, struck with wood, poured forth water for the thirsty people (Exodus 17:6). Concerning it the Apostle says:

“They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

For this reason also this distinguished leader circumcised the people with stone knives (Joshua 5:2–3). Those stone knives were buried with him as well, so that they might signify to later generations a profound mystery that would benefit them.

Thus we must understand this stone spiritually as well, although it was visibly set up, as a witness that would one day stand against unbelieving—that is, lying—Jews, of whom the Psalm says:

“The enemies of the Lord have lied to him” (Psalm 80:16).

For it was not without reason that, although God’s servant Moses—or rather God through Moses—had already made a covenant with the people, which was kept in the ark called the Ark of the Covenant, and although so many mysteries and commandments had been written in the books of the Law (Exodus 24:3 and following), it is nevertheless said here:

“Joshua made a covenant with the people on that day.”

The repetition of the covenant signifies the New Testament. The same is signified by Deuteronomy, which is interpreted as “the Second Law,” and by the tablets renewed after the first tablets had been broken (Exodus 34:1, 4). What was to be fulfilled in one way had to be signified in many ways.

The fact that the stone was set up beneath the terebinth signifies what the rod signifies in relation to the rock, so that water might flow forth; for here too the stone was not set up without wood. It was set up beneath it because he would not have been exalted on the cross unless he had first been subjected in humility. Or perhaps this signifies that, at the time when Joshua son of Nun did this, the mystery still had to be veiled.

The terebinth also exudes a medicinal tear, and this is the tree that the Septuagint translators placed here, although according to the other translators the reading is “oak.”

It is indeed surprising that, at least in his final words, by which Joshua, the man of God, addressed the people, he reproached them for nothing—not even for having spared those nations whom the Lord had commanded them to destroy utterly under the ban. For it is written:

“And it came to pass, after the children of Israel had become strong, that they made the Canaanites obedient, but they did not utterly destroy them” (Joshua 17:13).

At first Scripture testified that they had not been able to do this. But afterward, when they had become strong enough to make them obedient, their failure to destroy them was certainly contrary to the Lord’s command. Nothing of this kind had happened while Joshua was leading the army.

Why, then, did he not reproach them in his final address for neglecting the Lord’s command in this matter?

Perhaps the reason is that Scripture first said that they had not been able to do it. Even after they became strong, they must be thought to have remained afraid: if they wished to spare the enemies who were ready to obey, perhaps those enemies, driven by desperation, would have been compelled to fight more fiercely against them, and the Israelites might not have been able to defeat them.

The Lord therefore did not wish to hold this human fear against them, although it reveals a certain weakness of faith. If their faith had been strong, they would have done what followed when Joshua himself was fighting.

Because they did not possess such great faith, even after they had prevailed over their adversaries, they did not dare, out of fear, to fight them to the point of their destruction. As I have said, the Lord did not attribute this fear to them as malice, pride, or contempt for his command, but as something arising from weakness of spirit, when he addressed them through Joshua in his final speech.

Thus the Apostle also says:

“Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works.”

But concerning those who abandoned him in his danger not through malice but through fear, he says:

“At my first defense no one stood by me, but everyone deserted me; may it not be counted against them” (2 Timothy 4:14, 16).

## BOOK SEVEN. Questions on Judges

### QUESTION I. [Judges, chapter 1]

At the end of the Book of Joshua, the narrator briefly carried the history forward to the point at which the children of Israel turned aside to worship foreign gods. In this book the narrative returns to the sequence of events that followed the death of Joshua son of Nun. The book therefore does not begin at the time when the people fell away to worship idols, but with earlier intervening events, after which they reached that point.

### II. [Ib. I, 1–3]

“And it came to pass, after Joshua had died, that the children of Israel inquired of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0793] The printed editions read “inquired of the Lord” with the accusative; the manuscripts have “inquired in the Lord.” In the Septuagint: διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου, “through the Lord.” This type of expression is noted in Book 7 of the *Book of Expressions*.], saying: Who will go up with us against the Canaanite as commander, to defeat him [Note: [Col. 0793] Am., Er., and most manuscripts read “to fight him”; perhaps this should be “against him,” in accordance with the Septuagint, πολεμῆσαι πρὸς αὐτόν]? And the Lord said: Judah shall go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand [Note: [Col. 0793] Thus the Sorbonicus manuscript, in accordance with the Septuagint. Other codices have “into his hands.”].”

Here it is asked whether a certain man was called Judah, or whether the tribe itself was called by that name, as commonly happens. But those who asked the Lord were seeking a leader after Joshua’s death; hence it is thought that the name of an individual man is expressed.

Yet Scripture does not ordinarily name leaders when they are appointed without also mentioning their parentage. Moreover, it is certain that after Joshua the people of Israel had leaders, the first of whom was Othniel son of Kenaz. It is therefore more correctly understood that the name Judah signifies the tribe of Judah.

The Lord wished the Canaanites to begin to be crushed by that tribe. When the people had asked about a leader, the Lord’s answer served to show that God did not wish the entire people to wage war against the Canaanites. He therefore said, “Judah shall go up.”

The Scripture then continues:

“And Judah said to Simeon his brother”—

that is, one tribe to another. The sons of Jacob called Judah and Simeon, who were named individually among their other brothers, were not still alive. Rather, the tribe of Judah said to the tribe of Simeon:

“Come up with me into my lot, and let us fight against the Canaanite [Note: [Col. 0793] The printed editions have “against the Canaanites,” but the manuscripts have “against the Canaanite”; it is clear that Augustine read it this way in Book 7 of the *Book of Expressions*], and I too will go with you into your lot.”

It is clear that the tribe of Judah requested assistance from the other tribe and intended to repay it when they too began to possess what was necessary in their own lot.

### III. [Ib. I, 9–12]

“And Caleb said: Whoever strikes the City of Letters and captures it, I will give him my daughter Achsah as a wife” [Note: [Col. 0793] All the manuscripts have “my daughter as a wife,” omitting the name Achsah.].

This event was also mentioned in the Book of Joshua (Joshua 15:16). But it is rightly asked whether it occurred while Joshua was alive and is repeated here by recapitulation, or whether it occurred after his death, after the statement had been made, “Judah shall go up,” and Judah had begun to conquer the Canaanites, during which war all these events are narrated.

It is more credible that it happened after Joshua’s death, but that it was mentioned earlier by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation, as were other events. For now, when the deeds performed by the tribe of Judah against the Canaanites are being set forth, the order of the narrative runs as follows among the other military deeds of Judah:

“The sons of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanite who lived in the hill country, the south, and the plain. And Judah went to the Canaanite who lived in Hebron, and Hebron went out to meet him. The name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arbocsepher [Col. 0794] [Note: [Col. 0794] Am., Er., and Lov. have “Kiriatharbe or Sepher.” The manuscripts and Rat. have “Kiriathar Voxsepher.” In the Septuagint: Καριαθαρβοκσεφερ, *Kariatharbocsepher*.]. And he struck Sheshai, Ahiman, and Cholmi, the sons of Anak. And from there they went up against those who lived in Debir. The name of Debir formerly was the City of Letters. And Caleb said: Whoever strikes the City of Letters and takes it, I will give him my daughter as a wife.”

From this very clear sequence of events it is evident that this happened after Joshua’s death. At the time when the cities given to Caleb were being mentioned, the narrator took the opportunity to anticipate something that happened later.

Nevertheless, I do not think it was without reason that Scripture wished to mention twice the giving of Caleb’s daughter as the reward of the victor.

### IV. [Ib. I, 14–15]

Another question arises concerning Caleb’s daughter. In the Book of Joshua the account says of her:

“And it came to pass, as she entered, that she consulted with him, saying, ‘I will ask my father for a field.’ And she cried out from the donkey,”

and so forth; there she asked her father for a field, and it was granted to her (Joshua 15:18–19).

Here, however, the text says:

“And it came to pass, as he entered, that Othniel urged her to ask her father for a field” [Note: [Col. 0794] The Thuaneus codex here and below has “moved her.” The Greek Septuagint has ἐπέσεισεν αὐτήν, “urged her.”].

There is no contradiction between the statement there, “as she entered,” and the statement here, “as he entered”; they were entering along the road together.

Where the former passage says that “she consulted with him,” that is, with her husband, saying, “I will ask my father for a field,” and that she cried out from the donkey and asked for it, the present passage says that, when she consulted with him, she was urged to ask. One statement is made there and the other here.

Both could have been expressed as follows:

“She consulted with him, saying, ‘I will ask my father for a field’; and he urged her, and she cried out from the donkey.”

Moreover, in the earlier passage the field is said to have been requested, and the name of the field is not omitted. Here, however, although she was urged by her husband to ask for a field, she is not said to have asked for the field. Instead, crying out from the pack animal—which the earlier passage calls a donkey—she asks for the redemption of water, because she had been given land in the south.

The Scripture adds:

“And Caleb gave her, according to her heart’s desire, the redemption of the upper springs and the redemption of the lower springs.”

What this means is obscure, unless perhaps she asked for the field so that she might have from its produce the means to redeem water, since water was scarce in the regions to which she was being taken as a wife.

But when it says, “Caleb gave her the redemption of the upper springs and the redemption of the lower springs,” I do not see what we should supply except “streams”: upper streams, that is, in the hill country, and lower streams, in the plains or valleys.

### V. [Book I, 18–19]

“And Judah did not inherit Gaza and its territory, nor Ashkelon and its territory, nor Ekron and its territory, nor Azotus and its adjacent lands. And the Lord was with Judah, and he inherited the hill country, because he could not inherit the inhabitants of the valley, for Rechab opposed them, and he had iron chariots.”

When I was treating that passage in the Book of Joshua son of Nun where it is written, “And the Lord gave Israel all the land,” although they did not yet possess many parts of it, I said that “all the land was given” could be understood in this way: what was not given for possession was given for a certain useful exercise (*Questions on Joshua*, question 21). This is much more evident here, since the cities which Judah did not inherit are mentioned, and it is said, “And the Lord was with Judah, and he inherited the hill country, because they could not inherit the inhabitants of the valley.”

Who would not understand that this too belonged to the fact that the Lord was with Judah, lest he be exalted by suddenly possessing everything? For when Scripture adds, “because Rechab opposed them, and he had iron chariots,” it is said whose chariots he feared—not the Lord, who was with Judah, but Judah himself. If it is asked why he feared them while the Lord was with him, this is what should prudently be understood: that God, even when favorable, restrains [Note: [Col. 0795] Thus the manuscripts and the Ratramnus edition; the other editions read “checks” (*restringere*).] the excesses of excessive prosperity in the hearts of his own people, so that he turns enemies to their advantage—not only when enemies are defeated, but also when they are feared: the former to commend his generosity, the latter to restrain their pride. For certainly the angel of Satan is an enemy of the saints; yet the Apostle says that this angel was given to strike him, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (2 Corinthians 12:7).

### VI. [Book I, 20]

“And they gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had spoken; and from it he inherited three cities of the sons of Anak, and from it he drove out three sons of Anak.”

This was already stated in the Book of Joshua son of Nun (Joshua 15:13–14), since it happened while he was alive; but here it is recalled by way of recapitulation, when Scripture was speaking about the tribe of Judah, from which Caleb came.

### VII. [Book I, 21, 8]

It is asked how it can have been said, “And the sons of Benjamin did not dispossess the Jebusite who lived in Jerusalem, and the Jebusite lived with the sons of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day,” when earlier we read that the same city was captured and burned by Judah, after the Jebusites in it had been killed.

It must be recognized that this city was held in common by two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, as the division of the lands itself shows, which was made by Joshua son of Nun (ibid. 15:63; 18:28). For this is Jebus, which is Jerusalem. Therefore these two tribes remained attached to the temple of the Lord when the others—apart from Levi, which was the priestly tribe and received no territory in the division—separated themselves from the kingdom of Judah with Jeroboam.

It must therefore be understood that Judah did indeed capture and burn the city, killing those who had been found there; but not all the Jebusites were destroyed, either because some were outside that city or because they were able to flee. The surviving Jebusites were admitted by the sons of Benjamin, with whom Judah shared that city, and lived there together with them.

Thus, when it was said, “The sons of Benjamin did not dispossess the Jebusite,” it should be understood to mean that they were unable—or perhaps unwilling—to make them tributaries. Or alternatively, “he did not dispossess the Jebusite” was said because Benjamin did not hold the land possessed by the Jebusite without him.

### VIII. [Book I, 27]

“And Manasseh did not dispossess Beth-shean, which is a city of the Scythians.”

Today it is reportedly called Scythopolis. It may be asked how, in regions so far removed from Scythia, there could have been a city of the Scythians. But it may similarly be asked how Alexander the Macedonian could have founded the city of Alexandria so far from Macedonia. He did this, of course, while waging war widely and extensively. In the same way, when the Scythians once advanced by warfare into distant regions, they could have founded this city.

For it is recorded in the history of nations that the Scythians once held almost all Asia, when they were advancing to meet the king of the Egyptians who had voluntarily declared war against them. Terrified by their approach, he withdrew into his own kingdom.

### IX. [Book I, 27]

“And Manasseh did not dispossess Beth-shean, which is a city of the Scythians, nor its daughters.”

By “its daughters” he means the cities which it had established as a kind of metropolitan city.

### X. [Book I, 28]

“And it happened, when Israel grew strong, that he placed the Canaanite under tribute, but did not dispossess him.”

Something similar had already been stated in the Book of Joshua son of Nun, almost in the same words (Joshua 17:13). Accordingly, either it is said here by recapitulation, or it was said there by anticipation—that is, either the passage here recalls what had happened, or the passage there anticipates it.

### XI. [Book I, 34]

“And the Amorite oppressed the sons of Dan in the hill country, for he did not permit them to descend into the valley.”

This too was similarly either mentioned in the Book of Joshua son of Nun by anticipation (ibid. 19:48, according to the Septuagint), or recalled here by recapitulation.

### XII. [Book II, 1]

“And the angel of the Lord went up upon Mount Clauthmon.”

The writer of the book called the place by this name because he wrote afterward; for when the angel of the Lord went up upon it, it was not yet called by that name. It received its name from weeping, since in Greek *klauthmos* (κλαυθμός) means “weeping.”

There the people wept when they heard from this angel the words of the Lord taking vengeance upon them because they had been disobedient: they had not exterminated the peoples according to his command, even though they had prevailed over them, choosing to make them tributaries rather than kill and destroy them, as the Lord had ordered.

Whether they did this by disregarding God’s command or through fear—lest their enemies fight more fiercely against them to preserve their lives than they would fight to avoid paying tribute—they certainly sinned, either by despising what had been divinely commanded or by failing to trust that the one who had commanded them could assist them.

The reason he did not wish to say this to them through Joshua—if indeed this had already begun to happen while Joshua was alive [Note: [Col. 0796] The editions read, “had ordered it to happen while he was alive.” The Vatican manuscripts more correctly read, “had already begun to happen.”], rather than being mentioned beforehand as something that began after his death—was that he wished to reproach all of them through the angel. Not all of them had done this while Joshua was alive, although some may perhaps already have begun.

It is more credible, however, that nothing of this kind began while Joshua son of Nun was alive, and that the Israelites held under him only as much land as was sufficient for them to settle in, although within their allotted territories they had room to exterminate more enemies as they increased and grew stronger. Therefore, after Joshua’s death, when they had become strong enough to do this, they preferred to keep the peoples as tributaries according to their own will, rather than kill and destroy them according to God’s will. For this reason the angel was sent to rebuke them.

What is recalled in the Book of Joshua son of Nun (Joshua 13:51, 3) I consider more likely to have been mentioned by anticipation: either Joshua himself already knew prophetically that it would happen after his death, if the book called Joshua son of Nun was written by him, or, if it was written by someone else, the writer knew that it had already happened after Joshua’s death and mentioned it beforehand in that book.

### XIII. [Book II, 3]

What does it mean that, among the other words of the divine threat, the angel of the Lord says, “I will no longer cause the people whom I said I would drive out to migrate; I will not remove them from before you. And they will be straits for you, and their gods will be a stumbling block for you,” except that we should understand that some sins also arise from God’s anger?

God was indignant and threatened them because, by choosing to live among the nations whom the Israelites had not exterminated, the gods of those nations would become a stumbling block to them—that is, would cause them to stumble against the Lord their God and live under his displeasure. This is plainly a great sin.

### XIV. [Book II, 6, 8]

“And Joshua dismissed the people, and the sons of Israel went away, each to his own house and each to his inheritance [Note: [Col. 0797] The editions lacked the words “and each to his inheritance,” which we restore on the authority of the manuscripts.], to inherit the land.”

There can be no doubt that this is repeated by way of recapitulation (ibid. 24:28–29). For the death of Joshua son of Nun is also mentioned in this book, as though everything were briefly introduced from the beginning: how the Lord gave them the land, how they lived under the judges, and what they suffered. Then the narrative returns again to the succession of the judges, beginning with the first who was appointed.

### XV. [Book II, 10]

“And another generation arose after them, which did not know the Lord, nor the works that he had done for Israel.”

He explained what he meant by saying that they “did not know the Lord”: namely, they did not know him through those glorious and miraculous works by which Israel had come to know the Lord before them.

### XVI. [Book II, 13]

“And they served Baal and the Ashtaroth.”

It is commonly said that among the peoples of those regions Baal was the name for Jupiter, while Astarte was the name for Juno; the Punic language is thought to confirm this. For the Punic people seem to use *Baal* for “Lord.” Thus, by *Baal-samen*, they are understood to say something like “Lord of heaven,” since *samen* is their word for heaven.

Juno, without doubt, was called *Astarte* by them [Note: [Col. 0797] Three manuscripts read *Estart*; two others, *Astart*.].

Since these languages do not differ greatly from one another, it is reasonably believed that Scripture says here of the sons of Israel that they served Baal and the Ashtaroth because they served Jupiters and Junos. It should not be troubling that it did not say *Astarte*, that is, “Juno,” but used the name in the plural, as though there were many Junos. The meaning was intended to refer to the multitude of images, since each image of Juno was called Juno; thus he wished as many Junos to be understood as there were images.

I think that the reason for the variation is that he wished to mention Jupiter in the singular but Junos in the plural. For the same reason, if one considered the multitude of images, Jupiters too could be called in the plural.

We find this—in other words, “Junos” in the plural—in the Greek according to the Septuagint, whereas in the Latin it was in the singular. In the version that did not have the Septuagint translation but was from the Hebrew, we read *Astaroth*, and not *Baal* but *Baalim*.

If these names happen to mean something else in the Hebrew or Syriac language, it nevertheless remains certain that they were other gods, and false ones, whom Israel ought not to have served.

### XVII. [Book II, 10, 23, and III, 1, 4]

“And he sold them into the hand of their enemies round about.”

It is often asked why he said “sold,” as though some price were understood to have been paid. But we also read in the Psalm, “You sold your people for nothing” (Psalm 44:13), and in the prophet, “You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver” (Isaiah 52:3).

Why, then, were they sold if freely and without a price, and not rather given? Perhaps it is a manner of speaking in Scripture, so that even one who is given may be called “sold.”

The best sense of the words “You were sold for nothing” and “You sold your people without a price” is that those to whom God handed over his people were impious. They had not earned the people by worshiping God, so that their worship might seem to be the price.

But when it says, “You shall not be redeemed with silver,” it does not say “with a price,” but “with silver,” so that we understand the price of redemption to be of the kind the Apostle Peter describes: “You were not redeemed with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of the unblemished Lamb” (1 Peter 1:18–19). By “silver,” the Prophet signified every sort of money when he said, “You shall not be redeemed with silver,” because they were to be redeemed indeed by the price of Christ’s blood, but not by a monetary price.

When the Lord says, “And I will not continue to remove one man from before them, from the nations whom Joshua son of Nun left and permitted to remain in order to test Israel through them, whether they would observe the way of the Lord by walking in it [Note: [Col. 0798] The editions read “into it”; shortly afterward, “into the hand of Joshua.” In these places we follow the Septuagint with the manuscripts.], as their fathers observed it, or not”—and when it says that the Lord left these nations so as not to remove them at that time and did not hand them over to Joshua—it sufficiently shows why Joshua did not destroy all those nations by war: if that had happened, there would have been no nations by which these people could be tested.

They could have been left for their benefit if, when tested through them, they were found not to be rejected. If they proved to be such as the Lord had commanded them to be, those nations would then be removed from before them, if they lived accordingly, and there would be no need for them to be exercised by wars.

The words of the Lord should be understood to extend this far: “Because this nation has so greatly abandoned my covenant, which I commanded their fathers, and they have not obeyed my voice, I also will not continue to remove a man from before them”—that is, an adversary.

The remaining words belong to the writer, who explains what the Lord meant when he said that he would not remove a man from the nations whom Joshua son of Nun had left. Then, adding the reason why he had left them, he says: “And he left them to test Israel, whether they would observe the way of the Lord by walking in it, as their fathers observed it, or not.” By this he wished it to be understood that the fathers who had observed the way of the Lord were those who had lived with Joshua, that is, during the time when he was alive.

For earlier he had reported that another generation arose after those who had lived with Joshua, and that from them began the transgressions which offended the Lord. The nations had been left for the purpose of testing them—that is, proving them—and had not been exterminated by Joshua.

Then, lest anyone think that Joshua had done this on his own human initiative, so that those nations would be left, Scripture adds: “And the Lord left these nations, so as not to remove them quickly, and he did not deliver them into the hand of Joshua.”

Then it continues: “And these are the nations whom Joshua left”—[Note: The printed editions read “whom the Lord left.” But most manuscripts, and the better ones, read “whom Joshua left,” as does the Septuagint in the Complutensian edition; Theodoret likewise has this reading in *Questions on Judges*, question 8]—“to test Israel through them, all who did not know all the wars of Canaan; indeed, for the sake of the generations of the sons of Israel, to teach them war.”

The reason for this testing was therefore that they might learn to wage war—that is, that they might wage war with the degree of piety and obedience to God’s law with which their fathers had pleased the Lord God even in warfare. This does not mean that war is something desirable, but that piety is praiseworthy in war.

What follows, “But those who before them did not know them”—what does this refer to except the nations whom those who came before these people had not known through warfare, and who were left for their testing, that is, their proving?

Then, listing who they were, he says: “Five satrapies of the foreigners,” which he describes more clearly in the Books of Kings (1 Kings 6:5, 16). Satrapies are, as it were, small kingdoms governed by satraps [Note: The manuscripts read *satrapes*]. This name was, or is, a title of honor in those regions.

“And all the Canaanite,” he says, “and the Sidonian, and the Hivite dwelling in Lebanon, from Mount Hermon as far as Lebo-hamath” [Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The editions instead read “from Mount Hermon as far as Cabemath,” except for the Louvain edition, which has “Cabemeth”]. “And it happened that Israel was tested through them,” as though he were saying: “This happened so that Israel might be tested through them—to know whether they would obey the commandments of the Lord.”

This was not so that God, who knows all things, including the future, might know, but so that they themselves might know, and might either glory in their own conscience or be convicted by it, according as they obeyed or did not obey the commandments of the Lord, which he had commanded their fathers through Moses.
