Since they were thus shown to themselves as people who had not obeyed God, through those nations which had been left for their testing—that is, for their exercise and proving—God therefore said either those things through which the angel who was sent spoke openly and explicitly [Note: [Col. 0799] Here we follow the Erfurt and Louvain editions; B. and M. read, “and he spoke expressly.”], or the words mentioned shortly before: “Because this nation has so greatly abandoned my covenant, which I commanded their fathers, and they have not obeyed my voice, I also will not continue to remove a man from before them.”

In Deuteronomy, God is represented as speaking about these hostile nations: “I will not drive them out in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you. Little by little I will drive them out, until you multiply and grow and inherit the land” (Exodus 23:29–30).

The Lord could have fulfilled this promise toward those who obeyed him, so that the extermination of those nations would take place as the Israelites increased, since their growing population would not allow the lands from which the enemies were expelled to remain desolate.

But when he says, “lest the wild beasts multiply against you,” is it not remarkable if he wished the beastlike desires and lusts to be understood—those which usually arise from the sudden success of earthly prosperity? For God could not have been able to exterminate human beings while being unable either to destroy the beasts or prevent them from being nourished.

### XVIII. [Book III, 9]

“And the Lord raised up a savior for Israel, and he saved them.”

Then, as though the question were asked, “Which savior?” he says, “Gothoniel, the son of Kenaz.” Here we must take the word in the accusative case, as though it said *Gothonielem*.

It should be noted that a human being is also called a “savior,” through whom God saves people. For it says: “The sons of Israel cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up a savior for Israel, and he saved them—Gothoniel, the son of Kenaz, the younger brother of Caleb—and he heard them.”

Among the constructions called *hyperbata*—transposed arrangements of words—this is a rare type, because it also contains what the Greeks call *hysterologia* (ὑστερολογία), the placement of a later event before an earlier one. For when it later says, “and he heard them,” the sentence would be clearer if this were placed first.

The order is: “And the sons of Israel cried out to the Lord, and he heard them, and the Lord raised up a savior for Israel.” Then the words inserted here, “and he saved them,” followed later by “Gothoniel,” or “Gothoniel the son of Kenaz,” would be clearer if stated in this order: “And the Lord raised up a savior for Israel, Gothoniel the son of Kenaz, and he saved them.”

### XIX. [Book III, 11]

Scripture testifies that the Promised Land rested from wars for forty years under Gothoniel as judge. This was as long a period of peace as the beginnings of the Roman Empire experienced under King Numa Pompilius alone.

### XX. [Book III, 19–20]

It may be asked whether the judge Ehud lied when he killed Eglon, king of Moab. For when he alone was lying in wait for Eglon in order to strike him, he said to him, “I have a secret word for you, O king,” so that Eglon would send away all those who were with him.

When this had happened, Ehud said again, “I have a word from God for you, O king.”

But this need not be a lie, since Scripture commonly calls even an action a “word”; and in truth that is what it was. When he said, “a word from God,” it should be understood that God had commanded him to do this, for God had raised him up as a savior for his people, and in those times such things had to be done by divine command.

### XXI. [Book III, 17]

It is reasonably asked how King Eglon could have been very thin, while his fat closed over the wound when he was struck. This should be understood as an expression that is to be taken in the opposite sense, as when a grove is called a *lucus* because it gives no light, or when someone is said to abound although he does not, or when “he blessed the king” means “he cursed him,” as is written in the Book of Kings about Naboth (1 Kings 21:10, 13).

For in the translation that is not according to the Septuagint but is from the Hebrew, we find: “Now Eglon was exceedingly fat.”

### XXII. [Book III, 23]

“And Ehud went outside” [Note: Most manuscripts read “Ehud went outside.” Some, however, agree with the editions in reading “to the doors”], “and passed by the guards, and shut the doors of the upper room behind him, and locked them.”

This is said by way of recapitulation, since what had been omitted is supplied. For it should be understood that he did this first, and then descended from the upper room and passed by the guards.

### XXIII. [Book III, 25]

It may be puzzling how the servants of King Eglon opened with a key what Ehud had not locked with a key; or, if he had locked it with a key, how he could have failed to take the key with him, so that they would be unable to open it with a key.

Accordingly, either another key was brought, or it was a kind of lock that could be closed without a key but could not be opened without one. There are certain things of this kind, such as those called *veruclata* [Note: This is the reading in all the manuscripts; the editions have *verudata*].

### XXIV. [Book III, 30]

Under the judge Ehud, Israel had peace in the Promised Land for eighty years—that is, twice as long as the memorable period under the Roman king Numa Pompilius.

### XXV. [Book III, 31]

“And after him arose Shamgar son of Anath” [Note: The printed editions have *Sannegar*. The manuscripts have *Samegar*, and some of them read “son of Anead.” The Septuagint has “Shamgar son of Dinach”], “and he struck six hundred foreigners, apart from calves of oxen, and saved Israel.”

How this man fought for Israel after Ehud and was said to have saved Israel may be questioned. For the Israelites had not again been taken captive or placed under the yoke of slavery.

It should be understood that he is said to have “saved” them not because an enemy had inflicted some harm, but because he prevented the enemy from inflicting harm. It must be believed that the enemy had begun to attack and was driven back by this man’s victory.

But what the addition “apart from ox-goads” means is obscure. Perhaps he also killed oxen in battle, and thus it was said that he killed six hundred men apart from what he did with the oxen that were killed. But why “ox-goads”? Is this perhaps a customary Greek expression, by which even fully grown animals are called “calves”? For it is said that people in Egypt commonly speak in this way, just as among us hens of any age are called “chicks.”

The translation from the Hebrew, however, does not have “apart from calves of oxen,” as does the version according to the Septuagint. The Hebrew version instead has “killed six hundred men with a plowshare,” which the other version does not have.

### XXVI. [Book IV, 8]

What does Barak’s reply to Deborah mean when he says, “If you go, I will go; and if you do not go with me, I will not go, because I do not know the day on which the angel of the Lord will prosper with me,” as though he could not have learned the day from a prophetess? Nor did she tell him the day; she simply went with him.

And what does “the angel of the Lord will prosper with me” mean? Does it show that the actions of angels too are prospered—that is, assisted—by the Lord, so that they succeed? Or is it an expression meaning, “he prospers with me through the angel,” that is, “he brings prosperity to me through the angel”?

### XXVII. [Book IV, 15]

“And the Lord terrified Sisera and all his chariots.”

See how Scripture commends God’s action in human hearts, so that he brings about the outcome he has determined. Certainly he terrified, or struck Sisera with astonishment, so that he might hand him over.

### XXVIII. [Book IV, 22]

When Jael, the woman who killed Sisera, had spoken to Barak, who was seeking him, Scripture says of Barak himself that “he went in to her.” It should be observed that it does not follow that, whenever Scripture says of a man that he went in to a woman, he should immediately be understood to have had intercourse with her.

Scripture frequently says, “he went in to her,” intending nothing other than that he had intercourse with her. Here, therefore, “he went in to her” properly means that he entered her house, not that intercourse is to be understood from these words.

### XXIX. [Book V, 7–8]

In Deborah’s song it says:

“The inhabitants of Israel failed; they failed until Deborah arose, until a mother arose in Israel. They chose new gods as barley bread; then they stormed the cities of the rulers.”

The interwoven order of the words here creates obscurity and raises a question. How is it to be understood as saying, “They chose new gods as barley bread; then they stormed the cities of the rulers,” as though God favored them in storming the cities of the rulers precisely when they chose new gods as barley bread?

But elsewhere in Scripture we have often learned how transposed constructions occur. When the words are restored to their order, the meaning becomes clear.

The order here is therefore:

“The inhabitants of Israel failed; they failed, choosing new gods as barley bread, until Deborah arose, until a mother arose in Israel. Then they stormed the cities of the rulers.”

### XXX. [Book V, 8]

It may be asked how it can be said, “They chose new gods as barley bread,” since, although barley bread is inferior by comparison with wheat bread, it nevertheless nourishes and is a life-sustaining food. The new gods whom those who had abandoned the living God are said to have chosen cannot be counted among foods for the soul, but rather among poisons.

Or should the comparison be understood only to the extent that the statement means this: just as disgust often causes people to reject what ought to be chosen and delight in what ought to be rejected, so, through the fault of a perverse will, as though through the sickness of disgust, although God was their true God, they chose in the false gods nothing but novelty, rejecting the truth [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts. The editions instead have: “they chose false gods for themselves, nothing but novelty, and rejected the truth”]. Thus they chose deadly food as though it were barley bread, not thinking that they would perish from it, but believing that they would derive life from it as from harmless, though inferior, food.

The comparison is therefore based on their opinion and on the sickness of their mind, not on the truth. For those new gods cannot be compared with any food that gives life.

### XXXI. [Book VI, 8, 11]

“And it happened, when the sons of Israel cried out to the Lord because of Midian, that the Lord sent a prophet to the sons of Israel, and he said to them.”

The reason why the name of this prophet is not given—something very unusual in Scripture—remains hidden. Nevertheless, I do not think there was no reason.

After the words in which he reproached the people for their disobedience, Scripture continues: “And the angel of the Lord came and sat beneath the oak that was in Ophrah.” It is not unreasonable to understand that this angel was indicated under the name “man,” so that after he had spoken these words he came to the oak mentioned and sat there.

It is well known that angels are commonly called by the name “men” (Genesis 19:10). It is less familiar and less obvious, however, that one who was an angel should be called a prophet. Yet we read that one who was a prophet was called an angel (Matthew 11:10). If the prophetic words of angels are known—that is, words by which they foretold the future—why could an angel not now be called by the name “prophet”?

Nevertheless, as I said, no explicit and manifest testimony concerning this matter presents itself.

### XXXII. [Book VI, 12]

When the angel says to Gideon, “The Lord is with you, mighty in strength,” “mighty in strength” is in the nominative case, not the vocative. The meaning is, “The Lord, mighty, is with you,” not, “You are mighty.”

### XXXIII. [Book VI, 14]

It should be noted that, when speaking to Gideon, the angel says as though by the authority of the Lord, “Have I not sent you?” For who sent him except the one who sent the angel to him?

Deborah, however, says to Barak, “Has not the Lord, the God of Israel, commanded you?” (Judges 4:6). Here it is not said, “Has not the Lord sent you?” but, “Have I not sent you?”

### XXXIV. [Book VI, 15]

When Gideon replies to the angel, “In me, Lord”—that is, “Pay attention to me”—and asks, “With what shall I save Israel? Behold, my thousand is the humblest in Manasseh,” is he to be understood as having been placed over a thousand men, whom Scripture calls *chiliarchs* (χιλίαρχοι) in Greek? Or does it mean something else?

### XXXV. [Book VI, 18–22]

It should be noted that Gideon does not say to the angel, “I will offer a sacrifice to you,” but says, “I will offer my sacrifice and set it before you.” From this it should be understood that he wished to offer the sacrifice not to the angel but through the angel.

The angel himself clearly demonstrates this. He did not accept the sacrifice from him as though it were offered to himself, but said to him: “Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and place them upon that rock, and pour out the broth.” When Gideon had done this, the angel of the Lord extended the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. Fire came out from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes.

Thus the angel himself fulfilled the service of a minister in the sacrifice offered by Gideon. A human minister, as a human being, could have supplied fire without a miracle; the angel supplied it miraculously as an angel.

Finally, Gideon then recognized that he was the angel of the Lord, for Scripture immediately adds: “And Gideon saw that he was the angel of the Lord.” Before this, therefore, Gideon had been speaking with him as with a man, although he believed him to be a man of God, and wished to offer a sacrifice in his presence, as though he would be assisted by the presence of his holiness.

### XXXVI. [Book VI, 20]

It may be asked why Gideon dared to offer a sacrifice to God outside the place where God had commanded sacrifices to be offered. God had forbidden sacrifice to him anywhere except at his tabernacle (Deuteronomy 12:13); the temple later succeeded that tabernacle. In Gideon’s time, however, God’s tabernacle was at Shiloh, and therefore sacrifice could lawfully be offered only there.

It should be understood that Gideon initially thought the angel was a prophet, and consulted God through him about offering the sacrifice. If the angel had forbidden it, it certainly would not have been done. But because he approved it and consented that it should be done, Gideon followed God’s authority in carrying it out.

God established those lawful regulations in such a way that he gave laws not to himself but to human beings. Therefore, whatever he himself commanded beyond those regulations should be understood as being carried out not by transgressors but rather by the pious and obedient, as in Abraham’s case when he was commanded to sacrifice his son (Genesis 22:2).

Elijah likewise offered a sacrifice outside the tabernacle of the Lord in order to convict the priests of the idols (1 Kings 18:30–38). He should be understood to have done this by the Lord’s command, since God ordered him to do it through revelation and inspiration, as to a prophet.

Moreover, the practice of sacrificing outside the tabernacle had become so widespread that Solomon too is found to have sacrificed at the high places, and his sacrifice was not condemned (ibid. 3:4–15). Yet kings are censured when, among their praiseworthy deeds, they did not destroy the high places where the people had been accustomed to sacrifice contrary to God’s law; and the one who destroyed them is praised with greater commendation.

Thus God tolerated rather than prohibited the custom of his people, who sacrificed outside his tabernacle—not to foreign gods, but to the Lord their God—and even in this way he heard those who offered sacrifices.

But what Gideon did—who would not understand that it was arranged through the angel so that it might take place prophetically, with that rock being signified in the prophecy? No sacrifice was offered to the rock itself; rather, fire is said to have come from it, by which the sacrifice was consumed.

Whether through the water which the struck rock poured forth in the wilderness (Numbers 20:2), or through fire, the gift of the Holy Spirit is signified, which the Lord Christ poured out upon us in the richest abundance.

This gift is also signified by water in the Gospel, where the Lord himself says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The Evangelist then adds: “Now he said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:37–39).

It is also signified by fire, where, when he came upon those gathered together, we read: “There appeared to them divided tongues as if of fire, and one rested upon each of them” (Acts 2:3). The Lord himself also says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

### XXXVII. [Book VII, 6]

“And the number of those who lapped with their hand, with their tongue, was three hundred men.” Most Latin manuscripts do not have “with their hand,” but only “with their tongue,” because they understood what was said above—“like dogs”—in that way. The Greek, however, has both: “with their hand, with their tongue,” so that it may be understood that they snatched up water with their hand and cast it into their mouths. This was like the drinking of dogs, which do not place their mouths against the water and draw it in as cattle do, but seize it with their tongues and take it into their mouths. The same is understood to have been done by these men, except that they cast the water into their mouths with their hands and caught it with their tongues.

The translation from the Hebrew expresses this more clearly in these words: “And the number of those who had lapped, with their hand putting water into their mouth, was three hundred men.” For people do not ordinarily drink in such a way that, without the help of their hands, they draw water up with their tongues like dogs. Nor had these men been commanded to do this. Rather, when they had gone down to the water to drink, many drank kneeling, since that could be done more easily and with less effort. A few, however, because they bent down without kneeling and drank like dogs, did so with the water thrown into their mouths by hand.

Since their number was three hundred, this signifies the cross because of the Greek letter Τ (tau), by which this number is represented. Through this same sign it was also prefigured that the nations would believe more fully in the crucified one, since the letter is Greek. Hence the Apostle uses the name “Greeks” to signify all the nations when he says, “To the Jew first and to the Greek” (Rom. II, 9–10), and “to Jews and Greeks” (I Cor. I, 24). He often speaks in this way of circumcision and uncircumcision, because among the languages of the nations Greek is so prominent that all the nations are fittingly signified by it.

This number should also be noticed in Abraham’s household servants, through whom he rescued his brother from his enemies, when Melchizedek blessed him in a great mystery. The fact that eighteen are exceeded there—for three hundred and eighteen are reported (Gen. XIV, 14–20)—seems to me to signify the time at which this would also take place, namely, the third period, which was to occur under grace. The first period is before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. Each period is signified by the number six because of its perfection: three times six makes eighteen.

Thus, too, that woman had been ill for eighteen years whom the Savior found bent over, raised upright, and released from the devil’s bondage, as the Gospel indicates (Luke XIII, 11–13). The fact that these men were approved, through whom Gideon would conquer, so that they were said to resemble dogs in drinking, signifies that the Lord chose what is contemptible and of no account (I Cor. I, 28), since a dog is regarded as contemptible. Hence he says, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matt. XV, 26). David likewise, wishing to cast himself down as contemptible, called himself a dog when speaking to Saul (I Sam. XXIV, 15).

### XXXVIII. [Book VII, 11]

What is meant by the statement, “Gideon himself and Phurah his servant went down to the part of the camp where there were fifty,” which some Latin manuscripts have as “to that part in which there were guards in groups of fifty in the camp,” while others read, “to the fiftieth part of the camp”? The obscure wording has produced several interpretations. Either that was the part of the camp guarded by fifty watchmen, or, if “fifty at a time” are understood to have guarded all around, these men went down to one part where fifty were stationed.

### XXXIX. [Book VII, 13]

The man who told his companion the dream that Gideon heard, so that he might be confirmed concerning the future victory, said that he had seen a barley-loaf rolling through the camp, striking the tent of Midian and overturning it. I think this should be understood to mean that the Savior would confound the proud through what is contemptible in the world—which is signified by the barley-loaf.

### XL. [Book VII, 20]

When Gideon ordered his three hundred men to shout, “The sword for the Lord and for Gideon”—that is, for this Gideon—it signifies that the sword would accomplish what pleased the Lord and Gideon.

### XLI. [Book VIII, 26–27]

The question is commonly raised concerning what the *ephud*, or *ephod*, was. If it was the priestly garment, as most say—or rather an over-garment, called in Greek *ependyma* (ἐπένδυμα), or *epomis* (ἐπωμίς), which can more appropriately be rendered in Latin as a shoulder-garment—it is reasonably asked how Gideon could have made it from so much gold.

For the text reads:

“And the weight of the golden earrings which he requested was one thousand seven hundred shekels of gold, besides the bracelets, necklaces, and purple garments that were upon the kings of Midian, and besides the necklaces that were upon the necks of their camels. And Gideon made it into an ephod and set it up in his city, in Ophrah; and all Israel fornicated after it there, and it became a stumbling-block to Gideon and to his household.”

How, then, could this garment have been made from so much gold? Samuel’s mother also made for her son, as we read, an *ephud bar*, which some have interpreted as “a linen ephod,” when she gave him to the Lord to be brought up in the temple (I Sam. II, 18). There it is more clearly evident that this was a kind of garment.

Or was it said that he “set it up in his city” so that it might be understood from this that it had been made of gold? For the text does not say “he placed it,” but “he set it up,” since it was so solid and substantial that it could be made to stand—that is, once placed, it remained standing.

When Gideon had therefore made this illicit object, “all Israel fornicated after it,” that is, followed it contrary to the Law of God. [Col. 0806] Here it is not without reason asked: since it was not an idol—that is, an image of some false and foreign god—but an ephod, one of the sacred objects of the tabernacle belonging to the priestly vestment, how can Scripture call it fornication when the people followed and venerated it?

The reason is that, apart from the tabernacle of God, where were the objects God had commanded to be made there, it was not lawful to make anything similar elsewhere. Hence Scripture continues and says, “And it became a stumbling-block to Gideon and to his household,” that is, so that one might depart from the offended God. For it was in a certain sense a kind of idol: whatever was manufactured outside God’s tabernacle and worshiped as God was an idol. The very things commanded to be made in the tabernacle were directed rather to the worship of God than to be worshiped as God or as an image of God.

Nevertheless, by *ephud* or *ephod* one may understand, by the figure of speech in which the whole is named from a part, everything Gideon established in his city as though for the worship of God, resembling the tabernacle of God. This may be indicated by the fact that the ephod is the insignia of priestly honor, which Scripture frequently mentions. Gideon’s sin would then have been that he made something resembling the tabernacle of God outside it, where God was worshiped—not that he set up a solid-gold ephod to be adored, but that from the gold taken as spoil he made objects belonging to the ornaments or implements of the sanctuary. All these are signified by the term *ephod*, because of the excellence, as I have said, of the priestly garment.

The ephod itself, if it is the shoulder-garment of the priestly vestment, was not commanded to be made entirely of gold, although it did contain some gold. It was divinely ordered to be made from gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen (Exod. XXXIX, 2). But since the Septuagint translators arranged the passage so that, after all the objects Gideon had taken from the spoils were mentioned, they added, “And Gideon made it into an ephod,” the wording appears to suggest that it was made from all that had been mentioned. Yet the figure of speech in which a part is signified by the whole may also be understood there: “He made it into an ephod” may mean “he made an ephod from it,” or “he made out of it an ephod”—not consuming all of it for the ephod, but using from it as much as was sufficient.

For in the translation from the Hebrew it is read: “And Gideon made an ephod from it.” What is written as *ephud* among the Septuagint is reported to be called *ephod* in Hebrew.

Not all priests wore such a shoulder-garment, made of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, but only the high priest. Thus the garment which we mentioned as having been made for Samuel by his mother was certainly not of this kind, since when he was given to be brought up he was not the high priest but a child. Hence, as has been said, it is called *ephud bar*, or rather *ephud bat*, as those who know the Hebrew language assert, and this is interpreted as “a linen ephod.”

I think, however, that Gideon made the chief garment and ornament of the high priest, through which the other works of the sanctuary were also signified, since he had established in his city something resembling the sanctuary of God apart from the tabernacle. Because of this sin, it became a stumbling-block to him and to his household, so that—as Scripture later relates—his numerous sons perished (Judg. IX, 5).

### XLII. [Book VIII, 27–28]

A question must not be passed over: how did the land rest for forty years in the days of Gideon, when, after the victory by which he delivered the Hebrews, he made an abomination from the gold of the spoils, all Israel fornicated after it, and it became a stumbling-block to him and to his household?

How, then, after so great a crime committed by both Gideon and the people, did the land rest for forty years, when Scripture generally shows that, whenever the people fornicated against the Lord God, they lost peace rather than gained it and were subjected to their enemies rather than protected from their enemies’ attacks?

It should be understood that Scripture, as it often does, spoke by prolepsis—that is, by anticipation—when it said that Gideon made the ephod against the Law of God from the gold taken after the enemies had been defeated and overthrown. Scripture wished to say in one place both where the gold came from and what was done with it. But this sin occurred later, at the end of Gideon’s life, when the evils that Scripture subsequently connects with it also followed. Scripture first recalled how many years the land had rested in the days of Gideon, and then, by recapitulation—that is, by returning to the order it had interrupted—spoke first of the stumbling-block that had occurred last.

### XLIII. [Book VIII, 33]

“And it came to pass, when Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned away and fornicated after the Baals; and they established Baal-berith as a covenant for themselves, so that he might be their god.”

The Baals and Baal-berith are to be understood as idols. Thus the transgression and fornication committed by the people after Gideon’s death was greater than that committed during his lifetime because of the ephod. Although the ephod had been illicitly made, it nevertheless came from the sacred objects of the tabernacle. This later fornication after idols has not even the false defense of ancestral religion.

Therefore, if that ephod was made not at the end of Gideon’s life but earlier, God bore with it patiently so that peace continued in the land, because, although something forbidden had been made, it had not departed far from him who had commanded something of that kind to be made in his tabernacle and in his honor.

But God did not wish these graver offenses, and the people’s manifest fornication after idols, to remain unpunished.

### XLIV. [Book IX, 14, 13]

The bramble, that is, a certain kind of thorn-bush, is introduced as saying to all the trees that gathered to make it king:

“If in truth you anoint me as king over you, come and trust in my protection; but if not, let fire come out from the bramble and consume the cedars of Lebanon.”

The sense is obscure, but the proper punctuation makes it clear. It should not be read, “And if not, let fire come out from the bramble,” but should be divided as follows: “And if not”—and then it should continue—“let fire come out from the bramble.” That is: “If you do not trust in my protection,” or, “If you do not truly anoint me to reign over you, let fire come out from the bramble and consume the cedars of Lebanon.”

These are the words of one threatening what it can do if they refuse to have it reign over them. But because it does not say, “Fire will come out from the bramble and consume the cedars of Lebanon,” but rather, “Let fire come out and consume,” the passage becomes more obscure than if only the punctuation were hidden.

It is a more forceful threat, and in a certain sense one whose effect is more immediate, if someone says, “If you do not do what I want, may my anger rage against you”—that is, “Let it rage now; why should I restrain it?”—than if he says, “It will rage,” in the permissive form, threatening a future punishment.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “As if he were saying, ‘Let it rage,’ in the permissive form.”]

### XLV. [Book IX, 23]

“And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem.”

It cannot easily be determined whether this word signifies that God commanded or permitted the event. The Greek has here *exapesteilen* (ἐξαπέστειλεν) for “he sent forth,” the same word found in the Psalms where we read, “Send forth your light” (Ps. XLII, 3). In some passages, however, our translators have rendered the Greek *exapesteilen* as “sent,” not “sent forth.”

It may therefore be understood in this way: God sent forth an evil spirit as though it wished to go among them—that is, he gave the evil spirit power to disturb their peace. Indeed, it did not seem absurd that an evil spirit should also be sent by the Lord for the sake of just vengeance, since some have translated *exapesteilen* even as “he sent in.”

### XLVI. [Book IX, 32–33]

The words which Zebul, the ruler of the city of Shechem, sent by messengers to Abimelech also include the following:

“And now rise by night, you and the people who are with you, and lie in ambush in the field. And in the morning, as soon as the sun rises, you shall hasten and move against the city.”

Some Latin manuscripts have “you shall hasten,” while others have *manicabis*. The Greek has a phrase which could not be expressed in Latin by one word: “You shall rise at dawn.”

Perhaps “you shall hasten” comes from the morning time, although it is also commonly said of other times when one is urging someone to act quickly. I do not recall *manicabis* as a Latin word.

What is troubling is that, after saying “as soon as the sun rises,” the text adds, “you shall rise at dawn,” even though dawn—which in Greek is called *orthros* (ὄρθρος)—means the time before the sun, when it has already become customary to say that the sky is beginning to grow white.

It should therefore be understood that the word “morning” refers to dawn itself. “As soon as the sun rises” was added to express that the action was not to take place after the sun had already risen, but when the radiance of the rising sun had appeared.

For dawn does not become bright from any other source than when the light of the returning sun begins to reach the part of the sky that we see in the east. Hence in the Gospel one evangelist says that the same event occurred “at dawn, while it was still dark” (John XX, 1), while another says “at sunrise” (Mark XVI, 2). The light of dawn, however slight, was necessarily produced by the sun rising—that is, coming toward its rising and casting forth its radiance as its presence approached.

Some uneducated people have thought that this light was not from the sun but was the light first created, before God created the sun on the fourth day.

### XLVII. [Book X, 1]

“And after Abimelech there arose Thola son of Phua, son of his paternal uncle, a man of Issachar, to save Israel.”

He called him “the son of his paternal uncle,” saying “the son of his father’s brother,” although it would have been more orderly, customary, and clear to say “the son of the brother of his father.” For he was the son of his paternal uncle, as is found more clearly in the translation from the Hebrew.

Thus the expression “of his father’s brother” is not declined from the nominative “father of a brother,” but from “father’s brother,” which means “paternal uncle.” Whether one puts “this father of a brother” in the nominative, or “this father’s brother,” the genitive is “of this father’s brother.”

Another question, however, arises: how could Phua, a man of Issachar—that is, a man from the tribe of Issachar—have been Abimelech’s paternal uncle, when Abimelech had Gideon as his father, and Gideon belonged to the tribe of Manasseh? How, then, could Phua and Gideon have been brothers, so that Phua could be the paternal uncle of Abimelech, whose uncle’s son Thola succeeded Abimelech according to this account?

Gideon and Phua could therefore have had the same mother but different fathers. They would have been brothers as sons of one mother, not of one father. Women commonly married into tribes other than their own. Thus Saul, although he was from the tribe of Benjamin, gave his daughter to David, a man from the tribe of Judah (I Sam. XVIII, 27). The priest Jehoiada, certainly a man from the tribe of Levi, married the daughter of Joram the king, a man from the tribe of Judah (II Chron. XXII, 11).

[Note: Col. 0809. The manuscripts read “Judae,” or “Jude”; the Septuagint has “Iadaé.”]

This is why we read in the Gospel that Elizabeth and Mary were relatives (Luke I, 36), although Elizabeth was descended from the daughters of Aaron. From this it is understood that a woman from the tribe of Levi, one of the daughters of Aaron, married into the tribe of Judah. Thus a relationship arose between the two women, so that the flesh of the Lord was descended not only from a royal line but also from a priestly one.

### XLVIII. [Book XI, 24]

Among the other things Jephthah says through messengers to the king of the Ammonites, he also says:

“Will you not inherit whatever Chemosh your god has inherited for you? And shall we inherit everything that the Lord our God has inherited from before you?”

Some Latins thought this should be translated, “Will you not possess whatever Chemosh your god has given you as an inheritance?” This could appear to mean that Jephthah affirmed that this god, called Chemosh, had been able to give something as an inheritance to his worshipers.

Others have: “Will you not possess whatever Chemosh your god possessed?” This sounds as though he had been able to possess something.

Or was it perhaps said according to the passage that the nations were placed under angels, in accordance with the Song of Moses, the servant of God (Deut. XXXII, 8, according to the Septuagint)? Was the angel under whom the Ammonites were placed therefore called Chemosh? Who would dare affirm this, since the statement may be understood as having been made according to their belief, because he thought that their god possessed this land or had given it to them as a possession?

The meaning is clearer in the Greek wording: “Will you not inherit whatever Chemosh your god has inherited for you?” In the word “you,” it may be understood as though it said, “as it appears to you.” He has inherited it for you, because you think this, not because he was able to inherit anything.

Finally, in what follows, “And everything that the Lord our God has inherited from before you,” it does not say, “has inherited for us,” as though it meant “as it appears to us,” but that he has truly inherited it from before you, because he took it from them and gave it to these people. “This,” he says, “we shall inherit.”

### XLIX. [Book XI]

The matter of Jephthah’s daughter, whom her father offered to God as a burnt offering because he had made a vow during the war that, if he won, he would offer as a burnt offering whoever came out of his house to meet him, is usually regarded as a major and extremely difficult question.

Some wish to know what this means and inquire about it devoutly. Others, however, who attack these holy Scriptures with ignorant impiety, especially charge them with this: that the God of the Law and the Prophets was pleased even by human sacrifices.

We first answer their slanders in this way: the God of the Law and the Prophets—or, to speak more explicitly, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—was not pleased even by those sacrifices in which animals were offered as burnt offerings. Rather, because those sacrifices were symbolic and shadows of future things, he wished to commend to us the realities signified by them. There was also this useful reason why those sacrifices were changed and no longer merely commanded but forbidden: so that we would not think God was truly pleased by such things according to carnal sentiment.

But whether future things ought also to have been signified by human sacrifices is reasonably asked. This is not because we ought to shrink from or fear the deaths of people who would one day die, if those who willingly accepted such things being done to them were commended to God for eternal reward. But if that were true, this kind of sacrifice would not displease God. Scripture itself clearly testifies that it does displease him.

Although he wished and commanded that all the firstborn should be dedicated to him and belong to him, he nevertheless wished human firstborn to be redeemed (Exod. XIII, 2, 12–13), so that people would not believe that they ought to sacrifice to God the sons whom they had first brought forth.

Then Scripture speaks even more clearly, showing that God condemns human burnt offerings by forbidding them, detesting them among other nations and commanding his people not to imitate them:

“When the Lord your God has destroyed the nations which you are entering to possess their land, removing them from your presence, and you have dispossessed them and dwell in their land, take heed to yourself that you do not seek to follow them after they have been destroyed from before you. Do not seek their gods, saying, ‘As those nations do for their gods, so will I do also.’ You shall not do so to the Lord your God. For they have done for their gods the abominations which the Lord hates; for they burn their sons and their daughters in fire to their gods” (Deut. XII, 29–31).

What could be shown more clearly by these testimonies of Holy Scripture—to pass over other passages of this kind—than that the God from whom this Scripture was given to the human race not only does not love such sacrifices, but even hates them, sacrifices in which human beings are slaughtered?

He clearly loves and crowns the person who, being just and suffering injustice, struggles for the truth even to death, or is killed by enemies whom he has offended on account of justice, repaying good for evil—that is, love for hatred. The Lord calls such blood “righteous blood,” from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Matt. XXIII, 35).

Most especially, Christ himself shed his blood for us and offered himself as a sacrifice to God. He offered himself in such a way that he was killed by enemies for the sake of justice. In imitation of him, thousands of martyrs struggled for the truth even to death and were sacrificed by raging enemies. Scripture says of them, “As gold in the furnace he tested them, and as a holocaust offering he accepted them” (Wis. III, 6). Hence the Apostle also says, “For I am already being poured out as a sacrifice” (II Tim. IV, 6).

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have: “Such love, which the Lord calls righteous blood, is to be sought from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah.”]

But Jephthah did not make a burnt offering of his daughter to the Lord in this way; rather, he did so although animals had been commanded to be offered and human beings forbidden to be sacrificed.

What he did seems more like what Abraham did, which the Lord specifically commanded (Gen. XXII). God did not command by a general law that such sacrifices should ever be offered to him; indeed, he entirely forbade them. Thus there is a difference between what Jephthah did and what Abraham did: Abraham offered his son because he had been commanded to do so, whereas Jephthah did what the Law forbade and no special command ordered.

Furthermore, not only did God later show in his Law that he was not pleased by such sacrifices; he also showed it at that very time in the case of Abraham’s son. Although he had tested the father’s faith by giving the command, he nevertheless prevented him from killing his son and supplied a ram so that the sacrifice could lawfully be completed according to the ancient custom appropriate to that time.

If anyone is troubled by how Abraham could piously believe that God was pleased by such sacrifices, if they were illicitly offered to God, and therefore thinks that Jephthah too rightly believed that such a sacrifice could be acceptable to God, let him first consider that it is one thing to make a vow voluntarily and another to obey one who commands.

If a master establishes a practice in a household and orders a servant to do something extraordinary, and the servant does it with praiseworthy obedience, he is not for that reason free from punishment if he presumptuously undertakes to do it on his own.

In addition, Abraham had grounds for believing that he should not spare his son because of the divine command. He did not believe that God gladly accepted such victims, but that God had commanded this so that he might raise the slain boy and demonstrate something by it as a wise God. This is also stated about him in the Epistle called “to the Hebrews,” where his faith is praised because he believed that God could raise his son from the dead (Heb. XI, 17–19).

Jephthah, however, made a human sacrifice without God’s command or request and contrary to his lawful precept. For it is written:

“And Jephthah vowed a vow to the Lord and said: ‘If you truly deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, then whoever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon shall belong to the Lord, and I will offer him as a burnt offering.’”

By these words he certainly did not vow some animal that he could offer as a burnt offering according to the Law. It was not customary for animals to come out to meet commanders returning victorious from war. As for the many kinds of animals, dogs commonly run out to meet their masters, playing with them in affectionate service. Jephthah could not have had such animals in mind in his vow, lest he appear to have vowed something not only illicit but also contemptible and unclean according to the Law, thereby insulting God.

Nor does he say, “Whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me, I will offer it as a burnt offering,” but, “Whoever comes out, I will offer him.” There is no doubt that he had a human being in mind. Yet perhaps he did not specifically have his only daughter in mind, although, given the greatness of her father’s glory, who else could have come before him except perhaps his wife?

For he does not say “whatever comes out” but “whoever comes out from the doors of my house.” Scripture commonly uses the masculine gender for either sex, as when it is said of Abraham, “He rose from the dead one” (Gen. XXIII, 3), although his wife had died.

Since Scripture appears to have made no judgment about this vow and deed, as it judged openly in Abraham’s case when he offered his son because he had been commanded to do so, but merely left the matter for readers to judge—as with the deed of Judah, Jacob’s son, who unknowingly went in to his daughter-in-law and, insofar as it depended on him, committed fornication because he thought her a prostitute (Gen. XXXVIII, 15), a deed which Scripture neither approved nor condemned but left to be assessed and weighed in consultation with the justice and Law of God—we might therefore say that God was displeased by such a vow and that it was brought to its punishment by having Jephthah’s only daughter be the one to meet her father.

If he had hoped for and desired this, he would not have torn his clothes as soon as he saw her and said, “Alas, my daughter! You have hindered me; you have become a stumbling-block before my eyes.”

[Note: Col. 0812. The printed editions read “had vowed”; the better manuscripts read “had wished.”]

Furthermore, the Lord allowed his daughter the long delay of sixty days and did not prevent the killing of his only and beloved child, as he had prevented Abraham, until Jephthah struck himself with the most grievous bereavement by fulfilling what he had vowed, without in any way appeasing God by a human sacrifice.

We might therefore say that punishment was repaid to such a father so that the example of such a vow would not remain unpunished: otherwise people might think that they were making a great vow to God when they vowed human victims, and, what is more horrifying, their own children; or such vows might not be genuine but feigned, since those who made them would hope, by the example of Abraham, that God would prevent their fulfillment.

We could say this, I repeat, were we not held back from that judgment especially by two testimonies of the divine Scriptures. Since this deed is recorded for remembrance in books of such authority, we must investigate it more carefully and cautiously, insofar as the Lord helps us, lest we give a rash judgment in either direction.

One testimony is that in the Epistle to the Hebrews Jephthah is counted among such men that we hesitate to blame him. It is written:

“And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah, and David, and Samuel, and the prophets—who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced justice, and obtained promises” (Heb. XI, 32).

The other is that, where these things are related about him—namely, that he made such a vow and fulfilled it—Scripture first says:

“And the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, and passed through the watchtower of Gilead, and from the watchtower of Gilead he crossed over to the children of Ammon; and Jephthah vowed a vow to the Lord,”

followed by the other matters pertaining to this very vow. Thus everything that happened afterward appears to be understood as the work of the Spirit of the Lord who had come upon him.

These testimonies compel us to ask rather why the deed happened than to condemn it hastily.

First, however, the testimony I cited from the Epistle to the Hebrews, among the praiseworthy men recalled there, includes not only Jephthah but also Gideon. Scripture likewise says of Gideon, “The Spirit of the Lord strengthened Gideon” (Judg. VI, 34). Yet we cannot praise his deed—making an ephod from the gold of the spoils, after which all Israel fornicated, and which became a stumbling-block to Gideon’s household (Judg. VIII, 27). Indeed, because Scripture judges it here most openly, we do not hesitate to condemn it.

Nevertheless, this does no injury to the Spirit of the Lord who strengthened him so that he might overcome the enemies of his people with such ease. Why, then, is Gideon counted among those who “through faith conquered kingdoms, practicing justice,” unless because Holy Scripture, while truly praising the faith and justice of such people, is not thereby prevented from also truthfully noting any sins of theirs that it knows and judges ought to be noted?

When that same Gideon asked for a sign and, as he himself said, tested God with the fleece (Judg. VI, 39), I do not know whether he did not transgress the commandment that says, “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Deut. VI, 16). Nevertheless, even in his testing, the Lord revealed what he wished to announce: the fleece being wet while the entire ground around it was dry signified the first people of Israel, among whom were the holy ones, as though amid a spiritual rain of heavenly grace. Then, when the ground was wet and the fleece dry, it signified the Church spread throughout the whole world, possessing heavenly grace not in the fleece as though in a covering, but openly, while that earlier people had been separated from and dried up by the dew of the same grace.

Yet Gideon deserved this testimony in the Epistle to the Hebrews among the faithful and those who practiced justice because of the good and faithful life in which he is to be believed to have died.

Whether, then, because it is said, “The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah,” and the vow followed, together with the defeat of the enemies and the fulfillment of the vow, all these things should be attributed to the Spirit of the Lord, so that this sacrifice should be regarded as though the Lord had commanded it, as he commanded Abraham’s sacrifice, I would not readily say.

For a distinction can certainly be made in Gideon’s case: after the sin he committed by making the ephod, after which the entire people fornicated, no prosperity of his is recorded. After Jephthah made his vow, however, his notable victory followed—the very victory for which he had made the vow—and after attaining it he fulfilled what he had vowed.

Again, we must consider that Gideon, although not after making the ephod, nevertheless after testing the Lord—which was certainly a sin—brought salvation to the people by slaughtering and overcoming their enemies in a great victory. For it is written:

“And Gideon said to the Lord, ‘Let your indignation not be kindled against me, and I will speak once more, and I will test once more with the fleece,’”

and so forth.

He feared God’s anger because he knew that, by testing him, he was committing a sin—something God most clearly forbids in his Law. Yet this sin of his was followed by the evidence of a marvelous sign and by the great success of victory and the people’s deliverance.

God had already determined to help the afflicted people, and he used the mind of this leader whom he had chosen for that task—a mind not only faithful and devout but also failing and sinning—to announce what he wished and to accomplish what he had declared.

For God accomplished many things for his people not only through those who, even if they sinned, are nevertheless numbered among the just, but also through Saul himself, who was rejected in every respect. The Spirit of God came upon Saul also, and he prophesied—not when he was acting justly, but when he was raging against the holy and innocent man David (I Sam. XIX, 20–23).

The Spirit of the Lord acts through the good and the wicked, through those who know and those who do not know, accomplishing what he knows must be accomplished and has determined. Through Caiaphas also, the Lord’s most bitter persecutor, who did not know what he was saying, the Spirit uttered the notable prophecy that Christ had to die for the nation (John XI, 49–51).

Who acted, then, except the Spirit of the Lord, taking care to announce what was to come, so that this very matter—the fleece first being wet and afterward dry, and the ground first dry and afterward wet—would come to the mind of Gideon, who wished to test the Lord and did not believe what had already been told him, namely that the people’s salvation would be accomplished through his hand?

Thus his failure of faith should be attributed to his weakness and sin, while the fact that God used even such a mind for what had to be signified to the human race should be understood as belonging to God’s mercy and marvelous providence.

If, however, someone says that Gideon did and said everything knowingly, by prophetic revelation, so that such signs might be displayed through him; that he did not waver in faith, and believed what the Lord had already promised him; but that, in prophetic action, he wished to test Him by means of the fleece, and that his testing was therefore blameless, just as Jacob’s deception was (Gen. 27:15–16); and that when he said to the Lord, “Let not your indignation be angry with me,” he did not say this because he feared the Lord’s anger, but because he trusted that He would not be angry when Gideon did what, instructed by His Spirit, he understood as a prophet ought to do—let him say so, if he wishes, provided only that, whatever it may signify, he does not dare to excuse from sin the thing which Scripture itself condemned in the matter of the ephod. For it also appears that Gideon devised on his own initiative the sign whereby the three hundred men, whose number itself pertained to the sign of the cross, received earthen jars and enclosed burning torches in them; when the jars were broken, the suddenly flashing lights terrified so great a multitude of enemies (Judg. 7:16–22). Scripture does not say that the Lord instructed him to do this. Yet who but the Lord inspired Gideon’s mind and purpose to devise so great a sign? He prefigured that His saints would possess the treasure of evangelical light in earthen vessels, as the Apostle says: “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). When these vessels were broken, as it were, in the passion of martyrdom, a greater radiance of their glory shone forth, overcoming the impious enemies of evangelical preaching with Christ’s unexpected brightness.

Thus, whether through those who knew or through those who did not know, the Spirit of the Lord worked, in prophetic times, the prefiguration and proclamation of future things. Their sins must not therefore be said not to have been sins, because God, who knows how to use even our evils for good, also used their sins themselves to signify what He willed. Accordingly, if it was not a sin—whether to vow or to perform the killing of any human being, or even a parricidal sacrifice—because it signified something great and spiritual, then God prohibited such things and testified that He hated them for no reason. For those things which He commanded to be done are likewise referred to some signification of great spiritual realities. Why, then, would He prohibit those acts, since, on account of the same signification of those realities—the reason why these other acts were lawfully performed—they too could nevertheless lawfully be performed? Unless it is because human sacrifices, even when they signified something of the sort that ought rightly to be believed, were not pleasing to God: not when someone is killed by enemies because he wished to live rightly or refused to sin, for the sake of justice, but when one human being is sacrificed by another as a chosen victim, after the manner of an animal.

“But what if,” someone may say, “because animal victims, by the very fact that they had long been customary—even though those who rightly understood them referred them also to the signification of spiritual realities—nevertheless made people less attentive to seeking the great mystery of Christ and the Church; and for this reason [Col. 0816] God, wishing by a remarkable and unexpected deed to rouse human minds as though they were asleep, took care that something of this kind should be offered to Him, especially since He had forbidden such sacrifices to be offered to Him? In this way the very astonishment would give rise to a great question, and the great question would lift the pious mind to investigate the great mystery; and the human mind, piously searching the depth of prophecy, would draw up the Lord Christ like a fish on a hook from the depths of Scripture.”

We do not resist this reasoning and consideration. But the question of the vow-maker’s intention is one matter, and the question of God’s providence, which makes the best use of whatever intention he may have had, is another. Therefore, if the Spirit of the Lord, who came upon Jephthah, commanded him to make this vow—something the Scripture itself has not made explicit—then, if He did command it, since it is not permissible to despise His commands, not only is folly not to be blamed, but obedience is even to be praised. For even if a person kills himself—something which, to be sure, it is wicked to do by human will and deliberation—it must certainly be understood as done obediently rather than criminally, if it was commanded by God. We discussed this question sufficiently in the first book of *The City of God* (*The City of God*, book 1, chapter 21).

But if Jephthah, following human error, thought that a human sacrifice ought to be vowed, then his sin was justly punished in the case of his only daughter; and he himself seems sufficiently to show this by his words when he says, “Alas, my daughter, you have hindered me; you have become a stumbling-block before my eyes,” while also tearing his garments. Nevertheless, even here his error contains a certain praise of faith: he feared God, so that he would fulfill what he had vowed, and did not evade the sentence of divine judgment against him—either hoping that God would prohibit the act, as He did in Abraham’s case, or deciding that it was better to carry out God’s will, even when He did not prohibit it, once he had understood it, than to despise it.

Yet here too one may rightly ask whether it is not more truly understood that God did not wish this to be done, and that Jephthah would rather have obeyed God by not doing it, since God had shown that He did not wish such a thing in the case of Abraham’s son and in the lawful prohibition. Nevertheless, if Jephthah did not act for this reason, he would seem to have spared his only daughter for his own sake rather than to have followed God’s will. He therefore understood more readily, when his daughter came out to meet him, that God was exacting punishment, and he faithfully submitted himself to a just penalty, fearing a harsher vengeance as though it were imposed for evasion. For he believed that the soul of his good and virginal daughter would also be well received, since she had not vowed herself to be sacrificed, but had not resisted her father’s vow and will and had followed God’s judgment.

Just as death is not to be voluntarily inflicted by anyone upon himself or upon anyone else, so it is not to be refused when God commands it, since by His ordinance it must be undergone at some time. Nor does anyone who refuses to endure it labor to avoid it altogether, but only to postpone it.

[Note: [Col. 0816] The words that follow—namely, “But these things, as we hasten,” and continuing up to “now already”—are absent from the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts.]

For the present, as we hasten onward, what has been said concerning the foregoing question has seemed to us, in this respect, to have been discussed sufficiently, in whatever manner.

Now let us investigate, insofar as God assists us, and briefly consider what the Spirit of the Lord—whether through Jephthah’s ignorance or knowledge, [Col. 0817] through his imprudence or obedience, through his offense or faith—prefigured in this deed. This passage of the holy Scriptures admonishes and in some way compels us to think of a certain man powerful in strength. For Jephthah is described in this way, and his name is interpreted as “Opening.” The Lord Christ, as the Gospel indicates, “opened the understanding” of His disciples “so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45, 27).

Jephthah’s brothers rejected him and drove him from his father’s house, charging him with being the son of a prostitute, as though they themselves had been born of a lawful wife. The chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees did the same against the Lord. They appeared to boast of observing the Law, as though He were violating the Law and therefore were, so to speak, not a legitimate son. Although He had assumed a body from the holy Virgin, as is known to believers, His mother, insofar as her nation is concerned, may also be called that Jewish synagogue. Let whoever wishes turn through the prophetic books and see how often, and with what severe and indignant language, that people are reproved as an unchaste woman for their fornications.

Hence there is also that most recent passage in this book, whether in the statement that after Gideon made the ephod all Israel committed fornication, or in the statement that they went after the gods of the nations by whom they were surrounded. For this reason divine anger was stirred against them, and for eighteen years they were crushed by the children of Ammon (Judg. 8:27; 10:6–8).

But were not the priests, scribes, and Pharisees whom we have said were prefigured in those who persecuted and expelled Jephthah—as they persecuted and expelled the Lord Christ as though He were not a legitimate son—also born from that same people of Israel? The likeness is shadowed forth in this respect: as I have said, they regarded themselves as observers of the Law and thought that they had the right to expel, as illegitimate, the one who appeared to act against the commands of the Law, while they themselves were legitimate. In this sense that people is said to commit fornication: by not keeping the commands of the Law, it did not show fidelity to its husband.

Thus it is written concerning Jephthah: “And the sons of the wife grew strong, and they expelled Jephthah.” The word used here, “grew strong,” signifies figuratively “prevailed.” This was fulfilled in the Jews, who prevailed over Christ’s weakness, because He willed to endure from them the sufferings that were necessary—as Jacob, likewise signifying this same thing, prevailed over the angel with whom he wrestled to portend it (Gen. 32:24–28).

They therefore said to Jephthah, “You shall not inherit in our father’s house, because you are the son of a prostitute.” It was as though they were saying what the Gospel records: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath” (John 9:16). And, boasting as though they were legitimate sons, they said to the Lord, “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God” (John 8:41).

“And Jephthah fled from the face of his brothers and dwelt in the land of Tob.” He fled because He concealed how great He was; He fled because He remained hidden from them while they raged. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). He fled because they saw the weakness of the dying man but did not see the power of the risen one.

[Col. 0818] He dwelt in a good land, or, to express it more fully, a rich and fertile land. What is called in Greek ἀγαθόν (*agathon*, “good”) is called in Latin *opimum* (“rich” or “fertile”); and this is interpreted as “Tob.” Here, it seems to me, his resurrection from the dead is to be understood. For what land is richer than an earthly body clothed with the excellence of immortality and incorruption?

It is said of Jephthah that, after fleeing from the face of his brothers and dwelling in the land of Tob, outlaws gathered to him and went about with him. Although, even before the Passion, the Lord was reproached for eating with tax collectors and sinners, when He replied that the healthy do not need a physician, but the sick (Matt. 9:11–12); and although He was “numbered among the transgressors” (Isa. 53:12) when He was crucified among thieves and transferred one of them from the cross to paradise (Luke 23:33, 43), nevertheless, after He rose again and began to be, according to what we explained above, in the land of Tob, wicked men gathered to Him because of the forgiveness of sins. They walked with Him because they lived according to His commands.

This does not cease to happen even now and hereafter, until the wicked take refuge in Him, so that He may justify the ungodly who turn to Him, and the unrighteous may learn His ways (Ps. 50:15).

Now, when those who had rejected Jephthah—for he was a Gileadite—turned to him and sought him as the one through whom they might be delivered from their enemies, how clearly does this prefigure that those who rejected Christ would turn back to Him and find salvation in Him! This may refer either to those whom the apostle Peter accused of that very crime, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, and whom he urged to turn to Him whom they had persecuted: they were pierced in heart and desired salvation from the one whom they had alienated from themselves. For what is being delivered from enemies except being delivered from sins? Thus he said to them, “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins will be forgiven you” (Acts 2:22–38).

Or it may rather signify the calling of the people of Israel that is hoped for at the end. This seems more clearly indicated by the statement, “And it came to pass after days,” which certainly signifies “after a period of time.” It thereby suggests that we should not understand this as referring to what belonged to the Lord’s recent Passion, but to what would happen afterward. This also seems to be indicated by the fact that the elders of Gilead came to Jephthah, so that the later and final times may be understood through the elders’ age.

“Gilead” is interpreted as “Rejecting” or “Revelation.” Both meanings fit this matter very well, because at first they rejected the Lord Christ, and afterward He will be revealed to them.

Jephthah was sought as commander against the children of Ammon, whose defeat would bring deliverance to those who wished to fight against them under his command. Since “Ammon” is interpreted as “Son of my people” or “People of sorrow,” it certainly signifies either those enemies who, persisting in unbelief, were foretold from that very people, or all those predestined to Gehenna, where there will be “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 25:30), as though they were a people [Col. 0819] of sorrow.

Yet “people of sorrow” may also suitably be understood as the devil and his angels, either because they procure eternal misery for those whom they deceive, or because they themselves have been assigned to eternal misery.

Jephthah gave an elegant reply to the elders of Gilead, expressing the prophecy much more clearly: “Did you not hate me, and expel me from my father’s house, and drive me away from yourselves? Why, then, have you come to me when you are in distress?” Something similar was prefigured in Joseph, whom his brothers rejected by selling him (Gen. 37:28), and to whose aid and mercy they turned when they were afflicted by famine (Gen. 42–44).

Here, however, the signification of future things shines forth much more fully: it was not the very brothers who had expelled Jephthah who came to him, but the elders of Gilead, pleading with him on behalf of the entire people. The same nation is called Israel, whether in those who existed at that time and rejected Christ, or in those who afterward returned to His help. To the hostile people, drawing out and preserving its long hatred, whether in its ancestors or in its descendants, and finally converted in those who would be converted at the end, it is said: “Did you not hate me, and expel me from my father’s house?” For this seemed to those who persecuted Him to be what they had done: they had expelled Christ from the house of David, whose kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:33).

And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “We have not come to you in this way now.” It was as though the Jews converted to Christ were saying: “Then we came to persecute; now we come to follow.” They also profess that he will be their head against the enemies. He replies that, if he conquers their enemies, he will be their ruler—something Gideon refused when the Israelites wished to make him so. For he replied to them, “The Lord will rule over you” (Judg. 8:22–23).

A king is signified by the title “ruler”; but that people did not yet have a king in the time of the Judges. They began to have Saul (1 Sam. 10:1), and afterward his other successors, who are recorded in the books of Kings. For in Deuteronomy, when they are instructed what kind of king they should have, if they should desire one (Deut. 17:14), he is not there called “king,” but “ruler.”

But because this Jephthah prefigured the one who is the true King—and this was also written in the title affixed to His cross, which Pilate did not dare to erase or amend (John 19:19–22)—we must believe that the words “I will be your ruler” were spoken with reference to Him. They had said, “You will be our head,” because “Christ is the head of the man” (1 Cor. 11:3), and He Himself is “the head of the body, the Church” (Eph. 5:23).

Finally, after Jephthah delivered them from all their enemies, he did not become their king. We are therefore to understand that the statement belonged rather to the prophecy concerning Christ than properly to Jephthah himself. Scripture concludes its account of Jephthah in this way: “And Jephthah judged Israel for six years, and Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city, Gilead” (Judg. 12:7). He therefore judged Israel like the other Judges; he did not rule there as prince, like those contained in the books of Kings.

Moreover, after that same Jephthah had been appointed their commander, he sent messengers to the enemy first bearing words of peace. This is shown by what the Apostle says, [Col. 0820] in whom Christ was speaking: “If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, be at peace with all people” (Rom. 12:18). To examine all the very words that Jephthah sent would be too lengthy for us as we hasten onward. Nevertheless, insofar as they concern the signification of future things, they seem to me to be understood in such a way that Christ’s teaching may be discerned in them, admonishing us how we ought to walk—that is, how we ought to live—among those who have not been called according to the purpose. “The Lord knows those who are His” (2 Tim. 2:19).

Moreover, when Jephthah was about to defeat his enemies, “the Spirit of the Lord came upon him.” This signifies the Holy Spirit imparted to the members of Christ.

That he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, crossed the watchtower of Gilead, and went from the watchtower of Gilead across to the children of Ammon signifies the progress of Christ’s members toward victory over their enemies. For “Gilead” is interpreted as “Rejecting,” and “Manasseh” as “Necessity.” Those who are making progress must therefore pass beyond the rejecters—that is, those who despise—and must also pass beyond necessity, lest, when the one who is making progress has passed beyond those who despise, he yield to those who cause fear.

They must also pass beyond the watchtower of Gilead, since “Gilead” is also interpreted as “Revelation.” A watchtower is a height from which one looks out or looks down—that is, looks from above. The watchtower of Gilead therefore seems to me suitably to signify the pride of revelation. Hence the Apostle says, “And because of the greatness of the revelations, that I might not be exalted” (2 Cor. 12:7). This too must therefore be passed beyond; one must not remain there because of the danger of falling. Once these things have been passed beyond, the enemies are easily overcome. This is signified by the statement that he passed from the watchtower of Gilead to the children of Ammon, concerning whom we have already spoken as enemies.

And Jephthah made a vow and said: “If you will indeed deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, whoever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon shall be the Lord’s, and I will offer him as a burnt offering.”

Whoever considers what Jephthah may have thought in this passage according to human reasoning does not seem to think that he had his only daughter in mind. Otherwise, when he saw her come out to meet him, he would not have said, “Alas, my daughter, you have hindered me; you have become a stumbling-block before my eyes.” For “you have hindered me” is said as though he indicated that he had been prevented from fulfilling what he had intended.

But whom could he have first imagined coming out to meet him, since he had no other children? Did he imagine his wife, and did God prevent this from happening, while also ensuring that it would not go unpunished, so that no one afterward would dare such a thing, and so that, through the great providence of God, the mystery of the Church might be prefigured even by what occurred?

The prophecy is therefore fitted together from both elements: from what the vow-maker intended and from what happened against his will. For if he imagined his wife, the wife is the Church of Christ. “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery,” says the Apostle; “but I am speaking with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31–32).

But because the wife of this Jephthah could not be a virgin, [Col. 0821] in the fact that a daughter came out instead, the forbidden sacrifice of the rash vow-maker was not left unpunished, and the virginity of the Church was signified. Nor is it contrary to the truth that the same Church is signified by the name “daughter.” For whose type did that woman represent, when the Lord said to her, after she had been healed by touching His garment’s fringe, “Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Matt. 9:20–22)?

And certainly, in a matter no one disputes, He Himself called His disciples the sons of the bridegroom, most clearly indicating that He was the bridegroom: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them; but days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” [Note: [Col. 0821] This note is missing in Migne’s text.] (Matt. 9:15).

The Church, whom the blessed Apostle calls a “chaste virgin” (2 Cor. 11:2), will therefore be a burnt offering when, at the resurrection of the dead, what is written will be fulfilled in all: “Death is swallowed up in victory. Then He will deliver the kingdom to God the Father” (1 Cor. 15:54, 24). That kingdom is the Church itself, and the king is the one whose figure that vow-maker bore.

But because this will occur when the sixth age of the world has been completed, a postponement of sixty days was requested from the virginity. For the Church is gathered from all the ages. The first is from Adam to the Flood; the second from the Flood—that is, from Noah—to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the deportation to Babylon; the fifth from that deportation to the Virgin’s childbirth; the sixth from then until the end of this world.

Through these six ages, as through sixty days, the holy virgin Church mourned her virgin state. For although she is virginal, she nevertheless had sins to mourn; on account of them, this same virgin, spread throughout the whole world, says daily, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12). I think that she preferred to call the same sixty days “two months” because of the two men: one through whom death came, and the other through whom came the resurrection of the dead. On their account there are also said to be two Testaments.

As for the command that was established in Israel—that from year to year they should come together to lament Jephthah’s daughter, the Gileadite, for four days each year—I do not think it signifies anything after the burnt offering had been completed, which will result in eternal life. Rather, it signifies the former times of the Church, in which “those who mourn” were blessed.

The universality of the Church is represented by four days, on account of the four regions of the world throughout which she has been spread far and wide. As for the literal historical meaning, I do not think the Israelites decreed this except because they understood that God’s judgment in that matter had been brought forth chiefly to strike the father, so that no one afterward would dare to vow such a sacrifice. For why would mourning and lamentation have been decreed if that vow had been a cause for rejoicing?

But if the subsequent defeat of the people of Ephraim by that same Jephthah is also to be referred to God’s judgment, which will come at the end, as the Lord Himself says, “Those who did not wish me to reign over them, bring here and kill before me” (Luke 19:27), then the forty-two thousand who fell were not mentioned with an arbitrary number (Judg. 12:4, 6).

For just as the two months, because of their sixty days, signify the number six and the six ages, so there too the product of six times seven signifies the same thing insofar as it concerns the six ages of the world: six times seven is forty-two. Nor [Col. 0822] was it without significance that Jephthah himself judged the people for six years.

**L. [Judg. 13:4]** It may be asked how the angel spoke to Samson’s mother when announcing that she would have a son, since she was barren: “Now therefore beware, and do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean.” What is “unclean,” unless perhaps the dissolution of discipline that had begun in Israel had also caused them to stumble into eating those animals whose consumption God had prohibited (Deut. 14:3–19)? Why should we not believe that those who were even more easily led to transgress into the worship of idols could also have done this?

**LI. [Judg. 13:6]** When Samson’s mother told her husband how the angel had announced to her that she would have a son, she said: “And I asked him where he was from, and he did not announce his name to me.” It may be asked whether she spoke truthfully, since this is not read in the passage where the angel spoke to her. But we should understand that Scripture was silent there about what it recalled here.
