It may also be asked why she did not say, “I asked him what his name was, and he did not announce his name to me,” but said, “I asked him where he was from.” The addition, “and he did not announce his name to me,” then seems inconsistent. When she asked where he was from, she had not asked his name, but his place or city, since she thought he was a man. She even called him a man of God, although in appearance or form he resembled an angel—that is, because she saw him as exceptionally splendid, as she herself related.

But if the sentence is divided as follows—“And I asked him where he was from, and his name”—with “I asked him” understood again, followed by “he did not announce it to me”—there is no difficulty. What she says, “he did not announce it to me,” can refer to both: neither where he was from nor his name.

**LII. [Judg. 13:7, 5]** Likewise, when the same woman said that the angel had told her, “The child will be a Nazirite of God from the womb until the day of his death,” this is not read as having been said by the angel. Nor is the statement that is read as having been made—“He will begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines”—recalled by the woman.

Thus she omitted something she had heard; nevertheless, she must not be thought to have said anything she had not heard. Rather, Scripture did not set down all the angel’s words when it inserted into the narrative the fact that he spoke to the woman.

It was said, “from the womb until the day of his death,” because in the Law those who had made a vow were called Nazirites for a period of time, according to what Scripture commanded through Moses (Num. 6:2–21). Hence the command given to this man that no razor should come upon his head and that he should not drink wine or strong drink. Samson observed throughout his whole life what those called Nazirites observed for a fixed number of days when they made and fulfilled a vow.

**LIII. [Judg. 13:16, 15, 1]** Scripture says, “For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of God.” It is therefore clear that his wife too believed him to be a human being. Accordingly, when he said to him, “Let us constrain you now, and let us prepare before you a kid of the goats,” he invited him as a human being, but so that he might eat with him what he had made as a sacrifice.

For [Col. 0823] “to prepare a kid of the goats” is not ordinarily said except when a sacrifice is being made. Hence he replied in this way: “If you constrain me, I will not eat of your bread,” thereby showing that he had been invited to a meal. Then he added, “And if you make a burnt offering, you shall offer it to the Lord.”

He said, “If you make a burnt offering,” because Manoah had said, “Let us prepare before you a kid of the goats.” Not every sacrifice, however, was a burnt offering. A burnt offering was not eaten, because it was entirely consumed by fire; for this reason it was called a *holocaustum*, a whole-burnt offering.

Although the angel would not eat, he instructed them rather to make a burnt offering, not to him but to the Lord. This was especially appropriate because at that time the people of Israel had become accustomed to sacrificing to any false gods. For this reason they had then offended God, so that He delivered them to their enemies for forty years.

**LIV. [Judg. 13:16–23]** What does it mean that, after the angel who had spoken with Manoah and his wife had revealed himself to them, Manoah said to his wife, “We shall surely die, because we have seen God”? He was thinking, evidently as a human being, of that statement of the Law where it is written, “No one can see my face and live” (Exod. 33:20).

They therefore supposed that they had seen God, because of the great miracle that had occurred: the one who had previously spoken with them as though he were a man stood in the fire of the sacrifice. But did they call God the one who was in the angel, or did they call the angel himself God?

For it is written:

“And Manoah took the kid of the goats and the sacrifice, and offered it upon the rock to the Lord who works wonders; and Manoah and his wife were watching. And it came to pass, when the flame rose up from the altar toward heaven, that the angel of the Lord ascended in the flame. And Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell upon their faces upon the ground. And the angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah and his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the Lord, and Manoah said to his wife, ‘We shall surely die, because we have seen God.’”

Since, therefore, in these words he did not say, “We shall surely die, because we have seen the angel of the Lord,” but, “We have seen God,” the question arises whether they understood God in the angel, or called that same angel God.

The third possibility—that they had thought the one who was an angel was God—cannot be maintained, since Scripture says quite explicitly, “Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the Lord.”

But why was he afraid of death? Scripture in Exodus had not said, “No one sees the face of an angel and lives”; it had said, “my face,” when God was speaking. Or was Manoah so disturbed by recognizing God in the angel’s presence that he feared death for this reason?

His wife replied to him: “If the Lord had wished to kill us, He would not have received a burnt offering and sacrifice from our hand, nor would He have shown us all these things; nor would He have caused us to hear such things.” Did they believe that the angel himself had received the sacrifice because they saw him standing in the altar’s flame? Or did they understand that the Lord had received it because the angel did this in order to show that he was an angel?

Whichever of these may be the case, [Col. 0824] the angel had already said, “If you make a burnt offering, offer it to the Lord”—that is, not to me, but to the Lord. Therefore, the angel’s standing in the altar’s flame is to be understood as signifying rather that the Angel of the Great Counsel, in the form of a servant (Isa. 9:6)—that is, in the human being whom He was to assume—would not receive the sacrifice, but would Himself become the sacrifice.

**LV. [Judg. 15:8, 15]** What does it mean that Samson struck the foreigners “shin upon thigh”? For who has a shin above his thigh, since the shin is below, extending from the knee to the ankle? Moreover, if this referred to the place on the body where he wounded them, were all those whom he struck wounded in one and the same part of the body?

If that were credible, we might perhaps suppose that he fought with the shinbone of some animal as with a club and struck them with it upon the thigh, just as it is written of him that he killed a thousand with the jawbone of an ass. But, as I have said, it is not credible that, while fighting, he observed only one place in which to strike them. Nor does Scripture say, “He struck them with a shin upon the thigh,” but “the shin upon the thigh.”

The obscurity is therefore caused by an unusual expression. It is said as though one were to say, “He struck them in a most astonishing manner”—that is, so that, astonished and stupefied with wonder, they placed shin upon thigh: the shin of one foot upon the thigh of the other, as those who are stunned with amazement are accustomed to sit.

It is as though one were to say, “He struck them hand to jaw”—that is, with such slaughter that, in sorrowful astonishment, they would place their hand to their jaw. The translation made from the Hebrew also sufficiently shows that this is the meaning, for it reads: “He struck them with a great blow, so that, stupefied, they placed calf upon thigh.” This is equivalent to saying that they placed shin upon thigh, since the calf is, of course, situated behind along with the shin.

**LVI. [Judg. 15:12]** What does Samson mean when he says to the men of Judah, “Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves, and hand me over to them, lest you come against me yourselves”? Some have interpreted this expression as, “lest you come against me yourselves.”

But that he said this so that they would not kill him is indicated by what is written in the book of Kings, when Solomon ordered a man to be killed and said, “Go, meet him” (1 Kings 2:29). This is not understood because such an expression is not customary among us.

For when military authorities say, “Go, lift him up,” meaning “Kill him,” who would understand it except one who knows the customary usage of that speech? It is also commonly said among us, “He shortened him” [Note: [Col. 0824] The printed editions read *compediavit illi*; but most and better manuscripts read *compendiavit*.], meaning “He killed him.” No one understands this except one who is accustomed to hearing it.

This is the force common to all expressions: just as languages themselves are not understood except by learning them through hearing or reading, so it is with their customary forms of speech.

[ANNOTATIONS ON JOB]

[Col. 0825]

**CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING WORK**

Augustine did not indicate here the date of the subsequent little work except by the sequence of the *Retractations*. In that sequence, he assigned this work a middle place among the books composed around the year 400, and stated that he had reviewed it sometime before the work against Petilian’s Letter, which was written while Anastasius was seated in the Roman chair, according to book 2, chapter 51, and therefore no later than the year 402.

[Col. 0825]

[Note: [Col. 0825] See book 2, chapter 13, of the *Retractations*, vol. 1, col. 635, from the words “The book whose title is *Annotations on Job*” up to the words “to him upon the earth.” M.]

**OF THE HOLY BISHOP AURELIUS AUGUSTINE OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK OF ANNOTATIONS ON JOB** [Note: [Col. 0825] Written around the year of Christ 400.] [Note: [Col. 0825] This book was reviewed against two manuscripts of the Victorine library, one of the Royal library, one of the Navarre College, and against the Bec and Fleury manuscripts; against variant readings transcribed from one Belgian manuscript; and also against the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.] [Note: [Col. 0825] In addition, we compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

## [Job, chapter I]

“And his possessions were great upon the earth”: because he was active in those very works. “They held a feast every day, until their number was complete.” This is a sign of love. “And he offered sacrifices for them, according to their number.” One should understand that there were particular confessions, as though individual sacrifices, but another sacrifice for all and for every sin; this is signified when he says: [Note: [Col. 0825] Thus the Royal Manuscript. But the Victorinus codex has, “which signifies God.” Erasmus, Amerbach, and two manuscripts have, “which signifies the Lord.” Louvain has, “which signifies before the Lord.”] “Lest perhaps my sons have sinned and cursed God in their hearts.” “Lest perhaps” is properly added, because he suspected that they had cursed him in their hearts.

“And behold, the angels of God came, to stand before God.” The soul’s disposition toward truth could not otherwise be narrated than by being expressed, in a certain manner, temporally and locally. “And indeed the devil came with them.” Is “with them” said because he could hear only through them?

“And the Lord said to the devil, ‘From where have you come?’” The comparison of a past action with that from which he is thereafter permitted to act is the answer to the question; the question itself, however, is the divine power, in which he is not permitted to act as he wishes. “For inquiry will be made into the thoughts of the ungodly” (Wis. I, 9), in order to reveal him to us.

“But stretch out your hand and touch all that he has”: grant him power. “Unless he blesses you to your face.” This is an unfinished expression, that is: “If he does not bless you to your face after his possessions have been touched,” as though one should supply, “What do you command?” “And the devil departed from the presence of the Lord”: from consultation to action. “And enemies came and captured them.” In accordance with the saying, “who now works in the sons of disobedience” (Eph. II, 2), he stirred these men up as well. It should be noted, however, how he had power over human beings and over the elements, yet power granted by God.

“Naked I came out of my mother’s womb.” [Col. 0826] It should be noted how consolingly he speaks, although he mourned according to customary practice. [Note: [Col. 0826] Two manuscripts have “consolatory.”]

## [Job, chapter II]

“Behold, I deliver him to you; only preserve his soul”: so that he would not presume that he could take away his life. “And he took a potsherd for himself, to scrape away the discharge.” Through the Lord’s Passion this signifies the scraping away of the sins of those who confess.

## [Job, chapter III]

“And the night in which they said, ‘A man has been conceived.’” Certain higher powers, who were able to know this. “Let that night be darkness”: let it no longer endure what he has endured. “Let that night be darkness,” that is, let it be consigned to oblivion. “Nor let the Lord seek it from above”: let it not be restored through immortality; that is, let mortality perish. “Nor let light come upon it”: the light of remembrance.

“But let darkness and the shadow of death receive it”: this present life, which is a shadow of future punishment. The sense is that the righteous person, who is light, does not see it, but darkness—that is, sinners and the carnal tribulations of this life—does. “And let them trouble it as the bitterness of day”: the commandments of a good life, or the day of judgment, by which the carnal are disturbed. “And let darkness receive that night”: perpetual darkness.

“Let it not be among the days of the year”: among the spiritual righteous who enjoy the sun and are greater. “But let that night be sorrow”: because it causes sorrow to those who love it. “Nor let it be counted among the days of the months.” The righteous in the Church are associated with the moon as with something lesser; to them it is said, “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people” (I Cor. III, 1), so that Paul himself belongs among the days of the year.

“But let him who curses that day curse it”: the Lord, who will curse those who love carnal things. “Let the stars of that night grow dark”: those eminent in sins. “Let it remain, and let it not come into the light.” Because they will not be converted, he says this prophetically. [Note: [Col. 0826] The printed editions have “through the Prophet”; the manuscripts have “prophetically.”]

“Because he did not shut the doors of my mother’s womb”: the earthly city, which Babylon signifies. For the doors would be shut if the sinner were not praised in the desires of his soul (Ps. IX, 2, 4). “Why did I not die in the womb?” before I became prominent to you through some action. Conception pertains to hope. “Why did I come out of the womb and not immediately perish?” This figure, therefore, should be understood in the case of one who had grown old in such desires.

“And why did knees receive me?” so that I might be established there? “Why did I suck breasts?” nourishing teachings for wickedness. “Now surely, sleeping, I would be at rest”: by dying to this world. “With the kings honored by the earth”: in the Church. “Who gloried in swords.” Hence the saying, “and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 17). “Or with princes who had much gold”: wisdom. “Who filled their houses with silver”: with the Lord’s eloquence.

“Or like an untimely birth cast out of the womb”: so that he would never become prominent. “Or like infants who have not seen the light”: who did not attain to some nobility. “There the ungodly laid down their fury”: in death, away from this world. “There those weary in body rested”: either weary in body but not in spirit, or having reached the end of bodily existence. “They did not hear the voice of the exactor.” “The judge will hand you over to the exactor” (Luke XII, 58): this is the source of the statement; that is, their sins were forgiven—for he was speaking of the ungodly.

“There the small and the great are.” I think this is properly understood of one person, in accordance with the saying, “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. XIV, 11). “And the servant who does not fear his master”: either according to the saying, “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good” (Rom. XIII, 3), or according to the saying, “Perfect love casts out fear” (I John IV, 18).

“Why, then, is light given to those who are in bitterness?” the honor of sinners. “And life to souls that are in sorrows?” in the material of sorrows, that is, in sins. “Who desire death, and it does not come to them”: the obtaining of the fruit of sin. “Death is rest to a man whose life is hidden”: either because it is hidden before God or because it is known to few. This should be understood of that death by which we die to the world. In that death there is no rest.

“For God has shut him in”: by not giving him over to the desires of his heart. “For my groaning comes before my food”: before the joy of God’s foods, tribulations come first. “And I weep, constrained by fear”: seeing that I cannot avoid what I feared. “For the fear that I dreaded has come upon me”: adversities that arise from God’s mercy for correction. “Neither in peace, nor in quiet, nor in rest.” For the things he feared were false. “For wrath has come upon me”: vengeance, according to which the righteous person is scarcely saved (I Pet. IV, 18).

## [Job, chapter IV]

### The words of Eliphaz

“But who can bear the weight of your words?” Here he says that he is compelled to speak because he cannot endure Job’s statements. “Is not your fear foolish?” You ought to have been prepared for these things if you were truthfully advising others. Nor did you fear such things rightly, when you said, “For the fear that I dreaded has come upon me” (Job III, 25). “And your hope and the simplicity of your life are like foolishness”: by which these things are thought to be good.

“The roar of the lion and the voice of the lioness”: the devil himself and the city of pride, which the Prophets often also present in the form of a beast. “And the joy of dragons has been extinguished”: of the proud and the treacherous. “The myrmecoleon has perished because it had no food.” For at the end there will be none whom it may lead in and devour. The godly will be separated from the ungodly.

Here, however, he is mistaken because he understood of Job what he had heard prophesied about the devil. The myrmecoleon should be understood either because both aspects are present in him: he snatches away and secretly pursues the grain, which, when the eye has been removed, he causes not to germinate; or because he rules over the greedy and those who store up treasures on earth; or because he persecutes the righteous, like ants preparing food for themselves in summer for winter, food on which he will not feed when the good have been separated from the ungodly.

“And the cubs of lions were separated from one another.” The conspiracy of the rulers of that city has been scattered—those born from that civic association and from the devil—or because they devastated one another. Hence the saying, “Nation will rise against nation” [Note: [Col. 0828] Amerbach, Erasmus, and most manuscripts have “Nation will rise above or against nation.” The Gospel in Greek has *ethnos epi ethnos*, “nation against nation.”] (Mark XIII, 8).

“None of this would have happened to you”: either those losses, bereavement, and the wound of the blow; or grief of soul would not have pierced you, because you would also have consoled yourself if you had said sincerely to others, “Does not my ear receive from him magnificent things?” For he says that he speaks these things from revelation.

“And a spirit passed before my face.” He wishes it to be understood as though he had felt a breath; for in what follows he denies that it was a figure. It should also be remembered that the Spirit descended upon the Apostles in this way.

“For what? Will a man be clean before the Lord?” Either he says that he heard these things, or he says that he shuddered for this reason: no one is clean before the Lord; or he says that he saw in this way because no one is so clean before God that he sees God as he is. “Clean” should now be understood according to perfection, so that we may understand in a certain manner what he denies above: that a clean man perishes.

“If he does not trust his servants.” This occurred when Elijah said, “Lord, they have killed your prophets,” and he said to him, “I have left seven thousand men for myself” (III Kings XIX, 14, 18). For those seven thousand men were not already clean on that account. Angels and Prophets are called servants.

“And against his angels he found something perverse.” Either what is said against them, or what they themselves say. Nevertheless this can also be understood of the true angels.

“Those who dwell in houses of clay”: whose citizenship is not in heaven. “He struck them as a moth.” Either some corruption struck them like a moth, or God struck them—either by this moth or as a moth strikes, that is, secretly, inwardly, through corruption arising from themselves by means of carnal desires; this is what dwelling in houses of clay means.

“And from morning until evening they are no more.” Either they do not exist beyond this age, or they pass from prosperous circumstances to tribulation; for they have received punishment. “Because they could not help themselves, they perished”: since they place their hope in themselves. “They perished because they did not have wisdom”: they did not have the wisdom not to hope in themselves. [Note: [Col. 0828] Erasmus reads “in hoping.” M.]

## [Job, chapter V]

“But call, if anyone answers you.” For those who are clean before God are answered. “Indeed, anger kills the foolish”: indignation by which someone is distressed, as though something unjust had happened to him, while he does not consider that he is so unclean before God that the angels have not deemed it worthy either to answer him when he calls or to reveal themselves to him. Whoever does not consider this is foolish and is destroyed by irrational anger. Or a fool cannot hear or see angels for this reason: he has been killed by anger and slain by jealousy.

“Yet jealousy kills the one who goes astray”: jealousy for imitating sinners. “But I have seen fools putting down roots.” Here “fools” should be understood as the ungodly, so that, conversely, human wisdom is piety, as is said below. “And they are crushed upon the doors of the weak”: of the humble, when they have been received into the bridal chamber by the bridegroom and the foolish have remained outside (Matt. XXV).

“For the things they gathered, the righteous will eat.” This can be understood of the Jews, who gathered the prophecies that the Gentiles rather consumed; and of those who, while doing what others prescribe and do not do themselves, eat what others have prepared. “But they themselves will not be delivered from evil”: although they preach that such things should not be done. “Let their strength be exhausted”: the strength by which they grow proud against the weak. Let it be exhausted so that they may already begin to labor.

“For labor does not come forth from the earth”: let them not complain about the creature, but about themselves. “But man is born to labor.” He is said to be “born” according to the sense in which a person is turned from repose toward a laborious life.

“But the young of the vulture fly very high.” The vulture is rightly understood as the Lord, because by the height of prophecy he saw our mortality, upon which he would descend to feed, converting us into his body. The young of the vulture, therefore, are called the sons of the bridegroom; and “flying very high” means having their citizenship in heaven (Phil. III, 20), so that they may be freed from the labor in which man is born. For they followed the voice of the one who says, “Come to me, all you who labor” (Matt. XI, 28).

The young of the vulture can also be understood in an evil sense as the aerial powers, which feed on deaths, that is, on sins. Because such transgressing angels were not led into the humility of mortal existence, which is extremely laborious and in which man is born, they are very proud of it—that is, they fly very high.

“He gives rain upon the face of the earth”: as though he showed mercy to those who confess. “So that their hands do not accomplish truth”: let them not do what they promise, threatening to rule over the weak. “In the day darkness will meet them”: as with the Jews, who did not recognize who the Lord was. Or, “as in the night they will grope at midday”: like those who, although they saw the signs, nevertheless doubted, saying, “He is a prophet”; others, “He deceives the people” (John VII, 40, 12), when they were unwilling to see even by the light of a lamp.

“And let them perish in war”: in temptations. “And let the weak escape from the hand of the powerful”: of the devil. “But let the weak have hope.” Those who are strong seek the things of this world.

“Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves.” Here he is mistaken because it seems to him that Job suffers these things because of his sins, whereas Job is blessed for this reason: in this life, when he is reproved, he has the possibility of correction. [Note: [Col. 0829] Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions instead have, “it seems to him that Job suffers these things because of his iniquities.”]

“And in the seventh evil will not touch you.” The mystery of the Sabbath. “In famine he will deliver you from death.” For by the word he nourishes and makes one firm against temptations. “But in battle he will release you from the hand of the sword”: from the power of bonds.

“From the scourge of the tongue [Col. 0830] he will hide you”: so that you do not feel insults, not so that you do not suffer them. [Note: [Col. 0830] The printed editions have, “Will you not suffer the unjust?” The manuscripts have, “Will you not suffer?” followed by “the unjust,” and so forth.] “You will mock the unjust and the wicked”: as wisdom will mock the destruction of the wicked (Prov. I, 26). “And you will not fear fierce beasts”: that is, you will not fear the Jews, because the Gentiles will obey you. These things should be understood of the Lord.

Eliphaz is mistaken here because he thinks that what has been revealed to him should be understood of Job, whereas everything applies to the Lord. “For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field.” The stones of the field are mentioned because among the Gentiles there was no ordering of the Law, so that they were, as it were, stones from a building. “And the wild beasts will be at peace with you”: whether this refers to the Jews or to the Gentiles.

“Then you will know that your house will be in peace”: that is, the Church. “And your sons will be like every plant in the field”: without dryness. “And you will come to the tomb like ripe grain”: after the Passion.

“Behold, we have investigated these things in this way.” Here the authority of this prophecy is confirmed. “But you yourself know what you have done.” For God did not permit these things to happen to you unjustly.

## [Job, chapter VI]

### The words of Job

“But, as it appears, the words are evil.” For Job’s words do not arise from impatience with his afflictions, since they signify grief—not Job’s personal grief, but the grief he had concerning the whole human race.

“For the arrows of the Lord are in my body.” The words of God by which the soul is pierced when it is compelled to confession. “Their fury drinks my blood.” For they remove sin. When I begin to speak, they stimulate me; what I speak, they compel me to speak.

“For what? Will the wild ass bray in vain, unless it is seeking food?” so that it suffers hunger because it wished to be free. “Or will the ox bellow when it has food in the manger?” Food is prepared for the ass through the labor of the ox, just as for the Gentiles through the labor of the Prophets and Apostles, who were, of course, Jews. These words, therefore, belong to one desiring food—that is, assistance—not to one impatient of pain.

“Can bread be eaten without salt?” As though he were asked, “Why do you express these things by means of figures?” he answers, “Because if I were to say them in my own person, they would be tasteless.” “Or is there flavor in empty words?” He calls human speeches empty, because bread is the words of God, but heavenly bread.

“Thus my soul also cannot cease.” Just as bread cannot be eaten without salt, so now I perform a ministry through the word of God, because of the saying, “How will they hear without someone preaching?” (Rom. X, 14).

“For I see my foul foods, as there is the odor of a lion.” For my words are foul like a lion: either because of pride, through which those who boast consider themselves important; or because those who embrace carnal things have the foulness of a lion, delighting in their own words.

“But if he should grant it, and [Note: [Col. 0830] The printed editions, following the Vulgate, have, “Who will grant that?” The manuscripts have, “But if he should grant it and.” The Greek has, “For if he should grant it also.”] my request should come.” He calls the thing he was asking for his request. “And may the Lord grant my hope.” For one who trusts in the hope of consolation to come after tribulation is tested at the proper time. He rightly calls it “hope,” because when the thing has come, testing will no longer be necessary.

“Let my city be a tomb, over whose walls I was leaping.” He wishes that Babylon’s society be his tomb—not so that it might bury him, but so that he might know that it covers the dead, whoever they may be in it, while he had been proud of its foundation and protection, as it were.

“I will not spare.” For I have not lied: they are the holy words of my God. For he said nothing other than what he heard from God—that is, he prophesies generally concerning humanity, because it needs assistance in confession.

“For what is my strength, that I should endure?” This signified his wound. “Or what is my time, that my soul should endure?” Because, with death imminent, people are terrified so that they may be converted and confess to God the corruption of their sins; in consideration of this he says that he is compelled to confession.

“Is the strength of stones my strength?” He means those who are hard and impenetrable to the arrows of God’s words, and who are not moved to confess. “Or did I not trust in him when it was well with me?” that is, when I was immortal in the image of God. “But help has withdrawn from me”: I became mortal, wishing to trust in myself. “And the visitation of the Lord has despised me,” according to the saying, “Or the son of man, that you visit him?” (Ps. VIII, 5).

“My relatives did not regard me.” I shuddered at the angels. “Like a failing torrent.” For mercy once flooded through me, but I dried up and was not a spring for myself. “Or like waves they passed over me”: as though they were consolations taken as drink. “Those who feared me have now rushed upon me”: the devil with his angels.

“I have perished and have become an exile from my house”: either from the heavenly dwelling or from conscience. For this reason he sat outside, beyond his own house.

“Look at the roads of the Temanites; consider the paths of the Sabeans.” He signifies those who trust in temporal things, concerning whom—that is, concerning the man whom he signifies—he says that he does not presume. “But now you have risen against me without mercy”: thinking that human blessedness consists in abundance of carnal things. For they mocked him rather than sympathizing with him.

“But seeing my wound, fear.” Understanding what it signifies, fear future punishments. “For what? Have I asked anything of you? Or do I need your strength?” For the one who can save him is weak before him.

“Teach me, and I will be silent.” They ought therefore to have been patient with his instruction, because they could not teach him. “But, as I see, you speak the small words of the true man.” He calls “the true man” the one who signifies the person performing repentance by conversion to God, concerning whom they spoke small words.

“For I am not asking help from you.” The true man asks help from God. For he is true who confesses. Hence the saying, “Whoever does the truth comes to the light” (John III, 21). “Nor will I endure the expression of your speech.” He said that he could endure the speech of God, by which he might be instructed.

“Nevertheless you have rushed upon the orphan.” [Note: [Col. 0831] Louvain has “upon the insignificant one.” Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts have “upon the orphan,” in accordance with the Vulgate and the Greek.] As far as you are concerned, you wished to mock me, although you did not understand what he signifies. For they ought not to have mocked Job, whom they saw; therefore: “Nevertheless.” [Note: [Col. 0831] The printed editions have, “therefore they come nevertheless.” The Royal Manuscript has, “therefore they came nevertheless.” Other manuscripts have, “therefore nevertheless”: supply, “Job says.”]

“But now, looking on, cease from me”: since you have nothing to teach me. “And again, attend to justice.” For at first they seemed to themselves to be compelled to speak by justice. “For there is no iniquity in my mouth; and have not my jaws meditated wisdom?” He says that he did not accuse God, but introduced a man accusing his own iniquities, as his speech above was understood. He calls this meditation wisdom.

## [Job, chapter VII]

“Is not human life a temptation upon the earth?” Here he now shows more openly from whose significance he had spoken above. He calls temptation like an arena of contest, where a person either wins or is defeated.

“And his life is like that of daily laborers”: one who awaits a temporal wage, so that the life of those who await the fruit of their righteousness in the future is no longer upon the earth. “Or like a servant fearing his master and attaining a shadow.” This signifies Adam’s hiding from the face of the Lord and the covering of leaves, from which a shadow is made, which man obtained after abandoning God. “Or like a laborer awaiting the wages of his work.” This differs from the preceding image in that the former possessed the things, whereas this one desires to possess temporal things themselves.

“So I also awaited empty months.” He has already called temporal goods “empty,” referring to the shadow. “And nights of sorrows were given to me”: nights in which the light of wisdom is lost and which provide the material for punishments.

“If I sleep, I say, ‘When will it be day?’ and if I rise again, ‘When will it be evening?’” This is when a person experiences the desire for business during leisure and for leisure during business.

“But I am filled with pains from evening until morning”: at which he dies away from God. Hence also God, walking at evening, dismissed them (Gen. III, 7–8), which signifies those who grieve and have no expectation of remedy except morning. Of this it is said, “In the morning I will stand before you” (Ps. V, 5), that is, when after judgment God will be revealed in the morning to the righteous. Hence also the Lord is buried in the evening and rises in the morning (John XIX and XX). He can therefore compare this life to the morning star.

“And my body has grown together with the decay of worms”: with a multitude of worms. “I pour out clods of earth [Note: [Col. 0832] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions have, “At the bottom I pour out globes of earth.”], scraping away the discharge.” This is an expression of desires or anxieties in confession, in which the wicked rejoice, because they reduce to an occasion for sinning what others confess through repentance; hence they are dogs that licked Lazarus’s wounds (Luke XVI, 21).

“And my life is more fleeting than speech.” For I do less than I say. “Remember, therefore, that my life is spirit”: that is, in spiritual hunger. [Note: [Col. 0832] Erasmus and Louvain have “in life.” Amerbach and the manuscripts have “in hunger.”] “And I will not return to visible things.”

“The eye of the one who sees will not know me”: because I will be changed, so that by “the one who sees” we understand the envious devil. “Your eyes are upon me, and I do not remain.” For you kill in me the carnal life in which I existed.

“Like a cloud cleansed from heaven”: either cleansed through heaven, just as we say that iron has been cleansed; here he may have signified that help came to him from heaven so that he might be cleansed; or certainly, so that it would no longer be a cloud but would be thinned into clear air, as though cleansed by the sun’s rays, so that the obscurity of flesh and blood would not exist in heaven. For “flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” when “this corruptible” has put on incorruption and “death will be swallowed up in victory” (I Cor. XV, 50, 53, 54).

“For if a man descends to the underworld, he will not ascend again.” Remember, therefore, so that you may not descend. “And he will no longer return to his house”: that is, to his rest.

“Therefore I also will not spare my mouth”: confessing while there is time. “Am I the sea, or a dragon?” For you have not cast me away as you cast away the ungodly or the devil. “For you have set a guard over me”: so that I may not move toward disturbance, as the boundaries are set for the sea.

“Because I said, ‘My bed will comfort me’”: carnal things, in which he was resting. “And I will bring consolation to myself upon my couch.” I ought to refer my consolation to you.

“You terrify me through dreams, and you dismay me through a vision”: through the tribulations of this life, which are dreams, just as the good things of this life are also dreams. “You will release my soul from the spirit”: because of visible terrors, from which the soul that fears coming upon them will be delivered. “And I have thrust my bones away from death.” For my bones had gone into death, unless I had become stronger and patient through these terrors; this is the firmness of the bones.

“For I will not live forever, that I should endure patiently.” I corrected myself through the brevity of life and the fear of death. Hence the devil is unchangeable, because he does not die but is condemned. “The beginning of wisdom is fear” (Sir. I, 16): this is the point.

“Leave me, for my life is vanity”: because I do not endure temptations. Or, “because you have directed your understanding toward him”: for this reason he is rational. Hence the saying, “But we have the mind of the Lord” (I Cor. II, 16). He calls the gift of reason an extension of the intellect.

“And in rest you will judge him”: as worthy of rest. “How long will you not release me?” bound by tribulations. “Nor abandon me until I swallow my saliva?” Until, amid pain and scourges, I contain and swallow the flow of pleasures, warned by tribulations.

“If I have sinned, what can I do to you?” The sense is: “If I have sinned, I can do nothing to you.” Or perhaps human beings are burdensome to you by speaking? You, then, who know the mind, why did you establish man so that he would speak against you, so that he would be a burden to you? But if human sin harms you neither by deed nor by word, why do you not forget his sin, but instead cleanse it? Is it not because the things stated above are referred to your goodness? “What is man, that you have exalted him?”

His friends, not understanding these things, thought that God was reproached by him. For if you do not bring temptations upon me in order that I may restrain my flowing impulses and that you may thus provide for me, what other reason is there for correcting man? For his sin cannot harm you because he sins; nor do you experience his speech as adversarial, although you know the human mind and could certainly have refrained from establishing what is opposed to you.

“And why have you not forgotten my iniquity?” If the reason is not that these temptations should benefit me, so that everything might belong to your goodness, including your correction of me, why have you not forgotten it?

“Now I will go into the earth.” For when you cleanse my sin, I still have to go into the earth through bodily death. “For I will awaken, and I will no longer be”: in this earth.

## [Job, chapter VIII]

### The words of Baldad the Sauchite

“He sent their iniquities into the hand [Note: [Col. 0833] The printed editions have “into the hand”; shortly afterward, “or overthrow.” The manuscripts have “into the hand,” in accordance with the Greek; and afterward, “or reckoning.”]”: he sent them into the hand either in punishment or in reckoning, that is, he showed them to be debtors, namely sinners.

“And he will restore to you the life of righteousness”: the life owed to righteousness, that is, blessed life. “And your former things will be very small”: in comparison with the later things, which will be infinite.

“Or will not these teach you and report it to you?” For the authority of some people is greater. Here too he is about to speak concerning Christ, recounting what he had heard, just as Eliphaz recounted his revelation.

“Does papyrus flourish without water?” So also the ungodly will wither without God’s mercy. “While it still stands in its root, it is not cut down”: if it has no water. “Before every plant drinks, does it not wither?” unless it drinks; for the ungodly never truly flourished.

“And his tent will be filled with spiders”: useless works. But now he appears to be speaking of the Jews and the Lord. “And if he should support his house, it will not stand”: either by the holy Scriptures, or by hope in the Lord’s promise, or by the kingdom itself. “And when he begins, he will not endure”: to follow God; this happened to the Jews, who did not continue after beginning to follow him.

“For he is moist before the sun”: rotting through the flow of carnal things. [Note: [Col. 0834] The printed editions have “rotting”; the manuscripts have “rotting ones,” referring to the Jews.] “Before the sun,” however, means under tribulations; as above, “under” signifies “before,” just as we say, “Make before me.”

“And from his decay his shoot will rise.” If they had not been so evil, the Lord—who was born from them according to the flesh (Rom. IX, 5)—would not have been exalted through the Passion.

“He sleeps among gatherings of stones.” For their leaders will crucify him. “And he will live in the midst of pebbles”: among the humble, from whom the Apostles came.

“If he is swallowed up, the place will deny him.” If he hides that he is the Son of God, it will be said that he is not the Son of God. It is therefore necessary that he reveal himself; for in this place divine things cannot be recognized.

“But from the earth another will sprout”: either the Lord through rising again, or another race of the godly, that is, Christians.

“For the Lord will not approve the innocent.” Or, “Will he not reject?” Or: “Will he not approve the ungodly as innocent?” “Nor any gift”: that is, the sacrifices that the Jews had. “But he will fill the mouth of the truthful with laughter”: of those who confess. “And the tent of the ungodly will not endure”: either the temple itself or the kingdom.

[Ib. IX.] The words of Job. Truly I know that it is so—that is, because he has repaid me according to my iniquities—but not as you suppose; rather, because no one is righteous in his sight. They will not answer him one out of a thousand. For in everything he will convict them. He brings mountains into old age, and they do not know it—that is, into weakness; as it says, “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. VI, 8). He overturns them in anger. By becoming angry he overturns them, that is, so that they find something other than what they had desired, since “whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XIV, 11). He shakes the world from its foundations: through the calling that has taken place, by which the eminent in the world have been shaken. And its pillars will be moved. He commands the sun, and it does not rise: so that either wisdom may not be understood, or those who wrote may not be understood; as it says, “Seal the book” (Dan. XII, 4). He alone stretches out the heavens: the Church, which is properly God’s dwelling, which he stretches throughout the whole world; “alone,” to signify the unity of the Trinity. For certainly all things were made through the Son in the Holy Spirit. And he walks upon the sea as upon the earth. “Upon the earth,” that is, firmly establishing the Church in the world, or subjecting sinners to himself, among whom he is not submerged and by whose temptations he is not overcome. If he passes by me, I shall not see him. If he is higher than I, or if he has brushed past me in his speed, I shall not recognize him. It is necessary, therefore, that he both accommodate himself to my weakness and not abandon me. For if he delivers me to death, [Col. 0835] who will turn him away? He delivers to death when either he passes beyond or passes by so as to remain unknown. This is the death of the soul: not to know God. For his anger cannot be turned away. The anger of others can be turned away by someone more powerful. All other things beneath the heavens have been subjected to him, except heaven itself—that is, the rational creature. For if it had subjected all other things to itself, it would never be punished through those things which it had subjected to itself; but because God subjected them to it, it is punished through them when it offends the one who subjected them. [Note: [Col. 0835] In the Septuagint: *Kētē ta hypouranon*, “sea-monsters that are under heaven.” But we believe that corruption has entered their translation, which perhaps read *kēthoi tēs hyperēphanias*, “helpers of pride”; this agrees with the Hebrew text.]

But if I am also righteous, he will not hear me: when I appeal to him, presuming upon my righteousness. For, comparing it with the unchangeable and everlasting things that are with him, he will not hear me as though I were unrighteous. Therefore his mercy is necessary for me. I will plead his judgment: because I cannot judge myself to be righteous. Hence it says, “Nor do I judge myself; but the one who judges me is the Lord” (1 Cor. IV, 3–4). But if I call, and he does not answer, I shall not believe that he has heard my voice. When I plead his judgment, if he does not answer, I shall not believe that he has ever answered me; for he heard me for hidden reasons, not because of the merit of my supplication. Or certainly: I shall not believe that I have not been heard now, for at some time I have been heard. Or in this way: If he answers what I ask, I shall believe that I have indeed been heard; for if I do not believe, even though what I ask comes to pass, still I have not been heard, so that the petitioner’s faith is the sign of being heard.

Lest perhaps he crush me in the whirlwind. For this reason I seek his judgment, lest he crush me in the whirlwind. For he has brought about many of my tribulations without cause—their cause was hidden from me. Or certainly, this is the voice of one confessing: one who, under God’s scourges, confesses that he has not been corrected and therefore may be crushed in a whirlwind, as under a greater punishment. For he does not allow me to breathe: my tribulations are so numerous. Indeed, because he is able, he prevails. He conquers, so that I may do his will, not mine.

Even if I am righteous, my mouth will speak impiously: if I have considered myself righteous. Nevertheless, my life will be taken away. Although I do not know whether I have acted impiously, my life will nevertheless be taken away, so that I may suffer what I do not want or fail to do what I do want. There is one thing that I have said: anger destroys the great and powerful. That is, tribulations come upon human beings for this one reason: so that no one who presumes upon his own strength may seem great and powerful to himself.

For wicked men will be in great death: not in an ordinary death, in which even the righteous are found when they are afflicted and mocked by the wicked. The earth has been delivered into the hands of the impious: either the bodies of the righteous, but not their souls, when they are persecuted, or when the impious are permitted to rule. It may also be understood as the sinful person delivered into the devil’s hands according to his mortality. He covers the judgment he makes [Note: [Col. 0835] He was using a corrupt manuscript; for among the Septuagint it reads, “he will make the faces of judges”; in the Vulgate, “he covers the face of judges.”]: either the judgment of the impious person himself, or that of the righteous; for in this present time it is covered. Or certainly, he makes his judgment by this very act—that is, he punishes him by hiding his providence from him; as it says, “Because of the greatness of his anger he will not seek” (Ps. II, 25). Or he vindicates the righteous by hiding his judgment [Col. 0836] from his persecutor—that is, his providence—so that the sinner may be caught more tightly in the snares of his sins through impunity.

But if it is not so, who is he, then? This may be understood of the Lord, who was also mocked, whose earth—that is, whose body—was delivered into the hands of the Jews, and whose majesty was hidden while he carried out judgment. But if he is not the one, who then is he who does greater things than he himself did? Or thus: If God does not execute judgment upon the righteous or the impious, who can do so?

My life is lighter than a runner. He calls those who depart from righteousness fugitives, like the younger son who went off into a distant country (Luke XV, 13). Or like a flying eagle seeking food. From the higher regions, in which rational souls are blessed by nature—that is, from works of righteousness—they have bent themselves toward earthly pleasures.

But if I speak, I forget while I am speaking. Speech: just as the soul’s inclination was toward external things, so, while it advances toward what is outside, desiring to enjoy the creature, it forgets the Creator within. Bending down upon my face, I shall groan. For that bending is followed by pain. I am shaken in all my limbs: fear, by which he begins to turn back. And since I am impious, why have I not died, and why do I suffer? “I know,” he implies. Or he says that he suffers because he has not died to impiety.

And when I have been cleansed with clean hands: either with God’s hands or with his own—that is, through good works by regeneration. You have dipped me sufficiently in filth: brought me into this mortality. And my garment has become accursed to me: immortality, with which we desire to be clothed over (2 Cor. V, 4); but because we cannot possess it in this corruption, he therefore says, “My garment has become accursed to me.”

For you are not a man like me, with whom I might contend. I could demonstrate my righteousness to a human being; but in your judgment I am found unrighteous. Would that there were an arbiter for us! He seems to blaspheme, unless he is understood to be longing for “the Mediator of God and human beings” (1 Tim. II, 5), so that through him he may present his prayers. In this way he hears, placed between the two, and he accuses the human being. For “the Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22). He is the one who would accuse and the one who would hear between the two.

Let him remove his rod from me. Let the fear of the Law pass away, so that through the freedom and love of adoption I may be joined to him. For I am not with myself: because I cling to the things that are outside.

[Ib. X.]

I will bring forth words against myself. These are the words of one confessing. And I will say to the Lord, “Do not teach me to be impious.” Do not test me beyond what I can bear, nor allow things to happen to me by which I might be persuaded to impiety. Or, “Is it good for you if I act unjustly?” It is not good for you if I act unjustly; therefore you have not established me in this condition unjustly. Because you despise the work that your hands made? If you despise the work of your hands. Have you looked upon the counsel of the impious? But not upon that impiety which is apparent to human beings. And, “Have you looked upon the counsel of the impious?” Not because it pleases him that they should act unjustly.

Or, do you look as a human being looks? For certainly you do not look as a human being looks; therefore you have looked upon the counsel of the impious. There is an impiety that you alone see and that human beings do not see. Or is your life human? That is, brief, so that you cannot judge concerning perpetuity. [Col. 0837] And you have investigated my sins. For what is hidden from human beings could not be hidden from you. For you know that I have done nothing impiously. As far as human beings are concerned, I have done nothing impiously. But who is there who can snatch from your hands [Note: [Col. 0837] Thus the manuscripts, together with the Septuagint. The printed editions have, “who may be snatched away.”]?—from the hands of the one who judges. You judge as God does, when you see even those impieties that a human being does not see.

Afterward, having changed, you struck me: with the human being changed, not God; because the changed human being experiences God as changed, just as eyes changed by prolonged darkness experience the sun as changed. Remember that you fashioned me from clay. Therefore I need your mercy. You will turn me again into earth: by death, which is the punishment of sin.

Did you not milk me like milk? For even now, among mortal beings, he has shown mercy, when he formed human beings from human beings out of an unformed beginning. Since these things are therefore in you, I know that you can do all things, because they are of such great goodness that they also bring about the carnal substance. But if I have also sinned, you will preserve me: either so that you do not destroy me, or so that my sin does not remain hidden. And if I am righteous, I cannot breathe: in the sight of human beings. For you see the sins that are hidden from human beings. For I am full of reproach: in your sight. And I am seized like a lion for slaughter. There is a sin of pride that is hidden from human beings, since it can creep in even among praiseworthy deeds.

Again, having changed, you cruelly torment me: after the punishment of sin by which the human being became mortal. He speaks according to these tribulations that human beings suffer in this life, because most tribulations suddenly occur and disturb the quiet of mortal life itself, when it is in health or in security concerning temporal affairs, however much that security he attributes to God’s mercy. Restoring my torments upon me. For mortality itself is already a torment, and from it other tribulations arise.

Why, then, did you bring me out from the womb? From obscurity into recognition, which alone becomes the source of greater misery when it is overturned; he also recalled this birth above. And I would be as though I had not been: utterly unknown. Hence it says, “He calls those things that are not as though they were” (Rom. IV, 17), that is, according to obscurity. Or, is not the time of my life short? It is not on account of the length of my life that I have not died, since what I live is certainly short.

Spare me, until I rest a little. After the mercy by which you made me from clay, struck me with mortality when I was changed, and then consoled me by that very mortality, you afterward exercised me with tribulations. Spare me, therefore, so that I may rest in you, before I go to punishments from which return is not permitted. For from those he mentioned above one may return, if a person turns to God. He wishes to rest before he goes to eternal punishments, precisely so that he may not go there. It is as if we said to someone, “Correct yourself before you are condemned”: for once he has corrected himself, he will not be condemned.

Where there is no light, and where there is no seeing of the life of human beings. That is the life of human beings where the true light is, which illuminates every human being (John I, 9). One is the land of the living, another the land of the dying.

[Ib. XI.] The words of Sophar the Minaean. Or will an eloquent person appear righteous? For he thinks that Job abounds more in words [Col. 0838] than in deeds. Blessed is the human being born, short of life. He repeats to him his own opinion, which he wants understood as spoken loquaciously and emptily. Since there is no one who contradicts you. For when he was speaking, no one contradicted him.

But how the Lord speaks to you. Speak rather in such a way that God may have mercy on you. For it will be doubled upon you: by correcting and consoling. And then you will know that what you have sinned has been worthily repaid to you by the Lord: after correction, illumination follows. Or you will find the Lord’s footprint: so that you may wish to criticize God. Heaven is exalted, and what will you do? So that you may discover heaven’s mysteries. For you ought not criticize the one whose works you do not comprehend. Who will say to him, “What have you done?” For this too will have been rightly done if God has done it, because he cannot do anything except rightly.

For he himself knows the works of unrighteous human beings. It is not a work of unrighteousness. From this he wants it understood that this man, whom he considers unrighteous, foolishly criticized God; for he thought that this was how he spoke. But the human being wavers in his words in another way: now God pleases him, now he displeases him, whereas with God there is stability.

And a man born of a woman will be like a wild ass in the desert: through desire for freedom, impatient of a ruler and a trainer. And stretching out your hands toward him: so that he may accept your works. If there is anything unrighteous in your hand. He repeated the same two points, but with the order changed. And let unrighteousness not remain in your house. By “house” he meant the heart.

For then your face will shine like water: a pure conscience. Like a wave that does not pass away, and you will not be terrified: unless it touches everyone in this life. And your prayer will be like the morning star: it will go before the illumination; as though these things, pertaining to the prophecy of the holy city or to the people of God, are said as heard or revealed, just as the things said by his earlier friends were. And many will entreat your face. All these things concern the Church.

[Ib. XII.] The words of Job. But a righteous and blameless man has come into derision. This is to be understood of the Lord. The sense is: “It is therefore no wonder if I too have become a derision to you.” And his house, so that it might be devastated by the unrighteous: the Church by persecutors. Rather, let no one, though wicked, trust that he will remain unpunished, because judgment begins from the house of God (1 Pet. IV, 17). As though no inquiry were going to be made concerning them: let them not trust.

But nevertheless ask the four-footed creatures whether they will answer you. He rightly investigates the unrighteous, because from their works they were able to know the Creator and ought to have worshiped him. They ought not to have been taught by the response of creatures, since they had received reason by which they could know these things. If the soul of every living thing is not in his hand. From this, therefore, it is known that he created all things, because the soul of every living thing is in his hand. And the spirit of every human flesh: of all human flesh—that is, the rational soul.

For the ear judges words. Just as sense judges sensible things, so the spirit judges spiritual things—the spirit that ought to have known that the works of the Lord are in the Lord’s hand. In much time there is wisdom. Not, certainly, in much time, but with the Lord, from whom it must be sought. If he destroys, who will build? He destroys on account of power and closes on account of wisdom, so that a person may not reach it. If he restrains water, he will dry up the earth: wisdom itself, and by “earth,” the human being. But if he also releases it, he will destroy, overturning the earth. For sinners will be thrown into confusion by the deeds of many wise people.

He leads counselors away captive. For he subjects to himself those who seek counsel from him. But he sends the judges of the earth into terror: either the Jews, or Pilate, or those who judge with an earthly understanding. He places kings upon thrones: that is, the Apostles. And he girds their loins with a belt: that is, continence. He sends priests away captive: so that they may be led away by human beings; and by these the Jews are signified.

He changes the lips of the faithful. He changes them for the better, so that they may presume not upon their own righteousness but upon his grace. And he has known the understanding of the elders. He approves the understanding of the elders. Hence it says, “You have been known by God” (Gal. IV, 9), to which the contrary is, “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12). And he rightly began with faith and reached the gray hairs of understanding.

He reveals deep things from darkness: by opening the prophecies. And he brought the shadow of death into the light: that is, he made it known that this life is a shadow of death. Deceiving nations and destroying them: when they thought that they were harming the Church of God, although they were harming themselves; this is to be understood of the impious. Laying nations low and leading them into the way: toward humility, like that donkey. Reconciling the hearts of the rulers of the people of the earth: reconciling to himself either the Jews or the kings of the earth, who at first persecuted the Church.

But he led them astray into a way that they did not know [Note: [Col. 0839] The printed editions have “led out”; the manuscripts have “led astray.” The Septuagint has ἐπλάνησε, *eplanēse*, “he led astray.”]: by overthrowing the works of the Law, so that they might be understood simply; for this reason he appeared to them to be a sinner. By this error they were darkened like a drunken man.

[Ib. XIII.]

And I will accuse myself before him, if he wishes: so that he may accuse himself; this is confession. And you are all physicians of evils. For you cannot heal the good through consolation. Hear, therefore, the rebuke of my mouth: directed against you. And before his sight you utter deceit: when you wish to appear righteous, although you are not.

Or do you withdraw yourselves from being made judges? Can you conceal yourselves and refrain from judging, because I speak the truth about you? For if you do everything, you will be added to him: that is, even if you carry out all the commandments, he will find something in you for which to accuse you. For no one is righteous in his sight.

But if you have secretly shown respect to persons: your own persons, by justifying yourselves, not only before human beings but also before yourselves. The body is of clay: so that you may at least fear by considering your fragility.

Taking hold of my flesh with my teeth. I will not spare myself, so that I may accuse not only you but also myself. And I will place my soul in my hand: to be examined, so that I conceal nothing, or so that I may reckon up my sins. Though the one who is powerful, who also began, should kill me, even though he kills my sins, nevertheless I will speak, and before him I will accuse myself: I will not justify myself by hiding my sins.

Behold, I approach my judgment: so that I may judge myself; as though this itself were a person’s righteousness, not to spare himself in confession. Then I shall not be hidden from your face: as sinners hide themselves. Remove your hand from me: so that nothing remains in me to be chastised and love may be in me. And let your fear not terrify me.

How many are my iniquities? From this he may be seen to have said, “I will place my soul in my hand,” in order to reckon them up. Or do you think [Col. 0840] that I am opposed to you? Although I am certainly weak, is this what you fear—that, if I have been justified, I might be your equal, when I am like a leaf? Therefore there is some hidden cause, since this is not the reason.

And you have laid upon me the sins of youth. Let this be the reason why he says that his sins were hidden from him: because he became proud, which is the sin of youth. And you have placed my foot in fetters: in the bond of mortality. And you have examined the roots of my feet: my desires. He grows old like a wineskin: so that I cannot carry new wine; or, “so that I may be sewn together with a new cloth” [Note: [Col. 0840] Erasmus and Lovaniensis omit “so that.”], like a garment eaten by moths.

[Ib. XIV.]

For a human being born of a woman is short-lived and full of anger: of punishment [Note: [Col. 0840] Thus the manuscripts of better quality. The printed editions have, “living for a short time, full of full anger.”]. And you have brought him to judgment before you. Although he is so mortal, he nevertheless has something for which to render an account; for what he can do is required of him, however little he can do. For his months are counted before you. Precisely because he is temporal, he is convicted of sin; for you had made him eternal.

Depart from him; let him rest: according to the opinion of the carnal and animal person, for whom this life is the whole of the good. And therefore he wishes himself to be spared, so that he may enjoy this life. For there is hope for a tree. These words should be spoken ironically. There is certainly greater hope for a human being, which carnal people do not wish to believe.

But when a man dies, he departs. Here too, ironically. For in time the sea will diminish; afterward it is filled again. He is speaking about those places where the advance and retreat of the waters occur, or because all shores secretly diminish and increase according to the lunar hours—when the moon rises, the tide grows for us or for others up to the middle of the sky [Note: [Col. 0840] The printed editions have “up to the middle of the month.” The manuscripts more correctly have “up to the middle of the sky.”], and from there it diminishes.

As long as the sky exists, it will not be sewn together: for the new [Note: [Col. 0840] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have “it will not be sewn together for the new,” without a comma. M.], that is, for the sky itself. And would that you had guarded me in the underworld! So great is the hope of resurrection that I would already be free even from these uncertain conditions of life. And that you had hidden me until your anger had rested. Hence it says, “Hide yourself for a little while, until the Lord’s anger passes by” (Isa. XXVI, 20)—that is, until this mortality passes away and resurrection is reached.

For if a human being dies, he will live. For this is not life. When the days of his life have been completed: then he will live. Then you will call, and I will answer you: obedient to you, without the impediment of mortality. You have sealed my iniquities in a bag: so that you might repay them to me. You have noted if I have erred unwillingly: this too you have noted. To err unwillingly, however, is the punishment of sin.

And indeed, a mountain falling flows away. Thus also the human being fell from his height and firmness. And a rock grows old in its place: as the human being does in his nature and condition. And through the alluvion of frequent whirlpools: as though the human being too had been reduced to frailty when he is worn down by repeated floods of desire.

But you have destroyed the hope of the human being. He proceeded by degrees from mountain to rock, from rock to stones, from stones to sand, because carnal people suffer these diminutions. And he rightly said, “You have already destroyed.” For you have driven him to the end: to annihilation. So that this hope in which carnal people rejoice may perish.

You have changed his face and dismissed him: when the image of God in him was destroyed. And when he has had many children, he does not know it: because he dies, although his offspring continues. But his flesh grieves over him: that is, the carnal human being grieves carnally over such a condition of himself and mourns animally. The spiritual person knows that, although the outer human being is being corrupted, the inner human being is renewed day by day (2 Cor. IV, 16), because he perceives this happening within himself.

[Ib. XV.] The words of Eliphaz the Temanite. And he has filled his belly with sorrow. For the spirit of knowledge heals rather than causes pains through consolation; but you, who fill your belly with sorrow, do not answer with the spirit of knowledge.

Have you not cast off fear? You did not fear God, saying such things against him. And you chose the tongue of evil people: with which human beings curse. What then? Were you the first human being born? Because you are so proud. Or were you formed before the hills? The mountains too are to be understood by the name “hills,” that is, the powerful spirits, before all virtues.

But an old and decrepit person is also among us: one who knows even what we do not know is among us. What did your heart dare? And what did your eyes endure? They hoped. For what is a human being, that he should be without fault? You too said this.

If there is no faith in his holy ones: because of the uncertainties of the times, by which they are often deceived, so that they say many things and do not do them. And heaven is not clean before him: on account of those who dwell in heaven; or certainly, “heaven” is put for the holy ones themselves, because God dwells in them.

What the wise have said and their fathers have not hidden. For the Apostles also preached to the Jews. The earth was given to them alone: to inhabit. And no stranger came upon them: neither a holy human being nor an angel; that is, they will possess it in security. When they think that they are already at peace. He speaks as though he thinks this has happened to Job himself.

He does not believe that he will turn from darkness: he does not believe that he will turn from sins. And he has been appointed as food for vultures: for the aerial powers that feed upon the deaths of sinners. As a commander he will fall in the front line. He is bold and does not endure tribulations. Because [Note: [Col. 0841] “Because,” according to Erasmus and Lovaniensis. M.] he raised his hands against God. Or, “because he raised them”? And he ran against him insultingly: doing the opposite of what he commanded.

With the thick neck of his shield: presuming upon his protection. Because he covered his face with his fat. Through fatness—that is, through the exaltation of his pride—he hid God from himself. And he made a bridle over his thighs: so that he might be bound by his lusts and led by that bond to death.

For what they prepared for him, others take away: even the earthly kingdom itself, or whatever temporal hope the righteous will receive together with the whole world. And he will not become rich, nor will his substance remain: that is, the substance of the impious. He will not cast a shadow over the earth: that is, he will not become green. But the wind will dry up his shoot: temptation. His cutting-off will be corrupted before its time: before he expects it. Let him fall like the flower of the olive. Let him fall from peace, or because better things follow these, as fruit follows the flower.

For the testimony of the impious is death: a sign. And fire will consume the houses of those who accept gifts. For these are the impious who prefer temporal gifts to righteousness. He will conceive and in his belly will bring forth groaning. The things he hopes for advance toward his punishment.

[Col. 0842] [Ib. XVI.] The words of Job. I have heard many such things: not only the things you say. All of you are comforters of evils. You can console the wicked, because they imitate you, not the good; and this is a vocative. For I have heard nothing good from any of you.

What then? Is the spirit an order in words? Of pride. Or in what will it be troublesome to you? Even though you do not love what you say. And I speak according to you: as you deserve. If your soul were subjected in place of mine. If you suffered what I suffer, I would speak in words, not deeds; so that it is worthless to say what you do not do [Note: [Col. 0842] The manuscripts have “what you do”: without the negation.].

For if I speak, I shall not grieve over the wound. You have shown yourselves wise neither in speaking nor in keeping silent. For the wise, even when they speak, suffer with those whom they console; or, when speaking in their confession, they grieve over their own wound; or, when they are silent, they are silent prudently.

But now he has wearied me and made me foolish and corrupt: so that I might not speak against you. God has broken my pride, so that, having been made foolish, I may become wise. You have seized me, and I have been made a witness. You convicted me of my sins, and I myself am a witness against myself. And my lie rose up against me: when I seemed righteous to myself. I answered against my own face. Hence it says, “I will set you before your face” (Ps. XLIX, 21).

In anger he used me and cast me down. He blessed, using anger—not that he suffers it; but he cast me down as though I were proud. He growled at me with his teeth. He rebuked me, so that “teeth” may be understood as words. The arrows of his pirates fell upon me. The aerial powers whom God uses and permits either to exercise the good or punish the wicked. They are called pirates because they lie in wait for those sailing upon this sea.

He rushed upon me with the edge of his eyes. He did not conceal my sins, as though he were indicating that I should be punished. For he is like a light, showing the punishers whom they must punish. His appearance became my ruin. Or thus: He made me see my sin; previously it had not been brought home to my perception in this way.

He struck me sharply upon the knees, and they all rushed upon me together. For when God strikes, the angels of Satan rush upon a person. When I was at peace, he tore me apart. He tore me away from peace itself, or from myself, so that I might be mangled by adversaries and by those hostile to me. And, taking hold of my hair, he tore it apart: through my sins he divided me against myself.

He set me up as a target: at which they might shoot, as a target is usually set up for archers so that they may direct their arrows toward it. They surrounded me with spears, casting them into my kidneys; they did not spare me: on account of carnal desires, which he says were driven into him by evil persuasions from wicked angels.

They poured out my gall upon the earth: so that I might envy earthly goods in those who abound in them. They cast me down with a great prostration: so that we might not understand a merely carnal prostration. They sewed sackcloth to my skin: the inward sins by which he remembers that he had been among the good. And the shadow of death is upon my eyelids. I want to see, but carnal habit hinders me.

Let the earth not cover the blood of my flesh: that is, if my prayer has been defiled by desiring earthly things, let a heap of earth not be added to the bond of my mortality; he signified this by the name “blood.” That is, let me not be covered by the desire for earthly things with greater calamities of voluntary sin, which is that natural sin arising from the mortal condition. Nor let there be a place for my cry. Let the merit of my prayer be blocked.

And now, behold, my witness is in the heavens. He seems to be speaking of the Lord, because he had not yet descended to earth. And my confidant is in the heights: because of his participation in mortality. Let a man be judged together with the Lord. Let the Lord come, so that the man may be judged together with him, like John with Christ. In their judgment the difference between the perfect human being and God made human is understood.

As a son of man to his neighbor: the Lord, having assumed humanity, to the one who had fallen among robbers (Luke X, 30). For my years have been counted and have come to me: that I might be helped through Christ in the fullness of times (Gal. IV, 4). And I shall enter the way by which I shall not return: the way of renouncing the world.

[Ib. XVII.]

I have failed, shaken in spirit: the order is, “I have failed in spirit, shaken by labors.” I ask that I may be buried, and it does not happen to me: that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. For we groan, being burdened, in the condition in which we do not wish to be stripped but clothed over (2 Cor. V, 4); that is, we prefer to be changed rather than die. Yet this does not happen, although a human being desires it. For he owes death as the condemnation of sin.

I will offer prayers with labor, and what have I done? by obtaining [it] I have accomplished no small thing [Note: [Col. 0843] Thus the manuscripts of Bec and Fleury. The printed editions have: “I offer prayers with labor; and what have I done? I have not done it for myself.”]. Outsiders have stolen my goods. He signifies the immortality of which a person is stripped, the one who was left half-dead by robbers. And who is this? The one who will come to my aid, signifying the Lord. But he says, “Who is he?” because he was to be among human beings, so that he would scarcely be distinguished from them.

Let him be bound to my hand: by the bond of love, so that he may guard me and lead me where he wishes. Because you have hidden their heart from understanding. You hid those who did not recognize him. For this reason you will not exalt them: because they were not humble, they were therefore blinded and could not be exalted through the humility of Christ.

Let evils be announced to a part. For “a hardening in part has happened to Israel” (Rom. XI, 25), either because the things Christ announced seemed evil to them, so that they said, “He deceives the crowds” (John VII, 12), or because the things announced through the Prophets concerning Israel’s blindness did not happen to the whole people, but to a part.

And their eyes wasted away over their sons: in amazement at the miracles concerning which it was said, “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Matt. XII, 27). But you have made me a subject of discourse among the nations: the human being whom you redeemed—that is, the Church about which the nations would speak, or which would speak to the nations. And I have become a laughingstock to them: either to the nations, when they reviled it, or to the Jews, who spoke to the nations.

My eyes have been darkened by anger. The eyes of the Church—that is, the Apostles—were darkened when they were not understood by those who were being punished with this penalty. And I have been greatly overcome by all. For both Jews and Gentiles overcame the Church.

And the truthful were astonished [Note: [Col. 0843] “They were amazed,” according to Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice.
