M.], either at why power was given to the impious against the Church [Note: [Col. 0843] In B.: “the Church.” Erasmus, Lyons, Venice: “against the Church.” M.], or at why the Gospel was not recognized by the impious.

But let the righteous rise up over his enemy: he who falls temporarily through persecutions, so that afterward he may rule over the unbelieving. And let the pure of hands take courage: the courage of hope, so that he may confess Christ even in persecution.

For he did not find truth in you. For grace is necessary for all, both Jews and others. And the joints of my heart have been loosened: so that I may not conceal my sins.

They have made night into day: the impious. Hence it says, “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. V, 20). If I endure, the underworld will be my house: if I endure my sins, so as not to confess them. I have called destruction my father. I shall not be a son of life. But he called decay his mother and sister. Because they cling inseparably, as though they were related.

For what hope do I have now? “If I endure” is implied. Or, shall I see my goods? Those by which I was deceived and refused to turn, and endured the sinner.

### [Book XVIII]

The words of Bildad the Shuhite.

“And the light of the wicked will be extinguished.” Therefore do not wonder if your light too, like that of the wicked, has been extinguished.

“His light became darkness in the house”: the brightness of his house; that is, either the devil or the Antichrist.

“And the lamp over him will be extinguished”: a small and earthly light.

“Let the lowly receive his substance”: let the humble possess what he wished to possess [Note: The printed editions read *did not wish*; the manuscripts read *wished*.].

“For his foot has been thrust into a snare”: for he himself was captured while persecuting the Lord.

“He who thirsts has strengthened himself against him”: so that those who hunger and thirst for righteousness may conquer him.

“His cord is hidden upon the earth”: by which he may be caught—that is, the things apparently granted to him.

“And his capture is on the path”: along which he passes.

“Let pains destroy him all around”: from every side.

“And many will come in distress from hunger around his feet”: many who follow him, or who serve him.

“Let the branches of his feet be eaten”: his doctrines, that is, the way by which he proceeds.

“Let health be broken from his dwelling”: the tranquility of this life.

“And let the necessity of a royal cause seize him”: the appointed occasion of his punishment, which will contribute to God’s glory; for this reason his desire is now permitted to him. He says “a royal cause” because he will boast that he is Christ.

“Let it dwell in his tent during his night”: let the necessity of the royal cause torment his conscience; the appetite for tyranny—“during his night,” in the punishment of his blindness, when he is condemned.

“Let his beautiful things be sprinkled with sulfur”: let the things in which he took pleasure be consumed by foul-smelling fire.

“And from above his harvest will fall upon him”: from God.

“And let his name not be in the face of the streets where it was”: let him be removed from the memory of the people.

“And let there be no recognition of him among his people” [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read *his designation* (*cognominatio*).] Let him come to such abasement that he is not recognized by his own.

“And let the house of him not be preserved beneath heaven”: for some will indeed be preserved.

“But let others live among his people”: let his people be subjected to others.

### [Book XIX]

The words of Job.

“And you destroy me with words”: you weaken me, although you ought to have comforted me.

“Know only that God has done this to me”: with whom I can be convicted of sin, not with human beings.

“And he has surrounded me with his rampart”: a ditch surrounds walls; by it I have been compelled to confession.

“Behold, I laugh at reproaches, and I do not speak”: he indicates the usefulness of confession; for if he wished to laugh at his sin and not proclaim it, he would cry out and not be heard.

“He has placed darkness upon my face”: he has taken from me the illumination of my face, which happens to those who turn away.

“And he has taken the crown from my head”: the spiritual dignity given by wisdom.

“And he has shattered me on every side, and I departed”: I held everything, and he took it from me, against that power of restraint which I had received.

“And he regarded me as an enemy”: he judged me as though I would harm him if I were his equal.

“And they surrounded my tent”: my heart and conscience.

“My brothers have withdrawn”: in the hope of correction, because they are brothers—although at first they rejected my correction and followed those who advised them to pursue what belonged to others, that is, harmful things.

“And my friends have become merciless”: in spiritual evils, those who do not sympathize with their neighbors but rather mock them—although they would not mock people afflicted by bodily evils.

“And those who knew my name have forgotten me”: they do not recognize me, because I have been changed.

“The neighbors of my house, and my maidservants”: those with whom I used to share secrets; flatterers who withdraw from the one who confesses to God. Such people are said to act as servants.

“I called my servant, and he did not answer”: either the body, or those who served him for evil purposes.

“My mouth pleaded” [Note: The printed editions read *I pleaded*; the manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint, read *it pleaded*.] “and I begged my wife”: as though saying, “Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Psalm 41:12 [LXX/Latin numbering]). That is, he desired her to consent to him.

“I called, flattering, the children of my womb”: those whom he had begotten, persuading them to hope in the world.

“And those whom I had loved rose up against me”: in that life.

“My flesh has rotted in my skin”: through love of the things perceived externally, my inward parts have rotted. For certainly it is a small matter if we take this literally, as though he had had a scab.

“And my bones are in my teeth”: my firmness and strength are in words, not in deeds.

“Have pity on me, have pity on me, O my friends”: he appears to ask angels to intercede for him, or at least the saints to pray for the penitent.

“For the hand of the Lord is what has touched me”: he says that he was touched by the Lord’s hand so that he might feel pain from his wound, which previously left him without sensation.

“Why do you persecute me as the Lord does?”: you detest and abhor me as the Lord does; or you rebuke me, although I am already confessing.

“You are not satisfied with my flesh”: you are not pleased if I live carnally.

“With an iron stylus and lead”: so that, just as lead yields to an iron stylus, human hearts may yield to my words.

“Or let them be engraved upon rocks as a testimony”: so that those who are firm in evangelizing may learn them.

“For I know that the one who will restore me is eternal”: because he is able to repair me.

“Of which I am conscious within myself”: because I deserved them.

“Which my eye has seen, and no other”: that is, “No one knows what is happening in a person except the spirit that is in him” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

“And everything has been completed for me in my bosom”: in my inward parts, where no one sees, in my conscience.

“But if you also say, ‘What shall we say against him?’”: according to what was also said to spiritual people: “Keeping watch over yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

“And we shall find the root of the matter in him”: so that we may convict him from his own words [Note: Erasmus reads *from their words*.]

“For wrath will come upon the unrighteous”: he calls those unrighteous who exalt themselves over sinners and think that they cannot be such themselves.

### [Book XX]

The words of Zophar the Naamathite.

“For you do not understand more than I do”: he turns to the others who were consoling Job with him.

“I shall hear the instruction of my shame”: indirectly, he wishes Job to hear the instruction of his own shame; for then he can also attain the spirit of wisdom. This is a customary expression, as when we say, “It is good for me to be cautious, for otherwise things will go badly for me,” when we want someone else to be cautious.

“Do you know this from ancient times?”: from the beginning of the ages, you know these things.

“The eye will see, and will not add”: for it will not be seen.

“May the wicked destroy his children”: either his imitators or those whom he has deceived.

“And may his hands be kindled with pains”: may they be tormented by his works.

“His bones are filled with his youth”: he takes pride in his strength.

“He will hide it beneath his tongue”: he will not display it, like a deceitful person, so that he may use it secretly.

“He will spare it and will not abandon it”: loving it and unwilling to be without it, he will not pursue it. Or, the Lord will spare him, and he will not abandon it because of this impunity.

“And he will hold it in the middle of his throat”: like something that delights him.

“And he will not be able to help himself”: he will not thereby free himself.

“The gall of an asp is in his belly”: in his inward parts, in secret, he possesses the malice of harming.

“Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited out”: with torment in his inward parts and pressure of heart.

“An angel will drag him from his house”: whenever his hidden things are revealed through tribulations.

“And he will shine with the fury of dragons” [Note: Some manuscripts read *fury*; all, however, have *he will shine* afterward. Augustine thus appears to have read it, although the Septuagint now has *he will suck*, and the Vulgate *he will suck*.] The one who was initially hidden, exposed through tribulations, will now shine openly with the fury of dragons.

“Let the tongue of the serpent kill him”: let the devil deceive him.

“And let him not see the milking of the flocks”: let him not produce the fruits of sheep—that is, works of righteousness—so that he may understand that he can be redeemed through them.

“Nor the food of honey and butter”: good works performed with charity, cheerfulness of heart, and generosity in giving. For butter is rich milk.

“He labored in vain and to no purpose”: because he does not understand that these things must be done in a way that pertains to mercy.

Hence the Lord is also said to eat butter and honey (Isaiah 7:15), because these are offered to him in his humble members.

“What they produced was something hard”: something that cannot be chewed or swallowed. I do not know what the hard thing is; I think it is iniquity or pride.

“He will not be saved in his desire”: because he desired unjust things.

“There will be no remnants of his foods”: his desires have passed away.

“When he thinks that he is filled, he will be straitened”: it is not so much satisfaction from the fullness of his desires as pressure.

“If somehow he fills his belly”: such necessity will come upon him that he will doubt whether he can fill his belly, although these things are sought precisely to drive away need. He says this because the more he has, the more he desires.

“And he will send upon him the fury of wrath”: because he did not see him performing good works.

“Let a bronze arrow wound him”: a perpetual one.

“Let a missile pass through his body”: let temptation penetrate him, so that he is wounded both by what he hopes for and by what he abandons, as though pierced from breast to back.

“Let there be flashes of lightning in his tents”: sudden terrors in his thoughts.

“Let a stranger injure his house”: the devil, who is an intruder when he tempts—although a person also has temptations of his own.

“And let heaven disclose his iniquities”: the heavenly judgment.

“And the possession of his goods will come from the bishop” [Note: The printed editions read *from him himself*. The manuscripts read *from the bishop*, in agreement with the Septuagint, *para tou episkopou*, “from the bishop.”] God will grant these things to him.

### [Book XXI]

The words of Job.

“And let this consolation from you not be mine”: the consolation by which you think one should rejoice in temporal goods, since they are common to the devout and the impious; and if someone were wicked, you think that he is punished here through them. Job says that these goods remain with the wicked all the way to the grave, and that they are not punished through them.

“What then? Is my chastisement human?”: my chastisement is from God. Therefore he himself can also be comforted, not you.

“Or why should I not be angry?”: therefore do not console me in this way, for I certainly see the prosperity of the wicked.

“Look at me and be astonished”: as though I were saying empty things.

“For if I remember, I am troubled”: he confesses the indignities of human life, returning to his former feeling from the state in which he now is [Note: The manuscripts read *to the terrified state*. Ambrose and Erasmus read *to the terrified feeling*. Shortly afterward the Floriacensis manuscript has the reading printed here, *when he confesses*.]

“And my flesh is held by pains”: I suffer carnally.

“Why do the wicked live?”: he asks them for the reason, since they said that vengeance is exacted here upon the wicked.

“And their sheep remain as though by age”: how can they remain forever by age? They will not always be so.

“But their goods were in their hands”: he did not take their goods away when they said these things.

“Indeed, the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished”: temporal brightness, even if not in the way these men understood it.

“May his children lack his goods”: the goods he persuaded them to seek—temporal goods, whether those of the Antichrist or of the devil.

“May his eyes see his own death”: this also signifies that those who rejoice in such prosperity do not know its end; but in the future it will be brought home even to the perception of the wicked.

“For there is no will of his in his house after him”: because in their conscience they did not attain to the Lord through tribulations.

“Even if the number of his months is cut in half”: although he worshiped God in the present, because he did not also hope for the future, he does not possess the full number of months.

“For he himself judges murders”: when the wicked have persuaded others to impiety through love of carnal impieties, they certainly kill them in the future age. Human beings do not judge such murders, however; God alone does.

“Here he will die in the strength of his simplicity”: he seems to be pursuing hidden murders, mentioning one person who is generous and another who is miserly, because prosperous and generous people are thought to be good.

“His bowels are full of fat”: he possesses gladness.

“And their marrow is poured out”: the marrow of his bowels, because he does not keep his goods within himself but spends them either on himself or on others.

“Therefore I know that you boldly press upon me”: you do not speak with consideration.

“For you say, ‘Where is the house of the prince?’”: whether of the wicked man or of the proud man; for they thought that his goods were taken from him here, although many have even ended their lives full of such goods, and are to be punished through them [Col. 0848].

“And where is the covering in the tents of the wicked?”: honor.

“Ask those who pass along the road”: those who do not take pleasure in the road but pass along it.

“And you will not be ignorant of their signs”: either the signs which the wicked give to passersby, telling them what will happen to them; or the signs by which the wicked are recognized [Note: Thus Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice. In the Bolognese edition, *to him*.]

“Who will announce his way before him?”: no one announces his way before the wicked man unless the Lord announces it confidently, because he himself answers him.

“And yet the Lord himself also has been led down into the grave”: therefore the reward of devotion must not be hoped for here.

“And he kept watch over the heap”: for he himself rose first, before the heap of those who were to rise rose.

“The stones of the torrent were sweet to him”: those whom the world did not overthrow, that is, his disciples.

“And every person follows after him, and innumerable people go before him”: or, “every person after him,” that is, one person; and “innumerable before him,” those who are now counted among humanity [Note: Three manuscripts read *to be counted*.] Or, after him is the crowd of believers, and before him the patriarchs and prophets.

“How then do you console me in vain?”: by urging present goods or evils upon me.

### [Book XXII]

The words of Eliphaz the Temanite.

“Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?”: as though Job had said that he does not judge rightly, when God cannot be reproved except by an understanding superior to him, if indeed understanding is given to human beings by God.

“And will he come with you into judgment?”: so that you may be compared with him.

“Your light has been changed into darkness”: your dignity.

“And water has covered you while you slept”: the flood of tribulation has covered you while you were secure.

“Or does he distinguish through a cloud?”: as though he were unable to see through a cloud.

“A cloud is his hiding place, and he will not be seen”: the things on earth are hidden from him.

“And he traverses the circuit of heaven”: its shape, but not the earth.

“Do you therefore guard the path of the world?”: as though Job had thought that God does not care for human affairs.

“Because the immature were captured”: immature according to themselves; for they thought that they would remain forever.

“Or certainly before they reached wisdom”: but Job’s friends said this because they had heard it, not because they themselves understood it.

“And the thought of the wicked is far from him, and he fills their houses with good things”: the thought of the wicked is far from him because he does not act as the wicked hopes—that is, either because impiety pleases him, or because he does not see it.

“Those who see will be more righteous”: those who understand, although these men did not understand, thinking that the wicked are repaid here.

“And the blameless will mock them”: the wicked.

“Be harsh, if you endure patiently”: that is, be harsh.

“You will put iniquity far from your tent”: your conduct or life, although these men speak of such things carnally.

“And placing it upon a mound, upon a rock”: against what he said, “A river flows away from their foundations.”

“Because he humbled himself”: the light itself.

“And you will say, ‘He has been lifted up in pride’”: against the proud.

“Rescue the innocent, and you will be saved by the purity of your hands”: do not fail in good works, because God cares for human affairs.

### [Book XXIII]

The words of Job.

“And indeed I know that correction is from my hand”: from my sins.

“And my hand has become heavy upon my groaning”: therefore you struck me, so that I might suffer [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *you struck me*.]

“And that I may come as far as his throne”: so that I may be so holy as to reach the company of those who are his thrones. Then I can speak and hear the truth; hence the heavens are also called holy.

“And I shall know the reasons that he will speak to me”: the explanations by which he shows that he judges all things justly.

“And I shall perceive what he announces to me”: already near him.

“Will he be judged with me in great power?”: as though he would resist me through his power? Certainly not.

“Yet let him not abuse me in terror”: because of my sins, for which I now fear—while I am in terror—let him not abuse me.

“But when I have come to him”: in the freedom in which I shall be numbered among his thrones, I shall love everything, and his power will not resist me; although now he can use me as he wishes, since I am a sinner—that is, he can do with me what he wills, even in punishing me, yet justly.

“For truth and correction are from him”: that is, he does not correct unjustly.

“He brings my judgment to its conclusion”: even if he now chastises me, afterward he will make the judgment manifest.

“For if I walk first, afterward I shall not be”: let me neither hope arrogantly nor despair faithlessly; that is, let me not decline either to the right or to the left.

Hence: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Psalm 138:8). Who can drive me away from there? and so forth.

“On the left, what he does I shall not grasp”: he repeats what he said above. By “the left” he means that he will not grasp the one devoted to temporal things.

“He will turn to the right, and I shall not see”: therefore I must not be on the left. He said “he will turn” because he himself is in spiritual things, from which I turn away if I am on the left.

“He knows my way”: so that even if he leads me through tribulations, I will follow.

“He has tested me like gold”: in tribulations [Note: Three manuscripts read *in temptations*.]

“I shall go forth in his commandments”: I shall come out of my darkness, yet remain in his commandments.

“But if he himself has judged thus”: so that he may test me like gold through tribulations.

“Therefore I hastened to him”: because he afflicted me, I hastened to him after abandoning temporal things.

“And having been warned, I became concerned about him”: so that through these bodily punishments I might avoid eternal punishments.

“Therefore I shall be troubled before his face”: now I shall be troubled so as to take care, thinking of the future judgment, where his manifestation will be.

“And the Lord has softened my heart”: Job attributes even the fear by which he avoids future punishments to God’s mercy. For he would not know that punishments and darkness await the wicked unless the Lord softened his heart through present tribulations—contrary to the statement that God hardens Pharaoh’s heart (Exodus 7:3).

### [Book XXIV]

“Why are the times not hidden from the Lord?”: why, or therefore.

“They have crossed the boundaries”: Christ.

“And they have turned the poor away from the right way”: either so that they might imitate them, or so that they might conclude from this that there is no divine judgment, because they saw the wickedness by which these people harmed them being left unpunished while they abandoned righteousness.

“Together the meek of the earth were hidden”: with those who turned aside from the right way, the meek were hidden, so that they would not bring me help.

For there are three kinds of people in the Church when persecution arises: some consent, some flee, and some suffer. Job assumes the role of the last.

“And wild asses rushed upon me in the field”: foolish and untamed, and therefore proud, they rushed upon me as I confessed—that is, upon the Church.

“And they went out to their work”: for this is their work: to rush upon me. That is, they were appointed by God for this.

“Bread has become sweet to him among the young men”: he calls persecution sweet bread to the wicked persecutor, because he gladly enjoyed it when he inflicted it upon young men. We may understand “young men” either as lovers of pleasures, since such people easily consent to these things; or as those who have advanced so far in the Church that they have passed beyond the simplicity of childhood but have not yet reached that manly strength by which even a persecutor is despised.

“They reaped a field not their own before its time”: either he speaks of kinds of persecution, by which they frightened someone through the loss of a field; or the Church is to be understood as the field, which they wished to reap through persecutions before its maturity—that is, before the weeds could grow together with it, so that they might be separated at harvest (Matthew 13:29–30).

“They will be moistened by the dripping of the mountains”: fleeing naked to caves where the rocks drip.

“They snatched the orphan from the breast”: orphans and widows are often to be understood as representing the Church; it is the people under torment.

“And they humbled the one who had fallen”: one abandoned either by God’s help or by someone else’s. It is great savagery not to spare such people.

“In distress they lay wicked ambushes”: in times of need.

“They were driven from the city and from their houses”: others were driven out by them.

“But the soul of the little ones was greatly in groaning”: it was so.

“Yet God himself did not care for them”: for the wicked, by not caring for them now, caused them to despair of God’s judgment, because they were doing evil with impunity.

“And therefore they were handed over to darkness”: to ignorance of God’s judgment.

“And suddenly, like a thief, that day will seize them.”

“The eye of the adulterer watches for darkness”: he wishes to show into what darkness the wicked are handed over through impunity. He does not mean the darkness sought by adulterers and others who do evil at night so as not to be recognized by day, but the darkness that remains upon them even in the morning [Note: The printed editions read *evil*. The manuscripts read *morning*.]

“He digs through houses in the darkness”: he recalls other evil deeds.

“By day they sealed themselves up”: they concealed themselves.

“They did not know the light, because the shadow of death remains with them at once” [Note: Thus the printed editions and the manuscripts. The Septuagint has *not in the morning*.] The shadow of death did not leave them simply because night had departed.

“He is light upon the face of the water”: in comparison with the earth, those whom the light penetrates and who bear the image of lightness are to be regarded as brighter; and therefore the shadow of death is light upon them. They too bear it by the condition of the flesh.

Or, “He is light upon the face of the water” means, “upon those who confess in Baptism.”

“Let their portion be cursed upon the earth”: let what they have chosen be barren.

“For they snatched from the bosom of the orphans”: from the heart of the weak, the word through evil persuasion.

“Then his sin was remembered”: the sin he thought would pass into oblivion.

“Let every wicked person be crushed like an incurable tree”: like something that does not heal [Note: Lovaniensis reads *which is not healed*. Other printed editions and the manuscripts read *which does not heal*.]

“For he did no good to the barren woman”: to one who is without the consolation of children.

“Therefore, when he rises, he does not believe against his life”: he does not believe against his own life; for he ought to have believed that his life was evil and, for that very reason, to rise up against it.

“When he begins to be weakened, let him not hope for health”: let him not hope for health when he begins to suffer tribulation.

“But he falls into sickness”: such consolations the wicked seek in adversity, by which they become weaker.

“His height withered like mallow in the heat”: because he did not endure the heat of tribulation; mallow is mentioned because of its weakness.

Or, “like an ear falling of its own accord from straw”: because he was in his own height in the morning. For he chose for himself such consolations that would make him weaker still.

“Otherwise, who is there who will say that I speak falsely?”: if matters are otherwise.

### [Book XXV]

The words of Bildad the Shuhite.

“For what beginning is there except fear from him?”: this addition appears to agree with Job’s words: “Therefore I shall be troubled before his face; I shall consider and fear him” (Job 23:15).

“Let no one think there is delay for pirates”: without delay, they tempt according to his permission.

“For against whom will there be no ambushes from him?”: that is, when he himself permits it. By “ambushes” he means temptations.

“Or how will a human being be righteous before the Lord?”: therefore he permits the person to be tested justly.

“Or how will one born of woman be cleansed?”: unless he is cleansed by God, he is unclean.

“If he commands the moon, and it does not shine”: for if the reasons and orders of his providence require that the moon not shine, he will command it not to shine, and it will not shine.

“But why?”: Does he wish it to appear from this that the moon is not clean before him, because he commands it and it does not shine? Or perhaps the nature of the rational soul is figuratively indicated here. For the intelligible sun is that true light which illuminates every human being (John 1:9).

And since the moon shines more brightly to earthly eyes the farther it recedes from the sun, but when it approaches the sun it is extinguished for earthly beings, let us understand that the soul is divinely commanded, once it has overcome its earthly and mortal birth by which its splendor appears to those who see with earthly perception, to appear, approach, and be subjected to wisdom. Thus, rejoicing most secretly in its light [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions read *most secret*.], it must beware of doing its righteousness before human beings, so as to be seen by them (Matthew 6:1), but when it boasts, let it boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31).

“For the stars also are not clean before him”: in comparison with him.

### [Book XXVI]

The words of Job.

“Whom are you helping?”: or, whom will you assist? He had indignantly thought, as though their injustice deserved punishment by God.

But, speaking to himself, he recalls himself so as to leave their judgment to God rather than appear to stand beside God, or wish to help him as though he were weak, in restraining or correcting human beings; or to give him advice about what he should do with them; or to follow him, as though he could discover the reason why he permits deceitful people to be and to live, when he surpasses every soul seeking virtue with incomprehensible power; or as though he could announce anything to him about them, when human beings receive from him even their breath whenever they utter anything.

“Will the giants be reduced to nothing?”: therefore it is not surprising if God spares these people, when he does not reduce the giants to nothing.

And lest someone say, “But they have been thrust down to the underworld,” he adds that God sees the underworld; and yet he has placed them there where they deserved to be. So too with the righteous—whether now as they are, or afterward as they will be—although he never removes them from his presence, because everything is naked before him. You may also understand these nearest giants to be these proud comforters.

“Under the water, and their neighbors”: is “under the water” to be understood as “they are held,” or something similar?

“And there is no covering for destruction”: even destruction does not escape him.

“Stretching the north over nothing”: the north may signify the devil, and the earth the sinner, since hope is empty for both.

“Suspending the earth over nothing”: in the air.

“Binding the water in his clouds”: because of the obscurity of prophecy.

“And the cloud beneath him is not split”: beneath the truth possessed by the cloud, which is not divided for those who understand the Scriptures. For the Scriptures do not contradict one another, as those who do not understand think.

“He who holds the face of the sun” [Note: There is a mistake in Augustine’s manuscript: the Septuagint reads *of the throne*, while the Vulgate has *of the seat*.] so that the sun of righteousness would not be recognized by the wicked.

“And he stretches out his cloud over it”: the flesh that the Lord assumed.

“He has enclosed a command upon the face of the water”: the peoples.

“Until the completion of the light”: until the end of this life, that is, the end of the age; or until human beings are completed, that is, perfected—those of whom it was said, “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

“The pillars of heaven trembled and were astonished at his rebuke”: this happened to Peter through Paul (Galatians 2:11).

“By his strength he calmed the sea”: he quieted the world, from which the Church was suffering persecution.

Accordingly, the trembling of the pillars of heaven at his rebuke may also be understood in this way: the strongest members of the Church trembled on behalf of the weak at the Lord’s rebuke, when he permitted the temptations of persecution. For the pillar cries out: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

“By his understanding the whale was wounded”: he says that the devil was wounded by the pain with which the righteous did not yield to him.

“And the gates of heaven fear him”: either the angels, or those who have received the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

“By his command he killed the dragon, the deserter”: he had called him the whale as well. But now he shows how he was wounded, when those who renounced him received the command.

“Behold, these are the parts of his way”: by which one comes to God.

“But who will know the power of his thunder when he acts?”: by “thunder” he means the unmistakably clear voice of his manifestation. Or perhaps that voice which he gave through the Son of Thunder: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The order would then be: “When he acts, who will know the power of his thunder?”

### [Book XXVII]

“And the divine spirit is in my nostrils”: here it is shown prophetically that he speaks what he speaks and prophetically knows that his comforters are full of deceit.

“Far be it from me to call you righteous until I die”: even if you persecute me to death, because I freely rebuke you.

“For I will not separate the innocent; nor you, however” [Note: Erasmus reads *nor*, instead of *but not*.]

“For I am not conscious to myself of having committed anything unjust”: those who fear that something true may be brought against them commonly spare others.

“For what hope is there for the impious? Because he waits”: lest anyone think that he had wished evil upon his enemies, he here reveals the intention with which he spoke. He wants their impiety overthrown and their pride destroyed. This happens when the soul held guilty is released from impiety; it is released through the confession of the penitent person and the grace of the forgiving God.

Therefore, “What hope is there for the impious?” is a question, and the answer is: “Because he waits and trusts in the Lord,” if perhaps he may be released [Note: The Septuagint has *he will be saved*. The Vulgate renders this passage with the verb *he may set free*.] or if the Lord may hear his prayers.

Another meaning may indeed occur in these words, but it does not fit the book and the faith as a whole to make the impious’ position one of total despair, as though he had no hope whatsoever. Against this interpretation it is written: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the impious, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Romans 4:5).

And therefore what follows is understood to speak of the Lord’s grace.

“Or if necessity should come upon him”: for this reason we must wait for the grace of the one who releases.

“For did he have confidence in necessity—that is, in temptation—because of merits in God’s sight?”

“Or if he calls, will he hear him?”: if he calls as though trusting in his works, which are nothing.

“Therefore I shall announce to you what is in the hand of the Lord”: what God has ordained.

“Behold, you all know that you speak vainly of vain things”: for this reason grace must now be awaited. How could he appeal to the merits of his works while speaking vainly of vain things?

“But the possession of the powerful will come from the Almighty upon them”: so that the powerful may possess them—that is, the devil and his angels. He calls them powerful because these people will become weak by following vanity, so that those leaders and princes of vanity may prevail over them. Thus the Lord also calls him strong (Luke 11:21), for no other reason than that he holds the weak.

“And if his children are many, they will be for slaughter”: he calls his children those who imitate him in deceiving others—the persuader of false doctrines, destined for condemnation.

“But if they become young men, they will be in need”: that is, if they are confirmed in error, they will still be in need, for vanity has not satisfied them.

“And those who are around him will die by death”: those who are most like him in deceiving others.

“And he will not have mercy on their widows”: on the peoples whom he deceived with them, when their husbands have been left dead, as though he had kept faith with them in the promise of error.

“But if he gathers silver as earth”: that is, if prudent and wise people, while they are still earth and clay—that is, while they still think foolishly and carnally—agree with them, then, once corrected and gaining knowledge, they will turn to the righteous.

“For their houses will be like moths and spiders, which he has preserved”: the heart or conscience.

Or by “houses” he means the defenses with which they protect themselves—clever and hidden, but utterly weak—like the moth’s cocoon in which it hides, and the spider’s cave into which it withdraws, covering and closing itself.

“What he has preserved” is understood as referring to the spider itself in that cave, since not all spiders do this. It also refers to the voluntary and inward corruption of an evil thought, and to the useless works which the wicked person carefully preserved for himself in his house.

“The rich man will sleep and will not add”: after death he will not add riches to those very impieties.

“He opened his eyes, and he is not”: in the resurrection he will not find himself rich, as he had supposed.

“Heat will carry him away, and he will depart”: either the heat of the sea, the tribulation of the world; or the heat by which grasses without roots wither.

“And it will scatter him from his place”: either from his hope; or God will scatter him from his place, so that he is not in God’s place—that is, among the people whom God inhabited.

“And he will cast it upon him, and will not spare”: as though it were a mound of punishments.

“He will clap his hands over him”: as it is said, “I too will laugh at their destruction” (Proverbs 1:26). For he will not mourn over the destruction of the wicked.

### [On Job, XXVIII]

For there is a place for silver, from which it is obtained: the prudent, who are more active in practice. But the place for gold is where it is refined: the wise, who are engaged in contemplation. For iron comes from the earth. These metals are to be understood indiscriminately in a good sense; for that is why he mentioned iron, as though he were speaking above all of iron—although the strong may also be understood by iron. Indeed, there is no distinction in the wisdom of men who are in it [uncertain reading]. But bronze, like stones, is excluded, because everything is separated from the earth. [Note: We correct the text with the aid of the Regius manuscript: the printed editions read *seducuntur* (“are led astray”), whereas the required reading is *secluduntur* (“are separated”).] He shows that good people are temporarily mixed with the wicked because the good are separated from those very wicked people and are purified through them, like metals necessary for a work or a building, while the earth itself must be purified and shaped. Hence they too must be separated, so that after this separation the earth may have its own place and order, as do the wicked through condemnation according to their merits.

“And he himself found every end”: what each thing should be brought to. “Found” means “ordained.” “A stone of darkness and the shadow of death”: the stone—that is, the Old Testament—was given to darkness and the shadow of death, that is, to those who pursued carnal things, although they expected them from the one God. Therefore, in their pride, they did not cut through the torrent—that is, they did not pass through the slipping-away of temporal things to any firmness—but were carried along by that very falling.

“And a division of the torrent was made from the ash”: that is, from the person confessing his sins and not being proud of the merits of his works; this was accomplished through the grace of the New Testament. “A division of the torrent from the ash”: from human beings. “And they were shaken from among human beings”: by flatterers, when God did not rebuke them, as they lost their primacy through the very things that had been promised to them. [Note: Perhaps read *ob ipsa*, “because of the very things.”] “The earth from which bread came forth”: one must understand, “I mean those who were shaken, from whom, as from the earth, the Lord’s bread came forth.” “And he will set it on fire”: the Lord will set the unfaithful person before heavenly judgment. [Note: Three manuscripts read *Domini*, “of the Lord.”]

“The place of sapphire—its stones”: the order is, “the place of sapphire,” that is, the precious and necessary [stones] for the building of the heavenly city. “And its mounds are gold”: the gold belonging to it is not a little gold, but mounds of gold.

“The path that the bird has not known”: the humility of the Lord. “Nor has the eye of the vulture seen it”: of the devil. “The lion does not pass over it”: one who is proud through strength.

“Upon the hardest stone he stretches out his hand.” For God is able to raise up children for Abraham from stones (Matt. III, 9). “And he broke through the banks of the rivers”: so that he might water everything. By rivers he means preachers of the word. For they wished to be confined within their own banks, so as to preach only to the circumcision.

“My eye has seen every precious thing”: the human eye, through the Word made flesh. “He revealed the depth of the rivers.” The powers by which persecutions are endured in martyrdom are hidden and deep within a person until they are revealed by the trial of persecution. “And he displayed his power in the light”: in those to whom he said, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14). Through them, too, a considerable part of the Jews was converted.

“The abyss said, ‘It is not in me.’” Therefore, people established in the abyss will not be able to find wisdom in it, because it is not there. “Gold enclosed will not be given in exchange for it”: that is, treasure. “It will not be inferior to the gold of Ophir”: as though he were saying, “Seek it even in this way, if indeed it is not inferior to the gold of Ophir.” “Gold and glass will not be compared with it.” This may be understood either as some beautiful glass, or because there are people who value glass more highly than wisdom. “And vessels of gold are its exchange”: they are not, one must supply.

“And the lofty things and Gabis will not be remembered.” They will be consigned to oblivion in comparison with it. Or “the lofty things and Gabis” may mean proud things, which are not to be remembered, so that through humility you may draw wisdom from hidden things. [Note: The printed editions read *gravis*, corruptly in place of *Gabis*, a Hebrew word which the Septuagint indeed retained; Symmachus translated it *huperêmena* (“lofty things”); the Vulgate has *eminentia* (“high things”); Jerome, in his *Hebrew Names in Job*, interprets it as “the height of confusion”; while others think it denotes some unknown kind of precious stone.]

“Where has wisdom been found?” He says this because a human being could not find wisdom except through grace; therefore the heart must be turned toward God. “It is hidden from the eyes of every human being”: because it is not found among those without understanding.

“Perdition and death said”: the lost and the dead, while they live in delights. “The Lord established its way”: humility, which is hidden from the birds of heaven. “And he himself knows its place.” What is the place of wisdom, except the Father? For when it is said, “I am in him, and he is in me” (John X, 38), they are, as it were, mutually one another’s places. For he himself sees everything that is under heaven. He knows it in the manner in which he made it, not through sense-perception. [Note: Augustine appears to have read this as *ventorum libramenta atque mensuras* (“the balances and measures of the winds”), instead of *aquae*, or *aquarum mensuras* (“the measures of water” or “of the waters”), which is the true reading of Scripture.]

The whole creation is signified by a part. And he rightly said that all things were made by weight, measure, and number (Wis. XI, 21), in which the Creator is understood. When he made them, he counted them as he saw them. He did not see them outside himself in order to make them, but in himself, as an artisan does.

“And the way of storms by their voices”: “storms” is put for temptations; “temptations” for those who are tempted—just as one might speak of “the voices of shipwreck” instead of “the voices of those shipwrecked.” “Then he saw it and expounded it.” In predestination the Lord saw the way by which those who were tempted would turn back. “He prepared and investigated”: in predestination, not in action. [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript, of excellent quality, lacks the negative particle here.]

### [On Job, XXIX]

“Who will restore me to the months of former days?” These words seem to be spoken in the person of the Church together with Christ, its head, as though the whole Christ were speaking during a time of abundant tribulations and temptations—as in those days of which the Lord says, “The days will come when you will desire to see one of these days, and you will not see it” (Luke XVII, 22).

For at the time when the Lord was on earth there was no anxiety, although the Christian people were still small and consisted of those who had believed in him—among whom were more than five hundred brothers, to whom he also deigned to appear after the resurrection, as the Apostle says (I Cor. XV, 6). At that time, then, there was no anxiety that the Church might be badly governed by wicked people or torn apart by the plots of heresies or schisms. Nor had it yet suffered bodily persecutions; it had endured no adversities, whether inward or outward.

Job therefore speaks in the person of the human being—that is, of the people belonging to the New Testament—desiring those days, as the Lord had foretold. Perhaps for this reason he called them months, not years, because from the time when the Lord chose the disciples until the Passion there were months, not years.

“When his lamp shone over my head”: either the visibly present flesh of the Lord, or the word proceeding bodily from the mouth of one who was present. “When the word of the Lord watched over my house,” to guard my manner of life carefully. [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads, “when the Lord watched over my house.”]

“And my young men were around me”: those who humbly served by administering what was necessary. “When butter flowed along my ways”: through my conduct, the joy of faith and good works. “When my mountains abounded in milk”: the Prophets were suitably explained to the little ones.

“When I went out at dawn into the city”: either when brightness had already begun to shine after the darkness of fear had passed, or at the beginning of the Church, so that it was neither entirely hidden nor entirely manifest. “And a seat was placed for me in the squares”: authority to teach was carried to me by the crowds.

“When young men saw me, they hid themselves”: those devoted to desires. “But the old men rose”: the prudent. “And the powerful ceased to speak”: those who were proud of their doctrines.

“Because the ear heard, and it blessed me.” “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII, 45). “And the eye that saw me turned away”: the unbelieving Jews. “And the mouth of the widow blessed me”: the soul that renounced marriage with the devil. “Behold, the dead son, the only son of his mother, who was a widow, was being carried out” (Luke VII, 12).

“And I clothed myself with judgment as with a cloak”: in preferring spiritual things to carnal things, “let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI, 3), that is, with what intention it acts. For when the left side is covered, the right is exposed in the clothing of a cloak. This is what one does who judges rightly to what purpose his action should be referred.

“I sought the judgment that I did not know.” “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what will there be for us?” (Matt. XIX, 27). He says that it was part of his happiness that he had someone from whom he might inquire about the future judgment.

“I broke the jaws of the wicked”: so that they would no longer devour the people with the food of bread. “My age will grow old; like a palm tree, I shall live for a long time”: it will be prolonged, and I shall be like a palm tree in everlasting honor, height, and uprightness.

“And the dew will remain upon my harvest.” Once a field is sown and germinates, it is called a harvest. “My glory is new with me”: that is, the glory of the New Testament. “And my bow will proceed in my hand”: I shall do what I command. “And they did not add to my speech.” This signifies the perfection of the Gospel, for the word given to the Synagogue required addition.

“But they rejoiced when I spoke to them”: because the earlier speech contained fear, while the later contained love. “And if I also laughed at them, they did not believe”: concerning the things he spoke in parables, in such a way that they were not understood; nevertheless, they did not think that he was saying empty things merely because the words seemed to sound that way. This is Sarah’s laughter (Gen. XVIII, 10), which signified that they had done everything in prophecy; hence those who speak figuratively.

“I chose their way and sat as prince”: either by accepting mortality, or by dining with tax collectors and sinners—but in such a way that I was their prince for salvation. “And I lived as a king surrounded by the strong”: those who left their own things and followed him.

“As one comforting the mourners.” He refers to those who rejoiced in hope while they were sorrowful over the present life. “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matt. V, 5), as it is said; and, “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (II Cor. VI, 10). They cannot attain that greatness of which it is said, “Whoever does and teaches these things will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 19). [Note: We have restored from the manuscripts a negative omitted in the printed editions.]

### [On Job, XXX]

“But now the lowliest mock me; now those younger in age admonish me”: for such people were born later in the Church and make very little progress. He says “admonish me” because through ecclesiastical honors they receive the power to preach to the people, although they themselves do not practice what they preach.

“Whose parents I disdained.” He calls their parents those whose imitation made them sons—those to whom it was then said, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites” (Matt. XXIII, 13). “And the strength of their hands was as nothing to me”: the power of their parents, who at that time had such great influence that they crucified the Lord.

“In this all life perished”: because they did not correct themselves even at the end. “Unstable through poverty and hunger”: through various insatiable desires. “Who yesterday fled into the desert”: by resorting to an excuse based on the Law, which they did not understand simply; and because they had received it in the desert, they fled into “yesterday’s” desert. For just as “today” belongs to the New Testament, so “yesterday” belongs to the Old. Of the New it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV, 8), and, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7).

“Who gnawed the bark of trees”: because they took the figures of the Law, by which the wines were covered, as food. [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “by which useful things were covered.” M.] “Their food was the root of plants”: the sacraments that they had been commanded to celebrate bodily, as things clinging to the earth. From these, however, the fruit of simple understanding would arise and be carried above the earth into freedom, to which they could not attain.

“Dishonored, rejected, and lacking every good”: having lost the honor of primacy and the hope of the promise; for they had also lost the earthly gift on account of their merits, and they do not possess the kingdom of heaven.

“Who ate the roots of trees because of great hunger.” What was said of the roots of plants, on account of the fruit of grain, is to be understood here of the roots of trees, on account of the fruit of wine and oil. For the Church received all these spiritual fruits; their roots, entangled in the earth, were the sacraments that the Jews were compelled to observe bodily—Sabbath, circumcision, sacrifices, and other things of this kind, which were spiritual foods.

“Thieves rose up against me”: those who reached illicit honors, belonging properly to the righteous, through dark deceptions. “Their houses were caves of rocks”: they defended and concealed their desires with certain obscurities of the divine Books.

“And they cried out among the trees.” Their sins were manifest, although they tried to cover them with the obscurity of the Scriptures, as with the shadows of trees. Hence, “The cry of Sodom has risen up to me” (Gen. XVIII, 20). In many places Scripture uses “cry” for manifest sins: a word is whatever is conceived in the heart; a cry, when it proceeds into action.

“Who lived beneath the roots of the earth.” They may be understood as living not merely in the roots but even below the roots—those who keep the commandments carnally. Roots are not yet the fruits themselves, but the source from which the fruitful parts arise, whether of trees or of plants—provided, that is, that the species is fruitful, since roots are also spoken of in connection with non-fruit-bearing species.

“Sons of foolish and ignoble people”: the Jews. For above he called these people their parents on account of imitation, because they too walk under the name of God, whom they do not worship. He calls the Jews foolish and ignoble because, on the contrary, they not only confidently claimed to be guides of the blind but also claimed to be children of Abraham, boasting that they were noble through that father. But when they hear, “They are blind, guides of the blind” (Matt. XV, 14), they are shown to be foolish; and when they hear, “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham” (John VIII, 39), they are shown to be ignoble by their degeneration.

“Name and honor are extinguished from the earth.” They existed, but have been extinguished. “Now I am their lyre”: the lyre of those whose fathers they are, who had me at their ear but not in their heart. “And they have me as a tale”: an empty and useless story and hearing, although they both tell about me and hear me.

“They abhorred me and went far away”: they became far from righteousness by sinning, and by their evil behavior they abhorred the commandments of righteousness. “Nor did they spare spitting in my face.” The face of Christ is indeed abhorrent to those who recoil from his commandments with contempt. Or they made me known in a bad way through the perversity of their conduct.

“Opening his quiver, he afflicted me”: the hidden things of reality, from which temptations arise. “And they put a bridle in my face”: so that, against my will, I might consent to them, carrying them as they led me wherever they wished, down to their own depths.

“And those sprouting on the right rose up against me”: they arose both by favoring and by giving good advice, in order to satisfy their own desires, not by persecuting me. “They bound my feet with fetters”: with ecclesiastical offices, so that I could not flee from them.

“My paths were crushed”: so that they would not appear, along which the good customarily walk, seeking not their own interests but those of Christ (Phil. II, 20). “For he stripped me of my robe”: of my former authority, to which people are accustomed to yield; this happens when the multitude and the prevailing custom of sinners gain power.

“And he wounded me with his darts”: with commandments by which I see the evils and, because I cannot restrain them, am tormented. “He used me as he wished”: God used even my calamity and misery for his own righteousness, as he wished.

“I am wrapped in pains”: I suffer both in myself and in others. “Outside there are conflicts, within fears” (II Cor. VII, 5). “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Cor. XI, 29). “My pains are repeated; my hope departs like a breath”: they have turned toward the hope of temporal things, possessing what I promise as though it were something empty. “And my salvation has passed like a cloud”: they do not hope for the promised salvation because they love the present salvation.

“And now my soul will be poured out over me”: in prayer. [Note: The printed editions read *peccando*, “by sinning”; the manuscripts read *precando*, “in prayer.”]

“At night my bones were broken”: he says that the firmness he had possessed was taken from him. “And my sinews were dissolved”: his former actions. “With great strength he seized my robe”: to display his power, now by afflicting me and afterward by restoring me. “And like the edge of my garment he surrounded me”: he left me only a small amount of authority.

“In earth and ashes is my portion”: in penitence, because this is the end. “They stood and looked at me”: while I lay prostrate, the proud stood by, seeking something to criticize in me. “And you cast me away from salvation.” He grieves for those who have lost the hope of restoration.

“For the earth is the house of every mortal.” He therefore says that he fears death because his manner of life is not in heaven (Phil. III, 20), according to the many who are evil within the Church and live in an earthly manner.

“And would that I could kill myself”: so that I might die to the world. “Or ask another, and let him do this for me”: either a better angel, or God, through whom I might be corrected.

“I was expecting good things.” He grieves because these things happened to him suddenly. “My belly seethed, and it will not be silent”: his inner parts, or his memory, by which he recalls what he had first been and how he was afflicted, in groanings. “And I stood crying out in the assembly”: because the assembly of those who refused to correct themselves did not hear him.

“My skin became exceedingly black”: because of what he suffered outwardly. “My lyre has been turned into mourning”: his good works, by which, rejoicing, he praised God.

### [On Job, XXXI]

“I made a covenant with my eyes.” Have I begun to hope for visible things? “So that I would not think of a virgin”: one must supply, “God forbid.” Here he begins to recount the merits of the Church, in those who persevere to the end amid great temptations, while iniquity abounds and the love of many grows cold (Matt. XXIV, 12–13).

“And I will not think of a virgin”: of the incorruptibility of wisdom or righteousness. “And what other portion is there for God from above?” One must supply, “I will not think of it.” Or it may be taken this way: “And what is there, except that one?”

“If I walked with mockers”: it is now difficult for the good who are in the Church not to associate with such people. [Note: Erasmus, Lugdunensis, Venetus, and Lovaniensis read this as follows: “Now, for the good who are in the Church, it is difficult not to associate with such people.” In B: “Now concerning the good who are in the Church.” “It is difficult not to associate with such people.” M.] “Or if my foot hastened toward deceit”: hypocrisy.

“Let me sow, and let others eat my fruits”: as happened to the Jews, that is, saying things that others do rather than doing them themselves. “Let me be without a root upon the earth”: so that I may wither easily. For the person who does what he says is firm upon the earth as upon a rock.

“If my heart followed a woman”: so that it might seek its own glory among the people of God rather than God’s glory, which alone is rightly owed to him. “Or if I lay in wait at her doors”: if I deceitfully pursued the desires or fear of her people, by which they would be driven to serve me rather than God.

“May my wife please another”: may my reputation please the devil; for when we please him, we displease God. He rejoices in our evils. “And may my children be humbled”: my deeds, or those who imitate me.

“For the fury of my soul is untamed: to defile a man’s wife”—by claiming her for myself.

“And if I despised the judgment of my male servant or female servant when they were judged before me”: according to what is said, “If then you have judgments concerning worldly matters” (I Cor. VI, 4). By “servants” he means laypeople still devoted to worldly affairs.

“And if I also neglected a visitation, what answer will I give?” In tribulation, what conscience will I have, because I neglected this? “Were not they, just as I, conceived in the womb?” In the sacraments. For the same things are preached to everyone. [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read this passage as, “For the same things are preached in the sacraments to everyone.”] “And were we not likewise in the womb?” For one person does not renounce the world differently from another who is about to serve God fully.

“And from my mother’s womb I was their guide.” From its beginning the Church performs these things. [Note: The manuscripts read, “From its beginning it performs these things”; the printed editions read, “From the beginning I was.”]

“Or if I disregarded one perishing naked and did not cover him”: if I did not cover the one perishing through faith in the remission of sins, as though he lacked a tunic, veiling him from the nakedness of ugliness—that is, of sin. For he is already despairing because of the multitude of his sins. Hence also, “Blessed are those whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1).

“If the shoulders of the weak did not bless me”: through the hope of immortality, as though they were covered from above with a cloak. But lest they think that, after faith in the remission of sins, it is enough merely to be free from fear of past punishments and begin to hope for temporal things, he rightly adds: “They were warmed by the fleece of my sheep”—they were freed from the cold of earthly hope by considering those who, through renunciation, laid aside carnal things, after the example of a flock of shorn sheep (Cant. IV, 2).

“If I raised my hand against an orphan”: one who, because he could not find a father, might follow a creature or a human being. “Trusting that I had much help”: wishing to dominate them.

“May my shoulder depart from my neck”: this happens to those who separate themselves from the Church while wishing to dominate the peoples, so that they suffer a cutting-off corresponding to their cutting-off. By the shoulder or arm, actions are signified.

“For fear restrained me”: lest he raise his hand against the orphan. “And I could not bear its weight”: if I should wish to oppress the orphan.

“I made gold my strength.” Surely I did not presume upon the teaching or wisdom of God? “And if I trusted in a precious stone”: as though I trusted in my own works. “And if I rejoiced because my wealth was great”: as though it were my own, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (II Cor. X, 17).

“And if I placed my soul in innumerable things”: one must supply, “for all things, let my arm depart from my shoulder.” [Note: The Septuagint has “my hand”; the Vulgate supports this reading.] “Because I was loved by many.” [Note: Ambrosianus and Erasmus read, “because it was loved.”]

“And my heart was secretly deceived.” The order is: “If I placed my soul in innumerable things, and my heart was secretly deceived”—if I consented to such a thought as to presume upon myself.

“And if I kissed my hand, putting it to my mouth”: I rejoiced as though because of my own works.

“And if I rejoiced over the ruin of my enemy”: of the Church, as are those who persecute the Church.

“May my ear hear my curse”: may it come to my understanding. “May I be proclaimed a reproach in my people”: in the people of the saints, so that I may be separated as one mocked.

“And if my maidservants often said”: flatterers. “Who will give us that we may be satisfied with his flesh?”—when I was sufficiently good, so that they might imitate in me carnal prosperity. I did not, however, behave in this way; for, lest they say such things, I did not present myself as good in such matters.

“Outside, the guest did not remain wet”: I received the stranger in this world.

“And if, while sinning willingly, I concealed my sin.” For we sin voluntarily after we have received knowledge of the truth (Heb. X, 26).

“Or if I let the weak depart from my door with an empty bosom”: so that he left the door because his bosom was empty.

“Who will grant me an auditor? Who will make it possible for me to be heard?”

“If I did not fear the hand of the Lord”: the hand with which he wrote, “If you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you” (Matt. VI, 15).

“If I have any written indictment”—the order is, “If I have any written indictment.” “And if I did not tear it apart upon my shoulders, and, crowned, read it while lifting it upon my shoulders”: and, crowned, read it publicly—that is, against my own face. “I will set you before your face” (Ps. XLIX, 21). For I shall be confounded as the crown of the people, because I did not fulfill the commandment of the Lord, although I had already said that I had fulfilled it, first denying that I possessed the written indictment that was later brought against me.

“If the earth ever groaned over me”: the wage-earners of the Church, because I am evil. “Or if its furrows wept together”: the furrows that receive the seeds and from which fruits are given; because I am both evil and sowed evil seeds, therefore they wept together.

“Or if I alone ate its strength without payment”: the mercy by which the person being catechized participates with the one catechizing (Gal. VI, 6); that is, I alone, without repaying the one who gave it.

“Or if, deceiving the soul of the Lord of the earth, I grieved him”: not showing myself worthy of his Passion, since he poured out his soul for me. “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit who is in you” (Eph. IV, 30).

“Let nettles grow for me instead of wheat”: instead of spiritual teachers, teachers of itching ears, through the frictions of people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth (I Tim. VI, 5). “And let a thorn grow instead of barley”: instead of those who obey carnally, sinners and those who resist.

For Job was righteous in his own sight—in his own conscience.

### [On Job, XXXII]

“The words of Elihu the Buzite.” “God rejected him”—some manuscripts read, “God added to him”—“and not a man”: this is the reason, he says, why they kept silent. “And I will not answer him with your speeches.” For I shall say such things that he will be unable to answer me, just as he cannot answer you.

“Because I waited, and they did not speak”: as though he were turning toward Job, he says this. “My belly is like a wineskin full of new wine.” Scripture commends him because he is about to speak prophetically. “And like a ruptured bellows of a bronze-worker”: in order to dissolve hardness, I speak with force; hence he is also said to be angry. For there would have been no need for me to speak if you had answered him. Otherwise the moths will eat me as well”—either as they eat you, or as they eat all who show partiality to persons.

### [On Job, XXXIII]

“My heart is pure in my words”: it is not double. “The divine spirit that made me”: one must supply *is*, so that the sentence reads, “The divine spirit is the one who made me.”

“How then do you say, ‘I am righteous, and he did not hear me?’” as though Job had spoken to an adversary.

“For God speaks once”: as though the Lord had made the calling of all the righteous once for all, while divine providence acts temporally around each individual. “In a dream or in a night vision”: either in ignorance or in tribulation. “Or as a terrible fear falls upon people when they sleep in their chambers”: while they are secure.

“And he will rescue his body from ruin”: figuratively, as bones. “And he spared his soul from death”: when he has converted him, he will spare him.

“For war is coming, and again he will rebuke him in sickness on his bed”: after conversion he now tests him, lest he presume upon himself. “And the multitude of his bones wasted away”: his confidence in himself. “And he will not be able to eat any food”: consolation from temporal things.

“And he will renew his body like plaster on a wall”: a change of life; here also it is figurative, on account of the building—that is, into fellowship. “And he will soften his flesh like that of a child”: so that he will not be hardened by pride. According to Elihu’s view, Job in his humility is tested through renewal.

“And he entered with a cheerful face, with confession”: prepared for temptations. “Save my soul, so that I may not come into corruption”: here the temptation of death is meant. “Three times with a man”: of conversion, testing, and death.

“But he rescued my soul from death”: for this death still remains, “so that my soul may praise him in the light.” Therefore the prayers will now cease, because there will be no need. 

### [On Job, XXXIV]

“But Elihu answered and said.” How is “and he added” to be understood? “And you who possess knowledge, perceive with your ears”: with spiritual ears. “For the ear tests words”: this refers to the carnal ear.

“What is good, since Job said, ‘I am righteous’?” What good did he say by saying this? “And he has lied in my judgment.” Hence, “I was expecting good things” (Job XXX, 26): therefore, beyond hope—which is to say, he lied.

“Who is a man like Job?” These are still Job’s words. For he said, “The one who walks with God will not be visited.” Elihu thinks that Job was deceived because he did all those things while hoping for this; or at least because he does not think that the one who walks with the Lord is visited for good.

“Far be impiety from the Lord”: either that he should not visit for good the one who walks with him, or that, even if he visits him in temptation, he should act impiously and unjustly.

“He is impious who says to a king, ‘You act unjustly.’ But you ought not to say this, since you are not impious.” It is properly, “he who says it,” not “he who has said it,” lest he should already be impious on this account as well—just as one says, “He has done it,” of someone who does this.

“Most impiously, to princes”: as though he were saying to the angels, “Unless Michael is your prince, you act most impiously.” Or if “most impiously” is said of princes, how much more of a king?

“For they made bad use of their exclusion when the weak were excluded.” They made bad use of their exclusion when, because of weakness, they were excluded from that vision by which all things are seen to be divinely ordered and administered in the most orderly fashion. They acted badly in this respect because they preferred to follow their own spirit and to think that God did not care about these things. Hence it will vainly happen to them that, in their necessities, they cry out to and entreat a human being, when they ought to have entreated God.

“And there will be no place, and there is no shadow of death, where those who commit iniquity may hide.” The shadow of death does not exist for the purpose of hiding, as in, “The elders do not have wisdom” (Job XXXII, 9), because old age is not the cause of wisdom; and, “Do not greet a heretic” (Tit. III, 10), lest it be because he is a heretic.

“And he will overturn the night, and they will be humbled”: so that what was beneath them will be above them; that is, what had been subject to them will press upon them. “And he extinguished the wicked”: they seemed to themselves to shine. “And they did not know his acts of righteousness.” He says what good God brought forth from their iniquity: that the cry of the poor might be carried to him.

“He will himself give peace, and who will be able to condemn?” Not the kind of peace that human beings seek, which is disturbed by those tribulations. “If God justifies, who is the one who condemns?” (Rom. VIII, 33–34).

“And against a human being at once”: against Gentiles and Jews alike.

“Who makes a hypocritical man reign because of the perversity of the people”: to whom it is said, “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself?” (Rom. II, 21).

“Without me I shall see; you show me”: while reproving you, do I perhaps fail to see that I myself ought to be reproved? This should be pronounced interrogatively.

“If I have committed iniquity, I will not add to it”: corrected by you. “Does he demand it from you because you rejected it?” Because you reproved it.

“And the wise man will hear my word”: that God cares for everything. “But Job did not speak in wisdom”: thinking that something had happened to him unjustly by divine action.

## [Book of Job, Chapter XXXV]

“Why did you think this in judgment? Why did you judge this? Who are you, who said, ‘I am righteous,’ before the Lord’s presence? Before the Lord’s presence you said, ‘I am righteous.’ Both statements are blameworthy in a human being: the one, if it is said arrogantly, or if it is false that he is righteous, even according to human righteousness; the other, because a human being can never truly say that he is righteous before God’s presence, in comparison with whom everyone is unrighteous.

“Or do you say, ‘What benefit is it to you, or what can I do, if I have sinned?’ For Job seems to have said this to God, as though either his sin benefits God, so that through this suffering he is compelled toward impiety, when he says, ‘Do not teach me to be impious,’ or, ‘Is it good for you if I act wickedly?’ (Job 10:2–3); or as though he harmed God by sinning, and therefore God pursues him as though he were pressing down an enemy, lest he suffer any harm from him. For he had also said this: ‘If I have sinned, what can I do to you?’ (ibid. 7:20).

“Elihu therefore answered both points in the words that follow: ‘I will give you an answer, and to my three friends. Look toward heaven and see; look at the clouds, how high they are above you. If you have sinned, what do you do?’ He confirms what Job had said: ‘If I have sinned, what can I do to you?’ Or, if you have committed many injustices, what can you do? ‘You have committed many injustices’ is more than what he said above, ‘You have sinned.’ Yet what can you do to God, when you cannot even harm the clouds? And if you are righteous, what will you give him? Conversely, just as your righteousness benefits him nothing, so your injustice harms him nothing. Or what could he receive from your hand, even if you wished to give it, on account of sacrifices, which fools think God receives as though he needed them?

“Your impiety concerns a man like yourself, and your righteousness a son of man: the former harms, or the latter benefits.” Yet by these verses he confirms rather than refutes Job’s statement: “If I have sinned, what can I do to you?”

It is therefore necessary that he next show why, in this life, human beings are afflicted by the injuries of the wicked, among whom the devil also is numbered with his angels, the prince of all injuries and iniquities. Since sinners cannot harm God, why does he deliver them into the power of evil things, to be afflicted by them? He explains this afterward, saying:

“Because of the multitude they will cry out; they will shout because of the arm of the mighty. And he did not say, ‘Where is God, who made me?’” They suffer these things so that they may seek God, not so that they may cry out vainly. But when he says “who made me,” this serves as a sign that he will not abandon the one who seeks him, since he himself made him.

“Who appoints the night watches”: the periods of this age, ordered under definite powers, because in this night of error he will not leave human beings without protection—he who made them.

“Who separates me from the quadrupeds of the earth and makes me wiser than the birds of heaven.” Thus the Lord must be sought amid the afflictions of this life, so that we do not desire earthly goods from him; for we are already better than the beasts before we receive those goods.

“There they will cry out, and you will not hear.” “There,” he says, amid the multitude and the affliction of those crying out, and “because of the arm of the mighty”; or certainly “there” means “for this reason,” as in: “There have fallen those who work iniquity” (Psalm 35:13). And when he says “you will not hear,” he is speaking about that matter. “Because of the injuries of the wicked”: “they will cry out” must be supplied. For the Lord does not wish to see vain things. He does not wish to help those who ask for vain things, nor those who cry out in affliction for no other reason than that they are not prosperous in the iniquity of this age. They were separated from the quadrupeds of the earth for this reason, and made wiser than the birds of heaven.

“For the Almighty himself sees those who practice righteousness, and he will save me.” Just as he himself sees those who practice righteousness, since he perceives the innermost depths of the heart, so he saves them with that salvation which he himself sees in secret: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9). Therefore, even if the illusory salvation of human beings is disturbed, the Father who sees in secret nevertheless gives help in tribulation (Matthew 6:4).

“Judge him, if you can praise him as he is.” Job seemed to be saying this when he said: “Would that there were an arbiter for us!” (Job 9:33).

“And now, because he does not visit his anger, nor has he known sins with severity.” “He has known” means “for punishment.” Hence: “For I acknowledge my iniquity,” and in the same passage: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Psalm 50:5, 11). He has therefore known sins; for this reason human beings suffer tribulations in this age. But he has not known them “with severity,” because, correcting them in measured portions, he grants a place for repentance.

“And Job opened his mouth vainly; in his ignorance he multiplies words.”

## [Book of Job, Chapter XXXVI]

“Bear with me a little, that I may teach you; for there are still words within me, receiving my knowledge from afar.” For “as long as we are in this body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6).

“By my works, which are righteous, I will speak.” Otherwise God might say to him what he says to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take up my covenant in your mouth? But you have hated instruction” (Psalm 49:16–17). Here, therefore, one must speak by works; for knowledge is received from afar, partially and in a riddle. “But when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be abolished” (1 Corinthians 13:12); and it will no longer be “from afar,” because “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).
