“In truth, you will not understand words that are not unjust unjustly.” He says that the very things Job was suffering are God’s words, spoken in truth and not unjustly; but he thinks that Job understands them unjustly, since he supposes that Job complains of suffering undeservedly, although it was said even concerning the tribulation of the righteous: “It is time for judgment to begin from the household of the Lord” (1 Peter 4:17).

“And know that the Lord will not reject the innocent,” although “he reproves the one whom he loves and scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

“Strong in the strength of his heart, he does not make the impious alive,” although he may seem to spare him for a time. And rightly does he say, “strong in the strength of his heart,” because he will not make him alive when he seeks a late opportunity for repentance with tears and does not find it, nor bend toward mercy the one who judges forcefully, whom he now contemptuously disregards when he admonishes mercifully. [Note: At Col. 0865 the printed editions read *sero*; the manuscripts read *serae*. Below, at chapter 37, verse 4, the late repentance of unbelievers on the day of judgment is called *sera*.]

“And he will give judgment to the poor”: so that they may judge those from whom they suffer injustice. And he says “of the poor” rightly, so that by contrast you may understand the impious rich person, that is, the proud one.

“He will not remove his eyes from the righteous.” Even when he tests him as in a furnace through the trial of tribulation (Sirach 27:6), he will not remove from him the understanding by which God is known and worshiped. From this he sufficiently shows that the punishment of the impious is blindness itself, even when they seem to be spared.

“And with kings upon the throne”—“he made them sit” must be supplied—that is, the righteous. He calls those “kings” who rule their own flesh. Hence the saying: “What king, going to engage another king in battle…” (Luke 14:31), and so forth. “And he made them sit forever, and they will be exalted.” Here too what he said above must be supplied: “with kings upon the throne.” He said “they will be exalted” because they were humbled.

“And those who are fettered with chains.” The Apostle says that it is good for him to be released from this bond and to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), that is, from the restraints of this life, in which “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15).

“They will be caught in the cords of poverty.” They will be convicted by the long habits of carnal pleasures, which arise from the lack of those things by which mortal life is sustained and conducted.

“And their works are announced to them.” Not good works, certainly, but either those very works of desire about which it is said, “I know that good does not dwell in my flesh” (Romans 7:18)—which, even if they do not rule in our mortal body so that we obey them, nevertheless are not absent—or those works by which a human being deserved to come to these things through the transmission of sin.

“And their offenses, when they have grown strong.” These are the works he mentioned above. For they cannot easily be announced, that is, revealed, to the weak; rather, they are announced to those who have already progressed so far that they have passed beyond all that iniquity which is commonly known through the most open acts of disgrace and crime.

“But he will hear the righteous,” namely, the one who lives by faith (Habakkuk 2:4), so that he attributes to God’s grace, not to his own merits, not only the fact that he has been justified according to the measure of this life, but also what remains: that he may be freed from the whole evil of sins. Truth [Note: At Col. 0865, Er. and Lov. read *quem*; M.] announces this to the faithful when they have grown strong, when they are caught in the cords of poverty; for they are still fettered with chains, not yet exalted so as to sit upon the throne with kings forever.

“And he said that they will turn away from iniquity.” “He said”—God must be supplied. “If they hear and serve, they will complete their days in good things and their years in glory.” Then there will be no sin at all in human beings, because there will be no struggle with death, that is, no need arising from mortality, which came from sin, when it will already be said: “Where, O death, is your contention?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

“But he will not save the impious, because they did not wish to know the Lord.” This seems to apply especially to the Gentiles.

“And when they were admonished, they were disobedient.” This applies to the Jews and to all who resemble them through disobedience, even within the Church.

“And hypocrites will store up wrath in their hearts”—the wrath by which they crucified the Lord.

“They will not cry out, because he has bound them”—with the honor of his name above all the nations.

“Therefore let their soul die in youth”: in the pride by which they raised themselves up, as though on account of the merits of their works.

“And let their life be wounded by angels.” This is more suitably understood as referring to the messengers of truth, for some are “the fragrance of life leading to life,” and for others “the fragrance of death leading to death” (2 Corinthians 2:16).

“Because they afflicted the weak and powerless”: that “weak thing of God” which “is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

“But he will establish the judgment of the meek”: the Lord himself, delaying even the punishment of those who imitate his meekness, although that punishment will certainly come.

“And because the abyss deceived you from the mouth of the enemy.” It deceived you, as it appeared to his persecutors, when the depth of this age deceived Christ through the mouth of the false witness. He directs the speech to the Lord himself.

“They were poured out beneath it”—“they deceived you” must be supplied. For they are said to have been poured out beneath the abyss because they were weighed down by earthly desires.

“And your table descended, full of fatness”: the sacrament of his body and blood, the bread that descended from heaven (John 6:50).

“Judgment will not fail the righteous.” Although the poor eat and are satisfied, prepared, in the fullness of charity, to imitate the Lord’s sufferings, he nevertheless does not for that reason fail to execute judgment upon them promptly.

“And wrath will be upon the impious, because of the impiety of the gifts they received through iniquities.” He calls all gifts “gifts”—whatever temporal advantages are involved, for the sake of which iniquities are committed.

“Let not the inclination of your mind turn you away from the prayers of the weak,” who, when in distress, cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24). This is addressed to the Lord, not with the authority of one giving an admonition or the boldness of one issuing a command, but as prophetic speech proclaiming future events in the imperative mood, as in: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one” (Psalm 44:4).

“And all who have strength”: those presuming upon their works and wishing to establish their own righteousness (ibid. 10:3).

“Do not draw them out through the night.” It is clear that you separate them from your people, whether those proud ones who have been broken off from the olive tree, or the branches cut from the vine, from which heresies and schisms have arisen.

“So that the peoples may ascend on their behalf”: so that the weak things of this world may be grafted in, while the strong are confounded (1 Corinthians 1:27). “For whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

“But take care that you do nothing improper,” lest the name of the Lord God and his teaching be blasphemed when those whose judgment is just say: “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Romans 3:8).

“For you have chosen this above poverty.” You have chosen not only the poverty of one who confesses, but also, above this, the beauty of life and conduct, so that saving doctrine may be adorned in every respect.

“Behold, God will console,” or “will be strengthened,” “in his own strength.” For although he was crucified in weakness, “he lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

“For who is like that powerful one? Or who is there who can examine his works?”—as though judging him, when he himself is the judge of the living and the dead.

“Or who is there who says, ‘He acted unjustly’?” [Note: The printed editions read, “who says to him unjustly”; shortly afterward they read, “whom they praised.” We have substituted the reading of the manuscripts, which agrees with the Septuagint and the Vulgate.]

“Remember that his works are great, which men have praised”: the Evangelists and all preachers of the word whose lives correspond to their ministry.

“Every human being looks toward him,” mindful of human weakness.

“All who are pierced with compunction through repentance for sins are human beings.”

“Behold, God is great, and we shall not know him.” He is great because, “as sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). “We shall not know” is spoken from the person of those for whom a partial blindness has occurred “until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered” (ibid. 11:25).

“The number of his years is without limit”: this is said on account of eternity.

“But the drops of rain are countable for him.” For the fact that the Gospel has filled human preachers [Note: The Floriacensis codex reads, “that through human beings.”] is countable until the consummation of the age, until “knowledge which is partial” is abolished and “what is perfect” comes, face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12).

“Rain will be poured out along his paths.” For the ways of the wicked will not contain him.

“Clouds will flow, and they will become dark over very many people.” For although the Gospel has been veiled, it has been veiled among those who are perishing.

“He appointed a time for the beasts, and they know the order of their resting place.” For “the ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isaiah 1:3).

“Amid all these things his mind is not astonished.” “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 110:10).

“Nor is your heart changed from the body,” so that, lifted up from the earth, it may be directed upward toward the Lord.

“If he thinks of spreading out a cloud,” so that those who see may become blind (John 9:39).

“Just as he spread it out through the tabernacle.” For dwelling in mortal flesh as in a tabernacle, through it he was not recognized by his persecutors, while he yielded to them and stretched and spread it out upon the cross.

“Behold, he pours his light over everything,” which he had concealed; when a partial blindness came upon Israel, he pours it out over all the nations.

“And he covered the roots of the sea.” He reproved the desire of the world. For the light was not covered in order to conceal it, but in order to reveal it.

“For in these things he judged the peoples,” by showing them their sins through the light of truth.

“He will give food to many”: to those who recognize their sins when they are reproved, and who hunger and thirst for righteousness.

“In hands he covered the light.” [Note: The printed editions read *immanibus* (“with monstrous or savage ones”), but the manuscripts read *in manibus* (“in hands”). Augustine was troubled by this because the ancients consistently wrote the compound word *inmanis* with *n*, and so in old books one often finds *inmensus*, *inbutus*, *inlatus*, *inpunis*, and so forth. In the Greek Septuagint, moreover, the expression is ἐπὶ χειρῶν (*epi cheirōn*, “upon hands”).]

If the reference is to those who are *immanes* (“savage” or “monstrous”), he covered the light from people who do not forgive sins while wishing God to forgive them. But if the reference is to *manus* (“hands”), he covered it from those who exalt themselves on account of their hands—that is, their works—justifying themselves.

For he said that he covered the light so that it would not be seen by them, because “their foolish heart was darkened” (Romans 1:21).

“And he commanded concerning it in the opposite direction”: those who practice the truth, either by forgiving so that they may be forgiven, or by confessing their evil deeds so that they may be subjected to God’s grace, are to come to the light, so that their works may be revealed, because “they have been done in God” (John 3:21), not in themselves.

For he is opposite both to the savage person in mercy and to the proud person in humility.

“So that he might announce it concerning his friend”: concerning that light, that is, concerning what he covered in order to hide it from the savage and ungrateful person, so that he might announce it—that is, disclose it—not now to a servant under the Law but to one reconciled through grace; or “to his friend,” that is, to his imitator, because “the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20:28).

“Possession against those who strive to ascend”: so that those who draw themselves away from earthly things may possess the light itself. For it is announced to those who are still striving to ascend; once they have ascended, there will be no need of an announcer, since they will see face to face.

But when he says “those who strive to ascend,” he does not mean those who oppose him, but those who go out to meet him, as the Apostle says: “To meet Christ” (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

## [Book of Job, Chapter XXXVII]

“But my heart was also astonished at this”: with admiration.

“And it was torn from its place”: from earthly things in which it took delight, so that it might be directed upward toward the Lord.

“Hear the sound of his terror and of his voice.” From this it appears that he is speaking these things in the spirit. For he begins to say why his heart was torn from its place: namely, through the authority of the Gospel resounding terrifyingly throughout the whole world: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2).

“And they go forth at the noise of his mouth”: certainly toward those who are outside, in the pleasures of visible things.

“Under the whole heaven he circles, and his light is at the ends of the earth”: while the Church is spread through all nations.

“After him the voice will roar.” After his first coming, the final trumpet of his second coming will thunder in glory (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:15).

“With the sound of his majesty.” He has put “majesty” in place of “pride,” because his first coming was in humility.

“And he will not be able to be investigated when his voice has been heard.” Let the Lord therefore be sought now, while he can be found (Isaiah 55:6)—that is, while he can be grasped for salvation through sincere faith. For then he will not be able to be sought, when he comes to judge and his voice is heard saying: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41). For then the repentance of unbelievers will be late and fruitless.

“The strong one will thunder wondrously with his voice.” For the voice of his first coming came not from his strength but from our weakness, through his participation in mortality. Of him it was said: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

“For he did great things that we did not know.” These things belong to his first coming; and therefore he will come afterward as judge, to demand what he gave. “Things that we did not know” is spoken from the person of those who were unaware of the Lord’s divinity, looking upon the weakness of his flesh.

“Commanding the cloud, ‘Be upon the earth’”: commanding his flesh to be received through the sacrament in his memory (Luke 22:19–20), for the imitation of humility and the instruction of charity.

“And the storm of rain, and the storm of showers, of his power.” There is indeed a cloud over the earth; but when it is expressed so as to water hearts through the rain and showers of the word, this occurs not by our power but by his.

“In the hand of every person he marks.” Through his works he signifies to each person how guilty he is, so that every person may know his own weakness and cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24).

“But the beasts entered under the protection and rested in their shelter.” Sinners entered under the indulgence of grace and rested in their conscience, their sins having been forgiven.

“From the storehouses the storm came upon them”: temptation from the hidden order of things.

“And from the storehouses, cold”: judgment from secret places against those who do not persevere, so that their charity may grow cold “because of the abundance of iniquity” (Matthew 24:12–13). For this rightly happens to them when they place their hope not in God but in human beings.

“And from the spirit of God ice will be given.” Not only will those who place their hope in human beings grow cold through the abundance of the wicked, but some also become hard as ice through the good works in which the spirit of God is present—those for whom Paul is “the fragrance of death leading to death” (2 Corinthians 2:16).

“And who is capable of understanding these things, so as to grasp that ice is rightly and justly given by the spirit of God?” For just as those who praise human beings carnally grow cold through human iniquity by falling into despair, so those who carnally desire to be praised by human beings become hard through human righteousness by growing envious.

“But he governs the water as he pleases,” so that it may rain upon one city and not rain upon another (Amos 4:7). This concerns spiritual rain, according to the merits of souls that are subject or not subject to him.

“And the cloud watered the grain.” Let us therefore be grain, if we desire to be watered. [Note: In the printed editions the words “the cloud watered the grain. Let us therefore be grain” were missing; they have been restored with the help of the manuscripts.]

“He scattered his light-cloud.” This is the Gospel of his incarnation.

“And it itself is turned around the circuit, and it itself is handled throughout the world.”

“In the governing instruments, to perform everything that he has commanded them.” The governing instruments in which that cloud is turned around its circuit are the preachers of the word, through whom the Churches are governed so as to perform all God’s commands.

“These things have been established by him over the earth”: by our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Whether in the tribe or in his own land.” Whether in the tribe of Judah, from which he was born according to the flesh, suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven—for the Apostles and many brothers had been born from that people and were found near and saved, whether called by him before his Passion or through the Apostles after his Ascension, in Jerusalem itself and in the Churches of Judea that were in Christ, as the Apostle Paul recalls, on account of the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers—or whether in his own land.

“Or whether he wished to be found in mercy”: namely, whether he wished that cloud to be found in mercy by believing Gentiles. For what follows is: “But the Gentiles glorify God for his mercy” (Romans 15:9).

“Perceive these things with your ears, Job.” He seems to renew his attention, intending to speak about the calling of the Gentiles.

“Stand, and stir the power of the Lord.” Do not be moved in your mind by attributing anything to yourself.

“We know that God established his works,” clearly rejecting those who glory in their works.

“When he made light from darkness”: when he justified the impious. “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

“He knows the distinction of the clouds”: the distinction between Evangelists who believed before his Passion and those who believed after his Passion.

“And the great falls of the wicked.” He does not mean those who escaped after crucifying him, so that afterward they might repent and be baptized in him, but the fall of those who could not be corrected and who continued afterward to persecute the Church. Their falls are not small but great.

“But your garment is strong.” [Note: The Septuagint has *thermē* (“warm”); the Vulgate likewise has “warm.”]

This means proud dignity, as though spoken against one who dares to be exalted on account of his works.

“When the earth rests from the south, will you establish the heavens with him, which have been spread out equally for seeing?”

We appropriately understand “the earth from the south” as referring to those from the Jews who believed in Christ. For just as the sun is farther from the northern earth and nearer to the southern, so those whom the Apostle says were found near the light of the Evangelists (Ephesians 2:17) may not improperly be understood as “the earth from the south.”

As we customarily understand the heavens as the Evangelists, as in: “The heavens declare the glory of God”—for it was said concerning them, “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:2, 5)—so we rightly understand the earths as the peoples to whom the Gospel was preached.

And because the peoples who believed from Judea, after they rested when they departed from this earth [Note: In some manuscripts, “from this life”]—for they are no longer here—the authority of the Evangelists was nevertheless established in the Churches that are from the Gentiles, and the mercy of God was established, no longer with the assistance of the authority of the Churches of Judea that are in Christ, the meaning is therefore to be expressed as a question:

“Will you, when the earth from the south is at rest”—that is, when no Christian people from the Jews remains in this life—“establish with him the Evangelists and the books of the divine Scriptures, which through God’s mercy have been spread equally for seeing, not among the Jews alone but also among the Gentiles?”

For he commends God’s grace and mercy, lest anyone glory in merits, which was the pride of the Jews.

“Why then teach me what we should say to him, and let us cease from saying many things?” For, once convicted, they have nothing to say to him, since they possess no merit of their own but need his mercy.

“Are you perhaps a book or a scribe standing beside me, so that, standing, I may make a human being silent?” Why, then, do you not speak, if you have something to say? You do not receive my words as though I were dictating to you, so that you should say nothing; rather, we are conversing.

“Visible light is not for everyone, the light that shines in the clouds.” He returns to what he was saying about the hope of the forgiveness of sins and the illumination of grace through God’s mercy: for light shines in the clouds. Yet it is not proper to the clouds themselves; they are illuminated. One thing is that which shines by its own light, another that which shines because it has been illuminated.

“But it is not visible to everyone.” For many think that souls shine with their own light when they are wise. Hence come those who, “claiming to be wise, became fools” (Romans 1:22).

“And the spirit passes through, and will cleanse them.” Here he called “spirit” the one of whom it was said: “At the rebuke of the spirit of your wrath” (Psalm 17:16), and: “From your spirit, where shall I flee?” (Psalm 138:7). For through the corrections of temptations their merit is shown to human beings, because they themselves are darkness through their sins and lack the glory of God (Romans 3:22), so that they may wish to be illuminated by his light, giving honor to him, not to themselves. Thus, when pride has been put aside, they are cleansed from the great offense. For the Spirit of sanctification does not pass away but remains.

“From the north, a cloud of golden color.” From the most criminal impiety, far removed from God, the cleansed and converted nevertheless come, illuminated by wisdom. From where, if not through grace, by which merits are not considered but sins are forgiven? Hence the one who wished to be forgiven says: “I will teach transgressors your ways, and the impious will turn to you” (Psalm 50:15), like a cloud from the east or north, now golden in color, its darkness illuminated.

“In these things there is great glory and honor of the Almighty.” “To the one who is forgiven much, he loves much.”

“For he can also justify the impious, since he is almighty.”

“And we do not find another like him in strength.” For he alone did not commit sin, and “no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). For God alone is truthful, while “every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:11). Thus God, having become human, prevailed when he was judged.

“He who judges justly—do you not think that he hears him?” Therefore let no human being, despairing of pardon, add sins to sins, as though already condemned, because he is certain of God’s justice, under which he cannot remain unpunished. For God judges so justly that he also hears those who implore pardon—and all the more, the more justly he judges. For it is not the judgment of justice to mix repentant suppliants with those who refuse humility and the satisfaction of repentance.

“Therefore human beings will fear him,” if they remember that they are human beings, confessing their sins, because they are still human beings—those to whom it is said, “Are you not human beings?”

“And the wise in heart will also fear him,” lest, by attributing to themselves what they have received and saying that they are wise, they become fools. For what is given to the humble can be taken away from the proud.

Therefore the wise, although wise through illumination of the heart and not through boasting of the tongue, and although kings spiritually judging the earth, while themselves judged by no one (1 Corinthians 2:15), should nevertheless serve the Lord in fear and rejoice with trembling, lest they perish from the right way (Psalm 2:11–12).

For it is God who works in them both to will and to work, according to his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

### [There, chapter XXXVIII]

And after Elihu had ceased speaking, the Lord spoke to Job from the whirlwind of a cloud. Even if this voice came about in the same manner as when it came to Moses, or as when the Lord showed himself to the three disciples on the mountain (Matt. 17:1–5), nevertheless I think that what is signified by the wording “from the whirlwind of a cloud,” rather than simply “from a cloud,” is that Job was not questioned—that is, tested—through sound flesh, but through the tribulation and disturbance of the flesh.

“Who is this that hides counsel from me, enclosing words [Note: [Col. 0871] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The printed editions have: ‘who hides my counsel, despising words,’ etc.] in his heart and thinks that I give it?” Therefore no one can say that he suffers something harsh undeservedly; for if not in deeds, then at least in words there is sin; and if not in words, then at least in reckless presumption inwardly, in the heart, or in the words of one’s thoughts. And since these things are not hidden from God, no one who has been chastised should say that he receives discipline undeservedly, as though there were no further progress for him to make through it.

For it must be understood that at the beginning of this book Job was commended to the devil by God’s testimony, and at the end to his three friends, though God nevertheless knew how much was still lacking in him for perfection—a perfection to which paternal chastisements bring even men praiseworthy in this life and already pleasing to God—chastisements which the Apostle did not wish removed from him when he said: “My grace is sufficient for you; for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

“Gird your loins like a man.” This signifies that God’s servants suffer hard and bitter things in this world so that they may gather and bind all their affections away from the flow of earthly pleasures.

“I will question you, and you shall answer me. Where were you when I founded the earth?” Here he begins to commend the eminence of our Lord Jesus Christ, because in him is the salvation of all those struck by the serpent’s poisonous persuasion, lest anyone think that salvation exists in himself.

He is God—not as in the saying, “You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6), but one for whom being equal to the Father was not robbery (Phil. 2:6). And he is the Son of Man—not like the sons of men “in whom there is no salvation” (Ps. 145:3), but exalted above his companions (Ps. 44:8). For he is not merely righteous, like Job, Paul, and the Church, but also the one who justifies, like the Only-Begotten from the Father, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

Therefore, to indicate the distinction of his divine humanity, in whom the prince of this world found nothing (John 14:30)—because in his passion he was then paying the price for what he had not seized (Ps. 68:5)—and the justification of the saints through the forgiveness of sins, by which saints gathered into one become his body, the Church, of which Job is also a part according to the historical sense because he was justified, and a figure of the whole according to prophecy, he begins to say what he is going to say:

“Where were you when I founded the earth?” Is this because he did not yet exist, or because the earth was not founded through him as through the only Son? And does “the earth” mean this earth, or the Church itself? For she received the cornerstone (Eph. 2:20), about which he will soon speak.

“Tell me, if you know understanding.” For the things temporally accomplished by the Lord for our sake belong to understanding.

“Who set its measurements, if you know?” This refers to the distribution of spiritual gifts. “To each of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men’” (Eph. 4:7–8). “For if the whole body were an eye, where would be the hearing?” (1 Cor. 12:17). For according to the measure of each part he produces the growth of the body for its building up in love (Eph. 4:16) [Note: [Col. 0872] The manuscripts have “into love.”].

Or who is the one who stretched the measuring line over it, so that he might make it his inheritance, distinguishing it from those to whom he says, “I never knew you” (Matt. 7:23)? “For the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19).

Or upon what were its circles fixed? They bind it together so that it may not be dissolved. The divine Books are fixed upon the Lord, because whoever wishes to interpret them without him must necessarily drift and go astray.

And who is the one who placed the cornerstone upon it, “which the builders rejected” (Ps. 117:22)?

“When the stars were made together”: together baptized were so many thousands, shining among sinners like lights in darkness, through the word of life.

“All my angels praised me with a loud voice”: the Evangelists.

“I shut up the sea with doors”: peoples embittered by love of earthly things. But why “with doors”? Perhaps so that it would have not only a limit for exercising the righteous through persecutions, but also so that the righteous might be permitted to go out from it.

“When it raged from the womb of its mother, wishing to come forth”: when it grew angry in the assembly of the Babylonian city, fornicating through love of this age, wishing to extend its persecutions in order to destroy from the earth those of whom it was said, “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you take them away from evil” (John 17:15).

“I surrounded it with a cloud as a covering.” For not only the good, but also many wicked people and lovers of this age, have been subjected to the sacrament of Christ’s body; by its authority they are restrained from persecuting the saints.

“And I wrapped it in mist”: ignorance, by which they expect earthly happiness from it and fear earthly unhappiness; and therefore they fear those whom, if this were not so, they would persecute. For it was not only said, “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek him shall praise the Lord,” but also: “All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped” (Ps. 21:27, 30).

“And I set boundaries for it, imposing bars and doors”: boundaries by which its savagery might be restrained—not so that it would afflict nothing, but so far as it might exercise; bars so that the unjust might not advance; doors so that the righteous might go out from them.

“And I said, ‘Thus far you shall come, and you shall not cross over.’” Just as the devil himself received a limit to how far he might afflict Job, so the sea received a limit to how far it might persecute the Church.

“But in yourself your waves shall be shattered”: through alternating devastation by discord and wars.

“Or did I establish the morning light with you?” That is, did I predestine, with your counsel, the time of the resurrection?

“Or did the morning star know its order?” The words “with you” are to be supplied. He calls the Lord the morning star because of the rising of the resurrection’s morning. For this could not have been said of anyone else: “and until the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Pet. 1:19).

He himself recognized his order, so that he might be “the firstfruits of those who sleep,” “the firstborn from the dead” (1 Cor. 15:20), the head of the Church, with the body also to follow in the future resurrection of the saints.

“To grasp the wings of the earth”: it was said, “If I take my wings straight” (Ps. 138:9)—namely, the spiritual virtues of the faithful, by which they are lifted away from worldly allurements.

“To shake the wicked out of it.” For the reason that he rose first, recognizing his order so long beforehand, was to insinuate faith in the resurrection; and, preached everywhere through the Church’s wings by the ministry of messengers flying about, he will justly seize them for the work of judging the twelve tribes of Israel when he comes to shake the wicked out of the Church, who are now tolerated as mixed in with her before the judgment.

“And you, taking earth’s clay, fashioned an animal?” Whether he is recalling Adam himself, or what now, in the sixth age of the world, just as on the sixth day, has been made from sinners, as from the clay of the earth—man made according to the image of him who created him (Gen. 1:27; 2:7). The Church certainly did not do this; rather, she was made in him through the Word made flesh at the fitting time (John 1:3), through whom all things were made.

“And you placed him famous upon the earth?” This man, made in the sixth age of the world, was placed upon the earth more famously than the one made on the sixth day, before there were other human beings by whom he could be made famous—unless perhaps he is called famous because he has now become so widely known.

“And did you take light away from the wicked?” Like the one who came so that “those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

“Or did you shatter the arm of the proud?” Their power, like that of the one who chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong (1 Cor. 1:27).

“Or did you come to the source of the sea?” Like the one for whose coming everything hidden in the hearts of the wicked was opened through confession, and those who believed in him were justified. For what source of the sea should we understand better than the secret place from which all this most bitter impiety bursts forth—impiety that raises up immense waves of already manifest evil deeds, which people see in the open acts but cannot see at the source itself?

“Or do you walk in the tracks of the abyss?” The abyss here is rightly understood as the worldly life, whatever lies in the depth of evils, concerning which it is written: “When the sinner comes, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). For even the most despairing people, subjected to grace through the forgiveness of sins, were saved and emerged, and received Christ—not into the abyss in which they had been pressed down, but into its place, so that where he walked, trampling them down, Christ might walk while dwelling in them. Christ walks in the tracks of the abyss, which remain in them through the memory of their sins, so that, while recalling where they had been, they may love more greatly the one whom they received, from whom so much was forgiven them (Luke 7:41–47).

“Or are the gates of death opened to you in fear?” The gates of death are opened to all who die, but not in fear, as they were to that one man who died in order to destroy death. Or certainly, they are opened for resurrection.

“Or, when the gatekeepers of hell saw you, did they fear?” As they feared that one in whom the prince of the world found nothing worthy of death [Note: [Col. 0874] The Floriacensis codex has “the prince of death.” A little later Am. Er. and most manuscripts have “whom they unwillingly lost.”], whom they released so quickly, whom they admitted unwillingly.

The gatekeepers of the underworld are to be understood as certain lower powers appointed over death.

“Or did you know the breadth beneath heaven?” As the one who knew it and spread the Church throughout it.

“Tell me, then, how great each thing is.” For who could know this except the one whom he taught?

“Or in what land does the light dwell?” For he teaches this, because “the manifestation of his words gives light and grants understanding to the simple” (Ps. 118:130).

“Or what is the place of darkness?” He also teaches this, the one who says, “Come to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6). For by this he shows that those who withdraw become dark, when they refuse to be simple. “For the beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (Sir. 10:14). Hence those who did not glorify God or give thanks [Note: [Col. 0874] The Floriacensis codex has “the prince of death.” A little later Am. Er. and most manuscripts have “whom they unwillingly lost.”] “became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. 1:21), and they became a place of darkness.

Unless perhaps the place of darkness is the place that receives those who persist in sins, so that they themselves are the darkness whose place it is—something no human truly knows.

Likewise, the land in which the light dwells can be understood as that land of the living [Col. 0875]—that is, the blessedness that will receive those who persist in faith, hope, and love, who were once darkness but are now “light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

“If you lead me to their boundaries”: as far as those who are such extend. For where is there anything that the wisdom of God is not, which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)? Certainly no human being can be compared with it.

“And if you know their paths, do you know that you were then born, and that the number of your years is great?” And if you know the paths of the wicked—those who are either darkness or the place of darkness—because all who have already turned to God once walked in those paths before receiving from God the grace by which he justifies the ungodly, do you nevertheless know that the cause of your being born mortally in this world came into existence at the time when the first parents of all human beings entered those same paths? Through transgression, they summoned death by their hands and words, so that all might die in Adam.

For the number of someone’s years is not to be counted as so small from the time when that person appeared in this life, but from the time when the first mortal birth came into existence. For example, when Abraham was born, all the Hebrews were then born in him. Therefore the number of years is great for each person according to the origin of mortality, which arose in the paths of the wicked.

But who remembers having existed, or, while he existed, could have known that he was in his father’s loins? Indeed, no one even recalls the time when he was born not in his parents but in himself—although no one doubts that at that time he already existed, lived, and perceived.

That Wisdom which forms all things knows all this—not only the things above the heavens, but also these mortal things. And because Christ is “the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24), he knows these things: he who was also born mortally, not by mortal condition—for he was free among the dead—but through compassion for mortals, so that he might make them free from death.

“Or did you come to the treasures of snow?” That is, did you attain to that knowledge, as the one who knew even the hidden and secret causes of the scandals that were about to come at their appointed times? For that is why he calls them “treasures”: they serve to test and exercise the hearts of spiritual people, when he cried out, “Woe to the world because of scandals! For scandals must come; but woe to that person through whom the scandal comes!” (Matt. 18:7).

Those lifted high through pride freeze like snow and fall; and through their abounding iniquity the love of many grows cold. But those who courageously wait for the Lord (Ps. 26:14) and are fervent in spirit (Rom. 12:11) persevere to the end and will be saved (Matt. 24:13).

“Or have you seen the treasures of hail?” They are the wicked as hail, when they not only grow numb, having no fervor of spirit, but also, through hardened obstinacy, crush others by persecuting or rushing upon them.

“Which have been stored up for you for the time of enemies, and for the day of battle and war?” Who could fail to see from this whose person Job bears in prophecy? These things were not stored up for this one man alone, for the time of enemies and the day of battle and war, but certainly for the one people of God.

The time of enemies lasts until iniquity passes away. The more it abounds, the more fiercely one must fight and wage war against the devil, lest the love of those who persevere grow cold.

“And from where does the frost proceed?” Who knows this, except that these things are like the beginnings of birth pangs? For frost is extremely fine hail.

“And is the south wind scattered beneath heaven?” Although the south wind is felt to be burdensome to mortal flesh, I do not remember that in the holy Books it signifies anything evil anywhere, just as the north wind never signifies anything good: the former because it blows from the side where the light shines, the latter because it comes from the side farther removed from the light.

Therefore the south wind is scattered beneath heaven so that some help from God may be understood against all those iniquities, for as long as we are not yet in heaven but beneath heaven.

“Who prepared the channel of mighty rain and the way for the voices of the storm?” See how briefly these three things embrace what the Lord sets forth in the temptations: things to be despised by those who build upon rock, but destructive to those who build upon sand (Matt. 7:24–27).

He mentioned rain, a river, and the voices of the storm, by which we understand winds.

The one who is tempted by rain is the person who, from the very height of the divine Scriptures, perversely obtains an occasion for sin through misunderstanding. For example, hearing, “The one to whom little is forgiven loves little” (Luke 7:42–43), he may say to himself, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Rom. 3:8), and “Let us remain in sin so that grace may abound” (Rom. 5:20). There are many such ways in which people overthrow themselves by wrongly interpreting the divine word, promising themselves impunity when the mercy of God is commended in the divine Books.

He is tempted by the river when he is tempted by people who have understood and received these things in such a way. For by “river” he now means what is gathered from the rain and is called a torrent, when he says, “Who prepared a torrent for mighty rain?”—that it may fill it and run along it [Note: [Col. 0876] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “that it may be filled and that it may flow.”].

Such are the vessels of wrath made ready for destruction (Rom. 9:22), which receive the Scriptures in the manner I have described. Through them that destructive interpretation has a freer course, because fruitful fields do not receive it. And it drives, throws down, and drags along whatever it finds unstable with all the greater force, since it appears to have been accepted on divine authority.

He is tempted by winds when empty human persuasions of the proud blow through him—people who boast vain words from their own authority.

Therefore the one who is prepared for destruction by God’s judgment, by not obeying his words—which is to build upon sand—does not resist such winds; and by falling he becomes a way for the voices of the storm.

By “mighty rain,” I think, he means something difficult to grasp, that is, difficult to understand.

“That it might rain upon the earth where there is no man”: “Who prepared it?” is to be supplied. By “man” he seems to signify the Law, which was given to the Jews. Therefore we understand the Gospel’s rain as falling upon the Gentiles.

“In the desert where there is no human being”: among the Gentiles themselves, where there was no authority belonging to one who knew God.

“To satisfy the desolate and uninhabited place, and to make the green grass sprout.” “More are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1).

In all four of these verses, “Who prepared it?” is to be supplied.

“Who is the father of the rain?” Like the bridegroom who sent his children to water the earth by preaching the kingdom of heaven.

“And who gave birth to the clods of dew?” Those who receive that preaching well. For he says “clods of dew” in the same way that vessels made to receive wine are so called.

“From whose womb does the ice proceed?” Is ice to be understood positively, because of its firmness and restraint from flowing, so that “From whose womb does ice proceed?” has the same meaning as “Who is the father of the rain”? Or is “womb” used for a hidden place, so that ice proceeds from its womb, just as “God gave them over to a debased mind” (Rom. 1:28)?

Or rather, does ice proceed from the womb of the one who, by persuading others to the impiety with which he is inwardly filled, causes them to grow cold and hard after losing the warmth of love? For who knew this person as well as the one who said to those who were hard and resisted the Gospel, “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44)?

“Or who gave birth to the frost in heaven?” It descends like a river of water. What we understood concerning ice at the end should, I think, also be understood concerning frost. Yet the words “in heaven” have not been added without reason, so that those who preside may be understood from them—imitating, to be sure, the good messengers of truth who transform themselves “as ministers of righteousness” (2 Cor. 11:15).

This is the significance of what is added: “which descends like a river of water.”

“Or who melted the face of the wicked?” That is, who confounded it? Who except the one who also glorified those whom he justified (Rom. 8:30)?

“Or did you understand the bonds of the Pleiades, and open the enclosure of Orion? Or will you open Mazuroth [Note: [Col. 0877] Thus the manuscripts and the Septuagint. The printed editions have “Arcturus.”] in its season and bring evening over its building?”

Must astrology also be investigated in order for us to understand the characteristics of these constellations and thus understand this passage? I would be surprised if that fit our discussion, and certainly it would be far too lengthy; therefore we pass on to other matters.

Or, since certain stars are named, are all the stars to be understood through a figure of speech in which the part signifies the whole? (If Mazuroth is also a star, although we do not find the word interpreted in the Greek language; for it is sufficiently evident that the name is Hebrew.)

Thus, by a part standing for the whole, the saying “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3) is also understood. For the morning star was not created first among all creatures, so that “before the morning star” would mean “before every creature.” Rather, through the morning star all the stars are meant, which is a part standing for the whole; and through all the stars all times are understood. For it is written concerning the stars, “Let them be for signs and for seasons” (Gen. 1:14). Thus the Lord’s being born before all times, not being born in time, and therefore his coeternity with the Father, is indicated.

The mention, therefore, of the Pleiades, Orion, Mazuroth, and the Evening Star persuades us, by this abbreviation, to understand all the stars. If all the others may be understood through one morning star, how much more may they be understood when so many are named?

Why, then, is it said in one place, “Did you understand the bonds”; in another, “Did you open”; in another, “opening in its season”; and elsewhere, “You will bring evening over its rising”? Are these expressions proper to each of the things mentioned in order? Or could one rightly say, “You opened the enclosure of the Pleiades,” and “You understood the bonds of Orion”? The other two expressions can likewise be exchanged [Note: [Col. 0877] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have “can likewise be mentioned.” M.].

Just as in the Psalm, “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them” (Ps. 2:4): no meaning would be lost even if it were said, “He who dwells in the heavens will mock them, and the Lord will laugh at them.” For just as the one who dwells in the heavens is himself the Lord, so whether the name of the Pleiades or of Orion is used, the meaning is the same if all the stars are understood through either one.

Therefore, under the name of all the stars, all such people in the Church are to be understood as have their way of life in heaven (Phil. 3:20). Their bonds are understood as those by which they are joined both to one another and to God, lest they fall. “But love never falls” (1 Cor. 13:8).

Who could have known this except the one who revealed it, who said, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34), and, “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father” (John 14:21)?

Their enclosure is the enclosure formed by divine Scripture, which they do not transgress. But who opens it except the one to whom one passes, so that the veil may be removed?

The time of their opening is the time of their demonstration and manifestation, when the Lord will come, “bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and reveal the counsels of hearts”; and then each person’s praise will come from God (1 Cor. 4:5). For he alone will do this in his own time, because “when Christ who is our life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4).

He will bring them over their building, making them possess what they have built here. For “if anyone’s work which he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward” (1 Cor. 3:14).

“Do you know the changes of heaven?” Are they changes for the worse, like those who knew God but did not glorify him as God? They did not wish to be God’s dwelling places, and therefore they were changed when they became futile in their thoughts (Rom. 1:21).

Or are they changes for the better? For although we shall all rise, we shall not all be changed. But who will be changed is made clear when he says, “And we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51–52).

When the righteous are changed, heaven will be changed, because God’s throne is heaven (Matt. 5:34), and wisdom is the Word of God, and “the Word was God,” and the soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom.

Or is it rather both? For he did not say “the change of heaven,” but “changes.”

Or does he mean all the things that happen together beneath heaven [Note: [Col. 0878] The printed editions have “all the things that happen beneath heaven.” The word “are” is absent from the Floriacensis manuscript.]? For just as the changes of this heaven affect the things beneath heaven, so when the righteous are changed—whether for the worse or for the better—they affect carnal people in both directions.

“You will call the cloud with your voice”: either with the inner voice, or with the voice by which it was said, “Follow me” (John 21:19), or with the voice by which it was said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

“And in the trembling of mighty water they will obey you”: powerful peoples, when they hear, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for God is the one working in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13).

“You will send forth rivers [Note: [Col. 0878] In the Septuagint, *keraunous*, ‘thunderbolts’; in the Vulgate, ‘flashes of lightning.’] with force, and they will go.” “Rivers,” he says, “of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). By “force” he means confidence, by which persecutors were not afraid; for “those who use force seize the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 11:12).

“Or will they say to you, ‘What is it?’” That is, will they perhaps ask of you either the intention of your command, as Saul said, “What do you command me to do?” (Acts 9:6), or the hope of their reward, as they said, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?” (Matt. 19:27)?

“Who gave women wisdom for weaving and knowledge of varied patterns?” A woman also made garments for her husband in Solomon’s writings (Prov. 31:10–24).

Therefore these are to be understood as the works of the Churches, by which God is honored. For the weaving itself—that is, binding weak brothers together, as though they were a soft weft, with the strong and upright spiritual people, as by the interweaving of warp threads—is a great and singular work of the Churches [Note: [Col. 0879] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have “the chosen spiritual people.” M.].

And the knowledge of varied patterns serves this purpose: just as in a woven cloth there is a variety of colors that does not disturb the beauty of unity, so among the brothers there should be diverse gifts, yet they should cling together without the discord of envy, “bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).

“Or who numbers the clouds in wisdom?” For “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19). But which human being, he says, knows this?

“Or will you bend the instruments of heaven down to the earth?” The heavenly angels, through whom divine voices are usually proclaimed. For they did not fall like that one angel, but were bent down toward the earth through the curvature of obedience, especially since the Lord himself was also on earth. For the Evangelist says, “And angels ministered to him” (Matt. 4:11).

“And ash was spread out like earth, and he bound him to stones as food” [Note: [Col. 0879] In the Septuagint, “like a stone, a cube.”].

The humility of repentance was spread widely and abundantly so that the Lord, who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5:5), might cling to them as with the glue of love: a human being to human beings, so that he might be the mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5), giving himself to them as food through the sacrament of his body and blood, choosing the foolish things of the world as stones in order to confound the wise (1 Cor. 1:27).

For to angels he is food insofar as he is the Word of God with God; but in order to become food to stones, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

Therefore he will be glued to human beings, provided the humility of repentance precedes, just as ash is spread out, making a path for him.

Hence the one who said, “Therefore bear fruits worthy of repentance, and do not say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:8–9), announced that he was to be glued as food to these stones.

But if the humility of repentance does not precede, he will not be glued to them, because “he recognizes the exalted from afar” (Ps. 137:6).

“Or will you catch food for the lion, or fill the souls of dragons?” It was said of the devil, “You shall trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 90:13), because of his ambushes and anger. Therefore all his angels are compared with lions and dragons.

But he catches food for them and fills their souls who, after convicting the impious, hands them over to their power. They wish to conceal their impiety, but when they are brought forth, they are certainly caught, so that they may come under the power of the devil and his angels, to whom they consented.

“For they are fearful in their lairs”: in the hiding places of their ambushes. For if they were not fearful, who could stand? Yet they fear the command of the one under whom they cried out, “Have you come before the time to destroy us?”

And just as it is clear concerning the pigs that the demons would not have entered them unless they had been permitted (Mark 1:24; 5:11–13), so it must be understood that they can do nothing to anyone unless they are permitted. They are permitted by the justice by which all things are governed, whether for the purpose of testing, or as punishment imposed for condemnation or correction.

“And they sit in the forests, lying in wait.” For the will to do harm does not rest in them, even when power is not granted. They watch in ambush amid such a forest-like density of opportunities for the flesh to see who may be caught by the divine laws—that is, convicted of his sin—and thus become worthy to be assigned as their food.

“But who prepared food for the raven?” Its young cry to the Lord, wandering and seeking food, as it says in the Psalm: “To the young ravens who call upon him” (Ps. 146:9). This passage closely resembles that verse.

They cannot be understood in an evil sense, because they call upon him. Therefore they signify black people—that is, sinners not yet whitened by the forgiveness of sins.

But they are called young because they are already humble; they are called wandering because they have not yet known the truth, which nevertheless they devoutly seek when they cry to the Lord.

Food can be prepared for the raven because of the foreknowledge of the one who knows that each person, even one who is not yet humble, will be converted. Yet they are young—that is, humble—and they cry to the Lord.

### [Book of Job XXXIX.]

Have you known the time when the wild goats give birth among the rocks? *Trágos* (τράγος) is “goat,” and *élaphos* (ἔλαφος) “deer”; therefore *tragelaphus* is an animal compounded from goat and deer. It signifies, then, the mind serving the law of God according to the inner person. Yet it sees how much of a goat it still is in part, with another law in its members warring against the law of its mind and taking it captive under the law of sin (Rom. VII, 22–23). [Note: [Col. 0880] Lov. has *parat* (“prepares”). But Am., Er., and all our manuscripts have *peperit* (“gave birth”).]

But the one who placed solid foundations of examples in the Scriptures gives birth to rocks for such persons at the appointed time—foundations in which even those who are at rest may not despair of themselves, whose flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh—until, having overcome the serpent’s persuasions by the deer’s vitality, they live by the spirit and follow the spirit (Gal. V, 17–18), so that sin (from which the likeness of the goat is drawn) may not reign in their mortal body, to make them obey its desires (Rom. VI, 12).

Or have you guarded the births of the does? These are the churches, in the number of spiritual ones, persuading by motherly affection those who imitate them, whom serpent-like opinions can no longer harm. Yet even such persons are guarded, not presuming upon themselves but upon God. And have you counted the months of their gestation? For they give birth only through the Gospel, which the Lord proclaimed with the authority of his teaching during the appointed months from his baptism until his passion and ascension. And have you released their birth-pangs? For it was not without labor that it was said, “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19). These birth-pangs are released when the offspring has been delivered—that is, when the truth has been persuaded upon those for whom such groaning is made, through the Word of God acting within their consciences.

And have you nourished their young without fear? That is, without being timid in the milk of the sacraments. For they did not receive again the spirit of slavery in fear (Rom. VIII, 15). You will send forth their offspring: into the freedom of a richer spiritual pasture.

[Note: [Col. 0881] Thus the manuscripts, following the Septuagint. The printed editions, however, have *euntes* (“going”).] Their children will break loose: the bonds of worldly desires. They will multiply in grain: in the more solid food of wisdom, after the nourishment of milk. They will go out and will not return to them. They will go out as from the narrow confines of instruction which is handed on by human teachers to beginners; and they will not return to their mothers, no longer needing milk or requiring human teachers. Certainly, these three verses are not to be pronounced as questions.

But who is it that has set the wild donkey free? It is extraordinary if he does not signify by the wild donkey those few who, free from every worldly business, serve God. And who has loosed his bonds? The bonds of carnal and popular affections. For I have appointed the wilderness as his dwelling and his tents as a salt-land, from which he cries, “My soul thirsted for you” (Ps. LXII, 2). He mocks the multitude of the city, which Scripture calls Babylon, traveling along the broad way that leads to destruction (Matt. VII, 13), and he does not hear the complaint of the taskmaster: he owes nothing to anyone. He has considered the mountains of his pasture: the greatness of revelations. And he seeks every green thing: everything everlasting.

But will the unicorn be willing to serve you? He is proud in the dignity of this age, because Christ has also subdued such men and appointed them ministers of the Church. For *monoceros* (μονόκερως) means “unicorn,” and it signifies pride. Or will he sleep over your manger? As though upon the humility of the one who was even placed as an infant in a manger (Luke II, 7). One rests there in the security of the forgiveness of sins and in forgetfulness of the anxieties of a bad conscience. And will he bind his yoke with straps? Bearing a gentle yoke fastened with straps—that is, in the authority of those who have mortified and subdued the flesh. Hence John too was girded with a leather belt (Matt. III, 4), not with the rough ropes of sins.

Or will he plow furrows for you in the field? He will open the hearts of an obedient people for the attainment of the kingdom of God. But do you trust in him because his strength has been changed? So that even in the ministry of the Church he may no longer seek the vanity of human praise and honor, as he sought it in the world. Or will you entrust your works to him? As the one for whom the Apostle says that he acts as an ambassador, exhorting people on Christ’s behalf to be reconciled to God (II Cor. V, 20). And will you believe him, that he will return your seed to you? He will claim nothing from it for his own dominion. For he calls “seed” the work of sowing. And will he bring it into your threshing-floor? That he may be among those to whom the Lord himself commands that the Lord of the harvest be asked to send workers into his harvest (Luke X, 2)—not that he may wish to make a threshing-floor for himself, like the founder of heresies and schisms and all who seek not God’s glory but their own.

For it is exceedingly difficult that this unicorn should wish to do so; yet even this he grants and accomplishes in the human mind, he who alone works wonders (Ps. LXXI, 18), destroying plans and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive into his obedience (II Cor. X, 4–5).

The wing of the ostriches is mingled with the wings of the herodion and the hawk. The meaning is that those slow in understanding, signified by the ostriches because they cannot fly, have been granted—through the grace of the one who chose the foolish things of the world (I Cor. I, 27)—to equal the speed of the intellectually gifted who believe together, signified by the other birds mentioned.

And she leaves her eggs on the ground. He now begins to speak about the ostrich, that is, about those whom he signifies through this animal. For their slow wings would not be mingled with the wings of swift birds so that they might fly together unless they left their former hope upon the earth, which he signifies by the eggs. And they warm them in the dust. For even if what he hoped for in the world has not been achieved, it often comes to pass through the favor of lovers of the world, who are compared to dust.

And she forgets that a foot will crush them and a beast of the field will trample them. But if the hostile desire of someone or the wickedness of this world disturbs and crushes such a person’s hope—like the eggs he leaves upon the ground—he cares so little that, as though forgetful, he does not feel it. She is hardened toward her young, as though they were not hers. Even if the hope is no longer like eggs but has become an actual possession, like children already born—that is, temporal happiness—he firmly despises it, unwilling that it should be his happiness, because he desires the true one.

He labored in vain, without any fear. This is before his conversion. For he labors in hope of the world without fruit and, what is more foolish, without any fear, while he presumes upon uncertain things. Because God in his wisdom disregarded her and did not allot her understanding. What indeed is more foolish than to trust in vanity and labor to acquire things destined to perish, without any fear of losing them?

Many conceive this attitude when a long period of worldly happiness comes to them, especially if it is handed down in uninterrupted succession from grandparents and ancestors, so that they do not believe they can suddenly become unhappy. And because they commonly appear great upon the earth, yet do not enjoy, through a heavenly way of life, the wings of virtues, they are rightly compared to ostriches.

But attend to what follows: When the time comes, she will fly aloft and mock the horseman and rider. After the fullness of time had come (Gal. IV, 4), so that the rich of this age were commanded not to be high-minded or to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God (I Tim. VI, 17), they began to lift their hearts upward to the Lord and to mock the proud persecutors whom the Lord cast into the sea. Then the ostrich’s wing, mingled with swift birds, seeks the sky, and the other things said above about this animal come to pass.

Or have you surrounded the horse with strength? He appears to describe a martyr, an undaunted and joyful witness to saving faith—not through his own strength, however, but through that with which the Lord has surrounded him. And have you clothed his neck with neighing? “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the evil day” (Eph. VI, 11). And the boldness of his breast is his glory.

[Note: [Col. 0882] The Floriacensis manuscript has *audaciam*, “boldness” in the accusative.]

This is the boldness with which Isaiah dares and says (Isa. LXV, 1; Rom. X, 20):

[Note: [Col. 0882] In Lov., after *dicit*, there is added: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I appeared openly to those who were not asking about me.” The whole passage is absent from Am., Er., and our manuscripts.]

He goes forth and exults in the field.

[Note: [Col. 0883] The Septuagint has *anorussôn*, “digging.”] Going out into the light of freedom, he rejoices in the ease of good works within the breadth of charity. And he advances into battle with strength: against the temptations of adversity. Meeting the missile, he despises it, because armor has been placed around him, including that shield of faith in which the flaming darts of the enemy are extinguished (Eph. VI, 16). Nor does he turn away from the sword: whether from visible death, or from those who are hard in refusing consent to the truth and sharp in persecuting him. He does not turn away from them because he is commanded to love even them.

For over him the bow and sword rejoice. Through his confession, the threat of God is indeed affirmed, announcing from afar the invisible punishments, as well as the testimony of the Word, by which he fights all errors as though at close quarters. For it is one thing to threaten that the punishments of sinners will come in the distant future, like stretching a bow to shoot its arrows; it is another to fight present desires as though face to face, with the sword of the Word.

At the trembling of the lance and spear. What does it mean that the bow and sword rejoice over him at the trembling of the lance and spear? Is it because, unless he himself also trembles—that is, fears the future death hurled by divine justice—he cannot despise the present death threatened by the persecutor, so as to maintain an undaunted confession and proclaim the truth with confidence, against which enemies cannot prevail? In this way the bow and sword rejoice over him—that is, through him God’s teaching is freely affirmed, by which it threatens the wicked with future destruction and kills present iniquity.

For unless the joy of our hope were accompanied by the trembling of condemnation, that very security would become negligence and proud presumption in us; nor would it be said to us in the Psalm, “Rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. II, 11).

And in anger he overturns the earth. Being angry within himself, he overturns within himself earthly desires and carnal fears, by which each person is turned away from enduring suffering. Perhaps in this passage it is said, “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 5). With a most salutary anger each person ought to correct himself, saying, “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess to him.” Since confession is made with the mouth for salvation (Rom. X, 10), it immediately follows: “God is the salvation of my countenance” (Ps. XLI, 6–7).

Nor will he believe until the trumpet has sounded. Before the time of temptation, even if earthly trembling has been overturned, it does not appear, and it is not easy to believe it unless the time of temptation itself has taught it. But when the trumpet sounds, he will say, “Well done!” When the time of temptation comes, then his soul will truly please him if he glories in tribulations, because tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces tested character, and tested character produces hope (Rom. V, 3–4). Then, instead of angrily saying to his soul, “Why do you trouble me?”, he will say in exultation, “Praise the Lord, my soul” (Ps. CXLV, 2).

And from afar he smells the battle. Not as though it were among the visible human persecutors, but from afar—that is, far from the eyes—knowing that our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. VI, 12). This is why it is said “from afar.” Appropriately, however, it is said that he “smells,” because the things of the air are perceived by smell, whether good or bad.

He therefore smells the battle who understands that the ruler of the power of the air works in the sons of disobedience (Eph. II, 2), whose persecuting anger or ambushes he endures, so that he may fight against spiritual wickedness with spiritual weapons, not bodily weapons against flesh and blood—that is, against evil and lost human beings whom he sees with bodily eyes.

The thunder of the commanders and the shouting. “He smells” is to be supplied. I think “thunder” is said because of the air itself, in which spiritual wickedness enclosed there moves. These spirits are not called “rulers of the world” because they rule heaven and earth, but as the Apostle himself explains. For lest it be understood in this way, he immediately added what he meant by “rulers of the world”: “of this darkness,” he says—that is, of the ungodly. To those who were converted to the Lord he said, “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8).

It lies within each person’s will whether he is darkness or light. But when he is darkness, he is darkness in himself—that is, in the sins that belong particularly to him. When he is light, he is not light in himself but in the Lord, by whom he is illumined, so that, as Isaiah said, “his darkness may be like midday” (Isa. LVIII, 10). It is also said in the Psalms, “You will illumine my darkness” (Ps. XVII, 29).

Those whom the Apostle calls the rulers of darkness are also called “commanders” in this verse. For darkness—that is, the ungodly—are led by them to persecute the godly, meaning those who suffer persecution for righteousness, not those who suffer because of their own ungodliness and iniquities.

The martyr is said to smell the shouting of such commanders, not because any sound is heard by the bodily ears, but because he perceives by faith with the ears of his heart what great things the devil and his angels plot against God’s servants. Hence the Apostle says, “For we are not ignorant of his schemes” (II Cor. II, 11). Against this shouting of the commanders, the ears of unbelievers are of course deaf.

Does the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom? Just as, by the wisdom of God, which is Christ, the new person is gradually renewed and will have his way of life in the heavenly places. With wings outspread and motionless, looking toward the south: with the virtues of the twofold love unfolded and freed from every worldly impediment, remaining unshaken in faith—not presuming upon himself even in this, but hoping in God and directing his attention back to him, from whom that ardor of charity is inspired, so that he may preserve his strength for him (Ps. LVIII, 10), saying, “Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation. Indeed, he is my God and my Savior, my protector; I shall not be moved any further” (Ps. LXI, 2–3).

And is the eagle exalted at your command? As at the command of the one who says, “When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32). For he was going to die for us and raise his body to heaven through the resurrection: “Wherever the corpse is,” he says, “there the eagles will gather” (Matt. XXIV, 28). For he has satisfied with heavenly good things the desire of the one whose youth will be renewed like the eagle’s (Ps. CII, 5).

The exaltation of the eagle may also refer to what the Apostle says:

[Col. 0885] “For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God”—

so that the verse which follows there about the vulture may refer to what also follows there:

“or whether we are self-controlled, it is for you.”

For it follows:

“Or will the vulture remain sitting upon its nest on the rock?”

This appears to have been said with reference not to contemplating sublime things in an excess of mind, but to caring for those below through self-control, by which one accommodates oneself to human affairs, so that the ungodly—who are regarded as dead—may, having been justified through the Word, that is, as though devoured by the mouth, be converted into the body of the Church.

For the vulture feeds on the dead. Therefore it is above its nest, where it places, as though they were young, works necessary for this life. It is on the rock because, when the Apostle had said, “Whether we are self-controlled, it is for you,” he immediately added, “For the love of Christ compels us” (II Cor. V, 13–14); and “the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4).

And rightly it is said that, sitting, he will remain, in accordance with what was said: “I am constrained by both desires, having the wish to depart and to be with Christ—for that is much better—but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I, 23–24). Indeed, it is much more fitting that this should refer to the exaltation of the eagle, while the vulture sitting and remaining in the nest refers to “to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.”

And because the rock may also rightly be understood as the whole Church, on account also of Simon, who for this reason was called Peter by the Lord (Mark III, 16), the summit of the rock is the head of the Church. To this the following verse is added:

“Upon the summit of the rock and in the cavern.”

The summit refers to what is the head, while the cavern refers to the fact that our life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. III, 3). And when he is there, he seeks food, concerning which it was said to Peter, “Kill and eat” (Acts XI, 7), so that he might incorporate into the Church those from the Gentiles who would believe.

His eyes look from afar, and his young roll in blood. He stretches his attention far ahead, through the hope of future immortality, toward eternal life. Although his works roll about in the weakness of the flesh—that is, he is tossed by uncertain movements, since human ignorance does not know, from the merciful things he does, what may benefit each person before God—nevertheless, with eyes that look far ahead, he dispenses them in sincere charity for the sake of eternal salvation.

But when this kind of worker and steward finds those who, through the affection by which they renounce the devil, have already died to this age, he presents to them without any hesitation the ministry of the mouth in the work of speech, by which he transfers them, already fully prepared, into the body of the Church. Therefore it follows:

“Wherever there are corpses, there they are immediately found.”

### The Lord answered and said.

Since the Lord now seems to repeat his speech, although he himself had been speaking, it is understood that Job, at what had been said, was struck with astonishment in silence and had become still, so that he dared say nothing more. Therefore, in the two verses that follow, the Lord encourages him to answer.

“Does the one who disputes with the Almighty remain silent?” That is: Why are you silent while disputing with the Almighty? “Will the one who reproves God answer in this way?” The word “does” is to be supplied, so that the meaning is: Does the one who, while disputing, answers, reprove God? For one disputes with the Almighty by asking questions, not by convicting or refuting him. Therefore, because he is Almighty, one is not for that reason to refrain from disputing with him. For nothing is required from him through argument, as though from Truth itself, for the purpose of reproving him.

It can also be understood in this way: “Does the one who disputes with the Lord remain silent?” That is, because the one who disputes with the Almighty does not remain silent, one ought not to dispute with him in order to become quiet.
