For the person who disputes usually contradicts; but whoever contradicts God cannot be at rest—that is, he finds no rest—unless he consents without any contradiction to God’s will. “Will the one who reproves God answer in this way?” That is, when he answers God by disputing, he reproves God, and for this reason does not attain rest. Hence it was said, “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. IX, 20).

But had Job done anything of this kind? God does not receive him as contradicting him, as his friends, through lack of understanding, do, since God bears witness to him both at the beginning and at the end of the book.

Or was this said with reference to the person represented by Job—that is, the body of the Lord, which is the Church, in which there is a large number of weak people, not indeed those who have despaired, but those who are still endangered in their progress? Their feet are almost moved, and their steps are nearly poured out, while they are jealous of sinners and observe the peace of sinners. They say:

“How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High? Behold, these are sinners, and those who abound in the world have acquired riches. Have I purified my heart in vain and washed my hands among the innocent? And I have been scourged all day, and my chastisement has come in the morning” (Ps. LXXII, 2–14).

For Job himself seems rather to answer in the verses that follow.

### Job answered and said:

Why, then, do I bring judgment upon myself, having been admonished and rebuked by the Lord, hearing such things, when I am nothing? That is: Why do I bring judgment upon myself when the Lord admonishes and rebukes me, if I contradict him—hearing such things, that is, understanding with what justice and mercy he deals with me—when in myself I am indeed nothing?

What answer shall I give? That is: What can I contradict to the Truth?

I will place my hand upon my mouth. That is: I will restrain and curb my loquacity.

Once I have spoken, I will not add again.

Unless this is understood mystically, how has Job spoken once, since he spoke so many times? Or how will he not add again, when he is about to speak shortly afterward? But “speaking” here should be understood as the soul’s advance into these external things, by which it abandons God and resists him.

Hence a greater kind of advance is also called a “cry” in Scripture, when God says that the cry of Sodom has come to him (Gen. XVIII, 20). The opposite of that speech and cry is that most blessed silence of which it is said, “And he will be silent without fear of every evil.”

Therefore he rightly says that he spoke once in a continuous kind of speech throughout the whole life of the old person, when he was like a spirit that walks and does not return (Ps. LXXVII, 39). But now, placing his hand upon his mouth so that he may advance no further, he promises that he will not add again, lest he depart from God.

Amen.

# A Mirror of Sacred Scripture

[Col. 0887]

## Preface to the Book Entitled *The Mirror*

Gregory observes in book 2, chapter 1 of the *Moralia*, that Sacred Scripture has been set before us in the place of a mirror. Accordingly, when it devotes itself to recounting the deeds of illustrious men, it does not pass over their sins and falls in complete silence, so that suitable examples may be available to each person for the formation of conduct.

Nevertheless, Scripture possesses this function of a mirror also for another reason—or rather, it claims it especially in that part in which the precepts of life are contained. When these are set before one’s eyes, if there is any stain in one’s conduct, or if an unfeigned beauty and appearance of piety resides in the mind, it is more easily judged.

That these precepts were collected into a single book through the diligence of the holy doctor Augustine, to which he himself gave the name *The Mirror*, Possidius confirms in his *Life*, chapter 28. After listing the books that precede the *Retractations*, he adds:

“He who wished to benefit everyone, both those who wanted to read many books and those who were unable to do so, extracted from both Testaments of God, the Old and the New, after setting down a preface, the divine precepts or prohibitions pertaining to the rule of life, and made one book from them, so that whoever wished might read it and recognize in it how obedient or disobedient he was to God. He wished to call this work *The Mirror*.”

He reports that it was completed a short time before the invasion of Africa by the Vandals, which belongs to the year of Christ 428. From this you may understand that this work is approximately from the year 427, and that it is consequently numbered among the minor works published later than the books of the *Retractations* in ancient manuscripts, as was noted at the end of the *Retractations* in volume 1.

Cassiodorus Senator also indicates that he knew this book well, in book 1, chapter 16 of *On Divine Scripture*, in these words:

“The book of the same Augustine, almost a work of moral philosophy, which he collected from divine authority for the formation and correction of conduct and called *The Mirror*, should be read with great attention.”

Moreover, when the holy Doctor was preparing this pious work for the use of the common people, he wished to include only instructions that were easier to understand. We believe that this same purpose also led him to use a version not from the Greek of the Seventy, which he usually followed, but from the Hebrew, since he had finally discovered that the latter was clearer in many passages.

For this reason he praises it several times in his later books of *Questions on the Heptateuch*, and especially in book 4 of *On Christian Doctrine*. In that book, which he added to the other three in the year 426 or 427, he speaks as follows in chapter 7, when he is about to cite testimony from the prophet Amos:

“Not, however, according to the Seventy Interpreters, who, although they too interpreted by the divine Spirit, nevertheless appear to have said certain things differently for this reason: so that the reader’s attention might be more strongly urged to search out the spiritual meaning. Hence some of their expressions are also more obscure, because they are more figurative; but as they have been translated from the Hebrew into Latin speech by the presbyter Jerome, skilled in both languages.”

Furthermore, if any of the statements collected in the *Mirror* should perhaps appear contradictory, he had decided to reconcile and clarify them by proposing questions afterward. We have searched for these questions in vain in the manuscript codices. Since Possidius says nothing about this labor, although he did not think it appropriate to remain silent about the work itself or even about the preface of the *Mirror*, it is reasonably believed that Augustine was prevented from completing it.

Another *Mirror*, produced not long ago through the care of Jerome Vignier and published under Augustine’s name, arranges the statements of Scripture under certain fixed headings established for various matters concerning sacred doctrine. It therefore appears to have been prepared not so much for the formation of life as for the instruction of the mind. Consequently, it agrees less with the *Mirror* described both by Possidius’ words and by Augustine’s preface. Accordingly, just as we must regard this one of ours as genuine, so we must regard Vignier’s as spurious.

[Col. 0887]

## Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo: *A Mirror of Sacred Scripture*

[Note: [Col. 0887] Written around the year of Christ 427.]

[Note: [Col. 0887] It was found in only two Gallican manuscripts, one of the Royal Library and the other belonging to the Church of Chartres. With the help of these codices, and by collating the editions of Am., Er., and Lov. against them, it is restored in full in many places.]

[Note: [Col. 0887] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C, S)

### Preface

Who does not know that in the Holy Scriptures—that is, in the Canonical, Prophetic, Evangelical, and Apostolic books endowed with canonical authority—some things are set down so that they are merely to be known and believed? Such is the statement that “in the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1), and that “in the beginning was the Word” (John I, 1), and all the divine or human deeds that are narrated merely so that they may be known.

Other things, however, are set down as commands, so that they are to be observed and done, or as prohibitions, so that they are not to be done. Such are: “Honor your father and mother,” and, “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX, 12, 14; Matt. XV, 4; V, 27–28).

Among the things written by command and prohibition, some are veiled in sacramental mysteries. Many such things were commanded that people of the Old Testament were to do, but they are not now done by the Christian people; they are required and treated only in their meaning. Such is the Sabbath as visible rest (Deut. V, 12); such are unleavened loaves in bread without leaven and the Passover in the slaughter of sheep (Exod. XII); such are the many kinds of sacrifices and foods to be avoided, the new moons, and the annual solemnities that the Jews still observe; and such are those ordinances which do not properly pertain to works of righteousness but are understood to signify something.

For what Christian is compelled in the seventh year to return a slave to freedom and, if he does not wish to depart, to pierce his ear with an awl against the doorpost (Exod. XXI, 2, 6), and to observe other things of this kind?

Other commandments, however, are still to be done if they are commanded, and not to be done if they are prohibited. Such are the ones I mentioned: “Honor your father and mother,” and, “You shall not commit adultery.”

Accordingly, I have undertaken to compose this work concerning those things which have been set down in the sacred writings by command, prohibition, or permission in such a way that they still pertain, even now—that is, in the time of the New Testament—to the practice of a godly life and to conduct. As far as God helps me, I shall collect all such passages from the canonical books and heap them together into one volume, as into a mirror, so that they may easily be examined.

For it was necessary that our authors should set these things down as they did: commands were interwoven with their own narratives or arguments, and matters proper to the narrative with figurative matters, while the order of events was preserved, opponents were answered, those who needed instruction were taught, and those who grow weary of what is readily available and plain were, in a certain sense, renewed by the discovery of hidden things.

In this work, however, we neither lead an unbeliever to faith nor build him up in faith; nor do we exercise the ability and attention of learners through certain salutary difficulties. Rather, we admonish the person who already believes and wishes to obey God to look into this mirror, to consider how much he has progressed in good conduct and works, and how much is still lacking in him.

In this way he can give thanks both for what he has and make suitable efforts to obtain what he does not have; and, for the sake of preserving what must be preserved, he can apply the care and prayers of faithful devotion.

Among all the things that I have decided to set before the reader for examination, whatever may appear contradictory will afterward have to be explained and resolved through questions proposed later.

Certainly, although I have thought that the punishments of wrongdoers and the rewards of those who do right should be mentioned in some places, who does not know that in the New Testament they are unlike those in the Old?

Let us therefore begin with the Law given through Moses, taking up the divine precepts of the kind that we promised to recall.

## From the Book of the Law Called Exodus

[Col. 0890]

### Chapter XX

You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above or on earth below, nor of what is in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not adore them or worship them.

Likewise: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not hold guiltless the one who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain.

And shortly afterward: Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God will give you.

You shall not kill.

You shall not commit adultery.

You shall not steal.

You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor.

You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor desire his wife, nor his male slave, nor his female slave, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that belongs to him.

Likewise, after the Decalogue, these precepts for living are found in other places in the same book:

You shall not make gods of silver with me, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves.

[Note: [Col. 0890] The particle *mecum*, “with me,” is not found in the printed editions and is now absent from the Vulgate version. But the manuscripts of this work have it; the Hebrew text has it, and even the Vulgate version in the Corbie volume copied more than eight hundred years ago has it.]

And somewhat later:

### Chapter XXI

Whoever strikes a person intending to kill him shall die by death. But if he did not lie in wait for him, and God delivered him into his hand, I shall appoint for you a place to which he may flee. If anyone deliberately kills his neighbor by ambush, you shall drag him away from my altar so that he may die.

Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall die by death.

Whoever steals a person and sells him, having been convicted of the offense, shall die by death.

Whoever curses his father or mother shall die by death.

If men quarrel and one strikes his neighbor with a stone or with his fist, and the other does not die but lies in bed; if he gets up and walks outside supported by his staff, the one who struck him shall be innocent—provided, however, that he repays the cost of his labor and the expenses of physicians.

Whoever strikes his male slave or female slave with a rod, and the slave dies in his hands, shall be guilty of a crime. But if the slave survives for one day or two, he shall not be subject to punishment, because the slave is his property.

If men quarrel and someone strikes a pregnant woman, and she indeed suffers a miscarriage but survives, he shall be subject to a fine in whatever amount the woman’s husband demands and the arbiters determine. But if her death follows, he shall give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.

If anyone strikes the eye of his male or female slave and blinds it, he shall set the slave free in exchange for the eye he destroyed. If he knocks out a tooth of his male or female slave, he shall likewise set the slave free.

If an ox gores a man or woman with its horn and they die, it shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten; the owner of the ox shall also be innocent.

But if the ox was a habitual gorer from yesterday and the day before, and its owner had been warned but did not confine it, and it kills a man or woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner shall be killed.

But if a price is imposed upon him, he shall pay for his life whatever amount is demanded of him.

[Col. 0891] If it gores a son or daughter, the same judgment shall apply to it.

If it attacks a male slave or female slave, it shall pay thirty shekels of silver to the owner; but the ox shall be stoned.

If anyone opens a cistern, or digs one and does not cover it, and an ox or donkey falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall repay the value of the animals; but what has died shall belong to him.

If someone’s ox wounds another person’s ox and it dies, they shall sell the living ox and divide the price; they shall also divide the carcass of the dead one between them.

But if it was known that the ox was a habitual gorer from yesterday and the day before, and its owner did not guard it, he shall repay an ox for an ox, but he shall take the entire carcass.

[XXII.] If anyone steals an ox or a sheep and kills or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep. If a thief is found breaking into a house or digging through it, and, having been wounded, dies, the one who struck him shall not be liable for bloodshed. But if he did this after sunrise, he has committed murder, and he himself shall die. If he has nothing with which to make restitution for the theft, he shall be sold. But if what he stole is found alive with him—whether an ox, an ass, or a sheep—he shall restore double.

If anyone damages a field or vineyard and lets his animal loose to graze another’s property, he shall restore, as compensation for the damage, whatever is best in his own field or vineyard. If fire, having spread, finds ears of grain [Note: [Col. 0891] So here in all the manuscripts with which the Corbie volume of the Bible agrees. But in the Hebrew and in the Septuagint it reads “thorns.” So also does the Vulgate after the Roman correction made on the authority of Sixtus V.], and consumes heaps of produce or standing crops in the fields, the one who kindled the fire shall pay the damage.

If anyone entrusts money or a vessel to a friend for safekeeping, and it is stolen from the person who received it, then, if the thief is found, he shall restore double; if he is concealed, the master of the house shall be brought before the gods and shall swear that he did not stretch out his hand against the property of his neighbor to commit fraud, whether concerning an ox, an ass, a sheep, or a garment, or anything else that can cause damage. The matter of both parties shall come before the gods; and if they give judgment, he shall restore double to his neighbor.

If anyone entrusts to his neighbor an ass, an ox, a sheep, or any animal for safekeeping, and it dies, is injured, or is seized by enemies [Note: [Col. 0891] The printed editions have “by wild beasts.” The manuscripts, however, have “by enemies,” which is the more correct reading], with no one having seen it, there shall be an oath between them that he did not stretch out his hand against his neighbor’s property. The owner shall accept the oath, and the other shall not be compelled to make restitution. But if it was stolen, he shall restore the loss to the owner. If it was killed by a wild beast, he shall bring to him what was killed, and he shall not make restitution.

Whoever borrows any of these things from his neighbor, and it is injured or dies while the owner is absent, shall be compelled to make restitution. But if the owner was present, he shall not make restitution—especially if the animal had been hired for payment for his labor.

If anyone seduces a virgin who is not yet betrothed and sleeps with her, he shall provide her bride-price and take her as his wife. If the virgin’s father refuses to give her, he shall pay money according to the amount of the bride-price [Col. 0892] that virgins customarily receive.

You shall not allow sorcerers to live. Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death. Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be killed, except to the Lord alone.

You shall not grieve or oppress a stranger, for you too were strangers in the land of Egypt. You shall not harm a widow or an orphan. If you harm them, they will cry out to me, and I will hear their cry; my anger will be kindled, and I will strike you with the sword. Your wives shall become widows and your children orphans.

If you lend money to my poor people who dwell with you, you shall not press him like an exactor, nor oppress him with interest. If you take your neighbor’s garment as a pledge, return it to him before sunset; for it is the only covering he has for his body, and he has nothing else in which to sleep. If he cries out to me, I will hear him, because I am compassionate.

You shall not speak evil of the gods, and you shall not curse the ruler of your people. You shall not delay offering your tithes and firstfruits. You shall give me the firstborn of your sons.

A little later [XXIII.]:

You shall not receive a false report, nor join your hand to speak false testimony on behalf of the wicked. You shall not follow the crowd to do evil, nor agree in judgment with the opinion of the majority so as to depart from the truth [Note: [Col. 0892] The printed editions have “so as to depart from the true God.” “God” is absent from the manuscripts of this book and likewise from the sacred Scriptures.]. You shall not show partiality to the poor in judgment [Note: [Col. 0892] The manuscript of the Church of Chartres has here “in a matter”; thus it was also read in the Corbie Bible of the Vulgate version.].

If you encounter your enemy’s ox or his wandering ass, lead it back to him. If you see the ass of one who hates you lying beneath its burden, do not pass by, but help him with it. You shall not pervert the judgment of the poor. You shall flee falsehood. You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous, for I reject the wicked. You shall not accept gifts, which blind even the wise and overturn the words of the righteous.

You shall not trouble a stranger, for you know the souls of strangers, since you too were strangers in the land of Egypt.

And after some intervening material, when he was speaking about foreigners:

You shall not worship their gods, nor serve them. You shall not do their works, but you shall destroy them and shatter their statues; and you shall serve the Lord your God.

And after much else in the same book concerning the gods of the nations [XXXIV.]:

But destroy their altars, shatter their statues, and cut down their sacred groves. Do not worship a foreign god; “Jealous” is his name, he is a jealous God. Do not make a covenant with the inhabitants of those regions, lest, when they commit fornication with their gods and worship their images, someone invite you to eat of the things sacrificed. Nor shall you take wives for your sons from among their daughters, lest, after they have committed fornication, they make your sons commit fornication with their gods. You shall not make molten gods for yourself.

And a little later:

You shall offer the firstfruits of your land in the house [Note: [Col. 0892] The manuscripts have “into the house.”] of the Lord your God.

I have thought it worthwhile to gather these passages from the book of the Law called Exodus. Now let us examine the following book, Leviticus, in the same manner.

## FROM LEVITICUS

### [Chapter XVIII]

“Every man,” he says, “shall not approach his nearest blood relative to uncover his nakedness. I am the Lord. You shall not uncover your father’s nakedness or your mother’s nakedness; she is your mother, you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife, for it is your father’s nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, whether born of your father or of your mother, whether born at home or elsewhere. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son’s daughter or your daughter’s granddaughter, for it is your own nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter, whom she bore to your father, for she is your sister. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s sister, for she is your father’s flesh. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother’s sister, for she is your mother’s flesh. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your uncle, nor approach his wife, who is joined to you by kinship. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law, for she is your son’s wife; you shall not uncover her shame. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife, for it is your brother’s nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your wife and her daughter. You shall not take her son’s daughter or her daughter’s daughter to uncover her shame, for they are her flesh, and such intercourse is incestuous. You shall not take your wife’s sister as a rival wife during her lifetime, to uncover her nakedness while she is still alive. You shall not approach a woman suffering her menstrual period, nor uncover her uncleanness. You shall not lie with your neighbor’s wife, nor defile yourself by the mingling of semen. You shall not give any of your offspring to be consecrated to the idol Molech, nor profane the name of your God. I am the Lord. You shall not lie with a male as with a woman, for it is an abomination. You shall not lie with any animal, nor defile yourself with it. A woman shall not submit to an animal, nor mate with it, for it is a crime. You shall not defile yourselves by any of these things.”

And after a little while [XIX.]:

Let each person fear his mother and father.

And one verse later:

Do not turn to idols, and do not make molten gods for yourselves. I am the Lord your God.

And a little later:

You shall not gather the ears of grain that remain, nor collect the leftover grapes and fallen berries in your vineyard; but you shall leave them to be gleaned by the poor and by strangers. I am the Lord your God. You shall not steal. You shall not lie. No one shall deceive his neighbor. You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of your God. I am the Lord. You shall not slander your neighbor, nor oppress him by force. The wages of your hired laborer shall not remain with you until morning. You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear the Lord your God, for I am the Lord. You shall not do what is unjust, nor judge unjustly. You shall not show partiality to the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful; judge your neighbor justly. You shall not be an accuser or a whisperer among the peoples. You shall not stand against the blood of your neighbor. I am the Lord. You shall not hate your brother in your heart; but openly rebuke him, lest you bear sin on his account. You shall not seek revenge, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens. You shall love your friend as yourself. I am the Lord. Keep my laws.

And a little later [Col. 0894]:

You shall not eat with blood [Note: [Col. 0894] The printed editions have “meat with blood.” But the manuscripts lack the word “meat,” which is also absent from the Latin Bibles except the corrupt ones.]. You shall not practice divination, nor observe dreams. You shall not cut your hair in a circle, nor shave [Note: [Col. 0894] The Chartres manuscript has “nor uproot.” Others, following the Vulgate, have “nor shave.” If Augustine read it in this way, one is naturally surprised that he transferred this commandment into this collection, which was meant to contain only commandments equally applicable to the time of the Old and New Testaments. Moreover, the Septuagint translates: οὐδὲ φθερεῖτε τὴν ὄψιν τοῦ πώγωνος, “nor shall you mar the appearance of your beard.”] your beard. You shall not cut your flesh on account of the dead, nor make any figures or marks upon yourselves. I am the Lord.

Do not prostitute your daughter, lest the land be defiled and filled with wickedness.

And one verse later:

I am the Lord. Do not turn to magicians, nor inquire of diviners, lest you be defiled by them. I am the Lord your God.

Rise before a gray head, and honor the person of the old man, and fear your God. I am the Lord.

If a stranger dwells in your land and remains among you, do not reproach him; but let him be among you as a native, and you shall love him as yourselves, for you too were strangers in the land of Egypt. I am the Lord your God.

You shall do nothing unjust in judgment, in a rule, in weight, or in measure. Let the balance and weights be just and equal; let the bushel be just and the sextarius equal. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Keep all my commandments and all my judgments, and do them. I am the Lord.

### [XX.]

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

You shall speak these things to the children of Israel: If any man among the children of Israel, or among the strangers dwelling in Israel, gives any of his offspring to the idol Molech, he shall surely die; the people of the land shall stone him. I will set my face against him and cut him off from the midst of his people, because he gave some of his offspring to Molech and defiled my sanctuary and profaned my holy name.

But if the people of the land, acting negligently and treating my command as though it were insignificant, allow the man who gave some of his offspring to Molech to go free and refuse to kill him, I will set my face against that man and his family, and I will cut off both him and all who agreed with him in committing fornication with Molech from the midst of his people.

The soul that turns to magicians and diviners and commits fornication with them—I will set my face against that soul and destroy it from the midst of its people.

Sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am the Lord your God. Keep my commandments and do them. I am the Lord who sanctifies you.

Whoever curses his father or mother shall surely die. Whoever curses father or mother [Note: [Col. 0894] In the more carefully corrected Bibles: “whoever has cursed father and mother.”] shall have his blood upon him.

If a man commits adultery with another man’s wife and commits adultery with his neighbor’s spouse, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely die. Whoever lies with his stepmother and uncovers his father’s shame, both shall surely die; their blood shall be upon them. If anyone lies with his daughter-in-law, both shall die, for they have committed a crime; their blood shall be upon them. Whoever lies with a male as with a woman, both have committed an abomination; they shall surely die [Col. 0895]; their blood shall be upon them.

Whoever takes a woman together with her mother has committed a crime; he shall be burned alive together with them, and such a great abomination shall not remain among you.

Whoever lies with an animal or beast shall surely die; you shall also kill the animal. A woman who submits to any animal shall be killed together with it; their blood shall be upon them.

Whoever takes his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees her brother’s shame, they have done a wicked thing. They shall be killed in the sight of the people, because they have uncovered each other’s nakedness; and they shall bear their iniquity.

Whoever lies with a woman during her menstrual flow and uncovers her nakedness, and she exposes the source of her blood, both shall be destroyed from the midst of their people.

You shall not uncover the nakedness of your maternal aunt or paternal aunt. Whoever does this has exposed the shame of his own flesh; both shall bear their iniquity.

Whoever lies with his uncle’s or his mother’s brother’s wife and uncovers the shame of his kin, both shall bear their sin; they shall die without children.

Whoever takes his brother’s wife does an unlawful thing; he has uncovered his brother’s nakedness. They shall be without children.

And in another place:

A man or woman in whom there is a spirit of a python or of divination shall surely die; they shall stone them; their blood shall be upon them.

Likewise, in another place, when he was speaking about the high priest [XXI.]:

“He shall take a virgin as his wife,” he says. “He shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a prostitute, but a maiden from his own people, lest he mix the stock of his lineage with the common people of his nation; for I am the Lord who sanctifies him.”

And after much else [XXIV.]:

The man who curses his God shall bear his sin. Whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord shall surely die; the whole assembly shall stone him, whether he is a citizen or a stranger. Whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord shall surely die.

Whoever strikes and kills a human being shall surely die. Whoever strikes an animal shall pay its equivalent, that is, life for life. Whoever inflicts a blemish on any of his fellow citizens shall suffer as he has done: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; whatever blemish he inflicted, he shall be compelled to endure the same. Whoever strikes an animal shall repay another. Whoever strikes a human being shall be punished. Let there be equal judgment among you, whether a stranger or a citizen has sinned, for I am the Lord your God.

And after a little while [XXVI.]:

You shall not make an idol or a carved image for yourselves, nor erect pillars, nor set up a distinguished [Note: [Col. 0895] So the manuscripts, following the Vulgate. But the printed editions have “as a sign.”] stone in your land to worship it. For I am the Lord your God.

These passages are from Leviticus. Now we shall set down what seemed worth recalling from the book whose name is Numbers.

## FROM NUMBERS

### [Chapter XXVII]

When a man dies without a son, the inheritance shall pass to his daughter. If he has no daughter, his brothers shall be his heirs. But if he has no brothers [Col. 0896], you shall give the inheritance to his father’s brothers. But if he has no paternal uncles either, the inheritance shall be given to those who are nearest to him. This shall be a sacred law for the children of Israel, as the Lord commanded Moses.

And after much else [XXXV.]:

No one shall be condemned on the testimony of a single witness. You shall not accept payment from one who is guilty of bloodshed.

These are the passages we found in Numbers and thought should be examined. Next we shall consider Deuteronomy.

## FROM DEUTERONOMY

### [Chapter I]

There shall be no distinction of persons: you shall hear the small as well as the great, and you shall not accept anyone’s person, because the judgment is God’s.

And after much intervening material, where he repeats the Decalogue [IV.]:

Therefore guard your souls carefully. You did not see any likeness on the day when the Lord spoke to you at Horeb from the midst of the fire, lest, being deceived, you make for yourselves a carved likeness or an image of male or female; a likeness of any animals that are upon the earth, or of birds flying beneath heaven; or of reptiles that move upon the earth, or of fish that dwell in the waters beneath the earth. Lest, raising your eyes toward heaven, you see the sun, the moon, and all the stars of heaven, and, deceived by error, worship and serve them, which the Lord your God created for the service of all the peoples beneath heaven.

And a little later:

Take care, he says, lest you ever forget the covenant of the Lord your God that he made with you, and make for yourself a carved likeness of the things that the Lord forbade to be made; for the Lord your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.

And elsewhere [V.]:

You shall have no foreign gods in my sight. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor a likeness of anything in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship or serve them. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to many thousands who love me and keep my commandments.

You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for he shall not go unpunished who takes his name over an empty matter.

And a little later:

Honor your father and mother, he says, as the Lord your God commanded you, so that you may live long and prosper in the land that the Lord your God will give you. You shall not kill, nor commit adultery, nor steal, nor speak false testimony against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his house, nor his field, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that belongs to him.

And elsewhere in the same book [VI.]:

You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength.

And a little later:

When you have eaten and are satisfied, take great care not to forget the Lord, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery. You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him alone [Col. 0897], and swear by his name. You shall not follow foreign gods, any of the nations around you, for the Lord your God, who is in your midst, is a jealous God; lest the anger of the Lord your God be kindled against you and he remove you from the face of the earth. You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.

Likewise a little later, when he speaks about foreigners [VII.]:

Nor shall you form marriages with them: you shall not give your daughter to his son, nor take his daughter for your son, because she will seduce your son from following me, so that he may serve foreign gods instead. Then the anger of the Lord will be kindled, and he will quickly destroy you.

Rather, this is what you shall do to them: overthrow their altars, shatter their statues, cut down their sacred groves, and burn their carved images. And after a little while:

You shall burn their carved images with fire. You shall not covet the silver and gold from which they are made, nor take anything from them for yourself, lest you offend, because it is an abomination to the Lord your God. You shall not bring anything from the idol into your house, lest you become accursed, as it too is; you shall detest it as filth, and regard it as pollution and uncleanness, because it is accursed.

And elsewhere [VIII.]:

Observe and beware lest you ever forget the Lord your God and neglect his commands, judgments, and ordinances that I command you today; lest, after you have eaten and are satisfied, built beautiful houses and lived in them, and possessed herds and flocks, silver, gold, and an abundance of everything, your heart be lifted up and you remember no longer the Lord your God.

And a few verses later:

In the end, he says, he had mercy on you, lest you say in your heart, “My strength and the power of my hand have procured all these things for me”; but you shall remember the Lord your God, for he himself gave you strength.

And after a little while [XI.]:

So that you may eat and be satisfied. Beware lest your heart be deceived and you depart from the Lord your God, serve foreign gods, and worship them; then the Lord, angered, may shut up heaven.

And after a little while [XII.]:

Destroy all the places in which the nations whose land you are about to possess served their gods, upon high mountains and hills and beneath every leafy tree [Note: [Col. 0897] So the manuscripts, following the Vulgate. But the printed editions have “above.”]. Demolish their altars and shatter their statues; burn their sacred groves with fire and crush their idols; erase their names from those places.

And after some intervening material, when he was speaking about foreigners:

Beware lest you imitate them after they have been overthrown when you enter the land, and seek out their rites, saying, “Just as these nations served their gods, so I too will serve.” You shall not act in this way toward the Lord your God. For they have done to their gods all the abominations that the Lord rejects, offering their sons and daughters and burning them with fire. Whatever I command you, that alone you shall do for the Lord; you shall neither add anything nor take anything away.

### [XIII.]

If a prophet rises in your midst, or someone who claims to have seen a dream, and predicts a sign or portent, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, “Let us go and follow foreign gods whom you do not know, and serve them,” you shall not listen to the words of that prophet [Col. 0898] or dreamer. For the Lord your God is testing you, to make clear whether you love him or not with all your heart and all your soul.

You shall follow the Lord your God and fear him; you shall keep his commandments and hear his voice. You shall serve him and cling to him. But that prophet or maker of dreams shall be killed, because he spoke in order to turn you away from the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery, in order to make you stray from the way that the Lord your God commanded you. Thus you shall remove the evil from your midst.

If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or daughter, or the wife who rests upon your breast, or the friend whom you love as your own soul, tries to persuade you secretly, saying, “Let us go and follow foreign gods whom neither you nor your fathers have known, gods of all the surrounding nations, whether near or far, from one end of the earth to the other,” do not yield to him or listen to him. Your eye shall not spare him, so as to pity and conceal him; instead, you shall kill him immediately. Your hand shall be the first against him, and afterward the hand of all the people; he shall be killed by stoning, because he sought to draw you away from the Lord your God.

And a little later [XIV.]:

You shall not cut yourselves, nor make baldness over the dead, for you are a holy people to the Lord your God.

And elsewhere [XV.]:

If, he says, one of your brothers who dwells within one of the gates of your city, in the land that the Lord your God will give you, falls into poverty, you shall not harden your heart or close your hand; rather, you shall open it to the poor person and lend him whatever you see that he needs.

Beware lest a wicked thought steal upon you and you say in your heart, “The seventh year, the year of remission, is approaching,” and you turn your eyes away from your poor brother, unwilling to lend him what he requests; lest he cry out against you to the Lord and it become sin for you. You shall indeed give to him, and you shall do nothing deceitfully in relieving his needs, so that the Lord your God may bless you at all times and in everything to which you put your hand.

There will never cease to be poor people in the land where you dwell. Therefore I command you to open your hand to your needy and poor brother who lives with you in the land.

And after a little while [XVI.]:

You shall appoint judges and magistrates in all your gates that the Lord your God gives you, for each of your tribes, so that they may judge the people with just judgment; they shall not incline to either side. You shall not accept persons or gifts, for gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the righteous. You shall pursue justice, justice alone, so that you may live and possess the land that the Lord your God will give you.

And a little later:

You shall not make for yourself or set up a statue that the Lord your God hates.

Likewise, a little later [XVII.]:

When there is found among you, within one of the gates that the Lord your God will give you, a man or woman who does evil in the sight of the Lord your God and transgresses his covenant, going to serve foreign gods and worshiping them—the sun, the moon, or any of the host of heaven, which I have not commanded—and this is reported to you, and after careful inquiry you discover that it is true and that such an abomination has been committed in Israel, you shall bring the man or woman who committed this most wicked deed to the gates of your city, and they shall be stoned.

By the testimony of two or three witnesses the one who is to be killed shall perish. No one shall be put to death on the testimony of a single witness against him. The hands of the witnesses shall be the first to kill him, and afterward the hands of the rest of the people shall be raised against him, so that you may remove the evil from your midst.

Likewise, after a little while:

But the man who acts proudly and refuses to obey the command of the priest who at that time ministers to the Lord your God, or the decree [Note: [Col. 0899] Lov. has “by the decree,” as it was once read in certain Bibles. But Am. Er. and the manuscripts have “and the decree”; understand “refuses to obey.” For the Hebrew text reads approximately: “Whoever acts presumptuously, so as not to listen to the priest . . . or to the judge, shall die,” etc. The Greek Septuagint has: “so as not to obey the priest . . . or the judge,” etc.] of the judge—that man shall die. Thus you shall remove the evil from Israel, and all the people, hearing of it, shall fear, so that no one thereafter swells with pride.

And after some intervening material, when he was warning about foreigners [XVIII.]:

Beware, he says, lest you wish to imitate the abominations of those nations. Let there not be found among you anyone who passes his son or daughter through fire, or who consults diviners, observes dreams and omens; nor a sorcerer, enchanter, consulter of pythonic spirits, or diviner who seeks truth from the dead. For the Lord rejects all these things as abominations.

And after a little while [XIX.]:

One witness shall not stand against anyone, whatever the sin or crime may be; every matter shall be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.

If a false witness stands against a man, accusing him of transgression, both parties whose case it is shall stand before the Lord, in the presence of the priests and judges who are in office in those days. When, after very careful examination, they discover that the witness has spoken falsely against his brother, they shall do to him what he intended to do to his brother. Thus you shall remove the evil from your midst, so that the rest, hearing of it, may fear and never again dare to do such things.

You shall not pity him; but you shall exact life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, and foot for foot.

And elsewhere in the same book [XXI.]:

If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who does not obey the command of his father and mother, and, when disciplined, refuses to obey, they shall seize him and bring him to the elders of that city and to the gate of judgment. They shall say to them, “This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious; he refuses to listen to our warnings; he spends his time in revelry, debauchery, and banquets.” The men of the city shall stone him, and he shall die. Thus you shall remove the evil from your midst, and all Israel, hearing of it, shall fear.

And a little later [XXII.]:

You shall not see your brother’s ox or sheep wandering and pass by; instead, you shall lead it back to your brother. Even if your brother is far away and you do not know him, you shall take it into your house, and it shall remain with you until your brother seeks it and receives it. You shall do the same with an ass, a garment, and anything belonging to your brother [Col. 0900] that has been lost. If you find it, you shall not neglect it as though it were another’s.

If you see your brother’s ass or ox fallen on the road, you shall not disregard it, but shall help him raise it.

A woman shall not wear a man’s clothing, nor shall a man use a woman’s clothing; for whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord.

Likewise, a little later:

When you build a new house, you shall make a wall around the edge of its roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you be liable when someone falls from it and plunges downward.

And a little later:

If a man takes a wife and later hates her, and seeks occasions on which to dismiss her, accusing her of a very shameful charge, and says, “I took this woman as my wife, but when I approached her I did not find her a virgin,” then her father and mother shall take and bring with them the signs of her virginity to the elders of the city who are at the gate.

The father shall say, “I gave my daughter to this man as a wife; but because he hates her, he has brought against her a very shameful charge, saying, ‘I did not find your daughter a virgin.’ Yet here are the signs of my daughter’s virginity.” They shall spread the garment before the elders of the city.

The elders of that city shall seize the man and beat him. They shall also condemn him to pay one hundred shekels of silver, which he shall give to the girl’s father, because he has spread a shameful charge against a virgin of Israel. She shall remain his wife, and he shall not be able to dismiss her for all the days of his life.

But if what he alleges is true, and virginity is not found in the girl, they shall cast her outside the doors of her father’s house, and the men of her city shall stone her, and she shall die, because she committed a wicked deed in Israel by committing fornication in her father’s house. Thus you shall remove the evil from your midst.

If a man sleeps with another man’s wife, both shall die—that is, the adulterer and the adulteress—and you shall remove the evil from Israel.

If a man betroths a virgin, and someone finds her in the city and lies with her, you shall bring both of them to the gate of that city, and they shall be stoned: the girl, because she did not cry out, although she was in the city; the man, because he violated his neighbor’s wife. Thus you shall remove the evil from your midst.

But if a man finds in the field a girl who is betrothed, and seizes her and lies with her, he alone shall die. The girl shall suffer nothing, nor is she guilty of death, because just as a robber rises against his brother and kills him, so the girl suffered. She was alone in the field; she cried out, and there was no one to rescue her.

If a man finds a virgin girl who has no fiancé, and seizes her and lies with her, and the matter comes to judgment, the man who slept with her shall give the girl’s father one hundred shekels of silver and shall take her as his wife, because he violated her. He shall not be able to dismiss her for all the days of his life.

No man shall take his father’s wife, nor uncover her covering.

And a little later [XXIII.]:

There shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel, nor a male prostitute among the sons of Israel.

And a little later:

You shall not lend money to your brother at interest, nor grain, nor any other thing; but you may lend at interest to a foreigner.

And a few verses later:

When you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it, for the Lord your God will surely require it of you; and if you delay, it will be reckoned to you as sin. If you do not wish to promise, you will be without sin. But what has once gone forth from your lips you shall observe [Col. 0901] and do as you promised to the Lord your God; you spoke it by your own will and with your mouth.

And a little later [XXIV.]:

You shall not take the lower or upper millstone as a pledge, for he has pledged [Note: [Col. 0901] So the Speculum reads in all the books, with which the old Corbie volume of the Bible agrees. But in the Bibles corrected on the authority of Sixtus it reads “he has opposed.”] his life to you.

If a man is caught kidnapping one of his brothers, one of the children of Israel, and, having sold him, accepts [Note: [Col. 0901] The printed editions have “will accept.” The manuscripts have “accepting.” The Vulgate has “has accepted.”] payment, he shall be killed; thus you shall remove the evil from your midst.

And a few verses later:

When you reclaim from your neighbor something that he owes you, you shall not enter his house to take away his pledge. You shall stand outside, and he will bring out to you whatever he has. But if he is poor, the pledge shall not remain with you overnight; instead, you shall return it to him immediately before sunset, so that he may sleep in his garment and bless you, and you may have justice before the Lord your God.

You shall not deny the wages of your needy and poor brother, whether he is a stranger who dwells with you in the land and within your gates; rather, you shall pay him the price of his labor that same day, before sunset, because he is poor and sustains his life by it. Otherwise he may cry out against you to the Lord, and it will be reckoned to you as sin.

Fathers shall not be put to death for their sons, nor sons for their fathers; each person shall die for his own sin.

And a few verses later:

When you reap your grain in your field and, having forgotten a sheaf, leave it behind, you shall not return to take it; rather, you shall allow the stranger, the orphan, and the widow to take it, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the work of your hands.

If you gather the fruit of your olive trees, whatever remains on the trees you shall not return to gather; instead, you shall leave it for the stranger, the orphan, and the widow.

If you harvest your vineyard, you shall not gather the remaining grapes; they shall go for the use of the stranger, the orphan, and the widow.

Remember that you too were a slave in Egypt, and therefore I command you to do this.

## [XXV]

If a dispute arises between people and they appeal to the judges, then to the one whom they determine to be just they shall award the palm of justice; but the one whom they find guilty they shall condemn for his guilt. If, however, they judge the offender worthy of blows, they shall throw him down and have him beaten in their presence. The number of blows shall correspond to the measure of the offense, but only so that they do not exceed forty, lest your brother, horribly lacerated, die before your eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0901] In the sacred Bibles, *abeat* (“depart”) appears.]

And a little later:

If men have a quarrel among themselves and one begins to fight against the other, and the wife of one, wishing to rescue her husband from the hand of the stronger man, puts out her hand and seizes his genitals, you shall cut off her hand, and you shall not be moved by any mercy toward her.

You shall not have in your purse two kinds of weights, a larger and a smaller; nor shall there be in your house a larger measure and a smaller one. You shall have a just and true weight, and your measure shall be equal and true.

## And after many passages [XXVII]

Cursed is the man who makes a carved or cast image, an abomination to the Lord, the work of the hands of craftsmen, and sets it up in secret; [Col. 0902] and all the people shall answer and say, “Amen.”

Cursed is he who does not honor his father and mother; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Cursed is he who moves his neighbor’s boundary markers; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Cursed is he who causes a blind man to go astray on the road; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Cursed is he who perverts the judgment of the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Cursed is everyone who lies with his father’s wife and uncovers the covering of his bed; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Cursed is he who lies with any animal; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Cursed is he who lies with his sister, the daughter of his father or of his mother; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Cursed is he who lies with his mother-in-law; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Cursed is he who secretly strikes his neighbor; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Cursed is he who accepts gifts in order to strike down an innocent person; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Up to this point we have set down what seemed worth including from the books of Moses. In the books that follow, which are called Joshua, Judges, Kings, and Chronicles, one reads more a history of events than commandments for living. Nevertheless, I did not think that these very few passages from the Book of Joshua should be passed over in this work.

## OF JOSHUA

### [Chapter XXII]

Return and go to your tents and to the land of your possession, which Moses, the servant of the Lord, gave you beyond the Jordan—provided only that you carefully keep and fulfill in deed the commandment and the law that Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded you: that you love the Lord your God, walk in all his ways, observe his commandments, cling to him, and serve him with all your heart and soul.

And in another place [XXIII]:

“After you have entered,” he says, “among the nations that will remain among you, do not swear by the names of their gods, serve them, or worship them; but cling to the Lord your God, as you have done to this day.”

Many passages must also be set down from the Book of Psalms, although the same things are often repeated. But I shall exercise restraint as far as I can, so that this work—which above all ought to be committed to memory—does not extend to excessive length.

## OF THE PSALMS
In Psalm I. Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, who has not stood in the way of sinners, and who has not sat in the seat of mockers. But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night.

In Psalm II. Now therefore, kings, understand; be instructed, judges of the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice with trembling. Worship purely [Note: [Col. 0902] Here follows Jerome’s version. At first he undertook to correct the Psalms that the Church had long sung according to the Septuagint; afterward, in a new translation from the Hebrew, he rendered the entire Psalter into Latin. On this subject there survives his Letter to Sophronius; Augustine also mentions the same work in his Letter to Audax, now no. 261, §5. Finally, Jerome acknowledges this interpretation of the verse, “Worship purely,” and defends it in Book 1 against Rufinus. For the rest, compare Jerome’s Psalter according to the Hebrew, found in volume 7 of his works.], lest he become angry and you perish from the way. When his fury has blazed up shortly afterward, blessed are all who hope in him.

In Psalm IV. Sons of men, how long, my illustrious ones, will you love vanity shamefully, seeking falsehood? And a little later: Be angry, and do not sin; speak in your hearts upon your beds, and be silent. Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness, and trust in the Lord.

In Psalm V. For you are not a God who desires iniquity. Nor will the wicked dwell near you; the unrighteous will not stand in the presence of your eyes. You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak falsehood. The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit.

In Psalm XIV. Lord, who will sojourn in your tent? And who will dwell on your holy mountain? He who walks without blemish and practices righteousness, and speaks truth in his heart; who is not quick with his tongue, has done no evil to his friend, and has not taken up reproach against his neighbor. In his eyes the wicked is despised [Note: [Col. 0903] We have corrected this in accordance with the manuscripts; in the printed editions it read: “His eye despises the wicked.”], but he glorifies those who fear the Lord. He swears so as to bring affliction upon himself, and does not change. He has not given his money at interest, and has not accepted gifts against the innocent. He who does these things will not be moved forever.

In Psalm XXIII. Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who will stand in his holy place? He who is innocent in his hands and pure in heart, who has not lifted up his soul in vain and has not sworn deceitfully. He will receive blessing from the Lord, and righteousness [Note: [Col. 0903] The printed editions have “mercy.” The manuscripts, in accordance with Jerome’s Psalter, have “righteousness.”] from the God of his salvation.

In Psalm XXVI. The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the strength of my life; whom shall I dread? And four verses later [Note: [Col. 0903] In the earlier printed editions: “and the third verse later.” We restore “and four verses later” from the manuscripts.]: If armies should stand against me, my heart will not fear. If war should rise against me, in this I will trust. One thing I asked of the Lord, and this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life; that I may see the beauty of the Lord and attend upon his temple. And elsewhere: My heart said to you, “I have sought his face”; your face, Lord, I will seek. And afterward: Wait for the Lord; be strong, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord.

In Psalm XXVII. Do not hand me over with the ungodly and with those who work iniquity, who speak peace with their friends while evil is in their hearts.

In Psalm XXX. Be strengthened, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who await the Lord.

In Psalm XXXI. Do not become like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding. Bind their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you. Many are the pains of the wicked; but mercy will surround the one who trusts in the Lord. Rejoice in the Lord and exult, righteous ones; and be glad, all you upright in heart.

In Psalm XXXII. Praise the Lord, you righteous; praise is fitting for the upright. And elsewhere: Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom the Lord chose as his inheritance.

In Psalm XXXIII. I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth. In the Lord [Col. 0904] my soul will be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice. Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together. And a few verses later: Taste and see that the Lord is good; blessed is the man who hopes in him. Fear the Lord, you his holy ones, for there is no want for those who fear him. Lions have lacked [Note: [Col. 0904] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with Jerome’s Psalter. The printed editions here had “the rich have lacked.”] and suffered hunger; but those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing. Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life, loving to see good days? Guard your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. And seven verses later [Note: [Col. 0904] The printed editions have “and the fourth verse later.” But the manuscripts have “and seven verses later.” In the printed editions the number was generally expressed incorrectly, and differently from the manuscripts; it is enough to have noted this once.]: The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and he will save the crushed in spirit.

In Psalm XXXVI. Do not contend with the wicked, and do not envy those who work iniquity. For like grass they will quickly wither, and like green herbs they will dry up. Hope in the Lord and do good; sojourn in the land and be nourished by faith. And [Note: [Col. 0904] The printed editions omit “and”; it is found in the Royal Manuscript and in Jerome’s Psalter.] delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart. Roll [Note: [Col. 0904] Lovaniensis has “roll yourself.” Other printed and written codices have “roll,” in accordance with Jerome’s Psalter.] your way upon the Lord, and trust in him, and he himself will act. He will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like midday. Be silent before the Lord, and wait for him; do not contend with the one who prospers in his way, with the man who does what he devises. Abandon anger, and leave wrath; do not contend so as to do evil. For those who do evil will perish, but those who wait for the Lord will inherit the land. Yet a little while, and the wicked will be no more; you will consider his place, and it will not remain. But the meek will inherit the land and delight in an abundance of peace.

And a little later: Better is a little to the righteous man than the many riches of the wicked. For the arms of the wicked will be broken, but the Lord upholds the righteous.

And after a while: Turn away from evil and do good. And elsewhere: Wait for the Lord and keep his way; he will exalt you so that you may possess the land. Preserve simplicity and look upon what is upright, for at the end there will be peace for the man.

In Psalm XXXIX. Blessed is the man who has placed his trust in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0904] Thus in the manuscripts and in Jerome’s Psalter. But in the printed editions: “who has placed his trust in God.”], and has not turned aside toward proud displays and falsehood.

In Psalm XLIII. In the Lord we will rejoice all day long, and in your name we will give thanks forever. And a little later: All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we lied concerning your covenant. Our heart has not turned back, nor have our footsteps deviated from your path. For you have cast us down in the place of dragons, and covered us with the shadow of death. If we had forgotten the name of our God and spread out our hands to a foreign god, would God not investigate this? For he knows the thoughts of the heart. Because of you we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter.

In Psalm XLVI. Sing to God, sing; sing to our king, sing. For God is king of all the earth; sing skillfully.

In Psalm XLIX. Sacrifice praise to God, and pay your vows to the Most High. And call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me.

But to the wicked God said: What have you to do with recounting my precepts, so that you take my covenant upon your lips? You hate discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you consented with him, and your portion was with adulterers. You released your mouth to evil, and your tongue contrived deceit. Sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against the son of your mother you fashioned reproach. You did these things, and I was silent; you thought that I would become like you. I will rebuke you and set these things before your eyes. Understand this, you who forget God, lest I seize you and there be no one to deliver you. He who sacrifices confession glorifies me, and to the one who walks in an orderly way I will show the salvation of God.

In Psalm L. Cleanse me from my iniquity and from my sin. For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. And elsewhere: A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a broken and humbled heart you, O God, will not despise.

In Psalm LI. Why do you boast in wickedness, mighty man? The mercy of the Lord endures all day. Your tongue devises plots, making deceit like a sharp razor. You loved evil more than good, falsehood more than speaking righteousness. You loved every devouring word, deceitful tongue. But God will destroy you forever; he will terrify you, tear you from your tent, and uproot you from the land of the living. The righteous will see and fear, and will laugh at him: Behold the man who did not make God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and was strengthened by his plots. But I, like a flourishing olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God forever and ever. I will give thanks to you forever, for you have acted; and I will wait for your name, for it is good in the presence of your holy ones.

In Psalm LXI. Hope in him at all times, peoples; pour out your heart before him [Note: [Col. 0905] The printed editions have “your hearts.” The manuscripts, in accordance with Jerome’s Psalter, have “your heart.”]; God is our hope. Yet the sons of Adam are vanity, the sons of men are falsehood; together they act deceitfully on false balances. Do not trust in slander, and do not deceive yourselves through robbery. If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.

In Psalm LXIII. The righteous man will rejoice in the Lord and hope in him.

In Psalm LXVIII. For on your account I bore reproach; shame covered my face. I have become a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to the sons of my mother. For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproach of those reproaching you has fallen upon me. I wept over my soul in fasting, and it became a reproach to me. I made sackcloth my garment, and I became a byword to them. Those sitting at the gate spoke against me, and those drinking wine sang songs.

And somewhat later: I will praise the name of God in a song, and magnify him with thanksgiving. This will please God more than a young bull, putting forth horns and hooves. The meek will see and rejoice. [Col. 0906] You who seek God, your soul will live. For the Lord has heard the poor.

In Psalm LXXII. For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed everyone who plays the harlot away from you. But for me, it is good to draw near to God; I have placed my hope in the Lord God, so that I may recount all your proclamations.

In Psalm LXXV. Make vows and fulfill them to the Lord your God. All who surround him will bring gifts to the One who is fearsome, who takes away the spirit of princes, who is fearsome to the kings of the earth.

In Psalm LXXVII. Listen, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in a parable [Note: [Col. 0906] Thus the manuscripts and Jerome’s Psalter. The printed editions here have “in parables.”]; I will speak ancient riddles. And elsewhere: They will recount to their children, so that they may place their hope in God, not forget his thought, and keep his commandments.

In Psalm LXXX. Praise God, our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob. And elsewhere: Israel, if you hear me, let there be no foreign god among you, and do not worship a strange god. I am the Lord your God.

In Psalm LXXXI. How long will you judge unjustly and accept the faces of the wicked? Judge the poor and the orphan; do justice to the needy and the impoverished.

In Psalm LXXXIII. Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will still praise you. Blessed is the man whose strength is in you, whose paths are in his heart: passing through the valley of weeping, they will make it a spring. The teacher will also be clothed with blessing [Note: [Col. 0906] The printed editions have “the learned one.” The manuscripts, together with Jerome’s Psalter, have “the teacher.”]; they will go from strength to strength and will appear before God in Zion.

And a little later: For one day in your courts is better than thousands. I have chosen to be despised in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.

In Psalm XCI. It is good to give thanks to the Lord and sing to your name, O Most High.

In Psalm XCIII. Understand, you foolish among the people; and learn wisdom at last. And a little later: Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law, so that he may rest from the days of affliction until a pit is dug for the wicked.

In Psalm XCIV. Come, let us worship and bow down; let us bend the knee before the face of the Lord our Maker. And two verses later: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, as on the day of testing in the wilderness.

In Psalm XCV. Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord, bless his name; announce his salvation from day to day. Tell his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples. And six verses later: Bring to the Lord, families of the peoples, bring to the Lord glory and strength. Bring to the Lord glory for his name; lift up gifts and enter his courts. Worship the Lord in the beauty of the sanctuary.

In Psalm XCVI. You who love the Lord, hate evil. And three verses later: Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord, and give thanks to the memory of his holiness.

In Psalm XCVII. Shout for joy to the Lord, all the earth; raise your voices, praise, and sing.

In Psalm XCVIII. Exalt the Lord our God and worship the footstool of his feet, for he is holy [Note: [Col. 0906] Thus the manuscripts and Jerome’s Psalter. The printed editions have “for it is holy.”].

In Psalm XCIX. Shout for joy to the Lord, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness. Enter before him with praise. [Col. 0907] Know that the Lord himself is God; he made us, and we are his [Note: [Col. 0907] The printed editions have “and we are not his.” The manuscripts, in accordance with Jerome’s Psalter, have “and we are his.”]. And one verse later: Enter his gates with thanksgiving, his courts with praise; give thanks to him.

In Psalm C. I will walk in the simplicity of my heart in the midst of my house. I will not set before my eyes a word of Belial. I hated the one who practices deviations; he did not cling to me. A crooked heart will depart from me; I will know no evil. The one who speaks secretly against his neighbor—I will kill him [Note: [Col. 0907] In the earlier printed editions it read: “I did not set before my eyes the words of Belial . . . nor did a crooked heart cling to me. I did not know evil departing from me . . . I killed him.” We have corrected these verses in accordance with the manuscripts and Jerome’s Psalter.]. The proud in eyes and lofty in heart—I will not be able to remain with him. My eyes are upon the faithful of the land, so that they may dwell with me; the one who walks in a simple way, he will serve me. The one who does evil will not dwell in the midst of my house [Note: [Col. 0907] In Jerome’s Psalter: “the one who practices deceit.”]; the one who speaks falsehood will not please in the presence of my eyes. In the morning I will destroy all the wicked of the land, so that I may cut off from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity.

In Psalm CII. But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and to eternity upon those who fear him, and his righteousness upon children’s children, for those who keep his covenant and remember his precepts in order to do them.

In Psalm CIV. Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name; make his thoughts known among the peoples. Sing to him and sing psalms to him; speak of all his wonders. Rejoice in his holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord be glad. Seek the Lord and his strength; seek his face continually. Remember his wonders, which he performed, his signs, and the judgments of his mouth.

In Psalm CVII. My heart is ready, O God; I will sing and play the psaltery—indeed, my glory. Arise, psaltery and lyre; I will arise at dawn. I will give thanks to you among the peoples, Lord; I will sing to you among the nations.

In Psalm CX. I will give thanks to the Lord with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous and in the assembly. And elsewhere: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; good instruction belongs to all who practice it; its praise endures forever.

In Psalm CXI. Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he takes great delight in his commandments. And five verses later: The good man is merciful and lends; he will order his words with judgment, for he will not be moved forever. The righteous man will be in everlasting memory; he will not fear evil tidings. His heart is ready, trusting in the Lord; his heart is firm; he will not fear until he looks upon his enemies. He has distributed and given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn will be exalted in glory. The wicked man will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away. The desire of the wicked will perish.

In Psalm CXII. Praise the Lord, servants; praise the name of the Lord. May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever. From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise.

In Psalm CXIII. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see. They have ears, but they will not hear, etc. And a little later: May those who make them and all who trust in them become like them. Israel trusts in the Lord; he is their helper and protector. The house of Aaron trusts in the Lord; he is their helper and protector. Those who fear the Lord trust in the Lord; he is their helper and protector.

In Psalm CXV. I believed, therefore I spoke; I was afflicted greatly. And after a while: What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has repaid me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Glorious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones. And three verses later: I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise, and I will call upon the name of the Lord. I will fulfill my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people, in the courts of the house of the Lord, in your midst, Jerusalem.

In Psalm CXVI. Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him together, all peoples.

In Psalm CXVII. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. Let Israel now say: his mercy endures forever. Let the house of Aaron say: his mercy endures forever. Let those who fear the Lord say: his mercy endures forever. When I was afflicted, I called upon the Lord, and the Lord heard me in an open place. And five verses later: It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in man. It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes. And eight verses later: The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation. A voice of praise and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.

In Psalm CXVIII. Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who keep his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart. And elsewhere: I will walk in a broad place, because I have sought your precepts. I will speak of your testimonies before kings, and I will not be put to shame. I will delight in your commandments, which I have loved. I will lift up my hands toward your commandments, which I have loved, and I will speak of your precepts.

And four verses later: I have not turned aside from your law. I remembered your judgments from of old, Lord, and I was comforted. Horror seized me because of the wicked, because they abandoned your law. Your precepts were songs to me in the house of my sojourning. I remembered your name in the night, Lord, and kept your law. This happened to me because I kept your precepts. “The Lord is my portion,” I said [Note: [Col. 0908] The printed editions have “The Lord.” The manuscripts have “Lord.”], “that I may keep your word.” I entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your word. I considered my ways and turned my feet toward your testimonies. I hastened and did not neglect to keep your commandments. The cords of the wicked entangled me; I did not forget your law. At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for the judgments of your righteousness. I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your precepts.

And a few verses later: But I kept your precepts with my whole heart. Their heart has grown fat like grease, but I meditated on your law. It is good for me that I have been afflicted, so that I might learn your precepts. The law of your mouth is better for me than thousands of gold and silver.

And a few verses later: For your law is my meditation. And shortly afterward: But I will speak of your precepts. And shortly afterward: I have not forgotten your commandments. And two verses later: The proud have dug pits for me that were not in accordance with your law. And two verses later: They almost consumed me on the earth, but I did not abandon your precepts. And seven verses later: If your law had not been my delight, I might have perished in my affliction. I will never forget your precepts, for by them you have given me life. I am yours; save me, for I have sought your commandments. The wicked have waited for me in order to destroy me; I will consider your testimony. I have seen the end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad. How I have loved your law! It is my meditation all day long.

And a little later: I have restrained my feet from every evil path, so that I might keep your words. I have not departed from your judgments, because you instructed me.
