How sweet your word is to my throat—sweeter than honey to my mouth. I considered your precepts; therefore I hated every way of falsehood. Your word is a lamp for my foot and a light for my path.

And seven verses later: My soul is always in my hand, and I have not forgotten your law. The wicked have set a snare for me, but I have not strayed from your precepts. Your testimonies are my inheritance forever, for they are the joy of my heart. I inclined my heart to perform your righteous judgments, for the sake of eternal recompense. I hated the disorderly and loved your law. You are my protection and my shield; I have hoped in your word. Depart from me, evildoers, and I will keep the commandments of my God.

And seven verses later: You have counted all the wicked of the earth as dross; therefore I have loved your testimonies. My flesh bristled with fear of you, and I feared your judgments. I have practiced judgment and righteousness; do not abandon me to those who slander me.

And a few verses later: Therefore I have loved your commandments more than gold and topaz. Therefore I directed myself toward all your precepts; I hated every way of falsehood. Your testimonies are wondrous; therefore my soul has kept them.

And two verses later: I opened my mouth and drew breath, because I desired your commandments. And elsewhere: My zeal consumed me, because my enemies forgot your words. Your word is exceedingly well tested, and your servant loved it. I am small and despised, but I have not forgotten your precepts.

And three verses later: Your commandments are my will. And a little later: See my affliction and deliver me, for I have not forgotten your law. And six verses later: Many are those who persecute and afflict me; I have not declined from your testimonies. I saw those who transgressed against you and grieved, because they did not keep your word. See that I have loved your precepts, Lord; according to your mercy give me life.

And four verses later: I rejoice in your word like one who finds much spoil. I hated and detested falsehood; but I loved your law. Seven times a day I praised you for the judgments of your righteousness. Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling block for them. I awaited your salvation, Lord, and performed your commandments. My soul kept your testimonies and loved them exceedingly. I kept your precepts and testimonies, for all my ways are before you.

And eight verses later: Let your hand be my helper [Col. 0910], for I have chosen your precepts. I desired your salvation, Lord, and your law is my will [Note: [Col. 0910] Thus the manuscripts and Jerome’s Psalter. The printed editions have “my meditation.”]. And two verses later: I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments.

In Psalm CXIX. I was speaking of peace, but they were waging war against it.

In Psalm CXXI. Pray for the peace of Jerusalem; may it be well with those who love her. And two verses later: For the sake of my brothers and neighbors I was speaking of peace to you. For the sake of the house of the Lord our God I sought good things for you.

In Psalm CXXII. To you I lifted my eyes, who dwell in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God until he has mercy on us.

In Psalm CXXIV. Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; Jerusalem is immovable and inhabited forever.

In Psalm CXXVII. Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord, who walks in his ways [Note: [Col. 0910] The printed editions have “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.” We follow the manuscripts and Jerome’s Psalter.].

In Psalm CXXIX. I waited for the Lord; my soul waited, and I hoped in his word.

In Psalm CXXX. Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; I have not walked among great and wondrous things beyond me. If I have not composed and made my soul silent, like a weaned child with its mother, so is my soul as a weaned child with me. Hope, Israel, in the Lord, from now and forever.

In Psalm CXXXII. Behold, how good and how beautiful it is for brothers to dwell together as one.

In Psalm CXXXIII. Behold, bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy place [Note: [Col. 0910] The printed editions have “toward the holy places.” The manuscripts, in accordance with Jerome’s Psalter, have “toward the holy place.”], and bless the Lord.

In Psalm CXXXIV. Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, servants. You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing to his name, for it is fitting. And shortly afterward: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands. They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see, etc. And a little later: May those who make them and all who trust in them become like them. House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.

In Psalm CXXXV. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. Give thanks to the God of gods, for his mercy endures forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy endures forever. And at the end of the psalm: Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his mercy endures forever.

In Psalm CXXXVI. If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten. Let my tongue cling to my throat if I do not remember you, Jerusalem; if I do not place Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy.

In Psalm CXXXVIII. Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and did I not stand apart against your adversaries? I hated them with perfect hatred; they became enemies to me.

In Psalm CXXXIX. Do not grant, Lord, the desires of the wicked; do not let his crimes be brought forth and exalted. And four verses later: The talkative man will not prosper in the land.

In Psalm CXL. Let the righteous rebuke me in mercy and reprove me; let not the oil of bitterness make my head fat. And five verses later: For my eyes are toward you, Lord; in you I have hoped. Do not empty my soul.

In Psalm CXLI. With my voice I cried out to the Lord; with my voice I entreated the Lord. I will pour out my speech before him; I will announce my tribulation before him. And six verses later: I cried out to you, Lord; I said, “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living.”

In Psalm CXLII. I meditated on all your works; I spoke of the works of your hands. I spread out my hands to you; my soul is like thirsty land before you. And three verses later: Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I trust in you. Make known to me the way in which I walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you. Deliver me from my enemies, Lord; I have taken refuge in you.

In Psalm CXLIII. Deliver me and rescue me from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of falsehood. May our sons be like a flourishing plantation in their youth. Our daughters like corners adorned in the likeness of a temple. May our storehouses be full, overflowing from this into that. May our livestock be in thousands, innumerable in our streets; may our bulls be fat. May there be no breach, no going out, and no wailing in our streets. Blessed is the people whose condition is such; blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.

In Psalm CXLIV. I will exalt you, Lord, my God and king, and bless your name forever and beyond. Every day I will bless you, and I will praise your name continually forever. And two verses later: Generation after generation will praise your works, and they will proclaim your mighty deeds. I will speak of the beauty of the glory of your greatness and of the words of your wonders. They will speak of the strength of your terrible deeds, and they will recount your greatness. They will speak of the memory of your abundant goodness, and they will praise your righteousness.

And three verses later: And your holy ones will bless you. They will speak of the glory of your kingdom and tell of your mighty deeds, to make known to the sons of men his mighty deeds and the glory of the beauty of his kingdom.

And a little later: The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him; he will hear their cry and save them. The Lord guards all who love him, but he will crush all the wicked. My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord, and all flesh will bless his holy name forever and continually.

In Psalm CXLV. Praise the Lord, my soul; I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I exist. Do not trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation. And two verses later: Blessed is the one whose God of Jacob is his helper, whose hope is in the Lord his God.

In Psalm CXLVI. Praise the Lord, for he is good; a song of our God [Note: [Col. 0911] Thus the manuscripts and Jerome’s Psalter. The printed editions have “to our God.”], for it is fitting; praise is beautiful. And a few verses later: The Lord receives the meek; he humbles the wicked to the ground. Sing to the Lord with thanksgiving; sing to our God. And four verses later: He does not delight in the strength of a horse, nor is he pleased by the legs of a man. The Lord is pleased with those who fear him and await his mercy.

In Psalm CXLVIII. Let the kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth, young men and maidens, old men together with children, praise the name of the Lord.

In Psalm CXLIX. Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is in the assembly of the holy ones. Let Israel rejoice in its Maker; let the sons of Zion exult in their king. And three verses later: He will exalt the meek in Jesus. The holy ones will exult in glory; they will praise him on their couches. The exaltations of God will be in their throats.

In Psalm CL. Praise the Lord in his holy places; praise him in the strength of his power. Praise him for his mighty deeds; praise him according to the abundance of his greatness. And at the end of the psalm: Let everything that breathes praise the Lord.

These are the passages we have collected from the Book of Psalms, in which each person may examine his own life, if he desires to make progress. Here we admonish the reader to read what I have set down from the Psalms as though it were one continuous psalm, silently passing over my words, which I inserted for this purpose: so that, if he wishes, he may see where what I have set down is written—that is, at what verse or in what place of that same psalm. For if these are omitted, whoever examines only the words of the Psalms in continuous reading will be affected much more pleasantly, and therefore more profitably, by the divine utterances.

Now we shall collect from the books of Solomon whatever will appear necessary for this work, beginning with Proverbs. If this book is rightly understood, almost the whole of it will serve to form pious conduct. But I pass over the obscure passages: let readers and lovers of spiritual literature have those passages by which they may exercise themselves. In this work we have decided to include those passages whose meaning can readily be applied to the conduct of life. Although I may seem to many to have omitted passages that are utterly clear, some things are more obscure precisely where they are thought to be obvious. For what seems clearer, or what is more absurd if one wishes to take it literally, than what is written there: “Abstain from alien water, and do not drink from a foreign spring” [Note: [Col. 0912] The Vulgate version lacks this sentence, “from alien water,” etc.; yet it was familiar to Augustine, and he often explained it when dealing with the Donatists, who misused it perversely. It is found among the Septuagint at Proverbs 9:18. From their translation, the other testimonies set down below also came to his mind, except that the Septuagint expresses this one in the plural: *cheîres dè andreiôn ploutizousin*, “the hands of the strong make rich.”]? Or what value would it have for correcting conduct, unless a deeper meaning were required there, in the saying: “Poverty humbles a man, but the hands of the strong make rich” (Prov. X. 4)? For neither being poor nor being strong-handed lies within the power of good people, and both have happened to many very wicked persons; and, if this proverb is wrongly understood, it could incite poor but strong men to think that they ought to enrich themselves by robbery. Who, moreover, would not laugh if he thought that what is written there had been stated literally: “For sons are not born to the wicked” (ibid. XXIV. 20)?

We shall therefore leave aside all such passages, as well as those in which something is urged at somewhat greater length, when the thing urged and commanded is not obscure. Rather, what should be placed in this *Mirror* is what those may examine who are already persuaded that they ought to live well and laudably, but are seeking what they should desire and observe in order to do so. These, then, are the passages from Solomon’s Proverbs that we believe should be included.

## FROM THE PROVERBS

### [Chapter I]

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge. Fools despise wisdom and instruction. Hear, my son, your father’s discipline, and do not abandon your mother’s law.”

And fourteen verses later, when he was speaking about murderers:

“They lie in wait for their own blood,” he says, “and devise plots against their own lives. Thus the paths of every greedy man seize the lives of those who possess them.”

Again, four verses later:

“How long, little ones, will you love childishness, and fools desire what is harmful to them, and the imprudent hate knowledge? Then they will call upon me, and I shall not answer; they will rise early, and shall not find me, because they hated discipline and did not receive the fear of the Lord, nor submit to my counsel, and rejected all my correction. Therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way and be filled with their own counsels. The turning away of the little ones will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them. But whoever listens to me shall rest without terror and enjoy abundance, with the fear of evils removed.”

And three verses later [II]:

“For if you call upon wisdom and incline your heart to prudence; if you seek her as money and dig her out as treasures, then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God, because the Lord gives wisdom, and from his mouth come knowledge and prudence. He preserves the safety of the upright and protects those who walk simply, guarding the paths of justice and keeping watch over the ways of the holy. Then you will understand justice, judgment, equity, and every good path. If wisdom enters your heart and knowledge pleases your soul, counsel will guard you and prudence will preserve you, so that you may be delivered from the evil way and from the man who speaks perverse things—those who abandon the straight path and walk along dark ways, who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things, whose ways are crooked and whose steps are infamous. So that you may be delivered from the alien woman and from the foreign woman who makes her words smooth, who abandoned the guide of her youth and forgot the covenant of her God.”

And thirteen verses later [III]:

“Let mercy and truth not abandon you; bind them around your throat and write them on the tablets of your heart, and you will find grace and good discipline before God and human beings. Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean upon your own prudence. In all your ways think upon him, and he himself will direct your steps. Do not be wise in your own eyes. Fear God and depart from evil.”

And one verse later:

“Honor the Lord from your substance and from the first fruits of all your produce.”

And two verses later:

“My son, do not reject the Lord’s discipline, nor lose heart when you are corrected by him. For whom the Lord loves, he corrects, and he takes pleasure in him as a father does in a son. Blessed is the man who finds wisdom and who abounds in prudence. Her acquisition is better than trading in silver, and her first fruits are better than gold; she is more precious than all riches, and nothing that is desired can be compared with her.”

[Col. 0914] And ten verses later:

“My son, let these things not flow away from your eyes: keep the law and counsel.”

And nine verses later:

“Do not withhold doing good from one who can do it; if you are able, do it yourself also. Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I shall give to you,’ when you can give immediately. Do not plot evil against your friend when he trusts in you. Do not contend with a man without cause.”

And seven verses later:

“He himself will mock the mockers, but he will give grace to the gentle.”

And forty-three verses later [Note: [Col. 0914] I was reluctant to note the extremely frequent errors in the numbering of verses. Once these had been introduced into the Amerbach edition, subsequent editions thereafter consistently retained them, despite the resistance of manuscript copies. Nevertheless, it seems necessary here not to be silent about several of the more significant corrections. For in the printed editions, instead of “And forty-three verses later,” one read “And twenty-four verses later”; likewise, below, where you now have “And ninety-seven verses later,” they had “And several verses later”; and where it now reads “And fifty-seven verses later,” they had “And some verses later.” In these and almost countless other places we have restored the reading of the manuscripts, so that it may more easily be understood what kind of verses, and of what measure, those verses were that Augustine counted.] [IV]:

“Guard your heart with all vigilance, because from it life proceeds. Remove the perverse mouth from yourself, and let deceitful lips be far from you. Let your eyes look straight ahead, and let your eyelids precede your steps. Direct the path of your feet, and let all your ways be made firm. Do not turn aside to the right or to the left. Turn your foot away from evil. For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right, but the ways on the left are perverse. He himself makes your courses straight, and he will lead your journeys forward in peace.”

### [V]

“My son, attend to my wisdom and incline your ear to my prudence, so that you may guard your thoughts and your lips preserve discipline. For the lips of a prostitute drip with honey, and her throat is smoother than oil. But her end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet descend into death, and her steps penetrate to the underworld.”

And ninety-seven verses later [VI]:

“Do not let your heart desire her beauty, lest you be captured by her glances. For the price of a prostitute is scarcely one loaf of bread, but a woman takes the precious life of a man. Can a man conceal fire in his bosom so that his garments do not burn? Or can he walk upon burning coals without scorching his feet? So is he who enters another man’s wife: he will not be clean when he touches her. The guilt is not great when someone has stolen, for he steals to fill his hungry soul; yet when discovered he will repay sevenfold and give over all the substance of his house. But an adulterer, because of the poverty of his heart, destroys his own life.”

And four verses later [VII]:

“My son, keep my words and store up my commandments for yourself. Keep [Note: [Col. 0914] Manuscripts: ‘Examine.’] my commands and live, and keep my law as the pupil of your eye.”

And fifty-seven verses later [VIII]:

“Understand, little ones, shrewdness; and you foolish, pay attention.”

And two verses later:

“My throat will meditate on truth, and my lips will detest the impious” [Note: [Col. 0914] So the manuscripts read, in accordance with the Vulgate. But the printed editions had: “And my lips do not bear witness against the impious.”].

And three verses later [Col. 0915]:

“Receive my discipline, and not money; love instruction more than gold. For wisdom is better than all the most precious things, and nothing desirable can be compared with her.”

And two verses later:

“The fear of the Lord hates evil; it detests arrogance, pride, a crooked way, and a double-tongued mouth.”

And six verses later:

“I love those who love me, and those who keep watch for me early will find me. With me are riches and glory, magnificent wealth and justice. My fruit is better than gold and precious stone, and my produce is better than refined silver. I walk in the ways of justice, in the midst of the paths of judgment, to enrich those who love me and fill their treasures.”

And twenty-three verses later:

“Blessed is the man who hears me, who watches daily at my doors and keeps guard at the posts of my doorway. Whoever finds me will find life and draw salvation from the Lord. But whoever sins against me injures his own soul. All who hate me love death.”

And nine verses later [IX]:

“Abandon childishness and live, and walk in the ways of prudence. Whoever instructs a mocker does himself an injury, and whoever rebukes an impious man brings a stain upon himself. Do not rebuke a mocker, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you. Give an opportunity to the wise, and wisdom will be added to him. Teach the just man, and he will hasten to receive it. The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and the knowledge of the holy is prudence.”

And eighteen verses later [X]:

“Treasure gained by iniquity will not profit, but justice will deliver from death.”

And four verses later:

“He who gathers in the harvest is a wise son, but he who snores in summer is a son of disgrace.”

And four verses later:

“The wise in heart will receive commandments, but the fool is beaten by his lips. Whoever walks simply walks securely, but whoever corrupts his ways will be exposed. Whoever signals with his eye causes pain; the fool will be beaten by his lips. The mouth of the just is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the impious conceals iniquity. Hatred stirs up quarrels, but love covers all offenses. Wisdom is found on the lips of the wise, and a rod on the back of one who lacks sense. The wise conceal wisdom, but the mouth of the fool is near to disgrace.”

And four verses later:

“The way of life is for one who keeps discipline; but whoever abandons reproof goes astray. Lying lips conceal hatred. Whoever utters an insult is a fool. In much speaking sin will not be absent; but whoever restrains his lips is most prudent. The tongue of the just is refined silver; the heart of the impious is worth nothing. The lips of the just instruct many; but those who are unlearned will die in poverty of heart. The blessing of the Lord makes rich, and affliction will not be joined to it. As though laughing, the fool commits crime; but wisdom is prudence for a man. What the impious fears will come upon him; what the just desire will be given to them.”

And two verses later:

“As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the lazy person to those who sent him. The fear of the Lord adds days, but the years of the impious will be shortened. The expectation of the just is joy, but the hope of the impious will perish. The strength of the simple is the way of the Lord, and terror belongs to those who work evil. The just will never be shaken, but the impious will not dwell on the earth. The mouth of the just will bring forth wisdom; the tongue of the perverse will perish. The lips of the just consider what is acceptable, but the mouth of the impious speaks perverse things.”

### [XI]

“Deceitful scales are an abomination to God, but an accurate weight is his will. Where there is pride, there will also be disgrace; but where there is humility, there is wisdom. The simplicity of the just will guide them, and the treachery of the perverse will destroy them. Riches will not profit on the day of vengeance, but justice will deliver from death. The justice of the simple will direct his way, but the impious will fall through his own wickedness. The justice of the upright will deliver them, and the wicked will be caught in their own snares. When an impious man dies, there will be no hope thereafter, and the expectation of the anxious will perish.”

And five verses later [Note: [Col. 0916] The Royal manuscript has: “And three verses later.” The Chartres manuscript: “And four verses later.” Perhaps it should be read: “And eight verses later.”]:

“Whoever despises his friend is lacking in heart; but the prudent man will be silent. Whoever walks deceitfully reveals secrets, but whoever is faithful in spirit [Note: [Col. 0916] In the Royal manuscript, instead of *animi*, “in spirit,” it reads *amici*, “of a friend.” Both words are received together in Bibles corrected under the authority of Sixtus. Nevertheless, *amici* is absent from the ancient Corbie biblical manuscript.] conceals what has been entrusted. Where there is no governor, the people will fall; but there is safety where there is much counsel. The one who guarantees for a stranger will be afflicted by evil, but whoever avoids snares will be secure.”

And two verses later:

“A merciful man benefits his own soul, but whoever is cruel rejects even his own relatives.”

And three verses later:

“A perverse heart is an abomination to the Lord, but his will is with those who walk simply. Hand in hand, the wicked will not be innocent; but the offspring of the just will be saved.”

And two verses later:

“The desire of the just is wholly good; the expectation of the impious is fury. Some distribute their own goods and become richer; others seize what is not theirs and are always in want. The soul that blesses will be made fat, and whoever gives drink will himself also be given drink. Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples, but blessing will be upon the head of those who sell it. He rises early with good result who seeks good, but whoever searches out evil will be overcome by it. Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the just will sprout like a flourishing leaf.”

And four verses later:

“If the just man receives recompense on earth, how much more the impious and the sinner?”

### [XII]

“Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but whoever hates reproof is foolish. Whoever is good will receive grace from the Lord, but whoever trusts in his own thoughts acts impiously. A man will not be strengthened by wickedness, and the root of the just will not be moved.”

And several verses later [Note: [Col. 0916] The manuscripts have: “And ten verses later”; nevertheless, more verses appear to have intervened, unless perhaps these verses were unusually long.]:

“The desire of the impious is a stronghold of the worst things, but the root of the just will prosper. Because of the sins of the lips, ruin draws near to the wicked, but the just will escape from distress. Each person will be filled with good things from the fruit of his mouth, and he will be repaid according to the work of his hands. The way of the fool is right in his own eyes, but the wise man listens to counsel.”

And four verses later:

“There is one who makes a promise and is pierced, as it were, by the sword of conscience; but the tongue of the wise is health. The lip of truth will be firm forever, but the sudden witness [Col. 0917] prepares a lying tongue. Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but joy will follow those who make plans for peace. Nothing that happens to the just will grieve him, but the impious will be filled with evil. Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0917] The Vulgate has: “An abomination to the Lord.”], but those who act faithfully are pleasing to him. A cunning man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools provokes folly.”

And two verses later:

“Sorrow in a man’s heart will humble him, but a good word will make him glad. Whoever overlooks a loss for the sake of a friend is just; but the way of the impious will deceive them. The fraudulent man will not find gain, and the substance of a man will be the price of gold. In the path of justice there is life, but the crooked way leads to death.”

### [XIII]

“A wise son is his father’s instruction, but the mocker does not listen when he is rebuked. From the fruit of his mouth a man will be filled with good things, but the soul of transgressors is wicked. Whoever guards his mouth guards his soul, but whoever is thoughtless in speaking will experience evils. The lazy man wants and does not want, but the soul of those who work will be enriched. The just man detests a lying word, but the impious man brings shame and will be put to shame. Justice guards the way of the innocent, but wickedness overthrows sinners. One is as though rich when he has nothing, and another is as though poor when he possesses many riches. A man’s riches are the ransom of his soul; but the poor man does not endure reproof. The light of the just gives joy, but the lamp of the impious will be extinguished. Among the proud there are always quarrels, but those who do everything with counsel are guided by wisdom. Wealth acquired hastily will diminish, but what is gathered gradually by hand will increase. Hope that is delayed afflicts the soul; desire when it comes is a tree of life. Whoever disparages something binds himself for the future, but whoever fears the commandment will live in peace. The law of the wise is a fountain of life, so that he may turn away from the ruin of death. Good instruction gives grace; on the way of the despised there is a pit.”

And several verses later [Note: [Col. 0917] The Royal manuscript has: “And twelve verses later.”]:

“Whoever spares his rod hates his son, but whoever loves him diligently instructs him. The just man eats and fills his soul, but the belly of the impious is insatiable.”

And two verses later [XIV]:

“Whoever walks on the straight road and fears God will be despised by the one who walks on an infamous way. In the mouth of a fool is the rod of pride, but the lips of the wise guard them.”

And two verses later:

“A faithful witness will not lie; a deceitful witness brings forth a lie. The mocker seeks wisdom and does not find it; instruction is easy for the wise. Go away from a foolish man, and do not recognize the lips of imprudence [Note: [Col. 0917] The Vulgate has: “and he does not know the lips of prudence.”]. The wisdom of the shrewd person is to understand his way, but the imprudence of fools is wandering. The fool mocks sin; among the just grace will remain. A heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not have a stranger share in its joy. The house of the impious will be destroyed, but the tents of the just will flourish. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end leads to death. Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, [Col. 0918] and mourning takes possession of the end of joy.”

And three verses later:

“The wise man fears and turns away from evil; the fool leaps across it and is confident. The impatient man will work folly, and the cunning man is hateful.”

And four verses later:

“Whoever despises his neighbor sins, but whoever has mercy on the poor will be blessed. Those who work evil go astray; mercy and truth prepare good things. In every work [Note: [Col. 0918] The manuscripts have: “in every good work.”] there will be abundance, but where there are many words there is often want.”

And four verses later:

“In the fear of the Lord there is confidence of strength, and for his children there will be hope. The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, so that he may turn away [Note: [Col. 0918] In the more carefully corrected sacred Bibles: “so that they may turn away.”] from the ruin of death.”

And two verses later:

“Whoever is patient is governed by much prudence, but whoever is impatient exalts his own folly. The health of the heart is the life of the flesh, but envy is the rottenness of the bones. Whoever slanders the needy reproaches his Maker, but whoever has mercy on the poor honors him.”

And seven verses later [XV]:

“A gentle answer breaks anger, but a harsh word stirs up fury. The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge, but the mouth of fools pours forth folly.”

And seventeen verses later:

“The pestilent man does not love the one who rebukes him, nor does he walk with the wise.”

And twelve verses later:

“Better is a little with the fear of the Lord than great and insatiable treasures. Better is an invitation to vegetables with love than to a fattened calf with hatred. An angry man provokes quarrels, but the patient man calms those that have been stirred up. The way of the lazy is like a hedge of thorns, but the way of the just is without stumbling. A wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish man despises his mother.”

And two verses later:

“Thoughts are scattered where there is no counsel, but where there are many counselors they are confirmed. A man rejoices in the decision of his mouth, and an opportune word is best. The path of life is above the instructed man, so that he may turn away from the lowest underworld.”

And four verses later:

“He who pursues greed troubles his own house, but whoever hates gifts will live. The mind of the just meditates on obedience, but the mouth of the impious overflows with evils. The Lord is far from the impious, but he will hear the prayers of the just. The light of the eyes gladdens the soul; good report makes the bones fat. The ear that hears reproofs of life will dwell among the wise. Whoever rejects discipline despises his own soul, but whoever submits to reproof possesses a heart. The fear of the Lord is the discipline of wisdom, and humility precedes glory.”

### [XVI]

“It belongs to a man to prepare his mind, and to God to govern his tongue. All the ways of human beings are open to his eyes; the Lord is the weigher of spirits. Commit your works to the Lord, and your thoughts will be directed. The Lord has made everything for himself, even the impious for the evil day. Everyone who is arrogant is an abomination to the Lord; even if hand is joined to hand [Note: [Col. 0918] The Vulgate now reads: “hands joined to hand”; and below, after “he will not be innocent,” it inserts this sentence: “The beginning of the good way is to do justice,” etc. This is neither in the Hebrew nor in the ancient Corbie Bibles of the Vulgate version; it was taken from the Septuagint.], he will not be innocent. Iniquity is redeemed by mercy and truth, and evil is avoided through the fear of the Lord. When a man’s ways please the Lord, he will turn even his enemies toward peace. Better is a little with justice than many fruits with iniquity. A man’s heart arranges his way, but it belongs to the Lord to direct his steps. Divination is on the lips of a king; his mouth will not err in judgment. Weight and scales are the Lord’s judgments, and all the stones of the [sacculus, money] pouch are his work [Note: [Col. 0919] It should read *sacculi*, “of the pouch,” not *saeculi*, “of the age”; and a little below, *diligetur*, “will be loved,” not *dirigetur*, “will be directed.” These errors had also entered the sacred Bibles.]. Those who act impiously are abominable to a king, because the throne is established by justice. Just lips are the delight of kings; whoever speaks rightly will be loved. The king’s indignation is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it. In the brightness of the king’s face there is life, and his clemency is like the late rain. Acquire wisdom, because it is better than gold, and obtain prudence, because it is more precious than silver. The path of the just turns away from evils; whoever guards his soul keeps his way. Pride precedes destruction, and before a fall the spirit is exalted. It is better to be humbled with the gentle than to divide spoils with the proud. The instructed man will find good things in speech, and blessed is whoever hopes in the Lord. Whoever is wise in heart will be called prudent, and whoever is gentle in speech will receive greater things.”

And seventeen verses later:

“Better is a patient man than a strong man, and whoever rules his own soul is better than one who captures cities. Lots are cast into the lap, but they are directed by the Lord.”

### [XVII]

“Better is a dry morsel with joy than a house full of sacrifices with quarrelling. A wise servant will rule over foolish sons and will divide an inheritance among brothers. As silver is tested by fire and gold in the furnace, so the Lord tests hearts. An evil man obeys an iniquitous tongue, and a deceitful man submits to lying lips. Whoever despises the poor reproaches his Maker, and whoever rejoices in another’s ruin will not go unpunished. The crown of old men is their children’s children, and the glory of sons is their fathers. Well-composed words do not suit a fool, nor a lying lip a prince. A most pleasing jewel is the expectation of one who waits; wherever he turns, he will understand prudently. Whoever conceals an offense seeks friendship, but whoever repeats it a second time separates allies. Reproof benefits the prudent more than a hundred blows benefit a fool. The wicked man always seeks quarrels, but a cruel angel will be sent against him. It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool confident in his own folly. Whoever repays good with evil will not see evil depart from his house. Whoever releases water is the beginning of quarrels, and before suffering insult he abandons judgment. Both the one who justifies the impious and the one who condemns the just are abominable to God.”

And sixteen verses later:

“The impious man receives gifts from the bosom in order to pervert the paths of judgment. Wisdom shines on the face of the prudent; the eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth.”

And three verses later [Note: [Col. 0919] The manuscripts have: “And seventeen verses later,” an obvious error of the scribes; or else the copy of Proverbs that Augustine read contained more sayings at that place than the sacred Bibles.]:

“Whoever restrains his words is learned and prudent, and a man of educated spirit is precious.”

And two verses later [XVIII]:

“Whoever wishes to withdraw from a friend seeks opportunities; he will be reproachable at all times.”

[Col. 0920] And six verses later:

“To favor the person of the impious is not good, so that you may turn away from the truth of judgment.”

And six verses later:

“Whoever is slack and negligent in his work is a brother to one who dissipates his own work. The name of the Lord is a most fortified tower; the just man runs to it and will be exalted.”

And two verses later:

“Before he is crushed, a man’s heart is exalted; and before he is glorified, he is humbled.”

And seven verses later:

“The just man is the first to accuse himself; his friend comes and examines him. The lot puts an end to disputes and decides even among the powerful. A brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city, and judgments are like the bars of cities.”

And two verses later:

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruits. Whoever finds a good wife finds a good thing and will draw delight from the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0920] The printed editions added here: “Whoever drives away a good wife drives away a good thing; but whoever keeps an adulteress is foolish and senseless.” This has also now been inserted into the Vulgate from the Septuagint. But it is not found in the ancient Corbie Bibles or in the Hebrew, nor is it present in Augustine’s *Mirror* in the manuscripts, which immediately continue as follows: “with entreaties,” etc.].

“The poor man will speak with entreaties, but the rich man will answer harshly. A man who is friendly in companionship will be a closer friend than a brother.”

### [XIX]

“Better is a poor man who walks in his simplicity than a rich man who twists his lips and is foolish. Where there is no knowledge of the soul, there is no good; and whoever is hasty stumbles with his feet. A man’s folly undermines his steps, and in his heart he rages against God. Riches add many friends, but from the poor even those whom he had withdraw. A false witness will not go unpunished, and whoever speaks lies will not escape. Many honor the person of the powerful and are friends of one who gives gifts. The brothers of a poor man hate him; moreover, his friends have withdrawn far from him. Whoever pursues only words will have nothing, but whoever possesses understanding loves his own soul.”

And ten verses later:

“Laziness brings on sleep, and the slack soul will hunger. Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his soul, but whoever neglects his ways will be put to death. Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, and he will repay him in return. Discipline your son, and do not despair.”

And six verses later:

“A needy man is merciful, and a poor man is better than a lying man. The fear of the Lord leads to life, and in abundance he will dwell without visitation by the wicked one [Note: [Col. 0920] In the Vulgate: “the worst things,” although in the Corbie Bibles: “the worst thing.”].”

And two verses later:

“When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool becomes wiser; but if you rebuke a wise man, he will understand discipline. Whoever afflicts his father and drives away [Note: [Col. 0920] It should read “drives away,” as in the corrected Bibles. The Royal manuscript has here, instead of “flees,” “confounds.”] his mother is disgraceful and unhappy. Do not cease, my son, to hear instruction, nor ignore words of knowledge. An unjust witness mocks judgment, and the mouth of the impious devours iniquity. Judgments are prepared for mockers, and blows for striking the bodies of fools.”

### [XX]

“Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous; whoever delights in these will not be wise.”

And several verses later:

“Weight and weight, measure and measure: both are an abomination before God. A boy is known by his pursuits, whether his works are clean and upright.”

[Col. 0921] And two verses later:

“Do not love sleep, lest poverty oppress you; open your eyes and be filled with bread.”

And seventeen verses later:

“Weight and weight are an abomination before God; deceitful scales are not good.”

And twenty-five verses later [XXI]:

“Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard. A hidden gift extinguishes anger, and a gift in the bosom, the greatest indignation. It is joy for the just to practice judgment, but terror for those who work iniquity. A man who strays from the way of instruction will be counted among the assembly of giants.”

And nine verses later:

“Whoever guards his mouth and tongue guards his soul from distress. The proud and arrogant person who acts in anger is called unlearned. Desires kill the lazy, for his hands refused to work at all. All day he desires and longs, but the just man gives and does not cease. The sacrifices of the impious are abominable, because they are offered from crime. A lying witness will perish; a man who speaks well [Note: [Col. 0921] In the sacred Bibles: “an obedient man.”] will speak victoriously.”

And five verses later [XXII]:

“A good name is better than great riches.”

And fifteen verses later:

“Whoever is inclined to mercy will be blessed, for he has given of his bread to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0921] At this place the Septuagint inserts: “He who gives gifts will acquire victory and honor,” etc. This saying was inserted into the Vulgate, although it is neither in the Hebrew nor in the Corbie codex of the Vulgate version.].

“Drive out the mocker, and quarrelling will go out with him; causes and insults will cease.”

And four verses later:

“The lazy man says, ‘There is a lion outside; I shall be killed in the middle of the streets.’”

And three verses later [Note: [Col. 0921] The Royal manuscript has: “And two verses later.”]:

“Whoever slanders the poor in order to increase his riches will himself give to one who is richer and will be in want.”

And eight verses later:

“Do not use violence against the poor because he is poor, and do not crush the needy at the gate, because the Lord will judge his case and will pierce those who pierced his soul. Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his paths and take a stumbling-block for your soul. Do not be among those who pledge their hands and offer themselves as sureties for debts.”

And after some interval [XXIII]:

“Do not withdraw discipline from a boy, for if you strike him with a rod, he will not die. You will strike him with a rod, and you will free his soul from the underworld.”

And eight verses later:

“Do not be among the banquets of drinkers, nor among the feasts of those who bring together meats for eating.”

And twenty verses later:

“Do not look at wine when it becomes yellow, when its color shines in the glass. It enters smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent and spread poison like a basilisk.”

And seven verses later [XXIV]:

“Do not envy,” he says, “evil men, nor desire to be with them, because their mind meditates on robberies and their lips speak fraud.”

Again, sixteen verses later:

“Rescue those who are led to death, and do not cease to free those who are dragged to destruction. If you say, ‘Our strength is insufficient,’ the one who examines the heart understands; nothing escapes the Savior of your soul, and he will repay a man according to his works.”

Again, nine verses later:

“When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he is ruined, let your heart not exult, lest perhaps the Lord see it, be displeased, and turn his anger away from him. Do not contend with the worst men [Note: [Col. 0922] The Chartres manuscript has: “with the impious.”], nor envy the impious.”

And two verses later:

“Fear the Lord, my son, and the king, and do not mingle with slanderers, because their destruction will suddenly arise; and who knows the ruin of either of them?”

“These things also apply to the wise: To recognize a person in judgment is not good. Whoever says to an impious man, ‘You are just,’ the peoples will curse him and the tribes will detest him. Those who rebuke will be praised, and blessing will come upon them. He will kiss the lips of the one who answers with upright words.”

And two verses later:

“Do not be a false witness against your neighbor, nor deceive anyone with your lips. Do not say, ‘As he did to me, so I shall do to him; I shall repay each person according to his work.’ I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, nettles had entirely filled it, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed. When I saw this, I laid it to heart and learned discipline from the example.”

And twenty verses later [XXV]: “What your eyes have seen, do not bring forth hastily in a quarrel, lest afterward you be unable to correct it, when you have disgraced your friend. Plead your case with your friend, and do not reveal a secret to a stranger, lest perhaps, when he hears it, he insult you and never cease reproaching you. Golden apples in beds of silver is one who speaks a word at the proper time. A golden earring and a shining pearl is one who reproves a wise person and an obedient ear.”

And seventeen verses later: “Vinegar on soda is one who sings songs to a wicked heart.” [Note: [Col. 0922] Nothing is missing here in the Hebrew or in the ancient Corbie Bibles. But in printed Bibles this verse is supplemented with: “As a moth to a garment,” etc.] “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink; for you will heap burning coals upon his head, and the Lord will repay you.”

And ten verses later: “Like an open city without a surrounding wall, so is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speech.”

And two verses later [XXVI]: “As a bird flying elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0922] Printed editions have ‘to the heights.’ But the Carnotensis manuscript has ‘elsewhere,’ as it is read in uncorrupted Bibles.], and a sparrow going wherever it will, so an undeserved curse uttered against anyone will come upon him. A whip for a horse, a bridle for an ass, and a rod for the back of fools. Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself.”

And ten verses later: “As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly. Have you seen a man who seems wise to himself? There is more hope for a fool than for him.”

“The lazy man says, ‘There is a lion on the road, and a lioness in the paths.’ As a door turns on its hinge, so the lazy man turns in his bed. The lazy man hides his hands beneath his armpit, and he is weary if he turns them toward his mouth. The lazy man seems wiser to himself than seven men who speak judgments. Like one who seizes a dog by the ears is one who passes by impatiently and involves himself in another’s quarrel. As one is guilty who throws spears and arrows toward death, so is a man who deceitfully harms his friend and, when he has been caught, says, ‘I was only playing.’ When the wood is exhausted, the fire is extinguished; and when the whisperer is removed, quarrels subside. As coals to embers and wood to fire, so an angry man stirs up quarrels. The words of a whisperer are like simple things, yet they reach the innermost parts of the belly.”

And three verses later: “By his lips an enemy is recognized when he has devised deceit in his heart. When he lowers his voice, do not believe him, for there are seven evils in his heart. One who conceals hatred deceitfully will have his malice revealed in the assembly. One who digs a pit will fall into it; and one who rolls a stone, it will return upon him. A deceitful tongue does not love truth, and a slippery mouth works ruin.”

[XXVII.] “Do not boast about tomorrow [Note: [Col. 0923] The manuscript has ‘on the morrow.’], since you do not know what the coming day will bring forth. Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.”

And four verses later: “Open reproof is better than hidden love. The wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates.”

And three verses later: “Do not abandon your friend or your father’s friend.”

And several verses later: “Sheol and destruction are never filled; likewise, the eyes of human beings are insatiable. As silver is tested in the crucible and gold in the furnace, so a person is tested by the mouth of one who praises.” [Note: [Col. 0923] In Bibles printed from the press, this is followed by: “The heart of the wicked searches out evils,” etc.; this is absent from the Hebrew and from the ancient Corbie Bibles.]

“If you pound a fool in a mortar, as grain is pounded from above with a pestle, his folly will not be taken from him.”

And several verses later [Note: [Col. 0923] The Carnotensis codex has: ‘And twenty verses later.’] [XXVIII]: “A poor man who oppresses the poor is like a violent rainstorm that prepares famine. Those who abandon the law praise the wicked; those who keep it are inflamed against him. Wicked men do not understand judgment; but those who seek the Lord observe everything. Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man on perverse paths.”

And two verses later: “One who gathers wealth through interest and usury stores it up for the one who is generous to the poor. One who turns his ear away so as not to hear the law—his prayer will be accursed. One who leads the upright astray in an evil way will fall into his own destruction, and the innocent will possess his goods.”

And four verses later: “One who hides his crimes will not prosper; but one who confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy. Blessed is the person who is always cautious; but one who is hard-hearted will fall into evil.”

Again, twelve verses later: “A faithful man will be greatly praised; but one who hastens to become rich will not be innocent. One who shows partiality in judgment does not do well; for a piece of bread he abandons the truth. A man who hastens to become rich and envies others does not know that poverty will overtake him. One who reproves a man will afterward find favor with him, more than one who deceives by flattering speech. One who takes something from his father or mother and says, ‘This is not a sin,’ is a partner of a murderer. One who boasts and enlarges himself provokes quarrels; but one who hopes in the Lord will be healed.” [Col. 0924] “One who trusts in his own heart is a fool; but one who walks wisely will himself be saved. One who gives to the poor will not lack; one who despises the one who pleads will suffer want.”

And ten verses later [XXIX]: “A man who speaks to his friend with smooth and deceptive words spreads a net for his steps.”

And twenty-two verses later: “A servant cannot be instructed by words, because he understands what you say and disdains to answer. Have you seen a man quick to speak? There is more hope for folly than for his correction.”

And four verses later: “Humility follows the proud, and glory receives the humble. One who shares with a thief hates his own soul; he hears the one who adjures him, yet does not disclose it. One who fears a man will quickly fall; but one who hopes in the Lord will be lifted up. Many seek the face of a ruler, but judgment concerning each person proceeds from the Lord. The righteous detest an impious man, and the impious detest those who are on the straight path.”

And fourteen verses later [XXX]: “Two things I have asked; do not deny them to me before I die: Keep vanity and lying words far from me. Do not give me poverty or riches; grant me only what is necessary for my sustenance, lest, when I am filled, I be enticed to deny you and say, ‘Who is the Lord?’ or, compelled by poverty, I steal and swear falsely by the name of my God. Do not accuse a servant to his master, lest he curse you and you fall.”

And a little later [XXXI]: “Open your mouth, decide what is just, and judge the needy and the poor.”

Let these passages from Proverbs suffice. Next, turning to another book of Solomon, called Ecclesiastes, we shall likewise point out those things we find in it that are suitable for this work.

## ECCLESIASTES

[Chapter II.] “And I saw that wisdom surpassed folly as far as light differs from darkness. The eyes of the wise man are in his head; the fool walks in darkness.”

And a little later [IV]: “Guard your foot when you enter the house of God.” [Note: [Col. 0924] In the Vulgate version there is added: “and draw near in order to hear.”] “For obedience is much better than the sacrifices of fools, who do not know what evil they are doing.”

[V.] “Do not speak rashly, nor let your heart be quick to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven, and you are upon earth; therefore let your words be few. Dreams follow upon many cares, and folly is found in many words. If you have made a vow to God, do not delay to fulfill it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him. But whatever you vow, fulfill it. It is much better not to vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfill what was promised. Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, nor say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest perhaps God, angered by your words, destroy all the work of your hands. Where there are many dreams, there are many vanities and innumerable words; but you—fear God.”

And six verses later: “The miser is not filled with money, and one who loves riches will gain no fruit from them.”

[Col. 0925] And a little later [VII]: “It is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting, for in the former the end of all human beings is recalled, and the living considers what is to come. Anger is better than laughter, because through sadness of face the mind of the sinner is corrected. The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools where there is joy. It is better to be reproved by a wise man than to be deceived by the flattery of fools, for as the crackling of burning thorns beneath a pot, so is the laughter of a fool.”

And four verses later: “The patient man is better than the arrogant. Do not be quick to anger, for anger rests in the bosom of a fool. Do not say, ‘What do you think is the reason that former times were better than the present?’ For such a question is foolish.”

And three verses later: “Yet instruction and wisdom have this advantage: they give life to their possessor.”

And somewhat later [VIII]: “I keep the king’s command because of the oath sworn to God. Do not hasten to withdraw from his presence, nor persist in an evil undertaking.”

And a little later: “Because the sinner commits evil a hundred times and is sustained by patience, I have learned that it will be well with those who fear God, who revere his presence. It will not be well with the wicked, nor will his days be prolonged; but like a shadow they will pass away, those who do not fear the presence of God.”

And somewhat later [IX]: “I said that wisdom is better than strength.”

And four verses later: “Wisdom is better than weapons of war; and one who sins in one thing will lose many good things.”

And two verses later [X]: “Wisdom and a little glory are more precious than folly for a time.”

And thirteen verses later: “One who digs a pit will fall into it; and one who breaks through a hedge will be bitten by a serpent. One who moves stones will be afflicted by them; and one who splits wood will be wounded by it. If iron has become blunt, and is not as it was before but has been dulled, it will be sharpened with much labor, and after diligence wisdom will follow. If a serpent bites silently, the one who slanders secretly is no less dangerous. The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious, but the lips of a fool will bring him to ruin.”

And a little later [XI]: “Therefore rejoice, young man, in your youth; and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes. But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment. Remove anger from your heart, and put away wickedness from your flesh. For youth and pleasure are vanity.”

[XII.] “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth.”

And several verses later [Note: [Col. 0925] The Regius manuscript has: ‘And thirty-three verses later.’] “Fear God and observe his commandments.”

## THE SONG OF SONGS

There remains that book of Solomon whose title is *The Song of Songs*. But what can we transfer from it into this work, since the whole book commends the holy loves of Christ and the Church in figurative speech and proclaims them with prophetic grandeur? Except that, although it is exceedingly difficult to understand, we can nevertheless readily perceive in it how greatly that divine and divinely inspired charity should be desired [Col. 0926] and how highly it should be valued, since it is not said there only once but is repeated a second and a third time in different places [Chapters II, III, VIII]:

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and the stags of the fields, do not arouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes it. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field, if you raise love until it wishes it.” [Note: [Col. 0926] This passage and the other testimony immediately following are given according to the Septuagint; the rest are given according to the Vulgate.]

The Church, in which we certainly are, exhorts her daughters in these words—that is, she exhorts herself, constituted as she is in many members. She herself is the most fruitful field of God, whose powers and strengths are great, and to which the martyrs attained by loving Christ. For how far does he wish the love of his beloved to be raised in this intervening life, except as far as he himself taught by word and urged by his example when he said: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV.13)? And did he not bring to completion what he said? And lest this seem to pertain to him alone, John says in his Epistle: “Just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we also ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John III.16). This, then, is “until it wishes it.”

It is also read in the same Song [II]: “Order love within me.”

Christ himself also says there [VI]: “You are beautiful, my beloved, gentle and lovely as Jerusalem.”

And elsewhere [VII]: “How beautiful and how lovely you are, most beloved, in delights!”

And in another place [VIII]: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as Sheol.”

And one verse later: “Many waters could not extinguish love.” [Note: [Col. 0926] So the Vulgate reads in printed editions. But in the Corbie Bible manuscripts: “will not be able to extinguish.” In the Septuagint: *hydōr poly ou dynēsetai*, “much water will not be able.”] “Nor will rivers overwhelm it. If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, he would despise it as nothing.” [Note: [Col. 0926] Two manuscripts have “they will despise it.”]

## THE BOOK OF JOB

[Chapter XXIV.] “Those who know him do not know his days. Others have moved boundary markers, plundered flocks, and carried them away. They have driven off the orphan’s ass and taken the widow’s ox as a pledge.”

And five verses later: “They reap a field that is not theirs, and they harvest the vineyard of the one whom they have oppressed by force. They strip men naked, taking away their clothing, leaving them without covering in the cold.”

And two verses later: “They have used violence, plundering orphans, and robbed the poor people. From the naked, who go without clothing, and from the hungry they have taken ears of grain.”

And two verses later: “They have made men groan from the cities; the soul of the wounded cried out, and God does not permit this to go unavenged. They were rebels against the light; they did not know its ways, nor did they return to its paths.”

And twenty-one verses later: “Let him be crushed like a barren tree. For he fed the sterile woman, and did no good to the one who did not bear; he struck down the strong in his strength.”

[Col. 0927] And a little later [XXIX]: “The ear that heard blessed me, and the eye that saw bore witness to me, because I had delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the one who was perishing came upon me, and I consoled the widow’s heart. I clothed myself with justice, and I dressed myself in it as in a garment, and with my judgment as with a diadem. I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. I was a father to the poor; and the case I did not know, I investigated carefully. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth.”

And somewhat later [XXXI]: “If I walked in vanity and my foot hastened toward deceit, let him weigh me in a just balance, and let God know my innocence. If my steps turned aside from the way, and if my eye followed my heart, and a stain clung to my hands.” [Note: [Col. 0927] It should be read as in the better Bibles: “If my heart followed my eyes.”]

And two verses later: “If my heart was deceived concerning a woman, and if I lay in wait at the door of my friend.”

And two verses later: “For this is a wicked deed and the greatest iniquity. It is a fire devouring unto destruction and consuming all produce. If I disdained to enter into judgment with my male servant or female servant when they disputed against me.”

And four verses later [Note: [Col. 0927] The Regius codex has: “And six verses later.”]: “If I denied the poor what they desired, and made the eyes of the widow wait. If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it. For from my childhood compassion grew with me, and it came forth with me from my mother’s womb. If I looked down upon one who was perishing because he had no clothing, and upon the poor man without covering. If his sides did not bless me, and he was warmed by the fleeces of my sheep. If I raised my hand against the orphan, even when I saw myself superior in the gates.”

And five verses later: “If I thought gold was my strength, and said to refined gold, ‘My confidence.’ If I rejoiced over my great riches, and because my hand had found very much.”

And six verses later: “If I rejoiced at the ruin of the one who hated me, and exulted because evil had found him.”

And four verses later: “The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to the traveler. If I concealed my sin as a man and hid my iniquity in my bosom. If I feared a great multitude, and the contempt of relatives terrified me, and I did not remain silent, nor go out of the door. Who will grant me a hearer, that the Almighty may hear my desire, and that he who judges may himself write a book, so that I may carry it on my shoulder and bind it around myself [Note: [Col. 0927] The manuscripts omit ‘and bind it around me.’] like a crown? I will declare it at every one of my steps, and offer it as to a prince [Note: [Col. 0927] The Regius manuscript has ‘a prince.’]. If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it. If I ate its produce without payment and afflicted the souls of the farmers.”

Now let us gather from the books of the Prophets those passages necessary for this work. First, from those prophets who, because of the brevity of their books, are called the Minor Prophets. Thus, in the prophet Hosea we find the following.

## THE BOOK OF HOSEA

[Col. 0928]

[Chapter IV.] “Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a dispute with the inhabitants of the land. For there is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.”

And twelve verses later: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve me as priest.”

And fifteen verses later: “For they have abandoned the Lord by failing to keep him. Fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart.”

And seventeen verses later: “For they associated with prostitutes and sacrificed with effeminate men. And the people who do not understand will be beaten. If you commit fornication, Israel, at least let Judah not offend. Do not enter Gilgal, and do not go up to Beth-aven, nor swear, ‘As the Lord lives.’”

And several verses later [Note: [Col. 0928] The Regius manuscript has: “And eight verses later.”] [V]: “They will not set their thoughts on returning to the Lord their God, because a spirit of fornication is among them, and they have not known the Lord.”

And sixty-one verses later [VI]: “Your judgments will go forth like the light. For I desired mercy and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.”

And somewhat later [X]: “Sow for yourselves in righteousness and reap in the mouth of mercy; renew for yourselves the fallow ground. But it is time to seek the Lord, when he comes who will teach you righteousness.”

And seventy-eight verses later [XII]: “And you shall turn to the Lord your God” [Note: [Col. 0928] The Regius manuscript has: “Turn.”] “Keep mercy and judgment, and hope always in the Lord your God.”

And fifty-one verses later [XIII]: “But I am the Lord your God; I brought you out of the land of Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0928] The Vulgate has: “Your God from the land of Egypt,” omitting “brought you out,” which has been taken from the Septuagint.] “and you shall know no lord besides me, and there is no savior besides me.”

And thirty-nine verses later [XIV]: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have fallen because of your iniquity. Take words with you and return to the Lord. Say to him, ‘Take away all iniquity and receive what is good, and we will repay the calves of our lips.’”

## THE BOOK OF JOEL

[Chapter I.] “Awake, drunkards, and weep, and howl, all you who drink wine to sweetness, for it has perished from your mouth. For a nation has risen against my land, strong and without number.”

And somewhat later [II]: “Now therefore, says the Lord, ‘Return to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning; tear your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful.’”

## THE BOOK OF AMOS

[Chapter II.] “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Judah, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments. For their idols deceived them, after which their fathers went.”

And two verses later: “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of sandals. They crush the heads of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble. A son and his father went to the young woman, to profane my holy name.”

And one verse later: “And they drank, he says, the wine of the condemned in the house of their God.”

And somewhat later [V]: “For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: ‘Seek me, and you shall live.’”

And three verses later: “Seek the Lord, and live.”

And eight verses later: “They hated the one who reproved at the gate, and they abhorred the one who spoke uprightly. Therefore, because you plundered the poor and took select spoil from him.”

And three verses later: “For I know your many crimes and your mighty sins: enemies of the righteous, taking a bribe and crushing the poor at the gate.”

And two verses later: “Seek good and not evil, so that you may live; and the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as you have said. Hate evil and love good, and establish judgment at the gate; perhaps the Lord God of hosts will have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.”

And several verses later [VI]: “You who sleep on ivory beds and indulge yourselves on your couches; you who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; you who sing to the sound of the psaltery—like David, they thought they had instruments for song; drinking wine from bowls, anointed with the finest ointment, and suffering nothing over the ruin of Joseph.”

And somewhat later [VIII]: “Hear this, you who crush the poor and bring the needy of the land to an end, saying: ‘When will the harvest pass, that we may sell our goods, and the Sabbath, that we may open the grain, so that we may reduce the measure, increase the shekel, and adjust the dishonest scales; so that we may acquire the needy and the poor for silver and a pair of sandals, and sell the refuse of grain?’” [Note: [Col. 0929] In the sacred Bibles, “month.”]

## THE BOOK OF MICAH

[Chapter II.] “Woe to those who devise useless things and work evil upon their beds. In the morning light they do it, because their hands are against God. They coveted fields, seized them by force, and robbed houses; they oppressed a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.”

And somewhat later [III]: “Hear this, rulers of the house of Jacob and judges of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert everything that is right. You who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity. Its rulers judged for bribes; its priests taught for payment; and its prophets divined for money. Yet they rested upon the Lord, saying, ‘Is not God in our midst? Evil will not come upon us.’”

And somewhat later [VI]: “I will show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord seeks from you: namely, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk attentively with your God.”

And three verses later: “Even now there is fire in the house of the wicked, the treasures of iniquity, and a measure diminished and full of wrath. Shall I justify a wicked balance and deceitful weights in the bag? In these its rich men have been filled with iniquity; its inhabitants have spoken lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth.”

And twelve verses later [VII]: “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers in autumn, like one who gleans the grapes of the vintage. There is no cluster to eat; my soul desired the first-ripe figs. The holy man has perished from the earth, and there is no upright person among human beings. All lie in wait for blood; each man hunts his brother to death. They call the evil of their hands good. The prince makes a request, and the judge is ready to repay it, while the great man speaks the desire of his soul.”

## THE BOOK OF HABAKKUK

[Chapter I.] “Judgment has been turned against me, and contradiction is stronger. Therefore the law is torn apart, and judgment does not reach its end, because the wicked prevails against the just; therefore perverse judgment goes forth.”

And a little later [II]: “But the just man will live by his faith.”

“And as wine deceives one who drinks it, so will the proud man be; he will not be honored.”

And somewhat later: “What benefit is a sculpted image, because its maker has sculpted it, a molten image and a false likeness? For its maker trusts in his creation, making mute idols. Woe to one who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ or, ‘Rise!’ to a silent stone. Can it itself teach? Behold, it is covered with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all within it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth be silent before him.”

## THE BOOK OF ZEPHANIAH

[Chapter I.] “I will destroy,” he says, “from this place the remnant of Baal and the names of the temple-servants together with the priests; and those who worship upon the roofs the host of heaven, and worship and swear by the Lord, and swear by Milcom; and those who turn away from following the Lord; and those who have not sought the Lord or investigated him. Be silent before the face of the Lord, for the day of the Lord is near.”

And sixteen verses later: “And at that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are settled upon their dregs, who say in their hearts, ‘The Lord will do neither good nor evil.’”

And several verses later [Note: [Col. 0930] The Regius manuscript has: “And eighteen verses later.”] [II]: “Gather together, assemble, nation without favor, before the decree gives birth—like dust passing away—before the day passes, before the anger of the Lord’s fury comes upon you, before the day of the Lord’s fury comes upon you. Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth who have practiced his judgment. Seek the just, seek the humble; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury.”

And somewhat later [III]: “And I will leave in your midst a poor and needy people, and the remnant of Israel will hope in the name of the Lord. They will not commit iniquity [Col. 0931] nor speak lies, and a deceitful tongue will not be found in their mouth.”

## THE BOOK OF ZECHARIAH

[Chapter V.] Speaking of the scroll that he saw in the spirit: “And he said to me, ‘This is the curse that goes forth over the face of the whole earth, for every thief, as it is written there, will be judged, and every one who swears will likewise be judged by this. I will bring it forth,’ says the Lord of hosts, ‘and it will enter the house of the thief and the house of the one who falsely swears by my name; and it will remain in the midst of his house and consume him, its wood and its stones.’”

And somewhat later [VII]: “And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘Judge true judgment, and show mercy and compassion, each one to his brother. Do not oppress the widow, the orphan, the stranger, or the poor, and let no man devise evil against his brother in his heart.’”

Again, somewhat later [VIII]: “Speak truth, each one with his neighbor. Judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates. Let each of you not devise evil against his friend in your hearts, and do not love a lying oath. For all these are things that I hate, says the Lord.”

## THE BOOK OF MALACHI

[Chapter I.] “A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is my fear? says the Lord of hosts.”

And a little later [II]: “I have made you contemptible and lowly among all the peoples, because you have not kept my ways and have shown partiality in the Law. Is there not one father of us all? Has not one God created us? Why then does each one despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers? Judah has transgressed, and abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem, because Judah has profaned the holiness of the Lord, which he loved, and has taken the daughter of a foreign god. The Lord will destroy the man who does this, teacher and disciple, from the tents of Jacob, and the one who offers a gift to the Lord of hosts.”

“And again you have done this: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, weeping and groaning, so that I will no longer look upon the sacrifice, nor accept anything pleasing from your hand. And you said, ‘For what reason?’ Because the Lord has testified between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have despised; yet she is your companion and the wife of your covenant. Did not one make [them], and is there a remnant of his spirit? And what does each one seek except the offspring of God?” [Note: [Col. 0931] The Vulgate version has: “And what does one seek?” But the Septuagint: “What else besides offspring does God seek?”]

“Therefore guard your spirit, and do not despise the wife of your youth. When you hate her, send her away, says the Lord God of Israel; but iniquity will cover his garment, says the Lord of hosts. Guard your spirit, and do not despise her.”

“You have wearied the Lord with your words,” [Col. 0932] and you said, “In what way have we wearied him?” In this, when you said, “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him”; or else, “Where is the day of judgment?”

And fifteen verses later [III]: “And I will draw near to you in judgment,” he says, “and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers; against those who oppress the wages of the hired worker, widows” [Note: [Col. 0932] So the manuscripts read, in agreement with the Vulgate. But printed editions have: “and humble widows.”] “and orphans; against those who oppress the stranger and do not fear me, says the Lord of hosts. For I am the Lord, and I do not change; and you, sons of Jacob, have not been consumed. For from the days of your fathers you have departed from my statutes and have not kept them. Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord of hosts.”

And fifteen verses later: “Your words have prevailed against me, says the Lord. And you said, ‘What have we spoken?’” [Note: [Col. 0932] In the sacred Bibles, “against you” is added.] “You said, ‘It is futile to serve God; and what profit is there in keeping his commandments and walking mournfully before the Lord of hosts?’ Therefore now we call the arrogant blessed, for those who do iniquity are built up” [Note: [Col. 0932] Here and shortly below, the sacred Bibles have “impiety” instead of “iniquity.”] “and they have tested God and have been saved.”

“Then those who fear God spoke, each one with his neighbor. And the Lord attended and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the Lord and think upon his name.
