Do not be reluctant to visit the sick, for through such deeds you will be strengthened in love. In all your works remember your last things [Col. 0955], and you will never sin.

### [VIII.]

Do not quarrel with a powerful man, lest you fall into his hands. Do not contend with a wealthy man, lest he perhaps stir up a lawsuit against you [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions had “lest a lawsuit stand against you”; the Vulgate has “lest he bring a lawsuit against you.”]. For gold has destroyed many, and has reached the heart of kings and turned them.

Do not quarrel with a talkative man, and do not pile wood [Note: The Regius manuscript has “do not pile up”; in agreement with the Greek *kai mê epistoibasês*.] onto his fire.

And after two verses:

Do not despise a person turning away from sin, nor reproach him. Remember that we are all under correction. Do not scorn a person in his old age, for some of us also grow old. Do not rejoice over your dead enemy [Note: “Your enemy” is absent from the Greek text and from the Regius manuscript of the *Speculum*; but this codex later reads, “and we do not wish to come into the joy of enemies.”], knowing that we all die and do not wish to come into joy.

Do not despise the account of wise elders, and occupy yourself with their sayings. For from them you will learn instruction in understanding [Note: The printed Vulgate has “you will learn wisdom and instruction in understanding”; but the ancient Corbeiensis Bibles agree here with Augustine’s *Speculum* and with the Greek.], and how to serve the great without complaint.

Do not let the account of elders pass you by; for they too learned from their fathers. For from them you will learn understanding and an answer in time of need [Note: The sacred Bibles have “to give an answer.”].

And after sixteen verses:

Do not take counsel with fools, for they cannot love anything except what pleases them. Do not give counsel before a stranger, for you do not know what he will bring forth.

And after two verses:

Do not be jealous of the wife of your bosom.

And after seven verses:

Do not desire a virgin, lest you be scandalized by her beauty [Note: The Vulgate has “do not look upon her”; the Greek has *mê katamanthane*, “do not scrutinize.”]. Do not give your soul to prostitutes in any way, lest you destroy yourself and your inheritance.

And after two verses:

Turn your face away from a well-adorned woman, and do not gaze at another’s beauty.

And after twelve verses:

Do not abandon an old friend, for a new one will not be like him. New wine is a new friend; it will grow old, and you will drink it with enjoyment.

Do not be jealous of the glory and wealth of the sinner, for you do not know what his downfall will be. Do not let the injury of the unjust please you [Note: Thus the Carnutensis manuscript, in agreement with the Vulgate. The printed editions had “of the just.”].

And after two verses:

Keep far away from a person who has power to kill, and you will not suspect the fear of death. If you approach him, do not commit anything, lest he take your life.

And after four verses:

Deal with the wise and prudent. Let just men be your companions at table, and let your glory be in the fear of God.

And after fifty-three verses [Note: Thus the Regius manuscript; the Carnutensis has “after fifty-four verses.”]:

### [X.]

The race of human beings that fears God will be honored; but the race that passes beyond the commandments of the Lord will be dishonored among human beings. The ruler among his brothers is held in honor; and those who fear the Lord will be in his sight.

The glory of the rich, the honored, and the poor is the fear of God. Do not despise a just poor man [Col. 0956], and do not magnify [Note: The printed editions have “do not magnify”; we have corrected this according to the Regius manuscript, “you will not magnify,” although the same codex has shortly before “do not despise.” The Vulgate is more harmonious: “do not despise,” followed by “do not magnify.”] a sinful rich man.

Great, and judge, and powerful is he who is held in honor; and there is none greater than the one who fears God. Sensible servants will serve a free man; a prudent and disciplined person will not murmur when corrected.

And after five verses:

My son, preserve your soul in gentleness, and give it honor according to its merit.

And after six verses:

### [XI.]

Wisdom will exalt the head of the humble person, and will make him sit in the midst of the great. Do not praise a man for his appearance, nor despise a person by his outward look. Among flying creatures the bee is small, but its fruit has the beginning of sweetness.

Never glory in clothing, and do not exalt yourself on the day of your honor.

And after six verses:

Before questioning, do not reproach anyone; and when you have questioned, correct justly. Before hearing, do not answer a word; and in the midst of elders [Note: This should be read as in the Bibles corrected under the authority of Sixtus, “of speeches,” in agreement with the Greek *logōn*. Shortly afterward, where the text has “do not contend,” the manuscripts of this book, together with the Vulgate, prefer “do not be contended against.”] do not add to speaking.

Do not contend over a matter that does not trouble you, and do not take your stand in the judgment of sinners. My son, do not let your activities be many; and if you become rich, you will not be free from sin. For if you pursue too much, you will not overtake it; and if you run ahead, you will not escape.

And after twenty verses:

Do not remain in the works of sinners; but trust in God, and remain in your place.

And after several verses:

Before death, do not praise any person.

And after one verse:

Do not bring every person into your house, for the deceitful have many snares.

For just as the inward parts of infants belch forth [Note: The printed Vulgate has “of foul-smelling things”; the ancient Corbeiensis Bibles have “of putrid things.”], and just as a partridge is led into a pit and a doe into a snare, so also is the heart of the proud; and so is the one who observes, seeing the fall of his neighbor.

For the person who turns good things into evil lies in wait, and will place a blemish on the chosen. From one spark the fire is increased, and from one deceitful person bloodshed is increased. The sinful person lies in wait for blood.

Beware of the pestilent person, for he fabricates evil, lest he bring upon you mockery forever. Admit a foreigner to yourself, and he will overthrow you in confusion [Note: The sacred Bibles have “in a whirlwind.”], and estrange you from your own people.

### [XII.]

If you do good, know to whom you do good, and there will be much grace in your good deeds. Do good to the just, and you will find a great reward; and if not from him, certainly from God.

It is not well with those who persist in evil and do not give alms, for the Most High also hates sinners and has mercy on those who repent. Give to the merciful, and do not receive the sinner. Do good to the humble, and do not give to the impious.

Prevent bread from being given to him, lest he become more powerful than you through it; for you will find double evils in all good things [Note: The Regius manuscript has “in people who are not good.” The Vulgate, following the Greek, adds after “in all good things,” “whatever you do for him”; this is absent from the Corbeiensis Bibles.], since the Most High also hates sinners and will repay the impious with vengeance.

And after four verses [Col. 0957]:

Do not trust your enemy forever, for his wickedness grows rusty like bronze. And if he goes humbled and bent over, apply your mind [Note: Thus the Regius manuscript, in agreement with the Vulgate. The printed editions have “cast away your mind”; so also the Corbeiensis Bible.], and guard yourself from him.

Do not establish him beside you, nor let him sit at your right hand, lest, having turned, he stand in your place [Note: This phrase was expunged from the printed Vulgate: “lest, having turned, he stand in your place.” It is found in all the copies of this work and in the ancient Corbeiensis Bible, perhaps standing in place of what the Greek reads: *mê anatrepsas se stê epi ton topon sou*.]. Lest, having turned, he seek your seat in your place, and at the end you recognize my words and are pricked by my sayings.

Who will pity an enchanter bitten by a serpent, or any of those who approach wild beasts? So it is with one who associates with an unjust person and is wrapped up in his sins. He will remain with you for one hour; but if you turn away, he will not support you.

The enemy is gracious on his lips, but in his heart he lies in wait in order to overthrow you into a pit. The enemy weeps in his eyes; and if he finds an opportunity, he will not be satisfied with blood.

If evils befall you, you will find him there first. The enemy weeps in his eyes, and as though helping you, he will dig under your feet. He will shake his head and clap [Note: So also the ancient Corbeiensis Bible. But the current printed Vulgate has “he will clap.”] his hand; and while whispering many things, he will change his face.

And after sixty-one verses:

### [XIII.]

Good is the possession that has no sin in the conscience; but most evil is poverty in the mouth of the impious.

And after three verses:

### [XIV.]

Blessed is the man who has not fallen by a word from his mouth and has not been pricked by the sorrow of sin. Happy is the one who has not had sorrow in his soul and has not fallen away from his hope.

For a greedy and grasping person, possessions are without reason; and for an envious person, what use is gold?

And after fourteen verses:

My son, if you have means, do good to yourself, and offer obligations worthy of God. Remember that death does not delay, and the covenant of the underworld, because it has been shown to you. For the covenant of this world will die by death.

Before death, do good to your friend, and according to your means stretch out and give to the poor.

And after sixteen verses:

Blessed is the man who will remain in wisdom, who will meditate on his righteousness [Note: “His” is absent from the Regius manuscript; “his” is also absent after the word “understanding.”], and who will think upon God’s watchfulness in his understanding: the one who considers his ways in his heart and understands in his hidden places.

And after twenty-five verses:

### [XV.]

Foolish people will not grasp it, but sensible people will meet it. Foolish people will not see it, for it is far from pride and deceit. Lying men will not remember it, but truthful men will be found in it and will prosper until the vision of God.

Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, for wisdom has proceeded from God. Praise will stand beside the wisdom of God, and it will abound in a faithful mouth, and the ruler will grant it to him.

Do not say, “By God, it is absent.” For whatever he hates, do not do. Do not say, “He has planted me,” for impious people are not necessary to him.

God hates every accursed thing of error, and it will not be lovable to those who fear him. From the beginning God established the human being and left him in the hand of his own counsel. He added his commandments and precepts. If you wish to keep the commandments, they will preserve you, and you will make a pleasing pledge forever.

He has set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish. Before a human being are life and death, good and evil; whichever pleases him will be given to him.

For the wisdom of God is great, and he is mighty in power, seeing everyone without interruption. The eyes of God are upon those who fear him, and he himself knows every work of a human being. He commanded no one to act impiously, and he gave no one room for sinning.

For he does not desire a multitude of faithless and useless children.

### [XVI.]

And do not rejoice in impious children if they multiply; do not delight in them if the fear of God is not with them. Do not trust their life, and do not look upon their labors. For one who fears God is better than a thousand impious children, and it is better to die without children than to leave behind impious children.

And after twenty-one verses:

Do not say, “I shall be hidden from God, and who will remember me from on high?”

And shortly afterward:

### [XVII.]

The covenants are not hidden through their iniquity, and all their iniquities are before God. The almsgiving of a person is like a seal with him, and a person’s grace he will preserve like the apple of the eye. And afterward he will rise and repay them, repaying each one upon his head, and he will turn them into the inner parts of the earth.

But to those who repent he gave the way of justice, and he strengthened the failing to endure, and he appointed for them the portion of truth.

Turn to God, and abandon your sins; pray before his face, and lessen the stumbling-block [Note: The Greek agrees. But the Vulgate prefers “pray before the face of the Lord, and lessen the stumbling-blocks.” The Regius manuscript has “before his face.” In the following verse the same manuscript, together with the Carnutensis, has “Return yourself to God.” The Greek supports *epanage*, “return.”].

Return to God, and turn away from your injustice, and hate the accursed thing exceedingly.

And after nine verses:

How great is the mercy of God, and his propitiation for those who turn to him! For not all things can be in human beings, since the son of a human being is not immortal.

And after thirty verses:

### [XVIII.]

He has mercy on those who receive the instruction of mercy and on those who hasten in his judgments.

My son, do not give cause for complaint in good things, and in every gift do not give the sorrow of an evil word. Does not dew cool heat? So a good word is better than a gift. Is not a word plainly above a good gift? And both belong with a justified person [Note: Thus the manuscripts and the Corbeiensis Bible, in agreement with the Greek. The printed editions, with the Vulgate, have “but both.”].

A fool will reproach harshly, and a gift from an undisciplined person makes the eyes waste away. Before judgment, prepare justice for yourself; and before you speak, learn. Before sickness, apply medicine; and before judgment, examine yourself; and in the sight of God you will find propitiation.

Before sickness, humble yourself; and in the time of illness, show your conduct. Do not be hindered from praying always, and do not fear being justified even unto death, for the reward of God [Col. 0959] remains forever.

Before prayer, prepare your soul, and do not be like a person who tests God.

And after six verses:

A wise person will fear in all things, and in days of sin will beware of idleness.

And after five verses:

Do not go after your desires, and turn away from your own will. If you grant your soul its desires, it will make you a joy to your enemies. Do not delight in crowds, and do not take pleasure in excesses.

And after five verses:

### [XIX.]

And whoever despises small things will gradually fall. Wine and women make the wise apostatize, and expose those who are sensible.

And after several verses:

Whoever believes quickly is lighthearted and will be diminished; and whoever sins against his own soul will be held in contempt.

And after two verses:

Whoever hates talkativeness extinguishes wickedness.

And after eight verses:

You have heard a word against your neighbor; let it die within you, trusting that it will not burst you apart. At the face of a word the fool labors like the groaning of a woman giving birth. An arrow fixed in the fleshy thigh is like a word in the mouth [Note: The Vulgate has “in the heart.”] of a fool.

Correct your friend, lest he perhaps did not understand and say, “I did not do it”; or, if he did it, lest he do it again. Correct your neighbor, lest he perhaps did not say it; and if he did say it, lest he repeat it. Correct your friend, for an offense often occurs; and do not believe every word.

There is one who slips with his tongue, but not from his heart. For who is there who has not sinned with his tongue? Correct your neighbor before you threaten him; and give room to the fear of the Most High, because all wisdom is the fear of God, and in it is the fear of God.

And after five verses:

Better is a person who lacks wisdom but lacks understanding in the fear of God than one who abounds in understanding but transgresses the law of the Most High.

And after sixteen verses:

### [XX.]

How good it is to rebuke rather than to become angry!

And after several verses:

Whoever unjustly assumes power for himself will be hated.

And after eight verses:

A wise person makes himself beloved through his words.

And after sixteen verses:

The slip of a false tongue is like someone falling from a pavement; so the downfall of wicked people will come swiftly. A worthless person will be like an empty tale, and among the disciplined [Note: The sacred Bibles have “among the undisciplined.”] it will be constantly repeated.

A proverb from the mouth of a fool will be rejected, for he does not speak it at the proper time.

And after two verses:

There is one who loses his soul through embarrassment, and through an imprudent person he will lose it; he will destroy himself through partiality. There is one who, through embarrassment, makes a promise to a friend, and has gained him as an enemy for nothing.

A wicked reproach is a lie in a person, and it will constantly be in the mouth of the undisciplined. A thief is preferable to the constant presence of a lying person; but both will inherit destruction.

The manner of a lying person is without honor, and his shame is with him [Note: This should be read, in accordance with the Vulgate, “and their shame is with them”; or the first part of the verse should be corrected according to the Greek: “The way of a lying person.”] without interruption. A wise person will bring himself forth through his words.

And after four verses:

Hospitality-gifts and presents blind the eyes of judges, and, like a mute in the mouth, turn away their corrections. Hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure—what use is there in either? Better among human beings is the one who hides his folly [Col. 0960] than the one who hides his wisdom.

### [XXI.]

My son, you have sinned; do not add to it again, but also pray concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you. Flee sins as from the face of a serpent; and if you approach them, they will seize you.

His teeth are the teeth of a lion, killing the souls of human beings; every iniquity is like a two-edged sword; there is no healing for its wounds.

And after four verses:

Whoever hates correction is the imprint of a sinner; but whoever fears God will return to his heart.

And after five verses:

The way of sinners is paved [Note: In the more reliable Bibles, “made level,” where “made level” corresponds to the Greek *hōmalismenē*] with stones; and at their end are the underworld, darkness, and punishments. Whoever keeps justice will hold fast his understanding. The completion of the fear of God is wisdom and understanding.

And after several verses:

Whatever wise word a knowledgeable person hears, he will praise and add to himself; a luxurious person will hear it, dislike it, and throw it behind his back. The account of a fool is like a burden on the road, for grace will be found on the lips of the sensible.

The mouth of the prudent is sought in the assembly, and they will ponder his words in their hearts.

And after two verses:

Instruction is fetters on the feet of a fool, and like handcuffs upon his right hand. A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise person will scarcely laugh quietly. Instruction is a golden ornament for the prudent, and like a bracelet on the right arm.

And after eight verses:

In the mouth of fools is their heart, and in the heart of the wise is their mouth. When the impious person curses the devil, he curses his own soul. The whisperer will defile his soul and will be hated by everyone; and whoever remains [Note: So also in the ancient Corbeiensis Bibles. But the current printed Vulgate prefers “and whoever remains with him.”] will be hateful. The quiet and sensible person will be honored.

### [XXII.]

The lazy person is stoned with a muddy stone, and everyone will speak against his contemptible conduct.

And after four verses:

A prudent daughter is an inheritance for her husband; but the one who brings shame becomes an insult to her father. She who is bold brings shame upon her father and husband, and will not be diminished by the impious; but she will be dishonored by both.

Music during mourning is an untimely account; lashes and instruction are wisdom at every time. Whoever teaches a fool is like someone who glues a potsherd together. Whoever recounts a word to one who does not pay attention is like someone awakening a sleeper from deep sleep.

The one who speaks with a sleeper is the one who explains to a fool; and at the end he says [Note: The printed editions, following the Vulgate, have “who recounts wisdom to a fool, and at the end of the account says.” The manuscripts lack the words “wisdom” and “of the account”; these are also absent from the Greek.], “Who is this?”

Weep over the dead, for his light has failed; and weep over the fool, for understanding has failed him. Weep a little over the dead, because he has found rest; but the life of the most wicked is worse than death for the fool. The mourning of the dead lasts seven days; but for the fool and the impious, all the days of their life.

And after twenty-one verses:

Throwing a stone at birds will bring them down; so whoever reviles a friend will dissolve the friendship. Even if you draw a sword against a friend, do not despair, for there is a return. If you open your mouth with a grievous word against a friend, do not fear, for reconciliation is possible—except in the case of insult, reproach, pride, and the revelation of a secret, and a deceitful wound. In all these things a friend will flee.

And after ten verses:

Who will place a guard over my mouth and a sure seal over my lips, so that I may not fall because of them and my tongue may not destroy me?

### [XXIII.]

Lord, Father and ruler of my life, do not abandon me, and do not let me fall into these things. Who will set scourges over my thoughts and the instruction of wisdom in my heart, so that they may not spare me on account of their ignorances, and so that their offenses may not appear? Otherwise my ignorances will increase, and my sins will multiply, and my offenses will abound, and I will fall before my adversaries, and my enemy will rejoice.

Lord, Father and God of my life, do not abandon me to their thoughts. Do not give me haughtiness of my eyes, and turn every desire away from me [Note: The printed editions have “turn wicked desire away from me.” The word “wicked” is absent from the manuscripts and from the sacred Bibles.]. Take away from me the desires of the belly, and do not let the lusts of desire seize me; and do not hand me over to a shameless and undisciplined soul.

Hear the instruction of the mouth, children; and whoever keeps it will not perish by his lips, nor will he be scandalized in the most wicked works. The sinner is caught in his own vanity, and the proud and abusive person will be scandalized by them.

Do not accustom your mouth to swearing, for there are many falls in it. Let the naming of God not be constant in your mouth, and do not intermingle yourself with the names of the holy, for you will not be innocent with respect to them.

For just as a servant who is constantly questioned is not diminished by resentment, so everyone who swears and invokes names in everything will not be cleansed from sin. A person who swears excessively will be filled with iniquity, and a plague will not depart from his house.

And if he breaks it [Note: The printed editions have “and if he breaks it against his brother.” “Against his brother” is absent from the Greek and the Vulgate, as well as from the Regius manuscript, which instead of “breaks it” has “has sworn in vain.”], his offense will be upon him; and if he dissimulates, he sins twice. And if he swears in vain, he will not be justified, for his house will be filled with retribution [Note: The printed editions add “most evil,” a word lacking in the manuscripts and sacred Bibles.].

And after four verses:

Do not accustom your mouth to undisciplined speech [Note: The Carnutensis manuscript has “Do not accustom your mouth to speak undisciplinedly.” The Regius has “to undisciplined swearing or speech.” Finally, the Greek text reads in some Bibles “to reckless indiscipline,” and in others “to intemperance of swearing.”], for there is sinful speech in it.

Remember your father and your mother, for you stand in the midst of the great; lest God forget you in their sight, and, made foolish through your constant conduct, you suffer reproach, and would have preferred not to have been born, and curse the day of your birth.

A person accustomed to words of reproach will not be instructed throughout all his days. Two kinds abound in sins, and a third brings anger and destruction. A hot soul, like a burning fire, will not be extinguished until it swallows something; and a wicked person in the mouth of his flesh will not cease until he kindles a fire.

And after two verses:

Every person who violates his bed, despising his own soul and saying, “Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me, and walls cover me, and no one looks around. Whom should I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins, and will not understand, because his eye does not see”—the fear of such a person, and the eyes of people who fear him, drive the fear of God away from him.

He did not recognize that the eyes of the Lord are far brighter than the sun, observing all the ways of human beings and looking into the depths of the abyss and into the hidden parts of human hearts.

And shortly afterward:

### [XXV.]

What you did not gather in your youth, how will you find it in your old age? How beautiful is the judgment of gray hair, and for elders to know counsel! How beautiful is wisdom among the aged, and understanding and counsel among the honored! The crown of the old is great experience, and their glory is the fear of God.

And after ten verses:

The fear of God has placed itself above all things. Blessed is the one to whom it has been granted to possess the fear of God. To whom will the one who fears him be likened? [Note: The sacred Bibles have “the one who holds fast to him.”]

And after twenty verses:

Do not look upon the appearance of a woman, and do not desire a woman for her appearance.

Thirty-three verses later [XXVI]: A drunken woman causes great anger; her abuse and disgrace will not be concealed. A woman’s fornication will be recognized by the haughtiness of her eyes and by her eyelids. In the case of a daughter who does not turn away [Note: [Col. 0962] The printed editions read, “who does not take heed”; the manuscripts, together with the Vulgate, read, “who does not turn away.”], keep firm watch, lest, finding an opportunity, she use herself [Note: [Col. 0962] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Leuven edition read, “lest she abuse herself.” M.]. Guard against every irreverence of the eyes [Note: [Col. 0962] The Vulgate reads, “of her eyes.” Nevertheless, “her” is absent from the Corbie Bibles.]; and do not be surprised if she neglects you.

And four verses later: The grace of an attentive wife delights her husband, and her discipline makes his bones fat. A sensible and silent woman is a gift from God; there is no change in a well-instructed soul. Grace upon grace is a holy and modest woman. Yet no weighing is worthy of a self-controlled soul.

And twelve verses later: Whoever turns from righteousness to sin, God has prepared him for the sword.

And four verses later [XXVII]: Whoever seeks to become rich turns away his eye.

And three verses later: Sin will be crushed [Note: [Col. 0962] The Carnutes manuscript reads, “will be turned back.” The Vulgate reads, “Sin will be crushed together with the sinner’s offense.”]. If you do not hold fast in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown. As dust remains in the perforation [Note: [Col. 0962] The manuscripts read, “in the perforation,” or “in the piercing.” The Vulgate reads, “in the striking.”] of a sieve, so does a man’s perplexity remain in his thought. The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and temptation in tribulation tests righteous people. As cultivation from a tree reveals its fruit, so a word reveals the thought of a person’s heart. Do not praise a man before his speech; for this is the testing of human beings. If you pursue righteousness, you will grasp it and put it on like a robe of honor; you will dwell with it, and it will protect you forever, and on the day of recognition you will find security. Birds flock to their kind, and truth returns to those who practice it. The lion always lies in wait for prey; so do sins for those who practice wickedness. A holy man remains in wisdom like the sun, but a fool changes like the moon.

[Col. 0963] Among the senseless, keep your word for the proper time; but among thoughtful people be constant. The talk of sinners is hateful, and their laughter is in the sins of sin. Speech that swears excessively will set the hair on one’s head on end, and its irreverence is a stopping of the ears. The shedding of blood occurs in the quarrel of the proud, and their curse is grievous to hear. Whoever exposes the secrets of a friend loses trust and will find no friend to his liking. Love your neighbor and join yourself to him in faith; but if you expose his secrets, do not pursue him afterward. For just as a man destroys his friend, so does one who destroys his neighbor’s friendship. And just as one who releases a bird from his hand, so you have abandoned your neighbor [Note: [Col. 0963] The Regius manuscript reads, “So is the one who has abandoned.”], and you will not capture him. Do not pursue him, for he is far away. He has fled like a doe from a snare, because his soul has been wounded; and you will no longer be able to bind him to yourself.

And the agreement of the accursed is this: to expose a friend’s secrets is despair for an unhappy soul. The one who winks with his eyes contrives wickedness, and no one will cast him off. In the sight of your eyes his mouth will sweeten his words, and he will marvel at your sayings; but finally he will pervert his mouth and make your words a stumbling block. I have hated many things, but nothing so much as him; and the Lord will hate him.

And two verses later: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it; whoever sets a stone before his neighbor will stumble over it; and whoever prepares a snare for another will perish in it. The most wicked scheme will roll back upon the one who devises it, and he will not know from where it will come upon him. Mockery and insult are for the proud, and vengeance will lie in wait for him like a lion. Those who delight in the fall of the righteous will perish by a snare.

And three verses later [XXVIII]: Whoever wishes to take revenge will find vengeance from God, and He will preserve his sins. Forgive your neighbor who has wronged you, and then, when you pray, your sins will be released. A man harbors anger against another man and seeks healing from God! He shows no mercy to a person like himself, yet prays for his own sins! Though he himself is flesh, he harbors anger and asks God for reconciliation! Who will plead for his offenses? Remember the end, and cease from hostility; for decay and death are imminent in the commandments of God. Remember the fear of God, and do not be angry with your neighbor. Remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook your neighbor’s ignorance. Refrain from quarrels, and you will lessen sins. For an angry man kindles a quarrel; a sinful man will disturb friends and introduce hostility among those who live in peace.

And four verses later: A hastened contest kindles fire, a hurried quarrel sheds blood, and a tongue that gives testimony brings death. If you blow upon it [Note: [Col. 0963] The Vulgate reads, “If you blow upon a spark, as upon fire,” and so forth.], it will flare up like fire; and if you spit upon it, it will be extinguished: both proceed from the mouth. The whisperer and the double-tongued person are accursed, for they have disturbed many who were living in peace. The third tongue has stirred up many and scattered them from nation to nation. It has destroyed the walled cities of the wealthy and dug out the houses of great men. It has overthrown the strength of peoples and dissolved mighty nations. The third tongue has driven out married women [Note: [Col. 0963] Two manuscripts read, “has driven out strong women.”] and deprived them [Col. 0964] of their labors. Whoever watches that tongue will have no rest, nor will he have a friend in whom he may rest.

And after some verses [Note: [Col. 0964] The Regius manuscript reads, “and thirty-three verses later”]: Make a balance for your words and straight reins for your mouth; take care lest you slip with your tongue, fall before enemies lying in wait for you, and your fall become incurable, ending in death.

[XXIX] Whoever shows mercy lends to his neighbor, and whoever prevails by his hand observes the commandments. Lend to your neighbor in his time of need, and repay your neighbor again at his proper time. Confirm your word and act faithfully toward him, and at every time you will find what you need. Many have regarded a loan as a discovery and have caused trouble for those who helped them.

And thirteen verses later: Nevertheless, be stronger toward one who is humble in spirit, and do not drag him along on account of almsgiving. For the sake of the commandment, take in the poor man, and because of his poverty do not send him away empty-handed. Lose your money for the sake of your brother and friend, and do not hide it under a stone for destruction. Place your treasure in the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold. Enclose your almsgiving in the poor man’s heart, and it will plead for you against every evil; it will fight for you like a shield of the mighty and a spear against your enemy. A good man gives security for his neighbor, but whoever has lost shame will abandon him [Note: [Col. 0964] The Carnutes manuscript reads, “will abandon you.” But the others have the better reading, “will abandon him”; the neighbor is understood. For the Greek text has this sense: “And whoever has lost shame will abandon him.”]. Do not forget the kindness of a guarantor, for he has given his life for you. The sinner and the unclean flee from a guarantor. The sinner credits the guarantor’s possessions to himself and, ungrateful in understanding, abandons the one who has freed him. A man gives security for his neighbor, and when he has lost respect, he will be abandoned by him. A most wicked guarantee has ruined many who were diligent [Note: [Col. 0964] It should be read as in the sacred Bibles, “who were directing.”], and has agitated them like waves of the sea. It has made powerful men wander about and depart, and they have roamed among foreign nations. The sinner who transgresses the commandments of the Lord will fall into a wicked pledge.

And one verse later: Recover your neighbor according to your strength, and take care lest you fall.

And sixteen verses later [XXX]: Whoever loves his son applies the rod to him repeatedly, so that he may rejoice in his final days [Note: [Col. 0964] In the Vulgate, after “in his final days,” there is added, “and he will not feel his way at the doors of his neighbors”; this is absent from the Greek.]. Whoever teaches his son will be praised in him.

And ten verses later: An untamed horse turns out hard, and an undisciplined son turns out headstrong. Nurse your son, and he will make you afraid; play with him, and he will grieve you. Do not smile at him, lest you suffer, and in the end your teeth chatter. Do not give him power in his youth, and do not disregard his thoughts. Bend his neck in his youth, and strike his sides while he is still a child, lest he become hardened, refuse to believe you, and become a grief to your soul. Teach your son and work upon him, lest you be ashamed of his disgrace [Note: [Col. 0964] The Vulgate reads, “lest you stumble over his disgrace.”]. A poor man who is healthy and strong is better than a rich man who is weak and scourged by wickedness. The health of the soul in the holiness of righteousness is better than all gold and silver; and a healthy body [Col. 0965] is better than immense wealth. There is no wealth above the wealth of bodily health, and there is no delight above joy of heart. Better is death than a bitter life, and eternal rest than enduring sickness. Good things hidden in a closed mouth are like dishes set around a tomb.

And five verses later: Do not give sadness to your soul, and do not afflict yourself in your deliberation. Joy of heart is the life of a person and an unfailing treasure of holiness; and a man’s rejoicing is long life. Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God, and restrain yourself; gather your heart in His holiness, and drive sadness far from you. For sadness has killed many, and there is no usefulness in it. Jealousy and anger shorten one’s days, and worry brings on old age before its time.

And ten verses later [XXXI]: Whoever loves gold will not be justified, and whoever pursues corruption will be filled with it. Many have been given over to falls because of gold [Note: [Col. 0965] Greek: *eis ptōma charin chrusiou*, “to a fall because of gold.”], and their ruin has come through its appearance. Gold is a stumbling block for those who sacrifice; woe to those who pursue it, and every imprudent person will perish [Note: [Col. 0965] The Regius codex reads, “will be deceived.”] through it. Blessed is the rich man who has been found without blemish, who has not gone after gold and has not placed his hope in money and treasures. Who is he, and we shall praise him? For he has done wonders in his life. Who has been tested in it [Note: [Col. 0965] This agrees with the Greek *tis edokimast hē*; but the Vulgate prefers, “Who has been approved.”] and been found perfect? His glory will be eternal. Whoever could transgress and did not transgress, and could do evil and did not do it: therefore his good deeds have been established in the Lord, and the Church of the saints will recount his almsgiving.

And after some verses: Use what is set before you like a frugal man, so that, when you eat much, you are not hated. Stop first for the sake of discipline, and do not be excessive, lest you offend. Even if you sit among many, do not be the first to extend your hand to them, nor ask first to drink. How sufficient for a learned man is a little wine!

And after some verses: Do not provoke those who love wine, for wine has destroyed many.

And twenty-six verses later [XXXII]: Let the elder speak; for the first word becomes you, who love knowledge [Note: [Col. 0965] The Regius manuscript reads, “love knowledge.” The Carnutes manuscript reads, “of one who loves knowledge.” The Vulgate reads, “to one who loves knowledge.” Finally, the Greek means, “in diligent knowledge.”]; and do not interrupt music. Where there is no hearing, pour out your speech; and do not be presumptuously exalted in your wisdom.

And five verses later: Young man, speak in your own cause, scarcely except when it is necessary [Note: [Col. 0965] The Regius codex lacks the words “when it is necessary.” They are absent from the Vulgate, but not from the Greek text.]. If you are questioned twice, let your answer be brief. In many matters be like one who does not know, and listen while remaining silent and asking questions at the same time. Do not presume to speak among great men [Note: [Col. 0965] The Regius codex and the sacred Bibles lack the word “to speak.”]; and where there are old men, do not speak much. Before hail comes lightning, and before shame comes grace, and in place of reverence good [Col. 0966] favor will come to you [Note: [Col. 0966] In the Vulgate, verse 15 of chapter 5 begins: “And do not delay the hour of rising; but go ahead,” and so forth.]. Go ahead first into your house, and there take your ease, and there play, and carry out your thoughts, but not in sins and arrogant speech. And above all these things bless God, who made you and intoxicates you with all His good things. Whoever fears God will receive His instruction, and those who keep watch for Him will find blessing. Whoever seeks the law will be filled with it, but whoever acts deceitfully will stumble over it. Those who fear the Lord will find just judgment and will kindle righteousness like a light. A sinful person will avoid correction and will find comparison according to his own will. A man of counsel will not destroy understanding.

And four verses later: My son, do nothing without counsel, and afterward you will not regret it.

And a few verses later: Whoever believes in God will heed His commandments, and whoever trusts in Him will not be diminished.

[XXXIII] Evils will not meet the one who fears the Lord; rather, in temptation God will preserve him and deliver him from evils. A wise person does not hate commandments and ordinances, and is not tossed about like a ship in a storm. A sensible man believes the law of God, and the law is faithful to him. Whoever makes inquiry will prepare a saying.

And a little later [XXXIV]: Vain hope and falsehood belong to a senseless man, and dreams exalt the imprudent. As one who has grasped a shadow and follows the wind, so is one who attends to deceptive visions. This is the character of dreams: before a person’s face there is the likeness of a person. What can be cleansed from the unclean? And what truth can be spoken by a liar? Divination is error, omens are lies, and the dreams of those who do evil are vanity. Just as the heart of a woman in labor suffers fantasies, unless a visitation has been sent forth by the Most High, do not set your heart upon them. For dreams have caused many to wander and have brought down those who hoped in them. Without falsehood the word will be brought to completion, and wisdom will be contemplated in the mouth of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0966] The Vulgate reads: “The word of the law will be brought to completion, and wisdom will be made smooth in the mouth of the faithful.” The manuscript codices of the *Speculum* read, “in the faithful mouth.”].

And five verses later: I saw many things while recounting [Note: [Col. 0966] It should be read, “I saw while wandering,” or, as in the sacred Bibles, “I saw while wandering.”], and very many customary forms of speech. Several times I endangered myself to the point of death because of these things, and by the grace of God I was delivered. The spirit of those who fear God is sought, and in His regard they will be blessed [Note: [Col. 0966] The Vulgate reads, “he will be blessed.”]. For their hope is in the One who saves them, and the eyes of God are upon those who love Him. Whoever fears the Lord will fear nothing and will not be terrified, because He is his hope. Blessed is the soul of one who fears the Lord. Toward whom does he look, and who is his strength? The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear Him: He is the protector of power, the support of strength, the shelter from heat, and the shade at noon [Note: [Col. 0966] The Vulgate reads, “of midday.”]; the one who averts offense and helps in misfortune; who raises up the soul, enlightens the eyes, and grants health, life, and blessing.

The offering of one who sacrifices from iniquity is defiled, and the mockeries of the unjust are not pleasing. The Lord is only for those who wait upon Him [Col. 0967] in the way of truth and righteousness. The Most High does not approve the gifts of the unjust, does not look upon the offerings of the wicked, and will not be appeased for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices. Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father. The bread of the needy is the life of the poor; whoever defrauds him is a man of blood. Whoever takes away bread earned by sweat is like one who kills his neighbor. Whoever sheds blood and whoever defrauds a laborer are brothers. If one builds and another destroys, what do they gain except labor? If one prays and another curses, whose voice will God hear? What benefit does one receive from washing who is baptized after touching a dead person and then touches him again? So too, what benefit does a person gain by humbling himself if he fasts in his sins and then commits the same sins again? Who will hear his prayer?

[XXXV] Whoever keeps the law multiplies prayer. A saving sacrifice is to heed the commandments and turn away from every iniquity; to offer an atoning sacrifice for injustices, and, as a supplication for sins, to withdraw from injustice.

And a few verses later: You will not appear empty-handed in the presence of God. For all these things are done because of the commandments of the Lord. The offering of the righteous fattens the altar, and it is an odor of sweetness in the presence of the Most High. The sacrifice of the righteous is accepted, and the Lord will not forget its remembrance. Give glory to God with a good heart, and do not diminish the first fruits of your hands. In every gift make your face cheerful, and sanctify your tithes with rejoicing. Give to the Most High according to His gift, and with a good eye make your hands’ offering; for the Lord is one who repays, and He will repay you sevenfold. Do not offer wicked gifts, for He will not receive them. Do not look upon an unjust sacrifice, for the Lord is judge, and with Him there is no regard for a person’s status. The Lord will show no partiality against the poor man, but He will hear the prayer of the wronged. He will not despise the prayers of the orphan or of the widow when she pours out a lamenting speech. Does not a tear descend onto the cheek, and a cry rise from the cheek because of that which descends upon it [Note: [Col. 0967] The sacred Bibles read: “Do not the widow’s tears descend onto her cheek, and does her cry not rise against the one who causes them to descend?”]?

And four verses later: The prayer of one who humbles himself will pierce the clouds.

And a little later [XXXVII]: Be constant with a holy man, whoever you know to observe the fear of God, whose soul is like your soul.

And five verses later: And in all these things entreat the Most High to direct your way in truth.

And twenty-one verses later: My son, test your soul during your life; and if it is wicked, do not give it power. For not everything is suitable for everyone, and not every kind of thing pleases every soul. Do not be greedy at every feast, and do not pour yourself out over every food.

And four verses later [XXXVIII]: Honor the physician because of necessity, for the Most High created him. For healing is from God, and from the king he will receive a gift. The physician’s discipline will exalt his head, and in the presence of [Col. 0968] great men he will be praised. The Most High created medicine from the earth [Note: [Col. 0968] In the sacred Bibles, “medicines.”], and a prudent man will not reject it. Was not bitter water sweetened by wood? Its power is known to human beings, and the Most High gave humanity knowledge, to be honored in His wonders. Through these remedies He has eased their pain [Note: [Col. 0968] The Vulgate reads, “He will ease their pain, and the apothecary will prepare them.” Moreover, in verse 9, instead of “do not despair,” it reads, “do not despise yourself.”].

And four verses later: My son, do not despair in your illness; instead, pray to the Lord, and He Himself will heal you. Turn away from sin, and stretch out your hands, and cleanse your heart from every sin.

And one verse later: And make the offering fat, and give the physician his place, for the Lord created him; and let him not depart from you, since his works are necessary. For there is a time when you fall into their hands; but they will pray to the Lord to direct their rest and their health because of their conduct [Note: [Col. 0968] The manuscripts read, “because of their conversion.”].

And one verse later: My son, bring forth tears for the dead, and begin to weep as one who has suffered terribly. According to judgment, cover his body, and do not despise his burial. Because of the carrying away, bear his mourning bitterly for one day, and console yourself on account of the grief; and make mourning according to his merit for one or two days, because of detraction. For death hastens because of grief, and sorrow will conceal strength, and sadness of heart will bend the neck.

And one verse later: Do not give your heart over to sadness.

And nine verses later: The wisdom of the scribe appears in a time of leisure, and whoever is diminished in activity will acquire wisdom.

And a little later [XXXIX]: Say aloud: “Hear me, divine fruits of the waters, and flower like a rose planted beside a stream” [Note: [Col. 0968] The Vulgate has: “He says, ‘Hear me, divine fruits, and flower like a rose planted beside streams of water.’”]. Have the fragrance of Lebanon. Bloom like lilies, give fragrance, put forth leaves in grace, and praise the song; bless the Lord in His works. Give magnificence to His name and confess Him with the voice of your lips, in songs of the lips and on lyres; and thus you shall say in confession: “The works of the Lord are all exceedingly good.” At His word the water stood like a heap, and at the word of His mouth it was like reservoirs of water. For at His command pleasure comes to be, and there is no diminution in His salvation. Every work of flesh is before Him, and nothing is hidden from His eyes. From age to age He will look upon it [Note: [Col. 0968] The Vulgate reads, “He looks upon it.”], and nothing is wondrous in His sight. One must not say, “What is this?” or, “What is that?” For everything will be sought in its proper time.

And a little later [XL]: Grace is like a paradise in blessings, and mercy endures forever.

And twelve verses later: Brothers are a help in time of tribulation, and mercy will deliver them.

And a little later [XLI]: Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure—what use is there in either? Better is the person who hides his foolishness than the person who hides his wisdom.

And sometime later [LXIII]: Those who bless the Lord, exalt Him as much as you can; He is greater than every praise. As you exalt Him, be filled with strength.

And after much material [LI]: Draw near to me, you who are unlearned, and gather in the house of instruction. Why do you still delay, and why do you still speak of these things? Your souls thirst intensely. I opened my mouth and spoke: “Acquire wisdom for yourselves without silver” [Note: [Col. 0969] The word “wisdom” is absent from the manuscripts and also from the sacred Bibles.], and submit your necks to the yoke, and let your soul receive instruction. For it is near at hand to find it. See with your own eyes, for I have labored little and found much rest for myself. Take instruction in exchange for a great quantity of silver, and possess abundant gold through it. Let your soul rejoice in its mercy, and you will not be put to shame in its praise. Do your work before the appointed time, and it will give you your reward at its proper time.

We have thought these passages from the Book of Tobit should be included.

## From the Book of Tobit

[Chapter IV] You shall honor your mother all the days of her life. For you must remember what and how great dangers she suffered for you in her womb.

And two verses later: All the days of your life keep God in mind, and take care never to consent to sin or neglect the commandments of your God. From your substance give alms, and do not turn your face away from any poor person; for then it will happen that the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you. As far as you are able, be merciful. If you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, willingly strive to share even a little. For you are storing up a good reward for yourself on the day of necessity. For almsgiving delivers from every sin and from death, and does not allow the soul to go into darkness. Almsgiving will bring great confidence before the Most High to all who practice it. Take care, my son, to avoid every form of fornication, and apart from your wife never allow yourself to know such a crime. Never allow pride to rule in your mind or in your speech; for every ruin had its beginning in it. Whatever anyone has done for you, immediately return his wages to him; and do not let a laborer’s pay remain with you at all. What you hate to have done to you, see that you never do to another. Eat your bread with the hungry poor, and cover the naked with your garments.

And two verses later: Always seek counsel from a wise person. At every time bless God, and ask Him to direct your ways, and let all your plans remain in Him.

And seven verses later [Note: [Col. 0969] The Regius manuscript reads, “eight verses later.”]: Do not be afraid, my son. We lead a poor life, but we shall have many good things if we fear God, withdraw from every sin, and do what is good.

And after much material [XII]: Then Raphael said to them secretly: “Bless the God of heaven and confess Him before all the living, for He has shown His mercy toward you. For it is good to conceal the king’s secret, but to reveal and confess the works of God is honorable. Prayer with fasting is good, and almsgiving is better than storing up treasures of gold. For [Col. 0970] almsgiving delivers from death; it is what purifies sins and makes one find eternal life. But those who commit sin and iniquity are enemies of their own souls.”

And a little later [XIV]: “Hear, therefore, my children, your father: Serve the Lord in truth, and seek to do what is pleasing to Him. Command your children also to practice righteousness and almsgiving, so that they may remember God and bless Him at all times, in truth and with all their strength.”

Now, since not all the canonical books of the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0970] In the Regius codex: “the ancient books for this work”; the word “Testament” is omitted.] have supplied what is necessary for this work of ours, and those that did supply it did not do so from all their passages, but only from those in which we found clearer precepts of good conduct—whether useful things are commanded or contrary things prohibited—let us pass to the sacred evangelical and apostolic Scriptures. The four most famous and distinguished Gospels occupy the chief place in the canon of the New Testament; in the first of them, which is according to Matthew, let us examine those passages that are relevant to the work we have undertaken.

## From the Gospel According to Matthew

[Chapter V] When the Lord saw the crowds, He went up onto the mountain; and when He had sat down, His disciples came to Him. And opening His mouth, He taught them, saying:

Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.

Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.

Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.

Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.

Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

Blessed are you when people curse you [Note: [Col. 0970] The word “people” is absent from the Carnutes codex and also from the sacred Bibles.], persecute you, and, lying, say every evil thing against you because of me. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven; for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.

You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be salted? It is no longer useful for anything except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people.

You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden. Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. Thus let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to abolish, but to fulfill. Amen I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until everything has happened. Therefore, whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever practices and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

But I say to you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the [Col. 0971] scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

You have heard that it was said to the ancients, “You shall not kill”; but whoever kills will be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, “Raca,” will be liable to the council; and whoever says, “Fool,” will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.

Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer [Note: [Col. 0971] The Regius codex reads, “offer”; this agrees with the Greek *prosphere*.] your gift.

Be agreeable to your adversary quickly, while you are on the way with him, lest your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Amen I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last farthing.

You have heard that it was said to the ancients, “You shall not commit adultery.” But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

And if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. For it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be thrown [Note: [Col. 0971] The manuscripts read, “go.”] into Gehenna. And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. For it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna.

It was also said, “Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce.” But I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.

Again, you have heard that it was said to the ancients, “You shall not swear falsely”; but you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord. But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of His feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great king; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be, “Yes, yes; no, no.” Whatever is more than these comes from evil.

You have heard that it was said, “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.” But I say to you, do not resist evil; rather, if someone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also. And to anyone who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. And whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him another two. Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from one who wishes to borrow from you [Note: [Col. 0971] Thus the printed editions and the manuscript codices of this work; according to the Greek, *ton thelonta apo sou daneisthai*, “to lend to the one who wishes from you.” But the Vulgate reads, “from the one who wishes to borrow from you.” Later, where it reads “do not turn away,” the Regius codex has “do not turn”; the Greek has *mē apostraphēs*, “do not turn away.”].

You have heard that it was said [Note: [Col. 0971] The printed editions add here, “to the ancients”; this word is absent from the manuscripts and from the sacred Bibles.], “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” But I say to you, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes His sun rise upon the evil and the good and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.

For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the Gentiles do this? Therefore, you shall be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect.

## [VI.]

“Take heed that you do not practice your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.

“Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be honored by people. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

“And when you pray, do not pray like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in the synagogues and at the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by people. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, enter your room, and after closing your door pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

[Note: [Col. 0972] In the Chartres manuscript and the ancient Corbie Bibles, *cum orabis* (“when you pray”) stands in place of *cum oraveris*. In this same verse, after “door,” *your* is added in the Corbie Bibles and in the Greek.]

“But when praying, do not speak at excessive length, like the Gentiles; for they think that they will be heard because of their many words. Therefore do not become like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

[Note: [Col. 0972] The Regius codex reads: *quibus opus sit vobis* (“the things you need”); Greek: *hôn chreian echete* (“of which you have need”).]

“Pray, then, in this way:

‘Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth. Give us today our supersubstantial bread.

[Note: [Col. 0972] The printed editions read “daily”; but the manuscripts, together with the sacred Bibles, read “supersubstantial.”]

And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.’

For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins.

“And when you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites. For they disfigure their faces, so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

“Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal. For where your treasure is, there also is your heart.

“The lamp of the body is the eye.

[Note: [Col. 0972] Thus all the manuscripts of this *Speculum*. But the Vulgate reads: ‘The lamp of your body is your eye.’ The Greek wording, however, says nothing other than: ‘The lamp of the body is the eye.’]

“If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark. If, then, the light that is in you is darkness, how great will that darkness be?

“No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will support the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon.

“Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life—what you will eat—or about your body—what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they? And which of you, by being anxious, can add one cubit to his stature?

“And concerning clothing, why are you anxious? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor or spin. Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. If, then, God so clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith?

[Note: [Col. 0973] Thus the manuscripts, in agreement with the Vulgate, read “of little faith”; but the printed editions read “of least faith.”]

“Therefore do not be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’ or ‘What will we drink?’ or ‘With what will we be clothed?’ For the Gentiles seek all these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first, therefore, the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow; for tomorrow will be anxious about itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.”

## [VII.]

“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment by which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure by which you measure, it will be measured back to you.

“Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while, behold, there is a beam in your eye? Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye; and then you will see how to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.

“Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest they perhaps trample them under their feet and, turning around, tear you apart.

“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

“Or which of you is there who, if his son asks him for bread, would hand him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, would hand him a serpent? If you, then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?

“Therefore, whatever you wish people to do for you, you also do for them; for this is the Law and the Prophets.

“Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way spacious that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. How narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and there are few who find it.

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits. Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but a bad tree produces bad fruits. A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. Therefore, you will know them by their fruits.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven—he will enter the kingdom of heaven.

“Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who practice iniquity.’

“Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock. The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew and struck [Note: [Col. 0974] The manuscripts read ‘fell upon.’ The Greek is *prosépeson*.] against that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon rock.

“And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand. The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew and struck against that house; and it fell, and its ruin was great.”

A little later [X.]:

“You have received without payment; give without payment. Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff, for the laborer is worthy of his food.

“Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart. When you enter a house, greet it, saying, ‘Peace to this house.’

[Note: [Col. 0974] Thus the printed editions, in agreement with the Vulgate. But the manuscripts lack the words ‘saying, Peace to this house’; these words are found neither in the Greek text nor in Jerome. Indeed, when Jerome says of this passage, ‘He expressed covertly the greeting of the Hebrew and Syriac language,’ he indicates that Matthew did not explicitly state the formula of greeting, but only implicitly, namely in what follows: ‘Your peace will come upon it.’ The formula is explicitly stated by Luke, chapter 10, verse 5.]

“And if that house is worthy, your peace will come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you. And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, as you go out of the house or city, shake the dust from your feet. Truly I tell you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city.

“Behold, I send you like sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. But beware of people. For they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; and you will be led before governors and kings on my account, as a testimony to them and to the nations.

“When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you will speak; for what you are to speak will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.

“Brother will hand brother over to death, and father his son; and children will rise up against their parents and put them to death. And you will be hated by all people [Note: [Col. 0974] The word ‘people’ is absent from the Regius codex, as well as from the Greek text and the Vulgate; nevertheless it is found in the ancient Corbie Bibles.] because of my name. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.

“When they persecute you in this city, flee to another. Truly I tell you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes.

“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household?

“Therefore do not fear them. For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known. What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the rooftops. Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.

“Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Therefore do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows.

“Everyone, therefore, who acknowledges me before people, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before people, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.

“Do not suppose that I came to bring peace upon earth. I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I came to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his household.

“Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Whoever finds his life will lose it; and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.

“Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. And whoever gives one of these least ones even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple—truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward.”

A little later [XI.]:

“To what, then, shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace, who call to their companions and say: ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not beat your breasts.’ For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.’ And wisdom was justified by her children.

“And a little later:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

Likewise a little later [XII.]:

“If you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned the innocent.

“And a little later:

“Whoever is not with me is against me; and whoever does not gather with me scatters. Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.

“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit. Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. A good person brings forth good things from the good treasure [Note: [Col. 0976] The Vulgate does not have ‘of his heart,’ although the Greek text has *tês kardias*, with *autoû* added in certain manuscripts, as in Chrysostom.] of the heart; and an evil person brings forth evil things from the evil treasure. But I tell you that for every idle word people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

And after some interval [XV.]:

“Listen and understand. It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth—this defiles a person.”

And a little later:

“Peter, answering, said to him, ‘Explain this parable to us.’ But he said, ‘Are you also still without understanding? Do you not understand that everything entering the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the privy? But the things that proceed from the mouth come out of the heart, and these defile a person. For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things that defile a person; but eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person.’”

Likewise after some interval [XVI.]:

“Then Jesus said to his disciples: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a person give for his soul? For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his works.’”

Likewise somewhat later [XVIII.]:

“Truly I tell you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greater in the kingdom of heaven. And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.

“But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone pulled by an ass be hung around his neck and he be sunk into the depth of the sea.

“Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks! For it is necessary that stumbling blocks come; nevertheless, woe to the person through whom the stumbling block comes!

“If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is good for you to enter life maimed or lame [Note: [Col. 0976] The printed editions had omitted ‘or lame’; it is found here in the manuscripts and also in the sacred Bibles.] rather than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into eternal fire. And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is good for you to enter life with one eye rather than, having two eyes, to be cast into the Gehenna of fire.

“See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. For the Son of Man came to save what had perished.

“And a little later:

“If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. But if he does not listen to them, tell the Church. And if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.

“Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven. Again I tell you, if two of you agree on earth about any matter whatever that they may ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.”

Then Peter approached him and said, “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?” Jesus said to him, “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven.

“Therefore the kingdom of heaven has been compared to a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. When he began to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents.
