Since he had nothing with which to repay, his master ordered him to be sold, together with his wife, his children, and all that he possessed, and repayment to be made.

“Then that servant fell down and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’ Taking pity on that servant, his master released him and forgave him the debt.

“But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him one hundred denarii; and seizing him, he began to choke him, saying, ‘Repay what you owe.’ Then his fellow servant fell down and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’ But he was unwilling. Instead, he went away and had him put in prison until he repaid the debt.

“When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly distressed; and they came and reported to their master everything that had taken place. Then his master summoned him and said to him, ‘Wicked servant, I forgave you the whole debt because you begged me. Should you not therefore also have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?’

“And his master, becoming angry, handed him over to the torturers until he repaid the entire debt. So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.”

And a little later [XIX.]:

“The Pharisees approached him, testing him and saying, ‘Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?’ He answered and said to them, ‘Have you not read that the one who made [Note: [Col. 0977] The printed editions read: ‘that the one who made the human being.’ But the manuscripts lack the word ‘human being,’ which Augustine does not usually add, as we have already observed. Although this word now appears in the Vulgate, it is absent from the ancient Corbie Bibles and from the Greek text.] them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: “For this reason a man will leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh.” Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God, therefore, has joined together, let no human being separate.’

“They said to him, ‘Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and that she be dismissed?’ He said to them, ‘Because Moses permitted you, on account of the hardness of your hearts, to divorce your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.’

“His disciples said to him, ‘If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.’ He said, ‘Not everyone grasps this word, but only those to whom it has been given. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; and there are eunuchs who were made so by people; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who can grasp it grasp it.’

“Then children were brought to him so that he might lay hands on them and pray; but the disciples rebuked them. Jesus, however, said to them, ‘Allow the children, and do not prevent them from coming to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.’ And after he had laid his hands on them, he departed from there.

“And behold, someone approached and said to him, ‘Good Teacher, what good shall I do so that I may have eternal life?’ He said to him, ‘Why do you ask me about the good? One is good—God. But if you wish to enter life, keep the commandments.’ He said to him, ‘Which ones?’ Jesus said, ‘You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not give false testimony; honor your father and mother; and, you shall love your neighbor as yourself.’

“The young man said to him, ‘I have kept all these things [Note: [Col. 0978] The Vulgate in the printed editions adds: ‘from my youth’; the *Speculum* of Augustine does not have it here, nor do the ancient Corbie Bibles or the Greek text.] What do I still lack?’ Jesus said to him, ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.’

“When the young man heard the word, he went away sorrowful, for he had many possessions. Jesus then said to his disciples, ‘Truly I tell you, a rich person will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty. And again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.’

“When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying, ‘Who, then, can be saved?’ But Jesus looked at them and said, ‘With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.’

“Then Peter answered and said to him, ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?’ Jesus said to them, ‘Truly I tell you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for the sake of my name will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first.’”

And a little later [XX.]:

“Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

And somewhat later [XXII.]:

“Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.

“And elsewhere:

“‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the greatest and first commandment. The second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Upon these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets.”

And a few verses later [XXIII.]:

“Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: ‘The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat. Therefore whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do. They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them upon people’s shoulders, but they themselves do not wish to move them with their finger.

“They do all their works so that they may be seen by people. For they enlarge their phylacteries and lengthen their fringes. They love the first couches at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi.

“But do not be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher, and you are all brothers. And do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor be called teachers, for one is your teacher, Christ. The greater among you will be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

“And a little later:

“‘Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have abandoned the weightier matters of the Law—judgment, mercy, and faith. These you ought to have done, without omitting the others. Blind guides, who strain out a gnat but swallow a camel.

“‘Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, but inwardly they are full of robbery and every impurity.

[Note: [Col. 0979] The Regius manuscript reads: ‘they are full of robbery,’ and so forth. The Greek is *gémousin ex arpagês*. The Vulgate reads: ‘you are full of robbery and impurity,’ omitting ‘every,’ which is also absent from the Greek.]

“‘Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and dish, so that what is outside may also become clean.

“‘Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which appear outwardly beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.

“‘Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you build the tombs of the Prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say, “If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the Prophets.” Thus you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the Prophets. And you—fill up the measure of your fathers.

“‘Serpents, offspring of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna? Therefore [Note: [Col. 0979] The printed editions read: ‘therefore I tell you.’ But the manuscripts and the sacred Bibles lack ‘I tell you.’] behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city, so that upon you may come all the righteous blood poured out upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.’”

And a little later [XXIV.]:

“Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold; but whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

And after some interval:

“Be ready, because you do not know at what hour [Note: [Col. 0980] The sacred Bibles read: ‘because you do not know what hour.’] the Son of Man will come. Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom his master appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom, when his master comes, he finds acting in this way. Truly I tell you, he will appoint him over all his possessions.

“But if that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants, while eating and drinking with drunkards, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know; he will cut him in two and assign his portion with the hypocrites. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

And a little later [XXV.]:

“Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

Likewise a little later:

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty. All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.

“Then the king will say to those at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me.’

“Then the righteous will answer him, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you? Or when did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?’

“And the king, answering, will say to them: ‘Truly I tell you, insofar as you did it to one of these least of my brothers, you did it to me.’

“Then he will say also to those at his left hand: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.’

“Then they themselves also will answer, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?’

“Then he will answer them, saying: ‘Truly I tell you, insofar as you did not do it to one of these least ones, neither did you do it to me.’

“And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

And after some interval [XXVI.]:

“Keep watch and pray, so that you may not enter into temptation.”

# FROM THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK

## [CHAPTER VII]

Calling the crowd to him again, he said to them: “Listen to me, all of you, and understand. Nothing from outside entering a person can defile him; but the things that proceed from a person are what defile a person. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”

And when he had entered the house away from the crowd, his disciples questioned him about the parable. And he said to them: “Are you also so without understanding? Do you not understand that everything external entering a person cannot defile him [Note: [Col. 0981] The Venetian edition reads ‘defile’; and a little later, ‘defile.’ M.], because it does not enter his heart but the stomach [Note: [Col. 0981] The Vulgate reads: ‘but goes into the stomach.’] and exits into the privy, purifying all foods?”

And he said that the things proceeding from a person are what defile a person. For from within, from the heart of people, proceed evil thoughts [Note: [Col. 0981] The word ‘proceed’ is absent from the Vulgate, but it is found in the manuscripts of this *Speculum*. In these, the Regius manuscript, after ‘evil thoughts,’ continues: ‘from there they proceed.’], adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, greed, wickedness, deceit, indecency, an evil eye, blasphemies, pride, foolishness. All these evils proceed from within and defile a person.

And elsewhere [VIII.]:

“Calling the crowd together with his disciples, he said to them: ‘If anyone wishes to follow me [Note: [Col. 0981] The Regius codex, in agreement with the Greek, reads ‘to follow after me’; so also the ancient Corbie Bibles.], let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake and for the Gospel will save it. For what will it profit a person if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what will a person give in exchange for his soul?

“‘For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man also will put him to shame [Note: [Col. 0981] The Vulgate reads: *confundetur eum* (“will be ashamed of him”).] in the glory of his Father with his angels.’”

And elsewhere [IX.]:

“Taking a child, he placed it in the midst of them. And when he had embraced it, he said to them: ‘Whoever receives one of these children in my name receives me; and whoever receives me does not receive me, but him who sent me.’

“And a little later:

“‘For whoever gives you a cup of water to drink [Note: [Col. 0981] The printed editions added ‘cold’; this is absent from the manuscripts and from the sacred Bibles.] in my name, because you belong to Christ—truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward.

“‘And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone pulled by an ass were placed around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.’

“And after a little while:

“‘Have salt in yourselves, and maintain peace among yourselves.’”

And shortly afterward [X]:

The Pharisees approached and questioned him, asking, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?”—testing him. But he answered and said to them, “What did Moses command you?” They said, “Moses permitted a writ of divorce to be written and the wife to be dismissed.” Jesus answered them, “Because of the hardness of your hearts he wrote this commandment for you. But from the beginning of creation God made them male and female. For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

And again in the house his disciples questioned him about the same matter. And he said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her; and if a wife divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.” And four verses later:

“Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them. For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Amen I tell you: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will not enter it.” And embracing them and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them.

And as he was setting out on the road, a certain man ran up [Note: [Col. 0982] The Vulgate has procurrens, “running up.” The Greek, prodramōn, “running ahead” or “running up.”], knelt before him, and asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to receive eternal life?” But Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God. You know the commandments: You shall not commit adultery; You shall not murder; You shall not steal; You shall not bear false witness; You shall not defraud; Honor your father and mother.” He answered and said to him, “Teacher, I have kept all these things from my youth.” Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, “One thing is lacking to you: go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” But he was saddened by the saying and went away grieving, for he had many possessions.

And Jesus, looking around, said to his disciples, “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God!” The disciples were astonished at his words. But Jesus, answering again, said to them, “Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God for those who put their confidence in money! It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” They were even more amazed, saying to one another, “Then who can be saved?” Looking at them, Jesus said, “With human beings it is impossible, but not with God; for all things are possible with God.”

Peter began to say to him, “Look, we have left everything and followed you.” Jesus answered, “Amen I tell you: there is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or mother, or father, or children, or fields, for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this present time—houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and fields, with persecutions—and in the age to come, eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

And shortly afterward:

“You know that those who seem to rule over the Gentiles lord it over them, and their rulers exercise authority over them. But it is not so among you. Rather, whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be the slave of all. For the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

And somewhat later [XI]:

Jesus answered and said to them, “Have faith in God. Amen I tell you: whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be removed and cast into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that whatever he says will happen, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you: whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will come to you [Note: [Col. 0982] The Vulgate has et evenient, “and they will happen.”].

“And when you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your sins.”

[Col. 0983] Likewise, somewhat later [XII]:

Jesus answered and said to them, “Give back, therefore, to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.”

And elsewhere:

One of the scribes approached, having heard them disputing and seeing that he had answered them well, and asked him which commandment was first of all. Jesus answered him, “The first of all the commandments is: Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. This is the first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these.”

The scribe said to him, “Well said, Teacher; you have spoken the truth, that there is one God and there is no other besides him; and that he is to be loved with all the heart, all the understanding, all the soul, and all the strength; and to love one’s neighbor as oneself is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.” Jesus, seeing that he had answered wisely, said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And no one thereafter dared to question him.

And shortly afterward:

“Beware of the scribes, who want to walk about in long robes, to be greeted in the marketplace, and to sit in the first seats in the synagogues and in the places of honor at banquets. They devour widows’ houses under the pretense of lengthy prayer; they will receive the more severe judgment [Note: [Col. 0983] The Vulgate has accipient, “they will receive.”].”

And Jesus sat opposite the treasury and watched how the crowd put money into the treasury. Many rich people were putting in large amounts. When a poor widow came, she put in two small coins, which make a quadrans. Calling his disciples to him, he said to them, “Amen I tell you: this poor widow has put in more than all those who have put money into the treasury. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had—all her means of living.”

And shortly afterward [XIII]:

“When they lead you away and hand you over, do not deliberate beforehand what you are to say; rather, whatever is given to you in that hour, say it. For it is not you who are speaking, but the Holy Spirit.”

And a little later:

“You will be hated by all on account of my name. But whoever endures to the end will be saved.”

And elsewhere:

“Watch, keep awake, and pray; for you do not know when the time will be. It is like a man who has gone abroad, left his house, and given authority to his servants, assigning each his task, while commanding the doorkeeper to keep watch. Keep watch, therefore, for you do not know when the master of the house will come—whether in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning—lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping. And what I say to you I say to all: Keep watch.”

## FROM THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

[Chapter II.] “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will.”

And somewhat later [III]:

The crowds asked him, saying, “What then shall we do?” He answered and said to them, “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none; and let the one who has food do likewise.”

Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him, “Teacher, what shall we do?” He said to them, “Do nothing beyond what has been appointed for you.”

The soldiers also questioned him, saying, “And what shall we do?” He said to them, “Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your wages.”

And somewhat later [VI]:

“Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh. Blessed are you when people hate you, and when they exclude you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man. Rejoice on that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for their ancestors did the same things to the prophets.

“But woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation. Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep. Woe when all people bless you [Note: [Col. 0984] The word omnes, “all,” is now absent from the Vulgate; but it stood in the ancient Corbie Bibles and in the Greek.], for their ancestors did the same things to the false prophets.

“But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you. Bless those who curse you. Pray for those who slander you. To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also; and from the one who takes away your cloak, do not withhold your tunic as well. Give to everyone who asks you; and from the one who takes away what is yours, do not demand it back. And just as you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them.

“And if you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For sinners also do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? For sinners also lend to sinners, in order to receive an equal return.

“Nevertheless, love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return; and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, because he is kind toward the ungrateful and the wicked. Be merciful, therefore, just as your Father is merciful.

“Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Give, and it will be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, they will pour into your lap. For with the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

He also told them a parable:

“Can a blind person lead a blind person? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher; but everyone who is fully instructed will be like his teacher.

“Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the beam that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the splinter from your eye,’ while you yourself do not see the beam in your eye? Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the splinter from your brother’s eye.

“For there is no good tree that produces bad fruit, nor a bad tree producing good fruit [Note: [Col. 0985] The Regius codex has fructus bonos, “good fruits.”]. Each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thorns, nor are grapes harvested from a bramble. A good person brings forth good from the good treasure of the heart; and an evil person brings forth evil from the evil treasure. For from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.

“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say? Everyone who comes to me, hears my words, and does them—I will show you whom he is like. He is like a man building a house, who dug deeply and laid the foundation upon rock. When a flood came, the river broke against that house but could not shake it, because it had been founded upon rock. But the one who hears and does not act is like a man building his house upon the ground without a foundation. When the river broke against it, it immediately fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

And somewhat later [VII]:

“To whom, then, shall I compare the people of this generation, and to whom are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, saying: ‘We played the flute for you [Note: [Col. 0985] In the Regius manuscript, tibiis, “with flutes,” is absent here; nor is this word added in Matthew 11:17, although the Greek ēulēsamen, the verb found in both passages, does not simply mean ‘we sang,’ but ‘we played the flute for you.’], and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not weep.’

“For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.’ And wisdom has been justified by all her children.”

Likewise, somewhat later [VIII]:

“This, then, is the parable: The seed is the word of God. Those beside the road are the ones who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word away from their heart, so that they may not believe and be saved. Those on the rock are the ones who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; but they have no roots, because they believe for a time [Note: [Col. 0985] In the sacred Bibles, qui ad tempus, “who believe for a time.”], and in the time of trial fall away. The seed that fell among thorns represents those who have heard, but as they go on their way are choked by worries, riches, and pleasures of life, and bear no fruit. The seed in good soil represents those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, hold fast to it and bear fruit with endurance.

“No one who lights a lamp covers it with a vessel or puts it under a bed; rather, he puts it on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor concealed that will not be known and come into the open. Take care, therefore, how you hear [Note: [Col. 0985] The printed Vulgate has audiatis, “how you may hear.” In the ancient Corbie Bibles, however, it has auditis, “how you hear.”]. For to the one who has, it will be given; and from whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away.”

And somewhat later [IX]:

Having summoned the twelve Apostles, he gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases. And he sent them to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick. And he said to them, “Take nothing for the journey: neither staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money, and do not have two tunics. Whatever house you enter, remain there, and do not depart from there. And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.”

Likewise, somewhat later:

He said to all, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily [Note: [Col. 0986] In the Regius and Chartres manuscripts, quotidie, “daily,” is not added.], and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but loses himself and brings ruin upon himself [Note: [Col. 0986] The Vulgate has faciat, “and brings ruin upon himself.”]? For whoever is ashamed of me and my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his own majesty, and that of the Father and of the holy Angels.”

And elsewhere:

A thought arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, seeing the thoughts of their hearts, took a child, set him beside himself, and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For the one who is least among all of you is the greatest.”

And somewhat later:

He said to another, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” Jesus said to him, “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you go and announce the kingdom of God.”

Another said, “I will follow you, Lord; but first permit me to say farewell to those who are at home.” Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

And shortly afterward [X]:

“Behold, I send you like lambs among wolves. Carry neither purse, nor bag, nor sandals, and greet no one along the road. Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you.

“Remain in that same house, eating and drinking what they have, for the laborer is worthy of his wages. Do not move from house to house. Whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you; heal the sick who are in it, and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has drawn near to you.’

“But whatever city you enter and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust that clung to us from your city, we wipe off against you. Yet know this: the kingdom of God has drawn near.’ I tell you, on that day it will be more tolerable for Sodom than for that city.”

And shortly afterward:

“Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”

And shortly afterward:

A certain lawyer stood up, testing him, and saying, “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.”

And shortly afterward:

“Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbor to the man who fell among robbers?” He said, “The one who showed mercy toward him.” Jesus said to him, “Go, and you do likewise.”

And shortly afterward:

“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; yet one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

Likewise, shortly afterward [XI]:

“When you pray,” he said, “say: ‘Father, may your name be sanctified. May your kingdom come. Give us our daily bread today [Note: [Col. 0987] In the ancient Corbie Bibles, quotidie, “daily,” in accordance with the Greek to kath’ hēmeran, “according to each day.”]. And forgive us our sins, since we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And do not lead us into temptation.’”

And he said to them, “Who among you will have a friend and go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from the road, and I have nothing to set before him’? And the man inside, answering, says, ‘Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything.’ If he persists in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, nevertheless, because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs.

“And I say to you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

“What father among you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will offer him a scorpion? If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?”

And shortly afterward:

When he was saying these things, a certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked.” But he said, “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”

And shortly afterward:

As he was speaking, a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him; and he entered and reclined. The Pharisee began, thinking to himself, to say why he had not been baptized before dinner. And the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and the dish, but what is within you is full of plunder and wickedness. Fools! Did not the one who made the outside also make the inside? Nevertheless, give what remains as alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you.

“But woe to you Pharisees, because you tithe mint and rue and every vegetable, while passing over justice and the love of God. These things you ought to have done, without omitting the others. Woe to you Pharisees, because you love the first seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplace. Woe to you, because you are like unmarked tombs, and people walking over them do not know it.”

One of the lawyers answered and said to him, “Teacher, by saying these things you also insult us.” But he said, “Woe to you lawyers also, because you load people with burdens that they cannot carry [Note: [Col. 0988] Here the Regius codex has quae portari non possunt, “which cannot be carried.” So also the ancient Corbie Bible. The Greek text has dusbastakta, that is, “difficult to carry.”], while you yourselves do not touch the burdens with even one of your fingers.”

And elsewhere [XII]:

“Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.”

And shortly afterward:

“I say to you, my friends: Do not be afraid of those who kill the body and, after that, have nothing more they can do. But I will show you whom you should fear. Fear the one who, after killing, has authority to cast into Gehenna. Yes, I tell you, fear him.

“Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies, and not one of them is forgotten before God? Indeed, even all the hairs of your head are numbered. Therefore do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.

“I say to you: Everyone who acknowledges me before human beings, the Son of Man will also confess in him before the Angels of God; but whoever denies me before human beings will be denied before the Angels of God.

“And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but to the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven.

“When they bring you into synagogues, before magistrates and authorities, do not be anxious about how or what you should answer, or what you should say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.”

Someone from the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said to him, “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?”

And he said to them, “Take care and beware of all greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.”

And he told them this parable:

“The field of a certain rich man yielded abundant crops. And he thought within himself, saying, ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to store my crops?’ And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will gather all that has grown for me and my goods. And I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and feast.”’

“But God said to him, ‘Fool! This very night they are demanding your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?’ Thus it is with the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.”

And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you: Do not be anxious about your life—what you will eat—or about your body—what you will wear. Life is more than food, and the body more than clothing.

“Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap; they have neither storeroom nor barn, and God feeds them. How much more valuable are you than they? Which of you, by worrying, can add a single cubit to his stature? If, then, you cannot do even what is least, why are you anxious about the rest?

“Consider the lilies [Note: [Col. 0988] The printed editions have lilia agri, “the lilies of the field.” Agri is absent from the Regius manuscript and from the sacred Bibles, which likewise lack the same word in the following verse.]—how they grow. They neither labor nor spin. Yet I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith?

“And you, do not seek what you will eat or what you will drink, and do not be lifted up. For all these things the nations of the world seek; but your Father knows that you need them. Nevertheless, seek the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0989] The Vulgate now has quaerite primum regnum Dei et justitiam ejus, “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.” But in the ancient Corbie Bible it lacked the words primum, “first,” and et justitiam ejus, “and his righteousness”; these are also absent from the Greek text and from all the manuscripts of this *Speculum*.], and all these things will be added to you.

“Do not be afraid, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom. Sell what you possess and give alms. Make purses for yourselves that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there your heart will also be.

“And shortly afterward:

“You also must be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come [Note: [Col. 0989] In the manuscripts and in the ancient Corbie Bibles, venit, “he comes.” In the Greek, erchetai, “he comes.”].”

Peter said to him, “Lord, are you telling this parable to us, or to everyone?” The Lord said, “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise steward whom the master appoints over his household, to give them their measure of grain at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom, when his master comes, he finds doing so. Truly I tell you, he will appoint him over all that he possesses.

“But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat the menservants and maidservants, and to eat, drink, and become drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him apart and assign him his portion with the faithless.

“But the servant who knew his master’s will and did not prepare or act according to his will will be beaten severely. But the one who did not know and did things deserving blows will be beaten lightly. Everyone to whom much has been given, much will be demanded from him; and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, even more will be required.”

Likewise, shortly afterward:

“Hypocrites! You know how to interpret the face of earth and sky; how is it that you do not interpret this time? And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?”

And somewhat later [XIII]:

“Strive to enter through the narrow door; for many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.”

And elsewhere [XIV]:

He told a parable to those who had been invited, observing how they chose the places of honor at table, and said to them:

“When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you has been invited by him, and the one who invited both you and him comes and says to you, ‘Give this person your place’; and then you begin, with shame, to occupy the lowest place. But when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have honor before all those reclining with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

And he also said to the one who had invited him:

“When you make a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends, your brothers, your relatives, or rich neighbors [Col. 0990], lest they also invite you in return and repayment be made to you. But when you make a banquet, invite the poor, the disabled, the lame, and the blind; and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. For you will be repaid at the repayment [Note: [Col. 0990] The Vulgate has in resurrectione, “at the resurrection.” The Greek, en tē anastasei, “at the resurrection.”] of the righteous.”

And shortly afterward:

“If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.

“For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the necessary expense, to see whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, after he has laid the foundation and is unable to finish, all who see it will begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was unable to complete it.’

“Or what king, going to engage another king in war, does not first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while the other is still far away, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. Thus, therefore, none of you who does not renounce all that he possesses can be my disciple.”

And somewhat later [XVI]:

“And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings. The one who is faithful in very little is faithful also in much; and the one who is unjust in a little is unjust also in much. If, then, you were not faithful in unrighteous mammon, who will give you what is yours [Note: [Col. 0990] The passage is to be restored from the sacred Bibles in this form: “If, then, you were not faithful in unrighteous mammon, who will believe you concerning what is true? And if you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?”]?

“No servant can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.”

The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things and mocked him. And he said to them, “You are those who justify yourselves before human beings; but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God.”

And a few verses later:

“Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery.”

And shortly afterward [XVII]:

“It is impossible that stumbling blocks should not come; but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were placed around his neck and he were thrown into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble.

“Take heed to yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and turns back to you seven times in a day, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.”

And elsewhere [XVIII]:

He told this parable to certain people who trusted in themselves as righteous and despised others:

“Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. The Pharisee stood and prayed this within himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.’

“But the tax collector, standing far off, was unwilling even to lift his eyes toward heaven; rather, he beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

They also brought infants to him so that he might touch them. When the disciples saw this, they rebuked them. But Jesus called them and said, “Let the children come to me, and do not forbid them. For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Amen I tell you: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it.”

A certain ruler questioned him, saying, “Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” Jesus said, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. You know the commandments: You shall not murder; You shall not commit adultery; You shall not steal; You shall not bear false witness; Honor your father and mother.” He said, “I have kept all these things from my youth.”

When Jesus heard this, he said to him, “One thing is still lacking to you: sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” When he heard this, he became sorrowful, because he was very rich. Seeing him become sorrowful, Jesus said, “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

Those who heard this said, “Then who can be saved?” He said to them, “The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God.”

Peter said, “Look, we have left everything and followed you.” He said to them, “Amen I tell you: there is no one who has left house, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this present time, and in the age to come eternal life.”

And elsewhere [XIX]:

Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I repay it fourfold.” Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost.”

And somewhat later [XX]:

“Give back, therefore, to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.”

And elsewhere:

While all the people were listening, he said to his disciples, “Beware of the scribes, who want to walk about in long robes and love greetings in the marketplace, the first seats in the synagogues, and the places of honor at banquets. They devour widows’ houses while pretending to make lengthy prayers; they will receive the greater condemnation.”

### [XXI.]

And looking up, he saw the rich putting their gifts into the treasury; but he also saw a certain poor widow putting in two small coins. And he said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all the others. For all these contributed to the gifts of God out of their abundance; but she, out of what she lacks, put in all the means of living that she had.”

Likewise, in another passage: “Therefore, settle in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you will answer. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict. You will be handed over by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends, and they will put some of you to death; and you will be hated by all on account of my name. Yet not a hair from your head will perish. By your endurance you will possess your souls.”

And shortly afterward: “But take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts become weighed down with revelry, drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and that day suddenly come upon you. For it will come like a snare upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth. Therefore keep watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are about to happen, and to stand before the Son of Man.”

Likewise, shortly afterward [XXII.]: “A dispute also arose among them as to which of them seemed to be the greatest. But he said to them: ‘The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But you must not be so; rather, let the greater among you become like the younger [Note: [Col. 0992] The printed editions, together with the Vulgate, have ‘like the lesser.’ But the manuscripts have ‘like the younger’; so also the ancient Corbie Bibles, in accordance with the Greek, *hôs ho neôteros*.]; and the leader like the one who serves. For who is greater: the one reclining, or the one serving? Is it not the one reclining? But I am among you as the one who serves.’”

And in another passage: “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.”

## Concerning the Gospel According to John

[Cap. V.] “How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the one God?”

And shortly afterward [VIII.]: “Jesus said, ‘Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on do not sin any more.’”

And a little later: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”

And shortly afterward: “Truly, truly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

And elsewhere: “Truly, truly I tell you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.”

And shortly afterward [XII.]: “Whoever loves his life will lose it; and whoever hates his life in this world will preserve it for eternal life. If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.”

And in another passage: “For they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God.”

And elsewhere [XIII.]: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If I, then, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, so that, just as I have done for you, you also should do.”

And a little later: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you, so that you also may love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

And a little later [XIV.]: “If you love me, keep my commandments.”

And shortly afterward: “Whoever has my commandments [Col. 0993] and keeps them is the one who loves me; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him.”

And three verses later [Note: [Col. 0993] The Regius codex has: “And four verses later.”]: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.”

And a little later [XV.]: “Remain in me, and I in you. Just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not remain in me, he will be thrown out like a branch and will wither; and they will gather it, throw it into the fire, and it will burn. If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. In this my Father is glorified: that you bear much fruit and become my disciples. As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; remain in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be complete. This is my commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends.”

And a little later: “I command you these things, that you love one another.”

These are the passages from the four Gospels that I thought should be included in this work. From them it can be understood that the three evangelists—namely Matthew, Mark, and Luke—have given us more commands for living because they chiefly followed that part which is called the active life. But because John adhered more to the contemplative life, although his Gospel rises above the others, we nevertheless find in it far fewer moral commands. From this point we shall now mention, from that book which they entitled the Acts of the Apostles, what we have found—very little indeed. For it contains the history of events by which faith is built up, and examples rather than commands are written there.

## Concerning the Book of the Acts of the Apostles

[Cap. XV.] James, therefore, speaking, said: “For this reason I judge that those who turn to God from the Gentiles should not be troubled, but that we should write to them to abstain from the pollutions of idols, from fornication, from what has been strangled, and from blood.”

And shortly afterward: “For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you than these necessities: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from fornication. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.”

And after much else, when the apostle Paul was speaking to the leaders of the Church whom he had gathered [Note: [Col. 0993] The Regius manuscript has “whom he had consecrated.”], he said [XX.]: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops, to shepherd the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.”

And shortly afterward, to the same men [Col. 0994]: “I coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing [Note: [Col. 0994] The Corbie Bibles likewise read “silver, or gold”; but the printed Bibles have “and gold.”]; you yourselves know. For these hands served my needs and those who were with me. In every way I have shown you that by laboring in this manner we ought to support the weak and remember the word of the Lord Jesus, for he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

And in another passage, when James and those who were with him were speaking to the apostle Paul, they said to him [XXI.]: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and all are zealous for the Law. They have heard about you that you teach the Jews who live among the Gentiles to abandon Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the custom. What, then, is to be done? Certainly the multitude must assemble, for they will hear that you have arrived. Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have a vow upon themselves. Take these men, purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that what they have heard about you is false, but that you yourself walk in observance of the Law. But concerning those among the Gentiles who have believed, we have written, judging that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from fornication.”

We have found that these passages from the book of the Acts of the Apostles, insofar as they suit this work, are sufficient to place here. In them we see that the Apostles wished to impose none of the burdens of the old Law upon those who had believed from among the Gentiles, as far as abstinence from bodily pleasures is concerned, except that they should abstain from these three things: from what was sacrificed to idols, from blood, and from fornication.

Hence some people think that there are only three deadly sins: idolatry, homicide, and fornication—whereby adultery and every intercourse apart from that with one’s wife are certainly included. Are all the other sins, then, not deadly, although they separate people from the kingdom of God? Or was it said pointlessly and deceptively: “Neither thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers [Note: [Col. 0994] The printed editions have “wrongdoers.” But the Regius manuscript, like the sacred Bibles, has “revilers.], nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10)?

But we must restrain our argument and now proceed to the apostolic Epistles, and see what in them also can suitably be adapted to this work.

## Concerning the Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to the Romans

[Cap. I.] “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel. For it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written: ‘But the righteous person lives by faith’ [Note: [Col. 0994] Here and in Habakkuk 2:4, the Greek has *zēsetai*, ‘will live.’].

“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those people who suppress the truth [Note: [Col. 0994] The Vulgate adds here ‘of God,’ although this word is absent from the Greek] in unrighteousness. For what can be known about God is manifest among them, because God has manifested it to them. For his invisible attributes, from the creation of the world, are clearly perceived and understood through the things that have been made—his eternal power also and divinity [Col. 0995]—so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasoning, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and reptiles. Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their own bodies among themselves. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.

“Therefore God gave them over to degrading passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature. Likewise, the men, abandoning natural relations with women, burned with desire for one another, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving in themselves the due recompense for their error. And since they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what is improper: filled with all unrighteousness, wickedness, fornication, greed, and evil; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, senseless, faithless, without affection, without covenant, without mercy. Although they had known God’s righteous judgment, they did not understand that those who practice such things deserve death; they not only do them but also approve those who practice them.”

[II.] “Therefore you are without excuse, every human being who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge [Note: [Col. 0995] Am. and Er. have “who judge.” The Greek is *ho krinōn*]. We know that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who practice such things. Do you suppose, O human being, that when you judge those who practice such things and do them yourself, you will escape God’s judgment? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and forbearance? Do you not know [Note: [Col. 0995] In the ancient Corbie Bibles the participle is used: “not knowing”; in accordance with the Greek, *agnoōn*] that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?

“But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works: eternal life to those who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption; but wrath and indignation to those who are contentious [Note: [Col. 0995] The printed Vulgate has “who seek eternal life” and then “but to those who are contentious”; whereas the ancient Corbie Bibles have the same reading as this *Speculum*] and who do not obey the truth but obey unrighteousness. Tribulation and distress upon every soul of a human being who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek; but glory, honor, and peace for everyone who works good, for the Jew first and also for the Greek.”

And shortly afterward: “For it is not the hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law will be justified.”

Likewise, a little later: “You, therefore, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who boast in the Law, do you dishonor God by transgressing the Law? For ‘the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you,’ as it is written.”

And somewhat later [V.]: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace [Note: [Col. 0996] The sacred Bibles have “through faith into this grace”], in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. And not only that, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.”

And in another passage [VI.]: “Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. Nor present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness; but present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and your members to God as weapons of righteousness.”

And shortly afterward: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and to iniquity leading to iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification.”

And in another passage [VIII.]: “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.”

And shortly afterward: “They are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer together with him so that we may also be glorified together.”

And shortly afterward: “But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with endurance.”

And a few verses later: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God.”

And a little later: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us. For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities [Note: [Col. 0996] Here the sacred Bibles add “nor powers.”], neither things present nor things to come, neither might nor height nor depth nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

And in another passage [X.]: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For Scripture says: ‘Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.’ For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. For the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him. For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”

And in another passage [XI.]: “But stand by faith [Note: [Col. 0996] The Vulgate has “you stand.” The Greek is *estēkas*]; do not be high-minded, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either. See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you [Note: [Col. 0997] The Vulgate adds “of God” after “goodness”; this is absent from the Greek], if you remain in his goodness.”

And shortly afterward [XII.]: “Therefore I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your rational service. And do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may discern what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.

“For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. For just as in one body we have many members, and not all the members have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.

“Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, in proportion to faith; or service, in serving; or the one who teaches, in teaching; the one who exhorts, in exhortation; the one who gives, in generosity; the one who leads, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

“Let love be without hypocrisy: hating evil, clinging to what is good; loving one another with brotherly affection [Note: [Col. 0997] The Vulgate formerly had *charitatem*; but now, more correctly, *charitate*. Likewise, somewhat below, in place of *mihi vindictam* (“vengeance to me”), it has *mihi vindicta* (“vengeance is mine”).]; anticipating one another in honor; not sluggish in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord; rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, constant in prayer; sharing in the needs of the saints, pursuing hospitality.

“Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. Have the same mind toward one another. Do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Do not be wise in your own estimation. Repay no one evil for evil; provide what is good, not only before God but also before all people. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone. Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay,’ says the Lord.

“But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head. Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.”

[XIII.] “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God [Note: [Col. 0997] The sacred Bibles have “have been ordained”; the authorities are understood]. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist will bring judgment upon themselves.

“For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to bad. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it; for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do what is evil, be afraid, for it does not carry the sword without reason. It is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil.

“Therefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. For this reason you also pay taxes, for they are God’s ministers, serving for this very purpose. Pay everyone what is owed: tax to whom tax is owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, fear to whom fear is owed, honor to whom honor is owed.

“Owe no one anything, except to love one another. For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the Law. For ‘You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet’; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love does no evil to one’s neighbor. Therefore love is the fullness of the Law.

“And understand the present time: it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep. For our salvation is now nearer than when we believed. The night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably, as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in sexual debauchery and wantonness, not in strife and jealousy; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.”

[XIV.] “Welcome the one who is weak in faith [Note: [Col. 0998] The printed editions had “weak into faith.” But the manuscripts, in accordance with the Vulgate, have “weak in faith.” The preposition *in* is absent from the Greek.], not for disputes over opinions. One person believes that he may eat everything; but the one who is weak eats vegetables. Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats; for God has welcomed him.

“Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls; and he will stand, for God is able to make him stand. One person judges one day to be different from another; another judges every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord; and the one who eats, eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. And the one who does not eat abstains for the Lord and gives thanks to God.

“For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. If we live, we live for the Lord; and if we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. For it was for this that Christ died and rose again: that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.

“But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God [Note: [Col. 0998] The printed Vulgate has “before the tribunal of Christ”; but the ancient Corbie Bibles agree with this *Speculum*. In them also the following verse reads “every knee will bend to me,” in accordance with the Greek, *emoi kampsei*]. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.’ Therefore each of us will give an account of himself to God.

“Therefore let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: not to place a stumbling block or an occasion of offense before a brother. I know and am convinced in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself; but for the one who considers something unclean, for that person it is unclean. For if your brother is distressed because of food, you are no longer walking according to love. Do not destroy, by your food, the one for whom Christ died.

“Therefore do not let what is good for us be blasphemed. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by people [Col. 0999]. Therefore let us pursue what makes for peace and what makes for mutual edification [Note: [Col. 0999] The printed editions and the Vulgate add “let us preserve” after “for mutual edification”; this verb is absent from the manuscripts and from the ancient Corbie Bibles, and is not present in the Greek].

“Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. Everything is indeed clean, but it is evil for the person who eats through giving offense. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine, or to do anything by which your brother is offended [Note: [Col. 0999] The Carnutensian *Speculum* manuscript and the Corbie Bibles have “by which your brother offends.” The Greek is *proskoptei*, that is, “stumbles”], or is scandalized, or is made weak.

“You have faith [Note: [Col. 0999] Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read: “The faith that you have.” M.]—keep it to yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves. But the one who doubts, if he eats, is condemned, because he does not act from faith. And whatever is not from faith is sin.”

[XV.] “But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not please ourselves. Let each of us [Note: [Col. 0999] Thus the *Speculum* manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek, *hēmōn* (“of us”). But the Vulgate has *vestrum* (“of you”).] please his neighbor for the good, for edification. For Christ did not please himself, but, as it is written: ‘The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.’

“Whatever was written previously was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and through the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and consolation grant you to have the same mind toward one another according to Christ Jesus, so that with one mind and one mouth you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Therefore welcome one another, just as Christ also welcomed you, for the glory of God.”

And somewhat later: “For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. They were pleased to do so, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to minister to them in material things.”

And a few verses later: “I appeal to you, therefore, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0999] The Vulgate has “the love of the Holy Spirit.” “Holy” is absent from the *Speculum* manuscripts and from the Greek], to assist me in prayers for me to God.”

And shortly afterward [XVI.]: “I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause dissensions and offenses contrary to the teaching that you have learned, and to avoid them. For such people do not serve Christ our Lord, but their own belly; and through smooth words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent. For your obedience has become known everywhere. Therefore I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil.”

## Concerning the Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians

[Cap. I.] “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you. Rather, be perfected in the same mind and in the same judgment. For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those of Chloe’s household, that there are contentions among you.

“I mean this: each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I to Apollos,’ or ‘I to Cephas,’ or ‘I to Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

And shortly afterward: “It is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.’”

And in another passage [III.]: “For since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human standards? For when one says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ and another, ‘I to Apollos,’ are you not merely human?”

And shortly afterward: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.

“Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God.”

And after a few verses [IV.]: “Therefore do not judge before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God.

“Now, brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to go beyond what is written, so that none of you may become arrogant in favor of one against another. For who makes you different? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

And shortly afterward: “To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, naked and beaten, homeless, laboring and working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become as the refuse of this world, the scum of all things, to this very day. I do not write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children.”

Likewise, shortly afterward [V.]: “It is commonly reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not even occur among the Gentiles: that someone has his father’s wife.
