And you are puffed up, rather than mourning, so that the one who did this deed might be removed from your midst.

“For my part, although absent in body but present in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, the one who has acted in this way: when you are assembled, and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus, to hand such a person over to Satan [Note: [Col. 1000] Am., Er., and the Regius manuscript omit “to Satan”] for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, just as you are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

“I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators—not at all meaning the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or the rapacious, or those who serve idols; otherwise you would have had to leave the world. But now I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, [Col. 1001] or is a reviler, or a drunkard, or rapacious; with such a person you must not even eat.

“For what have I to do with judging those outside? Is it not those inside whom you judge? God will judge those outside. ‘Remove the evil person from among yourselves.’”

[VI.] “Does any one of you, having a case against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we will judge angels, let alone matters of this life?

“So if you have judgments concerning matters of this life, appoint as judges those who are of no account in the Church. I say this to your shame. Is there really no wise person among you who can judge between his brother? But brother goes to court against brother—and this before unbelievers?

“Indeed, it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer loss? But you inflict injury and cause loss, and this upon your brothers.

“Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have sexual relations with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God.”

And shortly afterward: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not. Or do you not know that the one who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, it says, ‘The two will become one flesh.’ But the one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit.

“Flee fornication. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body. Or do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price. Therefore glorify and bear the Lord in your body.”

### [VII.]

Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the wife her due; likewise also the wife to the husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same relationship, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But I say this as a concession, not as a command. I wish all people to be as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that.

[Note: [Col. 1001] The ancient Regius manuscript also reads “because of fornications,” in agreement with the Greek.]

But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn. But to those who are joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not separate from her husband; but if she has separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let a husband not dismiss his wife.

[Col. 1002] To the others I say—I, not the Lord—if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband.

[Note: [Col. 1002] Here the Vulgate adds “believing”; nevertheless, this word is absent from the Corbie Bibles and from the Greek.]

For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are holy. But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. In such a case the brother or sister is not subject to bondage; but God has called us to peace. For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? Rather, let each live as the Lord has allotted to him, as God has called each one. This is how I teach in all the churches.

Was someone called while circumcised? Let him not draw over the foreskin. Was someone called in the foreskin? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and the foreskin is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments. Let each remain in the calling in which he was called.

Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned about it. But even if you are able to become free, make use of the opportunity. For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise, the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave. You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Let each one, brothers, remain with God in the condition in which he was called.

[Note: [Col. 1002] The sacred Bibles read “brothers,” plural.]

Concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful. I therefore think that this is good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a person to remain as he is. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Nevertheless, such people will have tribulation in the flesh; but I am sparing you.

This, then, I say, brothers: the time is short. Henceforth let those who have wives be as though they had none; those who weep as though they were not weeping; those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing;

[Note: [Col. 1002] At this point the words “and those who buy as though they did not possess” are missing.]

and those who use this world as though they were not using it. For the form of this world is passing away.

I want you to be free from anxiety. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about the things of this world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided. The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy both in body and in spirit. But the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare over you, but with regard to what is honorable and what provides the opportunity to serve the Lord without impediment.

[Note: [Col. 1002] In the Regius Speculum manuscript, the reading is “to observe” (*observandi*); this word was also found in most Bibles before Sixtus’s correction. In the Corbie copies one reads “to observe the Lord” (*Domino observandi*), perhaps in place of *Domino obsecrandi*. The Greek reads: *allà pròs tò euschémōn, kaì euprosédron tō Kyriō aperispástōs*—“but for what is honorable and for serving the Lord attentively, without distraction.” Jerome translated this in the first book *Against Jovinianus*: “but for what is honorable, and for serving the Lord earnestly without any distraction,” although he says that the Greek idiom cannot be expressed in Latin.]

But if anyone thinks that he is behaving dishonorably toward his virgin, because she is past marriageable age, and it ought to happen in this way, let him do what he wishes: he does not sin if she marries. But the one who stands firm in his heart, having no necessity, yet has authority over his own will, and has decided in his heart to keep his virgin, does well. Therefore both the one who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and the one who does not give her in marriage does better.

A woman is bound by law for as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my advice. I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

### [VIII.]

Concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all possess knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known how he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, this person is known by him.

Concerning food sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world. And shortly afterward:

But knowledge is not in everyone. Some, through their conscience concerning the idol even now, eat the food as something sacrificed to an idol; and because their conscience is weak, it is defiled. Food, however, does not commend us to God. For neither, if we do not eat, will we be lacking; nor, if we eat, will we have an abundance.

But see to it that perhaps this freedom of yours does not become a stumbling-block to the weak. For if someone sees the one who possesses knowledge reclining in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be built up to eat the food sacrificed to idols? And the weak brother will perish through your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, by sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause my brother to stumble.

And shortly afterward:

### [IX.]

Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to lead about a sister, a woman, as do the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? Or do only I and Barnabas lack the right to do this? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not eat of the flock’s milk? Am I saying these things merely in human terms? Or does the Law also say this? For it is written in the Law of Moses: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.” Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he certainly say this for our sake? Indeed, it was written for our sake: because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes in hope of receiving a share.

If we sowed spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things? If others share in your authority, should not we do so even more? But we have not made use of this authority; rather, we endure everything so that we may not place any obstacle in the way of Christ’s gospel.

Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and that those who serve at the altar share with the altar?

[Note: [Col. 1004] The ancient Corbie Bibles agree. But the Vulgate now reads “share,” whereas this reading has “are made participants.”]

Thus also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the gospel should live from the gospel. But I have made use of none of these things. Nor have I written this so that it should be done for me. For it is better for me to die than that anyone should empty my glory. For if I preach the gospel, this is no ground for glory to me; necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.

What, then, is my reward? That, in preaching the gospel, I may offer the gospel of Christ without expense, so that I may not abuse my authority in the gospel.

[Note: [Col. 1004] The word “Christ” also appears in the Greek; nevertheless, it is not in the Vulgate.]

For although I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, so that I might gain the more. To the Jews I became as a Jew, so that I might gain the Jews; to those under the Law, as though I were under the Law—although I myself was not under the Law but under grace—

[Note: [Col. 1004] The Greek text lacks these words: “although I myself was not under the Law but under grace.” The Vulgate has only “but under grace”; these words, together with what precedes, seem likewise to have been imported from the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 6, verses 14 and 15.]

so that I might gain those who were under the Law; to those without the Law, as though I were without the Law—although I was not without the law of God, but was under the law of Christ—so that I might gain those who were without the Law. To the weak I became weak, so that I might gain the weak. I became all things to all, so that I might gain all.

[Note: [Col. 1004] The Vulgate reads “so that I might save them all.”]

But I do everything for the sake of the gospel, so that I may become a participant in it. Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it. Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things. They do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one.

I therefore run in this way, not as though toward something uncertain; I fight in this way, not as one beating the air. Rather, I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified.

### [X.]

For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud. And after a few verses:

But God was not well pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness. These things happened as examples for us, so that we might not be desirous of evil things, as they desired them. Nor become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” Nor commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day. Nor test Christ, as some of them tested him, and perished by serpents. Nor murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer.

All these things happened to them as examples; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Therefore let the one who thinks he stands beware lest he fall. No temptation has overtaken you except a human one. But God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear; rather, with the temptation he will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure.

Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols. And shortly afterward:

But the things that the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the Lord’s table and in the table of demons. Are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?

All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial. All things are lawful for me, but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own advantage, but that of the other.

Eat everything sold in the meat market, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. And shortly afterward:

But if someone says, “This has been sacrificed to idols,” do not eat it, for the sake of the one who pointed it out and for the sake of conscience. I mean not your own conscience, but the other person’s. For why should my freedom be judged by another’s conscience? If I partake with thanksgiving, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks?

Therefore, whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do everything to the glory of God. Be without offense to Jews, Greeks, and the church of God, just as I also please everyone in every way, not seeking my own advantage but that of the many, so that they may be saved.

### [XI.]

Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ. And shortly afterward:

Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head. But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head.

And after a little while:

But in giving this instruction I do not praise you, because you assemble not for the better but for the worse. For, first of all, when you assemble in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and to some extent I believe it. For there must also be heresies among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.

When you assemble together, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper. For each one takes his own supper beforehand to eat; and one is hungry, while another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and shame those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

And after several verses:

Therefore whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1005] The Vulgate, in agreement with the Greek, reads “this bread.”]

But let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink from the cup. For the one who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body. For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. Yet when we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.

Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not come together for judgment. I will arrange the remaining matters when I come.

And elsewhere:

### [XII.]

But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it, so that there might be no division in the body, but that the members might be mutually concerned for one another. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored,

[Col. 1006]

[Note: [Col. 1006] The Carnutensis manuscript reads “are honored,” in agreement with the Greek *doxazetai*, that is, “is glorified” or “is treated with glory.”]

all the members rejoice with it. Now you are Christ’s body and members individually.

And God has appointed some in the church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, administrations, kinds of tongues, interpretations of languages. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all miracles? Do all possess gifts of healings? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? But desire the greater gifts. And I will show you an even more excellent way.

### [XIII.]

If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, it benefits me nothing.

Love is patient; it is kind. Love does not envy; it does not act wrongly; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek what belongs to itself; it is not provoked; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never falls away.

And after several verses:

But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three; but the greatest of these is love.

### [XIV.]

Pursue love. And shortly afterward:

Since you are zealous for spirits, seek to abound for the building up of the church.

Again, shortly afterward:

Brothers, do not become children in your understanding; but be infants in malice and mature in your understanding.

And elsewhere:

What then is the matter, brothers? When you come together, each of you has a psalm, a teaching, an apocalypse, a tongue, an interpretation. Let everything be done for building up.

And after several verses:

Let women keep silent in the churches; for they are not permitted to speak, but are to be subordinate, as the Law also says. If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in the church. Or did the word of God come forth from you? Or did it reach you alone?

And shortly afterward:

### [XV.]

Do not be deceived: bad conversations corrupt good morals. Wake up, righteous ones,

[Note: [Col. 1006] The Greek reads: *Eknēpsate dikaíōs*—“Wake up rightly.”]

and do not sin. For some possess ignorance of God; I speak this to your shame.

And shortly afterward:

Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

### [XVI.]

Concerning the collections for the saints, as I ordered in the churches of Galatia, so you also should do. On the first day of the week, let each of you set something aside by himself, storing up whatever he has prospered in, so that collections may not be made when I come. When I am present, I will send those whom you approve by letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem. And if it is worthy that I go as well, they will go with me.

I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; for I will pass through Macedonia. Perhaps I will remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now merely in passing; but I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. I will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

But if Timothy comes, see to it that he may be without fear among you. And shortly afterward:

Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and be strengthened. Let everything you do be done in love.

## ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS

### [Chapter I]

For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience, that we conducted ourselves in the world in the simplicity

[Note: [Col. 1007] In the Bibles revised by order of Sixtus V, the word “of heart” is added after “in simplicity.” But this word was absent from the ancient Corbie copies, from the Greek, and from all the manuscripts of this *Speculum*.]

and sincerity of God, not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God.

And shortly afterward:

### [II.]

But if anyone has caused me grief,

[Note: [Col. 1007] Here “me” is absent from the Regius manuscript and from the Greek. It was eventually removed from the Vulgate, which had added it in the ancient Corbie Bibles and in most others.]

he has not caused me grief, but to some extent—all of you, so that I may not burden you. The rebuke inflicted by the majority is sufficient for such a person, so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and console him, lest perhaps such a person be swallowed up by excessive grief. Therefore I urge you to confirm your love toward him. For this reason I also wrote, so that I might learn by testing you whether you are obedient in everything.

But to whom you have forgiven anything, I also forgive. For what I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I did for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.

And elsewhere:

### [IV.]

Therefore, since we have this ministry,

[Note: [Col. 1007] The Vulgate now reads in its printed editions “since we have a ministry,” omitting the word “this.” But the ancient Corbie Bible read “since we have this ministration,” in agreement with the Greek *tēn diakonian tautēn*.]

according as we have received mercy, we do not lose heart. Rather, we renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in cunning and not adulterating the word of God, but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every human conscience before God.

And after a few verses:

For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Jesus.

And shortly afterward:

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be God’s and not from us. In everything we suffer affliction, but are not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken;

[Note: [Col. 1007] Lovanius inserted here from the Gembloux manuscript: “we are humbled, but are not put to shame.” This was found neither in our other manuscripts nor in other editions of the *Speculum*, nor in the sacred Bibles, except perhaps in certain interpolated copies.]

we are cast down, but do not perish, always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being handed over to death because of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. Thus death is at work in us, but life in you.

But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written, “I believed, and therefore I spoke,” we also believe, and therefore we speak.

And after six verses:

Therefore we do not lose heart. Although our outward person is being corrupted, nevertheless our inward person is being renewed day by day. For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing in us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure,

[Note: [Col. 1008] The Regius manuscript and the Corbie Bibles read “beyond all measure into sublimity,” in agreement with the Greek *kath’ hyperbolēn eis hyperbolēn*.]

while we do not contemplate the things that are seen but the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

And shortly afterward:

### [VI.]

As fellow workers, we also exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain.

[Note: [Col. 1008] The Regius manuscript reads “as those who urge you.”]

For he says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

We give no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be criticized. Rather, in everything we show ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in prisons, in riots, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as disciplined and yet not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.

And after a few verses:

Make room for us also. Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? What agreement does the temple of God have with idols?

For you are the temple of the living God, as the Lord says: “For I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they will be my people.” Therefore, “Come out from their midst and be separated,” says the Lord, “and do not touch what is unclean; and I will receive you, and I will be a father to you, and you will be my sons and daughters,” says the Lord Almighty.

### [VII.]

Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.

And shortly afterward:

For even if I caused you grief in the letter, I do not regret it. And if I did regret it, seeing that the letter, although it caused you grief for a time, now I rejoice—not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved unto repentance. For you were grieved according to God, so that you might suffer no harm from us. For grief according to God produces repentance leading to steadfast salvation.

[Col. 1009]

But the grief of the world produces death. For behold, this very fact—that you were grieved according to God—how much earnestness it produces in you!

And after a few verses:

### [VIII.]

We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia: that amid a great testing through affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deepest poverty abounded in the riches of their simplicity.

[Note: [Col. 1009] The Vulgate now reads “their abundance of joy was,” but “was” was absent from the Corbie Bibles, from the Greek, and from the manuscripts of this *Speculum*.]

For according to their ability—I bear them witness—and beyond their ability, they were willing, with much exhortation, begging us for the grace and fellowship of the ministry being performed for the saints. And not as we had hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us by the will of God, so that we urged Titus that, just as he had begun, so he should also complete this grace in you.

[Note: [Col. 1009] The Regius manuscript reads “complete it toward you”; shortly afterward it reads “your earnestness and love toward us,” omitting “also”; in both places it agrees with the Greek.]

But just as you abound in everything—in faith, speech, knowledge, every earnestness, and also your love for us—so you should abound in this grace as well. I do not say this as a command, but, through the earnestness of others, testing the genuineness of your love also.

[Note: [Col. 1009] The Ambrosian and Erfurt editions read “testing your good natural disposition.” The Greek has only one word, *gnēsion*, which signifies genuineness or sincerity.]

For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: although he was rich, he became poor for your sake, so that you might become rich through his poverty. I give advice in this matter. For this is beneficial for you, who began not only to do but also to desire it from the previous year.

Now, then, complete the work also, so that just as there was readiness of will, there may likewise be completion from what you have. For if the will is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. For it is not so that there should be relief for others and tribulation for you, but that there should be equality: at the present time, let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also supply your need, and equality may result, as it is written: “The one who had much did not have an excess, and the one who had little did not have less.”

But thanks be to God, who has given the same earnest care for you in Titus’s heart. For he accepted the exhortation; but being more earnest, he went to you of his own accord. We sent with him the brother whose praise in the gospel is spread through all the churches. And not only that, but he was also appointed by the churches as our traveling companion in this grace,

[Note: [Col. 1009] The Corbie Bibles likewise read “in this grace.” But the Vulgate now reads “for this grace.” The Greek has *syn tē chariti tautē*, “with this grace.”]

which is administered by us for the glory of the Lord and our intended willingness, avoiding this: that anyone should criticize us in this abundance which is administered by us.

[Note: [Col. 1009] The printed editions added here “for the glory of the Lord,” but this is absent from the manuscripts and from the sacred Bibles. A little farther below, instead of “after several verses,” the Regius manuscript reads “after nine verses.”]

For we provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings.

[Col. 1010]

And after several verses:

### [IX.]

For concerning the ministry being performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your readiness, about which I boast of you among the Macedonians: that Achaia has been prepared since the previous year, and your zeal has stirred up very many.

But I sent the brothers so that our boasting about you in this matter might not be emptied, so that, as I said, you may be ready; lest, if Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—we will not say you—should be put to shame in this matter.

Therefore I considered it necessary to urge the brothers to go ahead to you and prepare this promised blessing, so that it may be ready, as a blessing and not as an act of greed. But I say this: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings. Let each give as he has determined in his heart, not with sadness or from necessity. For God loves a cheerful giver.

God is able to make every grace abound toward you, so that, always having complete sufficiency in everything, you may abound in every good work, as it is written: “He dispersed; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever.”

[Note: [Col. 1010] The manuscripts and the ancient Corbie Bibles likewise read this way. But the printed editions had, as the Vulgate now does, “unto the age of ages,” although the Greek has only *eis ton aiōna*, “forever.”]

And he who supplies seed to the sower will also supply bread for eating, and will multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that, enriched in everything, you may abound in complete simplicity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God. For the ministry of this service not only supplies what the saints lack, but also abounds through many thanksgivings to the Lord, through the testing of this ministry; glorifying God in the obedience of your confession

[Note: [Col. 1010] The sacred Bibles add here “to the gospel of Christ.”]

and in the simplicity of your fellowship with them and with all, while they pray for you and long for you because of the surpassing grace of God in you. I give thanks to God

[Note: [Col. 1010] The Vulgate reads “Thanks be to God,” omitting “I give.” The Greek has *charis de tō Theō*, “but thanks be to God.”]

for his indescribable gift.

And elsewhere:

### [X.]

But “the one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends.

And after a little while:

### [XI.]

Are they ministers of Christ? And I—

[Note: [Col. 1010] “And I” is redundant. It was also repeated here in the Vulgate, but was rightly removed by the correctors of the Bibles, since the Greek text does not contain it.]

I speak as one less wise—I am more so. In far greater labors, in more abundant imprisonments, in beatings beyond measure, in frequent deaths: from the Jews five times I received forty lashes minus one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck; I was in the depth of the sea a night and a day.

Often on journeys, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in labor and hardship, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fastings, in cold and nakedness; besides the external matters, my daily burden: concern for all the churches.

Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire? If it is necessary to boast, I will boast of the things that belong to my weakness.

And shortly afterward:

### [XII.]

Therefore I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. For this reason I am pleased with weaknesses, insults, necessities, persecutions, and many distresses for Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1011] The sacred Bibles do not add “many.”]

For whenever I am weak, then I am powerful.

And after several verses:

Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not burden you. For I do not seek what belongs to you, but you. For children ought not to store up treasures for their parents, but parents for their children. But I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls, even if, loving you more, I am loved less.

And after several verses:

For I fear that perhaps, when I come, I may not find you such as I wish, and that I may be found by you such as you do not wish; that perhaps there may be among you quarrels, jealousies, hostilities, dissensions, slanders, whisperings, conceits, and disturbances; and that, when I come again, God may humble me before you, and I may mourn many of those who sinned previously and did not repent of the uncleanness

[Note: [Col. 1011] The sacred Bibles insert here “and fornication.”]

and shamelessness that they committed.

And elsewhere:

### [XIII.]

But let us pray to God that you do nothing evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is right.

[Note: [Col. 1011] The Vulgate reads “what is good.” The Greek has *to kalon*, “what is right” or “beautiful.”]

And after six verses:

Finally, brothers, rejoice; be made complete; be encouraged; be of the same mind; be at peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you.

## ON THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO THE GALATIANS

### [Chapter I]

If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant.

And after a little while [V.]: For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any value, nor uncircumcision, but faith that works through love. And elsewhere: But you have been called to freedom, brothers [Note: [Col. 1011] So the manuscripts of this *Speculum* read, in agreement with the Vulgate. The printed editions, however, have “in freedom.” In Greek it is *ep’ eleutheria* (“for freedom”).]; only do not turn freedom into an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another [Note: [Col. 1011] The word “Spirit” is absent from the ancient Corbie Bibles and from the Greek.]. For the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another. But I say [Note: [Col. 1011] The printed editions add after “But I say,” “in Christ,” which is found neither in the manuscripts nor in the sacred Bibles, unless perhaps in interpolated copies.]: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. For these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do whatever you wish. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law. Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity [Note: [Col. 1011] In the Vulgate “indecency” is inserted here; this word is absent from the ancient Corbie Bibles. It does occur in Jerome, but with the word “debauchery” omitted. In Greek, however, “adultery” is named first, then “fornication,” followed by the others listed here, with the term “indecency” omitted.], debauchery, the service of idols, sorcery, [Col. 1012] hostilities, strife, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 1012] The Vulgate has “will not inherit”; the Greek, *ou klēronomēsousin* (“will not inherit”).]. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, forbearance, goodness, kindness [Note: [Col. 1012] In the Vulgate two words are added—namely, “meekness” here and, lastly, “chastity”—so that the fruits of the Spirit become twelve. In the ancient Corbie Bibles there are no more than eleven, because “meekness” is omitted. In Greek there are no more than nine, because “patience” and “chastity” are absent, while the words “meekness” and “moderation” correspond to only one term, *praotēs*.], faith, moderation, self-control. Against such things there is no law. But those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another.

[VI.] Brothers, even if someone should be overtaken in some offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks that he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another. For each person will bear his own burden. Let the one who is being catechized share the word [Note: [Col. 1012] The Corbie Bibles likewise read this way, in agreement with the Greek, *ton logon*. The Vulgate now has the ablative, “the one who is catechized by the word.”] with the one who catechizes him in all good things. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. For the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit. Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due time we shall reap without failing. Therefore, while we have the opportunity, let us do good to all, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith.

## On the Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Ephesians

[Cap. IV.] I therefore entreat you, brothers—I, a prisoner in the Lord—to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. And elsewhere: Therefore I say and testify in the Lord that you should no longer walk as the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their heart. They, having lost hope, have given themselves over to indecency, for the practice of every impurity and greed [Note: [Col. 1012] Instead of “and greed,” the Vulgate now has “to greed”; the Corbie Bible, “in greed,” in agreement with the Greek, *en pleonexia*.]. But you did not learn Christ in this way, if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, as truth is in Jesus. Put off [Note: [Col. 1012] The Vulgate has “to put off,” although in the Corbie Bibles it had, in the first hand, “put off.” In Greek it is *apothesthai umas*, “for you to put off”; and consequently *ananeousthai*, “to be renewed,” and *endusasthai*, “to put on.” The Vulgate, changing these infinitives into imperatives, prefers “be renewed” and “put on.”] the old man according to your former way of life, which is being corrupted according to the desires of error. Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth. Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another. Be angry, and do not sin. Do not let the sun go down upon your anger. Do not give place to the devil. Let the one who was stealing steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one suffering need. Let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but only whatever word is good for the edification of the occasion [Note: [Col. 1013] The Vulgate has “for the edification of faith.” But all the manuscripts of this *Speculum* have “for the edification of the occasion,” in agreement with Jerome, who observes this in commenting on the passage: “For what we rendered,” he says, “as ‘for the edification of the occasion’—which is what is said in Greek, *tēs chreias*—the translator changed in the Latin books for the sake of euphony and wrote ‘for the edification of faith.’”], so that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption [Note: [Col. 1013] The Vulgate has “for the day of redemption,” supported by the Greek, *eis hēmeran* (“for the day”).]. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice. Be kind and compassionate toward one another, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you.

[V.] Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma. But let fornication and every impurity or greed not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, nor foolish talk, nor coarse joking, which is inappropriate, but rather thanksgiving. For know this with understanding: no fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—which is the service of idols—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Therefore do not become partners with them. For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light—for the fruit of light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth—testing what is pleasing to God. And do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, expose them. For the things they do secretly are shameful even to mention. But everything that is exposed is made manifest by the light. For everything that is made manifest is light. Therefore he says: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” [Note: [Col. 1013] In place of “upon you,” the Vulgate has “upon you” with the pronoun in a different form, “you”; although the Greek reads *epiphausei soi ho Christos*, “Christ will shine upon you,” or, as Jerome interprets it, “Christ will arise for you.”]. Therefore, brothers, see carefully how you walk—not as foolish people but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. For this reason do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1013] The printed Vulgate likewise reads this way. But in the ancient Corbie Bibles “Holy” is not added; Jerome, likewise following the Greek, omits it.], speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts [Col. 1014] to the Lord, always giving thanks for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ. Let wives be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife, just as Christ is the head of the Church, he himself the Savior of his body [Note: [Col. 1014] The pronoun “his” is absent from the manuscripts of this *Speculum*; it is not found in the Greek or in Jerome either.]. But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also let wives be subject to their husbands in everything. Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for it, in order to sanctify it, cleansing it by the washing of water in the word [Note: [Col. 1014] Jerome likewise has this, without the added word “of life.” That word, after “in the word,” is now read in the Vulgate, but not in the Greek text.], so that he might present the glorious Church to himself, without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but holy and immaculate. Thus husbands also ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. No one ever hated his own flesh; rather, he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church, because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. This mystery is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church. Nevertheless, let each of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife fear her husband.

[VI.] Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. “Honor your father and your mother”—which is the first commandment with a promise—“so that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived upon the earth.” And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but raise them in the discipline and correction of the Lord. Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your hearts, as you would Christ; not serving merely for outward appearance, as those who please human beings, but as slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with good will as though serving the Lord and not human beings, knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive it back from the Lord, whether slave or free. And you, masters, do the same toward them, giving up threats, knowing that both their Lord and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with him. Finally, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having accomplished everything, to stand. Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, praying at every time in the Spirit with every prayer and supplication, and keeping watch in it [Col. 1015] with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints, and for me, so that speech may be given to me when I open my mouth, with boldness to make known the mystery of the Gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains [Note: [Col. 1015] The printed editions have “in these chains,” so that. But the Royal manuscript and the sacred Bibles lack the pronoun “these.”], so that in it I may dare to speak as I ought.

## On the Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Philippians

[Cap. I.] For I shall be put to shame in nothing, but with all confidence, as always and now, Christ will be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death. For to me, living is Christ, and dying is gain. But if to live in the flesh is for me the fruit of labor, what I should choose I do not know. For I am constrained by the two: having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake. And six verses later: Only live worthily of the Gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or, being absent, hear about you, you are standing firm in one spirit, striving together for the faith of the Gospel, and in nothing frightened by your opponents. This is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation—and this from God. For it has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him, engaged in the same struggle that you saw in me and now hear about me.

[II.] If, therefore, there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort from love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any affection and compassion [Note: [Col. 1015] The Vulgate has “affection of compassion.” The Greek is *splanchna kai oiktirmoi*.], complete my joy by thinking the same way, having the same love, united in soul, sharing the same mind. Do nothing through strife or empty glory, but in humility consider one another superior to yourselves. Let each of you consider not his own interests but those of others. Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence but much more now in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will. Do everything without murmuring or hesitation, so that you may be blameless and innocent children of God, without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life, for my glory on the day of Christ [Note: [Col. 1015] The Greek text agrees. But the Vulgate reads “unto my glory on the day of Christ” (*ad gloriam meam in die Christi*).]; [Col. 1016] because I did not run in vain or labor in vain. But even if I am poured out upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and congratulate all of you. In the same way, you too rejoice and congratulate me. I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly, so that I too may be encouraged when I learn how things are with you. For I have no one so like-minded who will sincerely be concerned for you. For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know his proven character: that, as a son with his father, he served with me in the Gospel. Therefore I hope to send him as soon as I see how things stand with me. I trust in the Lord that I myself will also come to you shortly. But I considered it necessary to send Epaphroditus to you, my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, and your apostle and minister of my need, since he was longing for all of you and was distressed because you heard that he had been ill. For indeed he was ill almost to the point of death, but God had mercy on him—and not only on him but also on me, so that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow. Therefore I sent him all the more eagerly, so that when you see him you may rejoice again, and I may be without sorrow. Receive him therefore with all joy in the Lord, and hold such people in honor, because for the work of Christ he came near to death, risking his life in order to supply what was lacking in your service to me.

And a little later [III.]: Brothers, I do not consider myself to have grasped it. But, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus. Therefore, let as many as are mature think this way; and if you think differently in any respect, God will reveal this to you also. Nevertheless, with regard to what we have attained [Note: [Col. 1016] “This” is absent from the sacred Bibles; nor is the particle “and” found there after the word “let us think.”], let us continue in the same mind and remain within the same rule. Be imitators of me, brothers, and observe those who walk in this way, as you have us for a pattern. For many walk—of whom I often told you, and now even weeping I say it—who are enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction; their god is their belly; and their glory is in their shame. They set their minds on earthly things. But our citizenship is in heaven.

And thirteen verses later [IV.]: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all. The Lord is near. Be anxious about nothing, but in everything, by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is holy, whatever is lovely, whatever is of good report—if there is any virtue and if there is any praise [Note: [Col. 1016] In the Louvain edition “of discipline” had previously been added here, in agreement with the Vulgate; but the Amiens edition, Erasmus, and the Royal manuscript omit the word, in agreement with the Greek.], think about these things. What you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me, do these things, and the God of peace will be with you. I rejoiced greatly in the Lord because at last you have flourished again in your concern for me, as you were indeed concerned, but you were occupied. I do not say this because of want. For I have learned, in whatever circumstances I am, to be self-sufficient. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. Everywhere and in everything I have been instructed both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Nevertheless, you did well by sharing in my tribulation. You yourselves also know, Philippians, that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the account of giving and receiving except you alone. For even in Thessalonica, once and twice, you sent to meet my need. Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the abundant fruit credited to your account [Note: [Col. 1017] The printed editions formerly had, in agreement with the Vulgate, “in your account” (*in ratione vestra*). But the manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek and the ancient Bibles, have “to your account” (*in rationem vestram*).]. I have everything and abound. I have been filled, having received from Epaphroditus what you sent: a fragrant aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.

## On the First Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Thessalonians

[Cap. II.] You yourselves know, brothers, our entrance among you, that it was not in vain, but after suffering much [Note: [Col. 1017] The word “much” is absent from the sacred Bibles.] and being treated shamefully, as you know, at Philippi, we had confidence in our God to speak the Gospel of God to you amid great anxiety. For our exhortation was not from error, nor from impurity, nor in deceit. But just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the Gospel, so we speak—not as pleasing human beings, but God, who tests our hearts. For we were never found using flattering speech, as you know, nor with an occasion for greed—God is witness—nor seeking glory from human beings, either from you or from others. Although we could have been a burden to you as apostles of Christ, we became little children in your midst, as a nurse cherishes her own children. So, longing for you, we were eager to share with you not only the Gospel of God but also our own lives, because you had become very dear to us. For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: working night and day so as not to burden any of you, we proclaimed the Gospel of God to you. You and God are witnesses of how devoutly, justly, and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believed. As you know, we exhorted, comforted, and testified to each one of you, as a father does to his children, that you should walk worthily of God, who called you into his own kingdom and glory. For this reason we too give thanks to God without ceasing, because when you received from us the word of the hearing of God, you received it not as the word of human beings, but, as it truly is, the word of God, which is at work in you who believe. For you became imitators, brothers, of the churches of God that are in Judea in Christ Jesus, because you also suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen as they did from the Jews.

And elsewhere [IV.]: Finally, brothers, we ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so you should walk, that you may abound more and more. For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus. For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication; that each one of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God; and that no one transgress or defraud his brother in business, because the Lord is an avenger of all these things, as we told you before and testified. For God did not call us to impurity but to sanctification. Therefore, whoever rejects these things rejects not a human being but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in you. Concerning brotherly love, we have no need to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. Indeed, you do this toward all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we ask you, brothers, to abound more and more, to strive to live quietly, to attend to your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk honorably before those who are outside and desire nothing from anyone. But we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope.

And after several verses [V.]: Therefore let us not sleep as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep sleep at night, and those who are drunk are drunk at night. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, clothed with the breastplate of faith and love, and with the helmet of the hope of salvation. For God did not appoint us for wrath but for the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him. Therefore comfort one another and build one another up, just as you are doing. But we ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, preside over you in the Lord, and admonish you, and to hold them in the greatest love because of their work. Be at peace with them. We ask you, brothers: admonish the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient with everyone. See that no one repays evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good for one another and for all. Rejoice always. Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in everything, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you. Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies. Test everything; hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every appearance of evil.

## On the Second Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Thessalonians

[Cap. I.] We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing greatly and the love of each one of you for one another is increasing, so that we ourselves glory in you among the churches of God, because of your endurance and faith in all your persecutions and tribulations that you endure as an example of the just judgment of God, so that you may be considered worthy [Col. 1019] of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer. If nevertheless it is just with God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled, rest with us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. They will suffer eternal punishment unto destruction [Note: [Col. 1019] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have “they will suffer destruction.” The Vulgate has “they will suffer in destruction.”], from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his power, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed on that day. For this reason we also pray always for you, that our God may deem you worthy of his calling and fulfill every good purpose [Note: [Col. 1019] The printed editions added “his”; that word is absent from the manuscripts and from the sacred Bibles.] and work of faith in power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you and you in him, according to the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.

And elsewhere [III.]: We charge you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that they received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not disorderly among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without payment. Rather, in labor and toil, working night and day, we did so in order not to burden any of you—not as though we lacked authority, but so that we might offer ourselves as a pattern for you to imitate. For even when we were with you, we instructed you that if anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat. For we hear that some among you are walking disorderly, doing no work but meddling. Now we charge and exhort such people, in the Lord Jesus Christ, to work quietly and eat their own bread. But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good. If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, mark that person and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame. And do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

## On the Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Colossians

[Cap. III.] Therefore, if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory. Therefore put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols. Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. In these things you also once walked, when you lived in them. But now put away all these things as well: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy. Do not utter shameful speech from your mouth [Note: [Col. 1019] The Royal *Speculum* manuscript and the sacred Bibles lack the words “do not utter”; likewise they lack the word “of God,” which here in verse 10 appears after “in the knowledge.”]. Do not lie to one another, stripping off the old man with his deeds [Col. 1020] and putting on the new, who is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him. Here there is no Gentile and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free, but Christ is all and in all. Therefore, as God’s chosen, holy and beloved, put on compassion, kindness, humility, moderation, and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another if anyone has a complaint against another. Just as the Lord forgave you, so also do this [Note: [Col. 1020] The verb “do” is absent from the Royal manuscript and from the sacred Bibles.]. Above all these things put on love, which is the bond of perfection. And let the peace of Christ exult in your hearts; into this peace you were also called in one body. And be grateful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing yourselves in all wisdom with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God. Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him. Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives and do not be bitter toward them. Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing in the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation, so that they do not become fainthearted. Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything, not serving merely for outward appearance, as those who please human beings, but in simplicity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work from the heart, as for the Lord and not for human beings, knowing that you will receive from the Lord the repayment of the inheritance. Serve the Lord Christ. For the one who does wrong will receive back what he has done unjustly, and there is no partiality with God.

[IV.] Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Lord in heaven. Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it with thanksgiving. Pray at the same time for us also, that God may open for us a door for speech, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also imprisoned, so that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak. Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.

## On the First Epistle of Blessed Paul to Timothy

[Cap. I.] The goal of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. Some, having strayed from these things, have turned to empty talk, wishing to be teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions. But we know that the law is good if someone uses it lawfully, knowing this [Note: [Col. 1020] The Vulgate has “knowing this.” The Greek is *eidōs* (“knowing”).]: that the law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the wicked and defiled, patricides and matricides, murderers, fornicators, men who lie with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine, which accords with the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God, which has been entrusted to me.

[Col. 1021] And shortly afterward [II.]: Therefore, first of all, I ask that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all human beings, for kings and for all who are in high position, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity. Likewise, shortly afterward: Therefore I want men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger and disputation. Likewise, women should adorn themselves in becoming clothing, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or costly clothing, but—as is fitting for women professing piety—through good works. Let a woman learn in silence with all submission. But I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but to remain in silence.

And after several verses [III.]: Therefore a bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, well ordered, modest, hospitable, and able to teach; not given to wine, not violent, but gentle; not quarrelsome, not greedy, but managing his own household well, having children who are submissive with all chastity. But if anyone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he take care of the Church of God? He must not be a recent convert, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil. Moreover, he must also have a good testimony from those who are outside, so that he does not fall into reproach and the devil’s snare. Deacons likewise must be modest, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not pursuing disgraceful gain, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be tested, and then let them serve, being without accusation. Women likewise must be modest, not slanderers, sober, faithful in everything. Let deacons be husbands of one wife, managing their children and their own households well [Note: [Col. 1021] The Vulgate has “manage well.” The Lyon manuscript likewise has this reading.]. For those who have served well acquire for themselves a good standing [Note: [Col. 1021] The Vulgate has “will acquire.” But the manuscripts of this *Speculum* have “acquire,” supported by the Greek, *peripoiountai*.] and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

After twelve verses [IV.]:

“But the Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared, forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have come to know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.

“By setting these things before the brothers, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. But avoid profane and old-womanish fables. Train yourself for godliness. For bodily exercise is useful for a little; but godliness is useful for everything, holding the promise of life, both of the present life and of the life to come. This saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance. For to this end we labor and are reviled, because we hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of believers. Command and teach these things.

“Let no one despise your youth; rather, be an example of the faithful in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, and in purity. Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching. Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Meditate on these things; devote yourself to them, so that your progress may be evident to all [Note: The Regius manuscript reads, ‘may be evident in all things’; this agrees with the Greek *en pasin*]. Pay attention to yourself and to the teaching; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.”

[V.] “Do not rebuke an elder, but appeal to him as to a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, with complete purity.

“Honor widows who are truly widows. But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn [Note: All manuscripts of the *Speculum* read ‘let them learn,’ in agreement with the Greek *manthanétôsan*. The Vulgate has ‘let her learn,’ in the singular.] to manage their own household and to repay their parents in kind; for this is pleasing before God. But she who is truly a widow and desolate hopes in God and persists [Note: The Vulgate reads, ‘let her hope and persist.’ The Greek text has *elpiken kai pros menei*, ‘she has hoped and persists’; hence the Regius manuscript, through the frequent scribal change of *v* into *b*, reads *sperabit*, ‘she will hope’] in supplications and prayers night and day. But she who lives in luxury is dead while she lives. And command these things so that they may be blameless.

“But if anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

“Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one man, bearing witness through good works: whether she raised children, showed hospitality, washed the feet of the saints, assisted those suffering tribulation, and followed every good work.

“But avoid younger widows. For when they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have rejected their first faith. At the same time they also learn to go around from house to house—not only being idle, but also being talkative and saying things they ought not. I therefore wish younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give no occasion to the adversary for reviling. For some have already turned back after Satan.

“If any believer has widows [Note: In the old Corbie Bibles: ‘If any believer, male or female, has widows’; this agrees with the Greek *ei tis pistos e piste*, ‘if any believer, male or female’], let him assist them, so that the Church may not be burdened and may have enough for those who are truly widows.

“Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching. For Scripture says, ‘You shall not muzzle [Note: The Corbie Bibles likewise read ‘you shall not muzzle’; the present Vulgate reads, ‘you shall not bind.’] an ox while it is threshing’; and, ‘The laborer is worthy of his wages.’

“Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except before two or three witnesses. Rebuke sinners in the presence of all, so that the others also may have fear. I testify before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by inclining to either side. Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.

“Do not continue to drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.

“The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but some people’s sins follow afterward. Likewise, good works are manifest, and those that are otherwise cannot remain hidden.”

[VI.] “Let all who are under the yoke as slaves consider their masters worthy of all honor [Note: The Vulgate reads, ‘let them regard them as worthy’], so that the name of the Lord and the doctrine may not be blasphemed. But those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers; rather, they should serve them all the more because they are believers and beloved, sharing in the benefit. Teach and exhort these things.

“If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine that accords with godliness, he is arrogant [Note: Read, with the Vulgate, ‘he is arrogant,’ or ‘he is arrogant in his conduct’; the Greek has *tetuphotai*, ‘he is puffed up’], knowing nothing, but being diseased with disputes and quarrels about words. From these arise envy, contention, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and conflicts among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain.

“Godliness with contentment is indeed great gain. For we brought nothing into this world; and there is no doubt that we can take nothing out.
