But having food and clothing, let us be content with these things. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptations, into the snare of the devil, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into destruction and perdition. For the root of all evils is desire for wealth; by pursuing it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.

“But you, man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith; take hold of eternal life, to which you were called and for which you confessed the good confession before many witnesses [Note: The Greek text has *eis en*, ‘into which’].

“I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, to keep the commandment unstained and blameless until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. And after a few verses:

“Command those who are rich in this present age not to be proud, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who abundantly supplies us with all things for enjoyment; to do good, to become rich in good works, to be generous in giving, to share, and to store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life.

“O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some professing have fallen away from the faith. Grace be with you. Amen.”

## On the Second Letter of Blessed Paul to Timothy

[I.] “For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and sobriety. Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner; rather, share in the work of the Gospel according to the power of God. And after a few verses:

“Hold to the pattern of sound words that you heard from me in faith and love in Christ Jesus. Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.”

[Col. 1024] And shortly afterward [II.]:

“You therefore, my son, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And what you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust to faithful people who will be capable of teaching others also. Labor as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself. And even the one who competes in the arena is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully. The farmer who labors ought first to receive a share of the fruits.

“Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in all things. Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel, in which I suffer hardship even to chains, as though doing evil; but the word of God is not bound. Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with heavenly glory.

“This saying is trustworthy: For if we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him; if we deny him, he will also deny us; if we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.

“Remind them of these things, testifying before God. Do not contend about words, for it is useful for nothing except the overthrow of those who hear. Take care to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed worker [Note: The manuscripts read, ‘an irreproachable worker.’ A little later the Regius manuscript and the edition of Erasmus read, ‘avoid empty talk.’ The Corbie Bibles read likewise], handling the word of truth correctly.

“But avoid profane and empty talk; it will advance greatly toward ungodliness [Note: The Greek text supports this reading. The Vulgate instead prefers, ‘for they advance greatly’], and their speech will spread like gangrene. And after six verses:

“‘The Lord knows those who are his’; and, ‘Let all who invoke [Note: The Sacred Bibles read, ‘and let everyone who names’] the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.’

“In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some indeed for honor, others for dishonor. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.

“Flee youthful desires; pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart. Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate quarrels. The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with meekness those who resist [Note: The Vulgate reads, ‘those who resist the truth.’ The word ‘the truth,’ however, is absent from the Greek and from the manuscripts of this work, except the Gembloux manuscript], in the hope that God may perhaps grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth, and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will.”

[III.] “But know this: in the last days perilous times will come. People will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, without self-control, harsh, without kindness, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God, having an appearance of godliness but denying its power. Avoid such people.

“For among them are those who enter houses and take captive little women burdened with sins and led by various desires, always learning but never able to arrive at knowledge of the truth.

“And after eight verses:

“But you have followed my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, endurance, persecutions, and sufferings such as befell me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra; what persecutions I endured, and the Lord delivered me from all of them. Indeed, all who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution. But evil people and deceivers will advance from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.

“But remain in the things you have learned and that have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them. And because from infancy you have known the sacred Scriptures, which are able to instruct you for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction [Note: The Vulgate reads, ‘for rebuke’; the Greek has *pros epanorthosin*, ‘for correction’], and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work.”

[IV.] “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: proclaim the word; persist whether the time is favorable or unfavorable; reprove, exhort, rebuke with complete patience and teaching. For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires, having itching ears. They will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn to fables.

“But you, be watchful in all things, labor, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry [Note: Nothing more appears in the Greek Bibles; in the Latin texts, however, ‘be sober’ is added].

“For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is near. I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing.”

## On the Letter of Blessed Paul to Titus

[I.] “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might set right what remains and appoint presbyters in each city, as I directed you. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or disobedience. For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward; not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain [Note: The Regius manuscript reads, ‘not pursuing shameful gain’], but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, holding firmly to the trustworthy word that accords with the doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict.

“And after several verses:

“For this reason rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in faith and not pay attention to Jewish fables and commandments of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving [Col. 1026] nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him. They are detestable, unbelieving, and disqualified for every good work.”

[II.] “But you speak what is fitting for sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober, dignified, prudent, sound in faith, love, and endurance. Older women likewise are to have holy behavior, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, good teachers, so that they may teach the younger women prudence: to love their husbands, to love their children, to be prudent, chaste [Note: The Vulgate adds ‘sober’; no corresponding word occurs here in the Greek], managing their households, kind, subject to their own husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed.

“Likewise exhort younger men to be sober. In all things present yourself as an example of good works, in doctrine, integrity, and seriousness. Let your speech be sound and irreproachable, so that the one who is opposed may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about us [Note: The Regius manuscript reads, ‘about you’; this agrees with the Greek].

“Slaves are to be subject to their own masters, pleasing them in all things, not contradicting, not defrauding, but showing complete good faith, so that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in all things.

“For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people [Note: The Vulgate reads, ‘of our Savior’; ‘our’ is absent from the manuscripts of the *Speculum* and from the Greek text. In the Greek, moreover, the feminine article is used with the nominative *he soterios*, indicating that grace itself is saving or bringing salvation], training us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. He gave himself for us, so that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a people acceptable to him, zealous for good works.

“Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.”

[III.] “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey commands, to be ready for every good work; to slander no one, not to be quarrelsome, but gentle, showing all meekness toward all people.

“And after a few verses:

“The saying is trustworthy; and concerning these things I want you to affirm strongly, so that those who have believed in God may take care to preside over good works. These things are good and useful to people.

“But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, disputes, and quarrels about the law; for they are useless and vain. After one or two admonitions, avoid a heretical person, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment.”

## On the Letter of Blessed Paul to Philemon

“For I had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother. And shortly afterward:

“Whom I wished to keep with me, so that he might serve me on your behalf in the chains of the Gospel. But without your counsel I wanted to do nothing, so that your good deed might not be as though compelled, but voluntary.”

## On the Letter to the Hebrews

[III.] “See to it, brothers, that there is not perhaps in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, causing you to depart from the living God. Rather, exhort one another each day, as long as it is called ‘Today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become participants in Christ, provided that we hold the beginning of his substance firm to the end, while it is said:

“‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation.’

“And after a few verses [IV.]:

“Let us therefore fear lest, while the promise of entering into his rest remains, any of you should be judged to have fallen short. For the good news was announced to us just as it was to them; but the word they heard did not benefit them, because it was not united [Note: In the Corbie biblical manuscript and in the Complutensian edition one reads, ‘not being united,’ so that the participle refers not to the word but to those whom the word did not benefit. Certain Greek copies support this reading. Compare Theophylact’s Commentaries] with faith in those who heard it.

“And elsewhere:

“Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession.

“And after three verses:

“Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of grace, so that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help.”

And shortly afterward [VI.]:

“For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love that you showed in his name when you served the saints and continue to serve them. But we desire each one of you to show the same diligence for the fulfillment of hope [Note: Lov. reads ‘of faith’; other printed editions and manuscripts, together with the Sacred Bibles, read ‘of hope’] to the end, so that you may not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

“And after seven verses:

“For people swear by one greater than themselves, and every dispute among them is settled by an oath for confirmation.”

And somewhat later [X.]:

“Let us hold fast the unwavering confession of our hope—for he who promised is faithful—and let us consider one another for the provoking of love and good works, not abandoning our assembly, as is the custom of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching.

“For if we sin deliberately after receiving knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains for us, but a fearful expectation of judgment and a jealousy of fire that will consume the adversaries. Anyone who rejects the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as common the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?

“For we know the one who said, ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay’ [Note: The Vulgate reads, ‘Vengeance belongs to me, and I will repay’]; and again, ‘For the Lord will judge his people.’ It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God.

“But remember the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great contest of sufferings. On the one hand, you were made a spectacle through reproaches and tribulations; on the other, you became companions of those who were treated in this way. For you sympathized with prisoners and joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions [Col. 1028], knowing that you have a better and abiding substance.

“Therefore do not cast away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you need endurance, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise. For yet a little while, just a little, and ‘the one who is to come will come and will not delay. But my righteous one lives by faith’ [Note: In the Greek here and in Habakkuk 2:4 one reads *dzesetai*, ‘will live’]; and ‘if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him.’”

And somewhat later [XII.]:

“Therefore, since we too have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, let us lay aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith. For the joy set before him he endured the cross, despising its shame, and sits at the right hand of the throne of God.

“Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary and lose heart. You have not yet resisted to the point of blood in your struggle against sin, and you have forgotten the encouragement that speaks to you as to sons:

“‘My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him. For the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives.’

“Persevere in discipline. God offers himself to you as to sons. For what son is there whom his father does not correct? But if you are without discipline, of which all have become participants, then you are adulterers and not sons.

“Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we respected them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? They indeed disciplined us for a few days according to their own will; but he does so for what is useful, so that we may receive his sanctification. Every discipline at the present time seems to be not joy but sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who are trained by it.

“Therefore raise up your slack hands and strengthen your weakened knees; make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray but rather be healed. Pursue peace with everyone and holiness, without which no one will see God. See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, that no root of bitterness springing up above may cause trouble and through it many may be defiled, and that no fornicator or profane person be found among you, like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright.”

And elsewhere [XIII.]:

“Let brotherly love remain among you, and do not forget hospitality. For through it some, having received angels as guests, pleased God [Note: In the uncorrupt Bibles the Vulgate reads, ‘were hidden’].

“Remember prisoners as though imprisoned with them, and those who suffer ill-treatment as though you yourselves remained in the body. Let marriage be honored among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled; for God will judge fornicators and adulterers.

“Let your conduct be without greed; be content with present things. For he himself said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you,’ so that we may confidently say, ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what a human being can do to me.’

“Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Looking to the outcome of their conduct, imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

“Do not be carried away by various and foreign teachings. For it is good to establish the heart by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those who walk in them. We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him beyond the camp, bearing his reproach. For we have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come.

“Through him, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. Do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for God is pleased with such sacrifices.

“Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch as those who will have to give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not groaning; for this would not benefit you.

“Pray for us. For we are confident that we have a good conscience, wishing to conduct ourselves well in all things.”

## On the First Letter of Peter

[Cap. 1.] “Now, if necessary, you are distressed for a little while by various trials, so that the testing of your faith may be much more precious than gold, which is tested through fire.”

“And elsewhere:

“Therefore, girding up the loins of your mind, being perfectly sober, hope in the grace that is being offered to you at the revelation [Note: The ancient Corbie Bibles likewise read, in agreement with the Greek *en apokalypsei*, ‘at the revelation.’ The printed Vulgate has ‘for the revelation’] of Jesus Christ. As obedient children, do not conform yourselves to your former desires in your ignorance, but, according to the one who called you, the Holy One, be holy yourselves in all your conduct, because it is written, ‘You shall be holy, for I am holy.’

“And if you invoke as Father the one who judges without partiality according to each person’s work, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourn. And after several verses:

“Having purified your souls in obedience to love, love one another earnestly from a pure heart, having been born again [Note: The Regius manuscript omits ‘having been born again’].”

And after a few verses [II.]:

“Therefore, laying aside all malice, all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and every slander, like newborn infants desire the rational milk without deceit.

“And shortly afterward:

“Beloved, I urge you, as foreigners and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, by observing your good works they may glorify God on the day of visitation.

“Be subject to every human ordinance [Note: The translator appears to have read *taxei* instead of *ktisei*, which means ‘creation’] for God’s sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. For this is the will of God: that by doing good you silence the ignorance of foolish people. Live as free people, not using freedom as a covering for evil, but as servants of God.

“Honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king.

“Servants, be subject in all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the difficult. For this is grace: if, because of conscience toward God, someone endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is there [Note: The manuscripts, together with the Sacred Bibles, read this way. The printed editions have, ‘what grace is there.’ In the second part of the same verse the Vulgate does not have ‘and suffer’] if, when you sin and are struck, you endure it? But if, when you do good and suffer, you endure it patiently, this is grace before God.

“For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but handed himself over to the one judging unjustly [Note: The Greek has *to krinonti dikaios*, ‘to the one judging justly’]. He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness. By his bruise you have been healed [Note: The Vulgate reads, ‘by whose bruise.’ The Greek has *hou*, ‘whose’]. For you were like wandering sheep, but now you have returned to the shepherd and guardian of your souls.”

And elsewhere [III.]:

“Likewise, let wives be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they observe your chaste conduct in fear. Let their adornment not be outward—braiding the hair, wearing gold, or arranging garments—but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and gentle spirit, which is precious in the sight of God.

“For in this way the holy women of former times who hoped in God also adorned themselves, subject to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You are her daughters when you do good and fear no disturbance.

“Likewise, husbands, live with your wives according to knowledge, granting honor to the woman as to a weaker vessel, since they are also fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.

“Finally, all of you be of one mind, compassionate, loving the brotherhood, merciful, gentle [Note: The word ‘gentle’ is absent from the Regius manuscript and the Corbie Bibles. Nor does the Greek text have *modesti*; instead it has *philophrones*, ‘friendly-minded’], humble; not repaying evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but, on the contrary, blessing, because to this you were called, so that you may inherit a blessing.

“For whoever wishes to love life and to see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. Let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.

“And who is there who will harm you if you become imitators of what is good? But even if you suffer for righteousness, you are blessed. Do not fear their fear [Col. 1031], and do not be troubled. Rather, sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you, but with gentleness and fear, having a good conscience, so that in whatever they slander you, those who malign your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better, if such is the will of God, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.”

And after several verses [IV.]:

“Since Christ therefore suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, because whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins, so that for the remaining time in the flesh he may live not for human desires but for the will of God. For the past time was sufficient for fulfilling the will of the Gentiles, when you walked in debauchery, desires, wine-drinking, revelries, drinking bouts, drunkenness, and illicit idol worship [Note: The word ‘drunkenness’ is redundant and is absent from the more reliable Bibles].

“And after several verses:

“Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers. Above all, maintain continual mutual love among yourselves, because love covers a multitude of sins. Be hospitable to one another without murmuring. As each has received grace, administer it to one another, as good stewards of God’s manifold grace. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

“Beloved, do not be surprised [Note: Instead of ‘do not be surprised,’ the manuscripts read ‘do not marvel,’ which fits the Greek *me xenizesthe* no less well, that is, ‘do not be disturbed as by something new and unusual.’ A little later the translator renders *hos xenou* as ‘as though something new’; the words that precede it, ‘do not be afraid,’ are absent from the Sacred Bibles] by the fiery ordeal that is taking place among you for your testing; do not be afraid as though something new were happening to you, but rejoice insofar as you share in Christ’s sufferings, so that you may also rejoice and exult at the revelation of his glory.

“If you are reviled in the name of Christ, you will be blessed [Note: The Regius manuscript, agreeing with the Greek, does not add ‘you will be’], because the Spirit of honor, glory, and power of God—and the Spirit who is his—rests upon you. Let none of you suffer as a murderer, thief, evildoer, or coveter of what belongs to others. But if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; rather, let him glorify God in that name.

“For the time has come for judgment to begin with the household [Note: The Vulgate reads, ‘from the household.’ The Greek has *apo tou oikou*, ‘from the household’] of God. And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God? And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?

“Therefore let those who suffer according to the will of God entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.”

### [V.]

So I exhort the elders among you—I, a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, as well as a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed in the future—shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for the sake of shameful gain but willingly; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock from the heart. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.

Likewise, young men, be subject to the elders. And all of you mutually clothe yourselves with humility, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves, therefore, under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation. Cast all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you. Be sober; keep watch. For your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in faith, knowing that the same suffering is being inflicted upon your brotherhood throughout the world.

But the God of every grace, who called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered for a little while, will himself perfect, strengthen, establish, and ground you. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## Concerning the Second Epistle of Peter

### [Chapter I]

Through whom he has granted us the greatest and most precious promises, so that through these you may become sharers in the divine nature, having escaped the corruption of the desire that exists in the world. [Note: Thus the printed editions, following the Vulgate; the Corbie Bibles, however, had “through which.” The Speculum likewise has this in the Gembloux codex, but the Regius has “through which things,” following the Greek *di’ hōn*; although this may refer to the preceding words “glory and virtue” and be translated “through which.”] For this very reason, applying all diligence, furnish virtue in your faith; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, self-control; in self-control, endurance; in endurance, godliness; in godliness, brotherly affection; in brotherly affection, love.

For when these things are present and abound in you, they will not make you empty or fruitless in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: The printed editions have “if they are present with you”; so too does the present Vulgate. But the particle *if* was absent from the ancient Corbie Bibles and the Regius manuscript of the Speculum, and is unnecessary, provided that *vobiscum* is not read as one word. The Greek reads *tauta gar hymin hyparchonta*.] [Note: The Regius codex and the Corbie Bible, agreeing with the Greek, have “knowledge” rather than “in the knowledge.”] For whoever lacks these things is blind and gropes with his hand, having forgotten the cleansing of his former sins.

Therefore, brothers, make every effort to make your calling and election sure through good works. For if you do these things, you will never fall into sin.

And a little later [II.]:

Just as there will also be false teachers among you, who will secretly introduce destructive sects and deny God who bought them, [Note: Am. Er. and two manuscripts, following the Vulgate, have “who deny.”] bringing upon themselves swift destruction. Many will follow their debaucheries, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. In their greed they will exploit you with fabricated words. Their condemnation, determined long ago, is not idle, and their destruction does not sleep.

And elsewhere:

The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unrighteous for the day of judgment, to be punished—especially those who follow the flesh in polluted desire and despise authority: bold, self-pleasing, they are not afraid to introduce sects, blaspheming. [Note: The Regius codex and the Corbie Bible have “to do” instead of “to introduce”; but neither verb is explicitly expressed in the Greek text, which contains only *doxas ou tremousi blasphēmou­ntes*, a phrase which some understand as: “they do not fear to attack with insults glorious men,” that is, men distinguished by rank; or, “to attack glorious men with insults.” Compare the Epistle of Jude, verse 8, where the Vulgate reads: “But they despise authority and blaspheme majesties,” while the Greek has the same words, *doxas de blasphēmousin*.]

Whereas angels, though greater in strength and power, do not bring against themselves a condemnatory judgment, these people, like irrational animals, born by nature for capture and destruction, blaspheming what they do not understand, will perish in their corruption. They will receive the wages of unrighteousness, considering daytime indulgence a pleasure; they are stains and blemishes, reveling in their pleasures while feasting with you; they have eyes full of adultery and of unceasing sin; they entice unstable souls; they have a heart trained in greed; they are children of the curse. Abandoning the straight way, they have gone astray.

And after a few verses:

For, speaking proud words of vanity, they entice in the desires of the flesh, in debauchery, those who have barely escaped from those who live in error, promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption. For by whatever anyone is overcome, by that he is enslaved. For if, after escaping the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their later condition has become worse than the former.

For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What has happened to them accords with the true proverb: “The dog has returned to its own vomit,” and, “The washed sow to the mire.”

And after a while [III.]:

Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, awaiting and hastening the coming of the day of God?

And a little later:

Beloved, while you await these things, make every effort to be found by him spotless and blameless in peace, and consider the patience of our Lord to be salvation.

And elsewhere:

Therefore, brothers, knowing these things beforehand, guard yourselves, lest, carried away by the error of the foolish, you fall from your own steadfastness. But grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be glory, both now and unto the day of eternity. Amen.

## Concerning the Epistle of James

### [Chapter I]

Consider it all joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various trials, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance. But endurance must have a perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing. If anyone among you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach them, and it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing. For the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. Let that person not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord: he is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.

But let the humble brother glory in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because he will pass away like the flower of grass. For the sun rose with its heat and dried up the grass; its flower fell, and the beauty of its appearance perished. So also the rich person will wither in his ways. [Col. 1034]

Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life that God promised to those who love him. [Note: So the manuscripts read, along with the sacred Scriptures. The printed editions, however, had “he will receive life.”]

And a little later:

Therefore, my beloved brothers, do not go astray. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.

And after a few verses:

You know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. For human anger does not accomplish God’s righteousness. Therefore, putting away all filthiness and abundance of wickedness, receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, that person will be compared to someone observing the face of his birth in a mirror: he observed himself, went away, and immediately forgot what he was like. But whoever has looked carefully into the perfect law of freedom and has continued in it, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, that person will be blessed in his action. [Note: The Carnotensis codex has “in the law, perfect freedom.” But the Vulgate, supported by the Greek, has “into the perfect law of freedom.” In this same verse, the words *in it* after “has continued” are absent from the printed editions of Am. and Er., and also from the Greek.]

If anyone thinks that he is religious but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his heart, that person’s religion is worthless. Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction and to keep oneself undefiled from this age.

### [II.]

My brothers, do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality toward persons.

And after several verses:

Listen, my beloved brothers: has not God chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom that God promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor. Do not the rich oppress you by their power, and do they not themselves drag you before the courts? Do they not blaspheme the good name that has been invoked over you?

If, however, you fulfill the royal law according to the Scriptures, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.

And after a few verses:

For judgment will be without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy. But mercy triumphs over judgment. [Note: The Vulgate now reads, “But mercy exalts judgment.” The manuscripts of this Speculum, as well as the Corbie Bible, have *judicio*—“over judgment”—instead of *judicium*; this is not improper if the reading is *superexsultat*, as occurs frequently in other books of Augustine, in accordance with the Greek, *kai katakauchātai eleos kriseōs*. Erasmus has here *superexsultet*.]

And after a while [III.]:

Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you will receive a greater judgment. For we all offend in many ways. If anyone does not offend in speech, that person is perfect, able also to guide the whole body by a bridle. [Note: The printed editions have “for he is able.” But the manuscripts, following the Vulgate, have “he is also able.” The Greek reads, *dynatos chalinagōgēsai kai holon to sōma*, that is, “able to control by a bridle, and the whole body.”]

And elsewhere:

No human being can tame the tongue; it is an restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing. My brothers, this ought not to be so.

And after a few verses:

Who is wise and disciplined among you? Let that person show his works through good conduct, in the meekness of wisdom. [Note: Two manuscripts, together with the Vulgate, have “his operation.”] But if you have bitter zeal and there are disputes in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth. This is not the wisdom that descends from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. For where there is zeal and dispute, there are instability and every evil work. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, moderate, compliant, agreeing with what is good, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without hypocrisy. [Note: The Vulgate has “not judging, without hypocrisy.” The Greek text reads *adiakritos kai anupokritos*.] The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

### [IV.]

From where do wars and quarrels arise among you? Is it not from your desires, which wage war in your members?

And after a few verses:

You ask, and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, intending to spend it on your desires. Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of this age makes himself an enemy of God.

And a little later:

Therefore he says: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.” Submit yourselves, therefore, to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. Be miserable, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.

Do not slander one another, brothers.

And after a few verses:

There is one lawgiver and judge, who can destroy and set free. But who are you to judge your neighbor? Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into that city, spend a year there, trade, and make a profit,” although you do not know what will happen tomorrow. [Note: The Vulgate has “what tomorrow may be”; the Corbie Bible has “what tomorrow may produce.”]

For what is your life? It is a vapor that appears for a little while; afterward it will vanish. Instead, you ought to say: “If the Lord wills, and if we live, we will do this or that.” But now you boast in your arrogance. Every such boasting is evil. Therefore, for the one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin.

### [V.]

Come now, rich people: weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be a testimony against you and will consume your flesh like fire. You have stored up wrath for yourselves in the last days. [Note: The Regius manuscript and the printed editions of Am. and Er. omit “wrath for yourselves”; these words are also absent from the Greek.]

Behold, the wages of the laborers who harvested your fields, wages withheld by you, cry out; [Col. 1036] and their cry has entered the ears of the Lord of hosts. [Note: The Vulgate has “the wages that were withheld by you cry out.”]

You have feasted upon the earth and nourished your hearts in luxury. You have condemned and killed the righteous person; he did not resist you. [Note: It should be read, as in the more accurate Bibles, “you have condemned,” in accordance with the Greek *katedikasate*, that is, “you condemned.”]

Therefore, be patient, brothers, until the coming of the Lord.

And a little later:

You also be patient; strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord has drawn near. Do not groan against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged.

And elsewhere:

Above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath. Let your speech be “Yes, yes” and “No, no,” so that you may not fall under judgment. Is any one of you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing psalms. Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him. [Note: The ancient Corbie Bible likewise reads “will raise him up.” The printed editions and the present Vulgate have “will relieve him.”]

Therefore confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved. For the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful.

And after several verses:

My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back, he should know that whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.

## Concerning the First Epistle of John

### [Chapter I.]

If we say that we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth. But if we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from every sin.

If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous, so that he may forgive us our sins [Note: “Our sins” is absent from the Regius codex and from the Greek text.] and cleanse us from every unrighteousness. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.

### [II.]

My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins—not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.

And by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments. Whoever says that he knows him but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But whoever keeps his word, truly in that person the love of God has been perfected. By this we know that we are in him, if we remain in him. [Note: The sacred Bibles lack the words “if we remain in him.”] Whoever says that he remains in him ought also to walk as he walked.

And after several verses:

Whoever says that he is in the light while hating his brother is in darkness until now. Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no stumbling-block in him. But whoever hates his brother is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.

And a little later:

Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. [Note: The second part of verse 15 is missing here: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”] For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life; it is not from the Father but from the world. And the world is passing away, along with its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever. [Note: The printed editions had added, “just as God also remains forever”; this is absent from the manuscripts of the Speculum and from the sacred Bibles.]

And elsewhere:

Every lie is not from the truth.

And after a little while [III.]:

Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy.

Everyone who commits sin also commits lawlessness; and sin is lawlessness. And you know that he appeared to take away sins [Note: The sacred Bibles add “our”] and that there is no sin in him. Everyone who remains in him does not sin; and everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him.

Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous. Whoever commits sin is from the devil, because the devil has sinned from the beginning. The Son of God appeared for this purpose: to destroy the works of the devil.

Everyone who has been born from God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born from God. By this the children of God and the children of the devil are evident. Whoever is not righteous is not from God, nor is the one who does not love his brother, because this is the message that you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another. [Note: The Regius codex has “that we should love,” in agreement with the Greek.]

And after a few verses:

Do not be amazed, brothers, if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love remains in death. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.

By this we have known the love of God: that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. Whoever possesses the substance of the world [Note: The Vulgate has “the substance of this world,” with the demonstrative pronoun, which is nevertheless absent also from the Corbie Bible] and sees his brother in need but closes his compassion against him—how does the love of God remain in that person?

My little children, let us not love in word or tongue but in deed and truth. By this we know that we are from the truth, and before him we persuade our hearts: because if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things.

Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God; and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing before him. And this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he gave us commandment. [Col. 1038] Whoever keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in that person. And by this we know that he remains in us: by the Spirit whom he gave us.

### [IV.]

Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, about which you heard that it is coming, and now it is already in the world.

You are from God, little children, and you have conquered them. [Note: So the manuscripts of the Speculum read, in agreement with the Greek. The Vulgate has “you have conquered him.”] For greater is the one who is in you than the one who is in the world. They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them. We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error.

Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God; and everyone who loves has been born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.

And a little later:

Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us.

And again a little later:

Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God. And we have known and believed the love that God has in us. God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him.

By this the love of God is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world. There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. But whoever fears has not been perfected in love. [Note: So the manuscripts read, together with the sacred Bibles. The printed editions placed the negation in the first member of the statement: “Whoever does not fear is perfect in love.”]

Therefore, let us love God, because he first loved us. If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from him: that whoever loves God should love his brother also.

### [V.]

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born from God. And everyone who loves the one who begot him also loves the one who has been born from him. By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and do his commandments. For this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.

For everything that has been born from God conquers the world.

And after a little while:

This is the confidence that we have toward him: that whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us. And we know that he hears us.

And after three verses:

Whoever knows that his brother is committing a sin not leading to death, let him ask, and he will give him life—those who commit sins not leading to death. [Note: The edition of Am. has “he will ask”; shortly afterward, together with the other codices of this Speculum, it has “and he will give him life to those who sin not unto death,” in accordance with the Greek, *aitēsei kai dōsei autō zōēn tois amartanousi mē pros thanaton*. The Vulgate now has “let him ask, and life will be given to the one sinning,” although the ancient Corbie Bible had “and he will give life to the one sinning,” and so forth.]

There is sin leading to death; I do not say that anyone should pray concerning that. [Note: The manuscripts do not add “anyone,” nor is it present in the Greek.] Every unrighteousness is sin, and there is sin not leading to death. [Note: So the manuscripts of the Speculum read, except for the Regius manuscript, which, together with the Vulgate, lacks the negative particle here. Nevertheless, the particle is present in the Greek text and gives this sense in the ordinary gloss.]

We know that everyone who has been born from God does not sin; but the generation from God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him.

And elsewhere:

Little children, guard yourselves from idols.

## Concerning the Second Epistle of John

Not as though I were writing you a new commandment, but the one that we have had from the beginning: that we should love one another. And this is love: that we walk according to his commandments. This is the commandment: that, just as you heard from the beginning, you should walk in it.

And after a few verses:

Everyone who goes away and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in the teaching has both the Son and the Father. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, and do not say “Hail” to him. For whoever says “Hail” to him shares in his evil works.

## Concerning the Third Epistle of John

Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, and this also for strangers, who have borne witness to your love before the Church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God. [Note: The Greek text supports this reading. The printed Latin Vulgate prefers “doing well, you will send them”; the Corbie Bible has “doing well, sending them.”]

For they have gone out for the sake of his name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to receive such people, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.

And after a little while:

Beloved, do not imitate evil but what is good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God.

## Concerning the Epistle of the Apostle Jude

For certain men have slipped in, who long ago were designated for this judgment: ungodly people who turn the grace of our Lord into debauchery and deny the only ruler [Col. 1040] and our Lord Jesus Christ.

And a little later:

These are stains at their feasts, feasting with you without fear and feeding themselves.

And elsewhere:

These are grumblers, complainers, walking according to their desires; their mouth speaks blasphemy. [Note: The printed Vulgate has “speaks proud things”; the Corbie Bible has “speaks pride.” The Greek is *lalei huperogka*.] They admire persons for the sake of gain.

But you, beloved, remember the words foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They were saying to you that in the last time there would be mockers walking according to their own desires in ungodliness. [Note: The Corbie Bible has “of ungodliness” rather than “in ungodliness,” in accordance with the Greek. The present Vulgate nevertheless has “in ungodlinesses.”]

These are the ones who separate themselves, natural people, not having the Spirit. But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.

And some, indeed, convict as condemned; but others save by snatching them from the fire. To others show mercy with fear, hating even the tunic stained by the flesh.

## Concerning the Book of the Apocalypse of John

### [Chapter II.]

If human beings are meant to be understood as being admonished when the angels are admonished, we learn from all the same commands that false brothers are to be endured through patience for the sake of God’s name; that through repentance we are to return to our first good works; that persecutions for the faith are to be endured unto death; and that we are to serve in love. [Note: The Regius codex has “to burn” instead of “to serve.”]

Near the end of the book, when he was speaking about the holy city [XXI.]:

“Nothing unclean,” he says, “will enter it, nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood.”

And elsewhere [XXII.]:

“Blessed are those who wash their robes in the blood of the Lamb, so that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter the city through the gates. Outside are dogs, sorcerers, the sexually immoral, murderers, those who serve idols, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood. I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you.”

# [On the Harmony of the Evangelists]

[Col. 1039]

## Preface to the Books on the Harmony of the Evangelists

In this work Saint Augustine undertakes to defend the Gospel against the calumnies of the pagans. From the very time of its promulgation, the Holy Spirit had won for it great authority and faith among all peoples, both through the many miracles divinely accomplished and through his appearing in bodily form, as though to ratify it by his own divine power. Yet there were not lacking people who attacked it.

First, it endured the force of tortures and punishments with which the earliest Christians were cruelly persecuted. Then it faced the monstrous accusations directed equally against the teaching and the history that the four sacred writers had composed about Christ under divine inspiration. Both attacks were in vain.

Indeed, just as the adversaries of evangelical truth achieved nothing by their first efforts except to make that truth more certain and better established, when the divine Spirit supplied strength to the martyrs who asserted it with their blood, so that same Spirit kindled the minds of outstanding men with an ardor by which, refuting the calumnies of idolaters with great distinction in learning, they secured for the Gospel greater firmness and dignity.

Above all, the sacred historians were accused of being by no means in agreement with one another: “For this,” Augustine says, “they are accustomed to bring forward as the crowning proof of their vanity, that the Evangelists themselves disagree with one another” (*Book 1, chapter 7, no. 10*).

As for the pagans, the Manichaeans used to sing this tune concerning certain passages, falsely alleging—as may be seen in the books against Faustus—that these passages had been added to the Gospels. Yet it was not enough for Augustine to reconcile the matters over which those heretics raised controversy, against whom he chiefly defended the Old Testament. Rather, so that he might rightly be heard also as a champion of the New Testament, he undertook to demonstrate the complete agreement of the four Evangelists, both in recounting events and in the very order of their narrative.

It could scarcely have happened otherwise than that this study cost him great labor. Hence, in *Tractate 112 on John*, no. 1, he calls it “laborious writing”; and again, in *Tractate 117*, no. 2, he says that the matters there were disputed with the greatest effort.

Clearly, he lacked the aids available to all who later labored over the same subject. Yet even those later writers, following in his footsteps, scarcely discovered anything of importance that he had not already said. He completed this work, interrupting the books on the Trinity that he had already begun, through continuous labor, according to *Book 2 of the Retractations*, chapter 16, and in any event not before the end of the year 399. For in *Book 1*, chapter 27, he testifies that at that time idols were being destroyed by the authority of laws enacted by the emperors.

We have no explicit law on this matter earlier than those promulgated and enforced in Africa in the year 399 (*City of God*, book 18, chapter 54). Before those laws had been established, Augustine admitted that the right to overthrow images by no means belonged to him unless this was done with the consent of those to whom the images belonged (*Sermon 62*, chapter 11, no. 17).

He devotes the first book to refuting those who, while regarding Christ—or rather pretending to regard him—as a man of outstanding wisdom, undermined faith in the Gospel on the pretext that it had not been written by Christ himself but by his disciples, whom they claimed had attributed divinity to him and had not received from him the teaching they themselves proclaimed concerning the abandonment of the worship of the gods.

In the second book he considers the Evangelist Matthew in sequence up to the account of the supper; comparing Matthew with Mark, Luke, and John, he demonstrates that complete agreement is found among them. The third book concerns the agreement of the same four Evangelists from the account of the supper to the end of the Gospel. Finally, the fourth concerns those matters peculiar to Mark, Luke, and John.

In a Corbie codex written 900 or 1,000 years ago, the work is entitled: “Of Aurelius Augustine, bishop, on the Harmony of the Evangelists.” So it is also in most other manuscripts. In all of them, however, the books are divided into chapters, except for the first; the chapter headings are placed at the front of the books.

[Col. 1041]

[Note: See *Book 2, chapter 16, of the Retractations*, col. 636, from the words “During those same years” through col. 637, ending with the words “Divine authorities.” M.]

## The Four Books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Harmony of the Evangelists

[Note: Written around the year 400 after Christ.]

[Note: The four books *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* have been newly collated with four manuscripts of the Vatican Library; two of the Colbert Library; two each of the Bec and Cistercian collections; one from the Church of Laon; likewise one each from Saint Genevieve in Paris, the College of Navarre, and the canon-count D. de Saint George of Lyon; with the Corbie manuscript, written in an excellent hand 900 or 1,000 years ago; with the reliable Albinensis, Audoenensis, Fiscannensis, Floriacensis, Fossatensis, Gemmeticensis, Germanensis, Pratellensis, Remigiensis, Silvae-majorensis, and Vindocinensis manuscripts; and with variant readings collected from five Belgian manuscripts through the work of the theologians of Louvain; as well as with the older editions of Bad., or Rat., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C, S)

# BOOK ONE
[Col. 1041] Having briefly discussed the authority, number, order, and varying manner of composition of the Evangelists, Augustine, before treating their agreement, addresses in this book those who are either troubled by the fact that Christ himself wrote nothing, or invent that books on magic were written by him; and also those who loudly claim, contrary to the teaching of the Gospel, that Christ’s disciples not only attributed more to their master than was actually the case by calling him God, but also, by prohibiting the worship of the gods, taught something different from what they had learned from him. Against these people he vindicates the teaching of the Apostles from the utterances of the Prophets, demonstrating that the God of Israel alone is to be worshiped. He alone, because he forbade the worship of other gods alongside himself, was previously not accepted by the Romans; but at last he subjected the Roman Empire to his name and, as he had promised through his Prophets would happen, shattered idols among all nations through the preaching of the Gospel.

## CHAPTER I — The authority of the Gospels

[Col. 1041]

1. Among all the divine authorities contained in the holy Scriptures, the Gospel rightly holds preeminence. For what the Law and the Prophets foretold as future is shown in the Gospel to have been brought to pass and fulfilled. Its first preachers were the Apostles, who saw the Lord himself and our Savior Jesus Christ present in the flesh [Note: Badius, Erasmus, and most manuscripts: “whose.”]. They took care to proclaim to the human race, once they had received the commission to evangelize, not only those things which they remembered hearing from his mouth or seeing him do before their own eyes, but also those things which, before they had attached themselves to him as disciples, they were able to seek out and learn through the surest indications and most reliable testimony: events divinely accomplished and worthy of remembrance at his birth, infancy, or childhood, whether by him himself, by his parents, or by any others. Two of them, namely Matthew and John, also published in separate books written accounts of him containing those things which seemed worth committing to writing.

[Col. 1043] [Note: Four manuscripts: “revealed.”]

2. And so that it might not be thought to make any difference, for receiving and preaching the Gospel, whether it was announced by those who had followed the same Lord as disciples while he appeared here in the flesh, or by those who faithfully learned of him from them, divine providence arranged through the Holy Spirit that authority should be granted to some of those who followed the first Apostles not only to announce but also to write the Gospel. These are Mark and Luke. The other men who attempted or dared to write something about the deeds of the Lord or the Apostles did not prove in their own times to be such persons that the Church would place confidence in them and receive their writings into the canonical authority of the holy Books—not merely because they were not such men as ought to have been believed when they narrated these things, but also because they inserted into their writings certain falsehoods condemned by the Catholic and apostolic rule of faith and by sound doctrine.

## CHAPTER II — The order of the Evangelists and their manner of composition

3. These four Evangelists, therefore, are known throughout the whole world. Perhaps there are four because there are four parts of the earth, and by the sacrament of their number they signified, in a certain way, that Christ’s Church would be spread throughout the whole world. They are said to have written in this order: first Matthew, then Mark, third Luke, and last John. Thus, their order of knowing and preaching was one thing, and their order of writing another.

For in knowing and preaching, those who followed the Lord present in the flesh, heard him speak, saw him act, and were sent from his mouth to evangelize, were unquestionably first. But in composing the Gospel—which must be believed to have been divinely ordered—two of those whom the Lord chose before his Passion occupied the first and last places: Matthew the first, and John the last. The other two, who were not among that number but had nevertheless followed Christ speaking through those men, were placed in the middle like sons to be embraced, and thus were fortified on either side by the two others.

[Col. 1044] 4. Of these four, only Matthew is said to have written in the Hebrew language; the others in Greek. Although each seems to have followed his own particular order of narration, none of them is found to have wished to write as though unaware of the preceding writer, or to have omitted through ignorance things which another is found to have written. Rather, as each was inspired, he added the labor of his own work without superfluous cooperation.

Matthew is understood to have undertaken the account of the Lord’s incarnation according to the royal line, together with most of his deeds and sayings as they pertain to human life in the present. Mark, following him, seems to be, as it were, his attendant and abridger. For he said nothing in common with John alone; by himself, very little; with Luke alone, less; but with Matthew, very much, and in many passages almost as many things, in the very same words, whether agreeing with Matthew alone or with the others.

Luke, on the other hand, appears to have been more concerned with the Lord’s priestly lineage and person. For he ascends to David not by following the royal genealogy, but by passing through those who were not kings, reaching Nathan, the son of David (Luke 3:31), who himself was not a king. This differs from Matthew, who, descending through King Solomon (Matthew 1:6), followed the other kings in order, preserving in them a mystical number, about which we shall speak later.

## CHAPTER III — Matthew relates Christ chiefly to the royal person, Luke to the priestly person

5. For the Lord Jesus Christ, one true king and one true priest—one role for governing us, the other for atoning for us—showed that he had enacted his own prefiguration in these two persons, commended separately among the Fathers [Note: The printed editions read “among the ancient Fathers”; “ancient” is absent from the manuscripts.], whether in the title fixed above his cross, “King of the Jews,” whence Pilate replied under a mysterious impulse, “What I have written, I have written” (John 19:19–22)—for it had been foretold in the Psalms, “Do not alter the inscription of the title” (Psalm 74:1)—or, as concerns the person of the priest, in what he taught us to offer and receive. Hence he set forth beforehand the prophecy concerning himself, saying, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4) [Note: Two manuscripts: “the prophet.”].

Christ appears as king and priest in many other testimonies of the divine Scriptures as well. Hence David himself—who is not without reason more frequently called the son of David than the son of Abraham, and whom Matthew and Luke held in common, the one descending from him through Solomon, the other ascending to him through Nathan—although he was openly a king, nevertheless prefigured the person of a priest when he ate the bread of the Presence, which only priests were permitted to eat (1 Samuel 21:6; Matthew 12:3).

To this may be added the fact that Luke alone mentions that Mary had been revealed by the angel to be related to Elizabeth [Note: Thus the printed editions of Badius and Erasmus, supported by all the manuscripts. At Leuven: “mentions that she was manifestly related to Elizabeth.”], who was the wife of the priest Zechariah. The same writer says that Zechariah had her as a wife from the daughters of Aaron—that is, from the priestly tribe (Luke 1:36, 5).

6. Since, then, Matthew directed his attention to the king’s person and Luke to the priest’s, both chiefly commended Christ’s humanity. For Christ became both king and priest according to his humanity. God gave him the throne of David his father, so that his kingdom would have no end (Luke 1:32–33), and made him “the man Christ Jesus,” mediator between God and human beings, to intercede for us (1 Timothy 2:5).

Luke did not have a companion joined to him as an abridger, as Mark was joined to Matthew. This too perhaps was not without some hidden significance, because kings are not without the service of attendants [Note: Two manuscripts and the edition of Rat—namely, the edition revised through the work of Augustine of Regensburg—read: “without the service of a retinue.”]. Therefore, the one who undertook to narrate Christ’s royal person had a companion joined to him, as it were, who in some way followed his footsteps.

But because the priest entered the Holy of Holies alone, Luke, whose attention was directed toward Christ’s priesthood, did not have a companion following him who might in some way abridge his narrative.

## CHAPTER IV — John took care to express Christ’s divinity

7. These three Evangelists, nevertheless, differ chiefly in their treatment of those things which Christ accomplished temporally through human flesh. John, however, directed his attention above all to the Lord’s very divinity, by which he is equal to the Father, and took particular care to commend it in his Gospel insofar as he believed it sufficient for human beings.

Accordingly, he is borne far above the other three, so that you may see them, in a manner of speaking, moving on earth with Christ as man, while he has crossed the cloud that covers the whole earth and reached the clear heaven. From there, with the sharpest and most steadfast vision of the mind, he saw “in the beginning the Word, God with God, through whom all things were made,” and recognized that the same Word “became flesh so that he might dwell among us” (John 1:1, 3, 14): he assumed flesh, not that he was changed into flesh.

For unless the assumption of flesh had occurred while his divinity remained unchangeable, he would not have said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); for the Father and flesh are not one. John alone likewise recorded this testimony of the Lord concerning himself: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” [Note: The better manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek, ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακε τὸν πατέρα, read thus; the printed editions read: “Whoever sees me sees the Father.”], and, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:9–10); and, “That they may be one, just as we are one” (John 17:22); and, “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does the same” (John 5:19).

John placed in his Gospel almost alone any other statements that rightly disclose to those who understand them Christ’s divinity, in which he is equal to the Father. He was like one who had drunk more abundantly and, in a certain sense, more familiarly from the secret of Christ’s divinity, resting upon the Lord’s breast, on which he was accustomed to recline at his meal (John 13:23).

## CHAPTER V — The two virtues: John concerns himself with the contemplative, the other Evangelists with the active

8. Two virtues, therefore, have been set before the human soul: one active, the other contemplative; one by which we travel, the other by which we arrive; one by which we labor so that the heart may be cleansed for seeing God, the other by which we are at leisure and see God. The former is exercised in the precepts governing this temporal life, the latter in the teaching of that everlasting life.

Thus the former acts, while the latter rests, because the former is engaged in the cleansing of sins, the latter in the illumination of those who have been cleansed [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “in the illumination.”]. Accordingly, in this mortal life the former is found in the work of good conduct, while the latter is found more especially in faith, and among very few persons through a mirror in an enigma, and partially in some vision of immutable truth (1 Corinthians 13:12).

These two virtues are understood to have been prefigured in Jacob’s two wives. Concerning them I discussed, to the best of my ability and insofar as seemed sufficient for that work, in my Against Faustus the Manichaean (Book 22, chapter 52). For Leah is interpreted as “Laboring,” while Rachel means “Beginning seen” [Note: The printed editions, except Rat., have “beginning of sight.” The manuscripts have “beginning seen”; this is also how it is read in Book 22 Against Faustus, chapter 52, where the following interpretation is added: “or the Word,” Augustine says, “from which the beginning is seen.”].

From this, if you pay careful attention, it may be understood that the three Evangelists who treated more fully the Lord’s temporal deeds and sayings—those especially useful for shaping the conduct of the present life—were concerned with the active virtue. John, on the other hand, who narrated far fewer of the Lord’s deeds but recorded his sayings more carefully and abundantly, especially those that suggest the unity of the Trinity and the happiness of eternal life, maintained his purpose and preaching in commending the contemplative virtue.

## CHAPTER VI — Some have understood the four living creatures in Revelation as referring to the four Evangelists more aptly than others

9. Hence it seems to me that those who interpreted the four living creatures in Revelation as referring to the four Evangelists paid more plausible attention to the matter when they understood the lion as Matthew, the human being as Mark, the calf as Luke, and the eagle as John, than those who assigned the human being to Matthew, the eagle to Mark, and the lion to John.

They wished to derive a conjecture from the beginnings of the books, rather than from the whole purpose of the Evangelists, which ought to have been examined more carefully. For it is much more fitting that the one who chiefly commended Christ’s royal person should be signified by the lion. Thus, in Revelation the lion is mentioned together with the very royal tribe, where it is said, “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5).

According to Matthew, Magi are reported to have come from the East to seek and worship the king who appeared to them as having been born through the star. King Herod himself fears the infant king and, in order to kill him, slaughters so many children (Matthew 2:1–18).

As for Luke’s being signified by the calf, because of the priest’s great sacrifice neither of the two interpreters had any doubt. There the narrative begins with the priest Zechariah; there Mary’s relationship to Elizabeth is mentioned (Luke 1:5, 36); there the rites of the first priesthood are narrated as fulfilled in the infant Christ (Luke 2:22–24). Many other details can be carefully observed which show that Luke’s attention was directed toward the person of the priest.

Mark, therefore, who did not wish to narrate either the royal or the priestly lineage, relationship, or consecration, but is shown to have been concerned with the things accomplished by Christ as a human being, seems to be signified among those four living creatures by the figure of the human being alone.

These three creatures—the lion, the human being, and the calf—walk upon the earth. Hence these three Evangelists are chiefly occupied with the things Christ accomplished in the flesh and with the precepts he gave to those bearing mortal flesh for the conduct of mortal life. John, however, flies like an eagle above the clouds of human weakness and gazes upon the light of immutable truth with the sharpest and most steadfast eyes of the heart [Note: Treatise 36 on John, section 5].
