## CHAPTER VII — The reason for undertaking this work on the agreement of the Evangelists; a response to those who say that Christ wrote nothing and that his disciples lied by preaching him as God

10. Certain people attack these holy chariots of the Lord, by which he is carried throughout the world and subdues peoples beneath his gentle yoke and light burden, either with impious frivolity or with ignorant recklessness, seeking by their accusations to weaken the credibility of the truthful narrative. Through these narratives the Christian religion, disseminated throughout the world, has grown with such fertility that unbelievers scarcely dare any longer to mutter their accusations among themselves, overwhelmed by the faith of the nations and the devotion of all peoples.

Nevertheless, because some people are still held back from believing by their calumnious arguments, while others who already believe are disturbed by them as much as possible through continued agitation, and because some of our brothers desire to know what answer they should give to such questions, either for the advancement of their own knowledge or for refuting the empty talk of those people, we have undertaken this work—inspiring and assisting us is the Lord our God, which may he also make beneficial to the salvation of those others—to demonstrate the error or recklessness of those who think they can bring sufficiently clever accusations against the four books of the Gospel, each written separately by one of the four Evangelists.

To accomplish this, it must be shown that these same four writers do not contradict one another. For this is what they usually put forward as the crowning point of their vanity: that the Evangelists themselves disagree among themselves.

11. But first we must examine what usually troubles some people: why the Lord himself wrote nothing, so that it should be necessary to believe what others wrote about him.

This is said especially by those pagans who do not dare to blame or blaspheme the Lord Jesus Christ himself. They attribute to him the highest wisdom, but only as to a human being. They say, however, that his disciples attributed more to their master than was actually the case by calling him the Son of God, and the Word of God through whom all things were made, and by saying that he and God the Father are one; and similarly in the apostolic writings, where we have learned that he is to be worshiped together with the Father as one God.

They think he should be honored as an exceedingly wise man, but deny that he should be worshiped as God.

12. When they ask why he himself did not write, they seem prepared to believe of him only what he would have written about himself, not what others might have proclaimed about him according to their own judgment.

I ask them, then, why they have believed of certain highly renowned philosophers of theirs what their disciples left written and preserved in memory about them [Col. 1048], even though those philosophers themselves wrote nothing about themselves.

Pythagoras, for example, than whom Greece at that time had no more celebrated figure in the contemplative virtue, is said to have written nothing—not about himself, nor even about any other matter. Socrates, whom they in turn placed above everyone in the active virtue by which character is formed, went so far as to be proclaimed the wisest of all, even by the testimony of their god Apollo—and they do not fail to mention this—yet he treated the fables of Aesop in a few verses, applying his own words and meters to another person’s subject matter. He was so unwilling to write that he said he had done this only because he was compelled by the command of his divine spirit, as his most renowned disciple Plato records. Even in that work, however, he preferred to adorn another person’s ideas rather than his own.

What, then, is the reason they believe of those philosophers what their disciples commended in writing about them, but do not wish to believe of Christ what his disciples wrote about him—especially since they admit that he surpassed other human beings in wisdom, although they refuse to acknowledge him as God?

Did those men, whom they do not doubt were far inferior to Christ, manage to make truthful disciples of themselves, while Christ could not? If this is said, it is supremely absurd. Let them believe of the one whom they acknowledge as wise not what they themselves wish, but what they read in the writings of those who learned from that wise man the things they wrote.

## CHAPTER VIII — If Christ is believed to be wise on the testimony of rumor, why is he not believed to be God when a greater rumor proclaims it?

13. Next, let them say how they came to know or hear, at least, that he was exceedingly wise. If through rumor spreading abroad, is the rumor reported about him more reliable than his disciples, through whose preaching that very rumor has spread its fragrance throughout the whole world? [Note: Fourteen manuscripts: “the rumor about him has been reported.”] Finally, let them compare rumor with rumor and believe the rumor about him that is greater.

For the rumor that is spread with marvelous clarity concerning the Catholic Church—which they marvel to see disseminated throughout the world—far surpasses, beyond comparison, their feeble whispers. This rumor is so great and so renowned that these people, fearing it, gnaw at their timid and tepid objections within themselves, now more afraid of being heard than desirous of being believed. It proclaims Christ to be the only-begotten Son of God and God, through whom all things were made [Note: Erasmus and Leuven: “It is so great and so renowned that, fearing it, they ... proclaim Christ to be the only-begotten Son of God and God, whom they do not wish to be believed or proclaimed,” with almost all the manuscripts and the older edition of Rat. differing. We have restored the reading found here.].

If, then, they choose rumor as their witness, why do they not choose this rumor, which shines forth with such clarity? If they choose written testimony, why not the Gospel, which possesses such authority?

We certainly believe concerning their gods what is found both in their older writings and in their more celebrated tradition. If those gods are to be worshiped, why do they ridicule them in the theaters? But if they are to be ridiculed, then there is even more reason to ridicule them when they are worshiped in temples.

It remains for them either to wish to be witnesses concerning Christ—though by speaking about what they do not know they remove from themselves the merit of knowing what they say—or, if they claim to possess books which they assert that he wrote, to produce them for us. Surely, they must be extremely useful and beneficial books, since, as they themselves admit, the wisest man wrote them.

But if they are afraid to produce them, they are certainly bad. And if they are bad, the wisest man did not write them. Yet they confess Christ to be the wisest man. Therefore Christ did not write anything of that kind.

## CHAPTER IX — Some invent that Christ wrote books on magic

14. These people are so foolish that they say the books they believe he wrote contain the arts by which they think he performed those miracles whose fame has spread everywhere.

By holding this opinion they betray what they love and what they desire. They think Christ was wise for the very reason that he knew certain unlawful practices—practices condemned not only by Christian teaching but also, rightly, by the administration of the earthly state.

And certainly, if those who claim to have read such books of Christ have really read them, why do they themselves perform none of the things they marvel that he performed by means of such books?

## CHAPTER X — Some madly claim that the same books were addressed to Peter and Paul

15. What is more, some of those who either believe or wish others to believe that Christ wrote such things have fallen into such error, apparently by divine judgment, that they say the same books were addressed to Peter and Paul, as though marked with an epistolary title.

It is possible that either enemies of Christ’s name, or people who thought they could lend authority to such execrable practices by attaching them to so glorious a name, wrote such things under the names of Christ and the Apostles. In this most deceitful audacity they were so blinded that they rightly became objects of ridicule even to boys who, while still childishly occupying the rank of Lector, know the Christian Scriptures.

16. When they wished to invent that Christ had written something of this kind to his disciples, they considered to whom he could most plausibly have written—namely, to those who had adhered to him most familiarly, to whom such a secret might suitably have been entrusted. Peter and Paul occurred to them, I suppose because they saw them painted together with him in many places; for Rome celebrates the merits of Peter and Paul with especially solemn observance, also because they shared the same day of martyrdom [Note: Three manuscripts: “most renownedly and solemnly.” Erasmus and Leuven: “with greater renown and solemnity”; adding “and,” which is absent from the other manuscripts.].

Thus those people entirely deserved to fall into error who sought Christ and his Apostles not in the holy books but in painted walls. It is no wonder that, inventing things on the basis of painters’ inventions, they were deceived.

Throughout the entire period in which Christ lived in mortal flesh with his disciples, Paul was not yet his disciple. After his Passion, resurrection, and ascension; after the Holy Spirit had been sent from heaven; after many Jews had been converted and had embraced the faith wondrously; and after the stoning of Stephen, the deacon and martyr—when he was still called Saul and was fiercely persecuting those who believed in Christ—Christ called him from heaven and made him his disciple and Apostle (Acts 9:1–30).

How, then, could Christ have written books before his death to disciples whom he regarded as his most intimate companions, Peter and Paul, when Paul was not yet his disciple?

## CHAPTER XI — Against those who dream that Christ converted peoples to himself by magical art

[Col. 1050]

17. Let those who foolishly claim that he was able to accomplish such things by magical arts, and that by this very art he consecrated his name in order to convert peoples to himself, consider whether he could by magical arts have fulfilled such great Prophets through the divine Spirit before he was born on earth—Prophets who foretold such future things about him as we now read in the Gospel as past events and see at the present time throughout the world.

For if he used magical arts to cause himself to be worshiped even after his death, he was not a magician before he was born. A single nation had been assigned to him to prophesy his coming; the entire administration of that nation’s state was a prophecy of the king who was to come and establish a heavenly city from all nations.

## CHAPTER XII — After subduing the Jews, the Romans did not accept their God because he commanded that he alone be worshiped and that idols be destroyed

18. Accordingly, the only god of that Hebrew people, which—as I said—had been assigned to prophesy Christ, was the one God, the true God, who made heaven and earth and all that is in them. When they offended him, they were often subjected to their enemies. Now, too, on account of the most grievous crime of killing Christ, they have been utterly uprooted from Jerusalem itself, which was the capital of their kingdom, and subjected to the Roman Empire.

The Romans were accustomed to appease the gods of the nations they conquered by worshiping them [Note: Five manuscripts: “to appease them by worship.”] and to adopt their sacred rites. They refused to do this with the God of the Hebrew nation when they attacked or conquered it.

I believe they saw that if they accepted the rites of that God—who commanded that he alone be worshiped, with even the idols destroyed—they would have to abandon everything they had previously accepted as objects of worship, whose religious observances they believed had enlarged their empire.

In this matter the deceit of demons greatly misled them. For they ought certainly to have understood that, by the hidden will of the true God, in whose hands supreme power over all things lies, their kingdom had been given and increased—not by the favor of those gods. If those gods had possessed any power in this matter, they would rather have protected their own peoples from being defeated by the Romans, or would have subjected the Romans themselves, once conquered, to those peoples.

19. They cannot say that the gods of the nations they conquered loved and selected their piety and moral character. They will never say this if they recall their beginnings: the asylum for criminals and the fratricide of Romulus.

When Remus and Romulus established the asylum, so that anyone guilty of any crime who fled there might keep his offense unpunished, they did not give commands of repentance to heal the souls of the wretched. Rather, they armed, with the reward of impunity, the gathered band of frightened men against their own cities, whose laws they feared.

Nor, when Romulus killed his brother, who had committed no wrong against him, did he consider the justice of exacting punishment; he considered the establishment of his own dominion.

Did the gods love such conduct—favoring the enemies of their cities by favoring those who were hostile to them? On the contrary, they neither oppressed those cities by abandoning them nor helped these men by transferring themselves to their side, because they do not possess the power to give or take away kingdoms.

The one true God does this by a hidden judgment—not intending to make those immediately blessed to whom he has given an earthly kingdom, nor immediately wretched those from whom he has taken it, but making people blessed or wretched for another reason and from another source. He distributes temporal and earthly kingdoms to whomever he wishes and for as long as he wishes, according to the predetermined order of the ages, whether by permitting or by granting them.

## CHAPTER XIII — Why God allowed the Jews to be subjected

20. Hence they cannot say this either: “Why, then, did the God of the Hebrews, whom you call the supreme and true God, not only fail to subject the Romans to them, but did not even help the Hebrews themselves so that they would not be subjected by the Romans?”

Their evident sins came first, and because of those sins the Prophets had long before foretold that this would happen to them. Above all, they killed Christ in impious fury. Through that sin they had been blinded because of the merits of other hidden sins. The same prophetic testimony also foretold that Christ’s Passion would benefit the nations.

Nothing makes clearer that the kingdom, temple, priesthood, sacrifice, and that mystical anointing of the Hebrew people—which is called *χρῖσμα* (*chrisma*, “anointing”) in Greek, from which the name “Christ” shines forth, and on account of which that people called its kings “christs”—had been assigned solely to the purpose of announcing Christ beforehand than the fact that, once the resurrection of the slain Christ began to be preached to believing Gentiles, all those institutions ceased.

The Romans did not know that this happened through their victory; the Jews did not know that it happened through their subjugation.

## CHAPTER XIV — By the overthrow of idols and the conversion of all nations to his worship, the God of the Hebrews showed that he had not been conquered when they were defeated

21. Few of the pagans who remain notice the truly extraordinary fact that the God of the Hebrews—offended by those who were defeated and not accepted by those who conquered them—is now proclaimed and worshiped by all nations.

He is the God of Israel, of whom the Prophet addressed the people of God long beforehand in these words: “He who redeemed you, the God of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isaiah 54:5).

This was accomplished through the name of Christ, who came to human beings from the seed of Israel. Israel was the grandson of Abraham, from whom the Hebrew nation began [Note: Second Book of the Retractations, chapter 16]. To Israel also it was said, “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 28:14).

From this it is shown that the God of Israel is the one God who made heaven and earth and justly and mercifully cares for human affairs, in such a way that justice neither shuts out mercy nor mercy obstructs justice.

He was not conquered in his Hebrew people because he allowed their kingdom and priesthood to be attacked and destroyed by the Romans. For through the Gospel of Christ, the true king and priest, whose future coming was prefigured by that kingdom and priesthood, the same God of Israel is now everywhere destroying the idols of the nations. The Romans refused to accept his sacred rites precisely so that those idols would not be destroyed, just as they accepted the rites of the gods of other nations whom they conquered.

Thus he also removed the kingdom and priesthood of the prophetic nation, because the one who had been promised through it had already come; and through Christ the king he subjected the Roman Empire, by which that nation had been defeated, to his own name. He also converted it through the strength and devotion of the Christian faith to the overthrow of the idols on whose behalf its sacred rites had not been accepted.

22. I suppose Christ did not accomplish by magical arts, before he was born among human beings, the things that were destined to happen to him—things foretold through so many Prophets and even through the kingdom and priesthood of a certain nation.

The people of that kingdom, now destroyed and scattered everywhere by the wondrous providence of God, although they have remained without any royal or priestly anointing—in which anointing the name of Christ appears—nevertheless retain certain remnants of their observances.

That people, however, did not adopt the Roman rites of idol-worship even when conquered and subjugated; thus it bears the prophetic Books as a testimony to Christ, so that the truth of the Christ prophesied may be proved from the codices of his enemies [Note: Six manuscripts: “the truth is brought forth.”].

Why, then, do these wretched people still expose themselves by praising Christ maliciously [Note: The edition of Rat. and five manuscripts: “judge.”]? If some magical writings have been composed under his name, while Christ’s teaching is vehemently opposed to such arts, let them understand from this instead how great that name is—since even those who live contrary to his commands attempt, by adding his name, to honor their own wicked practices.

For just as, through various human errors, many people have founded various heresies against the truth under his name, so Christ’s enemies themselves perceive that, in persuading others of what they advance against Christ’s teaching, they possess no weight of authority unless they attach Christ’s name to it.

## CHAPTER XV — Pagans compelled to praise Christ, but insulting his disciples

23. Moreover, these vain praisers of Christ and devious detractors of the Christian religion do not dare to blaspheme Christ because some of their philosophers, as Porphyry of Sicily records in his books, consulted their gods about what answer they should give concerning Christ, and those gods were compelled by their oracles to praise Christ.

This is not surprising, since we also read in the Gospel that demons confessed him (Luke 4:41). It is written in our Prophets, moreover, “The gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95:5).

Thus, lest these people attempt to contradict the responses of their own gods, they restrain their blasphemies against Christ and pour them out upon his disciples. It seems to me, however, that those gods of the nations whom the pagan philosophers were able to consult would have been compelled to praise Christ’s disciples as well, if they had been asked about them.

## CHAPTER XVI — The Apostles taught nothing concerning the overthrow of idols that differed from Christ or the Prophets

24. Nevertheless, these people argue that the destruction of temples, the condemnation of sacrifices, and the breaking of idols are not brought about through Christ’s teaching but through that of his disciples, whom they claim taught something different from what they learned from him.

In this way they wish to undermine the Christian faith while honoring and praising Christ. For it was through Christ’s disciples that both Christ’s deeds and Christ’s sayings were announced, and upon these the Christian religion rests [Col. 1053]—a religion that was hostile to those people even when they were already very few and no longer attacking it, but still muttering against it.

But if they do not wish to believe that Christ taught such things, let them read the Prophets. They not only commanded that the superstitions of idols be overthrown, but also foretold that this overthrow would occur in Christian times.

If they deceived us, why is it being fulfilled with such manifest clarity? If they spoke the truth, why is such great divinity resisted?

## CHAPTER XVII — Against the Romans who rejected the God of Israel alone
25. Nevertheless, they must be asked more carefully whom they think the God of Israel is, and why they did not accept that he should be worshiped, as they accepted the gods of the other nations whom the Roman Empire conquered—especially since it is their opinion that all gods ought to be worshiped by the wise. Why, then, was this one rejected from the number of the others? If he is very powerful, why is he alone not worshiped by them? If he has little or no power, why, when their idols have been shattered, is he now almost alone worshiped by all nations? Those who worship greater and lesser gods whom they consider gods will never escape the bind of this question: they do not worship this God, who has prevailed over all those whom they worship. For if he possesses great power, why was he judged worthy of disapproval? If he possesses little or no power, how did he accomplish so much despite being rejected? If he is good, why is he alone separated from the other good gods? If he is evil, why is he alone not overcome by so many good gods? If he is truthful, why are his commands rejected? If he is a liar, why are his predictions fulfilled?

## CHAPTER XVIII—The God of the Hebrews was not accepted by the Romans because he wished to be worshiped alone

26. Finally, let them think of him whatever they wish. Do the Romans not even consider evil gods worthy of worship, when they built temples to Pallor and Fever? Do they not also advise that good demons (ἀγαθοὺς, “good”) should be invited, and evil demons (κακοὺς, “evil”) appeased? Whatever, then, they think of him, why did they judge that he alone should neither be invited nor propitiated for themselves? Who is this God—either so unknown that, among so many gods, he alone has not yet been discovered, or so well known that, among so many people, he is now alone worshiped?

Nothing therefore remains for them to say concerning why they refused to accept the worship of this God, except that he wished to be worshiped alone, while he prohibited the worship of the Gentile gods whom they were already worshiping. But they must be asked this very point even more insistently: whom, or what sort of being, do they think this God is, who did not wish the gods to be worshiped for whom they built temples and idols, and who had so much power that his will proved stronger for overthrowing their idols than their will proved for refusing to accept his worship?

Certainly the opinion of that philosopher of theirs is exposed—the one whom they affirmed even by an oracle to have been the wisest of all human beings. For it is the opinion of Socrates that each god ought to be worshiped in the manner in which that god himself has commanded that he be worshiped. Consequently, these people were placed under the greatest necessity not to worship the God of the Hebrews. For if they wished to worship him in another way than he himself had said he should be worshiped, they would not in fact be worshiping him, but something they themselves had invented. If, however, they wished to worship him in the way he had prescribed, they saw that they ought not to worship the other gods whom he prohibited from being worshiped.

Thus they rejected the worship of the one true God lest they offend many false gods, judging that the anger of those gods would harm them more than his benevolence would benefit them.

## CHAPTER XIX—That this is the true God

27. But let this have been a foolish necessity and a ridiculous timidity. Now we ask what people who approve the worship of all gods think about this God. For if he ought not to be worshiped, how are all gods worshiped when he is not worshiped? But if he ought to be worshiped, then not all ought to be worshiped, because unless he alone is worshiped, he is not worshiped.

Or perhaps they will say that he is not a god, while they call those beings gods who, as we believe, can do nothing except what is permitted by his judgment—not so that they may benefit anyone, but so that they may not even harm anyone except those whom he, who can do everything, judges ought to be harmed. Yet, as they themselves are compelled to admit, those beings certainly have less power than he.

For if the gods are those whose seers, consulted by human beings, did not—as I will not say deceive them—nevertheless give answers concerning matters close to private affairs, how is he not God whose seers not only gave fitting answers to the things about which they were consulted for the time being, but also, concerning the whole human race and all nations, foretold long beforehand matters about which they had not been consulted, matters that we now both read and see?

If they call that being a god through whom the Sibyl sang the fates fulfilled for the Romans [Note: In seven manuscripts, *facta* (“deeds”); *fata* (“fates”) in the others.], how is he not God who brought it about—as he had foretold—that the Romans and all nations would believe in one God through the Gospel of Christ and would overthrow all the idols of their ancestors?

Finally, if they call those beings gods who never dared through their seers to say anything against this God, how is he not God who, through his seers, not only commanded that their idols be overthrown, but also foretold that they would be overthrown among all nations by people who, having abandoned those gods, would be commanded to worship him alone and would obey that command?

## CHAPTER XX—Nothing against the God of the Hebrews is found to have been foretold by the pagan seers

28. Let them read, if they can, whether any of the Sibyls or any other of their seers foretold that this would happen: that the God of the Hebrews, the God of Israel, would be worshiped by all nations; that those who worshiped other gods had rightly rejected him beforehand; that the writings of his prophets would in future possess such exalted authority [Note: Six manuscripts read *futurum … sublimare* (“would in future exalt …”).] that even the Roman Empire, obeying them, would order the idols to be destroyed; and that they had warned people not to obey such commands. Let them read these things, if they can, in any books of their own seers.

For I pass over the fact that the things read in their books bear witness on behalf of our religion—that is, the Christian religion—since they could have heard them from holy angels and from our own prophets, just as even the demons were compelled to confess Christ present in the flesh. But I pass over these matters, because when we produce them they insist that they were fabricated by our people. They themselves must be pressed—entirely compelled—to produce something prophesied by the seers of their gods against the God of the Hebrews, just as we both observe so many and such great commands against their gods from the books of our prophets, recite their predictions, and display their fulfillment.

Those few of them who remain now prefer to grieve that these things have been fulfilled rather than acknowledge the God who was able to foretell what would be fulfilled. Yet, in their false gods—which are truly demons—they desire nothing else as a great benefit except that, after learning from their responses that something is going to happen to them, it should happen.

## CHAPTER XXI—This alone is the God who ought to be worshiped: although he prohibits the worship of others, others do not prohibit his worship

29. Since these things are so, why do these wretched people not understand that he is the true God whom they see separated from the company of their gods in such a way that the God whom they are compelled to acknowledge—who professes that all gods ought to be worshiped—cannot be worshiped by them along with the others?

Since they cannot be worshiped together, why is he not chosen who forbids the worship of these others, while those who do not forbid his worship are abandoned? Or, if they do forbid it, let it be read. For what ought to have been recited more often to their peoples in their temples, where nothing of this kind has ever resounded? Certainly the prohibition of so many against one ought to have been more widely known and more powerful than the prohibition of one against so many [Note: Five manuscripts read *potior* (“preferable”) rather than *potentior* (“more powerful”).].

For if the worship of this God is impious, then the gods are useless because they do not prohibit human beings from impiety. But if the worship of this God is pious, since it commands that these others not be worshiped, their worship is impious.

If they prohibit his worship so timidly that they fear being heard more than they dare to prohibit it [Note: The printed editions read *audere timeant* (“fear to dare”); the manuscripts more truly read *audiri timeant* (“fear being heard”). The demons, that is, feared that if they prohibited the worship of the true God, he would become known precisely through them.], who would not understand by this very fact, who would not perceive, that the one who publicly prohibits the worship of these others, who commanded, foretold, and brought about the overthrow of their idols, ought rather to be chosen than those concerning whom we do not know that they commanded anyone not to worship him, do not read that they foretold it, and do not see that they possessed any power to accomplish it?

I ask them to answer: who is this God who so persecutes all the gods of the Gentiles, who so exposes and extinguishes all their sacred rites?

## CHAPTER XXII—The opinion of the nations concerning our God

30. Why should I question people who have exhausted themselves by trying to think who this being is? Some say, “He is Saturn”—I suppose because of the sanctification of the Sabbath, since they assigned that day to Saturn.

Varro himself, than whom they find no one more learned among their own people, thought that the God of the Jews was Jupiter. He judged that it made no difference by what name he was called, provided that the same reality was understood. I suppose he was frightened by his supreme status. For since the Romans ordinarily worship nothing higher than Jupiter—as their Capitol testifies clearly enough—and since they consider him king of all the gods, when Varro noticed that the Jews worshiped the supreme God, he could suspect nothing other than Jupiter.

But whether those who think that Saturn, or those who think that Jupiter, is the God of the Jews, let them say when Saturn ever dared to prohibit the worship of another god—not even Jupiter himself, who is said to have driven him from his kingdom, though he was his father and Jupiter his son. If Jupiter pleased his worshipers as the more powerful and victorious god, then let them not worship Saturn, defeated and expelled. Yet Jupiter did not prohibit even him from being worshiped, and although he was able to conquer him, he nevertheless allowed him to be a god.

## CHAPTER XXIII—What the pagans have babbled about Jupiter and Saturn

31. “These,” they say, “are myths, either to be interpreted by the wise or laughed at. We, however, worship Jupiter, of whom Maro says:

> All things are full of Jupiter.”

(*Eclogue* 3.60.)

That is, “the spirit giving life to all things.” Varro therefore rightly thought that Jupiter was worshiped by the Jews, because the prophet says, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24).

What about the fact that the same poet speaks of the ether? How do they understand it? For he says:

> Then the almighty Father, Ether, with fertile rains,  
> Descended into the lap of his joyful consort.

(*Georgics* 2.324–325.)

They say, of course, that ether is not spirit but an elevated body by which heaven is extended above the air. Is the poet permitted, according to the Platonists, to speak at one time as though it were not a body but spirit, and at another time, according to the Stoics, as though God were a body?

What, then, do they worship in the Capitol? If spirit—or, finally, if the corporeal heaven itself—what is that shield of Jupiter doing there, which they call the aegis? Surely the origin of this name is explained by saying that Jupiter, having been concealed by his mother, was nourished by a she-goat. Or are the poets lying about this too? And are the Roman Capitols also works of the poets?

What is the meaning of this variety—not poetic, but plainly theatrical—in which they seek the gods in books according to the philosophers, but worship them in temples according to the poets?

32. Was Euhemerus also a poet, who most plainly reveals that Jupiter himself, Saturn his father, and Pluto and Neptune his brothers, were human beings, so that their worshipers ought to give thanks to the poets rather because they invented many things to adorn them rather than to dishonor them? Cicero nevertheless mentions that Euhemerus himself was translated into Latin by the poet Ennius (*On the Nature of the Gods*, book 1).

Was Cicero himself also a poet, when he admonishes the person with whom he is debating at Tusculum as though he were privy to hidden matters, saying:

> But if I should attempt to scrutinize ancient traditions and draw from what the writers of Greece have handed down, those very gods of the greater nations who are so regarded will be found to have departed from us and gone up to heaven. Ask where their tombs are pointed out in Greece; remember, since you have been initiated, what is handed down in the mysteries; then at last you will understand how widely this extends.

(*Tusculan Disputations* 1.)

Here he certainly admits plainly enough that these gods were human beings, though he benevolently supposes that they reached heaven. Yet he did not hesitate to say publicly that even this honor of popular belief had been conferred upon them by human beings, when speaking of Romulus:

> We have raised Romulus, who founded this city, to the immortal gods through benevolence and fame.

(*Against Catiline* 3.)

What, then, is surprising if earlier people did with Jupiter, Saturn, and the others what the Romans did with Romulus—and what, in more recent times, they also wished to do with Caesar? Virgil even added the flattery of poetry, saying:

> Behold, the star of Caesar, child of Dione, has appeared.

(*Eclogue* 9.47.)

Let them therefore see to it that perhaps historical truth displays the tombs of false gods on earth, while poetic vanity does not place their stars in heaven but invents them there. For that star is not truly Jupiter’s, nor that one Saturn’s; rather, after their deaths, human beings who wished to have them as gods assigned their names to stars established from the beginning of the world.

What, moreover, did chastity do so badly, or pleasure so well, that among the stars which revolve with the sun and moon, Venus possesses a star while Minerva does not?

33. But let Cicero the Academic have been more uncertain than the poets, although he dared to mention the tombs of the gods and commit them to writing—though he did not presume this from his own opinion, but reported it from the tradition of the sacred rites themselves.

Does Varro either invent as a poet, or cautiously propose as an Academic, what he says: that the sacred rites of such gods were composed from the life or death of each one, during which they lived or died among human beings?

Was Leon, that Egyptian priest, also a poet or an Academic, who revealed to Alexander of Macedon an origin of these gods different indeed from the Greek opinion, but nevertheless revealed it in such a way as to declare that they had been human beings?

34. But what does this have to do with us [Note: The printed editions read, “But what does it have to do with us if they say?” The words “if they say” are absent from the manuscripts.]? Let them say that they worship Jupiter, not a dead human being; that they dedicated the Capitol not to a dead man but to the spirit that gives life to all things and fills the world; and let them interpret his shield, made in honor of his nurse from goatskin, however they wish.

What do they say about Saturn? The Saturn whom they worship—is he not the one who first came from Olympus,

> Fleeing Jupiter’s weapons, an exile from a kingdom taken away,  
> He gathered the untutored race scattered among the high mountains,  
> Gave them laws, and preferred that the land be called Latium,  
> Since he had safely hidden in those regions?

(*Aeneid* 8.320–324.)

Does not the very image of him, fashioned with covered head, indicate him as though he were hiding? Did he not show the Italians agriculture, which he demonstrates by the sickle?

“No,” they say. “For even if he was a certain human being and king about whom these things are narrated [Note: The printed editions read *Nam tametsi fuerit ille* (“For even if he was that man”); the manuscripts read *Nam videris si fuit* (“For you may see whether he was”).], nevertheless we interpret Saturn as Universal Time, as his Greek name also indicates. For he is called χρόνος (*chronos*), which, with an aspirate added, is also the name for time; hence he is called Saturn in Latin, as though he were ‘sated’ with years.”

I do not know what should now be done with people who, while attempting to interpret the names and images of their gods in a better way, admit that their greater god and the father of the others is Time. For what else do they indicate than that all their gods are temporal, since they establish Time itself as their father?

35. Their more recent philosophers, the Platonists who lived in Christian times, were ashamed of this [Col. 1058] and attempted to interpret Saturn differently. They said that he was called χρόνος (*chronos*) as though from satiety of understanding, because in Greek satiety is called χόρος (*choros*), while understanding or mind is called νοῦς (*nous*). The Latin name also seems to support this, as though it were composed from a Latin first part and a Greek second part, so that Saturnus would mean as though he were *satur nous*—“full mind.”

They saw how absurd it would be if Jupiter were regarded as the son of Time, since they either believed or wished him to be believed an eternal god. According to this new interpretation—which, if their predecessors had possessed it, would surely not have escaped Cicero and Varro—they say that Jupiter is the son of Saturn, as though he were a spirit flowing from that supreme Mind. They wish him to be, as it were, the soul of this world, filling all heavenly and earthly bodies.

Hence comes what Maro says, which I mentioned shortly before: “All things are full of Jupiter.”

If these people could change human superstition as easily as they change this interpretation, would they not establish either no images at all, or at least Capitols for Saturn rather than for Jupiter? For they argue that no rational soul becomes wise except through participation in that supreme and unchangeable wisdom—not merely the soul of any human being, but even that of the world itself, which they call Jupiter.

We, for our part, not only grant but emphatically proclaim that there is a certain supreme wisdom of God, through participation in which every soul that truly becomes wise is made wise. Whether, however, this entire bodily mass called the world possesses a soul of some kind, or something like a soul—that is, rational life by which it is governed as each animal is governed—is a great and hidden question. This opinion ought neither to be affirmed unless it is discovered to be true, nor refuted unless it is discovered to be false.

But what does this have to do with a human being, even if the matter should always remain hidden from him? No soul becomes wise or blessed through any other soul, but only through that one supreme and unchangeable wisdom of God.

36. The Romans, however, who built a Capitol not for Saturn but for Jupiter—or the other nations who thought Jupiter ought to be worshiped especially above the other gods—did not hold what these people have concluded. According to their new opinion, if they had possessed any authority in such matters, they would have dedicated the highest citadels [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *artes* (“arts”), against the manuscripts and Ratramnus.] to Saturn rather; and they would have destroyed the astrologers, or genethliacs, above all, because these men placed Saturn—whom these interpreters call the maker of wise people—among the other stars as an evil god.

This opinion has prevailed so strongly against them in human minds that they do not even wish to name him, calling him “the old man” rather than Saturn. Their superstition is so fearful that the Carthaginians have now almost changed the name of their own street, calling it “the Street of the Old Man” more often than “the Street of Saturn.”

## CHAPTER XXIV—Not all worship the gods who reject the God of Israel; nor does one worship him who worships others

37. It is therefore known what the worshipers of idols are proved to worship, and what they attempt to disguise [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions read *colere* (“worship”) rather than *colorare* (“disguise”).].

But these recent interpreters of Saturn must also be asked what they think about the God of the Hebrews. They too approved the worship of all gods along with the nations, since they were ashamed, in their pride, to humble themselves beneath Christ for the remission of their sins.

What, then, do they think about the God of Israel? If they do not worship him, they do not worship all gods. If they do worship him, they do not worship him as he commanded himself to be worshiped, because they also worship others whom he prohibited from being worshiped.

For he prohibited these things through the very seers through whom he foretold that the things now suffered by their idols at the hands of Christians would come to pass. Whether angels were sent to those prophets, showing them figuratively the one true God, creator of all, to whom everything is subject, through a fitting appearance of visible things, and indicating how he commanded himself to be worshiped; or whether the minds of some among them were so exalted by the Holy Spirit that they saw those things with the vision with which the angels themselves see them—nevertheless, it is clear that they served that God who prohibited the worship of other gods.

They served him in the faithful piety of their kingdom and priesthood, through the rites signifying the true King and Priest who was to come, Christ.

## CHAPTER XXV—The false gods do not prohibit the worship of others alongside themselves. The God of Israel is proved to be the true God by his works and by his prophecies, which have been fulfilled

38. As for the gods of the Gentiles—whom these people wish to worship while refusing to worship the one who cannot be worshiped along with them—let them say why none of them is found to prohibit the worship of another, since they assign them different offices and functions and wish them to preside over matters properly belonging to each one.

If Jupiter does not prohibit the worship of Saturn because Saturn is not a human being whom Jupiter expelled from his kingdom, but either the body of heaven or a spirit filling heaven and earth—and therefore cannot prohibit the worship of the higher Mind from which he is said to have emanated; if, for the same reason, Saturn does not prohibit the worship of Jupiter, because he was not defeated by Jupiter in rebellion, as Saturn was by some Jupiter or other, fleeing whose weapons he came to Italy, but favors the first Mind’s soul generated from itself—then at least Vulcan ought to prohibit the worship of Mars, the adulterer of his wife, and Hercules ought to prohibit the worship of Juno, his persecutor.

What is this shameful agreement among them, that chaste virgin Diana does not prohibit the worship—not to mention Venus, but even Priapus? For if one human being wished to be both hunter and farmer, he would be the slave of both, yet he would be ashamed even to build neighboring temples for them.

Let them interpret Diana as whatever virtue they wish; let them also interpret Priapus as the god of fertility [Note: Lovaniensis reads *foeditatis* (“of foulness”); the other printed editions and our manuscripts read *feconditatis* (“of fertility”).]—provided, of course, that Juno would be ashamed to have such an assistant in making females fertile. Let them say what pleases them and interpret what they understand; nevertheless, let the God of Israel overturn all their arguments.

Since he prohibited the worship of all those gods, while no one prohibited the worship of him, and since he commanded, foretold, and brought about the overthrow of their idols and sacred rites, he has sufficiently shown that they are false and deceptive, while he is the true and truthful God.

39. Who would not marvel at these now few worshipers of many false gods, who refuse to obey the one about whom, when asked who this God is, they answer with whatever opinion they happen to form, yet do not dare deny that he is God? For if they deny it, they are very easily convicted by his works and by his prophecies and their fulfillment.

I am not speaking of those things which they consider themselves free not to believe: that in the beginning he made heaven and earth and everything in them (Genesis 1). Nor am I speaking of those very ancient events: that Enoch was translated (ibid. 5:24), that he destroyed the impious by the flood, and that through the wood he delivered Noah the righteous and his household (ibid. 7).

I begin with the works accomplished among human beings from Abraham onward. For through an angelic oracle a promise was made manifest to him, and we now see it being fulfilled. He was told, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (ibid. 22:18). From his seed came the people of Israel, and from that people came the virgin Mary, who bore Christ—in whom let them now dare to deny, if they can, that all nations are blessed.

This promise was also made to Isaac, Abraham’s son (ibid. 26:4), and to Jacob, Abraham’s grandson (ibid. 28:14), who was also called Israel. From him that entire people was both propagated and named, so that its God might be called the God of Israel—not because he is not the God of all nations, whether they do not know him or now know him, but because he wished the power of his promises to appear more clearly in that people.

That people was first multiplied in Egypt and, through Moses, delivered from that slavery by many signs and wonders. After defeating many nations, it also received the promised land, where it reigned through kings who arose from the tribe of Judah.

Judah was one of the twelve sons of Israel, Abraham’s grandson. From him they were called Jews. With the help of that same God, they accomplished many things and, under his scourging, endured many things because of their sins, until the seed should come to whom it had been promised that all nations would be blessed, and that they would willingly shatter the idols of their ancestors.

## CHAPTER XXVI—Idolatry overthrown through the name of Christ and the faith of Christians, in accordance with the prophecies

40. For what is fulfilled through Christians was not first foretold in Christian times, but long beforehand. The Jews themselves who remain enemies of the name of Christ—concerning whose future unbelief those prophetic writings are not silent—possess and read the prophet who says:

> Lord my God and my refuge in the day of troubles, to you the nations shall come from the ends of the earth, and they shall say: “Truly our fathers worshiped lies, idols, in which there is no profit.”

(Jeremiah 16:19.)

Behold, this is now happening. Behold, now the nations come from the ends of the earth to Christ, saying these things and shattering the idols.

For this too is a great thing that God provided for his Church, spread everywhere: that the Jewish people, deservedly conquered and scattered throughout the lands, might carry the books of our prophecies everywhere, so that we would not be thought to have fabricated these things, and might become witnesses to our truth even while hostile to our faith [Note: The printed editions read, “carried everywhere the books of our prophets.” More manuscripts read, “carried everywhere the books of our prophecies.”].

How, then, did Christ’s disciples teach what they had not learned from Christ, as foolish people babble in their folly, so that the superstition of the Gentile gods and idols might be destroyed? Can the disciples of Christ be said to have fabricated those prophecies that are now read in the books of Christ’s enemies?

41. For who overthrew these things except the God of Israel? To that very people it was said through divine words given to Moses:

> Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.

(Deuteronomy 6:4.)

> You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness of anything, either in heaven above or on earth below.

(Exodus 20:4.)

And, so that he might also overthrow these things when he received the power to do so, he commanded:

> You shall not worship their gods, nor serve them; you shall not act according to their works, but you shall utterly depose them and utterly shatter their idols.

(ibid. 23:24.)

Who, then, would say that Christ and Christians do not belong to Israel, when Israel was Abraham’s grandson, to whom first, and then to his son Isaac, and then to Israel himself, his grandson, it was said—as I have already recalled—“In your seed all nations shall be blessed”?

We now see this fulfilled in Christ, since from that people arose the virgin of whom the prophet of the people of Israel and of the God of Israel sang, saying:

> Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.

“Emmanuel” is interpreted as “God with us.”

(Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23.)

Therefore the God of Israel, who prohibited the worship of other gods, who prohibited the manufacture of idols, who commanded that they be overthrown, and who foretold through the prophet that nations would come from the ends of the earth saying, “Truly our fathers worshiped lies, idols in which there is no profit”—he himself, through the name of Christ and the faith of Christians, commanded, promised, and accomplished the overthrow of all these superstitions.

In vain, therefore, do these wretched people—who have been prevented from blaspheming Christ even by their gods, that is, by the demons who fear the name of Christ—wish to make this teaching foreign to him, the teaching by which Christians argue against idols and eradicate all those false religions wherever they can.

## CHAPTER XXVII—The remnants of idolaters are pressed to serve at last the true God, who everywhere overthrows idols

42. Let them answer concerning the God of Israel, whom the books of not only Christians but also Jews testify to have taught and commanded these things. Let them consult their own gods, who prohibited the blasphemy of Christ, concerning the God of Israel. If they dare, let them give some insulting answer concerning the God of Israel.

But whom will they consult? Or where will they now consult them? Let them read the books of their own gods. If they think that the God of Israel is Jupiter, as Varro wrote—let me speak for the moment according to their opinion—why, then, do they not believe Jupiter that idols ought to be destroyed?

If they think he is Saturn [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “If they think Saturn is God.” Ratramnus and the manuscripts more correctly read, “If they think Saturn,” with “the God of Israel” understood.], why do they not worship him? Or why do they not worship him in the way he commanded through the seers by whom he brought about what he foretold?

Why do they not believe him when he says that idols must be overthrown and other gods must not be worshiped? If he is neither Jupiter [Note: Lovaniensis reads *Jupiter*. The other printed editions and the manuscripts read *Jovis*, the genitive form used here as a nominative, as above in section 30.] nor Saturn—for if he were one of them, he would not speak so greatly against the sacred rites of their Jupiter and Saturn—who, then, is the one whom these people alone do not worship for the sake of their other gods, and who, after the other gods have been overthrown, so plainly brings it about that he alone is worshiped, with every proud height that had raised itself against Christ on behalf of the idols humbled, while it persecuted and killed Christians?

Now, certainly, they ask where they may hide when they wish to sacrifice, or where they may conceal their gods [Note: Ratramnus and Erasmus read *recludant* (“shut away”) rather than *retrudant* (“thrust back”).], lest Christians find and shatter them. From where has this come, except from fear of the laws and kings through whom the God of Israel exercises his power—laws and kings already subject to the name of Christ?

As he promised long beforehand through the prophet:

> All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him.

(Psalm 71:11.)

## CHAPTER XXVIII—The rejection of idols foretold

43. Surely what is repeatedly sung through the prophet is now being fulfilled: that he would abandon his impious people—not all of them, since many Israelites also believed in Christ, for his Apostles were from them—and would humble every proud and injurious person, so that he alone would be exalted, that is, manifested to human beings as alone high and powerful.

This would continue until idols were cast away by believers and hidden by unbelievers, when the earth is shattered by his fear—that is, when earthly people are broken by fear, fearing either his law or the laws of those who, believing in him and ruling the nations, prohibit such sacrilege.

44. The prophet says these things, which I have briefly set forth beforehand so that they might be more easily understood:

> And now you, house of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord. For he has dismissed his people, the house of Israel, because their land has been filled, as from the beginning, with auguries like those of foreigners, and many foreign children have been born to them. Their land has been filled with silver and gold, and there was no number to their treasures. Their land has been filled with horses, and there was no number to their chariots. Their land has been filled with the abominations of the works of their hands, and they worshiped what their fingers had made. And the human being bowed down, and the man humbled himself, and I will not forgive them. And now enter into the rocks and hide yourselves in the earth from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the majesty of his power, when he rises to shatter the earth. For the eyes of the Lord are exalted, but the human being is lowly; and the height of human beings shall be humbled, and the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day. For the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every injurious and proud person, and upon every high and humbled person [Note: The reading appears to be *et elatum* (“and the lifted-up”), since the Greek has μετέωρον (*meteōron*). Shortly afterward, the printed editions read, “and upon every lofty and lifted-up cedar of Lebanon.” The manuscripts, however, have “of the lofty and lifted-up”; in accordance with the Septuagint, τῶν ὑψηλῶν καὶ μετεώρων (*tōn hypsēlōn kai meteōrōn*). They continue, καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶν δένδρον βαλάνου Βασάν (*kai epi pan dendron balanou Basan*), “and upon every oak tree of Bashan”; here Augustine read *Libanou* (“of Lebanon”) instead of *balanou*. After the words “and upon every high hill,” verse 15 is omitted: “and upon every lofty tower, and upon every high wall.”], who shall be humbled; and upon every lofty and lifted-up cedar of Lebanon, and upon every tree of the oak of Bashan, and upon every mountain, and upon every high hill, and upon every ship of the sea, and upon every sight of beautiful ships. And the arrogance of human beings shall be humbled and fall, and the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day. And they shall hide all the works of their hands in caves, in the clefts of the rocks, and in the hollows of the earth, from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the majesty of his power, when he rises to shatter the earth. For on that day the human being shall cast away the golden and silver abominations that they made so that people might worship them—useless and harmful things—and they shall enter into the holes of the solid rock and into the clefts of the rocks, from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the majesty of his power, when he rises to crush the earth.

(Isaiah 2:5–21.)

## CHAPTER XXIX—Why should the pagans not worship the God of Israel, if they suppose that he is even placed over the elements?

45. What do they say about this God of Sabaoth, which is interpreted as “God of powers” or “of armies,” because powers and armies of angels serve him? What do they say about this God of Israel, because he is the God of that people from whom came the seed in which all nations would be blessed?

Why do they not worship him alone, when they insist that all gods ought to be worshiped? Why do they not believe him, since he has both exposed and overthrown other false gods?

I heard one of them say that he had read in some philosopher or other that, from what the Jews did in their sacred rites, he understood which God they worshiped:

> “The one,” he said, “who is placed over these elements from which this visible and corporeal world has been constructed.”

Yet in the sacred Scriptures of his prophets it is clearly shown that the God whom the people of Israel were commanded to worship is the one who made heaven and earth and from whom comes all true wisdom.

But why prolong this discussion, when what I am doing is sufficiently supported by the fact that, whatever their presumptuous opinion of this God may be, they cannot deny that he is God? For if he is placed over the elements from which this world consists, why is he not worshiped rather than Neptune, who is placed over the sea alone? Why not rather than Silvanus, who is placed over fields and forests alone? Why not rather than the Sun, who is placed over the day alone, or even over the heat of the entire heavens? Why not rather than the Moon, which shines with power over the night alone, or even over moisture? Why not rather than Juno, who is said to possess the air alone?

Certainly, whatever these overseers of parts may be, they must be beneath him who holds authority over all the elements and over the whole of this mass. Yet he prohibits all of them from being worshiped. Why, then, do these people, contrary to the command of their greater god, not only wish to worship them, but refuse to worship him because of them?

They still cannot find what they can consistently and clearly say about this God of Israel, nor will they ever find it until they discover that he is the one true God, by whom all things were created.

## CHAPTER XXX—The God of Israel, through the fulfillment of his prophecies, has now become known everywhere
46. Accordingly, a certain great Lucanian declaimer among them, in his poem, I believe himself also having long sought, whether through his own thoughts or through the books of his people, who the God of the Jews might be—and because he was not seeking piously, failing to find him—nevertheless preferred to call him an uncertain God, whom he did not discover, rather than no god at all, since he perceived such great proofs of him. For he says:

> And Judaea, devoted to the rites  
> of an uncertain God.  
> *(Lucan, Book 2, near the end.)*

And this holy and true God of Israel had not yet, through the name of Christ, accomplished throughout all nations such things as have come to pass everywhere down to the present day, after Lucan’s time. But now, who is so hard-hearted that he is not bent, or so sluggish [Note: [Col. 1064] Er. and Lov., “lukewarm” (*tepidus*). Rat. and the manuscripts, “sluggish” (*torpidus*).] that he does not catch fire, when what is written is being fulfilled: “There is no one who can hide himself from his heat”? For now the things foretold so long ago in that same psalm, from which I recalled this verse, are made manifest in the clearest light.

For by the name “heavens” the apostles of Christ are signified, because God presided in them so that they might proclaim the Gospel. The heavens, therefore, have now declared the glory of God, and the firmament has announced the work of his hands. Day has poured forth speech to day, and night has announced knowledge to night. Now there are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard. Now their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. Now he has placed his tabernacle in the sun—that is, in manifestation—which is his Church. For, in order to do this, he himself, as the passage continues, “came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber,” that is, the Word joined to human flesh came forth from the virginal womb. Now “he rejoiced like a giant and ran his course.” Now “his going forth was from the highest heaven, and his return as far as the highest heaven.” And therefore the verse I recalled shortly before follows most appropriately: “And there is no one who can hide himself from his heat” (Psalm 18:1–7).

And still these feeble men, chattering their petty objections, choose to be turned by this fire into ashes like straw rather than to be cleansed from their filth like gold, although the deceptive monuments of their false gods have already been frustrated, while the truthful promises of that uncertain God have now become certain realities.

### CHAPTER XXXI  
### Prophecy concerning Christ fulfilled

47. Let the evil flatterers of Christ, who do not wish to be Christians, therefore cease saying that Christ did not teach that their gods should be abandoned and their images shattered. The God of Israel, of whom it was foretold that he would be called the God of the whole earth—and is now called the God of the whole earth—foretold through the Prophets that this would happen, and fulfilled it through Christ at the appropriate time.

For certainly, if the God of Israel is now called the God of the whole earth, what he commanded must be carried out, since the one who commanded has become known. And because he became known through Christ and in Christ, so that his Church might be spread throughout the world and through it the God of Israel might be called the God of the whole earth, let those who wish read a little earlier in the same prophet—or rather, let me recall it as well. It is not so long that it ought to be passed over.

Many things are said about Christ’s presence, humility, and passion, and about his body, whose head he is—that is, about his Church—when she is called like a barren woman who did not give birth. For many years the Church, which was to exist among all nations in her children, that is, in her saints, did not appear, since Christ had not yet been proclaimed by the Evangelists to those to whom he had not been proclaimed by the Prophets. And it is said that the deserted woman would have more children than she who had a husband. By the name of this husband the Law is signified, or the King whom the first people of Israel received. The Gentiles had not received the Law at the time when the prophet was speaking, nor had the King of Christians yet appeared to the Gentiles, although from those Gentiles a far more fertile and numerous multitude of saints arose.

Thus Isaiah speaks, beginning with Christ’s humility [Note: [Col. 1065] Thus the Rat. edition, supported by the manuscripts. But Er. and Lov.: “humanity” (*humanitate*).] and afterward turning to address the Church, up to the verse we mentioned, where he says, “And he who redeemed you, he himself, the God of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth”:

> “Behold,” he says, “my servant shall understand [Note: [Col. 1065] Seven manuscripts: “shall understand understanding” (*intellectum intelliget*).], and he shall be exalted and greatly honored. Just as many shall be astonished at you, so shall your appearance be dishonored by all, and your honor by men. Thus many nations shall be astonished at him, and kings shall shut their mouths. For those to whom nothing was announced concerning him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand.  
>
> Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced him before him as a child, as a root in thirsty ground. He has neither appearance nor honor. And we saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty; but his face was rejected and disfigured, his condition despised by all men: a man under affliction, and one who knows how to bear infirmities. Therefore his face was turned away; he was insulted and held of no account.  
>
> He bears our infirmities, and for us he is in anguish. And we considered him to be in anguish, under affliction and punishment. But he was wounded because of our sins, and weakened because of our iniquities. The discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed. We all went astray like sheep, and the Lord delivered him over for our sins.  
>
> And because he was badly treated, he did not open his mouth. Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before the one who shears it he was without a voice; so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who shall declare his generation? For his life shall be taken from the earth; because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death.  
>
> Therefore I shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth. The Lord wills to cleanse him from his affliction. If you give yourselves for your offenses, you shall see offspring of very long life. And the Lord wills to take his soul away from pains, to show him light, and to form him through understanding, to justify the righteous man who serves many well; and he himself shall bear their sins.  
>
> Therefore he himself shall inherit many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong. Because his soul was delivered to death, and he was counted among the wicked; and he himself bore the sins of many, and was delivered over because of their iniquities.  
>
> Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; exult and cry aloud, you who do not give birth, because the deserted woman has many more children than she who has a husband. For the Lord has said: Enlarge the place of your tabernacle, and fasten your halls [Note: [Col. 1065] Er. and Lov.: “sheepfolds” (*caulas*). Rat. and nearly all the manuscripts: “halls” (*aulas*); this is supported by many manuscripts in Epistle 105, no. 15, where, however, after the Lov. edition, “curtains” (*aulaeas*) is read.]; do not spare. Extend your cords farther, and establish strong stakes. Extend again and again toward the right and toward the left. For your offspring shall inherit the nations, and you shall inhabit cities that had been deserted; you need not fear. For you shall prevail, and you shall not be ashamed that you were detested. For you shall forget your shame forever, and you shall not remember the disgrace of your widowhood, because I am the Lord who made you; the Lord is his name. And he who redeemed you, he himself, the God of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isaiah 52:13–54:5).

48. What can be said against this clear presentation and expression of events both foretold and fulfilled? If they think that Christ’s disciples lied about his divinity, will they doubt his passion? They are not accustomed to believe that he rose again; yet they readily believe that he suffered all those human things at human hands, because they wish him to be believed merely human.

He, therefore, was led like a sheep to slaughter; he was counted among the wicked; he was wounded because of our sins; by his bruise we were healed; his face was insulted and held of no account, struck with blows and smeared with spittle; his disfigured body was displayed on the cross. He was led to death because of the iniquities of the people of Israel. He had neither appearance nor beauty when he was struck on the face, crowned with thorns, and mocked while hanging there. Like a lamb before its shearer has no voice, so he did not open his mouth when the mockers said to him, “Prophesy to us, Christ” (Matthew 26–27; Mark 14–15; Luke 22–23; and John 18–19).

Surely he has now been exalted; surely he has now been greatly honored. Surely many nations are now astonished at him. Kings have now shut their mouths—the mouths with which they used to promulgate the harshest laws against Christians. Surely those to whom nothing was announced concerning him now see, and those who did not hear now understand (Romans 15:16–21). For the nations to whom the Prophets did not announce these things now see for themselves more clearly how truly they were announced through the Prophets. And those who did not hear Isaiah himself speaking now understand from his writings concerning whom he spoke.

For even among the Jewish people, who believed the report of the Prophets, or to whom was the arm of the Lord revealed?—that is, Christ himself, who was announced through them (John 12:37–38; Romans 10:16)—when with their own hands they were committing against Christ those crimes which the Prophets they possessed had foretold? Surely he now possesses many as his inheritance and divides the spoils of the strong, when he distributes, after expelling and exposing them, those things which the devil and demons possessed, through the construction of his churches and for all kinds of necessary uses.

### CHAPTER XXXII  
### The apostles’ teaching against idolatry vindicated from the prophecies

49. What, then, do the perverse flatterers of Christ and detractors of Christians say to these things? Did Christ use magical arts so that these events might be foretold so long beforehand through the Prophets? Or did his disciples invent them? [Note: [Col. 1066] Earlier editions read “be enlarged” (*dilatetur*). But the manuscripts read “rejoice” (*delectetur*), to which Augustine first alludes in “Rejoice, barren woman”; he will subsequently explain the Prophet’s other saying, “Enlarge the place of your tabernacle.”] Did they cause the Church, once barren and now possessing more children than that Synagogue which had received the Law or the King as a husband, to rejoice as she spread among the nations? Did they cause her to enlarge the place of her tabernacle so that, occupying all nations and languages, she might extend her cords farther than the boundaries of the Roman Empire reach, even to the Persians, Indians, and other barbarous peoples? Did they cause her name to be extended toward the right through true Christians and toward the left through false Christians among so many peoples? Did they cause her offspring to inherit the nations, and her now to inhabit cities that had been deserted by the true worship of God and by true religion? Did they cause her not to fear human threats and fury, when she was clothed in the blood of the martyrs like a purple honor, so that she might prevail over so many, so violent, and so powerful persecutors? Did they cause her not to be ashamed that she had been detested, when it was a great crime even to become or to be a Christian? Did they cause her to forget her shame forever, because where sin had abounded, grace abounded still more (Romans 5:20)? Did they cause her not to remember the disgrace of her widowhood, because, after being abandoned for a little while and subjected to reproach [Note: [Col. 1067] Thus, most suitably, the old Corbie manuscript; for this corresponds to the Prophet’s words quoted above: “You shall not remember the disgrace of your widowhood.” [“exposed to reproaches.”]], she now flourishes again in such eminent glory?

Finally, did Christ’s disciples invent the fact that the Lord who made her and rescued her from the dominion of the devil and demons is now called the God of Israel, the God of the whole earth—a fact that the Prophets, whose books are now in the hands of Christ’s enemies, foretold so long before Christ became the Son of man?

50. From this, then, let the perverse flatterers of Christ and the execrators of the Christian religion understand—something which leaves not even the slowest and dullest [Note: [Col. 1067] The ancient codices consistently read “dullest” (*obtunsissimis*).] minds in obscurity or doubt—that Christ’s disciples learned and taught against their gods those very things contained in Christ’s teaching. For the God of Israel, who is found in the books of the Prophets to have commanded that all the things these people wish to worship are to be abominated and overthrown, is himself now called the God of the whole earth through Christ and Christ’s Church, just as he promised so long beforehand.

If in their astonishing madness they suppose that Christ worshiped their gods and was able to accomplish such things through them, did the God of Israel also worship their gods—the God who fulfilled through Christ what he promised about being worshiped among all nations and about those gods being abominated and overthrown (Deuteronomy 7:5)? Where are their gods? Where are the prophecies of the fanatics and the divinations of the Python priests? Where are the auguries, auspices, haruspices, oracles of demons? Why is nothing from books of that kind produced—some warning or prediction against the Christian faith and against the evident truth of our Prophets, now so clearly established among all nations?

“We have offended our gods,” they say, “and they have abandoned us. Therefore the Christians prevailed against us, and the prosperity of human affairs, exhausted [Note: [Col. 1067] Lov.: “depressed” (*depressa*). The other editions, supported by the manuscripts: “exhausted” (*defessa*).] and diminished, is slipping away.” Let them read in the books of their own prophets that this would certainly happen to them through the Christians. But let them read it in a place where, even if Christ is not mentioned—for they wish him to have been a worshiper of their gods—at least the God of Israel, whom they acknowledge to be their destroyer, is condemned and detested.

But they will never produce such a passage, unless perhaps they fabricate one now. When they do produce it, it will be evident from the very fact that so great a matter, previously unknown, is being brought forward—something that surely ought to have been recited in the temples [Note: [Col. 1068] The Ratisbon edition adds: “in the ears” (*auribus*).] of all nations before the foretold event occurred, so that those who now wish [Note: [Col. 1068] Thus Rat. and several manuscripts. But Lov. and Er.: “do not wish” (*nolunt*).] to be Christians might have been instructed and warned in advance.

### CHAPTER XXXIII  
### Against those who complain that human prosperity has declined during Christian times

51. In the next place, concerning their complaint that human prosperity has declined during Christian times: if they read the books of their philosophers, who criticized the very things now being taken away from them even against their will and amid their grumbling, they will then find great praise for Christian times.

For what prosperity is being taken from them except what they were abusing most wickedly and extravagantly, to the great injury of the Creator? Or perhaps these are bad times because throughout almost all cities theaters, arenas of indecency, and public professions of vices [Note: [Col. 1068] The printed editions had “vicious persons” (*flagitiosorum*); the manuscripts read “vices” (*flagitiorum*).] are falling; and because marketplaces or walls in which demons were worshiped are also falling? Why are they falling, unless because of the scarcity of the resources with which they were constructed for wanton and sacrilegious use?

Did not Cicero, when praising a certain actor named Roscius, call him so skilled that he alone was worthy to enter the stage, and so good a man that he alone was worthy not to go there (Cicero, *Oration for Roscius*)? What else does this reveal most openly than that the stage was so disgraceful that the better a man was, the less he ought to be there? And yet their gods were appeased by such dishonor, which he considered something from which good men ought to keep away.

There is also an open confession by that same Cicero, where he says that Flora the Mother had to be appeased by the celebration of games (Cicero, *Against Verres*, act 5). At those games such indecency was customarily displayed that, in comparison with them, the others were respectable—although even from those other games good men were forbidden to take part.

What sort of Flora is this Mother? What kind of goddess is she, whom indecency conciliates and renders favorable when it is celebrated more frequently and allowed freer rein? How much more honorably did Roscius enter the stage than Cicero worshiped such a goddess!

If the reduced supply of resources spent on celebrating these things offends the gods of the nations, it is clear what sort of beings those are who take pleasure in such things. But if the gods themselves, being angry, diminish these things, they are angry more usefully than they are appeased.

Therefore, either let them accuse their philosophers, who criticized such practices in extravagant men, or let them break the gods who demanded such things from their worshipers—if indeed they can now find either gods to break or gods to conceal. Let them cease blasphemously attributing to Christian times the decline of worldly goods that were flowing into shameful and harmful activities, lest they remind us all the more of the reason for praising Christ’s power.

### CHAPTER XXXIV  
### Epilogue to the foregoing

[Col. 1069]

52. I would say much more on this subject, were I not compelled by the necessity of the work undertaken to bring this book to a close and return to the purpose proposed.
