When I began to resolve the Gospel questions in which the four Evangelists seem to some people not to agree with one another, after explaining as well as I could the intentions of each, I first encountered the question that some are accustomed to raise: why we produce no writings of Christ himself.

For they wish it to be believed that he himself wrote something else, I know not what, which they approve; that he thought nothing against their gods, but rather worshiped them by magical ritual; and that his disciples not only lied about him when they said that he was the God through whom all things were made, although he was nothing other than a human being, however outstanding in wisdom, but also did not teach concerning their gods what they had learned from him.

For this reason we pressed them especially concerning the God of Israel, who is worshiped by all nations through the Church of the Christians and has now everywhere overthrown their sacrilegious vanities, just as he foretold so long beforehand through his Prophets and fulfilled, through the name of Christ—in whom he had promised that all nations would be blessed—the things he had foretold.

From this they ought to understand that neither could Christ know or teach anything concerning their gods other than what the God of Israel commanded and foretold through his Prophets, through whom he promised and sent Christ himself. In Christ’s name, according to the promise he made to the fathers, when all nations would be blessed, it came about that the God of Israel himself was also called the God of the whole earth.

Nor did Christ’s disciples depart from the teaching of their Master when they forbade the worship of the gods of the nations, lest we either offer service to senseless images, enter into fellowship with demons, or serve the creature rather than the Creator with the obedience owed to religion.

### CHAPTER XXXV  
### The mystery of the Mediator proclaimed to the ancients through prophecy and to us through the Gospel

53. Since Christ himself is the Wisdom of God, through whom all things were created, and since no rational minds, whether of angels or human beings, become wise except by participation in him—to whom we cleave through the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured into our hearts—and since this Trinity is one God, divine providence provided for mortals, whose temporal life was occupied with things that arise and pass away, that this same Wisdom of God, by assuming a human being into the unity of his person, in whom he would be born, live, die, and rise again in time, might, through speaking and doing, suffering and enduring what was appropriate for our salvation, become both an example to human beings below of returning and an example to the angels above of remaining.

For unless something arose temporally in the nature of the rational soul—that is, unless something began to exist that previously was not—it would never pass from a most wretched and foolish life to one that was wise and supremely good. And so, since the truth of those who contemplate is enjoyed in eternal things, while faith belongs to those who believe in things that arise, the human being is cleansed through faith in temporal things so that he may grasp the truth of eternal things.

For one of their most distinguished philosophers, Plato, also says in the book they call the *Timaeus*: “As eternity is to what has arisen, so truth is to faith.”

Those two things above are eternity and truth; those two below are what has arisen and faith. Therefore, in order that we may be recalled from the lowest things to the highest, and that what has arisen may receive eternity, we must come to truth through faith.

And because all things that move toward the opposite are restored through some intermediary, and temporal iniquity was alienating us from eternal justice, there was need for a temporal intermediary justice. This intermediary was temporal from the lower things, but just from the higher things [Note: [Col. 1070] Thus the Ratisbon edition formerly read; but later editions, contrary to the manuscripts, altered this certainly genuine reading to: “This intermediary was temporal, mixed from lower and higher things.”]; and thus, without breaking away from the highest things, while adapting itself to the lowest, it would restore the lowest things to the highest.

Therefore Christ is called the Mediator of God and human beings, God and human between immortal God and mortal humanity (1 Timothy 2:5), reconciling humanity to God, remaining what he was and becoming what he was not. He is our faith in things that have arisen, who is truth in eternal things.

54. This great and ineffable mystery, this kingdom and priesthood, was revealed to the ancients through prophecy and proclaimed to their descendants through the Gospel. For it was necessary that what had long been promised through one nation should at some time be bestowed upon all nations.

Accordingly, the one who sent the Prophets before his descent also sent the apostles after his ascension. He is the head of all his disciples, as members of his body, through the human being whom he assumed. Therefore, when they wrote what he showed and said, it must by no means be said that he himself did not write, since his members carried out what they had learned under the direction of their head.

Whatever he wished us to read concerning his deeds and words, he commanded them to write as though they were his own hands. Whoever understands this partnership of unity and the ministry of concordant members in different offices under one head will not receive what he reads in the Gospel narrated by Christ’s disciples any differently than if he had seen the very hand of the Lord, which he carried in his own body, writing.

Let us therefore now examine what kind of things these are that they think the Evangelists wrote contrary to one another—something that may appear so to those who understand poorly—so that, once these questions have been resolved, it may also become clear from this that the members of that head, not only by thinking the same but also by writing things that agree, preserved genuine concord in the unity of his body.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1071]

In this book Augustine treats Matthew’s Gospel in sequence up to the account of the supper, and compares it with the Gospels of Mark, Luke, and John, demonstrating that perpetual agreement is found among the four Evangelists.

### PROLOGUE

1. Since in a lengthy and very necessary discourse, which we contained in one book, we refuted the vanity of those who think Christ’s disciples contemptible because, when they wrote the Gospel, we produce no writings of Christ himself—although they do not hesitate to honor him as a human being of wisdom far surpassing all others, even if they do not honor him as God—and since they wish him to appear to have written things of the sort that the perverse approve, rather than things whose reading and belief could correct them from their perversity, let us now see how the things that the four Evangelists wrote about Christ agree with one another and among themselves.

This is so that those who are more curious than capable may not take offense at the Christian faith on this account. After reading the Gospel books not casually but as though examining them with greater diligence, they imagine that they have detected certain inconsistencies and contradictions and judge that these should be asserted contentiously rather than considered prudently.

### CHAPTER I  
### Why Christ’s ancestors are commemorated down to Joseph, although Christ was not born from his seed but from the Virgin Mary

2. The evangelist Matthew began in this way: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). By this opening he sufficiently showed that he had undertaken to narrate Christ’s generation according to the flesh. According to this generation Christ is the Son of man, as he himself also very often calls himself (ibid. 8:20 and 9:6), commending to us what he mercifully deigned to become for our sake.

For that heavenly and eternal generation, according to which he is the only-begotten Son of God before every creature, since all things were made through him, is so ineffable that the prophet’s statement is understood to have been spoken concerning it: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8).

Matthew therefore sets out Christ’s human generation, recalling his ancestors from Abraham and bringing them down to Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born. For it was not right that he should think Joseph ought to be separated from Mary’s marriage on the ground that Christ was not born from intercourse with him but was born of a virgin.

This example most magnificently teaches married believers that, even when continence is preserved by mutual agreement, a marriage can continue and be called a marriage—not through sexual intercourse, but through the bond of affection—especially since a son could also be born to them without any carnal embrace, which is employed only for the begetting of children.

Nor was Joseph for that reason not to be called Christ’s father, because he did not beget him through intercourse, since he would rightly be the father even of one whom he had adopted from elsewhere rather than begotten from his own wife.

3. Christ was indeed thought to be Joseph’s son in another sense as well, as though he had been born entirely from Joseph’s flesh. But this was thought by those to whom Mary’s virginity was hidden. For Luke says: “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:23).

Yet Luke did not hesitate to call not only Mary his parent but both his parents, where he says: “The child grew and was strengthened, being filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was in him. And his parents went every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover.”

But lest anyone think that “parents” here should be understood as Mary’s blood relatives together with her mother, what will he answer to the fact that Luke himself likewise said earlier: “And his father and mother were astonished at the things that were spoken about him” (ibid. 2:40–41, 33)?

Since, then, Luke himself relates that Christ was born not from intercourse with Joseph but from the Virgin Mary, why does he call Joseph his father unless we rightly understand him to be Mary’s husband without bodily union, through the very bond of marriage, and for that reason also Christ’s father in a much closer sense, since Christ was born from his wife than if he had been adopted from elsewhere?

It is therefore clear that when Luke says “as was supposed, the son of Joseph,” he said this on account of those who thought that Christ had been born from Joseph in the same way as other human beings.

### CHAPTER II  
### How Christ is the son of David, although he was not born from intercourse with Joseph, the son of David

4. Accordingly, even if someone could demonstrate that Mary derived no blood relationship from David, it would be sufficient, on this reasoning, to understand Christ as the son of David in the same way that Joseph was rightly called his father. How much more, then, when the apostle Paul plainly says that Christ was “from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3)! We certainly ought not to doubt that Mary herself also derived some blood relationship from David’s stock.

Since the priestly line of this woman is not left unmentioned either—for Luke indicates that Elizabeth was her kinswoman and says that Elizabeth was of the daughters of Aaron (Luke 1:36, 5)—we must hold most firmly that Christ’s flesh was propagated from both lines, namely that of kings and that of priests. In these persons, among the Hebrew people, a mystical anointing was also represented, that is, chrism, from which the name “Christ” shines forth, foretold so long beforehand by that most evident sign as well.

### CHAPTER III  
### Why Matthew lists different ancestors of Christ from Luke

5. Those who are troubled by the fact that Matthew lists one set of ancestors, descending from David to Joseph (Matthew 1:1–16), while Luke ascends from Joseph to David with another set (Luke 3:23–38), can easily observe that Joseph could have had two fathers: one from whom he was begotten, and another by whom he was adopted [Note: [Col. 1072] *Retractations* II, chapter 16.].

For the practice of adoption was ancient even among that people of God, so that they made their own children whom they had not themselves begotten. Apart from the fact that Pharaoh’s daughter had adopted Moses (Exodus 2:10)—for she was a foreigner—Jacob himself adopted his grandsons born from Joseph, in the clearest words, saying:

> “Now therefore your two sons, who were born to you before I came to you, are mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine like Reuben and Simeon. But any children whom you beget afterward shall be yours” (Genesis 48:5–6).

Thus it also came about that there were twelve tribes of Israel, excluding the tribe of Levi, which served the temple. Together with Levi there were thirteen tribes, although Jacob had had twelve sons.

It is therefore understood that Luke took Joseph’s father in his Gospel not as the man from whom Joseph was begotten, but as the man by whom he had been adopted, and that he recalled his ancestors upward until he reached David.

Since it is necessary, with both Evangelists narrating the truth—Matthew and Luke—that one of them followed the ancestry of the father who had begotten Joseph and the other that of the father who had adopted him, whom can we more plausibly understand to have followed the ancestry of the adopter than the Evangelist who did not wish to say that Joseph was begotten by the man whose son he said Joseph was?

For Joseph was more suitably called the son of the man by whom he had been adopted than said to have been begotten by the man from whose flesh he had not been born. Matthew, however, by saying, “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob,” and continuing throughout with the word “begot,” until at the end he said, “Jacob begot Joseph,” clearly expressed that he had carried the line of begetters down to the father from whom Joseph was begotten, not adopted [Note: [Col. 1073] Thus in the manuscripts. But in the printed editions, “ancestry.”].

6. Even if Luke had said that Joseph was begotten by Heli, this word ought not to disturb us so that we would believe anything other than that one Evangelist had referred to the begetting father and the other to the adoptive father.

For someone may rightly be said to have begotten—not by flesh but by affection—the one whom he adopted as his son. Indeed, God did not beget us, to whom he gave the power to become his children, from his own nature and substance as he did the only-begotten Son, but certainly adopted us through love.

The Apostle is understood to use this word frequently for no other reason than to distinguish the Only-begotten, who existed before every creature and through whom all things were made, who alone was born from the substance of the Father and, according to the equality of divinity, is altogether what the Father is. He says that the Son was sent to assume flesh from that race from which we too are according to our nature, so that, by his participation in our mortality through love, he might make us participants in his divinity through adoption.

For he says:

> “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” [Note: [Col. 1073] Most and the older manuscripts: “so that we may receive” (*recipiamus*).] (Galatians 4:4–5).

And yet we are also said to have been born from God—that is, to have received the power to become his children, though we were already human beings. We become this through grace, not through nature. For if we were sons by nature, we would never have been anything else.

When John had said, “He gave them power to become the children of God, to those who believe in his name,” he continued: “who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God.” Thus those whom he said had been made children of God by receiving power—a thing signified by the adoption Paul mentions—he also said had been born from God.

And to show more clearly by what grace this had happened, he says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:12–14), as though he were saying: “What is astonishing if those who were flesh became children of God, when for their sake the Only-begotten became flesh, though he was the Word?”

There is, of course, this great distinction: when we are made children of God, we are changed for the better; but when the Son of God became the son of man, he was not changed for the worse, but assumed what was lower than himself.

James also says: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of first beginning of his creation” (James 1:18). Thus, lest we think from his use of the word “begot” that we become what he himself is, he sufficiently demonstrated that through this adoption a certain primacy in creation was granted to us.

## 7

It would therefore not be contrary to the truth even if Luke said that Joseph was begotten by the man by whom he had been adopted. For in this way too he begot him—not so that he might be a human being, but so that he might be a son—just as God begot us so that we might be his sons, although he had made us to be human beings. But he begot the Only-Begotten not merely so that he might be a Son, which the Father is not, but also so that he might be God, which the Father also is.

Yet plainly, if Luke too had used this word, it would have been altogether ambiguous which of them had mentioned the adoptive father and which the father who begot him from his own flesh. Likewise, even if neither of them had said “begot,” but one had called him the son of one man and the other the son of another, it would nevertheless have been ambiguous which of them had mentioned the man from whom he was born and which the man by whom he had been adopted.

But now, since one says, “Jacob begot Joseph,” while the other says, “Joseph, who was the son of Heli,” even the difference in their wording has elegantly indicated what each of them intended. This could easily, as I said, occur to a religious-minded person, who would judge that anything else ought rather to be investigated than that the evangelist should be believed to have lied. It would easily, I say, occur to him to consider for what reasons one man could have two fathers. This would also occur to those slanderous critics, if they had preferred to consider the matter rather than quarrel over it.

## CHAPTER IV

### Why forty generations, apart from Christ himself, are found in Matthew, although he divides them into three groups of fourteen

### 8

What must next be explained truly required an exceptionally attentive and painstaking reader in order to be noticed and understood. For it has rightly been observed that Matthew, who intended to indicate Christ’s royal person, named forty men in the sequence of the generations, apart from Christ himself.

This number signifies the period during which, in this world and upon this earth, we must be ruled by Christ according to the arduous discipline by which God chastises, as it is written, “every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). Concerning this the Apostle says that “through tribulation we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14: [Col. 1075] 21).

It is also signified by that iron rod of which we read in the Psalm, “You shall rule them with an iron rod,” after he had said above, “Yet I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain.” For the good too are ruled with an iron rod, concerning whom it is said, “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord; and if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the gospel of God? And if the righteous man will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Peter 4:17–18).

To these people the following also applies: “You shall shatter them like a potter’s vessel” (Psalm 2:9). The good are ruled by this discipline, whereas the wicked are crushed. They are mentioned as though they were the same people because of the one and the same sacraments, which the wicked share in common with the good.

**Note:** [Col. 1075] Two Vatican manuscripts, contrary to the others, read: “because of one faith and the same sacraments.”

### 9

Since, then, this number is a sacramental sign of that arduous period during which we struggle under the discipline of Christ the King against the devil, this too makes its meaning clear: the Law and the Prophets consecrated a fast of forty days—that is, the humbling of the soul—through Moses and Elijah, who fasted for forty days each (Exodus 34:28; 3 Kings 19:8). The Gospel did so through the Lord’s own fast, during which forty days he was also tempted by the devil (Matthew 4:1–2). What else did this signify than our temptation throughout the whole period of this world, prefigured in his flesh—the flesh which he graciously chose to assume from our mortality?

After his resurrection, too, he wished to remain on this earth with his disciples for no more than forty days (Acts 1:3), still mingling with their life through human association and receiving mortal human nourishment with them, although he was no longer destined to die. By those forty days he signified that, through his hidden presence, he would fulfill what he had promised when he said, “Behold, I am with you always, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

The reason why this number signifies this temporal and earthly life immediately presents itself, although there may perhaps be another, more hidden reason: the periods of the years proceed in four successive seasons, and the world itself is bounded by four regions, which Scripture sometimes mentions under the names of the winds: east and west, north and south (Zechariah 14:4). Forty, moreover, contains four times ten. And ten itself is completed by the number’s progression from one to four.

### 10

Thus, when Matthew received Christ the King, coming into this world and this earthly, mortal human life in order to rule us, struggling as we are amid temptation, he began from Abraham and enumerated forty men.

For Christ came in the flesh from that Hebrew people whom God separated from the other nations, taking Abraham away from his land and his kindred (Genesis 12:1–2). This especially pertained to prophesying and announcing him more distinctly: it was foretold from which people he would come.

Although he distinguished the generations by three sections of fourteen, saying that from Abraham to David there were fourteen generations, [Col. 1076] from David to the Babylonian captivity another fourteen, and from then until Christ’s birth yet another fourteen (Matthew 1:17), he nevertheless did not add them up by saying, “Altogether there are forty-two.” For one of those forefathers is counted twice: Jeconiah, at whom a turning toward foreign nations took place, when the migration to Babylon occurred.

When an order bends away from its straight course and, in turning aside, forms something like an angle, the object situated at the angle is counted twice: once at the end of the preceding order and once at the beginning of the deviation itself. This already prefigured Christ’s passage from circumcision to uncircumcision, as though migrating in some manner from Jerusalem to Babylon, and becoming for believers on both sides a kind of cornerstone.

At that time God was preparing these things in figure for things that would later come in reality. Jeconiah himself, at whom this prefigured angle occurs, is interpreted as “Preparation of God.” Thus the total is not forty-two, which three times fourteen would produce, but, because one is counted twice, forty-one generations—if we count Christ himself as well, Christ who, like a king, presides over this temporal and earthly life of ours that must be ruled, under the sign of the number forty.

### 11

Because Matthew wished to signify Christ descending to share our mortality, he therefore recounted the generations themselves from Abraham to Joseph and from Joseph to Christ’s birth by descending, at the beginning of his Gospel.

Luke, however, does not recount the generations at the beginning of his Gospel, but from Christ’s baptism; and he recounts them not by descending but by ascending, as though assigning Christ more particularly the role of a priest in the expiation of sins. It was there that a voice from heaven declared him, and there that John bore witness to him, saying, “Behold, he who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

By ascending, Luke also passes through Abraham and arrives at God, to whom we are reconciled once cleansed and expiated. It is rightly Luke who takes up the origin of adoption, because through adoption we become sons of God by believing in the Son of God. Through carnal generation, however, the Son of God rather became, for our sake, the son of man.

He made it sufficiently clear that he did not say “Joseph, the son of Heli” because Joseph had been begotten by Heli, but because he had been adopted by him, since he also called Adam the son of God, although Adam had been made by God; yet through the grace that he later lost by sinning, he had been placed in paradise as a son.

### 12

Accordingly, in Matthew’s generations the taking upon himself of our sins by the Lord Christ is signified; in Luke’s generations, the abolition of our sins by the Lord Christ is signified. For that reason Matthew recounts them by descending, while Luke recounts them by ascending.

When the Apostle says, “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh,” this is the taking upon himself of sins; but when he adds, “so that he might condemn sin in the flesh concerning sin” (Romans 8:3), this is the expiation of sins.

Therefore Matthew descends from David through Solomon, in whose mother David sinned (2 Samuel 11:4), whereas Luke ascends to David through Nathan, the prophet through whom God expiated David’s sin [Col. 1077] (2 Samuel 12:1–14).

**Note:** [Col. 1077] See also *Retractations* 2.16.

The very number that Luke traces most certainly indicates the abolition of sins. Since no iniquity of Christ—for he had none—is joined to the iniquities of human beings, which he took upon himself in his flesh, the number in Matthew, apart from Christ, is forty.

But because he joins us, cleansed and purified from every sin, to the righteousness of himself and of his Father, so that what the Apostle says may come to pass, “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17), therefore in Luke’s number both Christ, from whom the enumeration begins, and God, to whom it reaches, are counted. The number becomes seventy-seven, signifying the complete remission and abolition of every sin.

The Lord himself also clearly expressed this through the mystery of this number, saying that one must forgive the sinner not merely seven times, but even seventy times seven (Matthew 18:22).

### 13

Nor is it without reason that this number pertains to the cleansing of all sins, if it is examined more carefully. Ten is displayed as the number of righteousness in the Ten Commandments of the Law. Sin, moreover, is transgression of the Law; and transgression of the number ten is appropriately represented by eleven. Hence eleven curtains of goats’ hair were commanded to be made in the tabernacle (Exodus 26:7). Who could doubt that sackcloth pertains to the symbolism of sin?

And so, because the whole of time revolves in a cycle of seven days, all sins appropriately reach the number seventy-seven when eleven is multiplied by seven. In this number there is also complete remission of sins: our priest’s flesh expiates us, from whom this number now begins, and the Holy Spirit reconciles us to God, to whom this number now reaches—the Spirit who appeared in the form of a dove at this baptism, where this number is mentioned (Luke 3:22).

## CHAPTER V

### How Luke’s order accords with Matthew’s in those matters concerning Christ’s conception and infancy or childhood that one omits and the other recounts

### 14

After enumerating the generations, Matthew continues as follows:

“Now the generation of Christ was in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.”

How this happened—something that Matthew omitted—Luke explained after recounting John’s conception, narrating it in this way:

“In the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary. And the angel entered to her and said: ‘Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.’”

When she had seen him, she was troubled at his words and considered what sort of greeting this might be.

**Note:** [Col. 1077] The printed editions here and below read *audisset*, “had heard.” But most manuscripts, and those of better quality, consistently read *vidisset*, “had seen,” in accordance with the Greek text, *ē de idoûsa*, “but when she had seen.”

“And the angel said to her: ‘Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. [Col. 1078] He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.’

“But Mary said to the angel: ‘How will this happen, since I do not know a man?’

“And the angel answered and said to her: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the Power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born will also be called the Son of God.’”

**Note:** [Col. 1078] The printed editions read *ex te sanctum*, “the holy one from you.” The words *ex te*, “from you,” are absent from three Vatican manuscripts and from most Gallican manuscripts, and they do not appear in the Greek text.

“And the rest, which does not pertain to the matter now under discussion.”

Matthew therefore recalled this when he said of Mary, “She was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.” There is no contradiction because Luke explained what Matthew omitted, since both testify that Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit.

Nor is it contradictory that Matthew next connects what Luke omits. For Matthew continues and says:

“Joseph her husband, being a just man and unwilling to expose her, wished to dismiss her secretly. But while he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: ‘Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife, for that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he himself will save his people from their sins.’

“Now all this took place so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: ‘Behold, a virgin will have a child in her womb and will bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel,’ which is interpreted, ‘God with us.’

“Joseph rose from sleep and did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and he took his wife. But he did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son, and he called his name Jesus.

“When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, and the rest.”

**Note:** [Col. 1078] The printed editions read *vocabitur*, “will be called.” But the manuscripts read *vocabunt*, “they will call,” except for the Audoenensis manuscript, which reads *vocabis*, “you will call.” Thus the Greek exemplars vary between *kalesousin*, “they will call,” and *kaleseis*, “you will call.”

### 15

Matthew and Luke agree concerning the city of Bethlehem. But Luke explains how and for what reason Joseph and Mary came there, whereas Matthew omits this.

Conversely, Luke is silent about the Magi who came from the East, while Matthew speaks of them, weaving the narrative together in this way:

“Behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him.’ But when King Herod heard this, he was troubled,” and the rest, up to the point where it is written that the Magi, having received a response in a dream not to return to Herod, went back to their own country by another road.

Luke omits all this, just as Matthew did not narrate what Luke narrates: that the Lord was placed in a manger; that an angel announced his birth to the shepherds; that a multitude of the heavenly host appeared with the angel, praising God; that the shepherds came and found true what the angel had announced to them; that he received his name on the day of his circumcision; and what Luke further narrates after the days of Mary’s purification had been completed: that they brought him to Jerusalem, and concerning Simeon and [Col. 1079] Anna, and what they said about him in the temple after they had recognized him, having been filled with the Holy Spirit.

Matthew is silent about all these things.

### 16

It is therefore rightly asked when the events took place—whether those that Matthew omits and Luke recounts, or those that Luke omits and Matthew recounts.

For after narrating that the Magi who had come from the East returned to their own country, Matthew continues by saying that Joseph was warned by an angel to flee with the child into Egypt, lest he be killed by Herod; then, when Herod failed to find him, that Herod killed the boys two years old and under; and that after Herod’s death Joseph returned from Egypt and, hearing that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, settled with the child in the Galilean city of Nazareth.

Luke omits all these events.

Nor can it therefore appear contradictory that one evangelist says what the other omits, or that one recalls what the other does not say. The question is when the events Matthew connects concerning the journey to Egypt and the return from there after Herod’s death could have taken place, so that they were already living in the city of Nazareth—the city to which Luke says they returned after they had completed in the temple everything concerning the child according to the Law of the Lord.

Here, therefore, we must understand a principle that will apply to other matters of this kind as well, so that such passages may not similarly disturb and confuse us: each evangelist arranges his narrative so that it appears to be an ordered sequence omitting nothing. For when he leaves unmentioned the matters he does not wish to relate, he joins the matters he does wish to relate to those he has already narrated in such a way that they seem immediately to follow.

But when one evangelist relates what the other has left unsaid, careful attention to the sequence reveals the point at which the evangelist who omitted it could have passed over the event, in order to connect the events he intended to narrate to what preceded as though they followed without any intervening events.

Accordingly, we understand that when Matthew says that the Magi were warned in a dream not to return to Herod and went back to their own country by another road, he omitted there what Luke narrated as having taken place concerning the Lord in the temple, as well as what Simeon and Anna said. Luke, in turn, omitting the journey into Egypt—which Matthew narrates—connected the return to the city of Nazareth as though it followed continuously.

17. If anyone wishes to arrange into a single narrative all that, in the accounts of the two evangelists, is either said or omitted by one or the other concerning Christ’s birth and infancy or childhood, he may do so as follows:

“Now the birth of Christ took place in this way” (Matt. 1:18). There was in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah; and he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, whose name was Elizabeth. Both were righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.

Now it happened, while he was serving as priest before God in the order of his division, according to the custom of the priesthood, that he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and offer incense. And the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense. An angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. When Zechariah saw him, he was troubled [Col. 1080], and fear fell upon him. But the angel said to him:

“Do not fear, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. And you shall have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great before the Lord, and he will drink neither wine nor strong drink; and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. And he himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers toward their children, and the disobedient to the prudence of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfected people.”

And Zechariah said to the angel: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.”

And the angel answered and said to him: “I am Gabriel, who stand before God, and I have been sent to speak to you and announce this good news to you. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their proper time.”

And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they wondered that he was delaying in the temple. But when he came out, he was unable to speak to them; and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them, and remained mute. When the days of his service were completed, he went to his house.

After those days Elizabeth his wife conceived, and she kept herself in seclusion for five months, saying: “Thus has the Lord dealt with me in the days when he looked upon me, to remove my reproach among men.”

Now in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary. And the angel entered to her and said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.”

When she saw him, she was troubled by his saying, and considered what kind of greeting this might be. And the angel said to her: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

But Mary said to the angel: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?”

And the angel answered and said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is to be born will be called the Son of God. And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her who is called barren, because no word is impossible with God.”

And Mary said: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” And the angel departed from her.

Rising in those days, Mary went into the hill country with haste, to a city of Judah. And she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And it happened that, when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb; and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. And she cried out with a loud voice and said:

“Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And how has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting came into [Col. 1081] my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed, because those things will be fulfilled which were spoken to her by the Lord.”

And Mary said:

“My soul magnifies the Lord,  
and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior,  
because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid.  
For behold, from this time all generations will call me blessed,  
because he who is mighty has done great things for me,  
and holy is his name.  
And his mercy is from generation to generation  
for those who fear him.  
He has shown strength with his arm;  
he has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart.  
He has brought down the mighty from their throne  
and exalted the lowly.  
He has filled the hungry with good things,  
and sent the rich away empty.  
He has received Israel his servant,  
remembering his mercy,  
as he spoke to our fathers,  
to Abraham and to his seed forever.”

Mary remained with her about three months, and returned to her house (Luke 1:5, 36). And she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit.

But Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly. While he was considering this, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying:

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife, for that which has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”

Now all this took place so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled:

“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.”

When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him, and took his wife; and he did not know her (Matt. 1:18–25).

Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her. And it happened that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were calling him by his father’s name, Zechariah. But his mother answered and said: “By no means; he shall be called John.”

And they said to her: “There is no one among your relatives who is called by this name.” And they made signs to his father, asking what he wanted him to be called. And asking for a writing tablet, he wrote, saying: “John is his name.” And they all marveled. Immediately his mouth and tongue were opened, and he spoke, blessing God. And fear came upon all their neighbors; and throughout all the hill country of Judaea all these things were being reported. And all who heard them laid them up in their heart, saying: “What, then, will this child be?”

[Note: [Col. 1081] One of the Colbertine manuscripts has *Quis?* (“Who?”); other codices have *Quid* (“What?”), and likewise the ancient Corbie Bibles. The reason is evidently that the Greek has *ti* (“what?”), neuter in gender, agreeing with *to paidion*, which signifies “the child.”]

For the hand of the Lord was with him. And Zechariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel,  
because he has visited and accomplished redemption for his people.  
And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us  
in the house of David his servant,  
as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets  
who have been from of old:  
salvation from our enemies  
and from the hand of all who hate us;  
to show mercy to our fathers  
and to remember his holy covenant,  
[Col. 1082] the oath which he swore to Abraham our father,  
that he would grant us  
that, delivered from the hand of our enemies  
and serving him without fear,  
in holiness and righteousness before him  
all our days.  
And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High;  
for you will go before the face of the Lord  
to prepare his ways,  
to give knowledge of salvation to his people  
for the forgiveness of their sins,  
through the tender mercy of our God,  
by which the Dawn from on high has visited us,  
to shine upon those who sit in darkness  
and in the shadow of death,  
to guide our feet into the way of peace.”

And the child grew and became strong in spirit; and he was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel.

Now it happened in those days that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered. This registration was the first, when Quirinius was governor of Syria.

[Note: [Col. 1082] Some manuscripts and the Ratisbon edition have *a praeside* (“by the governor”); Erasmus and Louvain have *sub praeside* (“under the governor”). But in most and better manuscripts the preposition is absent: *praeside*, that is, “with him acting as governor,” in accordance with the Greek *hēgemoneuontos*.]

And everyone went to register, each to his own city. Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to register with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was with child.

And it happened, while they were there, that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth. And she bore her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging.

And shepherds were in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the brightness of God shone around them, and they were greatly afraid. And the angel said to them:

“Do not fear; for behold, I announce to you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people: for today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger.”

And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying:

“Glory to God in the highest,  
and on earth peace among people of good will.”

And it happened that, when the angels had departed from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem, and see this word that has come to pass, which the Lord has shown us.” And they came in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in the manger. When they saw him, they recognized what had been told them about this child.

And all who heard it marveled at the things that had been told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all that they had heard and seen, just as it had been told them.

And when the eight days had been completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb (Luke 1:57; 2:21).

And behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him.”

When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, [Col. 1083] he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. And they said to him: “In Bethlehem of Judaea; for so it is written through the prophet:

‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah,  
are by no means least among the rulers of Judah;  
for from you will go forth a ruler  
who will rule my people Israel.’”

Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: “Go and inquire carefully about the child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him.”

When they had heard the king, they departed. And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood over the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother; and falling down, they worshiped him. And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. And having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way (Matt. 2:1–12).

After they had departed, when the days of his mother’s purification had been completed according to the Law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the Law of the Lord: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” And they were to offer a sacrifice according to what was said in the Law of the Lord: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon; and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. And he came in the Spirit into the temple.

And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he himself took him into his arms, blessed God, and said:

“Now you dismiss your servant, Lord,  
according to your word, in peace;  
because my eyes have seen your salvation,  
which you have prepared before the face of all peoples:  
a light for revelation to the Gentiles,  
and the glory of your people Israel.”

And his father and mother were marveling at the things that were said about him. And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother:

“Behold, this one is appointed for the falling and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed—and a sword will pierce your own soul also—so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

And there was Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity; and she was a widow until the age of eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day. And coming at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 1083] The printed editions have “the redemption of Israel.” But the manuscripts, with great agreement, read “the redemption of Jerusalem”; with them also agrees the very ancient Corbie biblical codex. Moreover, the Greek text has *lutrōsin en Ierousalēm*, “redemption in Jerusalem,” with the preposition *in* added. Because of the concurrence with the *in* in the preceding word, it could easily have dropped out through the carelessness of copyists.]

And when they had completed everything according to the Law of the Lord (Luke 2:22–39), behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying:

“Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you; for Herod [Col. 1084] is going to seek the child in order to destroy him.”

He rose, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt. And he was there until the death of Herod, so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi, became extremely angry; and he sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its districts, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had carefully learned from the Magi. Then what had been spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:

“A voice was heard in Ramah,  
weeping and much lamentation,  
Rachel weeping for her children,  
and she refused to be comforted,  
because they are no more.”

But after Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel; for those who sought the child’s life are dead.”

He rose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judaea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee. And coming there, he lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: “He shall be called a Nazaraean” (Matt. 2:13–23).

But the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was in him. And his parents went every year to Jerusalem for the solemn feast of Passover. And when he was twelve years old, and they had gone up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast, after the days had been completed, as they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.

Thinking that he was in the company, they traveled a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances. And when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking him. And it happened that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and questioning them. And all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers. And when they saw him, they were amazed.

And his mother said to him: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow.”

And he said to them: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?”

And they did not understand the word that he spoke to them. And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them. And his mother kept all these words in her heart.

[Note: [Col. 1084] The printed editions have *conferens in corde suo* (“pondering them in her heart”). *Conferens* is absent from the manuscripts.]

And Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men (Luke 2:40–52).

## CHAPTER VI  
### On the order of John the Baptist’s preaching among all four Evangelists

18. From this point the preaching of John begins to be narrated, and all four mention it. For Matthew, after the words that I last cited, where he mentioned the testimony from the prophet, “He shall be called a Nazaraean,” continues and adds: “In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judaea,” and so forth (Matt. 3:1).

Mark, who narrated nothing about the Lord’s birth, infancy, or childhood, began his Gospel at this point—that is, with John’s preaching. For he began as follows:

“The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus [Col. 1085] Christ, the Son of God: as it is written in Isaiah the prophet, ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you. The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’ John was in the wilderness baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins,” and so forth (Mark 1:1–4).

And Luke, after the words where he said, “And Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men,” then proceeds to John’s preaching, saying:

“In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judaea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, Philip his brother tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came upon John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness,” and so forth (Luke 3:1–2).

The apostle John, moreover, preeminent among the four Evangelists, after speaking of the Word of God—who is himself the Son before all ages of creation, because all things were made through him—immediately introduced the preaching and testimony of John, saying: “There was a man sent by God, whose name was John” (John 1:6).

We must therefore now examine how the four Evangelists’ narratives concerning John the Baptist do not conflict with one another—not so that we must demand or require in every respect what we have just done concerning the beginnings of Christ’s birth from Mary, showing how Matthew and Luke agree with each other by making one account from both narratives. There we demonstrated to slower minds that, when either evangelist mentions what the other omits, or omits what the other mentions, this does not impede understanding the truthful narrative of the other. Thus, from this example—whether in the manner I have used, or in some other way that may be done more conveniently—everyone may see that the same can be done in other comparable passages.

19. Let us therefore now, as I said, examine the agreement of the four Evangelists concerning John the Baptist.

Matthew continues as follows: “In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judaea.” Mark did not say, “In those days,” because he had not previously set out any sequence of events in whose days he could be understood to be speaking, had he said, “In those days.”

Luke, however, expressed the very time of John’s preaching or baptism more distinctly by reference to earthly authorities, saying:

“In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judaea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, Philip his brother was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias was tetrarch of Abilene, under the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came upon John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.”

Nevertheless, we must not understand that Matthew, when he said “in those days,” meant these days—that is, the time of these authorities—but rather that he intended the expression “in those days” to be understood as referring to a much longer period.

For immediately after narrating that Christ had returned from Egypt following Herod’s death—which certainly occurred during Christ’s infancy or childhood, so that what Luke narrated about him when he was twelve years old in the temple of Jerusalem may be accommodated (Luke 2:42–50)—Matthew, having mentioned that the infant or child had been brought back from Egypt [Col. 1086], immediately added: “In those days John the Baptist came.” By this he surely did not indicate only the days of Christ’s childhood, but all the days from his birth up to the time when John began to preach and baptize, by which time Christ’s youthful age is found to have arrived. For Christ and John were of approximately the same age, and Christ is said to have been about thirty years old when he was baptized by John.

[Note: [Col. 1086] The manuscripts have *juvenalis aetas* (“youthful age”). This is used repeatedly in place of *juvenilis*.]

## CHAPTER VII  
### On the two Herods

20. But what Luke narrated commonly troubles some people: that in the days of John’s baptism Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, when the Lord, already a young man, was baptized (Luke 3:1–21); whereas Matthew says that, after Herod’s death, the child Jesus returned from Egypt. Both statements cannot be true unless it is understood that there were two Herods.

Since no one is unaware that this could have happened, with what blindness do those people rage who are more inclined to slander evangelical truth than to consider carefully enough that two men may have been called by the same name? The whole world is full of examples of this kind.

This later Herod is said to have been the son of the earlier Herod, just as Archelaus was the one whom Matthew records as having succeeded his deceased father in the kingdom of Judaea (Matt. 2:19–22), and just as Philip was the one whom Luke identifies as the brother of Herod the tetrarch and himself tetrarch of Ituraea.

That Herod who sought the life of the child Christ was a king. Another Herod, his son, was called not a king but a tetrarch—a Greek name signifying one appointed over a fourth part of a kingdom.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### How Matthew says that Joseph was afraid to go with the infant Christ to Jerusalem because of Archelaus, yet was not afraid to go into Galilee, where his brother Herod was tetrarch

21. Perhaps someone is troubled again by this: Matthew says that Joseph was afraid to go into Judaea with the returning child because Archelaus, the son of Herod, was reigning there in place of his father. How, then, could he go into Galilee, where another son of Herod, Herod the tetrarch, was ruling, as Luke attests?

But surely the times are not the same: the time when the child was feared is not the time that Luke now records. Those circumstances had changed so greatly that in Judaea itself Archelaus was no longer king, but Pontius Pilate was governor—not king of the Jews, but prefect. In his time, under Tiberius Caesar, the sons of Herod the Great did not possess a kingdom but a tetrarchy.

This had certainly not yet occurred when Joseph, fearing Archelaus who was reigning in Judaea, went with the child into Galilee, where their city Nazareth was also located.

## CHAPTER IX  
### How Matthew says that Joseph went into Galilee with the infant Christ because he feared Archelaus, who was reigning in Jerusalem in place of his father, while Luke says that he went into Galilee because Nazareth was their city

22. Or does this also cause difficulty: how Matthew can say that the child Jesus’ parents went into Galilee for this reason—that they did not wish to go into Judaea because of their fear of Archelaus—when they seem rather to have gone into Galilee [Col. 1087] because their city was Nazareth of Galilee, as Luke has not failed to mention?

It must be understood that, when the angel said to Joseph in a dream in Egypt, “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel,” Joseph first understood this as an order to proceed into Judaea. For the land of Israel could initially have been understood in that sense.

But after he learned that the son of Herod, Archelaus, was reigning there, he did not wish to expose himself to that danger, since “the land of Israel” could also be understood in such a way that Galilee was included in it, because the people of Israel inhabited Galilee as well.

This question can also be resolved in another way: Christ’s parents may have thought that, with the child about whom they had learned such things through angelic revelations, they ought to live nowhere except Jerusalem, where the Lord’s temple was. Thus, when returning from Egypt, they would have gone there and lived there, unless the presence of Archelaus frightened them away.

For they had not been divinely commanded to live there in such a way that they ought to disregard what they feared concerning Archelaus.

## CHAPTER X  
### How Luke says that his parents went with him every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover, while Matthew says that, because of fear of Archelaus, they were afraid to go there when returning from Egypt

23. Does someone also ask: How, then, as Luke narrates, did his parents go every year of Christ’s childhood to Jerusalem, if fear of Archelaus prevented them from approaching it?

It would not be difficult for me to resolve this, even if one of the Evangelists had indicated how long Archelaus reigned there. It could have happened that they secretly went up during the feast amid so great a crowd, intending to return immediately, while fearing to live there on other days. Thus they would neither have been irreligious by neglecting the solemnity nor conspicuous through continuous residence.

But since all have also been silent about the duration of Archelaus’s reign, another interpretation is available: when Luke says that they customarily went up to Jerusalem every year (Luke 2:41), we may understand that this practice began when Archelaus was no longer feared.

If some history outside the Gospel, which appears worthy of belief, reveals that Archelaus’s reign lasted somewhat longer, what I said above will suffice: the child’s parents feared living in Jerusalem, yet, because of the fear of God, they did not neglect the solemn feast, during which they could very easily remain hidden.

For it is not incredible that people, choosing suitable times—whether days or hours—might enter places in which they fear to be present.

## CHAPTER XI  
### How, when the days of Christ’s mother’s purification had been completed, they could go with him into the temple to perform the solemn rites, as Luke says, if, according to Matthew, Herod had already learned from the Magi that he had been born and, while seeking him, had killed so many infants

24. This also resolves the question for anyone who is troubled by the fact that, when that older Herod had already been alarmed and anxious at the Magi’s report that the king of the Jews had been born, they could safely go up with him into the temple after the days of his mother’s purification had been completed, so that the rites concerning him might be performed according to the Law of the Lord [Col. 1088], as Luke records.

Who does not see that even that one day could have been hidden from the king, who was occupied with many matters? But if it does not seem plausible that Herod, who was extremely anxious to learn what the Magi would report to him about the child, only realized after so many days that he had been deceived—so that, after the time of the mother’s purification had passed, the solemn rite of the firstborn had been performed concerning the infant in the temple of Jerusalem, and they had also departed for Egypt, it then occurred to him to seek the child’s life and kill so many little ones—if this is what causes difficulty, I will say nothing of how many and how great occupations could have burdened royal responsibility and either completely diverted or hindered him for many days from that purpose.

The causes by which this could have happened cannot be enumerated. Yet no one is so inexperienced in human affairs as either to deny or doubt that such causes could have been many and serious. Whose mind would not consider how many other, more terrifying matters—whether true or false—could have been reported to the king? A man who had feared that an infant king would oppose him or his sons after some years could have been driven by the terror of other dangers that seemed more immediate, and his mind, torn away from that concern, could have been occupied instead with guarding against dangers nearer at hand.

But let us set this aside. I say that, after the Magi reported nothing to Herod, he could have believed that they had been deceived by a deceptive appearance of a star and, after failing to find the one whom they thought had been born, had been ashamed to return to him. In this way, once his fear had subsided, he may have ceased to inquire after and pursue the child.

Thus, when they had come with him to Jerusalem after the mother’s purification, and the events recorded by Luke had taken place in the temple (Luke 2:22–39), the words of Simeon and Anna, who prophesied about him, would have restored the king’s former purpose when those who had heard them began to proclaim them. Joseph, warned in a dream, fled with the infant and his mother into Egypt.

Then, when the events that had taken place and the words that had been spoken in the temple became widely known, Herod realized that he had been deceived by the Magi. Thereafter, desiring to bring about Christ’s death, he killed many infants, as Matthew narrates (Matt. 2:3–16).

## CHAPTER XII  
### On John’s words among all four Evangelists

25. Matthew weaves his account of John together as follows:

“In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judaea and saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. For this is he who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, saying: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight’” (Matt. 3:1–3).

Mark and Luke likewise agree that this testimony from Isaiah concerns John (Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4). For Luke also recalled more of the following words from the same prophet when he narrated the Baptist John’s preaching.

The evangelist John, moreover, records that John the Baptist himself applied this same testimony from Isaiah to himself (John 1:23), just as Matthew now reported certain words of John that the others did not report.

“Preaching,” he says, “in the wilderness of Judaea and saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near”—the other evangelists omitted these words of John.

Now the words that Matthew next follows and adds [Col. 1089]—“For this is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah, saying: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight’”—are placed ambiguously. It is not clear whether Matthew himself has recalled this in his own person, or whether he continued to follow the words of that same John and added it, so that John is understood to have said the whole: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near; for this is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah,” and so forth.

This should not cause difficulty merely because he does not say, “For I am he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah,” but says, “For this is he who was spoken of.” Such a manner of speaking is also customary among the Evangelists themselves, Matthew and John.

Matthew said, “He found a man sitting at the tax booth” (Matt. 9:9), and did not say, “He found me.” And John says: “This is the disciple who bears witness to these things and wrote these things; and we know that his testimony is true” (John 21:24). He did not say, “I am he,” or, “My testimony is true.”

The Lord himself very often says “the Son of Man” (Matt. 9:6; 16:27) or “the Son of God” (John 5:25), and does not say “I.” And he says, “It was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day” (Luke 24:46), not, “It was necessary for me to suffer.”

John the Baptist, therefore, may also have said, after declaring, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” the words that follow about himself: “For this is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah,” and so forth. Matthew could then have woven the narrative together after his words in this way: “Now John himself had a garment of camel’s hair,” and so forth.

If this is so, it is not surprising that, when asked what he said about himself, as the evangelist John narrates, he answered: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:23), just as he had already said when commanding them to repent.

Concerning his clothing and food, then, Matthew continues as follows:

“Now John himself had a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.”

Mark says nearly the same thing in almost the same words; the other two are silent.

26. Matthew continues and says:

“Then Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: ‘Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Produce, therefore, fruit worthy of repentance; and do not think of saying among yourselves, “We have Abraham as our father.” For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Already the axe has been placed at the root of the trees; therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. I indeed baptize you in water for repentance; but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing shovel is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.’”

Luke also says all these things, expressing almost the same words of John. Wherever there is some variation in the wording, however, the same meaning is nevertheless maintained. For example, Matthew says that John said, “And do not think of saying among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’” whereas Luke says, “And do not begin to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’” Matthew has, “I indeed baptize you in water for repentance”; Luke inserts the crowds’ question about what they should do and John’s response concerning good works, as fruits of repentance—a matter Matthew omitted. Then, when they were considering in their hearts whether he himself were the Christ, Luke says that John answered them, “I indeed baptize you with water”; he did not say, “for repentance.”

Matthew then says, “But he who is coming after me is mightier than I”; Luke, “But one mightier than I is coming.” Likewise Matthew says, “Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry”; Luke, “Whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie.” Mark also says this, while omitting the rest. For after recalling John’s clothing and food, he continues: “And he preached, saying: ‘The one mightier than I is coming after me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy, bending down, to untie. I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.’”

Thus, concerning the sandals, Mark differs from Luke by adding “bending down.” Concerning the baptism, he differs from both because he does not say “and fire,” but only “with the Holy Spirit.” Matthew and Luke alike say, in the same order, “He will baptize you with the Spirit and fire,” except that Luke did not add “holy,” as Matthew said, “with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III, 3–12; Mark I, 6–8; and Luke III, 7–17). [Note: Luke now has the word “holy” added in both the Greek and Latin Bibles.]

The evangelist John bears witness with these three when he says: “John bears witness concerning him and cries out, saying, ‘This was he of whom I said, “He who comes after me has been made before me, because he was before me”’” (John I, 15). In this way he shows that John said this at the time when they recall him as having said it; but he repeated and recalled what he had already said when he stated, “This was he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me.’”

27. If, therefore, the question is which words John the Baptist actually spoke—whether those which Matthew recalls him as having spoken, or those which Luke recalls, or those few which Mark attributes to him while remaining silent about the rest—there is no reason for concern, in the judgment of anyone who understands prudently that the very meanings are what must be known for the truth, regardless of the words in which they were expressed.

For the fact that one writer follows a different order of words is certainly not contradictory. Nor is it contradictory if one says what another omits. As each remembered, and as each was disposed to express the same meaning more briefly or at greater length, so it is clear that they expressed it.

28. This is sufficiently evident in what is of greatest importance here: since the truth of the Gospel, through the Word of God—which remains eternal and unchangeable above every creature—was dispensed through a creature in temporal signs and human languages and attained the highest authority, we should not suppose that anyone is lying merely because, when several people remember what they heard or saw, the same event is reported neither in the same manner nor in the same words.

Nor should we suppose this merely because the order of the words is changed, or because different words are used in place of one another while nevertheless having the same force; or because something is said less fully, either because it does not occur to the person remembering or because it can be understood from what others say; or because, for the sake of narrating other matters which someone has decided to emphasize, each person undertakes to touch upon some things only in part rather than explain them completely, so that the appropriate limitation of time may suffice; or because, in order to illuminate and clarify the meaning, the person entrusted with the authority to narrate adds nothing to the events but does add something to the wording; or because, while retaining the event accurately, someone does not succeed—although attempting to do so—in reciting from memory all the words he heard exactly.

Whoever says that the Evangelists ought, through the power of the Holy Spirit, to have been granted this privilege, so that they would differ neither in the kind of words, nor in their order, nor in their number, does not understand that, the more the authority of the Evangelists surpasses that of other people, the more their example had to establish the security of truthful speakers generally. Thus, when several people happen to narrate the same event, none of them can rightly be accused of falsehood merely because he differs from another in a way that can be defended even by the precedent of the Evangelists.

Since it is not permissible either to believe or to say that any Evangelist lied, it will likewise be evident that the person who remembers an event and to whom something of the kind shown to have happened to the Evangelists occurs has not lied. And the more important it is for good morals to avoid lying, the more we ought to be governed by such eminent authority, lest we regard as lies the variations we find among certain narratives when they vary from one another as the Evangelists vary.

At the same time—and this is especially important for sound doctrine—we should understand that the truth to be sought and embraced concerns not so much the words as the events, since we approve as belonging to the same truth those who use different expressions but do not differ concerning the events and meanings.

29. What, then, should be considered contradictory in the passages from the Evangelists’ narratives that I have set side by side? Is it that one says, “Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry,” while others say, “to untie the strap of his sandal”? For it seems that carrying sandals and untying the sandal-strap are different not merely in words, or in the order of words, or in some manner of expression, but in the matter itself.

It is therefore reasonable to ask what John said he was unworthy to do: to carry the sandals, or to untie the sandal-strap. For if he said one of these, the person who was able to report what he said seems to have told the truth; but the one who reported the other, although he did not lie, will certainly be thought either to have forgotten or to have said one thing in place of another. Yet all falsehood ought to be absent from the Evangelists—not only falsehood expressed through lying, but also that arising through forgetfulness.

Therefore, if something different is properly understood from the statement “to carry the sandals,” and something different from “to untie the sandal-strap,” what else should rightly be understood except that John said both—whether at different times or consecutively?
