For he could have said: “Whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie, nor his sandals to carry”; then one Evangelist could have reported one part and others the other, while all nevertheless narrated the truth.

But if John intended nothing else, when speaking of the Lord’s sandals, than his superiority and his own humility, then whichever expression he used—whether concerning untying the sandal-strap or carrying the sandals—he nevertheless conveyed the same meaning. Whoever, even in his own words, expressed the same signification of humility through mentioning the sandals did not depart from the same intention.

Thus, when we speak of agreement among the Evangelists, this is a useful principle and one especially worthy of being committed to memory: it is not a lie when someone, saying something different from what the person about whom he is speaking said, nevertheless expresses that person’s intention—the same intention expressed by the one who recalls his words. In this way we learn profitably that nothing else should be sought except what the speaker intends.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### Concerning Jesus’ Baptism

30. Matthew continues and says:

“Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him. But John tried to prevent him, saying: ‘I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?’ But Jesus answered him: ‘Permit it for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.’ Then he permitted him.”

The other Evangelists also testify that Jesus came to John. Three of them mention that he was baptized, but they are silent about what Matthew says: that John said this to the Lord, or that the Lord answered John (Matt. III, 13–15; Mark I, 9; Luke III, 21; and John I, 32–34).

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Concerning the Words of the Voice from Heaven over the Baptized One

31. Matthew then continues:

“But after he was baptized, immediately he came up from the water. And behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’”

The other two, Mark and Luke, narrate this similarly. But concerning the words of the voice that came from heaven, they vary in expression while preserving the meaning. For what Matthew says was spoken—“This is my beloved Son”—the other two say, “You are my beloved Son.” Both expressions serve to explain the same meaning, as was discussed above.

The heavenly voice said one of these forms, but the Evangelist wished to show that what was said amounted to “This is my Son,” so that it might be indicated to those who were listening that he himself was the Son of God. Accordingly, he wished to report the words as “You are my Son,” as though it were said to them, “This is my Son.” The voice was not informing Christ of something he already knew; rather, those who were present were hearing it, and the voice itself was made for their sake.

Now, one Evangelist says, “in whom I am well pleased”; another, “with you I am well pleased”; another, “in you I have become well pleased” (Matt. III, 16–17; Mark I, 10–11; and Luke III, 22). If you ask which of these expressions sounded in that voice, accept whichever you wish, provided that you understand that those who did not report the same wording nevertheless reported the same meaning.

This variation in expression is also useful, so that a statement expressed in only one way may not be understood inadequately or interpreted contrary to the nature of the matter. If someone wishes to understand “in whom I am well pleased” as meaning that God appears to be pleased in the Son, he is corrected by the expression “with you I am well pleased.” Conversely, if someone understands from that one expression that the Father is pleased with human beings in the Son, he is corrected by the expression “in you I have become well pleased.”

It is therefore sufficiently clear that, whichever of the Evangelists preserved the words of the heavenly voice, the others varied the wording in order to explain the same meaning more familiarly. We should understand that all of them reported the statement as though it were: “In you I have established my good pleasure”—that is, “through you I will accomplish what pleases me.”

Some manuscripts according to Luke, however, have the voice sounding as it is written in the Psalm: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7). Although this is reportedly not found in the older Greek manuscripts, if it can be confirmed by certain trustworthy copies, what else should be understood except that both forms sounded from heaven, regardless of the order of the words?

## CHAPTER XV  
### How, According to the Evangelist John, John the Baptist Says, “I Did Not Know Him,” Although According to the Other Evangelists He Is Found Already to Have Known Him

32. What is said concerning the dove according to John does not narrate when the event occurred; rather, it reports the words of John the Baptist as he recalls what he saw. In this connection the question arises how the statement should be understood: “And I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me, ‘He upon whom you will see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (John I, 33).

For if John recognized him at the time when he saw the dove descending upon him, we must ask how he could have said to Jesus as he came to be baptized, “I ought rather to be baptized by you” (Matt. III, 14), since he said this before the dove descended.

It is therefore evident that, although he already knew him—for he even leaped in his mother’s womb when Mary came to Elizabeth (Luke I, 41)—he nevertheless learned through the descent of the dove something about him that he had not previously known: namely, that Jesus himself would baptize in the Holy Spirit by a particular divine power. Thus no human being who had received Baptism from God, even if he baptized someone, could say that what he administered was his own, or that the Holy Spirit was given by him.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Concerning Jesus’ Temptation

33. Matthew continues and says:

“Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And after he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. And the tempter approached him and said: ‘If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.’ But he answered and said: ‘It is written, “Man does not live by bread alone”’” [Note: The Rat. edition and one of the Colbertine manuscripts have “man will live,” in the future tense, corresponding to the Greek zēsetai, with the Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 8:3 supporting it.] “but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God,” and so on up to the statement: “Then the devil left him; and behold, angels approached and ministered to him.”

Luke narrates the whole of this similarly, although not in the same order. Hence it is uncertain what happened first: whether the kingdoms of the earth were first shown to him and afterward he was lifted onto the pinnacle of the temple, or this first and the other afterward. It makes no difference, however, provided that it is clear that all these things occurred. And when Luke expresses the same meanings in different words, it need not always be pointed out how nothing is lost to the truth.

Mark, for his part, testifies that Jesus was tempted by the devil in the wilderness for forty days and nights, but he is silent about what was said to him and what he answered. Likewise, what Luke omitted Mark did not omit: that angels ministered to him (Matt. IV, 1–11; Mark I, 12–13; and Luke IV, 1–13). John, however, omitted this entire passage.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Concerning the Call of the Apostles Who Were Fishing

34. Matthew continues his narrative:

“When he had heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.”

Mark says this as well, and so does Luke (Matt. IV, 12; Mark I, 14; and Luke IV, 14), although Luke says nothing here about John’s being handed over.

The Evangelist John, however, says that before Jesus went into Galilee, Peter and Andrew remained with him for one day, and that at that time Peter received the name by which he was called, whereas previously he had been called Simon. On the following day, when Jesus already wished to depart for Galilee, he found Philip and told him to follow him. From there the narrative proceeds to Nathanael. On the third day, when Jesus was in Galilee, he performed the miracle at Cana, changing water into wine (John I, 39–II, 11).

The other Evangelists omitted all these events, weaving into their narratives the fact that Jesus returned to Galilee. It is therefore understood that several days intervened during which the events concerning the disciples took place—events inserted by John.

This is not contrary to the passage in which Matthew reports that the Lord said to Peter, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18). We should not understand that Peter received this name at that time, but rather at the time when John recalls that Jesus said to him, “You shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted as “Peter” (John I, 42). Thus the Lord later addressed him by this name, saying, “You are Peter.” He did not say, “You shall be called Peter,” but “You are Peter”—a name that had already been given to him in the words, “You shall be called.”

35. Matthew then connects his narrative and says:

“And leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum by the sea, in the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali,” and so forth, until the discourse he delivered on the mountain comes to an end.

In this narrative sequence Mark bears witness with him concerning the calling of the disciples: Peter and Andrew, and shortly afterward James and John. But whereas Matthew immediately joined to this the account of the lengthy discourse that Jesus delivered on the mountain after healing many people and being followed by a large crowd, Mark inserted other events: Jesus was teaching them in the synagogue, and they were astonished at his teaching. Then Mark said what Matthew says after that lengthy discourse: that Jesus was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.

Mark also narrated the man from whom an unclean spirit was expelled, and then Peter’s mother-in-law. In these matters Luke agrees with him (Matt. IV, 13; VII, 29; Mark I, 16–31; and Luke IV, 31–39). Matthew, however, narrated nothing about this demon [Col. 1095]; concerning Peter’s mother-in-law he was not silent, but mentioned her later (Matt. VIII, 14–15).

36. In the passage we are now considering, the same Matthew says that, after the calling of the disciples while they were fishing—when he commanded them to follow him—Jesus went throughout Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel, and healing every disease. After crowds had gathered to him, he went up onto the mountain and delivered that lengthy discourse.

This gives room for understanding that the events which Mark narrates after the election of those same disciples occurred when Jesus was going throughout Galilee and teaching in their synagogues. This includes the event concerning Peter’s mother-in-law. Matthew later recalled what he had omitted, although he did not bring every omitted event back into the narrative.

37. It may reasonably cause difficulty that John says that Andrew first followed the Lord, together with another man whose name is not given, not in Galilee but near the Jordan. Then Peter received his name from him, and third, Philip was called to follow him. The other three Evangelists, however, say that these men were called while fishing, in accounts that agree sufficiently among themselves, especially Matthew and Mark.

Luke does not name Andrew, although it is understood that he was in the boat according to the narratives of Matthew and Mark, who briefly touch upon how the event happened. Luke explained it more fully, mentioning there also the miracle involving the catch of fish and the fact that the Lord first spoke to the crowds from the boat.

There also appears to be this difference: Luke recalls that the Lord said only to Peter, “From now on you will be catching people,” whereas the other two narrate that this was said to both brothers. But this could certainly have first been said to Peter when he was amazed at the enormous catch of fish, as Luke suggests, and then said to both, as the other two recall.

What we said about John must therefore be carefully considered. It cannot be regarded as a minor contradiction, since the place, the time, and the calling itself seem so different. For if, near the Jordan and before Jesus had gone into Galilee, two men followed him at the testimony of John the Baptist—one of them being Andrew, who immediately brought his brother Simon to Jesus and at that time received the name Peter—how do the other Evangelists say that Jesus found them fishing in Galilee and called them to discipleship (Matt. IV, 13–23; Mark I, 16–20; Luke V, 1–11; and John I, 35–44)?

The answer is that we must understand that, when they saw the Lord near the Jordan, they did not yet adhere to him inseparably. They merely came to know who he was, and, having marveled at him, returned to their own affairs.

38. At Cana of Galilee, too, after Jesus had changed water into wine, the same John says that his disciples believed in him. He narrates it as follows:

“On the third day there was a wedding at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding” (John II, 1–2).

If they believed in him at that time, as John says shortly afterward, then they were not yet disciples when they were invited to the wedding. But this was said according to the manner of expression by which we speak when we say that the apostle Paul was born at Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts XXII, 3); for he was not already an apostle at that time.

Thus, when we hear that Christ’s disciples were invited to the wedding, we should understand not that they were already disciples, but that they were to become disciples. They were certainly already Christ’s disciples when these events were narrated and written down; and therefore the narrator of past events spoke of them in this way.

39. The same John says:

“After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples; and there they remained not many days” (John II, 12).

It is uncertain whether Peter, Andrew, and the sons of Zebedee had already joined him. Matthew first narrates that Jesus came and dwelt in Capernaum, and afterward that he called them while they were fishing from their boats. John, however, says that his disciples came to Capernaum with him.

Or perhaps Matthew recapitulated what he had omitted. He does not say, “After this, as he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers,” but, without indicating any difference in the succeeding time, says, “As he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers,” and so forth.

It is therefore possible that Matthew later narrated not what happened later, but what he had previously omitted, so that they may be understood to have come with him to Capernaum, where John says that he, his mother, and his disciples came.

Or were they instead other disciples? Philip, for example, was already following him, having been called in such a way that Jesus said to him, “Follow me.” The order in which all twelve Apostles were called does not appear in the Evangelists’ narratives. Indeed, not only is the order of their calling absent, but the calling itself is not mentioned for all of them. Only Philip, Peter, Andrew, the sons of Zebedee, and Matthew the tax collector—who was also called Levi—are mentioned (Matt. IV, 18–22; IX, 9; Mark I, 16–20; II, 14; Luke V, 1–11; and John I, 35–44).

Nevertheless, Peter alone, and first, received a name from him individually (John I, 42). The sons of Zebedee he called not individually but together, naming both of them “sons of thunder” (Mark III, 17).

40. It should certainly be noted that the Gospel and apostolic Scriptures do not call only those twelve people his disciples. They call all those who, believing in him, were instructed by his teaching for the kingdom of heaven, “disciples.”

From this multitude he chose twelve, whom he also named Apostles, as Luke recalls. Shortly afterward Luke himself says:

“And coming down with them, he stood on a level place, with a crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people” (Luke VI, 13–17).

He certainly would not have called twelve men a crowd of disciples. Other passages of Scripture also clearly show that all who learned from him what pertained to eternal life were called his disciples.

41. It may be asked how he called fishermen two by two from their boats—first Peter and Andrew, and then, after proceeding a little farther, two other men, the sons of Zebedee, as Matthew and Mark narrate—when Luke says that both of their boats were filled by that great catch of fish and mentions Peter’s companions, James and John, the sons of Zebedee, being called to help when they could not draw in the full nets. They were all astonished at the great quantity of fish that had been caught, and although Jesus said only to Peter, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching people,” nevertheless they followed him after bringing the boats to land.

It must therefore be understood that what Luke indicates happened first. At that time they were not called by the Lord; only Peter was told that he would catch people.

This was not said as though he would never again catch fish. For even after the Lord’s resurrection we read that they went fishing (John XXI, 3). He said, therefore, that thereafter Peter would catch people; he did not say that he would no longer catch fish.

This leaves room for understanding that they returned, as was their custom, to fishing, so that afterward what Matthew and Mark narrate could take place: Jesus called them two by two and commanded them to follow him—first the two, Peter and Andrew, and then the other two, the sons of Zebedee.

At that time they followed him not after bringing the boats to land, as though they intended to return to their work, but as people following one who was calling and commanding them to follow him.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### Concerning the Time of His Withdrawal into Galilee

42. We must also inquire how the Evangelist John says that Jesus went into Galilee before John the Baptist was sent to prison.

After recalling that Jesus changed water into wine at Cana of Galilee, went down to Capernaum with his mother and disciples, and remained there not many days, John says that Jesus then went up to Jerusalem for the Passover. After this he came into the land of Judea with his disciples and stayed there with them and baptized. He then continues:

“John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there; and people were coming and being baptized. For John had not yet been sent into prison” (John II, 13; III, 22–24).

Matthew, however, says, “When he had heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee” (Matt. IV, 12). Mark likewise says, “After John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee” (Mark I, 14).

Luke says nothing about John’s being handed over, but nevertheless, after Christ’s baptism and temptation, he too says that Jesus went into Galilee, just as the other two do. He connects his narrative as follows:

“When every temptation had been completed, the devil departed from him until an opportune time. And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through the whole region” (Luke IV, 13–14).

It is therefore understood that these three Evangelists did not narrate anything contrary to the Evangelist John. Rather, they omitted the Lord’s first arrival in Galilee after his baptism, when he changed water into wine; at that time John had not yet been handed over. They connected their narratives with the Lord’s arrival in Galilee that occurred after John had been handed over.

The Evangelist John speaks of this return to Galilee as follows:

“When Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples—he left Judea and departed again into Galilee” (John IV, 1–3).

We therefore understand that John had by then been handed over, while the Jews had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John had made and baptized.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### Concerning the Lengthy Discourse Which, According to Matthew, He Delivered on the Mountain

43. Let us now examine whether the other Evangelists appear to contradict that lengthy discourse which the Lord delivered on the mountain according to Matthew.

Mark did not mention it at all, nor did he report anything similar to it, except for certain sayings which the Lord repeated in other places, not as a continuous discourse but scattered among his narrative. Nevertheless, Mark left a place in the structure of his account where we may understand that this discourse was delivered but omitted by him. He says:

“He was preaching in their synagogues and throughout all Galilee, and casting out demons.”

In this preaching which Mark says Jesus carried on throughout Galilee, this discourse delivered on the mountain is also understood to be included, the discourse mentioned by Matthew. For Mark continues:

“And a leper came to him, beseeching him, and kneeling down said to him: ‘If you will, you can cleanse me’” (Mark I, 39–40).

He then connects the rest of the account concerning the cleansing of this leper in such a way that the person he describes may be understood as the same one whom Matthew says was cleansed when the Lord descended from the mountain after that discourse.

Matthew says:

“When he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me’” (Matt. VIII, 1–2), and so forth.

44. Luke also remembers this leper (Luke V, 12–13), though not in this order. He follows the customary practice of recalling omitted events later, or anticipating events that occurred later, as the divine prompting supplied them—events previously known and later written down in remembrance.

Luke also narrated a lengthy discourse of the Lord. He began it in a manner similar to Matthew. Matthew says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven”; Luke says, “Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.”

Many of the statements that follow are likewise similar in Luke’s account. At the end of the discourse, the conclusion is found to be entirely the same: concerning the prudent man who builds upon a rock and the foolish man who builds upon sand. The only difference is that Luke mentions only the river striking the house, not the rain and winds as Matthew does.

It could therefore very easily be believed that Luke also inserted the same discourse of the Lord, while omitting certain sayings that Matthew included; adding others that Matthew did not report; and explaining some in different words while preserving the integrity of the truth.

45. This, as I said, could very easily be believed if it were not for the fact that Matthew says this discourse was delivered by the Lord while he was seated on the mountain, whereas Luke says it was delivered by the Lord while he was standing on a level place.

This difference makes it appear that one discourse was different from the other. What would prevent Christ from repeating elsewhere certain things he had already said, or from doing again certain things he had already done?

It is not, however, believed that the two discourses inserted by Matthew and Luke were separated by a long interval of time. This is reasonably inferred from the fact that both before and after them they narrate certain similar or identical events, so that it is not unreasonable to think that their narratives, in inserting these discourses, were concerned with the same places and days.

Matthew says:

“And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis and Jerusalem and Judea and from beyond the Jordan. Seeing the crowds, he went up onto the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,’” and so forth (Matt. IV, 25; VII, 29).

Here it may be understood that Jesus wished to avoid the large crowds and therefore went up onto the mountain, as though withdrawing from the crowds in order to speak only to his disciples.

Luke also appears to bear witness to this, narrating as follows:

“It happened in those days that he went out onto the mountain to pray, and he spent the night in the prayer of God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he also named Apostles: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon who is called the Zealot, Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became the betrayer.

“And coming down with them, he stood on a level place, with a crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the maritime region and Tyre” [Note: We follow the printed editions in reading “and the maritime region and Tyre.” Some manuscripts have “and the maritime region of Tyre,” omitting “and,” which is also absent from the Greek.] “and Sidon, who had come to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. Those who were troubled by unclean spirits were cured. And the whole crowd sought to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all.

“And he, lifting up his eyes toward his disciples, said: ‘Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God,’” and so forth (Luke VI, 12–49).

Here it may be understood that, when Jesus chose the twelve disciples from among the larger number on the mountain and named them Apostles—a detail Matthew omitted—he delivered the discourse that Matthew inserted and Luke omitted, namely, the one on the mountain. Then, after descending, he delivered another similar discourse on the level place, which Matthew omitted and Luke included. The two discourses may have been concluded in the same manner.

46. After concluding this discourse Matthew continues and says:

“When Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astonished at his teaching.”

The crowds may be understood to mean the groups of disciples from whom he had chosen the twelve.

When Matthew immediately adds, “But when he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him; and behold, a leper came and worshiped him,” this may be understood to have occurred after both discourses—not only after the one Matthew inserted, but also after the one Luke inserted.

For it is not apparent how much time elapsed after the descent from the mountain. Matthew wished to indicate only that, after that descent, great crowds were with the Lord when he cleansed the leper, not how much time had intervened—especially since Luke says that the same leper was cleansed while the Lord was already in the city, a detail Matthew did not take care to mention.

47. Nevertheless, the following possibility may also suggest itself: that at first the Lord was on some higher part [Col. 1100] of the mountain with his disciples alone, when he chose twelve of them; then that he descended with them—not from the mountain itself, but from the mountain’s summit into a level place, that is, onto some flat area situated on the mountainside, which could accommodate many crowds—and stood there until the crowds gathered around him. Afterwards, when he had sat down, his disciples approached him more closely, and, with them and the other crowds present, he delivered one sermon, which Matthew and Luke both report, though in different modes of narration, with the same truth of events and statements that both expressed.

For we have already pointed out—and anyone would naturally see this without being warned—that if one writer omits something another reports, this is not a contradiction; nor, if one reports something in a different way from another, so long as the same truth of events and statements is set forth. Thus, when Matthew says, “But when he had come down from the mountain,” this may also be understood as referring to that level place which could have been on the mountainside. Then Matthew narrates the cleansing of the leper, as do Mark and Luke in similar fashion.

## CHAPTER XX

### How Matthew can say that the centurion came to him on behalf of his servant, when Luke says that he sent friends to him

48. After this Matthew continues and says: “When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, asking him and saying: ‘Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is being severely tormented,’” and so forth, up to the place where he says, “And the servant was healed in that hour” (Matt. 8:5–13).

Luke also recalls this event concerning the centurion’s servant—not, as Matthew does, after the cleansing of the leper (which Luke recalls later), but after the conclusion of that longer sermon. He joins the events in this way: “When he had completed all his words in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. Now a certain centurion’s servant, who was ill, was at the point of death, and he was precious to him,” and so forth, up to the place where the servant was healed (Luke 7:1–10).

Here we must understand that, when he had indeed completed all his words in the hearing of the people, Christ entered Capernaum—that is, he did not enter before he had finished those words. But the interval of time after he had completed these sermons and before he entered Capernaum is not specified. It was during that interval that the leper was cleansed; Matthew places this event in its own position, whereas Luke recalls it later.

49. Let us therefore see whether Matthew and Luke agree concerning this centurion’s servant. Matthew says: “A centurion approached him, asking him and saying: ‘My servant lies at home paralyzed.’” This seems to conflict with what Luke says:

“When he had heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and save his servant. And when they had come to Jesus, they earnestly entreated him, saying: ‘He is worthy that you should grant this to him, for he loves our nation and he himself built our synagogue for us.’ Jesus was going with them; and when he was already not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying: ‘Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof. [Col. 1101] For this reason I did not even consider myself worthy to come to you; but say the word, and my servant will be healed.’”

If this is how the event took place, how can Matthew’s account be true—“A certain centurion approached him”—when the centurion himself did not approach, but sent friends? We must carefully observe that Matthew has not departed entirely from the customary manner of speaking.

We commonly say not only that someone has approached even before he has reached the place to which he is said to have approached—hence we say that someone has approached a little or approached a great deal, according to how near he is to reaching his intended destination—but we also often say that the very arrival for the sake of which someone approaches has taken place, even when the person who arrives does not see the one whom he reaches, as when he reaches someone through a friend whose favor he needs.

Custom has established this usage so firmly that even in ordinary speech those are called *perventores*—“those who reach”—who, through the intervention of suitable persons and by the art of canvassing, gain access to the otherwise inaccessible dispositions of powerful people. If arrival itself is customarily said to take place through others, how much more can approach take place through others? Approach often falls short of arrival, since someone may come very near without being able to reach the person in question.

Matthew therefore did not absurdly wish, even in ordinary language, to say briefly that the centurion approached the Lord through others: “A centurion approached him.”

50. Nevertheless, we should also attentively consider the profound mystical meaning of the holy Evangelist’s expression, according to what is written in the Psalm: “Approach him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6). Since Christ himself praised the centurion’s faith—the faith by which one truly approaches Jesus—to such an extent that he said, “I have not found such faith in Israel,” the prudent Evangelist preferred to say that the centurion himself approached Christ rather than those through whom he had sent his words.

Luke, for his part, disclosed the whole manner in which the event occurred so that from his account we might be compelled to understand how the other Evangelist, who could not lie, said that the centurion approached. Thus, too, the woman who suffered from an issue of blood, although she touched the fringe of Christ’s garment, nevertheless touched the Lord more truly than did the crowds that pressed around him (Luke 8:42–48). Just as she touched the Lord more truly the more she believed, so the centurion approached the Lord more truly the more he believed.

The remaining matters in this chapter—things one Evangelist reports and another omits—are needlessly examined in detail, since by the rule first commended they are found to contain no contradiction.

## CHAPTER XXI

### In what order the account of Peter’s mother-in-law was given

51. Matthew continues and says: “When Jesus had come into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. He touched her hand, and the fever left her; and she rose and ministered to them” (Matt. 8:14–15).

Matthew does not specify when this occurred—that is, what preceded or followed it. For it is not necessary to understand that it happened immediately after the event he has just narrated. Nevertheless, he is evidently recalling here something he had previously omitted. Mark relates it (Mark 1:29–31) before mentioning the cleansing of the leper, [Col. 1102] which he seems to have inserted after the sermon delivered on the mountain—a sermon about which he himself is silent.

Luke likewise narrates the event concerning Peter’s mother-in-law after this incident (Luke 4:38–39), and Mark does the same, even placing it before the sermon which he himself inserts at length and which may be regarded as the same sermon Matthew says was delivered on the mountain.

What difference does it make who places an event where—whether he inserts something according to its chronological order, recalls something previously omitted, or anticipates an event that occurred later—provided that he does not contradict either himself or another writer in reporting the same or different events? No one, however accurately and faithfully he knows events, has control over the order in which he recalls them. What comes to a person’s mind first or later does not occur as we choose, but as it is given. It is therefore sufficiently probable that each Evangelist believed he ought to narrate events in the order in which God wished the very things he was narrating to be brought to his memory—at least in matters whose order, whether one way or another, detracts nothing from the authority and truth of the Gospel.

52. Why, then, did the Holy Spirit, distributing to each person his own gifts as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11), and therefore undoubtedly governing and directing the minds of the saints, so that the books might be set at so lofty a summit of authority, in recalling what they were to write, permit one to arrange his narrative in one way and another in another way? Whoever seeks this with devout diligence will be able to discover it with divine assistance.

It is not, however, the purpose of the work we have now undertaken to investigate this. Our sole purpose is to demonstrate that the Evangelists contradict neither themselves nor one another, regardless of the order in which each of them could or wished to narrate the same events or different events in Christ’s deeds and words.

Therefore, where the order of time is not apparent, it should not matter to us what order of narration any one of them followed. Where the order is apparent, however, if something causes difficulty because it seems to contradict either the writer himself or another, it must certainly be examined and disentangled.

## CHAPTER XXII

### Whether Matthew, Mark, and Luke disagree concerning the order of the events they narrate next

53. Matthew therefore continues, saying: “When evening had come, they brought him many who were possessed by demons. He cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were ill, so that what had been spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘He himself took our weaknesses and bore our illnesses’” (Matt. 8:16–18).

The fact that Matthew joins the words “When evening had come” sufficiently indicates that this belongs to the time of the same day. Mark likewise, after saying of Peter’s mother-in-law, “And she ministered to them,” immediately adds:

“When evening had come, after the sun had set, they brought to him all who were ill and those possessed by demons. And the whole city was gathered at the door. He healed many who were afflicted with various diseases, and he cast out many demons; and he did not permit them to speak, because they knew him. And rising very early, while it was still dark, he went out and departed into a deserted place” (Mark 1:31–35).

Here Mark appears to have maintained the order, so that after the statement “When evening had come” he would then say, “And rising very early.” Yet it is not necessary that whenever “when evening had come” is said, the evening of that same day be understood, nor that whenever “[Col. 1103] at daybreak” is said, the dawn of that same night be meant. Nevertheless, the order of events may in any case seem to have been preserved here, because the sequence of times has been arranged.

Luke too, when he had narrated the event concerning Peter’s mother-in-law, does not himself say, “When evening had come,” but adds what has the same meaning:

“When the sun had set, all who had those sick with various diseases brought them to him; and he laid his hands on each of them and healed them. Demons also came out of many, crying out and saying, ‘You are the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he did not permit them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. When day had come, he went out and departed into a deserted place” (Luke 4:40–42).

Here too we see precisely the same sequence of times preserved that we found in Mark.

Matthew, however, who appears to have recalled this event concerning Peter’s mother-in-law not in the order in which it occurred but in the order in which he remembered what he had omitted, after narrating what happened that day, including the coming of evening, does not then add the dawn. Instead he narrates as follows: “When Jesus saw many crowds around him, he ordered them to go across the lake.”

This is a different event, not the one Mark and Luke connect with the evening and then the dawn. We must therefore understand that Matthew has inserted here another event he recalled: on some day, when Jesus saw many crowds around him, he ordered them to go across the lake.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### Concerning the man who said to the Lord, “I will follow you wherever you go,” and the neighboring events: the order in which Matthew and Luke narrate them

54. Matthew next adds: “And one of the scribes approached and said to him, ‘Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go,’” up to the place where he says, “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:19–22). Luke narrates this similarly.

But Luke places it after several other events, and he too does not specify the order of time, but follows the manner of one recalling events. It is uncertain whether he has inserted something he previously omitted or anticipated an event that occurred later than those that follow. He says:

“As they were traveling along the road, someone said to him, ‘I will follow you wherever you go.’” And he gives precisely the same reply that Matthew records.

Matthew says that this occurred when Jesus ordered them to go across the lake, whereas Luke says it occurred as they were traveling along the road. This is not contradictory, since they certainly traveled along the road in order to come to the lake.

Matthew and Luke entirely agree concerning the man who first asked to bury his father. Matthew first gives the words of the man who made this request concerning his father, and then the Lord’s words, “Follow me.” Luke first gives the Lord’s words, “Follow me,” and then the man’s request. This makes no difference to the meaning.

Luke also records that another man said, “I will follow you, Lord, but first permit me to say farewell to those at home” [Note: [Col. 1103] So the manuscripts and the edition of Regensburg, with which Augustine’s *Speculum* and the Corbie Bibles agree. At., Er., and Lov. read, “to those who are at home,” incorrectly.]. Matthew says nothing about him.

Luke then proceeds to another event, not to one that followed next in chronological order. “After this,” he says, [Col. 1104] “[the] Lord also appointed seventy-two others” (Luke 9:57; 10:1). “After this” is clear enough; but how long afterward the Lord did this is not apparent.

Nevertheless, during this interval occurred what Matthew next adds, for Matthew is still maintaining the chronological order, narrating as follows:

## CHAPTER XXIV

### Concerning his crossing the lake, where he slept in the boat, and the expulsion of the demons whom he permitted to enter the pigs: how the events and sayings agree among Matthew, Mark, and Luke

55. “And when he had entered the boat, his disciples followed him; and behold, a great disturbance arose on the sea,” up to the place where he says, “And he came into his own city.”

These two events, which Matthew narrates consecutively—the calming of the sea after Jesus, awakened from sleep, commanded the winds, and the case of those who were possessed by a savage demon and were driven into the wilderness after their chains had been broken—are likewise narrated by Mark and Luke (Matt. 8:23–34; Mark 4:36–5:17; Luke 8:22–37).

Some statements are expressed in different words by the different writers, but they are not different statements. For example, Matthew says that Jesus said, “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” Mark says, “Why are you afraid? Do you still lack faith?”—that is, perfect faith, like a mustard seed. Thus Mark too means “you of little faith.” Luke says, “Where is your faith?”

The whole statement could have been: “Why are you afraid? Where is your faith? You of little faith.” Thus one Evangelist recalls one part and another another part.

Likewise, when those who awakened him spoke, Matthew has, “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” Mark has, “Teacher, does it not concern you that we are perishing?” Luke has, “Master, we are perishing.” This is one and the same meaning: those awakening the Lord wished to be saved. There is no need to ask which of these expressions was actually spoken to Christ. Whether they said one of these three things, or other words that none of the Evangelists recorded but that had the same force and conveyed the same meaning, what difference would it make? It could also have happened that, since several of them were awakening him at once, all these words were spoken by different persons.

Likewise, after the storm had been calmed, Matthew reports them as saying, “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” Mark has, “Who, then, is this, that both the wind and the sea obey him?” Luke has, “Who, then, is this, that he commands even the winds and the sea, and they obey him?” Who does not see that the meaning is one? “Who, then, is this?” has exactly the same force as “What sort of man is this?” And where “he commands” is not stated, it is naturally understood, since obedience is rendered to one who commands.

56. Matthew says that there were two men afflicted by that legion of demons which was permitted to enter the pigs, whereas Mark and Luke mention one. You should understand that one of them was a person of greater prominence and renown, whose condition that region especially lamented and whose recovery it desired most earnestly.

The two Evangelists, wishing to indicate this, judged that only the man whose case had become more widely and notably famous need be mentioned. Nor is there anything troubling in the fact that the demons’ words are reported differently by the Evangelists, since all the statements can either be reduced to one meaning or understood as having all been spoken.

Nor is there any contradiction in Matthew’s use of the plural [Col. 1105] and the others’ use of the singular, since they themselves report that, when asked what his name was, he answered that he was “Legion,” because there were many demons.

Nor does Mark’s saying that the herd of pigs was near the mountain conflict with Luke’s saying that it was on the mountain. The herd was so large that part of it was on the mountain and part near the mountain. There were two thousand pigs, as Mark explicitly states.

## CHAPTER XXV

### Concerning the paralytic to whom he said, “Your sins are forgiven,” and, “Take up your pallet,” especially whether Matthew and Mark agree about the place where this occurred, since Matthew says it was in his own city, whereas Mark says it was in Capernaum

57. Matthew then continues, still preserving the order of time, and connects his narrative as follows:

“And he entered the boat, crossed over, and came into his own city. And behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed,” and so forth, up to the place where he says, “When the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings” (Matt. 9:1–8).

Mark and Luke also speak of this paralytic.

Matthew reports that the Lord said, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” Luke does not say “son,” but “man.” This serves to convey more precisely the Lord’s meaning: the sins were forgiven to a man who, simply because he was a man, could not say, “I have not sinned.” At the same time, the one who forgave the man’s sins was understood to be God.

Mark says what Matthew says, except that he does not include “Take courage.” The statement could indeed have been expressed in any of these ways: “Take courage, man; your sins are forgiven, son”; or, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven, man”; or in any other suitable order of words.

58. The following point may reasonably cause difficulty. Matthew narrates the event concerning this paralytic as follows: “And he entered the boat, crossed over, and came into his own city. And behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed.” Mark, however, does not say that this happened in Jesus’ own city—which is certainly called Nazareth—but in Capernaum. He narrates it in this way:

“And again he entered Capernaum after some days, and it was heard that he was in the house. Many gathered, so that there was no longer room, not even at the door, and he was speaking the word to them. And they came bringing him a paralytic who was carried by four men. Since they could not bring him to him because of the crowd, they uncovered the roof where he was; and, having opened it, they lowered the pallet on which the paralytic lay. When Jesus saw their faith,” and so forth (Mark 2:1–12).

Luke does not state in what place this occurred, but says:

“It happened on one of the days that he was sitting and teaching. Pharisees and teachers of the law were also sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem; and the power of the Lord was present to heal them. And behold, men were carrying on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they sought to bring him in and place him before him. Since they could not find by which way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and lowered him through the tiles, together with the bed, into the middle before Jesus. When he saw their faith, he said: ‘Man, your sins are forgiven,’” and so forth (Luke 5:17–26).

The question therefore remains [Col. 1106] between Mark and Matthew, since Matthew writes as though the event occurred in the Lord’s own city, whereas Mark says it occurred in Capernaum.

The difficulty would be greater if Matthew had also named Nazareth. But since Galilee itself could be called Christ’s city, because Nazareth was in Galilee, there is no difficulty. In the same way, the entire kingdom, although established in so many cities, is called the Roman city. And although the city of which it is written, “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:3), is established among so many nations, it is still called one city. Likewise, the former people of God, dwelling in so many cities, are called one house, the house of Israel (Isa. 5:7; Jer. 3:20; Ezek. 3:4).

Who, then, would doubt that Jesus did this in his own city when he did it in Capernaum, a city of Galilee, to which he had returned by crossing over from the region of the Gerasenes? Since he came into Galilee, he could rightly be said to have come into his own city, whatever town in Galilee he was in—especially since Capernaum so surpassed the other Galilean towns that it was regarded almost as a metropolis.

But if it were wholly impermissible to understand either Galilee itself, in which Nazareth was situated, or Capernaum itself, which stood out among the cities as the head of Galilee, as Christ’s city, we could say that Matthew omitted what occurred after Jesus came into his own city until he reached Capernaum, and then added this account of the paralytic’s healing. The Evangelists often do this: they omit intervening events and write as though the event they add immediately followed, without indicating that anything has been omitted.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Also concerning the calling of Matthew: whether he is the same person as the one whom Mark and Luke call Levi son of Alphaeus

59. Matthew then continues, saying:

“As Jesus was passing on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew, and said to him, ‘Follow me.’ And he rose and followed him” (Matt. 9:9).

Mark narrates the same event, likewise preserving the order after the healing of the paralytic:

“And he went out again beside the sea, and the whole crowd came to him, and he taught them. And as he was passing by, he saw Levi [Note: [Col. 1106] In most manuscripts, “Levi son of Alphaeus.” Likewise in the old Corbie Bibles.] son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax office, and he said to him, ‘Follow me.’ And he rose and followed him” (Mark 2:13–14).

There is no contradiction here, for this is Matthew, who is also Levi.

Luke likewise adds this after the healing of the same paralytic:

“After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax office, and he said to him, ‘Follow me.’ And leaving everything, he rose and followed him” (Luke 5:27–28).

It therefore seems more probable that Matthew recalls and reports here something he had omitted. For it must be believed that Matthew was called before the sermon delivered on the mountain. On that mountain Luke records that all twelve were chosen from among many disciples, and that Jesus also called them Apostles (Luke 6:13).

## CHAPTER XXVII

### Concerning the banquet at which he was accused of eating with sinners, and the fact that his disciples did not fast—which appears to be reported differently concerning who made the accusation—and concerning their words and the Lord’s replies: whether Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree

60. Matthew therefore continues and says:

“It happened, as he was reclining at table in the house, that behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples,” and so forth, up to the place where he says, “But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved” (Matt. 9:10–17).

Matthew does not specify whose house Jesus was reclining in with the tax collectors and sinners. It might therefore seem that he did not add this event in chronological order, but inserted something he remembered as having happened at another time—unless Mark and Luke, who narrate the event in essentially the same way, make clear that Jesus was reclining in the house of Levi, that is, Matthew’s house, and that all the statements that follow were made there.

Mark says the same thing while preserving the same order:

“It happened, as he was reclining in his house, that many tax collectors and sinners were reclining together with Jesus” (Mark 2:15–22).

When Mark says “in his house,” he clearly refers to the man of whom he had just been speaking, namely Levi.

Luke likewise, after saying, “He said to him, ‘Follow me.’ And leaving everything, he rose and followed him,” immediately adds: “And Levi made a great banquet for him in his house; and there was a large crowd of tax collectors and others who were reclining with them” (Luke 5:27–39). It is therefore clear in whose house these events took place.

61. Let us now examine the very words that all three Evangelists set down as having been spoken to the Lord or as his replies.

Matthew says: “When they saw this, the Pharisees said to his disciples, ‘Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?’”

Mark says almost exactly the same thing: “Why does your teacher eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”

Matthew has omitted what Mark adds, “and drink.” But what difference does that make, since the meaning is complete and equally indicates that they were dining together?

Luke appears to have recalled the matter somewhat differently:

“The Pharisees and their scribes murmured, saying to his disciples, ‘Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?’”

This does not mean that their teacher was intentionally excluded from the reference. Rather, Luke indicates that the accusation was made against everyone together, both Jesus and his disciples—not that it was spoken directly to him, but that it was addressed to them in a way that included both him and them.

For Luke himself says that the Lord replied, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” He would not have replied this way unless the words “you eat and drink” applied especially to him as well.

This is why Matthew and Mark report that the accusation was made concerning his disciples: even when it was spoken about the disciples, it was directed more pointedly against their teacher, whom they followed and imitated.

The meaning, therefore, is one and the same, and it is conveyed all the more effectively because the words vary while the truth remains.

Likewise, Matthew reports that the Lord replied:

“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill. Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

Mark and Luke retain essentially the same meaning in almost the same words, except that neither inserts the prophetic testimony, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.”

Luke, after saying, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,” adds “to repentance.” This serves to explain the meaning, lest anyone suppose that Christ loves sinners simply because they are sinners. The comparison with the sick likewise makes clear what God intends by calling sinners as a physician calls the sick: namely, that they may be healed from iniquity as from an illness. This takes place through repentance.

62. Likewise, Matthew says:

“Then the disciples of John approached him, saying, ‘Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently?’”

Mark similarly introduces the matter, saying:

“The disciples of John and the Pharisees were fasting; and they came and said to him, ‘Why do the disciples of John and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?’”

Mark may appear to have added the Pharisees, as though they had said this together with the disciples of John, whereas Matthew says that only John’s disciples said it.

But the very words that Mark records them as having spoken more strongly indicate that some people spoke about others. That is, the guests who were present came to Jesus because the disciples of John and the Pharisees were fasting, and they spoke to him about them.

Thus, when Mark says, “They come,” he is not referring to the people about whom he had inserted the statement, “The disciples of John and the Pharisees were fasting.” Rather, while those people were fasting, others who were troubled by this came and said to him, “Why do the disciples of John and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?”

Luke makes this still clearer. After reporting the Lord’s response concerning the calling of sinners as though they were sick, he says:

“But they said to him, ‘Why do the disciples of John fast frequently and make supplications, and likewise those of the Pharisees, while yours eat and drink?’”

Thus here too Luke, like Mark, narrates that some spoke about others.

Why, then, does Matthew say, “Then the disciples of John approached him, saying, ‘Why do we and the Pharisees fast’”? Because they too were present, and all of them, each as he was able, made the accusation competitively. The three Evangelists have conveyed their common meaning in different ways of speaking, but in a manner that does not depart from the truth.

63. Likewise, Matthew and Mark both include the statement about the bridegroom’s sons, that they will not fast as long as the bridegroom is with them. The difference is that Mark calls them “the sons of the bridechamber,” whereas Matthew calls them “the sons of the bridegroom.” This makes no difference to the matter, since by “the sons of the bridechamber” we understand not only the bridegroom’s sons but also the bride’s.

The meaning is therefore plainly the same, not two opposing meanings.

Luke does not say, “Can the sons of the bridegroom fast?” Instead he says, “Can you make the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” Here too he elegantly discloses the same meaning while indicating something additional.

For it is understood that those very people who were speaking would bring it about that the bridegroom’s sons fast in mourning, since they themselves would kill the bridegroom.

Matthew says “mourn”; Mark and Luke say “fast,” because later Matthew too says, “Then they will fast,” not “Then they will mourn.” Yet by that word he indicated that the Lord was speaking of the kind of fasting associated with the humility of affliction.

The other kind—the fasting that belongs to the joy of a mind suspended in spiritual things and, because of this, in a certain sense withdrawn from bodily food—the Lord is understood to have indicated through the later comparisons concerning the new cloth and the new wine. He shows that this kind of fasting is not suited to those who are occupied with animal and carnal concerns around the body and therefore still retain the old disposition. The other two Evangelists explained these comparisons in the same way.

It is already sufficiently clear that there is no contradiction if one writer says something another omits, whether it concerns a word or an event, provided that he either does not depart from the same meaning or that what he adds does not conflict with what another reports.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### Concerning the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter who was raised, and the woman who touched the fringe of his garment: whether the order in which these events are reported contradicts any of the Evangelists, and especially concerning the words of the ruler of the synagogue when he petitioned the Lord

64. Matthew next continues, still preserving the order of time:

“While he was speaking these things to them, behold, one ruler approached and worshiped him, saying, ‘My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live,’” and so forth, up to the place where he says, “And the girl arose, and this report spread throughout that whole region” (Matt. 9:18–26).

The other two, Mark and Luke, also report this event, but now depart from Matthew’s order. They recall and insert it elsewhere, namely at the point where Jesus returns by crossing over from the region of the Gerasenes, after the demons had been expelled and permitted to enter the pigs.

Mark joins the events in this way after the incident in the region of the Gerasenes:

“When Jesus had crossed over again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered around him, and he was beside the sea. And one of the rulers of the synagogue, named Jairus, came; and when he saw him, he fell at his feet,” and so forth (Mark 5:21–43).

We must therefore understand that the event concerning the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter did occur when Jesus had crossed over again in the boat to the other side, but how long afterward is not apparent.

For if there had been no interval, there would have been no time for the event Matthew has just narrated at his own banquet to take place. For, in the manner of the Evangelists, Matthew narrated as a separate event something that had happened concerning himself and in his house. After that event, nothing else immediately follows except this account of the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter.

Matthew connects the events in such a way that the transition itself clearly indicates that what follows happened next. After recalling above what Jesus had said about the new cloth and the new wine, he immediately adds: “While he was speaking these things to them, behold, one ruler approached.” If the ruler approached while Jesus was saying these things, then no other event or saying of his intervened.

In Mark’s narrative, however, there is clearly a place where other events could have been inserted, as we have already shown.

Luke likewise, after narrating the miracle that occurred in the region of the Gerasenes, turns to the account of the ruler’s daughter in a way that does not conflict with Matthew, who demonstrates that this event occurred after the comparisons concerning the cloth and the wine by saying, “While he was speaking these things.”

After Luke had finished narrating what occurred in the region of the Gerasenes, he passed to another event in this way:

“It happened, when Jesus had returned, that the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And behold, a man named Jairus, who was himself a ruler of the synagogue, came and fell at Jesus’ feet,” and so forth (Luke 8:40–56).

The crowd did indeed welcome the Lord immediately, since it was waiting for him to return. But the statement that follows—“And behold, a man named Jairus”—should not be understood as having occurred immediately. The event concerning the banquet of the tax collectors came first, as Matthew narrates. Matthew connects this event with that banquet in such a way that no other event can be understood to have followed immediately.

65. In the account we have now undertaken to examine, all three Evangelists agree without any question concerning the woman who suffered from an issue of blood. It makes no difference to the truth of the event that one writer omits something another reports, nor that Mark says, “Who touched my garments?” while Luke says, “Who touched me?”

One spoke in customary language, the other more precisely, but both express the same meaning. We more commonly say, “You are tearing me apart,” than “You are tearing my clothes,” although it is perfectly clear what we intend to be understood.

66. But when Matthew tells that the ruler of the synagogue announced to the Lord that his daughter was not dying, or near death, or at the point of death, but altogether dead, whereas the other two say that she was already close to death but not yet dead—so much so that they say those who came afterward announced that she had died, and therefore that the teacher should no longer be troubled, as though he had come in order to prevent her death by laying his hand upon her, not as one who could raise the dead—we must consider whether this appears contradictory. We must understand that, for the sake of brevity, Matthew preferred to say that the Lord had been asked to do what it is clear that he did: namely, to raise her from the dead. For he attends not to the father’s words concerning his daughter but to what is most important, his intention; and he put down words corresponding to that intention. The father had despaired to such a degree that he preferred her to come back to life, not believing that she could be found alive, rather than merely remain dying, as she had been when he left her.

Thus the other two recorded what Jairus said, whereas Matthew recorded what he wanted and thought. In either case, the request made to the Lord was that he should save the girl either while she was dying or by raising her after death. But since Matthew had undertaken to relate the whole matter briefly, he indicated that the father had said, in asking, what he certainly also wished and what Christ accomplished.

Indeed, if either of the other two had recorded that the father himself said what those who came from his house had said—that Jesus should no longer be troubled because the girl had died—then the words Matthew records would conflict with his thought. But as it is, although those messengers reported this and forbade the teacher to come any longer, it is not recorded that the father agreed with them. Accordingly, when the Lord said to him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be saved,” he did not rebuke one who was unbelieving, but strengthened more firmly one who was believing. His faith was like that of [Column 1111] the man who said, “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX, 23).

67. Since this is so, through these varied but not contradictory forms of expression used by the Evangelists we learn a plainly most useful and absolutely necessary lesson: in anyone’s words we should look for nothing except the intention, which the words ought to serve. Nor does anyone lie if he expresses in different words what another person intended, without repeating that person’s actual words. Otherwise, those wretched hunters of words might think that truth must somehow be bound to the points of letters, whereas in every sign of the mind—not only in words but in all other signs as well—it is the mind itself that must be sought.

68. As for the fact that some copies of Matthew read, “For the woman is not dead, but asleep,” although Mark and Luke testify that she was a girl of twelve years: understand that Matthew was speaking according to Hebrew usage. In other passages of Scripture too, not only those who have had intercourse with a man but women altogether, even untouched and chaste, are called *mulieres*, “women.” Thus it is written of Eve herself, “He formed her into a woman” (Genesis II, 22). Likewise, in the Book of Numbers, the women who had not known the bed of a male—that is, virgins—are ordered to be spared and not killed (Numbers XXXI, 18). In accordance with this usage, Paul too says that Christ himself was made “of a woman” (Galatians IV, 4). We should understand this rather than believe that the twelve-year-old girl was already married or had experienced sexual intercourse.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### On the two blind men and the demon who was mute, which Matthew alone records

69. Matthew continues and says: “As Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying, ‘Have mercy on us, Son of David,’” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “But the Pharisees were saying, ‘By the prince of demons he casts out demons’” (Matthew IX, 27–34).

Matthew alone includes this account of the two blind men and the mute demon. For the two blind men about whom the other Evangelists also relate a story (Mark X, 46–52, and Luke XVIII, 35–43) are not these men, although a similar event occurred. Indeed, if Matthew himself had not also remembered that other event (Matthew XX, 29–34), one might think that what he now relates had been reported by the other two as well.

We must carefully commit this to memory: some events are similar. This is demonstrated when the same Evangelist recalls both events. Thus, whenever we find such individual accounts in different Evangelists and encounter in them an apparent contradiction that cannot otherwise be resolved, we should recognize that the event is not the same but another similar event, or one that happened in a similar way.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### Where, taking pity on the crowds, he sent his disciples, giving them authority to perform healings, and gave them many instructions, ordering how they should live; here it must be considered how Matthew agrees with Mark and Luke, especially concerning the staff, which Matthew says is not to be carried, while Mark says that it alone is to be carried, and concerning footwear and clothing

70. From this point onward the order of events is not apparent. For after these two events, concerning the blind men and the mute demon, the account continues as follows:

“Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the kingdom of the Gospel, and healing every disease and every infirmity. But when he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and lying helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples: ‘The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send [Note: [Column 1112] Printed editions have *mittat*, “send.” The manuscripts, however, have *ejiciat*, “send out.” The Greek has *ekbalē*, “send out.”] laborers into his harvest.’ And having summoned his twelve disciples, he gave them authority over unclean spirits,” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “Truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward” (Matthew IX, 35–X, 42).

In this entire passage, which we are now recalling, he gave his disciples many instructions. But whether Matthew inserted it in chronological order, or whether the order of his narrative followed the order of his recollection, as has been said, is not apparent.

Mark seems to have touched upon this passage briefly. He enters it in this way: “And he went around the villages in the surrounding area, teaching. And he summoned the Twelve and began to send them out two by two; and he gave them authority over unclean spirits,” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “Shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them” (Mark VI, 6–11).

Before Mark related this, however, after the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter had been raised, he first related the passage in which the people in the Lord’s homeland wondered where he had obtained such wisdom and miraculous powers, since they knew his family. Matthew recalls this after the instruction to the disciples and after many other events (Matthew XIII, 54).

Thus it is uncertain whether Matthew, having omitted the event in the Lord’s homeland, later recalled it, or whether Mark anticipated it from memory: which of them preserved the order of events and which followed the order of his recollection.

Luke, immediately after the resurrection of Jairus’s daughter, adds this passage concerning the disciples’ authority and instruction (Luke IX, 1–6), as briefly as Mark. He too, however, does not present it in such a way that it clearly follows in the chronological order of events.

In the names of the disciples, Luke, who names them elsewhere [Note: [Column 1112] The Ratisbon edition and nineteen manuscripts read, “names them by another name.”], when they are first chosen on the mountain, does not differ from Matthew except in the name of Judas of James (Luke VI, 14–16). Matthew calls this man Thaddaeus; some copies, however, have Lebbaeus [Note: [Column 1112] Five manuscripts have *Lebdaeus*, corruptly, as is clear from the Greek text, which in Matthew 10:3 has *kai Lebbaîos ho epiklētheis Thaddaîos*, “and Lebbaeus who is called Thaddaeus.”]. But who has ever forbidden one person to be called by two or three names?

71. It is also customary to ask how Matthew and Luke could record that the Lord told the disciples not to carry a staff, when Mark says, “And he instructed them to take nothing for the journey except a staff,” and then adds, “no bag, no bread, and no money in their belts,” thereby showing that his account concerns the same event as that of the others, who said that a staff was not to be carried.

This can be resolved by understanding that the staff which, according to Mark, was to be carried is meant in one sense, while the staff which, according to Matthew and Luke, was not to be carried is meant in another. [Column 1113] The same applies to the word “temptation”: in one sense it is said, “God tempts no one” (James I, 13), and in another, “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy XIII, 3). The former is temptation leading astray; the latter is testing.

The word “judgment” is likewise understood in one way in the statement, “Those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 29), and in another way in, “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Psalm XLII, 1). The former is a judgment of condemnation; the latter, a judgment of discernment.

72. There are many other words that do not have a single meaning but, when appropriately placed in different contexts, are understood in different ways. Sometimes they are expressed with an explanation, as in the statement: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in wickedness, so that you may be mature in your understanding” (1 Corinthians XIV, 20). This could have been stated briefly in a compressed form: “Do not be children, but be children.”

Similarly: “If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise” (ibid. III, 18). What else does this mean but: “Let him not be wise, so that he may be wise”?

At other times statements are expressed in a compressed form so as to exercise the reader who investigates them. Thus Paul says to the Galatians: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another. For each person will bear his own burden” (Galatians VI, 2–5).

Unless you understand the word “burden” in different senses, you will undoubtedly think that the speaker contradicts himself—indeed, in words placed very close together in a single passage. For shortly before he said, “Bear one another’s burdens,” and afterward he said, “Each person will bear his own burden.” But some burdens consist in sharing weakness, while others consist in rendering an account to God for our actions. The former are shared with our brothers and sisters so that they may be supported together; the latter are borne individually by each person.

In the same way, the staff can be understood spiritually, as when the Apostle said, “I will come to you with a staff” (1 Corinthians IV, 21), and physically, whether it is used for a horse or for some other purpose. For the moment I pass over the other figurative meanings of this word.

73. We must therefore accept that both statements were spoken by the Lord to the Apostles: that they should not carry a staff, and that they should carry nothing except a staff.

When, according to Matthew, he said to them, “Do not acquire gold, silver, or money in your belts; no bag for the journey, no two tunics, no sandals, and no staff,” he immediately added, “For the laborer is worthy of his food.” This sufficiently shows why he did not want them to acquire or carry these things: not because they are unnecessary for sustaining this life, but because he was sending them in such a way that he demonstrated that these things were owed to them by the very people to whom they would proclaim the Gospel when they believed—like payment owed to soldiers, like the fruit owed to those who plant a vineyard, like the milk owed to shepherds from their flock.

Hence Paul says: “Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not partake of the flock’s milk?” From this he was speaking about the things necessary for preachers [Column 1114] of the Gospel. A little later he says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things? If others share in your authority, do we not do so even more? But we have not used this authority.”

It is therefore clear that the Lord did not command these things as though Evangelists ought to live from no other source than what those to whom they proclaim the Gospel provide. Otherwise the same Apostle would have acted contrary to this command, since he supported himself by the labor of his own hands so as to be a burden to no one (1 Thessalonians II, 9). Rather, the Lord gave them the authority by which they would know that these things were owed to them.

When something is commanded by the Lord, failure to do it is the fault of disobedience. But when authority is granted, anyone may choose not to use it and may, as it were, relinquish what is his by right.

Thus, when the Lord spoke to the disciples, he was doing what the Apostle himself later explained more clearly: “Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat what comes from the temple? Those who serve at the altar share in what belongs to the altar? In the same way, the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but I have used none of these rights” (1 Corinthians IX, 7–15). When he says that the Lord ordained this, but that he himself did not use it, he plainly shows that the right to use such support was granted, not that a necessity of serving was imposed.

74. In establishing this order—that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel—the Lord, as the Apostle says, was speaking to the Apostles so that, without anxiety, they would neither acquire nor carry the necessities of this life, whether great or small.

For this reason he included “and no staff,” indicating that all things were owed by his faithful to his ministers, who were to demand nothing superfluous. By adding, “For the laborer is worthy of his food,” he completely opened up and clarified where and why he was saying all these things.

He therefore signified this authority by the name “staff” when he said that they should take nothing for the journey except a staff. It could also have been expressed briefly in this way: “Carry none of the necessities with you—not even a staff, except a staff alone.” Thus the statement “not even a staff” can be understood to mean that they should not carry even the smallest things; while the addition “except a staff alone” can be understood to mean that, through the authority received from the Lord and signified by the name “staff,” even what they did not carry would not be lacking.

The Lord therefore said both things.
