But because one Evangelist did not record both, it is thought that the one who said that the staff, in one sense, was not to be carried contradicts the one who said that a staff, in another sense, was to be carried. Once the explanation has been given, however, this should no longer be thought.

75. Likewise, when Matthew says that sandals are not to be carried on the journey, he forbids the anxiety that makes people think they must carry them so that they will not be without them. The same must be understood concerning two tunics: none of them was to think that, in addition to the one he was wearing, he should carry another in case it should be needed, since he could receive one through that authority.

Accordingly, when Mark says that they were to be shod with sandals or soles, he indicates that this footwear has a mystical significance: the foot should be neither covered nor bare upon the earth. That is, the Gospel should neither be concealed nor rest upon earthly advantages.

And when he forbids them not merely to carry or possess two tunics but, more explicitly, to put on two tunics—saying, “and not to put on two tunics”—[Column 1115] what else does he teach them than to walk not in duplicity but in simplicity?

76. There is therefore no doubt that the Lord said all these things, partly literally and partly figuratively. But the Evangelists inserted different elements into their writings: some of the same things were included by two, by any three, or by all four of them. Even so, not everything that he said or did was written down.

If anyone thinks that the Lord could not place some sayings figuratively and others literally within one discourse, let him examine the rest of his teaching. He will see how rashly and without learning he makes such a judgment. For, to mention one point that occurs to me at present, such a person might think that the almsgiving itself, and everything else commanded in that passage, must be understood figuratively because the Lord says that the left hand should not know what the right hand is doing (Matthew VI, 3).

77. I remind the reader again—and the reader ought to remember this, so that he may not need such a reminder so often—that in various and different places in his discourses the Lord repeated many things that he had already said elsewhere. Otherwise, when the order of such passages does not agree with that found in another Evangelist, someone might think that one of them contradicts the other on this account. The reader should understand that something may be said again elsewhere after having already been said in another place.

This should be observed not only concerning sayings but also concerning deeds. There is nothing to prevent us from believing that the same event happened again. But to slander the Gospel by refusing to believe that something happened again, when no one can prove that it could not have happened again, is sacrilegious folly.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### Where John the Baptist sent his disciples to the Lord from prison: what Matthew and Luke say

78. Matthew continues and says: “When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went away from there to teach and preach in their cities. Now when John had heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “And wisdom was justified by her children” (Matthew XI, 1–19).

Luke also inserts this entire passage concerning John the Baptist: that he sent to Jesus, what sort of answer those whom he sent received, and everything the Lord said about John after they had departed (Luke VII, 18–35). He does not, however, place it in the same order. It is not apparent which of them here preserves the order of his recollection and which preserves the order of the events themselves.

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### Where he reproached the cities because they had not repented, as Luke also says; here it must be considered how Matthew agrees with Luke in the order itself

79. Matthew continues and says: “Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been performed, because they had not repented,” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “It will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you” (Matthew XI, 20–24).

Luke also recalls this passage (Luke X, 12–15), joining these words from the Lord’s mouth to a certain discourse that he has continued. Thus he appears more likely to be recalling them in the order in which they were spoken by the Lord, while Matthew follows the order of his recollection.

Alternatively, if Matthew’s statement, “Then he began to reproach the cities,” is understood [Column 1116] as referring to the specific moment indicated by the word “then,” rather than to the somewhat broader period during which these many events were done and said, anyone who believes this should also believe that the statement was made twice.

For even within one Evangelist there are passages in which the Lord is found to have said something twice. Thus, in Luke himself, the Lord’s instruction not to take a bag on the journey, together with similar instructions, is found in two places (Luke IX, 3, and X, 4). Why, then, should it be surprising if something else is said twice, separately by different Evangelists, in the same order in which it was spoken? The order appears different in the individual accounts because it was spoken both at the time when one Evangelist recalls it and at the time when the other recalls it.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### Where he calls them to take up his yoke and burden: how Matthew does not differ from Luke in the order of narration

80. Matthew continues: “At that time Jesus answered and said: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent,’” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew XI, 25–30).

Luke also recalls this passage, but only in part. He does not say, “Come to me, all you who labor,” or the words that follow. It is credible that the Lord said this once, but that Luke did not recall everything that was said.

Matthew says, “At that time Jesus answered and said,” after he had reproached the cities. Luke, however, after that reproach of the cities, inserts a few things—not many—and then adds this passage in the following way: “In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said” (Luke X, 21).

Thus, even if Matthew had not said, “At that time,” but “In that same hour,” Luke inserts so little in between that it would not be unreasonable to regard the saying as having been spoken in the same hour.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### Where the disciples plucked and ate ears of grain: how Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree with one another in the order of narration

81. Matthew continues and says: “At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath; and his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat,” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Matthew XII, 1–8).

This is also recorded by Mark and Luke without any question of contradiction (Mark II, 23–28, and Luke VI, 1–5). But they do not say, “At that time.” Perhaps Matthew therefore preserved the order of the events here, while the others followed the order of their recollection. Unless, of course, “At that time” is understood more broadly, meaning the period during which these many and varied events were taking place.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### Concerning the man whose withered hand was healed on the Sabbath: how Matthew’s account agrees with Mark and Luke, whether in the order of events or in the words of the Lord and the Jews

82. Matthew continues his account as follows: “And when he had passed on from there, he came into their synagogue. And behold, a man having a withered hand,” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “And it was restored to health like the other” (Matthew XII, 9–13).

Mark and Luke also do not omit this account of the man who had a withered hand and was healed (Mark III, 1–5, and Luke VI, 6–10).

One might think that [Column 1117] both the event concerning the ears of grain and the healing of this man occurred on the same day, since the Sabbath is mentioned here as well, unless Luke had made clear that the healing of the withered hand occurred on another Sabbath.

Accordingly, when Matthew says, “And when he had passed on from there, he came into their synagogue,” he certainly did not come except after he had passed on from there. But it is not stated how many days later he came into their synagogue after passing through that grainfield, or whether he went there directly and immediately. This leaves room for Luke’s account, which says that the man’s hand was healed on another Sabbath.

It may, however, cause difficulty that Matthew says they themselves asked the Lord, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” wishing to find an opportunity to accuse him. Yet he reports that the Lord put forward the example of the sheep, saying: “What man among you, if he has one sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable is a human being than a sheep? Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” Mark and Luke, however, report that the Lord himself asked them: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save a life or to destroy it?”

We must therefore understand that they first asked the Lord, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” Then, knowing their thoughts and that they were seeking an opportunity to accuse him, he placed in their midst the man whom he was going to heal and asked the question that Mark and Luke recall him asking. When they remained silent, he proposed the example of the sheep and concluded that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. Finally, after looking around at them with anger—as Mark says—and being grieved at the hardness of their hearts, he said to the man: “Stretch out your hand.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### Whether, after the man whose withered hand was healed, these three Evangelists depart from one another in such a way that they contradict each other in no respect in the order of the account itself

83. Matthew continues, weaving his account together as follows:

“But the Pharisees went out and took counsel against him, how they might destroy him. Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there; and many followed him, and he healed them all. And he charged them not to make him known, so that what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled,” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “And in his name the nations will hope” (Matthew XII, 14–21).

Matthew alone recalls this; the other two proceed to something else.

Mark appears to have preserved the order of events to some extent. He says that Jesus, having learned of the Jews’ malicious plot against him, withdrew to the sea with his disciples; crowds gathered to him; and he healed very many of them (Mark III, 7–12).

It is scarcely apparent where he began to move on to another subject—not one that followed in chronological order. Was it where he says that crowds gathered to him? For this could already have happened at another time. Or was it where he says that he went up onto a mountain?

Luke too seems to recall this when he says: “Now it happened in those days that he went out onto the mountain to pray” (Luke VI, 12). By saying “in those days,” he sufficiently indicates that this did not happen immediately.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### Concerning the mute and blind man who had a demon: how Matthew and Luke agree

84. Matthew therefore continues and says: “Then [Column 1118] a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to him; and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw” (Matthew XII, 22).

Luke recalls this not in the same order but after many other events, and says only that the man was mute, not that he was also blind (Luke XI, 14). But we should not suppose that he is speaking of another man merely because he omits something. For he too goes on to connect the events that Matthew relates.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### Where it was said to him that he cast out demons by Beelzebul: whether Matthew differs in no respect from the other two, especially Luke, in everything he said on that occasion concerning blasphemy against the Holy Spirit and the two trees

85. Matthew continues, saying:

“And all the crowds were amazed and said, ‘Can this be the Son of David?’ But the Pharisees, hearing this, said, ‘He casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.’ But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them: ‘Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste,’” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew XII, 23–37).

Mark does not introduce the statement that Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul immediately after the incident involving the mute man. Rather, after some other events that he alone records, he adds this as well—either recalling and inserting it at another point, or omitting something and then returning to this order (Mark III, 22–30).

Luke says almost exactly what Matthew says (Luke XI, 14–26). In calling the Spirit of God the “finger of God,” he does not depart from the same meaning; indeed, he teaches us something by this, so that we may know how to understand the expression wherever we read of the “finger of God” in Scripture.

There is no controversy concerning the things that Mark and Luke do not say here, nor concerning those that they express somewhat differently, since the meaning is the same.

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### What he answered those who asked for a sign, concerning the prophet Jonah, the Ninevites, and the Queen of the South, and concerning the unclean spirit that, after leaving a person, returns and finds the house cleansed: how Matthew agrees with Luke

86. Matthew continues and says:

“Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, ‘Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you,’” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “So will it also be for this evil generation” (Matthew XII, 38–45).

Luke also relates this in that section, though in a somewhat different order (Luke XI, 16–37). For he mentions above that they asked the Lord for a sign from heaven, after the miracle involving the mute man. He does not there report what the Lord answered them in response. But later, when the crowds had gathered, he says that this was the answer given to those whom he indicates were the same people he had mentioned earlier as seeking a sign from heaven.

He connects this passage after inserting the account of the woman who said to the Lord, “Blessed is the womb that carried you.” He introduces this woman after recalling the Lord’s discourse about the unclean spirit leaving a person, returning, and finding the house cleansed.

After that woman, when Luke says that the crowds received an answer concerning the sign they were seeking from heaven, he inserts the comparison with the prophet Jonah. Then, continuing the Lord’s own discourse, he recalls what was said about the Queen [Column 1119] of the South and the Ninevites. Thus he has recalled something that Matthew omitted, while omitting something that Matthew recorded in this passage.

Who, then, does not see that it is pointless to ask in what order the Lord said these things? We must learn this also from the Evangelists’ supreme authority: it is not a lie if someone arranges another person’s discourse in an order different from that in which the speaker delivered it, when the order itself makes no difference to the matter, whether it was this way or that.

Luke also indicates that this discourse of the Lord was longer, and in it he recalls certain statements like those Matthew includes in the discourse delivered on the mountain (Matthew V–VII). We understand that these were said twice—there and here.

After concluding this discourse, Luke moves on to another subject. Whether he preserved the order of events there is uncertain. For he connects the passage as follows: “While he was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him.” He does not say, “While he was speaking these things,” but simply, “While he was speaking.” For if he had said, “While he was speaking these things,” he would necessarily compel us to understand that he had narrated not only these matters in this order, but that the Lord had also performed them in this order.

## CHAPTER XL  
### Where his mother and brothers were announced to him: whether the order itself does not differ between Mark and Luke

87. Matthew therefore continues and says:

“While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him,” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother” (Matthew XII, 46–50).

We must undoubtedly understand this as having happened consecutively. For when Matthew turns to relate it, he first says, “While he was still speaking to the crowds.” What does “still” mean except that he was engaged in the very speech he had been delivering? He did not say, “And while he was speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers”; rather, he said, “While he was still speaking.” By these words he compels us to understand that they came while he was delivering the speech he had indicated above.

Mark too, after reporting what the Lord said concerning blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, says: “And his mother and brothers come” (Mark III, 31–35), omitting certain things that Matthew places at greater length than Mark and Luke at greater length than Matthew within the same sequence of the Lord’s discourse.

Luke, however, did not preserve the chronological order of this event. He anticipated it and related it earlier from memory. Indeed, he inserted it in such a way that it appears detached from the connection both with what precedes and with what follows.

After recalling certain parables of the Lord, he inserts this recollection concerning his mother and brothers as follows: “His mother and brothers came to him,” he says, “but they could not reach him because of the crowd.” He does not specify when they came to him.

Again, when he moves on from this passage, he speaks as follows: “Now it happened, he says, on one of the days that he got into a boat, and his disciples with him” (Luke VIII, 19–22). Here too, by saying “it happened on one of the days,” he sufficiently indicates that it is not necessary to understand this as the day on which the preceding event occurred, or as the day immediately following it.

Thus Matthew’s account of the Lord’s mother and brothers [Column 1120] contains no contradiction with the other two, either in the Lord’s words or in the order of the events themselves.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### What he spoke from the boat to the crowds concerning the seed of which some fell on the way, and so forth; concerning the seed among which weeds were sown, the mustard seed, and the leaven; and what he spoke in the house concerning the treasure hidden in the field, the pearl, the net cast into the sea, and the one who brings forth new and old things from his treasure: how Matthew agrees with Mark and Luke, both in what they say with him and in the order of narration

88. Matthew continues:

“On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. And great crowds gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat down; and the whole crowd stood on the shore. And he spoke many things to them in parables, saying,” and so forth, up to the passage where he says: “Therefore every scribe who has been instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matthew XIII, 1–52).

That this occurred immediately after the account of the Lord’s mother and brothers, and that Matthew also preserved the order in his narration, is suggested by the way he passes from that account. He connects the events by saying, “On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea, and great crowds gathered around him.”

When he says “on that day”—unless perhaps “day,” according to scriptural usage, signifies a period—he sufficiently indicates either that this happened consecutively or that not many events could have intervened. This is especially so because Mark also preserves this order (Mark IV, 1–34).

Luke, however, after relating the account of the Lord’s mother and brothers, moves on to another subject, but in doing so makes no connection that appears to contradict this order (Luke VIII, 22).

Of all the things Matthew relates that the Lord spoke, those which Mark and Luke also say with him present no question of contradiction. The things Matthew alone records are even less open to controversy. Nor, although one Evangelist follows an order somewhat different from another—partly the order of events and partly the order of recollection—do I see in the order itself what or whom any of them contradicts.

## CHAPTER LXII  
### Where he came into his homeland and they marveled at his teaching while despising his family: how Matthew agrees with Mark and Luke, especially whether the order of narration contradicts the other account in any respect
89. Matthew therefore continues: “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these parables, that he departed from there; and coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogues” [Note: [Col. 1120] Three manuscripts: “in their synagogue,” in accordance with the Greek text.], etc., up to the passage where he says: “And he did not perform many miracles there because of their unbelief” (Matthew 13:53–58). From the preceding discourse of parables he passes on in such a way as not to show that the sequence of events necessarily follows. This is especially so because Mark, proceeding from these parables not to the matter to which Matthew proceeds, but to another, and Luke likewise arranging his narrative in this way, make it more credible that what those two continuously append happened subsequently: namely, the boat [Col. 1121] in which Jesus was sleeping, and the miracle of the demons cast out among the Gerasenes (Mark 4:35; 5:17; Luke 8:22–37). Matthew has already inserted these two matters above by recalling them (Matthew 8:23–34). Let us now see whether what the Lord said in his own country, or what was said to him there, agrees with the other two, Mark and Luke. For John records, at very different and dissimilar points in his narrative, either that such things were said to the Lord (John 6:42), or that he said things like those which the other three recall at this point.

90. Mark indeed recalls here nearly all the same things as Matthew, except that he says that the Lord was called by his fellow citizens “the carpenter and son of Mary” (Mark 6:1–6), not, as Matthew says, “the carpenter’s son.” Nor is this surprising, since both could have been said: they believed him to be a carpenter precisely because they believed him to be a carpenter’s son. Luke, however, relates this same event more fully and recalls more things there. He inserts it not long after Christ’s baptism and temptation, undoubtedly anticipating something that happened later, after many intervening events. From this anyone may observe that, for the very great question which, with God’s help, we have undertaken to unravel concerning the agreement of the Evangelists, it is most necessary to recognize that they may either have omitted something or, without being ignorant of the order of the events, retained instead another order in their recollection. This can be understood most clearly from the fact that Luke, before narrating anything done by the Lord at Capernaum, anticipated the passage now under consideration, where his fellow citizens were both astonished at the power of his miracles and contemptuous of the lowliness of his birth. For Luke says that he said to them: “Certainly you will say to me: ‘Physician, heal yourself. The great things we have heard were done at Capernaum, do here also in your own country.’” Yet, according to Luke’s own narrative, nothing is as yet recorded as having been done at Capernaum. Since the passage is neither long nor difficult, and is most necessary, we insert it in full, showing the point from which he came to this narrative and how he did so. After stating that the Lord was baptized and tempted, Luke continues thus:

> “And when every temptation had been completed, the devil departed from him until a time. And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and a report concerning him went out through all the surrounding region. And he himself taught in their synagogues and was glorified by all. And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up; and, according to his custom, he entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day and stood up to read. And the book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him.” And when he had unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; because of this he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.’  
> 
> “And when he had folded the book, he returned it to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed upon him. And he began to say to them: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.’ And all bore witness to him and wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth; and they said: ‘Is this not Joseph’s son?’  
> 
> “And he said to them: ‘Certainly you will say to me this proverb: “Physician, heal yourself. The great things we have heard were done at Capernaum—do them here also in your own country”’” (Luke 4:13–23), and so forth, until he completes that entire passage of his narrative.

What, then, could be clearer than that Luke knowingly anticipated this event in his narrative, since he certainly knew—and himself mentions—that great things had already been done by Jesus at Capernaum, and certainly knew that he had not yet narrated the events that had occurred there? For Jesus’ baptism was not so far in the past that Luke could be thought to have forgotten that he had not yet mentioned anything about what had taken place at Capernaum. He has only just begun to narrate events after the baptism.

## CHAPTER XLIII — How Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree concerning Herod’s words when he heard of the Lord’s miracles, and concerning the order of the narrative

91. Matthew continues: “At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus and said to his servants: ‘This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore miraculous powers are at work in him’” (Matthew 14:1–2).

Mark says the same thing and in almost the same way, but not in the same order (Mark 6:14–16). After the Lord had sent out the disciples, telling them to take nothing on the journey except a staff, and after the discourse he recalls had ended, Mark added this account. Yet he does not create any necessity by which we would be forced to understand that this event also happened next; nor does Matthew. For Matthew says, “At that time,” not “On that day” or “At that hour.”

The difference is that Mark does not say that Herod made this statement, but says: “Some were saying that John the Baptist had risen from the dead.” Matthew, however, says of Herod himself: “He said to his servants.”

Luke also follows the same order of narration as Mark. Yet he too does not compel us to believe that this was the actual order of events. He recalls the same matter as follows:

> “Now Herod the tetrarch heard all that was happening through him, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead, by others that Elijah had appeared, and by still others that one of the ancient prophets had risen. And Herod said: ‘I beheaded John; but who is this about whom I hear such things?’ And he sought to see him” (Luke 9:7–9).

In these words Luke also confirms Mark, at least insofar as the statement that John had risen from the dead was attributed to others, not to Herod. But since Luke mentions that Herod was perplexed and later places these words in his mouth—“I beheaded John; but who is this about whom I hear such things?”—we must understand either that, after this perplexity, Herod confirmed in his mind what others were saying when he said to his servants, as Matthew narrates, “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore miraculous powers are at work in him”; or else these words should be pronounced in such a way as to show that he was still uncertain.

If Matthew had written, “Is this perhaps John the Baptist?” or “Could this be John the Baptist?” there would be no need to say anything about the manner of pronunciation by which his doubt and perplexity might be understood. But since those words are absent, the statement can be pronounced in either way: we may understand him to have spoken as one who, persuaded by the words of others, had become convinced; or we may understand him to have remained perplexed, as Luke relates.

This is especially so because Mark, who earlier said that others had stated that John had risen from the dead, nevertheless does not fail, at the end of the passage, to report Herod himself as saying: “John, whom I beheaded—he has risen from the dead.” These words too can be pronounced in two ways, so that they may be understood either as the words of one who is convinced or of one who is doubtful.

After Luke recalls this, he passes on to another subject. Matthew and Mark, however, take this occasion to narrate how John was killed by Herod.

## CHAPTER XLIV — The order in which these three Evangelists narrate John’s imprisonment and death

92. Matthew therefore continues and says:

> “For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother,” etc., up to the passage where he says: “And his disciples came and took his body” [Note: [Col. 1123] The printed editions have *his body*. The word *his* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text], “and buried it; and they came and reported it to Jesus” (Matthew 14:3–12).

Mark narrates this similarly (Mark 6:17–29). Luke, however, recalls it in a different order, placing it near the account of the Lord’s baptism. He too is therefore understood to have anticipated the event, taking the opportunity to narrate there something that happened much later.

After recalling John’s words about the Lord—that he held the winnowing shovel in his hand, would cleanse his threshing floor, gather the grain into his barn, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire—Luke immediately added something that did not happen immediately afterward. John the Evangelist makes this perfectly clear when he recalls that, after Jesus had been baptized, he went into Galilee, where he changed water into wine; that after staying in Capernaum for a few days, he returned to the land of Judea; and that there he baptized many near the Jordan, before John was sent to prison (John 2:1, 12; 3:22–24).

Who would not suppose, if he were less well educated in these writings, that after those words about the winnowing shovel and the cleansed threshing floor, Herod immediately became angry with John and sent him to prison? Yet we have already proved elsewhere that these events were not narrated in the order in which they occurred, and in this very passage it is not just anyone else but Luke himself who proves it (Luke 3:15–21).

For if John was sent to prison immediately after those words, how could Jesus, according to Luke’s own narrative, have been baptized after the account of John’s imprisonment? It is therefore clear that Luke, recalling the event because of the opportunity, anticipated it and placed it at the beginning of his narrative, before many events that he was going to narrate as having occurred before this happened to John.

Nor did the other two—Matthew and Mark—place the account of John’s imprisonment in their narratives according to the order of events as it appears even in their own writings. For they too say that, after John had been handed over, the Lord went into Galilee (Matthew 4:12; Mark 1:14). Then, after many things that he did in Galilee, they come to the account of Herod’s recognition or perplexity: that John, whom he had beheaded, had risen from the dead (Matthew 14:1–2; Mark 6:14–16). On this occasion they narrate everything that happened to John while he was imprisoned and killed.

## CHAPTER XLV — The order in which all the Evangelists come to the miracle of the five loaves, and how they come to it

93. Matthew continues. After saying that Christ had been informed that John had been killed, he connects his narrative as follows:

> “When Jesus heard this,” he says, “he withdrew from there in a boat to a deserted place by himself. And when the crowds heard this, they followed him on foot from the cities. And when he went out, he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick” (Matthew 14:13–14).

He records this as having happened immediately after John’s suffering. Consequently, the events mentioned earlier—those that moved Herod to say, “I beheaded John”—must be understood to have happened afterward. For those events must have occurred later, when the report reached Herod, causing him to be moved and to wonder who this person could be about whom he was hearing such things, since he himself had killed John.

After narrating John’s suffering, Mark recalls that the disciples who had been sent out returned to Jesus and reported to him all that they had done and taught. Mark alone records that the Lord told them to rest for a short while in a deserted place; that he went away with them in a boat; and that the crowds, seeing this, went ahead of them to that place. The Lord had compassion on them and taught them many things. As the hour grew late, the event took place in which all who were present were fed from five loaves and two fish (Mark 6:30–44).

All four Evangelists recall this miracle. Luke, who had already narrated John’s suffering much earlier (Luke 3:20), now, on the occasion we have described, recalls Herod’s perplexity about who the Lord was and immediately adds what Mark does: that the Apostles returned to him and reported all that they had done; that he took them away to a deserted place; that the crowds followed; that he spoke to them about the kingdom of God; and that he healed those who needed treatment. Then, as the day was declining, Luke too recalls the miracle of the five loaves (Luke 9:10–17) [Note: [Col. 1124] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have *on that very day*. M.].

94. John, however, differs greatly from those three Evangelists, because he dwells more on the discourses delivered by the Lord than on the deeds he performed miraculously. After recalling that Jesus had left Judea and gone again into Galilee—understood to have occurred at the time when the other Evangelists also say that he went into Galilee after John had been handed over—John, while Jesus was passing through Samaria, weaves into his narrative many things that he said on the occasion of the Samaritan woman whom he found at the well.

After two days, John says that Jesus left there for Galilee, then came to Cana of Galilee, where he had changed water into wine, and healed the son of a certain royal official (John 4:3, 5, 43–54).

John is silent about the other things that the others said Jesus did and said in Galilee. What they omit, however, he does report: that Jesus went up to Jerusalem for a festival and there performed the miracle involving a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years and had no one to put him into the pool in which those afflicted with various diseases were healed. On this occasion John recalls that Jesus said many things.

After this he says that Jesus crossed the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias, and that a great crowd followed him. Then Jesus went up onto a mountain and sat there with his disciples, near the Passover, the feast of the Jews. When he raised his eyes and saw the very large crowd, he fed them with five loaves and two fish (John 5–6:13), as the other Evangelists also say.

It is therefore certain that John omitted the events through which the others reached their account of this miracle. Nevertheless, as though proceeding by another route of narration, he and the three others—who were traveling almost alongside one another—meet at the miracle of the five loaves. The three others had kept silent about what John reported, while John, pursuing the Lord’s discourses at greater length, had made a kind of circuit through events they omitted; shortly afterward he meets them again at the common narration of the miracle of the five loaves, only to diverge from them once more into deeper matters.

## CHAPTER XLVI — How all four Evangelists agree concerning the miracle of the five loaves itself

95. Matthew continues and brings his narrative of the event of the five loaves forward in order as follows:

> “When evening came, his disciples came to him, saying: ‘This is a deserted place, and the hour has already passed; dismiss the crowds, so that they may go to the villages and buy food for themselves.’ But Jesus said to them: ‘They do not need to go; you give them something to eat,’” etc., up to the passage where he says: “The number of those who ate was five thousand men, besides women and children” (Matthew 14:15–21).

This miracle, which all four Evangelists recall (Mark 6:34–44; Luke 9:12–17), is thought to contain some discrepancies among them. It must therefore be examined and discussed, so that from this case we may also learn rules for interpreting other similar expressions, by which the same meaning and the same factual truth are preserved despite differences in wording.

The examination should begin not with Matthew, according to the order of the Evangelists, but rather with John, because he presents the account so explicitly that he even names the disciples with whom the Lord discussed the matter. He says:

> “When Jesus had therefore raised his eyes and seen that a very great crowd was coming to him, he said to Philip: ‘Where shall we buy bread so that these people may eat?’ But he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do.  
> 
> “Philip answered him: ‘Bread worth two hundred denarii would not be enough for them, so that each might receive even a little.’ One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, said to him: ‘There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish; but what are these among so many?’  
> 
> “Then Jesus said: ‘Make the people recline.’ Now there was much grass in the place. So the men reclined, numbering about five thousand. Jesus therefore took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those reclining; likewise, as much fish as they wanted. When they had been filled, he said to his disciples: ‘Gather up the fragments that remain, so that they may not be lost.’ So they gathered them and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves that remained to those who had eaten” (John 6:5–13).

96. It is not at issue here that John said what kind of loaves they were: he did not omit that they were barley loaves, whereas the others did. Nor is it at issue that John did not say that, besides the five thousand men, women and children were also present, which Matthew does say.

It should now be regarded as certain, and should be held as a rule in such questions, that no one ought to be troubled when one writer says what another omits. The question is how all the things they say can be true, so that one narrator, by relating a different detail, does not exclude another’s account.

If, according to John’s narrative, the Lord looked at the crowds and asked Philip, testing him, where food could be obtained for them, one might wonder how it can be true that, as the others narrate, the disciples first told the Lord to dismiss the crowds so that they could buy food for themselves in the nearby places. According to Matthew, Jesus answered them: “They do not need to go; you give them something to eat.” Mark and Luke agree with him, merely omitting the words, “They do not need to go.”

It is therefore understood that, after saying these words, the Lord looked at the multitude and said to Philip what John records, while the others omitted it.

Next, what Philip answered according to John is reported by Mark as the response of the disciples. Mark wishes it to be understood that Philip answered through the mouth of the others. They may also, as is very common, have used the plural number in place of the singular.

Thus Philip’s statement, “Bread worth two hundred denarii would not be enough for them, so that each might receive even a little,” is equivalent to Mark’s statement: “Shall we go and buy bread for two hundred denarii and give them something to eat?”

Mark also recalls that the Lord asked, “How many loaves do you have?” The others omitted this.

What Andrew suggested according to John concerning the five loaves and two fish is reported by the others in the plural instead of the singular, as spoken by the disciples collectively.

Luke compressed Philip’s response and Andrew’s response into one statement. When he says, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish,” he reports Andrew’s response. But when he adds, “Unless perhaps we ourselves go and buy food for all this crowd,” he seems to be referring to Philip’s response, except that he says nothing about the two hundred denarii. Yet this too can be understood as part of Andrew’s thought. After saying, “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish,” Andrew himself added, “But what are these among so many?” This amounts to saying, “Unless perhaps we ourselves go and buy food for all this crowd.”

97. From this entire variety of expressions, together with the agreement of the meaning and of the facts, it is sufficiently clear that we are beneficially taught to seek in words nothing except the intention of the speakers. All truthful narrators must attend to making that intention clear whenever they narrate something about a human being, an angel, or God. For the speakers’ intention can be expressed in words, so that the accounts do not disagree with one another in their substance.

98. It should certainly not be omitted here—because it may be relevant to other cases of this kind that arise—that Luke says the people were ordered to recline in groups of fifty, whereas Mark says in groups of fifty and of one hundred.

This causes no difficulty here because one writer mentions a part and the other the whole. The writer who also reports groups of one hundred reports what the other omitted; therefore there is no contradiction.

Nevertheless, if one writer had mentioned only groups of fifty and another only groups of one hundred, the accounts would appear very contradictory. It would not easily be recognized that both things had been said, but that one writer had mentioned one detail and the other the other detail. Yet who would deny that, on more attentive consideration, this should have been discovered?

I have said this because many things of this kind often occur which appear contradictory to those who pay little attention and judge rashly, although they are not contradictory.

## CHAPTER XLVII — How the Evangelists who relate the walking upon the waters agree with one another, and how they depart from the passage where the crowds were fed with the five loaves

99. Matthew continues and says:

> “And after dismissing the crowds, he went up onto the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone. But the boat was being tossed in the middle of the sea by the waves, for the wind was against it. During the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea. And when they saw him walking upon the sea, they were troubled, saying: ‘It is a ghost,’” etc., up to the passage where he says: “They came and worshiped him, saying: ‘Truly you are the Son of God’” (Matthew 14:23–33).

After narrating the miracle of the five loaves, Mark follows with the same account:

> “When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and he was alone on the land. And when he saw them laboring at the oars—for the wind was against them—” etc. (Mark 6:47–54).

Mark’s account is similar, except that he says nothing about Peter walking upon the waters.

We should guard against being troubled by Mark’s statement that, while walking upon the waters, the Lord “wanted to pass them by.” How could they have understood this unless he was going in another direction and wanted to pass them by as strangers, since they did not recognize him and thought he was a ghost?

Who would be so slow as not to notice that this can be referred to a mystical meaning? Nevertheless, when they were troubled and cried out, he came to their aid, saying: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.”

How, then, did he want to pass by those whom he strengthened in their fear, unless that intention to pass by served to elicit the cry to which help had to be given?

100. John too remains with these events for a while. After narrating the miracle of the five loaves, he likewise does not omit the account of the boat in distress and the Lord’s walking upon the waters. He connects the narrative as follows:

> “When Jesus therefore knew that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, he fled again to the mountain by himself. When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea. And when they had got into the boat, they came across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not come to them. The sea, however, rose because a great wind was blowing,” etc. (John 6:15–21).

Nothing here can appear contradictory except that Matthew says that, after dismissing the crowds, Jesus went up onto the mountain to pray there alone, whereas John says that he was on the mountain with the same crowds whom he had fed with the five loaves [Note: [Col. 1128] Some better manuscripts have this reading. Other manuscripts, twelve in number, have: *on the mountain with the same crowds from the five loaves*. The printed editions of Erasmus and Lovaniensis have: *he fled onto the mountain with the same crowds from the five loaves*.].

But since John himself says, after that miracle, that Jesus fled onto the mountain so that the crowds, who wanted to make him king, would not seize him, it is perfectly clear that they had come down from the mountain to lower ground when the loaves were distributed to the crowds.

Therefore there is no contradiction in his going up onto the mountain again, as both Matthew and John say. The difference is that Matthew says, “He went up,” whereas John says, “He fled.” This would be contradictory only if fleeing did not involve going up.

Nor is there any conflict between Matthew’s statement that he went up onto the mountain alone to pray and John’s statement: “When he knew that they were about to come and make him king, he fled again onto the mountain by himself.” The reason for praying is not opposed to the reason for fleeing. Indeed, by transforming in himself the body of our lowliness so that he might conform it to the body of his glory (Philippians 3:21), the Lord was also teaching that the time when there is cause to flee is itself a great reason for us to pray.

Nor is there any contradiction in the fact that Matthew first says that Jesus ordered the disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the water until he had dismissed the crowds, and that, after dismissing the crowds, he went up onto the mountain alone to pray; whereas John first recalls that Jesus fled alone onto the mountain and then says: “When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, and when they had got into the boat,” etc.

Who does not see that John, by recapitulation, later said that the disciples did what Jesus had already ordered before he fled onto the mountain? It is customary in speech to return, in a certain way, to something previously omitted.

But because the return itself occurred within such a brief space of time, it is not mentioned; and those who hear the account commonly suppose that what is said later also happened later.

In the same way, after saying that the disciples got into the boat and crossed the sea to Capernaum, John says that the Lord came to them, as they were laboring on the sea, walking upon the waters. This plainly happened earlier during the voyage by which they were going to Capernaum.

101. After narrating the miracle of the five loaves, Luke proceeds to another matter and departs from this order. He says nothing about that boat or about the Lord’s journey upon the waters. Instead, after saying, “And they all ate and were filled, and twelve baskets of their remaining fragments were taken up,” he immediately adds:

> “And it came to pass, when he was praying alone, that the disciples were with him; and he questioned them, saying: ‘Who do the crowds say that I am?’” (Luke 9:17–18).

He then narrates something else, not the event reported by the other three: that the Lord came walking upon the waters to the disciples who were sailing.

Nor should it be supposed that, on the mountain which Matthew says Jesus ascended in order to pray alone, he asked his disciples, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” Luke may seem to agree with Matthew because he says, “when he was praying alone,” whereas Matthew says, “he went up onto the mountain alone to pray.”

But Luke is speaking of an entirely different occasion: while Jesus was praying alone and the disciples were with him, he asked them this question. Luke alone says that he was alone, but not without the disciples, as Matthew and John say when the disciples departed from him to cross the sea ahead of him. Luke explicitly adds: “The disciples were with him.”

Thus Luke says that Jesus was alone without the crowds, which did not remain with him.

## CHAPTER XLVIII — How Matthew and Mark do not contradict John concerning what happened after they crossed the water

102. Matthew continues, saying:

> “And when they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesaret. And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent word throughout the whole region and brought to him all who were sick. And they begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and as many as touched it were made well.  
> 
> “Then scribes and Pharisees came to him from Jerusalem, saying: ‘Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread,’” etc., up to the passage where he says: “But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person” (Matthew 14:34–15:20).

Mark also recalls these events without any question of contradiction (Mark 7:1–23). Whatever is said differently by one writer does not depart from the same meaning.

After the boat from which the Lord had come walking upon the sea reached land, John, according to his custom, focuses on the Lord’s discourse. Taking the occasion of the bread, he recalls that Jesus said many things, especially profound and divine. After that discourse, his narrative rises loftily to another subject and then another (John 6:22–72).

Yet although John departs from the course followed by the other two, his transition to different matters does not conflict with their order. What prevents us from understanding that the people whom Matthew and Mark mention were healed by the Lord, and that Jesus said to those who followed him across the sea the things that John reports? For Capernaum, where John says they crossed the sea, lies beside the Lake of Gennesaret, the land to which Matthew says they came ashore.

## CHAPTER XLIX — The Canaanite woman who said, “The dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table,” and how Matthew and Luke agree with one another

103. Matthew therefore continues after the Lord’s discourse, in which he discussed the matter of unwashed hands with the Pharisees. He connects his narrative, preserving—so far as the transition itself indicates—the order of the events that followed:

> “And Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders and cried out, saying to him: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely tormented by a demon.’ But he did not answer her a word,” etc., up to the passage where he says: “‘O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.’ And her daughter was healed from that hour” (Matthew 15:21–28).

Mark also recalls the account of the Canaanite woman, preserving the same order of events and raising no question of contradiction, except that he says the Lord was in a house when the same woman came to him and begged on behalf of her daughter (Mark 7:24–30).

Matthew could easily be understood to have omitted the mention of the house while recalling the same event. But since he says that the disciples urged the Lord, “Send her away, because she is crying out after us,” he seems to signify nothing other than that the woman uttered her pleading cries behind the Lord as he walked.

How, then, could she have come to him in the house? We must understand that Mark said that she entered where Jesus was, after having first stated that he was in a house. But because Matthew says, “He did not answer her a word,” he allows us to recognize what both Evangelists omitted: that during this silence Jesus went out from that house. Thus the rest of the narrative follows, and there is no longer any disagreement.

What Mark records the Lord as having answered her concerning not giving the children’s bread to the dogs was said after the events that Matthew does not omit: namely, that the disciples pleaded with him on her behalf; that he answered that he had been sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel; and that she came—that is, followed after him—and worshiped him, saying, “Lord, help me.” Then came the statement that both Evangelists record.

## CHAPTER L — Whether Matthew and Mark agree concerning the feeding of the crowds with seven loaves

104. Matthew continues his narrative as follows:

> “And when Jesus had departed from there, he came beside the Sea of Galilee; and he went up onto the mountain and sat there. And great crowds came to him, having with them the mute, the lame, the blind, the weak, and many others. And they cast them at his feet, and he healed them, so that the crowds marveled, seeing the mute speaking, the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.  
> 
> “But Jesus called his disciples and said: ‘I have compassion on the crowd, because they have remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat,’” etc., up to the passage where he says: “Those who ate were four thousand men, besides children and women” (Matthew 15:29–38).

Mark also recalls this other miracle of the seven loaves and a few small fish, in almost the same order, except that he inserts something no one else mentions: the healing of a deaf man whose ears the Lord opened by spitting and saying, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened” (Mark 7:31–8:9).

105. It is not irrelevant to point out here, concerning this miracle of the seven loaves reported by Matthew and Mark, that if one of the two had mentioned it without also mentioning the miracle of the five loaves, he would have seemed to contradict the others.

Who would not have supposed that only one and the same event had occurred, but that it had not been narrated completely and truthfully—whether by that one writer, by the others, or by all of them? One might think either that the writer who mentioned seven loaves had made a mistake and should have mentioned five, or that those who mentioned five should have mentioned seven, or that both groups had lied or been misled by forgetfulness.

The same would be thought concerning the twelve baskets and the seven baskets, and concerning the five thousand and the four thousand who were fed. But because those who narrate the miracle of the seven loaves do not remain silent about the miracle of the five, no one is troubled, and everyone understands that both events occurred.

We have said this so that whenever something similar is found to have been done by the Lord—something that appears so contradictory to another Evangelist that it cannot at all be reconciled—nothing else may be understood except that both events occurred and that one was mentioned by one writer and the other by another. We made the same point concerning the groups of one hundred and fifty reclining, since if we did not also find both arrangements in one account, we would think that the individual Evangelists had said contradictory things [Note: [Col. 1131] See above, chapter 46.].

## CHAPTER LI — Matthew’s statement that Jesus came from there to the region of Magedan, how it agrees with Mark, and how he again answered those asking for a sign by referring to Jonah
106. Matthew continues and says: “And having dismissed the crowd, he got into the boat and came to the region of Magadan,” and so on up to the passage where he says: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matt. 15:39–16:4). Matthew himself also said this elsewhere (ibid. 12:39). Hence it must be held firmly, again and again, that the Lord often said the same things, so that when an apparent contradiction cannot otherwise be resolved, it may be understood that he said the same thing twice.

Mark, for his part, preserves this same sequence: after the miracle of the seven loaves, he adds this same account as Matthew does, except that Matthew says “Magadan,” whereas Mark says “Dalmanutha,” as it is read in some manuscripts (Mark 8:10–12). There is no doubt, however, that the same place is meant by both names. For many manuscripts, including those of Mark, have only “Magadan.”

Nor should it cause difficulty that Mark does not say that, when those seeking a sign from heaven asked him, he answered with the same reference to Jonah as Matthew, but says that the Lord answered them, “No sign will be given it.” For it must be understood that they were asking for the kind of sign they sought—that is, one from heaven. Mark omitted mentioning Jonah, which Matthew recorded.

## CHAPTER LII — How the account of the leaven of the Pharisees agrees with Mark, whether in substance or in sequence

107. Matthew continues: “And leaving them, he went away. And when his disciples had come across the sea, they forgot to take bread. He said to them: ‘Watch, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees,’” and so on up to the passage where he says: “Then they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (Matt. 16:5–12). Mark also arranges this same material in the same sequence (Mark 8:13–21).

## CHAPTER LIII — Whether Matthew, Mark, and Luke contradict one another in substance or sequence when he asked the disciples whom people said he was

108. Matthew continues: “Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi and asked his disciples, saying: ‘Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?’ [Note: [Col. 1131] The printed editions had omitted “I,” which is found here in manuscripts of the best quality and in the Greek.] But they said: ‘Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets,’” [Col. 1132] and so on up to the passage where he says: “And whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:13–19).

Mark narrates this in almost the same sequence, but first inserts the account of the blind man’s healing, which he alone records—namely, the man who said to the Lord, “I see people like trees walking” (Mark 8:22–29). Luke recalls this event after the miracle of the five loaves and inserts this account (Luke 9:18–20). As we have already shown above, the sequence of Luke’s recollection does not conflict at all with the sequence of the others.

What may cause difficulty is that Luke says the Lord asked his disciples whom people said he was while he was alone praying and they were with him, whereas Mark says that he asked them this while they were on the road. But this troubles only someone who thinks that he never prayed on the road. [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read: “He who thinks that he never prayed on the road.” The editions of Antwerp and Ratold, together with the manuscripts, do not have “he who thinks.”]

109. I also recall having already said that no one should suppose that Peter received his name here, where the Lord said to him, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” He received this name only where John records that it was said to him, “You shall be called Cephas,” which is translated “Peter” (John 1:42).

Nor, in the passage where Mark, naming the twelve disciples, says that James and John were called “sons of thunder,” should we suppose that Peter then received his name, because Mark says there that Jesus gave him the name Peter (Mark 3:16–19). He said this by recalling the event; it does not mean that it happened at that moment.

## CHAPTER LIV — Where he foretold his passion to the disciples: the agreement among Matthew, Mark, and Luke

110. Matthew continues and says: “Then he commanded his disciples that they should tell no one that he was Jesus Christ. From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and scribes,” and so on up to the passage where he says: “You do not understand the things that are of God, but those that are of men” (Matt. 16:20–23).

Mark and Luke attach this in the same sequence (Mark 8:30–33; Luke 9:21–22). Luke, however, says nothing about Peter’s opposition to Christ’s passion.

## CHAPTER LV — How these same three relate the Lord’s command that whoever wishes to follow him must come after him

111. Matthew continues: “Then Jesus said to his disciples: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me,’” and so on up to the passage where he says: “And then he will repay each according to his work” (Matt. 16:24–27).

Mark also adds this while preserving the same sequence. He does not, however, speak of the Son of Man coming with his angels to repay each according to his work. He does record that the Lord also said: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him the Son of Man will also be ashamed when he comes in his glory with the holy angels” (Mark 8:34–38). This can be understood as belonging to the same meaning as Matthew’s statement that he will repay each according to his [Col. 1133] work.

Luke likewise attaches the same material in the same sequence, using wording that is not greatly different, though he is very similar in the truth of the meaning (Luke 9:23–26). [Note: Ratold and two manuscripts read: “very similar in the truth of the statement.”]

## CHAPTER LVI — How the Lord showed himself on the mountain to three disciples with Moses and Elijah; how these three agree in sequence and substance, especially concerning the number of days, since Matthew and Mark say it happened after six days, whereas Luke says after eight

112. Matthew continues: “Amen, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. And after six days Jesus took Peter, James, and his brother John and led them up a high mountain by themselves,” and so on up to the passage where he says: “Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”

This vision of the Lord on the mountain before the three disciples, Peter, James, and John—where testimony was also borne to him from heaven by the voice of the Father—is recorded by three Evangelists in the same sequence and with entirely the same meaning (Matt. 16:28–17:9; Mark 8:39–9:9; Luke 9:27–36). The other details, according to the various forms of expression that we have demonstrated above in many places, may be seen by readers to differ without any difference in meaning.

113. As for the fact that Mark, like Matthew, says it happened after six days, while Luke says after eight, those whom this troubles should not be dismissed but instructed by an explanation.

When we state the number of days by saying, “After so many days,” we sometimes do not count the day on which we are speaking or the day on which the event we foretell or promise will occur, but count the intervening days, after which the event will truly take place in full and complete measure. Matthew and Mark did this: excluding the day on which Jesus said these things and the day on which he displayed the vision mentioned on the mountain, and counting the intervening days, they said, “After six days.” The other Evangelist, counting the final days—that is, the first and the last—said, “After eight days,” in the manner of speech by which a part is mentioned for the whole.

114. Likewise, Luke says concerning Moses and Elijah: “And it happened that, as they were departing from him, Peter said to Jesus: ‘Master, it is good for us to be here,’” and so forth. This should not be considered contrary to Matthew and Mark, who joined the statements in such a way as to make Peter appear to have proposed this while Moses and Elijah were still speaking with the Lord.

They did not state that he said it at that moment; rather, they omitted what Luke added: that, as Moses and Elijah were departing, Peter proposed to the Lord that three tents be made. Luke also added that, when they entered the cloud, a voice came from the cloud. The others did not say this, but neither did they contradict it.

## CHAPTER LVII — Where he spoke to them about Elijah’s coming: the agreement between Matthew and Mark

115. Matthew continues: “And the disciples asked him, saying: ‘Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?’ But he answered them: ‘Elijah indeed will come and restore all things. But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, [Col. 1134] but did to him whatever they wished; so also the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.’ Then the disciples understood that he had spoken to them about John the Baptist” (Matt. 17:10–13).

Mark also records this, preserving the same sequence and differing somewhat in wording, but never departing from the truth of the same meaning (Mark 9:10–12). He does not, however, add that the disciples understood that the Lord had indicated John by saying that Elijah had already come.

## CHAPTER LVIII — How these three agree, even in the sequence of their narratives, concerning the man who brought his son to him, whom the disciples had been unable to heal

116. Matthew continues and says: “And when he had come to the crowd, a man approached him, falling on his knees before him and saying: ‘Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is epileptic and suffers terribly,’” and so on up to the passage where he says: “But this kind is not driven out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17:14–20).

Mark and Luke also record this in the same sequence, without any question of contradiction (Mark 9:16–28; Luke 9:38–43).

## CHAPTER LIX — Where he told them of his passion and they were sorrowful, as all three record in the same sequence

117. Matthew continues, saying: “As they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them: ‘The Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.’ And they were greatly saddened” (Matt. 17:21–22).

Mark and Luke record this in the same sequence (Mark 9:29–31; Luke 9:44–45).

## CHAPTER LX — Where he paid the tribute from the fish’s mouth, which Matthew alone records

118. Matthew continues, saying: “And when they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma approached Peter and said to him: ‘Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?’ He said: ‘Yes,’” and so on up to the passage where he says: “You will find a stater; take it and give it to them for me and for you” (Matt. 17:23–26).

Matthew alone records this. After inserting it, he follows the same sequence in which Mark and Luke also proceed alongside him.

## CHAPTER LXI — Concerning the little child whom he set forth for imitation; the world’s scandals; the members of the body that cause scandal; the angels of little ones who see the Father’s face; the one sheep from the hundred; correcting a brother privately; loosing and binding sins; the agreement of two and the gathering of three; forgiving sins up to seventy-seven times; and the servant whose great debt was forgiven but who himself did not forgive his fellow servant: how Matthew does not contradict the others

119. Matthew therefore continues and says: “At that time the disciples came to Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you suppose, is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’ And Jesus called a little child, placed him in their midst, and said: ‘Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven,’” up to the passage where he says: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts” (Matt. 18).

From this somewhat longer discourse of the Lord, Mark, following the same [Col. 1135] sequence, included some but not all of it; he also inserted some things that Matthew does not say (Mark 9:33–49).

The whole discourse, as far as we have undertaken to consider it, is interrupted only by Peter, who asks how often he ought to forgive his brother. The Lord was speaking in such a way that it is sufficiently clear that Peter’s question and the answer given to him belong to this same discourse.

Luke records nothing in this sequence except the episode of the little child whom Jesus placed before the disciples as an example when they were thinking about their own greatness (Luke 9:46–48). If he said other things similarly that are included in this discourse, he recalled them elsewhere and as spoken on other occasions. Thus John records that after the resurrection the Lord said concerning the remission of sins: “Whose sins you retain are retained, and whose sins you forgive are forgiven” (John 20:23), whereas Matthew remembers the Lord saying this in the present discourse, and himself testifies that it had earlier been said to Peter (Matt. 16:19).

We must therefore remember, lest we be disturbed whenever the sequence of statements appears to conflict, that Jesus often said the same things in many places, as we have so often emphasized; otherwise it would always be necessary to issue this reminder.

## CHAPTER LXII — When he was asked whether it was lawful to divorce one’s wife: how Matthew and Mark agree, especially concerning the questions asked by the Lord or by the Jews and their answers, in which they seem to differ somewhat

120. Matthew continues his narrative in this way: “And it happened that, when Jesus had finished these sayings, he departed from Galilee and came into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. And great crowds followed him, and he healed them there. And the Pharisees approached him, testing him and saying: ‘Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause?’” and so on up to the passage where he says: “Let him who is able to accept this accept it” (Matt. 19:1–12).

Mark also records this, preserving the same sequence (Mark 10:1–12). We must carefully consider whether there appears to be a contradiction in the fact that Mark says the Pharisees were asked by the Lord what Moses had commanded them, and that, when questioned in this way, they answered him concerning the permission to issue a bill of divorce, whereas Matthew says that, after the Lord had declared in his own words that God had joined male and female and that therefore they ought not to be separated by man, they replied: “Why then did Moses command a bill of divorce to be given and the wife to be dismissed?”

Jesus again said to them: “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to divorce your wives; but from the beginning it was not so.” Mark, too, does not omit this answer of the Lord, but places it after they had answered his question concerning the bill of divorce.

121. As for the sequence or form of the words, we must understand that the truth of the matter is not affected whether, while the Lord was prohibiting separation and confirming his statement from the Law, they themselves raised the question of the bill of divorce permitted to them by the same Moses through whom it was also written that God had joined male and female (Gen. 2:24), or whether they gave this answer when he questioned them about Moses’ command.

For his intention was such that he would not explain [Col. 1136] why Moses had permitted it unless they had first mentioned it themselves. This intention is indicated by the question Mark records. Their intention, likewise, was to use Moses’ authority—as though, because he had commanded that a bill of divorce be given, they could thereby conclude that the Lord would certainly forbid separation. Indeed, they had approached him to test him with this very answer in mind.

Matthew expresses their intention in such a way that he does not record them as having been questioned, but as having voluntarily introduced Moses’ command by which they seemed to refute the Lord as he prohibited the separation of spouses.

Since, therefore, both Evangelists have made clear the intention of the speakers, to which their words must be subordinated, it does not matter how different their manner of narration was, provided that neither departed from the same truth.

122. It may also be understood in this way: as Mark says, when they first questioned him about dismissing a wife, the Lord in turn asked them what Moses had commanded them. When they answered that Moses had permitted them to write a bill of divorce and dismiss her, he responded to them from the Law itself, which had been given through Moses, explaining how God had instituted the union of male and female and saying what Matthew records: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female?” and so forth.

After hearing this, they repeated to him what they had answered when he first questioned them, saying: “Why then did Moses command a bill of divorce to be given and the wife to be dismissed?” Then Jesus showed that the reason was the hardness of their hearts.

For the sake of brevity, Mark places this earlier, as though it were given in response to their earlier answer, which Matthew omitted. He judged that nothing was lost to the truth, wherever the same words they had spoken twice were given back to them, since the Lord had given the same answer in those very words.

## CHAPTER LXIII — Concerning the little children upon whom he laid his hands, the rich man to whom he said, “Sell everything you have,” and the vineyard whose laborers were hired at different hours: how Matthew does not contradict the other two

123. Matthew continues: “Then little children were brought to him so that he might lay his hands on them and pray; but the disciples rebuked them,” and so on up to the passage where he says: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 19:13–20:16).

Mark preserves the same sequence as Matthew (Mark 10:13–31), but only Matthew inserts the account of the laborers hired for the vineyard.

After Luke had recorded the episode in which the disciples asked among themselves who was the greatest, he added the account of the man whom they had seen casting out demons even though he did not follow them. From that point he departs from these two Evangelists, where he says that Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:46–51). After inserting much other material, he again catches up with them when he records the rich man to whom he says, “Sell everything you possess” (ibid. 18:18–30), whom Matthew and Mark now record in the sequence in which they proceed together.

There, too, Luke does not omit the account of the little children before mentioning the rich man, just as the others do.

As for the rich man who asks what good he should do in order to obtain eternal life, there may [Col. 1137] seem to be a difference between Matthew’s wording, “Why do you ask me about the good?” and the wording of the others, “Why do you call me good?” The question, “Why do you ask me about the good?” may be referred more directly to what the man says when he asks, “What good shall I do?” For there he both mentions “good” and asks a question; “Good Teacher” is not yet a question.

Thus both statements can most appropriately be understood together: “Why do you call me good?” and “Why do you ask me about the good?”

## CHAPTER LXIV — Where he foretold his passion privately to the twelve disciples and the mother of the sons of Zebedee asked with her sons that one might sit at his right hand and the other at his left: how Matthew does not contradict the other two

124. Matthew continues and says: “As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside and said to them: ‘Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes; and they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified; and on the third day he will rise.’ Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached him with her sons, worshiping and asking something of him,” and so on up to the passage where he says: “Just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20:17–28).

Mark also preserves the same sequence. He says that the sons of Zebedee made the request, whereas Matthew expressly indicates that it was spoken through their mother, since she brought their desire before the Lord. Thus Mark briefly intimated that the sons themselves, rather than their mother, said what was said.

Finally, both according to Matthew and according to Mark, the Lord answered the sons rather than their mother.

After Luke had recorded, in the same sequence, what Jesus foretold to the twelve disciples concerning his passion and resurrection, he omits what these two record and, after other intervening material, catches up with them at Jericho (Luke 18:31–35).

As for what Matthew and Mark say concerning the rulers of the Gentiles who dominate their subjects—not so among the disciples, but rather that the one who is greatest will become the servant of the others—Luke says something similar, but not in that place (ibid. 22:24–27). The sequence itself indicates that the Lord said the same thing again.

## CHAPTER LXV — Concerning the healing of the blind men of Jericho: how Matthew does not conflict with Mark or Luke

125. Matthew continues: “And as they were going out from Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, two blind men sitting beside the road heard that Jesus was passing by, and cried out, saying: ‘Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David,’” and so on up to the passage where he says: “And immediately they received their sight and followed him” (Matt. 20:29–34).
