Mark also records this, but says that it happened to one blind man (Mark 10:46–52). The question is resolved in the same way as the question concerning the two men who were afflicted by a legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes was resolved above (see above, ch. 24, no. 56).

For that one of the two blind men whom Matthew has just mentioned was especially well known and famous in that city is sufficiently clear from the fact that Mark recorded both his name and his father’s name. This is not easily found in the case of the many others whom the Lord healed above, except when he also gave the name of Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue [Col. 1138], whose daughter Jesus raised (Mark 5:22–43).

This makes the point still clearer, since that ruler of the synagogue was certainly prominent in that place. Without doubt, therefore, this Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, having fallen from some great prosperity, was a man of exceptionally notorious and famous misery, since he was not only blind but also sat there begging.

This is why Mark wished to mention him alone: his healing gave this miracle as wide a fame as the man’s misfortune had possessed.

126. Luke, although he plainly records a miracle performed in exactly the same way, should nevertheless be understood to be recounting an equal miracle involving another blind man and displaying the same kind of event.

For Luke says that this happened when Jesus was approaching Jericho (Luke 18:35–43), whereas the others say it happened when he was leaving Jericho.

The name of the city and the similarity of the event might suggest that it happened only once. But the claim that the Evangelists contradict one another because one says, “As he approached Jericho,” while the others say, “As he was leaving Jericho,” certainly persuades only those who prefer to believe that the Gospel lies rather than that Jesus performed two similar miracles in similar ways.

Every faithful child of the Gospel easily sees what is more credible and what is more likely to be true. Even a contentious person, at least when warned, answers himself by reflection—whether by remaining silent or, if he refuses to be silent, by thinking about the matter.

## CHAPTER LXVI — Concerning the colt of the she-ass: how Matthew agrees with the others, who mention only the colt

127. Matthew continues and says: “And when they drew near Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them: ‘Go into the village opposite you, and immediately you will find a she-ass tied and a colt with her,’” and so on up to the passage where he says: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest” (Matt. 21:1–9).

Mark also narrates this, preserving the same sequence (Mark 11:1–10).

Luke remains in Jericho for a while, recording certain things that the others omitted—concerning Zacchaeus, the chief tax collector, and certain things spoken in parables. After this, he too catches up with them to record the colt on which Jesus sat (Luke 19:1–38).

Nor should it cause difficulty that Matthew mentions both a she-ass and a colt, while the others say nothing about the she-ass. Rather, we should recall the rule that we indicated above concerning the fifty and the hundred who reclined when the crowds were fed with five loaves (see above, ch. 46, no. 98).

Once that rule has been indicated, this should no longer trouble the reader—not even if Matthew had remained silent about the colt just as the others remained silent about the she-ass, so that it might seem especially contradictory that one said “she-ass” and the others “the colt of a she-ass.”

How much less should it trouble us here, where one mentioned the she-ass, about which the others were silent, while he did not remain silent about the colt, which they did mention? Wherever both events can be understood, there is no contradiction—even if one Evangelist mentions one event and another mentions another. How much less is there a contradiction when one mentions one event and another mentions both?

128. John, too, although he says nothing about the Lord’s sending his disciples to bring these animals to him, briefly inserts the account of the colt, [Col. 1139] together with the prophetic testimony that Matthew uses (John 12:14–15).

Even in this prophetic testimony, the Evangelists’ wording differs somewhat, but does not depart from the same meaning. It may cause difficulty, however, that Matthew presents the prophet as mentioning the she-ass, whereas neither John’s quotation nor the ecclesiastical manuscripts of the customary interpretation have this form.

The reason seems to me to be that Matthew is reported to have written his Gospel in the Hebrew language. It is clear that the interpretation called the Septuagint differs in some passages from what those who know Hebrew find in the Hebrew text and from what the individual translators rendered in the same Hebrew books.

If someone asks why the Septuagint interpretation, whose authority is so great, differs in many places from the truth found in the Hebrew manuscripts, I do not think anything more probable can be offered than that the translators of the Septuagint translated under the same Spirit under whom the words they were translating had been spoken. This is confirmed by their remarkable agreement, which is widely celebrated.

Therefore, by varying their wording in some places, while not departing from the same will of God to which those words belonged and to which their own words had to conform, they wished to demonstrate nothing other than what we now admire in the harmonious diversity of the four Evangelists: namely, that it is not a lie when someone narrates a matter in a different way, provided that he does not depart from the will of the one with whom he must agree and whose intention he must preserve.

Knowing this is useful for conduct, so that we may avoid and judge lies; it is also useful for the faith, so that we do not suppose that truth is protected as though by consecrated sounds, as if God had entrusted to us not only the event itself but also the exact words that must be used because of it.

Rather, the event that must be stated is placed before the words by which it is stated, so that we ought not seek those words at all if we could know the event without them, as God knows it, and as his angels know it. [Note: Twelve manuscripts and the edition of Ratold read: “the matter that must be learned, through the words by which it must be learned.”]

## CHAPTER LXVII — Concerning those expelled from the temple who were selling and buying: how these three do not conflict with John, who places the same event much earlier

129. Matthew continues and says: “And when he had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying: ‘Who is this?’ But the crowds were saying: ‘This is Jesus the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.’ And Jesus entered the temple of God and drove out all those selling and buying in the temple,” and so on up to the passage where he says: “But you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. 21:10–13; Mark 11:15–17; Luke 19:45–46; John 2:1–17).

All four record the expulsion of the sellers from the temple, but John places it in a very different sequence.

After John the Baptist’s testimony concerning Jesus, John recalls that Jesus went into Galilee, where he changed water into wine. Then, after mentioning that he spent a few days in Capernaum, he says that Jesus went up to Jerusalem when the Passover of the Jews was near and, having made a whip from cords, drove the sellers from the temple.

[Col. 1140] It is therefore clear that the Lord did this not once but twice: John records the first occasion, and the other three the last.

## CHAPTER LXVIII — Concerning the withered fig tree and the events narrated alongside it: how Matthew does not conflict with the others, especially Mark, concerning the sequence of the narrative

130. Matthew continues: “And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. But when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonders he performed and the children crying out in the temple and saying, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David,’ they were indignant and said to him: ‘Do you hear what these are saying?’ Jesus said to them: ‘Yes. Have you never read, “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise”?’ And leaving them, he went outside the city to Bethany and stayed there.

“Now, as he was returning to the city in the morning, he was hungry. And seeing a fig tree beside the road, he approached it and found nothing on it except leaves. And he said to it: ‘May no fruit ever come from you again.’ And immediately the fig tree withered. And when the disciples saw this, they marveled, saying: ‘How did it wither immediately?’ But Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Amen, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will do not only this to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, “Be taken up and cast into the sea,” it will happen. And whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive’” (Matt. 21:14–22).

131. Mark also relates this in sequence, but does not preserve the same order.

First, what Matthew says—that Jesus entered the temple and expelled the sellers and buyers—Mark does not mention at that point. Instead, after surveying everything, when evening had already come, he says that Jesus went out to Bethany with the twelve. On the following day, as they were leaving Bethany, Jesus was hungry and cursed the fig tree. Matthew also records this.

Mark then adds that Jesus came to Jerusalem and, after entering the temple, expelled the sellers and buyers, as though this had happened on another day rather than the first (Mark 11:11–17).

But because Matthew joins the events in this way—“And leaving them, he went outside the city to Bethany”—and then records that, as he returned to the city in the morning, he cursed the tree, it is more credible that Matthew preserved the temporal sequence concerning the expulsion of the sellers and buyers from the temple.

When he says, “And leaving them, he went outside,” whom could he mean by “leaving them” except those with whom he had just been speaking—those who were indignant that the children were crying out, “Hosanna to the Son of David”?

Mark therefore omitted what happened on the first day, when Jesus entered the temple, and inserted it later, after saying that he found nothing on the fig tree except leaves—an event that happened on the second day, as both Evangelists attest.

But Mark says that the disciples marveled that the tree had withered and that the Lord answered them concerning faith and the moving of the mountain into the sea not on the second day, when he said to the tree, “May no one ever again eat fruit from you,” but on the third day.

On the second day, Mark recorded that the sellers were expelled from the temple—an event that he had omitted from the first day. Thus, on that second day, he says that evening came and Jesus went out of the city; and, when they passed by in the morning, the disciples saw that the fig tree had withered from its roots [Col. 1141]. Peter remembered and said to him: “Rabbi, look, the fig tree that you cursed has withered.” Then Jesus answered concerning the power of faith.

Matthew, however, presents the entire sequence as though it had all happened on the second day: Jesus said to the tree, “May no fruit ever come from you again”; it immediately withered; and the disciples saw and marveled, receiving the answer concerning the power of faith.

It is therefore understood that Mark, on the second day, recorded what had happened on the first day but which he had omitted—namely, the expulsion of the sellers and buyers from the temple. Matthew, after recording what happened on the other day, when he returned from Bethany to the city in the morning and cursed the tree, omitted what Mark recorded: that Jesus came into the city, went out in the evening, and, when they passed by in the morning, the disciples marveled that the tree had become dry.

Matthew then attached to the event that occurred on the second day, when the tree was cursed, the event that occurred on the third day, when the disciples marveled at its withering and heard the Lord speak about the power of faith.

He joined the events in such a way that, unless we are compelled by Mark’s narrative to examine where and what Matthew omitted, the sequence cannot be recognized.

After Matthew had said: “And leaving them, he went outside the city to Bethany and stayed there. Now, as he was returning to the city in the morning, he was hungry. And seeing a fig tree beside the road, he approached it and found nothing on it except leaves. And he said to it: ‘May no fruit ever come from you again.’ And immediately the fig tree withered,” he omitted the other events belonging to that same day and immediately added: “And when the disciples saw this, they marveled, saying: ‘How did it wither immediately?’”

What they saw on one day, they marveled at on another.

It is understood, however, that the tree did not wither at the moment when they saw it, but immediately when it was cursed. For they did not see it as it was withering, but already completely withered; thus they understood that it had withered immediately at the Lord’s word.

## CHAPTER LXIX — When the Jews asked the Lord by what authority he did these things: how these three agree with one another
132. Matthew continues and says: “And when he had come into the temple, the chief priests and elders of the people approached him as he was teaching and said: ‘By what authority are you doing these things? And who gave you this authority?’ Jesus answered and said to them: ‘I too will ask you one question; if you tell me, I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. The baptism of John—where was it from?’” and so on, up to the passage where he says, “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matt. 21:23–27). The other two, Mark and Luke, have also set out the whole matter in almost the same words (Mark 11:27–33; Luke 19:47; 20:8). Nor do they seem to differ at all in sequence, except in the matter I discussed above: Matthew, omitting certain events belonging to the following day, has woven the narrative together in such a way that, unless one pays attention, he may be thought still to be describing the second day, while Mark is describing the third.

Luke, however, did not add this as one following the sequence of the days. Rather, after mentioning that those buying and selling had been driven from the temple, he omitted the fact that Jesus went out to Bethany, returned to the city, and what happened concerning the fig tree, as well as the answer given to the disciples’ amazement concerning the power of faith. After omitting these matters, he introduced the following words: “And he was teaching daily in the temple. But the chief priests and the scribes and the leaders of the people were seeking to seize him; and they did not find what they could do to him. For all the people were hanging upon his words, listening to him. And it happened on one of the days, while he was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, that the chief priests and the scribes came together with the elders and said to him: ‘Tell us, by what authority are you doing these things?’” and so on—matters which the other two also record.

Thus it is clear that their accounts do not conflict even in sequence, since the day which Luke says took place “on one of the days” is understood to be the day on which the others likewise report these events.

## CHAPTER LXX

### Concerning the two sons whom the father commanded to go to the vineyard, and concerning the vineyard leased to other tenants: how Matthew does not conflict with those two, whose sequence he follows, especially in this parable which all three relate concerning the vineyard leased to tenants, because of the answer given by those to whom the question was put, where there appears to be some variation

133. Matthew continues: “But what do you think? A man had two sons, and approaching the first he said, ‘Son, go and work today in my vineyard.’ But he answered and said, ‘I will not’; yet afterward, moved by repentance, he went. Approaching the other, he said likewise; but he answered and said, ‘I will, Lord,’ and he did not go,” and so on, up to the passage where he says, “And whoever falls upon this stone will be broken to pieces; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Matt. 21:28–44).

[Note: [Col. 1142] The printed editions have: “A certain man had.” “Certain” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek.]

Mark and Luke do not mention these two sons who were commanded to go and work in the vineyard. But what Matthew narrates afterward concerning the vineyard leased to tenants, who persecuted the servants sent to them, and afterward killed the beloved son and cast him outside the vineyard, they too do not omit, preserving the same sequence (Mark 12:1–11; Luke 20:9–18)—that is, after the Jews, when questioned about John’s baptism, said that they did not know, and he replied to them, “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

134. Therefore no question of contradiction arises here, except that Matthew, after saying that the Lord asked the Jews, “When the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” adds that they answered and said, “He will destroy those wicked men wickedly, and will lease the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruit at its proper seasons.”

Mark does not report that this was answered by them, but that the Lord, following upon his question, spoke these words, in a way answering himself: for he says, “What then will the lord of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others.”

It can easily be understood either that their words were added without the insertion of “They said” or “They answered,” although this was nevertheless understood; or that this answer was attributed rather to the Lord because, when they spoke the truth, he himself—the Truth—also answered concerning them.

135. What is more troubling is that Luke not only does not say that they gave this answer, but, attributing these words to the Lord just as Mark does, also reports an opposite answer from them: “God forbid.” For he narrates as follows: “What then will the lord of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy these tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said to him, “God forbid.” But he looked at them and said, “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’?”

How, then, according to Matthew, did those to whom he was speaking say, “He will destroy those wicked men wickedly, and will lease the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruit at its proper seasons,” when, according to Luke, they contradicted such words by saying, “God forbid”?

In fact, what the Lord says next concerning the stone rejected by the builders and made the cornerstone is introduced in such a way that those who contradicted the parable were convicted by this testimony. Matthew himself also records this saying in a manner suggesting that they had contradicted him, when he says, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’?” For what does “Have you never read?” mean except that they had answered something contrary to this?

Mark also indicates the same thing, reporting these words as follows: “Nor have you read this Scripture: ‘The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’?” According to Luke, this statement appears more clearly in its proper place, after their contradiction in saying, “God forbid.” For it has the same force as the wording he himself gives: “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’?” This conveys the intention of the statement, whether the wording is “Have you never read,” or “Have you not even read this,” or “What then is this that is written?”

136. It remains, therefore, for us to understand that among the crowd listening, some answered what Matthew records: “They say to him: ‘He will destroy those wicked men wickedly, and will lease his vineyard to other tenants.’” Others, however, gave the answer which Luke does not suppress: “God forbid.”

Those, therefore, who had answered the Lord with the former statement were answered by the others: “God forbid.” But the answer of those to whom these others said “God forbid” was attributed to the Lord by both Mark and Luke because, as I have said, the Truth itself spoke through them—whether through people who did not know, if they were wicked, as through Caiaphas, who, without knowing what he was saying, prophesied when he was high priest (John 11:49–51); or through people who knew, already understood, and believed.

For that multitude was also present through which that prophecy had already been fulfilled, when they came to meet him with great solemnity and cried out, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117:26; Matt. 21:9).

137. Nor should it trouble us that Matthew says that the chief priests and elders of the people approached the Lord and asked by what authority he did these things, and who had given him this authority, when he in turn questioned them about John’s baptism—where it was from, from heaven or from human beings—and when they answered that they did not know, he said, “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

For from that point Matthew continued the discourse in a connected manner and said, “But what do you think? A man had two sons,” and so forth. Without any interruption involving another matter or person, the discourse continues, according to Matthew, up to the point where he mentions the vineyard leased to tenants.

It may be supposed that he spoke all these words to the chief priests and elders of the people, by whom he had been questioned about his authority. Yet if they had asked as tempters and enemies, those who had believed cannot be understood to be among them—those who had clearly borne witness to the Lord from the prophet, and who could also at this point have answered, not in ignorance but in belief, “He will destroy those wicked men wickedly, and will lease the vineyard to other tenants.”

This should not trouble us so as to make us think that there were no believers among that crowd listening to the Lord’s parables at that time. Matthew omitted, for the sake of brevity, what Luke does not omit: namely, that this parable was spoken not only to those who had questioned him about his authority, but to the people.

For Luke says: “Then he began to speak this parable to the people: ‘A man planted a vineyard,’” and so forth. Among these people, therefore, we must understand that there could also have been those who listened to him as did those who had said, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” These were either themselves, or among those, who answered, “He will destroy those wicked men wickedly, and will lease the vineyard to other tenants.”

Mark and Luke attributed their answer to the Lord not only because he himself had said it, since he is the Truth [Note: [Col. 1144] Lovanius: “he himself had said it, who is the Truth.” The other books have: “because he is the Truth.”], which often speaks even through the wicked and the ignorant, moving the human mind by a certain hidden impulse—not by the merit of that person’s holiness, but by the right of its own power—but also because such people could have been of a kind that they were not without reason already reckoned as members in the Lord’s own body. Their voice could rightly be attributed to him whose members they were, since he had already baptized more people than John (John 4:1), and had crowds of disciples, as the Evangelists themselves frequently testify. Among these were also the five hundred brothers to whom the apostle Paul says he appeared after the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:6).

This is especially so because, according to Matthew himself, the wording is not “They say to him, ‘He will destroy those wicked men wickedly,’” in such a way that the plural pronoun “they” must be understood, as though this were the answer of those who had deceitfully questioned him about his authority. Rather, it says, “They say to him”—that is, to the Lord himself—with the singular pronoun, not the plural, as is evident in the Greek manuscripts without any ambiguity [Note: [Col. 1144] Greek: autō, “to him.”].

138. There is a saying of the Lord in the Evangelist John where what I am saying can be understood more easily. “Jesus was saying,” he writes, “to those Jews who had believed him: ‘If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.’ And they answered him: ‘We are Abraham’s offspring and have never been enslaved to anyone; how do you say, “You will be free”?’ Jesus answered them: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. But a slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. If, therefore, the Son sets you free, you will truly be free. I know that you are Abraham’s sons, but you are seeking to kill me, because my word finds no place in you’” (John 8:31–37).

He certainly would not have said “You are seeking to kill me” to those who had already believed in him, to whom he had said, “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples.” But because he had said this to those who had already believed in him, while the crowd present contained many enemies as well, even though the Evangelist does not specify who the speakers were, it is sufficiently clear from what they answered and from what they subsequently deserved to hear from him which words belonged to which persons.

Thus, just as according to John there were among that crowd those who had already believed in Jesus and also those who sought to kill him, so among the crowd of which we are now speaking there were those who had deceitfully questioned the Lord about the authority by which he did these things, and there were also those who had faithfully and sincerely acclaimed, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Accordingly, there were those who said, “He will destroy them and give his vineyard to others.”

This voice is rightly understood also to have been the Lord’s own, either because of the Truth which he himself is [Note: [Col. 1145] The manuscripts do not add “which he himself is.”], or because of the unity of his members with their Head.

There were also those who said to those giving such an answer, “God forbid,” because they understood that the parable had been spoken concerning themselves.

## CHAPTER LXXI

### Concerning the wedding feast of the king’s son, to which the crowds were invited: what sequence Matthew followed, in view of Luke, who reports something similar elsewhere

139. Matthew continues: “When the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they understood that he was speaking about them; and seeking to seize him, they feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet. And Jesus answered and spoke to them again in parables, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who made a wedding feast for his son, and sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding, and they were unwilling to come,’” and so forth, up to the passage where he says, “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 21:45–22:14).

Matthew alone narrates this parable concerning those invited to the wedding feast. Luke also records something similar, but it is not the same, as the sequence itself indicates, although that account does bear some resemblance to this one (Luke 14:16–24).

As for the fact that after the parable of the vineyard and the killing of the householder’s son Matthew adds that the Jews understood that everything had been said against them and began to plot against him, Mark and Luke also testify to this, preserving the same sequence (Mark 12:12; Luke 20:19). From that point they proceed to something else, adding next what Matthew also inserted in sequence after this parable, which he alone included, concerning the wedding feast.

## CHAPTER LXXII

### Concerning the coin to be returned to Caesar, whose image it bears, and concerning the woman who had married seven brothers: how these three agree

140. Matthew therefore continues: “Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel in order to trap him in his speech. And they sent their disciples to him with the Herodians, saying: ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and you do not care about anyone; for you do not regard the status of human beings. Tell us, then: what do you think? Is it lawful to pay the census-tax to Caesar, or not?’” and so on, up to the passage where he says, “And when the crowds heard this, they were astonished at his teaching” (Matt. 22:15–33).

Mark and Luke likewise narrate these two answers of the Lord: one concerning the coin, because the tax was to be paid to Caesar, and the other concerning the resurrection, because of the woman who had married seven brothers one after another. Nor do they differ in sequence (Mark 12:13–27; Luke 20:20–40).

After the parable concerning the tenants of the vineyard, and concerning the Jews against whom it was spoken, who were preparing a plot—matters all three record—Mark and Luke omit the parable concerning those invited to the wedding feast, which Matthew alone inserted. Then, following Matthew, they narrate these two matters, concerning Caesar’s tribute and the woman who had been successively married to seven men, in precisely the same sequence, without any question of contradiction.

## CHAPTER LXXIII

### Concerning the man to whom the two commandments of love of God and neighbor were entrusted: what sequence Matthew and Mark follow, so that they may not appear to differ from Luke

141. Matthew therefore continues and says: “But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they came together. And one of them, a lawyer, testing him, asked him: ‘Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?’ Jesus said to him: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets’” (Matt. 22:34–40).

Mark also records this, preserving the same sequence (Mark 12:28–34). Nor should it trouble us that Matthew says the man who questioned the Lord was testing him, whereas Mark omits this and concludes at the end by saying that the Lord told him, since he had answered wisely, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.”

For it may be that, although he approached as a tester, he was corrected by the Lord’s answer. Or we should not understand the testing as evil, as though he wished to deceive an enemy, but rather as cautious, as though he wished to examine someone still unknown. For it is not without reason that Scripture says, “One who readily believes is light-hearted and will be diminished” (Ecclus. 19:4).

142. Luke, however, inserts something of this kind not in this sequence but much earlier (Luke 10:25–37). Whether he is recalling this event, or whether it is another man with whom the Lord similarly dealt concerning these two commandments, is entirely uncertain.

It nevertheless appears rightly to be another man, not only because of the great difference in sequence, but also because Luke says that he himself answered the Lord when questioned, and in his answer mentioned these two commandments. When the Lord told him, “Do this, and you will live”—directing him to do what he himself had said was great in the Law—the Evangelist continues: “But he, wishing to justify himself, said: ‘And who is my neighbor?’”

Then the Lord narrated the story of the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers. Since the man in question is described as testing the Lord, answered the two commandments himself, and, after the Lord’s admonition, “Do this, and you will live,” is not commended as good—the words “But he, wishing to justify himself” make this clear—whereas the man whom Matthew and Mark mention in the same sequence is commended so highly that the Lord says to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God,” it is more credible that this is another man, not the same one.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

### Concerning the Jews’ being questioned about Christ, whose son they thought him to be: whether Matthew does not conflict with the other two, since according to him the question is, “What do you think about Christ? Whose son is he?” and they answer, “David,” whereas according to the other two it is, “How do the scribes say that Christ is David’s son?”

143. Matthew continues: “When the Pharisees had gathered, Jesus questioned them, saying: ‘What do you think about Christ? Whose son is he?’ They said to him, ‘David’s.’ He said to them: ‘How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying, “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies beneath your feet”? If David therefore calls him Lord, how is he his son?’ And no one was able to answer him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him any further” (Matt. 22:41–46).

Mark also records this immediately and in the same sequence (Mark 12:35–37). Luke merely omits the man who questioned the Lord about which commandment was first in the Law. After omitting this, he too preserves the same sequence and likewise narrates that the Lord questioned the Jews about how Christ was David’s son (Luke 20:41–44).

The meaning is not affected by the fact that, according to Matthew, after Jesus had asked them what they thought about Christ and whose son he was, they answered, “David’s,” and only then he added how David called him Lord. According to the other two, Mark and Luke, they are found neither to have been questioned nor to have answered.

We must understand that, after their answer, the Lord’s statement is conveyed by the two Evangelists: how he spoke it in the hearing of those whom he wished to instruct profitably by his teaching and turn away from the doctrine of the scribes. These scribes knew about Christ only that, according to the flesh, he was descended from David; they did not understand him to be God, which was why he was David’s Lord.

Therefore, as though speaking about those who were in error, the Lord addressed these others whom he wished to free from that error, and according to these two Evangelists he is reported to have said, “How do you say”—so that, as Matthew narrates it, this should be understood not as spoken to those people, but rather as spoken about them to those whom he wished to instruct.

## CHAPTER LXXV

### Concerning the Pharisees sitting on Moses’ seat and saying things they do not do, and the other things the Lord said against those same Pharisees: whether Matthew’s discourse agrees with the other two, especially Luke, who records a similar discourse elsewhere and not in this sequence

144. Matthew continues, maintaining the sequence of the narrative: “Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: ‘The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works. For they say and do not do,’” and so forth, up to the passage where he says, “You will not see me from now on until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Matt. 23).

Luke also records that the Lord delivered a similar discourse against the Pharisees, the scribes, and the lawyers, but in the house of a certain Pharisee who had invited him to a meal.

In order to narrate this, Luke had departed from Matthew near the passage where both had reported the Lord’s saying concerning the sign of Jonah—three days and nights—and concerning the queen of the South, the Ninevites, and the unclean spirit that returns and finds the house cleansed. After this discourse Matthew says, “While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him” (Matt. 12:39–46).

Luke, however, after mentioning in that discourse of the Lord certain things which Matthew omitted, departs from the sequence he had followed with Matthew in this way: “While he was speaking,” he says, “a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him; and he entered and reclined. But the Pharisee began to consider within himself why he had not washed before the meal. And the Lord said to him: ‘Now you Pharisees cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish.’”

From that point he says other things of the same kind against those Pharisees, scribes, and lawyers as Matthew says in the passage we have now undertaken to examine (Luke 11:29–52).

Although Matthew records these matters in such a way that, even though he does not name the house of the Pharisee, he does not specify a location that would conflict with that house, the Lord had already come to Jerusalem from Galilee. After his arrival, the preceding events are woven together in such a way that they may plausibly be understood to have taken place in Jerusalem. Luke, however, narrates his discourse while the Lord was still traveling toward Jerusalem.

It seems to me, therefore, that these are two similar discourses, one of which Luke and the other Matthew narrated.

145. It should certainly be considered how the statement “You will not see me from now on until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” is to be understood, since according to Matthew himself they had already said this (Matt. 21:9).

For Luke also says that this was the Lord’s answer to those who had warned him to leave because Herod wanted to kill him. There too he records that the Lord spoke precisely these words against Jerusalem itself, which Matthew gives here.

According to Luke, the account runs as follows: “On that very day some Pharisees approached, saying to him: ‘Go out and depart from here, because Herod wants to kill you.’ And he said to them: ‘Go and tell that fox, “Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third I am brought to completion”’ [Note: [Col. 1148] The printed editions have “and on the third day I am brought to completion.” The word “day” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek.]. Nevertheless, I must journey today and tomorrow and the following day, because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem. Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children as a bird gathers her brood beneath her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. But I say to you: you will not see me until the time comes when you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Luke 13:31–35).

Luke’s account does not seem to conflict with the fact that the crowds said, as the Lord approached Jerusalem, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” For according to Luke’s sequence he had not yet arrived there, and this had not yet been said.

But since Luke does not say that the Lord then departed from that place so as not to return until the time when this would already be said—for he continues on his journey until he comes to Jerusalem—and since the words, “Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third I am brought to completion,” are understood to have been spoken by him mystically and figuratively—for he did not suffer on the day which is the third from that day, although he immediately says, “I must journey today and tomorrow and the following day”—this certainly compels us also to understand mystically what he says: “You will not see me until the time comes when you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

He is referring to that coming of his in which he will come in glory. In this way, the words “I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third I am brought to completion” are referred to his body, which is the Church.

Demons are cast out when the nations, abandoning their ancestral superstitions, believe in him. Healings are completed when people live according to his commandments, after renouncing the devil and this world, until the end of the resurrection, by which the Church will be brought to completion as though on the third day—that is, perfected unto angelic fullness through the bodily immortality as well.

Therefore Matthew’s sequence should by no means be thought to have departed into something else. Rather, Luke should be understood either to have anticipated events that took place in Jerusalem and inserted them from memory before his narrative brought the Lord to Jerusalem, or to have reported that, while already approaching the city, he answered those who warned him to beware of Herod with words such as Matthew says he also spoke to the crowds when he had already arrived in Jerusalem and all the events narrated above had taken place.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

### When he foretold the destruction of the temple, how his sequence of narration agrees with the other two

146. Matthew continues and says: “And Jesus went out from the temple and was departing. His disciples approached him to point out the buildings of the temple. But he answered and said to them: ‘Do you see all these things? Amen, I say to you, not one stone here will be left upon another that will not be destroyed’” (Matt. 24:1–2).

Mark also records this in almost the same sequence, after a slight digression made in order to mention the widow who put two small coins into the treasury (Mark 12:41; 13:2)—an event which Luke alone also records.

According to Mark, after the Lord’s discussion with the Jews concerning how they should understand Christ as David’s son, the events concerning the need to beware of the Pharisees and their hypocrisy are narrated. Matthew treated this passage at great length and recorded more of what was said there. Therefore, after the same passage, which Mark touched upon briefly and Matthew arranged extensively, Mark added nothing further, as I have said, except the account of that very poor yet most generous widow. Then he adds [Col. 1150] the matters by which he again connects with Matthew, speaking of the future destruction of the temple.

Luke likewise, after the discussion concerning Christ and how he was David’s son, mentions briefly the need to beware of the hypocrisy of the Pharisees. From there, like Mark, he proceeds to the widow who put two small coins into the treasury. Then he adds the account of the future destruction of the temple, which Matthew and Mark [Note: [Col. 1150] After the words “which Matthew and Mark,” the manuscripts add: “when the Lord’s disciples privately asked him what sign there would be of his coming.”] also record (Luke 20:46–21:6).

## CHAPTER LXXVII

### Concerning the discourse he delivered on the Mount of Olives, when the disciples asked when the consummation would be: how these three agree with one another

147. Matthew continues, saying: “As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples approached him privately, saying: ‘Tell us when these things will be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age.’ And Jesus answered and said to them: ‘See that no one deceives you. For many will come in my name, saying, “I am Christ,” and they will deceive many,’” and so forth, up to the passage where he says, “And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

Let us now consider this lengthy discourse of the Lord according to the three Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, and Luke. For they preserve the same sequence and weave these matters together in parallel (Matt. 24:3–25:46; Mark 13:4–37; Luke 21:7–36).

Each of them does indeed include certain matters peculiar to himself, concerning which no suspicion of contradiction need be feared. But concerning what they report in common, we must see whether they might seem to contradict one another anywhere.

If something of this kind should occur, it cannot be said that the Lord said it elsewhere in a similar way, since the narratives of all three concern the same setting of events and times. It is of no importance for understanding or conveying the meaning that they do not all preserve the same sequence for the Lord’s sayings, provided that the things they report him to have said do not contradict one another.

148. Matthew says: “And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the consummation will come.” Mark likewise records it in the same sequence: “And the gospel must first be preached to all nations.” He does not add, “and then the consummation will come,” but his use of “first” signifies this very thing: “The gospel must first be preached to all nations,” because the disciples had asked about the end.

When he says, “The gospel must first be preached to all nations,” he clearly signifies “first,” that is, before the consummation comes.

149. Likewise, Matthew says: “Therefore, when you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand.” Mark says this as follows: “But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not to be—let the reader understand.”

By changing the wording, he explained the same meaning. It is “where it ought not to be” precisely because it ought not to be in the holy place.

Luke, however, does not say, “When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place,” or “where it ought not to be.” Rather, he says: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation has drawn near” [Col. 1151]. The abomination of desolation will therefore then be in the holy place.

150. Matthew says: “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and let the one who is on the housetop not come down to take anything from his house; and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his tunic.” Mark also records this in almost the same words.

Luke, however, says: “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains”—this agrees with the other two—but the rest he gives differently. He continues: “And let those who are in the midst of it depart, and let those who are in the regions not enter it; for these are days of vengeance, so that all things which are written may be fulfilled.”

What the other two say—“Let the one who is on the housetop not come down to take anything from his house”—appears sufficiently different from what Luke says—“Let those who are in the midst of it depart”—unless perhaps, because there will be great disturbance when so great a danger is imminent, those whom the siege has enclosed—something signified by the words “those who are in the midst of it”—will be on the housetops, stunned and wishing to see what is impending or by what means they might escape.

But how does he say “let them depart,” when he had previously said, “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army”? The following statement, “Let those who are in the regions not enter it,” seems to belong to an appropriate warning, and it can be observed: those who are outside should not enter it. But how can those who are in the midst of it depart, when the city is already surrounded by an army?

Or does “being in the midst of it” refer to the time when danger will press so urgently that, for the sake of preserving the present temporal life, escape will no longer be possible? Since the soul must then be prepared and free, neither occupied nor oppressed by carnal desires, does this signify what the other two say about the one who is on the roof, or on top of the house?

Thus, what Luke says, “Let them depart,” means that they should no longer be seized by desire for this life, but should be ready to migrate into another life. What the other two say, “Let him not come down to take anything from the house,” means that no affection should incline a person toward the flesh, as though he were about to obtain some advantage from it.

And what Luke says, “Let those who are in the regions not enter it,” means that those who have already placed themselves outside it through a good purpose of heart should not once again desire it through carnal longing. What the other two say is, “Let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his garment,” as though he were again to wrap himself in the cares from which he had been stripped.

151. But when Matthew says, “Pray, however, that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath,” Mark has stated one part and omitted the other: “Pray,” he says, “that it may not be in winter.” Luke, however, did not say this, but alone said something which seems to me to illuminate this very statement, which the others have expressed obscurely. For he says: “But take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with dissipation, drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly; for like a snare it will come upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth. Therefore keep watch, praying at all times that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are to come.” This is the flight that Matthew mentions, which ought not to take place in winter or on the Sabbath.

The cares of this life pertain to winter, as Luke expressly stated; dissipation and drunkenness, however, pertain to the Sabbath. For sorrowful cares are like winter, whereas dissipation and drunkenness overwhelm and bury the heart in carnal pleasure and indulgence. This evil is signified by the name “Sabbath” because it was—and still is—the most deplorable custom of the Jews to overflow with delicacies on that day, while they remain ignorant of the spiritual Sabbath.

Or, if something else is to be understood in Matthew’s and Mark’s words, Luke may also have said something else, provided that no question of contradiction is thereby raised. For we have not now undertaken to expound the Gospels, but to defend them against accusations of falsehood or deceit.

The other matters that Matthew included in this discourse in common with Mark pose no problem. Those that he shares with Luke, however, Luke did not place in this discourse, whose sequence agrees with Matthew’s; rather, elsewhere he either recalls and inserts such matters by anticipation, mentioning earlier what was said by the Lord later, or makes it understood that the Lord said them twice—once as Matthew relates, and then again according to Luke.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII  
### How what Matthew and Mark mention as occurring two days before the future Passover, and afterward say took place in Bethany, does not contradict John, who, together with them, relates the same event as having taken place in Bethany and says, “Six days before the Passover”

152. Matthew continues:

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, that he said to his disciples: You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (Matthew 26:1–2).

The other two, Mark and Luke, bear witness to this, not departing from the same sequence (Mark 14:1; Luke 22:1). They do not, however, indicate that this was said by the Lord; they omitted that detail. Speaking in his own person, Mark nevertheless says, “Now the Passover and Unleavened Bread were two days away,” and Luke, “The feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called the Passover, was approaching.” It was therefore approaching in such a way that it was two days away, as the other two more clearly agree.

John, however, mentioned the nearness of this same feast in three places while relating other events in the first two passages. In the third, his narrative appears to concern approximately the same period that the other three indicate, namely, the already impending passion of the Lord (John 11:55; 12:1; 13:1).

153. Yet to those who look at the matter with insufficient care, it may seem contradictory that Matthew and Mark, after saying that the Passover would take place after two days, then mention that Jesus was in Bethany, where the account is given of the precious ointment; whereas John says that Jesus came to Bethany six days before the Passover, intending to relate the same event concerning the ointment (John 12:1).

How, then, according to those two, was the Passover two days away, when, after saying this, they are found with John in Bethany relating the matter of the ointment, while John says that the Passover would be six days away? Those who are troubled by this do not understand that Matthew and Mark inserted the event concerning the ointment in Bethany by recapitulation—not after their statement about the two days, but because it had already occurred when six days still remained before the Passover.

Neither of them, after saying that the Passover would be two days away, added the account of what happened in Bethany in such a way as to say, “After this, when he was in Bethany.” Rather, Matthew says, “When Jesus was in Bethany,” while Mark says, “When he was in Bethany.” This is plainly understood to mean that the event occurred before the things were said that took place two days before the Passover.

Thus, as may be gathered from John’s narrative, Jesus came to Bethany six days before the Passover. There the meal took place at which the precious ointment is mentioned. From there he came to Jerusalem, seated on a donkey; afterward the events narrated as having occurred in Jerusalem after his arrival took place.

From the day on which he came to Bethany and the event concerning the ointment occurred until the day on which all these things were done and said, we understand—even though the Evangelists do not mention it—that four days elapsed, so that the day designated by the other two as two days before the Passover might arrive.

When Luke says, “The feast of Unleavened Bread was approaching,” he does not specify the two-day interval. We should understand the nearness he mentions as falling within that two-day interval. When John says, “The Passover of the Jews was near” (John 11:55), he does not mean that it was two days away, but six days before the Passover. Accordingly, after mentioning certain events that followed this statement, he then wished to show how near he had said the Passover was:

“Jesus therefore, six days before the Passover,” he says, “came to Bethany, where Lazarus had been dead, whom Jesus raised from the dead” (John 12:1–2). “They made him a supper there.”

This is the event that Matthew and Mark mention by recapitulation after they had already said that the Passover would be two days away. By recapitulating, therefore, they return to that day six days before the Passover, and relate what John says about the supper and the ointment. From there Jesus was to come to Jerusalem, and, after completing there the events that have been narrated, to arrive at the day two days before the Passover—from which these Evangelists had departed in order to recall by recapitulation what had previously happened in Bethany concerning the ointment. After completing that account, they return again to the point from which they had departed, namely, to narrate the Lord’s discourse, which he delivered two days before the Passover.

For if we remove from the middle the event in Bethany, which they narrated by departing from the sequence and recalling it through recapitulation, and join the sequence together, the narrative proceeds as follows according to Matthew, with the Lord saying:

“You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”

“Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the chief priest, who was called Caiaphas, and took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. But they said, ‘Not on the feast day, lest there be a tumult among the people.’ Then one of the Twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests” (Matthew 26:2–14), and so forth.

Between the statement, “Lest there be a tumult among the people,” and the statement, “Then one of the Twelve, who was called Judas, went,” Matthew inserted the account of Bethany, which he had introduced by recapitulation. Omitting that insertion, we have joined the narrative together in order to show that the chronological sequence is not contradictory.

According to Mark, likewise omitting the account of the supper in Bethany, which he too inserted by recapitulation, the narrative sequence runs as follows:

“Now the Passover and Unleavened Bread were two days away; and the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how they might seize him by deceit and kill him. For they said, ‘Not on the feast day, lest there be a tumult among the people.’ And Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him” (Mark 14:1–10), and so forth.

Here too, between the statement, “Lest there be a tumult among the people,” and the statement we added, “And Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve,” Mark inserted the account of Bethany, which he had introduced by recapitulation.

Luke, in fact, omitted the event that took place in Bethany altogether.

We have said this on account of the six days before the Passover mentioned by John when he narrated the event in Bethany, and the two days before the Passover mentioned by Matthew and Mark when, after their statement about the two days, they recalled the same event in Bethany that John had related.

## CHAPTER LXXIX  
### Concerning the supper in Bethany, where the woman anointed the Lord with precious ointment: how Matthew, Mark, and John agree with one another, and how they do not contradict Luke, who mentions a similar event as having occurred at another time

154. Matthew therefore continues from the point at which we had finished considering his narrative, and says:

“Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the chief priest, who was called Caiaphas, and took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. But they said, ‘Not on the feast day, lest there be a tumult among the people.’

“But when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him carrying an alabaster flask of precious ointment, and poured it over his head as he reclined,” and so on, up to the place where he says, “What she has done will also be told in remembrance of her” (Matthew 26:3–13).

Let us now consider the woman and the precious ointment that were involved in the event in Bethany. Although Luke also mentions a similar event, and the name of the man with whom the Lord was dining agrees—for he too calls him Simon—it is not contrary to nature or human custom for one person to have two names; still less is it impossible for two people to have one name. It is therefore more credible that the Simon in whose house this event occurred in Bethany was another man, not the leper.

Luke does not say that the event he narrates took place in Bethany. Although he does not mention the city or village where it occurred, his narrative nevertheless does not seem to concern the same place.

I therefore think that nothing else should be understood except that it was not a different woman who at that time approached Jesus’ feet—a sinful woman who kissed them, washed them with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment; to whom the Lord, using the comparison of the two debtors, said that many sins had been forgiven her because she loved much. Rather, it was the same Mary who did this twice: once, namely, as Luke narrated, when she first approached with that humility and those tears and earned the forgiveness of her sins (Luke 7:36–50).

John too, although he did not narrate how the event occurred in the manner Luke did, nevertheless commended and mentioned this same Mary when he had begun to speak of Lazarus’s being raised, before he came to Bethany. He narrates it there as follows:

“There was a certain man,” he says, “who was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha her sister. Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was ill” (John 11:1–2).

In saying this, John bears witness to Luke, who narrated that the event took place in the house of a certain Pharisee named Simon. Mary had therefore already done this.

What she did again in Bethany is another event, unrelated to Luke’s narrative, but narrated jointly by three Evangelists: John (John 12:1–8), Matthew, and Mark (Mark 14:3–9).

155. Let us therefore consider how this agrees among the three—Matthew, Mark, and John. There is no doubt that they narrate the same event as having taken place in Bethany, where, as all three mention, the disciples murmured against the woman as though the precious ointment had been wasted.

Matthew and Mark say that the Lord’s head was anointed with that ointment, whereas John says that his feet were. The rule we demonstrated when discussing the feeding of the crowds with five loaves shows that this is not contradictory. There, because someone mentioned that the groups sat down by fifties and by hundreds, no contradiction could be seen when one Evangelist said fifty and another a hundred. It could have seemed contradictory if one had mentioned only hundreds and another only fifties, yet it was necessary to understand that both events occurred. That example should teach us—as I pointed out there—that even when individual Evangelists mention individual details, we should understand both details as having occurred (above, chapter 46, §98).

Accordingly, here too let us understand that the woman anointed not only the Lord’s head but also his feet.

Unless, perhaps, someone is so absurd and malicious as to deny that anything could have remained in a broken alabaster flask from which she might also have anointed his feet, since Mark mentions that the head was anointed after the alabaster flask had been broken. But when such a person insists that it was broken in such a way that nothing remained in it, striving against the truth of the Gospel, how much better and more reverently does another insist that it was not broken in such a way as to empty it completely, striving on behalf of the truth of the Gospel?

If that malicious critic is so stubbornly blind that he attempts to break the harmony of the Evangelists over the broken alabaster flask, let him first accept that the feet were anointed before it was broken, so that what remained in the intact flask could also be used to anoint the head, when the breaking emptied it completely.

We recognize that orderly care begins from the head, but we also ascend in an orderly way from the feet to the head.

156. The remaining details of this event seem to me to pose no question. Some Evangelists say that the disciples murmured about the pouring out of the precious ointment, while John mentions Judas, and says that this was because he was a thief. I think it is clear that Judas himself is signified by the name “disciples,” by the same manner of expression that we indicated in the discussion of Philip and the five loaves, where the plural is used for the singular (above, §96).

It may also be understood that the other disciples either felt or said this, or were persuaded of it when Judas made the suggestion, and that Matthew and Mark expressed the intention of them all in their words; but that Judas said it because he was a thief, while the others said it out of concern for the poor. John, however, may have wished to mention it only of Judas, whose habit of stealing he believed should be disclosed on this occasion.

## CHAPTER LXXX  
### Where he sends the disciples to prepare the Passover for him to eat: how Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree with one another

157. Matthew continues:

“Then one of the Twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them, ‘What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?’ And they appointed for him thirty pieces of silver,” and so on, up to the place where he says, “And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and prepared the Passover” (Matthew 26:14–19).

Nothing in this chapter can be thought contrary to Mark and Luke, who relate the same events in a similar manner (Mark 14:10–16; Luke 22:3–13).

When Matthew says, “Go into the city to a certain man, and say to him: ‘The Teacher says, My time is near; I will keep the Passover with my disciples at your house,’” [Note: This difficulty does not occur in the Greek: *pros ton deina* (“to such-and-such a person”).] he means the person whom Mark and Luke call the master of the house or the owner of the house, in which the upper room was shown to them where they were to prepare the Passover.

Thus, when Matthew inserted the words “to a certain man,” he wished, for the sake of brevity, to indicate that person by a concise expression. If he had said that the Lord commanded them, “Go into the city and say to him, ‘The Teacher says, My time is near; I will keep the Passover at your house,’” it might have been understood as though the message were to be addressed to the city.

Accordingly, Matthew inserted the words “to a certain man” not as part of the Lord’s command, which he was narrating, but in his own person: the Lord ordered them to go to a certain man, so that it would not be necessary to state everything, since this seemed sufficient to convey the intention of the one giving the command.

Who does not know that no one ordinarily speaks by saying, “Go to a certain man”? If he said, “Go to anyone,” or “to whomever you please,” the expression could be complete, but there would be no particular person to whom they were being sent. Yet Mark and Luke show that the person was definite, although they silently omit his name. The Lord knew to whom he was sending them.

And so that those whom he sent might also be able to find him, he foretold the sign they were to follow: a man carrying a jar or pitcher of water. By following him, they would come to the house he intended.

Since here one could not say, “Go to anyone”—an expression that is grammatically complete but does not fit the factual reality being conveyed—how much less could one say here, “Go to a certain man,” which can never be said correctly in ordinary speech?

Nevertheless, it is clear that the disciples were sent by the Lord not to just anyone but to a certain man, that is, to a particular person. The Evangelist could properly have narrated this in his own person by saying, “He sent them to a certain man, to say to him, ‘I will keep the Passover at your house.’” He could also have said, “He sent them to a certain man, saying, ‘Go and say to him, I will keep the Passover at your house.’”

Accordingly, after placing the Lord’s words, “Go into the city,” Matthew himself inserted the words “to a certain man”—not because the Lord said this, but so that he might indicate to us, without naming him, that there was a certain man in the city to whom the Lord’s disciples were sent to prepare the Passover.

After this insertion of two words in Matthew’s own person, the sequence of the Lord’s words follows: “And say to him, ‘The Teacher says …’” For if one now asks, “To whom?” the proper answer is, “To that certain man whom the Evangelist indicated when, in his own person, he inserted the words ‘to a certain man.’”

The expression is less customary, but when understood in this way it is entirely complete. Or, if the Hebrew language, in which Matthew is said to have written, has some distinctive feature that makes the whole expression complete even when understood as spoken by the Lord, those who know that language may judge.

The expression could also be made clear in Latin in this way: “Go into the city to a certain man whom the man carrying a jar of water, when he meets you, will point out.” In this form the one giving the command could be obeyed without ambiguity. Likewise, he might say, “Go into the city to a certain man who lives at such-and-such a place, in such-and-such a house.” With the place and the house specified, the meaning could be understood and carried out.

But when someone says, without these and similar indications, “Go to a certain man and say to him,” the statement cannot be understood because it intends a particular person by saying “to a certain man” without explaining how he is to be recognized.

If we take the inserted expression as spoken in the Evangelist’s own person, the wording is indeed somewhat obscure because of the need for brevity, but it is nevertheless complete.

When Mark says “jar,” while Luke says “pitcher,” one has indicated the type of vessel and the other its capacity. Both, however, have preserved the truth of the meaning.

158. Matthew continues:

“When evening came, he reclined at table with the Twelve disciples; and as they were eating, he said: ‘Amen I say to you, one of you will hand me over.’ And being greatly saddened, they began individually to say: ‘Surely I am not the one, Lord?’” and so on, up to the place where he says:

“But Judas, who handed him over, answering, said, ‘Surely I am not the one, Rabbi?’ He said to him, ‘You have said so’” (Matthew 26:20–25).

In these matters that we have now proposed for consideration, the other Evangelists also raise no question, since they relate similar events (Mark 14:17–21; Luke 22:14–23; John 13:21–27).

# BOOK THREE

[Column 1157]

In this book the agreement of the Evangelists from the account of the supper to the end of the Gospel is demonstrated by bringing together and arranging in sequence the continuous narratives of each.

## PROLOGUE

1. Since the narrative of all four Evangelists has now reached the point at which they must proceed together to the end and cannot diverge much from one another—even if one happens to mention something that another omits—it seems to me that we can demonstrate the agreement of all the Evangelists more efficiently if, beginning at this point, we join together everything in all of them and arrange it into a single narrative and form.  
[Note: According to Rat. and Er., “and series” (*seriemque*).]

I therefore think that what we have undertaken can be explained more conveniently and easily if we begin the narrative by mentioning everything, together with the testimony of those Evangelists who each mentioned from among all these events whatever he could or wished to mention; yet all these matters were stated by all of them in such a way that it must be demonstrated that they are nowhere contradictory to one another.  
[Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the editions of Er. and Lov. read: “with the testimony of those same Evangelists, what each of them, etc.”]

## CHAPTER I  
### Concerning the Lord’s supper and the explicit identification of his betrayer: how the four Evangelists agree with one another

2. Let us therefore begin here according to Matthew:

“While they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body’” (Matthew 26:20–26).

Mark and Luke also mention this (Mark 14:17–22; Luke 22:14–23).

Luke mentions the cup twice: first before he gave the bread, and then after he had given the bread. What he said earlier he stated by anticipation, as he often does; what he placed in its proper sequence he had not mentioned earlier. Taken together, however, both passages produce the same meaning as that of the other two.

John says nothing here about the Lord’s body and blood, but plainly bears witness elsewhere that the Lord spoke much more extensively about this (John 6:32–64).  
[Note: The best manuscripts of Corbie and Rheims, along with a few others, omit “that the Lord spoke here”; nevertheless, they retain with the others the words “but plainly elsewhere much more extensively.”]

After John has mentioned that the Lord rose from the supper and washed the disciples’ feet, and has also given the reason why he did this—where the Lord had still indicated obscurely, through the testimony of Scripture, that he would be betrayed by the one who ate his bread—he comes to the passage that the other three likewise indicate:

“When Jesus had said this,” he says, “he was troubled in spirit, and testified and said: ‘Amen, amen I say to you, one of you will betray me.’”

The disciples therefore looked at one another, as John himself adds, uncertain of whom he was speaking (John 13:2–32).

And, as Matthew and Mark say, being saddened, they began to say to him individually, “Surely I am not the one?” But he answered, as Matthew continues:

“He who dips his hand with me into the dish is the one who will betray me.”

Matthew then continues:

“The Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written of him; but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed! It would have been good for that man if he had not been born.”

Mark also agrees in this order.

Then Matthew adds:

“But Judas, who betrayed him, answering, said, ‘Surely I am not the one, Rabbi?’ He said to him, ‘You have said so.’”

Here too it is not explicitly stated whether he was the one. For it can still be understood as though Judas were saying, “I did not say that.” It could also have been spoken by Judas and answered by the Lord in such a way that not everyone noticed the meaning.

3. Matthew then continues and inserts the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood given to the disciples, as do Mark and Luke.

But after he had handed over the cup, he spoke again about his betrayer. Luke continues:

“Nevertheless, behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table. And indeed, the Son of Man goes according to what has been determined; nevertheless, woe to that man through whom he will be betrayed!”

At this point we should understand that what John narrates follows, while the others omitted it, just as John omitted certain things that they said.

After the Lord had said, following the giving of the cup, what Luke records—“Nevertheless, behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table,” and so on—we join to it the passage according to John:

“Therefore one of his disciples was reclining at Jesus’ bosom, the one whom Jesus loved. Simon Peter therefore motioned to him and said to him, ‘Who is it of whom he speaks?’ When he had therefore reclined upon Jesus’ breast, he said to him, ‘Lord, who is it?’ Jesus answered: ‘It is the one to whom I shall give the morsel after dipping it.’ And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. And after the morsel, Satan then entered into him.”

4. Here we must consider whether not only Luke, who had already said that Satan entered into Judas’s heart when he made an agreement with the Jews to betray Jesus after receiving money, but also John himself may seem to contradict himself. For John had already said above, before Judas received the morsel:

“And supper having been made, when the devil had already put into his heart that Judas should betray him.”

How does he enter the heart except by implanting wicked persuasions into the thoughts of the wicked?  
[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “the persuasions of wicked thoughts.”]

But now we must understand that Judas was more completely possessed by the devil, just as, in the opposite direction, those who had already received the Holy Spirit received him more fully when, after the resurrection, Jesus breathed upon them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22), and later, when he was sent from above on the day of Pentecost, they certainly received him more fully.

“After the morsel, Satan then entered into him.” And, as John himself continues in sequence:

“Jesus says to him, ‘What you are doing, do quickly.’ But none of those reclining at table knew why he had said this to him. For some thought, because Judas had the money box, that Jesus had said to him, ‘Buy what we need for the feast,’ or that he should give something to the poor. When he had therefore received the morsel, he went out immediately. And it was night.

“When he had gone out, Jesus says: ‘Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. And if God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and he will glorify him immediately.’”

## CHAPTER II  
### Concerning Peter’s foretold denial: how it is shown that the Evangelists do not contradict one another

5. “‘Little children, I am with you only a little longer. You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, “Where I am going, you cannot come,” so now I say to you. I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, as I have loved you, so that you also may love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.’

“Simon Peter says to him, ‘Lord, where are you going?’ Jesus answered: ‘Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but you will follow afterward.’ Peter says to him: ‘Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.’ Jesus answered: ‘You will lay down your life for me? Amen, amen I say to you, the cock will not crow until you deny me three times’” (John 13:33–38).

The other three also mention this prediction of Peter’s denial; it is not John alone, whose Gospel I have just quoted (Matthew 26:30–35; Mark 14:26–31; Luke 22:31–34).

They do not all arrive at their mention of it from one identical occasion in the discourse. Matthew and Mark, in exactly the same order and at the same point in their narratives, both attach it after the Lord had left the house where they had eaten the Passover. Luke and John, however, place it before he had left there.

We could easily understand either that the first two inserted it by recapitulation or that the latter two stated it by anticipation, if we were not more troubled by the fact that they place before Peter’s declaration of confidence not merely different words but also different statements of the Lord—statements that would have moved Peter to express his presumption of dying either with the Lord or for the Lord. These differences more strongly compel us to understand that Peter expressed his confidence three times at different points in the Lord’s discourse, and that the Lord answered him three times that he would deny him three times before the cock crowed.

6. It is not incredible that Peter was moved to make such a presumption at somewhat separated intervals of time, just as he was moved to deny the Lord. Nor is it incredible that the Lord similarly answered him three times. After the resurrection, indeed, he questioned him three times in uninterrupted sequence whether he loved him, and when Peter answered the same thing three times, the Lord himself gave him one and the same command three times concerning the feeding of his sheep (John 21:15–17).

That Peter expressed his confidence three times, and that he heard from the Lord three times about his threefold denial, is made more credible by the very words of the Evangelists, who differently report the different statements made by the Lord.

Let us recall what I have just inserted from John’s Gospel. He had certainly said:
