“Little children, I am with you only a little longer. You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so now I say to you. I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, as I have loved you, so that you also may love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

Simon Peter says to him, “Lord, where are you going?”

It is plainly evident here that Peter was moved by those words to say, “Lord, where are you going?” because he had heard the Lord say, “Where I am going, you cannot come.”

Jesus answered that same Peter:

“Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but you will follow afterward.”

Then Peter said:

“Why,” he says, “can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”

The Lord answered this presumption by foretelling his future denial.

When Luke had mentioned that the Lord said, “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you all, that he might sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers,” he then added that Peter answered:

“Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.”

And the Lord said:

“I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow today until you deny three times that you know me.”

Who does not see how different this statement is from the other, and how different was the matter that moved Peter to make his presumption?

Matthew, however, says:

“And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Then Jesus says to them: ‘You will all be scandalized because of me on this night. For it is written, “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.” But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.’”

Mark says precisely the same.

What similarity do these words or statements have with those according to John or those according to Luke, in response to which Peter expressed his presumption?  
[Note: This is how it should be read, in agreement with the manuscripts and the edition of Regensburg; not as in Er. and Lov., which read: “What similarity do these words or the statement have …”]

Here, therefore, Matthew continues:

“But Peter, answering, said to him, ‘Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Amen I say to you, on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ Peter said to him: ‘Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.’ Likewise all the disciples said.”

### 7

Mark also recalls this almost in the very words, except that he expressed the Lord’s statement not generally but more precisely as to how it would happen: “Amen, I say to you, that you today, this very night, before the cock gives its voice twice, will deny me three times.” Since, then, all say that the Lord foretold that Peter would deny him before the cock crowed, but not all say how many times the cock would crow, Mark alone related this more explicitly.

Hence it seems to some that he does not agree with the others, because they pay too little attention; and their judgment is especially clouded when, with hostile intent, they set themselves against the Gospel. For Peter’s entire denial is a threefold denial. He remained in the same state of mental fear and in the same purpose of lying until, reminded of what had been foretold to him, he was healed by bitter weeping and anguish of heart.

But if this entire denial—that is, the threefold denial—began after the first cockcrow, the three Evangelists would appear to have spoken falsely: Matthew, who said, “Amen, I say to you, in this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times”; Luke, “I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow today until you deny three times that you know me”; and John, “Amen, amen, I say to you, the cock will not crow until you deny me three times.” In different words and different word-order they explained the same statement as having been made by the Lord: that Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed.

Again, if Peter had completed the entire threefold denial before the cock began to crow, Mark would plainly have reported the Lord as saying something superfluous: “Amen, I say to you, that you today, this very night, before the cock gives its voice twice, will deny me three times.” For what purpose would he say “before it gives its voice twice,” when, if that entire threefold denial were completed before the first cockcrow, it would necessarily be found completed both before the second and before the third, and before all the cockcrows of that same night—indeed, it would already have been proved complete before the first?

But because that threefold denial began before the first cockcrow, the three Evangelists attended not to when Peter would complete it, but to how great it would be [Note: [Col. 1162] Louvain has “when.” But the other, better editions and the manuscripts have “how great.”] and when it would begin—that is, that it would be threefold and that it would occur before the cockcrow. Although, in his mind, the whole denial can be understood as having occurred before the first cockcrow, nevertheless, while it began in words of denial before the first cockcrow, the entire threefold denial was completed before the second cockcrow. Yet in the disposition of Peter’s mind and in his fear, the whole denial had been conceived before the first cockcrow.

[Note: [Col. 1162] Thus in the manuscripts and in the Ratisponensian edition. But Erasmus and Louvain have *coepta est* (“it began”).]

It makes no difference over how many intervals of delay the threefold denial was uttered aloud, since his heart had already been wholly possessed by it before the first cockcrow. He had been imbued with so great a dread that, when questioned, he could deny the Lord not once only but a second and a third time.

Thus, for those who attend more correctly and carefully [Note: [Col. 1162] Six manuscripts add here, “it appears.”], just as the man who looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt. 5:28), so Peter, whenever he gave verbal expression to the fear which he had conceived so vehemently in his heart that it could persist until the third denial of the Lord, must be regarded as having undergone the entire threefold denial at the time when a fear sufficient for that threefold denial seized him.

Consequently, even if the words of denial began to break forth only after the first cockcrow, as his breast was assailed by questions, he would not absurdly or falsely be said to have denied three times before the cockcrow, since before the cockcrow such fear had taken possession of his mind [Note: [Col. 1162] In nearly all manuscripts and in the Ratisponensian edition, “her.”] as could lead him on to the third denial.

Still less, then, should it trouble us that the threefold denial, although begun in three utterances of denial before the cockcrow, was not completed before the first cockcrow. It would be like saying to someone, “This night, before the cock crows, you will write me a letter in which you will insult me three times.” If he began writing it before any cockcrow and finished it after the first cockcrow, it would not for that reason be said that the prediction had been false.

Mark, therefore, spoke more plainly concerning the intervals between the actual utterances, when he reported the Lord as saying, “Before the cock gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times.” It will become clear that this is how it happened when we come to the same place in the Gospel narrative, so that there too it may be shown that the Evangelists agree with one another.

### 8

But if the very words which the Lord spoke to Peter are sought, they cannot be found, and they are sought to no purpose, since the meaning for whose discovery the words are brought forward can be perfectly clear even in the differing wording of the Evangelists.

Therefore, whether Peter, moved by different occasions in the Lord’s speeches, expressed his confidence separately three times, and the Lord three times foretold his denial, as the more probable investigation indicates; or whether, by some arrangement of the narrative, the recollections of all the Evangelists can be brought together so as to demonstrate that the Lord foretold only once, to the presumptuous Peter, that he would deny him—no contradiction among the Evangelists can be detected here, just as there is none.

## CHAPTER III  
### How the statements made by the Lord before he left the house where they had dined are shown to contain no discrepancy

### 9

Let us now follow, as far as we can, the entire sequence from all the accounts.

Since, according to John, this had been foretold to Peter, John continues and weaves together the Lord’s discourse, in which he says: “Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many dwelling places,” and so forth. He recounts his splendid and exceedingly exalted discourse at length, until he comes continuously to the place where the Lord says:

“Righteous Father, and the world has not known you; but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me; [Note: [Col. 1163] The printed editions omitted the particle “and,” which is found here in the better manuscripts, as well as in the ancient Corbie Bibles and the Greek text.] and I made your name known to them, and I will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John 14–17).

When a dispute had arisen among them, as Luke records, about which of them seemed to be the greater, he said to them:

“The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But you must not be so; rather, let the greater among you become as the younger,

[Note: [Col. 1163] The printed editions have *sicut minor* (“as the lesser”). But the manuscripts have *sicut junior* (“as the younger”); so too the ancient Corbie Bibles and Augustine’s *Speculum*, in accordance with the Greek, ὡς ὁ νεώτερος (“as the younger”).]

and the leader as one who serves. For who is greater, the one reclining at table or the one serving? Is it not the one reclining? But I am among you as one who serves. You are those who have remained with me in my trials. And I appoint to you, as my Father appointed to me, a kingdom, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

Then, as Luke himself adds, the Lord said to Simon:

“Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.”

He said to him: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.”

And he said: “I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow today until you deny three times that you know me.”

And he said to them: “When I sent you without purse, bag, or sandals, did you lack anything?”

They said: “Nothing.”

Therefore he said to them: “But now, let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let the one who has no sword sell his tunic and buy one. For I tell you that this also which is written must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was reckoned among the transgressors.’ For the things concerning me are reaching their fulfillment.”

They said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords.”

But he said to them: “It is enough” (Luke 22:24–38).

“And after singing a hymn,” as Matthew and Mark record, “they went out toward the Mount of Olives.” Then Jesus said to them:

“You will all be scandalized because of me on this night. For it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.”

Peter, answering, said to him: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.”

Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you, in this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.”

Peter said to him: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.”

And all the disciples said the same (Matt. 26:30–35).

We have inserted these words according to Matthew; but Mark’s words are almost identical and equally numerous (Mark 14:26–31), except for the difference concerning the cockcrow, which we have already explained above.

## CHAPTER IV  
### How the agreement of Matthew, Mark, and Luke is demonstrated concerning what happened in the estate or garden to which they came from that house after supper, while John is silent about it

### 10

Matthew therefore continues the narrative and says: “Then Jesus came with them to an estate called Gethsemane” (Matt. 26:36–46). Mark says the same (Mark 14:32–42). Luke says the same without explicitly naming the estate, when he writes:

“And going out, he went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives; and his disciples also followed him. And when he had reached the place, he said to them: Pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Luke 22:39–46).

This is the place which they called Gethsemane. We understand that the garden mentioned by John was there. He narrates it thus:

“When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the brook Cedron, where there was a garden, into which he entered, he and his disciples” (John 18:1).

Then, according to Matthew:

“He said to the disciples: ‘Sit here, while I go there and pray.’ And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled. Then he said to them: ‘My soul is sorrowful unto death; remain here and keep watch with me.’ And going forward a little, he fell upon his face, praying and saying: ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.’

“And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter: ‘So you were unable to keep watch with me for one hour? Keep watch and pray, so that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.’

“Again, a second time, he went away and prayed, saying: ‘My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done.’ And he came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were weighed down. And leaving them, he went away again and prayed a third time, saying the same words.

“Then he came to his disciples and said to them: ‘Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go. Behold, he has drawn near who betrays me.’”

### 11

Mark also weaves together these events, in precisely the same manner and order, sometimes compressing certain statements more briefly and sometimes making something clearer.

For according to Matthew this speech may seem self-contradictory: after the third prayer he comes to his disciples and says to them, “Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go. Behold, he has drawn near who betrays me.”

How can he connect “Sleep now and rest” with “Behold, the hour has drawn near,” and therefore say, “Rise, let us go”? Moved by what appears to be a contradiction, readers try to pronounce the words “Sleep now and rest” as though they were spoken reproachfully, rather than permissively.

That would be correct if it were necessary. But since Mark recalled the matter in such a way that, after saying “Sleep now and rest,” he added, “It is enough,” and then continued, “The hour has come; behold, the Son of Man will be handed over,” it is clearly understood that, after saying to them “Sleep now and rest,” the Lord remained silent for a while, allowing what he had permitted to take place; and then he added, “Behold, the hour has drawn near.”

Thus, according to Mark, “It is enough” is placed after those words; that is, “It is enough that you have rested now.” But because that intervening silence of the Lord is not itself mentioned, it constrains the interpretation, so that another manner of pronouncing those words must be sought.

### 12

Luke omitted how many times he prayed. But he reported something which the others left unmentioned: that, while he was praying, he was strengthened by an angel, and that the sweat of his prolonged prayer was bloody, with drops falling to the ground.

Therefore, when he says, “And rising from prayer, he came to his disciples,” he did not specify which prayer it was. Nevertheless, he does not contradict those other two accounts in the least.

John, however, after saying that he entered the garden with his disciples, does not report what he did there until his betrayer came with the Jews to arrest him.

### 13

These three, therefore, narrated the same event in such a way that one person too could have narrated it three times [Note: [Col. 1165] The printed editions added “speak” here, superfluously, since “narrate” is very well understood.] with some variation, yet without contradiction.

Luke made clearer how far he had gone from them—that is, how far he had withdrawn—in order to pray, saying, “about a stone’s throw.”

Mark, for his part, first reported in his own words that the Lord asked, if it were possible, for that hour to pass from him—that is, the hour of the Passion, which he immediately signified under the name of “the cup.”

Then he expressed the Lord’s own words in this form: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup from me.” If you add to these words what the other two reported, and what Mark himself, speaking in his own person, likewise placed above, the meaning becomes clear:

“Father, if it is possible—for all things are possible for you—take this cup from me.”

This prevents anyone from thinking that he diminished the Father’s power when he said, “If it is possible.” For he did not say, “If you can do it,” but, “If it is possible”; and what he wills is possible.

Thus “if it is possible” was said as though he had said, “if you will.” Mark made clear in what sense “if it is possible” is to be understood when he said, “All things are possible for you.”

And what the other Evangelists reported him as saying—“Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will,” which has the same force as, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done”—plainly shows that “if it is possible” was said not because of any impossibility, but because of the Father’s will.

This is especially clear because Luke expressed the same thing more plainly: he did not say, “If it is possible,” but, “If you will.” To this clearer statement Mark’s words can be joined more clearly, so that the sense is:

“If you will—for all things are possible for you—take this cup from me.”

### 14

The fact that Mark recalls him as saying not merely “Father” but “Abba, Father” means that *Abba* is Hebrew, which in Latin is *Father*.

Perhaps the Lord said both words for the sake of some sacramental meaning, wishing to show that he had taken upon himself that sorrow in the person of his body—that is, the Church—for which he became the cornerstone, as it came partly from the Hebrews, to whom “Abba” pertains, and partly from the Gentiles, to whom “Father” pertains (Eph. 2:11–22).

The apostle Paul, likewise not passing over this sacramental meaning, says: “In whom we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15); and again: “God sent his Spirit into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father” (Gal. 4:6).

For it was necessary that the good teacher and true Savior, showing compassion to the weaker, demonstrate in himself that his martyrs ought not to despair if, at the time of their Passion, sorrow arising from human frailty should perhaps enter their hearts. They were to conquer it by placing God’s will above their own, since he knows what is beneficial for those whom he cares for.

It is not now the time to discuss this whole matter more fully. Our present concern is the agreement of the Evangelists, from whose diversity of wording we profitably learn that, in words intended to make the truth heard, we must seek not something other than the speaker’s meaning.

“Father” is therefore the same as “Abba, Father.” But “Abba, Father” expresses the sacramental meaning more clearly; “Father” alone is sufficient to signify unity.

We must believe that the Lord said “Abba, Father.” Yet the meaning would not be evident unless, when others said “Father,” it were demonstrated that those two Churches—one from the Jews and one from the Gentiles—are nevertheless one.

Accordingly, “Abba, Father” was said in the same sense in which the Lord says elsewhere: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold,” clearly signifying the Gentiles, while he also had sheep among the people of Israel.

But because he immediately added, “I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16), “Abba, Father” has the same force with respect to Israelites and Gentiles as “Father” alone has with respect to the one flock.

## CHAPTER V  
### How the things which all the Evangelists recall as done and said at his arrest are shown to contain no disagreement among them

### 15

While he was still speaking, as Matthew and Mark say, behold, Judas, one of the Twelve, came, and with him a large crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the elders of the people. [Note: [Col. 1166] The printed editions read “sent by the chief priests.” The word “sent” is absent from the better manuscripts and from the Greek.]

The one who betrayed him had given them a sign, saying: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him.” And immediately approaching Jesus, he said: “Hail, Rabbi.” And he kissed him (Matt. 26:47–56; Mark 14:43–50).

First, as Luke records, he said to him: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:47–53). Then, as Matthew records: “Friend, for what purpose have you come?” Then he said what John recalls:

“Whom do you seek?”

They answered him: “Jesus the Nazarene.”

Jesus said to them: “I am he.”

Judas, who betrayed him, was also standing with them. When, therefore, he said to them, “I am he,” they went backward and fell to the ground.

Again, therefore, he asked them: “Whom do you seek?”

They said: “Jesus the Nazarene.”

Jesus answered: “I told you that I am he. If, therefore, you seek me, let these men go,” so that the word which he spoke might be fulfilled: “Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none” (John 18:2–11).

### 16

Those who were around him, seeing what was about to happen, as Luke says, said to him: “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?”

And one of them struck the servant of the chief priest, as all four Evangelists say, and cut off his ear, which Luke and John specify as the right ear.

According to John, the one who struck him was Peter; the man whom he struck was named Malchus.

Then, as Luke records, Jesus answered: “Allow this far.” To this he added what Matthew recalls:

“Put your sword back into its place. For all who take up the sword will perish by the sword. Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would provide me at once with more than twelve legions of angels? How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?”

To these words may be added what John recalls him saying at that place: “Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?”

Then, as Luke says, he touched the ear of the man who had been struck and healed him.

### 17

It should not trouble us as though Luke’s account were contradictory because, when the disciples asked whether they should strike with the sword, Luke says that the Lord answered, “Allow this far,” as though this had been said after the blow, approving what had happened up to that point but not wishing anything further to occur.

Rather, in the words reported by Matthew, it is better understood that the entire action in which Peter used the sword displeased the Lord.

The more probable interpretation is that, when they asked him, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” he answered at once, “Allow this far”—that is, “Do not be disturbed by what is about to happen. They must be permitted to advance this far: that they may arrest me, and that what has been written about me may be fulfilled.”

But while there was an interval between the disciples’ question and the Lord’s answer, Peter, eager to defend him and stirred by an even greater devotion to the Lord, struck the blow.

Events which could happen simultaneously could not, however, be expressed simultaneously in words. Luke does not say, “Jesus answered,” unless he was answering their question, not Peter’s action. Matthew alone reported what judgment the Lord passed on Peter’s act.

Matthew also did not say, “Jesus answered Peter, ‘Put your sword back in its place,’” but, “Then Jesus said to him, ‘Put your sword back in its place,’” which shows that the Lord said this after the act had occurred.

The words which Luke gives, “Jesus answered and said, ‘Allow this far,’” must therefore be understood as the answer to those who had asked the question. But because, as we have said, the blow occurred between the questioners’ words and the Lord’s response, Luke judged that the event should be narrated in this order, inserting the blow between the question and the answer.

This is not, therefore, contrary to Matthew’s statement, “For all who take up the sword will perish by the sword”—that is, those who have used the sword.

It might seem contradictory if the Lord’s response could be shown to approve voluntary use of the sword, even only to the extent of one blow—not even a deadly wound. Nevertheless, the whole matter may also be understood consistently as having been said to Peter, so that Luke’s account and Matthew’s are joined as I have explained above:

“Allow this far”; and, “Put your sword back in its place. For all who take up the sword will perish by the sword,” and so forth.

I have already explained how “Allow this far” is to be understood. If it can be understood better in another way, let it be so, provided only that the truth of the Evangelists remains secure.

### 18

Matthew then continues and records that, at that hour, he said to the crowds:

“Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest me as though I were a robber? Every day I sat teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me.”

Then he also added the words which Luke records: “But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.”

All this happened, as Matthew says, so that the Scriptures of the Prophets might be fulfilled.

Then all the disciples abandoned him and fled, as Mark also says.

A certain young man followed him, clothed in a linen cloth, as Mark himself records; and when they seized him, he abandoned the linen cloth and fled from them naked.

## CHAPTER VI  
### How the events which occurred when the Lord was taken to the house of the chief priest, and those which occurred in that house during the night, especially Peter’s denial, are shown to agree in all the Evangelists

### 19

Having seized Jesus, they led him to Caiaphas, the chief priest, where the scribes and elders had assembled, as Matthew says (Matt. 26:57–75).

But first he was led to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, as John says (John 18:12–27).

Mark and Luke do not give the name of the high priest (Mark 14:53–72; Luke 22:54–62).

He was led away bound, while, as John records, the tribune, the cohort, and the servants of the Jews were present in that crowd.

Peter was following him from a distance as far as the courtyard of the chief priest; and, having entered, he sat with the servants to see the outcome, as Matthew says.

He was warming himself at the fire, as Mark says at this point in the narrative.

Luke also records that Peter was following from a distance: when a fire had been kindled in the middle of the courtyard and they had sat around it, Peter was among them.

John says that Simon Peter and another disciple were following Jesus. That other disciple was known to the high priest, and he entered with Jesus into the high priest’s courtyard, as John says.

Peter, however, was standing outside at the door, according to the same John.

The other disciple, who was known to the high priest, therefore went out, spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in, as John himself says.

Thus it happened that Peter too was inside, in the courtyard, as the other Evangelists say.

### 20

The chief priests and the entire council, as Matthew says, were seeking false testimony against Jesus so that they might put him to death, and they did not find any, although many false witnesses had come forward.

Their testimonies did not agree, as Mark says when he recounts the same event.

Finally two false witnesses came, as Matthew says, and declared: “This man said, ‘I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days’” (Matt. 26:57–68).

[Note: [Col. 1169] Most manuscripts have *aedificare* (“to build”), in accordance with the Greek, οἰκοδομῆσαι (“to build”).]

Mark also reports others as saying: “We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple made with hands, and after three days I will build another not made with hands.’” Therefore their testimony was not consistent, as Mark himself says in the same passage.

The chief priest rose and said to him: “Do you make no answer to what these men testify against you?”

But Jesus remained silent.

The chief priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.”

Jesus said to him: “You have said it.” This is Matthew’s account.

Mark says the same thing in different words, except that he does not mention the chief priest’s adjuration; but he shows that Jesus’ “You have said it” has the same force as “I am.”

For he continues, as Mark says: “But Jesus said to him, ‘I am. And you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.’”

Matthew also says this, but does not state that Jesus answered, “I am.”

Then the chief priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses?” Matthew records this and continues:

“Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?”

They answered: “He is liable to death.”

Mark also testifies to this.

Matthew then continues: “Then they spat in his face and struck him with blows. Others slapped his face, saying: ‘Prophesy to us, Christ. Who is the one who struck you?’”

Mark says this too; he also records that they covered his face.

Luke likewise bears witness to these events.

### 21

The Lord is understood to have suffered these things until morning in the house of the chief priest, to which he had first been brought; there Peter too was put to the test.

But the Evangelists do not all narrate Peter’s testing, which occurred amid these insults to the Lord, in the same order.

Matthew and Mark first report the insults and then Peter’s testing. Luke, however, explains Peter’s testing first and only afterward the insults to the Lord.

John begins by recounting Peter’s testing, inserts certain events concerning the Lord’s insults, and adds that from there he was sent to Caiaphas the high priest. Then John returns to the beginning and explains the testing of Peter which he had begun in the house to which Jesus was first brought; afterward he returns to the sequence in which Jesus was led to Caiaphas.

### 22

Matthew therefore continues:

“Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard, and a servant girl came to him, saying: ‘You also were with Jesus the Galilean.’

“But he denied it before everyone, saying: ‘I do not know what you are saying.’

“As he went out through the gate, another servant girl saw him and said to those who were there: ‘This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene.’

“And again he denied it with an oath: ‘I do not know the man.’

“After a little while those who were standing there came and said to Peter: ‘Truly, you also are one of them, for your speech makes you evident.’

“Then he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man. And immediately the cock crowed.”

This is Matthew’s account.

It is understood that, after he had gone outside, once he had already denied him, the cock crowed for the first time—a detail Matthew omits but Mark reports.

### 23

Peter did not deny him a second time outside before the gate, but after he had returned to the fire. It was unnecessary to mention when he returned.

Mark therefore narrates it as follows:

“He went out into the forecourt, and the cock crowed. When the servant girl saw him again, she began to say to those standing around: ‘This man is one of them.’

“But he denied it again.”

This servant girl was not the same one but another, as Matthew says.

It is also understood that, in the second denial, he was challenged by two people: by the servant girl mentioned by Matthew and Mark, and by another person whom Luke mentions.

Luke narrates it thus:

“Peter was following from a distance. When a fire had been kindled in the middle of the courtyard and they had sat around it, Peter was sitting among them. When a certain servant girl saw him sitting by the light and had looked closely at him, she said: ‘This man also was with him.’

“But he denied him, saying: ‘Woman, I do not know him.’

“After a little while another man saw him and said: ‘You also are one of them.’”

When Luke says, “After a little while,” Peter had already gone out through the gate, and the first cock had crowed; he had then returned, so that, as John says, standing by the fire, he might deny him again.

In his account of Peter’s first denial, John omits not only the first cockcrow, as the others do except Mark, but also the fact that the servant girl recognized him while he was sitting by the fire.

John says only this:

“The doorkeeper servant girl therefore said to Peter: ‘Are you also one of this man’s disciples?’

“He said: ‘I am not.’”

Then John inserts the events which took place with Jesus in the same house and which he thought should be mentioned, narrating them thus:

“Now the servants and attendants were standing around a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were warming themselves. Peter was also with them, standing and warming himself.”

Here it is understood that Peter had already gone outside and returned. At first he had been sitting by the fire; afterward, when he returned, he had begun to stand.

### 24

But perhaps someone may say: He had not yet gone out; rather, he had risen in order to go out. This could be maintained by someone who thinks that he denied the second time outside before the gate.

Let us therefore examine what follows in John:

“The high priest therefore questioned Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching.

“Jesus answered him: ‘I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews gather, and I have spoken nothing in secret. Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I said.’

“When he had said these things, one of the attendants standing nearby struck Jesus on the face, saying: ‘Is that how you answer the high priest?’

“Jesus answered him: ‘If I have spoken wrongly, testify concerning the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?’

“And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.”

This clearly shows that Annas was a high priest. For Jesus had not yet been sent to Caiaphas when the attendant said to him, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”

Luke also mentions these two high priests, Annas and Caiaphas, at the beginning of his Gospel (Luke 3:2).

After saying this, John returns to what he had begun concerning Peter’s denial—that is, to the same house where the events he narrated had taken place, and from which Jesus was sent to Caiaphas, to whom he had been led from the beginning, as Matthew said.

John had inserted these events and now, recapitulating what concerned Peter and returning to that narrative, speaks in such a way as to complete the threefold denial:

“Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. They therefore said to him: ‘Are you also one of his disciples?’

“He denied it and said: ‘I am not.’”

Here, then, we find that Peter denied a second time not outside before the gate, but standing by the fire inside the courtyard. This could not have happened unless he had already returned after going outside.

For he had not merely remained outside, where another servant girl saw him. Rather, when he went out, she saw him—that is, when he rose to go out, she noticed him and said to those who were there, meaning those who were together inside in the courtyard by the fire: “This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene.”

The man who had gone outside, hearing this, returned and, when they challenged him, swore: “I do not know the man.”

For Mark says the same concerning this servant girl: “She began to say to those standing around: ‘This man is one of them.’”

She was not speaking to him but to those who had remained there when he went out, though in such a way that he heard her. Hence, returning and standing again by the fire, he persisted in denying their words.

Then, when John says, “They said, ‘Are you also one of his disciples?’” we understand this to have been said to him when he had returned and was standing there.

This is also confirmed by the fact that not only the other servant girl whom Matthew and Mark mention in connection with the second denial, but also the other man whom Luke mentions, challenged Peter. Hence John says, “They therefore said to him.”

Accordingly, either, after the servant girl said to those who were with her in the courtyard, as Peter was going out, “This man is one of them,” he returned upon hearing it in order to clear himself, by denying it; or—and this is more credible—he did not hear what was said about him as he went out, and, after he returned, the servant girl and the other man whom Luke mentions said to him, “Are you also one of his disciples?” and he replied, “I am not.”

Then the man whom Luke mentions persisted and said, “You also are one of them,” to whom Peter replied, “Man, I am not.”

Nevertheless, when all the Evangelists’ testimony concerning this matter is compared, it is clearly established that Peter did not deny a second time outside before the gate, but inside in the courtyard by the fire.

Matthew and Mark, who mentioned that he went outside, omitted his return for the sake of brevity.

### 25

Let us now examine the agreement among the accounts concerning the third denial, which we have already remembered that Matthew alone explained. Mark follows and says:

> “And after a little while those who stood by again said to Peter, ‘Truly you are one of them, for you are also a Galilean.’ But he began to curse and to swear, ‘I do not know this man whom you speak of.’ And immediately the cock crowed a second time.”

Luke, following the same account, narrates it thus:

> “And after an interval of about one hour, another man insisted, saying, ‘Truly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.’ And Peter said, ‘Man, I do not know what you are saying.’ And immediately, while he was still speaking, the cock crowed.”

John, following the account of Peter’s third denial, explains it thus:

> “One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said, ‘Did I not see you in the garden with him?’ Peter therefore denied again, and immediately the cock crowed.”

Thus, what Matthew and Mark mean by “after a little while,” namely how long this interval was, Luke makes clear by saying, “After an interval of about one hour.” John, however, says nothing about this interval.

Likewise, Matthew and Mark speak not in the singular but in the plural of those who were dealing with Peter, whereas Luke speaks of one man and John likewise of one man, identifying him as the relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off. It is easy to understand either that Matthew and Mark used the plural instead of the singular, as is customary in speech, or that one man—especially as someone who knew Peter and had seen him—made the assertion, while the others, following his lead, pressed Peter along with him. Hence the two Evangelists used the plural number by way of abbreviation, whereas the other two wished to designate only the man who was foremost in the matter.

Now Matthew says that Peter himself was told, “Truly you also are one of them, for your speech makes you evident,” just as John maintains that the same Peter was told, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?” Mark, however, says that they spoke among themselves about Peter: “Truly he is one of them, for he is also a Galilean” [Note: It may be read, “But Mark, in certain manuscripts, says that they spoke among themselves,” and so forth. For shortly before, Augustine quoted this very passage from Mark in the same form as in the sacred Scriptures: “They said to Peter, ‘Truly you are one of them,’” and so forth. In that wording, they are reported as speaking not among themselves about Peter but to Peter himself.]. Luke likewise says not to Peter but about Peter: “Another man insisted, saying, ‘Truly this man also was with him, for he is also a Galilean.’”

We may understand that those who are said to have addressed Peter held the same meaning; for what was said about him in his presence had the same force as if it had been said to him. Or, alternatively, both forms of speech may have occurred, with some Evangelists remembering one form and others the other.

We understand that the cock crow occurred after the third denial, as Mark expressly states.

### 26

Matthew then follows, saying:

> “And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which he had said: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ And he went outside and wept bitterly.”

Mark says:

> “Peter remembered the word that Jesus had said to him: ‘Before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times.’ And he began to weep.”

Luke says:

> “And the Lord, turning, looked at Peter; and Peter remembered the word of the Lord, as he had said: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ And going outside, Peter wept bitterly.”

John says nothing about Peter’s remembrance and weeping.

What Luke says—that the Lord, turning, looked at Peter—must be considered more carefully. Although inner courts are also spoken of, Peter was in the outer court among the servants, who were warming themselves together at the fire. It is not credible that the Lord could be heard there by the Jews, so that this look could have been a physical one.

For after Matthew had said:

> “Then they spat in his face and struck him with blows; others slapped him in the face, saying, ‘Prophesy to us, Christ! Who is it that struck you?’”

he continued:

> “But Peter was sitting outside in the court.”

He would not have said this unless those things were being done with the Lord inside. And from Mark’s account it appears that they were being done not only in the inner parts of the house but also in its upper rooms. For after Mark had narrated such things, he continued:

> “And while Peter was below in the court…”

Just as Matthew’s statement, “But Peter was sitting outside in the court,” shows that those things were taking place inside, so Mark’s statement, “And while Peter was below in the court,” shows that what he had described was happening not only in the inner parts but also in the upper rooms [Col. 1173].

How, then, did the Lord look at Peter with a physical face? It seems to me that this look occurred by divine action, so that Peter was reminded how often he had already denied him and what the Lord had foretold to him. Thus, when the Lord looked upon him mercifully, Peter repented and wept for his salvation.

This is like our daily saying, “Lord, look upon me,” and saying of someone who has been delivered from danger or trouble by divine mercy, “The Lord looked upon him.” Likewise Scripture says, “Look upon me and hear me” (Ps. 12:4), and, “Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul” (Ps. 6:5). So, I think, it was said: “The Lord, turning, looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord.”

Finally, although the Evangelists usually more often say “Jesus” than “Lord” in their narratives, Luke here says “Lord”: “The Lord, turning, looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord.” Matthew and Mark, because they say nothing about this looking, say that he remembered not the word of the Lord but the word of Jesus. From this too we may understand that the look came from Jesus, not through human eyes but by divine action.

## CHAPTER VII  
### Concerning what happened in the morning before he was handed over to Pilate, how the Evangelists do not disagree among themselves; and concerning the testimony of Jeremiah which Matthew inserted because of the Lord’s price, although it is not found in the Scripture of that prophet

### 27

Matthew then follows and says:

> “When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus in order to put him to death. And having bound him, they led him away and handed him over to the governor Pontius Pilate” (Matt. 27:1–10).

Mark similarly says:

> “And immediately, when morning came, the chief priests, after taking counsel with the elders and scribes and the whole council, bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate” (Mark 15:1).

After Luke had finished narrating Peter’s denial, he recapitulated what had happened with the Lord, evidently now around morning, and connected his narrative as follows:

> “And the men who held him mocked him, beating him; and they covered him and struck his face, asking him, ‘Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?’ And blaspheming him in many other ways, they spoke against him. And when day came, the elders of the people and the chief priests and scribes gathered, and they led him into their council, saying, ‘If you are the Christ, tell us.’ And he said to them, ‘If I tell you, you will not believe me; and if I ask you, you will not answer me or release me. But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.’ Then they all said, ‘Are you therefore the Son of God?’ He said to them, ‘You say that I am.’ And they said, ‘What further testimony do we need? For we ourselves have heard it from his mouth.’ And the whole assembly of them rose and led him to Pilate” (Luke 22:63–23:1).

Luke narrated all these things. Here we understand that Matthew and Mark also narrated that the Lord was asked whether he was the Son of God and that he said, “I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power” [Note: The printed editions have “of the power of God.” Yet in the manuscripts we do not find the word “God” here [Col. 1174], nor is it represented in the ancient Corbie Bibles, whether in the Vulgate version of Matthew 26:64 or of Mark 14:62. In those passages it is also absent from the Greek text.], “and coming on the clouds of heaven.” This happened when day was already dawning, at the time when Luke says, “And when day came.” Thus Luke narrates similar events, although he also records something that the others omitted.

We understand that during the night the Lord was dealt with through false witnesses. Matthew and Mark briefly mentioned this, whereas Luke omitted it, since he narrated what happened around morning. Those two Evangelists—Matthew and Mark—connected their account of what was done with the Lord up to morning; but afterward they returned to narrating Peter’s denial. When that was completed, they returned to the morning, so that from there they might connect the remaining matters, until they carried forward their account of what had been done with the Lord, though they had not yet mentioned what had occurred in the morning [Note: In seven manuscripts, *perduxerant* (“had carried forward”).] (Matt. 26:59–75; Mark 14:55–72).

John also, after having recalled as much as he thought appropriate of what had been done with the Lord, and after recounting Peter’s entire denial, says:

> “So they led Jesus from Caiaphas into the praetorium. It was morning” (John 18:28).

Here we may understand either that there was some reason which compelled Caiaphas to be in the praetorium and prevented him from being present while the other chief priests were examining the Lord, or that there was a praetorium in his house [Note: The difficulty of this reading—apparently preserved from a corrupt exemplar—is addressed by noting that in the sacred Scriptures we read not “to Caiaphas” but “from Caiaphas,” Greek *apò toû Kaïpha*, as is discussed again in John, Tractate 114.]. Nevertheless, he was led to Caiaphas at the beginning and was brought before him at the end. But since they were now bringing him as one already convicted, and since Caiaphas had previously decided that Jesus should die, there was no delay before he was handed over to Pilate to be killed.

Matthew therefore narrates what was done with the Lord through Pilate as follows.

### 28

First he digresses to recall the end of Judas the betrayer, which he alone narrated, saying:

> “Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, repented and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, ‘I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.’ But they said, ‘What is that to us? You see to it.’ And throwing the silver pieces into the temple, he departed; and going away, he hanged himself. But the chief priests, taking the silver pieces, said, ‘It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.’ After taking counsel, they bought with them the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners. For this reason that field has been called *Acheldemach*, that is, ‘Field of Blood,’ to this day. Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: ‘And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one whose price was set by the sons of Israel’ [Note: In the sacred Scriptures: “by the sons of Israel.”], ‘and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me.’”

### 29

If anyone is troubled because this testimony is not found in the writing of the prophet Jeremiah, and therefore thinks that something is to be detracted from the Evangelist’s credibility, let him first know that not all copies of the Gospels have the words “spoken through Jeremiah,” but only “through the prophet.”

We may therefore say that those copies should rather be believed which do not contain the name Jeremiah. For this was spoken through the prophet Zechariah; hence the copies containing the name Jeremiah are thought to be erroneous, since they ought either to have contained the name Zechariah or no name at all, as in certain copies, but only “through the prophet who says”—meaning, of course, Zechariah.

Let whoever wishes make use of this defense. But this is why it does not satisfy me: more copies contain the name Jeremiah, and those who have examined the Gospel more carefully in the Greek copies report that they found it so in the more ancient Greek manuscripts. There was no reason for this name to be added and thereby produce an error; but there certainly was a reason for it to be removed from some copies—namely, the bold ignorance of those who, being troubled by the question of why this testimony was not found in Jeremiah, removed it.

### 30

What, then, are we to understand except that this occurred according to the more secret counsel of God’s providence, by which the minds of the Evangelists were governed?

It could have happened that, while Matthew was composing the Gospel, Jeremiah came to mind instead of Zechariah, as often happens. Yet Matthew would undoubtedly have corrected this, at least after being warned by others who could have read it while he was still alive, unless he considered that, since his memory was governed by the Holy Spirit, the name of one prophet had come to him in place of another not without reason, but because the Lord had determined that it should be written in this way.

Why, then, did the Lord determine this? The first and most useful reason should readily occur to us: it was thereby indicated that all the holy Prophets, speaking by one Spirit, agree with one another in wondrous harmony. Their unity is even greater than if everything spoken by all the Prophets had been uttered through the mouth of one person. Therefore everything that the Holy Spirit spoke through them must be accepted without hesitation; each statement belongs to all of them, and all belong to each.

Since what was spoken through Jeremiah belongs as much to Zechariah as to Jeremiah, and what was spoken through Zechariah belongs as much to Jeremiah as to Zechariah, why should Matthew have corrected himself after reading that he had written one name in place of another? Why should he not rather have followed the authority of the Holy Spirit—by whom he certainly felt his mind was governed more than we do—and leave the passage written as the Lord, by admonishing him, had determined it should be written? The purpose was to teach us that there is such harmony among the Prophets in their words that we may properly, indeed most appropriately, assign to Jeremiah what we find spoken through Zechariah.

For if today someone, wishing to report the words of a particular person, were to give the name of another person who had not spoken them [Note: In almost all manuscripts: “who had spoken them.”], but who was the closest friend and most intimate associate of the person whose words he intended to report; and if, immediately remembering that he had named one person instead of the other, he gathered himself and corrected himself but nevertheless said, “I spoke correctly”—what else would he be considering except that there was such harmony between the two, between the person whose words he intended to report and the other whose name came to him in place of the first, that this other person’s having said it was equivalent to the first person’s having said it?

How much more, then, should this be understood and emphasized concerning the holy Prophets, so that we might receive all their books as one book belonging to one author, in which no discrepancy of content is believed to exist, just as none is found, and in which the consistency of truth is greater than it would be if a single, however learned, person had spoken everything?

Therefore, the argument which unbelievers or ignorant people try to draw from this, as though it demonstrated disagreement among the holy Evangelists, should rather be taken up by the faithful and learned as demonstrating the unity even of the holy Prophets [Col. 1176].

### 31

There is another reason as well, which seems to me to require fuller treatment at another time, lest we extend the discussion beyond what the need to complete this work permits: why the name Jeremiah was allowed to remain in this testimony of Zechariah—or rather, why the authority of the Holy Spirit commanded that it remain.

In Jeremiah it is written that he bought a field from the son of his brother and gave him silver for it—not indeed under the designation of the price given by Zechariah, the thirty pieces of silver. Nevertheless, the purchase of a field is not mentioned by Zechariah. That the Evangelist interpreted the prophecy concerning the thirty pieces of silver as referring to what has now been fulfilled concerning the Lord, so that this was his price, is evident.

But that the matter also concerns what Jeremiah said about the purchased field could be signified mystically by the fact that the name placed here is not Zechariah’s—the prophet who spoke of the thirty pieces of silver—but Jeremiah’s, who spoke of the purchased field. Thus, when the Gospel has been read and the name Jeremiah found, and Jeremiah has then been read without finding the testimony about the thirty pieces of silver but with the purchased field nevertheless discovered, the reader is prompted to compare the two and to unfold from them the meaning of the prophecy and how it relates to what was fulfilled in the Lord.

For the statement Matthew added to this testimony—“which the sons of Israel priced, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me”—is found neither in Zechariah nor in Jeremiah. Therefore it should rather be understood as having been elegantly and mystically inserted in the person of the Evangelist, because through the Lord’s revelation he learned that this kind of prophecy belonged to the event concerning the price of Christ.

At Jeremiah’s command, the deed of the purchased field was to be placed in an earthen vessel (Jer. 32:9–44). Here the potter’s field is bought with the Lord’s price, and this is done as a burial place for foreigners—as a dwelling place of rest for those who, journeying as foreigners in this world, are buried with Christ through Baptism.

For Jeremiah also says that the Lord declared that the purchase of the field signified this: there would be a permanent dwelling in that land for those released from captivity.

I have set these matters out as if they were to be sketched [Note: Four manuscripts read “sampled” or “tasted”] when I urged consideration of what should be sought more carefully and attentively in these prophetic testimonies, brought together and compared with the Gospel narrative.

Matthew inserted these things concerning Judas the betrayer.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### Concerning what happened before Pilate, and how the Evangelists do not disagree with one another

### 32

Then Matthew continues and says:

> “Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying, ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’ Jesus said to him, ‘You say so.’ And while he was being accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Then Pilate said to him, ‘Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?’ And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor was greatly amazed.
>
> “Now on the solemn day the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner whom they wished. At that time they had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. Therefore, when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, ‘Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?’ For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy.
>
> “While he was sitting on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying, ‘Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for today I have suffered many things in a dream because of him.’
>
> “But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus. The governor answered and said to them, ‘Which of the two do you want me to release for you?’ They said, ‘Barabbas.’ Pilate said to them, ‘What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?’ They all said, ‘Let him be crucified.’ The governor said, ‘Why, what evil has he done?’ But they cried out all the more, saying, ‘Let him be crucified.’
>
> “When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that the tumult was increasing, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, ‘I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you will see to it.’ And the whole people answered, saying, ‘His blood be upon us and upon our children.’
>
> “Then he released Barabbas to them; but Jesus, after scourging him, he handed over to them to be crucified.”

Matthew narrated these events concerning the Lord before Pilate (Matt. 27:11–26).

### 33

Mark also agrees with him in almost the same words and events. He reports Pilate’s words to the people who were asking that, according to the custom of the feast, one prisoner be released, as follows:

> “But Pilate answered them and said, ‘Do you want me to release to you the king of the Jews?’”

Matthew says:

> “Therefore, when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, ‘Whom do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?’”

There is no question that Mark omits their request that someone be released to them. But one may ask what words Pilate spoke: whether those reported by Matthew or those reported by Mark. “Whom do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” seems one thing, and “Do you want me to release to you the king of the Jews?” another.

But since the Jews called kings “christs,” and since the man who said “this one or that one” clearly asked whether they wanted the king of the Jews—that is, the Christ—to be released to them, there is no difference in meaning. Mark omitted Barabbas because he wished to say only what concerned the Lord. Nevertheless, in their response he sufficiently shows whom they wanted released. “The chief priests,” he says, “stirred up the crowd so that he would release Barabbas to them.”

He then continues:

> “But Pilate again answered and said to them, ‘What then do you want me to do with the king of the Jews?’”

It is therefore sufficiently apparent that Mark wishes to convey by saying “the king of the Jews” what Matthew conveys by saying “Christ.” For kings were not called christs except among the Jews. Matthew likewise says in this passage:

> “Pilate said to them, ‘What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?’”

Mark therefore continues:

> “But they cried out again, ‘Crucify him!’”

This corresponds to Matthew’s, “They all said, ‘Let him be crucified.’”

Mark continues:

> “But Pilate said to them, ‘Why, what evil has he done?’ And they cried out all the more, ‘Crucify him!’”

Matthew did not say this. But since Matthew said, “When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that the tumult was increasing,” and also said that he washed his hands before the people in order to signify his innocence of the righteous man’s blood, while Mark and the others omit this, Matthew sufficiently shows that the governor also dealt with the people so that Jesus might be released.

Mark briefly signified this when he reports that Pilate said, “Why, what evil has he done?” He then concludes his account of what was done with the Lord before Pilate as follows:

> “But Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas to them and handed Jesus over, after he had been scourged, to be crucified.”

Mark narrated these events before the governor (Mark 15:2–15).

### 34

Luke narrates what happened before Pilate as follows:

> “They began to accuse him, saying, ‘We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding the payment of taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.’”

The other two Evangelists did not say this, although they did say that he was accused. Luke therefore also disclosed the very charges they falsely brought against him.

He omitted what Pilate said to him: “Do you answer nothing? See how many things they accuse you of.” But he clearly continues and says what the others also said:

> “Pilate questioned him, saying, ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’ And he answered him, ‘You say so.’”

Matthew and Mark recalled this before saying that Jesus was addressed while he did not answer those accusing him.

The truth is not affected by the order in which Luke reported these things, just as it is not affected when one Evangelist omits something another records. Luke continues:

> “Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, ‘I find no cause in this man.’ But they insisted, saying, ‘He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee even to this place.’
>
> “When Pilate heard of Galilee, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem in those days.
>
> “When Herod saw Jesus, he rejoiced greatly, for he had wanted for a long time to see him, because he had heard many things about him, and he hoped to see some sign performed by him. He questioned him with many words, but he answered him nothing. The chief priests and scribes also stood there, persistently accusing him.
>
> “Herod despised him, together with his soldiers, and mocked him, clothing him in a white garment, and sent him back to Pilate. And Herod and Pilate became friends with one another on that very day, for previously they had been enemies.”

All these things—namely, that the Lord was sent from Pilate to Herod and what happened there—Luke alone records, even though he says something similar that may be found in other parts of the other narratives. The others wished to relate only what happened before Pilate, up to the point when the Lord was handed over to be crucified.

Luke therefore returns to what was happening before the governor, from which he had digressed in order to narrate what had happened before Herod, and continues:

> “Pilate, having summoned the chief priests and the rulers and the people, said to them, ‘You brought me this man as one who was turning the people away; and behold, having examined him in your presence, I found in this man none of the charges of which you accuse him. Nor did Herod; for I sent you to him, and behold, nothing deserving death has been done by him. Therefore, having chastised him, I will release him.’
>
> “Now he was obliged to release one to them at the feast. But the whole crowd cried out together, saying, ‘Take this man away, and release Barabbas to us’—a man who, because of a certain uprising that had occurred in the city and because of murder, had been sent into prison.
>
> “Pilate spoke to them again, wishing to release Jesus. But they shouted back, saying, ‘Crucify him, crucify him!’ He said to them a third time, ‘Why, what evil has this man done? I find no cause of death in him. Therefore I will chastise him and release him.’ But they pressed him with loud cries, demanding that he be crucified, and their voices prevailed.”

Matthew attested in very few words to this effort by Pilate, by which he repeatedly dealt with them in his desire to release Jesus, when he says:

> “When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that the tumult was increasing…”

He would not have said this unless Pilate had made great efforts, although he did not say how many times he had attempted to rescue Jesus from their fury.

Luke therefore concludes his account of what happened before the governor as follows:

> “And Pilate pronounced sentence that their request should be granted. He released to them the man who, because of murder and rebellion, had been sent into prison and whom they had requested; but he handed Jesus over to their will” (Luke 23:2–25).

### 35

Let us now consider the same events according to John—that is, what was done through Pilate.

> “They themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover. Therefore Pilate went out to them and said, ‘What accusation do you bring against this man?’ They answered and said to him, ‘If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.’”

We must see to it that this is not contrary to what Luke says: that definite charges were brought against him. Luke states what they were:

> “They began to accuse him, saying, ‘We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding the payment of taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.’”

In John’s account, however, the Jews seem unwilling to state the charges when Pilate said to them, “What accusation do you bring against this man?” For they answered:

> “If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.”

They apparently wished Pilate, following their authority, to stop asking what was being charged against him, and to believe him guilty merely because he had deserved to be handed over to Pilate by them.

We must therefore understand that both statements were made: this one and the one Luke records. Many things were said and many answers given; each Evangelist selected from them as much as seemed appropriate and included in his narrative what he judged sufficient. John himself also says certain things that were brought against him, which we shall examine in their proper places.

He therefore continues:

> “Pilate said to them, ‘Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.’ The Jews therefore said to him, ‘It is not lawful for us to kill anyone’—so that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what death he was going to die.
>
> “Pilate therefore entered the praetorium again, called Jesus, and said to him, ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’ Jesus answered, ‘Do you say this of your own accord, or have others told you about me?’”

This might appear not to agree with what the others report—“Jesus answered, ‘You say so’”—unless John subsequently shows that this too was said. Thus he shows that the words he now records were omitted by the other Evangelists rather than not spoken by the Lord.

Consider what follows:

> “Pilate answered, ‘Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests handed you over to me. What have you done?’ Jesus answered, ‘My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here.’
>
> “Pilate therefore said to him, ‘So you are a king?’ Jesus answered, ‘You say that I am a king.’”

Here we reach the point recorded by the other Evangelists. John then continues with words of the Lord which the others omit:

> “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.”

Pilate said to him:

> “What is truth?”

After saying this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them:

> “I find no cause in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man to you at the Passover. Do you want me, therefore, to release to you the king of the Jews?”

They all cried out again, saying:

> “Not this man, but Barabbas!”

Now Barabbas was a robber.

> “Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him. And the soldiers, weaving a crown of thorns, placed it on his head and clothed him in a purple garment. They came up to him and said, ‘Hail, king of the Jews!’ and they struck him with slaps.
>
> “Pilate went out again and said to them, ‘Behold, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no cause in him.’ Jesus therefore went out, bearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment, and Pilate said to them, ‘Behold the man!’
>
> “When the chief priests and the servants saw him, they cried out, saying, ‘Crucify, crucify!’”

[Note: The printed editions add “him,” but this word is absent from the manuscripts and from the ancient Corbie Bibles, nor is it found in the Greek. We have therefore removed it, as well as certain other small words, especially where the printed editions did not consistently or universally preserve them despite the repetition of the same sentence, on the authority of the ancient copies.]

Pilate said to them:

> “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no cause in him.”

The Jews answered him:

> “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

This may correspond to what Luke records among the Jews’ accusations:

> “We found this man subverting our nation,”

with the addition:

> “because he made himself the Son of God.”

John therefore continues:

> “When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid. And he entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus, ‘Where are you from?’ But Jesus gave him no answer. Pilate therefore said to him, ‘Will you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you and authority to release you?’ Jesus answered, ‘You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.’
>
> “From that point Pilate sought to release him. But the Jews cried out, saying, ‘If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.’”

This can correspond to what Luke narrates in the same account of the Jews’ accusation. After they had said, “We found him subverting our nation,” Luke added:

> “and forbidding the payment of taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.”

This resolves the question that might have led one to think John said that the Jews brought no charge against the Lord when they answered him:

> “If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.”

John then continues:

> “When Pilate heard these words, he led Jesus outside and sat down on the tribunal in the place called the Stone Pavement, in Hebrew *Gabbatha*. It was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour. And he said to the Jews, ‘Behold your king!’ But they cried out, ‘Take him away, take him away, crucify him!’ Pilate said to them, ‘Shall I crucify your king?’ The chief priests answered, ‘We have no king but Caesar.’ Then he handed him over to them to be crucified.”

John narrated these events concerning what was done with the Lord through Pilate (John 18:28–19:16).

## CHAPTER IX  
### Concerning the mockery inflicted on him by Pilate’s cohort, and how Matthew, Mark, and John, the three who report it, do not disagree among themselves
36. It now remains for us to examine the Lord’s Passion according to the testimony of the four Evangelists. Matthew begins it as follows:

“Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the praetorium and gathered the whole cohort around him. They stripped him and put a scarlet cloak around him; and plaiting a crown of thorns, they placed it on his head, and a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’” (Matt. 27:27–31).

Mark says this at the same point in his narrative:

“But the soldiers led him inside the courtyard of the praetorium and called together the whole cohort. They clothed him in purple and put on him a plaited crown of thorns. They began to salute him, ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ They struck his head with a reed, spat upon him, and, kneeling, worshiped him” (Mark 15:16–20).

Thus Matthew’s statement, “They put a scarlet cloak around him,” is understood to be what Mark expressed by saying that they clothed him in purple. For that cloak, used by the mockers in place of royal purple, was scarlet, a kind of red-purple very similar to crimson. It is also possible that Mark mentioned the purple color that the cloak possessed, although it was scarlet. Luke omitted this. John, however, before saying that Pilate handed him over to be crucified, mentions it as follows:

“Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him. And the soldiers, plaiting a crown of thorns, placed it on his head and wrapped him in a purple garment. They came up to him and said, ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ and they struck him with their hands” (John 19:1–3).

It is therefore evident that Matthew and Mark mentioned this by way of recapitulation, not [Col. 1182] as something that happened after Pilate had already handed him over to be crucified. For John clearly says that these things were done while he was still before Pilate; consequently, the others recalled what they had passed over.

This also concerns what Matthew says next:

“They spat upon him, took the reed, and struck his head. And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak, put his own clothes on him, and led him away to crucify him.”

The stripping of the cloak and putting on of his own clothes is understood to have happened at the end, when he was already being led away. Mark says this as follows:

“And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple garment and put his own clothes on him.”

## CHAPTER X  
### How Matthew, Mark, and Luke do not contradict John when they say that someone was compelled to carry his cross, while John says that Jesus himself carried it

37. Matthew continues:

“As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon. They compelled him to carry his cross” (Matt. 27:32).

Mark likewise says:

“And they lead him out to crucify him. They compel a passerby, a certain Simon of Cyrene, coming from the countryside—the father of Alexander and Rufus—to carry his cross” (Mark 15:20–21).

Luke says:

“And as they led him away, they seized a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming from the countryside, and laid the cross upon him to carry behind Jesus” (Luke 23:26).

John, however, narrates:

“They took Jesus and led him out. And carrying the cross for himself, he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull, in Hebrew Golgotha, where they crucified him” (John 19:16–18).

This indicates that he himself was carrying the cross when he went out to the place just mentioned. But that Simon was compelled along the way is what the other three commemorate; the cross was subsequently given to him to carry as far as the place of execution. Thus we find that both events occurred: first what John said, and afterward what the other three reported.

## CHAPTER XI  
### Concerning the drink given to him before his crucifixion was mentioned, and how Matthew and Mark agree

38. Matthew continues:

“And they came to a place called Golgotha, which means the Place of the Skull.” On this place they agree with complete clarity. Matthew then adds:

“And they gave him wine to drink mixed with gall; and when he had tasted it, he would not drink” (Matt. 27:33–34).

Mark narrates this as follows:

“And they offered him wine flavored with myrrh; but he did not accept it” (Mark 15:23).

Matthew’s phrase “mixed with gall” is to be understood as referring to bitterness, for he used “gall” as a term for bitterness. Wine flavored with myrrh is extremely bitter, although it is also possible that both gall and myrrh made the wine exceedingly bitter.

When Mark says, “He did not accept it,” this is understood to mean that he did not accept it in order to drink it. He did taste it, as Matthew testifies. Thus Matthew’s statement, “He would not drink,” is expressed by Mark as “He did not accept it,” while Mark passes over the fact that he tasted it.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Concerning the division of his garments, and how all the Evangelists agree

[Col. 1183]

39. Matthew continues:

“After they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots, and sitting there they kept watch over him” (Matt. 27:35–36).

[Note: Here Augustine silently passes over the words found in the Vulgate version, “so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘They divided my garments among themselves,’” and Nicolaus of Lyra long ago observed that these words are absent from the ancient books and, according to Jerome, do not belong to Matthew’s text. They are nevertheless found in the old Corbie Bibles.]

Mark says the same thing:

“And crucifying him, they divided his garments, casting lots over them to determine what each should take” (Mark 15:24).

Luke says:

“And dividing his garments, they cast lots; and the people stood watching” (Luke 23:34–35).

The three have stated this briefly. John, however, explains more distinctly how it happened:

“So the soldiers, when they had crucified him, took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier, and also the tunic. Now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout. Therefore they said to one another, ‘Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be,’ so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, saying, ‘They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots’” (John 19:23–24).

## CHAPTER XIII  
### Concerning the hour of the Lord’s Passion, and how Mark and John do not disagree over the third and sixth hours

40. Matthew continues:
