“And they placed above his head the charge against him, written: ‘This is Jesus, the King of the Jews’” (Matt. 27:37).

Before saying this, Mark says:

“Now it was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark 15:25).

He adds this after speaking of the division of the garments. The matter must be considered with the greatest care, lest it produce a serious error. Some suppose that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, and that darkness began from the sixth hour and lasted until the ninth, so that three hours are understood to have elapsed between his crucifixion and the beginning of the darkness.

This could indeed be understood quite correctly, unless John said that, at about the sixth hour, Pilate sat on the tribunal at the place called the Lithostrotos, and in Hebrew Gabbatha. He continues:

“Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour, and he says to the Jews, ‘Behold your king.’ But they cried out, ‘Take him away, take him away, crucify him!’ Pilate says to them, ‘Shall I crucify your king?’ The chief priests answered, ‘We have no king except Caesar.’ Then he handed him over to them to be crucified” (John 19:13–16).

If, then, at about the sixth hour, while Pilate was sitting on the tribunal, he was handed over to the Jews to be crucified, how was he crucified at the third hour, as some have supposed by failing to understand Mark’s words?

41. First, let us see at what hour he could have been crucified; afterward we shall see why Mark said that he was crucified at the third hour.

It was about the sixth hour when he was handed over for crucifixion by Pilate, who, as has been said, was sitting on the tribunal. It was not yet the full sixth hour, but approximately the sixth—that is, the fifth hour had been completed and something of the sixth had begun.

They would never say “five and a quarter,” “five and a third,” “five and a half,” or anything [Col. 1184] of that kind. For Scripture has this custom: it speaks of the whole by reference to a part, especially when indicating times. Thus, regarding those eight days after which they say that he ascended the mountain (Luke 9:28), Matthew and Mark, looking to the intervening days, said, “After six days” (Matt. 17:1; Mark 9:1).

This is especially clear because John spoke so carefully that he did not say “the sixth hour,” but “about the sixth hour.” If he had not spoken in this way, but had simply said “the sixth hour,” we could have understood him according to Scripture’s usual manner, as I have said, of referring to the whole by a part. In that case, after the fifth hour had been completed and the sixth had begun, the events narrated concerning the Lord’s crucifixion could have taken place, until the sixth hour was completed while he hung on the cross and darkness came. Matthew, Mark, and Luke all testify to this darkness (Matt. 27:45; Mark 15:33; Luke 23:44).

42. Let us now ask why Mark said, after mentioning that “those who crucified him divided his garments, casting lots over them to determine what each should take,” and then adding, “Now it was the third hour, and they crucified him.”

He had already said, “And crucifying him, they divided his garments” (Mark 15:24). The other Evangelists likewise testify that the garments were divided after he had been crucified. If Mark wished to indicate the time when this event occurred, it would have been enough to say, “Now it was the third hour.” Why did he add, “and they crucified him,” unless he wished to signify something by way of recapitulation—something that could be discovered when the Scripture was read at a time when the hour at which the Lord was suspended on the cross was known throughout the churches, so that either an error could be corrected or a falsehood refuted?

Since he knew that the Lord was suspended by the soldiers, not by the Jews, as John makes perfectly clear (John 19:23), he wished secretly to show that those who cried out for him to be crucified were more truly responsible for his crucifixion than those who, in the performance of their duty, rendered service to their ruler.

It is therefore understood that it was the third hour when the Jews cried out for the Lord to be crucified, and it is most truthfully demonstrated that they crucified him when they cried out. This is especially so because they did not want to appear to have done it themselves; for this reason they handed him over to Pilate, as their words sufficiently indicate according to John.

When Pilate had said to them, “‘What accusation do you bring against this man?’ they answered him, ‘If he were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you.’ Pilate therefore said to them, ‘Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.’ The Jews said to him, ‘It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death’” (John 18:29–31).

What they especially did not wish to appear to have done, Mark shows that they did at the third hour. He judged most truly that the Jews’ murderous tongue was more responsible for the Lord’s death than the soldiers’ hands.

43. Anyone who says that it was not the third hour when the Jews first cried out in this way shows himself to be madly hostile to the Gospel—unless perhaps he can resolve the question in some other way. For he has no means of proving that it was not then the third hour. Therefore one must believe the truthful Evangelist rather than the contentious suspicions of human beings.

“From where,” you ask, “do you prove that it was the third hour?”

I answer: because I believe [Col. 1185] the Evangelists.

If you also believe them, show how the Lord could have been crucified both at the sixth hour and at the third. John’s narrative compels us to acknowledge the sixth hour, while Mark mentions the third. If both of us believe them, show how both events could have occurred in another way, and I shall gladly rest satisfied. I do not love my own opinion, but the truth of the Gospel.

Would that others might discover further solutions to this question. Until that happens, use this one with me, if you please. If no other solution can be found, this one alone will suffice; if another can be found, we shall choose it once it has been demonstrated.

Only do not suppose that it follows that one of the four Evangelists lied, or that he erred at such a great and holy summit of authority.

44. If someone says that he proves it was not the third hour when the Jews cried out because, after Mark says, “But Pilate, answering again, said to them, ‘What then shall I do with the King of the Jews?’” and they again cried out, “Crucify him,” Mark inserts no delay in his narrative, but proceeds immediately to the point at which the Lord was handed over by Pilate for crucifixion—something John records as having occurred at about the sixth hour—let him understand that many events took place in between which Mark omitted.

During this interval Pilate was trying to rescue him from the Jews and was striving with the utmost persistence, by every means available to him, against their insane determination.

Matthew says:

“Pilate says to them, ‘What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?’ They all say, ‘Let him be crucified.’”

We say that it was then the third hour.

But Matthew continues:

“Pilate, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing, but rather that a riot was arising…”

We understand that two hours were consumed both in Pilate’s efforts to rescue the Lord and in the tumult of the Jews resisting those efforts. The sixth hour had begun, though it had not yet ended, when the events narrated from the moment Pilate handed over the Lord until the darkness began took place.

As for what Matthew mentioned earlier—“While he was sitting on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying, ‘Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him’” (Matt. 27:22–24, 19)—Pilate had sat on the tribunal later. But while narrating the earlier events, Matthew recalled what he had said about Pilate’s wife and wished to insert it there, where he judged it appropriate, in order to indicate the principal reason why Pilate did not wish to hand him over to the Jews even at the end.

45. Luke narrates that, after Pilate had said, “Having chastised him, therefore, I will release him,” the whole crowd cried out, “Take this man away, and release Barabbas for us.” Perhaps they had not yet said, “Crucify him.”

Again, according to Luke, Pilate spoke to them, wishing to release Jesus; but they shouted in response, saying, “Crucify, crucify him.” It is understood that this was then the third hour.

Luke continues:

“But he said to them a third time, ‘Why, what evil has this man done? I have found no cause of death in him. Therefore I will chastise him and release him.’ But they persisted with loud voices, demanding that he be crucified; and their [Col. 1186] voices prevailed” (Luke 23:16–23).

This itself sufficiently indicates that there was a great tumult. From the length of the delay before he said to them a third time, “Why, what evil has this man done?” one may understand how much time elapsed—enough for the truth to be investigated.

Afterward, when Luke says, “They persisted with loud voices, and their voices prevailed,” who does not see that this happened because they realized that Pilate did not wish to hand the Lord over to them? Since he strongly resisted doing so, he did not yield in a moment; rather, two hours and something more passed during his hesitation.

46. Ask John as well, and see how great was Pilate’s hesitation and refusal to undertake so shameful a service. John narrates these events much more fully [Note: Several manuscripts read “narrates more fully, although…” And below, instead of “Then, when he had scourged him,” manuscripts with broad agreement read, “Nevertheless, when he had scourged him.”], although he too certainly does not mention everything during which two hours and part of the sixth hour elapsed.

“Then, when he had scourged Jesus and permitted him to be mistreated by the soldiers in mock clothing and through many acts of mockery” (I believe he did this in the hope of calming their fury at least in this way, so that they would not continue raging all the way to death), “Pilate went out again and says to them, ‘Behold, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no cause in him.’ Jesus therefore came out wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. And he says to them, ‘Behold the man!’”

He hoped that they might be appeased when they saw him in that apparently disgraceful condition. But John adds:

“When therefore the chief priests and the attendants saw him, they cried out, saying, ‘Crucify, crucify him!’”

We say that this was then the third hour.

Consider what follows:

“Pilate says to them, ‘Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no cause in him.’ The Jews answered him, ‘We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.’ When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid. He entered the praetorium again and says to Jesus, ‘Where are you from?’ But Jesus gave him no answer. Therefore Pilate says to him, ‘Are you not speaking to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you, and authority to release you?’ Jesus answered, ‘You would have no authority against me unless it had been given you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.’ From that point Pilate was seeking to release him.”

How much time, then, do we suppose was consumed while Pilate was seeking to release him? How many things were omitted that were said either by Pilate or in opposition by the Jews, until they said something that moved him and caused him to yield?

The narrative continues:

“But the Jews cried out, saying, ‘If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.’

When Pilate heard these statements, he brought Jesus out and sat on the tribunal at the place called the Lithostrotos, and in Hebrew Gabbatha. Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour.”

From the Jews’ first cry, “Crucify him,” when it was the third hour, until Pilate sat on the tribunal, two hours had passed amid Pilate’s delays and the Jews’ agitation; the fifth hour had been completed and something of the sixth had begun.

He therefore says to the Jews, “Behold [Col. 1187] your king.”

But they cried out, “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!”

Yet Pilate was not already so shaken that he yielded easily through fear of accusation. At that time his wife had sent to him while he was sitting on the tribunal. Matthew, who alone mentions this, anticipated the event and inserted it before reaching that point in his narrative, placing it where he judged it appropriate.

Still trying to accomplish something, Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your king?”

The chief priests answered, “We have no king except Caesar.”

“Then he handed him over to them to be crucified” (John 19:4–16).

As he proceeded, as he was crucified with the two robbers, as his garments were divided and that tunic was subjected to the casting of lots [Note: Two manuscripts read, “and the lot was cast for that tunic.”], and as he was mocked with various insults during these events—for the insults were hurled while the other actions were taking place—the sixth hour was completed, and darkness came, which Matthew, Mark, and Luke mention.

47. Let impious obstinacy now collapse, and let it believe that the Lord Jesus Christ was crucified both at the third hour by the Jews’ tongue and at the sixth hour by the soldiers’ hands. For amid the Jews’ tumult and Pilate’s agitation, two hours and more passed from the cry in which they said, “Crucify him.”

But Mark, who is especially devoted to brevity, wished briefly to indicate Pilate’s intention and efforts on behalf of the Lord’s life. After saying, “But they again cried out, ‘Crucify him,’”—where he showed that they had already cried out when they wanted Barabbas released—he added, “But Pilate was saying to them, ‘Why, what evil has he done?’” (Mark 15:13–14).

In this way he briefly indicated what had taken place over a long period. Still remembering what he wished to be understood, he did not say, “Pilate said to them,” but “Pilate was saying to them, ‘Why, what evil has he done?’” If he had said “said,” we would understand that it had been spoken only once. Because he says “was saying,” he sufficiently indicated to those who understand that it had been said repeatedly and in many ways, until the sixth hour began.

Let us therefore consider how briefly Mark said this in comparison with Matthew; how briefly Matthew said it in comparison with Luke; how briefly Luke said it in comparison with John—although each mentioned different events; and finally, how briefly John himself spoke in comparison with the events that took place and the delays accompanying them.

Without the madness of resistance, let us believe that two hours and something could have elapsed during that interval.

48. Anyone who says that, if this were so, Mark could have said that it was the third hour at the time when it actually was the third hour—when the Jews’ cry for the Lord’s crucifixion had sounded—and could also have said that they themselves crucified him at that time, imposes his own arrogant rules upon narrators of the truth.

He could speak in this way only if he himself were narrating the events and if he assumed that everyone ought to narrate them in the same manner and order in which he had narrated them.

Let the plan of the evangelist Mark therefore prevail over this person’s plan. Mark judged that the statement should be placed where it appears, because divine inspiration suggested that location. Their memories were guided by the one who guides the waters, as Scripture says, according to his will.

Human memory flows through various thoughts, and it is not within anyone’s [Col. 1188] power to determine what will come to mind or when. Since those holy and truthful men entrusted the apparently accidental movements of their memories, for the sake of narrative order, to God’s hidden power—to whom nothing is accidental—no human being should say, standing far removed from God’s sight and far estranged from him, “This ought to have been placed here,” when he is profoundly ignorant of why God wished it to be placed there.

“For even if our gospel is veiled,” the Apostle says, “it is veiled among those who are perishing” (2 Cor. 4:3). After saying, “To some we are the fragrance of life leading to life, and to others the fragrance of death leading to death,” he immediately adds, “And who is sufficient for these things?” (2 Cor. 2:16)—that is, who is sufficient to understand how justly this happens?

The Lord says the same thing:

“I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

This is the depth of the riches of God’s knowledge and wisdom, by which, from the same lump, one vessel is made for honor and another for dishonor. To flesh and blood it is said:

“O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20–21).

Who, then, understands the Lord’s purpose even in this matter? Or who was his counselor? (Rom. 11:33–34.) He so governed the hearts of those who remembered the events and raised them to such a summit of authority in the Church that, through the very things that may appear contradictory in their writings, many would be blinded, being rightly handed over to the desires of their hearts and to a depraved mind (Rom. 1:24, 28), while many others would be exercised in refining a godly understanding according to the hidden justice of the Almighty.

For the prophet says to the Lord:

“Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep. The foolish person does not know, and the senseless does not understand these things” (Ps. 91:6–7).

49. I ask and admonish those who read these things, which we have labored over with the Lord’s assistance, to remember this discussion, which I have judged should be inserted here, whenever they encounter a similar difficulty among questions, so that the same points need not be repeated so often.

Anyone who wishes to pay attention without the hardness of impiety will easily see how appropriately Mark placed this statement about the third hour. There each person may recall at what hour the Jews crucified the Lord—those who wanted to transfer the crime itself either to the Roman rulers or to the soldiers, at the point where the action performed by the soldiers’ attendants is mentioned.

For Mark says:

“And crucifying him, they divided his garments, casting lots over them to determine what each should take.”

Who, if not the soldiers, as John makes clear?

Therefore, so that no one might turn away from the Jews and direct the thought of so great a crime toward those soldiers, Mark says:

“Now it was the third hour, and they crucified him.”

Thus diligent investigation will show that those who could be found crying out at the third hour for him to be crucified were the ones who more truly crucified him, while the deed performed by the soldiers occurred at the sixth hour.

[Note: The printed editions add “did this”; the manuscripts lack it.]

50. Nevertheless, there are some who wish to understand the Preparation mentioned by John—“Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour”—as the third hour of the day, when Pilate sat on the tribunal. In this way, the third hour would have been completed when he was crucified; after he had already been hanging on the cross, three further hours would have elapsed before he gave up his spirit. Thus, from the hour at which he died—that is, the sixth hour [Col. 1189] of the day—darkness would have come until the ninth.

They say that on that day, which was followed by the Sabbath, there was the Preparation of the Jews’ Passover, because the Unleavened Bread was beginning with that same Sabbath. Nevertheless, they say that the true Passover, which was already being enacted in the Lord’s Passion—not the Jews’ Passover, but that of Christians—began to be prepared, that is, began to have its “Preparation,” from the ninth hour of the night, when the Lord was being prepared to be killed by the Jews.

For *parasceve* means “preparation.” From that ninth hour of the night until his crucifixion, the sixth hour of the Preparation according to John coincided with the third hour of the day according to Mark. Thus Mark would not have mentioned by recapitulation the hour at which the Jews cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him,” but would have meant precisely the third hour at which the Lord was fastened to the cross.

What believer would not favor this solution to the question, provided that some plausible point can be identified at the ninth hour of the night from which we may appropriately understand the Preparation of our Passover—that is, the preparation for Christ’s death—to have begun?

If we say that it began when the Lord was seized by the Jews, it was still the early part of the night. If we say that it began when he was led to the house of Caiaphas’s father-in-law, where he was also examined by the chief priests, the cock had not yet crowed, as we infer from Peter’s denial, which took place when the cock was already heard. If we say it began when he was handed over to Pilate, it was clearly already morning.

It remains, therefore, for us to understand that this Preparation of the Passover—the preparation for the Lord’s death—began when all the chief priests before whom he was first examined answered and said, “He is guilty of death,” as found in Matthew and Mark (Matt. 26:66; Mark 14:64). Their statement concerning Peter’s denial is then understood, by way of recapitulation, to refer to something that had occurred earlier.

It is not an unreasonable conjecture that, at the time when, as I have said, they pronounced him guilty of death, it could have been the ninth hour of the night. From that hour until the hour when Pilate sat on the tribunal, it was approximately the sixth hour—not of the day, but of the Preparation, that is, of the preparation for the Lord’s sacrificial offering, which is the true Passover. Thus, when the sixth hour of that Preparation was complete—coinciding with the completed third hour of the day—the Lord was suspended on the cross.

Whether this interpretation is preferred, or whether one chooses to understand Mark as recalling the third hour and mentioning it especially to condemn the Jews in the Lord’s crucifixion—since they could be understood to have cried out for him to be crucified, so that we might regard them as having crucified him rather than those by whose hands he was suspended on the cross—just as the centurion came closer to the Lord than did those friends whom he sent [Note: See above, Book 2, chapter 20], there can be no doubt that the question concerning the hour of the Lord’s Passion has been resolved.

This question especially tends both to provoke the shamelessness of contentious people and to disturb the inexperience of the weak.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Concerning the two robbers crucified with him, and how all the Evangelists agree

51. Matthew continues:

“Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left” [Col. 1190] (Matt. 27:38).

Mark and Luke say the same (Mark 15:27; Luke 23:33). John creates no difficulty, although he does not call them robbers. He says:

“And with him two others, one on each side, and Jesus in the middle” (John 19:18).

There would be a contradiction if, when the others called them robbers, John had called them innocent men.

## CHAPTER XV  
### Concerning those who insulted the Lord, and how Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree

52. Matthew continues:

“Those who passed by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying, ‘You [Note: The printed editions add “vah!”; the older manuscripts and the Greek text lack this particle.] who destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.’”

Mark agrees with this in almost the same words.

Matthew then continues:

“Likewise the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said, ‘He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him, for he said, “I am the Son of God”’” (Matt. 27:39–43).

Although Mark and Luke use different words, they agree in meaning: one omits what the other records (Mark 15:29–32; Luke 23:35–37).

Neither is silent about the chief priests’ insulting the Lord while he hung on the cross, although Mark says nothing of the elders. Luke, because he says “the rulers” and does not add “of the priests,” embraces all the leading men under a more general designation, so that the scribes and elders can also be understood there.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Concerning the insults of the robbers, and how Matthew and Mark do not contradict Luke, who says that one insulted him and the other believed

53. Matthew continues:

“And the robbers who were crucified with him also reproached him” (Matt. 27:44).

Mark does not differ, saying the same thing in other words (Mark 15:32).

Luke may appear to contradict them unless we remember a very common form of expression. Luke says:

“But one of the robbers who were hanging there blasphemed him, saying, ‘If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.’”

He then continues and connects the account in this way:

“But the other answered and rebuked him, saying, ‘Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.’ And he said to Jesus, ‘Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.’ And Jesus said to him, ‘Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise’” (Luke 23:39–43).

How, then, could Matthew say, “The robbers who were crucified with him reproached him,” or Mark, “Those who were crucified with him reviled him,” when, according to Luke’s testimony, one of them reviled him, while the other both restrained him and believed in the Lord?

We must understand that Matthew and Mark, briefly passing over this event, used the plural number instead of the singular. Thus in the Epistle to the Hebrews we read, in the plural, “They shut the mouths of lions,” although only Daniel is [Col. 1191] understood to be meant; and “They were sawn in two,” although tradition relates this of Isaiah alone (Heb. 11:33–37).

In the Psalm also, where it says, “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together as one,” the plural number is used in place of the singular. This is explained in the Acts of the Apostles: “kings” refers to Herod, and “rulers” to Pilate, who used the testimony of that same Psalm (Ps. 2:2; Acts 4:26–27).

But since pagans too commonly attack the Gospel, let them observe how their own authors spoke of “the Phaedras, Medeas, and Clytemnestras,” although there was only one of each.

What, for example, is more commonplace than for someone to say, “The country people are insulting me,” even if only one person is doing so?

It would be a contradiction of Luke’s explicit statement about one only if the others had said that both robbers reviled the Lord. In that case one could not be understood under the plural number. But when it is said simply “the robbers,” or “those who were crucified with him,” and the word “both” is not added, this could be said if both had done it; yet because one did it, the customary form of expression could also signify him by the plural number.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Concerning the vinegar drink, and how all the Evangelists agree
54. Matthew continues and says: “Now from the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour” (Matt. 27:45–49). The other two also attest this (Mark 15:33–36; Luke 23:44–45); Luke additionally stated the cause of the darkness, namely, that the sun was darkened.

Matthew continues: “And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani? That is, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ But some of those standing there and hearing him said: ‘This man is calling Elijah.’” Mark agrees almost word-for-word, and in meaning he agrees not almost, but entirely.

Matthew continues: “And immediately one of them ran, and taking a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him drink.” Mark likewise says: “But one ran, and filling a sponge with vinegar and putting it around a reed, gave him drink, saying: ‘Let be; let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.’” Matthew, however, reported that it was not the man who offered the sponge with vinegar, but the others, who said this about Elijah: “But the others were saying: ‘Let be; let us see whether Elijah will come to save him.’” From this we understand that both he and the others said this.

Luke, before narrating the reviling by the robbers, mentioned the vinegar in this way: “But the soldiers also mocked him, approaching and offering him vinegar, and saying: ‘If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself’” (Luke 23:36–37). He wished to include in a single statement what the soldiers did and said. It should not be troubling that he did not say that one of them offered the vinegar; for he used the type of expression discussed above, putting the plural for the singular (above, ch. 16).

John also mentioned the vinegar, saying: “After this, Jesus, knowing that all things had now been completed, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said: ‘I thirst.’ Now a vessel was set there, full of vinegar; and they, putting a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop, offered it to his mouth” (John 19:28–29). But since John records Jesus saying, “I thirst,” and says that a vessel full of vinegar was there, it is not surprising if the others passed over these details.

## CHAPTER XVIII—How the words uttered by the Lord when he was immediately about to die do not set Matthew and Mark against Luke, or all three against John

55. Matthew continues: “But Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up his spirit” (Matt. 27:50). Mark similarly says: “But Jesus, having uttered a loud cry, expired” (Mark 15:37).

Luke explained what he said in that loud voice: “And crying out with a loud voice, Jesus said: ‘Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.’ And saying this, he expired” (Luke 23:46).

Just as John omitted the first cry, “Eli, Eli,” which Matthew and Mark reported, so he also omitted this one, which Luke alone indicated, while those other two signified it by the expression “a loud voice”: namely, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” Luke himself likewise attested that he said this with a loud voice, so that we might understand this to have been the loud cry mentioned by Matthew and Mark.

But John said that Jesus spoke words which none of the other three recorded—“It is finished”—after he had received the vinegar. We understand that he said this before that loud cry. For John’s words are: “When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is finished’; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John 19:30).

Between his saying, “It is finished,” and his saying, “and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit,” that loud cry was uttered, which John omitted but the other three recorded. The order appears to have been this: first he said, “It is finished,” when what had been prophesied concerning him had been accomplished; and, as though he had waited for this—for certainly he would die whenever he wished—he then commended and gave up his spirit.

Whatever order anyone may think could have been used, we must take the greatest care that no one suppose one Evangelist contradicts another merely because one omitted what another reported, or reported what another omitted.

## CHAPTER XIX—How Matthew and Mark do not disagree with Luke concerning the rending of the veil, and in what order it occurred

56. Matthew continues: “And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matt. 27:51). Mark says likewise: “And the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38).

Luke similarly says: “And the veil of the temple was torn down the middle” (Luke 23:45), but not in the same order. Wishing to attach one miracle to another, after saying, “The sun was darkened,” he immediately thought he should add, “And the veil of the temple was torn down the middle.” Thus he anticipated what occurred when the Lord expired, and then, returning to the narrative, dealt with the vinegar, the loud cry, and the death itself—events understood to have occurred after the darkness and before the rending of the veil.

Matthew, after saying, “But Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up his spirit,” immediately added, “And behold, the veil of the temple was torn.” He thereby clearly indicated that it was torn at the moment when Jesus gave up his spirit. If he had not added “and behold,” but had simply said, “And the veil of the temple was torn,” it would be uncertain whether he and Mark had mentioned this by way of recapitulation while Luke preserved the order, or whether Luke had recapitulated what they had placed in sequence.

## CHAPTER XX—How Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree concerning the astonishment of the centurion and those who were with him

57. Matthew continues: “And the earth shook, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened; and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose; and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many.” Since he alone reported these events, there is no need to fear that they might appear to contradict the others.

He continues: “But the centurion and those who were with him keeping watch over Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, were greatly afraid, saying: ‘Truly this was the Son of God’” (Matt. 27:51–54).

Mark says: “But when the centurion who stood facing him saw that he had expired in this way, after crying out, he said: ‘Truly this man was the Son of God’” (Mark 15:39).

Luke says: “But when the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying: ‘Truly this man was righteous’” (Luke 23:47).

There is no contradiction in Matthew’s saying that the centurion and those with him were astonished when they saw the earthquake, while Luke says that he was astonished that Jesus expired after uttering that cry, thereby showing how much authority he possessed over the time of his death. For Matthew not only said, “when he saw the earthquake,” but also added, “and the things that were happening.” This shows that Luke still had room to say that the centurion was astonished at the Lord’s very death, since that too was among the marvelous things that then occurred.

Even if Matthew had not added those words, it would still have been necessary to understand that, since many extraordinary things had occurred and the centurion and those with him could have been astonished at all of them, the narrators were free to mention whichever thing they wished him to have admired. They do not contradict one another when one says that he admired one thing and another says that he admired another, since he had admired everything.

As for one saying that the centurion said, “Truly this was the Son of God,” and another, “Truly this man was the Son of God,” this will not trouble anyone who remembers the many similar statements discussed and explained above. Both expressions converge upon the same meaning; and the fact that one omitted the word “man,” while another included it, is in no way contradictory.

It may seem more different that Luke does not say the centurion declared, “He was the Son of God,” but rather, “He was righteous.” Yet we must either understand that both statements were made by the centurion, with one narrator recording one and another recording the other, or perhaps understand Luke to have expressed the centurion’s meaning concerning how he called Jesus the Son of God.

For perhaps the centurion had not understood him to be the Only-Begotten, equal to the Father; rather, he called him the Son of God because he believed him to be righteous, just as many righteous people are called sons of God.

When Luke himself says, “But when the centurion saw what had happened,” he included under that expression everything marvelous that had occurred at that hour, as though he were mentioning a single marvelous event whose members and parts were all those miracles.

As for Matthew’s addition of those who were with the centurion, while the others omitted them, who would not see that this is not contradictory according to the well-known principle that one narrator may state what another omits?

And when Matthew says, “They were greatly afraid,” while Luke does not say, “He was afraid,” but “He glorified God,” who would not understand that he glorified God through fear?

## CHAPTER XXI—How Matthew, Mark, and Luke, who said that the women stood at a distance, do not contradict John, who named one of them as standing near the cross

58. Matthew continues: “There were also many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him; among them was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee” (Matt. 27:55–56).

Mark says: “There were also women looking on from a distance; among them was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joseph, and Salome; and when he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and many other women who had come up with him to Jerusalem” (Mark 15:40–41).

I see nothing between these accounts that could be considered contradictory. For what bearing on the truth does it have that some women were named together and others individually?

Luke likewise weaves his narrative together as follows: “And the whole crowd of those who had come together for this spectacle, and who saw what was happening, returned, beating their breasts. But all his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him from Galilee saw these things” (Luke 23:48–49).

Thus Luke agrees sufficiently with the two preceding Evangelists concerning the women’s presence, although he names none of them individually. He also agrees with Matthew concerning the crowd that was present together, saw what was happening, beat their breasts, and returned, although Matthew appended separately: “But the centurion and those who were with him.” Luke is therefore found to have spoken alone only about his acquaintances, who stood at a distance.

John too mentioned the women’s presence before the Lord gave up his spirit, narrating as follows: “Now standing beside the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus therefore saw his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved, he said to his mother: ‘Woman, behold, your son.’ Then he said to the disciple: ‘Behold, your mother.’ And from that hour the disciple took her into his own care” (John 19:25–27).

In this matter, unless Matthew and Mark had most explicitly named Mary Magdalene as well, we could say that some women stood at a distance and others near the cross; for none of them except John mentioned the Lord’s mother. But now how are we to understand that the same Mary Magdalene both stood at a distance with the other women, as Matthew and Mark say, and was near the cross, as John says?

The answer is that the interval was so great that they could be called both near, because they were present within his sight, and far away in comparison with the crowd standing closer around the centurion and soldiers.

We may also understand that those who had been present together with the Lord’s mother began to leave after he entrusted her to the disciple, in order to withdraw from the density of the crowd and view the remaining events from farther away. Thus the other Evangelists, who mention them after the Lord’s death, spoke of them as already standing at a distance.

## CHAPTER XXII—How all agree concerning Joseph, who asked Pilate for the Lord’s body, and how John does not contradict himself

59. Matthew continues: “When evening had come, a certain rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who himself was also a disciple of Jesus, came. He approached Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus; then Pilate ordered that the body be given” (Matt. 27:57–58).

Mark says: “And when evening had already come, since it was Preparation Day, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph from Arimathea, a noble councillor, who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God, came and boldly entered before Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. But Pilate wondered whether he had already died; and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he had already died. When he had learned this from the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph” (Mark 15:42–45).

Luke says: “And behold, a man named Joseph, who was a councillor, a good and righteous man—he had not consented to their counsel and action—from the city of Arimathea, a city of Judea, who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God, approached Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus” (Luke 23:50–52).

After John had narrated the breaking of the legs of those who had been crucified with the Lord and the piercing of the Lord’s side with a spear—events which he alone reported—he adds, in agreement with the others: “After these things Joseph of Arimathea, because he was a disciple of Jesus, though secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate to take away the body of Jesus; and Pilate permitted it. Therefore he came and took the body of Jesus” (John 19:38).

Nothing appears here in which any one of them contradicts another. Yet someone may perhaps ask how John does not contradict himself when, in agreement with the others, he testifies that Joseph asked for the body of Jesus, while alone stating that he had been a secret disciple of the Lord because of fear of the Jews. The question is rightly raised: why did the man who was a secret disciple because of fear dare to ask for his body, when none of those who followed him openly would have dared to do so?

We must understand that Joseph did this out of confidence in his position, which enabled him to enter Pilate’s presence familiarly. Yet in carrying out that final service for the dead, he cared less about the Jews, although ordinarily he avoided their hostility when listening to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXIII—How the three do not disagree with John concerning his burial

60. Matthew continues: “And having received the body, Joseph wrapped it in a clean linen cloth and placed it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn in the rock; and he rolled a large stone to the entrance of the tomb and departed” (Matt. 27:59–60).

Mark says: “Joseph bought a linen cloth, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen cloth and placed him in a tomb that had been hewn out of rock; and he rolled a stone to the entrance of the tomb” (Mark 15:46).

Luke says: “And taking it down, he wrapped it in a linen cloth and placed him in a tomb hewn in the rock, in which no one had yet been placed” (Luke 23:53).

No question of disagreement can arise from these three accounts. John, however, records that the Lord’s burial was attended to not by Joseph alone, but also by Nicodemus. Beginning, accordingly, with Nicodemus, he narrates: “Nicodemus also came, who had first come to Jesus by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.” Then, adding Joseph himself, he says: “So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the Jewish custom of burial. Now there was a garden in the place where he was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb, in which no one had yet been placed. Therefore, because it was the Preparation Day of the Jews, since the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus there” (John 19:39–42).

Here too there is no contradiction for those who understand correctly. Those who omitted Nicodemus did not assert that the Lord was buried by Joseph alone, even though they mentioned Joseph alone. Nor, because they said that Joseph wrapped him in one linen cloth, did they prevent us from understanding that Nicodemus could have brought and added other linen cloths, so that John might truthfully say that he was wrapped not in one cloth but in linen cloths.

Moreover, because the cloth placed around the head was also linen, as were the bands with which the whole body was bound, it could most truthfully be said—even if there had been only one shroud there—that “they bound him in linen cloths.” For “linen cloths” is a general term for things woven from flax.

## CHAPTER XXIV—How all agree concerning the events surrounding the time of the Lord’s resurrection

61. Matthew continues: “But Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb” (Matt. 27:61).

Mark says this as follows: “But Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph were watching where he was placed” (Mark 15:47). From this it is clear that they disagree in nothing.

62. Matthew continues: “On the next day, which is after the Preparation Day, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate, saying: ‘Lord, we remember that that deceiver said while he was still alive, “After three days I will rise.” Therefore command that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples come and steal him and say to the people, “He has risen from the dead”; and the last deception will be worse than the first.’ Pilate said to them: ‘You have a guard; go, guard it as you know how.’ So they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone together with the guards” (Matt. 27:62–66).

Matthew alone narrates this; none of the others reports anything that appears contrary to it.

63. Matthew then continues and says: “In the evening of the Sabbath, as it begins to dawn toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and, approaching, rolled away the stone and sat upon it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow. From fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men.

“But the angel answered and said to the women: ‘Do not be afraid, you; for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord had been placed. And going quickly, tell his disciples that he has risen; and behold, he goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him. Behold, I have told you’” (Matt. 28:1–15).

[Note: The printed editions have *in prima sabbati*, “on the first day of the week.” But the manuscripts of the best quality—Corbeiensis, Floriacensis, and others—consistently have *in primam*. The Greek has *eis mian sabbatōn*, “toward the first [day] of the week.”]

Mark agrees with this (Mark 16:1–11). But it may be asked how, according to Matthew, the angel was sitting on the stone after it had been rolled away from the tomb, whereas Mark says that when the women entered the tomb they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and were astonished.

This difficulty disappears if we understand either that Matthew omitted the angel whom the women saw when they entered, while Mark omitted the one whom they saw outside sitting on the stone; so that they saw two angels and heard individually from the two what the angels said about Jesus—first from the one whom they saw outside sitting on the stone, and then from the one whom they saw inside the tomb sitting on the right.

They were encouraged to enter by the words of the one sitting outside, who said: “Come and see the place where the Lord had been placed.” When they came and entered, as stated, they saw the one whom Matthew omits but Mark mentions, sitting on the right, and from him they likewise heard such things.

Or certainly, when the women are said to have entered the tomb, we should understand this as entering within some enclosure of masonry, which it is credible had surrounded the place at some distance in front of the rock in which the burial chamber had been hewn. Thus they saw sitting in that same space on the right the one whom Matthew says was sitting on the stone that the earthquake had rolled away from the entrance of the tomb—that is, from the place of the burial chamber hewn in the rock.

64. It may also be asked how Mark can say: “But they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and fear had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid,” when Matthew says: “And they went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples.”

The explanation may be that they did not dare say anything to anyone—namely, to respond to the angels themselves concerning what they had heard from them—or perhaps to the guards whom they saw lying there.

The joy mentioned by Matthew is not contrary to the fear of which Mark speaks. We must understand that both occurred in their minds, even if Matthew had not mentioned the fear. Since Matthew himself says, “They went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy,” he leaves no remaining question on this point.

65. A serious question also arises concerning the very hour at which the women came to the tomb. Matthew says: “In the evening of the Sabbath, as it begins to dawn toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.” What then does Mark mean when he says: “And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen”?

In this he does not disagree with the other two, Luke and John. What Luke calls “very early” and John calls “in the morning, while it was still dark,” is what Mark means by “very early, when the sun had risen”—that is, when the sky in the eastern part had already begun to grow light. This occurs only when the rising sun is near, for that radiance is what is commonly called dawn.

Thus Mark does not contradict John, who says that it was still dark. As the day begins, remnants of darkness become increasingly faint as the light rises.

Nor should Mark’s words, “very early,” be understood as though the sun itself were already visible above the earth. Rather, it is like what we usually say to people when we wish to indicate that something should be done earlier. When we say, “In the morning,” lest they think we mean a time when the sun is already visibly above the earth, we often add, “very early,” so that they understand the time also called dawn.

It is likewise customary, after the cock has crowed repeatedly and people begin to conjecture that day is already near, to say, “It is morning.” Then, after they have considered the matter and see the sky reddening or brightening because the sun is already rising—that is, already approaching these regions—they may add, having said “It is morning”: “It is very early morning.”

What difference does it make, then, provided that whether in one way or the other we understand Mark to call “morning” what Luke calls “at dawn,” and “very early morning” what Luke calls “very early at dawn,” and what John calls “morning while it was still dark”—with the sun already rising, that is, beginning by its rising to illuminate the sky?

How, then, does Matthew agree with these three, since he says not “at dawn” or “in the morning,” but “in the evening of the Sabbath, as it begins to dawn toward the first day of the week”? This must be investigated more carefully.

By “evening,” which is the first part of the night, Matthew wished to signify the whole night, at the end of which the women came to the tomb. The reason he is understood to have called it by that name is that from evening onward it was permissible to bring the spices, since the Sabbath had passed.

Therefore, because they were prevented by the Sabbath from doing this earlier, he named the night from the time at which it began to be lawful for them to act, at whatever point during that night they wished to do so.

Thus “in the evening of the Sabbath” was said as though he had said, “during the night of the Sabbath,” that is, during the night following the day of the Sabbath. His very words sufficiently indicate this. For he says: “In the evening of the Sabbath, as it begins to dawn toward the first day of the week.”

This cannot be the case if “evening” signifies only the first part of the night, that is, merely the beginning of the night. For it is not that beginning which begins to dawn toward the first day of the week, but the night itself, which begins to end with the light.

The end of the first part of the night is the beginning of the second; light, however, is the end of the entire night. Hence one cannot say that evening begins to dawn toward the first day of the week unless by “evening” the whole night is understood, the night which light brings to an end.

It is a customary manner of expression in divine Scripture to signify the whole by a part.

[Note: In manuscript B the word *significare* is absent. We have followed Erasmus and Lovaniensis. M.]

Thus by “evening” he signified the night, whose end is dawn. At dawn those women came to the tomb; consequently, they came during the night signified by the term “evening.” The whole night was signified by that term, as I have said; and therefore, at whatever point during that night they had come, they would have come during that night. Since they came at the final part of the night, they undoubtedly came during that night.

“Evening, as it begins to dawn toward the first day of the week,” can therefore mean only the whole night itself. They came in that evening because they came during that night; and they came during that night because they came during whatever part of that night, even its final part.

66. The three-day period during which the Lord died and rose again also cannot be correctly understood except according to this manner of expression, by which the whole is commonly signified by a part.

[Note: Here the printed editions inserted: “Hence a great account is given of the Lord’s saying”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]

He himself said: “For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matt. 12:40).

The periods are counted either from the time when he gave up his spirit or from the time when he was buried, but the reckoning does not become fully clear unless we take

[Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *computentur* (“let the periods be counted”); below, they read “unless [we take] up to the middle day.”]

 the middle day—that is, the whole Sabbath, together with its night—as a complete day, while understanding by a part standing for the whole the other two days—which placed it in the middle—namely, the Preparation Day and the first day of the week, which we call the Lord’s Day.

What help is there in the fact that some, constrained by this difficulty and ignorant of how greatly this manner of expression—that is, the part for the whole—contributes to resolving questions in the sacred Scriptures, wished to count as a night the three hours from the sixth to the ninth during which the sun was darkened, and as a day the other three hours during which light was restored to the earth, from the ninth hour until sunset?

The night of the coming Sabbath follows. If it is counted together with its day, there will already be two nights and two days. Then, after the Sabbath, follows the night of the first day of the week, that is, the night preceding the dawning of the Lord’s Day, during which the Lord rose. There will therefore be two nights and two days, and one additional night—even if the whole of it could be understood as intended, without our demonstrating that dawn is its final part.

[Note: The printed editions have *primi sabbati*, “of the first Sabbath”; and shortly afterward, *diei dominicae*, “of the Lord’s Day.”]

Consequently, even after those six hours have been counted—three during which the sun was darkened and three during which it shone again—the reckoning of three days and three nights will not stand.

It remains, therefore, that according to that most customary Scriptural manner of expression, in which the whole is understood from a part, we take the final day to be the period of the Preparation Day during which the Lord was crucified and buried, and from that final part understand the whole day together with its night, which had already passed.

The middle day, that is, the Sabbath, we take not from a part but as a complete whole. The third day, in turn, we take from its first part—that is, from the night—as a whole together with its daylight period. In this way there will be three days.

This is like the eight days after which he ascended the mountain: Matthew and Mark, attending to the intervening whole days, said, “After six days,” while Luke said, “After eight days” (above, book 2, ch. 56, no. 113).

[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *primum diem*, “the first day.”]

67. Let us now examine the remaining matters, and see how they agree with Matthew.

Luke says most clearly that two angels were seen by the women who came to the tomb. We had understood that each was mentioned by one of the two Evangelists: one by Matthew, namely, the one sitting outside on the stone; the other by Mark, namely, the one sitting inside on the right.

But Luke narrates as follows:

“Now it was the Preparation Day, and the Sabbath was beginning to dawn. The women who had come with him from Galilee followed, and they saw the tomb and how his body had been placed. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments; and on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

“On the first day of the week, very early, they came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared. They found the stone rolled away from the tomb; and entering, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.

“And while they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood beside them in shining clothing. As they were afraid and inclined their faces toward the ground, they said to them: ‘Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he spoke to you when he was still in Galilee, saying that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, be crucified, and rise on the third day.’

“And they remembered his words, and returning from the tomb, they announced all these things to the eleven and to all the others” (Luke 23:54–24:12).

[Note: The printed editions read *et ecce*, “and behold”; the manuscripts have *et ecce*, in accordance with the Greek.]

How, then, were the angels each seen sitting—one, according to Matthew, outside on the stone, and the other, according to Mark, inside on the right—when according to Luke two stood beside the women, although they said similar things?

We can still understand that one angel was seen by the women, both according to Matthew and according to Mark, as we said above. We may take their entering the tomb to mean that they entered some space enclosed by a wall, so that one could enter before the rocky burial chamber itself. There they saw an angel sitting on the stone rolled away from the tomb, as Matthew says; and this is what Mark means by “sitting on the right.”

Then, while they looked inside at the place where the Lord’s body had lain, they saw two other angels standing, as Luke says. These spoke similar words to encourage their minds and strengthen their faith.

68. Let us also consider what John says, and whether or in what way it agrees with these accounts.

John narrates as follows:

“On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came in the morning, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb. Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them: ‘They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have placed him.’

“Then Peter and the other disciple went out and came to the tomb. The two were running together, but the other disciple ran ahead faster than Peter and came first to the tomb. Bending down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter.

“Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been over his head, not lying with the linen cloths but separately, rolled up in one place.

“Then the other disciple also entered, the one who had come first to the tomb; he saw and believed. For they did not yet know the Scripture, that he had to rise from the dead.

“Then the disciples went away again to their own homes. But Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping. While she was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.

“They said to her: ‘Woman, why are you weeping?’ She said to them: ‘Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have placed him.’

“When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her: ‘Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?’ Supposing that he was the gardener, she said to him: ‘Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him away.’

“Jesus said to her: ‘Mary.’ Turning, she said to him in Hebrew, ‘Rabboni,’ which means ‘Teacher.’

“Jesus said to her: ‘Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brothers and say to them: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God.”’

“Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples: ‘I have seen the Lord,’ and that he had said these things to her” (John 20:1–18).

In John’s account, the day or time at which they came to the tomb agrees with the other accounts. The fact that two angels were seen also agrees with Luke. But the fact that Luke says the angels were seen standing, while John says they were sitting, together with the other details that Luke does not mention, may appear contradictory unless they are carefully considered in relation to how and in what order the events occurred.

69. Therefore, let us arrange in a single narrative, as far as the Lord may assist us, how all these events surrounding the time of the Lord’s resurrection could have occurred, according to the testimony of all the Evangelists.

At dawn on the first day of the week, as all agree, they came to the tomb. What Matthew alone records had already happened: the earthquake, the stone rolled away, and the guards terrified, so that some of them lay there as though dead. Then, as John says, Mary Magdalene came—undoubtedly more fervent in her love than the other women [Note: [Col. 1201] The printed editions read *cum caeteris mulieribus* (“with the other women”). The manuscripts lack the word *cum* (“with”).] who had ministered to the Lord—so that John was not unjustified in mentioning her alone, leaving unmentioned those who were with her, as the others testify.

She therefore came, and when she saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb, before she examined anything more carefully, assuming without hesitation that Jesus’ body had been taken away, she ran, as John himself says, and announced it to Peter and to that same John. He was the disciple whom Jesus loved. They began running to the tomb; and John, arriving first, bent down and saw the linen cloths lying there, but did not enter. Peter, however, following him, entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths lying there, and the napkin that had been on his head [Col. 1202], not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up separately. Then John also entered, saw the same things, and believed what Mary had said: that the Lord had been taken away from the tomb.

“For they did not yet understand the Scripture, that he had to rise from the dead.” Then the disciples went back again to their own homes. “But Mary was standing outside at the tomb, weeping”—that is, before that place of the rock-hewn tomb, yet still within the area into which they had already entered; for there was a garden there, as John himself records (John 19:41).

Then they saw an angel sitting on the right, upon the stone that had been rolled away from the tomb—the angel about whom Matthew and Mark tell. “Then he said to them: Do not be afraid, you; for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord had been laid. And go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen; and behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him. Behold, I have told you.” Mark likewise did not omit similar words.

While Mary was weeping at these words, she bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels, as John says, sitting in white garments, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed. “They say to her: Woman, why are you weeping? She says to them: Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have placed him.”

Here we should understand that the angels rose, so that they might also appear to be standing, as Luke records that they were seen, and that, according to the same Luke, they said to the frightened women, who had inclined their faces toward the ground:

“Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he spoke to you when he was still in Galilee, saying: The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and rise again on the third day.”

And they remembered his words.

After this Mary turned around and saw Jesus standing, as John says, but she did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus says to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing that he was the gardener, she says to him: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him.” Jesus says to her: “Mary.” She turned and said to him: “Rabboni”—which means “Teacher.” Jesus says to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God.”

Then she went out from the tomb—that is, from the place where the garden area lay before the excavated rock. With her went the other women, whom, according to Mark, trembling and fear had seized; and they said nothing to anyone.

Then, according to Matthew, “behold, Jesus met them, saying: Greetings. They approached, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.” Thus we understand that they came to the tomb twice and received the angels’ address twice, as well as that of the Lord himself: once there, when Mary supposed him to be the gardener; and now again, when he met them on the road, so that by this repetition he might strengthen them and restore them from their fear.

“Then he said to them: Do not be afraid. Go, announce to my brothers that they should go into Galilee; there they will see me.”

Then Mary Magdalene came [Col. 1203] announcing to the disciples that she had seen the Lord and that he had said these things to her—not she alone, but also the other women whom Luke mentions, “who announced all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. And these words appeared before them like nonsense, and they did not believe them.” Mark also bears witness to this. For after recording that the women had gone out from the tomb trembling and frightened and had said nothing to anyone, he added that the risen Lord appeared in the morning of the first day of the week, first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons; and that she went and announced it to those who had been with him, while they were mourning and weeping; and that when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe.

Matthew also inserted the fact that, while the women who had seen and heard all these things were departing, some of the guards who had lain there as though dead came into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened—that is, whatever they themselves had been able to perceive. The chief priests, having assembled with the elders and taken counsel, gave the soldiers a large sum of money so that they would say that his disciples had come and stolen him while they were sleeping. They also promised them protection from the governor who had entrusted them with the guard. Having taken the money, the soldiers did as they had been instructed, and this report has been spread among the Jews to the present day.

## CHAPTER XXV

How, when he later manifested himself to the disciples, all the Evangelists do not contradict one another, with their testimonies compared, and with the Apostle Paul and the Acts of the Apostles

70. We must now consider how the Lord appeared to the disciples after the resurrection—not only so that the agreement of the four Evangelists may also become clear in this matter (Matthew 28, Mark 16, Luke 24, and John 20–21), but also so that they may be shown to agree with the Apostle Paul, who speaks about this matter in his First Epistle to the Corinthians as follows:

“For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures; and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve [Note: [Col. 1203] The printed editions read *undecim* (“eleven”). But the manuscripts have *duodecim* (“twelve”), in agreement with the Greek, *toîs dôdeka* (“to the twelve”).]; afterward he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom the greater number remain until now, though some have fallen asleep; afterward he appeared to James, then to all the Apostles; and last of all [Note: [Col. 1203] Ten manuscripts read *novissimo* (“last”); the printed editions agreed with these below, §85.], as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me” (1 Corinthians 15:3–8).

None of the Evangelists, however, followed this order. We must therefore consider whether the order they followed contradicts this one. For neither did Paul say everything, nor did they say everything; we need only see whether, in what they all said, there is any contradiction among them.

Of the four Evangelists, Luke alone does not say that the Lord was seen by the women, but mentions only the angels. Matthew, however, says that he met them as they were returning from the tomb. Mark likewise says that he was first seen by Mary Magdalene [Col. 1204], as does John; but he does not say how he appeared to her, which John explains.

Luke, as I have said, not only leaves unmentioned the fact that he appeared to the women, but also says that two men, one of whom was Cleopas, spoke with him before recognizing him, as though the women had announced that they had seen nothing except angels who said that he was alive. For he narrates as follows:

“Behold, two of them were traveling that same day to a village that was sixty stades from Jerusalem, named Emmaus. They were speaking with each other about all these things that had happened. And it came to pass, while they were speaking and reasoning together, that Jesus himself, drawing near, went with them; but their eyes were held so that they might not recognize him.

“And he said to them: What are these words that you are discussing with one another as you walk, and why are you sad? One of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering, said to him: Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?

“To whom he said: What things? And they said: About Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to condemnation to death and crucified him. But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel. And now, besides all these things, today is the third day since these things happened.

“Yet some women from our company have terrified us. They were at the tomb before dawn, and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who say that he is alive. Some of our men also went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but they did not see him.” [Note: [Col. 1204] The earlier printed editions read *non invenerunt* (“they did not find [him]”). But the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read *non viderunt* (“they did not see [him]”), supported by the Greek, *ouk eidon*.]

Luke reports these things in a way that allows us to remember and reconstruct what had been said by the women, or by the disciples who had run to the tomb, when they were told that his body had been taken away from there.

Luke himself says only that Peter ran to the tomb and, stooping down, saw only the linen cloths lying there, and went away wondering at what had happened. He mentions this about Peter before narrating the story of the two men whom he encountered on the road, after narrating the women who had seen the angels and heard from them that Jesus had risen—as though Peter had then run to the tomb.

But Luke is understood to have inserted this account of Peter by way of recapitulation. Peter ran to the tomb at the same time as John, when the women—especially Mary Magdalene—had merely announced to them that the body had been taken away. She had made this announcement when she saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb. Afterward came the events concerning the vision of the angels and of the Lord himself, who appeared twice to the women: once at the tomb, and again when he met them as they were returning from the tomb.

This occurred before he appeared to the two men on the road, one of whom was Cleopas. For Cleopas, speaking with the Lord whom he did not yet recognize, did not say that Peter had gone to the tomb. Rather, he said: “Some of our men went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said.” This too is understood to have been said by way of recapitulation, namely, what the women had first announced to Peter and John concerning the Lord’s body having been taken away.

Therefore, when Luke himself says that Peter ran to the tomb, and reports that Cleopas said that some of them had gone to the tomb, he is understood to attest to John that two men went to the tomb. He mentioned Peter alone at first because Mary had first announced it to him.

Likewise, it may seem troubling that Luke says Peter, without entering, saw only the linen cloths as he stooped down and then departed wondering, whereas John says that he himself—namely, the disciple whom Jesus loved—saw this: that he did not enter the tomb, to which he had arrived first, but, after bending down, saw the linen cloths lying there; yet he also says that he himself later entered.

Peter, then, should likewise be understood to have first seen the cloths while stooping down, as Luke records and John omits; afterward he entered, yet entered before John, so that all may be found to have spoken truly without any contradiction.

71. The order of events, then, which could have occurred—how the Lord, in addition to having already spoken with the women, also appeared to the male disciples—must be set out and demonstrated according to the testimony not only of the four Evangelists but also of the Apostle Paul.

Among all the men whom the four Evangelists and the Apostle Paul mention, Peter is understood to have been the first to whom he appeared. But if he appeared to one of them before Peter, though all have omitted it, who would dare either to assert or to deny it? For Paul did not say, “He appeared first to Cephas”; rather, he said: “He appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve, afterward he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once.”

It is not clear which twelve he means, any more than which five hundred. For it is possible that these twelve were some group from the crowd of disciples. If he had meant those whom he called Apostles, he would no longer have said “twelve,” but “eleven,” as some manuscripts also read. I believe that confused readers corrected the text, thinking that it referred to the twelve Apostles, who, after Judas had perished, were eleven.

But whether the manuscripts that read “eleven” are more accurate, or Paul intended some other twelve disciples [Note: [Col. 1205] The manuscripts read: “or whether the Apostle Paul intended some other twelve.”], or whether he wished that sacred number [Note: [Col. 1205] Five manuscripts read: “or whether he wished the mystery of that number.”] to remain even in the eleven—because the number twelve among them was so mystical that another person, namely Matthias, had to be appointed in Judas’s place to preserve the mystery of that same number (Acts 1:26)—whatever the case may be, nothing follows from it that appears contrary either to the truth or to any of these most truthful narrators.

Nevertheless, it is reasonably believed that, after he appeared to Peter, he appeared next to these two men, one of whom was Cleopas, concerning whom Luke gives a complete account, while Mark briefly touches upon it as follows:

“After this he appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking, going into the countryside.”

We may reasonably understand that village also to have been called a settlement. What is now called Bethlehem itself was previously called a city, although it now possesses greater honor because the name of the Lord, who was born there, has been so widely proclaimed throughout the Churches of all nations.

In the Greek manuscripts, however, we more often find *agron* (“field”) than “village” [Note: [Col. 1206] *Eis agron* (“into a field”).]. By the name “field,” not only villages but also municipalities and colonies outside the city are customarily designated, the city being the head and, as it were, the mother of the others; hence it is called a metropolis.

72. When Mark says that the Lord appeared to them “in another form,” Luke says that their eyes were held so that they would not recognize him. Something had happened to their eyes, and it was allowed to remain until the breaking of the bread, for the sake of a certain mystery, so that another appearance might be shown to them in him and they would recognize him only in the breaking of the bread, as Luke’s narrative demonstrates.

In keeping with the condition of their minds—which still did not know that Christ had to die and rise again—their eyes suffered something similar: not because reality deceived them, but because they were unable to perceive the truth and were supposing something other than what was real. This was so that no one might think he had recognized Christ if he were not a participant in his body—that is, in the Church, whose unity the Apostle commends in the sacrament of the bread, saying: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

Thus, when he offered them the blessed bread, their eyes were opened and they recognized him: opened, certainly, to the knowledge of him, when the obstacle by which they were prevented from recognizing him had been removed. For they were not walking with their eyes closed; rather, something was present that prevented them from recognizing what they were seeing—something such as darkness or some kind of moisture commonly causes.
