This is not because the Lord could not transform his flesh so that it truly had another appearance, unlike the one they were accustomed to behold. For before his passion he was also transformed on the mountain, so that his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2). He who made true wine from true water (John 2:7–11) can make a true body of whatever kind he wishes from any body. But he had not done this when he appeared to those two in another form.

For he did not appear to them as he was [Note: [Col. 1206] The printed editions read: “For he did not appear to them otherwise than as he was, but as he was.” The manuscripts lack the words “otherwise than as he was, but”; these had been imprudently added because the verb *apparuit*, which Augustine here uses in the sense of “was seen,” was not properly understood. Augustine proves by this reasoning that, when Christ was seen by the two men in another form, his flesh had not therefore been transformed so as truly to present another appearance: if the eyes of those who saw him were held so that they would not recognize him, it follows that he was not seen by them in the very appearance that he presented.], because their eyes were held so that they would not recognize him.

It is not incongruous, however, to understand that this impediment in their eyes came from Satan, so that Jesus would not be recognized. Yet Christ permitted it to remain until the sacrament of the bread, so that, once they had shared in the unity of his body, the removal of the enemy’s impediment might be understood, and Christ might be recognized.

73. We must believe that these are the same men about whom Mark also narrates, because he says that they went and announced it to the others. Luke says that they rose at that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon. Then they too narrated what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread.

There was therefore already a report that Jesus had risen, made by the women and by Simon Peter, to whom he had already appeared. For these two found those to whom they came in Jerusalem speaking about this.

It is possible, then, that earlier, out of fear, they had been unwilling to say on the road that they had heard he had risen, when they had said only that the women had seen angels. Since they did not know with whom they were speaking, they might reasonably have been anxious that, if they spread reports everywhere about Christ’s resurrection, they might fall into the hands of the Jews.

But when Mark says, “They announced it to the others, and they did not believe them,” while Luke says that the others were already saying that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon, what are we to understand except that there were some present who were unwilling to believe this?

Who does not see that Mark omitted what Luke explained in his narrative—namely, what Jesus had spoken with them before they recognized him, and how they recognized him in the breaking of the bread? For immediately after saying that he appeared to them in another form as they went into the countryside, Mark added: “And they went and announced it to the others, and they did not believe them”—as though they could announce one whom they had not recognized, or recognize one whose appearance had been different.

How they recognized him, then, so that they could announce him, Mark undoubtedly omitted. This should be kept in mind so that we may become accustomed to observing the Evangelists’ practice: they omit things they do not mention and join together things they do mention, in such a way that those who lack experience in considering this matter may otherwise fall into the greatest error and suppose that the Evangelists do not agree with one another.

74. Luke continues and says:

“While they were speaking about these things, Jesus stood in the midst of them and said to them: Peace be with you; it is I, do not be afraid. But they were troubled and terrified, and supposed that they saw a spirit. And he said to them: Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.”

John is understood also to mention this showing of the Lord after the resurrection, speaking as follows:

“When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst and said to them: Peace be with you. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side.”

Accordingly, the words that Luke records and John omits can be joined to these words of John. Luke continues:

“While they still did not believe and were marveling because of joy, he said: Do you have anything here to eat? They offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, he took the leftovers and gave them to them.”

The words that Luke omits can likewise be joined to these, while John records them:

“Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. He said to them again: Peace be with you. As the Father sent me, I also send you. When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them: Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained.”

To these we may again join what John omitted and Luke records:

“And he said to them: These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms about me must be fulfilled. Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them: For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things. And I send [Note: [Col. 1208] The manuscripts have this form, in agreement with the Greek, *apostellô*. The printed editions have the future tense, *mittam* (“I will send”).] the promise of my Father upon you. But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

See how Luke also mentioned the promise of the Holy Spirit, which we do not find made by the Lord except in the Gospel of John (John 14:26 and 15:26). This should not be passed over without notice, so that we may remember how the Evangelists mutually attest to certain things that they themselves do not say, yet know to have been said.

After this Luke omits all the events that took place and mentions nothing except when Jesus ascended into heaven. Yet he joins this to the preceding words as though it followed them, although the event occurred on the fortieth day, as Luke himself narrates in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:2–9), whereas the preceding events took place on the first day of the week, the day on which the Lord rose.

As for John’s statement that the Apostle Thomas was not with them at that time, while according to Luke the two men, one of whom was Cleopas, returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, along with those who were with them, it must undoubtedly be understood that Thomas had gone out from there before the Lord appeared to them while they were speaking these things.

75. John now records another manifestation of the Lord to the disciples, eight days later, when Thomas was present, who had not previously seen him.

“And after eight days,” he says, “his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came when the doors were closed, stood in the midst, and said: Peace be with you. Then he said to Thomas: Put your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing. Thomas answered and said to him: My Lord and my God. Jesus says to him: Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

We might recognize this second appearance of the Lord to the disciples—that is, the second one John records—in Mark, who briefly touches upon it in his customary manner, if we were not troubled by what he says there: “Last of all, while the eleven were reclining, he appeared.”

This is not problematic merely because John omitted their reclining, since he could have passed over that detail. The difficulty is that Mark says “last of all,” as though he did not appear to them afterward, whereas John is still going to narrate a third manifestation of him [Col. 1209] at the Sea of Tiberias.

There is also the fact that Mark says: “Reproaching them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had risen.” This refers to the two to whom he appeared as they were going into the countryside, after he had risen; and to Peter, to whom it has been established from Luke that he appeared first; perhaps also to Mary Magdalene and the other women who were with her, when he appeared to them at the tomb and met them on the road as they were returning from it.

For Mark constructs his narrative as follows. After briefly mentioning the two to whom he appeared as they were going into the countryside, and that they announced it to the others but were not believed, he says: “Last of all, while the eleven were reclining, he appeared and reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had risen.”

How, then, can this be “last of all,” as though they never saw him afterward? The final appearance was the one in which the Apostles saw the Lord on earth, when he ascended into heaven. This occurred on the fortieth day after his resurrection.

Was he then going to reproach them because they had not believed those who had seen him risen, when they themselves had already seen him so many times after the resurrection, and especially on the very day of his resurrection—that is, on the first day of the week, already near evening—as Luke and John record?

It therefore remains for us to understand that Mark intended to mention, in his customary brief manner, the same day of the Lord’s resurrection—that is, the first day of the week—when, after dawn, Mary and the other women with her saw him; when Peter also saw him; when the two men, one of whom was Cleopas, saw him, and whom Mark himself also appears to mention; and when, already near evening, the eleven—except Thomas—and those who were with them were present; when the two men reported to them what they had seen.

Mark therefore intended to mention this event as well, in his customary brevity. For this reason he said “last of all,” because on that very day this was the final event, at the beginning of the night, after the two men had returned to Jerusalem from the village where they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread. They found, as Luke says, the eleven and those who were with them already speaking about the Lord’s resurrection and about his having appeared to Peter. They too reported what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread.

But there were certainly some present who did not believe. Hence Mark’s statement is true: “They did not believe them.” While they were reclining, then, as Mark says, and while they were still speaking about these things, as Luke says, the Lord stood in the midst of them and said: “Peace be with you,” as Luke and John relate. The doors were closed when he entered to them, as John alone records.

Thus, among the words of the Lord that Luke and John say he spoke to the disciples at that time, we must insert the reproach that Mark records: that they had not believed those who had seen him risen.

76. But another difficulty arises: how can Mark say that the Lord appeared while the eleven were reclining, if this was the beginning of the night of the Lord’s day, as Luke and John remember?

John clearly says that the Apostle Thomas was not with them then. We believe that he had gone out before the Lord entered to them, after the two men returning from the village had spoken with the eleven, as Luke’s account indicates.

Luke’s narrative provides a place where it may be understood that, while they were speaking about these things, Thomas first went out and afterward the Lord entered. But Mark, who says, “Last of all, while the eleven were reclining, he appeared,” seems to require us to admit that Thomas was there as well.

Unless perhaps, although one was absent, he still wished to call them “eleven,” because that apostolic fellowship was then designated by this number, before Matthias was appointed in Judas’s place.

Or, if it is difficult to accept the passage in this way, let us understand it as follows: after the many manifestations by which he presented himself to the disciples over forty days, he appeared also, finally, while the eleven were reclining—that is, on the fortieth day itself. Since he was about to ascend from them into heaven, he wished particularly on that day to reproach them because they had not believed those who had seen him risen before they themselves saw him.

After all, once he had ascended, the nations would believe the Gospel preached by them even though they had not seen him. After this reproach Mark continues:

“And he said to them: Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned.”

Since they were going to preach that whoever did not believe would be condemned—and would not believe precisely what he had not seen—were they not the first to be reproved because, before they had seen the Lord, they had not believed those to whom he had appeared earlier?

77. That this was the Lord’s final bodily appearance on earth to the Apostles is also suggested by what Mark says next:

“And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.”

Then he adds:

“And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat at the right hand of God. But they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.”

When he says, “And the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven,” he seems sufficiently to indicate that this conversation with them on earth was his final one, although the wording does not compel that conclusion entirely. For he does not say, “After he had spoken these things to them,” but “after he had spoken to them.” Thus, if necessity required it, the statement could allow that this was not his final conversation, nor that this was the final day on which he was present with them on earth. The words “after he had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven” could refer to everything he spoke with them throughout those days.

But since what we have said above more strongly persuades us that this was the final day than that the ten who were present in Thomas’s absence should be called eleven, we should believe that, after this conversation recorded by Mark, and with the words that follow—whether spoken by the disciples or by the Lord himself—recorded in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:4–8), the Lord was taken up into heaven, on the fortieth [Col. 1211] day after the day of his resurrection.

78. Although John acknowledges that he omitted many things Jesus did, he nevertheless wished to record a third manifestation of him to the disciples after the resurrection, at the Sea of Tiberias: to seven disciples, namely Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two others whom he did not name, while they were fishing.

At that time, at his command, they cast the nets on the right side and drew in 153 large fish. At that time also he asked Peter three times whether he loved him, entrusted his sheep to him to feed, foretold his own passion, and said concerning John: “So I will have him remain until I come.” [Note: [Col. 1211] The Louvain edition reads *si* (“if”), in accordance with the Greek text, *ean*. But Rat., Erasmus, and all the manuscripts read *sic* (“so”); and it is clear from what follows below, book 4, section 20, that Augustine read it in this way.]

John brought his Gospel to an end at this point.

79. It must now be asked when he was first seen by the disciples in Galilee; for this third appearance which John narrates also took place in Galilee, at the Sea of Tiberias. This is readily perceived by anyone who recalls the miracle of the five loaves, which John himself begins to narrate in this way: “After these things Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, that is, the Sea of Tiberias” (John 6:1).

But where can it be supposed that he ought first to have been seen by the disciples after the resurrection, if not in [Col. 1212] Galilee? Let the words of that angel be recalled who, according to Matthew, speaks in this way to the women coming to the tomb: “Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord was laid. And go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen; and behold, he goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him. Behold, I have told you” (Matthew 28:5–7).

Likewise, according to Mark—whether it was the same angel or another—he says: “Do not be terrified. You seek Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him. But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he told you” (Mark 16:6–7).

These words seem to say that Jesus was not going to show himself to the disciples after the resurrection anywhere except in Galilee. Yet Mark himself does not mention this appearance, although he says that, early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, and that she announced it to the disciples—those who had been with him, mourning and weeping—but that they did not believe her. After this, he appeared to two of them as they were going into the countryside, and they announced it to the others. This took place, as Luke and John jointly attest, in Jerusalem on that same day of the resurrection, at the beginning of the night. He then comes to the appearance which he calls the last, when the eleven were reclining at table. After this, he says, he was taken up into heaven—a thing we know occurred on the Mount of Olives, not far from Jerusalem. Thus Mark nowhere records the fulfillment of what he testifies was foretold by the angel.

Matthew, however, says nothing else and mentions no other place at all, either before or afterward, where the disciples saw the Lord after he had risen, except in Galilee, according to the angel’s prediction. Finally, after indicating what the angel had said to the women, and after adding, as they departed, what had been done concerning the guards who had been corrupted into telling a lie, he immediately proceeds as though nothing else followed—for in fact the angel had said: “He has risen, and behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him,” so that it might seem that nothing else ought to follow:

“But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted. And Jesus came and spoke to them, saying: ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age’” (Matthew 28:16–20).

Thus Matthew closed his Gospel.

80. Accordingly, if the narratives of the others, when considered, did not compel a more careful investigation, we would suppose nothing else than that the Lord was first seen by the disciples after the resurrection nowhere except in Galilee. Likewise, if Mark had been silent about that angelic prediction, one might suppose that Matthew said that the disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain, and worshiped the Lord there so that what he had related as commanded and foretold by the angel might appear to have been fulfilled.

But now Luke and John clearly show that the Lord was seen by his disciples in Jerusalem on the very day of his resurrection—Jerusalem being so far from Galilee that he could not have been seen by them in both places on the same day. Mark, too, while narrating that angelic prediction in the same way, nowhere mentions that the Lord was seen by the disciples in Galilee after the resurrection. These facts strongly compel us to ask how the words “Behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him” are to be understood.

For if Matthew himself had not said at all that the eleven disciples went to the mountain in Galilee where Jesus had appointed them, and that they saw and worshiped him there, we would not think that anything in this prediction had been fulfilled literally, but that the whole had been foretold in a figurative sense—just as, according to Luke, it is said: “Behold, today and tomorrow I cast out demons and perform healings, and on the third day I am brought to completion,” which certainly was not fulfilled literally [Note: [Col. 1212] See above, book 2, chapter 75, no. 145.].

Likewise, if the angel had said, “He goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him first,” or “There alone you will see him,” or “You will see him nowhere but there,” Matthew would unquestionably conflict with the other Evangelists. But since it was said, “Behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him,” and it was not stated when this would happen—whether as soon as possible, before he had been seen by them elsewhere, or afterward, once they had seen him somewhere besides Galilee—and since Matthew’s statement that the disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain, does not specify the day, nor does his narrative order connect the events in such a way as to compel us to understand that this happened first, he does not conflict with the narratives of the others. Rather, he gives them room to be understood and accepted.

Nevertheless, the fact that the [Col. 1213] Lord commanded them to see him not where he was first going to show himself, but in Galilee, where he necessarily appeared afterward—through the angel who said, “Behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him,” and through the Lord himself, who said, “Go and tell my brothers to go into Galilee; there they will see me”—makes every believer attentive to ask in what mystery these words are to be understood.

81. First, however, we must consider when he could also have been seen bodily in Galilee, since Matthew says: “But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted.”

For it is clear that this did not happen on the very day on which he rose: Luke and John agree most plainly that he was seen in Jerusalem on that day at the beginning of the night; Mark, however, does not speak so plainly. When, then, did they see the Lord in Galilee?

Not according to what John says, at the Sea of Tiberias; for there were seven of them, and they were found fishing. Rather, it was according to what Matthew says, when the eleven were on the mountain to which Jesus had gone before them in accordance with the angel’s prediction. His narrative appears to say that they found him there, since he had gone before them according to the appointment.

It was therefore neither on the day of his resurrection nor during the following eight days, after which John says that the Lord appeared to the disciples, when Thomas first saw him, since he had not seen him on the day of the resurrection. For if those same eleven had already seen him on the mountain in Galilee within those eight days, how could Thomas, who had been among those eleven, have first seen him after the eight days?

Unless someone says that those who were eleven there were not the eleven who were already then called Apostles, but eleven disciples drawn from the larger number of disciples. For only those eleven were still called Apostles, but they were not the only disciples. It is therefore possible that not all of them, but some of them, were there, together with other disciples, so that the number eleven was completed; and thus Thomas was not there, since he first saw the Lord after those eight days.

When Mark mentioned those eleven, he did not simply say “the eleven,” but “he appeared,” he says, “to the eleven.” Luke likewise says: “They returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them.” He too shows that those eleven were the Apostles. For when he added “and those who were with them,” he sufficiently made clear that the eleven were called by this more prominent designation, while the others were with them. Accordingly, those are understood to be the men who were already called Apostles.

It could therefore have happened that, from the number of Apostles and the other disciples, eleven disciples were assembled who saw Jesus on the mountain in Galilee during those eight days.

82. But another difficulty presents itself. For when John mentioned that the Lord was seen not by eleven on a mountain, but by seven who were fishing at the Sea of Tiberias, he says: “This is now the third time that Jesus was manifested to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.”

But if we accept that, within those eight days and before Thomas saw him, the Lord was seen by some eleven disciples, this manifestation at the Sea of Tiberias will not have been [Col. 1214] the third, but the fourth. We must take care, however, lest anyone suppose that John said “the third” as though only three manifestations of the Lord had occurred. Rather, this must be understood as referring to the number of days, not to the number of manifestations—not to consecutive days, but to days separated by intervals, as he himself attests.

For on the very first day of his resurrection, apart from the fact that he was seen by the women—that is, apart from what is clear in the Gospel—he manifested himself three times: once to Peter, again to the two of whom one was Cleopas, and a third time to many who were already speaking together at the beginning of the night. But John refers all of this to a single day and counts it once.

He counts a second time—that is, on another day—when Thomas saw him; and a third time at the Sea of Tiberias. This means the third day of his manifestations, not the third manifestation.

Accordingly, after all these events we are compelled to understand that what Matthew describes then took place: the eleven disciples saw him on the mountain in Galilee to which he had gone before them according to the appointment, so that what he had foretold both through the angel and through himself might also be fulfilled literally.

83. We therefore find in the four Evangelists ten instances in which it is recorded that the Lord was seen by human beings after the resurrection.

Once, by the women at the tomb (John 20:14).

A second time, by the same women as they were returning from the tomb on the road (Matthew 28:9).

A third time, by Peter (Luke 24:35).

A fourth time, by the two who were going to a village (ibid. 15).

A fifth time, by several in Jerusalem, when Thomas was not present (John 20:19–24).

A sixth time, when Thomas saw him (ibid. 26).

A seventh time, at the Sea of Tiberias (ibid. 21:1).

An eighth time, on the mountain in Galilee, according to Matthew (Matthew 28:16–17).

A ninth time, in the account of Mark, “last of all, while they were reclining,” since they were no longer on earth to dine with him (Mark 16:14).

A tenth time, on that very day—not now on earth, but lifted up in the cloud, when he ascended into heaven. Mark and Luke mention this. Mark, after the appearance to them while they were reclining, continues in this way: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven” (ibid. 19). Luke, omitting everything that could have taken place during the forty days in which he acted with the disciples, silently joins to that first day of his resurrection, when he appeared to many in Jerusalem, the final day on which he ascended into heaven. He narrates it in this way: “And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he withdrew from them, and was carried up into heaven” (Luke 24:50–51).

Thus they saw him, in addition to what they had seen while he was on earth, while he was also being carried up into heaven. Therefore, the Gospel books record that he was seen by human beings this many times before he ascended into heaven: nine times on earth, and once in the air as he ascended.

84. But not everything was written down, as John admits (John 21:25). For his intercourse with them was frequent during the forty days before he ascended into heaven (Acts 1:3). Yet he did not appear to them throughout all forty consecutive days. For John says that after the first day of his resurrection another eight days intervened, after which he appeared to them again.

The third time, at the Sea of Tiberias, may perhaps have been on the immediately following [Col. 1215] day; there is nothing contradictory in this. And afterward, whenever he wished, he appeared to them, appointing what he had also foretold earlier: that he would go before them into the mountain of Galilee.

Indeed, throughout those forty days he appeared as often as he wished, to whom he wished, and in whatever manner he wished. Thus Peter says, when he was preaching about him to Cornelius and those who were with him: “We ate and drank with him after he had risen from the dead, for forty days” (Acts 10:41).

This does not mean that they had eaten and drunk with him every day for forty days, since that would conflict with John, who inserts those eight days during which he did not appear to them before he was manifested for the third time at the Sea of Tiberias. From that point onward, even if he appeared to them and dined with them every day, there is no contradiction.

Perhaps for this reason it was said, “for forty days,” since four times ten has a symbolic meaning referring either to the whole world or to the whole temporal age. For those first ten days, which include the eight days, can, in the manner of Scripture, be counted as the whole without inconsistency.

85. Let us therefore also consider what the apostle Paul says, to see whether it raises no difficulty: “He rose,” he says, “on the third day according to the Scriptures, and appeared to Cephas.” He did not say, “He appeared first to Cephas,” since that would conflict with the Gospel, where it is read that he first appeared to the women.

“Then,” he says, “to the twelve” [Note: [Col. 1215] Lov. has “eleven.” But the manuscripts consistently have “twelve” in this testimony of the Apostle, as do the editions of Rat. and Er. at this place, although these same manuscript codices shortly afterward read “with those eleven.”]—whichever twelve they were, at whatever hour, yet on the very day of the resurrection.

“Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once.” Whether these were gathered together with the eleven behind closed doors because of fear of the Jews, after Thomas had gone out and Jesus came to them; or whether it happened at some time after those eight days, there is no difficulty.

“Then,” he says, “he appeared to James.” We must not understand this to mean that he was then first seen by James, but that he appeared to him individually in some particular manifestation.

“Then to all the Apostles”—not then for the first time to them either, but so that he might now associate more familiarly with them until the day of his ascension.

“Last of all,” he says, “as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me” (1 Corinthians 15:4–8). But this occurred from heaven, after a considerable interval following his ascension.

86. Let us now examine the matter we postponed: for what mystery did he, according to Matthew and Mark, give this command after rising, “I will go before you into Galilee; there you will see me” (Matthew 26:32; 28:7; Mark 14:28; 16:7)? Even if this was fulfilled, it was fulfilled only after many other events, although the command was given—without prejudice to what necessity may require—in such a way that either this [Col. 1216] alone or this first might have been expected to occur.

There can therefore be no doubt that, since this is not the voice of the Evangelist narrating that the event happened in this way, but the voice of the angel speaking at the Lord’s command and afterward of the Lord himself, while the Evangelist narrates only that this was said by the angel and by the Lord, the saying must be understood prophetically.

For “Galilee” is interpreted either as “Transmigration” or as “Revelation.” First, according to the meaning of “transmigration,” what else can the words “He goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him” be understood to mean than that the grace of Christ was going to transmigrate from the people of Israel to the Gentiles?

The Apostles would not have been believed when preaching the Gospel to them unless the Lord himself had prepared the way for them in the hearts of human beings. This is understood by the words, “He goes before you into Galilee.”

But the fact that they would rejoice and marvel as difficulties were broken through and overcome, and as a door was opened to them in the Lord through the illumination of believers, is understood by the words, “There you will see him”—that is, there you will find his members; there, in those who receive you, you will recognize his living body.

According to the other interpretation, by which “Galilee” means “Revelation,” this is to be understood not in the form of a servant, but in the form in which he is equal to the Father (Philippians 2:6–7). He promised this to those who love him in John when he said: “And I will love him, and I will show myself to him” (John 14:21).

This is not according to what they were already seeing, and what, even after rising with his scars, he later displayed not merely to be seen but also to be touched. Rather, it is according to that ineffable light “which enlightens every human being coming into this world,” according to which “he shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not comprehended him” (John 1:9, 5).

He went before us to the place from which, when he came to us, he did not depart, and to which, when he went before us, he did not abandon us. That will be the revelation that is true Galilee, when we shall be like him; there we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

It will also be the happier transmigration from this age into that eternity, if we embrace his commandments in such a way that we deserve to be separated to his right hand. For then the wicked will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25:33, 46). They will transmigrate from here to there, and there they will see him in a manner in which the ungodly do not see him.

“For the wicked will be taken away,” it says, “so that he may not see the glory of the Lord” (Isaiah 26:10); and “the wicked shall not see the light.” “This,” however, he says, “is eternal life: that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). In that eternity he will be known, and through the form of a servant he will lead his servants to the point where, as free persons, they may contemplate the form of the Lord.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1215]

## On the matters peculiar to Mark, Luke, and John

### PROLOGUE

1. Now, since we have examined Matthew’s narrative continuously and compared the other three with it to the end, showing that they conflict neither with themselves nor with one another, let us similarly examine Mark. Apart from what he said together with Matthew—concerning which we have already completed whatever discussion seemed necessary—let us inspect [Col. 1216] and compare the rest of his account, so that it may be shown to conflict with none of them up to the Lord’s Supper. For from that point onward we have already examined and treated how all the accounts of all four agree with one another to the end.

## CHAPTER ONE

### How, in Mark’s Gospel, apart from what he said together with Matthew, no contradiction [Col. 1217] is demonstrated from the beginning up to the passage, “And they enter Capernaum, and immediately on the sabbaths he was teaching them,” which he shares with Luke

2. Mark therefore begins in this way: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet,” and so on, up to the passage where he says: “And they enter Capernaum, and immediately, entering the synagogue on the sabbath, he was teaching them” (Mark 1:1–21).

Throughout this entire sequence, all the earlier material has been considered together with Matthew. Mark said this together with Luke because Jesus entered Capernaum and taught them in their synagogue on the sabbaths (Luke 4:31); but it raises no difficulty.

## CHAPTER TWO

### Concerning the man from whom the unclean spirit was expelled while convulsing him, and how Mark does not contradict Luke, who related this event with him

3. Mark continues and says: “And they were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes. And there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out, saying: ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us?’” and so on, up to the passage where he says: “And he was preaching in their synagogues and throughout all Galilee, and casting out demons” (Mark 1:22–39).

Although in this entire passage there are certain things that he said together only with Luke, they have already been treated when we followed Matthew’s continuous narrative, because they occurred within that sequence in such a way that I did not think they should be passed over.

But Luke says concerning the unclean spirit that it came out of the man in such a way that it did him no harm. Mark, however, says: “And the unclean spirit, tearing him, cried out with a loud voice and came out of him.” It can therefore seem contradictory. For how could it tear him—or, as some manuscripts read, convulse him—if, according to Luke, it did him no harm?

But Luke himself also says: “And when the demon had thrown him into their midst, it came out of him and did him no harm” (Luke 4:33–35). From this it is understood that Mark’s phrase “convulsing him” means what Luke expressed by “when it had thrown him into their midst.” What Luke immediately adds—“and it did him no harm”—is understood to mean that this tossing about and convulsion of the limbs did not weaken him, as demons sometimes depart after inflicting injury on certain limbs [Note: [Col. 1217] Seven manuscripts read, “with limbs amputated or torn away.” Others have “or crushed.”].

## CHAPTER THREE

### Concerning the name Peter: how it is repeatedly emphasized without contradicting John, who said when he received this name

4. Mark continues: “And a leper came to him, beseeching him, and, kneeling, said to him: ‘If you will, you can make me clean,’” and so on, up to the passage where he says: “And they cried out, saying: ‘You are the Son of God.’ And he sternly charged them not to reveal him” (Mark 1:40; 3:12).

Luke says something similar to this final statement, but without any question of contradiction (Luke 4:41).

Mark continues: “And going up into a mountain, he called to himself those whom he himself wished, and they came to him. And he made twelve to be with him, and that he might send them to preach; and he gave them authority to heal diseases and to cast out demons. And he gave Simon the name Peter,” and so [Col. 1218] on, up to the passage where he says: “And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled” (Mark 3:13–5:20).

I know that I have already discussed the names of the disciples when I was following Matthew’s order (above, book 2, chapters 17 and 53). Here again I warn the reader lest anyone suppose that Simon received the name Peter only now, so that this would conflict with John, who records that it had been said to him long before: “You shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted as Peter (John 1:42).

John recalled the very words of the Lord by which he gave him the name. Mark, however, recalled the matter here by way of summary when he said, “And he gave Simon the name Peter.” For when he wished to enumerate the names of the twelve Apostles and was obliged to mention Peter, he briefly indicated that Peter had not previously been called by this name, but that the Lord had given it to him—not at that moment, but when John recorded the Lord’s own words.

The rest raises no contradiction for anyone, and it has already been treated.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### How the statement, “The more he commanded them to be silent, the more they proclaimed it,” does not contradict his foreknowledge, which is commended in the Gospel

5. Mark continues: “And when Jesus had crossed over again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered around him, and he was by the sea,” and so on, up to the passage where he says: “And the Apostles, returning to Jesus, reported to him everything they had done and taught” (Mark 5:21; 6:30).

He said this last part together with Luke, without any disagreement (Luke 9:10); the rest has already been treated.

Mark continues: “And he said to them: ‘Come away by yourselves into a deserted place and rest a little,’” and so on, up to the passage where he says: “The more he commanded them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it, and they were astonished beyond measure, saying: ‘He has done all things well; he has made the deaf hear and the mute speak’” (Mark 6:31; 7:37).

In these matters there appears to be nothing in Mark that contradicts Luke, and we already considered all the earlier material when we compared it with Matthew.

But care must be taken lest anyone think that this final statement from Mark’s Gospel conflicts with all the passages that show, through many of his other deeds and sayings, that he knew what was happening within human beings—that their thoughts and intentions could not be hidden from him. John says this most plainly: “But Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people, and because he had no need for anyone to testify about a person; for he himself knew what was in a person” (John 2:24–25).

But why should it be surprising that he saw the present intentions of human beings, when he also foretold Peter’s future denial [Note: [Col. 1218] The printed editions have “future denial.” The manuscripts do not add “denial”; in its place, “intention” is to be understood.]—an intention which Peter certainly did not yet have when he confidently declared himself ready to die for him or with him (Matthew 26:33–35)?

Since this is so, how is it not contrary to such great knowledge and foreknowledge of his that Mark says: “He commanded them not to tell anyone; but the more he commanded them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it”?

For if he knew that they would proclaim it all the more the more he commanded them not to proclaim it, as one who knew both the present and future [Col. 1219] intentions of human beings, why did he give this command?

The answer is that he wished to show the sluggish how much more zealously and fervently they ought to proclaim him, since he commands them to preach while those who were forbidden could not keep silent.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### Concerning the man of whom John reported that he cast out demons in Christ’s name without joining the disciples, and to whom Jesus said, “Do not forbid him”; how this does not contradict the saying, “Whoever is not with me is against me”

6. Mark continues: “In those days, when there was again a great crowd and they had nothing to eat” [Note: [Col. 1219] The printed editions added “with Jesus,” but this is absent from the manuscripts and from the sacred Scriptures], and so on, up to the passage where he says:

“John answered him, saying: ‘Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name who does not follow us, and we forbade him.’ But Jesus said: ‘Do not forbid him. For there is no one who performs a mighty deed in my name and can quickly speak evil of me; for whoever is not against you is for you’” (Mark 8:1; 9:39).

Luke narrates this similarly (Luke 9:49–50), except that he does not include the words: “For there is no one who performs a mighty deed in my name and can quickly speak evil of me.” There is therefore no question of any contradiction between them.

But we must see whether this might be thought contrary to the Lord’s saying: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matthew 12:30; Luke 11:23).

For how was this man not against him, since he was not with him? John reported that he did not follow with them. If whoever is not with him is against him, how was this man not against him? Or, if he was against him, how does he say to the disciples, “Do not forbid him; for whoever is not against you is for you”?

Will someone say that the distinction lies in the fact that here he says to the disciples, “Whoever is not against you is for you,” whereas there he spoke of himself: “Whoever is not with me is against me”?

But surely someone cannot be apart from him if he is associated with his disciples as with his members. Otherwise, how will these sayings be true: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40), and “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40)?

Or can someone not be against him if he has been against his disciples? What then becomes of: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16), and “Whatever you did not do for one of the least of mine, you did not do for me” (Matthew 25:45), and “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), when he was persecuting his disciples?

Clearly, what is meant is that someone is not with him to the extent that he is against him, and is not against him to the extent that he is with him.

For example, this very man who performed mighty deeds in Christ’s name and was not associated with the fellowship of Christ’s disciples was with them to the extent that he performed mighty deeds in his name, and he was not against them to that extent. But to the extent that he did not adhere to their fellowship, he was not with them, and to that extent he was against them.

But because the disciples had forbidden him to do what he was doing in the respect in which he was with [Col. 1220] them, the Lord said to them, “Do not forbid him.” They ought to have forbidden what lay outside their fellowship, in order to persuade him toward the unity of the Church—not what he shared with them, namely, commending the name of their Master and Lord by the expulsion of demons.

In the same way the Catholic Church does not condemn the common sacraments in heretics. In these they are with us, and are not against us. But it condemns and forbids division and separation, or any position opposed to peace and truth. In this they are against us, because in this they are not with us; they do not gather with us, and therefore they scatter.

## CHAPTER SIX

### How, on the occasion of the man who cast out demons in Christ’s name, although he did not follow with the disciples, Mark reported that the Lord said more than Luke, and how it is shown that this pertains precisely to the fact that he forbade the man to be prevented from performing a mighty deed in his name

7. Mark continues and says:

“For whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you are Christ’s, truly I say to you, he shall not lose his reward. And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea. And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished,” and so on, up to the passage where he says:

“Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:40–49).

Mark recalls these words as spoken by the Lord after he forbade the disciples to prevent the man who was casting out demons in his name, although he did not follow with the disciples. He includes [Col. 1220] some things that none of the other Evangelists included, some that Matthew also included, and some that both Matthew and Luke included. But the latter placed them in connection with other occasions and in a different order of events, not at this point, where the man was mentioned who did not follow Christ with the disciples but cast out demons in his name.

For this reason it seems to me that here too, according to Mark’s account, the Lord said things that he also said elsewhere because they sufficiently pertained to this very statement of his by which he forbade the prevention of mighty deeds being performed in his name, even by someone who did not follow him with the disciples.

He connects the statements in this way: “For whoever is not against you is for you. Whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you are Christ’s, truly I say to you, he shall not lose his reward.”

Thus he shows that the man about whom John had reported, and from whom this discourse arose, was not so separated from the fellowship of the disciples as to condemn it like a heretic. Rather, he was like people who do not yet dare to receive Christ’s sacraments but nevertheless favor the Christian name, to the point that they also receive Christians and serve them for no other reason than that they are Christians. It is of such people that he says they do not lose their reward.

This does not mean that they should already regard themselves as safe and secure because of the goodwill they show toward Christians, even if they are not washed in Christ’s baptism and incorporated into his unity. Rather, it means that they are already being governed by God’s mercy in such a way that they may also arrive at these things [Note: [Col. 1221] The printed editions read “at this”; the manuscripts read “at these things.”] and thus depart from this age secure.

Before they are joined to the number of Christians, they are certainly more useful than those who, although already called Christians and instructed in the Christian sacraments, give such advice that those whom they persuade to follow it are dragged with them into eternal punishment. In the language of bodily members, the Lord commands that such people be torn away from the body, as a hand or eye that causes stumbling—that is, from the fellowship of unity itself—so that one may come to life without them rather than go with them into Gehenna.

They are separated from those from whom they are separated precisely when they do not consent to those who, by persuading them to evil, cause them to stumble. If their perversity becomes known to all the good with whom they have fellowship [Note: [Col. 1221] In most manuscripts, “there is acquaintance” rather than “there is fellowship.”], they are entirely separated from the fellowship of all and from participation in the divine sacraments themselves.

But if they are known in this way to some while their perversity remains unknown to many, they must be tolerated as chaff is tolerated on the threshing floor before the winnowing. Thus no consent is given to participation in their iniquity, nor is the fellowship of the good abandoned on their account.

This is what those do who have salt in themselves and have peace among themselves.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### From this point up to the Lord’s Supper, from which the consideration of all the accounts began, no question concerning Mark has been treated

8. Mark continues: “And rising from there, he came into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan, and crowds again gathered around him, and, as he was accustomed to do, he taught them again,” and so on, up to the passage where he says:

“For they all gave out of what they had in abundance; but she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had, her whole livelihood” (Mark 10:1; 12:44).

Throughout this entire sequence, all the earlier material was considered so that nothing might appear to contradict it, when we compared the other accounts with Matthew’s order. But this account of the poor widow who put two small coins into the treasury is given by only two: Mark and Luke (Luke 21:1–4), and they agree without any question.

From this point up to the Lord’s Supper, from which we began to examine and treat all the details of all the accounts, Mark says nothing that compels comparison with anyone else in order to investigate whether anything appears contradictory.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

### Concerning Luke’s Gospel, and how its beginning agrees with the beginning of the book of the Acts of the Apostles
9. Let us now proceed in order with the Gospel of Luke, except for those passages which it has in common with Matthew and Mark, since all those have already been treated. Luke therefore begins as follows:

“Since many have undertaken to arrange an account of the events that have been fulfilled among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having followed everything from the beginning [Note: [Col. 1221] Four manuscripts read “all things.” The others, along with the printed editions, have “everything”; so also the ancient Corbie Bible. According to the Greek, *pâsin* (“all”).], to write them out carefully and in order for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may recognize the truth of the matters about which you have been instructed” (Luke 1:1–4).

This opening does not yet belong to the narrative of the Gospel. It does, however, admonish us to understand that the same Luke also wrote the book called the Acts of the Apostles—not merely because the name Theophilus occurs there as well, for it could have happened that there was another Theophilus, and even if he were the same person, someone else might have written something to him, just as Luke wrote the Gospel—but because there too he begins in such a way as to say:

“In the first account, O Theophilus, I dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when, giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he commanded them to preach the Gospel” [Note: [Col. 1222] Thus in several manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read, “until the day when he chose the apostles.”] (Acts 1:1–2).

He thereby made it understood that he had already written one of the four Gospel books, whose authority in the Church is supreme. Nor, because he said that he had dealt with everything Jesus began to do and teach until the day when he commanded the apostles, should it be thought that in his Gospel he wrote down everything Jesus did and said while living on earth with the apostles. Otherwise he would contradict John, who says that Jesus did many other things which, if they were written down, the whole world could not contain the books (John 21:25). It is also clear that the other evangelists have related quite a few things which Luke himself did not touch upon in his narrative.

Thus, he dealt with everything by selecting from everything those matters about which he would make his account, judging them suitable and sufficient for the function entrusted to him. And when he says that many have undertaken to arrange an account of the events that have been fulfilled among us, he seems to indicate certain people who were unable to complete the task they had undertaken. He therefore says that it seemed good to him to write carefully and in order because many had undertaken it; but we must understand him to mean those whose authority does not exist in the Church, since they were entirely unable to complete what they had undertaken.

This man, however, not only carried his narrative as far as the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, so that he might have a place worthy of his labor among the four authoritative writers of the Gospel Scriptures; he also subsequently wrote what was accomplished through the apostles—so much as he judged sufficient for building up the faith of readers or hearers—in such a way that his alone was regarded in the Church as a trustworthy book narrating the acts of the apostles, while all those who had dared to write the apostles’ deeds and words without the faith that was required were rejected. For Mark and Luke wrote at a time when they could be approved not only by the Church of Christ but also by the apostles themselves, who were still living in the flesh.

## CHAPTER IX

### How it is shown that Luke’s account of the catch of fish does not belong to what John appears to have narrated after the Lord’s resurrection; and that from there up to the Lord’s Supper, where everything concerning all of them was considered to the end, no question from Luke’s Gospel was treated

10. Luke therefore begins to narrate the Gospel as follows:

“There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the course of Abijah; and his wife was from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth,” and so on, up to the passage where he says:

“When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon, ‘Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch’” (Luke 1:5–5:4).

This entire passage raises no question of contradiction. John does indeed seem to say something similar, but that event is entirely different: it took place after the Lord’s resurrection at the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:1–11). There, not only is the time very different, but the event itself is greatly different. For there, when the nets were cast on the right side, they caught 153 fish, and they were large. Yet it belonged to the evangelist to say that, although they were so large, the nets were not torn—clearly with reference to the event Luke records, where the nets were breaking because of the great multitude of fish.

Luke said nothing else resembling John’s account except around the Lord’s passion and resurrection. We have treated that entire passage, from his Supper to the end, in such a way that, by comparing all the testimonies, we demonstrated that they disagree in nothing.

## CHAPTER X

### How the evangelist John differs from the other three

11. John is the one who remains, and there is no one left with whom he may be compared. For whatever each one says individually, when the others have not said it, can scarcely give rise to any question of contradiction.

Accordingly, it is quite clear that these three—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—were chiefly concerned with the humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, according to which he is both king and priest. And therefore Mark, who in the mystery of the four living creatures (Revelation 4:6–7) seems to represent the person of a man, either appears more to be Matthew’s companion, because he says more things in common with him on account of the royal person, which is not usually solitary, as I mentioned in the first book (Book 1, chapter 3), or—and this is the more probable understanding—he proceeds together with both of them.

For although he agrees with Matthew in more matters, in some others he agrees more closely with Luke. Thus it is shown that what Christ is as man belongs both to the lion and to the calf—that is, both to the royal person represented by Matthew and to the priestly person indicated by Luke—and that Mark bears a figure pertaining to both.

The divinity of Christ, however, by which he is equal to the Father, insofar as he is the Word and God with God, and “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14), and insofar as he and the Father are one (ibid. 10:30), was chiefly undertaken for commendation by John. Like an eagle, he lingers over those things which Christ spoke in a more exalted manner, and as it were descends to earth only rarely.

Finally, although he clearly testifies that he knew Christ’s mother, he says nothing of Christ’s birth together with Matthew and Luke, nor does he mention his baptism together with the three. Instead, commending John’s testimony alone in a lofty and exalted manner, he leaves them and proceeds with him to the wedding at Cana of Galilee. Although the evangelist himself mentions that she was his mother, he nevertheless says to her, “What have I to do with you, woman?” (ibid. 2:1–11). He was not rejecting the woman from whom he received flesh; rather, at that moment he was chiefly indicating his divinity, as he was about to turn water into wine—a divinity which had also made that woman, but had not itself been touched by her.

12. After a few days spent in Capernaum, he returns to the temple, where John records him as speaking about the temple of his body:

“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (ibid. 2:12–22).

Here he especially indicates not only that God, the Word made flesh, was in the temple, but also that he himself raised that same flesh from the dead—not, of course, except according to that which is one with the Father and does not work separately. In nearly all the other passages, Scripture perhaps says only that God raised him; nor is it expressed anywhere else in such a way that, when God raised Christ, Christ himself also raised himself, because he is one God with the Father—as in this passage where he says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

13. Then, together with Nicodemus, how great and how divine were the things he spoke! From there he proceeds again to John’s testimony and commends the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices only because of the bridegroom’s voice. There he admonishes us that the human soul does not shine by its own light, nor is blessed except through participation in unchangeable wisdom.

From there he goes to the Samaritan woman, where the water is mentioned of which whoever drinks will never thirst forever. From there he returns again to Cana of Galilee, where he had made wine from water. There he records that he said to the royal official whose son was ill, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe” (ibid. 3:1–4:54)—wishing to raise the mind of the believer above all mutable things to such a degree that he would not even have the faithful seek miracles themselves, although they are performed divinely through the mutability of bodies.

14. From there he returns to Jerusalem, and a sick man who had been ill for thirty-eight years is healed. What things are said on this occasion, and how long they are said! There it is stated:

“The Jews were seeking to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God.”

Here it is sufficiently shown that he did not say that God was his Father in the ordinary way in which holy men customarily say it, but indicated that he was equal to him. For a little earlier, when they were accusing him concerning the Sabbath, he had said to them:

“My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

They were enraged there—not because he called God his Father, but because he wished to be understood as equal to him when he said, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” He showed that, since the Father works, it follows that the Son also works, because the Father does not work without the Son. For there, a little later, he says to them, who were already angry with him for this reason:

“Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (ibid. 5).

15. Finally John descends to join those three who were walking on earth with the same Lord, when five thousand men were fed with five loaves. Yet he alone records that, when they wanted to make him king, he alone fled to the mountain.

In this event, I see nothing else that he wished to impress upon the rational soul except that he reigns over our mind and reason insofar as he is on high, having no communion of nature with human beings, alone because he is the only-begotten of the Father. This mystery escaped carnal people creeping along below, because it is exceedingly lofty. Hence he himself also fled from them to the mountain, since they sought his kingdom with an earthly mind. Elsewhere also he says, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

John alone likewise records this, as though soaring above earthly things on an ethereal flight and rejoicing in the light of the Sun of righteousness. From that same mountain, after the miracle of the five loaves, he remained for a little while with the same three until they had crossed the sea. When he walked upon the waters, he immediately raised himself again into the word of the Lord—how great, how extended, how long, how heavenly and exalted a word, arising from the occasion of the bread! He had said to the crowds:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled. Work not for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life.”

From there he continued for a very long time with such lofty and exalted words. Then those who afterward did not walk with him fell from this height of the word. Those who were able to understand remained attached to him, for he said:

“It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (ibid. 6).

For certainly the Spirit profits also through the flesh [Note: [Col. 1225] Thus in seventeen manuscripts. The printed editions read, “and the Spirit profits the flesh.”]; and the Spirit alone profits; but the flesh without the Spirit profits nothing.

16. Then, when his brothers—that is, his relatives according to the flesh—suggested that he go up for the feast, so that he might become known to the multitude, with what height did he answer:

“My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready. The world cannot hate you; but it hates me, because I testify concerning it that its works are evil.”

This is therefore the meaning of “Your time is always ready”: you desire this day of which the prophet says, “But I have not wearied, following you, Lord, and I have not desired the day of man; you know” (Jeremiah 17:16). It means to fly toward the light of the Word and to desire that day which Abraham longed to see; he saw it and rejoiced (John 8:56).

After he had gone up to the temple for the feast, John records what he said there—how wonderful, how divine, how exalted! He said that they could not come where he was going; that they both knew him and knew where he was from; and that the one who sent him was true, though they did not know him—as if he were saying, “You know where I am from, and you do not know where I am from.”

What else did he wish to be understood by this except that, according to the flesh, he could have been known to them—his people and his homeland [Note: [Col. 1225] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and Lovaniensis read, “both by his people and by his homeland.” Manuscript M.]; but according to his divinity he was unknown? There too he spoke about the gift of the Holy Spirit and showed who he was, since he would be able to give so exalted a gift (John 7).

17. Again, as he was returning there from the Mount of Olives, John narrates how many and how great were the things he spoke, after he had forgiven the adulterous woman, whom those testing him had brought before him as though she were to be stoned. When he was writing with his finger on the ground, perhaps indicating that such people were to be written on the earth, not in heaven, where he admonished the disciples to rejoice that they were written (Luke 10:20); or perhaps, by humbling himself, as he showed by the inclination of his head, he was making signs upon the earth; or perhaps the time had already come for his law to be written upon earth that would bear fruit, and not upon barren stone as before.

After this, therefore, he said that he was the light of the world, and that whoever followed him would not walk in darkness but would have the light of life. He also said that he was the Beginning—the very one who was speaking to them. By this name he certainly distinguished himself from that light which he made, as the light through which all things were made, so that what he had said—“I am the light of the world”—would not be understood in the same way as when he said to the disciples, “You are the light of the world.”

For they were like a lamp, which must not be placed under a bushel but upon a lampstand (Matthew 5:14–15), just as he says also of John the Baptist, “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35). But he himself was like the beginning, of which it is said, “We have all received from his fullness” (ibid. 1:16). There he said that he was the Son, the truth [Note: [Col. 1226] Thus all manuscripts and Erasmus. Lovaniensis reads, “the Son of truth.” The Ratian edition reads, “and the truth.”], which, unless it liberates, no one will be free (ibid. 8:1–36).

18. Afterward, when he had given sight to the man blind from birth, John lingers over the occasion in a lengthy discourse concerning sheep, the shepherd, and the door, and concerning his power to lay down his life and take it up again. In this he displayed the supreme power of his divinity.

Then, when the Feast of Dedication was taking place in Jerusalem, he records that the Jews said to him:

“How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly.”

Taking this as an opportunity for discourse, John narrates the exalted things he also said. There he said:

“I and the Father are one.”

From there John goes on to proclaim that Lazarus had been raised by him. There Christ said:

“I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even though he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die.”

In these words, what do we recognize except the height of his divinity, in whose eternal participation we shall live?

From there John again meets Matthew and Mark in Bethany (Matthew 26:6–13; Mark 14:3–9), where the event took place involving the precious ointment with which Mary poured oil over his feet and his head (John 9:1–12:8). From this point onward, up to the Lord’s passion and resurrection, John proceeds with the three evangelists, although the narrative concerns the same places.

19. As for the Lord’s discourses, John does not cease to rise toward those things which Christ also spoke from this point onward in an exalted and prolonged manner. When Gentiles wished to see him through Philip and Andrew, he delivered an elevated discourse which none of the other evangelists included. There he again mentions in a splendid way the light that illuminates and makes sons of light (ibid. 12:20–50).

Then, at the very Supper, about which none of the evangelists was silent, how many and how exalted are the words of Christ that John records and the others omit! He speaks not only of the commendation of humility, when he washed the disciples’ feet, but, after the betrayer who had been identified by the morsel went out, John lingers over the astonishing and extremely lengthy discourse of Christ, with the eleven remaining with him.

There Christ said:

“Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”

He spoke many things about the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom he was about to send to them; about his glorification which he had with the Father before the world existed; and about his making us one in himself, just as he and the Father are one—not so that he, the Father, and we should be one, but that we should be one as they are one.

He said many other wondrous and exalted things. Who does not perceive that, even if we were capable of discussing them as they deserve, we have nevertheless not undertaken to do so in this work (John 13–17)? Perhaps they must be presented elsewhere; here certainly they are not to be expected.

For we wish to commend to lovers of the word of God and students of holy truth the fact that, although John was a herald and preacher in his Gospel of the same Christ who is true and truthful, as were the other three who wrote the Gospel and the other apostles who did not undertake to write the narrative itself but fulfilled the duty of their office in that preaching, John nevertheless was carried far higher into the things of Christ from the very beginning of his book.

He was rarely together with the others: first, near the Jordan, because of the testimony of John the Baptist; then across the Sea of Tiberias, when Christ fed the crowds with five loaves and walked upon the waters; third, in Bethany, where he was anointed with precious ointment through the devotion of a faithful woman; and finally, until he encountered them at the time of the passion, which he necessarily had to narrate together with them.

Yet there he presented the Lord’s Supper itself, about which none of them was silent, much more richly, as though drawing from the storeroom of the Lord’s breast, where he habitually reclined.

Then he strikes Pilate with loftier words, saying that Christ’s kingdom was not of this world, that he had been born a king, and that he had come into this world for this purpose: to bear witness to the truth (ibid. 18:36–37).

After the resurrection, he avoids Mary with mystical profundity [Note: [Col. 1227] Erasmus, Lovaniensis, and the manuscripts read “visiting.” But the Ratian edition, more correctly, reads “avoiding.”], saying:

“Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (ibid. 20:17).

He also gave the disciples the Holy Spirit by breathing upon them (ibid. 22), so that the Spirit himself, consubstantial and coeternal with the Trinity, would not be thought to belong only to the Father and not also to be the Spirit of the Son.

20. Finally, when commending his sheep to Peter, who loved him and confessed that love three times, he says that he wished that same John to remain until he came (ibid. 21:15, 23). Here, too, it seems to me that he taught through a profound mystery that this very evangelical ministry of John [Note: [Col. 1227] Two manuscripts read, “this very hidden ministry.” Shortly afterward, three manuscripts and the Ratian edition read, “is carried by the sublimity of the word.”], by which he is carried sublimely into the clearest light of the Word, where the equality and unchangeableness of the Trinity can be seen, and by which it can be most clearly discerned and known in what special respect the man by whose assumption the Word was made flesh differs from the others, cannot be clearly seen and understood until the Lord himself comes.

For this reason he will remain until he comes. He remains now in the faith of believers, but then he will be contemplated face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12), when our life appears and we also appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4).

But whoever thinks that it can happen to a person still living this mortal life that, once every cloud of bodily and carnal imaginings has been removed and dispersed, he may possess the serene light of unchangeable truth, cling to it firmly and unfalteringly with a mind wholly withdrawn from the habits of this life, and understand neither what he should seek nor who is to seek it—let him instead believe the lofty and wholly trustworthy authority that, as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord and walk by faith, not yet by sight (2 Corinthians 5:6–7).

Thus, steadfastly retaining and guarding faith, hope, and love, let him direct his attention toward sight, on the basis of the pledge we have received, the Holy Spirit, who will teach us all truth (John 16:13), when God, who raised Jesus Christ from the dead, will give life also to our mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in us (Romans 8:10–11).

Before that which is dead because of sin is given life, it is undoubtedly corruptible and weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15). And if, when aided, the mind at times rises above this cloud by which the whole earth is covered (Ecclesiasticus 24:6)—that is, above this carnal darkness by which all earthly life is covered—it is as though struck by a swift flash of lightning, and returns to its weakness, while the desire remains by which it may be raised again, without possessing sufficient purity by which it may be fixed there.

The more each person is capable of this, the greater he is; the less he is capable of it, the lesser he is. But if the human mind has not yet experienced anything of this kind, though Christ dwells in it through faith, it must devote itself to diminishing and bringing to an end the desires of this age through the practice of moral virtue. It should walk, as though in the company of those three evangelists, with Christ the mediator.

Let it hold faithfully, with great joy of hope, to him who is always the Son of God but for our sake became the Son of man, so that his eternal power and divinity, adapted to our weakness and mortality, might make for us from ourselves, in him and toward him, the way.

Let him be ruled by Christ the King, so that he may not sin; and, if he should happen to sin, let him be cleansed by that same Christ the Priest. Thus, nourished in the practice of a good way of life [Note: [Col. 1228] Seven reputable manuscripts and Eugyppius read, “with wings nourished,” instead of “nourished.”], and carried up from earth on the two wings of a twofold love as on two powerful wings, let him be illuminated by that same Christ the Word—the Word who was in the beginning, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1)—even if only through a mirror and in an enigma, yet far more sublimely than by any bodily likeness.

Therefore, although in those three evangelists the gifts of the active life shine forth, while in John’s Gospel the gifts of the contemplative life shine forth for those capable of discerning them, even John’s Gospel, because it is partial, will remain until the perfect comes (1 Corinthians 13:12, 9–10).

“To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit” (ibid. 12:8). One savors the day for the Lord (Romans 14:6); another drinks something more clearly from the Lord’s breast; another is carried up to the third heaven and hears ineffable words (2 Corinthians 12:2–4). Yet all, as long as they are in the body, are away from the Lord (ibid. 5:6).

And for all the faithful who possess a good hope, whose names are written in the book of life, what was said is preserved:

“I also will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

Nevertheless, during this pilgrimage, the more anyone has advanced in understanding or knowledge of this matter, the more carefully he must guard against the devil’s vices: pride and envy.
