Let him remember that this very Gospel of John, the more greatly it raises us toward the contemplation of truth, so much the more greatly commands us concerning the sweetness of love. And because that command is most true and salutary—“The greater you are, the more humble yourself in everything” (Ecclesiasticus 3:20)—the evangelist who commends Christ far more highly than the others washes the disciples’ feet in his presence (John 13:5).

# [ON THE LORD’S SERMON ON THE MOUNT]

[Col. 1229]

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOKS ON THE LORD’S SERMON ON THE MOUNT

This work belongs to the year of Christ 393 or 394 and was composed by Augustine during the period of his presbyterate. For in the first book of the *Retractions*, chapter 19, after reviewing the discussion on Faith and the Creed which he held at the council of Hippo-Regius in the year 393, Augustine recalls his unfinished book on Genesis. Since he assigns it no chronological indication other than one that can be derived from the council mentioned earlier, he next makes mention of this work in the following words:

“At the same time I wrote two volumes on the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount according to Matthew.”

In one volume he explains the first part of that sermon, contained in Matthew chapter 5; in the other, the later part contained in chapters 6 and 7.

Why, then, he undertook to treat this sermon before all others from the whole Gospel, he seems to indicate at the beginning of the work: namely, that he had understood it to be complete with respect to all the commandments by which the Christian life is formed. He explains all these commandments in the order in which they are reported by Matthew, demonstrating that they pertain to and correspond in sequence with the first seven statements concerning the blessed at the beginning of the sermon.

Many years later, when Pollentius was examining this work more closely, he encountered several difficulties concerning a wife who had separated from her husband. He submitted them to the holy Doctor, who resolved them in the first book on *Adulterous Marriages*.

[Col. 1229]

[Note: [Col. 1229] See Book 1, chapter 19, of the *Retractions*, column 614, from the words “At the same time I wrote on the Lord’s Sermon” through column 617, ending with the words “which the Lord spoke.” M.]

## THE TWO BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE LORD’S SERMON ON THE MOUNT ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

[Note: [Col. 1229] Written approximately in the year of Christ 393.]

[Note: [Col. 1229] In correcting these books, we used the Albinensis, Arnulfensis, Cistercian, Colbertinus, Corbeiensis, Floriacensis, Gemmeticensis, Lyrensis, Michaelinus, Pratellensis, Sagiensis, and Vindocinensis manuscripts; two Vatican manuscripts; two Bec manuscripts; and the variant readings of the Louvain theologians from six Belgian manuscripts. We also used the above-mentioned editions of Erasmus and Lovaniensis, to which were added the complete edition of Johannes Amerbach, produced at Basel in 1506, and another by Jacobus Mareschallus, published at Lyon in 1520. In addition, we consulted excerpts of Abbot Eugyppius in Corbeiensis and Germanensis manuscripts, as well as the collection of Florus in another Corbeiensis manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 1229] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

# BOOK ONE

### The first part of the sermon delivered by the Lord on the mountain, contained in Matthew chapter 5, is explained

## CHAPTER I

1. The sermon which our Lord Jesus Christ spoke on the mountain, as we read in the Gospel according to Matthew—if anyone considers it devoutly and soberly—I think he will find in it, insofar as it concerns the best way of life, a perfect standard for the Christian life. We dare to promise this without rashness, reasoning from the very words of the Lord himself.

For the sermon concludes in such a way that it appears to contain all the commandments that pertain to forming a life. For he says:

“Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house upon rock: the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them, I will compare him to a foolish man who built his house upon sand: the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, and it fell; and its ruin was great.”

Since, therefore, he did not say merely, “Whoever hears my words,” but added, saying, “Whoever hears these words of mine,” he sufficiently indicated, as I think, that these words which he spoke on the mountain instruct the lives of those who wish to live according to them so perfectly that they are rightly compared to one who builds upon rock.

I have said this so that it may appear that this sermon is complete with respect to all the commandments by which the Christian life is formed. The matter will be treated more carefully in its proper place.

2. The beginning of this sermon is introduced as follows:

“When he saw the crowds, he went up on the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying.”

If it is asked what the mountain signifies, it is properly understood to signify the greater commandments of righteousness, since the commandments given to the Jews were lesser. Yet it was one and the same God who, through the holy prophets and servants, according to the most orderly distribution of times, gave lesser commandments to a people who still had to be bound by fear, and through his Son gave greater commandments to a people whom it was now fitting to liberate by love.

When lesser commandments are given to the lesser and greater commandments to the greater, they are given by the one who alone knows how to provide the human race with medicine appropriate to its times.

Nor is it surprising that greater commandments are given for the sake of the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 1231] Seven manuscripts read, “for the sake of the kingdom of earth.”], while lesser commandments were given for the sake of an earthly kingdom, by the same one God who made heaven and earth.

Of this righteousness, which is greater, the prophet says:

“Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Psalm 35:7).

This appropriately signifies that it is placed upon a mountain by the one teacher alone who is capable of teaching such great matters.

He teaches while seated, which pertains to the dignity of the teaching office. His disciples approach him so that those who were nearer to his words in bodily terms might also be nearer in spirit to the fulfillment of his commandments.

“And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying.”

This circumlocution by which it is written, “Opening his mouth,” perhaps commends the fact that the sermon would be somewhat longer in duration—unless perhaps it is not without significance that he is now said to have opened his mouth, since in the Old Law he used to open the mouths of the prophets.

3. What, then, does he say?

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

We read that it was written concerning the desire for temporal things:

“All is vanity and presumption of spirit” (Ecclesiastes 1:14, according to the Septuagint).

“Presumption of spirit” signifies boldness and pride. In ordinary speech, proud people are also said to have great spirits—and rightly so, since spirit is also called wind. Hence it is written:

“Fire, hail, snow, ice, storm-spirit” [Note: [Col. 1231] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, except Marcellinus, read “spirits of storms.”] (Psalm 148:8).

Who does not know that the proud are called inflated, as though distended by wind? Hence also the apostle says:

“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1).

Therefore the poor in spirit are rightly understood here as the humble and God-fearing—that is, those who do not possess an inflated spirit [Note: [Col. 1232] Lovaniensis, together with four manuscripts, reads “an inflated spirit.” The other codices read “a puffing spirit.”].

There was no other appropriate beginning for blessedness, since it was destined to reach the summit of wisdom:

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus 1:16).

For, conversely:

“Pride is written as the beginning of every sin” (ibid. 10:15).

Let the proud therefore desire and love earthly kingdoms. But:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

## CHAPTER II

4. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance.”

I believe that this means the earth of which it is said in the Psalm:

“You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Psalm 141:6).

It signifies a certain solidity and stability of an eternal inheritance, where the soul rests through a good disposition, as in its proper place, just as the body rests upon the earth; and from it is nourished by its food, just as the body is nourished from the earth. This is the rest and life of the saints.

The meek are those who yield to wickedness and do not resist evil, but overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21).

Let the unmeek therefore quarrel and fight for earthly and temporal things. But:

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess as an inheritance the earth from which they cannot be expelled.”

5. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

Mourning is sorrow over the loss of loved ones. When people are converted to God, they lose those things which they had embraced as dear in this world; for they do not rejoice in the things in which they formerly rejoiced. Until the love of eternal things comes to be formed in them [Note: [Col. 1232] In the Corbie codex, “the sweetness of eternal things.” A little below, the printed editions read, “as they lose temporal things”; two Belgian manuscripts read, “as they lose temporal mourning.” But the reading is better in one Vatican manuscript and ten Gallican manuscripts: “as they lose the temporal”—with “joy” understood.], they are wounded by a certain sadness.

They will therefore be comforted by the Holy Spirit, who is called the Paraclete especially for this reason—that is, the Comforter—so that those who lose temporal things may enjoy eternal joy.

6. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.”

Here he speaks of lovers of the true and unshakable good. They will be satisfied with that food of which the Lord himself says:

“My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34),

which is righteousness; and with that water of which, as he likewise says, whoever drinks will have within him a spring of water welling up into eternal life (ibid. 4:14).

7. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy” [Note: [Col. 1232] The printed editions read, “for God will have mercy on them.” The word “God” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Gospel.].

He calls blessed those who help the afflicted, because they are repaid in such a way that they are freed from affliction.

8. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

How foolish, then, are those who seek God with these outward eyes, when he is seen with the heart, as it is written elsewhere:

“And seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wisdom 1:1).

For a pure heart is a simple heart. And just as this light cannot be seen except by clean eyes, so God is not seen unless that by which he can be seen is pure.

[Col. 1233] **9. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.** There is perfection in peace, where nothing is opposed; and therefore the peacemakers are sons of God, because nothing resists God [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus in Am. Er. and all manuscripts. Lov. has, “nothing in these resists God.”]. And, of course, sons ought to bear the likeness of their father. Those who are peacemakers within themselves are people who bring all the movements of their soul into order and subject them to reason—that is, to the mind and spirit—and who, having subdued their carnal desires, become the kingdom of God. In this kingdom everything is so ordered that what is chief and excellent in a human being rules over the other elements, which we share with animals, without opposition; and that very thing which is excellent in a human being—that is, the mind and reason—is subjected to what is superior, namely, truth itself, the only-begotten Son of God. For the lower cannot rule unless it first subjects itself to the higher.

This is the peace given on earth to people of good will (Luke 2:14); this is the life of the perfected and complete wise person. From such a most peaceful and orderly kingdom the ruler of this age was cast out—the one who exercises dominion over the perverse and disordered. Once this peace has been established and strengthened within, whatever persecutions the one cast out has stirred up externally increase the glory that is according to God. They do not weaken anything in that structure; rather, as his engines fail, they reveal how great is the strength built within. Therefore what follows is: **Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.**

## CHAPTER III

**10.** Now all these are eight statements. For from this point onward he addresses those who were present, saying: **Blessed will you be when they curse you and persecute you.** The preceding statements, however, he directed generally. He did not say, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of heaven,” but, “for theirs,” he says, “is the kingdom of heaven.” Nor did he say, “Blessed are the meek, for you shall possess the earth,” but, “for they shall possess the earth.” And so he spoke through the others up to the eighth statement, where he says: **Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.**

From that point he begins to address those present, although what was said above also applied to those who were listening in his presence, and what is subsequently said as though specifically addressed to those present also applies to those who were absent or who would come later. For this reason the number of these statements must be carefully considered.

Blessedness begins with humility: **Blessed are the poor in spirit**—that is, those who are not puffed up, while the soul submits to divine authority, fearing that after this life it may go on to punishment, even if in this life it perhaps seems blessed to itself.

From there it proceeds to knowledge of the divine Scriptures, where the soul must make itself meek through reverence, lest it dare condemn as absurd what seems so to the unlearned, and become unteachable through obstinate disputes.

Then it begins to understand by what bonds it is held captive in this age through carnal habit and sins. Thus, at this third stage, which is the stage of knowledge, the loss of the highest good is mourned, because one has become attached to the lowest things.

At the fourth stage [Col. 1234] there is labor, when the soul applies itself intensely to tear itself away from the things with which it has become entangled through a deadly sweetness. Here, therefore, one hungers and thirsts for righteousness, and great fortitude is necessary [Note: [Col. 1234] In ten manuscripts, *est* is not inserted], because what is held with delight is not abandoned without pain.

At the fifth stage, those who persevere in labor are given counsel for escape. Unless each person is helped by one who is superior, he is in no way capable of freeing himself from such entanglements of misery. The just counsel is that whoever wishes to be helped by someone more powerful should help one who is weaker, in whom he himself is more powerful. Thus: **Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.**

At the sixth stage is purity of heart, arising from a good conscience in good works and making one capable of contemplating that highest good which can be perceived only by a pure and serene understanding.

Finally, the seventh is wisdom itself—that is, contemplation of truth—which brings the whole human being into peace and receives the likeness of God. This is concluded in the words: **Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.**

The eighth returns, as it were, to the beginning, because it displays and proves the complete and perfected state. Thus the kingdom of heaven is named in the first and eighth statements: **Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven**; and **Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.**

This is what is meant when it is said: **Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?** (Romans 8:35). There are therefore seven things that bring perfection; the eighth glorifies and demonstrates what has been perfected, so that through these stages the others may be perfected, beginning again from the head, as it were.

## CHAPTER IV

**11.** It seems to me, then, that the sevenfold working of the Holy Spirit, of which Isaiah speaks (Isaiah 11:2–3), corresponds to these stages and statements. But the order differs: there the enumeration begins with the higher qualities, whereas here it begins with the lower. There it begins with wisdom and ends with the fear of God; yet the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.

Therefore, if we count them step by step as ascending, the first there is the fear of God, the second piety, the third knowledge, the fourth fortitude, the fifth counsel, the sixth understanding, and the seventh wisdom.

The fear of God corresponds to the humble, of whom it is said here, **Blessed are the poor in spirit**—that is, those who are not puffed up or proud. To them the Apostle says, **Do not be high-minded, but fear** (Romans 11:20), that is, do not be exalted.

Piety corresponds to the meek. For the person who seeks devoutly honors the Holy Scripture, does not criticize what he does not yet understand, and therefore does not resist—which is what it means to be meek. Hence it is said here: **Blessed are the meek.**

Knowledge corresponds to those who mourn, who have already learned from the Scriptures by what evils they are held bound—evils which, in ignorance, they pursued as though they were good and useful. Of them it is said here: **Blessed are those who mourn.**

Fortitude corresponds to those who hunger and thirst. They labor, desiring joy from true goods and wishing to turn their love away from earthly and bodily things. Of them it is said here: **Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.**

Counsel corresponds to the merciful. For this is the one remedy for escaping such great evils: that we forgive as we wish to be forgiven, and help others where we can, just as we desire to be helped in what we cannot do. Of them it is said here: **Blessed are the merciful.**

[Col. 1235] Understanding corresponds to the pure in heart, as to an eye that has been cleansed, by which one may perceive what the bodily eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor entered into the human heart (Isaiah 64:4; 1 Corinthians 2:9). Of them it is said here: **Blessed are the pure in heart.**

Wisdom corresponds to the peacemakers, in whom everything has already been ordered and no movement rebels against reason; rather, everything obeys the human spirit, while the spirit itself obeys God [Note: [Col. 1235] *Retractationes*, chapter 19, no. 1]. Of them it is said here: **Blessed are the peacemakers.**

**12.** The one reward, which is the kingdom of heaven, is given different names according to these stages. At the first stage, as was fitting, the kingdom of heaven is placed first; it is the perfect and highest wisdom of the rational soul. Thus it is said: **Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven**—as though it were said, “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.”

An inheritance is given to the meek, as though it were the father’s testament to those who seek with piety: **Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.**

To those who mourn there is consolation, as to those who know what they have lost and in what they have been immersed: **Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.**

To those who hunger and thirst there is satisfaction, as to those who are refreshed after laboring and struggling courageously for salvation: **Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.**

To the merciful there is mercy, as to those who use true and excellent counsel, so that what they display toward the weaker may be displayed toward them by one more powerful: **Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.**

To the pure in heart is given the ability to see God, as though they carried a pure eye for understanding eternal things: **Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.**

To the peacemakers is given the likeness of God, as though they were perfectly wise, formed according to God’s image, and renewed through the regeneration of the new human being: **Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.**

These things can indeed be fulfilled in this life, just as we believe they were fulfilled in the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1235] *Ibid.*, no. 2]. But the complete transformation into an angelic form, which is promised after this life, cannot be expressed in words.

**Blessed, therefore, are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.** This eighth statement, which returns to the beginning and declares the perfected human being, is perhaps also signified by circumcision on the eighth day in the Old Testament; by the Lord’s resurrection after the Sabbath, which is certainly the eighth day and also the first; by the celebration of the octave days, which we celebrate in the regeneration of the new human being; and by the number of Pentecost itself.

For when the number seven is multiplied by seven, producing forty-nine, the eighth is added, as it were, so that fifty may be completed and one may return, as it were, to the beginning. On that day the Holy Spirit was sent; on that day we are led into the kingdom of heaven and receive the inheritance, and are comforted, nourished, shown mercy, cleansed, and brought into peace. Thus perfected, we endure all the troubles inflicted from without for the sake of truth and righteousness [Col. 1236].

## CHAPTER V

**13.** “Blessed will you be,” he says, “when they curse you and persecute you, and say every evil thing against you, lying, because of me. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven.”

Let anyone who seeks the pleasures of this age and the resources of temporal things in the Christian name take notice that our blessedness is within, as it is said in prophetic speech of the ecclesial soul: **All the beauty of the king’s daughter is within** (Psalm 44:14). For externally, curses, persecutions, and slanders are promised. Yet from these there is a great reward in heaven, which is experienced in the hearts of those who endure—those who can already say: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:3–5).

It is not profitable merely to suffer these things, but to endure them for Christ’s name not only with an even temper, but also with exultation. For many heretics, deceiving souls under the Christian name, suffer many such things. But they are excluded from this reward because it was not said merely, **Blessed are those who suffer persecution**; rather, it was added, **for righteousness’ sake**. Where sound faith is absent, righteousness cannot exist, because **the righteous person lives by faith** (Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 1:17).

Nor should schismatics claim any share in this reward, because likewise where love is absent, righteousness cannot exist. For **love does no harm to one’s neighbor** (Romans 13:10); if they possessed it, they would not tear apart the body of Christ, which is the Church (Colossians 1:24).

**14.** It may be asked what difference there is between “when they curse you” and “they will say every evil thing against you,” since to curse is to say evil. But a curse is cast in one way when it is uttered insultingly in the presence of the one being cursed, as was said to our Lord: **Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?** (John 8:48). It is uttered in another way when the reputation of an absent person is damaged, as it is likewise written of him: **Some were saying, ‘He is a prophet’; but others were saying, ‘No, he deceives the people’** (John 7:12).

To persecute means to inflict violence or to attack through ambush. This was done by the one who betrayed him and by those who crucified him.

The fact that this too was not stated without qualification—“and they will say every evil thing against you”—but that **lying** was added, and also **because of me**, I think was added for the sake of those who wish to boast of their persecutions and the disgrace of their reputation. They therefore claim that Christ pertains to them because many evil things are said about them, even when those things are true, as when they are said about their error. And if some false things are occasionally alleged—as often happens through human recklessness—they nevertheless do not suffer these things because of Christ. For the person who is not a Christian according to the true faith and Catholic discipline does not follow Christ.

**15.** “Rejoice,” he says, “and exult, for your reward is great in heaven.”

I do not think that “heaven” here means the higher regions of this visible world [Col. 1237]. For our reward, which ought to be unshaken and eternal, must not be placed in things that are mutable and temporal. Rather, I think “in heaven” means in spiritual firmaments, where eternal righteousness dwells. In comparison with these heavens, the unrighteous soul is called earth; when it sinned, it was told: **You are earth, and to earth you shall return** (Genesis 3:19).

Of these heavens the Apostle says: **Our citizenship is in heaven** (Philippians 3:20). Those who rejoice in spiritual goods therefore already experience this reward; but it will then be perfected in every respect, when this mortal nature also puts on immortality.

“For so,” he says, “they persecuted the prophets who were before you.” He has now used “persecution” in a general sense, including curses and the tearing apart of one’s reputation. He rightly encouraged them by example, because those who speak the truth commonly suffer persecution; yet the ancient prophets did not, through fear of persecution, cease proclaiming the truth.

## CHAPTER VI

**16.** Very appropriately, then, the following comes next: **You are the salt of the earth.** He shows that those who pursue an abundance of temporal goods or fear their lack must be judged foolish, since they lose eternal things, which can neither be given nor taken away by human beings.

Therefore, if the salt has become foolish, by what shall it be salted? That is, if you, through whom the peoples are in a certain sense to be seasoned, have lost the kingdoms of heaven through fear of temporal persecutions, who will be the people through whom error is removed from you, when God has chosen you as those through whom he removes the error of others?

Thus salt that has become foolish is good for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled by people. It is not, therefore, the person who suffers persecution who is trampled by people, but the person who, by fearing persecution, becomes foolish. For only what is lower can be trampled; but the person who, although enduring many things in the body on earth, is fixed in heaven in the heart is not lower.

**17.** **You are the light of the world.** Just as above he said “the salt of the earth,” so now he says “the light of the world.” Here too “earth” must not be understood as the earth that we tread with bodily feet, but as the people who dwell on earth—or even sinners, whom the Lord sent apostolic salt to season and whose stinks to extinguish.

Nor should “world” here be understood as heaven and earth, but as the people who are in the world or love the world; the Apostles were sent to enlighten them.

**A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden**—that is, founded upon the distinguished and great righteousness which is also signified by the mountain on which the Lord teaches.

**Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a measure.** What are we to think? Is it said to be under a measure merely so that the lamp’s concealment is intended, as though he were saying, “No one lights a lamp and hides it”? Or does the measure signify something, so that placing the lamp under a measure means making bodily advantages more important than the preaching of truth—so that a person does not preach the truth because he fears suffering some inconvenience in bodily and temporal matters?

The measure is well spoken of, either because of the retribution of measure, since each person receives what he has done in the body, as the Apostle says: **There he will receive what each has done in the body** (2 Corinthians 5:10); and as it is said elsewhere concerning this bodily measure: **With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you** (Matthew 7:2). Or it is because temporal goods, which are accomplished in the body, both begin and pass away within a fixed measure of days, which the measure may signify, whereas eternal and spiritual things are not confined by any such limit [Note: [Col. 1238] *Retractationes*, chapter 19, no. 3]. For **God does not give the Spirit by measure** (John 3:34).

Thus whoever obscures and covers the light of good teaching with temporal advantages places the lamp under a measure.

But he places it **on a lampstand** when he subjects his body to the service of God, so that the preaching of truth is higher and the service of the body lower. Yet through that very service of the body the teaching shines with greater elevation, since it is conveyed to learners through bodily actions—that is, through the voice, the tongue, and the other movements of the body in good works.

He therefore places the lamp on a lampstand when the Apostle says: **I do not fight as one beating the air; but I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified** (1 Corinthians 9:26–27).

When he says, **so that it may shine for all who are in the house**, I think “house” means the habitation of human beings—that is, the world itself—because above he said, **You are the light of the world**. Or, if someone wishes to understand “house” as the Church, that too is not absurd.

## CHAPTER VII

**18.** “Let your light,” he says, “shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

If he had said only, “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works,” he would seem to have set the goal in human praise, which hypocrites seek, as do those who pursue honors and grasp at the most empty glory. Against such people it is said: **If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ** (Galatians 1:10); and through the prophet: **Those who please people are put to shame, because God has treated them as nothing**; and again: **God has broken the bones of those who please people** (Psalm 52:6); and again the Apostle says: **Let us not become desirous of empty glory** (Galatians 5:26); and elsewhere: **Let a person test himself, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another** (Galatians 6:4).

He therefore did not say merely, “so that they may see your good works,” but added, “and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” Thus the fact that a person pleases people through good works must not have its end in pleasing people; rather, it must be referred to the praise of God. The person should therefore please people so that God may be glorified in him.

This benefits those who offer praise, so that they honor not the human being but God. The Lord demonstrated this in the case of the man who was carried [Note: [Col. 1238] In eleven manuscripts and in the editions of Am. and Er., “whom he carried.” In Mar., “whom they carried.”]. When the crowds marveled at his power after the paralytic had been healed, the Gospel says: **They were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings** (Matthew 9:8).

The Apostle Paul, his imitator, says: **They were only hearing that the one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy; and they glorified God in me** (Galatians 1:23–24) [Col. 1239].

**19.** After encouraging his hearers to prepare themselves to endure everything for the sake of truth and righteousness, and not to hide the good they were to receive but to learn with such benevolence that they might teach others, referring their good works not to their own praise but to the glory of God, he now begins to instruct and teach them what they are to teach.

It is as though they were asking: “Look, we are willing both to endure everything for your name and not to hide your teaching. But what exactly is this which you forbid us to hide and for which you command us to endure everything? Are you perhaps going to say something different from what is written in the Law?”

“No,” he says. **Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish, but to fulfill.**

## CHAPTER VIII

**20.** There are two meanings in this statement, and both must be treated. When someone says, “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it,” he either means adding what it lacks or doing what it contains. Let us consider first the meaning I have placed first.

A person who adds what is lacking certainly does not abolish what he finds; rather, by perfecting it, he confirms it. Therefore he continues and says: **Amen I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one apex will pass from the Law until all things come to pass.**

For while even those things that are added for perfection are coming to pass, much more are those that were given beforehand for the beginning coming to pass.

When he says, **not one iota or one apex will pass from the Law**, nothing else can be understood except a forceful expression of perfection [Note: [Col. 1239] *Retractationes*, chapter 19, no. 3], since perfection is demonstrated through each individual letter. Among the letters, iota is smaller than the others because it is made with a single stroke; an apex is even a small mark at the top of a letter. By these words he shows that even the smallest matters in the Law are brought to fulfillment.

Then he adds: **Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.** The least commandments are therefore signified by one iota and one apex.

Whoever loosens them and teaches accordingly—that is, according to what he has loosened, not according to what he has found and read—will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Perhaps for this reason he will not be in the kingdom of heaven, since only the great can be there.

But whoever does and teaches accordingly [Note: [Col. 1239] In the Greek he read *houtō* (“in this way”) instead of *houtos* (“this person”).]—that is, whoever does not loosen them and teaches according to what he has not loosened—will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

Whoever will be called great in the kingdom of heaven must therefore also be in the kingdom of heaven, to which the great are admitted. This is the point of what follows.

## CHAPTER IX

**21.** **For I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven**—that is, unless you fulfill not only those least commandments of the Law that initiate a person, but also these commandments that I add, since I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, [Col. 1240] you will not enter the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 1239] *Retractationes*, chapter 19, no. 4].

But you say to me: “When he spoke above about those least commandments, he said that whoever loosened one of them and taught according to his loosening would be called least in the kingdom of heaven, while whoever did them and taught accordingly would be called great and, because he is great, would already be in the kingdom of heaven. Why, then, is anything added to the least commandments of the Law, if a person can already be in the kingdom of heaven because whoever does them and teaches accordingly is great?”

Therefore that statement must be understood in this way: **Whoever does and teaches accordingly will be called great in the kingdom of heaven**—that is, not according to those least commandments, but according to what I am about to say.

What is this? **So that your righteousness may exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees**, he says, **because unless it exceeds theirs, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.**

Therefore the person who loosens those least commandments and teaches accordingly will be called least. The person who does those least commandments and teaches accordingly is not yet to be regarded as great or fit for the kingdom of heaven; nevertheless, he is not as least as the person who loosens them.

To become great and fit for that kingdom, he must both do and teach as Christ now teaches—that is, so that his righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees.

The righteousness of the Pharisees is that they do not kill; the righteousness of those who are to enter the kingdom of God is that they do not become angry without cause. Not killing is therefore the lesser commandment. Whoever loosens it will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Whoever fulfills it by not killing will not immediately be great or fit for the kingdom of heaven, but he has nevertheless ascended one step. He will be perfected if he also does not become angry without cause. When he has fulfilled that, he will be much farther from murder.

Therefore the person who teaches that we must not become angry does not abolish the Law against killing; rather, he fulfills it, so that we preserve innocence both outwardly, by not killing, and in the heart, by not becoming angry.

**22.** “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’; and whoever kills will be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Racha,’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.”

What is the difference between being liable to judgment, being liable to the council, and being liable to the fire of Gehenna? The last sounds most serious and suggests that certain stages have been established, moving from lesser to greater offenses until one arrives at the fire of Gehenna.

Therefore, if being liable to judgment is less serious than being liable to the council, and being liable to the council is less serious than being liable to the fire of Gehenna, then becoming angry with one’s brother without cause must be understood as less serious than saying “Racha,” and saying “Racha” as less serious than saying “Fool.” For the guilt itself would not have degrees unless the sins too were recounted in stages.

**23.** One word here is obscure, because “Racha” is neither Greek nor Latin; the others are ordinary words in our language.

Some have wished to derive an interpretation of this word from Greek, supposing that *Racha* means “ragged,” because a rag is called *rhakos* (ῥάκος) in Greek. Yet when they are asked [Col. 1241] what “ragged” is in Greek, they do not answer *Racha*. Moreover, the Latin translator could have put “ragged” where he put *Racha*, rather than using a word that is absent from Latin and uncommon in Greek.

It is therefore more probable that what I heard from a certain Hebrew is correct, when I asked him about it. He said that it was a word signifying nothing, but expressing the movement of an indignant spirit.

Grammarians call such expressions interjections—parts of speech signifying the emotion of a disturbed mind. For example, a grieving person says “Alas!” or an angry person says “Hem!” Such words belong properly to their respective languages and are not easily transferred into another language. This is certainly why both the Greek and Latin translators put down the word itself, since they could not find a way to interpret it.

**24.** There are therefore stages in these sins. First, a person becomes angry and retains in his heart the movement he has conceived. If this disturbance forces out an indignant sound—not signifying anything, but bearing witness by its eruption to the movement of the mind that strikes the person with whom he is angry—that is certainly more serious than if the rising anger were suppressed in silence.

If not only the sound of indignation is heard but also a word that designates and marks a definite insult against the person to whom it is directed, who would doubt that this is more serious than merely producing the sound of indignation?

Thus in the first case there is one element: anger alone. In the second there are two: anger and the sound signifying anger. In the third there are three: anger, the sound signifying anger, and within the sound itself the expression of a definite insult.

Now consider also the three forms of liability: judgment, the council, and the fire of Gehenna.

In judgment, there is still an opportunity for defense. In the council, although there too is usually judgment, the distinction itself requires us to acknowledge that something different is meant here. The council appears to concern the pronouncement of the sentence: the question is no longer whether the accused should be condemned, but the judges confer among themselves about the punishment by which the person, already established as deserving condemnation, ought to be punished.

The fire of Gehenna has neither an uncertain condemnation, as judgment does, nor merely the penalty of one already condemned, as the council does. For in the fire of Gehenna both the condemnation and the punishment of the condemned person are certain.

There therefore appear to be certain stages both in sins and in liability. But by what invisible means punishments are assigned according to the merits of souls, who can say? We must therefore understand the difference between the righteousness of the Pharisees and the greater righteousness that leads into the kingdom.

Although killing is more serious than inflicting an insult by a word, there murder makes a person liable to judgment, whereas here anger makes a person liable to judgment—the least serious of those three sins. There, human beings were conducting an investigation into homicide; here, everything is left to divine judgment, whose final punishment for the condemned is the fire of Gehenna.

If someone says that homicide is punished with a more severe punishment under the greater righteousness, while an insult is punished by the fire of Gehenna, he is forced to understand that there are different degrees of Gehenna.

**25.** In these three statements, the words that are understood but not spoken must also be considered.

The first statement [Col. 1242] contains all the necessary words, so that nothing is left implicit: **Whoever is angry with his brother without cause,** he says, **will be liable to judgment.**

In the second, when he says, **Whoever says to his brother, “Racha,”** the words “without cause” are understood, and the statement is joined to what follows: **will be liable to the council** [Note: [Col. 1242] *Retractationes*, chapter 19, no. 4].

In the third, where he says, **Whoever says, “Fool,”** two things are understood: “to his brother” and “without cause.”

This explains how the Apostle can call the Galatians fools (Galatians 3:1), while also calling them brothers: he does not do so without cause. The word “brother” must therefore be understood here because later he speaks of how even an enemy must be treated according to the greater righteousness.

## CHAPTER X

**26.** Then the following comes next: **Therefore, if you bring your gift to the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother [Note: [Col. 1242] Am. Er. and several manuscripts have “be reconciled to your brother.” Lov. has “reconcile yourself.” The latter is most correct, supported by the Greek *diallagēthi*]; and then come and offer your gift.**

It is clear from this that the earlier passage referred to a brother, since the following statement is connected with it in such a way as to bear witness to what came before. For he does not say, “But if you bring your gift to the altar”; he says, **Therefore, if you bring your gift to the altar.**

If it is not lawful to become angry with one’s brother without cause, or to say “Racha,” or to say “Fool,” it is much less lawful to retain something in the heart so that indignation may be turned into hatred. This also concerns what is said elsewhere: **Do not let the sun go down upon your anger** (Ephesians 4:26).

We are therefore commanded, when we are bringing a gift to the altar, that if we remember our brother has something against us, we should leave the gift before the altar, go and be reconciled to our brother, and then return and offer the gift.

If this is understood literally, someone might perhaps think that it must be done only if the brother is present, since it is not possible to delay longer when one is commanded to leave one’s gift before the altar. But if the brother is absent and, as may happen, is even across the sea, it is absurd to believe that the gift must be left before the altar until one has traveled over lands and seas and then offered it to God.

We are therefore compelled to take refuge entirely in the spiritual meaning, so that what is said may be understood without absurdity.

**27.** Spiritually, then, we may understand the altar as faith itself in the inner temple of God, whose sign is the visible altar. Whatever gift we offer to God—whether prophecy, teaching, prayer, a hymn, a psalm, or any other such spiritual gift that occurs to the mind—cannot be acceptable to God unless it is supported by the sincerity of faith and placed upon it firmly and immovably, as though upon an altar [Note: [Col. 1242] Here Lov. adds “altar”; the other codices lack the word], so that what we say may remain whole and undefiled.

For many heretics, having no altar—that is, no true faith—have spoken blasphemies instead of praise, weighed down by earthly opinions and casting their vow, as it were, upon the earth.

But the intention of the person offering must also be sound. Therefore, when we are about to offer something of this kind in our heart—that is, in the inner temple of God—for, as the Apostle says, **the temple of God is holy, which you are** (1 Corinthians 3:17), and, [Col. 1243] **that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner person** (Ephesians 3:17)—if it comes to mind that our brother has something against us, that is, if we have injured him in some way, then he indeed has something against us.

For we have something against him if he has injured us. In that case there is no need to go to be reconciled; you will not ask forgiveness from someone who has done you an injury, but will simply forgive him, as you desire the Lord to forgive what you yourself have done.

We must go to be reconciled when it comes to mind that we may have injured our brother in some way. But we must go not with bodily feet, but with movements of the soul, so that with humble feeling you may prostrate yourself before the brother to whom you have run in loving thought, in the presence of the one to whom you are about to offer your gift.

In this way, even if he is present, you will be able to soften him with a sincere disposition and restore him to friendship by asking forgiveness—provided you have first done this before God, going to him not with sluggish bodily movement but with the swiftest affection of love. Then, returning—that is, directing your intention back to what you had begun to do—you will offer your gift.

**28.** Who does this—who either does not become angry with his brother without cause, does not say “Racha” without cause, or does not call him a fool without cause, all of which is committed with the greatest arrogance—or, if he has stumbled in one of these matters, humbly begs forgiveness, which is the one remedy—unless he is not puffed up by the spirit of empty boasting? [Note: [Col. 1243] Lov. has: “begs forgiveness; whoever does not do this is puffed up by the spirit of empty boasting.” But our reading is clearer and is supported by the other books.]

**Blessed, therefore, are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.**

Now let us see what follows.

# CHAPTER XI

**29.** “Be well disposed toward your adversary quickly,” he says, “while you are with him on the way, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the attendant, and you be thrown into prison. Truly I tell you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last quadrans.”

I understand the judge to be the Father; for “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). I understand the attendant to be an angel: “And angels,” he says, “ministered to him” (Matthew 4:11); and we believe that he will come with his angels to judge the living and the dead. I understand the prison to mean, plainly, the punishments of darkness, which elsewhere he calls “outer” darkness (ibid. 8:12): perhaps because the joy of divine rewards is inward, within the mind itself—or even if something more secret may be understood—which is said to the servant who has earned well, “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid. 25:23). In the same way, under the arrangements of civic administration, a person who is thrown into prison is sent out either by the judge’s secretary or from his court.

**30.** As for paying the last quadrans, it may reasonably be understood either as expressing that nothing is left unpunished—just as in ordinary speech we say “to the dregs” when we wish to indicate something so exact that nothing has been left over—or as signifying earthly sins by the name “the last quadrans.” For earth is found to be the fourth and last part of the distinct elements of this world: begin with [Col. 1244] heaven, count the air as the second, water as the third, and earth as the fourth. Thus it may fittingly be understood as saying, “Until you pay the last quadrans”—until you atone for earthly sins. For the sinner also heard, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19).

But when it says, “Until you pay,” I wonder whether it does not signify the punishment called eternal. For from where is that debt paid when there is no longer any opportunity for repentance and more righteous living? Perhaps “until you pay” is placed here in the same sense as in the passage, “Sit at my right hand until I place all your enemies beneath your feet” (Psalm 109:1). For he will not cease sitting at the right hand when his enemies have been placed beneath his feet. Or consider the Apostle’s statement, “For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies beneath his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25): he will not cease to reign when they have been placed beneath his feet.

Accordingly, just as in that passage—“He must reign until he places his enemies beneath his feet”—the meaning is that he will reign forever, since they will always be beneath his feet, so here we may understand the statement, “You will not come out from there until you pay the last quadrans,” to mean that he will never come out, because he is always paying the last quadrans while enduring the everlasting punishments for earthly sins.

I do not say this in such a way as to seem to have removed the need for a more careful treatment of how Scripture speaks of the punishments of sins as eternal. In any case, they should be avoided rather than known, however they are to be understood.

**31.** But let us now see who this adversary is, toward whom we are commanded quickly to be well disposed while we are with him on the way. He is either the devil, or a human being, or the flesh, or God, or his commandment.

I do not see how we are commanded to be well disposed toward the devil—that is, to be united or consenting with him. Some have translated the Greek word **εὑνοῶν** (*eunoōn*) as “being of one mind,” others as “consenting.” But we are not commanded to show goodwill toward the devil; for where there is goodwill, there is friendship. Nor would anyone say that friendship with the devil ought to be established. Nor is it advantageous to be in agreement with him, since by renouncing him once for all we have declared war against him, and by conquering him we shall be crowned. Nor ought we to consent to him, for if we had never consented to him, we would never have fallen into these miseries.

As for a human being, although we are commanded, so far as it depends on us, to live at peace with everyone—and goodwill, agreement, and consent can certainly be understood here—I still do not see how we are handed over by a human being to the judge, when I understand Christ to be the judge, before whose tribunal all must appear, as the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 5:10). How, then, will the one who is to be handed over to the judge be handed over by someone who will appear before the judge together with him?

Or, if someone is handed over to the judge because he has injured another person, even though the injured person is not the one who hands him over, it is much more suitably understood that the law itself hands the guilty person over to the judge whose law he violated when he injured another. For if someone has harmed another by killing him, there is no longer any time in which he can be reconciled with that person, since he is no longer with him on the way—that is, in this life. Yet for that reason he is not beyond healing through repentance and through fleeing with a sacrifice of a contrite heart to the mercy of the one who forgives sins to those converted [Col. 1245] to him, and who rejoices more over one repentant person than over ninety-nine righteous persons (Luke 15:7).

I see even less how we could be commanded to be well disposed, united, or consenting toward the flesh. Sinners are more likely to love their flesh, to be in agreement with it, and to consent to it. Those who subject it to slavery, however, do not themselves consent to it; rather, they compel it to consent to them.

**32.** Perhaps, then, we are commanded to consent to God and to be well disposed toward him, so that we may be reconciled to the one from whom we have turned away by sinning, and who can therefore be called our adversary. Those whom he resists are rightly called his adversaries: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6); and, “The beginning of every sin is pride, but the beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15, 14). The Apostle also says, “For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Romans 5:10).

From this it may be understood that no nature is evil and hostile to God, since those who were enemies are themselves reconciled to him. Therefore, whoever in this way—that is, in this life—has not been reconciled to God through the death of his Son will be handed over by him to the judge, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” Thus the remaining statements written in this chapter follow, and we have already discussed them.

Only one difficulty stands in the way of this interpretation: how can it rightly be said that we are with God on the way, if in this passage he himself is to be understood as the adversary of the ungodly, to whom we are commanded quickly to be reconciled? Perhaps the answer is that, since he is everywhere, even while we are on this way we are necessarily with him. For the Psalm says:

“If I ascend into heaven, you are there;  
if I descend into the underworld, you are present;  
if I take up my wings straight ahead  
and dwell in the farthest parts of the sea [Note: [Col. 1245] Am., Er., and Lov. read “at the farthest part”; the manuscripts, as also the Mar. edition, read “in the farthest parts,” following the Greek Septuagint, *eis ta eschata*.],  
even there your hand will lead me,  
and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 138:8–10).

Or, if it is unacceptable to say that the ungodly are with God—although God is present everywhere, just as we do not say that the blind are with the light, even though light surrounds their eyes—one possibility remains: that the adversary here is understood to be God’s commandment.

For what is so opposed to those who wish to sin as God’s commandment, that is, his law and divine Scripture, which has been given to us for this life so that it may be with us on the way? We must not contradict it, lest it hand us over to the judge; rather, we must quickly consent to it. No one knows when he will depart from this life.

Who, then, consents to divine Scripture except one who reads or hears it devoutly, granting it the highest authority? Such a person does not hate what he understands merely because he perceives it to oppose his sins; instead, he loves his correction and rejoices that his diseases are not spared until they are healed. If something sounds obscure or absurd to him, he does not thereby stir up contentious disputes, but prays that he may understand, while remembering that goodwill and reverence are owed to so great an authority.

But who does this except one who approaches the opening and learning of his father’s testament [Col. 1246]—not harshly, threatening lawsuits, but gently, with devotion?

“Blessed, therefore, are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance.”

Let us consider what follows.

# CHAPTER XII

**33.** “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

The lesser righteousness is not to commit adultery through bodily intercourse; the greater righteousness of the kingdom of God is not to commit adultery in the heart. Whoever does not commit adultery in the heart will much more easily guard against committing adultery in the body.

The one who gave this command therefore confirmed the Law; for he did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. It should be carefully observed that he did not say, “Everyone who desires a woman,” but “who looks at a woman in order to desire her”—that is, who directs his attention to her with this purpose and disposition, that he may desire her. This is no longer merely to be tickled by the pleasure of the flesh, but to consent fully [Note: [Col. 1246] Almost all manuscripts read “plainly.”] to lust, so that the unlawful desire is not restrained but, if opportunity is given, is satisfied.

**34.** There are three things by which sin is completed: suggestion, pleasure, and consent.

Suggestion occurs either through memory or through the bodily senses, when we see, hear, smell, taste, or touch something. If it is pleasurable to enjoy it, the unlawful pleasure must be restrained. For example, when we are fasting and, on seeing food, the appetite of the palate rises, this occurs only through pleasure. Yet we do not consent to it; by the authority of governing reason we restrain it [Note: [Col. 1246] The Mar. and Lov. editions, against the other books, read: “if we restrain it.”].

If consent takes place, however, there will be complete sin, known to God in our heart even if it is not revealed to human beings by an external act.

These stages are thus such that suggestion comes, as it were, from the serpent—that is, from a slippery and shifting, namely temporal, motion of bodies [Note: [Col. 1246] Ten manuscripts read “corporeal motion.”]. For even if such phantasms move about within the soul, they have been drawn from the body outside; and if some hidden bodily motion, besides these five senses, touches the soul, it too is temporal and slippery. Therefore, the more secretly it slips in so as to reach thought, the more fittingly it is compared to the serpent.

These stages are therefore like the event described in Genesis: suggestion and a kind of persuasion come, as it were, from the serpent; pleasure arises in the carnal appetite, as in Eve; and consent arises in reason, as in the man. Once these have taken place, the human being is expelled, as from paradise—that is, from the most blessed light of righteousness—into death, and entirely justly (Genesis 3:1).

For the one who persuades does not compel. All natures, in their proper order and through their proper stages, are beautiful; but one must not descend from the higher things, in which the rational mind has been ordered, to lower things. No one is compelled to do this; and therefore, if someone does it, he is punished by God’s just law [Note: [Col. 1246] Thus the manuscripts and Mar. At Am., Er., and Lov., “he is punished without just defense.”].

Before habit is formed, pleasure is either nonexistent or so slight as to be almost nonexistent [Note: Thus Am., Er., and the manuscripts, with only one exception. At Mar. and Lov., “before consent.”]. To consent to it is a great [Col. 1247] sin when the pleasure is unlawful.

Once someone has consented, he commits sin in his heart. If the matter also proceeds to an act, the desire seems to be satisfied and extinguished. But afterward, when suggestion returns, a greater pleasure is kindled—though it is still much less than the pleasure that repeated acts turn into a habit. Habit is exceedingly difficult to overcome. Nevertheless, even habit itself can be conquered if a person does not abandon himself and is not afraid of Christian warfare, with Christ as his leader and helper. Thus the man is subjected to Christ, and the woman to the man, in the original peace and order [Note: [Col. 1247] Am., Er., and Lov. have “authority”; the manuscripts, with Mar. agreeing, have “peace.”] (1 Corinthians 11:3; Ephesians 5:23).

**35.** Just as sin is reached through three stages—suggestion, pleasure, and consent—so sin itself has three forms: in the heart, in the act, and in habit, like three deaths.

The first is as though in the house: when the heart consents to lust. The second has already been brought outside, as though beyond the gate: when consent proceeds to an act. The third occurs when the mind is weighed down by the force of evil habit like a mass of earth, as though already rotting in a tomb.

Everyone who reads the Gospel recognizes that the Lord raised these three kinds of dead. Perhaps such a reader also considers the different forms taken by the voice of the one raising them: in one place he says, “Girl, arise” (Matthew 9:25); elsewhere, “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke 7:14); elsewhere, “He groaned in spirit, and wept, and groaned again, and afterward cried out with a loud voice, ‘Lazarus, come out’” (John 11:33–44).

**36.** Accordingly, by the name of adulterers mentioned in this chapter we must understand every carnal and lustful desire. Since Scripture so frequently calls idolatry fornication, while the Apostle Paul calls greed idolatry (Colossians 3:5; Ephesians 5:5), who could doubt that every evil desire is rightly called fornication? The soul neglects the higher law by which it is governed and is corrupted by the shameful pleasure of lower natures, as though prostituted for payment.

Therefore, whoever feels that carnal pleasure is rebelling against his right will through sinful habits, by whose untamed [Note: [Col. 1247] Ten manuscripts read “untamed” (*indomita*).] violence he is dragged into captivity, should recall as far as possible what kind of peace he lost by sinning and cry out, “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Romans 7:24–25).

When he cries out that he is wretched, he implores the helper’s aid through mourning. Recognition of one’s own wretchedness is no small approach to blessedness. Therefore, “Blessed also are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

# CHAPTER XIII

**37.** Then the text continues: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna.”

Here great courage is required to cut off the members. Whatever is signified by the eye is certainly something that is loved intensely [Col. 1248]. Those who wish to express their affection strongly commonly say, “I love him as my own eyes,” or even, “more than my own eyes.”

The addition of the word “right” may perhaps serve to intensify the force of the love. Although the bodily eyes are ordinarily directed toward seeing, and if both are directed they can see equally, people nevertheless fear losing the right eye more.

The meaning, then, may be this: Whatever you love so greatly that you regard it as your right eye—if it causes you to stumble, that is, if it becomes an obstacle to true blessedness—tear it out and cast it away from you. For it is better that one of those things which you love so greatly that they cling to you as members should perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna.

**38.** But because the text next speaks of the right hand and says similarly, “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna,” it compels us to inquire more carefully what he meant by the eye.

In this inquiry, nothing occurs to me that fits better than a beloved friend. For we can rightly call a member what we love intensely. We may also understand the eye as a counselor, because it is like one who shows the way; and, in divine matters, because it is the right eye. The left eye, then, would be a beloved counselor in earthly matters relating to the needs of the body. If such a counselor causes one to stumble, it would be superfluous to say that he should be cast away, since even the right eye must not be spared.

In divine matters, a counselor causes one to stumble if, under the name of religion and doctrine, he attempts to lead someone into a destructive heresy.

The right hand, therefore, should likewise be understood as a beloved helper and minister in divine works. For just as contemplation is understood in the eye, so right action is understood in the hand; while the left hand signifies the works necessary for this life and for the body.

# CHAPTER XIV

**39.** It was said, “Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.”

This is the lesser righteousness of the Pharisees. It is not contradicted by what the Lord says: “But I say to you, whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a woman released [Col. 1249] from her husband commits adultery.”

The one who commanded that a certificate of divorce be given did not command that a wife be divorced. Rather, he said, “Whoever divorces her, let him give her a certificate of divorce,” so that the thought of the certificate might restrain the rash anger of a man casting out his wife. The one who required delay before the divorce indicated, as far as he could, even to hard-hearted people, that he did not desire separation.

Therefore, when the Lord himself was asked about this elsewhere, he replied, “Moses did this because of the hardness of your hearts” (Matthew 19:8). However hard-hearted a man might be who wanted to divorce his wife, the thought that, once the certificate of divorce had been given, she could marry another without danger would easily calm him.

To reinforce the principle that a wife should not be divorced readily, the Lord therefore excepted only the cause of fornication. He commands all other troubles, should any arise, to be endured firmly for the sake of marital fidelity and chastity. He also calls the man who marries a woman released from her husband an adulterer.

The Apostle Paul indicates the duration of this rule: it must be observed as long as her husband lives; after his death, he grants permission to marry (Romans 7:2–3). He himself maintained this rule, and here he shows not his own advice, as in some exhortations, but the commandment of the Lord when he says:

“To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a woman should not depart from her husband; but if she does depart, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let the husband not divorce his wife” (1 Corinthians 7:10–11).

I believe the corresponding form is that, if he divorces her, he should not marry another, but should be reconciled to his wife. It is possible that he may divorce his wife on account of fornication, which the Lord wished to be excepted.

Now, if she is not permitted to marry another while the husband from whom she departed is alive, and he is not permitted to marry another while the wife whom he divorced is alive, it is much less lawful to commit illicit sexual acts with just anyone.

Certainly, those marriages should be judged more blessed in which the spouses, whether after producing children or even while disregarding this earthly offspring, are able by mutual agreement to maintain continence between them. For this does not violate the command by which the Lord forbids the spouse to be divorced. One who lives with her not carnally but spiritually does not divorce her. At the same time, the Apostle’s statement is observed: “It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” (ibid. 29).

# CHAPTER XV

**40.** What more commonly troubles the minds of the inexperienced—who nevertheless are eager to live according to Christ’s commandments—is that elsewhere the Lord himself says:

“Whoever comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26).

To those who understand less fully, this may seem contradictory: here he forbids a wife to be divorced except on account of fornication, while elsewhere he says that no one can be his disciple unless he hates his wife. If he were speaking about sexual intercourse, he would not place father, mother, and brothers under the same condition.

Yet how true it is that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matthew 11:12)! How much force is required for a person to love his enemies and hate his father, mother, wife, children, and brothers! The one who calls us to the kingdom of heaven commands both.

It is easy, with him as our guide, to show how these statements are not contradictory; but once they are understood, it is difficult to fulfill them—although, with the help of that same Lord, this too becomes very easy.

The eternal kingdom to which he has deigned to call his disciples, whom he also calls brothers, does not contain relationships of this kind, which belong to time. “There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither male nor female, neither slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all” (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11). The Lord himself also says, “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22:30).

Therefore, whoever wishes already here to contemplate the life of that kingdom must hate not the people themselves but these temporal relationships by which this passing life is supported—a life carried on through birth and death. Whoever does not hate them does not yet love that life in which there will be no condition of being born and [Col. 1250] dying, which binds earthly marriages.

**41.** Accordingly, if I were to ask a thoroughly good Christian who nevertheless has a wife—even though he still begets children with her—whether he would want to have a wife in that kingdom, remembering God’s promises and that life in which “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53–54), he would reply, with great or at least some love already stirred in him, and with an expression of horror, that he emphatically would not want this.

But if I were again to ask whether he would want his wife to live there with him after the resurrection, once she had received the angelic transformation promised to the saints [Note: [Col. 1250] Thus the manuscripts and the printed editions, except Mar. and Lov., which read “immortality”], he would reply that he wanted this just as emphatically as he had rejected the former.

Thus a good Christian is found to love in one woman God’s creature, which he desires to be reformed and renewed, while hating the corruptible and mortal union and coupling—that is, loving in her what is human and hating what is wifely.

He likewise loves an enemy not insofar as the enemy is an enemy, but insofar as he is a human being, wishing for him what he wishes for himself: that he may reach the kingdom of heaven corrected and renewed.

The same must be understood of father, mother, and the other bonds of blood: in them we hate what the human race has received through birth and death [Note: *Retractations* I, chapter 19, section 5], but we love what can be brought with us to those kingdoms, where no one says, “My father,” but all say to the one God, “Our Father”; nor does anyone say, “My mother,” but all say to that Jerusalem, “Our mother”; nor does anyone say, “My brother,” but all, from among everyone, say, “Our brother.”

Our marriage with him, when we have all been gathered together into one, will be, as it were, that of one spouse—he who freed us from the prostitution of this world by the shedding of his blood.

Therefore Christ’s disciple must hate those things that pass away in the people whom he desires to accompany him to the things that will always remain—and he must hate them in those people all the more deeply the more he loves them.

**42.** A Christian can therefore live harmoniously with his spouse in several ways: by satisfying with her the carnal need which the Apostle says is granted according to permission, not according to command [Note: In all the manuscripts, “not according to obligation”]; by the begetting of children, which can already be praiseworthy to some degree; or by possessing a fraternal relationship without any bodily union, having a wife as though he did not have one—which is the most excellent and sublime condition in Christian marriage.

Even so, he must hate in her the designation of temporal necessity [Note: [Col. 1250] Am., Er., and Lov. read, “he must hate in her all temporal necessities.” The manuscripts have, “he must hate in her the designation of temporal necessity.” Mar. likewise has this, although *necessitudinis* seems to be the reading intended instead of *necessitatis*], and love the hope of eternal blessedness.

Without doubt, we hate what we hope will at some time no longer exist, such as this present life of the world. If we did not hate this temporal life, we would not desire the future life, which is not subject to time.

The soul has been placed in this present life, of which it is said, “Whoever does not hate even his own life cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26). This life requires corruptible food, of which the Lord [Col. 1251] himself says, “Is not the soul more than food?” (Matthew 6:25)—that is, is not this life, for which food is necessary, more than food?

And when he says that he must “lay down his life for his sheep” (John 10:15), he is speaking of this life, declaring that he will die for us.

# CHAPTER XVI

**43.** Another question arises here: since the Lord permits a wife to be divorced on account of fornication, how are we to understand fornication in this passage? Is it to be understood in the sense in which everyone understands it—that we should regard as fornication the acts committed in sexual misconduct? Or should it be understood in the way Scripture commonly calls every unlawful corruption fornication, as was said above, including idolatry and greed, and therefore every transgression of the law arising from unlawful desire [Note: [Col. 1251] *Retractations* I, chapter 19, section 6]?

But let us consult the Apostle, so that we do not speak rashly. He says:

“To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.”

It may happen that she departs for the reason for which the Lord permits divorce.

Or, if a woman may divorce her husband even apart from the cause of fornication, while a man may not, what shall we say about the Apostle’s later statement, “And let the husband not divorce his wife”? Why did he not add “except on account of fornication,” which the Lord permits, unless he wishes a similar arrangement to be understood: if he divorces her—which is permitted on account of fornication—he should remain without a wife or be reconciled to his wife?

A husband would not be wrongly reconciled with that woman to whom the Lord said, when no one had dared to stone her, “Go, and from now on do not sin” (ibid. 8:11).

For when someone says, “It is not lawful to divorce a wife except on account of fornication,” he compels a man to retain his wife if there has been no cause of fornication. If such a cause has occurred, however, he does not compel him to divorce her; he permits it.

This is like saying, “It is not lawful for a woman to marry another man unless her husband has died.” If she marries before her husband’s death, she is guilty; if she does not marry after his death, she is not guilty. She was not commanded to marry, but permitted to do so.

If, then, the same form applies to this marital law between man and woman—so much so that the Apostle says not only of the woman, “A woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man,” but also does not remain silent about the man, saying, “Likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman”—if the form is the same, it should not be understood that a woman may divorce her husband except on account of fornication any more than a man may.

**44.** We must therefore consider how far we should understand fornication, and, as we began to do, consult the Apostle. He continues:

“To the rest I say—not the Lord.”

First we must see who “the rest” are. Above, he was speaking in the person of the Lord to those who are married; now, in his own person, he speaks to “the rest.” Perhaps, then, he means those who are not married. But this does not follow. He adds:
