“If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not divorce her.”

Thus even now he is speaking to those who are married. What, then, does he mean by “the rest,” unless above he was speaking to those who were joined in such a way that both shared the faith of Christ, whereas now he speaks to “the rest,” that is, to those who are joined in such a way that [Col. 1252] both are not believers?

What does he say to them?

“If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not divorce her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, let her not divorce her husband.”

If, then, he does not command this in the person of the Lord but gives advice in his own person, the matter is good in such a way that if someone acts otherwise, he is not a transgressor of a command. Shortly afterward he says the same about virgins: he does not have a command from the Lord, but gives advice. He praises virginity in such a way that whoever wishes may embrace it, yet if someone does not do so, he is not judged to have acted against a command.

One thing is commanded, another is advised, and another is forgiven.

A woman is commanded not to depart from her husband; if she departs, she must remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. Otherwise, then, she may not act.

A believing man, however, is advised not to divorce an unbelieving wife who consents to live with him. He is therefore permitted to divorce her, because the Lord’s command is not that he must not divorce her, but the Apostle’s advice is that he should not do so.

This is like the advice given to a virgin not to marry. If she marries, she does not follow the advice, but she does not act against a command.

There is forgiveness when it is said, “I say this according to permission, not according to command.”

Accordingly, if an unbelieving spouse may be divorced, although it is better not to divorce her, and yet according to the Lord’s command a spouse may not be divorced except on account of fornication, then unbelief itself is also fornication.

**45.** What do you say, Apostle? Certainly that a believing man should not divorce an unbelieving woman who consents to live with him.

“Yes,” he says.

Since the Lord also commands that a man should not divorce his wife except on account of fornication, why do you say here, “I say this, not the Lord”?

Because the idolatry followed by unbelievers, and every harmful superstition, is fornication. The Lord permitted a wife to be divorced on account of fornication. But because he permitted it and did not command it, he gave the Apostle room to advise that whoever wished should not divorce an unbelieving wife, so that perhaps she might thereby become a believer.

“For the unbelieving husband,” he says, “is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the brother” [Note: [Col. 1252] The printed editions read “in the believing wife” and shortly afterward “in the believing brother.” The manuscripts in both places lack the word “believing,” which is absent from the Apostle’s Greek text; nor was it present in the Latin, as Augustine testifies below, chapter 22].

I believe that by then it had happened that some women had come to the faith through believing husbands, and some men through believing wives. Although he did not mention names, he nevertheless encouraged them by examples, thereby strengthening his advice.

He continues:

“Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (1 Corinthians 7).

There were already Christian children, whether sanctified through the influence of one parent or through the agreement of both. This would not have happened unless, when one spouse became a believer, the marriage had not been dissolved and the unbelief of the other spouse had been tolerated until the opportunity for belief.

This, then, is his advice—the advice to which I believe the words refer: “If you spend anything more, when I return I will repay you” (Luke 10:35).

**46.** If unbelief is fornication, and idolatry is unbelief, and greed is idolatry, then there can be no doubt that greed also is fornication.

Who, then, can rightly separate any [Col. 1253] unlawful desire from the category of fornication, if greed is fornication? From this it is understood that, because of unlawful desires—not only those committed in sexual misconduct with other men or women, but absolutely any desires that cause a soul misusing the body to stray from God’s law and to be corrupted ruinously and shamefully—a husband may divorce his wife without guilt, and a wife may divorce her husband.

For the Lord makes an exception for the cause of fornication. As was considered above, we are compelled to understand this fornication in a general and universal sense.

**47.** When he says, “Except on account of fornication,” he does not specify whose fornication it is, whether the man’s or the woman’s. For it is not only the husband who may divorce a fornicating wife; whoever divorces a wife who herself forces him to fornicate divorces her on account of fornication.

For example, if a wife compels a man to sacrifice to idols, the man who divorces her divorces her on account of fornication—not only on account of hers, but also on account of his: hers, because she is committing fornication; his, so that he may not commit fornication.

Nothing is more unjust, however, than to divorce a wife on account of fornication if the husband himself is also convicted of committing fornication. For the statement comes to mind, “In whatever judgment you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge” (Romans 2:1).

Therefore, whoever wishes to cast away his wife on account of fornication must first be cleansed of fornication himself. I would say the same correspondingly about a woman.

**48.** When he says, “Whoever marries a woman released from her husband commits adultery,” it may be asked whether, just as the man who marries her commits adultery, so too does the woman whom he marries.

She is also commanded to remain unmarried or to be reconciled to her husband. But the text says, “if she departs from her husband.” There is a great difference between her divorcing him and her being divorced.

If she herself divorces her husband and marries another, she appears to have abandoned her former husband out of a desire to change her marriage; this is certainly an adulterous thought.

If, however, she is divorced by the husband with whom she wished to remain, the man who marries her does indeed commit adultery according to the Lord’s judgment. But whether she herself is held guilty of such a crime is uncertain.

Yet it is very difficult to see how, when a man and woman join themselves by mutual agreement, one of them can be an adulterer while the other is not.

Moreover, if the man commits adultery by marrying a woman released from her husband, even though she did not divorce him but was divorced, she makes him commit adultery—something the Lord nevertheless forbids.

From this it follows that whether she has been divorced or has divorced her husband, she ought to remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.

49. Again it is asked whether, if a man, with his wife’s permission—whether she is barren or unwilling to endure intercourse—takes another woman, provided she is neither another man’s wife nor separated from her husband, he can be free from the charge of fornication. An example is indeed found in the history of the Old Testament; but now the commandments are greater, to which the human race has advanced by that stage of development. Those earlier cases are to be examined in order to distinguish the periods of the divine dispensation, which has provided help to the human race in the most orderly manner—not, however, in order to appropriate them as rules for living [Note: [Col. 1253] In the Corbie manuscript, “to appropriate it as a rule for living.”]. Yet it may still be asked whether what the Apostle says—“The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife”—can be understood to have such force that, with the permission of his wife, who has authority over the marital body, a husband may have intercourse with another woman who is neither another man’s wife nor separated from her husband. But this must not be thought so, lest women also appear able, with their husbands’ permission, to do what everyone’s moral sense rejects.

50. Nevertheless, certain circumstances may arise in which a wife, with her husband’s consent, might seem obliged to do this on behalf of her husband. It is reported that something of this kind happened at Antioch approximately fifty years ago, in the time of Constantius [Note: [Col. 1254] Approximately A.D. 343; for he was writing this around A.D. 393.]. At that time Acyndinus, who was prefect and had also been consul, was demanding from a certain man a debt of one pound of gold owed to the treasury. Moved, I do not know by what impulse—for such conduct is often dangerous in those who possess authority, to whom everything is permitted, or rather seems to be permitted—he threatened, swearing and emphatically declaring that if the man did not pay the specified gold by the appointed day, he would be put to death.

The man was therefore held under severe guard and could not free himself from that debt. The dreaded day began to draw near. As it happened, he had a very beautiful wife, but she possessed no money with which she could help her husband. A certain rich man became inflamed by the woman’s beauty and, learning that her husband was in such danger, sent word to her, promising that, if she would sleep with him for one night, he would give her a pound of gold.

She, knowing that she did not have authority over her own body, but that her husband did, went to him and said that she was prepared to do this on behalf of her husband—provided that he, the master of the marital body, to whom the whole of that chastity was owed, wished it to be done for his life, as though it were something belonging to him. He thanked her and ordered that it be done, in no way judging the intercourse adulterous, since no lust was involved and the husband's great love, at his command and with his consent, demanded it.

The woman went to the rich man’s estate and did what the shameless man wanted. But she gave her body only to her husband—not to one who desired intercourse in the usual sense, but to one who desired to live. She received the gold; but the giver fraudulently withdrew what he had given and substituted a similar container filled with earth.

When the woman, now back in her own home, discovered this, she rushed into public, intending to proclaim what she had done with the same love for her husband by which she had been compelled to act. She appealed to the prefect, confessed everything, and showed the fraud to which she had been subjected. The prefect then first declared himself guilty, since his threats had brought the matter about; and, as though pronouncing judgment against another person, ordered that a pound of gold be paid into the treasury from Acyndinus’s property. As for the woman, he ordered her to be brought into possession of that land from which she had received earth in place of gold.

I am not arguing the matter in either direction. Let each person judge it as he wishes; for this is not a story drawn from divine authorities. Nevertheless, once the event has been narrated, human moral sense does not reject so completely what was done by that woman at her husband’s command as it recoiled earlier, when the case was presented without any example. In this Gospel passage, however, nothing ought to be considered more carefully than that fornication is so great an evil that, although marriage bonds are so tightly joined, this one cause alone is excepted as grounds for dissolution. What fornication is has already been discussed.

**CHAPTER XVII**

51. “Again,” he says, “you have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not swear falsely, but you shall render your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; No, no’; and whatever is more than this is from evil.”

The righteousness of the Pharisees consists in not swearing falsely. He confirms this righteousness of the kingdom of heaven by forbidding oaths. For just as one who does not speak cannot speak falsely, so one who does not swear cannot swear falsely.

Nevertheless, since a person swears when he calls upon God as witness, this passage must be considered carefully, lest the Apostle appear to have acted contrary to the Lord’s command when he often swore in this manner. He says, “As for the things I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying” (Gal. 1:20); and again, “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying” (2 Cor. 11:31). There is also this: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of his Son, how unceasingly I remember you always in my prayers” (Rom. 1:9–10).

Perhaps someone might say that an oath is present only when something is said by the thing invoked in the oath: that the Apostle did not swear because he did not say “by God,” but said, “God is my witness.” It is ridiculous to think this. Yet, for the sake of contentious or exceedingly slow-minded people [Note: [Col. 1255] In eleven manuscripts, “for the sake of slanderous or much slower-minded people.”], so that no one may think there is a difference, let him know that the Apostle also swore in this manner when he said, “I die every day, by your glory” (1 Cor. 15:31).

No one should suppose that this means, “Your glory makes me die every day,” as when we say, “He was made learned through that teacher’s instruction,” meaning that he was perfectly instructed through that teacher’s teaching. The Greek copies settle the matter: they read, Νὴ τὴν καύχησιν ὑμετέραν, “By your boasting,” an expression spoken only by one who is swearing.

The Lord’s command, then, is to refrain from swearing, lest anyone desire an oath as though it were a good thing and, through the habit of frequent swearing, slip by custom into perjury. Therefore, whoever understands that an oath belongs not among good things but among necessities should restrain himself as much as he can, so that he uses it only under compulsion, when he sees that people are slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe unless it is confirmed by an oath [Note: [Col. 1255] In three manuscripts, “unless it is confirmed.”].

This is the meaning of the command, “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; No, no.’” This is good and should be desired. “Whatever is more than this is from evil”: that is, if you are compelled to swear, know that the compulsion arises from the weakness of those whom you are trying to persuade of something useful. That weakness is certainly an evil, from which we pray to be delivered every day when we say, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13).

Accordingly, he did not say, “Whatever is more than this is evil”; for you do not do evil when you use an oath properly—although an oath is not good in itself, it is necessary in order to persuade another person of what you are rightly urging. Rather, he said, “it is from evil,” namely, from the weakness of the person who compels you to swear. But no one knows except one who has experienced it how difficult it is both to extinguish the habit of swearing and never rashly to do what necessity sometimes compels one to do.

52. It may also be asked why, after saying, “But I say to you, do not swear at all,” he added, “neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne,” and the rest, up to “nor by your head.” I think this was because the Jews did not believe themselves bound by an oath if they swore by these things. They had heard, “You shall render your oaths to the Lord,” and therefore did not think they owed an oath to the Lord if they swore by heaven, or earth, or Jerusalem, or their own head. This resulted not from any fault in the one giving the command, but from their misunderstanding.

The Lord therefore teaches that nothing among God’s creatures is so insignificant that anyone should think he may swear falsely by it, since divine providence governs created things from the highest to the lowest, beginning with God’s throne and extending even to a white or black hair.

“Neither by heaven,” he says, “because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet.” That is: when you swear by heaven or earth, do not imagine that you do not owe your oath to the Lord, because you are shown to be swearing by him whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is earth.

“Neither by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King.” This is better than if he had said “my city,” although that is what is understood. And since he himself is certainly Lord, whoever swears by Jerusalem owes his oath to the Lord.

“Nor shall you swear by your head.” What could anyone think belonged more to him than his own head? Yet how is it ours, when we have no power to make even one hair white or black? Whoever wishes to swear by his head therefore owes his oath to God, who ineffably possesses all things and is present everywhere.

Here the remaining cases are also understood, although they could not all be stated. We have already recalled the Apostle’s saying, “I die every day, by your glory.” To show that he owed this oath to the Lord, he added, “which I have in Christ Jesus.”

53. Yet, for the sake of those who are fleshly, I say that one must not suppose that when heaven is called God’s throne and earth his footstool, God has placed bodily members in heaven and on earth as we do when we sit. That seat signifies judgment. Since, in the whole body of the universe, heaven possesses the greatest beauty and earth the least, it is as though the divine power is more present to the excellence of beauty, while it orders what is least at the outermost and lowest places: thus God is said to sit in heaven and to tread upon the earth.

Spiritually, however, the name “heaven” signifies holy souls, and “earth” sinful souls. Since “the spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15), he is appropriately called God’s throne. The sinner, however, to whom it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. 3:19), is ordered among the lowest things because divine justice assigns what is fitting to each person’s merits. And the one who did not wish to remain in the law is punished under the law [Note: [Col. 1257] The Arnulfing manuscript reads, “is placed under the law.”]; he is appropriately understood as God’s footstool.

**CHAPTER XVIII**

54. To bring this summary to a close, what could be said or imagined that would require greater labor and effort, in which the faithful mind might exercise all the powers of its diligence, than overcoming a vicious habit? Let it cut off the members that hinder the kingdom of heaven and not be broken by the pain. Let it endure everything in marital fidelity which, although extremely burdensome, does not involve the crime of unlawful corruption—that is, fornication.

For example, if someone has a wife who is barren, or physically deformed, or disabled in her limbs, or blind, deaf, or lame; or if she is worn out by illnesses, pains, and sicknesses; or whatever else, apart from fornication, can be imagined as exceedingly horrible—let him endure it for the sake of fidelity and companionship. Let him not merely refrain from dismissing such a wife; even if he does not have a wife, let him not marry one who has been released from her husband, even if she is beautiful, healthy, wealthy, and fertile.

If these things are not permitted, let him consider it much less permissible to approach any other unlawful intercourse. Let him flee fornication in such a way that he withdraws himself from every shameful corruption.

Let him speak truthfully, commending it not through frequent oaths but through the integrity of his conduct. Let him flee to the citadel of Christian warfare and, as though from a higher position, cast down the countless armies of evil habits rebelling against him. A few have been mentioned so that all the others might be understood.

But who would dare undertake such great labors except one who burns with such love of righteousness that, as though inflamed by the most vehement hunger and thirst, and considering no life worth having until he is satisfied by it, he does violence to the kingdom of heaven? Otherwise he could not be strong enough to endure all those things that the lovers of this age consider laborious, difficult, arduous, and altogether burdensome in the cutting off of their habits.

Blessed, therefore, are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.

55. Yet when anyone experiences difficulty in these labors, making his way through hard and rough paths, surrounded by various temptations, and seeing on every side the burdens of his former life rise up [Note: [Col. 1257] So the manuscripts and Mar. read. At., Am., Er., and Lov. read, “the troubles of his former life.”], he may fear that he will not be able to complete what he has begun. Let him then seize upon counsel so that he may deserve assistance.

What other counsel is there than to bear the weakness of others and to help as much as he can the person who desires divine help for his own weakness? Let us therefore consider, in due order, the commandments concerning mercy.

The meek and the merciful may seem to be the same; but the difference is that the meek person, who was discussed above, does not contradict, out of piety, the divine judgments pronounced against his own sins, nor those words of God which he does not yet understand. He does not, however, offer any benefit to the person whom he neither contradicts nor resists. The merciful person, on the other hand, does not resist in such a way that he allows the other to become worse through resistance; rather, he does so for the other’s correction.

**CHAPTER XIX**

56. The Lord continues and says: “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also; and whoever wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well; and whoever compels you to go one thousand paces, go with him another two. Give to everyone who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you.”

The righteousness of the Pharisees is the lesser righteousness of not exceeding moderation in revenge, lest anyone return more than he has received. This is nevertheless a great step. For no one is easily found who, having received a blow with the fist, wishes to return only one blow; or who, having heard one insulting word, is content to return one word of equal force.

A person either takes revenge without measure because he is disturbed by anger, or because he considers it just that the person who caused the injury should first be injured more severely than the one who had not injured him was injured.

The law restrained such an attitude to a considerable degree, for it is written, “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.” These words indicate a limit, so that revenge does not exceed the injury. This is the beginning of peace; perfect peace, however, is entirely to refuse revenge.

57. Between that first condition—beyond the law—in which a greater evil is returned for a lesser evil, and what the Lord said to those whom he was perfecting, namely, that no evil should be returned for evil, there is an intermediate position: that as much should be returned as was received. Through this, in the course of the appointed times, a transition was made from the greatest discord to the greatest harmony.

Whoever first inflicts harm from a desire to injure and hurt—see how far he is from the person who does not repay even when injured. Whoever has done no evil to anyone first, but, after being injured, repays with something more severe, whether in intention or in deed, has withdrawn somewhat from the height of iniquity and advanced toward the height of righteousness; nevertheless, he does not yet possess what the law given through Moses commanded.

Whoever returns only as much as he received is already giving something. For the guilty person does not deserve as great a punishment as the innocent person suffered who was injured by him. The one who came to fulfill the law rather than abolish it perfects this initial righteousness—not severe, but merciful.

He left the two remaining steps for us to understand and preferred to speak of the highest summit of mercy. For there is still something that a person may do who does not fulfill this greatness of the commandment belonging to the kingdom of heaven: he may return not as much, but less—for example, one blow for two, or cut off an ear for an eye that has been torn out.

Ascending from this, the person who returns nothing at all draws near to the Lord’s command, but is not yet there. For it still seems little to the Lord if, for the evil you have received, you return no evil, unless you are also prepared to receive more.

Therefore he did not say, “But I say to you, do not return evil for evil,” although this too is a great commandment. Rather, he said, “Do not resist evil,” so that you would not merely refrain from returning what has been inflicted upon you, but would not resist further injury either.

This is what he explains immediately afterward: “But if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also.” He did not say, “If anyone strikes you, do not strike him”; he said, “Prepare yourself to be struck again.”

Those who serve people they greatly love—children or any other beloved persons who are sick, infants, or deranged—understand that this belongs to mercy. They often suffer much from them, and, if their recovery requires it, offer themselves to suffer even more, until the weakness of age or illness passes.

Since the Lord, the physician of souls, was instructing them in caring for their neighbors, what else could he teach them except to bear patiently the weaknesses of those whose well-being they wished to promote? Every wickedness arises from weakness of soul, because nothing is more innocent than the person who is perfect in virtue.

58. It may be asked what is meant by the right cheek. The Greek copies, which deserve greater confidence, have it this way; many Latin copies have “cheek” only, without “right.”

The face is that by which each person is recognized. We read in the Apostle: “You endure it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face.” He immediately adds, “I speak according to dishonor” (2 Cor. 11:20–21), explaining what it means to be struck in the face: to be despised and held in contempt.

The Apostle does not say this so that they should not tolerate such people, but to show himself all the more to be one who loved them in such a way that he wished to spend himself for them (ibid. 12:15).

Since a face cannot literally be called right or left, yet honor can exist both according to God and according to this world, the distinction is made as though between a right cheek and a left cheek. Thus, whenever a disciple of Christ is despised because he is a Christian, he should be much more prepared to be despised in whatever worldly honors he possesses.

The same Apostle, when people were persecuting the Christian name in him, would not have offered the other cheek to those striking his right cheek if he had remained silent about the dignity he possessed in this world. By saying, “I am a Roman citizen” (Acts 22:25), he was prepared to have that status despised in himself by those who had despised the precious and saving name borne by him.

Did he therefore endure chains any less afterward, although Roman citizens could not legally be bound? Or did he wish to accuse anyone of this injury? And if some spared him because of the name of Roman citizenship, he nevertheless did not thereby fail to offer himself to be struck, since by his patience he wished to correct those whom he saw honoring the left side in him—the things of this world—more than the right.

The only thing to consider is the spirit in which he did everything: how benevolently and mercifully he acted toward those from whom he suffered these things.

When he was struck on the cheek at the high priest’s command, his words, “God will strike you, whitewashed wall,” appeared insulting. To those who understand little, they sound like an insult; to those who understand, they are a prophecy. A whitewashed wall is hypocrisy—that is, a pretense displaying priestly dignity and concealing beneath that name, as beneath a white covering, an interior shamefulness resembling mud.

He wonderfully preserved what belonged to humility when, after being told, “Do you insult God’s high priest?” he replied, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people’” (Acts 23:3–5).

There he showed with what tranquility he had said what appeared to have been spoken in anger. His immediate and gentle reply was impossible for those who are indignant and disturbed. In that very statement he spoke truthfully to those who understood: “I did not know that he was the high priest”—as though he were saying, “I knew another high priest, for whose name I endure these things, one whom it is not lawful to curse; and you curse him, since in me you hate nothing except his name.”

Thus such things should not be made into a false show [Note: [Col. 1260] Twelve manuscripts read, “to insult.”], but one must be prepared for everything in the heart itself, so that one may sing the prophetic words: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8).

Many know how to offer the other cheek, but do not know how to love the one by whom they are struck. Yet the Lord himself, who certainly first fulfilled the commandments he taught, did not offer the other cheek when a servant of the high priest struck him. Instead he said, “If I have spoken evil, bear witness concerning the evil; but if I have spoken well, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23).

Nevertheless, his heart was prepared—not only to be struck on the other cheek for the salvation of all, but also to be crucified in his entire body.

59. The same is rightly understood of what follows: “Whoever wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.” This command concerns preparation of the heart, not ostentation of the deed [Note: [Col. 1260] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have “display” instead of “ostentation.”].

What is said about the tunic and the cloak is to be done not only with those articles, but with everything that we can say is temporally ours by some legal right. If this is commanded concerning necessities, how much more fitting is it to despise superfluities?

Nevertheless, the things I called ours must be included within the category specified by the Lord himself when he says, “If anyone wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic.” All those things, then, are to be understood about which someone can contend with us in court, so that they pass from our legal right into the right of the person who is contending, or on whose behalf the contention is made: clothing, a house, land, an animal, and money in general.

Whether this should also be understood of slaves is a major question. A Christian ought not to possess a slave in the same way as a horse or silver, although it may happen that a horse is worth more than a slave, and that something made of gold or silver is worth much more.

But if that slave is educated or governed by you, his master, in a more upright, honorable, and God-fearing manner than he could be by the person who wishes to take him away, I do not know whether anyone would dare say that he ought to be despised like clothing.

For one human being ought to love another as himself. The Lord of all commands this person, as the following words show, to love even his enemies.

60. We must carefully observe that every tunic is a garment, but not every garment is a tunic. The word “garment,” therefore, signifies more than the word “tunic.” Accordingly, I think the passage was phrased, “Whoever wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well,” as though it said, “Whoever wishes to take your tunic, give him whatever other clothing you have as well.” For this reason some have interpreted the Greek word ἱμάτιον as “cloak.”

61. “And whoever compels you,” he says, “to go one thousand paces, go with him another two.” This is meant not so much as an instruction about what to do with one’s feet as about being prepared in spirit.

In the Christian narrative itself, which possesses authority, you will find no such thing done by the saints or by the Lord himself when, in the human nature he graciously assumed, he offered us an example of how to live. Yet in almost every place you will find them prepared to endure with equanimity whatever had been wickedly inflicted upon them.

Do we understand this, then, as a figurative expression? “Go with him another two”: did he wish three to be completed, a number signifying perfection, so that each person may remember, when doing this, that he is fulfilling perfect righteousness by mercifully bearing the weaknesses of those whom he wishes to become healthy?

This may also be the reason why he presented these commandments through three examples. The first is if anyone strikes you on the cheek; the second, if anyone wishes to take your tunic; the third, if anyone compels you to go one thousand paces. In this third example, double is added to the single measure so that three may be completed.

If this number does not signify perfection here, as has been suggested, let us understand instead that the commandment begins with what is more tolerable and gradually increases until it reaches the point of bearing another amount equal to the first.

First he wished the other cheek to be offered when the right cheek had been struck, so that you would be prepared to endure less than you had already endured. Whatever the right cheek signifies is certainly more valuable than what the left signifies; and if someone who has endured something in a more valuable matter endures something also in a less valuable one, the latter is less.

Next, he commands the person who wishes to take the tunic to be given the cloak as well. This is either an equal amount or not much more, but it is not double.

Finally, regarding one thousand paces, he commands that two thousand be added, so that one bears an additional double amount. Thus he signifies that whether a wicked person wishes to be against you in something somewhat less than what has already occurred, in something equal to it, or in something greater, it must be endured with equanimity.

**CHAPTER XX**

62. In these three kinds of examples, I see no kind of injury omitted. Everything in which we suffer some wickedness falls into two categories: one cannot be restored; the other can.

In the case of what cannot be restored, people usually seek the consolation of revenge. What good does it do to strike back after being struck? Is what was injured in the body thereby restored intact?

But an inflamed spirit desires such nourishment. A sound and steadfast spirit, however, is not helped by it; rather, it judges that the weakness of another should be borne mercifully, instead of seeking to alleviate through another person's punishment its own weakness, which does not exist.

63. This does not prohibit the kind of revenge that serves correction; for that too belongs to mercy. Nor does it obstruct the intention by which a person is prepared to endure more from the one whom he wishes to correct.

Yet no one is fit to administer such correctional punishment unless he has overcome, by the greatness of his love, the hatred with which those who desire to avenge themselves commonly burn [Note: [Col. 1261] Eight manuscripts read, “by the gentleness of his love.”].

Parents are not to be thought hateful toward a little child when the child is beaten for doing wrong, so that he will not do wrong again. The perfection of love itself is set before us in imitation of God the Father when the following words are said: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you.” Yet it is said of God through the prophet: “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he accepts” (Prov. 3:12).

The Lord also says: “The servant who does not know his master’s will and does things worthy of blows will receive few blows; but the servant who knows his master’s will and does things worthy of blows will receive many blows” (Luke 12:47–48).

Therefore the matter is not sought except so that the person to whom authority has been granted according to the order of things may administer punishment, and may do so with the disposition of a father toward a little child whom, because of his age, he cannot yet hate.

From this we obtain a most suitable example, by which it is sufficiently clear that sin can be punished out of love rather than left unpunished. The person against whom punishment is directed should be wished to become blessed through correction, not miserable through punishment. Yet one must be prepared, if necessary, to endure patiently further injuries inflicted by the person one wishes to correct, whether one has authority to restrain him or not.

64. Great and holy men, who already knew very well that the death which separates the soul from the body is not to be feared, nevertheless, taking into account the attitude of those who feared it, punished certain sins with death. This was done both so that the living might be struck by a useful fear and so that, for those punished by death, death itself would not be harmful, but rather the sin—which might have increased had they continued to live.

Those to whom God had granted such judgment did not judge rashly. This is why Elijah put many people to death, both by his own hand (1 Kings 18:40) and by fire obtained from heaven (2 Kings 1:10). Many other great and divine men, moved by the same spirit to provide for human affairs, did this no less deliberately.

When the disciples, following Elijah’s example, recalled to the Lord what he had done and asked that they too be given power to call down fire from heaven to consume those who would not offer them hospitality, the Lord rebuked in them not the example of the holy prophet but their ignorance in administering punishment, an ignorance that still remained in those who were immature (Luke 9:52–56). He recognized that they desired punishment not out of love for correction but out of hatred.

Afterward, once he had taught them what it meant to love one’s neighbor as oneself, and after the Holy Spirit had been poured out—sent from above, as he had promised, when ten days had been completed after his ascension (Acts 2:1–4)—such punishments did not disappear, although they occurred much more rarely than in the Old Testament.

There, for the most part, people were held under the domination of fear because they were servants; here, they were chiefly nourished in freedom through love. Thus, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, Ananias and his wife Sapphira fell dead at the words of the Apostle Peter and were not restored to life, but were buried (ibid. 5:1–10).

65. If the heretics who oppose the Old Testament do not wish to believe this book [Note: [Col. 1262] The Manichaeans.], let them look to the Apostle Paul, whom they read together with us. He speaks of a certain sinner whom he handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, “so that the soul may be saved” (1 Cor. 5:5).

If they do not wish to understand death here—for perhaps the matter is uncertain—let them at least acknowledge that the Apostle inflicted some punishment through Satan. The added words, “so that the spirit may be saved,” clearly show that he did this not out of hatred but out of love.

Or, in those books to which they themselves attribute great authority, let them observe what we are saying. There it is written that the Apostle Thomas called down upon a certain man, who had struck him on the cheek, the punishment of a most horrible death, while commending his soul so that mercy might be shown him in the world to come.

A dog brought to the tables at which the Apostle was dining the hand torn from the rest of the body of the man who had been killed by a lion.

We are free not to believe this writing, since it is not in the catholic canon. Yet those who, through I know not what blindness, rage most fiercely against the bodily punishments found in the Old Testament both read it and honor it as perfectly incorrupt and entirely true, without understanding at all in what spirit and according to what distribution of times those punishments were inflicted.

66. In this kind of injury, then—the kind expiated by punishment—Christians must maintain this rule [Note: [Col. 1263] Three manuscripts read, “this Christian rule.” Shortly afterward, almost all the manuscripts read, “hatred arise,” omitting the preposition “in.”]: after receiving an injury, hatred must not arise, but the mind must be prepared, through compassion for the other’s weakness, to endure more. Nor should it neglect correction, for which it may use advice, authority, or power.

There is another kind of injury, one that can be restored intact. It has two forms: one concerns money, the other service. Accordingly, the examples that follow are respectively about returning a garment and about being compelled to go one thousand or two thousand paces. A garment can be returned, and a person whom you have helped through your labor can also help you, if necessary.

Unless perhaps the matter should instead be divided in this way: the first example, concerning the struck cheek, signifies everything inflicted by wicked people that cannot be restored except by punishment; the second, concerning the garment, signifies everything that can be restored without punishment. This may be why he added, “Whoever wishes to contend with you in judgment,” since what is taken through legal judgment is not thought to be taken by force in such a way as to require revenge.

The third example may be composed of both forms, since something may be restored either without punishment or with punishment. Someone who violently demands unpaid service without any legal judgment—like one who wickedly compels a person to assist him unlawfully against that person’s will—can both pay the penalty for his wickedness and return the service if the person who endured his wickedness demands it.

In all these kinds of injury, therefore, the Lord teaches that the Christian ought to possess a most patient and merciful spirit, one most ready to endure more.

67. Since it is not enough merely not to harm someone unless one also provides as much benefit as one can, he adds accordingly: “Give to everyone who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you.”

He says, “To everyone who asks you,” not “everything to everyone who asks,” so that you give what you can give honestly and justly. What if someone asks for money with which he intends to oppress an innocent person? What if, finally, he asks for sexual violation?

But not to pursue the countless possibilities that are innumerable: what must be given is that which, so far as a human being can know or reasonably believe, harms neither you nor another person. And when you justly deny someone what he asks, you should explain the justice of the denial, so that you do not send him away empty-handed.

Thus you will give to everyone who asks you, although you will not always give what he asks. Sometimes you will give something better, when you correct the person asking for something unjust.

68. But what he says, “Whoever wishes to borrow from you, do not turn away,” must be referred to the disposition of the mind. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Everyone who receives borrows, even if he himself will not repay; for since God repays more abundantly to the merciful, everyone who bestows a benefit lends at interest. Or, if one does not wish to call “borrower” anyone except the person who will repay what he receives, it should be understood that the Lord has embraced these two kinds of giving. For either we give what we give freely, or we lend it to someone who will repay. And often people who are ready to give because of the divine reward promised to them become reluctant to give what is requested as a loan, as though they would receive nothing from God, since the person who receives repays the thing given. Accordingly, divine authority rightly exhorts us to this kind of bestowing a benefit when it says, “And whoever wishes to borrow from you, do not turn away”: that is, do not for this reason withdraw your willingness from the one who asks, because your money will lie idle [Note: [Col. 1264] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have, “because your money empties you.”], and God will not repay you once the person has repaid; but when you do this at God’s command, it cannot be fruitless in the sight of the one who commands these things.

## CHAPTER XXI

69. Then he adds and says: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor, and you shall hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the pagans do this very thing? Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is perfect.”

For without this love, by which we are commanded to love even our enemies and persecutors, who can fulfill the things stated above? The perfection of mercy, by which the greatest assistance is given to the suffering soul, cannot extend beyond love of one’s enemy; and therefore the passage concludes in this way: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is perfect.” Yet this is to be understood in such a way that God is perfect as God, and the soul is perfect as a soul.

70. That there is nevertheless some degree in the righteousness of the Pharisees, which belongs to the ancient Law, is understood from the fact that many people hate even those by whom they are loved—for example, dissolute sons hate parents who restrain their dissipation. Thus a person ascends to some degree when he loves his neighbor, although he still hates his enemy. But by the command of the one who came to fulfill the Law, not to abolish it, he will complete goodwill and kindness when he extends them even to love of his enemy. For although that degree is something, it is nevertheless so small that it can be shared even with tax collectors. Nor should the words spoken in the Law, “You shall hate your enemy,” be understood as the voice of one commanding a just person, but of one permitting the weak.

71. Here a question certainly arises that must in no way be concealed: to those who consider them less carefully and soberly, many other passages of Scripture appear opposed to this command of the Lord, by which he urges us to love our enemies, do good to those who hate us, and pray for those who persecute us. For many imprecations against enemies are found in the Prophets, and these are thought to be curses, such as, “Let their table become a snare” (Ps. 68:23), and the other things said there; and, “Let his sons become orphans, and his wife a widow” (Ps. 108:9), along with the other things said above or below in that same psalm by the Prophet in the person of Judas. Many other passages are found throughout Scripture that seem contrary both to this command of the Lord and to the apostolic commandment that says, “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14). For it is also written of the Lord that he cursed the cities that did not receive his word (Matt. 11:20–24; Luke 10:13–15); and the Apostle mentioned above said of a certain person, “The Lord will repay him according to his works” (2 Tim. 4:14).

72. But these matters are easily resolved, because the Prophet, by way of imprecation, foretold what would happen—not by the desire of one wishing it, but by the spirit of one who foresaw it. The same is true of the Lord and of the Apostle. Indeed, in their words too we find not what they wished for, but what they foretold. For when the Lord says, “Woe to you, Capernaum,” he means nothing other than that, on account of its unbelief, something evil would happen to it. The Lord did not wish this out of malevolence, but saw it through his divinity. And the Apostle does not say, “May the Lord repay him,” but, “The Lord will repay him according to his works”: this is the language of one announcing what will happen, not of one pronouncing a curse. Likewise, concerning that hypocrisy of the Jews, already mentioned, whose overthrow he saw impending, he said, “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” (see above, ch. 19, §58).

The Prophets, moreover, very often foretell the future in the figure of one pronouncing an imprecation, just as they frequently sang of future things in the figure of the past tense. For example: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things?” (Ps. 2:1). He did not say, “Why will the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things,” although he was not recalling things as though they had already happened, but was looking ahead to things that would come. The same is true of the passage, “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 21:19). Here too he did not say, “They will divide my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they will cast lots.”

No one, however, brings a charge against these words except someone who does not perceive that such variation of figures in speech takes nothing away from the truth of events, but adds very much to the feelings of those who speak.

## CHAPTER XXII

73. But what the apostle John says presses the question more forcefully: “If anyone knows that his brother has committed a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and the Lord will give life to the one whose sin does not lead to death. There is a sin leading to death; I do not say that anyone should pray for that” (1 John 5:16). For he plainly shows that there are certain brothers for whom we are not commanded to pray, although the Lord commands us to pray even for our persecutors.

This question cannot be resolved unless we acknowledge that among brothers there are certain sins more serious than the persecution of enemies. That “brothers” signifies Christians can be proved by many testimonies of the divine Scriptures. Yet the clearest passage is where the Apostle says: “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the brother.” He did not add “our brother,” but considered it evident that, by the name “brother,” he intended a Christian who had an unbelieving wife. Therefore shortly afterward he says, “But if the unbelieving person departs, let him depart; a brother or a sister is not enslaved in such circumstances” (1 Cor. 7:14–15).

I therefore think that a brother’s sin leading to death occurs when, after coming to know God through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, someone attacks the brotherhood and is driven by the fires of envy against the very grace by which he was reconciled to God [Note: [Col. 1266] *Retractationes*, ch. 19, §7.]. But a sin not leading to death occurs when someone has not withdrawn love from his brother, but through some weakness of mind has failed to perform the duties owed to brotherhood.

For this reason the Lord also says on the cross, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). They had not yet become participants in the grace of the Holy Spirit or entered into the fellowship of holy brotherhood. And blessed Stephen prays in the Acts of the Apostles for those by whom he is being stoned (Acts 7:59), because they had not yet believed in Christ and were not fighting against that common grace.

And for this reason, I think, the apostle Paul does not pray for Alexander: he was already a brother and had sinned unto death—that is, by attacking the brotherhood through envy. But he prays for those who had not broken love, although they had succumbed through fear, that they might be forgiven. For he says:

“Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works. You too must avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words.”

Then he adds for whom he prays, saying:

“At my first defense no one stood by me, but everyone deserted me; may it not be held against them” (2 Tim. 4:14–16).

74. This distinction separates Judas, who betrayed, from Peter, who denied—not because the penitent should not be forgiven, lest we oppose that saying of the Lord in which he commands that a brother who asks his brother for forgiveness must always be forgiven (Luke 17:3), but because the stain of Judas’s sin was so great that he could not submit to the humility of asking pardon, even though an evil conscience compelled him both to acknowledge and to confess his sin.

For when Judas said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,” he nevertheless ran in despair to the noose more readily than he humbly asked for forgiveness (Matt. 27:4–5). Therefore it makes a great difference what kind of repentance God forgives. Many people confess their sin much more quickly and become so angry with themselves that they strongly wish they had not sinned; yet they do not lower themselves to humble and break their hearts and implore forgiveness. Because of the greatness of their sin, we must believe that they already possess this disposition of mind concerning their condemnation.

75. And this is perhaps what it means to sin against the Holy Spirit: after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, to attack brotherly love through malice and envy. The Lord says that this sin is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

Hence one may ask whether the Jews sinned against the Holy Spirit when they said that the Lord cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. Are we to understand this as spoken against the Lord himself, since he says elsewhere concerning himself, “If they called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more the members of his household” (Matt. 10:25)? Or, because they had said it out of great envy, ungrateful both for the benefits then present, although they were not yet Christians, are they nevertheless to be thought to have sinned against the Holy Spirit on account of the magnitude of their envy?

This cannot be inferred from the Lord’s words. For although in the same passage he says, “Whoever speaks an evil word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come,” it may be that he warned them for this purpose: that they should approach grace, and, after receiving grace, should not sin in the way they were then sinning.

For at that time they spoke an evil word against the Son of Man, and this could be forgiven them if they turned, believed in him, and received the Holy Spirit. Once they had received him, however, if they wished to envy the brotherhood and attack the grace they had received, this would not be forgiven them, either in this age or in the age to come.

For if he had condemned them in such a way that no hope remained for them, he would not have judged that they should still be warned, adding these words: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. 12:24–33).

76. Let us therefore understand the command to love our enemies, do good to those who hate us, and pray for those who persecute us in such a way that, in the case of certain sins of brothers, we understand that we are not commanded to pray. Otherwise, through our ignorance, divine Scripture would appear—as cannot happen—to disagree with itself.

But whether, just as we are not to pray for certain people, we should also pray against some, has not yet become sufficiently clear. For the general command is, “Bless, and do not curse,” and, “Repay no one evil for evil” (Rom. 12:14, 17). But for whomever you do not pray, you do not pray against him either. You may see that his punishment is certain and his salvation utterly hopeless; and you do not fail to pray for him because you hate him, but because you perceive that you can accomplish nothing and do not wish your prayer to be rejected by the most just Judge.

But what are we to make of those against whom we have received accounts of prayers by the saints—not prayers that they might be corrected, for in that form prayer was rather made for them, but prayers directed toward their final condemnation? Not like the prayer against the Lord’s betrayer through the Prophet, for that—as has been said—was a prediction of future events, not a wish for punishment; nor like the Apostle’s prayer against Alexander, for enough has already been said about that; but as we read in the Apocalypse of John, where the martyrs pray that they may be avenged (Rev. 6:10), although the first martyr prayed that his killers might be forgiven.

77. But this should not disturb us. For who would dare to assert that, when those holy candidates asked to be avenged, they were asking for vengeance against the people themselves, rather than against the kingdom of sin? For the sincere and complete justice and mercy of the martyrs’ vengeance consists in the overthrow of the kingdom of sin, under whose reign they endured such great sufferings.

The Apostle strives for its overthrow when he says, “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12). The kingdom of sin is destroyed and overthrown partly through the correction of people, so that the flesh may be subjected to the spirit, and partly through the condemnation of those who persist in sin, so that justice may be so ordered that, when the just reign with Christ, the condemned can no longer trouble them.

Consider the apostle Paul. Does he not seem to avenge in himself the martyr Stephen when he says, “I do not fight as though beating the air; but I discipline my body and bring it into subjection” (1 Cor. 9:26–27)? For in himself he was surely overthrowing and weakening, and disposing as conquered, that by which he had persecuted Stephen and the other Christians [Note: [Col. 1268] Eleven manuscripts read, “bound” (*vinctum*).]

Who, then, can prove that the holy martyrs did not ask the Lord for such vengeance upon themselves, since they could quite properly wish for the end of this age, in which they endured such great sufferings, as their own vindication?

Those who pray in this way pray for their enemies who are capable of being healed, and they do not pray against those who have chosen to be incurable [Note: [Col. 1268] Two manuscripts read, “and they pray against them,” omitting the negation.]. For God, when he punishes them, is not a malicious torturer but a most just disposer of things.

Therefore, without any doubt, let us love our enemies, do good to those who hate us, and pray for those who persecute us.

## CHAPTER XXIII

78. What follows accordingly, “So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven,” is to be understood according to the rule by which John also says, “He gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12). For there is one Son by nature, who is entirely incapable of sinning. We, however, become sons by receiving power, insofar as we fulfill the things commanded by him.

Therefore apostolic teaching calls this adoption, by which we are called to an eternal inheritance so that we may be coheirs with Christ (Rom. 8:17; Gal. 4:5). We become sons through spiritual regeneration and are adopted into the kingdom of God, not as strangers, but as those made and created by him. Thus one benefit is that, through his omnipotence, he caused us to exist when previously we were nothing; another is that he adopted us, so that, as sons, we might enjoy eternal life with him through our participation in him.

Accordingly, he does not say, “Do these things because you are sons,” but, “Do these things so that you may be sons.”

79. When he calls us to this through the Only-Begotten, he calls us to his likeness. For he, as he says next, makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust.

You may understand “his sun” not as this sun visible to bodily eyes, but as that wisdom of which it is said, “For she is the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26), and of which it is also said, “The sun of righteousness has risen for me,” and again, “For you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise” (Mal. 4:2). You may likewise understand the rain as the watering of the teaching of truth, because Christ appeared to the good and the evil, and the Gospel was preached to the good and the evil.

Or you may prefer to understand this sun as the one revealed not only to human eyes but also to the bodily eyes of animals, and this rain as that by which fruits are produced, fruits given for the nourishment of the body. I consider this the more plausible interpretation. For that spiritual sun does not rise except for the good and the holy; this is precisely what the wicked lament in the book entitled *The Wisdom of Solomon*: “The sun has not risen for us” (Wis. 5:6). And that spiritual rain waters only the good, because the vineyard is used to signify the wicked, concerning which it is said, “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6).

But whether you understand one or the other, it occurs through God’s great goodness, which we are commanded to imitate if we wish to be sons of God. For who is so ungrateful as not to recognize how much comfort the light of this visible sun and the physical rain provide in this life? We see that this comfort is commonly supplied both to the just and to sinners in this life.

He does not say, “the one who makes the sun rise upon the good and the evil,” but adds “his”—that is, the sun which he himself made and established, taking nothing from anyone in order to make it, just as Genesis says concerning all the lights (Gen. 1:16). He alone can properly say that all things he created from nothing are his. By this we are reminded how generously, at his command, we ought to grant our enemies the things that we did not create but received from his gifts.

80. Who, then, can either be capable of or prepared to endure injuries from the weak, insofar as this benefits their salvation; prefer to suffer more of another’s wrongdoing rather than repay what he has suffered; give to everyone who asks him something either what is requested, if he possesses it and can rightly give it, or good advice or a benevolent disposition; not turn away from one who wishes to borrow; love his enemies, do good to those who hate him, and pray for those who persecute him?

Who, then, does these things unless he is fully and perfectly merciful? By this one means misery is avoided, with the assistance of the one who says, “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6). “Blessed, therefore, are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy.”

But I think it is appropriate that the reader, fatigued by such a long volume, should now take a little rest and refresh himself, so that the remaining matters may be considered in another book.

# BOOK TWO

On the latter part of the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, contained in chapters 6 and 7 of Matthew.

## CHAPTER I

1. Mercy, with whose treatment the first book concluded, is followed by purity of heart, from which this book takes its beginning. Purity of heart is like the eye [Note: [Col. 1269] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “like the eye” (*tanquam oculus*).] by which God is seen; and one must take as much care to possess this eye in its simplicity as the dignity of the object that can be seen by such an eye demands.

Even when this eye has been purified to a considerable degree, it is difficult for some stains to fail to creep in from those things that commonly accompany our good actions, such as human praise. If people do not live rightly, that is harmful; but to live rightly and not wish to be praised—what else is that than to be hostile to human affairs, which are certainly more miserable the less people delight in a right life?

Therefore, if those among whom you live do not praise you for living rightly, they are in error. But if they do praise you, you are in danger—unless you possess a heart so simple and pure that you do not do the things you rightly do for the sake of human praise, and you rejoice more for those who praise what is right, because they take pleasure in what is good, than for yourself. For you would live rightly even if no one praised you.

You should also understand your praise to be useful to those who praise you only if they honor not you yourself in your good life but God, whose most holy temple is everyone who lives well. Thus what David says may be fulfilled: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. 33:3).

It therefore belongs to a pure eye not to look toward human praise in doing what is right, and not to refer what you do rightly to human praise—that is, not to do something rightly for the purpose of pleasing people. For then it will also be desirable to pretend to be good, if one pays attention only to being praised by people; and since a person cannot see the heart, he can praise what is false as well.

Those who do this—that is, those who pretend to goodness—are double-hearted. Therefore the heart is not simple, that is, pure, unless it rises above human praise and looks only to him when it lives rightly, striving to please the one who alone examines the conscience. Whatever proceeds from the purity of that conscience is more praiseworthy in proportion as it desires human praise less.

2. “Take care,” he says, “not to practice your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them.” That is: take care not to live rightly with the intention of being seen by people, and not to establish your good in this, that people may see you. “Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

This does not mean that you will have no reward if you are seen by people, but if you live rightly for the purpose of being seen by people. For where then would be what was said at the beginning of this sermon: “You are the light of the world”? A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do people light a lamp and place it under a basket, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for everyone in the house. “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works.” But he did not end there, for he added, “and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:14–16).

Here, however, because he condemns the possibility that this should be the end of right actions—that is, that we should act rightly for the purpose of merely being seen by people—after saying, “Take care not to practice your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them,” he added nothing. From this it is clear that he did not forbid right action before people, but forbade doing right before people for the possible purpose of being seen by them—that is, of looking toward this and placing the end of our intention there.

3. The Apostle also says, “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10), while elsewhere he says, “Please everyone in everything, just as I also please everyone in everything” (1 Cor. 10:32–33). Those who do not understand this think the statements contradictory, although he said that he did not please people because he did not act rightly for the purpose of pleasing people, but for the purpose of pleasing God. He wished to turn people’s hearts toward God precisely by pleasing people.

Thus he rightly said that he did not please people, because in this very matter he looked toward pleasing God. And he rightly commanded that people should be pleased—not so that this should be sought as the reward of right actions, but because no one who does not offer himself as an example to those whom he wishes to save can please God. No one can imitate someone who does not please him.

Thus, just as someone could speak without absurdity who said, “In this work by which I seek a ship, I am not seeking a ship but my homeland,” so the Apostle could appropriately say, “In this work by which I please people, I am not pleasing people but God, because I do not seek this for its own sake, but refer it to the purpose that those whom I wish to be saved may imitate me.”

He says the same concerning the offering made for the saints: “Not because I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. 4:17). That is: “What I seek is not your gift itself, but your fruit.” For by this sign it could become evident how much progress they had made toward God, when they willingly offered what he sought from them not for the enjoyment of receiving gifts, but for the fellowship of love [Note: [Col. 1271] All the manuscripts read, “they did.”].

4. Moreover, when he adds, “Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven,” he demonstrates nothing other than that we must take care not to seek human praise as the reward for our works—that is, not to think that such praise makes us blessed.

## CHAPTER II

5. “Therefore, when you give alms,” he says, “do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be glorified by people.”

“Do not,” he says, “wish to become known in this way, like the hypocrites.” It is clear that hypocrites do not possess in their hearts what they display before human eyes. For hypocrites are pretenders, like those who speak the parts of other persons, as in theatrical performances. The person who plays the role of Agamemnon in a tragedy, for example, or that of anyone else belonging to the history or fiction being performed, is not actually that person; he pretends to be him and is called a hypocrite.

Thus, in the Church or in all human life, whoever wishes to appear to be what he is not is a hypocrite. He pretends to be just but does not display justice, because he places the entire fruit in human praise. Even pretenders can obtain this praise while deceiving those to whom they appear good and by whom they are praised.

But they do not receive a reward from God, who examines the heart, except the punishment of their deceit. “They have received,” he says, “their reward from people.” And it will rightly be said to them, “Depart from me, workers of deceit. You bore my name, but you did not do my works.”

Those, therefore, have received their reward who give alms for no other reason than to be glorified by people—not if they are glorified by people, but if they give precisely so that they may be glorified, as was explained above. Human praise should not be sought by one who acts rightly, but should follow the one who acts rightly, so that those who can also imitate what they praise may progress—not so that the person whom they praise may think that he has benefited them in some way.

6. “But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

If you understand the left hand to mean unbelievers, it might seem that there is no fault in wishing to please believers. Yet we are absolutely forbidden to establish the fruit and end of a good work in the praise of any people whatsoever.

As far as concerns the purpose that those who are pleased by your right actions may imitate you, these actions must be displayed not only to believers but also to unbelievers, so that by praising our good works they may honor God and come to salvation.

But if you understand the left hand as an enemy, so that your enemy is not to know when you give alms, why did the Lord himself mercifully heal people while hostile Jews stood around? Why did the apostle Peter, after taking pity on and healing the disabled man at the Beautiful Gate, also endure the anger of his enemies against himself and against the other disciples of Christ (Acts 3–4)?

Furthermore, if an enemy must not know when we give alms, how are we to act toward that enemy in order to fulfill the command, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Prov. 25:21)?

7. There is a third opinion commonly held by worldly people, so absurd and laughable that I would not mention it unless I had discovered that many are held by this error. They say that the left hand signifies one’s wife: since women are usually more miserly with household money, the wife is to be kept unaware when her husband compassionately spends something on the needy, because of domestic quarrels.

As though only men were Christians, and this command had not also been given to women! To which left hand, then, is a woman commanded to conceal her act of mercy? Or is a wife also to be the left hand of her husband? This is said with the greatest absurdity.

Or if someone thinks that husband and wife are mutually one another’s left hands, and that one of them spends something from the household resources against the will of the other, such a marriage will not be Christian. Rather, whoever among them wishes to give alms at God’s command must regard the person who opposes him as an enemy of God’s command and therefore count that person among unbelievers.

Yet the command concerning such people is that a faithful husband should win his wife, or a faithful wife her husband, by good conduct and behavior. Therefore they should not conceal their good works from one another; through these they are to invite one another, so that each may invite the other into fellowship with the Christian faith.

Nor should thefts be committed so that God may be won over. If something must be concealed for as long as the other person cannot bear it calmly because of weakness, although the action is not unjust or unlawful, it is nevertheless readily apparent from consideration of the whole chapter that this is not what is now signified by the left hand; in this same consideration we will also discover what he calls the left hand.

8. “Take care,” he says, “not to practice your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

Here he has named righteousness in general, and then explains it in particular. One part of righteousness is the work performed through almsgiving, and therefore he connects the statements by saying, “Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be glorified by people.”

This refers back to what he said above: “Take care not to practice your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them.” What follows, “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward,” refers back to what he stated earlier: “Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

Then he continues, “But when you give alms.” When he says, “But you,” what else does he mean than, “Not as they do”? What, then, does he command me? “But when you give alms,” he says, “do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

Therefore, they act in such a way that their left hand knows what their right hand is doing. What is condemned in them is thus forbidden to you. What is condemned in them is that they act in such a way as to seek human praise.

Accordingly, nothing seems more likely to be signified by the left hand than the pleasure taken in praise. The right hand, however, signifies the intention of fulfilling the divine commands. Therefore, when the desire for human praise mixes with the conscience of the person giving alms, the left hand becomes aware of the work of the right hand.

Thus, “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” means: let the desire for human praise not mix with your conscience when, in giving alms, you strive to fulfill the divine command.

9. “So that your alms may be in secret.” What is “in secret” except in the good conscience itself, which cannot be displayed to human eyes or disclosed in words? For many people tell many lies.

Therefore, if the right hand acts inwardly and in secret, everything external, visible, and temporal belongs to the left hand. Let your alms therefore be in your very conscience, where many people give alms with good will even when they do not possess money or anything else that ought to be given to the needy.

Others give outwardly but do not give inwardly. They wish to appear merciful either out of ambition or for the sake of some temporal thing; in them only the left hand should be considered to be acting.

Others occupy a middle position between the two. They give alms with an intention directed toward God, yet some desire for praise or for some frail and temporal thing inserts itself into this excellent will.

But our Lord prohibits with much greater force the left hand’s acting alone in us, since he also forbids it to be mixed with the works of the right hand. This means that we must take care not only to give alms out of the desire for temporal things alone, but also not to attend to God in this work in such a way that the desire for external advantages mixes or joins itself to our intention.

For the subject is the purification of the heart, and unless the heart is simple, it will not be pure. But how will it be simple if it serves two masters, and does not purify its vision through a single intention directed toward eternal things, but clouds it also with love for mortal and fragile things?

“Let your alms therefore be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” Entirely and most truly, this is exactly right. For if you expect a reward from the one who alone examines the conscience, the conscience itself should be sufficient for you to merit the reward.

Many Latin copies read, “And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly.” But since we do not find “openly” in the Greek copies, which are earlier [Note: [Col. 1274] Today it is found in the Greek copies, not in the Latin ones.], we have not thought it necessary to discuss the matter here.

## CHAPTER III

10. “And when you pray,” he says, “you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, so that they may be seen by people.”

Here too, it is not wrong to be seen by people; what is wrong is doing these things for the purpose of being seen by people.
