The same point is repeated so often unnecessarily, since one rule must already be observed: we must understand that the danger is not that people know these things, nor that we should avoid them for that reason, but that they should be done with the intention of seeking in them the reward of pleasing people.

The Lord himself also preserves the same words when he adds, in the same way, “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward.” By this he shows that he forbids the desire for that reward which fools enjoy when they are praised by people.

### 11

“But when you pray,” he says, “go into your rooms.” What are these rooms except the heart itself, which is also signified in the Psalm when it says, “What you say in your hearts, and be pricked in your chambers” (Psalm 4:5)? “And shutting the doors,” he says, “pray to your Father in secret.” It is not enough to enter the rooms if the door stands open to intruders, through which things outside thrust themselves in improperly and seek our inner parts. By “outside” we mean all temporal and visible things, which enter our thoughts through the door—that is, through bodily sensation—and, as we pray, drown out our prayers with a crowd of empty phantasms.

The door must therefore be shut—that is, resistance must be offered to bodily sensation—so that spiritual prayer may be directed to the Father. This prayer takes place in the innermost recesses of the heart, where the Father is prayed to in secret. “And your Father,” he says, “who sees in secret, will repay you.” This too had to be concluded with such a clause: for he is not now instructing us to pray, but how to pray; nor, above, to give alms, but with what intention to give them. He is prescribing the cleansing of the heart, which nothing cleanses except a single and undivided intention directed toward eternal life through the pure love of wisdom alone.

### 12

“But when praying,” he says, “do not speak at length, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard because of their many words.” Just as it belongs to hypocrites to make themselves objects of display in prayer, whose reward is to please human beings, so it belongs to the Gentiles—that is, to the nations—to think that they will be heard because of their many words. Indeed, all excessive talk comes from the Gentiles, who devote themselves more to exercising the tongue than to cleansing the mind. They try to transfer this kind of empty effort even to bending God through prayer, supposing that, like a human judge, he can be brought by words to a particular decision.

“Do not therefore be like them,” says the one true Teacher. “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” If many words are spoken in order to instruct and teach one who is ignorant, what need is there of them with regard to the Knower of all things? Everything that exists speaks and declares itself to him by the very fact that it exists; and things that are going to exist do not lie hidden from his art and wisdom, in which all things that have passed and all things that will pass are present, without passing away.

### 13

Yet since he himself is also going to utter a few words by which he will teach us to pray, it may be asked why even these few words are necessary for one who knows everything before it happens and, as has been said, knows what we need before we ask him.

The first answer is that we ought not to act upon God by words, as though we were to obtain what we want through them, but through the realities we carry in our minds and through the intention of our thought, with pure love and simple affection. Nevertheless, our Lord taught us the realities themselves through words, so that, committing them to memory, we might recall them at the proper time for prayer.

### 14

But again it may be asked whether prayer should be offered through realities or through words: what need is there of prayer itself, if God already knows what we need? There is need of it because the very intention of prayer calms and purifies our heart and makes it more capable of receiving the divine gifts that are poured into us spiritually.

God does not hear us because of the ambition of our petitions. He is always ready to give us his light—not visible, but intelligible and spiritual. We, however, are not always ready to receive it, because we are inclined toward other things and held fast by desire for temporal matters. In prayer, therefore, the heart turns toward him who is always ready to give, provided that we receive what he gives. In this turning, the inner eye is purified, as the things desired temporally are excluded, so that the vision of the simple heart may bear the simple light that shines divinely **[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and one Corbie manuscript read, “the light of divinity.”]** without any setting or change.

It must not merely bear that light, but also remain in it—not only without distress, but with ineffable joy. In this way the blessed life is truly and sincerely brought to perfection.

## Chapter IV

### 15

Now we must consider what he commanded us to pray for—the one through whom we learn both what to pray for and obtain what we pray for.

“Pray therefore in this way,” he says:

> Our Father who are in heaven,  
> hallowed be your name;  
> your kingdom come;  
> your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth;  
> give us today our daily bread;  
> and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors;  
> and do not bring us into temptation,  
> but deliver us from evil.

Since in every petition goodwill must first be secured from the one to whom we make our petition, and then what we are asking must be stated, goodwill is ordinarily secured by praising the one to whom the prayer is directed; this is ordinarily placed at the beginning of the prayer. In this instance our Lord commanded us to say nothing other than, “Our Father who are in heaven.”

Many things have been said in praise of God, which anyone may consider as he reads them, since they are spread variously and extensively throughout all the holy Scriptures. Yet nowhere is the people of Israel found to have been commanded to say, “Our Father,” or to pray to God as Father. Rather, the Lord was presented to them as to servants—that is, to people still living according to the flesh.

I say this with reference to the time when they received the commandments of the Law, which they were ordered to observe. For the Prophets often show that our same Lord could also have been their Father, if they had not strayed from his commandments. Thus there is the passage, “I have begotten and raised children; but they have rejected me” (Isaiah 1:2); and the passage, “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81:6) **[Note: Ten manuscripts read: “and sons of the Highest; but you will die like human beings, and fall like one of the princes.”]**; and the passage, “If I am Lord, where is my fear? And if I am Father, where is my honor?” (Malachi 1:6).

There are many other passages in which the Jews are reproved because, by sinning, they refused to be children. This excludes the passages spoken prophetically about the future Christian people, who were to have God as Father, in accordance with the Gospel saying, “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12). The apostle Paul, however, says, “As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave,” and he recalls that we have received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15–23; Galatians 4:1–6).

### 16

Since our being called to an eternal inheritance, so that we may be fellow heirs with Christ and enter into the adoption of children, is not the result of our merits but of God’s grace, we place this same grace at the beginning of our prayer when we say, “Our Father.”

This name also awakens love: for what should be dearer to children than their father? It also awakens a submissive affection when human beings say to God, “Our Father,” as well as a certain confidence in obtaining what we are about to ask. Before we asked for anything, we received so great a gift that we were permitted to say to God, “Our Father.” For what will he not now give to children who ask, when he has already given them the very thing that makes them children?

Finally, how deeply this should touch the mind: whoever says, “Our Father” must take care not to be unworthy of so great a Father. If some commoner were permitted to call an elderly senator his father, he would undoubtedly tremble and scarcely dare to do so, considering the lowliness of his birth, his lack of resources, and the degraded status of a common person. How much more, then, must one tremble to address God as Father if one’s conduct is so stained and so filthy that God would have far greater reason to expel such a person from his fellowship than that senator would have to reject the poverty of any beggar?

The senator despises in the beggar something to which he too could be reduced by the fragility of human affairs; but God never falls into sordid conduct. Thanks, therefore, to his mercy, for he requires of us that he be our Father—a relationship that can be obtained at no expense, but solely through a good will.

Here too the rich, or those noble according to worldly standards, are admonished not to grow proud against the poor and the lowly when they have become Christians, since they say together to God, “Our Father.” They cannot say this truly and devoutly unless they recognize that they are brothers.

## Chapter V

### 17

Let the new people, therefore, using the voice of the New Testament and called to an eternal inheritance, say, “Our Father who are in heaven”—that is, in the holy and righteous.

God is not contained by spatial dimensions. The heavens are indeed the excellent bodies of the universe, but they are nevertheless bodies, and bodies can exist only in a place. Yet if God’s place is believed to be in heaven, as in the higher regions of the universe, then the birds, whose life is closer to God, would have better merit.

It is not written, “The Lord is near to lofty people,” or to those who live on mountains. Rather, it is written, “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 33:19), which refers more properly to humility.

But just as the sinner was called “earth” when it was said to him, “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Genesis 3:19), so, conversely, the righteous may be called “heaven.” For it is said to the righteous, “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17). Therefore, if God dwells in his temple and the saints are his temple, it is rightly said of him, “who are in heaven”—that is, “who are in the holy.”

This comparison is most appropriate, so that the spiritual difference between the righteous and sinners may be understood as corresponding to the bodily difference between heaven and earth.

### 18

For the sake of signifying this, when we stand for prayer we turn toward the east, from which the heavens arise—not as though God dwelled there and had abandoned the other parts of the universe **[Note: Erasmus, the Lyons edition, and the Venetian edition read, “not as though God were there and had abandoned the other parts of the universe.” M.]**—for he is present everywhere, not by the distances of places but by the power of his majesty **[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “by the majesty of his power.”]**.

Rather, this is done so that the mind may be reminded to turn toward a more excellent nature, that is, toward God, when the body itself—which is earthly—is turned toward the more excellent body, that is, toward the heavenly body.

This also accords with the stages of religion and is greatly beneficial, so that people of every understanding, both children and adults, may form a proper conception of God. Therefore, those who are still devoted to visible beauties and cannot think of anything incorporeal—since they necessarily prefer heaven to earth—hold a more tolerable opinion if they believe that the God whom they still conceive bodily is in heaven rather than on earth.

Then, when they eventually learn that the dignity of the soul surpasses even a heavenly body, they will seek him more in the soul than even in a heavenly body. And when they learn how great the difference is between the souls of sinners and those of the righteous, just as, while they still thought carnally, they did not dare to place him on earth but placed him in heaven, so afterward, with better faith or understanding, they will seek him more in the souls of the righteous than in those of sinners.

Thus it is rightly understood that the words, “Our Father who are in heaven,” are spoken of the hearts of the righteous, as in his holy temple. At the same time, the person who prays should desire that the one whom he invokes should also dwell within him; and when he desires this, he should hold fast to righteousness. By this gift God is invited to inhabit the mind.

### 19

Now let us see what should be requested. We have been told who is being addressed and where he dwells.

The first of all the things requested is this: “Hallowed be your name.” This is not requested as though God’s name were not holy, but so that it may be regarded as holy by human beings. That is, God should become known to them in such a way that they do not consider anything holier, and fear offending nothing more than him.

For when it is said, “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75:1), this should not be understood as though God were lesser in one place and greater in another. His name is great wherever he is named according to the greatness of his majesty. His name is holy wherever it is uttered with reverence and fear of offending him.

This is what is now taking place, while the Gospel is still becoming known among diverse nations and commending the name of the one God through the ministry of his Son.

## Chapter VI

### 20

Next comes, “Your kingdom come.” As the Lord himself teaches in the Gospel, the day of judgment will come when the Gospel has been preached among all nations (Matthew 24:14). This pertains to the sanctification of God’s name.

The words, “Your kingdom come,” do not mean that God is not reigning now. Someone might perhaps say that “come” means “come upon the earth.” But surely he is already reigning upon the earth and has always reigned upon it from the foundation of the world.

“Come,” therefore, should be understood as “be manifested to human beings.” For just as present light is absent to the blind and to those who close their eyes, so God’s kingdom, although it never departs from the earth, is nevertheless absent to those who do not know it.

No one, however, will be permitted to remain ignorant of God’s kingdom when his Only-Begotten has come from heaven—not only intelligibly but also visibly, in the Lord’s human nature—to judge the living and the dead **[Note: Retractations I.19.8.]**.

After that judgment—that is, when the righteous have been distinguished and separated from the unrighteous—God will inhabit the righteous in such a way that no one will need to be taught through a human being. Rather, all will be, as it is written, “taught by God” (Isaiah 54:13; John 6:45).

Then the blessed life will be perfected in every respect in the saints forever, just as the heavenly angels are now most holy and most blessed, wise and blessed solely because God illumines them. The Lord also promised this to his own: “In the resurrection,” he says, “they will be like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30).

### 21

Therefore, after the petition in which we say, “Your kingdom come,” there follows, “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth.”

That is: as your will is done in the angels who are in heaven, so that they cling to you in every way and enjoy you, with no error clouding their wisdom and no misery hindering their blessedness, so may it be done in your saints who are on earth and have been made from earth with respect to the body, although they are to be taken from earth into a heavenly dwelling and transformation.

This is also indicated by the angels’ proclamation: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). When our good will has gone before—the will that follows the one who calls us—God’s will is perfected in us as it is in the heavenly angels, so that no adversity resists our blessedness, which is peace.

Likewise, “Your will be done” is rightly understood as, “Let your commandments be obeyed”; and “as in heaven so also on earth” means, “by angels, and so also by human beings.” For the Lord himself says that God’s will is done when his commandments are obeyed, when he says, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34), and often, “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). He also says, “Behold my mother, and behold my brothers; whoever does the will of God is my brother, and sister, and mother” (Matthew 12:49–50).

Those who do God’s will therefore have God’s will done in them—not because they cause God to will, but because they do what he wills, that is, they act according to his will.

### 22

There is also this interpretation: “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth” means, “as in the holy and righteous, so also in sinners.”

This too may be understood in two ways. It may mean that we should also pray for our enemies—for what else are they to be regarded as, against whose will the Christian and Catholic name increases? In that case the words would mean: “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth,” as though it said, “Let sinners do your will as the righteous do, so that they may be converted to you.”

Or they may mean: “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth,” so that each person may receive what is his due. This will occur at the final judgment, when a reward is given to the righteous and condemnation to sinners, as the sheep are separated from the goats (Matthew 25:33–46).

### 23

There is also an interpretation that is not absurd but highly consonant with our faith and hope: heaven and earth may be understood as spirit and flesh.

Since the Apostle says, “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7:25), we see God’s will being done in the mind, that is, in the spirit. But when death has been swallowed up in victory and this mortal body has put on immortality—which will occur through the resurrection of the flesh and the transformation promised to the righteous, according to the preaching of the same Apostle (1 Corinthians 15:42, 55)—then God’s will will be done on earth as in heaven.

That is, just as the spirit does not resist God but follows and does his will, so the body also will not resist the spirit or soul, which is now troubled by the body’s weakness and inclined toward carnal habit. This will be the fullness of peace in eternal life: not merely will willing be possible for us, but also the accomplishment of the good.

“For to will,” he says, “lies close at hand for me; but to accomplish the good does not” (Romans 7:18). For God’s will has not yet been done on earth as in heaven—that is, not yet in the flesh as in the spirit.

God’s will is also done amid our misery, when through the flesh we suffer what is owed to us by the law of mortality, which our nature earned by sinning. But we must pray that, as it is done in heaven, so it may also be done on earth: that is, just as according to the inner person we delight together with the law (Romans 7:22), so, when the body has been transformed, no part of us may oppose this delight through earthly pains or pleasures.

### 24

Nor is it contrary to the truth to understand, “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth,” as meaning, “as in our Lord Jesus Christ, so also in the Church”—as in the man who fulfilled the Father’s will, so also in the woman who was betrothed to him.

For heaven and earth may appropriately be understood as man and woman, since the earth becomes fruitful when fertilized by heaven.

## Chapter VII

### 25

The fourth petition is: “Give us today our daily bread.” “Daily bread” may mean all the things that sustain the necessities of this life, concerning which, when giving his instruction, he said, “Do not be anxious about tomorrow”; and this is why “today” has been added. Or it may mean the sacrament of Christ’s body, which we receive daily. Or it may mean the spiritual food of which the same Lord says, “Work for the food that does not perish,” and, “I am the bread of life, who came down from heaven” (John 6:17, 41).

Which of these three is more probable may be considered. For someone may perhaps wonder why we pray to obtain things necessary to this life, such as food and clothing, when the Lord himself says, “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat or what you shall wear.” Can a person fail to be anxious about a thing for whose attainment he directs prayer to God with such earnestness? For prayer must be directed with such intensity of mind that everything said about shutting the rooms is referred to this end, as is also what he says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” He certainly did not say, “Seek first the kingdom of God, and then seek these things”; rather, “All these things,” he says, “will be added to you”—that is, even though you do not seek them. But how one can rightly be said not to seek what one most earnestly entreats God to receive, I do not know whether it can be found.

### 26

With regard to the sacrament of the Lord’s body, let those who, especially in eastern regions, do not receive communion at the Lord’s Supper daily not raise a question because this bread is called daily. Let them therefore be silent, and not defend their own opinion even by ecclesiastical authority **[Note: At this point the Louvain edition adds, “let them be content,” which is absent from the other printed codices and the manuscripts.]**. For they do this without scandal; they are not forbidden to do so by those who preside over the churches, nor are they condemned as disobedient. Thus it is proved that daily bread is not understood in that sense in those regions; for those who do not receive it every day would be charged with the crime of a great sin.

But, as stated, let us argue nothing one way or the other about these persons. Certainly, those who reflect must observe that we have received from the Lord a rule for prayer, which ought not to be transgressed either by adding anything or by omitting anything. Since this is so, who would dare say that we should say the Lord’s Prayer only once? Or, even if a second or third time, only until the hour when we communicate in the Lord’s body, and that afterward we should not pray thus during the remaining parts of the day? For we could no longer say, “Give us today,” what we have already received; nor could anyone compel us to celebrate that sacrament even in the last part of the day.

### 27

It remains, therefore, that we should understand daily bread as spiritual bread, namely the divine precepts, which ought to be meditated upon and practiced daily. For of these the Lord says, “Work for the food that does not perish.” This food is called daily for as long as this temporal life is conducted through days departing and succeeding one another. And indeed, as long as the affection of the mind alternates now toward higher things and now toward lower—that is, now toward spiritual things and now toward carnal things **[Col. 1281]**—like one who is at one time fed with food and at another suffers hunger, daily bread is necessary, so that the hungry person may be refreshed and the one who has fallen back may be raised up.

Therefore, just as our body in this life, before that transformation, is refreshed by food because it experiences loss, so the mind, because through temporal affections it suffers a kind of loss from its attention to God, should be refreshed by the food of the commandments. “Give us today” is said for as long as “today” is said, that is, in this temporal life. For after this life we shall be filled with spiritual food forever, so that it will not then be called daily bread, because there will be no succession of days—the movement of time by which one day follows another—from which it might be called daily. But just as it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice” (Psalm 94:8), which the Apostle interprets in the Epistle to the Hebrews as “as long as it is called today” (Hebrews 3:13), so here too we should understand, “Give us today.” If anyone wishes to understand this statement also of the necessary nourishment of the body or of the sacrament of the Lord’s body, all three must be understood together: namely, that we ask at once for daily bread necessary for the body, the sacred visible bread, and the invisible bread of the word of God **[Note: Thus most manuscripts. The printed editions read, “and the visible sacrament and the invisible bread of the word of God.”]**.

## Chapter VIII

### 28

The fifth petition follows: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” That debts mean sins is clear, either from the saying of the same Lord, “You shall not depart from there until you pay the last farthing” (Matthew 5:26), or from the passage in which he called debtors those reported to him as killed in the collapse of a tower, or those whose blood Herod mingled with sacrifices. For he said that people thought they were debtors beyond measure—that is, sinners—and added: “Amen I say to you, unless you repent, you will likewise perish” (Luke 13:1–5).

Here, then, no one is being required to forgive monetary debtors, but whatever another has sinned against him. We are commanded to forgive money rather by the precept stated above: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and contend with you in court, let him have your cloak also” (Matthew 5:40). Nor is it necessary there to forgive every monetary debtor his debt, but the one who refuses to repay, even to the point of wishing to litigate. “But the servant of the Lord,” as the Apostle says, “must not quarrel” (2 Timothy 2:24). Therefore, one who, whether voluntarily or after being summoned, refuses to repay money owed must be forgiven it.

For he will refuse to repay for one of two reasons: either because he has nothing, or because he is greedy and covets another’s property. Both concern poverty: the former is poverty of means, the latter poverty of mind. Whoever therefore forgives such a person a debt forgives one in need and performs a Christian work, while retaining this rule: he must be ready in his mind to lose what is owed to him. For if he acts in every way moderately and gently to have it restored to him, not so much intent on the gain of money as on correcting the person—for it is undoubtedly harmful to that person to have the means to repay and not repay—not only will he not sin, but he will also be of great benefit, lest, in wishing to make another’s money a gain **[Col. 1282]**, that person suffer the loss of faith, which is so much more serious that there is no comparison.

From this it is understood that even in this fifth petition, in which we say, “Forgive us our debts,” the reference is not indeed to money, but to everything by which anyone sins against us, and thereby also to money. For one who refuses to repay you money owed, when he has the means to repay, sins against you. If you do not forgive that sin, you cannot say, “Forgive us, as we also forgive.” But if you forgive it, you see that the person commanded to pray with this prayer is also admonished to forgive money.

### 29

It may indeed be considered that, since we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,” we are then convicted of having acted contrary to this rule if we do not forgive those who ask pardon, because we wish to be forgiven by the most gracious Father when we ask pardon. But by the other precept, by which we are commanded to pray for our enemies (Matthew 5:44), we are not commanded to pray only for those who ask pardon. For those who are such are no longer enemies. Yet no one can truly say that he prays for one whom he has not forgiven. Therefore it must be acknowledged that all sins committed against us must be forgiven, if we wish the sins we commit to be forgiven us by the Father. For, I think, enough has been said above about vengeance (above, Book I, chapters 19 and 20).

## Chapter IX

### 30

The sixth petition is: “And do not bring us into temptation.” Some manuscripts have “lead us,” which I think has the same force; for both have been translated from the one Greek expression, εἰσενέγκῃς, “bring in” or “lead in.” Many people pray in this way: “Do not allow us to be led into temptation,” thereby explaining how “lead us” is said. For God does not himself lead anyone in, but permits one to be led in when he has withdrawn his aid, in an order most hidden and according to merits. He also often judges, for manifest reasons, that the person whom he abandons is worthy to be permitted to be led into temptation.

But it is one thing to be led into temptation and another to be tempted. For no one can be proved without temptation, whether to himself, as it is written, “One who has not been tempted, what does he know?” (Ecclesiasticus 34:9, 11), or to others, as the Apostle says: “You did not despise my temptation in my flesh” (Galatians 4:13–14). From this he himself knew them to be steadfast: they had not been turned from love by the tribulations which had happened to the Apostle according to the flesh. But we are known to God even before all temptations, since he knows all things before they occur.

### 31

Therefore, what is written, “The Lord your God tempts you, that he may know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13:3), is expressed in that manner in which “that he may know” stands for “that he may make you know,” just as we call a day cheerful because it makes people cheerful, cold sluggish because it makes people sluggish, and in countless similar expressions found in ordinary speech, in the discourse of teachers, or in the holy Scriptures.

The heretics who oppose the Old Testament do not understand this, and think that he of whom it is said, “The Lord your God tempts you,” should be charged with the fault of ignorance—as though it were not written in the Gospel concerning the Lord: “But he said this, testing him; for he himself knew what he was about to do” (John 6:6). For if he knew the heart of the one whom he was testing, what was it that he wished to see by testing him? Certainly this was done so that the one being tested might become known to himself and condemn his own despair, after the crowds had been filled with the Lord’s bread, when he had thought that they had nothing to eat.

### 32

Therefore we do not pray here that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be brought into temptation: as if someone who must necessarily be tested by fire were to pray, not that he not be touched by fire, but that he not be burned up. For “the furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus 27:6). Thus Joseph was tempted by the enticement of adultery, but was not brought into temptation (Genesis 39:7–12); Susanna was tempted, and she too was neither led nor brought into temptation (Daniel 13:19–24); and so were many others of both sexes—but Job above all.

When those heretical enemies of the Old Testament have wished to ridicule with sacrilegious mouth his admirable steadfastness in God his Lord, they press above all the point that Satan asked that he be tempted (Job 1:11). They ask people incapable of understanding such matters how Satan could have spoken with God, without considering—for they cannot, blinded as they are by superstition and contentiousness—that God does not occupy a spatial area by bodily mass, so as to be in one place and not another, or to have one part here and another elsewhere; rather, he is present everywhere by his majesty, not divided into parts but perfect everywhere.

But if they regard carnally what is said, “Heaven is my throne and earth the footstool of my feet” (Isaiah 66:1)—to which the Lord also bears witness when he says, “Do not swear, either by heaven, because it is God’s throne, or by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet” (Matthew 5:34–35)—what wonder is it if the devil, stationed on earth, stood before God’s feet and said something before him?

For when are they able to understand that there is no soul, however perverse, which can nevertheless reason in any way, in whose conscience God does not speak? For who wrote the natural law in human hearts but God? Of this law the Apostle says: “For when Gentiles, who do not have the Law, do by nature the things of the Law, these, though not having the Law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or even excusing one another, on the day when the Lord will judge the hidden things of human beings” (Romans 2:14–16).

Therefore, if every rational soul, even though blinded by desire, nonetheless, when it thinks and reasons, owes whatever is true in that reasoning not to itself but to the light of truth itself, by which it is however faintly illumined according to its capacity so that it perceives something true in reasoning, what wonder is it if the devil’s soul, perverted by wicked desire, is reported to have heard in God’s voice—that is, in the voice of truth itself—whatever true thing it thought concerning the righteous man when it wished to tempt him? Whatever is false, however, is attributed to that desire from which it received the name devil.

Moreover, God has often spoken through bodily and visible creation **[Col. 1284]**, whether to good persons or bad, as Lord and ruler of all and as the one who orders things according to each thing’s merits: for example, through angels who also appeared to human sight, and through prophets saying, “Thus says the Lord.” What wonder, then, if God is said to have spoken with the devil, even if not in the thought itself, at least through some creature suited to such a work?

### 33

Let them not think it a matter of dignity, and as if a merit of righteousness, that God spoke with him. For he spoke with an angelic soul, although foolish and desirous, just as if he spoke with a human soul foolish and desirous. Or let them say how he spoke with that rich man whose most foolish desire he wished to rebuke, saying: “Fool, this night your soul is demanded of you; whose will be the things you have prepared?” (Luke 12:20). Certainly the Lord himself says this in the Gospel, to which those heretics, willing or unwilling, bow their necks.

But if they are troubled because Satan asked God that the righteous man be tempted, I do not explain why it happened; rather, I compel them to explain why the Lord himself said in the Gospel to his disciples, “Behold, Satan has asked to sift you like wheat,” and said to Peter, “But I have prayed that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). When they explain this to me, they simultaneously explain to themselves what they ask of me. But if they cannot explain it, let them not dare rashly to blame in some book what they read in the Gospel without offense **[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “what they do not understand without offense.”]**.

### 34

Temptations, then, occur through Satan, not by his power but by the Lord’s permission, either to punish people for their sins or, through the Lord’s mercy, to prove and exercise them. And it makes a great difference into what sort of temptation one falls. Judas, who sold the Lord, did not fall into the sort into which Peter fell when, terrified, he denied the Lord.

There are also, I believe, human temptations: when someone with a good intention nevertheless, through human frailty, goes wrong in some plan, or is irritated with a brother out of zeal to correct him, yet somewhat more than Christian tranquillity demands. Of these the Apostle says: “Let no temptation overtake you except a human one”; and he also says: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but will make with the temptation also the outcome, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13). In this statement he sufficiently shows that we should pray not that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be led into temptation. For we are led in if temptations occur which we cannot bear. But since dangerous temptations, into which it is harmful to be brought and led, arise either from favorable temporal circumstances or adverse ones, no one is broken by the distress of adversity who is not captivated by the pleasure of prosperity.

### 35

The final and seventh petition is, “But deliver us from evil.” For we must pray not only that we may not be led into evil, from which we are free and for which the sixth petition is made, but also that we may be delivered from that evil into which we have already been led. When this has happened, nothing fearful will remain, nor will any temptation be feared at all. Yet, so long as in this life we carry about this mortality into which we were led by the serpent’s persuasion, we must not hope that this can happen; nevertheless, we must hope that it will happen at some time. This is the hope that is not seen, concerning which the Apostle said, “But hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. VIII, 24). Yet the wisdom granted even in this life to God’s faithful servants must not be despaired of. It consists in this: whatever, by the Lord’s revelation, we have understood must be avoided, let us avoid with the utmost vigilant care; and whatever, by the Lord’s revelation, we have understood must be desired, let us desire with the most fervent love. Thus, when the remaining burden of this mortality has been laid down in death itself, the blessedness begun in this life—and toward attaining and possessing which all our effort is now directed—will at the proper time be perfected in every part of the human being.

### Chapter X

### 36

The distinction among these seven petitions must be considered and commended. Since our life is now conducted temporally, while eternal life is hoped for, and since eternal things have priority in dignity, although one passes to them after first living through temporal things, the answers to the first three petitions, although they begin in this life—which is lived in this present age—for the sanctification of God’s name began with the Lord’s own advent in humility; and the coming of his kingdom, in which he will come in glory, will be manifested not after the age has ended but at the end of the age; and the perfection of his will, “as in heaven and on earth”—whether by heaven and earth you understand the righteous and sinners, or spirit and flesh, or the Lord and the Church, or all these together—will be completed in the perfection of our blessedness and therefore at the end of the age, nevertheless all three will remain forever.

For the sanctification of God’s name will be everlasting, his kingdom has no end, and eternal life is promised to our perfected blessedness. These three, therefore, will remain consummated and increased in that life which is promised to us.

### 37

The remaining four things for which we ask seem to me to belong to this temporal life. The first of them is, “Give us this day our daily bread.” By the very fact that the bread is called daily—whether spiritual bread is meant, or bread in the sacrament, or visible bread as food—it belongs to the time indicated by the word “today.” This is not because spiritual food is not eternal, but because what is called daily in Scripture, whether amid the sound of speech or through whatever temporal signs it is presented to the soul, will then no longer exist, when all will be “taught by God” (Isa. LIV, 13; John VI, 45), and we will drink in the ineffable light of truth itself, signifying it not through the movement of bodies but through purity of mind.

Perhaps it is also for this reason that it is called bread, not drink: bread is changed into nourishment by being broken and chewed, just as the Scriptures feed the soul by being opened and expounded; but drink, already prepared as it is, passes into the body. Thus, for the present, truth is bread when it is called daily bread; but then it will be drink, when there is no need for the labor of disputing and speaking—of breaking and chewing, as it were—but only for the drinking in of pure and lucid truth.

Now our sins are forgiven, and now we forgive; this is the second of the remaining four petitions. Then there will be no forgiveness of sins, because there will be no sins. Temptations afflict this temporal life, but they will not exist when what was said has been perfected: “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your presence” (Ps. XXX, 21). The evil from which we desire to be delivered, and deliverance itself from evil, likewise belong to this life: a life which, by God’s justice, we have deserved as mortal, and from which by his mercy we are delivered.

### Chapter XI

### 38

It also seems to me that this number seven of the petitions corresponds to that sevenfold number from which the whole sermon proceeded. If the fear of God is that by which the poor in spirit are blessed, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven, let us ask that God’s name be sanctified among human beings, with pure fear remaining throughout the ages of ages (Ps. XVIII, 10).

If piety is that by which the meek are blessed, because they will possess the earth by inheritance, let us ask that his kingdom come—either into ourselves, so that we may become meek and not resist him, or from heaven upon the earth in the glory of the Lord’s advent, in which we will rejoice and be praised [Note: [Col. 1286] The editions of Mar. and Lov. read *laudabimus*, “we will praise.” Am. and Er. read *laetabimur*, “we will rejoice.” But the manuscripts read *laudabimur*, “we will be praised.”], when he says, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34). “In the Lord,” says the prophet, “my soul will be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. XXXIII, 2).

If knowledge is that by which those who mourn are blessed, because they will be comforted, let us pray that his will may be done “as in heaven and on earth.” For when the body, like earth, has consented in complete and perfect peace to the spirit, like heaven, we will not mourn. There is no other mourning of this present time except when these contend against one another and force us to say, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind,” and to testify to our grief in tearful speech: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII, 23–24).

If fortitude is that by which those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed, because they will be filled, let us pray that our daily bread may be given to us today, so that, strengthened and sustained by it, we may be able to come to that fullest satisfaction.

If counsel is that by which the merciful are blessed, because they will receive mercy, let us forgive our debtors their debts and pray that ours may be forgiven.

If understanding is that by which the pure in heart are blessed, because they will see God, let us pray not to be led into temptation, lest we have a divided heart by failing to desire the one simple good to which we may refer all that we do, and instead pursuing temporal and earthly things at the same time [Note: [Col. 1286] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “temporal and eternal things.”].

For temptations arising from things that seem grave and calamitous to human beings have no power over us if those arising through the allurements of things that people consider good and joyful have no power over us.

If wisdom is that by which the peacemakers are blessed, because they will be called sons of God (Matt. V, 3–9), let us pray that we may be delivered from evil. For this deliverance itself will make us free—that is, sons of God—so that by the Spirit of adoption we may cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII, 15; Gal. IV, 6).

### 39

It must certainly not be passed over carelessly that, among all the statements in which the Lord commanded us to pray, he judged that one especially should be commended which concerns the forgiveness of sins. In it he wanted us to be merciful, which is the one counsel for escaping misery.

In no other statement do we pray in such a way as though we were making a pact with God. For we say, “Forgive us just as we also forgive.” If we lie in this pact, the whole prayer has no fruit. For he says:

“If you forgive people their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins.”

### Chapter XII

### 40

The command concerning fasting follows, and it pertains to the same purification of the heart that is now under discussion. In this practice too we must beware lest some display and desire for human praise creep in—something that divides the heart and prevents it from being pure and single-minded for understanding God.

“But when you fast,” he says, “do not become like the hypocrites, sorrowful; for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

It is clear from these commands that all our intention is directed toward inward joys, lest by seeking our reward outwardly we be conformed to this age and lose the promise of a blessedness all the more solid and secure because it is inward, by which God chose us to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. VIII, 29).

### 41

In this chapter it must be observed above all that vanity can exist not only in the splendor and display of bodily things, but also in the very filth and mournful squalor of appearance; and it is more dangerous when it deceives under the name of service to God.

Therefore, someone who shines through excessive bodily adornment and dress, or through the splendor of other things, is easily convicted by the things themselves of being a pursuer of the world’s display, and no one is deceived by his deceptive appearance of holiness.

But someone who, in professing Christianity, draws people’s eyes to himself through unusual squalor and filth—when he does this by choice and does not suffer it from necessity—may be judged from his other actions as to whether he does this out of contempt for excessive adornment or from some ambition. For the Lord also commanded that wolves be guarded against beneath sheep’s clothing; but, he says, “You will know them by their fruits.”

When certain things are taken away from such people or denied to them—things they have either obtained through this covering or desire to obtain—it must then become clear whether there is a wolf in sheep’s clothing or a sheep in its own.

A Christian ought not therefore to charm people’s eyes with excessive adornment merely because hypocrites also frequently adopt a modest and necessary appearance in order to deceive the unwary. Nor should those sheep put aside their own skins if wolves sometimes cover themselves with them.

### 42

The question is therefore often asked what he meant when he said, “But when you fast, anoint your heads and wash your faces, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting.” No one would rightly command that, although we wash our faces as part of our daily custom, we should also have our heads anointed when we fast. If everyone admits that this would be disgraceful, the command to anoint the head and wash the face must be understood as referring to the inner person.

To anoint the head therefore pertains to joy, while to wash the face pertains to cleansing. Thus the one who rejoices inwardly in mind and reason anoints the head. We rightly understand “head” here as that which is preeminent in the soul and by which the other elements of the human being are plainly ruled and governed. This is what the person does who does not seek joy outwardly in order to rejoice carnally in human praise.

The flesh, which ought to be subject, cannot in any way be the head of the whole human nature. “No one has ever hated his own flesh,” as the Apostle says when he commands love for one’s wife (Eph. V, 25–33); but “the head of the woman is the man,” and the head of the man is Christ (I Cor. XI, 3).

Let him therefore rejoice inwardly in his fasting, by the very fact that in fasting he turns away from the pleasure of the world so as to be subject to Christ; this is the person who, according to this command, desires to have an anointed head.

In this way he will also wash his face—that is, cleanse his heart—with which he will see God, without a veil interposed because of the weakness contracted through filth, but firm and stable because it is pure and single-minded.

“Wash yourselves,” he says, “be clean; remove wickedness from your souls and from before my eyes” (Isa. I, 16). Our face must therefore be washed of those impurities by which God’s gaze is offended. For “with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, we will be transformed into the same image” (II Cor. III, 18).

### 43

The thought of things necessary for this life also frequently wounds and defiles our inward eye, and often divides the heart, so that when we seem to act rightly with other people, we do not do so with the heart that the Lord commands—that is, not because we love them, but because we want to obtain some advantage from them on account of the necessity of the present life.

We ought to do good to them for the sake of their eternal salvation, not for the sake of our temporal advantage. “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to gain” (Ps. CXVIII, 36). For “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I, 5).

But whoever assists a brother because of his own necessity in this life does not assist him out of love. He is looking after not the one whom he ought to love as himself, but himself; or rather, he is not even looking after himself, since by this he creates for himself a divided heart, which prevents him from seeing God. In that vision alone blessedness is certain and perpetual.

### Chapter XIII

### 44

It rightly follows that the one who is intent on cleansing our heart commands us:

“Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and consuming destroy [Note: [Col. 1288] This is how the manuscripts and Mar. read, as does Cyprian in Book 3 of *To Quirinus*. Am., Er., and Lov. read, “where rust and moth destroy,” and what follows, omitting, as they usually do, the remaining words of Scripture [Col. 1289], which throughout this work we restore from the manuscripts with great care], and where thieves dig through and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor consuming destroy, and where thieves do not dig through or steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will also be.”

Therefore, if the heart is on earth—that is, if someone acts with that heart in order to obtain an earthly advantage—how will what rolls about on earth be pure? But if it is in heaven, it will be pure, because whatever is heavenly is pure.

Something becomes dirty when it is mixed with an inferior nature, even though it is not dirty in its own kind. Pure silver, for instance, soils gold if it is mixed with it. Thus our mind is soiled by desire for earthly things, even though the earth itself is pure in its own kind and order.

We must not understand “heaven” in this passage as something bodily, because every body is to be regarded as earth. Whoever stores up treasure in heaven must despise the whole world. We must therefore establish and place our treasure and our heart in that heaven of which it is said, “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord” (Ps. CXIII, 16)—that is, in the spiritual firmament—not in what will pass away, but in what always remains. “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. XXIV, 35).

### 45

He shows here also that he gives all these commands concerning the cleansing of the heart when he says:

“The lamp of your body is your eye. Therefore, if your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark. Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?”

This passage must be understood so that we recognize that all our actions are then pure and pleasing in God’s sight if they are done with a single heart—that is, with an intention directed above, toward that end which is love, since “love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. XIII, 10).

We must therefore understand “eye” here as the very intention with which we do whatever we do. If it is pure and upright, and looks toward what ought to be looked toward, all our actions performed according to it must necessarily be good.

He called all these actions “the whole body,” because the Apostle also calls our members certain actions that he condemns and commands to be put to death, saying, “Therefore put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, avarice” (Col. III, 5), and other things of this kind.

### 46

It is therefore not what someone does but with what intention he does it that must be considered. This is the light in us, because it is evident to us that we do what we do with a good intention; for “everything that is made manifest is light” (Eph. V, 13).

The actions themselves that proceed from us for the benefit of human society have an uncertain outcome, and therefore he called them darkness. I do not know, when I hand money to someone in need who asks for it, what he will do or suffer as a result. It may happen that he either does something evil with it or suffers some evil because of it—something I did not want to happen when I gave it, and with that intention I did not give it.

Thus, if I acted with a good intention in doing what was known to me when I did it, and for that reason it is called light, my action is illuminated, whatever its outcome may have been. Since the outcome is uncertain and unknown, it has been called darkness.

But if I acted with a bad intention, even the light itself is darkness. It is called light because everyone knows with what intention he acts, even when he acts with a bad intention. But that light itself is darkness because the single intention is not directed upward; it is turned toward lower things and, as though with a divided heart, casts a shadow.

Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be? That is: if the very intention of the heart with which you do what you do—and which is known to you—is soiled and blinded by desire for earthly and temporal things, how much more so is the action itself, whose outcome is uncertain, dirty and dark?

Even if what you do without an upright and pure intention turns out well for someone else, how you did it is charged to you, not how it turned out for him.

### Chapter XIV

### 47

What follows—“No one can serve two masters”—must be referred to this same intention. He explains it immediately, saying:

“For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will endure the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon.”

These words must be carefully considered. He next shows who the two masters are when he says, “You cannot serve God and Mammon.”

Among the Hebrews, *mammon* is said to mean riches. The Punic name corresponds to this, for profit is called *mammon* in Punic. But whoever serves Mammon serves the one who, having been placed over these earthly things on account of his perversity, is called by the Lord the ruler of this age (John XII, 31; XIV, 30).

A person will therefore either hate this one and love the other—that is, God—or endure the one and despise the other. Whoever serves Mammon endures a harsh and destructive master. Entangled in his own desire, he is subjected to the devil. He does not love him—for who is there who loves the devil?—but he nevertheless endures him, just as in some great household a man who is joined to another man’s female slave, because of his own desire, endures harsh slavery even if he does not love the one whose slave he loves.

### 48

He said, “He will despise the other,” not, “He will hate him.” For scarcely anyone’s conscience can hate God [Note: [Col. 1290] *Retractations*, chapter 19, no. 8]. But he despises him—that is, he does not fear him, as though he were confident of his goodness.

The Holy Spirit recalls us from this negligence and destructive security when he says through the Prophet, “Son, do not add sin upon sin and say, ‘The mercy of God is great’” (Ecclus. V, 5–6); and, “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. II, 4).

For whose mercy can be remembered as being so great as that of the one who forgives all sins to those who turn, and makes the wild olive share in the richness of the olive tree? And whose severity is so great as that of the one who did not spare the natural branches, but broke them off because of unbelief (ibid. XI, 17–24)?

But whoever wishes to love God and take care not to offend him must not suppose that he can serve two masters. Let him free the intention of his heart from all duplicity. For then he will think of the Lord in goodness and seek him with a simple heart (Wis. I, 1).

### Chapter XV

### 49

“Therefore,” he says, “I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear.”

This is lest, even though superfluous things are no longer sought, the heart be divided on account of necessities themselves, and our intention be twisted toward obtaining them when we perform some action that appears merciful. That is, when we wish to seem to assist someone, we may instead pay attention to our own advantage there rather than to his benefit. For this reason we may not think that we are sinning, since what we want to obtain is not superfluous but necessary.

The Lord warns us to remember that God has given us much more by making and composing us from soul and body than he has given us in food and clothing—the care of which he does not want to divide our heart.

“Is not the soul,” he says, “more than food?” This is so that you may understand that the one who gave the soul will much more easily give food. And the body is more than clothing—that is, it is worth more—so that you may similarly understand that the one who gave the body will much more easily give clothing.

### 50

At this point it is commonly asked whether this food belongs to the soul, since the soul is incorporeal while this food is bodily. But we must understand that “soul” here is used for this present life, whose support is this bodily food.

In this sense the statement was also made, “Whoever loves his soul will lose it” (John XII, 25). Unless we understand this as referring to the present life—which must be lost for the kingdom of God, as the martyrs clearly were able to do—this command will contradict the statement:

“What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI, 26).

### 51

“Look,” he says, “at the birds of heaven, because they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns; and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they?” That is, are you not of greater value?

For surely a rational animal, such as a human being, has been assigned a higher place in the order of nature than irrational creatures, such as birds.

“Which of you,” he says, “by being anxious can add one cubit to his stature?” And concerning clothing, why are you anxious? The one by whose power and dominion it has come about that your body was brought to this stature can also clothe it by his providence.

That it was not by your own care that your body came to this stature can be understood from the fact that, even if you care and wish to add one cubit to this stature, you cannot. Leave the care of clothing your body, therefore, to the one whose care you see has brought it about that you possess a body of such stature.

### 52

A lesson concerning clothing also had to be given, just as one was given concerning food. Accordingly he continues:

“Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They do not labor or spin. But I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. If, then, God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith?”

These examples, however, are not to be examined as allegories, so that we ask what the birds of heaven or the lilies of the field signify. They have been set forth so that greater things might be commended through lesser ones.

The same applies to the example of the judge who neither feared God nor respected human beings, yet yielded to a widow who repeatedly appealed to him and considered her case—not out of piety or humanity, but to avoid being wearied.

That unjust judge in no way allegorically represents God. Nevertheless, the Lord wanted it to be inferred from this how much God, who is good and just, cares for those who entreat him: even an unjust human being cannot despise those who batter him with continual prayers, if only to avoid their persistence (Luke XVIII, 2–8).

### Chapter XVI

### 53

“Therefore,” he says, “do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the Gentiles seek all these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be supplied to you.”

Here he shows most clearly that these things are not to be sought as though they were our goods in such a way that we ought to do good for their sake if we do anything good; nevertheless, they are necessary.

He made clear the difference between the good that ought to be sought and the necessity that must be received when he said, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be supplied to you.”

The kingdom and righteousness of God are therefore our good. This is what must be desired, and in it the goal must be established, for its sake we must do whatever we do.

But because we are engaged in this life so that we may be able to reach that kingdom, and because this life cannot be lived without these necessities, he says, “These things will be supplied to you, but seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.”

When he said “first,” he indicated that the latter must be sought afterward—not in time, but in rank: the one as our good, the other as our necessity; and the necessity for the sake of that good.

### 54

We should not, for example, evangelize in order to eat, but eat in order to evangelize. For if we evangelize for the sake of eating, we value the Gospel less than food; our good will then lie in eating, and evangelizing will be our necessity.

The Apostle also forbids this when he says that it is lawful for him, and permitted by the Lord, that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel—that is, should receive from the Gospel the things necessary for this life—yet that he himself had not used this power.

There were many who wanted an opportunity to acquire and sell the Gospel. Wishing to cut off this opportunity from them, the Apostle supported himself by the work of his own hands (Acts XX, 34). Concerning them he says elsewhere, “So that I may cut off the opportunity from those who seek an opportunity” (II Cor. XI, 12).

Even if he had lived from the Gospel, by the Lord’s permission, as the other good apostles did, he would not for that reason have established the goal of evangelizing in that livelihood. Rather, he would have placed the goal of that livelihood in the Gospel itself. That is, as I said above, he would not evangelize in order to reach food and whatever other necessities there are, but would take these things in order to fulfill the Gospel, so that he might evangelize not unwillingly but by choice.

For he rejects this when he says:

“Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat the things that come from the temple, and that those who serve the altar share with the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. But I have used none of these things.”

From this he shows that it was permitted, not commanded; otherwise he would be held to have acted against the Lord’s command.

Then he continues:

“But I have not written these things so that they should be done in my case. It would be better for me to die than for anyone to make my glory void.”

He said this because he had already decided, on account of certain people seeking an opportunity, to support himself by the work of his own hands.

“For if I evangelize,” he says, “I have no glory”—that is, if I evangelize so that these things may be done for me, if I evangelize for the sake of reaching them and establish the goal of the Gospel in food, drink, and clothing.

But why does he have no glory? “For necessity,” he says, “is laid upon me”—that is, so that I evangelize because I have nothing from which to live, or so that I may acquire temporal profit from preaching eternal things. In this way necessity, not willingness, will be in the Gospel.

“For woe is me,” he says, “if I do not evangelize.” But how ought he to evangelize? Clearly, in such a way that he places his reward in the Gospel itself and in the kingdom of God. In this way he can evangelize not under compulsion but willingly.

“For if I do this willingly,” he says, “I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (I Cor. IX, 13–17). That is, if, compelled by lack of those things necessary for temporal life, I preach the Gospel, others will receive the reward of the Gospel—those who, when I preach the Gospel, love the Gospel itself—but I will not receive it, because I do not love the Gospel itself; rather, I have placed its price in those temporal things.

It is wicked for this to happen: that someone should minister the Gospel not as a son but as a slave entrusted with a stewardship, distributing what belongs to another and receiving nothing from it for himself except rations, which are given from outside not as participation in the kingdom but for the support of wretched servitude.

Yet elsewhere he also calls himself a steward. A slave adopted into the number of sons can indeed faithfully administer to his fellow heirs the thing in which he has earned a share as co-heir.

But here, when he says, “If unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship,” he wished such a steward to be understood as one who administers what belongs to another and receives nothing from it himself.

### 55

Therefore, whatever thing is sought for the sake of something else is without doubt inferior to that for whose sake it is sought. For that other thing is first, on account of which you seek this thing; not this thing, which you seek on account of the other.

Accordingly, if we seek the Gospel and the kingdom of God for the sake of food, we make food primary and the kingdom of God secondary, so that if food is not lacking, we do not seek the kingdom of God. This is to seek food first and the kingdom of God afterward—that is, to place the former first and the latter second.

But if we seek food in order to have the kingdom of God, we do what was said: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be supplied to you.”

### Chapter XVII

### 56

Those who seek first the kingdom and righteousness of God—that is, who place this before other things, so that they seek everything else for its sake—should not be anxious that the things necessary for this life on account of the kingdom of God will be lacking.

For he said above, “Your Father knows that you need all these things.” Therefore, when he had said, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness,” he did not say, “Then seek these things,” although they are necessary. Rather, he said, “All these things will be supplied to you”—that is, they will follow if you seek those things, without any impediment on your part.

This is so that, while seeking these things, you may not be turned away from the other; or so that you may not establish two goals, desiring both the kingdom of God for its own sake and these necessities, but may desire these rather for the sake of that. In this way they will not be lacking to you.

For you cannot serve two masters. The person tries to serve two masters who desires both the kingdom of God as a great good and these temporal things. But he cannot have a single eye and serve the one Lord God unless, whatever other things there are, he takes the necessities for the sake of this one thing—that is, for the sake of the kingdom of God.

Just as all those serving in the military receive provisions and pay, so all those who evangelize receive food and clothing. But not all soldiers serve for the safety of the state; some serve for the sake of what they receive. Similarly, not all who minister to God serve for the salvation of the Church, but for the sake of these temporal things, which they receive as provisions and pay—or for the sake of both this and that.

But it has already been said, “You cannot serve two masters.” Therefore, with a single heart, we must do good to all solely for the sake of the kingdom of God. In this action we must not think either of temporal reward alone or of temporal reward together with the kingdom of God.

He designated all these temporal things by the name “tomorrow” when he said, “Do not think about tomorrow” [Note: [Col. 1294] Nearly all the manuscripts read, “Do not be anxious about tomorrow.”]. The day called tomorrow belongs only to time, in which the future succeeds the past.

Therefore, when we do something good, let us think not of temporal things but of eternal things. Then the work will be good and perfect.

“For tomorrow,” he says, “will be anxious for itself”—that is, when it is necessary, you will take food, drink, or clothing, when the necessity itself has begun to press. These things will be present, because our Father knows that we need all of them.

“Sufficient for the day,” he says, “is its own evil”—that is, it is enough that the necessity itself will compel us to take these things. I think it is called “evil” for this reason: it is punitive for us, for it belongs to the weakness and mortality that we deserved by sinning [Note: [Col. 1294] *Retractations*, chapter 19, no. 9].

Do not therefore add anything more burdensome to this temporal punishment of necessity, so that you not only suffer the lack of these things but also serve God for the sake of satisfying that lack.

57. At this point we must be especially careful lest, when we see a servant of God taking precautions that these necessities should not be lacking, either for himself or for those entrusted to his care, we judge him to be acting contrary to the Lord’s command and to be anxious about tomorrow. For the Lord himself, although angels ministered to him (Matt. 4:11), nevertheless, for the sake of example—so that no one afterward might be scandalized when he noticed one of his servants providing these necessities—deigned to have a purse [Col. 1295] with money [Note: [Col. 1295] Eight manuscripts: “in which the money was carried.”], from which whatever was needed for necessary uses could be supplied. Judas, who betrayed him, was the keeper—and thief—of this purse, as it is written (John 12:6).

Similarly, the apostle Paul may seem to have thought about tomorrow when he said:

> “Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also must do. On the first day of every week, let each of you put something aside at home, storing up whatever he chooses, so that collections may not take place when I come. And when I arrive, I will send those whom you approve by letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it is appropriate that I go also, they will travel with me. I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia—for I shall pass through Macedonia—and perhaps I will remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on my way wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you now only in passing; I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. But I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost” (1 Cor. 16:1–8).

Likewise, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that the necessities of food were provided for the future because a famine was imminent. For we read:

> “In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch, and there was great rejoicing. When we had gathered together, one of them, named Agabus, rose and signified through the Spirit that a great famine was going to occur throughout the whole world, which also happened under Claudius Caesar. The disciples [Note: [Col. 1295] Am., Er., and Lov.: “those coming down.” Mar. and the manuscripts more correctly have “the disciples.”], according to what each had in abundance, determined that each should send something for service to the brothers living in Judea; and they did so, sending it to the presbyters by the hand of Barnabas and Saul” (Acts 11:27–30).

And when provisions were placed on board for the same apostle Paul as he sailed—provisions that were offered to him (ibid. 28:10)—it does not seem that food was supplied for only one day.

Furthermore, when the same apostle writes, “Let the one who was stealing steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to share with the one who is in need” [Note: [Col. 1295] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek text of the Apostle. Am., Er., and Lov. read: “so that he may have something good to share with the one who is in need.”] (Eph. 4:28), those who misunderstand do not think that he is keeping the Lord’s command, which says, “Look at the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns,” and, “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they do not labor or spin,” since here he commands them to labor, working with their hands so that they may have something they can also give to others.

And when he often says of himself that he worked with his own hands so as not to burden anyone (1 Thess. 2:9; 2 Thess. 3:8), and when it is written that he joined Aquila because of their common trade, so that they might work together to earn their living (Acts 18:2–3), he does not seem to have imitated the birds of the air and the lilies of the field.

From these and similar passages of Scripture it is sufficiently clear that our Lord does not disapprove if someone provides these things in the human manner; rather, he disapproves if someone serves God for the sake of these things, so that in his works he looks not to the kingdom of God but to acquiring them.

58. This entire command is therefore [Col. 1296] brought under the following rule: even in providing for these things, we must think about the kingdom of God; but in serving the kingdom of God, we must not think about these things. Thus, even if they should sometimes be lacking—as God often permits for the sake of our training—they not only do not weaken our purpose, but also confirm it after it has been tested and proved.

“For,” he says, “we glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:3–5).

When recalling his own tribulations and labors, the same apostle mentions that he suffered not only imprisonment, shipwreck, and many other such hardships, but also hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness (2 Cor. 11:23–27).

When we read this, we should not suppose that the Lord’s promises faltered, so that the Apostle suffered hunger, thirst, and nakedness while seeking the kingdom and righteousness of God, even though we have been told, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” For he who is the physician to whom we have once wholly entrusted ourselves knows these things as aids: when to add them and when to remove them, judging what is expedient for us. He governs and directs us, consoling and training us in this life, and after this life establishing and strengthening us in perpetual rest.

For when a human being often withholds food from his animal, he does not abandon it to his care; rather, he does so precisely as an act of care.

## CHAPTER XVIII

59. Since, however, when these things are either provided for the future or, when there is no reason to spend them, kept in reserve, it is uncertain with what intention this is done—for it may be done with a simple heart or with a double one—he most appropriately adds at this point:

> “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

At this point I think nothing else is commanded to us except that, when it is uncertain with what intention certain actions are performed, we interpret them in the better sense.

What is written, “You will know them by their fruits,” was said of manifest deeds that cannot be performed with a good intention: such things as sexual immorality, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and anything of that kind. Concerning these we are permitted to judge, as the Apostle says: “For what have I to do with judging those outside? Are you not to judge those who are inside?” (1 Cor. 5:12).

With regard to kinds of food, since any human food may be consumed without the fault of desire, with a good intention and a simple heart, the same Apostle forbids those who ate meat and drank wine to be judged by those who abstained from such foods:

> “Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats.”

There too he says:

> “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls” (Rom. 14:3–4).

Concerning such matters, which may be done with a good, simple, and magnanimous spirit, although they may also be done without goodness, they wanted, while still human beings, to pass judgment in the hidden realm of the heart [Col. 1297]—things over which God alone judges.

60. This also pertains to what he says elsewhere:

> “Do not judge anything before the proper time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the intentions of hearts; then each person will receive praise from God” (1 Cor. 4:5).

There are therefore certain intermediate actions whose intention we do not know, because they may be performed either well or badly. It is rash to judge these, especially in such a way as to condemn them. Their time of judgment will come when the Lord brings to light the things hidden in darkness and discloses the intentions of hearts.

The same Apostle says elsewhere:
