> “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but some also follow afterward” (1 Tim. 5:24–25).

He calls “manifest” those deeds whose intention is clear; these go before judgment, that is, if judgment follows upon them, it is not rash. Those that are hidden come afterward, because they too will not remain concealed when their proper time arrives.

The same must be understood of good deeds. For he adds:

> “In the same way, good works are manifest; and those that are otherwise cannot remain hidden.”

Let us therefore judge what is manifest, but leave judgment concerning what is hidden to God, because these things too—whether bad or good—cannot remain concealed when the time comes for them to be revealed.

61. There are two circumstances in which we must guard against rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what intention something has been done, or when it is uncertain what sort of person someone who now appears good or bad will eventually become.

Suppose, for example, that someone, complaining of stomach trouble, refuses to fast, and you, not believing him, attribute this to the vice of gluttony. You will judge rashly.

Again, if you recognize obvious gluttony and drunkenness, and rebuke the person as though he could never be corrected or changed, you will likewise judge rashly.

Let us therefore not rebuke what we do not know the intention of; nor let us rebuke what is manifest in such a way that we despair of healing. Thus we shall avoid the judgment about which it is now said, “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”

62. What he says may cause difficulty: “For with the judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure you measure, in that measure it will be measured back to you.” For if we judge with rash judgment, will God also judge us rashly? Or if we measure with an unjust measure, is there an unjust measure with God by which it will be measured back to us?

I think that the word “measure” signifies judgment itself. God in no way judges rashly or repays anyone with an unjust measure. Rather, this was said because the rashness with which you punish another must itself punish you.

Unless, perhaps, one should think that injustice harms the person against whom it proceeds but does no harm to the person from whom it proceeds. On the contrary, it often does no harm to the one who suffers the injury, while it must harm the one who inflicts it.

What harm did the persecutors’ injustice do to the martyrs? It did immense harm to the persecutors themselves. Even if some of them were corrected, at the time when they were persecuting, their own wickedness blinded them.

So too, rash judgment often does no harm to the one [Col. 1298] rashly judged; but to the one who judges rashly, the rashness itself must do harm.

I think the same rule applies to the saying, “Everyone who strikes with the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). How many strike with the sword and yet do not perish by the sword, as Peter himself did not? But let no one suppose that he escaped this punishment because his sins were forgiven—although nothing would be more absurd than to think that the punishment of the sword could have been greater, had it befallen Peter, than the punishment of the cross, which did befall him.

What, then, will he say about the robbers who were crucified with the Lord? One of them, who deserved pardon, deserved it after he had been crucified (Luke 23:33–43); the other did not deserve it at all. Or perhaps all those whom they had killed had been crucified, and therefore they deserved to suffer this themselves? It is ridiculous to think so.

What else, then, does the saying “Everyone who strikes with the sword will perish by the sword” mean, except that the soul dies through the very sin it commits?

## CHAPTER XIX

63. Since at this point the Lord warns us about rash and unjust judgment—for he wants us to do everything we do with a simple heart directed toward the one God, and since it is uncertain with what disposition many things are done, so that it is rash to judge them—especially since those judge rashly and criticize readily who love to blame and condemn more than to reform and correct, a vice that arises either from pride or from envy, he accordingly adds and says:

> “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye?”

For example, if that person sinned through anger, while you rebuke him through hatred, the difference between anger and hatred is like the difference between a speck and a beam. Hatred is aged anger, as though by the very passage of time it had acquired such strength that it deserved to be called a beam.

It may happen that, if you are angry with someone, you want him to be corrected; but if you hate someone, you cannot want him to be corrected.

64. “How can you say to your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while behold, there is a beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.”

That is: first drive hatred from yourself, and then you will be able to correct the one you love.

And he rightly says, “Hypocrite.” To accuse vices is the duty of good and benevolent men; when wicked people do this, they are acting in another’s role, like hypocrites who conceal what they are beneath a mask and display in the mask what they are not.

By the name “hypocrites,” therefore, understand pretenders. This class of pretenders is truly dangerous and troublesome: while they receive accusations of every vice with hatred and envy, they also want to appear to be giving advice.

We must therefore watch carefully and piously. Whenever necessity forces us to rebuke or reprimand someone, we should first consider whether the vice is one we have never possessed or one from which we have already been freed. If we have never possessed it, let us remember that we are human beings and could have possessed it. If we have possessed it and no longer do, let the memory of our common weakness touch us, so that mercy, not hatred, [Col. 1299] precedes the rebuke or reprimand.

Whether our action proves effective for the correction of the person on whose account we do it, or for his corruption—for the outcome is uncertain—we shall nevertheless remain secure in the simplicity of our eye.

But if, on examining ourselves, we find that we are in the same vice as the person we were preparing to rebuke, let us not rebuke or reprimand him. Rather, let us groan with him and invite him not to obey us, but to strive together with us [Note: [Col. 1299] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, except Mar., have “to be cautious.”].

65. The same applies to what the Apostle says:

> “To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews; to those under the Law I became as one under the Law—though I myself am not under the Law—in order to win those under the Law; to those outside the Law I became as one outside the Law—not being outside the law of God, but under the law of Christ—in order to win those outside the Law. To the weak I became weak, in order to win the weak. I have become all things to all people, so that I might win all”—

He certainly did not do this through pretence, as some wish to understand it, thereby shielding their detestable pretence with the authority of so great an example. Rather, he did it through love: he considered the weakness of the person whom he wished to help as though it were his own.

For he also makes this clear when he says:

> “Although I am free from all, I made myself a servant to all, so that I might win more” (1 Cor. 9:19–22).

To make clear that this is done not through pretence but through love—by which we sympathize with weak human beings as though we ourselves were weak—he gives this instruction elsewhere:

> “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another” (Gal. 5:13).

This cannot happen unless each person regards the weakness of another as his own, so that he bears it with equanimity until the one whose salvation he cares for is freed from it.

66. Rebukes should therefore be used rarely and only in great necessity; even in these, however, we must exert ourselves so that God, not ourselves, may be served. For this is the goal: that we do nothing with a double heart, removing from our own eye the beam of envy, wickedness, or pretence, so that we may see to remove the speck from our brother’s eye.

We shall see it with the eyes of the dove, such as are praised in the bride of Christ (Song 4:1), whom God chose for himself as a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27)—that is, pure and simple [Note: [Col. 1299] I Retractations, chapter 19, section 9.].

## CHAPTER XX

67. Since, however, some who desire to obey God’s commands may be deceived by the word “simplicity,” and may think that it is just as wrong sometimes to conceal the truth as it is to tell a falsehood, thereby causing greater harm by disclosing things that those to whom they are disclosed cannot bear than they would cause by concealing them entirely and always, he very rightly adds:

> “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart.”

For although the Lord told no falsehood, he nevertheless showed that he concealed certain truths when he said:

> “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” [Col. 1300] (John 16:12).

And the apostle Paul says:

> “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not able to bear it. Indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

68. In this command, by which we are forbidden to give what is holy to dogs and to throw our pearls before pigs, we must carefully ask what is holy, what the pearls are, and who the dogs and pigs are.

“Holy” is that which it is impious to violate or corrupt. The attempt and intention to commit such a crime are held guilty, even though the holy thing itself remains by nature inviolate and incorruptible.

“Pearls” are whatever spiritual things should be highly valued. Because they lie hidden, they are drawn, as it were, from the depths, and are found beneath the coverings of allegories, like pearls in opened shells.

It is therefore possible to understand the same thing as both holy and a pearl: holy because it must not be corrupted, and a pearl because it must not be despised.

Someone tries to corrupt what he does not want to remain whole; he despises what he considers worthless and regards as beneath him. Hence whatever is despised is said to be trampled.

Therefore, because dogs leap forward to tear apart whatever they attack and do not allow what they tear to remain whole, the Lord says, “Do not give what is holy to dogs.” Although the holy thing cannot be torn apart or corrupted, and remains whole and inviolate, we must consider the intention of those who resist sharply and with hostility and who, insofar as they can, would try, if possible, to destroy the truth.

Pigs, however, although they do not attack by biting in the manner of dogs, nevertheless defile things by trampling them indiscriminately:

> “Do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart.”

We therefore appropriately understand dogs as representing opponents of the truth and pigs as representing those who despise it.

69. When he says, “Turning, they will tear you apart,” he does not say that they will tear apart the pearls themselves. By trampling them, they tear apart the person who has already thrown the pearls, even when they turn in order to hear something more.

You will not easily find anything that can please someone who has trampled pearls—that is, who has despised divine discoveries obtained through great labor. I do not see how anyone who teaches such people can avoid being torn apart by indignation and anger.

Both animals are unclean: the dog and the pig. We must therefore be careful not to disclose anything to someone who cannot grasp it. It is better for him to seek what is closed than to attack or neglect what is open.

No other reason can be found why people fail to accept things that are clear and important except hatred and contempt. Because of the one, they are called dogs; because of the other, pigs.

All this uncleanness, however, is conceived through love of temporal things—that is, through love of this world, which we are commanded to renounce so that we may be clean.

Therefore, someone who desires to have a clean and simple heart should not consider himself guilty if he conceals something which he himself cannot grasp [Col. 1301]. Nor should it be inferred from this that lying is permitted. When the truth is concealed, it does not follow that a falsehood must be spoken.

Our first task, then, is to remove the obstacles that prevent understanding. For if someone cannot grasp the truth because of his uncleanness, he must be cleansed, by word or deed, insofar as this can be done by us.

70. When our Lord is found to have said certain things that many who were present did not accept, either because they resisted or because they despised them, we must not suppose that he gave what was holy to dogs or threw pearls before pigs. He did not give these things to those who could not grasp them, but to those who could, and who were present at the same time; the latter should not have been neglected because of the uncleanness of the others.

When tempters questioned him and he answered them in such a way that they had nothing to contradict—although they wasted away in their own poison rather than being filled with his food—others who were able to understand nevertheless heard many useful things because of the occasion provided by those men.

I have said this so that, if someone is unable to answer a questioner, he may not think himself excused by this saying if he claims that he does not wish to give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls before pigs.

Anyone who knows how to answer ought to answer, at least for the sake of those others in whom despair may arise if they believe that the question posed cannot be solved. This applies to useful matters that concern instruction for salvation.

Many things may be asked by idle people that are superfluous, empty, and often harmful. Yet even concerning these something should be said—namely, the reason why such questions ought not to be asked should itself be disclosed and explained.

Concerning useful matters, therefore, one should sometimes answer what is asked, as the Lord did when the Sadducees questioned him about a woman who had had seven husbands and asked whose wife she would be in the future resurrection. He answered that in the resurrection they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven.

At other times the questioner should himself be questioned about something else; if he answers, he thereby supplies himself with the answer to what he had asked. If he refuses to answer, those present will not think it unjust if he too does not hear an answer to his question.

Thus those who questioned him to test whether tribute should be paid were themselves asked whose image was on the coin they had produced. Since they answered the question put to them—that the coin bore Caesar’s image—they in a certain sense answered their own question to the Lord. Therefore, on the basis of their answer, he concluded:

> “Then give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matt. 22:15–34).

When the chief priests and elders of the people asked by what authority he did these things, he questioned them about John’s baptism. Since they did not want to say what they saw would be used against them, and yet did not dare to say anything bad about John because of those standing around, he said:

> “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matt. 21:23–27).

This appeared entirely just to those present. They said that they did not know what they did know, but did not want to say.

And it was indeed just that those who wanted an answer to the question they had asked should first do toward him what they requested that he do toward them. If they had done so, they would certainly have answered themselves.

They themselves had sent people to John asking who he was—or rather, priests and Levites had been sent, thinking that he was the Christ. John denied that he was and bore witness concerning the Lord (John 1:19–27). If they had been willing to acknowledge this testimony, they themselves would have shown by what authority Christ did these things. They had asked as though they did not know, in order to find an opportunity for accusation.

## CHAPTER XXI

71. Since, then, it had been commanded that what is holy should not be given to dogs and that pearls should not be thrown before pigs, a hearer might object, conscious of his ignorance and weakness, and hearing himself commanded not to give what he felt he had not yet received. He might therefore say:

> “What holy thing do you forbid me to give to dogs, and what pearls do you forbid me to throw before pigs, when I do not yet see that I possess these things?”

He most appropriately adds:

> “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.”

Asking pertains to obtaining the healing and strengthening of the soul, so that we may be able to fulfill what is commanded. Seeking pertains to finding the truth.

Since the blessed life is completed through action and knowledge, action requires the capacity of strength, while contemplation requires the manifestation of things. The first of these must therefore be asked for, and the second sought, so that the one may be given and the other found.

But in this life knowledge belongs first to the way rather than to possession itself [Note: [Col. 1302] Er. and Lov. read “possession”; but the manuscripts and older printed editions more correctly have “of possession.”]. Once someone has found the true way, he will arrive at possession itself, which nevertheless is opened to the one who knocks.

72. To make these three things—asking, seeking, and knocking—clear, let us use an example. Suppose someone cannot walk because his feet are weak. He must first be healed and strengthened for walking; this is what “Ask” refers to.

But what benefit is it if he can now walk, or even run, if he wanders along mistaken paths? The second step, then, is that he find the way leading to the place where he wishes to arrive.

Once he has taken that way and reached the very place where he wishes to dwell, if he finds it closed, it will have done him no good that he was able to walk, or that he walked and arrived, unless it is opened. This is what is meant by, “Knock” [Note: [Col. 1302] I Retractations, chapter 19, section 9.].

73. The one who makes promises without deceiving has given and continues to give great hope. He says:

> “Everyone who asks receives; and the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.”

Perseverance is therefore necessary, so that we may receive what we ask for, find what we seek, and have what we knock at opened to us.

Just as he spoke about the birds of the air and the lilies of the field so that we would not despair of food and clothing being provided for us, causing hope to rise from lesser [Col. 1303] things to greater things, so here too he says:

> “Or what person is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?”

How do evil people give good things? He called those who still love this world and are sinners “evil.” The things they give are to be called good according to their judgment, because they regard them as good.

Indeed, these things are also good in the order of nature, but they are temporal and belong to this frail life. And whoever is evil gives them not from his own possession: “The earth is the Lord’s and all its fullness” (Ps. 23:1), the Lord who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them (Ps. 145:6).

How much more, then, should we hope that God will give good things to us when we ask him, and that we cannot be deceived into receiving one thing instead of another when we ask him, since even we, although evil, know how to give what is asked of us?

We do not deceive our children; and whatever good things we give, we give not from our own possession but from his.

## CHAPTER XXII

74. The strength and vigor required for walking along the way of wisdom consist in good morals, which lead all the way to the purification and simplicity of the heart. After speaking about this for a long time, he concludes:

> “Therefore, whatever you wish that people would do for you, do the same for them; for this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 7:12).

In the Greek copies we find:

> “Therefore, whatever you wish that people would do for you, do the same for them.”

I think that the Latins added the word “good” to make the meaning clear. For the following objection arose: if someone should desire that something shameful be done to him, and should refer this saying to that desire—for example, if someone wished to be urged to drink excessively and stuff himself with cups, and then did this first to the person from whom he wished it to be done to himself—it would be ridiculous to think that he had fulfilled this saying.

Since this difficulty arose, as I think, one word was added to clarify the matter. After it had been said, “Therefore, whatever you wish that people would do for you,” the word “good” was added.

If it is absent from the Greek copies, those copies too should be corrected—but who would dare to do this?

We must therefore understand that the saying is complete and entirely perfect even if this word is not added. For what is said—“whatever you wish”—must not be understood in the ordinary and indiscriminate sense, but in its proper sense.

For “will” exists only in good things. In evil and shameful actions the proper term is “desire,” not “will.”

This is not because Scripture always speaks with strict propriety, but whenever necessary it uses the proper word so precisely that it does not allow another meaning to be understood.

75. This command appears to pertain to love of neighbor, but not also to love of God, since elsewhere he says that there are two commands on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend [Note: [Col. 1303] In the edition of Mar. and ten manuscripts: “and all the Prophets.”].

For if he had said, “Whatever you wish to be done to you, do this also,” that single saying would have embraced both commands. For it would immediately [Col. 1304] be said that each person wishes to be loved both by God and by human beings. Therefore, when he was commanded to do to others what he wished to be done to himself, he would certainly be commanded to love God and human beings.

But since the saying is expressed more specifically concerning human beings—“Therefore, whatever you wish that people would do for you, do the same for them”—it seems to say nothing other than, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

We must not, however, overlook what he adds here: “For this is the Law and the Prophets.” In the case of the two commands, he does not merely say, “The Law and the Prophets depend on them,” but adds, “the whole Law and the Prophets” [Note: [Col. 1304] Here again “all” is added in two Vatican manuscripts.], meaning the whole prophecy.

Since he does not add that here, he leaves room for the other command, which concerns love of God.

Here, however, because he is expounding the commands of a simple heart—and because one must fear that a person may have a double heart precisely toward those by whom the heart can be concealed, namely, other human beings—the command had to be stated in this form.

Almost no one wishes another person to act toward him with a double heart. But it is impossible for a person to give something to another with a simple heart unless he gives it without expecting any temporal advantage from that person, and with the intention we discussed sufficiently above when speaking about the simple eye.

76. Once the eye has been cleansed and made simple, it will be fit and capable of looking upon and contemplating its inner light. For this is the eye of the heart.

The person who has such an eye does not place the goal of his good works—so that they may truly be good—in pleasing human beings. Even if it happens that they please them, he refers this rather to their salvation and to the glory of God, not to his own empty boasting.

Nor does he perform something good for the salvation of his neighbor in order to acquire from it what is necessary for passing through this life.

Nor does he rashly condemn a person’s intention and will in an action whose intention and will are not apparent.

Whatever services he renders to another, he renders with the intention with which he wishes them rendered to himself: namely, without expecting any temporal advantage from that person.

Thus the heart in which God is sought will be simple and clean.

> “Blessed, therefore, are the clean of heart [Note: [Col. 1304] Many manuscripts here and elsewhere have “the clean-hearted,” but not consistently.], for they will see God” (ibid. 5:8).

## CHAPTER XXIII

77. Since this, however, belongs to few people, he now begins to speak about seeking and possessing wisdom, which is the tree of life. For the seeking and possessing—that is, contemplating—of this wisdom, the eye has been led through all the preceding instruction, so that it can now see the narrow way and the constricted gate.

Therefore he next says:

> “Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is broad and the way spacious that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. How narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it!”

He does not say this because the Lord’s yoke is harsh or his burden heavy, but because few are willing to bring their labors to an end [Col. 1305] [Note: [Col. 1305] In B.: “few are willing to be brought to an end.” We have followed Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov.; M.]. They have too little faith in the one who cries out:

> “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:28–30).

From this the discourse took its beginning, with its discussion of those who are humble and gentle in heart.

Many reject this easy yoke and light burden; few undertake them. Consequently, the way that leads to life is narrow, and the gate through which one enters it is constricted [Note: [Col. 1305] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, except Mar., read: “because many reject the easy yoke and light burden, and few undertake them; and thus the way is narrow.”].

# CHAPTER XXIV

**78.** Those, then, who promise wisdom and knowledge of the truth—which they do not possess—are especially to be guarded against, such as the heretics, who for the most part commend themselves by their small numbers. And therefore, after saying that few are those who find the narrow gate and the difficult way, lest they should insinuate themselves under the name of “the few,” he immediately added:

> “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.”

Yet these do not deceive the single eye that knows how to recognize a tree by its fruits. For he says:

> “By their fruits you shall know them.”

Then he adds the comparisons:

> “Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but a bad tree produces bad fruits. A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits. For every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire. Therefore, by their fruits you shall know them.”

**79.** At this point, the error of those who suppose that these two trees signify two natures must be especially guarded against: one belonging to God, and the other neither belonging to God nor deriving from God. This error has already been discussed more fully in other books, and, if what has been said is still insufficient, it will be discussed further. For the present, however, it must be shown that these two trees do not support their view.

First, that he is speaking about human beings is so clear that anyone who reads what precedes and follows must marvel at their blindness. Next, they attend to what is said: “A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits,” and therefore they think that neither can a bad soul be changed for the better, nor a good one for the worse—as though it had been said, “A good tree cannot become bad, nor can a bad tree become good.” But what was said is: “A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits.”

The tree itself is the soul, that is, the person himself; the fruits, however, are the person’s works. Therefore a bad person cannot perform good works, nor a good person bad works. If a bad person wishes to perform good works, let him first become good.

Thus, in another passage, the Lord himself states the matter more explicitly:

> “Either make the tree good, or make the tree bad.”

If by these two trees he were representing two natures, he would not say, “Make”: for what human being can make a nature? Moreover, there too, after mentioning the two trees themselves, he added:

> “Hypocrites, how can you speak good things, being evil?” (ibid. XII, 33–34)

Therefore, so long as someone is evil, he cannot produce good fruits; for if he produces good fruits, he will no longer be evil.

Thus it could most truthfully be said, “Snow cannot be hot”: once it begins to be hot, we no longer call it snow but water. It can therefore happen that what was snow is no longer snow; but it cannot happen that snow is hot. Similarly, it can happen that one who was evil is no longer evil; yet it cannot happen that an evil person does good. Even if such a person is sometimes useful, he himself does not accomplish this; rather, it is brought about in him by divine providence, as was said concerning the Pharisees:

> “Whatever they tell you, do, but do not do according to their works.”

The fact that they spoke good things, and that what they said was heard and done profitably, was not their achievement:

> “For they sit,” he says, “on Moses’ seat” (ibid. XXIII, 3).

By divine providence, therefore, while preaching God’s law, they could be useful to their hearers, though not to themselves.

[Col. 1306] Concerning such people it is said elsewhere through the prophet:

> “You have sown wheat, and you shall reap thorns” (Jeremiah XII, 13).

[Note: [Col. 1306] Nine manuscripts read: “You sow wheat, and you reap thorns.”]

For they command good things but do evil. Those who heard them and did what they said were not, therefore, gathering grapes from thorns; rather, through the thorns they were gathering grapes from a vine—as when someone puts his hand through a hedge, or certainly gathers a grape from a vine that has become entangled in a hedge. That fruit belongs not to the thorns but to the vine.

[Note: [Col. 1306] So Erasmus. In B.: “or certainly gathers a grape from a vine that has become entangled in a hedge.” M.]

**80.** It is rightly asked, however, which fruits he wants us to observe by which we may recognize the tree. Many count among the fruits certain things that belong to the sheep’s clothing, and in this way are deceived by wolves: such things as fasting, prayers, and almsgiving. If hypocrites could not also perform all these things, he would not previously have said:

> “Beware of practicing your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them.”

After stating this, he proceeds to discuss the three things themselves: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting.

Many give much to the poor, not out of mercy but from ambition. Many pray—or rather, appear to pray—not looking toward God but desiring to please human beings. Many fast and display a remarkable abstinence before those to whom such practices seem difficult and worthy of honor. By such deceptions they ensnare people, displaying one thing in order to deceive and bringing forth another in order to plunder or destroy those who, beneath this sheep’s clothing, cannot see the wolves.

These, then, are not the fruits by which he instructs us to recognize the tree. When such things are done truthfully with a good intention, they are properly the clothing of sheep; when they are done with an evil intention and in error, they do nothing but conceal wolves. Yet the sheep ought not therefore to hate their own clothing, because wolves often hide themselves in it.

**81.** The fruits by which, when discovered, we may recognize the bad tree are identified by the Apostle:

> “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, strife, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, heresies, sects, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

[Note: [Col. 1306] Seven manuscripts add “sects” (*sectae*); the word had been omitted in the printed editions.]

And the fruits by which we may recognize the good tree he himself immediately identifies:

> “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians V, 19–23).

It should certainly be understood that “joy” is used here in its proper sense. Evil people are properly said not to rejoice but to exult wildly, just as we said above that “will” is used in its proper sense—a will which evil people do not possess—where it was said:

> “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do likewise for them.”

Because of this proper meaning of the word, in which joy is spoken of only with reference to the good, the prophet also says:

> “There is no joy for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isaiah LVII, 21, according to the Septuagint).

“Faith” likewise is used here in a specific sense—not just any faith, but true faith. The other qualities listed here also have certain semblances of themselves among evil people and deceivers, so that they may deceive completely unless someone already possesses a cleansed and single eye with which to recognize them. Thus, in the best order, the discourse first dealt with cleansing the eye, and then stated the things that must be guarded against.

# CHAPTER XXV

**82.** But although someone may have a clean eye—that is, may live with a simple and sincere heart—he still cannot see another person’s heart. Whatever cannot be revealed in deeds or words is disclosed through trials.

There are two kinds of trial: either the hope of obtaining some temporal advantage, or the fear of losing one. Above all, care must be taken lest, while striving toward wisdom—which can be found in Christ alone, in whom “all the treasures of wisdom [Col. 1307] and knowledge are hidden” (Colossians II, 3)—we be deceived by heretics, or by anyone who misunderstands, or by lovers of this age, even through the very name of Christ.

For this reason what follows offers a warning:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven—he will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

We must not therefore think that someone already belongs among those fruits merely because he says to our Lord, “Lord, Lord,” and thus regard him as a good tree. Rather, those fruits consist in doing the will of the Father who is in heaven, whose will the Lord himself graciously offered himself as an example for fulfilling.

**83.** It may rightly be asked how this statement agrees with the Apostle’s words:

> “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus,’ and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians XII, 3).

For we cannot say that those who possess the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven, if they persevere to the end; nor can we say that those who say, “Lord, Lord,” yet do not enter the kingdom of heaven, possess the Holy Spirit.

How, then, does no one say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit? It is because the Apostle used the verb “says” in a specific sense, so as to signify the will and understanding of the speaker. The Lord, however, used the verb in a general sense when he said:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Even one who neither wishes nor understands what he says appears to say it. But a person properly “says” something when he expresses his will and mind through the sound of his voice.

Similarly, the “joy” mentioned shortly before among the fruits of the Spirit is used in a specific sense.

[Note: [Col. 1307] Am., Er., and Lov. add “of the holy [Spirit],” a reading absent from Mar. and the manuscripts.]

It is not used in the same way as when the same Apostle says:

> “It does not rejoice over iniquity” (1 Corinthians XIII, 6),

as though anyone could rejoice over iniquity. Such a state is the troubled exultation of the soul, not joy; for joy belongs only to the good.

Thus even those who do not perceive with their understanding and perform with their will what they utter may be said to say it—if they merely produce the sound with their voice. It is in this sense that the Lord says:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

But those truly and properly say it whose utterance does not conflict with their will and mind. It is with this meaning that the Apostle said:

> “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

**84.** It is especially relevant that, while striving toward contemplation of the truth, we must not be deceived merely by the name of Christ through those who possess the name but not the deeds, nor even by certain deeds and miracles. The Lord performed such things on account of unbelievers, yet he warned us not to be deceived by them, imagining that invisible wisdom is present wherever we have seen a visible miracle.

He therefore adds:

> “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will say to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity.’”

He will therefore know only the one who works righteousness.

He also forbade his own disciples to rejoice in such things—that is, in the fact that the demons had been subjected to them:

> “But rejoice,” he says, “because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20);

I believe this means in that heavenly city, Jerusalem, in which only the righteous and holy will reign.

> “Or do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God?” (1 Corinthians VI, 9)

**85.** But perhaps someone may say that the unrighteous cannot perform those visible miracles, and may rather believe that those who will say, “In your name we prophesied, and cast out demons, and performed many mighty works,” are lying.

[Col. 1308] Let him read, then, how many things the Egyptian magicians performed while resisting God’s servant Moses (Exodus VII–VIII). Or, if he does not wish to read this because they did not perform them in the name of Christ, let him read what the Lord himself says about false prophets:

> “Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or ‘There,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise and will give great signs and wonders, so that even the elect will be led astray. Behold, I have told you beforehand” (Matthew XXIV, 23–25).

**86.** How pure and single the eye must be, then, in order to find the way of wisdom, when so many deceptions and errors of evil and perverse people obstruct it—people whom we must all elude in order to arrive at the most certain peace and unshakable stability of wisdom!

For we must greatly fear that, through zeal for arguing and disputing, someone may fail to see what can be seen by the few, so that the noise of those who contradict remains small—unless he himself also obstructs his own vision.

To this also pertains what the Apostle says:

> “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting those who think differently with modesty, lest God perhaps grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy II, 24–25).

Therefore:

> “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew V, 9).

**87.** We must pay very close attention to how terrifyingly the conclusion of this entire discourse is brought forward:

> “Everyone, therefore, who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock.”

No one establishes what he hears or understands except by doing it. And if Christ is the rock, as many testimonies of Scripture proclaim (1 Corinthians X, 4), the person who builds upon Christ is the one who does what he hears from him.

> “The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew and struck that house, and it did not fall,”

[Note: [Col. 1308] So the manuscripts. But the printed editions, except Mar., read: “They could not move it.”]

for it had been founded upon the rock.

Such a person therefore fears neither obscure superstitions—for what else is signified by rain when it is used to represent something evil?—nor human rumors, which I think are compared with winds, nor the stream of this life, flowing over the earth through carnal desires. For by these three things, one who is led astray by prosperity is broken by adversity. None of them is feared by the person whose house is founded upon the rock—that is, by the one who not only hears the Lord’s commands but also does them.

The person who hears and does not do is dangerously exposed to all these things. He has no stable foundation; by hearing and not doing, he builds a ruin.

For he adds:

> “And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand. The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew and struck that house, and it fell; and its ruin was great.”

And it happened that, when Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astonished at his teaching:

> “For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes” (Matthew VII, 24–29).

[Note: [Col. 1308] Am., Er., and Lov. add “and Pharisees.” We have found this neither in any manuscript here nor in Mar. It does occur in the Vulgate version, but is absent from the Greek text.]

This is what I previously said was signified by the prophet in the Psalms, when he said:

> “I will act boldly in him: the words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm XI, 6–7).

Because of this number, I was also prompted to refer these commandments to those seven statements that he set forth at the beginning of this discourse when he spoke of the blessed, and to those seven operations of the Holy Spirit that the prophet Isaiah mentions (Isaiah XI, 2–3). But whether this order is to be considered in these matters, or some other order, we must do what we have heard from the Lord if we wish to build upon the rock.

[Col. 1307] **HERE ENDS THE FIRST PART OF THE THIRD VOLUME.**
